Decision trees are computationally efficient, handle both numerical and categorical data, and can naturally represent non-linear decision boundaries. In the medical imaging domain, decision trees have been used for tasks ranging from tumor detection to disease staging, offering a balance between accuracy and interpretability.

Despite their individual strengths, both ARM and decision trees face limitations when applied in isolation to medical image classification. ARM, while capable of generating expressive rules, may produce a large number of redundant or irrelevant rules without an embedded classification mechanism. Decision trees, although effective classifiers, may overlook subtle but clinically significant associations among features that do not directly impact the immediate split criteria. A hybrid approach that integrates ARM with decision tree algorithms has the potential to leverage the strengths of both methods: ARM can uncover latent, high-value associations in the image feature space, while the decision tree can utilize these associations to construct a concise, accurate, and interpretable classification model.

In the proposed hybrid framework, ARM is applied to the extracted medical image features to generate association rules that reveal meaningful patterns and correlations. These rules are then used to augment the feature representation or guide the splitting criteria in the decision tree construction process. This synergy can enhance classification accuracy by incorporating domain-relevant patterns discovered through ARM, while retaining the transparent decision-making process characteristic of decision trees. Moreover, such a hybrid model can facilitate clinical adoption by producing outputs that are both data-driven and readily interpretable by healthcare professionals.

The motivation for this research stems from the dual need for high diagnostic performance and interpretability in medical image analysis. While many state-of-the-art classification models achieve impressive accuracy, their lack of transparency limits their utility in sensitive medical contexts where understanding the rationale behind a decision is as important as the decision itself. By combining ARM and decision tree algorithms, the proposed method aims to bridge this gap, offering a robust and explainable classification approach suitable for various medical imaging applications. Through rigorous experimentation and evaluation, this study seeks to demonstrate that the hybrid approach can outperform traditional single-method classifiers in both accuracy and interpretability, thereby contributing to the advancement of trustworthy AI in healthcare.
conclusion: The proposed hybrid approach integrating Association Rule Mining with the Decision Tree algorithm demonstrates significant potential for improving medical image classification accuracy and interpretability. By leveraging the rule discovery capability of Association Rule Mining, the system effectively identifies relevant feature patterns, while the Decision Tree provides a structured and transparent classification process. Experimental results indicate enhanced performance compared to using either technique independently, particularly in handling complex and high-dimensional medical image datasets. The method offers not only accurate predictions but also interpretable decision paths, which are critical in clinical decision support systems. Furthermore, its adaptability to various medical imaging modalities underscores its versatility. Future work may focus on optimizing rule selection, incorporating deep learning features, and testing on larger, more diverse datasets to further validate generalizability. Overall, the hybrid model presents a promising framework for robust, explainable, and efficient medical image classification.

title: A study of collider signatures for two Higgs doublet models with a Pseudoscalar mediator to Dark Matter
abstract: We investigate collider phenomenology of two Higgs doublet models (2HDM) extended by a pseudoscalar mediator that couples to fermionic dark matter. Such frameworks naturally evade stringent direct detection bounds while offering distinctive signals at the LHC. We perform a systematic analysis of production and decay channels involving the pseudoscalar, focusing on mono‑X signatures and heavy Higgs cascade decays. Theoretical constraints from perturbativity, unitarity, and vacuum stability are imposed, along with current limits from Higgs measurements and flavour observables. Using Monte Carlo simulations and realistic detector effects, we explore discovery prospects for representative benchmark scenarios. Our results highlight parameter regions where collider searches are complementary to astrophysical probes, and demonstrate that targeted analyses can significantly enhance sensitivity to this class of dark sector models.
introduction:
The existence of dark matter (DM) is supported by a wide range of astrophysical and cosmological observations, including galactic rotation curves, gravitational lensing, and measurements of the cosmic microwave background. However, its particle nature remains one of the most compelling open questions in fundamental physics. A promising avenue to address this mystery lies in searching for signals of DM production at high-energy colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Collider searches offer a controlled environment in which to probe DM interactions with Standard Model (SM) particles, potentially revealing mediator states that couple the visible and dark sectors.

Among the various theoretical frameworks proposed to describe DM interactions, simplified models have gained attention for their ability to capture essential phenomenology with a minimal set of parameters. In particular, models featuring a pseudoscalar mediator are of significant interest. Pseudoscalar mediators naturally evade stringent constraints from direct detection experiments, as their couplings to fermions lead to spin-dependent or momentum-suppressed scattering cross-sections off nuclei. This makes collider searches a complementary and, in some cases, leading probe of such scenarios.

A theoretically well-motivated and phenomenologically rich setting for pseudoscalar mediators arises in extensions of the Higgs sector, notably the two Higgs doublet model (2HDM). In a 2HDM, the scalar sector of the SM is extended by introducing an additional SU(2)\(_L\) doublet, leading to a richer spectrum of physical Higgs bosons: two CP-even scalars \(h\) and \(H\), a CP-odd pseudoscalar \(A\), and a charged Higgs pair \(H^\pm\). When a pseudoscalar mediator to the dark sector is introduced in such a framework, it can mix with the CP-odd state of the 2HDM, resulting in novel collider signatures that differ from those in minimal pseudoscalar simplified models.

The 2HDM with a pseudoscalar mediator to DM provides several theoretical benefits. It is renormalizable, gauge invariant, and can be embedded in ultraviolet-complete theories such as supersymmetry. Moreover, the additional scalar degrees of freedom lead to distinctive phenomenology, including resonant and non-resonant production channels, cascade decays among the Higgs states, and modified couplings to SM particles. These features open up a variety of search strategies at the LHC, ranging from missing transverse energy (\(E_T^{\mathrm{miss}}\)) signatures in association with heavy-flavor quarks or electroweak bosons, to multi-Higgs final states.

From an experimental perspective, LHC searches for DM have traditionally focused on mono-X signatures, in which a pair of invisible particles recoils against a single visible object such as a jet, photon, or electroweak gauge boson. In the context of pseudoscalar mediators coupled via a 2HDM structure, additional processes become relevant. For example, heavy Higgs bosons can decay into a pseudoscalar mediator and a Z boson, or into combinations of lighter scalars and pseudoscalars, yielding final states with leptons, jets, and missing energy. The interplay between visible and invisible decay modes, together with the possibility of resonant production of heavy Higgs states, enhances discovery prospects and provides complementary probes of the parameter space.

Theoretical and experimental studies have begun to map the collider phenomenology of such models, but a comprehensive analysis of their distinctive signatures, especially in light of current and future LHC datasets, remains timely. This work aims to explore the collider signatures of two Higgs doublet models with an additional pseudoscalar mediator to dark matter, focusing on production mechanisms, decay patterns, and search strategies that exploit both standard and non-standard final states. By systematically studying these signatures, we seek to identify optimal channels for discovery and to clarify the complementarity between collider searches and other experimental approaches to dark matter.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the collider phenomenology of two Higgs doublet models (2HDMs) extended by a pseudoscalar mediator that couples to a fermionic dark matter candidate. Our analysis was motivated by the pressing need to explore theoretically well-motivated scenarios that can simultaneously address the electroweak symmetry breaking sector and provide a viable dark matter framework. By embedding the pseudoscalar mediator within a 2HDM structure, we ensured gauge invariance and renormalizability, while also allowing for rich collider signatures distinct from those of minimal dark matter models.

We have systematically explored the parameter space consistent with current theoretical and experimental constraints, including perturbativity, unitarity, electroweak precision observables, flavour bounds, and limits from direct and indirect dark matter searches. Particular attention was devoted to regimes where the pseudoscalar mediator has a mass below, near, or above the electroweak scale, leading to qualitatively different decay patterns and production channels at the LHC.

Our collider study focused on both standard Higgs boson searches and dedicated channels sensitive to the mediator’s pseudoscalar nature. In particular, mono-X signatures (with X = jet, Z, or Higgs) and associated production with top quarks were examined, as these channels provide complementary probes of the model. We have shown that the interplay between scalar and pseudoscalar states in the extended Higgs sector can significantly modify the event rates and kinematic distributions compared to simplified pseudoscalar mediator models. The mixing between the pseudoscalar mediator and the CP-odd Higgs state of the 2HDM induces characteristic patterns in angular distributions and transverse momentum spectra, which can be exploited to enhance discrimination from the Standard Model backgrounds.

Through detailed simulations, we have identified benchmark scenarios that remain viable under current LHC Run 2 bounds yet predict observable signals at the High-Luminosity LHC. These scenarios illustrate that, even in the presence of strong constraints from missing transverse energy searches, there exist regions of parameter space where visible decays of the pseudoscalar into Standard Model particles dominate, opening up complementary search strategies. Our results highlight the importance of combining missing energy searches with resonance and multi-object final state analyses to fully cover the model’s phenomenology.

Furthermore, we have emphasised that the collider reach is intricately linked to the dark matter sector. The relic density requirement and limits from direct detection experiments impose correlations among couplings and masses that directly impact production cross sections and branching ratios. In particular, the pseudoscalar nature of the mediator suppresses spin-independent scattering rates, relaxing direct detection constraints and allowing for larger couplings to quarks, thereby enhancing collider signals.

In summary, our study demonstrates that two Higgs doublet models with a pseudoscalar portal to dark matter offer a theoretically consistent and phenomenologically rich framework that can be effectively probed at current and future colliders. The distinctive interplay between the extended Higgs sector and the dark matter mediator leads to novel signatures beyond those of simplified models, underlining the necessity of tailored search strategies. Continued exploration of these scenarios, in conjunction with advances in dark matter detection experiments, will be essential for uncovering or constraining this compelling class of theories in the coming years.

title: Avoiding the Geometric Boundary Effect in Shear Measurement
abstract: We investigate methods to mitigate the geometric boundary effect in shear measurement, a source of systematic error arising from finite observational fields and irregular survey geometries. Using simulated shear fields with controlled boundaries, we quantify biases introduced by standard estimators and explore corrections based on window function deconvolution and apodization techniques. Our results show that boundary-induced biases can reach several percent in common survey configurations, but are effectively reduced to below 0.5% with optimized weighting schemes. We further demonstrate the applicability of our approach to realistic survey masks. These findings provide a practical framework for improving shear measurements, thereby enhancing the precision of weak gravitational lensing analyses.
introduction:
Weak gravitational lensing has emerged as a powerful tool for probing the large-scale distribution of matter in the Universe and constraining cosmological models. By measuring the minute, coherent distortions in the shapes of background galaxies induced by foreground mass concentrations, it is possible to infer the underlying matter density field and its statistical properties. The accuracy of such shear measurements is critical, as upcoming wide-field surveys such as LSST, Euclid, and the Roman Space Telescope aim to achieve percent-level precision in cosmological parameter estimation. In this context, systematic biases in shape and shear estimation must be understood and mitigated to levels well below the statistical uncertainties.

One source of systematic error that has received comparatively less attention is the so-called geometric boundary effect. This effect arises when shear is estimated in finite, irregularly shaped regions of an image or survey footprint. The discontinuity of the observed field at the boundaries introduces biases in shape measurement algorithms, particularly those that rely on Fourier-space techniques or on statistical correlation functions. Truncated isophotes, incomplete point spread function (PSF) corrections near edges, and anisotropic survey masks can all exacerbate this problem. For example, galaxies located near the edge of a detector or masked region may have poorly constrained ellipticities, while spatial filtering operations can mix modes across the boundary in a way that contaminates the recovered shear signal.

The geometric boundary effect is particularly relevant for realistic survey geometries, which inevitably contain gaps between detectors, irregular tiling patterns, and masking due to bright stars, cosmic rays, or image defects. In addition, the effect is scale-dependent: it can impact both small-scale shear measurements, which are sensitive to local galaxy configurations, and large-scale statistics, where survey geometry can couple to the underlying shear field. Despite its importance, mitigation strategies for boundary-induced biases have not yet reached the same level of maturity as those for other systematic effects, such as PSF modeling errors or noise bias.

In this work, we investigate the origin and magnitude of the geometric boundary effect in shear measurement and propose practical methods to avoid or correct for it. Our aim is to enable robust shear estimation across complex survey geometries, ensuring the fidelity of cosmological inferences from future weak lensing data.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the origin, impact, and mitigation of the geometric boundary effect in shear measurement, with particular attention to its implications for weak lensing analyses and related observational programs. The geometric boundary effect, arising from the finite extent and irregular shapes of survey regions, can bias shear estimators through incomplete sampling of the shear field and anisotropic mode coupling. Our investigation demonstrates that this effect is not merely a technical nuisance but a significant source of systematic error that can propagate into cosmological inferences if left unaddressed.

Through a combination of analytic modeling, numerical simulations, and controlled tests on mock survey geometries, we have quantified the magnitude of the boundary-induced bias under various observational scenarios. Our results show that the bias scales non-trivially with both the shape of the survey footprint and the spatial correlation properties of the underlying shear field. In particular, elongated or highly fragmented survey regions exacerbate the leakage of power between modes and increase the sensitivity of shear estimates to poorly constrained boundary-adjacent modes. These findings highlight the necessity of incorporating survey geometry explicitly into the design of shear measurement pipelines.

We have also evaluated a set of mitigation strategies aimed at reducing or eliminating the geometric boundary effect. Among these, the use of apodization windows tailored to the survey footprint and the development of modified shear estimators that down-weight or correct for boundary regions proved particularly effective. In simulation, such approaches reduced boundary-induced biases to below the statistical error floor for survey areas comparable to current wide-field weak lensing datasets. Importantly, we find that mitigation does not require sacrificing large fractions of survey area, provided that the apodization or correction scheme is optimized jointly with the power spectrum or correlation function estimator.

Our analysis further underscores the value of forward-modeling the survey geometry in cosmological parameter estimation. By embedding realistic survey masks and boundary treatments directly into the theoretical prediction stage, one can avoid post hoc corrections and maintain consistency between measurement and model. This approach naturally accommodates complex survey boundaries and can be integrated with existing Markov Chain Monte Carlo or likelihood analysis frameworks.

Looking ahead, the methods presented here are directly relevant to upcoming large-scale surveys, such as those to be conducted by the Rubin Observatory, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, where unprecedented statistical precision will render even subtle geometric effects significant. As survey footprints become more complex due to joint analyses across multiple instruments and observing strategies, the robust control of geometric boundary effects will be essential for achieving the scientific goals of precision cosmology.

In summary, we have identified the geometric boundary effect as a quantifiable and correctable source of bias in shear measurement, developed and validated practical mitigation techniques, and demonstrated their efficacy in realistic survey configurations. By incorporating these strategies into future analyses, the cosmological community can safeguard the integrity of shear-based inferences and fully exploit the statistical power of next-generation surveys.

title: Relations for a periodic array of flap-type wave energy converters
abstract: This study investigates the hydrodynamic performance of a periodic array of flap-type wave energy converters (WECs) using linear potential flow theory. Analytical relations are derived to describe wave interaction, diffraction, and radiation within the array, accounting for periodicity and flap motion. The formulation employs eigenfunction expansions to represent the wave field and enforces boundary conditions on the flaps and free surface. Expressions are obtained for hydrodynamic coefficients, power capture width, and array interaction factors, enabling assessment of spacing and phase control effects. The results provide insight into optimal configurations for maximizing energy absorption while minimizing detrimental interactions, offering a theoretical framework for the design and performance evaluation of large-scale periodic arrays of flap-type WECs in regular wave conditions.
introduction:
Wave energy has emerged as a promising renewable resource with the potential to make a significant contribution to the global energy portfolio. Among the various technologies developed to harness this resource, wave energy converters (WECs) of the flap-type—also referred to as oscillating wave surge converters (OWSCs)—have attracted considerable attention due to their high efficiency in intermediate water depths and their relatively low visual impact. These devices typically consist of a large, bottom-hinged panel that oscillates in response to the horizontal motion of water particles induced by incident waves. The resulting motion is converted into useful power through a power take-off (PTO) system. 

In practical applications, the deployment of WECs in arrays is generally preferred over isolated units, as arrays can increase overall energy capture, improve economic viability, and facilitate grid integration. However, the hydrodynamic interactions between multiple devices in an array can be complex and have significant implications for performance. Constructive interactions can enhance the power output of individual units, while destructive interference effects can lead to reduced efficiency. Furthermore, wave scattering, diffraction, and radiation from each device can alter the local wave field, influencing both the dynamics of neighbouring WECs and the environmental impact of the installation.

For flap-type WECs, the hydrodynamic behaviour in an array setting is particularly influenced by the periodicity of the configuration. A periodic array, characterised by uniform spacing and identical device geometry, allows for the application of analytical and semi-analytical methods to describe the wave-structure interactions. Such approaches exploit the inherent symmetry of the problem to derive relations that can predict the response of the array to regular incident waves. The development of these relations is crucial for understanding and optimising the performance of large-scale wave farms, as they provide a framework for assessing the influence of array geometry, wave conditions, and PTO characteristics on overall energy extraction.

Previous studies have investigated the hydrodynamics of periodic arrays of various WEC types, including point absorbers and oscillating water columns, often employing linear potential flow theory to model the fluid motion. For flap-type converters, research has addressed single-device performance and some aspects of multiple-device interaction, but comprehensive analytical treatments of strictly periodic arrays remain limited. The derivation of closed-form or semi-analytical relations for such systems not only enhances theoretical understanding but also reduces the computational effort required for preliminary design and optimisation studies compared to fully numerical simulations.

This work focuses on establishing relations for a periodic array of flap-type wave energy converters, based on linear wave theory and appropriate boundary conditions for the device geometry and motion. The derived expressions aim to capture the essential hydrodynamic interactions within the array and provide a basis for further analysis of power capture and wave field modification. By developing these relations, the study contributes to the design methodology for efficient and environmentally responsible wave energy farms employing flap-type converters.
conclusion:
The present study has examined the hydrodynamic behaviour and performance characteristics of a periodic array of flap-type wave energy converters (WECs) through the derivation and analysis of analytical relations. By considering the periodicity of the system and employing linear potential flow theory, expressions have been developed to relate the motion of individual flaps within the array to the incident wave field, as well as to quantify the resulting wave scattering and power capture. The formulation incorporates the mutual interactions between devices, which are shown to play a significant role in determining the overall efficiency of the array.

The results indicate that the power absorption of each flap is not solely a function of the incident wave conditions but is also strongly influenced by the spacing, phasing, and hydrodynamic coupling with neighbouring units. Constructive and destructive interference effects within the array can lead to significant variations in both the captured power and the transmitted and reflected wave fields. The derived relations provide a systematic means of predicting these effects for arbitrary array configurations, thereby offering a valuable tool for preliminary design and optimisation.

It has been demonstrated that, for given wave conditions, there exists an optimal arrangement of flap spacing and operating parameters that maximises the total absorbed power while minimising detrimental interference losses. In particular, the analytical framework captures the trade-off between individual flap performance and collective array efficiency, enabling the identification of configurations that balance these competing factors. The approach also facilitates the investigation of directional wave incidence, revealing that array performance can be highly sensitive to incident wave angle, especially for closely spaced flaps.

The theoretical predictions obtained from the derived relations show good agreement with previously reported numerical and experimental findings for similar systems, lending confidence to the applicability of the method. While the model is based on linear theory and thus neglects viscous and nonlinear effects, it provides an essential first-order understanding of the hydrodynamic interactions in periodic flap arrays. Its relative simplicity compared to fully numerical simulations makes it particularly suitable for parameter studies and early-stage design assessments.

Future work could extend the present formulation to include more realistic features such as irregular wave spectra, nonlinear flap dynamics, and mooring system effects. Additionally, the integration of the hydrodynamic model with control strategies for power take-off systems would enable assessment of the combined influence of array configuration and operational tuning on overall performance. Investigations into the environmental impact of such arrays, including their influence on wave climate and sediment transport, would also be a valuable complement to the present analysis.

In summary, the derived relations for periodic arrays of flap-type WECs offer a robust and efficient means to characterise and optimise their performance. By capturing the essential physics of hydrodynamic interactions, they contribute to the development of more effective and economically viable wave energy extraction systems, supporting the broader goal of advancing renewable ocean energy technologies.

title: Spectral and spatial observations of microwave spikes and zebra structure in the short radio burst of May 29, 2003
abstract: We present a detailed analysis of the fine spectral and temporal structure of a short solar radio burst observed on May 29, 2003, in the microwave range. Using high time resolution (5 ms) and high spectral resolution (10 MHz) observations from the Solar Broadband Radio Spectrometer (SBRS) at Huairou, we identify a complex superposition of narrowband, short-duration spike emission and a well-defined zebra pattern structure. The event occurred during the impulsive phase of a compact flare, with the emission concentrated in the 5.2–7.6 GHz range. The zebra structure consists of several nearly parallel, quasi-equidistant stripes with frequency separations of 200–300 MHz, persisting for about 0.2 s. The spikes, with durations of 8–15 ms and bandwidths of 40–60 MHz, are distributed both inside the zebra stripes and in the continuum background, often clustering in groups and showing a high degree of polarization (>85% right-circular). The combined spectral morphology suggests that the zebra pattern may result from double plasma resonance (DPR) conditions in an inhomogeneous coronal loop, while the spikes are consistent with small-scale, coherent electron cyclotron maser or Bernstein mode emission triggered by localized energetic electron injections. Spatial information from simultaneous Nobeyama Radioheliograph observations at 17 and 34 GHz indicates that the radio source was compact and co-spatial with the flaring loop-top region, coinciding with hard X-ray emission sources observed by RHESSI. The temporal correlation between spikes and zebra stripes implies a close physical connection, possibly reflecting modulation of the emission process by propagating wave disturbances or intermittent particle acceleration. This event provides rare, high-quality evidence of the coexistence of microwave spikes and zebra patterns in the same burst, offering important constraints on models of coherent solar radio emission and the fine structuring of the coronal plasma in flare energy release sites.
introduction:
Fine spectral structures in solar radio emission provide key diagnostics of the physical conditions and processes in the solar corona. Among these structures, microwave spikes and zebra patterns are of particular interest, as they are signatures of coherent plasma emission mechanisms operating in regions of strong magnetic fields and energetic particle populations. Spikes are characterized by extremely short durations, narrow bandwidths, and high brightness temperatures, often interpreted as manifestations of small-scale, transient energy release events and associated with fine structuring of the acceleration region. Zebra structures consist of multiple, almost parallel, emission stripes in dynamic spectra, generally attributed to double plasma resonance or related mechanisms that involve wave–particle interactions in magnetized plasma.

While both types of fine structure have been extensively studied at metric and decimetric wavelengths, observations in the microwave range are relatively rare due to the high instrumental requirements for temporal, spectral, and spatial resolution. The detailed study of such phenomena in the microwave domain can yield quantitative constraints on magnetic field strength, plasma density, and the geometry of the emission source in the low corona. High-cadence imaging spectroscopy is particularly valuable, as it enables the association of spectral features with spatially resolved sources, shedding light on the dynamics of the underlying flare processes.

On May 29, 2003, a short but intense solar radio burst was recorded, exhibiting a rich variety of fine structures, including pronounced microwave spikes and a well-defined zebra pattern. The event occurred during a period of heightened solar activity and was accompanied by a compact flare in an active region with strong magnetic fields. The availability of simultaneous spectral and spatial observations at high resolution makes this burst an exceptional case for investigating the origin and relationship of these fine structures. In particular, the combination of dynamic spectra and interferometric imaging allows a direct comparison of the temporal and spectral properties with the morphology and evolution of the radio sources.

In this work, we present a detailed analysis of the spectral and spatial characteristics of the microwave spikes and zebra structure observed in the May 29, 2003 event. We aim to determine the physical parameters of the source regions, examine the possible emission mechanisms, and explore the connection between spikes and zebra stripes in the context of flare energy release and particle acceleration. The results contribute to a better understanding of coherent microwave emission processes and the fine structuring of flare-associated radio sources in the solar corona.
conclusion:
The analysis of the short radio burst observed on May 29, 2003, has provided new insights into the fine structure of solar microwave emission, in particular the simultaneous occurrence of zebra structure and narrowband spikes within a compact temporal and spectral interval. The high spectral resolution data reveal that the emission consisted of several quasi-parallel zebra stripes superimposed with clusters of millisecond-duration spikes, indicating that different emission processes were operating either concurrently or in rapid succession within the same coronal volume. The spatially resolved observations, obtained from interferometric measurements, confirm that the source region was highly localized, with an apparent size much smaller than the instrumental beam, implying that the actual emission sites were extremely compact and possibly structured on sub-arcsecond scales.

The spectral morphology of the zebra structure, including the frequency separation of the stripes and their temporal evolution, is consistent with interpretations based on the double plasma resonance (DPR) mechanism. In this scenario, the emission arises from upper-hybrid waves amplified at resonances between the electron cyclotron frequency and the upper-hybrid frequency in a non-uniform coronal magnetic field. The observed frequency spacing suggests magnetic field strengths of several hundred gauss in the source region, in agreement with expectations for low coronal heights above an active region. The superposed microwave spikes, with bandwidths of only a few tens of megahertz and durations of a few milliseconds, point to coherent emission from small-scale, transient acceleration sites, possibly associated with rapidly evolving magnetic reconnection or turbulence.

The close temporal and spatial relationship between the zebra structure and the spikes suggests that both phenomena may be manifestations of a common energy release process, modulated by different plasma conditions or wave–particle interaction regimes. It is plausible that the same population of energetic electrons, injected during a brief reconnection episode, could excite both the DPR-related zebra stripes and the spike bursts through different instabilities. Alternatively, the spikes may represent secondary processes occurring in regions adjacent to the primary zebra source, triggered by the same magnetic disturbance.

This event highlights the diagnostic power of combined spectral and spatial observations in the microwave range for probing the fine structure of solar radio bursts. The May 29, 2003 burst demonstrates that even very short-duration events can display a rich variety of coherent structures, revealing complex plasma conditions and magnetic configurations in the flaring corona. The inferred source sizes, magnetic field strengths, and plasma densities derived from the fine structure parameters provide valuable constraints for models of particle acceleration and wave generation.

Future observations with higher temporal, spectral, and spatial resolution, particularly from new generation solar radio instruments, will be essential to disentangle the detailed relationships between different types of fine structures, to confirm the physical connection between zebra patterns and spikes, and to further refine diagnostic techniques for coronal magnetic and plasma parameters based on coherent microwave emission.

title: A Tunable Base Station Cooperation Scheme for Poisson Cellular Networks
abstract: We propose a tunable base station cooperation scheme for downlink cellular networks modeled by a homogeneous Poisson point process. The scheme enables flexible coordination among neighboring base stations by adjusting a cooperation parameter that governs the extent of joint transmission. This tunability allows network operators to balance performance gains from cooperation against the associated signaling and resource overhead. Using tools from stochastic geometry, we derive analytical expressions for the coverage probability and average spectral efficiency under the proposed scheme, accounting for inter-cell interference and random user locations. The analysis reveals how the cooperation parameter influences key performance metrics, providing insights into optimal configuration under varying network densities and signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio thresholds. Simulation results validate the analytical findings and demonstrate that moderate cooperation levels can achieve significant performance improvements over non-cooperative operation with manageable overhead. The proposed framework offers a tractable and adaptable approach for designing cooperative strategies in large-scale, irregular cellular deployments.
introduction:
The rapid proliferation of mobile devices and the increasing demand for high data rates have driven the evolution of cellular networks toward higher spectral efficiency, more uniform service quality, and improved user experience. In contemporary and future wireless systems, such as 5G and beyond, the density of base stations (BSs) is expected to grow significantly, leading to increasingly irregular network topologies. This densification, while beneficial in terms of reducing path loss and increasing spatial reuse, also intensifies inter-cell interference, which remains a key limiting factor in network performance. Interference management has therefore emerged as a central research problem, motivating the development of techniques that allow base stations to coordinate their transmissions in order to mitigate interference and enhance coverage.

Base station cooperation, also referred to as coordinated multi-point (CoMP) transmission and reception, has been recognized as a promising approach to improve network throughput and fairness by enabling BSs to share information and jointly serve users. In its ideal form, full cooperation among all BSs can completely eliminate inter-cell interference, transforming the network into a large distributed multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system. However, full cooperation requires extensive backhaul capacity, tight synchronization, and significant computational resources, making it infeasible for large-scale deployments. Consequently, practical cooperation schemes typically involve only a subset of BSs, often based on geographical proximity or channel conditions, thereby trading off cooperation gains against implementation complexity.

A fundamental challenge in designing such schemes lies in determining the size and composition of the cooperating BS set for each user. If too few BSs are involved, the interference mitigation and diversity benefits are limited; if too many are included, the overhead imposed on the backhaul network and the complexity of coordination may outweigh the performance gains. Moreover, the optimal cooperation level can vary across the network and over time, depending on factors such as user location, traffic load, and network topology. This has led to an interest in tunable cooperation mechanisms that can adapt to changing conditions, offering a flexible balance between performance and resource consumption.

Stochastic geometry has emerged as a powerful analytical tool for the performance evaluation of large-scale wireless networks with random spatial configurations. In particular, modeling BS locations as a homogeneous Poisson point process (PPP) provides a tractable framework for deriving key performance metrics, such as coverage probability and average rate, while capturing the irregularity of practical deployments. The PPP model has been widely used to study interference-limited networks, and it offers a natural setting in which to analyze cooperation schemes whose performance depends on the spatial distribution of BSs and users.

Recent studies have applied stochastic geometry to investigate fixed cooperation schemes, such as serving each user with its nearest \(N\) BSs or with those within a fixed radius. These works have provided valuable insights into the achievable gains and limitations of cooperation in random networks. However, most existing models lack a mechanism to smoothly adjust the cooperation level in response to network conditions. As a result, they cannot capture the potential benefits of tunable cooperation, nor can they fully characterize the tradeoff between cooperation gains and resource overhead.

In this work, we propose a tunable base station cooperation scheme for Poisson cellular networks that allows the level of cooperation to be continuously adjusted via a single control parameter. The scheme is based on a selection criterion that interpolates between non-cooperative transmission and full cooperation, enabling a broad spectrum of operational modes. By varying the tunable parameter, network operators can adapt the cooperation region to optimize performance under different deployment scenarios and traffic conditions. This flexibility is particularly valuable in heterogeneous networks, where BS densities, transmit powers, and backhaul capabilities may vary significantly across the network.

We develop a stochastic geometry framework to analyze the proposed scheme, deriving expressions for the coverage probability and other relevant performance metrics as functions of the tunable parameter. The analysis reveals how the cooperation level influences both the desired signal power and the residual interference, and it quantifies the associated tradeoffs in a mathematically tractable manner. Our results demonstrate that the tunable cooperation scheme can yield substantial performance gains over non-cooperative operation, while avoiding the excessive overhead of full cooperation. Furthermore, by appropriately selecting the cooperation parameter, it is possible to target specific quality-of-service objectives or to adapt to temporal variations in the network.

The main contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a novel tunable cooperation criterion that generalizes existing fixed cooperation schemes and enables adaptive coordination among BSs in a Poisson network. Second, we provide a comprehensive analytical characterization of the scheme using tools from stochastic geometry, highlighting the impact of the tunable parameter on coverage probability. Third, we illustrate, through numerical examples, how the proposed approach can be optimized for various network configurations and performance objectives.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on BS cooperation in random cellular networks and outlines the limitations of existing approaches. Section III describes the system model, including the Poisson spatial framework and the proposed tunable cooperation scheme. Section IV presents the analytical derivations of the performance metrics, while Section V discusses numerical results and optimization strategies. Section VI concludes the paper and outlines possible directions for future research.
conclusion:
This work has proposed a tunable base station cooperation scheme for downlink Poisson cellular networks, enabling a flexible trade-off between cooperation gains and resource expenditure. By modeling base station locations as a homogeneous Poisson point process and incorporating a cooperation parameter, we derived analytical expressions for key performance metrics, including coverage probability and average user rate. The tunable parameter allows network operators to interpolate smoothly between non-cooperative transmission and full cooperation, adapting to varying traffic loads, interference conditions, and backhaul constraints.  

Our analysis demonstrates that moderate cooperation levels can yield substantial improvements in coverage and spectral efficiency without incurring the significant overhead associated with full coordination. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides a tractable means of quantifying the marginal benefits of increasing cooperation, offering insights into optimal network configuration under different operating regimes. Numerical simulations validated the accuracy of our analytical results and confirmed the robustness of the scheme across a range of system parameters.  

Overall, the tunable cooperation approach offers both theoretical and practical advantages, combining mathematical tractability with implementation flexibility. Future work will extend the model to incorporate user mobility, heterogeneous base station deployments, and more sophisticated channel models, further enhancing its applicability to next-generation cellular networks. The results presented here suggest that adaptive cooperation strategies can be a key enabler for improving performance in spatially random wireless systems.

title: Training Future Engineers to Be Ghostbusters: Hunting for the Spectral Environmental Radioactivity
abstract: This paper presents an innovative educational approach that integrates environmental radioactivity monitoring with advanced spectral analysis to train future engineers as adept “ghostbusters” of invisible radiation. The program combines theoretical instruction in nuclear physics, environmental science, and signal processing with hands-on laboratory and field activities. Students employ high-resolution gamma spectrometry and portable detection systems to identify and quantify naturally occurring and anthropogenic radionuclides in diverse environments. Emphasis is placed on interpreting complex spectra, distinguishing overlapping peaks, and understanding background contributions. Field exercises simulate real-world scenarios, fostering problem-solving skills, teamwork, and adherence to radiological safety protocols. Data analysis projects require students to apply statistical methods, calibration techniques, and uncertainty assessment, bridging the gap between measurement and environmental impact evaluation. By embedding these activities in the curriculum, the initiative not only enhances technical competence but also promotes environmental responsibility and public communication skills. The results demonstrate that immersive, spectrum-focused training significantly improves students’ ability to detect, analyze, and contextualize environmental radioactivity, preparing them to address contemporary challenges in environmental monitoring, nuclear safety, and radiological emergency response.
introduction:
The safe management of environmental radioactivity is a critical component of protecting human health and ecosystems in the context of an increasingly industrialized and technologically advanced society. While natural sources of radiation have always been present, anthropogenic activities—ranging from nuclear power generation and medical isotope production to industrial applications—have introduced additional radioactive materials into the environment. Detecting and quantifying these radionuclides requires sophisticated instrumentation, rigorous analytical methodologies, and a workforce equipped with both theoretical understanding and practical skill. In this regard, the training of future engineers to competently identify, measure, and interpret spectral data from environmental radioactivity is of paramount importance.

Spectral analysis, particularly gamma spectrometry, provides a non-destructive and highly sensitive means of determining the presence and activity of specific radionuclides. Interpreting spectral signatures demands an understanding not only of nuclear physics, but also of detector technologies, calibration procedures, and statistical data treatment. For engineers tasked with environmental monitoring, emergency response, or nuclear decommissioning, these competencies enable accurate assessments that inform remediation strategies and regulatory compliance. However, the inherently abstract nature of nuclear phenomena, combined with the complexity of spectral data, can make the learning process challenging for students without direct exposure to real-world applications.

To bridge this gap, innovative pedagogy is required—approaches that engage students in active problem-solving and simulate the investigative processes of professional practice. The metaphor of “ghostbusting” environmental radioactivity provides a creative framework for teaching, framing radionuclides as invisible entities whose presence must be revealed through careful detection and analysis. By adopting this thematic approach, students are encouraged to think like scientific detectives, applying engineering principles to locate, identify, and quantify “spectral ghosts” in the environment. Such experiential, scenario-based learning not only reinforces technical concepts but also fosters critical thinking, teamwork, and decision-making under uncertainty.

This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of an educational program aimed at training engineering students in the detection and analysis of environmental radioactivity through spectral methods. Drawing on the “ghostbuster” analogy, the program integrates theoretical instruction with laboratory exercises and field simulations. The results demonstrate how thematic, context-rich pedagogy can enhance student engagement, deepen conceptual understanding, and better prepare future engineers to address the complex challenges of environmental radiological monitoring.
conclusion:
The exploration of innovative pedagogical approaches to environmental radioactivity has demonstrated that framing the task as a “spectral hunt” can effectively engage engineering students in both the scientific and societal dimensions of radiological monitoring. By integrating hands-on instrumentation training with problem-based learning scenarios inspired by popular culture, students were encouraged to adopt the dual role of technical specialists and critical thinkers, capable of identifying, characterizing, and interpreting low-level environmental radiation signals. This approach fostered not only competence in the use of spectrometric tools and data analysis software, but also an appreciation of the broader environmental and ethical implications of their measurements.

The “ghostbusting” analogy, while playful, served as a pedagogical bridge, transforming abstract nuclear physics concepts into tangible investigative challenges. Students developed enhanced skills in spectral identification, background discrimination, and uncertainty quantification, which are essential for contemporary environmental engineering practice. Moreover, the collaborative, inquiry-driven format promoted communication skills and interdisciplinary awareness, preparing future engineers to work effectively in teams addressing complex environmental issues.

The results suggest that embedding such thematic, context-rich activities into engineering curricula can demystify radiation science, reduce apprehension toward nuclear topics, and cultivate a generation of professionals equipped to handle both the technical and societal demands of environmental radioactivity monitoring. Importantly, the approach underscores the value of creativity and narrative in STEM education, without compromising scientific rigor. Future work should explore scalability, adaptation for remote or resource-limited settings, and assessment of long-term retention of knowledge and skills. In an era where environmental monitoring is increasingly critical, training engineers to be adept “spectral investigators” offers a promising pathway toward both technical excellence and public trust in environmental stewardship.

title: Status of indirect searches for New Physics with heavy flavour decays after the initial LHC run
abstract: We review the status of indirect searches for New Physics via heavy flavour decays following the initial LHC run. Precision measurements of rare processes, CP violation, and mixing observables are compared with Standard Model predictions. While most results show remarkable agreement, some tensions persist, motivating further scrutiny with upcoming higher-luminosity data to probe potential beyond-Standard-Model effects.
introduction:
The study of heavy flavour decays has long been recognised as one of the most sensitive probes for physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). Processes involving beauty and charm hadrons, as well as rare kaon decays, provide a unique window into virtual effects of new particles and interactions, even when such states are too heavy to be produced directly in high-energy collisions. This sensitivity arises from the fact that flavour-changing neutral currents (FCNCs) and CP-violating transitions are strongly suppressed in the SM, often occurring only at loop level and being further diminished by the structure of the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa (CKM) matrix. As a result, potential contributions from new physics (NP) can compete with or even dominate over the SM amplitudes, leading to observable deviations in branching fractions, angular distributions, or CP asymmetries.

The advent of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has dramatically advanced the experimental study of heavy flavour decays. With its unprecedented luminosity and production rates for heavy quarks, and the dedicated capabilities of experiments such as LHCb, as well as contributions from ATLAS and CMS, the first LHC run (Run 1) delivered a wealth of precision measurements. These include rare decay modes such as \( B_s^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^- \), detailed angular analyses of semileptonic decays like \( B \to K^* \ell^+ \ell^- \), and improved determinations of CKM parameters through tree- and loop-dominated processes. The interplay between these results and those from earlier flavour experiments, notably the B factories and the Tevatron, has led to stringent constraints on a wide class of NP scenarios.

From a theoretical perspective, heavy flavour observables are interpreted within the framework of the SM effective field theory (SMEFT) or, more specifically, the weak effective Hamiltonian for quark flavour transitions. This approach allows for a clean separation between short-distance coefficients—potentially modified by NP—and long-distance hadronic matrix elements, which can be computed using lattice QCD, QCD sum rules, or other nonperturbative methods. Global fits to flavour observables provide a coherent means to test the internal consistency of the SM and to identify possible patterns indicative of new interactions, such as those mediated by heavy gauge bosons, leptoquarks, or supersymmetric particles.

The significance of indirect searches through heavy flavour physics lies in their complementary role to direct searches at high-energy colliders. While direct searches may be limited by available centre-of-mass energy and luminosity, indirect effects can reveal mass scales well beyond the direct reach, in some cases up to tens of TeV, depending on the type of interaction. Moreover, the flavour structure of potential NP—whether it aligns with the SM’s minimal flavour violation (MFV) hypothesis or exhibits new sources of flavour and CP violation—can be probed with high precision. This makes heavy flavour decays an essential component of the broader particle physics programme aimed at uncovering the nature of physics beyond the SM.

The completion of Run 1 of the LHC marks a natural point to assess the current status of these indirect searches. The combination of multiple decay channels, the confrontation of experimental data with state-of-the-art theoretical predictions, and the emergence of some intriguing tensions in certain observables motivate a careful and comprehensive review. In this work, we summarise the key experimental achievements in heavy flavour physics from Run 1, examine their theoretical interpretation, and discuss the implications for NP models. We place particular emphasis on rare decays and CP violation in the beauty and charm sectors, as well as on the constraints these results impose on extensions of the SM. Finally, we outline the prospects for future measurements in the upcoming LHC runs and at other facilities, which will further sharpen the sensitivity of indirect searches for new physics.
conclusion:
The first run of the LHC has marked a significant step forward in the exploration of heavy flavour processes as a probe for physics beyond the Standard Model. Measurements from the LHCb experiment, complemented by results from ATLAS, CMS, and earlier flavour factories, have dramatically improved the precision of numerous observables in the heavy quark sector. Rare decays, CP-violating asymmetries, and mixing parameters in the beauty and charm systems have been determined with unprecedented accuracy. In many cases, the experimental uncertainties are now at or below the level of the corresponding theoretical uncertainties, underscoring the importance of continued advances in lattice QCD and other non-perturbative techniques.

From the perspective of indirect searches, the absence of clear deviations from Standard Model predictions in key flavour-changing neutral current processes, such as \( B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^- \) and \( B \to K^{(*)} \ell^+ \ell^- \), has placed stringent constraints on a wide class of New Physics scenarios. Supersymmetric models, models with extended Higgs sectors, and scenarios with new flavour-violating couplings are now strongly limited in their viable parameter space. Similarly, the precise determination of the CKM matrix elements and the unitarity triangle shows remarkable consistency with the Standard Model, further restricting the room for large contributions from new heavy states.

Nevertheless, a number of intriguing tensions persist. Anomalies in certain angular observables of rare semileptonic \(B\) decays, hints of lepton flavour universality violation, and discrepancies in some charm CP asymmetries continue to motivate theoretical and experimental scrutiny. While each of these effects individually falls short of a discovery threshold, their collective pattern may be indicative of subtle New Physics effects, especially if they are confirmed and refined with larger data sets. The interplay between different decay modes and between high– and low–energy measurements will remain essential in disentangling potential new contributions from Standard Model hadronic effects.

The initial LHC run has thus provided both strong confirmation of the Standard Model’s flavour sector and a set of high-precision benchmarks against which future measurements will be judged. The upcoming higher-energy and higher-luminosity runs of the LHC, together with upgrades to LHCb and the advent of Belle II, will significantly extend sensitivity to rare processes and small deviations. Continued progress in theoretical calculations, particularly in controlling hadronic uncertainties, will be crucial for maximising the discovery potential of these measurements. Heavy flavour physics will remain a central pillar of the indirect search programme, offering a unique window into possible New Physics at energy scales beyond the direct reach of current colliders.

title: SMOT: Single-Shot Multi Object Tracking
abstract: We present SMOT, a Single-Shot Multi Object Tracking framework that unifies detection and tracking within a single, end-to-end trainable network. Unlike conventional tracking-by-detection pipelines that separate object localization from temporal association, SMOT jointly optimizes both tasks, enabling real-time performance without sacrificing accuracy. Our approach leverages a shared backbone for feature extraction and introduces a lightweight temporal correlation module to maintain identity consistency across frames. By eliminating the need for post-processing data association, SMOT reduces latency and computational overhead. Extensive experiments on standard MOT benchmarks demonstrate that SMOT achieves competitive tracking accuracy and robustness under challenging scenarios, including occlusions and appearance changes, while maintaining high throughput suitable for deployment in real-world applications.
introduction:
Multi-object tracking (MOT) is a fundamental problem in computer vision with wide-ranging applications, including autonomous driving, video surveillance, sports analytics, and human-computer interaction. The objective of MOT is to simultaneously detect multiple targets and maintain their consistent identities across frames in a video sequence. Traditional MOT approaches typically decompose the problem into two stages: object detection and data association. In this paradigm, detectors identify objects in each frame, and a separate association module links detections over time. While this pipeline has been effective, it often suffers from error propagation between stages, increased computational cost, and sensitivity to occlusions or missed detections.

Recent advances in deep learning have spurred interest in end-to-end formulations that jointly perform detection and tracking. These approaches aim to exploit shared feature representations and temporal context to improve robustness and efficiency. However, most existing end-to-end methods either require recurrent processing over multiple frames or rely on post-processing steps, limiting their real-time applicability. In high-speed or resource-constrained scenarios, the ability to track multiple objects in a single forward pass without sacrificing accuracy is highly desirable.

In this work, we propose **SMOT** — *Single-Shot Multi Object Tracking*, a novel framework that unifies detection and tracking within a single-stage architecture. SMOT processes each frame independently while embedding temporal cues that enable identity preservation without explicit sequence modeling. By leveraging a unified representation space for both localization and identity embedding, SMOT achieves competitive accuracy with significantly reduced latency. Our contributions include a streamlined architecture for joint tasks, a training strategy that balances detection and tracking objectives, and extensive experiments demonstrating that SMOT delivers real-time multi-object tracking performance on challenging benchmarks.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced SMOT, a single-shot framework for multi-object tracking that unifies detection and association within a single network. By jointly optimizing these tasks, SMOT achieves competitive accuracy while maintaining real-time performance. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing identity switches and improving tracking robustness in challenging scenarios. Our approach simplifies the traditional multi-stage tracking pipeline, lowering computational overhead and enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments. Future work will explore integrating richer temporal context and adaptive appearance modeling to further enhance long-term tracking stability. SMOT offers a promising direction for efficient, end-to-end multi-object tracking solutions.

title: Linearizability Criteria for Systems of Two Second-Order Differential Equations by Complex Methods
abstract: We investigate the linearizability of systems of two second-order ordinary differential equations using complex-analytic techniques. By representing the system as a single complex equation, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for transformation into a linear form via complex point transformations. The approach unifies and extends existing real-variable criteria, providing a more compact framework for analysis. Explicit linearization conditions are obtained in terms of the system’s coefficients and their derivatives. Several illustrative examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the method and its computational advantages over purely real approaches in identifying linearizable nonlinear systems.
introduction:
The study of nonlinear differential equations occupies a central place in the analysis of complex dynamical systems arising in mathematics, physics, and engineering. Among the wide variety of approaches to understanding such systems, the problem of linearization—transforming a nonlinear system into an equivalent linear one through an appropriate change of variables—has attracted sustained interest. Linear systems are generally more tractable, both analytically and numerically, and their qualitative behavior is well understood. Consequently, establishing criteria under which a nonlinear system can be linearized is of significant theoretical and practical importance.

For scalar second-order ordinary differential equations, the theory of linearization by point transformations has been developed extensively, tracing back to the pioneering work of Sophus Lie. Lie’s symmetry methods provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the linearizability of certain classes of equations, expressed in terms of the invariance properties of the equation under continuous transformation groups. These results have been extended in various directions, including higher-order equations and systems of equations. However, systems of two second-order ordinary differential equations present additional challenges, due to the increased complexity of their symmetry structures and the coupling between the components.

One fruitful approach to studying such systems is to employ complex methods, by representing the system as a single complex-valued second-order equation. This perspective not only reduces the notational and computational burden but also reveals additional structure that may be obscured in the purely real formulation. In particular, complex analysis techniques, combined with Lie symmetry theory, can lead to compact formulations of linearizability conditions, and in some cases, to new insights into the geometry underlying the transformation to linear form.

The idea of using a complex variable to encode two real variables is natural when the system exhibits certain symmetries or when the coupling between components has a form compatible with complex differentiation. In such cases, the real and imaginary parts of a complex-valued equation correspond directly to the two real equations of the system. Linearization can then be studied in the complex domain, where the transformation theory may be simpler or more transparent. Once linearizability criteria are established in the complex setting, they can be translated back into real form, providing explicit conditions on the coefficients of the original system.

Recent research has extended the complex method to various classes of systems, including those with cubic or higher-order nonlinearities in the first derivatives, as well as systems arising in mechanics and control theory. These studies have demonstrated that the complex approach can yield linearizability criteria that are not only elegant but also computationally efficient to verify. Moreover, the geometric interpretation of complex transformations as conformal mappings offers a natural framework for understanding the invariants associated with the system.

The present work focuses on deriving linearizability criteria for systems of two second-order ordinary differential equations using complex methods. We consider the general form of such systems that can be represented as a single complex equation, and we apply Lie’s theory in the complex domain to obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for linearization via complex point transformations. Our approach unifies and extends previous results, offering a systematic procedure for identifying linearizable systems within this framework. In addition, we discuss the correspondence between complex and real formulations, ensuring that the criteria are accessible to those working directly with real systems.

By combining classical symmetry analysis with the structural advantages of complex representation, this study contributes to the broader program of classifying and understanding nonlinear systems through their transformation properties. The results presented here are expected to be of interest to researchers in differential equations, mathematical physics, and applied mathematics, particularly those concerned with the integrability and solvability of coupled nonlinear systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the problem of determining linearizability criteria for systems of two second-order ordinary differential equations by employing complex analytic methods. By representing the coupled real system in terms of a single complex equation, we have been able to exploit the structure and symmetry inherent in the complex formulation to derive conditions under which the original nonlinear system can be transformed into a linear one via complex point transformations. This approach has the advantage of reducing the algebraic and differential complexity associated with purely real-variable techniques, while also revealing deeper geometric and analytic connections.

The main achievement of the study lies in the systematic derivation of necessary and sufficient conditions for linearizability in the complex domain, and the subsequent translation of these conditions into the real setting. This translation is essential, since the original problem is posed in terms of real-valued dependent and independent variables, but the complex representation serves as a unifying framework. The criteria obtained here generalize known results for single second-order equations to the coupled case, and highlight the role played by the Cauchy–Riemann equations, complex symmetry generators, and the associated Lie algebraic structure.

By framing the system in complex form, we have shown that the linearizability problem can be naturally related to the existence of a maximal eight-dimensional Lie point symmetry algebra in the complex setting, which corresponds to the projective group of transformations. The equivalence between the complex-symmetry-based criteria and their real counterparts ensures that the method is not only theoretically sound but also practically applicable. In particular, our results demonstrate that the complex method provides a straightforward pathway to identifying the linearizing transformations, circumventing some of the more cumbersome computations that arise in the real-variable approach.

Several illustrative examples have been presented to demonstrate the applicability of the derived criteria. These examples confirm that the method correctly captures both systems that are linearizable and those that are not, and that it can recover the linearizing transformations explicitly when they exist. The examples also underline the fact that the complex approach can handle certain coupled nonlinearities more elegantly, as the coupling terms often take on a simpler form in the complex representation.

The broader significance of these findings lies in the potential for extending complex methods to more general classes of systems, including higher-order equations, partial differential equations, and systems with variable coefficients or nonlocal terms. The complex formulation naturally incorporates rotational symmetries and conformal mappings, suggesting that the scope of applicability may be wider than the specific class of systems considered here. Moreover, the link between complex analysis and the geometry of the solution space opens avenues for further exploration, such as the use of complex differential invariants in classification problems.

In conclusion, the study affirms that complex methods provide a powerful and elegant framework for the linearization of systems of two second-order ordinary differential equations. The criteria obtained are both necessary and sufficient, and are readily applicable in practice. Beyond their immediate utility, these results contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between symmetry, geometry, and integrability in nonlinear systems. Future work will aim to extend these ideas to more general settings, to explore algorithmic implementations for automated detection of linearizability, and to investigate the relationship between complex linearization and other integrability techniques, such as the Painlevé analysis and the method of differential constraints. Through such developments, the complex approach may become an integral part of the standard toolkit for the analysis and simplification of nonlinear differential systems.

title: Fractal aspects of hadrons
abstract: We investigate the fractal characteristics of hadronic structures within the framework of quantum chromodynamics. By analyzing scaling behaviors in parton distribution functions and hadronic form factors, we identify self-similar patterns suggestive of underlying fractal geometry. Employing both phenomenological models and numerical simulations, we quantify fractal dimensions associated with spatial and momentum-space distributions. Our results indicate that fractal features emerge naturally from non-perturbative dynamics, potentially offering new insights into confinement and the internal complexity of hadrons. These findings suggest that fractal analysis may provide a complementary perspective for describing hadronic structure beyond conventional approaches.
introduction:
In recent decades, the study of hadronic structure has undergone significant conceptual and methodological evolution, driven by advances in experimental precision and theoretical frameworks. Hadrons, as bound states of quarks and gluons governed by the non-abelian dynamics of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), exhibit a rich internal complexity that remains only partially understood. Traditional descriptions, while successful in capturing many phenomenological aspects, often rely on simplified geometrical or statistical models that may conceal deeper patterns embedded in the spatial and momentum distributions of their constituents. One intriguing avenue of investigation is the possibility that hadrons exhibit fractal-like properties, characterized by self-similarity across different scales of resolution. Such an approach offers an alternative perspective on the organization of quark-gluon degrees of freedom, complementing and potentially extending conventional QCD analyses.

The concept of fractals, introduced and formalized in the context of mathematics and statistical physics, refers to structures whose complexity persists across scales, often described by non-integer dimensions. Fractal geometry has been successfully applied in diverse areas ranging from condensed matter systems to turbulence and astrophysics, providing a language to describe irregular, scale-invariant phenomena. In high-energy physics, the idea that scattering processes or internal partonic distributions might bear fractal signatures has been occasionally proposed, particularly in the context of multiparticle production and parton cascades. This connection arises naturally from the renormalization group viewpoint, in which scale transformations play a central role, and from the branching nature of parton evolution as described by perturbative QCD.

Deep inelastic scattering (DIS) experiments and high-energy hadron-hadron collisions have revealed that the internal structure of hadrons depends on the probing scale, a phenomenon encapsulated in the scaling violations of structure functions. While perturbative QCD provides a quantitative account of this evolution through the DGLAP equations, the underlying cascade of partons generated as the resolution increases bears a qualitative resemblance to fractal processes. The repeated splitting of partons into lower-energy offspring, governed by probabilistic rules, can produce distributions whose statistical properties are invariant under changes of scale within certain regimes. This observation motivates the exploration of fractal dimensions as descriptors of hadronic structure, potentially bridging phenomenological parameterizations with fundamental QCD dynamics.

The fractal approach to hadronic structure is not intended to replace QCD but to serve as an interpretive and heuristic framework. By associating a fractal dimension to the spatial or momentum-space distribution of partons, one can quantify the degree of complexity or irregularity inherent to the hadron’s internal landscape. Such dimensions may be extracted from experimental data, for instance through scaling analyses of form factors, multiplicity distributions, or transverse momentum spectra. Furthermore, the identification of fractal behaviour could illuminate the transition between perturbative and non-perturbative regimes, where the coupling strength becomes large and confinement effects dominate, potentially giving rise to new forms of scale invariance.

Historically, several models have hinted at such features. The statistical self-similarity of jet fragmentation, the intermittency patterns observed in multiparticle production, and the scaling properties of parton distribution functions in certain kinematic limits all point toward a deeper geometrical organization. In particular, the phenomenon of intermittency, characterized by power-law scaling of fluctuations in phase space, has been interpreted as a manifestation of fractal behaviour in the hadronization process. Similarly, the color flux-tube picture of confinement, with its string-like dynamics, may exhibit fractal-like transverse structures when probed at varying resolutions.

The present work aims to investigate the fractal aspects of hadrons in a systematic manner, drawing on both theoretical considerations and analysis of experimental observables. We will discuss the mathematical foundations of fractal geometry as they pertain to QCD systems, review existing evidence for fractal scaling in hadronic processes, and propose methodologies for quantifying fractal dimensions from data. By framing hadronic structure in this way, we hope to provide a complementary viewpoint that enriches the standard QCD narrative, offering potential insights into the emergent complexity of strong interactions.

Ultimately, the study of fractal properties in hadrons lies at the intersection of geometry, dynamics, and phenomenology. It compels us to reconsider the notion of structure in a quantum field theory context, where scale dependence is intrinsic and where complexity may be more than a byproduct of our descriptions—it may be a fundamental feature of the strongly interacting world.
conclusion:
The present study has explored the fractal aspects of hadronic structure, emphasizing the potential of fractal geometry as a complementary framework for describing the internal dynamics and spatial complexity of strongly interacting particles. By examining scaling properties in parton distribution functions, transverse momentum spectra, and form factors, we have shown that certain features of hadrons exhibit self-similarity over specific kinematic ranges. This self-similarity, quantified through effective fractal dimensions, offers an alternative language for characterizing the emergent complexity arising from Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at both perturbative and non-perturbative scales.

The analysis indicates that fractal dimensions extracted from experimental data are not universal constants but rather scale-dependent parameters, reflecting the underlying evolution equations of QCD.
