This observation suggests that the fractal description is not merely a mathematical curiosity, but a manifestation of the dynamical processes governing hadronic matter. In particular, the correspondence between fractal-like scaling and the parton cascade picture reinforces the view that the apparent irregularities in hadron structure are governed by deep symmetry principles and renormalization group behavior.

Moreover, the fractal perspective provides a unifying viewpoint for phenomena that are often treated separately, such as the scaling violations in deep inelastic scattering and the multiplicity distributions in high-energy collisions. By framing these within a common scaling paradigm, one gains a more coherent understanding of how hadronic complexity arises from simple fundamental interactions. The consistency between phenomenological fits using fractal models and available high-precision data supports further development of this approach.

Future investigations may benefit from integrating fractal analysis with lattice QCD simulations, enabling a bridge between analytic scaling descriptions and fully non-perturbative calculations. Additionally, extending the fractal framework to describe multi-hadron systems and collective effects in heavy-ion collisions could reveal new scaling laws and universality classes. Overall, the fractal aspects of hadrons open a promising avenue for deepening our comprehension of strong interactions, offering both conceptual insights and practical tools for interpreting the wealth of experimental data in hadronic and nuclear physics.

title: OntoVerbal: a Generic Tool and Practical Application to SNOMED CT
abstract: OntoVerbal is a generic tool designed to generate natural language verbalizations from ontologies, aiming to improve comprehensibility and facilitate knowledge sharing among domain experts. The system supports multiple ontology formats and languages, offering configurable templates and modular architectures for adaptability across domains. We present its practical application to SNOMED CT, a comprehensive clinical terminology, demonstrating how OntoVerbal can aid in interpreting complex medical concepts. Evaluation with healthcare professionals indicates improved clarity and usability of ontology content, highlighting the potential of OntoVerbal to bridge the gap between formal knowledge representations and end-user understanding in diverse knowledge-intensive domains.
introduction:
Ontologies have become central to the representation, integration, and reuse of knowledge in a wide range of domains, particularly in the biomedical and healthcare sectors. They offer a formal, explicit specification of conceptualisations, enabling consistent interpretation of terms and relationships across heterogeneous systems. Among the most significant of these resources is SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Clinical Terms), a comprehensive, multilingual clinical healthcare terminology that supports the structured representation of clinical content in electronic health records (EHRs) and other health information systems. SNOMED CT’s scope and granularity make it a powerful tool for semantic interoperability, clinical decision support, and data analytics. However, the complexity of its structure, the size of its vocabulary, and the formalism of its representation in Description Logics present substantial challenges for human users who need to explore, understand, and communicate its content.

While ontologies are typically designed for machine processing, their successful adoption in practice depends on the ability of domain experts—clinicians, researchers, policy-makers—to interact with them effectively. This requires not only user-friendly interfaces for querying and browsing, but also mechanisms to convey the meaning of ontology entities in natural language. The task of generating verbal, human-readable descriptions from formal ontology content—often referred to as ontology verbalisation—has attracted increasing research interest. By rendering complex logical axioms into coherent natural language sentences, ontology verbalisation facilitates comprehension, supports quality assurance, and enhances communication among stakeholders with varying levels of technical expertise.

Existing approaches to ontology verbalisation range from template-based methods to more flexible natural language generation (NLG) systems. Template-based methods are straightforward to implement and can produce predictable output, but they may lack expressiveness and adaptability across different ontologies. More sophisticated NLG frameworks can generate richer, more varied descriptions, but they often require substantial domain-specific configuration and linguistic resources. In the biomedical domain, where terminologies are vast and highly specialised, the challenge is compounded by the need to maintain accuracy and preserve the precise meaning of the formal definitions, while producing output that is intelligible to clinicians and other non-technical users.

SNOMED CT offers a pertinent case study for ontology verbalisation due to its scale, complexity, and critical role in clinical data exchange. With more than 350,000 active concepts and an intricate web of hierarchical and non-hierarchical relationships, it is not trivial for users to discern the intended meaning of a given concept from its logical definition alone. Although SNOMED CT provides fully specified names and synonyms for concepts, these labels often do not convey the full semantics encoded in the concept’s relationships and attributes. For example, the defining characteristics of a concept such as “Fracture of femur” involve not only the anatomical location but also the nature of the injury, relationships to body structures, and, in some cases, associated morphology or causative agents. Translating these definitions into plain language can help practitioners validate the ontology’s content, identify potential inconsistencies, and apply it more effectively in clinical documentation and decision support.

The motivation for developing a generic ontology verbalisation tool arises from the need to bridge the gap between formal ontology representations and their human interpretation. A generic tool should be able to process ontologies expressed in standard formats (e.g., OWL), adapt to different domains without extensive re-engineering, and generate natural language descriptions that are accurate, coherent, and contextually appropriate. Such a tool would not only benefit ontology engineers and domain experts during the development and maintenance of ontologies, but also serve as an educational and communication aid for end users in operational settings.

This paper presents OntoVerbal, a generic, configurable tool for the automatic generation of natural language descriptions from formal ontologies, and demonstrates its application to SNOMED CT. OntoVerbal is designed to be ontology-agnostic: it leverages the semantic structure of the ontology to produce descriptions without relying on extensive domain-specific handcrafting, while allowing customisation to reflect domain conventions and linguistic preferences. By separating the core verbalisation engine from domain-specific configuration, OntoVerbal supports reuse across diverse ontologies, from biomedical terminologies to environmental or engineering knowledge bases.

In the context of SNOMED CT, OntoVerbal takes as input the ontology’s logical definitions and produces human-readable descriptions that integrate concept labels, hierarchical information, and definitional relationships. The generated descriptions aim to capture the essential meaning of each concept in a form that is accessible to clinicians and other stakeholders, while remaining faithful to the underlying formal semantics. This facilitates a range of use cases: assisting clinicians in selecting the most appropriate terms for clinical documentation, enabling ontology curators to review and refine concept definitions, and supporting training and onboarding of new users.

The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we describe the architecture and methodology of OntoVerbal, highlighting the design principles that enable its generic applicability. Second, we report on the adaptation and application of OntoVerbal to a large-scale, complex ontology—SNOMED CT—illustrating the practical considerations and challenges encountered. Third, we discuss the implications of ontology verbalisation for improving usability, quality assurance, and adoption of biomedical terminologies, and outline directions for future research in this area.

By addressing the need for a flexible, reusable approach to ontology verbalisation, and by demonstrating its utility in a demanding real-world setting, this work contributes to the broader goal of making formalised knowledge more accessible and actionable for human users. In doing so, it supports the integration of ontological resources into everyday workflows, thereby enhancing the value they bring to both research and practice.
conclusion:
This work has presented OntoVerbal, a generic, ontology-driven natural language generation tool, and demonstrated its practical application to SNOMED CT. The motivation underpinning the development of OntoVerbal lies in the growing need for human-readable, context-appropriate verbalisation of complex biomedical ontologies, which are otherwise only accessible to domain experts familiar with their formal logical structures. By providing a flexible and reusable architecture, OntoVerbal addresses the challenge of bridging the gap between formal ontology representations and the variety of linguistic and pragmatic requirements encountered in real-world clinical and research settings.

The generic design of OntoVerbal enables its application across domains and ontologies by separating knowledge modelling from linguistic realisation. Its modular pipeline supports customisation at multiple levels, from ontology parsing and semantic interpretation to sentence planning and surface realisation, allowing adaptation to different target audiences, languages, and presentation purposes. The case study with SNOMED CT has served both as a proof of concept and as a rigorous test of the tool’s scalability, performance, and capacity to cope with the breadth and complexity of a large-scale, hierarchically rich, and clinically critical terminology.

Through the SNOMED CT application, we have shown that OntoVerbal can generate coherent, semantically faithful, and context-sensitive textual descriptions of concepts, relationships, and constraints. The evaluation indicated that these generated descriptions can improve comprehensibility for users less familiar with formal ontology syntax, while retaining precision for expert users. Importantly, the generation process preserved the intended meaning of the underlying axioms, demonstrating that natural language renderings can remain faithful to the source semantics without oversimplification. In addition, the flexibility of the system to accommodate domain-specific linguistic conventions underscores its potential for deployment in diverse settings, from clinical decision support to ontology curation and education.

Our findings suggest that ontology verbalisation, when supported by a robust and customisable tool like OntoVerbal, can play a significant role in enhancing transparency, user engagement, and adoption of semantic technologies in biomedicine. By reducing the cognitive barrier to understanding formal knowledge structures, such tools can facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration and support the broader dissemination of ontology-driven resources.

Future work will focus on extending OntoVerbal’s multilingual capabilities, integrating adaptive generation strategies based on user profiles, and exploring interactive verbalisation modes that allow users to query and refine generated descriptions dynamically. Further evaluation with end-users in clinical environments will be crucial to assess the impact of verbalisation on decision-making, training, and ontology maintenance workflows. In addition, applying OntoVerbal to other large biomedical ontologies and cross-domain settings will help validate its generality and uncover requirements for further refinement.

In conclusion, OntoVerbal offers a practical, scalable, and adaptable solution to the challenge of making complex ontological knowledge accessible through natural language. Its demonstrated effectiveness with SNOMED CT illustrates both the feasibility and the value of integrating ontology verbalisation into the broader ecosystem of semantic technologies, paving the way for more user-friendly and semantically transparent applications in healthcare and beyond.

title: Deep Deformation Network for Object Landmark Localization
abstract: We propose a Deep Deformation Network (DDN) for accurate and robust object landmark localization, integrating deep feature learning with geometric shape modeling in an end-to-end framework. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on separate stages for feature extraction and shape fitting, our method jointly optimizes both components, enabling the network to learn deformation-aware representations directly from data. The DDN consists of a convolutional feature extraction module followed by a geometric deformation layer that models non-rigid shape variations via a set of learned basis shapes. This design allows the network to capture complex appearance changes while enforcing spatial coherence among landmarks. We train the model using a combination of landmark localization loss and deformation regularization, facilitating generalization across object categories and imaging conditions. Experiments on challenging benchmark datasets, including facial landmark and human body joint localization tasks, demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming existing deep learning and shape-constrained methods. Furthermore, the DDN exhibits strong robustness to occlusion, pose variation, and low-resolution inputs. Our results highlight the effectiveness of integrating geometric constraints within deep architectures for precise and reliable landmark localization in diverse real-world scenarios.
introduction: Accurate object landmark localization is a fundamental problem in computer vision, with applications spanning face alignment, human pose estimation, and medical image analysis. Traditional approaches often rely on handcrafted features and shallow models, which struggle to cope with large variations in appearance, pose, and illumination. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated remarkable capability in learning hierarchical feature representations directly from raw data, enabling more robust and precise localization. However, effectively capturing complex, nonlinear deformations of objects remains challenging, particularly when limited annotated data is available. To address these issues, we propose a Deep Deformation Network that jointly learns semantic feature extraction and deformation modeling in an end-to-end manner. By integrating a deformation-aware module into a deep convolutional architecture, our method can explicitly model geometric transformations while preserving semantic consistency. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that the proposed approach achieves superior accuracy and generalization, highlighting its potential for a wide range of landmark localization tasks.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a Deep Deformation Network for accurate and robust object landmark localization. By integrating a global shape prediction module with a local deformation refinement stage, the proposed framework effectively captures both coarse structural information and fine-grained local variations. This two-stage design enables the network to handle large pose variations, occlusions, and intra-class deformations more effectively than conventional single-stage approaches. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of localization accuracy and robustness. Moreover, the architecture is end-to-end trainable, facilitating joint optimization of global and local components without the need for hand-crafted features or separate post-processing. The results suggest that incorporating hierarchical shape modeling within deep networks is a promising direction for object landmark detection. Future work will explore extending the framework to handle real-time applications, multi-object scenarios, and unsupervised or semi-supervised settings, further enhancing its applicability to complex real-world visual understanding tasks.

title: Shaping the $g^{(2)}$ autocorrelation and photon statistics
abstract: We investigate methods for tailoring the second-order intensity autocorrelation function, \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \), to control photon statistics in quantum and classical light fields. By engineering temporal and spectral properties, we demonstrate transitions between sub-Poissonian, Poissonian, and super-Poissonian regimes. Experimental and theoretical results reveal strategies for shaping \( g^{(2)} \) profiles, enabling customized photon correlations for applications in quantum communication, metrology, and photonic information processing.
introduction:
The second-order intensity autocorrelation function, \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \), is a central tool in quantum optics for characterizing the statistical properties of light. Originally introduced in the context of the Hanbury Brown and Twiss (HBT) experiment, \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \) provides direct insight into the underlying photon statistics, distinguishing between classical thermal fields, coherent states, and nonclassical states such as single-photon emitters. In particular, the value of \( g^{(2)}(0) \) serves as a criterion for photon bunching, antibunching, or Poissonian statistics, enabling the identification of quantum light sources and the quantification of their deviation from classical behavior.

Control over photon statistics is essential for a wide range of applications, from quantum communication and computation to precision metrology. Tailoring \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \) enables the engineering of optical fields with desired temporal correlations, which can enhance performance in protocols requiring reduced photon number fluctuations or specific timing characteristics. For example, antibunched light is a key resource for quantum key distribution and optical quantum logic, while bunched or super-thermal light can improve sensitivity in certain sensing schemes. Consequently, there is significant interest in methods to shape both the instantaneous and delayed photon correlations.

Recent advances in nanophotonics, cavity quantum electrodynamics, and integrated photonics have provided new degrees of freedom to manipulate the emission properties of quantum emitters and nonlinear media. Temporal modulation, spectral filtering, and tailored excitation schemes have been shown to reshape the \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \) profile, allowing transitions between different statistical regimes. Moreover, hybrid approaches combining multiple control mechanisms hold promise for precise and dynamic tuning of photon correlations.

In this work, we investigate strategies for shaping the second-order autocorrelation function and the associated photon statistics, bridging theoretical modeling with experimental considerations. We focus on how the interplay between source dynamics, optical filtering, and detection can be exploited to achieve targeted correlation profiles. By elucidating the connection between physical control parameters and the resulting \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \), we aim to provide a framework for designing light fields with tailored statistical properties, paving the way for optimized performance in emerging quantum technologies.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the controlled shaping of the second-order intensity autocorrelation function, \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \), and its impact on the photon statistics of light fields. By systematically varying the temporal and spectral properties of the source, as well as the post-processing and detection schemes, we demonstrated that the functional form of \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \) can be tailored to exhibit features corresponding to sub-Poissonian, Poissonian, and super-Poissonian statistics. This capability is of particular relevance for quantum optical applications where the temporal profile of photon correlations directly influences performance metrics such as indistinguishability, heralding efficiency, and noise resilience.

Our results highlight that the shaping of \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \) is not solely determined by the intrinsic emission process, but can also be engineered through external modulation and filtering. This provides a versatile framework for bridging the gap between source physics and application requirements. By controlling the autocorrelation profile, it becomes possible to emulate or suppress certain statistical behaviours, thereby enabling experimental flexibility without altering the underlying quantum emitter.

Furthermore, we have shown that the manipulation of \( g^{(2)} \) can be used as a diagnostic tool for disentangling contributions from multi-photon events, background noise, and detector effects. This approach offers a pathway toward more accurate characterisation of quantum light sources and may facilitate the benchmarking of emerging single-photon technologies. The interplay between theoretical modelling and experimental implementation presented here underscores the importance of comprehensive control over both field statistics and measurement protocols.

In summary, the ability to shape \( g^{(2)}(\tau) \) opens new opportunities for tailoring photon statistics to specific quantum information, metrology, and communication tasks. Future work will extend these concepts to the spatial domain, multi-mode fields, and higher-order correlation functions, paving the way for fully programmable quantum light sources with custom-designed statistical properties.

title: Improving exploration strategies in large dimensions and rate of convergence of global random search algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates enhanced exploration strategies for global random search algorithms in high-dimensional optimization problems, where traditional approaches suffer from slow convergence and premature stagnation. We propose novel sampling mechanisms that balance global exploration and local refinement through adaptive probability distributions and dimension-dependent perturbations. Theoretical analysis establishes improved bounds on the rate of convergence under mild regularity conditions. Extensive numerical experiments on benchmark functions demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve faster convergence and higher solution quality compared to standard random search variants. The results highlight the effectiveness of tailored exploration strategies in mitigating the curse of dimensionality.
introduction:
Global optimization problems arise in a wide range of scientific and engineering applications, where the objective function may be nonconvex, multimodal, and expensive to evaluate. In such contexts, deterministic methods often fail to provide satisfactory solutions, particularly when the search space is high-dimensional and the structure of the objective function is poorly understood. Random search algorithms, which rely on stochastic sampling strategies to explore the domain, have emerged as a flexible and robust class of methods capable of escaping local optima and providing asymptotic guarantees of convergence to the global optimum. However, their practical efficiency is highly dependent on the balance between exploration and exploitation, as well as on the speed at which they converge to high-quality solutions.

In high-dimensional settings, exploration becomes particularly challenging due to the curse of dimensionality: the volume of the search space grows exponentially with dimension, rendering naive uniform sampling ineffective. Traditional random search algorithms may waste a large proportion of their computational budget exploring regions of negligible relevance, leading to slow convergence rates. As a result, developing exploration strategies that guide sampling toward promising regions while maintaining sufficient diversity is essential for improving algorithmic performance.

Recent research has proposed various enhancements to random search, such as adaptive sampling distributions, hybrid deterministic–stochastic frameworks, and surrogate-based guidance. While these approaches have shown promise, a systematic understanding of their impact on convergence rates, especially in large-dimensional spaces, remains incomplete. In particular, there is a need to rigorously quantify how modifications to the exploration mechanism influence the probability of visiting near-optimal regions and the expected time to convergence.

The present work addresses these challenges by investigating improved exploration strategies for global random search algorithms in large-dimensional spaces, with an emphasis on their rate of convergence. We analyze both theoretical and empirical aspects, providing performance guarantees under reasonable assumptions and validating the results through numerical experiments. By establishing a clearer link between exploration design and convergence behavior, our study contributes to the development of more efficient stochastic search techniques capable of tackling high-dimensional global optimization problems.
conclusion: This work has examined enhanced exploration strategies for high-dimensional search spaces and their impact on the convergence rate of global random search algorithms. By refining sampling distributions and integrating adaptive mechanisms, we demonstrated improved coverage of the search domain and reduced stagnation in local regions. Analytical results and empirical evaluations confirmed that these strategies accelerate convergence without compromising solution quality. The proposed methods offer a scalable approach to addressing the curse of dimensionality and provide a foundation for further theoretical development. Future research will investigate hybrid frameworks combining deterministic guidance with stochastic exploration to further enhance performance in complex optimization problems.

title: Distributed Cooperative Manipulation under Timed Temporal Specifications
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of distributed cooperative manipulation of an object by multiple robotic agents under timed temporal specifications. We propose a control framework that enables a team of manipulators to coordinate their motions while satisfying high-level tasks expressed in Metric Interval Temporal Logic (MITL). The approach integrates decentralized planning with compliant force/position control, ensuring safe interactions, load sharing, and temporal constraint fulfillment without requiring centralized coordination or global knowledge. A distributed synthesis procedure guarantees that local controllers collectively satisfy the global specification within prescribed time bounds. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments, showing accurate task execution, robustness to uncertainties, and scalability with respect to the number of agents and task complexity.
introduction:
The coordinated manipulation of objects by multiple robotic agents has emerged as a fundamental capability in advanced manufacturing, automated assembly, warehouse logistics, and field operations. In contrast to single-arm manipulation, distributed cooperative manipulation leverages the combined capabilities of multiple manipulators, mobile bases, or aerial robots to handle objects that are too large, heavy, or unwieldy for a single agent. By sharing the manipulation task, agents can achieve higher payload capacities, improved dexterity, and greater flexibility in object positioning and orientation. However, the inherent complexity of coordinating distributed agents in a dynamic environment introduces significant challenges in control, planning, and task allocation, particularly when strict temporal constraints must be satisfied.

In many practical scenarios, cooperative manipulation must adhere not only to spatial goals but also to timing requirements. For example, in collaborative manufacturing, multiple robotic arms may need to lift and align a component within a narrow time window to synchronize with an assembly line. In search and rescue operations, aerial and ground robots might be required to transport debris or critical supplies according to deadlines dictated by safety considerations. These tasks are naturally expressed using temporal logic formalisms, which allow for specifying desired behaviors over time in a mathematically rigorous manner. Timed temporal logic, in particular, extends classical temporal logic by incorporating explicit time bounds on task execution, enabling the specification of requirements such as “the object must be delivered to the target location within 15 seconds” or “alignment must be maintained for at least 5 seconds.”

The integration of timed temporal specifications into distributed cooperative manipulation presents both theoretical and practical difficulties. On the one hand, the distributed nature of the system implies that no single agent has complete knowledge of the global state at all times, and communication delays or failures can hinder coordination. On the other hand, the manipulation task involves continuous-time, nonlinear dynamics that must be controlled in a way that guarantees satisfaction of discrete-time temporal logic constraints. Bridging this gap between continuous cooperative control and discrete temporal reasoning requires the development of frameworks that can systematically synthesize control and communication strategies from high-level timed specifications, while ensuring robustness to uncertainties and disturbances.

Existing research on cooperative manipulation has primarily focused on kinematic and dynamic control schemes, impedance and force control strategies, and decentralized coordination protocols. While these approaches have achieved impressive results in terms of stability, robustness, and adaptability, they often lack formal guarantees with respect to high-level task specifications, especially those involving explicit timing constraints. Conversely, the literature on temporal logic planning, including linear temporal logic (LTL) and metric temporal logic (MTL), has produced powerful methods for synthesizing controllers that satisfy complex task specifications. However, these methods are often developed for discrete or simplified dynamical models, and their extension to continuous, high-dimensional, and coupled systems such as cooperative manipulators remains an open research problem.

Recent advances in formal methods for robotics have begun to address the synthesis of controllers for multi-agent systems under temporal logic constraints, including some results on timed specifications. Nevertheless, the majority of these studies consider either abstracted models that neglect the physics of cooperative manipulation, or they assume centralized computation and perfect communication, which are unrealistic in many real-world settings. For distributed cooperative manipulation, the added complexity of shared object dynamics, coupled control inputs, and interaction forces necessitates new approaches that are both computationally tractable and physically realizable.

In this work, we address the problem of distributed cooperative manipulation under timed temporal specifications by developing a framework that unifies formal methods for temporal logic synthesis with distributed control strategies for physical multi-robot manipulation. Our approach enables a team of robotic agents to manipulate a shared object while satisfying high-level, time-critical task specifications expressed in a timed temporal logic formalism. We explicitly account for the continuous dynamics of the manipulators and the manipulated object, as well as the distributed nature of the system, where each agent has only partial information and limited communication capabilities. By combining symbolic reasoning over timed specifications with low-level cooperative control, we provide formal guarantees of specification satisfaction, even in the presence of bounded uncertainties.

The contributions of this paper are threefold: (i) we propose a novel distributed control synthesis method that bridges continuous cooperative manipulation dynamics with timed temporal logic constraints; (ii) we present a decentralized coordination protocol that ensures satisfaction of time-critical tasks without requiring centralized control; and (iii) we validate our approach through simulation and experimental studies involving multiple robotic manipulators performing cooperative transport and assembly tasks under strict timing requirements. Through this integration of distributed manipulation and timed specification satisfaction, we aim to advance the capabilities of autonomous multi-robot systems in complex, real-world environments.
conclusion: This work presented a distributed control framework for cooperative manipulation under timed temporal logic specifications. By integrating local planning with consensus-based coordination, the proposed method enables multiple manipulators to satisfy complex temporal constraints without centralized supervision. Formal guarantees ensure correctness with respect to both spatial and timing requirements. Simulation results demonstrated robustness to communication delays and disturbances. Future work will address experimental validation with physical robotic systems and explore extensions to heterogeneous teams and more expressive temporal logic specifications.

title: A Cram\'er-Wold theorem for elliptical distributions
abstract: We establish a Cramér–Wold type theorem for the class of elliptical distributions in finite dimensions. Specifically, we show that an elliptical distribution is uniquely determined by the distributions of its one-dimensional projections, extending the classical Cramér–Wold device beyond the Gaussian framework. Our approach exploits the structural representation of elliptical laws and properties of their characteristic generators, yielding necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiability from projected data. The results cover both degenerate and non-degenerate cases, and include stability under weak convergence. Applications are discussed for statistical inference, including estimation and testing in multivariate models with elliptical symmetry. This work provides a unified perspective linking projection characterizations and structural features of elliptical distributions.
introduction:
The Cramér–Wold theorem is a classical and fundamental result in probability theory, providing a powerful characterization of multivariate distributions through their one-dimensional projections. In its standard form, it states that a probability distribution on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is uniquely determined by the collection of distributions of all of its linear combinations. This theorem has found numerous applications across statistics, econometrics, and related fields, most prominently in proving convergence in distribution for multivariate random vectors by verifying the convergence of all one-dimensional projections. The elegance and generality of the Cramér–Wold device make it a cornerstone of the theory of weak convergence and distributional characterization.

While the theorem holds in full generality for arbitrary distributions, its consequences can be refined when attention is restricted to specific parametric or semiparametric families. In particular, elliptical distributions form an important and widely used class of multivariate distributions that generalize the multivariate normal distribution while preserving many of its appealing geometric and probabilistic properties. Elliptical distributions arise naturally in a variety of contexts, including robust statistics, finance, signal processing, and spatial data analysis, where their ability to model symmetric dependence structures and heavy tails is especially valuable.

An elliptical distribution in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is characterized by the property that its level sets of equal density are ellipsoids centered at a location parameter. This class includes, besides the multivariate normal, distributions such as the multivariate Student’s \(t\), the Kotz distribution, and certain symmetric stable distributions. The definition can be formulated in terms of a stochastic representation involving a location vector, a scale matrix, and a spherically symmetric random vector. The radial component controls tail behavior, while the orientation and scaling are encoded in the dispersion structure. Many statistical procedures for elliptical families rely on their projection properties and on the fact that any linear transformation of an elliptically distributed vector is again elliptical.

Given the intrinsic connection between projections and elliptical structure, it is natural to investigate whether a version of the Cramér–Wold theorem can be established that is tailored to the elliptical setting. Such a refined theorem could yield more efficient characterization results, simplify proofs in asymptotic theory, and deepen understanding of dependence structures within these families. Moreover, since elliptical distributions are fully determined by their characteristic generators and dispersion matrices, one might expect that fewer projections, or projections of specific types, suffice to characterize the distribution within this family.

The aim of this paper is to develop and prove a Cramér–Wold type theorem for elliptical distributions, identifying minimal conditions under which the distribution is uniquely determined by its projections. We will place our results in the context of the classical theorem, examine their implications for statistical inference, and illustrate their utility through examples and applications.
conclusion: We have established a variant of the Cramér–Wold theorem tailored to elliptical distributions, demonstrating that equality of one-dimensional projections suffices for distributional equality. This result extends classical characterizations, clarifies structural properties of elliptical families, and provides a useful tool for inference and modeling within this broad and practically significant class of multivariate distributions.

title: Analysis of Multipoint Correlations in Direct Numerical Simulation
abstract: Direct numerical simulation (DNS) provides a unique framework for investigating turbulent flows by resolving all relevant spatial and temporal scales without modeling assumptions. In this study, we present a detailed analysis of multipoint correlations in turbulent velocity fields obtained from high-resolution DNS of incompressible, homogeneous isotropic turbulence. The focus is on quantifying the spatial structure and scale interactions through two-point and three-point correlation functions, as well as higher-order moments, enabling characterization of anisotropy, intermittency, and coherent structures. By systematically varying the Reynolds number and domain resolution, we examine the scaling behavior of multipoint statistics and their convergence properties. The results reveal distinct departures from classical Kolmogorov scaling in the inertial range, particularly in higher-order correlations, indicating persistent small-scale intermittency. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that three-point correlations capture asymmetries in the turbulent cascade not accessible through two-point statistics alone. Comparisons with theoretical predictions and experimental measurements show good agreement at moderate scales, while discrepancies at extreme scales suggest limitations in current phenomenological models. These findings highlight the importance of multipoint diagnostics in improving turbulence modeling approaches and provide a comprehensive dataset for validating closure schemes in large-eddy simulations and Reynolds-averaged turbulence models.
introduction:
The study of turbulent flows remains one of the central challenges in fluid mechanics, owing to their inherently multiscale, nonlinear, and stochastic nature. Over the past decades, significant progress has been made through both experimental investigations and advances in computational capabilities. Among computational approaches, direct numerical simulation (DNS) has emerged as a powerful tool, enabling the resolution of the full range of dynamically relevant scales without resorting to turbulence modeling. By solving the Navier–Stokes equations numerically with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution, DNS provides access to complete flow field data, allowing for detailed investigations of turbulent structures and their statistical properties. Such data are particularly valuable for the analysis of multipoint correlations, which characterize the spatial and temporal relationships between fluctuations at different locations in the flow.

Multipoint correlations are essential for understanding the organization of turbulent motions beyond what can be inferred from one-point statistics. While single-point quantities, such as mean velocity profiles or turbulence intensities, offer insight into the local state of the flow, they do not capture the spatial coherence and topology of turbulent structures. Two-point correlations, structure functions, and higher-order multipoint statistics provide information on energy transfer mechanisms, anisotropy, and the nature of coherent structures across scales. These quantities are directly related to spectral energy distributions and can offer a bridge to theoretical frameworks such as Kolmogorov’s hypotheses and generalized scaling laws. Furthermore, multipoint correlations are fundamental for the development and validation of turbulence models, particularly those involving nonlocal closures or scale interactions, as they describe how fluctuations at distinct points influence one another.

The analysis of multipoint statistics poses several challenges. First, the high dimensionality of the correlation space increases rapidly with the number of points considered, making both the computation and interpretation nontrivial. Second, the accurate estimation of such correlations requires large sample sizes to achieve statistical convergence, especially for higher-order quantities. DNS datasets, despite their completeness, are still limited by computational cost, particularly at high Reynolds numbers where the range of scales is broad. Careful design of simulations, including domain size, resolution, and sampling strategy, is therefore critical to ensure that the computed correlations are physically meaningful and statistically robust.

Existing literature has addressed multipoint correlations in various canonical turbulent flows, including homogeneous isotropic turbulence, channel flows, and boundary layers. These studies have revealed important features such as the spatial extent of coherent motions, the scale dependence of intermittency, and the role of large-scale structures in modulating small-scale activity. However, many open questions remain, particularly regarding the universality of observed patterns across different flow configurations and Reynolds numbers, and the connection between multipoint correlations and underlying dynamical processes.

In this work, we present a detailed analysis of multipoint correlations obtained from high-resolution DNS of turbulent flows. By systematically examining correlations across a range of spatial separations and orientations, we aim to elucidate the structural organization of turbulence, quantify anisotropy and inhomogeneity effects, and explore implications for turbulence modeling. The results contribute to a deeper understanding of the spatial structure of turbulence and provide a comprehensive dataset for future theoretical and modeling efforts.
conclusion:
The present study has examined the statistical structure of turbulent flows by analyzing multipoint correlations obtained from direct numerical simulations (DNS). By systematically investigating two-point, three-point, and higher-order correlations in both physical and spectral space, we have sought to elucidate the mechanisms of scale interactions and the spatial organization of turbulent structures. The results demonstrate that multipoint correlation functions provide a richer and more nuanced description of turbulence than conventional second-order statistics alone, capturing essential features of intermittency, anisotropy, and non-local interactions across scales.

Our analysis confirms that two-point correlations remain valuable for quantifying energy-containing scales and the rate of spatial decorrelation; however, they are insufficient to fully characterize the complex topologies present in high-Reynolds-number flows. The inclusion of three-point correlations reveals asymmetries in the distribution of velocity increments and unambiguously highlights the role of triadic interactions in energy transfer. These findings are consistent with the predictions of the Navier–Stokes equations in Fourier space, where nonlinear terms inherently couple three wavenumbers. The DNS data further indicate that the strength and sign of the three-point correlations vary systematically with separation distance and orientation relative to the mean flow, providing direct evidence of anisotropy induced by large-scale structures.

The extension to higher-order multipoint correlations has allowed us to probe the intermittent nature of turbulence and the non-Gaussian statistics of velocity gradients and increments. In particular, fourth-order correlations have exposed the clustering of intense events and their spatial alignment, offering quantitative measures of coherent structure interactions. These statistics also illuminate the degree to which small-scale motions are modulated by larger-scale flow features, reinforcing the concept of scale-dependent organization in turbulent cascades. Such insights support and extend phenomenological models that posit a hierarchy of eddy interactions and the persistence of large-scale influence deep into the inertial range.

An important methodological outcome of this work is the demonstration that multipoint correlation functions can be robustly extracted from DNS data through careful averaging strategies and statistical convergence checks. The high spatial resolution and temporal sampling afforded by DNS have been essential in resolving fine-scale features without contamination from modeling assumptions, thus ensuring that the observed patterns are intrinsic to the Navier–Stokes dynamics. Nevertheless, the computational expense of DNS inherently limits the Reynolds numbers accessible in the present study, and future work should explore hybrid approaches—combining DNS, large-eddy simulation (LES), and experimental measurements—to extend these analyses to more extreme turbulent regimes.

The implications of our findings are twofold. First, on a fundamental level, they provide direct, quantitative evidence for the multifaceted nature of turbulence, where energy transfer, intermittency, and anisotropy are deeply intertwined and cannot be fully captured by low-order statistics alone. This has consequences for theoretical modeling, where closure schemes in Reynolds-averaged or LES frameworks may benefit from incorporating information drawn from multipoint statistics, potentially improving predictions of turbulent transport and mixing. Second, on a practical level, the ability to characterize and quantify multi-scale interactions and coherent structure dynamics can inform engineering applications ranging from aerodynamic design to environmental flow prediction, where accurate modeling of turbulent transport processes is critical.

In summary, the systematic analysis of multipoint correlations in DNS has yielded new insights into the structural and dynamical complexity of turbulent flows. By moving beyond traditional two-point measures, we have uncovered clear signatures of triadic and higher-order interactions, quantified the modulation of small scales by large-scale structures, and provided a framework for connecting these statistics to physical mechanisms of turbulence. While the present results are necessarily constrained by computational feasibility, they lay the groundwork for more comprehensive studies that integrate higher Reynolds number simulations, experimental data, and theoretical developments. Continued advances in computational power and data analysis techniques will enable increasingly detailed exploration of multipoint statistics, bringing us closer to a complete statistical theory of turbulence that faithfully represents the full hierarchy of interactions governing fluid motion.

title: Self-Driving Car Steering Angle Prediction Based on Image Recognition
abstract: This paper presents a method for predicting steering angles in self-driving cars using image recognition techniques. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is trained on a dataset of road images paired with corresponding steering commands. The proposed model automatically extracts spatial features from raw images, enabling end-to-end mapping from visual input to steering output. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach achieves high accuracy and robustness under varying road and weather conditions. The findings highlight the potential of deep learning-based vision systems to enhance autonomous driving performance and decision-making in real-world scenarios.
introduction:
The rapid advancement of autonomous driving technology has attracted significant attention from both academia and industry in recent years. A core component of an autonomous vehicle’s control system is the ability to accurately predict steering commands based on sensory input, enabling safe and reliable navigation in diverse driving environments. Among various modalities, visual data from forward-facing cameras has proven particularly valuable, as it provides rich contextual information about the road, surrounding vehicles, pedestrians, and environmental conditions. Leveraging image recognition techniques to infer steering angles offers a promising approach that draws upon developments in computer vision and deep learning.

Traditional methods for steering control often rely on handcrafted features and explicit lane detection algorithms, which can be sensitive to environmental variability such as lighting changes, weather conditions, and occlusions. In contrast, end-to-end learning approaches utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or other deep architectures to directly map raw pixel data to steering commands, thereby reducing the need for manual feature engineering. This paradigm shift has been enabled by advances in GPU computing, the availability of large-scale driving datasets, and the refinement of neural network architectures capable of learning hierarchical visual representations.

However, several challenges remain in achieving robust steering angle prediction from images. Variations in road geometry, complex traffic scenarios, and the presence of visual noise can degrade model performance. Furthermore, overfitting to specific datasets or environments may limit generalization to unseen conditions, raising safety concerns for real-world deployment. Addressing these challenges requires careful network design, data augmentation strategies, and evaluation protocols that faithfully capture the diversity of driving situations.

This study investigates a deep learning-based framework for predicting continuous steering angles directly from camera images in a simulated driving environment. By employing state-of-the-art image recognition techniques, the proposed approach aims to learn a robust mapping from visual input to steering control, minimizing reliance on explicit intermediate representations. The contributions of this work include the design and training of an optimized convolutional architecture, the application of data preprocessing and augmentation to enhance generalization, and a comprehensive evaluation of performance across varied driving scenarios. The findings highlight the potential and limitations of vision-based steering prediction for future self-driving systems.
conclusion:
This study presented a method for predicting steering angles in self-driving cars using image recognition techniques, demonstrating the potential of deep learning models to interpret visual input for autonomous navigation. By leveraging convolutional neural networks to process real-time images from a forward-facing camera, the proposed approach effectively captured relevant road features such as lane markings, curves, and surrounding vehicles. Experimental results indicated that the model achieved a high degree of accuracy in predicting steering angles, with smooth output behavior that is essential for safe and comfortable vehicle control. The findings suggest that integrating vision-based steering prediction into autonomous driving systems can enhance their ability to operate in diverse driving conditions without reliance on extensive sensor arrays.  

While the results are promising, several limitations remain. The model’s performance may be influenced by environmental factors such as varying lighting, weather conditions, and occlusions. Furthermore, the dataset used, although sufficient for experimental validation, could be expanded to include more diverse road scenarios to improve generalization. Future work will focus on incorporating temporal information from video sequences, fusing vision with complementary sensor data, and exploring advanced architectures to further enhance prediction robustness.  

In conclusion, the research reinforces the viability of image recognition-based steering angle prediction as a core component of self-driving technology. With continued refinement, such approaches could contribute significantly to safer, more adaptive, and more efficient autonomous vehicles, ultimately supporting broader adoption of self-driving systems in real-world transportation networks.

title: Raw Report on the Model Checking Contest at Petri Nets 2012
abstract: This raw report presents the results and observations from the Model Checking Contest held during the Petri Nets 2012 conference. The contest aimed to provide a fair and comprehensive evaluation of model checking tools using a diverse set of Petri net models and verification tasks. Participating tools were assessed on performance, scalability, and correctness across multiple categories, including state space generation and property verification. The report details the benchmark suite, experimental methodology, and comparative outcomes, offering insights into current tool capabilities and limitations. These results contribute to fostering progress in verification techniques and promoting reproducible, transparent evaluation within the model checking community.
introduction:
The Model Checking Contest (MCC) is an annual event that aims to provide a fair, systematic, and comprehensive evaluation of verification tools for concurrent systems, with a specific focus on models expressed as Petri nets. It serves both as a competitive benchmark and as a collaborative forum for tool developers and researchers to exchange ideas, assess progress, and identify challenges in the field of formal verification. The edition held in conjunction with the Petri Nets 2012 conference continued this tradition by offering a diverse set of models and verification tasks, enabling the comparison of tools under uniform conditions.

Model checking, as a formal verification method, plays an essential role in ensuring the reliability and correctness of systems where concurrency, synchronization, and resource sharing are critical. Petri nets, with their well-defined semantics and expressive power, constitute a natural modeling formalism for such systems. However, the complexity of verification tasks, often exacerbated by state space explosion, makes it imperative to develop and evaluate efficient algorithms and data structures. The MCC provides a structured platform to measure the effectiveness of these approaches across a broad spectrum of case studies.

The 2012 contest incorporated both “known” models, which were made available to participants in advance, and “surprise” models, disclosed only at the event itself. This combination is intended to assess tools in two complementary dimensions: their optimization and tuning capabilities when prior knowledge is available, and their generic applicability and robustness when faced with unseen problems. Verification tasks included state space generation and the evaluation of a set of formulae expressed in temporal logics, covering reachability, invariants, and other behavioral properties.

By gathering a variety of tools in a single evaluation campaign, the MCC not only produces a comparative ranking but also yields valuable raw data on performance, scalability, and coverage. Such data can inform the research community about the current state of the art, highlight promising techniques, and reveal limitations that may spur further investigation. The contest also fosters reproducibility and transparency, as the models, property specifications, and evaluation methodology are publicly documented.

This report presents a detailed account of the MCC at Petri Nets 2012. It describes the organization of the contest, the selection and characteristics of the models, the categories of verification tasks, and the participating tools. Furthermore, it provides the raw results obtained during the evaluation, without interpretation or bias, to serve as a factual basis for subsequent analysis. By making these results available in an open and structured form, the report aims to support ongoing efforts in the verification community to advance the capabilities and applicability of model checking techniques for Petri nets and related formalisms.
conclusion:
The Model Checking Contest at Petri Nets 2012 has provided an invaluable opportunity to assess the current state of the art in model checking tools, particularly in the context of Petri net models of varying size, structure, and complexity. By bringing together a diverse set of tools and benchmarks, the contest has created a common ground for fair, transparent, and reproducible evaluation, enabling both tool developers and end users to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of available approaches. The raw results gathered during the event offer a rich source of data for future analysis and comparative studies, while also highlighting areas where further methodological refinement may be beneficial.

One of the most significant outcomes of this edition has been the confirmation that no single tool universally dominates across all categories and model types. The variability in performance observed across different models and property types underscores the importance of maintaining a heterogeneous ecosystem of verification techniques. Tools based on decision diagrams, SAT/SMT solving, explicit state exploration, and structural reductions each demonstrated notable advantages in specific contexts, reinforcing the view that method selection should be guided by the particular characteristics of the verification problem at hand. The contest has thus served not only as a competition, but also as a mechanism for knowledge exchange between communities employing different verification paradigms.

The raw report also reveals progress over previous editions in the capacity of tools to handle larger state spaces and more complex temporal properties. Several participating tools showcased improved scalability and efficiency, reflecting sustained research efforts in algorithmic optimization and data structure engineering. However, the results also expose persistent challenges, particularly in handling certain classes of models that exhibit high concurrency, complex synchronizations, or large parameterized families. These challenges point to fertile ground for future research, both in refining existing approaches and in exploring hybrid or novel verification strategies.

From an organizational perspective, the contest format has proven effective in stimulating the development of benchmark suites that are representative, diverse, and challenging. The inclusion of both “known” models, familiar to tool developers, and “surprise” models, introduced without prior notice, has helped to balance the benefits of targeted optimization against the need for generality and robustness. This dual approach has ensured that performance results are reflective not only of specialized tuning but also of the adaptability of tools to new problem instances. Furthermore, the transparency of the evaluation process, supported by detailed public dissemination of raw data, strengthens the credibility and reproducibility of the findings.

Looking forward, the continuation of the Model Checking Contest promises to play a pivotal role in driving innovation in the field. The expansion of the benchmark repository, the refinement of property specification languages, and the integration of new verification challenges such as probabilistic reasoning or timed analysis could further enhance the scope and impact of future editions. By sustaining a collaborative, competitive, and methodologically rigorous environment, the contest will continue to serve as both a proving ground for emerging techniques and a catalyst for advancing the capabilities of model checking tools in the Petri net domain and beyond.

In sum, the 2012 contest has contributed substantially to the empirical understanding of model checking performance, fostered constructive interaction between research groups, and charted a path for ongoing progress in verification technology.

title: On Flexible Prismatic Polyhedra
abstract: We investigate families of flexible prismatic polyhedra derived from trapezoidal-faced suspensions. Using geometric constraints, we construct examples exhibiting continuous isometric deformations while preserving face shapes and edge lengths. The analysis extends to configurations with varying face arrangements and symmetries, revealing novel classes of nonrigid structures. These results contribute to the understanding of flexibility in polyhedral geometry and suggest further connections between suspension mechanisms and prismatic form.
introduction:
The study of polyhedral geometry has long attracted mathematicians, engineers, and architects, owing both to its aesthetic appeal and to the depth of its theoretical challenges. Among the many branches of this subject, the investigation of polyhedra capable of continuous deformation without altering the shapes of their faces—so‑called flexible polyhedra—has emerged as a particularly intriguing area of research. While rigid polyhedra obey Cauchy’s rigidity theorem, which asserts that convex polyhedra with rigid faces and edges are themselves rigid, the discovery of non‑convex examples that violate this principle has broadened our understanding of spatial structures. The seminal work of Bricard in 1897, which classified all flexible octahedra, provided some of the earliest examples of nontrivial flexibility. Since then, a variety of flexible forms, including suspensions, toroidal structures, and prismatic frameworks, have been identified and analysed.

Within this broader context, prismatic polyhedra—polyhedral surfaces composed of consecutive polygonal cross‑sections connected by trapezoidal or other quadrilateral faces—occupy a distinctive niche. These forms can be viewed as generalisations of prisms, in which polygonal layers are arranged in series, and flexibility, when it occurs, is manifested as a coordinated rotation and translation of the layers relative to one another. The geometric regularity of prisms makes them natural candidates for both theoretical exploration and practical application. In architectural and mechanical design, prismatic frameworks are valued for their modularity and scalability, and the possibility of controlled flexibility opens new avenues for deployable structures, kinetic facades, and reconfigurable mechanisms.

The existence of flexible prismatic polyhedra challenges intuition and invites a deeper examination of their geometric constraints. Classical rigidity results do not directly prohibit non‑convex prismatic forms from flexing, yet the conditions under which such flexibility arises are subtle. In particular, the interplay between the geometry of the cross‑sections, the nature of the connecting faces, and the spatial arrangement of successive layers determines whether a prismatic polyhedron can undergo a continuous isometric deformation. Recent advances in computational geometry and kinematic modelling have made it possible to explore these structures systematically, revealing previously unknown families of flexible prismatic configurations.

Interest in flexible prismatic polyhedra is not purely theoretical. In robotics and deployable mechanisms, prismatic linkages model a range of motion patterns that can be exploited for compact storage and rapid deployment. In materials science, arrays of prismatic cells can be used to design metamaterials with tunable mechanical properties, where flexibility can serve as a means of absorbing energy or adapting to external constraints. Understanding the geometric foundations of such flexibility is therefore a prerequisite for informed design. Moreover, from a mathematical standpoint, flexible prismatic polyhedra offer a fertile testing ground for conjectures about rigidity, symmetry, and the topology of polyhedral surfaces.

Despite their potential significance, flexible prismatic polyhedra have received less attention than other flexible forms, such as Bricard octahedra or Miura‑ori patterns. Much of the existing literature treats specific instances or highly symmetric cases, leaving open the question of how general such flexibility can be and how it may be classified. The lack of a comprehensive framework for describing and predicting flexibility in prismatic arrangements has hindered both theoretical progress and practical exploitation. There is thus a clear need for systematic methods that can identify flexible configurations, characterise their motion, and relate them to known classes of flexible polyhedra.

In this work, we aim to contribute to this emerging field by presenting a detailed analysis of flexible prismatic polyhedra, identifying the geometric conditions that permit continuous deformation while preserving face geometry. Our approach builds on established results in polyhedral kinematics, adapts techniques from linkage theory, and employs computational verification to confirm flexibility in nontrivial cases. By situating flexible prismatic polyhedra within the broader taxonomy of flexible surfaces, we seek to clarify their relationship to other known structures and to highlight the distinctive features of their motion.

The paper is organised as follows. We begin by reviewing relevant background on flexible polyhedra and existing examples of prismatic flexibility. We then introduce our formal model for prismatic polyhedra, defining the parameters and constraints that govern their geometry. Subsequent sections present families of flexible configurations, derive the conditions under which they arise, and analyse their deformation paths. Finally, we discuss implications for both theoretical geometry and applied design, and outline directions for future research. Through this study, we hope to advance the understanding of flexibility in polyhedral structures and to encourage further exploration of the rich design space offered by prismatic forms.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined the geometry, construction, and flexibility of a class of prismatic polyhedra that admit continuous deformations without altering the shapes of their constituent faces. Building upon prior investigations into flexible polyhedral structures, we have identified a family of configurations in which prismatic segments are joined in such a way that the overall framework retains a constant combinatorial structure while allowing for nontrivial flexion. Through explicit parametrization of the vertex coordinates, we demonstrated that these polyhedra satisfy the necessary geometric constraints for flexibility, including invariance of edge lengths and planarity of faces throughout the motion. 

Our analysis extends known examples by presenting new arrangements with higher-order symmetry, as well as asymmetric cases, thereby broadening the catalogue of flexible forms. The results highlight the role of angular relationships between adjacent prismatic segments in enabling mobility, and show that flexibility can persist even in the absence of obvious symmetry. These findings contribute to the understanding of how local constraints propagate through the global structure of a polyhedron, and suggest potential applications in deployable structures, mechanical linkages, and architectural design. 

Future work may address the classification of all such prismatic flexible forms, explore their rigidity boundaries, and investigate their realizations in physical models. The methods developed here may also be adapted to study flexibility in other polyhedral families, deepening the interplay between combinatorics, geometry, and motion in three-dimensional structures.

title: Universality and programmability of quantum computers
abstract: We investigate the concepts of universality and programmability in quantum computation, highlighting their foundational significance for both theoretical computer science and practical quantum technologies. Universality refers to the capacity of a quantum computational model to approximate any unitary transformation to arbitrary precision, given a suitable set of quantum gates. Programmability, in contrast, addresses the ability to implement a wide range of computational tasks within a fixed hardware architecture through adaptable control sequences or software-level instructions. We review established notions of universality, including gate set universality and measurement-based universality, and clarify their relationship to classical analogues. Furthermore, we examine the constraints imposed by physical realizations, such as noise, decoherence, and limited qubit connectivity, on achieving practical programmability. By synthesizing insights from quantum complexity theory and experimental architectures, we identify criteria for assessing both the theoretical and operational completeness of a quantum computing platform. This analysis underscores the interplay between abstract computational models and the engineering challenges of building truly general-purpose quantum processors.
introduction: Quantum computation has emerged as a transformative paradigm that harnesses the principles of quantum mechanics to process information in fundamentally new ways. Central to this field are the notions of universality and programmability, which together define the scope and flexibility of quantum devices. Universality refers to the ability of a computational model to implement any operation within a given class, typically formalized as the capacity to approximate any unitary transformation to arbitrary accuracy using a finite set of quantum gates. Programmability, in turn, captures the extent to which a quantum computer can be configured, through software-like control, to execute a broad range of algorithms without hardware modification. These concepts are deeply intertwined: a universal quantum computer must be programmable to exploit its full potential, yet practical programmability is constrained by noise, decoherence, and architectural limitations. Theoretical frameworks, such as the Solovay–Kitaev theorem, establish universality for discrete gate sets, while recent advances in variational and measurement-based models highlight alternative routes to programmable architectures. Understanding the interplay between universality and programmability is essential for bridging the gap between abstract models and physical implementations, guiding both the design of quantum processors and the development of efficient quantum compilers and control protocols.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the principles underlying universality and programmability in quantum computation, highlighting both their theoretical foundations and practical implications. Universality, defined as the ability of a finite set of quantum gates to approximate any unitary operation to arbitrary accuracy, remains a cornerstone of quantum computing theory. We have discussed how various universal gate sets, such as those built from single-qubit rotations and entangling two-qubit gates, provide the structural basis for implementing any quantum algorithm. Programmability, in turn, extends this notion by considering the flexibility of quantum architectures to execute a broad class of algorithms without hardware redesign, thereby paralleling the versatility of classical computing systems.  

Our analysis underscores that while universality is an intrinsic property of the computational model, programmability is shaped by both hardware constraints and software abstractions. Current advances in quantum technologies, including error correction, compilation techniques, and reconfigurable control systems, are progressively bridging theoretical universality with practical programmability. Nevertheless, challenges remain, especially in scaling architectures to maintain coherence, fault tolerance, and efficient resource use.  

The interplay between universality and programmability will be decisive in determining the trajectory of quantum computing toward general-purpose applicability. Future research should therefore address not only the identification of optimal universal sets and fault-tolerant protocols, but also the development of robust programming models that can fully exploit the potential of quantum hardware. By aligning theoretical universality with practical programmability, the field can move closer to realizing quantum computers as flexible, reliable, and widely usable computational devices.

title: Robust Stochastic Bayesian Games for Behavior Space Coverage
abstract: We propose a novel framework for robust stochastic Bayesian games that ensures comprehensive coverage of behavior spaces in multi-agent systems operating under uncertainty. Traditional Bayesian game formulations often focus on equilibrium computation without explicitly addressing the diversity of agent behaviors that may emerge in stochastic, partially observable environments. Our approach integrates robust optimization principles with stochastic game modeling to generate strategies that are resilient to model misspecification and adversarial perturbations while systematically exploring the feasible behavior space. We formalize the problem as a constrained optimization over belief-dependent policies, introducing a coverage metric that quantifies the extent to which sampled strategies span the space of possible agent behaviors. An iterative policy synthesis algorithm is developed, combining uncertainty-aware belief updates with diversity-promoting regularization. We evaluate the method in simulated multi-agent domains with incomplete information, demonstrating superior performance in both robustness to environmental variations and breadth of behavioral coverage compared to baseline Bayesian and robust game-theoretic approaches. These results suggest that robust stochastic Bayesian games offer a principled pathway toward building adaptive, resilient, and behaviorally diverse multi-agent decision-making systems in uncertain and dynamic contexts.
introduction:
Multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly deployed in complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments, ranging from autonomous driving and robotic swarms to distributed resource management and human–machine collaboration. In such settings, the interaction between agents is inherently strategic: each agent’s decisions influence and are influenced by the behaviors of others. Accurately modeling and reasoning about these interactions is critical for ensuring robust performance, safety, and adaptability. Game-theoretic models, and in particular stochastic games, provide a principled framework for representing sequential decision-making among multiple agents with potentially conflicting objectives under uncertainty. However, the practical application of stochastic games to real-world problems remains challenging due to incomplete information, high-dimensional and continuous behavior spaces, and the need to anticipate a diverse range of opponent strategies.

Bayesian games extend classical game theory to settings of incomplete information, where agents possess private types that capture hidden preferences, capabilities, or intentions. By modeling uncertainty over these types through probability distributions, Bayesian games allow agents to reason strategically without full knowledge of others’ internal states. When combined with the temporal dynamics of stochastic games, stochastic Bayesian games (SBGs) emerge as a powerful formalism for multi-agent decision-making under uncertainty. In SBGs, agents maintain beliefs over latent types and update them as the game unfolds, enabling adaptive strategies that respond to observed behaviors. Despite their conceptual appeal, the design and learning of effective policies in SBGs remains computationally demanding, particularly when the space of possible opponent behaviors is large or continuous.

A fundamental challenge in applying SBGs to real-world domains lies in achieving *behavior space coverage*—the ability to anticipate and respond to a sufficiently rich and representative set of possible opponent policies. Limited coverage can lead to brittle strategies that perform well against a narrow set of behaviors but fail catastrophically when confronted with novel tactics. This is especially problematic in safety-critical applications, where encountering unmodeled behaviors is inevitable. Existing approaches often rely on handcrafted opponent models, limited policy libraries, or narrow training distributions, which may not generalize well to the full diversity of realistic behaviors. Consequently, there is a pressing need for methods that can systematically explore and represent the opponent behavior space while maintaining robustness to distributional shifts.

Robustness in the context of SBGs refers to the capacity of an agent’s strategy to maintain desirable performance even when the true opponent behaviors deviate from prior expectations. This requires not only accurate belief updates but also principled mechanisms for hedging against worst-case scenarios. Robust game-theoretic methods have been proposed in zero-sum and cooperative settings, but their integration with SBGs for comprehensive behavior space coverage remains underexplored.
