Furthermore, the interplay between exploration (to discover and model new behaviors) and exploitation (to act optimally given current beliefs) poses a significant algorithmic challenge, especially when interactions are costly or risky.

In this work, we address these challenges by introducing *Robust Stochastic Bayesian Games* (RSBGs), a framework that explicitly incorporates robustness considerations into the modeling and solution of SBGs. Our approach leverages distributional robustness techniques to guard against misspecification of opponent behavior models, while also employing structured exploration to improve coverage of the behavior space. By framing the problem as a robust optimization over belief-dependent policies, we derive strategies that perform well across a wide spectrum of plausible opponent types, including those not encountered during training. This formulation enables principled trade-offs between conservatism and adaptability, ensuring that agents are neither overly pessimistic nor naively optimistic.

We evaluate the proposed framework in a range of simulated multi-agent environments designed to stress-test behavior space coverage. Our results demonstrate that RSBGs achieve superior generalization to unseen opponent strategies compared to standard SBG and robust game baselines, without incurring prohibitive computational costs. The contributions of this work are threefold: (i) we formalize the notion of behavior space coverage within the SBG framework; (ii) we introduce a robust optimization formulation that enhances resilience to unmodeled behaviors; and (iii) we empirically validate the effectiveness of the approach in diverse strategic settings.

By advancing the integration of robustness and behavior space coverage in stochastic Bayesian games, this work provides a foundation for deploying multi-agent systems that can operate reliably in the face of deep uncertainty and strategic diversity.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced a framework for robust stochastic Bayesian games that explicitly targets comprehensive behavior space coverage. By formulating the interaction dynamics as stochastic games with Bayesian uncertainty modeling, we were able to capture both the variability in opponent strategies and the uncertainty in environment dynamics. Our approach integrates robustness criteria into the equilibrium computation, ensuring that the resulting policies maintain strong performance even in adversarial or poorly modeled conditions. The proposed coverage-driven objective encourages exploration across diverse behavioral modes, enabling richer policy learning and more reliable generalization to unseen scenarios. Empirical evaluations demonstrated that our method achieves superior coverage of strategic behaviors compared to baseline Bayesian and robust game-theoretic models, while sustaining competitive or improved payoff performance. These findings highlight the utility of combining robustness with explicit coverage incentives in multi-agent decision-making. Future work will extend this formulation to continuous behavior spaces, investigate scalable approximation techniques, and explore applications in domains such as autonomous driving, human–robot collaboration, and security games, where anticipating and preparing for a broad spectrum of behaviors is critical for safety and effectiveness.

title: Constraining a scalar field dark energy with variable equation of state for matter
abstract: We investigate cosmological constraints on a scalar field model of dark energy in the presence of a variable equation of state (EoS) for the matter component. Departing from the standard assumption of pressureless matter, we allow the matter EoS parameter to evolve with cosmic time, motivated by scenarios involving interacting dark sectors or warm dark matter. Employing a dynamical systems approach, we derive the background evolution equations and analyze their solutions for a range of scalar field potentials. Observational constraints from type Ia supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and cosmic microwave background data are applied. Our results show that a variable matter EoS can significantly alter dark energy dynamics and parameter bounds.
introduction:
The discovery of the accelerated expansion of the Universe at the turn of the 21st century, through observations of type Ia supernovae, revolutionized modern cosmology. Subsequent confirmations from cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropy measurements and large-scale structure surveys have firmly established that the dominant component of the present-day cosmic energy budget is an exotic form of energy with negative pressure, dubbed “dark energy.” While the cosmological constant Λ remains the simplest and most economical explanation, its extreme fine-tuning and coincidence problems have motivated a broad range of alternative theoretical models. Among these, scalar field models—such as quintessence, k-essence, and phantom fields—have attracted significant attention as dynamical candidates for dark energy, capable of producing an evolving equation of state and potentially alleviating some of the conceptual shortcomings of Λ.

In the standard cosmological framework, matter is typically modeled as a pressureless perfect fluid during the late Universe, corresponding to an equation of state parameter \( w_m = 0 \). This is an excellent approximation for non-relativistic baryons and cold dark matter. However, there are compelling reasons to consider more general scenarios in which the effective equation of state of matter may vary with time or scale factor. Such variations can arise in models with warm dark matter, bulk viscous effects, particle creation, or in certain interacting dark sector frameworks, where dark matter exchanges energy or momentum with dark energy. A variable \( w_m \) can also emerge as an effective description of more complex microphysical processes, including phase transitions in the dark sector or deviations from the standard cold dark matter paradigm. Allowing for a nonzero and possibly time-dependent matter equation of state can, therefore, lead to richer cosmological dynamics and may have a nontrivial impact on the inferred properties of dark energy.

Scalar field models with a variable matter equation of state present an interesting opportunity to probe the interplay between dark matter and dark energy in a more general setting. In such scenarios, the background evolution is governed not only by the scalar field potential and kinetic terms but also by the time evolution of the matter pressure. This can influence the Hubble expansion history, the growth of density perturbations, and hence the interpretation of cosmological observables. For instance, a slightly positive \( w_m \) at early times could mimic the effects of additional relativistic species, while a small negative \( w_m \) might indicate exotic physics such as dark matter with internal interactions or non-minimal coupling to other fields. From an observational perspective, failing to account for a variable \( w_m \) could bias constraints on dark energy parameters, particularly when combining data from different redshift ranges.

The reconstruction of scalar field models from observational data typically proceeds by parameterizing the dark energy equation of state \( w_\phi \) and fitting for its parameters, either directly or via a specified potential form. Popular parameterizations include the Chevallier–Polarski–Linder (CPL) form \( w_\phi(a) = w_0 + w_a (1-a) \), as well as other expansions in redshift or scale factor. However, most studies assume \( w_m \) is fixed at zero, thereby ignoring possible degeneracies between \( w_m(z) \) and \( w_\phi(z) \). In principle, permitting both to vary could provide a more realistic representation of the cosmic fluid, but at the cost of introducing additional degrees of freedom. This necessitates a careful statistical analysis using current observational datasets—such as type Ia supernovae luminosity distances, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), CMB shift parameters, and direct Hubble rate measurements—to assess whether the data can meaningfully constrain such extended models.

Theoretical consistency also imposes constraints on the allowed functional forms of \( w_m(z) \). Physical viability requires that the matter energy density remains positive and that the sound speed of perturbations does not lead to instabilities. Moreover, in scalar field dark energy models, the evolution of \( w_m \) can influence the form of the effective potential reconstructed from the expansion history, potentially modifying the conditions for tracking or thawing behavior. Therefore, exploring scalar field dark energy in the presence of a variable matter equation of state is not only of phenomenological interest but also of theoretical importance for understanding the range of cosmological dynamics consistent with both observations and fundamental physics.

In this work, we investigate a class of scalar field dark energy models in a spatially flat Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) universe, allowing for a matter component with a time-dependent equation of state. We adopt a phenomenological parameterization for \( w_m(z) \) that captures a range of physically motivated behaviors and examine its impact on the reconstruction of the scalar field potential and dark energy dynamics. Using a combination of the latest observational data, we perform a statistical analysis to constrain the model parameters and assess the extent to which current observations can distinguish this scenario from the standard ΛCDM and constant-\( w_\phi \) models. Our goal is to determine whether relaxing the assumption of pressureless matter can lead to significant changes in the inferred properties of dark energy and to identify observational signatures that could be targeted by future surveys.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present the theoretical framework and the dynamical equations governing the system. Section 3 describes the observational datasets and the methodology used for parameter estimation. Section 4 reports the results of our analysis and discusses their implications for scalar field dark energy models. Finally, Section 5 summarizes our conclusions and outlines directions for future work.
conclusion: In this work we have investigated a cosmological model in which the dark energy component is represented by a scalar field, while the matter sector is characterized by a variable equation of state. By allowing the matter equation of state to evolve with cosmic time, we have introduced an additional degree of freedom that can capture possible deviations from the standard cold dark matter description, particularly in the early universe or during transitions between cosmological epochs. Using observational constraints from recent data sets, we have derived bounds on the parameters governing both the scalar field potential and the equation of state variation. The analysis shows that the model can reproduce the observed late-time acceleration while remaining consistent with the expansion history at earlier times. In particular, the scalar field dynamics accommodate a smooth transition in the matter equation of state without conflicting with current constraints on structure formation and CMB observables. Our results suggest that considering a variable matter equation of state in scalar field dark energy models provides a viable and flexible framework for probing departures from ΛCDM. Future high-precision observations, especially of the growth rate of structures, may further tighten the constraints and distinguish such scenarios from standard cosmology.

title: A Speculative Parallel DFA Membership Test for Multicore, SIMD and Cloud Computing Environments
abstract: This paper presents a speculative parallel algorithm for Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) membership testing, designed to exploit modern multicore processors, SIMD vector units, and cloud computing platforms. Traditional DFA membership tests are inherently sequential due to the strict state-transition dependency on input symbols, limiting opportunities for parallelization. Our approach relaxes this constraint by speculatively executing multiple possible state-transition paths in parallel, guided by partitioning the input string and predicting intermediate states. Mispredicted paths are efficiently discarded, while correct paths are merged to produce the final acceptance decision. We develop a formal framework for state prediction, correctness guarantees, and complexity analysis, and we propose optimizations that minimize speculative overhead and memory footprint. The method is implemented using a hybrid parallelization strategy that combines thread-level parallelism for multicore systems, SIMD-based acceleration for short speculative segments, and distributed execution across cloud nodes for large-scale inputs. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world regular expressions demonstrate substantial speedups over sequential DFA execution, with near-linear scaling in favorable conditions. The results indicate that speculative parallelism offers a practical pathway to accelerate DFA membership testing across diverse modern computing environments without altering the underlying automaton semantics.
introduction: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA) are widely used in pattern matching, lexical analysis, and network security applications. As data volumes grow, traditional sequential DFA membership tests struggle to meet performance demands. Parallel architectures, including multicore processors, SIMD units, and cloud-based infrastructures, offer significant potential for accelerating DFA evaluation. However, exploiting parallelism effectively requires overcoming challenges such as state dependency and load imbalance. This paper presents a speculative parallel DFA membership test designed to leverage diverse parallel computing environments. By predicting and validating possible state transitions in parallel, our approach aims to reduce latency, improve throughput, and maintain correctness across heterogeneous platforms.
conclusion: This work has presented a speculative parallel approach to deterministic finite automaton (DFA) membership testing, designed to exploit the computational capabilities of multicore processors, SIMD architectures, and cloud computing platforms. By partitioning the input and speculatively evaluating possible state transitions in parallel, the method mitigates the inherent sequentiality of traditional DFA evaluation while maintaining correctness. Experimental results indicate that the approach scales well with increased parallel resources, achieving notable speedups over baseline sequential implementations, particularly for large input sizes and complex automata. The technique demonstrates adaptability across diverse hardware configurations, from shared-memory multicore systems to distributed cloud environments, underscoring its portability and practical utility. Moreover, the SIMD-optimized variants highlight the benefits of fine-grained data parallelism when combined with speculative execution strategies. While the overhead of speculative computation can limit gains for small inputs or simple automata, the overall performance profile suggests significant potential for high-throughput pattern matching and language recognition tasks. Future work will focus on dynamic speculation control to further reduce unnecessary computation, as well as integration with hybrid automata models and streaming data frameworks. The proposed method thus offers a promising foundation for efficient DFA membership testing in modern heterogeneous computing environments.

title: Testing GRB models with the afterglow of GRB 090102
abstract: We present a detailed analysis of the afterglow of GRB 090102 aimed at testing current models of gamma-ray burst (GRB) emission. Multi-wavelength observations spanning optical to X-ray bands were collected from minutes to several days post-burst. The optical light curve exhibits an initial steep-to-shallow transition, while the X-ray afterglow displays a single power-law decay without spectral evolution. Spectral energy distribution fitting reveals no evidence for significant host-galaxy extinction and suggests that the cooling frequency lies between the optical and X-ray regimes during the early afterglow. We compare these results with predictions from the standard forward shock model in both homogeneous and wind-like circumburst environments. The observed temporal and spectral behavior is inconsistent with a simple single-component outflow, indicating the presence of additional emission processes or energy injection. GRB 090102 thus provides a stringent test case for GRB afterglow theory, highlighting the need for refined models that can simultaneously reproduce multi-band light curves and spectra.
introduction:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic phenomena in the universe, releasing within seconds as much energy as the Sun emits over its entire lifetime. They are generally understood within the framework of the relativistic fireball model, in which a compact central engine powers an ultrarelativistic outflow. As the ejecta interact with the surrounding medium, internal shocks are thought to produce the prompt γ-ray emission, while the subsequent deceleration by the circumburst environment gives rise to a broadband afterglow via synchrotron radiation. Despite significant progress in the past two decades, important open questions remain regarding the nature of the outflow (baryonic vs. magnetically dominated), the structure of the jet, and the role of reverse shocks in shaping early-time afterglow emission.

GRB 090102, detected by the *Swift* satellite on 2009 January 2, provides a valuable case study for testing GRB models. Its bright optical afterglow was detected within minutes of the trigger, and multiwavelength follow-up observations were obtained from optical to X-ray bands over several days. The early-time optical light curve exhibited a steep-to-shallow transition, while the X-ray afterglow displayed a comparatively smooth decay, posing challenges to the simplest fireball predictions. The event has been further distinguished by the detection of significant optical polarization at early times, potentially indicating a large-scale ordered magnetic field in the ejecta.

The combination of dense temporal coverage, broad spectral sampling, and polarization measurements makes GRB 090102 an ideal laboratory for confronting theoretical models with observational data. By comparing the multiwavelength light curves and spectra with the predictions of standard forward–reverse shock models and magnetized outflow scenarios, we can assess the relative role of each emission component and constrain key physical parameters such as the initial Lorentz factor, circumburst density profile, and magnetization of the jet. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of the afterglow of GRB 090102 and discuss its implications for the physics of GRB outflows and their interaction with the surrounding medium.
conclusion:
The multiwavelength study of GRB 090102 presented here has allowed us to place meaningful constraints on theoretical models of gamma-ray burst afterglows. The combined optical, X-ray, and radio data demonstrate a complex temporal evolution that departs in several respects from the simplest expectations of the standard forward-shock model. In particular, the early steep-to-shallow transition in the optical light curve, coupled with the comparatively smooth decay in the X-ray band, challenges the assumption of a single emission region and a homogeneous circumburst density profile. The disparity between the optical and X-ray temporal slopes also suggests that a purely adiabatic expansion in a constant-density medium is insufficient to explain the observations.

Our analysis indicates that models incorporating additional components—such as long-lived reverse shock emission, energy injection from a sustained central engine, or evolving microphysical parameters—can more naturally reproduce the observed behaviour. The early-time optical excess is consistent with a reverse-shock contribution, which would account for the rapid initial fading and subsequent flattening. Meanwhile, the X-ray light curve can be accommodated within a forward-shock framework if moderate energy injection is invoked, delaying the onset of the asymptotic decay phase. Such a scenario is also supported by the inferred spectral indices, which point to different cooling regimes in the optical and X-ray bands during the first few hours after the burst.

Comparisons with other well-observed events reveal that GRB 090102 shares features with bursts that exhibit strong reverse-shock signatures, although its X-ray evolution is less extreme. This suggests that the diversity of afterglow behaviours may reflect a continuum of physical conditions—varying magnetisation of the outflow, circumburst density profiles, and central engine activity—rather than discrete classes of events. The polarimetric detection reported for this burst further strengthens the case for a magnetised ejecta, which could enhance the reverse-shock emission and influence the early-time light curve morphology.

While our modelling efforts have narrowed the range of viable scenarios, degeneracies remain, particularly between the effects of energy injection and changes in microphysical parameters. Future observations that combine early-time polarimetry, rapid multi-band photometry, and broad-band spectroscopy will be critical for breaking these degeneracies. For GRB 090102, the available data already demonstrate the value of densely sampled, multiwavelength follow-up in exposing departures from the simplest theoretical expectations.

In summary, GRB 090102 provides an important test case for afterglow models, illustrating the need for flexible frameworks that can incorporate multiple emission components and evolving parameters. Its afterglow behaviour underscores the limitations of one-zone, constant-parameter descriptions, and highlights the potential of coordinated observations to probe the physical conditions in relativistic outflows.

title: Multipath Error Correction in Radio Interferometric Positioning Systems
abstract: Multipath interference presents a significant challenge to the accuracy and reliability of Radio Interferometric Positioning Systems (RIPS), as reflected signals distort phase measurements critical for precise localization. This paper proposes a novel multipath error correction framework combining adaptive signal modeling with spatial filtering techniques to mitigate phase biases. The method exploits the geometry of interferometric baselines and temporal stability of direct-path signals to isolate and suppress multipath components without requiring additional hardware. Simulation and experimental results in both controlled and outdoor environments demonstrate substantial improvements in positioning accuracy, with reductions in root-mean-square error exceeding 40% compared to conventional approaches. The proposed technique enhances robustness under severe multipath conditions, enabling more reliable RIPS deployment in urban, indoor, and obstructed environments where traditional systems suffer significant performance degradation.
introduction:
Radio interferometric positioning systems (RIPS) have emerged as a promising technique for achieving high-accuracy localization in a variety of environments, ranging from indoor industrial settings to outdoor navigation and tracking applications. Unlike conventional time-of-arrival or received signal strength–based methods, RIPS exploits the phase differences of continuous wave signals received at spatially separated nodes to estimate relative distances with sub-centimeter precision. This approach offers robustness against certain types of noise and hardware imperfections, while enabling scalable, cooperative localization without strict synchronization requirements. However, in practical deployments, the accuracy of RIPS is significantly challenged by multipath propagation, a phenomenon in which transmitted signals reach the receiver via multiple paths due to reflection, diffraction, and scattering from surrounding objects.

Multipath effects distort the measured phase of the received signals, introducing biases that cannot be mitigated solely by increasing signal-to-noise ratio or by simple filtering. In environments with strong reflectors, such as urban canyons, warehouse interiors, or metallic infrastructure, the resultant phase errors can accumulate, leading to substantial degradation in positioning accuracy. Traditional error mitigation techniques in radio localization—such as antenna diversity, frequency hopping, or statistical filtering—are only partially effective for RIPS, since the interferometric phase measurement is inherently sensitive to coherent signal superposition.

Recent research has explored various strategies to address multipath in RIPS, including advanced signal models that account for multiple propagation components, joint estimation of line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight parameters, and exploitation of spatial and frequency diversity. While these methods have shown promise, they often involve increased computational complexity, additional hardware, or restrictive assumptions about the environment. This makes them challenging to implement in resource-constrained nodes or dynamic scenarios where environmental conditions change rapidly.

The present work investigates novel multipath error correction techniques tailored to RIPS that aim to balance accuracy, computational efficiency, and implementation feasibility. By integrating improved signal modeling with adaptive estimation algorithms, the proposed methods seek to identify and compensate for multipath-induced phase distortions in real time. Experimental validation in both controlled and realistic settings demonstrates the potential of the approach to enhance positioning accuracy without substantial modifications to existing hardware. This contribution advances the practical deployment of RIPS in multipath-dense environments, supporting a broader range of applications that demand precise and reliable localization.
conclusion: This study demonstrated effective multipath error correction in radio interferometric positioning systems through advanced signal processing and modeling techniques. Experimental results confirmed significant accuracy improvements under challenging propagation conditions. The proposed approach enhances system robustness, offering practical benefits for high-precision applications. Future work will extend the method to dynamic environments and integrate adaptive algorithms for real-time performance optimization.

title: The Entropic Dynamics of Relativistic Quantum Fields
abstract: We investigate the formulation of relativistic quantum field theory within the framework of entropic dynamics, wherein quantum behavior emerges from principles of inference and information geometry. By generalizing the entropic updating of probability distributions to field configurations in spacetime, we derive covariant dynamical equations consistent with the Klein–Gordon field. The approach naturally incorporates constraints reflecting relativistic causality and local symmetries, leading to a probabilistic interpretation without invoking a fundamental wavefunction ontology. We further analyze the role of the information metric in defining field evolution and explore implications for vacuum structure, particle excitations, and the emergence of classical field behavior.
introduction:
The study of relativistic quantum fields lies at the intersection of quantum theory and special relativity, providing the foundational framework for our understanding of high-energy particle physics, quantum field theory (QFT), and the structure of the vacuum. Traditionally, the dynamics of such fields are derived from variational principles applied to Lorentz-invariant Lagrangians, yielding deterministic equations of motion for field operators in the Heisenberg picture or, equivalently, path integrals over field configurations. While this approach has been extraordinarily successful in predicting and explaining a wide range of phenomena, it leaves open deep conceptual questions regarding the statistical and informational underpinnings of quantum field dynamics. In particular, the interplay between quantum uncertainty, relativistic causality, and entropy production suggests that an alternative perspective—one grounded in the principles of inference and information theory—may shed new light on the nature of relativistic quantum fields.

In recent years, entropic methods have emerged as powerful tools for deriving dynamical laws in physics from principles of probabilistic inference. The program of entropic dynamics (ED) seeks to reconstruct the dynamical equations governing physical systems by treating them as rules for updating probability distributions in response to limited information. In this framework, the laws of physics are not fundamental postulates but emergent constraints on the consistent processing of information. Originally developed in the context of non-relativistic quantum mechanics, ED has been shown to reproduce the Schrödinger equation from purely inferential premises, without recourse to a quantization procedure. The key idea is to regard the state of a system as a probability distribution over its possible configurations, evolving under the guidance of entropy maximization subject to physically motivated constraints.

Extending ED to relativistic quantum fields involves significant conceptual and technical challenges. Unlike particle mechanics, where configuration space is finite-dimensional, a field configuration is specified by a function over space, yielding an infinite-dimensional configuration space. Moreover, relativistic invariance imposes stringent requirements on the formulation: the dynamics must respect Lorentz symmetry, causal structure, and the absence of a preferred foliation of spacetime. In the standard QFT formalism, these requirements are met by constructing field operators and correlation functions that transform covariantly under the Poincaré group. In an ED framework, however, one must ensure that the probabilistic updating rules and the definition of information constraints are themselves compatible with relativistic covariance.

A central motivation for exploring the entropic dynamics of relativistic quantum fields is to provide a foundation in which quantum fluctuations, statistical inference, and spacetime symmetries are integrated into a single coherent picture. While conventional QFT treats the vacuum as the lowest-energy eigenstate of the Hamiltonian, ED invites an interpretation of the vacuum as a maximally uninformative probability distribution subject to relativistic constraints. Excited states, scattering processes, and even particle creation can then be understood as manifestations of updated inferences in light of new information, rather than as purely dynamical evolutions in Hilbert space. This shift in perspective offers potential conceptual advantages, including a more transparent treatment of measurement, decoherence, and the emergence of classicality from quantum fields.

From a technical standpoint, the ED approach to relativistic quantum fields requires the formulation of an appropriate statistical manifold representing the space of possible field configurations. The geometry of this manifold, as encoded by an information metric such as the Fisher–Rao metric, provides the natural arena for defining entropic time and dynamical trajectories. Constraints on the updating process—such as local conservation laws, energy–momentum relations, and relativistic causality—play the role of generating the field equations. In favorable cases, the resulting dynamics may be expressed in a form equivalent to the functional Schrödinger equation for quantum fields, but now interpreted as an emergent law of inference rather than a postulated physical axiom.

An additional layer of complexity arises from the need to reconcile entropic time with relativistic time. In standard ED for non-relativistic systems, time is introduced as a parameter that tracks the accumulation of small entropic changes. In a relativistic setting, time is intertwined with space in a four-dimensional manifold, and simultaneity is frame-dependent. The challenge is to define a notion of entropic evolution that is consistent with relativistic covariance, possibly by introducing local proper times associated with spacelike hypersurfaces and ensuring that the probabilistic updates respect the causal structure of spacetime. This approach naturally connects with the Tomonaga–Schwinger formalism, in which quantum states evolve with respect to deformations of a spacelike hypersurface, providing a promising bridge between ED and the standard covariant description of quantum fields.

The entropic dynamics perspective also invites reconsideration of the role of constraints and symmetries in quantum field theory. In conventional formulations, symmetries are imposed at the level of the action or the commutation relations of field operators. In ED, symmetries emerge as invariances of the information constraints and the corresponding probability updating rules. This suggests that gauge invariance, Lorentz covariance, and other fundamental symmetries may be reinterpreted as properties of the underlying informational structure, rather than as independent postulates. Such a viewpoint could have implications for our understanding of quantum gravity, where the reconciliation of dynamical spacetime geometry with quantum principles remains an open challenge.

In this work, we develop a formulation of the entropic dynamics of relativistic quantum fields, with a focus on scalar fields as the simplest testing ground for these ideas. We begin by constructing the statistical manifold of field configurations and defining the appropriate information metric. We then specify the constraints that encode relativistic causality and energy–momentum relations, and use the method of maximum entropy to derive the corresponding dynamical laws. The resulting framework reproduces the functional Schrödinger equation for a relativistic quantum field, while providing an alternative interpretation grounded in inference and probability theory. We conclude by discussing the implications of this formulation for the interpretation of quantum field theory, the emergence of particles and interactions, and possible extensions to gauge fields and curved spacetimes.
conclusion:
In this work, we have explored the formulation of relativistic quantum field theory within the framework of entropic dynamics, emphasizing the role of inference and information geometry in deriving field evolution. By treating quantum fields as epistemic constructs whose dynamics arise from entropic updating constrained by relativistic covariance, we have shown that key structures of quantum field theory—such as canonical commutation relations and unitary evolution—can be recovered without postulating them a priori. The probabilistic description emerges naturally from the interplay between the geometry of the underlying configuration space and the symmetries imposed by Lorentz invariance.  

Our analysis demonstrates that entropic dynamics provides a coherent and flexible foundation for addressing conceptual challenges, including the reconciliation of quantum uncertainty with relativistic causality. The framework accommodates local field updates while maintaining global consistency, with the entropic time parameter serving as a covariant ordering of events. Moreover, the approach suggests novel avenues for incorporating constraints from interacting fields and curved spacetime, potentially deepening the connection between quantum theory and gravitation.  

The synthesis presented here underscores the interpretive clarity gained by grounding quantum field theory in principles of inference rather than ontological postulates. It highlights the potential of entropic dynamics as both a unifying formalism and a heuristic tool for extending quantum theory to regimes where conventional formulations encounter difficulties. Future work will focus on explicit models of interacting fields, the role of renormalization in the entropic context, and the extension to quantum fields in dynamic geometries.

title: Can Uncertainty Management be Realized in a Finite Totally Ordered Probability Algebra?
abstract: This paper investigates whether uncertainty management can be effectively achieved within a finite, totally ordered probability algebra. Such algebras, while computationally attractive, impose constraints on probability representation and combination. We analyze structural properties, focusing on their capacity to model gradations of belief, support inference, and preserve consistency under probabilistic operations. Limitations arising from finiteness and total ordering are examined, and implications for reasoning under uncertainty are discussed. Our findings indicate inherent trade-offs between expressive power and tractability, raising questions about their suitability for complex uncertainty management tasks.
introduction:
Uncertainty is an inherent feature of reasoning, decision-making, and knowledge representation in complex systems. From artificial intelligence to risk assessment and expert systems, the ability to manage and reason with incomplete, imprecise, or ambiguous information has been a central concern for decades. Probability theory, in its classical form, has long been employed as the dominant framework for representing uncertainty, offering a mathematically rigorous basis for modeling degrees of belief and predicting outcomes. However, the standard real-valued probability calculus assumes a continuous probability space, which may be computationally expensive or impractical for certain applications. This has motivated the exploration of alternative probabilistic models that operate on finite and discrete structures, while retaining essential inferential capabilities.

One such alternative is the probability algebra framework, in which probabilities are represented as elements of an ordered algebraic structure equipped with suitable operations for combination and revision. In particular, totally ordered probability algebras have been proposed as a means of simplifying uncertainty management, providing a finite chain of probability values that can be manipulated according to specified algebraic rules. By restricting the set of possible probability values to a finite set, one can potentially achieve computational efficiency, ease of implementation, and compatibility with qualitative reasoning methods. Such finite totally ordered structures have been considered in various contexts, including approximate reasoning, symbolic probability, and qualitative decision theory.

Despite these advantages, the adoption of finite totally ordered probability algebras for uncertainty management raises important theoretical questions. Chief among them is whether such algebras can adequately capture the essential behaviors and requirements of probabilistic reasoning. In particular, the algebra must support coherent operations for combining independent pieces of evidence, updating beliefs in light of new information, and maintaining consistency with probabilistic axioms. When the set of probability values is finite, certain desirable properties—such as closure under multiplication or the ability to represent arbitrary conditional probabilities—may be compromised. Furthermore, the total order constraint imposes a rigid ranking among probability values, which could limit the expressiveness of the system when compared to richer, partially ordered or continuous models.

The interplay between finiteness and total order thus poses a fundamental challenge: can uncertainty management, as it is understood in probabilistic and AI reasoning frameworks, be faithfully realized under these constraints? This question is not only of theoretical interest but also of practical significance. Many real-world systems, especially those embedded in hardware with limited precision or operating under strict time constraints, require efficient yet reliable mechanisms for handling uncertainty. If a finite totally ordered probability algebra can be shown to support the core operations of uncertainty management without introducing unacceptable distortions or anomalies, it could serve as a viable alternative to conventional probabilistic models in such settings.

Previous research has examined related issues in the context of ordinal probability theory, ranking functions, and finite-valued logics. These studies have highlighted both the potential and the limitations of discrete, ordered representations of uncertainty. However, a systematic investigation into whether a finite totally ordered probability algebra can satisfy the necessary conditions for general-purpose uncertainty management remains incomplete. Key concerns include the preservation of consistency under evidence combination, the avoidance of information loss in belief updating, and the compatibility of the algebraic operations with intuitive and normative probabilistic reasoning principles.

In this work, we address these concerns by formally analyzing the structure and behavior of finite totally ordered probability algebras in the context of uncertainty management. We seek to clarify the extent to which such algebras can emulate the inferential capabilities of continuous probability spaces, and to identify the inherent trade-offs imposed by finiteness and total order. Our analysis contributes to the broader understanding of discrete models for uncertainty, offering insights relevant to both theoretical foundations and practical implementations in computational reasoning systems.
conclusion:
This study has examined the feasibility of realizing uncertainty management within the framework of a finite, totally ordered probability algebra. By exploring the structural constraints inherent in such algebras, we have shown that while they offer appealing simplicity and computational tractability, they also impose significant limitations on expressive power and inferential accuracy. The total ordering guarantees comparability among all probability values, which simplifies decision-making processes; however, the finiteness of the set introduces unavoidable granularity. This discretization can lead to distortions in probability updates, loss of subtle distinctions between closely related events, and potential inconsistencies when applying standard probabilistic rules such as Bayes’ theorem.

Our analysis indicates that certain desirable properties of uncertainty management—such as precise representation of marginal changes in belief, or the preservation of nuanced likelihood ratios—cannot be fully preserved under finite total orders without sacrificing coherence or completeness. While it is possible to approximate traditional probabilistic reasoning within this algebraic framework, these approximations may accumulate errors over sequences of inferences, thereby undermining long-term reliability.

Nevertheless, finite totally ordered probability algebras may still hold value in domains where computational simplicity, bounded representational cost, or qualitative ranking is more important than exact probabilistic fidelity. They could serve as effective models for resource-limited reasoning systems or for contexts where only ordinal information is available. Future work should explore hybrid approaches that blend finite ordinal structures with richer probabilistic semantics, aiming to balance tractability and accuracy. Ultimately, the results suggest that while full uncertainty management in the classical sense cannot be fully realized in such an algebra, carefully constrained applications remain both possible and potentially useful.

title: Fitting the Two-Higgs-Doublet model of type II
abstract: We present a detailed phenomenological analysis of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM) of type II, focusing on its compatibility with current experimental constraints from collider data, flavour physics, and electroweak precision observables. In this framework, one Higgs doublet couples exclusively to up-type quarks and the other to down-type quarks and charged leptons, leading to a rich scalar sector with five physical Higgs bosons: two CP-even, one CP-odd, and a charged pair. We perform global fits to the model parameters, incorporating the latest LHC measurements of the 125 GeV Higgs boson signal strengths, direct searches for additional scalars, and bounds from rare B-meson decays and leptonic processes. The parameter space is further constrained by theoretical requirements such as perturbativity, vacuum stability, and unitarity. Our results highlight the regions of parameter space consistent with all constraints, identifying the viable ranges for the mixing angle α, the ratio of vacuum expectation values tan β, and the masses of the additional Higgs states. We discuss the implications for future collider searches, emphasizing benchmark scenarios that maximize discovery potential. This comprehensive fit provides an updated and consistent picture of the type II 2HDM in light of current data, guiding both experimental strategies and theoretical developments.
introduction:
The discovery of a scalar particle with a mass of approximately 125 GeV by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has marked a milestone in particle physics, confirming the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking as described in the Standard Model (SM). Nevertheless, the SM leaves several open questions, including the origin of the matter–antimatter asymmetry, the nature of dark matter, and the hierarchy problem. These shortcomings motivate the exploration of extensions of the scalar sector. Among the simplest and well-motivated extensions is the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM), in which the SM Higgs sector is augmented by an additional SU(2)\(_L\) doublet. This extension leads to a richer scalar spectrum, consisting of two CP-even neutral Higgs bosons, one CP-odd neutral Higgs boson, and a charged Higgs pair.

The 2HDM of type II, in particular, assigns one scalar doublet to couple to up-type quarks and the other to down-type quarks and charged leptons, thereby avoiding tree-level flavour-changing neutral currents through a discrete \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) symmetry. This structure appears naturally in the Higgs sector of the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) and has been extensively studied in phenomenological contexts. Current LHC data, together with precision electroweak measurements and flavour observables, impose stringent constraints on the model’s parameter space. A global fit incorporating these diverse datasets enables a comprehensive assessment of the model’s viability and identifies regions consistent with experimental results. In this work, we perform a detailed fit of the type II 2HDM, confronting theoretical constraints with the latest experimental bounds, and discuss the implications for collider phenomenology and future searches.
conclusion:
In this work, we have performed a detailed investigation of the parameter space of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM) of type II, confronting theoretical consistency requirements with current experimental constraints. By combining bounds from perturbative unitarity, vacuum stability, and electroweak precision observables with the latest measurements from collider searches and flavour physics, we have delineated the viable regions in terms of the scalar masses, mixing angles, and the ratio of vacuum expectation values, \( \tan\beta \). Our analysis incorporates both the measured properties of the observed 125 GeV Higgs boson and the non-observation of additional scalar states, ensuring compatibility with the most up-to-date ATLAS, CMS, and flavour sector results.

The global fits indicate that the alignment limit, in which the light CP-even Higgs mimics the Standard Model Higgs, remains strongly favoured, particularly under the assumption of mass degeneracy among the heavy Higgs states to satisfy electroweak precision constraints. Nonetheless, moderate deviations from perfect alignment are still permissible in certain regions of parameter space, especially for intermediate values of \( \tan\beta \) and heavier scalar spectra. The charged Higgs mass is subject to stringent lower bounds from \( B \to X_s \gamma \) and other flavour processes, pushing it above several hundred GeV in most viable scenarios. Direct searches for heavy neutral scalars further restrict low- and high-\( \tan\beta \) regimes, though parameter combinations with suppressed couplings to gauge bosons and fermions can evade current limits.

The interplay between collider and flavour constraints has proven crucial in shaping the allowed 2HDM-II parameter space. Our fits show that scenarios with sizable mass splittings among the non-standard Higgs bosons are increasingly disfavoured, as they induce large contributions to the oblique parameters. This reinforces the preference for a near-degenerate heavy Higgs sector in phenomenologically viable configurations. Furthermore, the inclusion of up-to-date Higgs signal strength measurements significantly narrows the room for extended Higgs dynamics to alter the observed production and decay rates.

Looking forward, the ongoing accumulation of LHC Run 3 data, together with prospective measurements from future \( e^+e^- \) colliders and improved determinations of flavour observables, will further refine the picture. In particular, enhanced sensitivity to heavy Higgs production and precision Higgs couplings will be decisive in testing the residual parameter space identified here. Our study underscores the continued relevance of the 2HDM-II as a benchmark framework for beyond-the-Standard-Model Higgs sectors, while highlighting the increasingly tight constraints imposed by the synergy of theoretical and experimental inputs.

title: Hybrid Charmonium and the $\rho-\pi$ Puzzle
abstract: We investigate the role of hybrid charmonium states in addressing the longstanding $\rho$–$\pi$ puzzle in charmonium decays. Employing QCD-inspired models and recent lattice results, we explore possible mixing between conventional $c\bar{c}$ and $c\bar{c}g$ configurations. Our analysis suggests that hybrid admixtures can naturally suppress certain hadronic decay modes of $\psi'$ while preserving $J/\psi$ decay patterns. This framework offers a consistent explanation of experimental branching ratios and provides testable predictions for future high-luminosity experiments.
introduction:
The study of charmonium, the bound states of a charm quark and its antiquark (\(c\bar{c}\)), has long served as a valuable probe of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) in the nonperturbative regime. Since the discovery of the \(J/\psi\) in 1974, the spectroscopy and decay patterns of charmonium states have been extensively examined, providing insight into the interplay between perturbative quark–gluon dynamics and long-range confinement effects. While potential models based on nonrelativistic QCD have successfully described much of the observed charmonium spectrum, a number of anomalies persist in their decay properties. Among these, the so‑called \(\rho\)–\(\pi\) puzzle remains one of the most intriguing.

The \(\rho\)–\(\pi\) puzzle refers to the unexpectedly strong suppression of hadronic decays such as \(\psi(2S) \to \rho\pi\) relative to the corresponding \(J/\psi \to \rho\pi\) decay, when compared with perturbative QCD expectations. According to the so‑called “12% rule,” which assumes that the ratio of hadronic decay widths for excited and ground‑state charmonium mirrors the ratio observed in their leptonic widths, the branching fractions for \(\psi(2S)\) decays to light hadrons should be approximately an order of magnitude smaller than for the \(J/\psi\). Experimentally, however, the \(\psi(2S) \to \rho\pi\) channel is suppressed by more than an order of magnitude beyond this prediction, while other hadronic modes do follow the expected scaling. This selective suppression challenges the standard picture of charmonium decays as proceeding predominantly through three‑gluon annihilation, modulated by phase space and wavefunction effects.

Several theoretical approaches have been proposed to explain this discrepancy, including destructive interference between decay amplitudes, final‑state interaction effects, and mixing between conventional charmonium and other nearby states. In particular, the possibility that higher charmonium states contain significant admixtures of hybrid configurations—bound states of a \(c\bar{c}\) pair with an excited gluonic field—has attracted considerable attention. Hybrid charmonium states are predicted by lattice QCD and flux‑tube models to occur in the mass region above open‑charm threshold, and their presence could alter decay patterns through modified couplings to light hadrons. If the \(\psi(2S)\) or nearby vector states possess hybrid components, the interference between conventional and hybrid decay amplitudes might naturally account for the anomalous suppression observed in the \(\rho\pi\) channel.

In this work, we revisit the \(\rho\)–\(\pi\) puzzle in the context of hybrid charmonium mixing. We review the relevant experimental data, outline the theoretical framework for hybrid–conventional state mixing, and analyze the consequences for hadronic decay branching ratios. Our aim is to assess whether hybrid admixture provides a viable and quantitatively consistent explanation for the observed anomalies, and to identify experimental signatures that could confirm or refute this hypothesis in forthcoming measurements.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the role of hybrid charmonium configurations in addressing the long-standing $\rho$–$\pi$ puzzle in charmonium decays. By considering the possible admixture of conventional $c\bar{c}$ states with gluonic excitations, we have explored how such hybrid components can modify decay amplitudes and branching ratios, thereby influencing the observed suppression patterns in vector–pseudoscalar channels. Our analysis indicates that the inclusion of hybrid states, particularly near the mass region of the $\psi(2S)$, can naturally account for deviations from the naïve perturbative QCD expectations, which predict scaling of hadronic widths according to wavefunction overlaps at the origin.

The phenomenological implications of this scenario are twofold. First, hybrid admixtures can lead to destructive interference between conventional and hybrid decay amplitudes, selectively suppressing certain exclusive channels such as $\rho\pi$. Second, the mass proximity of hybrid and conventional states in the charmonium spectrum enhances the likelihood of significant mixing, consistent with lattice QCD indications of low-lying vector hybrid states. This provides a dynamical mechanism for the suppression that does not require fine-tuning of parameters beyond reasonable model expectations.

While our treatment has been largely qualitative, guided by experimental data and theoretical constraints, the results highlight the utility of hybrid configurations in resolving anomalies in charmonium decays. More refined calculations, incorporating explicit mixing matrix elements from lattice simulations and improved determinations of decay constants, will be essential for a quantitative test of this proposal. Furthermore, future high-statistics measurements of exclusive $\psi(nS)$ decays, particularly into vector–pseudoscalar and vector–vector final states, will provide critical input for validating the hybrid mixing hypothesis.

In summary, the hybrid charmonium framework offers a coherent and physically motivated explanation for the $\rho$–$\pi$ puzzle, grounded in QCD dynamics and supported by emerging theoretical and experimental evidence. Continued investigation along these lines promises not only to clarify the nature of this specific decay puzzle, but also to deepen our understanding of gluonic degrees of freedom in the meson spectrum.

title: Electronic emission of radio-sensitizing gold nanoparticles under X-ray irradiation : experiment and simulations
abstract: Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) are promising radio-sensitizing agents due to their high atomic number and strong photoelectric absorption, enhancing local energy deposition under X-ray irradiation. We report combined experimental and Monte Carlo simulation studies of electron emission from citrate-stabilized AuNPs exposed to monochromatic and polychromatic X-ray sources. Electron yields were measured using an electron spectrometer under controlled irradiation conditions, enabling identification of core-level photoelectrons, Auger electrons, and secondary electron distributions. Simulations, performed with Geant4-DNA, reproduced the measured spectra and provided insight into electron transport and energy dissipation at the nanoscale. Results show significant enhancement of low-energy electron production compared to bulk gold, attributed to nanoparticle surface effects and finite size geometry. The agreement between experiment and simulation validates the computational approach for predicting dose enhancement in biological environments. These findings contribute to a quantitative understanding of AuNP-mediated radiosensitization mechanisms and support the rational design of nanoparticle-based strategies for improved radiotherapy efficacy.
introduction:
Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) have attracted considerable attention in recent years as potential agents for enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of radiotherapy. Their high atomic number (Z = 79) leads to an increased probability of photoelectric interactions under X-ray irradiation, thereby amplifying local dose deposition in the vicinity of the nanoparticles. This phenomenon, known as radiosensitization, has been proposed as a means to selectively increase damage to tumour tissues while sparing surrounding healthy cells. In addition to physical dose enhancement, the emission of low-energy secondary electrons from AuNPs plays a central role in initiating localized chemical and biological damage, particularly through the production of reactive oxygen species and direct DNA strand breaks.

A quantitative understanding of electron emission processes is therefore essential for elucidating the mechanisms underlying nanoparticle-mediated radiosensitization. Experimental characterization of the emitted electron spectra provides direct insight into the energy distribution and yield of these electrons, while computational modelling enables the exploration of microscopic interactions that are challenging to probe experimentally. Monte Carlo simulations, in particular, are widely used to describe radiation transport and electron cascades at the nanoscale, allowing for a detailed analysis of the contributions from photoelectrons, Auger electrons, and secondary electrons.

Despite significant progress, discrepancies remain between experimental measurements and simulation predictions, especially in the low-energy regime where electron transport and surface effects are complex. Understanding these differences is critical for refining theoretical models and for accurately predicting biological outcomes of nanoparticle-assisted radiotherapy. In this work, we investigate the electron emission from radio-sensitizing AuNPs under X-ray irradiation by combining controlled experimental measurements with detailed Monte Carlo simulations. By systematically comparing observed spectra with simulated results, we aim to assess the accuracy of current modelling approaches and to identify key factors influencing electron yield and energy distribution. Our findings contribute to the optimization of nanoparticle design and to the development of predictive tools for enhanced radiotherapeutic strategies.
conclusion: The combined experimental and simulation results presented here provide a comprehensive picture of the electronic emission processes from radio-sensitizing gold nanoparticles under X‑ray irradiation. Measurements confirmed that gold nanoparticles produce a significant yield of low-energy electrons, whose spectra and intensities are in good agreement with Monte Carlo simulations, validating the modeling framework. The analysis highlights the role of secondary electron cascades and surface effects in enhancing local dose deposition, a key mechanism underlying radiosensitization. Discrepancies at very low energies point to the need for refined descriptions of surface plasmon contributions and electron transport at the nanoscale. Overall, our findings strengthen the quantitative link between nanoparticle-induced electronic emission and potential therapeutic gain in radiotherapy. The validated simulation approach can be extended to optimize nanoparticle size, shape, and composition for maximal radiosensitizing efficiency, and to guide the integration of gold nanoparticles into clinically relevant irradiation protocols.

title: Two-mode squeezed states in cavity optomechanics via engineering of a single reservoir
abstract: We propose a scheme to generate two-mode squeezed states of mechanical oscillators in a cavity optomechanical platform by engineering a single, common reservoir. The approach exploits tailored optomechanical interactions to create an effective dissipative process that drives the mechanical modes into a stationary entangled state, without requiring direct coupling between them. By appropriately tuning the cavity drive frequencies and amplitudes, we realize a reservoir that selectively damps a Bogoliubov mode of the mechanical system, thereby stabilizing strong two-mode squeezing. The method is robust against thermal noise and parameter fluctuations, and operates in the steady state, removing the need for fast control or post-selection. Our results provide a resource-efficient route to macroscopic quantum correlations, relevant for quantum information processing, precision sensing, and fundamental tests of quantum mechanics.
introduction:
Cavity optomechanics explores the interaction between confined electromagnetic fields and the mechanical motion of mesoscopic or macroscopic objects, mediated by radiation pressure or dispersive coupling. Over the past decade, this field has emerged as a fertile platform for probing quantum phenomena at the interface between microscopic and macroscopic scales, enabling ground-state cooling of mechanical resonators, observation of quantum backaction, and quantum-limited sensing. A particularly compelling aspect of optomechanics lies in its potential for generating and controlling nonclassical states of light and motion, which are essential resources for quantum information processing, quantum communication, and tests of the foundations of quantum mechanics.

Among the variety of nonclassical states, squeezed states have received significant attention. Squeezed states of a single mode exhibit reduced fluctuations in one quadrature below the standard quantum limit, at the expense of increased fluctuations in the orthogonal quadrature, and are instrumental in precision metrology and gravitational-wave detection. Extending this concept to two modes leads to two-mode squeezed states, in which strong correlations between the quadratures of two distinct modes give rise to entanglement. Such states are a key ingredient in continuous-variable quantum information protocols, including quantum teleportation, dense coding, and quantum key distribution. In the context of optomechanics, two-mode squeezing can involve optical–optical, mechanical–mechanical, or optomechanical pairs of modes, opening avenues for coherent interconversion of quantum information between disparate physical carriers.

Conventional approaches to generating two-mode squeezed states in optomechanical systems often rely on coherent parametric interactions, such as simultaneous driving of multiple cavity modes or modulation of system parameters at appropriate frequencies. These schemes are typically implemented in the resolved-sideband regime, where the cavity linewidth is much smaller than the mechanical frequency, allowing selective enhancement of desired sideband processes. While coherent schemes can achieve high degrees of squeezing and entanglement, they are generally sensitive to thermal noise, dissipation, and parameter fluctuations. Moreover, their performance is often limited by the requirement of phase stability between multiple driving tones and by the competition between desired nonlinear interactions and unwanted processes induced by the same drives.

An alternative and increasingly fruitful strategy for generating nonclassical states exploits engineered dissipation. In this reservoir engineering paradigm, the system is coupled to a carefully tailored environment such that the desired quantum state emerges as the unique steady state of the dissipative dynamics. The environment effectively “cools” the system into the target state, thereby making it robust against certain types of noise and insensitive to the initial conditions. In optomechanics, reservoir engineering has been successfully applied to generate single-mode squeezed states of light and motion, entangled optical and mechanical modes, and mechanical states with nonclassical correlations. Typically, these proposals involve coupling the system to multiple engineered reservoirs or employing multiple cavity modes to achieve the necessary interference between dissipative channels.

A particularly appealing goal is the generation of two-mode squeezed states using only a single engineered reservoir, as this can significantly simplify the experimental architecture and reduce susceptibility to technical noise. In such schemes, the single reservoir is designed to interact with a suitable combination of system modes such that the dissipative dynamics directly cool the relevant collective quadratures into a two-mode squeezed state. This approach obviates the need for multiple independent baths or complex feedback loops, and can, in principle, operate in parameter regimes where coherent schemes are ineffective.

Recent theoretical and experimental progress has demonstrated the feasibility of single-reservoir engineering in various quantum platforms, including trapped ions, superconducting circuits, and optical cavities. In cavity optomechanics, however, the realization of steady-state two-mode squeezing via a single engineered reservoir remains challenging. The main difficulty lies in tailoring the reservoir’s spectral properties and coupling structure to match the collective mode operators that define the two-mode squeezed state, while simultaneously suppressing detrimental heating processes. Achieving this requires precise control over drive frequencies and amplitudes, as well as careful consideration of the interplay between optomechanical interaction strengths, cavity dissipation rates, and mechanical decoherence.

In this work, we present a scheme for generating two-mode squeezed states in a cavity optomechanical system through the engineering of a single common reservoir. Our approach relies on driving an optical cavity mode in a configuration that couples two mechanical modes (or, alternatively, two optical sidebands) to the same dissipative channel, with appropriately chosen relative phases and amplitudes. By working in a regime where the engineered dissipator dominates over intrinsic mechanical damping, we show that the system relaxes into a steady state that closely approximates an ideal two-mode squeezed vacuum. We analyze the performance of our scheme under realistic experimental conditions, including finite thermal occupancies and imperfections in the reservoir coupling, and we identify optimal parameter regimes for maximizing the degree of squeezing and entanglement.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we describe the model Hamiltonian and the derivation of the effective master equation governing the system’s dynamics under the influence of the engineered reservoir. In Sec. III, we analyze the steady-state properties of the system, focusing on the achievable two-mode squeezing and entanglement. In Sec. IV, we discuss the robustness of the scheme against various imperfections and outline potential experimental implementations. Finally, in Sec. V, we summarize our findings and highlight possible extensions of the present work to more complex multimode settings and hybrid quantum systems.
conclusion: We have proposed and analyzed a scheme for generating two-mode squeezed states in a cavity optomechanical system through the engineering of a single dissipation channel. By tailoring the system–reservoir interaction, the mechanical modes are driven into a steady-state entangled configuration without the need for multiple independent baths or time-dependent control. Our results demonstrate that high degrees of squeezing and robust entanglement can be achieved under realistic parameters, even in the presence of thermal noise. This approach simplifies experimental implementation while offering scalability to multimode scenarios. The method provides a versatile platform for continuous-variable quantum information processing and precision measurements, and can be extended to other hybrid quantum systems where engineered dissipation is a practical route to nonclassical state preparation.

title: Dissipative discrete breathers in rf SQUID metamaterials
abstract: We investigate the existence and dynamical properties of dissipative discrete breathers (DBs) in one- and two-dimensional arrays of radio-frequency superconducting quantum interference devices (rf SQUIDs), a class of nonlinear superconducting metamaterials. Each SQUID, driven by an external alternating magnetic field and coupled inductively to its neighbors, exhibits strong nonlinearity due to the Josephson element. Using numerical simulations of the corresponding driven-dissipative equations, we demonstrate that spatially localized, time-periodic excitations can be robustly generated from appropriate initial conditions. These dissipative DBs persist in the presence of losses and external driving, and their stability is examined through Floquet analysis. We explore their dependence on coupling strength, driving amplitude, and frequency, and discuss their role in dynamically tuning the local and global magnetic response of the metamaterial. Our results indicate that rf SQUID arrays offer a versatile platform for studying nonlinear localization in superconducting networks.
introduction:
Nonlinear metamaterials have attracted considerable attention over the past two decades due to their ability to exhibit tunable electromagnetic properties not found in naturally occurring media. Among the diverse classes of artificial structures, superconducting metamaterials based on radio-frequency (rf) superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) have emerged as a particularly promising platform. These systems combine the intrinsic nonlinearity of the Josephson effect with the low-loss, coherent dynamics of superconductors, enabling the exploration of a wide range of nonlinear wave phenomena in both classical and quantum regimes. An rf SQUID consists of a superconducting loop interrupted by a single Josephson junction; when arranged in periodic arrays, such elements interact magnetically through their mutual inductance, giving rise to collective dynamic states that can be tuned via external magnetic fields or currents.

An important class of nonlinear excitations in discrete lattices is the so-called discrete breather (DB), also referred to as an intrinsic localized mode. These are time-periodic, spatially localized oscillations that arise in nonlinear, discrete systems due to the interplay of nonlinearity and lattice discreteness. Discrete breathers have been extensively studied theoretically and experimentally in mechanical, optical, and electrical lattices, as well as in systems of coupled pendula and micromechanical arrays. In superconducting metamaterials, the inherent nonlinearity of each rf SQUID, combined with relatively weak coupling between neighboring elements, provides an ideal environment for the formation of DBs. Moreover, due to the low dissipation in superconductors, such localized excitations can persist for long times, making them accessible to experimental observation and exploitation.

In realistic systems, however, dissipation and external driving are unavoidable. Dissipative discrete breathers (DDBs) are localized states sustained by a balance between energy input from an external drive and energy loss to the environment. In driven-dissipative lattices, DDBs have been observed in various contexts, where they can act as robust carriers of energy or information. In rf SQUID metamaterials, the presence of an alternating external magnetic flux can serve as a coherent drive that compensates for dissipative losses, stabilizing localized oscillations. The study of DDBs in such superconducting systems is of both fundamental and practical interest: it sheds light on the nonlinear dynamical response of metamaterials and may lead to novel functionalities such as controllable localization, energy storage, or signal processing at microwave frequencies.

Previous works on rf SQUID arrays have demonstrated rich nonlinear dynamics, including multistability, bistable switching, and complex spatiotemporal patterns. Theoretical analyses have predicted the existence of discrete breathers in these systems in the Hamiltonian limit, while numerical simulations have indicated that DDBs can survive in the presence of realistic dissipation and driving. Experimental advances in the fabrication of large-scale, high-quality superconducting arrays now make it possible to probe these phenomena directly. Nevertheless, a systematic exploration of dissipative discrete breathers in rf SQUID metamaterials, including their stability regimes, bifurcation structure, and dependence on system parameters, remains incomplete.

In this work, we investigate the existence, stability, and dynamical properties of dissipative discrete breathers in one- and two-dimensional rf SQUID metamaterials driven by an external alternating magnetic flux. By employing a combination of numerical simulations and analytical techniques, we map the parameter regions where DDBs can be excited and sustained. We analyze their spatial profiles, frequency spectra, and robustness to perturbations, and we elucidate the role of key parameters such as the SQUID nonlinearity, coupling strength, and dissipation rate. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of nonlinear localization in superconducting metamaterials and point toward potential applications in tunable, low-loss microwave devices based on engineered nonlinear excitations.
conclusion: We have demonstrated the existence and stability of dissipative discrete breathers in rf SQUID metamaterials, arising from the interplay of nonlinearity, discreteness, and loss. Numerical simulations reveal robust, spatially localized oscillations persisting under realistic parameters. These findings highlight the potential of rf SQUID arrays for tunable, energy-localizing functionalities in superconducting metamaterials, and open avenues for experimental observation and exploitation of nonlinear localization in engineered electromagnetic media.

title: Denotational cost semantics for functional languages with inductive types
abstract: We present a denotational framework for assigning cost semantics to higher-order functional languages extended with general inductive types. Our approach integrates traditional denotational semantics with an explicit accounting of computational resources, enabling precise, compositional reasoning about program execution costs. The language under study supports algebraic data types, pattern matching, and recursive definitions, features that pose significant challenges for existing cost models due to their rich structural and computational behavior. We model inductive types using initial algebra semantics and augment the standard interpretation with cost annotations that capture both the structural decomposition of data and the operational steps required for evaluation. This yields a semantics that is both extensional, in the sense of respecting program equivalence, and intensional, in capturing complexity properties. We show that the semantics is sound with respect to a standard operational cost model, and we establish compositionality results that allow modular cost analysis of higher-order programs. Several examples illustrate how our framework supports reasoning about asymptotic complexity directly from denotational definitions, without recourse to low-level operational reasoning. This work lays a foundation for principled, mathematically robust cost analysis of expressive functional languages, bridging the gap between semantic theory and practical resource-aware program verification.
introduction: Reasoning about the computational cost of functional programs is essential for both theoretical analysis and practical optimisation. Denotational cost semantics provides a compositional framework in which the meaning of a program includes information about the resources it consumes. This approach has been successfully applied to core functional languages, enabling precise reasoning about time complexity and supporting formal verification of cost bounds. However, most existing work has focused on languages with simple types, leaving the treatment of rich inductive data types—such as lists, trees, and user-defined variants—less developed. Inductive types are central to functional programming, enabling expressive and modular program design, but they also introduce significant challenges for compositional cost models, particularly in accounting for recursive computations and data-dependent control flow. In this work, we present a denotational cost semantics for a typed functional language with general inductive types. Our semantics captures both the extensional meaning and the associated cost, supports compositional reasoning, and aligns with operational intuitions. We demonstrate its applicability through examples and prove correspondence and soundness results, laying a foundation for cost analysis in realistic functional languages.
conclusion: We have presented a denotational cost semantics for functional languages with inductive types, providing a compositional framework for reasoning about resource usage. Our approach supports precise cost analysis, enabling formal verification of complexity properties and guiding the design of efficient functional programs with rich data structures.

title: Approximate quantum state reconstruction without a quantum channel
abstract: We propose a method for approximate quantum state reconstruction that circumvents the need for a direct quantum channel between the source and the receiver. Our approach leverages classical communication of measurement outcomes from multiple, randomly chosen bases, combined with efficient post-processing algorithms, to infer an approximate density matrix of the original state.
