In recent years, technical developments, including the implementation of PMTs with reduced gain settings, the use of optical filters, and improved data analysis algorithms, have opened the possibility of safe and scientifically productive observations under increased NSB levels. Nevertheless, quantitative studies of the impact of moonlight on key performance parameters—such as sensitivity, energy threshold, angular resolution, and systematic uncertainties—are essential to establish reliable operational guidelines.

This work presents a systematic investigation of the influence of moonlight on MAGIC observations. We analyse data taken under varying lunar illumination and angular separations, characterise the corresponding changes in instrument response, and assess the feasibility and limitations of extending routine operations into bright moonlight conditions. The results provide a foundation for optimising the duty cycle of the MAGIC telescopes while maintaining high-quality scientific output.
conclusion: The analysis presented demonstrates that moonlight, while traditionally considered a limiting factor for Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes, can be mitigated to a significant extent in the operation of the MAGIC telescope. Through systematic observations under varying lunar illumination and zenith angles, we quantified the impact of increased night-sky background on trigger rates, image cleaning thresholds, and overall sensitivity. Our results indicate that, although elevated background light leads to a modest degradation in energy threshold and sensitivity, careful adjustment of hardware parameters and analysis cuts preserves a substantial fraction of the instrument’s performance. The findings confirm that observations can be extended into periods of moderate moonlight without compromising the scientific integrity of the data, thereby increasing the telescope’s annual duty cycle. This capability is particularly valuable for time-critical studies of transient and variable gamma-ray sources, where continuous monitoring can yield crucial insights. Future work will refine background suppression techniques and explore real-time adaptive configurations to further optimize performance under bright conditions. Overall, these results expand the operational envelope of MAGIC and highlight the importance of flexible observational strategies in maximizing the scientific return from ground-based gamma-ray astronomy.

title: Using Ants as a Genetic Crossover Operator in GLS to Solve STSP
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to solving the Symmetric Travelling Salesman Problem (STSP) by integrating ants as a genetic crossover operator within a Guided Local Search (GLS) framework. The method leverages ant-based path construction to generate high-quality offspring, enhancing solution diversity and convergence speed. Experimental results demonstrate improved performance over conventional GLS implementations.
introduction:
The Symmetric Travelling Salesman Problem (STSP) is a well-known NP-hard combinatorial optimisation problem with extensive applications in logistics, manufacturing, and network design. Numerous heuristic and metaheuristic approaches have been proposed to obtain near-optimal solutions within reasonable computational times, including Genetic Local Search (GLS) algorithms that combine the global exploration capabilities of genetic algorithms with the exploitation power of local search procedures. A critical component of GLS is the crossover operator, responsible for generating new candidate solutions by recombining information from parent tours. The design of effective crossover operators is essential for preserving high-quality building blocks while ensuring diversity in the population.  

Ant Colony Optimisation (ACO) has proven effective for the TSP by simulating the pheromone-guided path construction behaviour of real ants, which naturally balances exploration and exploitation. This study proposes a novel approach that integrates ant-based solution construction as a crossover mechanism within the GLS framework for the STSP. Instead of traditional crossover operators, ants use pheromone trails derived from parent tours to probabilistically generate offspring, potentially enhancing the search process. By embedding this biologically inspired operator into GLS, the method aims to exploit the structured learning of ACO while retaining the intensification benefits of local search. The proposed hybrid is evaluated on benchmark STSP instances to assess its performance relative to conventional GLS strategies.
conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates that integrating ant-based mechanisms as a genetic crossover operator within GLS effectively addresses the STSP, yielding improved solution quality and convergence speed. Experimental results confirm its potential to exploit collective foraging behavior for enhanced search diversification. Future work will explore adaptive parameter tuning and hybridization with other metaheuristics to further strengthen performance across diverse problem instances.

title: DA-NAS: Data Adapted Pruning for Efficient Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automating the design of high-performing deep neural networks. However, many NAS methods are computationally expensive, requiring extensive training and evaluation of candidate architectures. Recent approaches have sought to improve efficiency through weight sharing and search space reduction, yet these often overlook the role of dataset-specific characteristics in guiding the search. In this work, we propose **DA-NAS** (Data Adapted Neural Architecture Search), a novel framework that integrates *data-adapted pruning* into the NAS process to accelerate search while preserving competitive accuracy. DA-NAS leverages statistical and structural properties of the target dataset to identify and prune unpromising operations and connections early in the search, dynamically refining the search space in a task-aware manner. Our method operates in three stages: (1) initial dataset profiling to extract discriminative features and complexity indicators, (2) iterative pruning of low-utility architectural components based on their relevance to the profiled data, and (3) focused NAS within the reduced search space using a differentiable search strategy. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet demonstrate that DA-NAS achieves up to 40% reduction in search cost compared to baseline NAS approaches, with negligible or no loss in accuracy. Furthermore, the architectures discovered by DA-NAS exhibit improved parameter efficiency and faster inference times, particularly on resource-constrained devices. Our ablation studies confirm that the data-adapted pruning mechanism is the primary contributor to these gains, effectively aligning the search process with dataset-specific requirements. DA-NAS opens a promising direction for integrating data-centric insights into NAS, enabling efficient and adaptive architecture design for diverse application domains.
introduction: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automating the design of high-performing deep neural networks. However, the computational cost of NAS remains prohibitive, often requiring extensive training of numerous candidate architectures. Existing pruning techniques reduce network complexity, but they are typically applied post hoc and without consideration of dataset-specific characteristics. In this work, we propose DA-NAS, a data-adapted pruning framework that integrates pruning directly into the NAS process. By leveraging dataset-driven insights, DA-NAS selectively removes redundant components early in the search, enabling more efficient exploration of the architecture space. Our approach achieves competitive accuracy while substantially reducing search time and computational demands, making NAS more accessible for real-world applications.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced DA-NAS, a data-adapted pruning framework designed to enhance the efficiency of Neural Architecture Search by integrating dataset-specific characteristics into the search and pruning process. By jointly considering architectural relevance and data-driven pruning signals, DA-NAS effectively reduces the search space while preserving, and in some cases improving, model accuracy. Our experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DA-NAS achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art NAS methods, with substantially lower computational cost. The results highlight the importance of tailoring search strategies to the statistical properties of the target dataset, enabling more informed pruning decisions and faster convergence. Furthermore, the proposed approach maintains flexibility, making it applicable to a variety of search algorithms and network families. Future work will explore extending DA-NAS to multi-objective optimization scenarios, such as balancing accuracy, latency, and energy consumption, as well as investigating adaptive pruning schedules. We believe that data-adapted strategies like DA-NAS offer a promising path toward sustainable and scalable neural architecture design.

title: Detecting Security threats in the Router using Computational Intelligence
abstract: The increasing dependence on networked systems has made routers a critical target for cyberattacks, necessitating robust and adaptive security mechanisms. This paper presents a computational intelligence-based approach for detecting security threats within routers, aiming to enhance real-time threat identification and mitigation. The proposed system integrates machine learning algorithms with network traffic analysis to identify anomalies indicative of malicious activity, including intrusions, denial-of-service attempts, and unauthorized access. By leveraging supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, the model adapts to evolving threat patterns and reduces false positives compared to traditional rule-based systems. A dataset comprising simulated and real-world traffic was used to train and validate the model, ensuring its applicability to diverse network environments. Experimental results demonstrate high detection accuracy, low latency, and scalability, making the approach suitable for deployment in modern router architectures. The study highlights the effectiveness of computational intelligence in proactive network defense and underscores its potential for integration into firmware-level security solutions. This work contributes to advancing intelligent, autonomous router security capable of addressing emerging cyber threats in dynamic network landscapes.
introduction:
The proliferation of internet-connected devices and the rapid expansion of network infrastructures have significantly increased the reliance on routers as critical components in modern communication systems. Routers serve as the primary gateway between local networks and the external internet, facilitating the routing of data packets and enabling seamless connectivity. However, their pivotal role also makes them a prime target for malicious actors seeking to exploit vulnerabilities for unauthorized access, data interception, denial-of-service attacks, and other security breaches. Traditional security measures, such as static firewall rules and signature-based intrusion detection systems, often struggle to keep pace with the evolving sophistication of cyber threats. These conventional methods can be limited in detecting zero-day attacks, adaptive malware, and subtle anomalies that deviate from normal network behavior.

The complexity of detecting security threats in routers is exacerbated by the dynamic nature of network traffic, the diversity of protocols, and the increasing use of encrypted communications. Attack patterns are no longer confined to predictable signatures but can manifest as subtle statistical deviations or context-dependent anomalies. Moreover, with the advent of the Internet of Things (IoT), the number of devices connected through routers has surged, widening the attack surface and introducing heterogeneous data flows. This environment necessitates a more adaptive and intelligent approach to threat detection—one that can learn from data, identify patterns in real time, and generalize to previously unseen attacks.

Computational intelligence, encompassing techniques such as machine learning, neural networks, fuzzy logic, and evolutionary algorithms, offers promising solutions to these challenges. These methods excel at modeling complex, nonlinear relationships in high-dimensional data, enabling the identification of subtle indicators of compromise that may elude rule-based systems. For instance, supervised learning algorithms can be trained on labeled datasets of benign and malicious traffic to classify new flows accurately, while unsupervised techniques can uncover anomalous patterns without prior knowledge of attack signatures. Furthermore, hybrid approaches that integrate multiple computational intelligence paradigms can enhance robustness and detection accuracy.

The integration of computational intelligence into router-based security systems can facilitate proactive defense mechanisms capable of evolving alongside emerging threats. By embedding intelligent detection modules within routers, it becomes possible to analyze traffic at the network edge, reducing latency and mitigating attacks before they propagate further into the network. Such capabilities are particularly vital in scenarios where centralized monitoring is impractical or where real-time responsiveness is critical.

This paper investigates the application of computational intelligence techniques for detecting security threats in routers, focusing on their ability to adapt to the dynamic nature of network environments and detect a wide range of attack types. Through the design, implementation, and evaluation of intelligent detection models, this work aims to contribute to the development of resilient, efficient, and autonomous network defense strategies that address the limitations of traditional security approaches.
conclusion: This study demonstrated that computational intelligence techniques can effectively detect security threats in routers, enhancing network protection and resilience. By leveraging advanced algorithms, abnormal patterns were identified with high accuracy. Future work will refine detection models, enabling real-time responses and broader applicability to emerging network security challenges.

title: Phonon-limited electron mobility in Si, GaAs and GaP with exact treatment of dynamical quadrupoles
abstract: We present first-principles calculations of phonon-limited electron mobility in Si, GaAs, and GaP, incorporating an exact treatment of dynamical quadrupole contributions to long-range electron–phonon interactions. Using density-functional perturbation theory with a fully converged interpolation of electron–phonon matrix elements, we evaluate scattering rates and mobilities over a wide temperature range. The inclusion of dynamical quadrupoles yields measurable corrections to scattering by long-wavelength acoustic phonons, particularly in polar and near-polar semiconductors. Our results show improved agreement with experimental mobilities, especially at low temperatures where long-range effects are most pronounced. This work establishes the quantitative importance of dynamical quadrupoles for predictive transport calculations in technologically relevant semiconductors.
introduction:
The electron mobility in semiconductors is a central parameter governing the performance of a wide range of electronic and optoelectronic devices. It quantifies the ease with which charge carriers respond to applied electric fields and therefore affects switching speeds, power consumption, and signal-to-noise characteristics in integrated circuits, sensors, and communication systems. In intrinsic or lightly doped semiconductors at room temperature, the dominant scattering mechanism limiting electron mobility is often the interaction with lattice vibrations, i.e., phonons. A quantitative and predictive description of phonon-limited mobility, grounded in first-principles methods, is essential both for understanding fundamental transport phenomena and for guiding the design of materials and devices with tailored charge transport properties.

In the last decade, density-functional theory (DFT) combined with density-functional perturbation theory (DFPT) has enabled accurate calculations of electron–phonon (e–ph) coupling parameters and scattering rates without resorting to empirical fitting. These developments, together with advances in Wannier interpolation techniques, have made it possible to compute phonon-limited mobilities for technologically relevant materials with unprecedented accuracy. However, certain subtleties in the long-wavelength limit of the e–ph interaction remain challenging, particularly in polar and partially polar semiconductors where macroscopic electric fields are induced by atomic displacements. The long-range part of the e–ph interaction in such systems is typically treated by separating the dipolar contribution—associated with Born effective charges—from the short-range remainder. This approach captures the leading-order divergence in the e–ph matrix elements for longitudinal optical (LO) phonons, as in the Fröhlich model. Yet, at next-to-leading order in the phonon wavevector, additional multipolar terms emerge, notably the dynamical quadrupoles, which describe the change in the dipole moment induced by strain gradients.

Dynamical quadrupoles originate from the microscopic displacement patterns of the lattice and are a manifestation of the spatial variation of the induced polarization beyond the dipole approximation. Their importance has been recognized in the context of flexoelectricity, Raman scattering, and long-wavelength phonon dispersions. In the realm of charge transport, they contribute to the non-analytic behavior of the e–ph coupling at small phonon momenta, modifying scattering rates in a way that can be relevant for accurate mobility predictions. While earlier studies have incorporated quadrupolar effects using model assumptions or partial treatments, a fully ab initio, exact inclusion of dynamical quadrupoles in e–ph calculations for mobility has so far been lacking.

Silicon, gallium arsenide (GaAs), and gallium phosphide (GaP) are paradigmatic semiconductors with widespread applications and well-characterized transport properties. Silicon, an elemental, non-polar semiconductor, serves as the backbone of modern electronics, and its phonon-limited mobility is largely determined by acoustic phonon scattering. GaAs, a polar III–V compound with a direct band gap, exhibits high electron mobility due to relatively low effective mass and weaker acoustic scattering, but is strongly influenced by polar-optical phonon interactions. GaP, another III–V compound with an indirect band gap, presents an intermediate case with mixed characteristics. These materials thus provide an ideal testbed for systematically investigating the role of dynamical quadrupoles in electron–phonon interactions and their impact on transport.

In this work, we present a first-principles study of the phonon-limited electron mobility in Si, GaAs, and GaP, with an exact treatment of dynamical quadrupoles within the framework of DFPT. We employ a recently developed formalism that extends the long-wavelength expansion of the e–ph coupling to include quadrupolar terms without approximation, ensuring a rigorous description of the non-analytic behavior of the perturbation potential. By combining this formalism with maximally localized Wannier function interpolation, we obtain e–ph matrix elements on ultra-dense Brillouin zone grids, enabling converged evaluation of scattering rates and mobilities via the linearized Boltzmann transport equation.

Our results allow us to assess the quantitative impact of dynamical quadrupoles on mobility for each material, and to elucidate the physical mechanisms by which quadrupolar fields influence electron scattering. Beyond their specific numerical effect in the systems considered, the methodologies and insights developed here are broadly applicable to a wide range of semiconductors and insulators, including emerging materials for nanoelectronics, photonics, and thermoelectrics. This work thus contributes both to the fundamental understanding of electron–phonon interactions and to the advancement of predictive computational transport theory.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a comprehensive first-principles study of phonon-limited electron mobilities in Si, GaAs, and GaP, incorporating an exact treatment of dynamical quadrupole contributions to the long-range electron–phonon interaction. By extending the perturbative formalism beyond the conventional dipole approximation, we have accounted for the full multipolar structure of the long-wavelength coupling, thereby removing approximations that can obscure subtle scattering mechanisms in polar and nonpolar semiconductors. Our results demonstrate that, while the quadrupole terms have a negligible impact on the mobility of GaAs at room temperature—where polar optical phonon scattering dominates—they produce measurable corrections in Si and GaP, particularly at low temperatures where acoustic phonon scattering is paramount. The inclusion of dynamical quadrupoles yields mobilities in closer agreement with experimental measurements for these materials, underscoring the importance of capturing all relevant long-range interactions in quantitative transport predictions.

We have also analyzed the temperature dependence of the mobility within this refined framework, highlighting differences in the relative importance of intravalley and intervalley processes among the three compounds. The methodology developed here is fully general and can be applied to other semiconductors, including emerging materials where higher-order multipole effects may be enhanced by reduced dimensionality or complex bonding environments. Our findings indicate that accurate modeling of charge transport from first principles requires going beyond the dipole approximation when aiming for predictive fidelity, especially in materials with significant anisotropy or subtle electron–phonon coupling pathways. This work provides a robust foundation for future studies of phonon-limited mobility and related transport phenomena, supplying both methodological advances and quantitative benchmarks for theory–experiment comparisons.

title: Statistics of general functions of a Gaussian field -application to non-Gaussianity from preheating-
abstract: We present a general formalism for computing the statistical properties of arbitrary functions of a Gaussian random field, with particular emphasis on applications to the study of non-Gaussianity generated during the preheating phase after inflation. Our approach is based on expressing the target function as a series expansion in orthogonal polynomials with respect to the Gaussian measure, enabling analytic evaluation of correlation functions of any order. This method is applicable to functions that are strongly non-linear, discontinuous, or highly non-analytic, for which standard perturbative techniques fail. We derive explicit formulae for the two-point and higher-order correlation functions in both real and Fourier space, and we discuss the scaling behaviour of the associated polyspectra. The formalism is then applied to models of preheating in which the curvature perturbation is generated by a complicated, non-linear mapping from the Gaussian inflaton fluctuations. We demonstrate that such mappings can produce significant non-Gaussian signatures even when the underlying field is nearly scale-invariant and Gaussian. Our results provide a systematic framework for predicting and characterising non-Gaussian features arising from general non-linear processes in the early universe, and are relevant for interpreting present and future cosmological data.
introduction:
The statistical properties of cosmological perturbations play a central role in our understanding of the early Universe. In the simplest inflationary scenarios, the primordial curvature perturbations are generated from quantum fluctuations of a light scalar field and are well described by a Gaussian random field, whose statistical properties are fully characterized by its two-point correlation function or power spectrum. However, a variety of mechanisms can lead to significant deviations from Gaussianity, leaving imprints in higher-order correlation functions such as the bispectrum or trispectrum. These non-Gaussian signatures provide valuable information about the physics of the early Universe, probing interactions, particle content, and dynamics beyond the minimal inflationary paradigm.

One particularly interesting source of non-Gaussianity arises during the preheating phase that can follow inflation. In many models, the inflaton field decays non-perturbatively into other fields through parametric resonance or tachyonic instabilities. These processes are inherently non-linear and can lead to strongly non-Gaussian distributions of the resulting field fluctuations. In such scenarios, the relevant cosmological observables may not be given directly by a Gaussian field, but rather by some non-linear function of it. For example, the curvature perturbation may depend quadratically or in a more complicated way on an underlying Gaussian isocurvature field. Understanding the statistical properties of such general functions of Gaussian fields is therefore essential for accurate predictions and for interpreting observational data.

The problem of determining the statistical features of a non-linear transformation of a Gaussian field is in principle straightforward: the Gaussian probability distribution of the underlying field is known, and the transformation can be applied to obtain the distribution of the derived quantity. However, in practice, the complexity of the transformation, the need to compute spatial correlations, and the presence of divergences or cutoffs make the problem non-trivial. In the cosmological context, one is often interested not only in the probability distribution function but also in correlation functions in Fourier space, which determine the signatures in the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure. Moreover, the functional dependence on the Gaussian field can be highly non-polynomial, especially in models of preheating where mode amplification and rescattering generate intricate field configurations.

In this work, we develop a general formalism for studying the statistics of arbitrary functions of a Gaussian random field, with particular emphasis on applications to non-Gaussianity generated during preheating. Our approach allows us to compute the leading-order contributions to correlation functions in a systematic way, without assuming a specific functional form beyond smoothness conditions. We illustrate the method with concrete examples inspired by preheating dynamics, demonstrating how the resulting non-Gaussian features differ from those in standard inflationary models. This framework provides a bridge between the microphysics of the post-inflationary era and the statistical descriptors accessible to cosmological observations, offering new opportunities to probe the physics of the very early Universe.
conclusion:
In this work we have developed a general statistical framework for computing the properties of arbitrary functions of a Gaussian random field, with particular emphasis on applications to the study of non-Gaussianity generated during the preheating phase of the early universe. By formulating the problem in terms of the joint probability distribution of the underlying Gaussian field and its derivatives, we have been able to derive closed-form expressions for the correlation functions and higher-order moments of transformed fields. This approach allows us to treat a wide class of non-linear mappings between the Gaussian field and the observable quantities, without resorting to perturbative expansions that may fail in the strongly non-linear regime characteristic of preheating.

Our analysis clarifies the connection between the statistical structure of the primordial Gaussian fluctuations and the non-Gaussian observables that arise from non-linear processes in the post-inflationary era. In particular, by expressing the n-point functions of the transformed field in terms of integrals over the Gaussian measure weighted by the non-linear mapping function, we have shown how the shape and amplitude of non-Gaussianity are determined by both the functional form of the transformation and the correlation properties of the original field. This formalism is exact for any deterministic function of the Gaussian field, and it naturally extends to situations where the mapping is defined piecewise or has discontinuities, as can occur in certain preheating scenarios.

Applying this general framework to preheating, we have considered models in which the curvature perturbation receives a contribution from a secondary scalar field that undergoes explosive particle production through parametric resonance. The resulting relation between the preheating field fluctuations and the curvature perturbation is highly non-linear and model-dependent. Our method enables a direct computation of the resulting probability density function (PDF) and correlation functions of the curvature perturbation, capturing the full non-Gaussian structure without relying on small-parameter expansions. This is particularly important because in preheating the induced non-Gaussianity can be large and of non-standard shape, rendering the usual local-type ansatz inadequate.

We have demonstrated that for several representative mappings motivated by lattice simulations of preheating, the resulting bispectrum and trispectrum can exhibit features—such as oscillatory scale dependence and sign changes—not commonly found in slow-roll inflationary models. These features arise naturally from the non-monotonic and sometimes sharply peaked functional dependence of the curvature perturbation on the Gaussian preheating field. Our results therefore provide a concrete link between microphysical processes during preheating and potentially observable signatures in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) or large-scale structure (LSS) data.

An important outcome of our work is the recognition that the statistical properties of the transformed field can be highly sensitive to rare events in the tail of the Gaussian distribution when the mapping function has strong amplification in certain ranges of the input field. In such cases, the non-Gaussianity is dominated by contributions from regions of field space that occupy a small fraction of the total volume, but contribute disproportionately to higher-order moments. This insight may have implications for the interpretation of observational constraints, as it suggests that bounds on non-Gaussianity derived under the assumption of weak deviations from Gaussianity may not straightforwardly apply to scenarios with tail-dominated statistics.

Furthermore, our formalism makes it transparent how the scale dependence of the underlying Gaussian correlations propagates through the non-linear mapping to produce scale-dependent non-Gaussianity in the transformed field. This is relevant for preheating models where the resonance band structure imprints specific scales in the field fluctuations. The resulting non-Gaussianity is then not only large in amplitude but also carries characteristic scale-dependent signatures that can serve as discriminants between different preheating mechanisms.

From a methodological perspective, the approach we have outlined is broadly applicable beyond the specific context of preheating. Any cosmological or astrophysical process in which an observable depends non-linearly on an underlying Gaussian field—be it in the context of biased galaxy formation, weak gravitational lensing, or reionization—can be addressed within the same statistical framework. This generality underscores the utility of our results for a wide range of problems in cosmology.

In summary, we have provided an exact and versatile method for calculating the statistical properties of arbitrary functions of Gaussian fields, and have illustrated its power in the context of non-Gaussianity from preheating. Our findings highlight several key points: (i) non-linear mappings can generate highly non-trivial and large non-Gaussian signatures even when the underlying field is Gaussian; (ii) the shape and scale dependence of the resulting non-Gaussianity are direct probes of the functional form of the mapping and the correlation structure of the input field; (iii) rare events in the Gaussian tail can dominate the statistics in strongly non-linear cases; and (iv) the framework is adaptable to a variety of cosmological scenarios. Looking ahead, combining this formalism with detailed numerical simulations of preheating can yield precise predictions for the statistical signatures imprinted on cosmological observables, thereby opening a pathway to constraining or detecting preheating through forthcoming high-precision CMB and LSS surveys.

title: Westerlund 1: bound or unbound?
abstract: Westerlund 1 (Wd 1) is among the most massive young star clusters in the Milky Way, hosting a rich population of evolved massive stars and offering a unique laboratory for studying cluster formation and evolution. Whether Wd 1 is gravitationally bound or in the process of dispersing remains an open question with significant implications for theories of massive cluster survival. We present new high-precision radial velocity measurements for a sample of bright cluster members, combined with updated estimates of the cluster’s structural parameters from deep near-infrared imaging. By comparing the observed velocity dispersion to predictions from virial equilibrium models, we assess the cluster’s dynamical state while accounting for the contribution of unresolved binaries and stellar mass loss. Our analysis suggests that the current velocity dispersion is marginally consistent with a bound configuration, though the inferred virial mass is sensitive to assumptions regarding the binary fraction and the spatial distribution of stars. We discuss the potential influence of early gas expulsion and tidal interactions on the long-term stability of Wd 1, concluding that while the cluster may remain bound for several crossing times, it is likely evolving toward a more diffuse state on timescales of tens of Myr.
introduction:
Westerlund 1 (Wd 1) is one of the most massive young star clusters known in the Milky Way, with an estimated age of 3–5 Myr and a stellar mass of order 5 × 10⁴ M⊙. Its extreme mass, compact size, and rich population of evolved massive stars make it an important laboratory for studying the formation, early evolution, and dynamical fate of massive stellar systems in the Galactic disk. Whether Wd 1 is gravitationally bound or already dispersing is a key question, as the answer has implications for our understanding of cluster survivability, the efficiency of star formation, and the contribution of such systems to the field stellar population.

Massive clusters form in giant molecular clouds, and their subsequent evolution depends critically on the interplay between internal dynamics and external influences such as gas expulsion, tidal forces, and encounters with molecular clouds. Theoretical models and simulations suggest that rapid removal of residual gas can unbind a young cluster unless the star formation efficiency is sufficiently high or the gas is expelled slowly. Observationally, determining whether a cluster is bound requires accurate measurements of its structural parameters, stellar velocities, and total mass. The advent of high-resolution spectroscopy and astrometry allows for increasingly precise assessments of cluster kinematics, enabling robust constraints on their dynamical state.

Wd 1 presents both opportunities and challenges in this context. Its high extinction and location in a crowded region of the Galactic plane complicate membership determination and kinematic measurements. Nevertheless, recent spectroscopic and astrometric surveys have begun to yield radial velocities and proper motions for a significant number of its members, allowing for estimates of its internal velocity dispersion. Comparing these kinematic measurements to the expectations from virial equilibrium provides a direct test of whether the cluster is currently bound. In addition, the spatial distribution of members and the presence of mass segregation offer further insight into its dynamical history.

This study aims to combine available photometric, spectroscopic, and astrometric data to evaluate the bound or unbound nature of Westerlund 1. By assessing its present-day mass, velocity dispersion, and structural parameters in the context of dynamical models, we seek to clarify its evolutionary status and contribute to a broader understanding of the fate of massive young clusters in the Milky Way.
conclusion:
Our analysis of the dynamical state of Westerlund 1 suggests that, despite its extreme youth and richness, the cluster is likely to remain gravitationally bound for at least several tens of Myr. Using updated radial velocity measurements and proper motion constraints, we find that the observed velocity dispersion is consistent with the stellar mass inferred from photometric and spectroscopic studies, once allowance is made for unresolved binaries and measurement uncertainties. The resulting virial ratio lies below the threshold expected for rapid dispersal, indicating that the cluster has not undergone the kind of violent relaxation or gas expulsion that would readily unbind it. While some degree of mass segregation is evident, and the presence of massive binaries may inflate the measured velocity dispersion, the corrections applied here strengthen the case for long-term stability.

Nevertheless, important caveats remain. The internal kinematics are still only partially sampled, particularly in the dense core where crowding and extinction limit the completeness of the dataset. Moreover, the cluster’s location in the Galactic disk exposes it to tidal perturbations from the Galactic potential and passing molecular clouds, which could erode its mass over Gyr timescales. The current mass function appears to be only mildly depleted at low masses, but future dynamical evolution may preferentially remove these stars, potentially altering the cluster’s survivability.

Comparisons with N-body models of massive young clusters suggest that Westerlund 1 occupies a parameter space consistent with progenitors of long-lived bound systems such as globular clusters, albeit at lower total mass. If its initial conditions were indeed close to virial equilibrium, and if external perturbations remain modest, it could persist for hundreds of Myr, contributing to the rare population of massive bound clusters in the Milky Way.

In summary, the weight of current evidence points toward Westerlund 1 being gravitationally bound at present, with a significant probability of remaining so in the future. Continued high-precision astrometric monitoring, combined with deep spectroscopy, will be essential to refine its dynamical mass, constrain the binary population, and detect any subtle signatures of expansion or dissolution. Such studies will not only elucidate the fate of Westerlund 1, but also inform our broader understanding of the early dynamical evolution of massive star clusters.

title: RiPPLE: A Crowdsourced Adaptive Platform for Recommendation of Learning Activities
abstract: RiPPLE is a crowdsourced adaptive learning platform designed to recommend personalized learning activities to students while fostering collaborative knowledge construction. Leveraging learner-generated content, RiPPLE enables students to create, share, and evaluate questions and resources, which are then tagged with relevant concepts. The platform integrates adaptive recommendation algorithms that model individual learners’ knowledge states and engagement patterns to suggest suitable activities aimed at improving mastery and retention. By combining crowdsourcing with adaptive learning, RiPPLE addresses limitations of traditional systems that rely solely on expert-authored materials or static learning paths. The platform also provides educators with analytics for monitoring student progress and identifying misconceptions at both individual and cohort levels. Evaluation in authentic university settings demonstrates that RiPPLE enhances student engagement, promotes active learning, and supports diverse learning needs through scalable personalization. This paper presents the design principles, system architecture, and empirical findings, highlighting RiPPLE’s potential as a sustainable, learner-centered educational technology.
introduction:
In recent years, the rapid growth of online and blended learning environments has transformed the way learners access educational content and interact with peers and instructors. The proliferation of digital resources, ranging from open educational materials to massive open online courses (MOOCs), has created unprecedented opportunities for learners to engage with diverse forms of content at their own pace. However, this abundance of choice also presents a significant challenge: learners often struggle to identify the most relevant, engaging, and effective learning activities that align with their current knowledge, skills, and interests. Similarly, educators face difficulties in curating and recommending appropriate resources for heterogeneous cohorts of students with varying levels of prior knowledge, learning preferences, and goals.

Adaptive learning technologies have emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges by tailoring the learning experience to individual needs. By leveraging learner data, such systems can provide personalized recommendations for learning activities, scaffold content delivery, and dynamically adjust the learning path. While existing adaptive learning platforms have demonstrated positive effects on learning outcomes, many remain limited in their adaptability, scalability, and ability to incorporate diverse sources of content. Furthermore, such systems are often designed in a top-down manner, relying heavily on instructor-generated resources and predefined adaptation rules, which can limit their responsiveness to emerging learner needs and new pedagogical opportunities.

Crowdsourcing approaches have shown potential to complement traditional adaptive systems by harnessing the collective intelligence of learners themselves. Through collaborative tagging, rating, and contribution of learning materials, crowdsourcing can enable a richer and more diverse pool of educational resources that evolve in response to community input. In educational contexts, crowd-based content curation not only increases the variety of available materials but also fosters learner engagement, as students take an active role in shaping the learning environment. However, the integration of crowdsourced content with adaptive recommendation algorithms remains an underexplored area, with few systems effectively combining the scalability and diversity of crowdsourcing with the personalization capabilities of adaptive technologies.

RiPPLE (Recommendation in Peer-Learning Environments) has been developed to address this gap by providing a crowdsourced adaptive platform for the recommendation of learning activities. RiPPLE enables students to contribute, tag, and rate learning activities, while simultaneously leveraging these interactions to generate personalized recommendations through adaptive algorithms. This dual approach empowers learners to co-create the educational resource base while benefiting from tailored guidance that directs them toward the most relevant activities for their learning trajectory. By integrating learner-generated content into the recommendation process, RiPPLE seeks to create a virtuous cycle in which the quality and relevance of content improve over time, and recommendations become increasingly accurate and personalized.

The design of RiPPLE is grounded in principles from learning sciences, educational data mining, and human-computer interaction. It draws on the idea that peer learning and active participation in content creation can enhance motivation, deepen understanding, and develop metacognitive skills. At the same time, it recognizes the importance of algorithmic support in navigating complex learning spaces. Through the combination of crowdsourcing and adaptivity, RiPPLE aims to address key limitations of existing systems: the static nature of instructor-curated content, the lack of responsiveness to rapidly changing learning needs, and the underutilization of learner contributions in shaping adaptive pathways.

This paper presents the motivation, design, and evaluation of the RiPPLE platform. We first situate RiPPLE within the broader landscape of adaptive learning and crowdsourced educational technologies, reviewing relevant literature and identifying the specific challenges that our approach seeks to overcome. We then describe the system architecture, including the mechanisms for crowdsourced content generation, metadata enrichment, and adaptive recommendation. Following this, we report on empirical evaluations conducted in authentic learning contexts, focusing on user engagement, recommendation accuracy, and perceived usefulness. Finally, we discuss implications for the design of future adaptive learning systems, limitations of the current approach, and potential directions for further research.

By bridging the strengths of crowdsourcing and adaptivity, RiPPLE represents a novel contribution to the field of technology-enhanced learning. It offers a scalable and dynamic model for supporting personalized learning in diverse educational settings, empowering both learners and educators to collaboratively curate and navigate the ever-expanding universe of digital learning resources.
conclusion:
This study has presented RiPPLE, a crowdsourced adaptive learning platform designed to recommend learning activities tailored to students’ individual needs while fostering a collaborative learning environment. By integrating principles from learning sciences, recommender systems, and crowdsourcing, RiPPLE offers an innovative approach to addressing a persistent challenge in education: how to provide timely, personalised, and pedagogically sound learning recommendations at scale. The platform empowers learners not only to consume content but also to contribute by creating, evaluating, and curating activities, thereby positioning students as active participants in the co-construction of their learning environment.

The evaluation of RiPPLE demonstrated its capacity to generate recommendations that adapt to students’ evolving knowledge states, leveraging peer-generated resources without compromising quality. The crowdsourced nature of the platform expands the diversity and relevance of available learning activities, while the adaptive recommendation algorithms ensure that learners receive suggestions aligned with their current understanding and learning goals. The dual emphasis on adaptivity and participation distinguishes RiPPLE from traditional adaptive systems, which often rely on static or expert-authored content, and from purely social learning platforms, which lack fine-grained personalisation.

Our findings underscore the potential of combining crowdsourcing with adaptive technologies to create more engaging and effective learning experiences. Students reported that the platform’s recommendations were relevant and helpful, and that contributing to the pool of activities enhanced their engagement and sense of ownership over the learning process. Moreover, the system’s analytics provided actionable insights to both students and instructors, supporting formative assessment and targeted intervention.

However, the study also surfaced challenges that warrant further investigation. Ensuring the pedagogical quality of crowdsourced activities remains a critical concern; while peer review and rating mechanisms help filter content, additional scaffolding and instructor oversight may be needed to maintain high standards. Furthermore, sustaining student participation in content creation requires careful consideration of motivational factors, such as recognition, feedback, and integration into course assessment. The adaptive algorithms themselves could also benefit from incorporating a broader range of learner data, including affective and behavioural indicators, to refine recommendations further.

The work on RiPPLE contributes to the growing body of research exploring hybrid models that blend human and algorithmic intelligence in support of learning. By demonstrating the feasibility and benefits of a crowdsourced adaptive recommendation system, it opens avenues for scaling personalised learning in diverse educational contexts. Future research will focus on longitudinal deployments across disciplines, integration with institutional learning management systems, and the exploration of advanced analytics to enhance both recommendation accuracy and the learning experience.

In conclusion, RiPPLE exemplifies how the synergy of crowd contributions and adaptive recommendation technologies can create a dynamic, learner-centred ecosystem. By placing learners at the heart of both content generation and consumption, the platform not only addresses individual learning needs but also cultivates a collaborative, participatory culture that can enrich education at scale.

title: Impact of Free Carriers on Modulational Instability in Silicon-on-insulator Nanowaveguides
abstract: We investigate the influence of free carriers on modulational instability (MI) in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) nanowaveguides, considering both free-carrier absorption and dispersion induced by two-photon absorption. A generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation incorporating carrier dynamics is solved analytically and numerically. Results show that free carriers significantly modify MI gain spectra, leading to reduced gain and altered bandwidth compared to the carrier-free case. The suppression is more pronounced at higher input powers and in longer waveguides, where carrier accumulation is substantial. In certain regimes, carriers induce new instability bands due to dispersion changes. These findings provide insight into nonlinear dynamics in SOI nanowaveguides and are relevant for optimizing all-optical signal processing in integrated photonic circuits.
introduction:
Silicon-on-insulator (SOI) nanowaveguides have emerged as a prominent platform for integrated nonlinear photonics due to their high refractive index contrast, strong optical confinement, and compatibility with complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) fabrication processes. The large nonlinear parameter and tight mode confinement achievable in SOI structures enable a wide range of nonlinear optical phenomena at relatively low power levels, including self-phase modulation (SPM), four-wave mixing (FWM), soliton dynamics, and modulational instability (MI). Among these, MI plays a central role in the initiation of spectral broadening and the generation of correlated photon pairs, and it is also closely related to the onset of optical rogue waves and supercontinuum generation. Understanding the mechanisms governing MI in silicon nanowaveguides is therefore of both fundamental and practical interest.

In conventional optical fibers, MI arises from the interplay between Kerr nonlinearity and anomalous group-velocity dispersion (GVD), leading to the exponential amplification of perturbations on a continuous-wave (CW) or quasi-CW background. The gain spectrum and threshold conditions for MI in such systems are well described by the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) under the assumption that only instantaneous nonlinear responses are significant. However, in SOI nanowaveguides operating in the telecommunication wavelength range, nonlinear dynamics are complicated by the presence of two-photon absorption (TPA) and the subsequent generation of free carriers. TPA is enhanced in silicon due to its indirect bandgap and strong field confinement, and the carriers generated contribute to both free-carrier absorption (FCA) and free-carrier dispersion (FCD). These effects introduce additional nonlinear loss and phase modulation terms into the propagation dynamics, which can significantly influence MI behavior.

The impact of free carriers on nonlinear processes in silicon nanophotonics has been extensively studied in the context of pulse propagation, optical switching, and wavelength conversion. Free carriers, with lifetimes typically ranging from tens of picoseconds to several nanoseconds depending on recombination mechanisms and waveguide geometry, act on a slower timescale than the optical field. As a result, they impart a non-instantaneous nonlinear response, in contrast to the ultrafast Kerr effect. FCD alters the refractive index in a manner that can counteract or enhance the Kerr-induced phase shift, depending on the sign and magnitude of the carrier-induced index change. FCA, on the other hand, introduces wavelength-dependent attenuation that can suppress the growth of sidebands associated with MI. The combined action of these processes modifies the MI gain spectrum, potentially shifting the phase-matching condition and altering both the bandwidth and peak gain.

Previous theoretical and experimental studies have shown that free carriers can either suppress or enhance MI, depending on the operating regime and waveguide parameters. In the normal dispersion regime, where Kerr-only MI is absent in the absence of higher-order effects, FCD can provide an effective nonlinearity that enables phase matching, giving rise to a distinct form of carrier-induced MI. Conversely, in the anomalous dispersion regime, where Kerr MI is naturally supported, the free-carrier effects generally reduce the gain and narrow the bandwidth, although under certain conditions they can lead to new instability bands. The interplay between GVD, Kerr nonlinearity, TPA, FCD, and FCA thus leads to a rich variety of MI behaviors unique to semiconductor waveguides.

Despite these advances, a comprehensive understanding of how free carriers affect MI in realistic SOI nanowaveguide geometries remains incomplete. Many existing analyses rely on simplified models that neglect higher-order dispersion, carrier dispersion dynamics, or the spectral dependence of nonlinear coefficients. Furthermore, experimental studies are often limited by the difficulty of isolating free-carrier effects from other nonlinear processes, particularly in the presence of ultrashort pulses where self-steepening and Raman scattering may also contribute. There is therefore a need for a systematic investigation that combines an extended theoretical framework with parameters relevant to practical waveguide designs, in order to quantify the influence of free carriers on MI gain spectra, threshold conditions, and sideband evolution.

In this work, we analyze the impact of free carriers on modulational instability in SOI nanowaveguides, incorporating both FCD and FCA into a generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation framework that also accounts for TPA and higher-order dispersion. We derive analytical expressions for the MI gain in the presence of free carriers, identify the regimes where carrier effects dominate, and compare these predictions with numerical simulations for typical SOI waveguide parameters. Our results reveal how free carriers reshape the MI spectrum across different dispersion regimes, and provide guidelines for engineering waveguide dimensions and operating conditions to either mitigate or exploit carrier-induced effects. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of nonlinear dynamics in semiconductor photonic platforms and informs the design of devices for applications such as broadband light generation, parametric amplification, and on-chip quantum photonics.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the influence of free carriers on the modulational instability (MI) dynamics in silicon-on-insulator nanowaveguides. By incorporating free-carrier absorption and dispersion into the nonlinear propagation model, we demonstrated that carrier generation significantly modifies both the MI gain spectrum and its dependence on pump power and waveguide geometry. Our analysis reveals that free carriers tend to suppress MI by introducing additional loss and phase shift, leading to reduced gain and narrower bandwidth. This effect is more pronounced at higher pump powers and in dispersion regimes where the contribution of carrier-induced phase modulation is substantial. Furthermore, the interplay between Kerr nonlinearity, dispersion, and carrier dynamics can shift the frequency of maximum MI gain. These findings provide deeper insight into the role of nonlinear absorption processes in integrated photonic platforms and can inform the design of nanowaveguides for applications requiring controlled parametric amplification and wavelength conversion in the presence of carrier effects.

title: Parametric (quasi-Cherenkov) cooperative radiation produced by electron bunches in natural or photonic crystals
abstract: We investigate the generation of parametric (quasi-Cherenkov) cooperative radiation by relativistic electron bunches traversing natural and photonic crystals. The study focuses on the regime where the emission process is enhanced by coherent interaction of the bunch with the periodic medium, leading to superradiant effects. Using a self-consistent theoretical framework based on Maxwell’s equations and the dynamics of charged particles, we analyze the temporal and spectral characteristics of the emitted radiation under dynamical diffraction conditions. The influence of crystal structure, diffraction geometry, and bunch parameters on the cooperative emission intensity and angular distribution is examined. Numerical simulations reveal that, for sufficiently short and dense bunches, the radiation intensity scales quadratically with the number of electrons, significantly exceeding the incoherent limit. Differences between natural and photonic crystals in tuning the emission frequency and directionality are discussed. The results demonstrate the potential of crystal-based cooperative radiation sources for generating high-brightness, tunable electromagnetic pulses in the X-ray and terahertz ranges.
introduction:
The interaction of relativistic charged particles with periodic media gives rise to a variety of coherent radiation phenomena that have been the subject of sustained theoretical and experimental investigation over the past several decades. Among these, parametric, or quasi-Cherenkov, radiation occupies a distinctive place. This effect arises when a charged particle traverses a crystal and the virtual photon field associated with the particle is diffracted by the periodically modulated dielectric susceptibility of the medium. The resulting emission bears close analogy to Cherenkov radiation in that it is determined by a phase-matching condition between the particle velocity and an eigenmode of the medium, but it is mediated by the crystal’s reciprocal lattice vectors rather than by uniform dielectric dispersion. In natural crystals, this process is governed by the atomic-scale periodicity, whereas in artificial photonic crystals, the relevant periodic structure can be engineered over a broad range of wavelengths.

Traditionally, studies of parametric (quasi-Cherenkov) radiation have focused on spontaneous emission from individual relativistic electrons or incoherent ensembles. In such cases, the radiated intensity scales linearly with the number of particles, and the spectrum and angular distribution are dictated by the crystal geometry, diffraction conditions, and beam energy. More recently, attention has turned to situations in which electron bunches of sufficiently high density produce radiation coherently, leading to intensities that scale as the square of the particle number. This coherent regime is of particular interest when the bunch length is comparable to or shorter than the emitted wavelength, enabling constructive interference of the fields generated by different electrons.

An especially rich domain emerges when cooperative effects come into play: the self-consistent interaction between the bunched electron beam and the electromagnetic field in the periodic medium can lead to collective instabilities, superradiant emission, and nonlinear saturation phenomena. Such “cooperative radiation” processes have been extensively studied in free-electron lasers and in beam–plasma systems, but their manifestation in the context of parametric (quasi-Cherenkov) emission remains comparatively unexplored. In crystals, the interplay between multiple scattering of photons, the dynamical diffraction of the emitted wave, and the feedback on the electron motion can give rise to distinctive cooperative dynamics not present in uniform media.

Photonic crystals, with their tunable band structures and ability to create photonic band gaps, offer additional flexibility for tailoring the dispersion and diffraction conditions that govern quasi-Cherenkov emission. By adjusting lattice constants, refractive index contrasts, and geometries, it is possible to bring the cooperative regime into experimentally accessible parameter ranges for a given electron beam energy. Furthermore, the strong dispersion near photonic band edges can enhance the interaction time between the electrons and the radiation field, potentially increasing the efficiency of cooperative emission.

The present work is devoted to a theoretical and numerical investigation of parametric (quasi-Cherenkov) cooperative radiation generated by short, high-density electron bunches traversing natural and photonic crystals. We analyze the coupled dynamics of the electron bunch and the electromagnetic field under conditions of dynamical diffraction, taking into account both spontaneous and induced emission processes. Particular attention is paid to the dependence of the cooperative emission characteristics on crystal parameters, beam properties, and diffraction geometry. The results provide insight into the feasibility of using crystal-based structures as compact, tunable sources of intense, coherent radiation in the X-ray to terahertz ranges, and they extend the conceptual framework of cooperative radiation to encompass quasi-Cherenkov processes in periodic media.
conclusion:
The present study has examined the features of parametric (quasi-Cherenkov) cooperative radiation generated by relativistic electron bunches traversing natural and photonic crystals. By employing a self-consistent theoretical framework that accounts for the dynamical diffraction of emitted photons and the collective interaction of the electron ensemble with the electromagnetic field, we have elucidated the conditions under which cooperative effects substantially enhance the radiation yield. The analysis demonstrates that, under appropriate bunch length, density, and crystal geometry, the emitted intensity scales quadratically with the number of electrons, reflecting the coherent nature of the process.

Distinctive characteristics of the radiation—such as its angular distribution, polarization properties, and spectral line shape—were shown to depend sensitively on the crystal’s dispersion relation and on whether the diffraction occurs in the Laue or Bragg geometry. In photonic crystals, the engineered periodicity allows for tailored dispersion and diffraction conditions, enabling control over the emission frequency and directionality. The comparison with natural crystals highlights the potential advantages of photonic structures in achieving higher efficiencies and tunable emission characteristics.

Our results further indicate that the cooperative regime is especially pronounced when the electron bunch duration is shorter than the inverse of the spectral width of the parametric radiation, ensuring phase synchronism across the bunch. Under such conditions, superradiant-like behavior emerges, offering prospects for compact, high-brightness radiation sources in the X-ray and terahertz ranges.

These findings not only deepen the understanding of quasi-Cherenkov cooperative radiation mechanisms but also provide practical guidelines for experimental realization. Advances in high-quality crystal fabrication and ultrafast electron beam technology make the proposed regimes experimentally accessible. Future work will focus on incorporating beam emittance effects, exploring three-dimensional photonic crystal architectures, and extending the analysis to nonlinear regimes, thereby paving the way for novel coherent radiation sources based on electron–crystal interactions.

title: Breaking down the link between luminous and dark matter in massive galaxies
abstract: We investigate the connection between luminous and dark matter in a representative sample of massive galaxies, combining deep spectroscopic observations with high-resolution imaging and state-of-the-art dynamical modeling. Our analysis utilizes integral field unit data to map stellar kinematics out to several effective radii, enabling robust constraints on the total mass profiles. By decomposing these profiles into stellar and dark matter components, informed by stellar population synthesis models for mass-to-light ratios, we quantify the relative contributions of baryons and dark matter as a function of radius and galaxy mass. We find that within one effective radius, stellar mass dominates, but dark matter fractions increase systematically with radius, reaching over 50% at ~4 effective radii. The transition scale correlates with total stellar mass and central velocity dispersion, suggesting a link between baryonic assembly history and halo structure. Comparisons with ΛCDM-based hydrodynamical simulations indicate broad agreement in the dark matter distribution, though observed central dark matter fractions are slightly higher than predicted, potentially reflecting variations in feedback efficiency or merger history. Our results underscore the importance of combining spatially extended kinematic measurements with detailed stellar population analyses to disentangle the interplay between luminous and dark matter, offering new constraints on galaxy formation models in the high-mass regime.
introduction:
Understanding the interplay between luminous and dark matter is fundamental to deciphering the formation and evolution of massive galaxies. Luminous matter, primarily composed of stars and gas, traces the baryonic processes that shape galactic structures, while dark matter, detectable only through its gravitational influence, dominates the mass budget and governs the large-scale dynamics. In the current cosmological framework, massive galaxies are thought to form within extended dark matter halos, with baryonic collapse and feedback processes modulating the efficiency of star formation. However, the relative spatial distribution and coupling between these components remain incompletely understood, particularly at the high-mass end where early formation epochs and complex merger histories may imprint distinctive signatures.

Observational studies using stellar kinematics, gravitational lensing, and X-ray measurements have provided valuable constraints on the total mass profiles of massive galaxies. These analyses indicate that dark matter fractions within the optical regions vary systematically with stellar mass, size, and morphological type. Yet, disentangling luminous and dark matter contributions is challenging due to uncertainties in stellar population models, anisotropy in kinematics, and projection effects. Recent advances in integral field spectroscopy and high-resolution simulations offer new opportunities to probe the co-evolution of baryons and dark matter across cosmic time. By combining these approaches, we can better quantify the scaling relations, structural dependencies, and physical mechanisms underlying the observed mass distributions. This work aims to refine our understanding of the luminous–dark matter connection in massive galaxies, providing insights into both galaxy assembly and the nature of dark matter itself.
conclusion: Our analysis demonstrates that the interplay between luminous and dark matter in massive galaxies is more intricate than simple scaling relations suggest. The results indicate that baryonic processes, particularly feedback and star formation efficiency, significantly influence the distribution of dark matter in galaxy interiors. This coupling evolves with cosmic time, reflecting the complex assembly histories of massive systems. Future high-resolution observations and simulations will be essential for disentangling these components, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of galaxy formation and the co-evolution of luminous and dark matter.

title: Neural ODEs with stochastic vector field mixtures
abstract: We introduce a novel framework for modeling dynamical systems by extending Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) with stochastic vector field mixtures. In our approach, the instantaneous dynamics are represented as a probabilistic mixture of multiple learnable vector fields, enabling the system to capture multimodal, heterogeneous, and uncertainty-aware evolution patterns. The mixture components are parameterized by neural networks, while mixture weights are sampled from a stochastic process conditioned on the current state and time. This formulation unifies continuous-time deep learning with latent stochasticity, allowing the model to represent complex trajectories beyond the scope of deterministic Neural ODEs. We derive efficient training algorithms leveraging stochastic variational inference and demonstrate the approach on synthetic and real-world datasets. Empirical results show improved predictive accuracy, better uncertainty quantification, and enhanced robustness to noise, highlighting the potential of stochastic vector field mixtures for modeling complex temporal phenomena.
introduction:
Neural ordinary differential equations (Neural ODEs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning continuous-time dynamics from data, offering a flexible alternative to traditional discrete-layer neural networks. By parameterizing the derivative of the hidden state with a neural network, Neural ODEs enable the representation of latent trajectories that evolve according to smooth vector fields. This approach has led to advances in modeling time series, physical systems, and generative processes, where the dynamics are assumed to be deterministic and governed by a single learned vector field. However, many real-world phenomena exhibit variability and uncertainty that cannot be captured adequately by purely deterministic dynamics. In such scenarios, the assumption of a single fixed vector field is restrictive, as it fails to account for stochastic influences, structural variability, or multimodal patterns in the underlying system.

Stochastic modeling offers a natural way to address this limitation, as it allows for the representation of inherent randomness in the governing dynamics. Classical stochastic differential equations (SDEs) extend ODEs by incorporating noise terms, effectively modeling systems where the evolution depends both on deterministic drift and stochastic diffusion. While Neural SDEs have been proposed to learn such dynamics from data, they typically assume a fixed form of stochasticity, often Gaussian, and may not capture situations where the randomness stems from switching or mixing between qualitatively different dynamical regimes. In many domains, such as climate modeling, neuroscience, and financial systems, the underlying process may transition between distinct modes of behavior, each with its own characteristic vector field, in a way that is itself stochastic.

One promising approach to capturing these complexities is to model the system’s dynamics as a stochastic mixture of multiple vector fields. In this setting, the instantaneous derivative of the state is drawn from a distribution over vector fields, allowing the model to express multimodal and non-Gaussian uncertainty in the dynamics. This formulation generalizes both deterministic Neural ODEs, which correspond to mixtures with a single component and no randomness, and certain classes of Neural SDEs, where the noise term can be interpreted as inducing continuous perturbations to a primary vector field. By explicitly representing multiple candidate vector fields and specifying a stochastic mechanism for selecting or weighting them through time, we can more naturally model systems with regime switching, heterogeneous subpopulation dynamics, or latent control signals.

The idea of mixtures in dynamical systems has antecedents in switching linear dynamical models, mixture-of-experts architectures, and piecewise-smooth systems. However, the combination of mixture modeling with continuous-time neural parameterizations opens up new possibilities. In the Neural ODE framework, each vector field can be parameterized by its own neural network, or by a shared architecture conditioned on a discrete or continuous latent variable. The stochastic mixture weights may themselves be governed by a latent process, such as a Markov chain, Gaussian process, or another Neural ODE. This flexibility enables the representation of both abrupt switches between modes and smooth interpolations among them, depending on the application.

From a probabilistic perspective, stochastic vector field mixtures induce a distribution over trajectories, rather than a single deterministic path. This distribution can capture epistemic uncertainty arising from limited data, aleatoric uncertainty inherent to the system, and structured variability due to unobserved modulatory factors. Learning in this setting typically involves inferring both the parameters of the vector fields and the latent mixing process from observed trajectories. This poses challenges in terms of identifiability, computational efficiency, and numerical stability, as the integration of the dynamics must now account for stochasticity in the vector field selection in addition to any continuous noise processes.

Recent advances in stochastic adjoint methods, variational inference for latent SDEs, and efficient sampling of continuous-time processes provide tools for addressing these challenges. Nonetheless, the study of Neural ODEs with stochastic vector field mixtures remains at an early stage, with many open questions regarding their expressive power, generalization properties, and suitability for different classes of dynamical systems. In particular, there is a need to understand the trade-offs between representing uncertainty through mixtures of vector fields versus through additive noise, and how these choices affect extrapolation, interpretability, and robustness to distributional shifts.

In this work, we propose a general framework for Neural ODEs with stochastic vector field mixtures, unifying deterministic Neural ODEs, Neural SDEs, and switching dynamical systems under a single modeling paradigm. We formalize the notion of a stochastic mixture over parameterized vector fields, describe several parameterizations for the mixture components and mixing processes, and develop learning algorithms based on variational inference and stochastic backpropagation through continuous-time solvers. Our approach accommodates both discrete and continuous mixtures, allowing for the modeling of abrupt regime changes as well as more gradual, probabilistically weighted transitions. We demonstrate that this framework can capture complex multimodal dynamics that are not well represented by existing deterministic or purely diffusive models.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the concept of stochastic mixtures of neural vector fields in continuous time, providing a probabilistic interpretation and connections to related models. Second, we propose practical architectures and inference methods that enable scalable learning of such models from irregularly sampled and noisy data. Third, we empirically evaluate the approach on synthetic and real-world datasets, illustrating its ability to model systems with multiple regimes, structured variability, and non-Gaussian uncertainty. By bridging ideas from Neural ODEs, stochastic processes, and mixture modeling, our work expands the expressive capacity of continuous-time neural models and opens new avenues for the data-driven study of complex dynamical systems.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced a framework for Neural Ordinary Differential Equations driven by stochastic mixtures of vector fields, extending the expressive power of continuous-time deep learning models. By allowing the dynamics to evolve under a probabilistic selection or blending of multiple learned vector fields, our method captures richer temporal behaviours and accounts for uncertainty in the underlying generative process. We formulated the approach within a principled mathematical setting, demonstrating how mixture weights can be parameterised and learned jointly with the constituent vector fields, and how stochasticity can be injected in a controlled manner to balance flexibility and stability. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world sequence modelling tasks showed that the proposed model outperforms standard Neural ODE baselines in predictive accuracy and uncertainty quantification, particularly in regimes characterised by multi-modal or switching dynamics. Ablation studies highlighted the importance of both the mixture structure and the stochastic components in achieving these gains. Beyond performance, the framework offers interpretability benefits, enabling decomposition of complex trajectories into meaningful dynamical modes. Future work could explore more sophisticated mixture priors, Bayesian inference schemes, and applications to domains such as system identification or control under uncertainty. Overall, our results suggest that stochastic vector field mixtures provide a powerful and versatile extension to Neural ODEs, bridging the gap between deterministic continuous-time models and the stochastic, heterogeneous dynamics observed in many natural and engineered systems.

title: Comparing neural network training performance between Elixir and Python
abstract: This study investigates the comparative performance of neural network training implemented in Elixir and Python, focusing on execution speed, scalability, and resource utilization. We evaluate representative models using equivalent architectures and datasets, employing established deep learning frameworks available in each language. Benchmark results indicate that while Python, with its mature ecosystem and optimized libraries, achieves faster training times in most configurations, Elixir demonstrates competitive performance in distributed training scenarios due to its lightweight concurrency model.
