This turning-point criterion, established through the pioneering work of Chandrasekhar, Harrison, Wheeler, and others, relies on the fact that for spherically symmetric stars the normal modes of radial oscillation can be computed and their frequencies traced as functions of the stellar parameters. The mode with the lowest frequency vanishes at the stability boundary, providing a clear and computationally accessible criterion.

When rotation is introduced, the stability problem becomes more complex. Rotation modifies the equilibrium structure through centrifugal flattening and changes the distribution of angular momentum, while also coupling radial and nonradial perturbations. For uniformly rotating stars, full stability analyses require solving the linearized Einstein field equations for axisymmetric perturbations, a task that is computationally demanding and sensitive to the choice of perturbation variables and gauge conditions. Moreover, in rapidly rotating stars, purely radial modes in the nonrotating limit become coupled to polar-led nonradial modes, leading to quasi-radial oscillations whose stability properties are less straightforward to diagnose.

Given these challenges, approximate methods for assessing the stability of rotating relativistic stars have been sought. One notable approach is the extension of the turning-point method to sequences of rotating configurations. Friedman, Ipser, and Sorkin formulated a general criterion applicable to uniformly rotating perfect-fluid stars: along sequences of constant angular momentum, an extremum of the gravitational mass signals the onset of secular instability. This method, while powerful, does not directly yield the point of dynamical instability, which can occur at higher central densities. The exact determination of the dynamical instability threshold requires mode calculations, but in practice such computations for rapidly rotating relativistic stars remain technically challenging.

A quasi-radial stability criterion aims to bridge the gap between the simplicity of the turning-point method and the rigor of full dynamical analysis. By focusing on the fundamental quasi-radial mode—an oscillation mode that, in the limit of zero rotation, reduces to the purely radial fundamental mode—one can track its squared frequency along sequences of rotating models. The point at which this frequency vanishes marks the onset of dynamical instability. Approximate schemes for estimating this frequency, such as perturbative expansions in the rotation rate or numerical time evolutions of perturbed configurations, can thus provide a practical tool for stability assessment.

In recent years, advances in numerical relativity and high-precision equilibrium codes have made it possible to construct extensive datasets of rapidly rotating stellar models for a wide variety of EOS candidates. This progress invites a systematic re-examination of stability criteria, especially in the quasi-radial regime. A robust quasi-radial criterion could serve not only as a diagnostic for theoretical modeling but also as input for astrophysical scenarios involving accreting neutron stars, merger remnants, and proto-neutron stars formed in core-collapse supernovae, where rapid rotation is prevalent.

In this work, we develop and test a quasi-radial stability criterion for uniformly rotating relativistic stars, grounded in the analysis of the fundamental quasi-radial mode and applicable across a wide range of rotation rates up to the mass-shedding limit. We compare the stability thresholds predicted by this criterion with those obtained from the turning-point method and, where available, from full dynamical simulations. Our goal is to assess the accuracy and practical utility of a quasi-radial approach, and to clarify its domain of validity for astrophysical applications.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined the problem of quasi-radial stability in rotating relativistic stars, with the aim of formulating a practical criterion that extends the well-known stability conditions for nonrotating configurations to the case of uniform rotation. By constructing sequences of equilibrium models within the framework of general relativity and employing realistic equations of state, we have identified the relevant turning points in the mass–central density and mass–angular momentum parameter space that signal the onset of instability against axisymmetric perturbations. Our analysis has demonstrated that the stability limit for rotating stars can be expressed in terms of a generalized turning-point criterion, applicable to sequences of constant angular momentum, which reduces to the standard static limit in the appropriate nonrotating case.

The results indicate that for uniformly rotating configurations, the onset of instability is shifted to higher central densities and larger gravitational masses relative to the nonrotating sequence, reflecting the stabilizing influence of centrifugal support. The criterion we propose, based on the extremum of the gravitational mass along constant-angular-momentum sequences, captures this shift quantitatively and provides a simple diagnostic for assessing stability without resorting to full perturbative mode calculations. Comparisons with available linear stability analyses confirm that the proposed quasi-radial criterion reproduces the critical points within a small margin, lending confidence to its utility in astrophysical applications.

An important outcome of our study is the clarification of the interplay between rotation and the stiffness of the equation of state in determining the stability thresholds. For stiffer equations of state, the maximum permissible mass and the corresponding critical rotation rates are higher, and the quasi-radial stability boundary is correspondingly displaced. In contrast, softer equations of state yield lower stability limits and more modest rotational enhancements. These trends are consistent with expectations from the underlying balance between pressure gradients, gravitational attraction, and centrifugal effects, and they underscore the necessity of incorporating realistic microphysics when applying the criterion to observed neutron stars.

The quasi-radial stability criterion developed here has several potential applications. In the context of neutron star astrophysics, it can be used to delineate the stability limits of rapidly rotating pulsars, to constrain the maximum mass of supramassive configurations, and to provide input for modelling the end stages of accretion-induced spin-up in X-ray binaries. Furthermore, it offers a framework for interpreting gravitational-wave signals from the post-merger remnants of binary neutron star coalescences, where rapid rotation and strong-field gravity are both at play. By enabling a rapid assessment of whether a given remnant is likely to be stable or to undergo collapse to a black hole, the criterion can help link observational signatures to the underlying stellar parameters.

While the focus of the present work has been on uniformly rotating, axisymmetric configurations, the approach can be extended to include differential rotation, which is expected in many astrophysical scenarios, particularly in the aftermath of mergers. Incorporating magnetic fields and finite-temperature effects would also broaden the applicability of the criterion. Future work will address these extensions and seek to refine the stability boundary through comparison with fully dynamical numerical relativity simulations.

In summary, we have provided a consistent and computationally tractable quasi-radial stability criterion for rotating relativistic stars, grounded in the turning-point method and validated against perturbative results. This tool offers both theoretical insight into the structure and stability of rapidly rotating compact objects and practical utility in interpreting current and forthcoming astrophysical observations.

title: Singlet Scalars as Dark Matter and the Muon g-2 Anomaly
abstract: We investigate singlet scalar extensions of the Standard Model as a unified framework for explaining both the dark matter abundance and the muon anomalous magnetic moment. We analyze parameter regions consistent with relic density, collider bounds, and precision measurements. Our results show viable scalar masses and couplings accommodating current data, offering testable predictions for upcoming direct detection and collider experiments.
introduction:
The nature of dark matter (DM) and the persistent discrepancy in the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon, \(a_\mu = (g-2)_\mu/2\), remain two of the most compelling indicators of physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). Cosmological and astrophysical observations, from galaxy rotation curves to precise measurements of the cosmic microwave background, strongly support the existence of non-baryonic DM constituting about 27% of the energy density of the Universe. Yet, the SM lacks a viable particle candidate that can account for this component. Concurrently, recent high-precision measurements from the E821 experiment at Brookhaven and the ongoing E989 experiment at Fermilab report a deviation between the experimental value of \(a_\mu\) and its SM prediction at the level of \(4.2\sigma\), suggesting potential contributions from new particles or interactions.

Among the theoretical frameworks proposed to address these open questions, extensions of the SM scalar sector have received considerable attention. In particular, models introducing singlet scalar fields—scalars that are invariant under the SM gauge group—offer minimal and phenomenologically rich scenarios. Such singlet scalars can serve as stable DM candidates when protected by an additional symmetry, often a discrete \(Z_2\), and can interact with SM particles via a Higgs portal coupling. This simplicity allows for consistent relic abundance, compatibility with direct detection constraints, and potential explanations for anomalies in precision observables.

The muon \(g-2\) anomaly can be addressed in models where the singlet scalar is accompanied by additional particles or extended gauge symmetries, which can mediate new loop contributions to \(a_\mu\). In this context, the so-called 331 models—based on the \(SU(3)_C \times SU(3)_L \times U(1)_X\) gauge group—provide a compelling framework. They naturally predict an extended scalar sector, new gauge bosons, and exotic fermions, some of which can couple to the muon and modify its magnetic moment. Incorporating a singlet scalar dark matter candidate into a 331 model therefore offers an intriguing possibility to simultaneously address both the DM puzzle and the muon \(g-2\) anomaly.

In this work, we explore the viability of singlet scalar dark matter in a 331 model, focusing on the interplay between relic abundance, direct detection limits, and contributions to \(a_\mu\). We systematically analyse the parameter space consistent with current experimental constraints and discuss prospects for future tests.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the possibility that a singlet scalar field can simultaneously account for the observed dark matter abundance and contribute to resolving the long-standing discrepancy in the muon anomalous magnetic moment, \( (g-2)_\mu \). By embedding the singlet scalar into a minimal extension of the Standard Model, we explored the parameter space consistent with cosmological and collider constraints, as well as precision measurements. Our analysis shows that, for scalar masses in the sub-TeV range and with appropriate portal couplings to the Higgs sector, it is possible to achieve a thermal relic density compatible with current Planck data while producing loop-induced contributions to \( (g-2)_\mu \) that reduce the tension between theory and experiment.

We have identified regions of parameter space where both phenomena are addressed without violating bounds from direct detection experiments such as XENONnT and LZ, and from Higgs invisible decay searches at the LHC. The interplay between the relic density requirement and the muon magnetic moment constraint imposes non-trivial correlations among the scalar mass, the Higgs portal coupling, and potential new lepton-specific interactions. In particular, scenarios with enhanced couplings to the muon sector can yield sizable contributions to \( (g-2)_\mu \) while remaining viable in light of present data.

Future experimental developments will further probe these models. Upcoming direct detection experiments with improved sensitivity will test much of the allowed parameter space, while more precise measurements of \( (g-2)_\mu \) and Higgs properties will sharpen constraints. Our results demonstrate that singlet scalar extensions remain a compelling and economical framework for addressing two of the most pressing anomalies in particle physics, motivating continued theoretical and experimental investigation into their phenomenological implications.

title: Convex Optimal Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: We present a convex optimization framework for optimal uncertainty quantification, enabling rigorous bounds on quantities of interest under incomplete probabilistic information. By formulating uncertainty propagation as a tractable convex program, the approach accommodates general constraints on moments, support, and dependence structures of input variables. The method yields sharp, computationally efficient bounds that are guaranteed by construction, avoiding reliance on sampling-based approximations. Applications to engineering models and stochastic systems demonstrate its versatility and accuracy. This framework provides a systematic, scalable tool for robust decision-making under uncertainty with provable optimality guarantees.
introduction:
Uncertainty quantification (UQ) has emerged as a central theme in the analysis, design, and verification of complex systems across science and engineering. As models become increasingly sophisticated and data-driven, it becomes imperative to assess the reliability of predictions, to propagate uncertainties from inputs to outputs, and to provide rigorous bounds on quantities of interest. Traditional approaches to UQ, such as Monte Carlo simulation, polynomial chaos expansions, and Bayesian inference, offer powerful tools for characterizing uncertainty when probabilistic descriptions are fully specified. However, in many practical scenarios, the available information about system inputs is incomplete, imprecise, or inconsistent, rendering classical probabilistic methods either inapplicable or insufficiently robust. In such contexts, optimal uncertainty quantification (OUQ) has been proposed as a framework for deriving the best possible bounds on performance measures, given only partial information.

OUQ formalizes the problem of uncertainty assessment as an optimization problem over admissible probability measures and model responses, constrained by whatever information is available — such as bounds, moments, or structural properties of the system. By avoiding unwarranted assumptions about unknown aspects of the input distribution, OUQ produces rigorous, data-consistent bounds that are valid under all admissible scenarios. This worst-case perspective is especially relevant for safety-critical applications, where underestimating risk can lead to unacceptable consequences.

While the OUQ framework is general and expressive, its direct application often leads to infinite-dimensional optimization problems, which are computationally intractable in their raw form. A natural and fruitful direction is to identify cases in which the OUQ problem admits a convex reformulation. Convex optimization enjoys strong theoretical guarantees, efficient numerical algorithms, and a rich duality theory, making it a powerful tool for large-scale and safety-critical analysis. Convexity ensures that any local optimum is global, and that solutions can be computed reliably even in high-dimensional settings. Recognizing and exploiting convex structure within OUQ problems can therefore bridge the gap between rigorous uncertainty bounds and practical computational feasibility.

Recent advances in convex analysis, measure theory, and optimization have opened new possibilities for rendering OUQ problems tractable. For example, when the constraints on admissible measures are convex, and the objective — often an extremal expectation of a performance function — is linear in the measure, the resulting problem can be expressed as a convex program, sometimes reducible to finite-dimensional form via representation theorems. Moreover, dual formulations offer interpretable certificates for the optimal bounds, linking the solutions to generalized moment problems and robust optimization.

This work develops a systematic approach to convex optimal uncertainty quantification, identifying structural conditions under which OUQ reduces to convex optimization and demonstrating computational methods for solving these formulations efficiently. By uniting the rigor of the OUQ framework with the tractability of convex optimization, we aim to extend the applicability of uncertainty quantification to settings with limited information, high stakes, and stringent computational constraints. The results provide both theoretical insights into the geometry of admissible uncertainty sets and practical algorithms for computing sharp, reliable bounds in complex systems.
conclusion: This work has presented a convex optimization framework for uncertainty quantification that rigorously characterizes bounds on quantities of interest under limited or incomplete information. By formulating the problem in a convex setting, we ensure both computational tractability and provable optimality of the resulting bounds. The approach accommodates a broad class of admissible probability measures and constraint structures, enabling systematic and interpretable quantification of uncertainty across diverse applications. Numerical examples illustrate the method’s accuracy, stability, and efficiency compared to traditional sampling-based techniques. Future work will extend the framework to high-dimensional settings, incorporate additional structural priors, and explore adaptive algorithms for large-scale problems. Overall, this study demonstrates that convex optimal formulations offer a powerful, generalizable tool for reliable uncertainty quantification in complex systems.

title: Modeling sidelobe response for ground-based mm-wavelength telescopes with the geometrical theory of diffraction
abstract: We present a modeling framework for predicting sidelobe response in ground-based millimeter-wavelength telescopes using the geometrical theory of diffraction (GTD). The approach accounts for diffraction from structural features such as support legs, subreflector edges, and shielding panels, enabling accurate estimation of far-field antenna patterns beyond the main beam. Comparisons with measured beam maps demonstrate that GTD-based simulations capture key sidelobe structures and relative amplitudes. This method provides a computationally efficient tool for evaluating design trade-offs, mitigating stray light contamination, and improving calibration strategies in high-sensitivity mm-wavelength astronomical observations.
introduction:
Accurate characterization of the sidelobe response is of central importance in the design and operation of ground-based millimeter-wavelength telescopes. Sidelobes—responses of the antenna pattern outside the main beam—can introduce unwanted contamination from bright sources such as the Sun, Moon, or ground emission into astronomical observations, thereby limiting the achievable sensitivity and dynamic range. For instruments engaged in precision measurements, such as cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments or surveys of faint extragalactic sources, uncontrolled sidelobe pickup can lead to systematic errors that are difficult to remove in post-processing. Understanding and mitigating these effects requires predictive models that capture the relevant physical mechanisms over the full spatial domain of the antenna response.

At millimeter wavelengths, telescope optics are often large compared to the wavelength, enabling the use of high-frequency asymptotic methods to model electromagnetic scattering. Physical optics (PO) methods provide accurate predictions of the main beam and near sidelobes by integrating induced surface currents, but become computationally prohibitive for modeling far-out sidelobes, where multiple reflections, diffraction from structural edges, and scattering from support elements can contribute. In these regions, the Geometrical Theory of Diffraction (GTD) and its uniform extensions offer an efficient alternative, describing the propagation of rays and their diffraction from edges and tips without requiring a full-wave solution.

The GTD framework extends geometrical optics by introducing diffraction coefficients that account for the generation of new ray fields when incident rays encounter discontinuities in surface geometry. This approach captures the essential physics of edge diffraction from elements such as subreflector rims, feed-support legs, and shielding structures, which can dominate the far sidelobe response. When applied to ground-based mm-wavelength telescopes, GTD can be used to trace paths by which radiation from bright off-axis sources reaches the detectors, whether through single or multiple diffraction and reflection events. The resulting models can guide design choices—such as the shaping of baffles and shields—and provide inputs to data analysis pipelines for sidelobe subtraction.

Previous studies have demonstrated the utility of GTD for predicting straylight in radio and microwave antennas, but relatively few have targeted the specific geometries, frequency ranges, and environmental conditions of modern ground-based mm-wave instruments. The combination of large reflectors, complex support structures, and the need to suppress ground pickup to levels many tens of decibels below the main beam presents unique challenges. This work aims to develop and validate a GTD-based modeling approach tailored to these systems, capable of efficiently producing full-sky sidelobe maps and identifying dominant scattering mechanisms. By integrating GTD predictions with measured beam patterns, the methodology enables improved control of systematic errors in demanding astronomical applications.
conclusion:
The analysis presented in this work demonstrates the applicability and effectiveness of the geometrical theory of diffraction (GTD) in modeling sidelobe responses for ground-based millimeter-wavelength telescopes. By incorporating both geometric optics and edge-diffraction contributions, the developed framework captures key features of the sidelobe structure arising from interactions of the propagating field with structural elements such as subreflector edges, support legs, and shielding structures. The GTD-based approach enables the prediction of far-field patterns with a computational efficiency that is well suited for iterative optical design studies and for diagnosing performance impacts from structural modifications.

Comparisons with measured beam maps validate the model’s ability to reproduce both the angular location and relative amplitude of dominant sidelobe features. In particular, the inclusion of higher-order diffraction terms and multiple-edge interactions was found to be important for accurately representing sidelobe patterns at the dynamic range required for precision cosmological measurements. The results underscore the sensitivity of sidelobe levels to small geometric perturbations, reinforcing the importance of incorporating realistic structural details into electromagnetic models of telescope optics.

The methodology developed here bridges the gap between purely numerical full-wave simulations, which are computationally intensive at millimeter wavelengths for large structures, and simplified empirical treatments, which may not capture the relevant physics. By leveraging the asymptotic foundations of GTD, the model remains tractable while retaining physical interpretability, making it a useful tool for both design optimization and systematic error assessment.

Future work will extend the present approach to include hybrid formulations that combine GTD with physical optics for improved accuracy in transitional regions, as well as to model the impact of scattering from surface roughness and panel gaps. The integration of the GTD model into end-to-end instrument simulations will further enable the quantification of stray light contamination in science data products.

In summary, the presented GTD-based sidelobe modeling framework provides a robust, flexible, and computationally efficient means to predict and analyze sidelobe responses in ground-based mm-wavelength telescopes. Its demonstrated agreement with experimental data indicates strong potential for application in the design and characterization of current and next-generation instruments, ultimately supporting the stringent control of systematic effects required for high-precision astrophysical observations.

title: Safe-FinRL: A Low Bias and Variance Deep Reinforcement Learning Implementation for High-Freq Stock Trading
abstract: We propose **Safe-FinRL**, a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for high-frequency stock trading that addresses the dual challenges of bias and variance in policy estimation. Traditional DRL trading agents often suffer from unstable learning dynamics and overfitting to market noise, leading to suboptimal performance in live deployment. Safe-FinRL integrates a variance-reduced policy gradient method with bias-controlled value estimation, supported by robust risk-sensitive reward shaping. Our architecture incorporates temporal attention for high-resolution market data and employs adaptive position sizing to mitigate drawdowns under volatile conditions. Extensive experiments on high-frequency U.S. equity datasets demonstrate that Safe-FinRL achieves superior Sharpe ratios, lower maximum drawdowns, and more consistent returns compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The results indicate that simultaneously controlling bias and variance in DRL-based trading yields improved generalization to unseen market regimes, enhancing both profitability and safety for automated high-frequency trading systems.
introduction:
High-frequency trading (HFT) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in modern financial markets, characterized by the rapid execution of a large number of trades within extremely short time frames. Leveraging millisecond-level latency, advanced algorithmic strategies, and vast streams of market data, HFT firms aim to exploit small price discrepancies to generate consistent returns. While the potential for profit in HFT is considerable, the domain is distinguished by its complexity, volatility, and susceptibility to both market microstructure noise and overfitting. In this challenging environment, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has attracted significant attention as a promising approach for developing adaptive trading agents capable of learning optimal decision-making policies directly from high-dimensional market data.

DRL offers a model-free framework in which an agent interacts with the market environment, sequentially observing states, executing actions, and receiving rewards, with the goal of maximizing cumulative returns. Unlike traditional rule-based or supervised learning approaches, DRL enables agents to adaptively adjust strategies in response to evolving market conditions. However, the adoption of DRL in high-frequency trading faces several critical challenges. Chief among these are the high variance and bias in policy estimation, the instability of training in non-stationary environments, and the difficulty of balancing risk-sensitive objectives with profit maximization. In particular, standard DRL algorithms often suffer from high variance in gradient estimates, leading to unstable policy updates, and biases introduced by function approximation and finite samples, which may cause suboptimal convergence.

Existing DRL-based financial trading frameworks such as FinRL have demonstrated the feasibility of applying deep learning and reinforcement learning techniques to stock trading tasks. These frameworks provide modular pipelines for data processing, environment design, and algorithm integration. Nonetheless, when applied to high-frequency contexts, they frequently exhibit limitations in terms of risk control, execution stability, and resistance to overfitting. Bias in value estimation can result in overly optimistic strategies that perform well in backtests but fail in live markets, while high variance in policy updates can produce erratic decision-making that amplifies transaction costs and slippage. Moreover, the frequent and rapid decision cycles inherent to HFT exacerbate the accumulation of estimation errors, making the mitigation of both bias and variance crucial for robust performance.

The financial market's stochastic and partially observable nature compounds these difficulties. Price movements are influenced by a multitude of latent factors, including order book dynamics, institutional trading flows, and macroeconomic events, most of which are not fully captured in historical price and volume data. This partial observability introduces additional uncertainty into the learning process, increasing the risk of model miscalibration. Market microstructure noise, arising from bid-ask spread fluctuations, order execution delays, and hidden liquidity, further distorts the agent’s perception of the environment. Consequently, an effective DRL implementation for HFT must incorporate mechanisms that explicitly address uncertainty, reduce variance in policy evaluation, and constrain bias in value function approximation.

The Safe-FinRL framework proposed in this study aims to address these challenges by extending the conventional FinRL architecture with low-bias, low-variance algorithmic enhancements and integrated safety constraints. The concept of safety in this context encompasses both financial risk management—such as drawdown control and tail risk minimization—and algorithmic robustness, ensuring that learned policies generalize beyond specific training datasets. Safe-FinRL leverages techniques including ensemble value estimation to reduce variance, double estimators to mitigate overestimation bias, and distributional reinforcement learning to capture the stochastic nature of returns. Additionally, it incorporates risk-sensitive reward shaping and constraint-based optimization to align the agent’s objectives with realistic trading risk tolerances.

A key innovation of Safe-FinRL lies in its synergy between statistical learning theory and practical trading constraints. By grounding algorithmic choices in bias–variance trade-off principles, the framework ensures that policy evaluation is both statistically sound and operationally viable. This is particularly important in high-frequency environments, where the rapid pace of trading amplifies the consequences of model error. The framework also integrates advanced data preprocessing pipelines, including market feature engineering tailored to high-resolution tick data and robust normalization procedures to mitigate the impact of outliers and structural breaks.

The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we present a systematic analysis of bias and variance sources in DRL-based high-frequency trading and formalize their impact on trading performance. Second, we design and implement the Safe-FinRL framework, incorporating algorithmic enhancements that jointly address these sources while embedding risk management principles into the learning process. Third, we conduct extensive empirical evaluations using real high-frequency stock market data to benchmark Safe-FinRL against baseline DRL trading frameworks and traditional quantitative strategies, demonstrating substantial improvements in profitability, risk-adjusted returns, and stability.

By merging low-bias and low-variance learning techniques with domain-specific safety considerations, Safe-FinRL advances the state of the art in DRL-driven HFT. The proposed approach not only improves the statistical reliability of learned trading policies but also enhances their practical deployability in real-world, high-speed market environments. This work contributes to the growing body of research at the intersection of machine learning, financial engineering, and algorithmic trading, offering a robust foundation for the development of next-generation autonomous trading agents capable of thriving in the most demanding market conditions.
conclusion: This study presented **Safe-FinRL**, a low-bias, low-variance deep reinforcement learning framework tailored for high-frequency stock trading. By integrating advanced policy optimization techniques with robust risk-control mechanisms, the proposed approach addresses two persistent challenges in financial DRL applications: unstable learning dynamics and excessive variance in returns. Through empirical evaluation on high-frequency market datasets, Safe-FinRL demonstrated superior performance compared to baseline algorithms, achieving more consistent profitability while effectively mitigating drawdowns. The incorporation of adaptive exploration, regularization, and safety layers proved essential in stabilizing policy updates and reducing overfitting to transient market patterns. Furthermore, the modular architecture facilitates flexible integration with diverse market environments and data modalities, enhancing its practical applicability for real-world trading systems. While the results indicate strong potential, several avenues for future research remain, including extending the framework to multi-asset portfolios, incorporating market impact modeling, and exploring hybrid model-based/model-free strategies. Overall, Safe-FinRL contributes to the growing body of research on safe and efficient DRL in finance, offering a balanced trade-off between performance and risk that is critical for deployment in high-frequency trading contexts, where rapid decision-making and reliability are paramount. This work underscores the viability of safety-aware DRL as a core component in next-generation algorithmic trading solutions.

title: Phase diagram of matrix compressed sensing
abstract: We investigate the phase diagram of matrix compressed sensing, focusing on the recovery of low-rank matrices from undersampled linear measurements. Using tools from statistical physics and information theory, we characterize the fundamental limits of exact and approximate reconstruction in the high-dimensional regime. By applying the replica method and state evolution analysis to a generalized approximate message passing algorithm, we identify sharp phase transitions separating regions of successful recovery, partial recovery, and failure. Our results reveal the interplay between rank, sampling ratio, and measurement noise, and provide quantitative predictions for algorithmic performance. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions and highlight the existence of computational gaps between information-theoretic and algorithmic thresholds, offering guidance for the design of efficient recovery methods in practical scenarios.
introduction:
The recovery of structured signals from a limited number of measurements has become a central theme in modern signal processing, statistics, and machine learning. Compressed sensing (CS) theory has shown that sparse vectors can be reconstructed exactly from far fewer linear measurements than traditionally assumed necessary, provided that appropriate recovery algorithms are used and certain conditions on the measurement process are satisfied. This paradigm has inspired an extensive body of work on low-dimensional models for high-dimensional data, uniting ideas from convex optimization, information theory, and random matrix theory. In many applications, however, the objects of interest are not vectors but matrices with inherent low-rank structures, such as in collaborative filtering, quantum state tomography, and multi-task learning. The natural extension of CS to this setting, known as matrix compressed sensing (MCS), seeks to recover low-rank matrices from incomplete or undersampled linear measurements.

Matrix compressed sensing encompasses and generalizes two related problems: low-rank matrix completion, in which the measurements correspond to a subset of matrix entries, and standard compressed sensing, which can be seen as the special case of rank-one matrices. In the general MCS framework, we observe a set of linear measurements of an unknown matrix \(X_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}\) (or \(\mathbb{C}^{n \times m}\)), modeled as
\[
y_\mu = \langle A_\mu, X_0 \rangle + \xi_\mu, \quad \mu = 1, \dots, M,
\]
where each \(A_\mu\) is a known sensing matrix, \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\) denotes the Frobenius inner product, and \(\xi_\mu\) represents measurement noise. The goal is to reconstruct \(X_0\) from \(\{y_\mu\}\) when \(M\) is much smaller than \(nm\), exploiting the assumption that \(X_0\) has low rank \(r \ll \min(n,m)\). Recovery guarantees, algorithmic design, and the fundamental limits of such problems depend intricately on the interplay between the rank, the dimensions, the number of measurements, and the measurement ensemble.

Understanding the phase diagram of MCS—i.e., the regions in the space of problem parameters that separate possible from impossible recovery—has both theoretical and practical importance. In the noiseless setting, one may ask: for a given oversampling ratio \(\alpha = M/(nm)\) and relative rank \(\rho = r/\min(n,m)\), is exact recovery possible in principle? In noisy scenarios, one is interested in the asymptotic reconstruction error as a function of \(\alpha\), \(\rho\), and noise level. Such phase diagrams provide a concise summary of the intrinsic difficulty of the problem, delineating fundamental limits set by information theory, as well as the performance boundaries achievable by specific algorithms.

In vector compressed sensing, phase transitions have been characterized in detail for various recovery methods, most notably for \(\ell_1\)-minimization and approximate message passing (AMP) algorithms, using tools from statistical physics such as the replica method. These analyses reveal sharp boundaries in the measurement–sparsity plane, beyond which perfect recovery occurs with high probability. Similar ideas have been applied to low-rank matrix estimation problems, including matrix completion and robust principal component analysis. However, the general matrix compressed sensing problem, where measurements are arbitrary random linear projections, has received comparatively less attention from the perspective of precise phase diagram characterization.

From a statistical physics viewpoint, MCS can be formulated as an inference problem on a bilinear factorization of the unknown matrix: \(X_0 = UV^\top\), where \(U\) and \(V\) have dimensions \(n \times r\) and \(m \times r\), respectively. The measurements then become linear in the elements of \(U\) and \(V\), but the overall inference problem remains nonconvex. Bayesian formulations, which posit prior distributions on \(U\) and \(V\), allow for the derivation of asymptotically exact predictions for the achievable mean-squared error in the large-system limit, when the measurement operators are drawn from suitable random ensembles. Techniques such as the replica method provide a route to compute these performance metrics and to identify the associated phase transitions. Complementary to the theoretical analysis, algorithmic schemes—most prominently, variants of AMP adapted to bilinear models—offer practical recovery methods whose performance can approach the Bayes-optimal limits under certain conditions.

Characterizing the phase diagram of MCS thus serves multiple purposes. It enables the benchmarking of algorithms against fundamental limits, guiding the choice of methods for given regimes of undersampling and rank. It informs the design of measurement schemes by quantifying the trade-off between the number of measurements, the attainable accuracy, and the computational complexity. It also sheds light on the nature of the computational gap—if any—between what is information-theoretically possible and what is achievable in polynomial time. In some inference problems, such gaps manifest as “hard” phases, where recovery is possible in principle but known algorithms fail; determining whether such phases exist in MCS is an important open question.

In this work, we present a detailed analysis of the phase diagram of matrix compressed sensing in the context of random measurement ensembles. Using the replica method, we derive expressions for the asymptotic free energy and associated order parameters, which characterize the typical reconstruction performance in the large-system limit. We identify the boundaries between phases of perfect recovery, partial recovery, and complete failure, and compare these theoretical predictions with numerical simulations of AMP-based algorithms. Our results unify and extend previous studies on vector compressed sensing and matrix completion, providing a comprehensive view of the interplay between measurement density, matrix rank, and noise in determining the feasibility of low-rank matrix recovery.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the phase diagram of matrix compressed sensing, focusing on the interplay between measurement rate, matrix dimensions, and structural priors in determining the feasibility of accurate recovery. By employing tools from statistical physics—specifically the replica method—and validating our theoretical predictions with extensive numerical experiments, we have identified distinct regions in parameter space corresponding to successful recovery, partial recovery, and failure. The resulting phase diagram provides a comprehensive view of the fundamental limits of matrix compressed sensing under low-rank and other structured constraints.

Our analysis highlights the existence of sharp phase transitions separating these regimes, with the transition boundaries depending sensitively on both the rank fraction and the measurement noise level. In the noiseless case, the theoretical thresholds match closely with those obtained from empirical reconstructions using convex and non-convex algorithms, suggesting that the asymptotic predictions are relevant even for moderate problem sizes. In the presence of noise, we observe a continuous degradation in recovery performance, and the phase diagram elucidates the trade-off between measurement rate and achievable reconstruction accuracy.

An important outcome of this study is the clarification of the gap between information-theoretic limits and algorithmic performance. In some regions of the phase diagram, no known polynomial-time algorithm achieves the optimal recovery threshold, indicating the existence of computational barriers. Our results suggest that algorithmic advances—possibly leveraging problem-specific structure beyond low rank—are needed to bridge this gap.

The framework developed here can be extended in several directions. Future work could address more general matrix structures, such as joint sparsity or block low-rank patterns, and incorporate more realistic sensing models encountered in applications like imaging, recommendation systems, and quantum state tomography. Furthermore, the methodology could be adapted to study adaptive measurement schemes, where the sensing process is guided by intermediate reconstructions.

In summary, the phase diagram derived in this work serves as both a theoretical benchmark and a practical guide for designing and analyzing matrix compressed sensing systems. By delineating the boundaries of recoverability, it informs practitioners of the measurement resources required under various structural assumptions, and it motivates further research into algorithms capable of approaching the fundamental limits identified here.

title: Real Image Inversion via Segments
abstract: We propose a novel framework for real image inversion that leverages semantic segmentation to guide the reconstruction process. Unlike existing approaches that treat an image holistically, our method decomposes the target into semantically coherent segments and inverts each region individually within a shared latent space. This segmentation-driven strategy preserves fine-grained details and local structures while maintaining global consistency. We integrate boundary-aware blending to seamlessly combine inverted segments, reducing artifacts at region interfaces. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior fidelity and editability compared to state-of-the-art inversion methods. The segment-wise formulation also facilitates localized edits, enabling precise control over specific regions without degrading the rest of the image.
introduction:
The task of inverting real images into the latent space of generative models has become an essential research direction in computer vision and image synthesis. With the advent of high-quality generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models, it is now possible to synthesize photo-realistic images from compact latent codes. However, the inverse problem—mapping an arbitrary real image back into the latent space—remains challenging due to the inherent mismatch between the distribution of real images and that of synthetic samples generated by trained models. Accurate inversion is crucial for a wide range of downstream applications, including image editing, semantic manipulation, restoration, and hybrid generation, where precise control over image attributes is desired.

Conventional approaches to real image inversion often treat the image as a whole and attempt to optimize or predict a single latent code that reconstructs the entire scene. While such methods can capture global structures, they frequently struggle to preserve fine-grained details and local textures, especially when the generative model’s latent space has limited capacity to represent diverse real-world variations. This incompatibility can lead to compromises in either perceptual fidelity or latent consistency, ultimately constraining the quality and flexibility of edits.

Recent advances have explored more structured representations, acknowledging that natural images are inherently composed of semantically meaningful regions. Segmenting an image into distinct parts—such as foreground objects, background, or finer semantic components—enables a more localized inversion process. By assigning separate latent codes to different segments, one can better align the generative model’s capabilities with the complex variations present in real images. This decomposition not only improves reconstruction fidelity but also enhances controllability, as edits can be applied to specific segments without unintended changes to the rest of the image.

Segmentation-based inversion approaches leverage either pre-computed semantic masks from off-the-shelf segmentation networks or jointly optimize segmentation and inversion in an end-to-end fashion. The former benefits from mature segmentation techniques, while the latter offers potential adaptability to the target generative model. Both strategies aim to bridge the gap between the rigid structure of global latent codes and the flexibility required for fine detail preservation. Furthermore, by associating each segment with its own latent representation, these methods can exploit the generative model’s latent space more effectively, mitigating reconstruction artifacts and enabling more nuanced edits.

In this work, we propose a novel framework for real image inversion via segments that integrates semantic decomposition with latent optimization. Our approach segments the input image into semantically consistent regions and performs localized inversion for each region, aligning them within a shared generative space. This segment-wise inversion not only yields high-fidelity reconstructions but also facilitates targeted manipulations, as each segment’s latent code can be edited independently. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior reconstruction accuracy and editing flexibility compared to global inversion baselines, highlighting the advantages of segment-based latent representations for real image inversion.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a novel approach for real image inversion using segment-based decomposition, enabling more accurate and semantically consistent reconstructions. By leveraging localized segment representations, our method preserves fine-grained details while maintaining global structural coherence. Experimental results demonstrate improved fidelity and editability over existing techniques. This framework opens promising directions for controllable image manipulation, domain adaptation, and enhanced generative modeling, offering a robust foundation for future research in image-based content creation and understanding.

title: Latest Cosmological Constraints on Cardassian expansion models including the updated Gamma-ray bursts
abstract: We present updated constraints on Cardassian expansion models by incorporating the latest cosmological observations, including recently calibrated gamma-ray burst (GRB) data. In addition to GRBs extending the Hubble diagram to high redshift, we employ Type Ia supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and baryon acoustic oscillation measurements to test the viability of both original and modified polytropic Cardassian scenarios. Using a joint likelihood analysis, we obtain tighter bounds on the key model parameters, significantly reducing degeneracies previously reported. The inclusion of the updated GRB sample improves constraints at redshifts beyond those probed by supernovae, allowing a more precise assessment of departures from the standard ΛCDM expansion. Our results show that while current data remain consistent with ΛCDM within 1σ, small deviations characteristic of Cardassian cosmology cannot yet be ruled out, highlighting the importance of high-redshift probes in testing non-standard cosmological models.
introduction:
The accelerated expansion of the Universe, first revealed by Type Ia supernovae observations, remains one of the most compelling challenges in modern cosmology. While the standard ΛCDM model attributes this phenomenon to a cosmological constant or dark energy component, alternative scenarios have been proposed that modify the Friedmann equation without invoking exotic energy sources. Among these, the Cardassian expansion models introduce an additional nonlinear term in the energy density, allowing for late-time acceleration driven solely by matter. This framework offers a phenomenological approach to cosmic acceleration that can be tested against a variety of cosmological observations.  

Recent years have witnessed significant improvements in observational data, extending well beyond the redshift reach of Type Ia supernovae. In particular, gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) have emerged as valuable distance indicators at high redshift, complementing supernova constraints and enabling tighter bounds on cosmological parameters. The calibration of GRB luminosity relations, aided by improved datasets and statistical techniques, has enhanced their reliability as cosmological probes.  

In this work, we revisit the latest cosmological constraints on Cardassian expansion models by incorporating updated GRB data alongside other complementary datasets. By combining low- and high-redshift observations, we aim to place stringent limits on model parameters and assess the viability of the Cardassian framework in light of contemporary astrophysical measurements.
conclusion: In this work, we have revisited the cosmological constraints on Cardassian expansion models by incorporating the most recent gamma-ray burst (GRB) data, alongside other up-to-date cosmological probes. The inclusion of the updated GRB sample, calibrated in a cosmology-independent manner, has allowed us to extend the redshift reach of our analysis well beyond that provided by Type Ia supernovae alone, thereby offering a more stringent test of the high-redshift behavior of the models. Our joint analysis, combining GRBs with cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations, and Type Ia supernova data, yields tighter bounds on the model parameters compared to earlier studies. The results indicate that the modified Friedmann equation in the Cardassian framework remains a viable alternative to dark energy in explaining the late-time acceleration of the Universe, with the best-fit parameters consistent with a matter-dominated early epoch transitioning smoothly to accelerated expansion at low redshift. However, the allowed parameter space has been notably reduced, with some regions previously permitted now disfavored at high confidence levels. We also find no significant tension between the constraints derived from GRBs and those from other probes, supporting the robustness of GRBs as complementary cosmological tools. Future high-precision GRB measurements, especially at z > 6, will further enhance the discriminating power between Cardassian and ΛCDM scenarios. Overall, our findings underscore the importance of incorporating diverse and extended-redshift datasets in testing modified cosmological models and suggest that the Cardassian paradigm remains consistent with current observations, though continued scrutiny with forthcoming data will be essential.

title: Search for the Lepton-Flavor Violating Decays Upsilon(3S) -> e tau and Upsilon(3S) -> mu tau
abstract: We report on a search for the lepton-flavor violating decays Υ(3S) → eτ and Υ(3S) → μτ using a data sample of approximately 122 million Υ(3S) decays collected with the BABAR detector at the PEP-II asymmetric-energy e⁺e⁻ collider. The τ leptons are reconstructed in both leptonic and hadronic final states. No significant excess over the expected background is observed. We set 90% confidence level upper limits on the branching fractions: 𝔅(Υ(3S) → eτ) < 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ and 𝔅(Υ(3S) → μτ) < 4.1 × 10⁻⁶. These results improve upon previous bounds and constrain models of new physics.
introduction:
The study of rare and forbidden processes provides a sensitive probe for physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). In the SM, lepton flavor is conserved in charged lepton interactions, and charged lepton flavor violating (CLFV) decays are forbidden at tree level. While neutrino oscillations imply that lepton flavor is not an exact symmetry, the rates for CLFV processes induced by neutrino mixing are suppressed by factors of order \((\Delta m_\nu^2 / M_W^2)^2\), yielding branching fractions far below observable levels (\(\mathcal{O}(10^{-54})\)). Therefore, any experimental observation of a CLFV decay would constitute unambiguous evidence for new physics.

Many extensions of the SM predict enhanced CLFV rates within reach of current experiments. Supersymmetric models, leptoquark scenarios, models with compositeness, or those incorporating heavy neutrinos or extended Higgs sectors can produce CLFV branching fractions several orders of magnitude larger than the SM prediction, in some cases up to \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-6})\). While most experimental searches have focused on CLFV in muon and tau decays, heavy quarkonium states such as the bottomonium resonances \(\Upsilon(nS)\) provide an alternative and complementary laboratory. In these systems, CLFV can occur via virtual exchange of new heavy particles coupling to both quark and lepton currents, leading to decays such as \(\Upsilon(nS) \to \ell^\pm \tau^\mp\) (\(\ell = e, \mu\)).

The \(\Upsilon(3S)\) resonance is particularly well-suited for such searches. It is a narrow \(b\bar{b}\) bound state with a precisely known mass and width, produced copiously in \(e^+e^-\) collisions at \(B\)-factory experiments. The clean event environment, combined with well-understood detector performance and the ability to fully reconstruct many \(\tau\) decay modes, enables sensitive probes of rare decay modes with suppressed backgrounds. Furthermore, the relatively small total decay width of the \(\Upsilon(3S)\) allows for stringent limits on rare processes in terms of branching fractions.

Previous searches for CLFV in \(\Upsilon\) decays have set upper limits on branching fractions at the level of \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-5}\), depending on the final state and dataset. However, the large samples of \(\Upsilon(3S)\) decays collected by modern \(B\)-factory detectors such as BABAR and Belle allow for significant improvements in sensitivity. In this work, we present a search for the CLFV decays \(\Upsilon(3S) \to e^\pm \tau^\mp\) and \(\Upsilon(3S) \to \mu^\pm \tau^\mp\), using a data sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity of \(XX\) fb\(^{-1}\) recorded at the \(\Upsilon(3S)\) resonance with the BABAR detector at the PEP-II asymmetric-energy \(e^+e^-\) collider.

The analysis reconstructs \(\tau\) leptons in both leptonic and hadronic decay modes and exploits kinematic constraints from the well-defined initial state to suppress backgrounds from generic \(\Upsilon(3S)\) decays and continuum \(e^+e^- \to q\bar{q}\) and \(\tau^+\tau^-\) processes. The results are interpreted in terms of upper limits on the branching fractions for these CLFV decays, providing new constraints on models of new physics that predict enhanced rates for such processes.
conclusion:
We have conducted a search for the charged lepton–flavor–violating decays \(\Upsilon(3S) \rightarrow e^\pm \tau^\mp\) and \(\Upsilon(3S) \rightarrow \mu^\pm \tau^\mp\) using a high-statistics data sample collected with the [detector name] at the [facility name]. The analysis employed rigorous event selection criteria to suppress backgrounds from Standard Model processes, including \(\tau^+\tau^-\) production and other \(\Upsilon(3S)\) decays, as well as continuum \(q\bar{q}\) events. Signal extraction was performed via unbinned maximum likelihood fits to kinematic observables sensitive to the two-body decay signature, with systematic uncertainties evaluated from control samples and alternative modeling assumptions.

No statistically significant excess of events above the expected background was observed in either the \(e\tau\) or \(\mu\tau\) channels. In the absence of a signal, we set upper limits on the branching fractions at the 90% confidence level of  
\[
\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon(3S) \rightarrow e^\pm \tau^\mp) < X.X \times 10^{-6},
\]
\[
\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon(3S) \rightarrow \mu^\pm \tau^\mp) < Y.Y \times 10^{-6},
\]
where the quoted limits include both statistical and systematic uncertainties. These results improve upon previous constraints by factors of [improvement factor], representing the most stringent limits to date on such processes in the \(\Upsilon(3S)\) system.

The absence of a signal is consistent with Standard Model expectations, in which charged lepton–flavor violation is heavily suppressed due to the tiny neutrino masses. The new limits provide valuable constraints on a variety of new physics scenarios, including models with extended Higgs sectors, supersymmetry with slepton mixing, and leptoquark exchanges, which can enhance such decays to levels within experimental reach.

Future searches with larger data samples at current or next-generation \(e^+e^-\) colliders will further probe these channels, extending sensitivity by at least an order of magnitude. Such efforts remain an important component of the broader program to search for physics beyond the Standard Model through rare heavy quarkonium decays.

title: Modeling Personalized Item Frequency Information for Next-basket Recommendation
abstract: Next-basket recommendation aims to predict the items that a user is likely to purchase in their next shopping session, enabling personalized and timely suggestions in e-commerce platforms. While recent approaches have leveraged sequential modeling techniques to capture temporal purchase patterns, they often overlook personalized item frequency information, which reflects a user’s habitual purchasing tendencies. In this work, we propose a novel framework that explicitly models personalized item frequency as a complementary signal to sequential behavior for next-basket recommendation. Our method first constructs individualized frequency profiles from historical transactions, capturing long-term user preferences and periodic needs. We then integrate these profiles into a sequential neural recommendation architecture through a dual-channel design: one channel models short-term sequential dependencies using recurrent and attention-based mechanisms, while the other encodes frequency-aware preference representations. A fusion layer adaptively balances the contributions from these channels, allowing the model to account for both transient interests and stable, recurring demands. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that incorporating personalized item frequency significantly improves recommendation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art sequential methods. Our analysis further reveals that frequency modeling particularly benefits the prediction of recurrent and low-salience items, which are often missed by purely sequence-driven approaches. The proposed framework offers a principled way to unify short-term dynamics and long-term frequency patterns, and can be readily extended to other temporal recommendation scenarios. This work underscores the importance of habitual behavior modeling in enhancing the relevance and reliability of next-basket recommendations.
introduction:
Recommender systems have become an indispensable component of numerous online platforms, assisting users in navigating overwhelming volumes of content by providing personalized suggestions. Among the various recommendation scenarios, next-basket recommendation (NBR) focuses on predicting the set of items a user will purchase or interact with in their next transaction, given their historical purchase sequences. This task has gained increasing attention in both academic research and industrial applications, particularly in e-commerce and grocery retail, where understanding and anticipating user needs over time can significantly improve user satisfaction and business revenue.

Traditional recommendation methods, such as collaborative filtering and matrix factorization, have been extended to sequential settings through models that capture temporal dynamics and sequential dependencies in user behavior. More recently, deep learning approaches, including recurrent neural networks (RNNs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and self-attention-based architectures, have demonstrated strong performance in NBR by modeling complex patterns in the sequence of user interactions. These models are adept at capturing item co-occurrence patterns and temporal order, enabling the system to infer which items are likely to appear together in a future basket.

However, existing NBR models often underexplore a critical aspect of user behavior: personalized item frequency information. In repeated purchase scenarios, the frequency with which a user interacts with or purchases specific items over time can be a strong signal of preference strength, habitual consumption, or replenishment needs. For example, a user who purchases milk every week is more likely to include milk in their next basket compared to a user who bought milk only once in the past. Similarly, certain items may exhibit periodic or irregular purchase intervals unique to each user. Ignoring such personalized frequency patterns can lead to suboptimal recommendations, particularly in domains where consumable or replenishable goods are prevalent.

While some approaches attempt to incorporate global popularity or item frequency statistics across all users, these measures fail to capture individual-level variations. Global frequency may highlight universally popular products but cannot distinguish between items a specific user consistently buys and those they have tried only occasionally. Personalized frequency modeling requires capturing not only whether a user has interacted with an item, but also how often and at what intervals, thereby enriching the representation of user preferences with habitual and long-term behavioral cues.

Incorporating personalized item frequency information into NBR presents several challenges. First, frequency patterns must be integrated with sequential dependency modeling in a way that preserves temporal context while also emphasizing habitual tendencies. Second, frequency signals can vary significantly across items and users, with some items displaying stable, repeated patterns and others showing sporadic occurrences; thus, the modeling approach needs to adaptively weigh the importance of frequency signals. Third, overemphasis on frequency can lead to overly conservative recommendations dominated by frequently purchased staples, potentially reducing diversity and serendipity. Balancing the exploitation of frequency information with the exploration of novel or complementary items is therefore essential.

Recent studies in sequential recommendation have begun to explore auxiliary information such as time intervals, recency, and contextual factors to enhance prediction accuracy. Nonetheless, explicit modeling of personalized item frequency as a first-class signal remains underdeveloped. Integrating this dimension into NBR has the potential to improve performance by aligning recommendations more closely with users’ long-term habits and replenishment needs, thereby increasing both accuracy and user satisfaction.

Motivated by these observations, this work proposes a novel framework for modeling personalized item frequency information in the next-basket recommendation task. Our approach explicitly encodes user-specific purchase frequencies and integrates them with sequential modeling techniques to capture both habitual and contextual aspects of user behavior. We hypothesize that such a design can more accurately predict future baskets by leveraging the complementary strengths of frequency-based preference signals and sequential dependency learning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting the value of personalized item frequency modeling in advancing next-basket recommendation research.
conclusion:
In this work, we addressed the problem of enhancing next-basket recommendation by explicitly modeling personalized item frequency information. While conventional sequential and basket-based recommendation approaches primarily focus on temporal dynamics and co-occurrence patterns, they often overlook the nuanced role of user-specific frequency preferences in shaping future purchase behavior. To bridge this gap, we proposed a novel framework that integrates personalized frequency representations with sequential modeling, enabling the recommendation system to capture both short-term intent and long-term habitual tendencies.

Our approach introduces a dedicated frequency modeling component that encodes the historical occurrence patterns of items for each user, and incorporates this signal into the recommendation process alongside temporal and contextual features. By doing so, the model is able to distinguish between items that are repeatedly purchased due to persistent personal needs and those that appear sporadically due to transient interests. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrated that this integration leads to consistent improvements over strong baselines, validating the importance of item frequency information as a complementary signal for next-basket prediction.

The experimental results further revealed that the benefit of personalized frequency modeling is particularly pronounced in domains where repeated consumption is intrinsic, such as grocery shopping or subscription-based services. In these contexts, frequency-aware recommendations not only enhance predictive accuracy but also improve the perceived relevance of suggestions, as they align more closely with users’ established consumption rhythms. Moreover, our ablation studies confirmed that both the design of the frequency representation and its fusion with sequential dynamics contribute critically to the observed performance gains.

Beyond accuracy, the proposed method offers interpretability advantages. By explicitly modeling item frequency, the system can provide intuitive explanations for its recommendations, such as highlighting habitual purchases or identifying deviations from established patterns. This transparency can foster greater trust and engagement from users, and may also assist in downstream applications like inventory management or personalized promotions.

Looking ahead, there are several promising directions for extending this work. One avenue is to explore adaptive mechanisms that can dynamically adjust the influence of frequency information based on evolving user behavior or contextual changes. Another is to investigate richer forms of frequency modeling that account for periodicity, seasonality, or cross-item dependencies in repeated purchases. Additionally, integrating external knowledge sources, such as product category hierarchies or demographic profiles, could further enhance the personalization capabilities of the framework.

In summary, our study underscores the value of incorporating personalized item frequency into next-basket recommendation models. By capturing this often-overlooked aspect of user behavior, we can deliver recommendations that are not only more accurate but also more aligned with the enduring patterns and preferences that define individual consumers.

title: Media Usage in Post-Secondary Education and Implications for Teaching and Learning
abstract: This paper examines patterns of media usage among post-secondary students and explores the implications for teaching and learning in higher education. Drawing on survey data and qualitative interviews, the study investigates how students engage with digital and traditional media for academic and personal purposes, and how these practices influence learning behaviours and expectations. Findings indicate a strong preference for online resources, mobile technologies, and multimedia content, alongside continued use of print materials for specific tasks. The integration of media into academic work is shaped by factors such as accessibility, perceived reliability, and alignment with course requirements. Implications for teaching include the need to design learning environments that leverage diverse media formats, promote critical media literacy, and support flexible, student-centred pedagogies. The study contributes to understanding the evolving media ecology in higher education and its potential to enhance engagement, collaboration, and academic success.
introduction:
The rapid evolution of digital technologies over the past two decades has profoundly transformed the landscape of post-secondary education. Contemporary students engage with a diverse range of media—ranging from traditional print resources to interactive learning platforms, social media networks, and immersive digital environments—both within and beyond formal learning contexts. This shift in media usage patterns has significant implications for teaching and learning, as it influences not only how students access and process information, but also how they communicate, collaborate, and construct knowledge. Understanding the nature and extent of media usage in post-secondary settings is thus essential for educators, administrators, and policymakers seeking to design effective pedagogical strategies that align with the realities of twenty-first-century learning.

Media usage in higher education is shaped by a convergence of technological affordances, institutional practices, and student preferences. The proliferation of mobile devices, high-speed internet, and cloud-based applications has enabled continuous connectivity, making learning resources accessible at any time and from any location. At the same time, the integration of learning management systems (LMS), video conferencing tools, and open educational resources (OER) into curricula reflects an institutional recognition of the pedagogical potential of digital media. However, the ubiquity of digital media also raises questions about information overload, the quality and credibility of online content, and the potential for distraction in technology-rich environments. These tensions underscore the need for nuanced analysis of how media are used and the pedagogical frameworks that can harness their benefits while mitigating potential drawbacks.

Research on media usage in post-secondary education has documented a spectrum of practices, from the consumption of digitized lectures and e-books to participation in collaborative online projects and the creation of multimodal assignments. Studies suggest that students increasingly value flexibility, interactivity, and personalization in their learning experiences, often blending formal academic resources with informal, user-generated content. Social media platforms, for instance, are used not only for social interaction but also for peer support, information sharing, and professional networking. Yet, patterns of use vary widely across disciplines, demographic groups, and individual learners, reflecting differences in digital literacy, access to technology, and learning preferences. This variability presents both opportunities and challenges for educators aiming to create inclusive, equitable, and engaging learning environments.

The implications of these trends are far-reaching. Effective integration of media into teaching requires more than the mere adoption of new tools; it demands pedagogical innovation, critical engagement with media content, and the cultivation of students’ abilities to evaluate, synthesize, and apply information from diverse sources. Moreover, as higher education institutions navigate an increasingly competitive and globalized educational market, the strategic use of media can play a central role in enhancing student engagement, supporting lifelong learning, and fostering the competencies needed for success in a digital society. This paper examines current patterns of media usage among post-secondary students, explores their pedagogical implications, and offers recommendations for leveraging media to enhance teaching and learning outcomes.
conclusion:
The findings discussed in this paper highlight the increasingly central role that diverse forms of media play in post-secondary education, both as tools for delivering content and as platforms for fostering engagement, collaboration, and independent learning. The pervasive integration of digital technologies into students’ academic and personal lives creates opportunities for more flexible, multimodal, and interactive learning experiences. At the same time, it presents challenges related to equity of access, information literacy, and the need for pedagogical approaches that move beyond simple content transmission toward active and critical engagement with media.

The patterns of media usage observed among post-secondary learners underscore the necessity for instructors to adapt teaching strategies that align with students’ technological proficiencies and preferences while also guiding them to use media critically and responsibly. Incorporating a thoughtful mix of traditional and emerging media can help address varied learning styles and promote deeper understanding. However, maximizing the educational potential of these tools requires intentional instructional design, consideration of discipline-specific needs, and an awareness of the cognitive and social implications of constant connectivity.

Moreover, the rapid evolution of media platforms demands ongoing professional development for educators, ensuring they remain informed about new technologies and their pedagogical affordances. This process must be coupled with institutional support that fosters experimentation, collaboration, and the sharing of best practices. As media use becomes more embedded in higher education, ethical considerations—including data privacy, digital well-being, and the cultivation of respectful online discourse—should be integral to teaching and learning strategies.

In sum, media usage in post-secondary education is not merely a reflection of broader societal trends but a transformative factor in shaping the learning environment. The challenge for educators and institutions lies in harnessing the affordances of media to enhance student learning outcomes while mitigating potential drawbacks. This requires a balanced approach that blends innovation with critical reflection, ensuring that technology serves pedagogical goals rather than dictating them. As higher education continues to evolve in response to technological change, sustained research, dialogue, and adaptive practice will be essential to fully realize the potential of media-rich learning environments and to prepare students for thoughtful participation in a complex, digitally mediated world.

title: Algorithms for the minimum sum coloring problem: a review
abstract: The minimum sum coloring problem (MSCP) is a combinatorial optimization variant of the classical graph coloring problem, where integers are assigned to vertices such that adjacent vertices receive different integers and the sum of the assigned colors is minimized. This problem arises in diverse applications, including scheduling, resource allocation, and frequency assignment. Due to its NP-hard nature, the MSCP has been tackled through a variety of exact, heuristic, and metaheuristic algorithms. This review surveys recent advances in algorithmic approaches to the MSCP, emphasizing their design principles, computational performance, and applicability to large-scale instances. We categorize methods into exact algorithms, constructive heuristics, local search techniques, and hybrid metaheuristics, highlighting key innovations and comparative results. Challenges such as scalability, solution quality, and benchmark standardization are discussed, along with potential research directions aimed at improving efficiency and bridging the gap between theoretical developments and practical applications.
introduction:
The minimum sum coloring problem (MSCP) is a well-studied combinatorial optimization problem that arises in graph theory and has numerous practical applications. Given an undirected graph \( G = (V, E) \), the problem consists of assigning a positive integer color to each vertex such that adjacent vertices receive distinct colors, and the sum of the assigned colors is minimized. Formally, if \( c: V \rightarrow \mathbb{N}^+ \) is a proper coloring, the objective is to minimize \( \sum_{v \in V} c(v) \). The MSCP can be viewed as a variant of the classical graph coloring problem (GCP), where the goal is to minimize the number of colors used, known as the chromatic number. In contrast, the MSCP focuses on minimizing the total sum of color indices, which leads to different optimization strategies and solution characteristics.
