The MSCP is motivated by a variety of real-world applications in scheduling, resource allocation, frequency assignment, and VLSI design. For example, in scheduling scenarios, tasks may need to be assigned to time slots (colors) so that conflicting tasks do not occur simultaneously, while earlier or lower-numbered slots are preferable due to lower associated costs. Similarly, in communication networks, assigning frequencies to transmitters with minimal total interference cost can be modeled as a minimum sum coloring problem. The weighted nature of the objective function makes the MSCP more sensitive to the choice of smaller color indices, thereby encouraging solutions that not only avoid conflicts but also prioritize low-cost assignments.

From a computational perspective, the MSCP is NP-hard, even for restricted graph classes such as bipartite graphs. This hardness result follows from the NP-hardness of the classical GCP, of which MSCP is a generalization. Consequently, exact algorithms are limited to small- and medium-sized instances, while heuristic and metaheuristic approaches dominate the treatment of large-scale problems. The theoretical challenges lie not only in the combinatorial explosion of possible colorings but also in the fact that two colorings with the same number of colors can have significantly different sums, which complicates the search for optimal solutions.

Research on the MSCP has developed along multiple complementary directions. Early work focused on exact algorithms, including branch-and-bound and integer linear programming formulations, aimed at solving small instances to optimality and investigating structural properties of optimal solutions. Later, heuristic methods such as greedy algorithms, constructive heuristics, and local search procedures were proposed to obtain good-quality solutions with reduced computational effort. The emergence of metaheuristics — including simulated annealing, tabu search, genetic algorithms, ant colony optimization, and hybrid approaches — has further expanded the range of solvable instance sizes and improved solution quality. More recently, population-based and hybrid metaheuristics have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance for large and complex graphs.

In addition to algorithmic developments, several studies have addressed theoretical aspects of the MSCP, such as bounds on the chromatic sum, relationships between the MSCP and other coloring variants, and complexity results for special graph classes. Benchmark datasets and standardized evaluation protocols have been proposed to facilitate fair comparisons of algorithms, leading to a more structured body of empirical results. The availability of such benchmarks has helped identify strengths and weaknesses of different approaches and has guided the design of more efficient solution strategies.

Despite the considerable progress over the past decades, the MSCP remains an active research area. The increasing complexity of real-world networks and the demand for cost-sensitive optimization continue to drive interest in more effective and scalable algorithms. Moreover, hybridization strategies that combine exact methods with powerful heuristics, as well as the integration of problem-specific knowledge into general-purpose metaheuristics, represent promising avenues for further advances. The purpose of this review is to provide a comprehensive overview of the algorithms developed for the MSCP, analyzing their methodological foundations, performance characteristics, and applicability. By synthesizing the existing literature, this survey aims to highlight current trends, identify open challenges, and suggest directions for future research in this important optimization problem.
conclusion:
The minimum sum coloring problem (MSCP) has attracted increasing attention in recent decades due to its theoretical complexity and practical applications in areas such as scheduling, resource allocation, and frequency assignment. This review has examined the main classes of algorithms proposed to solve the MSCP, including exact methods, constructive heuristics, local search approaches, metaheuristics, and hybrid strategies. Each class exhibits distinct strengths and limitations, and their performance is often influenced by the structural properties of the input graphs as well as by the trade-off between solution quality and computational effort.

Exact algorithms, primarily based on branch-and-bound and integer linear programming formulations, are capable of producing optimal solutions for small and moderately sized instances, but their scalability remains limited by the NP-hard nature of the problem. Heuristic and constructive methods offer rapid generation of feasible colorings, often serving as good starting points for more sophisticated improvement procedures. Local search and metaheuristics, such as tabu search, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, and ant colony optimization, have demonstrated the ability to find high-quality solutions within reasonable computation times, particularly when carefully tailored to exploit graph-specific features. Recent advances in hybrid approaches, which combine complementary strategies—such as integrating global search with local refinement or coupling exact methods with heuristics—highlight the potential of exploiting algorithmic synergies to improve both robustness and efficiency.

Despite significant progress, several open challenges remain. Benchmarking is complicated by the diversity of test instances and evaluation metrics, making direct comparison of results difficult. Furthermore, the design of algorithms that can maintain high performance across a wide spectrum of graph types is still an open research issue. Advances in parallel computing, machine learning, and adaptive parameter control offer promising avenues for overcoming current limitations, particularly in scaling solution approaches to large, complex networks. Moreover, deeper theoretical insights into the structure of optimal and near-optimal colorings could inform the development of more effective algorithmic components.

In summary, the body of research on the MSCP has yielded a rich set of algorithmic tools and strategies, yet there is considerable scope for innovation. Future work that integrates theoretical analysis, algorithmic design, and empirical evaluation—while fostering reproducibility and standardized benchmarks—will be crucial to advancing our understanding and capability to solve the minimum sum coloring problem efficiently in both academic and practical contexts.

title: An improved effective field theory formulation of spin-1 Ising systems with arbitrary coordination number z
abstract: We present an improved effective field theory (EFT) formulation for spin-1 Ising systems with arbitrary coordination number \( z \). The approach incorporates higher-order spin correlations without uncontrolled decoupling approximations, enabling accurate treatment of multi-spin interactions. By systematically extending the cluster expansion and self-consistency conditions, the method yields precise estimates of thermodynamic quantities and critical parameters over a wide range of \( z \). Comparisons with exact and numerical results demonstrate significant improvements over conventional EFT. The formulation provides a versatile framework applicable to diverse lattice geometries and interaction schemes in spin-1 Ising models.
introduction:
The Ising model and its various extensions have long served as fundamental tools in the theoretical study of cooperative phenomena in statistical physics. Since its original formulation for spin-\(\frac{1}{2}\) systems, the Ising model has been generalized to incorporate higher spin values, competing interactions, quenched disorder, and external fields in order to capture the rich diversity of phase transitions observed in real materials. Among these generalizations, the spin-1 Ising model, often referred to as the Blume–Capel (BC) model when a single-ion anisotropy term is included, occupies a central position. This model has been widely applied to study magnetic systems with uniaxial anisotropy, multi-component fluids, \(^3\)He–\(^4\)He mixtures, and a variety of other physical systems where the spin variable can take on three discrete values \((S_i = -1, 0, +1)\).

Analytical approaches to the spin-1 Ising model face the challenge of accurately incorporating spin correlations while retaining computational tractability. Exact solutions are available only for one-dimensional systems or certain special cases, and numerical simulations such as Monte Carlo methods, while powerful, can be computationally demanding for large systems or for extensive parameter scans. Consequently, approximate analytical methods—most notably mean-field theory (MFT) and effective field theory (EFT)—have played a significant role in advancing our understanding.

The conventional MFT, despite its conceptual simplicity, neglects spin–spin correlations altogether, often leading to overestimation of critical temperatures and inaccurate predictions of critical exponents. EFT methods improve upon MFT by partially incorporating nearest-neighbor spin correlations through the use of differential operator techniques or exact spin identities. In the context of spin-1 systems, EFT has been successfully applied to calculate phase boundaries, tricritical points, and thermodynamic quantities, yielding results in better agreement with numerical simulations than MFT. However, standard EFT formulations typically rely on decoupling approximations that truncate higher-order spin correlation functions, which can limit accuracy, especially for low-dimensional systems or in the presence of strong fluctuations.

A further limitation of many existing EFT treatments for spin-1 systems is their focus on specific lattice types with fixed, small coordination numbers \(z\). While such approaches provide valuable insights, they are less adaptable to systems with arbitrary local geometry or to theoretical studies where \(z\) is treated as a continuous parameter interpolating between low- and high-dimensional limits. An EFT formulation capable of handling arbitrary coordination numbers without significant loss of accuracy is therefore of considerable interest. Such a formulation would not only unify the treatment of different lattice structures but also facilitate systematic studies of the dependence of thermodynamic properties on coordination number.

Recent developments in EFT for spin-\(\frac{1}{2}\) systems have demonstrated that improved treatments of spin correlations—by retaining higher-order terms in the correlation hierarchy or by employing more accurate closure schemes—can significantly enhance predictive capability. Extending these improvements to spin-1 systems, however, is nontrivial due to the increased number of spin states and the more complex structure of the spin identities. In particular, the presence of the nonmagnetic \(S_i = 0\) state introduces additional correlation functions involving quadratic spin operators, which must be treated on equal footing with the linear terms to preserve consistency.

In this work, we present an improved effective field theory formulation for spin-1 Ising systems with arbitrary coordination number \(z\). Our approach builds upon the exact spin identities for spin-1 variables and systematically incorporates multi-spin correlations without resorting to oversimplified decoupling schemes. By introducing a compact operator formalism, we derive a closed set of equations for the relevant correlation functions that remain valid for any \(z\). This formulation allows for the calculation of key thermodynamic quantities, such as magnetization, quadrupolar moment, and critical temperature, with improved accuracy across a wide range of coordination numbers.

The proposed method is benchmarked against exact solutions in one dimension, high-temperature series expansions, and Monte Carlo simulation results for two- and three-dimensional lattices. We demonstrate that our improved EFT yields results that are consistently closer to numerical data than those obtained from conventional EFT or MFT, particularly in predicting phase boundaries and tricritical points. Moreover, the ability to treat \(z\) as a continuous parameter enables a smooth interpolation between different lattice geometries, offering a unified framework for the analysis of spin-1 systems.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we outline the spin-1 Ising model and review the conventional EFT approach. Section 3 details our improved EFT formulation, including the derivation of the self-consistent equations for arbitrary \(z\). Section 4 presents numerical results and comparisons with other methods. Finally, Section 5 summarizes our findings and discusses potential extensions of the present work to more complex spin systems.
conclusion: In this work, an improved effective field theory formulation for spin-1 Ising systems with arbitrary coordination number \( z \) has been developed. By incorporating higher-order spin correlations exactly within a systematic framework, the approach overcomes limitations of conventional decoupling approximations. The method yields more accurate predictions for thermodynamic quantities and critical behavior across a wide range of \( z \) values. Its generality allows application to diverse lattice geometries and interaction schemes, providing a versatile tool for exploring complex spin-1 systems in statistical physics.

title: Zitterbewegung and a formulation for quantum mechanics
abstract: We present a formulation of quantum mechanics incorporating Zitterbewegung, treating it as a fundamental dynamical feature. The approach unifies particle motion and internal oscillations, offering new insights into relativistic quantum behavior and potential experimental signatures in condensed matter systems.
introduction: The phenomenon of *Zitterbewegung*, or “trembling motion,” was first predicted by Schrödinger in the context of the Dirac equation for relativistic electrons. It arises from the interference between positive- and negative-energy components of the wavefunction, producing a rapid oscillatory motion at the Compton scale. While initially regarded as a purely theoretical curiosity, Zitterbewegung has gained renewed interest due to its analogues in condensed matter systems, such as graphene and trapped ions, where effective Dirac-like dynamics emerge. Understanding this effect offers deeper insight into the structure of quantum theory and the role of relativistic corrections. In this work, we develop a formulation for quantum mechanics that naturally incorporates Zitterbewegung, elucidating its connection to fundamental operators and providing a framework to explore its manifestations across different physical regimes.
conclusion: This work has explored the role of Zitterbewegung in shaping a deeper formulation of quantum mechanics. By linking rapid oscillatory motion to underlying spinor structure, we have highlighted novel interpretative and mathematical consequences. The proposed framework offers new insights into particle dynamics and fundamental symmetries, suggesting avenues for further theoretical development and potential experimental probes of relativistic quantum behavior.

title: Stability of de Sitter Solutions in Non-local Cosmological Models
abstract: We investigate the stability of de Sitter solutions in a class of non-local cosmological models motivated by infrared modifications of gravity. Employing a dynamical systems approach, we derive conditions under which perturbations decay, ensuring background stability. Both scalar and tensor sectors are analyzed, revealing parameter regimes admitting stable accelerating solutions. Our results clarify the role of non-local terms in sustaining late-time cosmic acceleration without introducing ghost or tachyonic instabilities.
introduction:
The accelerating expansion of the Universe, first indicated by observations of distant type Ia supernovae and later confirmed by measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies and large-scale structure surveys, remains one of the most profound puzzles in modern cosmology. Within the standard cosmological model, this acceleration is explained by invoking a cosmological constant \(\Lambda\) or, more generally, a dark energy component with negative pressure. The simplest theoretical realization of such a scenario is the \(\Lambda\) Cold Dark Matter (\(\Lambda\)CDM) model, in which the late-time dynamics are dominated by a constant energy density, leading to an asymptotic de Sitter (dS) phase. While the \(\Lambda\)CDM framework provides an excellent fit to current observational data, it faces well-known theoretical challenges, including the cosmological constant problem and the coincidence problem. These issues motivate the investigation of alternative explanations for cosmic acceleration, including modifications of general relativity.

Among the broad spectrum of modified gravity theories, non-local models have attracted significant attention in recent years. Such models incorporate terms in the gravitational action that are non-local in spacetime, typically involving inverse differential operators acting on curvature invariants. Non-locality arises naturally in various contexts, such as quantum corrections to gravity, string field theory, and effective field theory descriptions of infrared modifications of gravity. By introducing scale-dependent modifications at large distances, non-local models offer a promising framework to address the late-time acceleration without resorting to an unnaturally small cosmological constant. In particular, non-local terms involving the inverse d’Alembertian of the Ricci scalar or more general curvature combinations have been proposed as viable candidates for dark energy.

An important feature of many non-local cosmological models is the existence of de Sitter solutions, which may correspond to the asymptotic state of the Universe at late times. The stability properties of these solutions are of central importance: a stable de Sitter attractor would provide a natural explanation for the observed acceleration, whereas instability could lead to qualitatively different cosmic evolution. Stability analysis also serves as a crucial theoretical consistency check, ensuring that small perturbations around the background solution do not grow without bound, which would jeopardize the model’s physical viability.

In the context of local modified gravity theories, the stability of de Sitter solutions has been extensively studied, often by analyzing the dynamics of homogeneous perturbations or the behavior of cosmological perturbation modes. Non-local models, however, present additional challenges. The presence of non-local operators results in equations of motion that are integro-differential in nature, complicating both their analytical and numerical treatment. A common strategy to address these difficulties is the localization of the non-local theory, whereby additional auxiliary fields are introduced to rewrite the action in a local form at the cost of enlarging the dynamical system. This reformulation allows the application of standard dynamical systems techniques to investigate the stability of cosmological solutions.

Recent works have demonstrated that certain non-local models can yield stable de Sitter solutions under specific parameter choices, while others exhibit instability or require fine-tuning. The detailed stability properties depend sensitively on the functional form of the non-local terms, the choice of auxiliary field variables, and the matter content of the Universe. Moreover, the stability analysis must take into account both background-level perturbations and, in some cases, the full spectrum of cosmological perturbations, as instabilities can manifest in scalar, vector, or tensor modes.

The purpose of the present work is to perform a systematic stability analysis of de Sitter solutions in a broad class of non-local cosmological models. Building on the localized formulation, we derive the autonomous dynamical system governing the evolution of the auxiliary fields and the Hubble parameter. We identify fixed points corresponding to de Sitter solutions and analyze their stability by examining the eigenvalues of the linearized system. Our study covers models with different non-local structures and parameter regimes, allowing us to map out the regions of stability in the model space. By clarifying the stability conditions, we aim to provide theoretical guidance for the construction of viable non-local modifications of gravity that can account for the observed cosmic acceleration while remaining free from pathological behaviors.

This work is organized as follows. In the next section, we review the class of non-local models under consideration and present their localized form. We then derive the background cosmological equations and identify de Sitter solutions. The subsequent section is devoted to the linear stability analysis of these solutions. Finally, we summarize our results and discuss their implications for the viability of non-local cosmological models.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the stability properties of de Sitter solutions arising in a class of non-local cosmological models motivated by infrared modifications of gravity. By employing a dynamical systems approach combined with linear perturbation analysis, we have identified the conditions under which such backgrounds remain stable against homogeneous and inhomogeneous perturbations. Our analysis demonstrates that the non-local terms can significantly alter the stability domain compared to their local counterparts, in some cases enlarging the parameter space that admits stable accelerating solutions. In particular, we have shown that the effective mass scale associated with the non-local operator plays a critical role in determining the fate of perturbations, with certain ranges leading to damped modes and others to growing instabilities.

We have also examined the influence of matter components and found that their presence can either stabilize or destabilize the de Sitter phase depending on the coupling structure. These results suggest that non-local modifications not only provide viable mechanisms for late-time cosmic acceleration but also offer rich phenomenology in the context of early- and late-universe dynamics. Future work should extend the current framework to include non-linear effects, explore possible observational imprints in the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure, and investigate the interplay between stability requirements and the theoretical consistency of the underlying non-local theory. Our findings underscore the importance of stability analyses in assessing the cosmological viability of non-local gravitational models.

title: Search for Baryonic Resonances Decaying to Xi pi in Deep-Inelastic Scattering at HERA
abstract: A search for narrow baryonic resonances decaying into \(\Xi \pi\) final states is performed using deep-inelastic \(ep\) scattering data collected with the H1 detector at HERA. The analysis is based on an integrated luminosity of approximately \( \mathcal{L} \) = XXX pb\(^{-1}\) in the kinematic region \(2 < Q^{2} < 100\ \text{GeV}^2\) and \(0.05 < y < 0.7\). Invariant mass spectra of \(\Xi^-\pi^-\), \(\Xi^-\pi^+\), \(\bar{\Xi}^+\pi^+\), and \(\bar{\Xi}^+\pi^-\) combinations are examined for signals of exotic pentaquark states. No statistically significant narrow structures are observed beyond the well-established \(\Xi(1530)^0\) resonance. Upper limits on production cross sections are determined at 95% confidence level, providing new constraints on models predicting such states in deep-inelastic scattering.
introduction:
The study of baryon spectroscopy provides critical insights into the non-perturbative regime of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), where quark confinement and the formation of hadronic bound states are governed by strong interactions. In addition to well-established three-quark baryons, QCD does not preclude the existence of more complex configurations, such as pentaquark states, which could manifest as narrow resonances in specific decay channels. The search for such exotic states has been motivated by both theoretical models, including the chiral soliton model, and experimental observations reported in various production environments.

In particular, the cascade (\(\Xi\)) baryon family, containing two strange quarks, offers an experimentally accessible sector in which to investigate possible exotic resonances. States decaying to \(\Xi \pi\) are of special interest, as they include known members of the \(\Xi(1530)\) isospin quartet, as well as potential exotic states with strangeness \(S = -2\) and atypical quark content. Reports from fixed-target experiments have suggested the existence of narrow \(\Xi\pi\) resonances beyond the conventional spectrum, though subsequent searches in different experimental settings have yielded mixed results.

Deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) at the electron–proton collider HERA provides a complementary environment for such searches. The high center-of-mass energy and wide kinematic range allow the study of baryon production in a regime where the struck quark hadronizes in the presence of a colored proton remnant. This environment may enhance the production of unusual baryonic configurations relative to other processes. Moreover, the HERA detectors offer precise tracking and particle identification capabilities, enabling reconstruction of multi-strange baryons and their decay products over a broad phase space.

In this work, we present a search for narrow baryonic resonances decaying to \(\Xi^- \pi^-\) and \(\Xi^- \pi^+\) (and their charge conjugates) in DIS events recorded with the H1 detector at HERA. The analysis focuses on invariant mass spectra of reconstructed \(\Xi \pi\) combinations, with the aim of confirming the presence of established states and probing for possible exotic signals. The results are compared to expectations from known baryon production and to previous experimental claims, providing new constraints on the existence of such resonances in the HERA kinematic domain.
conclusion: A search for narrow baryonic resonances decaying into \(\Xi^-\pi^-\) and \(\Xi^-\pi^+\) (and their antiparticle channels) has been performed using deep-inelastic \(ep\) scattering data collected with the H1 detector at HERA. The analysis covers an invariant mass range extending from threshold up to 2.4 GeV, with a mass resolution of a few MeV in the region of interest. Clear signals corresponding to the well-established \(\Xi^0(1530)\) and \(\overline{\Xi}^0(1530)\) states are observed in the neutral combinations, demonstrating the sensitivity of the reconstruction and selection procedure. No statistically significant narrow signal is found in the doubly charged or other neutral combinations beyond these known states. In particular, no evidence is seen for exotic pentaquark candidates previously reported by other experiments near a mass of 1860 MeV. Upper limits at the 95% confidence level are set on the production rates of such states relative to the \(\Xi^0(1530)\), under the assumption of similar kinematic distributions. These limits are sensitive to narrow states with natural widths much smaller than the detector resolution. The results presented here provide stringent constraints on the existence of narrow baryonic resonances in the \(\Xi\pi\) system in deep-inelastic scattering at HERA energies, and complement searches performed in other experimental environments and reaction channels.

title: High-dimensional Anomaly Detection with Radiative Return in $e^{+}e^{-}$ Collisions
abstract: We present a study of high-dimensional anomaly detection techniques applied to radiative return events in $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions. By exploiting initial-state radiation, the effective center-of-mass energy is reduced, enabling exploration of a broad range of invariant masses without varying the beam energy. We employ modern machine learning methods to identify deviations from Standard Model predictions in multi-observable feature spaces. The approach is validated using simulated datasets incorporating realistic detector effects, demonstrating sensitivity to a variety of new physics scenarios, including narrow resonances and non-resonant enhancements. Our results highlight the potential of high-dimensional, model-independent searches with radiative return as a powerful tool for precision studies and discovery at future $e^{+}e^{-}$ facilities.
introduction:
Anomaly detection plays a critical role in the search for physics beyond the Standard Model (SM) at high-energy particle colliders. While traditional searches are typically designed to target well-defined theoretical models, there is growing interest in model-independent approaches that can identify unexpected deviations from the SM in high-dimensional datasets. Such methods are especially relevant in the era of precision measurements at lepton colliders, where clean experimental environments and well-understood backgrounds enable sensitive probes of rare processes. In this context, $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions offer unique opportunities for both targeted and agnostic searches for new phenomena.

One promising avenue for uncovering new physics signatures in $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions is the use of radiative return events. In these processes, the initial-state radiation (ISR) of a high-energy photon reduces the effective center-of-mass energy of the collision, thereby allowing the exploration of a continuum of lower-energy interactions without requiring dedicated changes to the accelerator energy. Radiative return has been employed extensively in precision measurements of hadronic cross sections, the study of narrow resonances, and the determination of fundamental parameters such as the hadronic contributions to the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. However, its potential as a tool for high-dimensional, model-independent anomaly detection remains largely unexplored.

The kinematics of radiative return events are particularly favorable for anomaly detection. The emission of an energetic ISR photon modifies the event topology and constrains the invariant mass of the recoiling system. This enables the reconstruction of a wide range of effective collision energies from a single dataset collected at a fixed nominal energy. As a result, radiative return provides an intrinsic scan over possible resonance masses and production thresholds, opening the possibility to detect new particles or interactions not anticipated in the SM. Moreover, because ISR photons can be measured with high precision in modern detectors, the reconstruction of the effective hadronic system is relatively robust against experimental uncertainties.

High-dimensional anomaly detection methods, often based on machine learning techniques, are designed to identify statistically significant deviations in the joint distribution of multiple kinematic observables. In collider physics, these methods can operate directly on reconstructed final-state objects such as leptons, jets, and photons, exploiting correlations that may be difficult to capture with traditional cut-based analyses. The combination of such methods with radiative return has the potential to enhance the discovery reach for new states that may appear at lower effective energies, even if their production cross sections are small or their decay signatures are unconventional.

Despite these advantages, the application of anomaly detection to radiative return data presents several challenges. The high dimensionality of the observable space, while rich in discriminating power, introduces the risk of overfitting and complicates the estimation of statistical significance. Furthermore, the SM background processes in radiative return events can vary significantly as a function of the effective collision energy, requiring careful modeling and validation. Anomaly detection algorithms must therefore be designed to account for these dependencies, ensuring that any observed deviations are not artifacts of mismodeled backgrounds or detector effects. This necessitates the integration of detailed Monte Carlo simulations, advanced statistical techniques, and rigorous control regions.

The motivation for pursuing this line of investigation is twofold. First, historical precedent shows that unexpected discoveries often arise in kinematic regions or channels not originally targeted by theory-driven searches. Second, the upcoming generation of $e^{+}e^{-}$ colliders — such as the proposed FCC-ee, CEPC, and ILC — will collect unprecedentedly large datasets with exquisite detector performance, providing fertile ground for data-driven anomaly searches. Radiative return will naturally occur in these datasets, allowing the exploration of a broad range of invariant masses without additional beam time. By leveraging high-dimensional analysis techniques, we can maximize the information extracted from these events and enhance the sensitivity to new phenomena.

In this work, we develop and evaluate a framework for high-dimensional anomaly detection in radiative return events from $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions. We focus on final states with well-measured ISR photons and fully reconstructible recoil systems, enabling precise determination of the effective collision energy. We employ machine learning algorithms tailored to identify local deviations from the SM in the multidimensional space of observables, and we assess their performance using simulated datasets representative of future collider conditions. Our study aims to quantify the discovery potential of this approach, highlight its challenges, and outline strategies for robust application in forthcoming experiments. By combining the kinematic versatility of radiative return with the power of high-dimensional anomaly detection, we propose a novel pathway for uncovering new physics in the precision frontier of $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions.
conclusion: We have presented a high-dimensional anomaly detection framework leveraging radiative return events in $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions to enhance sensitivity to physics beyond the Standard Model. By exploiting the kinematic constraints of photon-tagged processes, our method reduces background complexity and enables robust modeling in multi-observable spaces. The combination of machine learning techniques with precise QED predictions allows for efficient identification of rare or unexpected signatures without explicit signal hypotheses. Our results demonstrate that radiative return provides a powerful probe for subtle deviations in collider data, offering a complementary pathway to conventional searches and motivating further applications to forthcoming $e^{+}e^{-}$ facilities.

title: A New Biometric Template Protection using Random Orthonormal Projection and Fuzzy Commitment
abstract: This paper proposes a novel biometric template protection scheme combining Random Orthonormal Projection (ROP) with the Fuzzy Commitment approach to enhance both security and recognition performance. The ROP method transforms original biometric feature vectors into a cancellable form using randomly generated orthonormal matrices, ensuring diversity and revocability. Subsequently, the transformed features are bound with error-correcting codes within the fuzzy commitment framework to safeguard against inversion and provide tolerance to intra-class variability. The proposed scheme effectively addresses key requirements of biometric template protection, including non-invertibility, revocability, and unlinkability, while maintaining high matching accuracy. Experimental evaluations on publicly available biometric datasets demonstrate that the method achieves competitive recognition rates with significantly improved resilience against various attacks, making it suitable for practical secure biometric authentication systems.
introduction:
Biometric recognition systems have gained significant attention in recent years due to their ability to provide reliable and convenient authentication based on physiological or behavioral traits such as fingerprints, iris patterns, or voice. Unlike traditional password-based systems, biometric traits cannot be easily lost or forgotten, making them a compelling choice for security-critical applications. However, the inherent permanence and uniqueness of biometric data also introduce serious privacy and security concerns. Once compromised, biometric templates cannot be reissued or replaced like passwords, rendering them vulnerable to misuse and identity theft. This has motivated extensive research into biometric template protection schemes that safeguard stored templates while preserving recognition performance.  

Existing template protection approaches can be broadly categorized into feature transformation methods and biometric cryptosystems. Feature transformation methods apply repeatable but non-invertible functions to biometric features, enabling template diversity and revocability. Biometric cryptosystems bind or generate cryptographic keys from biometric data, often employing error-tolerant schemes to accommodate intra-user variability. Despite progress, many existing solutions suffer from trade-offs between security, discriminability, and computational efficiency.  

In this work, we propose a novel biometric template protection scheme that integrates random orthonormal projection with the fuzzy commitment scheme. The random orthonormal projection serves as a cancellable transformation that preserves the inter-class separability of the biometric features while providing resistance against inversion attacks. The fuzzy commitment component securely binds the transformed features to a randomly generated key, leveraging error-correcting codes to tolerate within-class variations. This combined approach ensures template confidentiality, revocability, and high recognition accuracy. We evaluate the proposed method on benchmark biometric datasets, demonstrating its robustness against common attacks and its effectiveness in maintaining system performance, thereby offering a practical and secure solution for next-generation biometric authentication systems.
conclusion: This paper presented a novel biometric template protection scheme that integrates Random Orthonormal Projection with the Fuzzy Commitment framework. The proposed method addresses key challenges in biometric systems, including security, revocability, and recognition performance. Random orthonormal projection effectively transforms biometric features into a non-invertible domain, preserving discriminative information while enhancing resistance to inversion attacks. The fuzzy commitment scheme further secures the transformed templates by binding them with error-correcting codes, ensuring reliable authentication despite intra-user variations. Experimental evaluations demonstrated that the approach maintains high matching accuracy while providing strong protection against template compromise. Moreover, the use of random projections enables straightforward template revocation and reissuance without requiring changes to the original biometric data. This combination offers a practical and efficient solution for secure biometric systems. Future work will explore optimizing projection parameters and extending the framework to multimodal biometrics for enhanced robustness and universality.

title: Gamow shell model description of proton scattering on $^{18}$Ne
abstract: The Gamow shell model (GSM) in the coupled-channel representation is applied to describe low-energy proton scattering on the weakly bound nucleus $^{18}$Ne. The model incorporates the coupling between discrete states and the particle continuum, allowing a unified treatment of nuclear structure and reaction dynamics. Using a realistic GSM interaction, elastic and inelastic scattering cross sections are calculated and compared with available experimental data. The role of resonant and non-resonant continuum states in shaping the scattering observables is analyzed, providing insight into the underlying reaction mechanisms and the structure of unbound states in $^{19}$Na.
introduction:
The study of exotic nuclei near the drip lines has become a central topic in contemporary nuclear physics, driven by advances in radioactive ion beam facilities and the development of theoretical frameworks capable of describing open quantum systems. In such systems, the proximity of particle emission thresholds leads to a strong coupling between bound states, resonances, and the continuum of scattering states. This coupling plays a decisive role in determining nuclear structure and reaction dynamics and requires a unified treatment of structure and reactions beyond the traditional shell model paradigm. For weakly bound or unbound nuclei, the interplay between short-range nuclear forces and the long-range Coulomb interaction, as well as the coupling to decay channels, produces novel phenomena such as halo structures, threshold effects, and continuum-induced correlations.

The Gamow Shell Model (GSM) has emerged as a powerful theoretical approach for describing such open quantum systems in a fully microscopic and unified way. Built upon the Berggren ensemble, the GSM expands the many-body wave functions in a single-particle basis that includes bound, resonant, and scattering states on equal footing. This formalism allows for the consistent treatment of the coupling to the particle continuum, which is essential for describing both nuclear structure and reaction observables within the same framework. In particular, the GSM in the coupled-channel representation (GSM-CC) extends the method to describe nuclear reactions by explicitly coupling discrete many-body states of the composite system to scattering channels composed of a projectile and a target nucleus. This makes the GSM-CC well suited for the study of nucleon scattering on exotic nuclei, where the structure of the target and the reaction dynamics are strongly intertwined.

Proton scattering on proton-rich nuclei provides a sensitive probe of the nuclear potential, the distribution of single-particle strength, and the role of the continuum in shaping nuclear properties. The $^{18}$Ne nucleus, with $Z=10$ and $N=8$, lies close to the proton drip line and exhibits a rich spectrum of excited states, some of which are weakly bound or resonant. Its structure is characterized by the interplay between the $sd$-shell configurations and the coupling to the continuum of unbound proton states. Elastic and inelastic proton scattering on $^{18}$Ne thus offers a valuable testing ground for theoretical models that aim to describe the structure and reactions of proton-rich nuclei in a consistent framework.

From an astrophysical perspective, reactions involving $^{18}$Ne are of particular importance in the context of explosive hydrogen burning, such as the rapid proton capture process (rp-process) occurring in type I X-ray bursts. In these environments, $^{18}$Ne can participate in breakout reactions from the hot CNO cycles, influencing nucleosynthesis pathways toward heavier nuclei. Accurate theoretical predictions of cross sections and resonance parameters for proton-induced reactions on $^{18}$Ne are therefore essential for improving astrophysical reaction rate estimates. However, the experimental investigation of such reactions is challenging due to the short half-life of $^{18}$Ne and the low intensities of radioactive beams, making reliable theoretical modeling a crucial component of the analysis.

In recent years, the GSM-CC has been successfully applied to describe nucleon scattering on light exotic nuclei, reproducing both spectroscopic properties and reaction observables without the need to adjust parameters separately for structure and reaction calculations. In these applications, the effective two-body interaction is typically constrained by experimental data on bound states and resonances, while the continuum coupling is treated exactly within the Berggren basis. Such an approach naturally accounts for the dynamical polarization of the target nucleus due to the presence of the projectile and for the reorganization of the many-body wave function in the scattering process. In the case of $^{18}$Ne, the inclusion of continuum effects is expected to be particularly important for low-energy proton scattering, where near-threshold states can significantly affect the energy dependence of the cross section.

The present work aims to provide a comprehensive GSM-CC description of proton scattering on $^{18}$Ne, focusing on the elastic and inelastic channels at low and intermediate energies. By employing a realistic model space and a well-constrained effective interaction, we seek to elucidate the role of continuum coupling in shaping the scattering observables and to assess the predictive power of the GSM-CC for reactions on proton-rich nuclei. In doing so, we contribute both to the development of reaction theory for open quantum systems and to the understanding of nuclear structure and dynamics in the vicinity of the proton drip line.
conclusion: We have applied the Gamow shell model in the coupled-channel representation to investigate proton scattering on $^{18}$Ne, treating bound, resonant, and continuum states on the same footing. Using a realistic interaction constrained by the mirror nucleus $^{18}$O, we achieved a unified description of structure and reaction observables without adjustable scattering parameters. The calculated elastic cross sections and resonance properties reproduce the main experimental features, including the positions and widths of low-lying resonances, and provide insight into the role of continuum coupling in this weakly bound system. In particular, we find that coupling to non-resonant scattering channels significantly modifies resonance widths and shapes, underscoring the necessity of an open quantum system framework. This work demonstrates the predictive power of the Gamow shell model for light, proton-rich nuclei near the drip line and establishes a solid basis for future extensions to more complex reaction channels and heavier systems in the $sd$ shell region.

title: The masses of higher spin fields on AdS_4 and conformal perturbation theory
abstract: We investigate the masses of higher spin fields in \( \mathrm{AdS}_4 \) arising from weakly broken higher spin symmetry in the context of conformal perturbation theory. Starting from a three-dimensional conformal field theory with an infinite tower of conserved currents, we introduce a double-trace deformation that triggers a renormalization group flow between distinct fixed points. The breaking of current conservation induces small anomalous dimensions, which in the dual \(\mathrm{AdS}_4\) description correspond to nonzero masses for higher spin gauge fields. We compute these mass shifts perturbatively in the deformation parameter and establish explicit relations between CFT anomalous dimensions and AdS masses. Our results provide a detailed quantitative test of the AdS/CFT correspondence in non-supersymmetric settings and offer new insight into the dynamics of higher spin theories subject to controlled symmetry breaking.
introduction:
The study of higher spin gauge theories has attracted considerable attention in recent years, both as a testing ground for ideas in quantum gravity and as an arena for exploring the AdS/CFT correspondence beyond the realm of low-spin fields. In the context of AdS\(_4\)/CFT\(_3\), Vasiliev’s theory provides a consistent interacting framework for an infinite tower of massless fields of arbitrarily high spin, dual to free or critical vector models on the boundary. Deforming the boundary theory away from these exactly solvable limits typically induces small but finite masses for the bulk higher spin fields, thereby breaking the higher spin symmetry in a controlled fashion. Understanding the origin and magnitude of these masses is essential for elucidating the structure of the duality and the fate of higher spin symmetry under relevant perturbations.

Conformal perturbation theory offers a natural tool for this problem, allowing one to compute the leading corrections to operator dimensions in the boundary theory and to translate them into bulk mass shifts via the AdS/CFT dictionary. In particular, double-trace deformations of the CFT correspond to modified boundary conditions for bulk scalar fields, which in turn affect the dynamics of the entire tower of higher spin currents. By systematically analyzing these perturbations, one can extract precise quantitative predictions for the mass spectrum of higher spin modes in AdS\(_4\).

In this work, we develop this approach in detail, focusing on the interplay between conformal perturbation theory and bulk higher spin masses. Our results shed light on the mechanism of higher spin symmetry breaking and provide a concrete framework for testing the AdS\(_4\)/CFT\(_3\) correspondence in the presence of controlled deformations.
conclusion: In this work we have analyzed the masses of higher spin fields on AdS\(_4\) using conformal perturbation theory, clarifying their dependence on boundary deformations. Our results demonstrate the precise mechanism by which symmetry breaking generates mass shifts, in agreement with holographic expectations. The approach provides a systematic framework for computing corrections beyond the leading order and can be extended to more general backgrounds. These findings strengthen the link between bulk higher spin dynamics and boundary conformal data, offering a pathway for further exploration of interacting higher spin theories.

title: Learning Invariant Representations across Domains and Tasks
abstract: Learning robust and generalizable representations is a central challenge in machine learning, particularly when models are deployed across domains and tasks with differing data distributions. This work investigates methods for learning invariant representations that preserve task-relevant information while discarding spurious correlations tied to specific domains. We present a unified framework that combines domain-adversarial training, task-conditioned feature disentanglement, and contrastive alignment to encourage invariance both across domains and across heterogeneous task objectives. Our approach is evaluated on multi-domain, multi-task benchmarks spanning vision and language, demonstrating improved generalization to unseen domains and tasks compared to state-of-the-art baselines. We provide theoretical analysis showing that our method minimizes an upper bound on the joint generalization error, simultaneously reducing domain shift and task-specific bias. Empirical results indicate that learned representations maintain high discriminative power while exhibiting reduced sensitivity to nuisance factors. This work advances the understanding of how to systematically align latent spaces across diverse settings, enabling more reliable transfer in real-world, dynamically changing environments.
introduction:
The ability to learn representations that generalize across distinct domains and tasks is a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning. In many practical scenarios, data are collected under heterogeneous conditions, with variations in distribution stemming from differences in acquisition environments, sensor modalities, or population demographics. Furthermore, predictive models are often expected to perform well on multiple related tasks, each with its own label space and statistical characteristics. Traditional supervised learning paradigms, which assume that training and test data are drawn from the same distribution and that the model is optimized for a single task, struggle to meet these demands. As a result, there has been growing interest in developing methods that can extract invariant representations—features that capture the underlying factors of variation relevant to prediction while discarding spurious correlations tied to specific domains or tasks.

Invariant representation learning aims to disentangle the information in the data into components that are stable and transferable, and those that are domain- or task-specific. By isolating the stable factors, models can be more robust to distribution shifts and can leverage knowledge acquired in one context to improve performance in another. This capability is critical in settings where collecting labeled data for every possible combination of domain and task is infeasible. For example, in medical imaging, a classifier trained to detect disease in scans from one hospital should ideally perform well on data from other hospitals, even when the imaging devices or patient populations differ. Similarly, in natural language processing, a sentiment analysis model trained on reviews from one platform should generalize to reviews from another, despite differences in vocabulary and style.

Existing approaches to learning invariant representations span several related research areas, including domain adaptation, domain generalization, transfer learning, and multi-task learning. Domain adaptation methods typically assume access to labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled or sparsely labeled data from a target domain, and seek to align the feature distributions across domains. Domain generalization extends this to the more challenging setting in which no target domain data are available during training, requiring the model to learn features that are inherently domain-agnostic. Transfer learning focuses on reusing knowledge acquired from one task to accelerate or enhance learning in a different task, often by fine-tuning pretrained models. Multi-task learning, on the other hand, jointly learns multiple tasks by sharing representations, with the goal of exploiting task relatedness to improve performance on all tasks.

While these paradigms have led to significant progress, they often address domain or task variation in isolation, without fully exploiting the potential synergies between them. In real-world applications, however, domain and task shifts often occur simultaneously: a model may be deployed to new domains and new tasks at the same time. For instance, an autonomous driving system trained to detect pedestrians and traffic lights in sunny weather in one city may need to detect cyclists and road signs in rainy weather in another city. Addressing such combined shifts requires methods that can learn representations invariant to both domain-specific and task-specific factors, enabling effective cross-domain, cross-task transfer.

Several recent works have begun to explore this intersection, proposing frameworks that integrate ideas from multi-task learning and domain generalization. These approaches often rely on disentangling latent factors, adversarial training to remove domain or task information from the features, or meta-learning strategies that simulate domain and task shifts during training. Nevertheless, achieving robust invariance remains challenging. One difficulty lies in determining which aspects of the data should be preserved for generalization and which should be suppressed, especially when domain and task variations interact in complex ways. Furthermore, the trade-off between invariance and discriminative power must be carefully managed: overly aggressive removal of domain or task information can harm performance, while insufficient invariance can lead to poor generalization.

This work addresses the problem of learning invariant representations across both domains and tasks in a unified framework. We formalize the joint setting in which multiple source domains and multiple tasks are available during training, and the goal is to generalize to unseen combinations of domains and tasks. Our approach builds on the intuition that invariant factors are those that consistently support predictive performance across all observed domains and tasks, and that these factors can be identified by explicitly modeling and penalizing the variability of representations with respect to domain and task changes. By leveraging structured regularization and shared latent spaces, we aim to disentangle stable, transferable features from those that are specific to individual domains or tasks. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets spanning vision and language, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior generalization in scenarios involving simultaneous domain and task shifts, outperforming strong baselines from both the domain adaptation/generalization and multi-task learning literatures. This unified perspective contributes to bridging the gap between these traditionally separate research areas, and advances the broader goal of building learning systems that are truly robust to the diversity and complexity of real-world environments.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated methods for learning invariant representations that generalize across both domains and tasks. By jointly modeling domain-invariant features and task-specific nuances, our approach bridges the gap between domain adaptation and multi-task learning. Experimental results across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that encouraging invariance while retaining discriminative capacity leads to robust performance under distribution shifts and varying task requirements. The proposed framework consistently outperformed baselines in scenarios with limited labeled data in target domains, highlighting its potential for real-world applications where data heterogeneity is common. Future work will explore scalability to larger, more complex settings, and the integration of additional modalities to further enhance generalization. Overall, our findings underscore the importance of principled representation learning strategies for building models that remain reliable and effective across changing environments and evolving task demands.

title: Hearts Gym: Learning Reinforcement Learning as a Team Event
abstract: We present *Hearts Gym*, a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) environment inspired by the classic card game Hearts, designed to explore cooperative-competitive dynamics in team settings. Unlike standard RL benchmarks that focus on individual agent optimization, *Hearts Gym* emphasizes interdependent decision-making, partial observability, and strategic communication among teammates. The environment supports flexible team configurations, enabling the study of coordination protocols, emergent strategies, and adversarial counterplay. We provide a modular API for seamless integration with popular RL frameworks, along with baseline implementations using policy gradient and value-based methods. Experimental results demonstrate that team-aware training significantly outperforms independent learning in both win rate and stability. *Hearts Gym* offers a challenging yet accessible platform for advancing research on multi-agent collaboration, competition, and mixed-motive reinforcement learning.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a central paradigm in artificial intelligence, enabling agents to learn effective behaviors through trial-and-error interaction with dynamic environments. While much of the research focus has been on single-agent settings, real-world decision-making often involves multiple agents interacting in cooperative, competitive, or mixed-motive contexts. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has therefore become an increasingly important area of study, with applications ranging from autonomous vehicles and distributed control to strategy games and social simulations. However, learning in multi-agent settings introduces additional challenges such as non-stationarity, credit assignment, and coordination, making it a richer yet more complex domain for both research and education.

Games have long served as valuable testbeds for RL due to their well-defined rules, controllable complexity, and measurable performance outcomes. Card games in particular offer an intriguing balance of stochasticity, partial observability, and strategic depth. Hearts, a trick-taking card game traditionally played by four individuals, is a compelling environment for studying MARL because it combines elements of competition and temporary cooperation, requires reasoning under uncertainty, and demands adaptive strategies in response to other players’ evolving policies. Unlike fully cooperative or purely adversarial games, Hearts embodies a dynamic structure in which players may align temporarily against a leading opponent while ultimately pursuing individual victory. This makes it well suited for exploring the subtleties of emergent behavior, opponent modeling, and shifting alliances in a learning context.

Despite the rich potential of such environments, most RL education and research tools focus on either simplified grid worlds or highly complex domains such as StarCraft II or robotic control. This leaves a gap for approachable yet strategically rich environments that can be used to teach and experiment with MARL concepts in a controlled and reproducible manner. To address this gap, we introduce *Hearts Gym*, an open-source simulation environment tailored for MARL research and pedagogy. Hearts Gym provides a formalized interface for agents to play the game of Hearts, enabling researchers, educators, and students to investigate reinforcement learning algorithms in a domain that is both accessible and strategically challenging.

By framing Hearts as a “team event” in the educational setting, we position the learning experience itself as a multi-agent endeavor: students can develop and test agents collaboratively, engage in competitions to benchmark strategies, and collectively analyze the emergent dynamics. This dual level of teamwork—both among simulated agents in the environment and among human participants in the learning process—offers a unique pedagogical opportunity. Hearts Gym thus serves as both a research platform for studying MARL phenomena and a learning scaffold that fosters collaborative problem-solving, critical thinking, and hands-on experimentation with reinforcement learning principles. Through this work, we aim to bridge the gap between approachable gameplay environments and the complex realities of multi-agent learning, advancing both the study and teaching of reinforcement learning in multi-agent contexts.
conclusion:
This work introduced *Hearts Gym*, a collaborative multi-agent environment designed to teach and explore reinforcement learning (RL) concepts through the game of Hearts. By framing RL as a team-oriented event, the platform not only supports individual agent development but also emphasizes coordination, strategy adaptation, and the dynamic interplay between competitive and cooperative behaviors. Our approach integrates accessible tooling with pedagogical structure, enabling learners to experiment with state representations, reward shaping, and policy optimization in a socially engaging context. 

Through illustrative scenarios and baseline experiments, we demonstrated how Hearts Gym can serve both as a research testbed and an educational resource, bridging the gap between theoretical understanding and practical implementation. The results underscore the value of multi-agent card games in revealing emergent behaviors, strategic negotiation, and the trade-offs inherent to exploration versus exploitation. 

Looking forward, Hearts Gym offers fertile ground for extending RL research into areas such as opponent modeling, transfer learning between agents, and human–AI collaboration. We anticipate that its emphasis on teamwork will inspire novel instructional methods and foster deeper engagement with RL fundamentals. By combining play, competition, and cooperation, Hearts Gym provides a versatile and motivating framework for advancing both learning outcomes and multi-agent RL research.

title: A new reduced order model of linear parabolic PDEs
abstract: We present a novel reduced order modeling approach for linear parabolic partial differential equations, aimed at achieving high computational efficiency without compromising accuracy. The method combines projection-based techniques with an optimized basis selection strategy to capture dominant dynamical features using significantly fewer modes. Rigorous error analysis demonstrates stability and convergence, while numerical experiments on benchmark problems confirm substantial reductions in computational cost. The proposed framework offers a flexible and robust tool for real-time simulation, control, and parameter estimation in large-scale parabolic PDE applications.
introduction:
Partial differential equations (PDEs) of parabolic type arise in a wide range of scientific and engineering contexts, including heat conduction, diffusion processes, groundwater flow, and option pricing in financial mathematics. These equations typically describe the evolution of a state variable over time under the influence of spatial diffusion and possibly additional reaction or convection terms. Linear parabolic PDEs, in particular, form a fundamental class of problems for which theoretical analysis and numerical simulation are well developed. Nevertheless, when such models are applied to large-scale systems with high spatial resolution or complex geometries, the computational cost associated with their numerical solution can become prohibitively high, especially when repeated simulations are required as in optimization, control, uncertainty quantification, or real-time forecasting.

In many practical settings, the full-order numerical discretization of a linear parabolic PDE—whether by finite difference, finite element, or spectral methods—leads to a high-dimensional system of ordinary differential equations. Time integration of such systems, particularly over long time horizons or for many parameter configurations, can be computationally expensive in both CPU time and memory usage. The need to evaluate solutions rapidly and accurately has motivated the development of reduced order modeling (ROM) techniques. These methods aim to replace the original high-dimensional dynamical system with a surrogate model of much lower dimension, while preserving essential features of the dynamics. By projecting the full-order solution onto a carefully chosen low-dimensional subspace, ROMs can achieve significant reductions in computational cost without substantial loss of accuracy.

Among the various approaches to reduced order modeling, the Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) and related projection-based methods have been widely adopted. The POD constructs an orthonormal basis from snapshots of the full-order solution, capturing the most energetic modes in a least-squares sense. When combined with Galerkin projection, this yields a reduced dynamical system of dimension equal to the number of retained modes. Balanced truncation, Krylov subspace methods, and reduced basis methods form other important classes of ROMs, each with their own advantages in terms of stability, error control, and computational efficiency. Despite the success of these approaches, challenges remain. For example, the construction of the reduced basis often requires expensive offline computations, and the resulting ROM may exhibit instabilities or reduced accuracy when applied outside the parameter regime used for training. Furthermore, for time-dependent problems such as parabolic PDEs, the preservation of stability and accuracy over long time intervals is a nontrivial requirement.

Recent research has sought to address these difficulties by developing new formulations that exploit the specific structure of linear parabolic problems. For instance, certain operator-theoretic properties, such as self-adjointness, coercivity, and contractivity of the semigroup generated by the PDE, can be leveraged to design more robust ROMs. Additionally, advances in data-driven modeling, such as dynamic mode decomposition and operator inference, have opened new possibilities for obtaining reduced models directly from data, bypassing some of the limitations of projection-based methods. Nevertheless, there remains a need for reduced order models that combine rigorous theoretical foundations, computational efficiency, and robustness across a wide range of operating conditions.

The present work introduces a new reduced order modeling framework tailored to linear parabolic PDEs. The proposed method builds upon the projection-based paradigm but incorporates a novel basis construction and system approximation strategy that explicitly accounts for the temporal smoothing and dissipative nature of parabolic dynamics. By integrating analytical insights from the theory of semigroups with numerical techniques inspired by balanced truncation, the method achieves improved stability and accuracy, particularly for problems with slowly decaying modes or with parameters varying over wide ranges. Moreover, the computational procedure is designed to be efficient both in the offline stage, where the reduced basis is constructed, and in the online stage, where the reduced model is repeatedly evaluated.

The main contributions of this work are threefold. First, we derive a reduced basis generation algorithm that exploits the spectral properties of the spatial differential operator, ensuring that the most dynamically relevant modes are captured with minimal computational effort. Second, we formulate a reduced system approximation that preserves key stability properties of the original PDE discretization, thereby enabling long-time integration without spurious growth of numerical errors. Third, we demonstrate, through a series of numerical experiments on benchmark parabolic problems, that the proposed method outperforms standard POD–Galerkin ROMs in terms of accuracy, stability, and computational speed.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the formulation of linear parabolic PDEs and their standard numerical discretizations, emphasizing the structural properties relevant to model reduction. Section 3 presents the proposed reduced order modeling methodology in detail, including the basis construction, projection, and system approximation steps. Section 4 reports numerical experiments that illustrate the performance of the method on representative test problems. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the findings and discusses possible extensions to nonlinear and time-varying problems.
conclusion: In this work, we have developed a new reduced order model for linear parabolic partial differential equations that achieves substantial computational savings while maintaining high accuracy. By combining projection-based techniques with tailored basis construction, the method efficiently captures the dominant dynamics of the underlying system. Numerical experiments demonstrate its robustness across a range of problem settings, with errors remaining consistently low compared to full-order simulations. The proposed approach is straightforward to implement, adaptable to different boundary and initial conditions, and scalable to higher-dimensional problems. These results suggest that the model offers a practical and reliable tool for real-time simulation, control, and optimization of systems governed by parabolic PDEs, and provide a foundation for future extensions to nonlinear and time-varying problems.

title: Decoupling of heavy sneutrinos in low-scale seesaw models
abstract: We investigate the decoupling behavior of heavy sneutrino states in low-scale seesaw frameworks, focusing on their impact on low-energy observables. Within the context of supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model, we analyze one-loop corrections to charged-lepton flavor-violating processes and Higgs-sector parameters, assessing the interplay between large sneutrino masses and small neutrino Yukawa couplings. Using an effective field theory approach, we demonstrate that heavy sneutrinos decouple in the limit of large soft-breaking masses, while non-decoupling effects persist for specific parameter configurations. Our results clarify the conditions under which heavy sneutrinos leave measurable imprints, providing guidance for probing low-scale seesaw scenarios at future experiments.
introduction: Low-scale seesaw models provide an attractive framework to explain the smallness of neutrino masses while potentially offering rich phenomenology accessible at current or future experiments. In such scenarios, the introduction of heavy singlet neutrinos or sneutrinos can significantly affect low-energy observables, including lepton flavour violating processes and Higgs sector dynamics. However, the extent to which these heavy states decouple from the effective theory depends sensitively on their masses, mixings, and supersymmetry-breaking parameters. Heavy sneutrinos, in particular, can induce sizeable loop contributions even when their masses lie well above the electroweak scale, challenging the naive expectation of decoupling. Understanding their role is therefore crucial for precise predictions and for interpreting experimental results in terms of underlying model parameters. In this work, we examine the decoupling behaviour of heavy sneutrinos in low-scale seesaw models, focusing on their impact on phenomenology and effective couplings.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined the decoupling behaviour of heavy sneutrinos in the context of low-scale seesaw models, with particular emphasis on their impact on low-energy observables and the stability of the effective theory. By analysing the one-loop contributions to neutrino masses, lepton flavour violating processes, and Higgs sector parameters, we have shown that the decoupling of heavy scalar singlets is non-trivial when the seesaw scale lies close to the TeV range. Our results indicate that, while the Appelquist–Carazzone theorem ensures the suppression of heavy degrees of freedom in many scenarios, specific features of supersymmetric seesaw embeddings — such as soft SUSY-breaking parameters and the structure of the sneutrino mass matrix — can delay or modify the decoupling pattern.

In particular, we have demonstrated that for heavy sneutrino masses well above the electroweak scale, but with sizeable trilinear couplings or mass mixings, residual effects can persist in low-energy observables, potentially within reach of current or future experiments. This is especially relevant in extended models where the light–heavy sneutrino mixing is enhanced, leading to corrections to the Higgs mass prediction and to lepton flavour violating decay rates that do not vanish rapidly with the heavy mass scale. Our analysis also clarifies the parametric dependence of these effects, providing analytic estimates and numerical benchmarks that can be used to assess the phenomenological viability of specific low-scale seesaw realisations.

Furthermore, we have explored the interplay between the decoupling behaviour and the naturalness of the electroweak scale. We find that in certain regions of parameter space, the incomplete decoupling of heavy sneutrinos can exacerbate fine-tuning issues, whereas in others the seesaw-induced corrections remain sufficiently suppressed to preserve naturalness. The framework developed here can be straightforwardly applied to other supersymmetric neutrino mass models, and extended to include higher-loop effects and non-minimal gauge sectors.

Overall, our study highlights the importance of carefully assessing the decoupling properties of heavy scalar states in low-scale seesaw models, both for accurate phenomenological predictions and for a consistent interpretation of experimental results in the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

title: Separation Logic with Linearly Compositional Inductive Predicates and Set Data Constraints
abstract: We introduce an extension of separation logic supporting **linearly compositional inductive predicates** enriched with **set-based data constraints**. Our framework captures complex heap structures whose spatial composition aligns with linear decomposition of shape parameters, while simultaneously reasoning about associated data value sets. We formalize the syntax and semantics, ensuring soundness with respect to heap models combining shape and data. We develop a proof system enabling modular reasoning and show decidability for a significant fragment via an automata-theoretic approach. Applications include verification of programs manipulating linked data structures with element sets, such as lists, trees, and skip lists. Experimental evaluation demonstrates expressive power and practical efficiency in automated verification tasks.
introduction:
Separation Logic has emerged as a powerful formalism for reasoning about programs that manipulate complex, dynamically allocated data structures. By extending Hoare logic with assertions that can describe disjointness of heap regions, Separation Logic enables concise and modular proofs of memory safety and functional correctness. Over the past two decades, its applicability has been broadened through the incorporation of inductively defined predicates, allowing succinct specifications of recursively defined data structures such as linked lists, trees, and graphs. These inductive predicates capture structural invariants in a way that aligns closely with programmers’ intuitions, which in turn facilitates automated verification.

A central strength of inductively defined predicates in Separation Logic lies in their ability to express recursive shape properties. However, when reasoning about program fragments that manipulate multiple instances of a data structure, or that transform a data structure into another of related shape, compositionality becomes a challenge. Classical inductive predicates are typically defined in a way that does not guarantee linear compositionality: combining two heap segments that satisfy a predicate does not necessarily yield a larger segment that satisfies the same predicate, unless additional constraints are explicitly established. This lack of linear compositionality can hinder modular verification, as reasoning about combined structures often requires unfolding and refolding predicates, which in turn increases proof complexity and reduces automation potential.

Recent work has sought to address this limitation by introducing variants of inductive predicates that preserve compositionality properties under disjoint union of heaps. In particular, *linearly compositional inductive predicates* are designed such that the satisfaction of a predicate over disjoint heap fragments can be combined in a straightforward, linear manner to yield satisfaction over the union. This property is especially useful for modular reasoning: one can verify properties of substructures independently, and then reason about the whole by combining the results without revisiting the internal details of the substructures. Such an approach aligns well with the principles of local reasoning—the hallmark of Separation Logic—while extending its benefits to richer inductive specifications.

In practice, purely structural reasoning is often insufficient. Many real-world programs maintain not only shape invariants of heap-allocated structures, but also intricate data invariants over the values stored in them.
