This redundancy in message propagation improves robustness to packet loss and topology changes, while avoiding the overhead of maintaining complex routing structures. The simplicity and fault-tolerance of gossip protocols make them particularly attractive for large-scale MWSNs, where scalability and resilience are paramount.

Despite these advantages, existing gossip-based dissemination schemes are often designed for small data items, such as sensor readings or control messages, and may not directly address the unique challenges of code propagation. Code dissemination entails transferring significantly larger payloads, requiring mechanisms to ensure completeness, integrity, and efficiency, even in the presence of node mobility and constrained resources. Furthermore, excessive redundancy, while beneficial for reliability, can lead to unnecessary energy consumption and network congestion if not carefully managed.

In this work, we propose GCP (Gossip-based Code Propagation), a novel protocol tailored for large-scale MWSNs that leverages the strengths of gossip-based dissemination while addressing the specific requirements of code updates. GCP incorporates adaptive gossiping strategies, fragmentation and reassembly of code images, and energy-aware transmission control to achieve high propagation reliability with minimal overhead. Through extensive simulations and experimental validation, we demonstrate that GCP achieves efficient, resilient, and scalable code dissemination in challenging mobile wireless sensor network environments.
conclusion: In this work, we presented GCP, a gossip-based code propagation protocol tailored for large-scale mobile wireless sensor networks. By leveraging the inherent robustness and scalability of gossip mechanisms, GCP enables efficient and resilient dissemination of code updates in highly dynamic environments characterized by node mobility, intermittent connectivity, and constrained resources. Through analytical modeling and extensive simulation, we demonstrated that GCP achieves high delivery ratios with reduced communication overhead compared to traditional flooding-based approaches, while maintaining low update latency. The probabilistic nature of gossiping mitigates network congestion and energy expenditure, extending the operational lifetime of the network. Furthermore, GCP’s decentralized design ensures that no single point of failure can compromise the update process, making it well-suited for mission-critical and large-scale deployments. Our results indicate that GCP maintains performance even under high mobility scenarios, confirming its adaptability to real-world conditions where topology changes frequently. Future work will explore adaptive gossip parameters that respond to network conditions in real time, as well as integration with security mechanisms to ensure integrity and authenticity of propagated code. Overall, GCP offers a practical, scalable, and energy-aware solution for maintaining software consistency in mobile wireless sensor networks of unprecedented size and dynamism.

title: The limitations of discrete-time approaches to continuous-time contagion dynamics
abstract: Discrete-time formulations are widely employed to model contagion dynamics due to their algorithmic simplicity and ease of simulation. However, many real-world spreading processes—ranging from infectious disease transmission to information diffusion—evolve in continuous time. This paper examines the conceptual and practical limitations that arise when discrete-time approaches are applied to inherently continuous-time contagion phenomena. We analyze how time discretization can distort key dynamical properties, including the timing of transmission events, the distribution of inter-event intervals, and the estimation of reproduction numbers. Using both synthetic and empirical network data, we demonstrate that coarse temporal resolution may introduce biases in parameter inference, misrepresent critical thresholds, and mischaracterize transient behaviors. Furthermore, we show that certain discrete-time update schemes impose artificial synchrony, potentially producing spurious oscillations or altering outbreak probability. Our findings highlight the importance of aligning model assumptions with the temporal nature of the process under study. We discuss methodological strategies for mitigating discretization artifacts and argue for greater use of continuous-time frameworks when accurate representation of contagion dynamics is essential.
introduction:
The modeling of contagion processes—whether in epidemiology, information diffusion, or systemic financial risk—has long relied on mathematical frameworks that capture the evolution of interacting agents over time. A fundamental distinction in this literature lies between discrete-time and continuous-time formulations. In continuous-time models, changes occur at stochastic intervals governed by hazard rates or transition intensities, allowing for an exact representation of processes whose underlying mechanisms are inherently asynchronous. In discrete-time models, by contrast, the system is updated at fixed time steps, and transition probabilities are specified over these intervals rather than as instantaneous rates. Both approaches have proven valuable, yet the choice between them has profound consequences for the accuracy, interpretability, and predictive power of contagion models.

Discrete-time approaches are often favored for their simplicity, computational tractability, and ease of alignment with data that are naturally recorded in regular intervals, such as daily case counts, quarterly financial reports, or scheduled social media activity summaries. These models are frequently easier to implement, especially when the temporal resolution of the available data matches the model’s update interval. Furthermore, discrete-time formulations can be readily simulated using synchronous updating schemes, which are simple to parallelize and do not require specialized algorithms for event scheduling.

However, when the underlying contagion dynamics unfold in continuous time—as is the case for the transmission of infectious diseases, the spread of information through social contacts, or the cascading failures in interbank networks—discretization can introduce systematic distortions. Fixed time steps implicitly assume that events are synchronized to the update grid, which can alter the ordering of events and artificially inflate or suppress the likelihood of certain transitions. This is particularly problematic when the timescale of the contagion process is on the same order or shorter than the chosen time step, leading to aggregation of events and loss of temporal detail. Moreover, discrete-time transition probabilities are not directly comparable across studies with different time steps, complicating the interpretation of estimated parameters and their relation to underlying mechanisms.

The limitations of discrete-time approximations are compounded in networks where contagion dynamics depend sensitively on the temporal structure of contacts. In such settings, the precise timing of interactions can determine whether a susceptible node becomes infected before or after it has the opportunity to interact with others, thereby influencing the course of the contagion. Discrete-time models, by aggregating multiple events into a single update, may fail to capture these causal sequences. Even when the time step is chosen to be small, the computational burden of simulating large networks over fine-grained intervals can become prohibitive, and numerical artifacts may persist.

Continuous-time formulations address many of these issues by representing contagion processes as continuous-time Markov chains or related stochastic processes, where each event occurs at a random time drawn from an exponential distribution with a parameter determined by the current state of the system. This framework preserves the exact ordering of events and allows for rigorous analytical treatment of transmission dynamics. Nonetheless, continuous-time models require more sophisticated estimation and simulation methods and may demand high-resolution temporal data that are not always available.

This paper critically examines the limitations of discrete-time approaches when applied to inherently continuous-time contagion dynamics. We analyze the sources and magnitudes of approximation errors introduced by time discretization, identify conditions under which these errors become significant, and discuss the implications for inference, prediction, and policy evaluation. By contrasting discrete- and continuous-time representations both analytically and through simulation, we aim to provide clearer guidance on model choice and highlight the trade-offs between computational convenience and dynamical fidelity. Our findings underscore the importance of aligning modeling assumptions with the temporal nature of the underlying contagion process, particularly in contexts where accurate representation of event timing is crucial.
conclusion: This study has examined the limitations inherent in discrete-time formulations of contagion processes that are fundamentally continuous in nature. We have shown that time discretization can introduce systematic biases in estimated transmission rates, distort temporal correlations, and misrepresent the speed and variability of outbreak trajectories. Such artifacts become pronounced when the chosen time step is not well aligned with the intrinsic timescales of the dynamics. While discrete-time models offer analytical tractability and computational convenience, their use requires caution, especially for high-resolution or rapidly evolving systems. Future work should focus on hybrid or adaptive-time methods that preserve the fidelity of continuous-time dynamics while retaining modeling flexibility, thereby improving the accuracy and interpretability of contagion modeling across diverse domains.

title: Revisiting Wedge Sampling for Budgeted Maximum Inner Product Search
abstract: Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is a fundamental problem in large-scale recommendation, retrieval, and representation learning. Among the many strategies for approximate MIPS, wedge sampling has emerged as a simple yet effective technique, offering probabilistic guarantees while exploiting sparsity. However, its performance under strict computational budgets remains underexplored. In this work, we revisit wedge sampling from the perspective of budgeted MIPS, where only a fixed number of inner product evaluations can be afforded. We present a refined analysis of the trade-off between sampling allocation and retrieval accuracy, revealing previously uncharacterized regimes in which wedge sampling is near-optimal. Building on these insights, we propose adaptive budget allocation strategies that dynamically adjust sampling probabilities based on intermediate results, improving recall without increasing cost. Extensive experiments on real-world recommendation and embedding datasets demonstrate that our methods consistently outperform baseline wedge sampling and other budgeted MIPS approaches, particularly in high-dimensional and skewed data settings. Our results establish wedge sampling as a competitive and theoretically grounded solution for budget-constrained MIPS, and open avenues for integrating adaptive sampling into broader large-scale retrieval frameworks.
introduction: Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is a fundamental problem with numerous applications in recommendation systems, information retrieval, and machine learning. Given a query vector, the task is to efficiently identify database vectors with the largest inner products. While exact solutions can be computationally prohibitive at scale, approximate techniques have been widely explored. Wedge sampling is a probabilistic approach that offers attractive trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. However, its behavior under strict computational budgets remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we revisit wedge sampling in the context of budgeted MIPS, providing a refined analysis, proposing algorithmic enhancements, and empirically demonstrating improved performance. Our results clarify its practical utility for large-scale, resource-constrained retrieval scenarios.
conclusion: In this work, we revisited wedge sampling for budgeted maximum inner product search, providing new insights into its efficiency and accuracy under constrained computational budgets. By refining the sampling strategy and analyzing its probabilistic guarantees, we demonstrated improved performance over prior baselines, particularly in high-dimensional, sparse settings. Our empirical results confirmed that careful budget allocation can yield competitive retrieval quality while significantly reducing computation. These findings suggest that wedge sampling remains a strong candidate for scalable similarity search, with potential for further enhancement through adaptive and data-aware budget strategies.

title: LP Rounding for k-Centers with Non-uniform Hard Capacities
abstract: We study the *k*-center problem with non-uniform hard capacities, a fundamental facility location problem in which one seeks to open at most *k* centers in a metric space to minimize the maximum distance from any client to its assigned center, subject to the constraint that each open center can serve at most a specified number of clients. While the uncapacitated *k*-center problem admits a simple 2-approximation, the capacitated variant is substantially more challenging, particularly when capacities vary across potential center locations and must be respected exactly (hard capacities). We present a new linear programming (LP) relaxation for the problem, together with a rounding algorithm that converts fractional solutions into integral ones while losing only a constant factor in the objective. Our approach builds on a refined clustering framework and a novel capacity-aware rounding method that preserves feasibility without requiring capacity scaling or violation. We prove that our algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation guarantee, improving upon previously known bounds for the non-uniform hard-capacity setting. Our analysis introduces a capacity-respecting exchange argument that may be of independent interest in other capacitated location problems. Furthermore, we show that the integrality gap of our LP relaxation is bounded by a small constant, even for general metrics, and we provide matching hardness evidence under standard complexity assumptions. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method produces solutions that are consistently close to optimal and significantly better than heuristic baselines. This work advances the understanding of LP-based methods for capacitated clustering and suggests new directions for approximation algorithms in settings with heterogeneous and tightly constrained resources.
introduction:
Clustering problems are fundamental in theoretical computer science, operations research, and data analysis, arising naturally in numerous applications such as facility location, network design, and resource allocation. Among these, the *k*-center problem is one of the most widely studied: given a set of points and a distance metric, the task is to choose at most *k* centers so as to minimize the maximum distance from any point to its assigned center. This objective captures the goal of ensuring that all clients are served within a minimal service radius, making it particularly relevant in contexts where fairness or worst-case performance is of primary concern.

A rich body of work has examined the *k*-center problem under various constraints and generalizations. A particularly important variant incorporates *capacities* on the centers, limiting the number of clients each center can serve. This models realistic situations where facilities have resource limitations, such as bandwidth, storage, or staffing constraints. In the *uniform capacity* setting, all centers share the same capacity bound, while in the *non-uniform capacity* setting, capacities may vary from center to center. The latter is both more general and more challenging, as it captures heterogeneity in facility capabilities and leads to more complex combinatorial structure.

Within the capacitated *k*-center problem, one may distinguish between *hard* and *soft* capacities. Under hard capacities, a center cannot be opened more than once; one must respect the given capacity bound for each individual facility location. In contrast, soft capacities allow opening multiple copies of the same facility, effectively increasing capacity at a location at proportional cost. Hard capacity constraints are often more realistic in practice—for example, a physical warehouse cannot be duplicated at the same site—but they are also more difficult to handle algorithmically, as they preclude certain natural relaxations and rounding strategies.

The combination of *non-uniform* and *hard* capacity constraints presents a particularly challenging variant: the *k*-center problem with non-uniform hard capacities. This setting has been recognized as significantly more difficult than the uniform or soft-capacity counterparts. Several hardness results indicate that achieving constant-factor approximations is nontrivial, and naive extensions of known techniques for uniform capacities fail to yield strong guarantees. The non-uniformity breaks symmetries that are often exploited in algorithm design, while hard capacities eliminate flexibility in assignment, leading to intricate feasibility issues during solution construction.

Linear programming (LP) relaxations are a central tool in the design of approximation algorithms for facility location and clustering problems. LP formulations allow encoding the combinatorial problem as a set of linear constraints over fractional variables, representing fractional openings of facilities and fractional assignments of clients. Solving the LP yields an optimal fractional solution, which must then be *rounded* to an integral solution that respects the problem constraints, ideally without increasing the objective too much. For capacitated *k*-center problems, LP-based approaches have been explored, but the rounding step becomes substantially more complex when capacities are hard and non-uniform. In particular, standard dependent rounding and filtering techniques may violate capacity constraints or require opening more than *k* facilities.

In this work, we study LP rounding techniques tailored to the *k*-center problem with non-uniform hard capacities. Our aim is to develop a rounding algorithm that converts a fractional LP solution into a feasible integral solution while preserving a good approximation ratio. We build on a natural LP relaxation for the problem, strengthening it with additional valid inequalities to better capture the combinatorial structure of feasible solutions. Our rounding procedure carefully balances the need to respect both the global cardinality constraint (at most *k* centers) and the individual capacity bounds, while controlling the blowup in the covering radius.

Our contributions are twofold. First, we present a refined LP formulation that admits a polynomial-time solution and yields fractional solutions with structural properties conducive to rounding. Second, we design and analyze a rounding algorithm that produces an integral solution with a constant-factor approximation guarantee for the maximum service distance, matching or improving upon the best known bounds for this problem class. Our method exploits a clustering-based decomposition of the fractional solution, combined with a capacity-aware matching procedure that assigns clients to opened centers without exceeding capacities.

The results demonstrate that LP rounding, when guided by problem-specific structural insights, can overcome the significant obstacles posed by non-uniform hard capacities in *k*-center problems. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, our techniques have potential applicability in practical large-scale facility location scenarios where capacities are heterogeneous and duplicating facilities is infeasible. By advancing the understanding of LP-based methods in this challenging setting, we contribute both to the theory of approximation algorithms and to the toolkit available for solving realistic clustering problems under stringent capacity constraints.
conclusion: We presented an LP rounding framework for the k-center problem with non-uniform hard capacities, achieving improved approximation guarantees over previous methods. Our approach carefully integrates distance-based clustering with capacity-aware rounding, ensuring feasibility while minimizing the maximum assignment distance. By exploiting structural properties of the fractional LP solution, we circumvent key obstacles posed by non-uniform capacities and hard constraints. The resulting algorithm is both conceptually simple and analytically robust, offering new insights into the interplay between geometry and capacity limitations. These techniques open avenues for further research on capacitated location problems, particularly in extending to other metrics, dynamic settings, and related optimization models.

title: A Unified Framework for Task-Driven Data Quality Management
abstract: Ensuring high-quality data is essential for reliable decision-making in data-intensive applications, yet prevailing data quality management approaches often treat quality dimensions in isolation from the downstream tasks they support. This paper introduces a unified framework for task-driven data quality management that explicitly aligns quality assessment, improvement, and monitoring processes with the requirements of specific analytical or operational tasks. The framework integrates quality dimensions—such as accuracy, completeness, timeliness, and consistency—into a coherent model that quantifies their impact on task performance. By adopting a task-centric perspective, it enables prioritization of quality improvement efforts based on measured or estimated contributions to task outcomes, rather than generic quality scores. The proposed approach combines formal modeling, adaptive quality metrics, and iterative feedback from task execution to guide targeted interventions in data pipelines. We validate the framework through empirical studies in diverse domains, including predictive maintenance, clinical decision support, and real-time logistics optimization. Results demonstrate that task-driven quality management can yield significant performance gains while reducing unnecessary data cleansing effort. This work advances the state of the art by bridging the gap between abstract data quality theory and the practical needs of data-driven systems, offering a principled and scalable methodology for organizations to manage data quality as a strategic, task-dependent asset.
introduction:
In the era of data-driven decision-making, the quality of data has emerged as a fundamental determinant of the effectiveness, efficiency, and reliability of analytical and operational processes. Organizations across diverse sectors—ranging from healthcare and finance to manufacturing and e-commerce—are increasingly reliant on complex data ecosystems to inform strategic choices, automate workflows, and fuel machine learning models. However, the proliferation of heterogeneous, large-scale, and dynamically evolving datasets has intensified the challenges associated with ensuring that data is fit for its intended use. Traditional data quality management (DQM) approaches, which often emphasize generic quality dimensions such as completeness, accuracy, timeliness, and consistency, provide valuable baselines but risk overlooking the nuanced, task-specific requirements that ultimately determine whether data can support a given decision or computational process. This gap underscores the need for frameworks that explicitly align data quality assessments and interventions with the objectives and constraints of the tasks they are meant to serve.

Conventional DQM strategies frequently operate in a task-agnostic manner, applying uniform quality metrics across datasets without adequate consideration of the contextual factors that define “quality” in a particular application. For instance, the acceptable level of missing values in a dataset may differ dramatically between a predictive maintenance model in manufacturing, where certain sensor readings are critical for safety, and a recommendation system in e-commerce, where similar gaps may be tolerable or easily imputed. Similarly, the timeliness of data updates may be paramount in real-time fraud detection but less critical in periodic market trend analyses. Without a systematic mechanism to integrate task requirements into quality management processes, organizations risk allocating resources inefficiently—either over-investing in aspects of quality that have negligible impact on performance or under-addressing factors that critically impair outcomes.

A task-driven perspective on data quality management seeks to bridge this disconnect by framing quality not as an abstract, uniform ideal but as a property defined relative to a specific use case. This approach requires rethinking both the assessment and remediation phases of DQM. Assessment involves evaluating data in light of the functional, operational, and performance criteria of the task, potentially redefining quality dimensions or weighting them differently. Remediation involves prioritizing interventions based on their expected impact on task performance rather than on generalized benchmarks. The challenge lies in developing a unified framework that can systematically capture the interplay between task characteristics, data properties, and quality dimensions, while remaining adaptable to diverse domains and rapidly changing requirements.

Recent advances in machine learning, semantic modeling, and automated data profiling provide promising tools for operationalizing task-driven DQM. For example, performance sensitivity analysis can be employed to quantify the relationship between variations in specific quality attributes and changes in task outcomes. Ontology-based representations can formalize task requirements and data semantics, enabling more precise alignment between them. Furthermore, the growing emphasis on explainability and accountability in AI-driven systems amplifies the importance of transparent, task-aware quality management processes, as stakeholders increasingly demand justifications for decisions informed by data.

Despite these developments, the literature remains fragmented, with limited integration of task-specific considerations into a cohesive, end-to-end DQM framework. Existing models often address isolated aspects—such as quality assessment for a particular domain or automated cleaning techniques tailored to specific error types—without providing a generalized methodology that can be applied consistently across diverse contexts. Consequently, practitioners face difficulties in adapting available methods to new tasks, and researchers lack a common foundation for comparing and advancing task-driven approaches.

This paper addresses this gap by proposing a unified framework for task-driven data quality management that explicitly links data quality dimensions, assessment methods, and remediation strategies to the requirements of the target task. The framework integrates principles from information quality theory, task analysis, and performance-driven optimization, offering a structured methodology for aligning data quality efforts with task objectives. By grounding quality management in the realities of task execution, the proposed approach aims to enhance both the efficiency and the effectiveness of data-dependent processes. The remainder of this paper details the conceptual foundations of the framework, its operational components, and its application to representative use cases, illustrating its adaptability and impact across domains.
conclusion: This paper presented a unified framework for task-driven data quality management, integrating quality assessment, improvement, and monitoring into a cohesive process guided by downstream task requirements. By aligning data quality dimensions with specific task objectives, the framework enables targeted interventions that maximize the utility of available data while minimizing unnecessary processing. The approach supports both proactive and adaptive strategies, allowing dynamic responses to evolving data conditions. Experimental results and case studies demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing performance across diverse application domains. Future work will explore automated feedback loops between task performance and quality metrics, as well as scalability to large, heterogeneous datasets. Overall, this framework offers a principled basis for data quality management that is both context-aware and performance-driven.

title: Double injection, resonant-tunneling recombination, and current-voltage characteristics in double-graphene-layer structures
abstract: We analyze the electronic transport and recombination processes in double-graphene-layer (double-GL) structures under conditions of double carrier injection and resonant-tunneling recombination. The study is motivated by the unique band structure of graphene, which enables efficient tunneling between closely spaced layers separated by an ultrathin insulating barrier. Using a self-consistent model that incorporates interlayer potential distribution, carrier injection from contacts, and momentum-conserving tunneling, we derive analytic expressions for the steady-state carrier densities and recombination rates. We show that when the applied bias aligns the Dirac points of the two layers, resonant tunneling leads to a sharp enhancement of interlayer recombination, strongly affecting the current-voltage (I–V) characteristics. The interplay between double injection and resonant tunneling results in pronounced nonlinearity, including regions of negative differential resistance. We further examine the role of carrier heating and broadening effects on the tunneling resonance and demonstrate that these factors can significantly modify the peak-to-valley ratio in the I–V curves. The results suggest that double-GL structures with optimized barrier thicknesses and doping profiles can operate as high-speed electronic or optoelectronic devices, exploiting the resonant-tunneling-assisted recombination for signal modulation. Our findings provide guidance for the design of graphene-based resonant tunneling diodes and photodetectors, and they elucidate the fundamental transport mechanisms governing double-injection regimes in two-dimensional layered systems.
introduction:
Double-graphene-layer (double-GL) structures have attracted significant attention in recent years due to their unique electronic properties and potential applications in high-speed and optoelectronic devices. Consisting of two closely spaced monolayer graphene sheets separated by a thin insulating barrier, such heterostructures enable quantum mechanical tunneling of carriers between the layers. The atomically thin nature of graphene, combined with its linear energy dispersion and high carrier mobility, provides a platform for realizing novel transport regimes not accessible in conventional semiconductor heterostructures. Among these regimes, resonant tunneling and double injection of carriers play a central role in determining the recombination processes and the resulting current–voltage (I–V) characteristics.

In double-GL systems, resonant tunneling can occur when the energy bands of the two graphene layers are properly aligned by an applied bias or electrostatic gating. In this condition, electrons and holes can tunnel between layers with minimal scattering, leading to sharp features in the I–V characteristics, including negative differential resistance (NDR). Such behavior is of considerable interest for applications in oscillators, amplifiers, and fast switching devices. The recombination of injected carriers through resonant tunneling is a key process that governs the steady-state and dynamic response of the structure. In particular, when both layers are populated with carriers of opposite type—electrons in one layer and holes in the other—double injection can take place, enabling significant interlayer recombination rates mediated by tunneling.

The interplay between double injection and resonant-tunneling recombination distinguishes double-GL heterostructures from more conventional double-barrier semiconductor devices. In graphene-based systems, the absence of a bandgap and the symmetric electron–hole dispersion lead to qualitatively different tunneling spectra and bias dependencies. The current transport in such structures is not solely dictated by the density of states and barrier transparency, but also by many-body effects, screening, and the specific momentum conservation constraints imposed by the two-dimensional Dirac spectrum. As a result, the I–V characteristics can exhibit a rich variety of regimes, from quasi-linear behavior at low bias to pronounced NDR peaks associated with resonant alignment, followed by a rapid suppression of current due to detuning.

Understanding the mechanisms of double injection, resonant-tunneling recombination, and their impact on the I–V response is essential for both fundamental physics and technological development. Accurate modeling of these processes can guide the design of double-GL devices with tailored electrical and optoelectronic properties, including frequency-tunable terahertz sources, fast photodetectors, and logic elements. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework to describe the recombination dynamics and current transport in double-GL structures under various biasing conditions, highlighting the role of interlayer coupling, carrier injection balance, and resonance conditions. We analyze the resulting I–V characteristics, discuss their dependence on structural and material parameters, and compare our findings with available experimental data.
conclusion:
In this work, we have analyzed the mechanisms of double injection, resonant-tunneling–assisted recombination, and their impact on the current–voltage characteristics of double–graphene–layer (double-GL) structures. By developing a theoretical framework that accounts for the interlayer resonant tunneling of electrons and holes, as well as their subsequent recombination dynamics, we have identified the key parameters governing the device response under various biasing conditions. Our results demonstrate that resonant tunneling between aligned electron and hole subbands in adjacent graphene sheets can lead to a pronounced enhancement of the interlayer recombination rate, particularly when the applied bias brings the Dirac points into energetic resonance. This enhancement manifests itself as distinct features in the current–voltage characteristics, including sharp peaks and regions of negative differential resistance.

The analysis shows that double injection, where both electrons and holes are simultaneously transferred between layers, can significantly alter the carrier distributions and the electrostatic potential profile in the structure. The interplay between double injection and resonant tunneling sets the threshold and amplitude of the current peaks, as well as the onset of strong recombination-induced current saturation. The theoretical model predicts that at moderate temperatures and for realistic barrier thicknesses, the combined effect of these processes can be tailored by adjusting the interlayer voltage, barrier properties, and carrier doping, offering a pathway to control the non-linear transport response.

Our findings suggest that the observed features in the I–V characteristics of double-GL devices are not solely determined by single-particle tunneling, but result from a complex balance between injection, tunneling resonance, and recombination kinetics. This has important implications for the design of graphene-based tunneling transistors, oscillators, and detectors operating in the terahertz and infrared ranges, where sharp resonances and high-speed carrier dynamics are advantageous. Future work may extend the present analysis to include many-body effects, hot-carrier phenomena, and the influence of optical pumping, further broadening the potential application space. Overall, the interplay of double injection and resonant-tunneling–assisted recombination provides a rich mechanism for engineering the transport properties of double-graphene-layer structures, enabling novel device functionalities.

title: Classical tests in brane gravity
abstract: We investigate the classical tests of general relativity within the framework of brane-world gravity, focusing on the Randall–Sundrum type II scenario. Modifications to the Schwarzschild geometry induced by extra-dimensional effects are derived, and their impact on light deflection, perihelion precession, and radar echo delay is analyzed. Using perturbative methods, we obtain corrections to the standard general relativistic predictions and compare them with current observational bounds. The results constrain the brane tension and the magnitude of bulk-induced Weyl curvature terms. Our analysis shows that solar-system measurements place stringent limits on deviations from general relativity, providing a useful probe of extra-dimensional physics in gravitational phenomena.
introduction:
The study of gravity has undergone profound developments since the advent of Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which replaced Newtonian gravitation with a geometric description of spacetime curvature. For over a century, general relativity (GR) has withstood a wide range of experimental and observational tests, particularly in the so‑called classical regime, comprising phenomena within the Solar System and involving weak gravitational fields. These classical tests include the perihelion precession of Mercury, the deflection of light by the Sun, the gravitational redshift of light, and the Shapiro time delay. Each of these experimental verifications has not only confirmed the predictions of GR to high precision but also served as a benchmark for assessing alternative theories of gravity.

In recent decades, motivated by attempts to unify gravity with the other fundamental interactions and to address outstanding cosmological problems, extensions of GR have been proposed in a variety of theoretical frameworks. Among these, higher‑dimensional theories have attracted considerable attention. Inspired by string theory and M‑theory, brane world models posit that our observable universe is a four‑dimensional hypersurface (the “brane”) embedded in a higher‑dimensional “bulk” spacetime. In these scenarios, standard model fields are confined to the brane, while gravity can propagate into the extra dimensions. The resulting modifications to the gravitational field equations can have measurable consequences at both cosmological and astrophysical scales.

One of the most influential realizations of this idea is the Randall–Sundrum (RS) brane world model, which demonstrates how extra dimensions can be large or even infinite in extent without contradicting current observational constraints. The effective four‑dimensional Einstein equations on the brane acquire additional terms arising from the embedding in the bulk and from the projection of the bulk Weyl tensor. These corrections can alter gravitational dynamics, particularly in the vicinity of massive bodies, and thus lead to deviations from GR predictions in the weak‑field limit. Consequently, the classical tests of GR provide a natural and stringent arena in which to probe the viability of brane gravity models.

The importance of examining classical tests in the context of brane world scenarios stems from the dual role they play: on one hand, they serve as a necessary consistency check for any modified gravity theory; on the other, they provide a potential observational window into extra‑dimensional physics. The extraordinary precision achieved in Solar System measurements—such as modern radar ranging to planets and spacecraft tracking, very‑long‑baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations of light deflection, and atomic clock experiments measuring gravitational time dilation—means that even small deviations from GR can, in principle, be detected or tightly constrained.

Previous analyses have explored the impact of brane‑induced corrections on planetary motion, light propagation, and time delay, often leading to bounds on the parameters that characterize the extra dimensions, such as the brane tension or the bulk curvature scale. However, many of these studies employ simplifying assumptions, and a systematic treatment of the classical tests within a unified formalism remains of considerable interest. Moreover, recent observational advances motivate revisiting these calculations with updated experimental limits, thereby refining the constraints on brane models.

In this work, we investigate the classical tests of general relativity in the context of a specific brane gravity framework, focusing on the weak‑field solutions of the effective gravitational field equations on the brane. We derive the modifications to standard GR predictions for perihelion precession, light deflection, and radar echo delay, and compare them with the most precise current experimental data. Our goal is to determine the extent to which classical Solar System tests can constrain the parameters of the brane model under consideration, and to assess whether any allowed deviations might be detectable with foreseeable improvements in measurement accuracy.

By systematically confronting brane gravity predictions with classical tests, we aim to clarify the extent to which extra‑dimensional effects are compatible with well‑established empirical facts, and to delineate the parameter space in which such theories remain viable. This approach not only strengthens the empirical foundations of gravitational theory but also contributes to the broader effort to bridge the gap between high‑energy theoretical models and precision gravitational physics.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the implications of classical tests of general relativity within the framework of brane gravity scenarios. By analyzing light deflection, perihelion precession, and radar echo delay, we have identified the extent to which extra-dimensional corrections could manifest in solar system experiments. Our results show that, within current observational precision, the deviations from general relativity are strongly constrained, placing stringent bounds on the brane tension and the induced modifications to the Schwarzschild geometry. These findings reinforce the consistency of general relativity at accessible scales while leaving open the possibility of detectable signatures in higher-precision or strong-field regimes. Future observational campaigns, particularly those involving spacecraft tracking and pulsar timing, may further tighten these bounds or reveal subtle anomalies. The study thus provides a useful bridge between theoretical developments in higher-dimensional gravity and empirical tests, highlighting the continued relevance of classical experiments in probing fundamental physics.

title: VUV-synchrotron absorption studies of N$_2$ and CO at 900 K
abstract: High-resolution vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) absorption spectra of molecular nitrogen (N$_2$) and carbon monoxide (CO) have been recorded at a temperature of 900 K using synchrotron radiation as a tunable, intense light source. The measurements cover the 90–115 nm range with a resolving power up to 100,000, enabling precise determination of rotationally resolved line positions and intensities. Elevated-temperature spectra reveal extensive hot-band structure and enhanced population of high rotational levels, providing new constraints for spectroscopic models and potential energy curves. For N$_2$, transitions to the $b^1\Pi_u$ and $c'_4\ ^1\Sigma_u^+$ states were analyzed, while for CO, Rydberg and valence states converging to the first ionization limit were examined. Absolute cross sections were derived and compared with existing room-temperature data, yielding improved temperature-dependent parameters relevant to astrophysical and planetary atmosphere modeling. The results extend the database of high-temperature VUV spectra for diatomic molecules of fundamental and applied interest.
introduction:
High-temperature spectroscopic data for simple diatomic molecules are of critical importance in a wide range of scientific and technological contexts, from astrophysical modeling to plasma diagnostics and atmospheric re-entry simulations. Among these molecules, nitrogen (N\(_2\)) and carbon monoxide (CO) are of particular significance due to their abundance in planetary atmospheres, interstellar media, and combustion environments. Their electronic spectra, especially in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) region, are of central interest for understanding radiative processes, photodissociation pathways, and energy transfer mechanisms under elevated thermal conditions. Accurate laboratory measurements of absorption cross sections at high temperatures are therefore essential for refining theoretical models and for interpreting observational data from both terrestrial and extraterrestrial sources.

At room temperature, the spectroscopy of N\(_2\) and CO in the VUV has been extensively investigated, leading to well-established term values, oscillator strengths, and predissociation rates for many electronic states. However, at elevated temperatures, the populations of higher rotational and vibrational levels increase significantly, giving rise to new absorption features and altered line shapes. These changes can strongly influence the integrated absorption cross sections and the onset of continuum absorption. High-temperature data are also needed to validate ab initio calculations that incorporate rotational-vibrational excitation, as well as to provide inputs for non-equilibrium models of high-enthalpy flows. Despite their importance, high-resolution VUV absorption measurements at temperatures approaching 900 K remain comparatively scarce, owing to the experimental challenges associated with generating and maintaining uniform, high-temperature gaseous samples in the VUV beam path, and with achieving sufficient spectral resolution and signal-to-noise ratios in this spectral region.

The VUV region, ranging approximately from 100 to 200 nm in wavelength (10–6 eV photon energy), encompasses the first allowed electronic transitions of N\(_2\) and CO, including the well-known Lyman–Birge–Hopfield and \(b^1\Pi\)–\(X^1\Sigma^+\) systems, as well as numerous Rydberg series converging to the ionization limits. These transitions are sensitive to both rotational and vibrational excitation, and their intensities and profiles can be markedly different at elevated temperatures. For example, hot-band transitions originating from thermally populated excited vibrational states become more prominent, and perturbations between closely spaced energy levels can be enhanced by increased rotational congestion. Detailed measurements in this regime can thus provide stringent tests for multi-state coupled-channel models and for potential energy curves derived from high-level quantum chemistry.

Synchrotron radiation sources offer unique advantages for such studies, providing a continuous, intense, and tunable VUV photon flux with high spectral brightness. Coupled with high-resolution monochromators, synchrotron-based absorption spectroscopy enables precise determination of line positions, widths, and strengths over a broad spectral range. Furthermore, the stability and reproducibility of synchrotron output facilitate quantitative absorption cross-section measurements even in the challenging VUV domain, where conventional light sources are limited. Recent developments in windowless gas cells, heated absorption paths, and differential pumping techniques have further expanded the capability to probe high-temperature samples without significant contamination of the ultrahigh vacuum environment required for VUV beamlines.

Previous high-temperature VUV studies of N\(_2\) and CO have typically been limited either in spectral range or in resolution, often focusing on specific band systems or on integrated absorption over broad features. For example, studies using shock-tube techniques have achieved high temperatures but with transient conditions and modest spectral resolution, while some synchrotron-based measurements have examined heated gases but at temperatures lower than 900 K or with limited rotational resolution. Consequently, there remains a need for systematic, high-resolution, and wide-range VUV absorption measurements of these molecules under steady-state high-temperature conditions.

In this work, we report VUV-synchrotron absorption spectra of N\(_2\) and CO at a nominal temperature of 900 K, recorded over a broad spectral range encompassing several electronic band systems. The measurements were performed at high spectral resolution, enabling us to resolve individual rotational lines and to characterize hot-band transitions in detail. By comparing the spectra with room-temperature data and with theoretical simulations, we extract information on temperature-dependent line shifts, predissociation broadening, and changes in band intensities. The data contribute to the refinement of spectroscopic constants for excited states, to the validation of potential energy curves and coupling parameters, and to the construction of high-temperature absorption cross-section databases.

Our results address critical gaps in the available spectroscopic data for N\(_2\) and CO, providing a benchmark for modeling environments such as the upper atmospheres of planets, the interstellar medium subjected to shock heating, and the high-temperature regions of combustion and plasma systems. Furthermore, the experimental approach demonstrated here establishes a framework for future high-resolution VUV studies of other molecular species under extreme thermal conditions, thereby extending the reach of laboratory astrophysics and high-temperature molecular physics.
conclusion:
High-resolution VUV-synchrotron absorption measurements of N$_2$ and CO at 900 K have been presented, yielding comprehensive datasets on line positions, oscillator strengths, and predissociation linewidths for a range of electronic transitions. By employing a heated windowless absorption cell and exploiting the broad spectral coverage and high brightness of synchrotron radiation, we have extended previous room-temperature studies into a largely unexplored high-temperature regime. The elevated temperature populates a wide range of rotational and some vibrational levels, enabling the observation of hot-band transitions and high-$J$ lines that are absent or extremely weak at ambient conditions. This has allowed a more complete characterization of the rotational dependence of oscillator strengths and line broadening, including the identification of perturbations due to state interactions that become more prominent at high $J$.

For N$_2$, the measurements reveal significant $J$-dependent variations in line positions and widths within the $b$–$X$ and $c$–$X$ bands, consistent with earlier perturbation analyses but now extended to much higher rotational excitations. The high-temperature data improve the determination of molecular constants and predissociation rates, particularly for levels near avoided crossings with dissociative states. For CO, the $A$–$X$, $B$–$X$, and $C$–$X$ systems have been recorded with sufficient resolution to resolve individual rotational lines up to $J \approx 50$. The extracted oscillator strengths show systematic trends with $J$ that can be linked to rotational perturbations and intensity borrowing, and the linewidth data provide new constraints on the lifetimes of upper-state levels, especially those influenced by spin-orbit and non-adiabatic couplings.

The present results have direct implications for astrophysical and planetary atmospheric modelling. Accurate high-temperature absorption cross sections are essential for interpreting spectra of warm molecular gas in diverse environments, from the upper atmospheres of exoplanets and solar system bodies to shock-heated interstellar clouds. The extended rotational coverage and hot-band identifications will improve the accuracy of radiative transfer calculations under non-equilibrium conditions, where elevated rotational temperatures are common. In addition, the predissociation parameters obtained here contribute to a better understanding of molecular photodissociation rates at high temperatures, which influence the chemical balance in such environments.

Beyond their immediate application, these measurements provide valuable benchmarks for ab initio calculations of excited-state potential energy curves, couplings, and transition moments. The observed perturbations and their $J$-dependence offer stringent tests for theoretical models aiming to reproduce rovibronic structure over a wide range of energies. The ability to reproduce both the line positions and intensities for highly excited rotational levels remains a critical challenge, and the present dataset should stimulate further theoretical developments.

In summary, VUV-synchrotron absorption spectroscopy at elevated temperatures has yielded a rich set of experimental data for N$_2$ and CO, significantly extending the scope of previous work. The combination of broad spectral coverage, high resolution, and high temperature enables a deeper understanding of molecular structure and dynamics in conditions relevant to high-energy environments in nature and technology.

title: On Lipschitz-like property for polyhedral moving sets
abstract: We investigate the Lipschitz-like property for parameter-dependent polyhedral sets. Using variational analysis and geometric characterizations, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions ensuring stability of feasible points under perturbations. Applications to parametric optimization and equilibrium models are discussed, demonstrating the practical relevance of the derived criteria for sensitivity analysis and robust solution behavior.
introduction:
Variational analysis and generalized differentiation provide a powerful framework for studying stability properties of solution mappings to parameterized problems. Among these properties, the Lipschitz-like behavior—also referred to as the Aubin property—plays a central role in sensitivity analysis, as it ensures a uniform bound on the variation of feasible solutions with respect to perturbations in parameters. This property has been extensively investigated for multifunctions arising from variational inequalities, optimization problems, and equilibrium systems, with numerous characterizations available in terms of coderivatives and other generalized differential constructions.

A particularly important class of problems involves so-called moving sets, where the feasible set itself depends on a parameter. Such situations arise naturally in state-constrained control, contact mechanics, and economic equilibria, where the constraint set shifts or deforms in response to changes in the underlying data. When the moving sets possess a polyhedral structure—defined, for example, by finitely many linear inequalities depending on parameters—the analysis benefits from the rich geometric and combinatorial properties of polyhedra. In this context, the main challenge lies in formulating verifiable conditions under which the associated feasible-set mapping exhibits the Lipschitz-like property around a given reference point.

Earlier contributions have addressed the Aubin property for solution mappings to generalized equations with polyhedral graphs, using tools from Robinson’s theory of strong regularity and metric regularity. However, the case of parameterized polyhedral sets does not always fit directly into these frameworks, especially when the dependence on parameters is nontrivial and the representation of the set changes locally. This raises the question of how to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for Lipschitz-like behavior that are both geometrically transparent and computationally tractable.

The present work is devoted to a systematic study of the Lipschitz-like property for mappings defined by polyhedral moving sets. We aim to bridge the gap between general coderivative-based criteria and specialized results available for fixed polyhedral sets or affine variational inequalities. Our approach combines variational analysis techniques with a careful examination of the parametric structure of the defining inequalities. In doing so, we provide new characterizations that admit direct verification from the data of the problem, as well as insights into the role of active constraints and critical faces in determining stability. The results extend and unify several known criteria, and they open the way to further developments in the analysis of polyhedral multifunctions arising in optimization and related fields.
conclusion: We have established sufficient conditions ensuring the Lipschitz-like property for parameter-dependent polyhedral sets. The results extend existing criteria and offer practical verifiability through explicit geometric characterizations. These findings contribute to stability analysis in variational systems, providing a robust framework for studying sensitivity of solutions under polyhedral structure.

title: Can an underestimation of opacity explain B-type pulsators in the SMC?
abstract: We investigate whether an underestimation of stellar opacity can account for the presence of B-type pulsators in the low-metallicity environment of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). Current stellar models, adopting standard opacity tables, fail to predict the observed incidence of Slowly Pulsating B (SPB) stars and β Cephei variables at the SMC’s metallicity (Z ≈ 0.002). We compute non-adiabatic pulsation models for main-sequence B stars, systematically modifying the iron-group opacity profile near the Z-bump (T ≈ 2×10⁵ K). Our analysis shows that moderate opacity enhancements, particularly in the iron contribution, can significantly extend the instability strips toward lower metallicities, allowing the excitation of both SPB and β Cephei modes in the SMC. The required opacity increase is within the uncertainties suggested by recent experimental and theoretical studies. These results support the hypothesis that opacity underestimation may be a key factor in explaining pulsations in low-Z environments, and highlight the need for improved opacity measurements to refine stellar pulsation theory and reconcile models with extragalactic observations.
introduction:
B-type pulsators, such as β Cephei and Slowly Pulsating B (SPB) stars, are main-sequence stars whose variability is driven by the κ-mechanism operating in the so‑called iron-group opacity bump around temperatures of 200,000 K. The excitation of pulsation modes in these stars is highly sensitive to the local opacity, which in turn depends on the abundance of heavy elements—particularly iron, nickel, and related species. In the Milky Way, the instability strips of these pulsators are well reproduced by theoretical models using current opacity data and solar-like metallicities. However, in low-metallicity environments such as the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), theory predicts a significant reduction in the number of excited modes, and in some cases, the complete absence of β Cephei stars, due to the diminished iron-group opacity.

Observations over the last two decades have challenged these predictions. Photometric surveys of the SMC have revealed both β Cephei and SPB candidates, despite the low average metallicity (Z ≈ 0.002–0.004). The presence of these pulsators in the SMC therefore poses a problem for standard stellar models: according to current opacity calculations, the iron-group bump at such low heavy-element content should be insufficient to drive the observed variability. This discrepancy suggests that either the input physics in the models is incomplete or inaccurate, or that the chemical composition in these stars is somehow enhanced relative to the average SMC values, perhaps through processes such as diffusion or accretion.

One possible explanation is that the opacities used in stellar models are underestimated in the relevant temperature range. Over the past decade, experimental and theoretical work has indicated that certain opacity sources, particularly for iron and nickel, may be systematically underpredicted. Laboratory measurements of the monochromatic opacity of iron at conditions approaching those in stellar interiors have yielded values significantly higher than those from standard opacity tables, such as OPAL or OP. In addition, revisions to atomic data and line-broadening treatments have been shown to affect the calculated Rosseland mean opacities in the iron-bump region. If the true opacities in the driving zone are indeed higher than assumed, the κ-mechanism could remain efficient even at low overall metallicities, potentially explaining the existence of B-type pulsators in the SMC.

In this context, it becomes crucial to assess the extent to which an underestimation of opacity could reconcile theory with observation. By examining the sensitivity of pulsation excitation to modifications in the iron-group opacity profile, and by comparing the resulting instability domains with those inferred from SMC observations, we can test whether such an adjustment provides a viable solution. This investigation not only bears on the specific case of B-type pulsators in the SMC, but also has broader implications for stellar physics: accurate opacities are fundamental to modelling stellar structure and evolution across the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated whether an underestimation of stellar opacities could account for the presence of B-type pulsators observed in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), whose low metallicity environment challenges current theoretical predictions. Using updated stellar models and systematically enhanced opacity profiles in the iron-group element bump region, we examined the excitation of β Cephei and Slowly Pulsating B (SPB) modes under SMC-like conditions. Our results confirm that standard opacity data fail to produce unstable modes at the observed metallicities, consistent with previous studies. However, we find that a moderate increase in opacity—particularly near the temperatures where Fe, Ni, and other iron-group elements contribute most strongly—can restore mode instability in models representative of the SMC population.

The degree of enhancement required is non-uniform across the relevant temperature range, suggesting that any physical opacity revision would need to be selective rather than global. This is in qualitative agreement with recent experimental and theoretical work indicating possible underestimations in the contribution of specific ions. Nonetheless, the magnitude of the opacity increase necessary in our models, while plausible in light of these studies, is still at the upper limit of current uncertainties.

Our findings imply that opacity underestimation offers a viable, though not exclusive, explanation for the apparent discrepancy between observation and theory. Additional processes, such as rotational mixing or local metallicity variations, may act in concert with opacity effects. Future work combining refined opacity calculations, improved abundance determinations in the SMC, and extended mode identification for a larger sample of pulsators will be essential to fully resolve this issue. Ultimately, confronting stellar models with high-precision observational constraints remains a powerful approach to probing the microphysics governing stellar interiors.

title: PLG-IN: Pluggable Geometric Consistency Loss with Wasserstein Distance in Monocular Depth Estimation
abstract: We propose **PLG-IN**, a novel monocular depth estimation framework that introduces a pluggable geometric consistency loss based on the Wasserstein distance. Unlike conventional photometric or pixel-wise losses, our approach enforces structural alignment between predicted and target depth maps in a transport-based metric space, improving robustness to illumination changes and textureless regions. The geometric loss is modular and can be integrated into existing depth estimation networks without architectural modifications. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PLG-IN consistently enhances depth accuracy and preserves fine structural details, achieving competitive performance while maintaining computational efficiency across diverse training settings.
introduction:
Monocular depth estimation aims to infer scene depth from a single RGB image, a task that is inherently ill-posed due to the loss of geometric information during projection from the 3D world to the 2D image plane. Accurate depth prediction underpins a broad range of applications in robotics, autonomous driving, augmented reality, and scene understanding. In recent years, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and, more recently, vision transformers have substantially advanced performance on this task by learning powerful image representations from large-scale datasets. However, monocular depth estimation remains challenging, particularly in unconstrained environments, due to ambiguities in scale, occlusion handling, textureless regions, and varying camera intrinsics.

To address these challenges, many approaches have incorporated geometric constraints into learning frameworks. Supervised methods leverage ground-truth depth maps obtained via LiDAR or structured light sensors, but such data acquisition is costly and often impractical at scale. Self-supervised methods, on the other hand, exploit photometric reprojection losses and geometric relationships between multiple views, enabling training from readily available monocular or stereo video sequences. Despite their success, photometric consistency losses are sensitive to illumination changes, non-Lambertian surfaces, and dynamic scenes, often leading to suboptimal depth predictions.

Geometric consistency losses have emerged as an effective means to regularize depth estimation by enforcing agreement between predicted depth maps and the underlying 3D scene geometry. These losses typically operate by projecting depth predictions into a common frame and penalizing discrepancies. While this strategy improves robustness to photometric artifacts, existing formulations often rely on pixel-wise differences or simple L1/L2 distances between warped depth maps, which may insufficiently capture the global structure of depth distributions. Moreover, such metrics are sensitive to noise and fail to fully exploit the geometric relationships between estimated and target depth maps in a distributional sense.

Optimal transport theory, and in particular the Wasserstein distance, offers a principled way to measure differences between probability distributions by considering the cost of transporting mass from one distribution to another. Unlike point-wise metrics, the Wasserstein distance is sensitive to the underlying geometry of the data space, making it well-suited for comparing depth maps where spatial relationships are important. Recent studies in related domains, such as generative modeling and domain adaptation, have demonstrated the advantages of incorporating Wasserstein-based losses to capture structural discrepancies.

In this work, we propose **PLG-IN**, a *Pluggable Geometric Consistency Loss* based on the Wasserstein distance, designed to enhance monocular depth estimation in both supervised and self-supervised settings. Our key insight is to treat depth maps as spatial probability distributions and to measure their geometric consistency via an optimal transport formulation. By modeling the alignment between predicted and reference depth distributions in a way that respects spatial structure, PLG-IN mitigates the limitations of conventional pixel-wise losses and provides a richer supervisory signal.

The proposed PLG-IN module is *pluggable* in the sense that it can be seamlessly integrated into existing monocular depth estimation pipelines without architectural modifications. It complements photometric and smoothness losses in self-supervised frameworks, as well as regression losses in supervised ones, by introducing a geometry-aware term that encourages globally consistent depth predictions. We further derive an efficient approximation of the Wasserstein distance that is computationally feasible for high-resolution depth maps, enabling practical deployment in large-scale training.

We evaluate PLG-IN on standard monocular depth estimation benchmarks, including KITTI and NYU Depth V2, demonstrating consistent improvements over strong baselines in both supervised and self-supervised settings. Qualitative analysis reveals that our approach better preserves object boundaries, maintains structural coherence in textureless regions, and recovers more accurate depth in challenging scenarios. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) we introduce a novel pluggable geometric consistency loss based on the Wasserstein distance for monocular depth estimation; (2) we propose an efficient implementation suitable for high-resolution training; and (3) we provide extensive empirical validation showing PLG-IN’s effectiveness and generality.

By bridging optimal transport theory with geometric consistency modeling, PLG-IN offers a principled and flexible means to enhance depth estimation performance, paving the way for more robust and accurate monocular 3D perception systems.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced **PLG-IN**, a pluggable geometric consistency loss framework that integrates the Wasserstein distance into monocular depth estimation to enhance depth prediction accuracy and structural coherence. By leveraging the Wasserstein metric, our method captures fine-grained geometric discrepancies between predicted and ground-truth depth maps, enabling more stable and informative gradient signals during training. The pluggable design ensures compatibility with various backbone architectures and loss formulations, making PLG-IN easily adaptable to existing pipelines without extensive modification. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PLG-IN consistently improves performance across multiple evaluation metrics, particularly in preserving object boundaries and recovering scene geometry under challenging conditions. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the geometric consistency component and its synergy with the Wasserstein-based formulation. These results highlight the potential of incorporating transport-based metrics into depth estimation to bridge the gap between pixel-level supervision and holistic scene understanding. Future work will explore extending this framework to self-supervised and multi-view settings, as well as investigating more efficient approximations of the Wasserstein distance for large-scale, real-time applications.

title: Selective linear or quadratic optomechanical coupling via measurement
abstract: We investigate a scheme for selectively realizing linear or quadratic optomechanical coupling through measurement-based techniques. By tailoring the optical measurement basis, we engineer effective Hamiltonians in which the mechanical displacement couples either linearly or quadratically to the optical field. Our approach exploits quantum correlations and conditional dynamics to suppress unwanted terms, enabling flexible control over the interaction form without altering the physical device. Numerical simulations demonstrate high-fidelity selection of the desired coupling regime in experimentally realistic conditions. This method provides a versatile tool for quantum state preparation, mechanical sensing, and exploring nonlinear quantum effects in cavity optomechanical systems.
introduction:
Optomechanical systems, in which optical and mechanical degrees of freedom interact via radiation pressure, have emerged as an important platform for exploring fundamental aspects of quantum physics as well as enabling applications in precision measurement, sensing, and quantum information processing. The canonical example consists of an optical cavity with a mechanically compliant element, such as a membrane or a movable mirror, whose displacement shifts the cavity resonance frequency. This interaction naturally leads to a coupling between the intracavity field and the mechanical position that is typically linear to first order in displacement. Such linear optomechanical coupling underpins a wide range of phenomena, including sideband cooling, quantum-limited displacement detection, and the generation of entanglement between light and mechanics.

In addition to this linear regime, there is growing interest in accessing quadratic optomechanical coupling, in which the relevant interaction depends on the square of the mechanical displacement. Quadratic coupling enables qualitatively different capabilities: it allows for quantum non-demolition (QND) measurements of the mechanical energy, preparation of nonclassical mechanical states, and access to phonon-number-resolved dynamics. Systems with intrinsic quadratic coupling have been realized, for instance, in “membrane-in-the-middle” geometries or using higher-order optical modes, but the strength of such coupling is often much weaker than that of the linear term, and achieving selective access to purely quadratic interactions without residual linear contributions remains experimentally challenging.

The ability to switch between or selectively address linear and quadratic couplings in a single device would be highly advantageous, both for exploring fundamental physics and for implementing flexible quantum technologies. However, in standard cavity optomechanics, the form of the coupling is dictated by the device geometry and is fixed once the system is fabricated. Recent theoretical and experimental work has suggested that measurement-based techniques, leveraging interference between different optical modes or measurement back-action, can be used to engineer effective interactions that differ from the bare Hamiltonian. Such approaches open the possibility of dynamically tailoring the form of the optomechanical coupling without physically altering the device structure.

In the measurement-based paradigm, one uses the quantum correlations between the optical outputs and the mechanical motion, together with appropriate detection schemes, to reconstruct and control the mechanical dynamics. By choosing suitable optical probes, detection quadratures, and signal processing, it is possible to suppress or enhance specific contributions to the measured signal. For example, destructive interference between signals from multiple cavity modes can cancel the leading-order (linear) dependence on displacement, thereby isolating the quadratic term. Conversely, constructive interference can be used to maximize sensitivity to the linear term while rejecting quadratic contributions. This selective measurement effectively realizes a tailored optomechanical interaction at the level of the detected signal, even if the underlying physical coupling remains unchanged.

Such measurement-induced engineering of the coupling form has several appealing features. It can be implemented in situ, without modifying the optomechanical device itself, by adjusting only the optical probing and detection configuration. It is compatible with a variety of cavity geometries and mechanical elements, and can be reconfigured dynamically to alternate between different measurement regimes. Moreover, by working at the measurement level, one can exploit quantum-limited detection techniques and correlated optical noise to mitigate measurement back-action and enhance sensitivity.

In this work, we investigate a general scheme for selectively realizing effective linear or quadratic optomechanical coupling via measurement. We consider a setup in which two optical cavity modes couple to the same mechanical displacement, with distinct coupling coefficients and detunings. By appropriately combining the outputs of these modes in a balanced detection scheme, we show that the measured signal can be made proportional either to the mechanical displacement or to its square. We analyze the conditions under which the unwanted term can be cancelled to leading order, taking into account realistic imperfections such as mismatched coupling rates and finite detection efficiency. We further examine the impact of quantum noise and back-action on the measurement sensitivity in both regimes.

Our results provide a versatile route to engineer the form of the optomechanical coupling in a purely measurement-based manner, offering a flexible tool for quantum control of mechanical motion. This approach enables new experimental possibilities, from QND measurements of phonon number to high-bandwidth displacement sensing, within the same optomechanical platform.
conclusion: We have investigated a measurement-based strategy for selectively accessing either linear or quadratic optomechanical coupling in a generic cavity–mechanical system. By tailoring the detection scheme to exploit interference between different optical pathways, the effective measurement operator can be engineered to emphasize or suppress specific orders of the mechanical displacement. This approach allows the extraction of purely linear or purely quadratic information from a system whose intrinsic interaction may naturally contain both contributions. Our analysis demonstrates that the selectivity is robust against moderate imperfections in detection efficiency and phase stability, and can be implemented with standard homodyne or heterodyne techniques. Importantly, the scheme does not require modification of the physical optomechanical device, relying instead on flexible post-selection and signal processing, making it broadly applicable across platforms. This capability enables enhanced metrological performance in scenarios where one coupling type is advantageous, and facilitates studies of quantum nonlinearities in mechanical motion without spurious contamination from undesired coupling orders. The proposed measurement protocol thus provides a versatile tool for controlling the effective form of the optomechanical interaction, with potential applications ranging from precision sensing to the preparation and characterization of nonclassical mechanical states.

title: High-spin structures of 124-131Te: Competition of proton and neutron pair breakings
abstract: High-spin states in the isotopes \(^{124-131}\)Te have been investigated through γ-ray spectroscopy following heavy-ion induced reactions. The level schemes have been extended significantly, and new transitions have been placed based on γ–γ coincidence relationships and directional correlation measurements. The observed structures reveal a complex interplay between proton and neutron pair breaking mechanisms as angular momentum increases.
