Integrating template matching into deep architectures can enhance interpretability and robustness while retaining the expressive power of CNNs. In this work, we propose a novel ResNet block that embeds features through differentiable template matching, enabling pattern-specific responses within the residual framework. This approach bridges handcrafted feature concepts with modern deep learning design.
conclusion: This work introduced a novel ResNet block formulation that performs feature embedding through template matching, integrating similarity-based representations directly into the residual learning framework. By replacing or augmenting conventional convolutional operations with template correlation, the proposed design enables the network to capture structured, interpretable patterns while preserving the depth and compositional power of ResNet architectures. Experimental results indicate that this approach can enhance feature discrimination and robustness, particularly in scenarios where repetitive or prototypical structures are prevalent. The method maintains computational efficiency by leveraging optimized correlation computations and compatibility with existing deep learning toolchains. Future work will explore adaptive template learning, multi-scale matching strategies, and applications to domains requiring high invariance to transformations, further extending the utility of template-based embedding within deep residual networks.

title: Efficient data-driven gap filling of satellite image time series using deep neural networks with partial convolutions
abstract: Satellite image time series are often affected by missing data due to cloud cover, sensor malfunctions, or transmission errors, hindering their utility for environmental monitoring and change detection. Traditional gap-filling methods rely on temporal interpolation or auxiliary data, which may fail to capture complex spatial–temporal patterns. In this study, we present an efficient, data-driven approach for reconstructing missing regions in satellite image sequences using deep neural networks with partial convolutions. Partial convolutions enable the model to condition feature extraction exclusively on valid pixels, thereby improving robustness to irregularly shaped and spatially extensive gaps. Our framework leverages multi-temporal context, incorporating adjacent time steps to guide the reconstruction process while preserving fine spatial structures. We evaluate the method on multispectral satellite datasets with artificially and naturally occurring gaps, comparing against state-of-the-art inpainting and interpolation techniques. Results demonstrate superior reconstruction accuracy, visual fidelity, and computational efficiency, highlighting the potential of partial convolution-based deep learning for scalable, high-quality gap filling in large-scale satellite image time series.
introduction:
Satellite-based Earth observation has become an indispensable tool for monitoring environmental processes, mapping land cover, and assessing changes in ecosystems over time. Advances in sensor technology and the increasing availability of high-resolution imagery from missions such as Landsat, Sentinel, and MODIS have enabled the generation of dense time series that capture spatial and temporal dynamics at unprecedented scales. However, the utility of these datasets is often impaired by missing data, caused by factors such as cloud cover, sensor malfunctions, atmospheric effects, and orbital constraints. These gaps can severely limit the accuracy of downstream analyses, reduce the reliability of change detection, and hinder the derivation of continuous environmental indicators.

Traditional gap-filling methods for satellite image time series rely on a variety of strategies, including spatial interpolation, temporal smoothing, and model-based approaches such as harmonic analysis or regression against auxiliary variables. While these methods can be effective in certain settings, they often struggle in heterogeneous landscapes, under complex temporal dynamics, or when large contiguous regions are missing. Moreover, they may require strong assumptions about the underlying data distribution, limiting their ability to generalize across different geographic regions, seasons, or sensor types.

Recent developments in deep learning offer new opportunities for addressing the gap-filling challenge. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in particular have demonstrated remarkable success in image inpainting tasks, where missing regions are reconstructed based on surrounding context. However, standard convolution operations treat missing pixels as valid inputs, which can introduce artifacts and bias the reconstruction, especially in cases with extensive or irregular gaps. To mitigate this, partial convolution techniques have been proposed, wherein the convolution is conditioned only on valid pixels within the receptive field, accompanied by an updated mask that tracks which pixels have been filled. This approach has shown promise in computer vision applications, enabling more accurate and visually coherent reconstructions in natural images.

In the context of satellite image time series, partial convolutions offer an appealing framework for leveraging both spatial and temporal correlations while explicitly handling missing data. By integrating these operations into deep neural network architectures, it becomes possible to progressively reconstruct missing regions in a manner that respects the underlying spatio-temporal structure of the data. Furthermore, a data-driven approach allows the model to learn complex patterns of variation from large-scale archives, potentially outperforming handcrafted gap-filling algorithms and adapting to diverse environmental conditions.

This study proposes an efficient, data-driven method for gap filling in satellite image time series using deep neural networks with partial convolutions. We evaluate the approach on multi-temporal datasets affected by realistic data gaps, examining its ability to reconstruct missing information across a range of spatial extents and temporal contexts. By combining the strengths of modern deep learning with a principled treatment of missing data, our work aims to advance the state of the art in producing complete, high-quality Earth observation time series for scientific and operational applications.
conclusion: This study presented an efficient data-driven approach for gap filling in satellite image time series by leveraging deep neural networks with partial convolutions. The proposed method effectively addressed the challenges posed by missing or corrupted pixels, outperforming conventional interpolation-based techniques in both quantitative accuracy and visual fidelity. By explicitly conditioning convolutions on valid data regions, the model demonstrated strong robustness to irregular gap patterns and varying gap sizes, which are common in real-world remote sensing scenarios due to cloud cover or sensor malfunctions. Experimental results across diverse satellite datasets confirmed the approach’s generalization capability and its potential to preserve fine spatial structures while maintaining temporal consistency. Moreover, the architecture’s ability to integrate spatial and temporal cues without extensive pre-processing makes it a promising candidate for large-scale, automated gap-filling pipelines. While this work focused on optical imagery, the framework is readily adaptable to other modalities, such as SAR or multispectral data, and could benefit further from incorporating domain-specific priors. Future research will explore hybrid models combining partial convolutions with attention mechanisms to enhance contextual reasoning, as well as strategies for uncertainty quantification to support downstream applications in environmental monitoring and change detection.

title: A transition mass for black holes to show broad emission lines
abstract: We investigate the existence of a characteristic black hole mass above which active galactic nuclei (AGN) are capable of producing prominent broad emission lines in their optical and ultraviolet spectra. Broad emission lines, originating in rapidly moving gas close to the central engine, are a defining feature of Type 1 AGN, yet their occurrence is not universal. By combining a large, heterogeneous sample of AGN from recent spectroscopic surveys with reliable black hole mass estimates derived from stellar velocity dispersions, reverberation mapping, and single-epoch scaling relations, we examine the dependence of broad-line detectability on black hole mass, luminosity, and Eddington ratio. Our analysis reveals a statistically significant transition at a black hole mass of approximately \(M_{\mathrm{BH}} \sim 10^{7.5} M_{\odot}\), above which the fraction of AGN exhibiting broad lines rises sharply. This threshold appears robust against selection effects and persists after controlling for bolometric luminosity, suggesting a physical origin rather than a purely observational bias. We discuss possible interpretations, including changes in the structure or survival of the broad-line region (BLR) with black hole mass, the role of radiation pressure in BLR dynamics, and the influence of accretion mode transitions. The results imply that the BLR may be absent or severely diminished in lower-mass black holes, even when accreting efficiently, potentially due to disk-wind launching constraints or the inability to maintain the high-velocity, high-density gas required. This transition mass offers new insight into the co-evolution of black holes and their host galaxies, and into the physical conditions governing BLR formation.
introduction:
Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) residing at the centers of galaxies are often surrounded by dense, fast-moving gas that produces broad emission lines in their spectra. These broad emission lines (BELs), typically observed in active galactic nuclei (AGN), arise from the so-called broad-line region (BLR), where gas velocities reach thousands of kilometers per second. The presence or absence of BELs is a defining feature in AGN classification, distinguishing, for example, Type 1 AGN, which exhibit both broad and narrow emission lines, from Type 2 AGN, where only narrow lines are visible. While orientation and obscuration effects in the unified model of AGN explain some of this diversity, there is increasing evidence that intrinsic physical parameters of the central engine, such as black hole mass and accretion rate, play a significant role in determining the detectability of the BLR.  

One emerging hypothesis is that there exists a critical, or “transition,” black hole mass below which the BLR cannot be sustained or is too weak to produce detectable BELs. This idea stems from theoretical considerations of the BLR’s origin, which link its structure to the accretion disk’s ability to launch and maintain outflows or winds. At lower masses, the characteristic size of the BLR inferred from reverberation mapping relations becomes smaller, and the ionizing luminosity may drop below the threshold needed to keep the gas in the BLR ionized and dynamically supported. Moreover, observational surveys have revealed a population of low-mass AGN candidates that conspicuously lack broad lines, despite showing other signs of nuclear activity, suggesting a possible mass-dependent cutoff.  

Determining whether such a transition mass exists has important implications for AGN physics, black hole demographics, and the interpretation of emission-line surveys. It may help to reconcile discrepancies between optical and X-ray AGN classifications, inform models of BLR formation, and constrain the growth pathways of SMBHs in the low-mass regime. In this work, we investigate the evidence for a transition mass in black holes, explore the physical mechanisms that could drive the disappearance of BELs below this mass, and consider the observational strategies required to identify and characterize such a threshold.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the existence of a characteristic black hole mass above which broad emission lines are likely to be observed in active galactic nuclei. By combining theoretical expectations for the structure of the broad-line region (BLR) with empirical scaling relations between black hole mass, accretion rate, and BLR size, we find evidence for a transition mass scale that separates systems capable of sustaining a BLR from those in which it is absent or severely diminished. Our analysis suggests that this threshold arises from the interplay between gravitational potential, ionizing luminosity, and the dynamical conditions required to maintain high-velocity line-emitting gas. Below the critical mass, the combination of lower luminosity and reduced BLR radius likely leads to the suppression of broad lines, consistent with observations of low-luminosity AGN and certain narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. Above the threshold, the physical conditions favour a stable, optically thick BLR, yielding the characteristic broad Balmer and high-ionization lines. This framework provides a natural explanation for the empirical distribution of emission-line widths across the mass spectrum and may clarify the observed dichotomy between broad-line and narrow-line AGN. Future spectroscopic surveys, particularly those targeting intermediate-mass black holes, will be essential to refine the value of the transition mass and to test its dependence on Eddington ratio and host galaxy properties. Our results underscore the importance of black hole mass as a fundamental parameter in AGN unification schemes and suggest that the presence or absence of broad lines can be understood, at least in part, as a consequence of crossing a physically motivated mass threshold.

title: Understanding 3D Object Articulation in Internet Videos
abstract: We present a novel framework for understanding 3D object articulation from unconstrained Internet videos. Unlike prior methods relying on controlled capture or pre-defined models, our approach leverages noisy, in-the-wild video data to infer part structure, articulation parameters, and motion patterns. We introduce a robust pipeline that combines self-supervised keypoint discovery, motion segmentation, and differentiable rendering to jointly estimate object geometry and kinematics. Experiments on diverse object categories demonstrate that our method generalizes across viewpoints, backgrounds, and articulation types. This work contributes toward scalable, annotation-free learning of 3D articulated object models directly from the vast, varied visual content available online.
introduction:
The ability to understand and model the articulation of three-dimensional objects is fundamental to numerous applications in computer vision, robotics, augmented reality, and human–computer interaction. Articulation refers to the ways in which components of an object can move relative to one another, often constrained by joints, hinges, or other mechanical linkages. Examples abound in everyday life: a laptop lid rotating about its hinge, the swinging arms of a humanoid figure, or the opening and closing of a pair of scissors. Accurate estimation of such articulated motion from visual data enables richer scene understanding, facilitates physical interaction between autonomous systems and their environments, and supports realistic animation and simulation of objects in virtual spaces.

Traditional approaches to 3D articulation analysis have relied heavily on carefully curated datasets, often captured in laboratory settings with controlled lighting, fixed camera configurations, and limited object categories. These datasets, while valuable, impose constraints on the diversity of object types, articulation patterns, and environmental conditions that can be represented. Moreover, many existing methods assume access to complete 3D shape information, either in the form of CAD models or high-fidelity depth scans, which may not be available in unconstrained settings. As a result, there remains a considerable gap between the capabilities of current articulation estimation techniques and the demands of real-world scenarios.

In contrast, the proliferation of user-generated video content on the internet offers a vast and largely untapped resource for learning about 3D object articulation. Online platforms host millions of videos depicting a wide variety of objects undergoing articulated motion, captured across diverse viewpoints, backgrounds, and lighting conditions. These videos include instructional demonstrations, product showcases, mechanical repairs, and everyday activities, providing an unprecedented breadth of examples that span both common and rare object categories. By leveraging this abundance of visual data, it becomes possible to study articulation in a manner that is not only scalable but also reflective of the complexity and variability inherent in real-world environments.

However, extracting meaningful articulation information from internet videos presents significant challenges. First, such videos are typically captured with consumer-grade devices, resulting in motion blur, compression artifacts, and varying frame rates. The camera motion is often unconstrained, leading to complex interactions between object motion and viewpoint changes. Second, internet videos rarely come with annotations specifying object parts, joint types, or motion trajectories, making supervised learning approaches difficult to apply directly. Third, the diversity of object appearances and the occlusions caused by object self-motion or interactions with other objects increase the difficulty of robustly detecting and tracking relevant parts over time.

Recent advances in deep learning, particularly in self-supervised and weakly supervised representation learning, open up new possibilities for addressing these challenges. By exploiting temporal consistency, geometric constraints, and prior knowledge about physical articulation, models can begin to infer 3D structure and motion without requiring exhaustive manual annotation. Furthermore, the integration of multi-view cues available in videos, even from a moving camera, can enable the reconstruction of articulated motion in three dimensions. Advances in differentiable rendering, neural implicit representations, and correspondence learning provide additional tools for building systems that can learn articulation from raw video streams.

A deeper understanding of 3D object articulation in internet videos would have far-reaching implications. In robotics, it could enable systems to learn how to manipulate unfamiliar objects by observing demonstrations, reducing the need for task-specific programming. In augmented and virtual reality applications, it could lead to more realistic and interactive simulations of objects encountered in the real world. In content creation and digital preservation, it could facilitate the generation of accurate 3D models of historical artifacts or mechanical devices from archival footage. Additionally, insights gained from large-scale analysis of articulation patterns could inform the design of more efficient and adaptable mechanical systems.

This work aims to bridge the gap between controlled laboratory studies of object articulation and the complex, uncontrolled settings represented in internet videos. We propose a framework for discovering, modeling, and evaluating 3D articulated object motion from large-scale, in-the-wild video collections. Our approach combines advances in unsupervised part discovery, motion segmentation, and 3D reconstruction to produce interpretable models of object articulation without reliance on pre-existing CAD models or dense manual annotations. By systematically exploring the capabilities and limitations of current techniques in this challenging domain, we seek to advance the understanding of how objects move and interact in the real world, and to lay the foundation for future systems that can learn from the vast, dynamic visual record available online.
conclusion: In this work, we explored the problem of understanding 3D object articulation from internet videos, a domain characterized by unconstrained conditions, diverse object categories, and significant variability in motion and appearance. We presented a framework that leverages both visual and temporal cues to infer part-level geometry and motion, enabling the recovery of detailed articulation models without reliance on specialized capture setups. By integrating robust feature extraction with motion-aware 3D reconstruction techniques, our approach demonstrates strong generalization to real-world video data, surpassing prior methods in both qualitative realism and quantitative accuracy. The results highlight the potential of large-scale, in-the-wild video corpora as rich resources for learning complex object kinematics. Beyond the immediate applications in graphics, robotics, and augmented reality, our findings open avenues for richer semantic understanding of dynamic scenes. Future work may investigate incorporating multi-view internet imagery, expanding to non-rigid deformations, and exploiting language-vision pretraining to further enhance performance. Overall, this study establishes a step toward scalable, data-driven modeling of articulated objects, bridging the gap between controlled laboratory settings and the complexity of everyday visual experience.

title: Theory input for $t\bar{t}j$ experimental analyses at the LHC
abstract: We present theoretical predictions relevant for the analysis of top–antitop pair production in association with a hard jet ($t\bar{t}j$) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This process constitutes a significant fraction of inclusive $t\bar{t}$ events and plays a crucial role in precision measurements of the top quark mass, studies of QCD radiation patterns, and searches for physics beyond the Standard Model. We provide next-to-leading order QCD calculations matched to parton showers, including full top quark decays with spin correlations and off-shell effects, thereby enabling a realistic comparison with experimental data. Particular attention is devoted to the definition of observables sensitive to the kinematics of the additional jet, and to the impact of theoretical input on the extraction of fundamental parameters. We investigate the dependence of predicted distributions on renormalisation and factorisation scale choices, as well as on parton distribution functions, and quantify associated uncertainties. The interplay between matrix-element and parton-shower emissions is examined for key differential observables, highlighting regions where fixed-order accuracy is essential. Our results, implemented in a flexible Monte Carlo framework, provide a solid and systematically improvable baseline for ongoing and future $t\bar{t}j$ measurements at $\sqrt{s}=13$ and 14 TeV, supporting both Standard Model precision tests and new physics searches involving top quarks.
introduction: The production of a top–antitop quark pair in association with an additional jet ($t\bar{t}j$) is a key process studied at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Precise theoretical predictions for $t\bar{t}j$ observables are essential for accurate measurements of Standard Model parameters and for constraining possible new physics. These processes probe QCD in complex multi-scale regimes and affect backgrounds in Higgs and beyond-Standard Model searches, motivating detailed theoretical input for experimental analyses at current and future LHC runs.
conclusion: In this work, we have provided precise theoretical predictions relevant for $t\bar{t}j$ production at the LHC, incorporating higher-order QCD corrections and realistic event selection criteria. Our results demonstrate the importance of these corrections for accurate modeling of differential distributions and for reducing theoretical uncertainties. The improved predictions are directly applicable to current and future $t\bar{t}j$ measurements, enabling more robust comparisons between theory and experiment. This work thus supports precision tests of the Standard Model and contributes to the sensitivity of searches for possible new physics in the top-quark sector.

title: Internal stresses and breakup of rigid isostatic aggregates in homogeneous and isotropic turbulence
abstract: We investigate the internal stresses and breakup mechanisms of rigid isostatic particle aggregates suspended in homogeneous and isotropic turbulence through direct numerical simulations combined with a discrete-element representation of the aggregate geometry. The aggregates are modeled as mechanically stable networks of primary particles connected by rigid bonds, whose failure is governed by a critical tensile stress criterion. Turbulent flow fields are generated at moderate Taylor-scale Reynolds numbers, and the fully resolved hydrodynamic forces and torques on each primary particle are computed. From these, the internal force network is reconstructed to quantify the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of tensile stresses within the aggregate. The statistics of maximum internal stress are analyzed as a function of aggregate size, morphology, and orientation relative to the turbulent strain-rate eigenframe. We find that turbulent fluctuations produce intermittent stress concentrations significantly exceeding those predicted by mean-flow arguments, with the largest stresses associated with rare, intense straining events. Breakup probability is shown to depend sensitively on the interplay between aggregate geometry and the multiscale structure of turbulence, with elongated or anisotropic aggregates experiencing higher stress amplification. The critical stress for breakup is reached through cooperative loading of bonds in regions of high local curvature of the aggregate backbone. Our results provide quantitative insight into the mechanisms by which homogeneous and isotropic turbulence drives the mechanical failure of rigid isostatic aggregates, offering a predictive framework for breakup rates in natural and industrial particulate suspensions where cohesion is dominated by rigid interparticle contacts.
introduction: The breakup of rigid isostatic aggregates in turbulent flows is a key process in environmental and industrial contexts, affecting particle size distributions and suspension stability. In homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, velocity fluctuations generate hydrodynamic stresses that may exceed the mechanical strength of aggregates, leading to fragmentation. Understanding the relationship between turbulent stress statistics and aggregate breakup requires coupling fluid dynamics with aggregate mechanics. This work investigates internal stress distributions within rigid isostatic aggregates suspended in turbulence, aiming to clarify the mechanisms and thresholds governing their breakup under realistic flow conditions.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the internal stresses and breakup dynamics of rigid isostatic aggregates subjected to homogeneous and isotropic turbulence. By combining theoretical analysis with numerical simulations, we have quantified how hydrodynamic stresses, transmitted through the aggregate network, depend on both the turbulent flow statistics and the aggregate geometry. The results elucidate the link between the microscopic force distribution within aggregates and the macroscopic breakup rates observed under turbulent conditions.

Our analysis confirms that even in the absence of gross deformation, rigid isostatic aggregates experience substantial internal stress heterogeneity, arising from the intermittent nature of turbulent velocity gradients. The load paths through the contact network lead to stress concentrations at specific bonds, which can exceed the average hydrodynamic forcing by significant factors. This stress localization is found to be largely governed by the connectivity and spatial arrangement of primary particles, with more anisotropic structures exhibiting higher peak stresses for the same external conditions.

The statistical characterization of turbulent forcing revealed that breakup is primarily driven by rare, intense fluctuation events rather than by the mean shear level. The distribution of internal stresses inherits the non-Gaussian features of the turbulent strain-rate field, resulting in a finite probability of extreme stress values capable of overcoming cohesive bond strengths. Consequently, the breakup process is inherently stochastic, and the mean breakup time is strongly influenced by the tail behaviour of the stress probability density function.

We have shown that the critical turbulent dissipation rate required for breakup scales with the cohesive strength of the bonds and inversely with the degree of stress amplification within the aggregate. This amplification factor, in turn, is determined by the aggregate’s isostatic topology and the statistical alignment between its principal structural axes and the instantaneous strain eigenvectors of the turbulence. The framework developed here offers predictive capability for breakup rates when both the turbulent statistics and aggregate structural descriptors are known.

The findings have direct implications for modelling particle size distributions in turbulent suspensions, with relevance to environmental processes, industrial colloids, and aerosol science. In particular, they highlight the necessity of accounting for internal force transmission and structural heterogeneity, rather than relying solely on simplified estimates of hydrodynamic stress based on aggregate size. Future work should extend the present analysis to non-isostatic aggregates with redundant bonds, where force chains and load redistribution may alter the breakup statistics, and to conditions where particle inertia or non-Newtonian carrier fluids modify the turbulent stress field.

In summary, the present study provides a mechanistic understanding of how homogeneous and isotropic turbulence induces internal stresses in rigid isostatic aggregates, and how these stresses lead to breakup. By linking turbulent flow intermittency to microscopic failure mechanisms, we bridge the gap between fluid dynamic forcing and aggregate mechanical response, offering a foundation for more accurate and physically grounded breakup models.

title: Local field reconstruction from rotating coil measurements in particle accelerator magnets
abstract: We present a method for reconstructing the local magnetic field in particle accelerator magnets from rotating coil measurements. The approach combines harmonic analysis of the measured signals with a spatial reconstruction technique that captures both amplitude and phase information of the field components. By processing data from multiple coil orientations, the method resolves three-dimensional field variations with high accuracy. Numerical simulations and experimental validation on a dipole magnet demonstrate reliable reconstruction of local field maps, enabling improved magnet characterization and quality control in accelerator design and operation.
introduction:
The accurate characterization of magnetic fields in particle accelerator magnets is essential for ensuring beam stability, optimizing machine performance, and meeting stringent design specifications. In high-energy accelerators, the quality of the magnetic field directly impacts beam optics, dynamic aperture, and overall operational efficiency. Small deviations from the ideal field configuration can lead to significant deterioration of beam quality, making precise field measurement and analysis a critical aspect of accelerator physics and engineering. Among the various diagnostic techniques available, the rotating coil method has emerged as a widely adopted and reliable tool for determining the integrated multipole content of accelerator magnets.

Traditionally, rotating coil measurements provide information in terms of integrated field harmonics, expressed as a multipole expansion around a reference radius. This information is invaluable for magnet acceptance testing, quality control, and alignment, but it inherently represents an average of the field along the magnet’s length. In many cases, however, understanding the local field variation along the longitudinal axis is equally important. Longitudinal field profiling is necessary for diagnosing manufacturing defects, studying fringe field effects, and informing correction strategies in complex magnet assemblies. Direct local field measurements are challenging due to limited access, mechanical constraints, and the need for high spatial resolution without perturbing the magnet environment.

Recent developments in data processing and inversion techniques have opened the possibility of reconstructing the local field distribution from integrated measurements, extending the utility of rotating coil data beyond its conventional application. By combining a sequence of measurements taken with short coils or by exploiting the axial segmentation of the measurement system, it is possible to infer the three-dimensional field structure with high precision. Such reconstruction requires a careful mathematical formulation, robust handling of measurement noise, and an understanding of the physical constraints imposed by Maxwell’s equations.

This work presents a methodology for local field reconstruction in particle accelerator magnets using rotating coil measurements. The approach builds on the conventional multipole analysis framework while introducing an inversion algorithm capable of resolving longitudinal field variations. The method is validated through both simulated data and experimental measurements on representative accelerator magnets. The results demonstrate that detailed field maps can be obtained without the need for invasive probes, enabling improved diagnostics and quality assurance. The proposed technique enhances the diagnostic capability of existing rotating coil systems and provides a pathway to more comprehensive magnet characterization in accelerator facilities.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a comprehensive framework for reconstructing the local magnetic field distribution in particle accelerator magnets from rotating coil measurements. By integrating the theoretical foundations of multipole expansion techniques with an enhanced treatment of spatial sampling, we have demonstrated that it is possible to recover not only the global harmonic content of the field but also its variation along the magnet aperture with high fidelity. This capability is of particular significance for the characterization and quality assurance of modern accelerator magnets, where stringent field homogeneity requirements must be met to ensure beam stability and performance.

Our methodology builds upon established harmonic analysis approaches but extends them by incorporating rotation-synchronized data acquisition and advanced inversion algorithms capable of mitigating the effects of measurement noise, coil misalignments, and finite longitudinal resolution. Through both simulated and experimental case studies, we have shown that the proposed reconstruction method can reliably reproduce localized field perturbations that would be obscured in conventional integral measurements. The agreement between reconstructed field maps and independent Hall probe scans validates the accuracy of the technique within the expected uncertainty bounds.

One of the key findings is that local field reconstruction enables the identification and quantification of manufacturing imperfections and assembly tolerances that manifest as localized multipole errors. This level of diagnostic detail opens the possibility of targeted corrective actions, such as shimming or mechanical adjustments, before magnet installation. Furthermore, the ability to resolve the longitudinal evolution of the field provides valuable input for beam dynamics modelling, particularly in accelerators where fringe field effects and three-dimensional field components play a non-negligible role.

While the present study has focused on a specific class of rotating coil probes and measurement geometries, the underlying reconstruction principles are general and can be adapted to other probe designs, rotation schemes, and magnet types. Future work will address the extension of the algorithm to dynamic measurements under powered cycling, as well as its integration with automated data processing pipelines for large-scale magnet testing facilities. Additionally, exploring the combination of rotating coil data with complementary diagnostics, such as stretched wire or fluxgate measurements, may further enhance reconstruction robustness and spatial resolution.

In summary, the proposed local field reconstruction approach significantly enhances the diagnostic capabilities of rotating coil measurements in accelerator magnet metrology. By bridging the gap between global harmonic analysis and spatially resolved field mapping, it provides a powerful tool for both magnet development and operational quality control. The demonstrated accuracy, versatility, and potential for adaptation suggest that this technique can play an important role in meeting the increasingly demanding specifications of next-generation particle accelerators.

title: Fort Formation by an Automaton
abstract: This paper investigates the autonomous construction of fortified structures by a mobile automaton operating in a discrete, two-dimensional environment. The study models the automaton as a finite-state agent endowed with local sensing and limited memory, capable of manipulating unit blocks to form enclosed configurations. We formalize the concept of a “fort” as a contiguous arrangement of blocks satisfying predefined geometric and connectivity constraints, including perimeter closure and internal accessibility. The proposed algorithm enables the automaton to coordinate block placement through iterative exploration, obstacle negotiation, and adaptive path planning, without reliance on global positional information. Simulation experiments evaluate the system’s performance under varying environmental conditions, such as irregular terrain and resource distribution. Results demonstrate that the automaton consistently constructs valid forts with efficiency scaling sublinearly in relation to the number of available blocks. Furthermore, robustness tests reveal resilience to partial block loss and environmental perturbations. The work contributes to the broader understanding of decentralized construction mechanisms, with potential applications in robotic swarming, disaster response infrastructure, and extraterrestrial habitat assembly. Future research directions include multi-agent extensions and optimization of construction time.
introduction:
The autonomous construction of defensive or protective structures has long been a subject of interest in both robotics and artificial intelligence research. Fort formation, in particular, presents a compelling challenge, as it requires the integration of spatial reasoning, environmental perception, and adaptive planning within a dynamic context. An automaton tasked with fort formation must be capable of interpreting its surroundings, identifying suitable locations, and executing a sequence of coordinated actions to assemble structural elements into a coherent and functional whole. Such capabilities are relevant not only to defense-oriented applications, but also to disaster response, planetary exploration, and the development of self-organizing robotic swarms.  

Recent advances in autonomous systems, including improvements in sensor technologies, distributed control algorithms, and machine learning, have enabled increasingly complex construction tasks to be undertaken without direct human intervention. However, fort formation remains a nontrivial problem due to uncertainties in terrain, the need for structural stability, and the potential presence of adversarial conditions. Existing approaches often rely on predefined blueprints or centralized control, which can limit adaptability and scalability in unstructured environments.  

This work investigates a model in which a single automaton, governed by finite-state or rule-based logic, incrementally constructs a fort through local decision-making and feedback from its environment. By formalizing the problem within a computational framework, we aim to analyze the efficiency, robustness, and emergent properties of such autonomous construction processes, thereby contributing to the broader understanding of self-directed robotic assembly in complex and unpredictable settings.
conclusion: The investigation into fort formation by an automaton has demonstrated that complex defensive structures can emerge from the execution of simple, local rules. Through iterative simulation and analysis, it was shown that coordinated behavior arises without centralized control, leading to stable, adaptive formations that respond to environmental constraints. The results highlight the potential of automata-based models for understanding and replicating collective construction, with implications for robotics, artificial intelligence, and the study of self-organizing systems. Furthermore, the adaptability observed in formation patterns suggests applications in scenarios requiring rapid, autonomous deployment of protective barriers. Future work could explore optimization of rule sets for efficiency, resilience under dynamic conditions, and integration with sensory feedback. Overall, this study reinforces the viability of decentralized approaches to complex spatial organization in both natural and engineered contexts.

title: Dualized Simple Type Theory
abstract: We introduce Dualized Simple Type Theory (DSTT), a type-theoretic framework extending classical simple type theory with a systematic dualization of its logical and functional constructs. By incorporating dual types and dual inference rules, DSTT captures both constructive and co-constructive reasoning within a unified system. This duality enables symmetric treatment of introduction and elimination forms, supports bidirectional translation between primal and dual derivations, and provides a natural setting for modeling phenomena such as coinduction, continuation-passing, and polarity-sensitive logics. We present the syntax, typing rules, and categorical semantics of DSTT, along with metatheoretic results including normalization, consistency, and duality preservation. Applications demonstrate how DSTT generalizes existing type systems while offering novel expressive power for both theoretical exploration and practical programming language design.
introduction:
Simple type theory, originally formulated by Church, provides a foundational framework for reasoning about functions, predicates, and higher-order constructions in logic and computer science. Its well-structured hierarchy of types eliminates certain paradoxes of untyped systems and underpins many formal systems used in mathematics and programming languages. However, as applications expand into areas such as categorical logic, duality theory, and symmetric computational models, it becomes natural to consider extensions that systematically incorporate dual notions alongside the standard ones.  

Dualized simple type theory arises from the observation that many constructions in logic and computation admit categorical duals: products correspond to coproducts, conjunction to disjunction, and universal quantification to existential quantification. By explicitly integrating such duals into the type-theoretic framework, we obtain a system in which primal and dual forms coexist and interact under well-defined inference rules. This dualization not only enriches the expressive power of the theory but also reveals structural symmetries often hidden in the conventional formulation.  

The present work develops a formal account of dualized simple type theory, specifying its syntax, semantics, and proof-theoretic properties. We explore its categorical underpinnings, establish consistency and normalization results, and illustrate its utility in representing bidirectional reasoning patterns and dual computational processes, thereby extending the versatility of simple type theory.
conclusion: This work has introduced and developed the framework of Dualized Simple Type Theory, demonstrating how dualization principles can be systematically integrated into the foundations of typed λ-calculus. By extending the traditional simple type theory with a coherent dual structure, we have shown that expressive power is enhanced while preserving desirable meta-theoretic properties such as consistency and strong normalization. The dualized formulation clarifies symmetries between constructive and co-constructive reasoning, offering a unified basis for both intuitionistic and dual-intuitionistic logics. Our results suggest that this framework can serve as a robust foundation for future explorations in categorical semantics, proof theory, and programming language design, where dualities play a central role in structuring computation and reasoning.

title: Higher-Order Low-Rank Regression
abstract: We propose a novel framework for higher-order low-rank regression, addressing the challenge of modeling multiway structured data in high-dimensional settings. Our method extends classical low-rank regression to tensor-valued predictors and responses, exploiting multilinear algebra to capture complex interactions while controlling model complexity. We develop efficient optimization algorithms with theoretical guarantees and demonstrate their effectiveness through simulations and real-world applications. Experiments show superior predictive accuracy and interpretability compared to existing methods, highlighting the advantages of incorporating higher-order low-rank structures in regression analysis.
introduction:
In many scientific and engineering domains, modern data are naturally represented as multi-dimensional arrays, or tensors, rather than as simple vectors or matrices. Examples arise in neuroimaging, where measurements capture spatial, temporal, and spectral dimensions simultaneously; in chemometrics, where spectral data vary across multiple experimental conditions; and in recommender systems, where user-item interactions are recorded over time or contexts. These higher-order data structures preserve rich dependencies across modes, offering the potential for more accurate modeling and prediction. However, their complexity also poses significant challenges for conventional statistical learning methods, which are often designed for vector- or matrix-valued inputs.

Regression analysis is a fundamental tool for modeling relationships between predictors and responses, yet standard approaches typically require vectorizing tensor predictors, thereby discarding their inherent multiway structure. This vectorization can lead to prohibitively high-dimensional parameter spaces, making estimation unstable and computationally expensive, especially when the sample size is modest relative to the number of parameters. Moreover, ignoring the tensor structure may obscure meaningful interactions among modes, reducing both predictive accuracy and interpretability.

Low-rank modeling has emerged as a powerful framework for addressing such issues. By constraining coefficient tensors to have low multilinear rank, one can achieve substantial dimensionality reduction while retaining the core structural information in the data. Low-rank regression models exploit the idea that the relationship between tensor predictors and responses can often be captured by a small number of latent factors across each mode. This approach not only improves statistical efficiency but also facilitates interpretation in terms of mode-specific patterns. Existing work in this area has developed methods based on Tucker decompositions, CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decompositions, and related tensor factorizations to enforce low-rank structures in the regression coefficients.

Despite these advances, several challenges remain. First, many existing methods focus on second-order (matrix) data or treat higher-order cases by unfolding tensors into matrices, which can compromise the integrity of the multiway structure. Second, optimization over low-rank tensor manifolds can be computationally demanding, particularly for large-scale problems. Finally, there is a need for a unified framework that accommodates different tensor orders, supports various types of responses, and balances model expressiveness with statistical and computational tractability.

In this work, we propose a general higher-order low-rank regression framework that directly models tensor-valued predictors without resorting to matricization. Our approach imposes a multilinear rank constraint on the regression coefficient tensor, leveraging tensor decomposition techniques to achieve parsimonious representations. We develop efficient estimation algorithms that scale to large data sets and demonstrate how the framework can be adapted to handle diverse regression settings, including continuous, binary, and count responses. Through both simulated and real-world applications, we show that the proposed method yields improved predictive performance and interpretable latent structures compared to existing alternatives. This contribution advances the state of the art in tensor-based regression and provides a flexible foundation for analyzing complex multiway data.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated higher-order low-rank regression as a principled framework for modeling multidimensional structured data. By leveraging tensor representations and low-rank constraints, our approach effectively captures complex interactions while mitigating overfitting and reducing computational cost. The proposed methodology extends classical regression models to higher-order settings, enabling richer feature exploitation in domains such as signal processing, computer vision, and neuroscience. Experimental results confirmed significant improvements over conventional methods in both predictive accuracy and efficiency. Future research may explore adaptive rank selection, integration with deep architectures, and scalable optimization strategies to further broaden the applicability and robustness of higher-order low-rank regression.

title: Magnetic phases of mass- and population-imbalanced ultracold fermionic mixtures in optical lattices
abstract: We investigate the magnetic phases of ultracold fermionic mixtures with both mass and population imbalance in optical lattices, focusing on the strong-coupling regime of the Hubbard model. Using a combination of dynamical mean-field theory and exact diagonalization, we map out the phase diagram as a function of interaction strength, imbalance parameters, and temperature. We find that mass imbalance enhances antiferromagnetic ordering at half filling, while population imbalance induces ferrimagnetic and canted antiferromagnetic phases. The competition between these effects leads to rich magnetic behavior, including phase separation. Our results provide experimentally relevant predictions for realizing tunable quantum magnetism in optical lattice setups.
introduction:
Ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices provide an exceptionally clean and controllable platform for simulating strongly correlated quantum many‑body systems. By tuning lattice geometries, interaction strengths, and particle densities, it is possible to emulate paradigmatic condensed matter models and explore regimes that are difficult to access in solid‑state materials. In particular, fermionic mixtures loaded into optical lattices have emerged as versatile quantum simulators of the Hubbard model and its extensions, enabling the study of Mott insulating phases, magnetic ordering, and exotic quantum magnetism. The high degree of control over system parameters allows for systematic investigations of the interplay between kinetic energy, interaction energy, and quantum statistics.

While the majority of experimental and theoretical studies have focused on balanced mixtures—either with equal particle numbers or with identical tunneling amplitudes—recent advances have enabled the realization of mass‑ and population‑imbalanced systems. Mass imbalance can be engineered by combining different fermionic atomic species, such as \( ^6\mathrm{Li} \) and \( ^{40}\mathrm{K} \), or by applying species‑dependent optical lattices to the same atomic species in different internal states. Population imbalance, on the other hand, can be introduced by preparing unequal spin‑state populations. Both types of imbalance break certain symmetries of the standard Hubbard model, leading to qualitatively new physics. In particular, they can give rise to unconventional magnetic phases, modify phase boundaries, and generate competition between different ordering tendencies.

In the presence of mass imbalance, the disparity in tunneling amplitudes between the two fermionic components leads to anisotropic effective spin interactions in the strong‑coupling limit. This can favor Ising‑type over Heisenberg‑type correlations and modify the stability of antiferromagnetic order. Population imbalance acts as an effective Zeeman field, polarizing the system and potentially stabilizing ferrimagnetic or canted antiferromagnetic phases. The combined effect of mass and population imbalance introduces an additional layer of complexity, as it couples spin and charge degrees of freedom in nontrivial ways.

Understanding the magnetic phases of such imbalanced systems is of both fundamental and practical interest. On the fundamental side, it sheds light on the role of symmetry breaking and frustration in correlated electron systems. Practically, it informs the design of quantum simulators that aim to mimic complex materials, such as itinerant magnets or systems with spin‑dependent transport. In this work, we investigate the ground‑state magnetic properties of mass‑ and population‑imbalanced ultracold fermionic mixtures in two‑dimensional optical lattices, mapping out the resulting phase diagrams and identifying characteristic features of the emergent magnetic order.
conclusion: We have investigated the magnetic phases of mass- and population-imbalanced ultracold fermionic mixtures in optical lattices, revealing how imbalance modifies ordering tendencies and phase boundaries. Our results demonstrate the emergence of novel magnetic configurations absent in balanced systems, driven by interplay between kinetic and interaction energy scales. These findings enrich the understanding of strongly correlated imbalanced mixtures and offer guidance for future experimental exploration of quantum magnetism in optical lattices.

title: 2-tape 1-way Quantum Finite State Automata
abstract: We introduce and investigate the computational properties of 2-tape 1-way Quantum Finite State Automata (2T1QFAs), a quantum extension of classical 2-tape finite automata operating under a unidirectional input head movement. In this model, two parallel input tapes are read synchronously by a finite-state quantum control, enabling quantum superposition and interference across correlated tape contents. We formally define the machine model, specifying its unitary evolution and measurement protocols, and explore its language recognition capabilities in comparison to both classical and single-tape quantum counterparts. Our results demonstrate that 2T1QFAs can recognize certain non-regular languages with bounded error, exceeding the power of 1-tape quantum finite automata while maintaining strict space constraints. We also provide constructions illustrating quantum advantages in succinctness and computational efficiency. These findings contribute to the understanding of how limited quantum resources and multi-tape configurations can enhance automata-theoretic models, offering insights into the fundamental limits of quantum finite-state computation.
introduction:
Quantum computation has emerged as a powerful paradigm that extends the classical theory of computation by exploiting principles of quantum mechanics such as superposition, interference, and entanglement. Within this domain, quantum finite state automata (QFAs) have been studied as quantum analogues of classical finite state machines, providing a minimalistic yet insightful model for understanding the computational capabilities and limitations of quantum devices with constrained memory. QFAs, in their various forms, have been shown to recognize certain languages with fewer states or in ways fundamentally distinct from their classical counterparts, highlighting the potential advantages of quantum information processing even in highly restricted settings.

Early research in quantum automata focused on one-way QFAs, in which the input is scanned from left to right in a single pass, and the machine’s internal state evolves unitarily with possible intermediate measurements. These models, while limited in computational power compared to classical deterministic or probabilistic finite automata, exhibit intriguing differences in state complexity and language recognition boundaries. Variants such as measure-once and measure-many QFAs have been extensively explored, leading to a deeper understanding of how quantum interference can be harnessed in sequential computation.

Multiple-tape finite automata, in the classical setting, extend the capability of the single-tape model by allowing simultaneous access to multiple input streams. In particular, the 2-tape finite state automaton (2TFA) has been studied as an intermediate model between the single-tape automaton and more powerful computational devices like Turing machines. The two tapes may contain related or independent strings, enabling the machine to correlate symbols across tapes in a single step. The 2-tape model has found applications in language recognition problems that are cumbersome or impossible to solve efficiently with a single tape, while still maintaining finite-state control.

The integration of the multi-tape concept into the quantum finite automaton framework is a natural and promising direction. A 2-tape 1-way quantum finite state automaton (2T1QFA) can be defined as a quantum device that reads two tapes in parallel, moving unidirectionally, and updates its finite internal quantum state according to a unitary transformation conditioned on the pair of symbols currently being read. This model preserves the finite-state nature of traditional automata but potentially benefits from quantum parallelism and interference effects across two synchronized input streams. Such a setting could offer both a richer structure for algorithmic design and a refined lens for analyzing the boundaries of quantum regular language recognition.

Investigating 2-tape 1-way QFAs is motivated by several factors. First, from a theoretical standpoint, it enables the systematic study of how quantum mechanics interacts with the additional structural resources provided by multiple tapes. Second, it opens the possibility of recognizing certain nonregular languages or achieving more compact state complexity for specific regular languages compared to classical 2TFAs or single-tape QFAs. Third, it offers insight into the role of correlated input streams in quantum computation, which could parallel scenarios in quantum communication and distributed quantum information processing.

This work aims to formalize the model of 2-tape 1-way quantum finite state automata, examine their computational properties, and compare their expressive power to both classical and single-tape quantum counterparts. By defining precise operational semantics, constructing illustrative examples, and establishing theoretical bounds, we contribute to the foundational understanding of quantum automata theory in the multi-tape setting. Our results not only extend the landscape of QFA research but also shed light on how minimal quantum resources, when combined with structured input access, can lead to qualitatively new computational phenomena.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated the computational properties of 2-tape 1-way quantum finite state automata, highlighting their structural features and potential advantages over classical counterparts. By leveraging quantum parallelism and dual-tape processing, these automata demonstrate enhanced pattern recognition capabilities within strict space constraints. Our analysis suggests that such models can recognize certain languages more efficiently than comparable classical systems. Future research may explore complexity boundaries, error reduction techniques, and practical implementations, further clarifying their role in quantum automata theory and applications.

title: Diffractive Higgs boson photoproduction in peripheral collisions
abstract: We investigate diffractive Higgs boson photoproduction in peripheral hadronic collisions, where strong electromagnetic fields enable photon-induced interactions. Using the impact factor formalism, we evaluate cross sections for proton–proton and nucleus–nucleus systems at LHC energies, incorporating gluon ladder exchange in the perturbative QCD framework. Results indicate that peripheral collisions can provide a clean environment for Higgs production with suppressed hadronic backgrounds, offering a complementary channel to central collisions for probing Higgs properties and QCD dynamics.
introduction: The study of Higgs boson production mechanisms provides critical insights into the Standard Model and potential new physics. Among these mechanisms, diffractive processes offer a unique environment, characterized by color-singlet exchange and rapidity gaps, which can suppress background contributions. In high-energy hadronic interactions, photoproduction in peripheral collisions—where the impact parameter exceeds the sum of the radii of the colliding particles—allows quasi-real photons from the electromagnetic fields of one hadron to interact with the other. This regime minimizes strong overlap and enhances the relative contribution of photon-induced reactions. Diffractive Higgs boson photoproduction, involving the exchange of a colorless gluonic system, could be probed in proton–proton and proton–nucleus collisions at the LHC or future colliders. Investigating this process may yield valuable constraints on gluon distributions at small momentum fractions and test models of diffraction, complementing central exclusive production studies and broadening the phenomenology of Higgs boson generation in hadronic environments.
conclusion: We have investigated the diffractive photoproduction of the Higgs boson in peripheral collisions, focusing on the role of coherent photon-induced interactions. Using an approach based on the equivalent photon approximation and diffractive gluon distributions, we estimated cross sections for different collision systems and energies. Our results indicate that, despite the small production rates, the process offers a clean experimental environment due to the absence of underlying event activity and the presence of rapidity gaps. Such features could provide complementary information to standard Higgs production channels, particularly in probing the gluon content at small momentum fractions. Future high-luminosity runs and dedicated forward detectors may enhance the feasibility of observing this rare but potentially informative production mechanism.

title: Transformers are Adaptable Task Planners
abstract: We investigate the capacity of transformer-based models to function as adaptable task planners across diverse domains. By framing planning as a sequence modeling problem, we evaluate transformers on tasks requiring dynamic goal adaptation, multi-step reasoning, and integration of heterogeneous inputs. Our experiments span simulated environments, natural language instructions, and structured data, demonstrating robust generalization to novel planning scenarios. Results show that transformers can rapidly adjust strategies in response to changing constraints without task-specific fine-tuning. These findings highlight the potential of transformers as unified architectures for flexible, context-aware planning, bridging the gap between language understanding and autonomous decision-making.
introduction:
Recent advances in artificial intelligence have established transformer-based architectures as the prevailing foundation for a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal applications. Originally introduced for sequence transduction tasks such as machine translation, transformers have since demonstrated exceptional generalization capabilities, enabling them to achieve state-of-the-art performance in tasks as diverse as text summarization, question answering, code generation, and image captioning. This rapid expansion of applicability has been driven by the architectures’ ability to model long-range dependencies, leverage large-scale pretraining, and adapt flexibly to downstream objectives. While much research has focused on their representational capacity and scaling properties, a growing body of evidence suggests that transformers are not only powerful pattern recognizers but also adaptable task planners capable of decomposing complex instructions into coherent sequences of intermediate steps.

Task planning—the process of breaking down a high-level goal into a structured sequence of actions—has traditionally been associated with symbolic AI and classical planning algorithms. These methods rely on explicit modeling of states, actions, and transitions to derive optimal or feasible plans. In contrast, transformer models operate in a fundamentally different paradigm: they learn implicitly from vast corpora of human-generated sequences, without explicit planning modules or handcrafted rules. Nevertheless, large language models (LLMs) based on transformers have been observed to exhibit emergent planning-like behaviors, generating multi-step reasoning chains, conditional action sequences, and adaptive strategies in interactive settings. This phenomenon raises fundamental questions about the extent to which such models internalize generalized procedural knowledge and how this capacity can be harnessed for practical decision-making tasks.

Several factors contribute to this adaptability. First, the self-attention mechanism enables transformers to dynamically focus on relevant parts of an input, allowing them to integrate contextual cues when formulating responses. This contextual integration is crucial for planning, where the relevance of prior steps and anticipated outcomes must be weighed continuously. Second, large-scale pretraining exposes models to a wide variety of task structures, from instructional texts to narratives and dialogues, facilitating the abstraction of procedural patterns. Third, fine-tuning and prompt engineering techniques have demonstrated that relatively small adjustments in input formulation can steer model behavior toward more goal-directed and structured outputs, effectively eliciting planning capabilities without architectural changes.

The recognition of transformers as adaptable task planners has significant implications for both research and application. In domains such as robotics, autonomous systems, and human-computer interaction, the ability to generate coherent multi-step plans from natural language instructions can dramatically reduce the need for handcrafted control sequences or domain-specific planners. Similarly, in knowledge work and creative domains, transformer-based systems can assist in organizing complex workflows, coordinating collaborative processes, or optimizing sequences of actions toward efficiency or creativity. However, the adaptability of these models also raises critical concerns regarding reliability, interpretability, and control. Unlike explicit planning algorithms, the internal decision-making processes of transformers are opaque, making it challenging to diagnose errors or guarantee adherence to constraints.

This paper explores the hypothesis that transformers, particularly large language models, can function as adaptable task planners across a range of domains. We examine the mechanisms enabling this behavior, the conditions under which it emerges, and its limitations. Through a combination of empirical evaluation and theoretical analysis, we aim to characterize the planning capacity of transformers, identify strategies for enhancing their robustness, and outline the implications for future AI systems that unify perception, reasoning, and action generation within a single, flexible architecture. By doing so, we contribute to a deeper understanding of how these models can bridge the gap between language understanding and goal-directed behavior.
conclusion: This work has examined the capacity of transformer-based architectures to function as adaptable task planners across diverse domains. By leveraging their attention mechanisms and ability to encode long-range dependencies, transformers can integrate heterogeneous inputs, reason over complex sequences of actions, and adjust plans in response to dynamic constraints. Our analysis demonstrates that such models are not only effective in structured planning environments, but also robust when confronted with unstructured or noisy information. Moreover, their adaptability arises from both pretraining on broad datasets and fine-tuning for domain-specific objectives, enabling rapid transfer to novel tasks. These findings suggest that transformers bridge the gap between static planning algorithms and flexible, context-aware decision-making systems. Future research should explore the balance between model scale, interpretability, and efficiency, as well as investigate hybrid architectures that combine symbolic reasoning with learned representations. Ultimately, transformers hold significant promise as general-purpose planning agents in increasingly complex, real-world scenarios.

title: Sparse Nerves in Practice
abstract: Sparse nerve complexes provide a combinatorial framework for representing the topological structure of high-dimensional data while reducing computational overhead. In this work, we investigate practical strategies for constructing and applying sparse nerves in computational topology and data analysis. We formalize a family of sparsification schemes based on selective sampling of simplex-generating sets, guided by both geometric proximity and data-driven relevance metrics. Our approach balances fidelity to the underlying homotopy type with significant reductions in simplex count, enabling scalable computation of persistent homology. We evaluate these methods on synthetic manifolds and real-world datasets, including sensor network coverage models and high-dimensional embeddings from machine learning pipelines. Empirical results demonstrate that sparse nerves can preserve key topological invariants while achieving orders-of-magnitude savings in memory and runtime. Furthermore, we explore the trade-offs between sparsity, stability under perturbations, and interpretability of resulting summaries. These findings suggest that sparse nerve constructions are not merely a theoretical convenience but a practical tool for large-scale topological data analysis, with potential applications in streaming contexts and distributed computation.
introduction: Sparse nerve complexes have emerged as a powerful tool in topological data analysis, offering a means to capture combinatorial structure while reducing computational overhead. By selectively retaining simplices that preserve essential topological features, sparse nerves balance fidelity and efficiency, enabling scalable analysis of high-dimensional and large-scale datasets. Practical applications span sensor networks, shape reconstruction, and machine learning, where data complexity often prohibits full nerve computation. Despite theoretical advances, the translation of sparse nerve methods into practical workflows remains underexplored. Questions persist regarding stability, accuracy, and the trade-offs between sparsity and representational completeness. This paper investigates the implementation and performance of sparse nerves in applied settings, providing empirical evaluation, methodological refinements, and guidance for practitioners seeking to integrate these structures into data-driven analysis.
conclusion: This study has demonstrated the practical implications of sparse nerve architectures, highlighting their efficiency and adaptability in varied computational contexts. By leveraging sparsity, these models achieve reduced resource demands without compromising performance. The findings suggest promising avenues for real-world deployment, particularly in constrained environments. Future work should explore adaptive sparsity mechanisms to further enhance robustness, ensuring broader applicability across diverse domains where efficiency is paramount.

title: Formation and fate of low metallicity stars in IllustrisTNG50
abstract: We investigate the formation pathways, spatial distribution, and evolutionary outcomes of low-metallicity stars in the IllustrisTNG50 cosmological magnetohydrodynamical simulation. Using a metallicity threshold of \(Z/Z_\odot < 0.1\), we identify stellar populations across a representative sample of galaxies spanning a wide range of masses and morphologies at \(z=0\). We trace these stars back to their birth environments, quantifying the relative contributions from in-situ formation in low-metallicity gas and accretion through minor and major mergers. Our analysis shows that low-metallicity stars predominantly originate at early cosmic times (\(z > 3\)) in low-mass progenitors, with a substantial fraction subsequently incorporated into more massive galaxies via hierarchical assembly. In present-day massive galaxies, such populations are preferentially located in extended stellar halos, while in dwarf systems they remain centrally concentrated. We further examine the age–metallicity relation and kinematic signatures, finding evidence for distinct orbital anisotropies linked to formation channels. These results highlight the role of early star formation in chemically primitive environments and the lasting imprint of hierarchical growth on the spatial and dynamical properties of low-metallicity stellar populations.
introduction:
The chemical composition of stars encodes the history of galaxy formation and evolution. In particular, low metallicity stars, typically defined as having [Fe/H] ≲ –1, are fossil records of the early Universe, preserving information about the first episodes of star formation, the initial mass function, and the efficiency of metal enrichment. Their ages, kinematics, and spatial distributions provide constraints on the assembly histories of galaxies and the role of early accretion and feedback processes. Observations in the Milky Way and nearby galaxies have revealed that such stars are preferentially found in stellar halos, dwarf galaxies, and the outer regions of disks, and often exhibit abundance patterns indicative of enrichment by core-collapse supernovae from Population II progenitors.

Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations offer a powerful tool to study low metallicity stars in a fully self-consistent context, linking their formation to the growth of structure across cosmic time. The IllustrisTNG project is a suite of large-scale simulations that model galaxy formation within the ΛCDM cosmological framework, including prescriptions for star formation, chemical enrichment, and feedback from supernovae and active galactic nuclei. The highest resolution run, TNG50, combines a relatively large cosmological volume with unprecedented mass and spatial resolution, enabling the study of both the global statistical properties of low metallicity stars and their detailed spatial and kinematic distributions within individual galaxies.

Despite the wealth of observational studies, several questions remain open: What are the typical formation sites of low metallicity stars in a cosmological context? How do their spatial and dynamical properties evolve over time? To what extent do they originate in situ versus being accreted from satellite galaxies? By leveraging the capabilities of TNG50, we can trace the birth environments of these stars, follow their subsequent dynamical evolution, and quantify the relative contributions of different formation channels.

In this work, we investigate the formation and fate of low metallicity stars in TNG50 galaxies across a range of stellar masses. We analyse their birth properties, spatial distributions, and kinematics, and examine the role of accretion and mergers in shaping their present-day characteristics. Our results aim to bridge theoretical predictions with current and future observations from large stellar surveys.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the formation pathways, evolutionary histories, and eventual fates of low-metallicity stars in the TNG50 run of the IllustrisTNG simulation suite. By combining the high spatial and mass resolution of TNG50 with detailed tracking of the chemical enrichment of the interstellar medium, we have been able to characterize the environments in which metal-poor stellar populations originate, as well as the subsequent physical processes that shape their distribution and survival until the present day.

Our analysis shows that the majority of low-metallicity stars form at early cosmic times, typically at redshifts \( z > 3 \), in low-mass progenitor galaxies that have experienced limited chemical enrichment. These stars are often associated with rapid, bursty star formation episodes triggered by early gas accretion and minor mergers, before substantial feedback-driven outflows enrich the surrounding medium. A significant fraction of such stars form ex-situ and are later accreted into larger halos through hierarchical assembly. This process leads to the widespread presence of low-metallicity populations in the stellar halos of Milky Way–mass galaxies at \( z=0 \).

We find that the spatial distribution of these stars at present day is highly dependent on their origin. Stars formed in-situ in the main progenitor tend to reside in the inner halo and thick disk, whereas accreted metal-poor stars are more prevalent in the outer halo and tidal streams. Dynamical heating, mergers, and tidal stripping redistribute these populations over time, erasing much of the initial correlation between metallicity and galactocentric radius. Nevertheless, the imprint of their early formation in chemically unevolved environments persists in their low metal abundances.

By tracing individual star particles from formation to \( z=0 \), we have also quantified the survival rate of low-metallicity populations. While the vast majority remain bound to their host galaxies, a non-negligible fraction is stripped into the intracluster light in dense environments, especially for galaxies in massive halos. In lower-mass systems, metal-poor stars are more centrally concentrated and thus less susceptible to complete removal, although they can still be redistributed to large radii through repeated minor mergers.

Our results highlight the importance of hierarchical galaxy formation in shaping the present-day demographics of low-metallicity stars. The mass assembly history of the host galaxy strongly influences both the fraction of ex-situ stars and their spatial configuration.
