Moreover, the limited chemical evolution of low-mass progenitors at early times is a key driver of the abundance patterns observed today. This connection between early star formation in primitive environments and present-day stellar populations offers a crucial link between high-redshift galaxy evolution and local archaeological surveys.

The TNG50 results presented here are consistent with observational constraints from the Milky Way and Local Group, including the presence of extended metal-poor halos and distinct kinematic substructures. They also predict that galaxies of similar mass but differing merger histories will display significant diversity in their low-metallicity content. Future observational campaigns targeting resolved stellar populations in nearby galaxies, combined with improved chemical tagging, will provide stringent tests of these predictions.

In summary, low-metallicity stars in TNG50 are relics of the earliest stages of galaxy formation, preserved through a complex interplay of star formation, feedback, and hierarchical assembly. Their spatial and kinematic properties at the present day encode a rich record of their diverse origins, and their study provides a powerful tool for reconstructing the assembly histories of galaxies across cosmic time.

title: Gravitational portals in the early Universe
abstract: We investigate the theoretical possibility and cosmological implications of gravitational portals—hypothetical nonlocal connections mediated by spacetime curvature—operating in the high-energy conditions of the early Universe. Such portals, arising naturally in certain extensions of general relativity and quantum gravity frameworks, could facilitate effective interactions between otherwise decoupled sectors, including hidden matter fields or exotic particle species. We develop a phenomenological model in which transient, curvature-induced wormhole-like structures emerge during epochs of extreme density and temperature, particularly near the Planck scale. Employing semiclassical gravity and effective field theory techniques, we estimate portal formation rates, stability criteria, and decay channels, and assess their potential to alter thermal histories and particle abundances. We further explore signatures in primordial perturbations, gravitational wave backgrounds, and relic particle spectra. Our results suggest that even rare portal events could leave imprints on cosmological observables, thereby offering a novel probe of trans-Planckian physics. This work highlights the interplay between quantum gravitational effects and early-Universe dynamics, and motivates targeted searches in future cosmological and high-energy observations to constrain or detect the influence of gravitational portals.
introduction:
The study of the early Universe offers a unique arena for testing fundamental physics beyond the Standard Model and general relativity. Among the more speculative but compelling possibilities is the existence of “gravitational portals”—hypothetical nonlocal or transdimensional connections mediated purely by gravitational interactions. Such portals, if realized in nature, could have played a significant role in shaping the thermal history, matter content, and large-scale structure of the cosmos. They may arise naturally in certain frameworks, including higher-dimensional theories, string-inspired models, and scenarios involving semiclassical wormholes or spacetime foam. In these contexts, gravitational couplings can provide the only viable channel for energy exchange between otherwise sequestered sectors.

In the high-energy environment of the early Universe, gravitational portals could facilitate interactions between visible matter and hidden sectors without invoking additional gauge forces. This mechanism might account for phenomena such as the production of dark matter particles with extremely weak couplings, the transfer of entropy between sectors, or the generation of specific nonthermal distributions. The cosmological consequences of such processes are potentially observable through imprints on the cosmic microwave background, altered predictions for big bang nucleosynthesis, or distinctive patterns in the matter power spectrum.

The theoretical treatment of gravitational portals requires tools from quantum field theory in curved spacetime, semiclassical gravity, and, in some cases, full quantum gravity. Constraints arise from both direct cosmological observations and laboratory-based searches for deviations from Newtonian gravity at short distances. However, the extreme weakness of gravitational couplings makes such portals challenging to probe, necessitating indirect inference through precision cosmology.

In this work, we explore the possible roles of gravitational portals during the earliest epochs of cosmic evolution. We outline their theoretical underpinnings, classify relevant model frameworks, and assess their phenomenological implications. By confronting these ideas with current observational limits, we aim to delineate the viable parameter space and identify potential signatures that could be targeted by next-generation cosmological surveys.
conclusion:
The investigation of gravitational portals in the context of the early Universe offers novel insights into the interplay between high-energy gravitational phenomena and particle physics beyond the Standard Model. In this work, we have examined the theoretical underpinnings of gravitational portal frameworks, highlighting their potential to mediate interactions between the visible sector and hidden sectors during the high-temperature, high-curvature epoch following the Big Bang. Our analysis demonstrates that such couplings, arising naturally in certain extensions of general relativity and quantum gravity approaches, could have left measurable imprints on cosmological observables, including relic abundances, primordial spectra, and anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background.

Through a combination of analytical treatments and numerical modelling, we have shown that gravitational portals can operate efficiently in regimes where thermal contact between sectors is otherwise suppressed. In particular, we have identified parameter spaces in which portal-mediated processes contribute significantly to the freeze-in or freeze-out of hidden sector species, thereby influencing dark matter genesis scenarios. The sensitivity of these processes to the curvature scale and expansion history underscores the importance of a precise treatment of early-Universe dynamics when assessing the viability of portal-based models.

We have also explored the potential role of gravitational portals in generating non-trivial correlations between cosmological sectors, which could manifest as distinctive signatures in gravitational wave backgrounds. These features may arise from phase transitions, particle production events, or symmetry-breaking processes mediated by the portal interactions. Future observational facilities, particularly those capable of probing the milli- to deci-hertz gravitational wave regime, could provide critical tests of these predictions, complementing particle physics searches.

Our findings suggest that gravitational portals constitute a theoretically well-motivated and potentially observable bridge between high-energy gravity and hidden-sector physics. They enrich the landscape of mechanisms available for explaining dark matter, baryogenesis, and other outstanding cosmological puzzles. However, the complexity of the relevant parameter space, combined with the limitations of current observational precision, demands a concerted effort to refine models, improve numerical simulations, and develop targeted observational strategies.

In conclusion, gravitational portals in the early Universe represent a promising frontier for unifying aspects of cosmology and fundamental physics. By integrating advances in theoretical modelling with forthcoming observational data, the next decade may witness decisive progress in testing these scenarios, potentially revealing new sectors of nature that interacted with our own only through the most universal force: gravity.

title: Functional renormalization group study of the two-flavor linear sigma model in the presence of the axial anomaly
abstract: We investigate the two-flavor linear sigma model incorporating the axial \(U_A(1)\) anomaly using the functional renormalization group. Employing a scale-dependent effective action, we analyze the chiral phase structure and the influence of the anomaly on critical behavior. Our results indicate that the anomaly term significantly modifies the fixed-point structure, potentially altering the order of the chiral transition. The study provides nonperturbative insight into the interplay between chiral symmetry breaking and axial anomaly effects.
introduction: The two-flavor linear sigma model provides an effective low-energy description of chiral symmetry breaking in QCD. Incorporating the axial anomaly is essential for capturing the correct mesonic spectrum. We employ the functional renormalization group to investigate its influence on critical behavior and phase structure at finite temperature.
conclusion:
In this work, we have applied the functional renormalization group to investigate the two-flavor linear sigma model in the presence of the \(U(1)_A\) axial anomaly. By systematically incorporating the anomaly term into the effective average action and analyzing the resulting flow equations, we have explored its impact on the chiral phase structure and the universality class of the transition. Our study confirms that the anomaly explicitly breaks the axial symmetry, modifying the effective potential and the infrared fixed-point structure. For a sufficiently strong anomaly, the system exhibits a second-order chiral phase transition consistent with the \(O(4)\) universality class, in agreement with expectations from symmetry arguments and lattice QCD results. In contrast, a weakening of the anomaly strength near the critical temperature can lead to significant deviations, including the possibility of a first-order transition.

The functional renormalization group framework has allowed us to follow the scale evolution of couplings and masses beyond mean-field approximations, capturing fluctuation effects relevant near criticality. Our results highlight the sensitivity of the chiral dynamics to the temperature dependence of the anomaly, which may arise from topological fluctuations in QCD. This suggests that precise determination of the anomaly’s behavior is essential for a quantitative description of the QCD phase diagram.

Future extensions could include coupling to quark degrees of freedom, finite chemical potential, and explicit symmetry-breaking effects, providing a more complete picture of the interplay between anomaly dynamics and chiral symmetry restoration in hot and dense matter.

title: The Complexity of Bisimulation and Simulation on Finite Systems
abstract: We investigate the computational complexity of deciding bisimulation and simulation equivalence on finite-state systems. While bisimulation provides a robust notion of behavioral equivalence, simulation captures preorder relations relevant in verification. We present refined upper and lower bounds for both problems, emphasizing the impact of structural restrictions such as bounded degree and acyclicity. Our results unify and extend prior work, offering a clearer complexity landscape. Additionally, we discuss algorithmic implications for model checking, highlighting trade-offs between expressiveness and computational feasibility in practical verification tasks.
introduction: Bisimulation and simulation are fundamental notions in the theory of concurrent and reactive systems, providing formal means to compare the behavior of state-transition systems. These relations capture behavioral equivalence or refinement, enabling rigorous reasoning about system correctness, abstraction, and minimization. In the finite-state setting, they play a central role in model checking, verification, and synthesis, where efficient algorithms are crucial for handling large systems arising in practice. While bisimulation offers a symmetric equivalence relation preserving branching structure, simulation constitutes a preorder capturing one-sided behavioral inclusion. The computational complexity of deciding these relations has been extensively studied, revealing a rich landscape of algorithmic techniques and complexity bounds. Classical algorithms achieve near-linear or \(O(m \log n)\) performance for bisimulation and polynomial-time procedures for simulation, where \(n\) and \(m\) denote the number of states and transitions, respectively. However, subtle differences in the underlying definitions, as well as constraints on the system model, can significantly affect complexity. This paper revisits the complexity of bisimulation and simulation on finite systems, aiming to unify existing results, clarify boundary cases, and explore new algorithmic insights that bridge theory and practice in system verification.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the computational complexity of bisimulation and simulation relations on finite systems, with particular attention to their algorithmic characterizations and implications for system verification. By systematically analyzing the structural properties of state-transition graphs, we have clarified the inherent difficulty of deciding these equivalence and preorder relations under varying constraints. Our study has shown that while bisimulation checking can be performed in polynomial time for finite systems, the complexity can rise significantly in the presence of succinct or parameterized representations. Similarly, simulation, though often more permissive than bisimulation, exhibits comparable computational behavior, with certain restricted cases admitting more efficient algorithms.  

These findings underscore the nuanced trade-offs between expressiveness and tractability in behavioral equivalence checking. They also highlight the importance of selecting appropriate notions of equivalence according to the verification goals and the structural characteristics of the models under consideration. Beyond theoretical interest, our results provide guidance for the design of practical verification tools, suggesting when optimizations or alternative equivalences may be beneficial. Future work could extend these analyses to probabilistic or quantitative variants of bisimulation and simulation, as well as to infinite-state systems where decidability boundaries shift. Overall, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the algorithmic landscape surrounding fundamental behavioral relations in finite-state verification.

title: Going Deeper with Convolutions
abstract: This paper explores advanced convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures that extend beyond traditional convolutional layers to enhance representational capacity while maintaining computational efficiency. We investigate the use of factorized convolutions, multi-scale feature aggregation, and inception-style modules to capture richer spatial and contextual information. By decomposing convolutions into smaller, more efficient operations, our approach reduces parameter count and mitigates overfitting without sacrificing accuracy. Experimental evaluations on benchmark image classification datasets demonstrate significant improvements over baseline CNNs, achieving competitive or superior performance with reduced inference cost. We further analyze the trade-offs between depth, width, and filter diversity, providing insights into architectural design principles. The results highlight the potential of deeper yet efficient convolutional designs for a wide range of computer vision tasks.
introduction:
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as a fundamental architecture in computer vision and related domains, enabling significant advances in tasks such as image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. The success of CNNs stems from their ability to learn hierarchical feature representations directly from raw data, capturing low-level edges and textures in early layers and progressively abstracting to higher-level concepts in deeper layers. However, as the demand for higher accuracy and richer representations has grown, so too has the need for architectures that can efficiently increase depth and complexity without incurring prohibitive computational costs or overfitting.

Traditional approaches to improving CNN performance often involve stacking more convolutional layers to increase depth. While deeper networks have demonstrated superior representational power, they also present challenges, including vanishing gradients, increased training time, and the risk of redundancy in learned features. Furthermore, simply increasing depth may not be the most effective way to capture multi-scale contextual information, which is crucial for recognizing complex patterns in visual data. This has motivated the exploration of architectural innovations that enable networks to “go deeper” in a more structured and computationally efficient manner.

One influential direction in this regard is the development of modules that combine convolutions of different receptive field sizes within the same layer, allowing the network to process information at multiple scales simultaneously. This approach mitigates the limitations of fixed-size convolution kernels and enables richer feature extraction without an excessive increase in parameters. By integrating parallel convolutional and pooling operations and concatenating their outputs, such architectures can capture both fine-grained details and broader contextual cues in a single composite representation. This strategy not only increases the effective depth of the network but also enhances its width, promoting feature diversity.

The “Going Deeper with Convolutions” paradigm, exemplified by the Inception architecture, represents a milestone in this evolution. It introduces a carefully designed module that factorizes convolutions and employs dimensionality reduction techniques to balance representational capacity with computational efficiency. This design enables the construction of very deep networks that remain tractable to train and deploy, even on large-scale datasets such as ImageNet. By systematically combining multiple convolutional pathways and leveraging bottleneck layers, the approach achieves a favorable trade-off between accuracy and resource usage.

In this work, we examine the principles underlying deeper convolutional architectures, with a focus on the design choices that facilitate both depth and efficiency. We analyze the impact of multi-scale feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and factorized convolutions on network performance, and provide empirical evidence of their advantages in various visual recognition benchmarks. Through this investigation, we aim to contribute to the understanding of how to construct CNNs that are not only deeper but also more effective and computationally feasible.
conclusion: This work has explored the concept of going deeper with convolutions, emphasizing the benefits of increased network depth and architectural refinements in enhancing representational capacity. By systematically integrating more convolutional layers and carefully designed modules, we demonstrated how complex hierarchical features can be captured more effectively, leading to improved performance across diverse visual recognition tasks. The analysis underscored the importance of balancing depth with computational efficiency, avoiding redundancy, and mitigating vanishing gradient issues through architectural innovations. Our findings suggest that deeper convolutional networks, when paired with appropriate regularization and optimization strategies, can achieve superior generalization without incurring prohibitive computational costs. Future research may extend these principles to emerging domains, explore automated architecture search for optimal depth, and investigate hybrid models combining convolutional backbones with attention mechanisms. Ultimately, deepening convolutional architectures remains a powerful and evolving direction for advancing the state of the art in computer vision.

title: Quantum turbulence: From superfluid helium to atomic Bose-Einstein condensates
abstract: Quantum turbulence, characterized by the complex dynamics of quantized vortices, offers a unique window into turbulence in systems governed by quantum mechanics. In superfluid helium, turbulence emerges from the interaction and reconnection of vortex lines, producing energy cascades reminiscent of classical turbulence yet constrained by quantization of circulation. Recent advances in atomic Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs) have enabled controlled generation, visualization, and analysis of quantum turbulent states at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution. These systems, with tunable interactions and geometry, provide complementary insights into vortex dynamics, energy spectra, and dissipation mechanisms absent in classical fluids. This paper reviews key experimental and theoretical progress in both superfluid helium and atomic BECs, highlighting commonalities and distinctions in turbulence development, decay, and statistical properties. By bridging results across these platforms, we identify universal features of quantum turbulence and outline open questions, particularly concerning the crossover between quantum and classical regimes and the role of finite temperature effects in energy dissipation.
introduction:
Quantum turbulence (QT) refers to the complex, disordered motion of quantized vortices in quantum fluids, offering a striking counterpart to classical turbulence while embodying fundamentally distinct physics. In classical fluids, turbulence is characterized by a continuous vorticity field and an energy cascade across a broad range of scales. By contrast, in quantum fluids such as superfluid helium and atomic Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs), circulation is quantized in units of Planck’s constant divided by the particle mass, and vorticity is confined to topological line defects with a fixed core size. This quantization imposes discrete structural constraints on turbulent flows, yet many statistical properties bear remarkable similarity to their classical counterparts.

The study of QT has a dual motivation: to deepen our understanding of turbulence as a universal phenomenon, and to probe the unique consequences of quantum mechanics at macroscopic scales. Superfluid helium, with its well-established two-fluid model, has provided a long-standing platform for exploring vortex dynamics and energy spectra in regimes unattainable in classical fluids. More recently, atomic BECs have emerged as highly tunable systems for QT research, enabling direct imaging of vortex configurations, control over interaction strength, and the creation of tailored flow geometries. These advances have opened new avenues for connecting microscopic vortex dynamics to macroscopic turbulent behavior.

Comparative investigations across these systems reveal both common scaling laws and system-specific features, highlighting the interplay between quantization, dissipation mechanisms, and dimensionality. By bridging traditional low-temperature physics and ultracold atomic gases, QT research offers a fertile testing ground for fundamental concepts in fluid dynamics, statistical physics, and quantum many-body theory.
conclusion: Quantum turbulence bridges the physics of superfluid helium and atomic Bose–Einstein condensates, revealing universal features alongside system-specific dynamics. Studies in helium have illuminated the role of quantized vortices, energy spectra, and dissipation mechanisms at very low temperatures, while condensate experiments offer unprecedented control over geometry, interactions, and dimensionality. Together, these platforms have advanced our understanding of vortex reconnections, cascade processes, and the interplay between classical and quantum turbulence. Despite significant progress, key questions remain regarding the crossover between quantum and classical regimes, the nature of turbulence in reduced dimensions, and the role of finite temperature effects. Continued synergy between experiments, theory, and numerical simulations promises to deepen insight into turbulence in quantum fluids, with implications for diverse physical systems and potential applications in precision sensing and quantum technologies.

title: Segmentation of large images based on super-pixels and community detection in graphs
abstract: We present a novel approach for segmenting large images by integrating super-pixel over-segmentation with community detection in graphs. Initially, the image is decomposed into super-pixels to reduce computational complexity while preserving important boundaries. A weighted graph is then constructed, where nodes represent super-pixels and edges encode similarity measures based on color, texture, and spatial proximity. Community detection algorithms are applied to partition the graph into coherent regions corresponding to meaningful image segments. This method effectively balances segmentation accuracy with scalability, handling high-resolution images without excessive memory use. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, while significantly reducing processing time for large-scale image analysis.
introduction:
The segmentation of large-scale images has become an increasingly important task in a wide range of computer vision applications, including remote sensing, medical imaging, digital pathology, and high-resolution scene understanding. As imaging devices and acquisition technologies advance, the size and resolution of images continue to grow, enabling the capture of fine-grained details but also posing significant challenges for efficient and accurate image processing. Traditional pixel-by-pixel segmentation methods often struggle with the computational and memory demands required for processing such large images, leading to a growing need for approaches that can balance precision with scalability.

Super-pixel methods have emerged as an effective strategy to address this challenge by grouping pixels into perceptually meaningful atomic regions that preserve important boundary information while reducing the number of elements to be processed. Each super-pixel aggregates pixels with similar color, texture, and spatial proximity, thereby capturing local structural information and reducing the complexity of subsequent analysis. This representation not only accelerates processing but also provides a more natural unit for higher-level vision tasks, as super-pixels often align well with object boundaries. Popular algorithms such as Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) and its variants have demonstrated high efficiency and adaptability to different image domains, making super-pixels a widely adopted preprocessing step for image segmentation.

In recent years, the integration of graph-based methods with super-pixel representations has gained considerable attention. In such approaches, super-pixels are modeled as nodes in a graph, and edges are defined based on spatial adjacency or similarity measures between regions. This abstraction allows the application of a rich set of graph-theoretic tools to analyze the relationships among image regions and to identify meaningful groupings. Community detection in graphs, a concept widely studied in network science, offers a promising paradigm for segmentation in this context. By identifying communities—densely connected subsets of nodes within a graph—it becomes possible to group super-pixels that belong to the same semantic or structural region in the original image.

Community detection has traditionally been applied to social networks, citation networks, and other relational datasets; however, its principles are equally applicable to image analysis. Algorithms such as modularity maximization, spectral methods, and statistical inference frameworks can uncover hierarchical and non-hierarchical community structures. When applied to super-pixel graphs, these methods can naturally exploit the connectivity patterns among image regions, enabling segmentation that is both computationally efficient and capable of capturing global structural relationships in the image. Furthermore, community detection approaches can scale to large graphs and can be adapted to incorporate multi-scale information, which is particularly advantageous when dealing with large, high-resolution images.

Despite these advantages, the application of community detection to image segmentation presents several challenges. The definition of similarity measures between super-pixels must balance the influence of spatial proximity, color homogeneity, and texture descriptors to ensure that the resulting graph faithfully represents the image structure. Moreover, large images may result in graphs with tens or hundreds of thousands of nodes, requiring efficient algorithms and data structures to handle the associated computational load. Another consideration is the resolution of segmentation: while super-pixels reduce complexity, overly coarse super-pixel partitioning may obscure fine details, whereas excessively fine partitioning may negate computational benefits.

To address these challenges, recent research has explored hybrid strategies that integrate domain-specific image features, adaptive super-pixel generation, and scalable community detection algorithms. These strategies aim to achieve a balance between segmentation quality and computational efficiency. For example, adaptive thresholds in graph construction can control edge density to optimize the performance of community detection algorithms, while hierarchical community detection can produce multi-scale segmentations suitable for different analysis tasks. Additionally, parallel and distributed computing frameworks can be leveraged to process large image graphs in reasonable time frames.

The combination of super-pixel representation and community detection in graphs thus offers a compelling framework for the segmentation of large images. By reducing the number of primitives from individual pixels to coherent regions and by leveraging the capacity of community detection to uncover structural groupings, such methods are well positioned to handle the increasing size and complexity of modern image datasets. This approach aligns with the broader trend in computer vision toward graph-based representations, which provide a flexible and powerful foundation for integrating spatial and semantic information.

In this work, we investigate a segmentation methodology that constructs a super-pixel-based graph from large images and applies community detection algorithms to identify coherent image regions. We examine the impact of different super-pixel generation parameters, graph construction strategies, and community detection methods on segmentation performance. Our goal is to demonstrate that this combination not only reduces computational demands but also yields accurate and meaningful segmentations, even for images of substantial size and complexity. By systematically analyzing these components, we aim to contribute a practical and scalable solution to the problem of large image segmentation, with potential applicability across diverse domains where high-resolution imagery plays a central role.
conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates that combining super-pixel segmentation with community detection in graphs offers an effective framework for processing large images. By reducing the number of primitives through super-pixel decomposition, the method significantly decreases computational complexity while preserving essential structural and semantic information. The subsequent transformation of super-pixels into graph nodes enables the exploitation of community detection algorithms to identify cohesive regions, leading to accurate and meaningful segmentation results. Experimental evaluations indicate that this strategy achieves a favorable balance between segmentation quality and efficiency, particularly for high-resolution images where traditional pixel-based methods are computationally prohibitive. Furthermore, the graph-based representation facilitates the integration of additional features and contextual relationships, enhancing the adaptability of the method to diverse image domains. These findings suggest that the synergy between super-pixel preprocessing and graph community analysis is a promising direction for large-scale image segmentation. Future work will focus on optimizing graph construction and exploring advanced community detection techniques to further improve scalability, robustness, and applicability to real-time scenarios.

title: Tracking in dense environments and its inefficiency measurement using pixel $dE/dx$
abstract: Tracking charged particles in dense environments, such as the cores of high-energy jets or heavy-ion collisions, presents significant challenges due to high hit occupancies and overlapping trajectories. In this work, we investigate tracking inefficiencies in such conditions using pixel detector ionization measurements, quantified through the specific energy loss ($dE/dx$). By exploiting the correlation between $dE/dx$ and particle multiplicity, we develop a method to identify missing tracks and measure the associated inefficiency. The approach is validated using simulated and experimental data, demonstrating sensitivity to tracking losses in high-density regions. Our results highlight the potential of pixel $dE/dx$ as a complementary tool for performance monitoring and detector optimization in future high-luminosity experiments.
introduction:
The reconstruction of charged particle trajectories is a fundamental task in high-energy and nuclear physics experiments, providing the basis for precise momentum measurements, vertex reconstruction, and particle identification. Tracking algorithms exploit the spatial and temporal information recorded in detector subsystems to associate individual hits with the passage of charged particles. In modern collider experiments, silicon pixel detectors positioned in close proximity to the interaction point deliver high-resolution measurements of particle positions, enabling efficient reconstruction even in the presence of substantial background activity. However, as instantaneous luminosities increase and event multiplicities rise, tracking in dense environments becomes increasingly challenging.  

Dense environments occur in a variety of contexts, such as the cores of high-energy jets, the vicinity of secondary vertices from heavy-flavor decays, or the complex topologies arising in heavy-ion collisions. In these regions, the density of charged particle tracks is high enough that multiple trajectories may traverse the same detector elements, leading to overlapping signals. This can result in ambiguities in hit assignment, degraded pattern recognition performance, and ultimately a reduction in tracking efficiency. Furthermore, the proximity of trajectories can cause hit merging in pixel detectors, where signals from two or more particles are recorded as a single cluster, complicating both the determination of the number of particles and the precise measurement of their parameters.  

An important aspect of studying tracking performance in such conditions is the quantification of inefficiencies. Traditional efficiency measurements rely on well-identified reference tracks or samples with low occupancy, but these approaches may not fully capture the specific losses that occur in dense environments. One promising method to probe these effects is the use of ionization energy loss measurements, $dE/dx$, provided by pixel detectors themselves. While $dE/dx$ is conventionally used for particle identification at low momenta, in the context of dense environments it can also serve as a diagnostic tool to identify merged clusters or anomalously high charge depositions indicative of multiple traversing particles.  

The pixel $dE/dx$ measurement is derived from the total collected charge in a cluster of pixels associated with a reconstructed track segment. In cases where two charged particles deposit energy in the same cluster, the measured charge will typically exceed that expected from a single minimum-ionizing particle. By comparing the observed $dE/dx$ distribution to the expectation for isolated tracks, one can infer the fraction of clusters affected by merging, and thus estimate the associated tracking inefficiency. This approach has the advantage of being sensitive to losses that are otherwise difficult to measure, particularly for particles that fail to be reconstructed altogether due to shared hits.  

In high-luminosity hadron collider experiments, where the number of simultaneous proton–proton interactions per bunch crossing can be large, the ability to quantify and correct for such inefficiencies is critical for maintaining physics performance. Accurate knowledge of tracking efficiency in dense environments impacts measurements of jet substructure, heavy-flavor production, and searches for new physics signatures characterized by collimated decay products. Moreover, the methodology based on pixel $dE/dx$ can be applied in both proton–proton and heavy-ion collision analyses, providing a versatile tool for performance studies across a wide range of event topologies.  

This paper presents a study of tracking in dense environments, focusing on the development and application of a pixel $dE/dx$-based technique to measure the associated inefficiency. We describe the underlying principles of the method, validate it using simulated samples, and apply it to collision data to extract quantitative estimates of efficiency losses in high-density regions. The results provide valuable input for the optimization of tracking algorithms and detector design in future high-occupancy scenarios.
conclusion: In this study, we have investigated the performance of tracking in dense environments and evaluated inefficiencies using pixel $dE/dx$ measurements. By correlating the specific energy loss with reconstructed track properties, we identified characteristic signatures of tracking loss and confusion in high-occupancy regions. The analysis demonstrates that pixel $dE/dx$ provides a sensitive probe of track merging and hit-sharing effects, enabling a quantitative assessment of reconstruction performance under challenging conditions. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating such measurements into efficiency studies, particularly for precision physics in high-luminosity environments. Future work will focus on refining the method, extending it to different detector configurations, and integrating it into real-time quality monitoring frameworks.

title: Training Autoregressive Speech Recognition Models with Limited in-domain Supervision
abstract: We investigate strategies for training autoregressive speech recognition models when only limited in-domain transcribed data is available. While large-scale pretraining on out-of-domain corpora provides strong initialization, mismatches in acoustic conditions and linguistic patterns can degrade performance. We propose a two-stage framework combining self-supervised pretraining, domain-adaptive fine-tuning, and targeted data augmentation to bridge this gap. Our method leverages pseudo-labeling with confidence filtering to exploit unlabeled in-domain audio, reducing reliance on costly manual annotation. Experiments on multiple low-resource domain settings demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline fine-tuning, with relative word error rate reductions of up to 18%. Analysis reveals that gains stem from improved robustness to domain-specific variance in both acoustic and lexical distributions. This approach offers a practical path to deployable ASR in resource-constrained scenarios.
introduction:
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have witnessed substantial progress in recent years, driven by advances in deep learning architectures, large-scale pretraining, and the availability of massive speech-text corpora. State-of-the-art models, particularly those based on autoregressive sequence-to-sequence frameworks, have achieved remarkable performance across a variety of languages and acoustic conditions. Autoregressive ASR models generate transcriptions one token at a time, conditioning each prediction on the preceding context. This design enables them to capture complex dependencies between acoustic features and linguistic structures, often resulting in highly accurate and natural transcriptions. However, their performance is strongly influenced by the match between training and deployment domains. When deployed in domains with mismatched acoustic conditions, speaking styles, or vocabulary, autoregressive ASR models can experience significant degradation.

In many practical scenarios, collecting large quantities of high-quality, in-domain speech-text pairs is expensive or infeasible. For example, domain-specific applications such as medical dictation, legal transcription, or customer service analytics may involve specialized terminology, restricted access to data due to privacy regulations, or the need for expert annotation. As a result, practitioners often rely on models pretrained on out-of-domain data and subsequently adapted to the target domain with limited in-domain supervision. While transfer learning and domain adaptation techniques have been extensively studied for ASR, adapting autoregressive models poses specific challenges. Their sequential nature means that adaptation must preserve both the acoustic-linguistic alignment learned during pretraining and the autoregressive dependencies that underpin accurate decoding.

A straightforward approach to domain adaptation involves fine-tuning all or part of the model parameters on the available in-domain data. However, when the in-domain dataset is small, full fine-tuning may lead to overfitting, catastrophic forgetting of general-domain knowledge, or instability in training. Moreover, autoregressive models often have large parameter counts, making full fine-tuning computationally expensive and potentially impractical in resource-constrained environments. These issues have motivated research into parameter-efficient adaptation strategies, such as freezing most of the pretrained parameters and updating only a small subset, introducing lightweight adapter modules, or leveraging regularization techniques to retain general-domain performance.

Another line of work seeks to exploit unpaired in-domain data—speech without transcripts or text without corresponding audio—to improve domain adaptation. Semi-supervised learning methods, such as self-training with pseudo-labels or consistency regularization, have shown promise in enhancing performance when labeled data is scarce. However, these methods depend heavily on the quality of the initial model and the robustness of the adaptation procedure. For autoregressive models, errors in pseudo-labels can accumulate during decoding, reinforcing incorrect predictions and limiting the gains from unlabeled data.

Recent advances in self-supervised speech representation learning have further shifted the ASR landscape. Models such as wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT learn powerful acoustic representations from large amounts of unlabeled speech, which can then be fine-tuned for recognition tasks with relatively little supervision. While these approaches have reduced the dependence on labeled data, fine-tuning on specialized domains still requires careful management to avoid overfitting and to ensure that the model adapts to domain-specific characteristics without losing generalization ability.

Despite these developments, there remains a gap in understanding how best to train autoregressive ASR models for a new domain when only limited in-domain supervision is available. In particular, questions remain regarding the optimal balance between preserving general-domain knowledge and incorporating domain-specific patterns, the choice of parameter-efficient adaptation mechanisms, and the integration of unlabeled in-domain data. Addressing these questions is critical for deploying robust ASR systems in specialized domains where data scarcity is the norm.

In this work, we investigate strategies for training and adapting autoregressive speech recognition models under limited in-domain supervision. We focus on methods that leverage pretrained models, parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques, and semi-supervised learning with unlabeled in-domain data. Through systematic experiments across multiple domains and adaptation scenarios, we aim to identify practical approaches that achieve strong in-domain performance while maintaining generalization. Our findings contribute to the design of ASR systems that are both accurate and adaptable, enabling their application in diverse and data-constrained environments.
conclusion:
In this work, we investigated strategies for training autoregressive speech recognition models under conditions of limited in-domain supervision. By systematically combining large-scale out-of-domain pretraining with targeted adaptation on scarce in-domain transcriptions, we demonstrated that it is possible to achieve substantial performance gains without requiring extensive labeled resources from the target domain. Our experiments showed that carefully designed fine-tuning schedules, coupled with data augmentation and regularization, effectively mitigate overfitting and preserve generalization. Moreover, we found that leveraging intermediate representations learned from diverse speech corpora enables the model to adapt more rapidly and robustly to domain-specific acoustic and linguistic characteristics.

The proposed approach offers a practical pathway for deploying high-quality speech recognition systems in scenarios where collecting and annotating large in-domain datasets is infeasible, such as low-resource languages, specialized vocabularies, or privacy-sensitive environments. While the focus here was on autoregressive architectures, the underlying principles may extend to other sequence-to-sequence models and modalities. Future work will explore more sophisticated domain adaptation techniques, including semi-supervised learning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, as well as strategies for dynamically balancing in-domain and out-of-domain signals during training. Overall, our findings underscore the viability of limited-supervision training pipelines and highlight promising directions for building adaptable, high-performance speech recognition systems in resource-constrained settings.

title: Secure Index Coding with Side Information
abstract: We investigate the problem of secure index coding in the presence of side information, where a sender broadcasts encoded messages to multiple receivers, each possessing prior knowledge of a subset of messages. Building on classical index coding theory, we introduce security constraints to prevent an eavesdropper, with partial side information, from learning any additional messages beyond its initial knowledge. We characterize achievable secure index codes under various side information structures and identify conditions under which optimal secure coding rates match those of the insecure setting. Our approach combines combinatorial encoding design with information-theoretic secrecy analysis, yielding constructive schemes and converse bounds. The results provide fundamental limits and practical guidelines for secure and efficient broadcast communication with side information.
introduction:
The rapid growth of modern communication networks has created an ever-increasing demand for efficient and secure methods of data dissemination. In many practical scenarios, a single sender must broadcast information to multiple receivers, each of which possesses partial knowledge of the overall data set. This prior knowledge, often referred to as *side information*, can be exploited to reduce the amount of transmitted data, thereby improving bandwidth efficiency and reducing latency. The *index coding* problem, first formalized by Birk and Kol in the context of satellite communications, captures this setting and has since become a fundamental topic in information theory and network coding. In its classical form, index coding focuses on minimizing the broadcast rate by leveraging side information available at the receivers. However, as communication systems increasingly operate in adversarial environments, it is necessary to augment this framework with robust security guarantees.

Security in index coding is motivated by scenarios in which broadcast transmissions are susceptible to interception by unauthorized parties, or where some receivers may not be fully trusted. For instance, content distribution networks, wireless broadcast channels, or satellite downlinks often operate in open environments where eavesdroppers can overhear transmitted signals. In such settings, the index coding scheme must not only satisfy the decoding requirements of legitimate receivers but also ensure that unintended parties cannot glean any useful information about the messages they are not entitled to receive. This dual requirement naturally leads to the notion of *secure index coding*, which integrates principles from both network coding security and traditional cryptography into the index coding paradigm.

The study of secure index coding introduces new challenges that do not arise in the classical formulation. First, security constraints can conflict with the goal of minimizing broadcast length. For example, coding strategies that are optimal in the absence of security considerations may inadvertently leak information to eavesdroppers. Second, the presence of side information at both legitimate receivers and potential adversaries complicates the design space. An eavesdropper’s side information may come from prior transmissions, compromised nodes, or other channels, and must be carefully modeled to provide meaningful security guarantees. Third, security requirements can be framed under different notions, such as information-theoretic secrecy, which demands that an adversary’s uncertainty about protected messages remains maximal, or computational secrecy, which assumes limitations on the adversary’s computational resources.

Existing research on secure index coding has explored a variety of security models and performance metrics. In the information-theoretic setting, the goal is often to achieve *perfect secrecy*, meaning that the mutual information between the protected messages and the eavesdropper’s observations is zero. Achieving such strong guarantees typically requires the use of randomness in the encoding process, sometimes in the form of shared keys or publicly known random variables. More relaxed notions of security, such as weak secrecy, allow for negligible information leakage and may enable more efficient codes. Another important distinction in the literature is between *universal security*, where the scheme must be secure against all possible eavesdroppers with a given side information pattern, and *instance-specific security*, where the adversary’s side information is fixed and known to the sender.

The interplay between efficiency and security in index coding has significant practical implications. In wireless networks, for example, reducing the number of transmissions not only conserves spectrum but also reduces the exposure of the transmitted data to potential interception. At the same time, the broadcast nature of such channels makes them inherently vulnerable to eavesdropping, making security a critical design objective. In content delivery scenarios, secure index coding can enable personalized services in which different users receive overlapping but not identical content, all delivered in a bandwidth-efficient and privacy-preserving manner.

From a theoretical standpoint, secure index coding connects to several well-studied areas in information theory and coding theory. It can be viewed as a special case of secure network coding, with the additional structure that all communications originate from a single source and are broadcast over a noiseless channel. It also relates to combinatorial optimization problems, such as finding minimum-length index codes under graph-theoretic formulations, now augmented with constraints that capture security requirements. These connections enable the adaptation of tools from graph theory, linear algebra, and entropy inequalities to analyze and design secure index coding schemes.

The present work focuses on developing new frameworks and coding strategies for secure index coding with side information, under a general adversarial model that accounts for both the legitimate receivers’ and the eavesdropper’s side information. We aim to characterize the fundamental limits of secure index coding in terms of achievable broadcast rates and to provide explicit constructions that meet these limits in various scenarios. Our approach draws on both combinatorial and information-theoretic techniques, enabling us to unify and extend existing results in the literature. By doing so, we seek to deepen the understanding of how security constraints alter the structure of optimal index codes and to identify trade-offs between security level, code length, and computational complexity.

In summary, secure index coding with side information lies at the intersection of efficient communication and robust security, addressing the dual imperatives of bandwidth optimization and data protection in modern broadcast systems. As networks grow in scale and heterogeneity, the need for communication strategies that are both efficient and secure will only intensify. Through the development of general models, tight bounds, and practical coding schemes, this work contributes to the theoretical foundations and practical applicability of secure index coding, paving the way for its deployment in a wide range of emerging communication scenarios.
conclusion:
In this work, we investigated the problem of secure index coding in the presence of side information, focusing on both information-theoretic secrecy guarantees and efficient code constructions. We considered a setting in which a sender wishes to broadcast messages to multiple receivers, each possessing some prior side information, while ensuring that an eavesdropper gains no additional knowledge about the confidential messages beyond what is already known. By extending the classical index coding framework to incorporate security constraints, we characterized achievable rate regions under different secrecy models, including perfect secrecy and weak secrecy, and analyzed the trade-offs between security, code length, and decoding performance.

Our results demonstrate that side information at legitimate receivers can be leveraged not only to reduce the code length, as in traditional index coding, but also to enhance security without requiring additional shared keys. We derived new bounds on the minimum length of secure index codes and proposed explicit constructions that achieve these bounds in several important cases. We also showed that in certain network configurations, secure index coding can be achieved with no rate penalty relative to the insecure case, provided that the side information satisfies specific structural properties.

Furthermore, we analyzed the interplay between security and side information patterns through graph-theoretic representations, revealing that the presence of certain subgraph structures directly enables or limits the feasibility of secure coding schemes. This perspective offers valuable insight into the design of secure broadcast protocols in realistic communication scenarios, where side information is naturally available due to prior transmissions or network topology.

The proposed secure index coding schemes are not only theoretically optimal in several regimes but also practically implementable, making them suitable for applications in wireless broadcast, caching systems, and content delivery networks where both bandwidth efficiency and confidentiality are critical. Our findings suggest that carefully exploiting side information patterns can significantly reduce the overhead typically associated with securing broadcast transmissions.

Future work may extend these results to dynamic settings with time-varying side information, multi-round communication, or adversaries with partial interference capabilities, as well as to coding schemes resilient to collusion among receivers. The integration of secure index coding with physical-layer security techniques and network coding frameworks also presents promising directions for achieving robust, low-complexity, and scalable secure communication solutions.

title: Toward a well defined monopole creation operator
abstract: We revisit the definition of monopole creation operators in non-Abelian gauge theories, addressing ambiguities related to gauge invariance and locality. By constructing a well-defined operator within a lattice formulation, we clarify its transformation properties and physical interpretation. Our approach enables consistent analytical and numerical studies of monopole condensation as a signal of confinement.
introduction:
Magnetic monopoles, hypothetical particles carrying isolated magnetic charge, have played a central role in deepening our understanding of gauge theories and topological structures in field theory. Since Dirac’s pioneering work, which demonstrated that the existence of monopoles would explain electric charge quantization, the search for a consistent formulation of monopole operators has remained an active area of theoretical research. In non-Abelian gauge theories, monopoles emerge naturally in certain grand unified models and in the study of confinement mechanisms via dual superconductivity. Lattice gauge theory has provided a fruitful framework for investigating monopole condensation, where the existence of a suitable monopole creation operator is essential to probe the relevant order parameters.

However, defining such an operator in a well-controlled and gauge-invariant manner poses significant challenges. Many proposed constructions, while operationally useful, face ambiguities related to gauge fixing, dependence on the choice of Dirac strings, or ultraviolet regularization. In the continuum, the definition must ensure locality (up to the unavoidable nonlocality dictated by the monopole’s long-range field) and compatibility with the underlying symmetries of the theory. On the lattice, additional complications arise from discretization artifacts and the nontrivial mapping between continuum and lattice variables.

A rigorous and unambiguous definition of the monopole creation operator is not merely of technical interest. It is a prerequisite for quantitatively testing the dual superconductivity picture of confinement, for comparing results across different formulations, and for providing a bridge between analytical and numerical approaches. In this work, we revisit the conceptual foundations of monopole operators, propose a construction free from certain long-standing ambiguities, and explore its implications for both continuum and lattice gauge theories.
conclusion: In this work we have discussed the construction of a well-defined monopole creation operator, addressing ambiguities present in earlier formulations. By refining its definition within a consistent theoretical framework, we established clear transformation properties and ensured gauge invariance. Our analysis demonstrates that the operator correctly captures the physical features associated with monopole excitations, providing a reliable tool for studying confinement mechanisms. These results open the way to more precise nonperturbative investigations and possible applications in lattice gauge theory and related quantum field contexts.

title: Detection of the secondary eclipse of WASP-10b in the Ks-band
abstract: We report the detection of the thermal emission from the hot Jupiter WASP-10b through observations of its secondary eclipse in the Ks-band (2.14 μm). The data were obtained using the OMEGA2000 camera at the 3.5 m telescope of Calar Alto Observatory over a continuous monitoring sequence covering the predicted eclipse event. After applying careful reduction procedures, including sky background subtraction, flat-field correction, and differential photometry using a set of stable comparison stars, we derived a high-precision light curve. The secondary eclipse is detected with a depth of \(0.137 \pm 0.022\%\), corresponding to a planet-to-star flux ratio of \((1.37 \pm 0.22) \times 10^{-3}\) in the Ks-band. The mid-eclipse time is consistent, within uncertainties, with the expected phase for a circular orbit, placing a constraint on the orbital eccentricity of \(e \cos \omega = 0.0023 \pm 0.0018\). The measured brightness temperature of \(T_B = 1647^{+97}_{-131}\) K is significantly higher than the equilibrium temperature predicted under the assumption of zero albedo and full heat redistribution, suggesting inefficient day–night energy transport and possible contributions from reflected starlight or atmospheric thermal inversions. This detection represents one of the few ground-based measurements of a secondary eclipse for a relatively faint system (\(K = 10.7\)), demonstrating the feasibility of characterizing the atmospheric properties of exoplanets from the ground in the near-infrared. Our results provide important constraints for atmospheric models of WASP-10b and contribute to the growing sample of hot Jupiters with measured thermal emission.
introduction:
Transiting exoplanets offer a unique opportunity to probe the physical and atmospheric properties of planets outside our Solar System. When a planet passes in front of its host star, the resulting primary transit allows for measurements of its radius, orbital inclination, and, when combined with radial velocity data, its mass and bulk density. The complementary event, the secondary eclipse—when the planet passes behind the star—enables the direct measurement of the planet’s emitted and reflected flux. Observations of secondary eclipses in different wavelength bands provide critical constraints on the atmospheric temperature, composition, and energy redistribution processes of close-in exoplanets.

Hot Jupiters, gas giants in close orbits around their host stars, are particularly well-suited for such studies because their high equilibrium temperatures produce significant thermal emission in the near- and mid-infrared. The near-infrared Ks-band (centered at roughly 2.14 μm) is especially valuable for probing the dayside thermal emission of these planets, complementing longer-wavelength data obtained with space-based facilities. Ground-based observations in the Ks-band, while challenging due to the bright and variable sky background and atmospheric absorption, have become increasingly successful in recent years owing to advances in instrumentation, observing strategies, and data reduction techniques.

WASP-10b is a transiting hot Jupiter orbiting a relatively active K-dwarf star with a period of approximately 3.09 days. Discovered by the Wide Angle Search for Planets (WASP) survey, WASP-10b has a mass of about 3 Jupiter masses and a radius slightly smaller than Jupiter’s, resulting in a high bulk density. The system’s proximity (about 140 pc) and the brightness of its host star in the near-infrared make it an attractive target for secondary eclipse observations from the ground. The planetary atmosphere is expected to be strongly irradiated, and Ks-band photometry can help determine its dayside brightness temperature and provide insights into its atmospheric structure.

Secondary eclipse measurements in the Ks-band are of particular interest for constraining the efficiency of heat transport from the dayside to the nightside. For tidally locked hot Jupiters, the degree of day–night temperature contrast depends on the interplay between radiative cooling timescales and atmospheric dynamics. A relatively deep eclipse in the Ks-band would imply a high dayside temperature, suggesting inefficient heat redistribution, while a shallower eclipse could indicate a more homogeneous atmospheric temperature distribution. Furthermore, combining Ks-band detections with optical and mid-infrared data allows for the construction of a broadband emission spectrum, which can be compared with atmospheric models to infer chemical abundances and the presence of thermal inversions.

Despite the scientific potential, detecting the secondary eclipse of WASP-10b from the ground is challenging due to both the small expected depth of the signal—on the order of a few tenths of a percent—and the variability introduced by the active host star. Precise photometry, careful treatment of systematic effects, and robust statistical analysis are essential to achieve a reliable detection. In this work, we present the detection of the secondary eclipse of WASP-10b in the Ks-band using ground-based near-infrared observations. We describe our observations and data reduction methods, detail the modeling of the light curve and treatment of correlated noise, and discuss the implications of the measured eclipse depth for the atmospheric properties of WASP-10b. Our results add to the growing body of ground-based secondary eclipse measurements and demonstrate the feasibility of probing exoplanet atmospheres from the ground in the near-infrared.
conclusion:
We have presented the detection of the secondary eclipse of the hot Jupiter WASP‑10b in the Ks‑band, obtained through high‑precision ground‑based photometry. Our observations reveal a measurable decrease in flux during the predicted occultation phase, consistent with the planet passing behind its host star. The measured eclipse depth corresponds to a brightness temperature significantly higher than the planet’s equilibrium temperature under the assumption of zero albedo and efficient heat redistribution, suggesting that the dayside atmosphere may be subject to inefficient heat transport or additional sources of thermal emission.

The timing of the secondary eclipse is consistent, within the uncertainties, with expectations from a circular orbit, providing no compelling evidence for significant orbital eccentricity. This result aligns with recent radial velocity and transit timing measurements, which have similarly constrained the eccentricity to low values. Consequently, the eclipse timing supports the interpretation that tidal circularisation has already occurred for this close‑in giant planet, in agreement with theoretical predictions for its age and orbital separation.

Our Ks‑band detection provides a valuable constraint on the planetary spectral energy distribution in the near‑infrared. When combined with existing optical and infrared measurements, these data can inform atmospheric models, particularly in relation to the presence or absence of strong molecular absorption features and the efficiency of energy redistribution between the planetary hemispheres. The relatively high brightness temperature inferred here may indicate that WASP‑10b possesses a temperature inversion in its atmosphere or a low Bond albedo, both of which could be further tested through multi‑wavelength eclipse observations.

This work demonstrates the capability of modern ground‑based facilities to detect secondary eclipses of relatively faint transiting exoplanets in the near‑infrared, even for systems with moderate transit depths. Such observations are critical for expanding the sample of exoplanets with measured dayside emission, enabling comparative studies across a wider range of planetary masses, radii, and host star types. In particular, the case of WASP‑10b highlights how secondary eclipse detections can yield insights into atmospheric physics and orbital dynamics beyond what is accessible from primary transit observations alone.

Future follow‑up of WASP‑10b at multiple infrared wavelengths, ideally with space‑based platforms or next‑generation ground‑based instruments, will help to disentangle the degeneracies between atmospheric composition, albedo, and heat redistribution efficiency. Ultimately, building a comprehensive observational picture of systems like WASP‑10b will contribute to a more complete understanding of the diversity of hot Jupiter atmospheres and their evolutionary pathways.

title: Neutrino Oscillation as a constraint in the dynamics of Pop III Gamma Ray Bursts
abstract: We investigate the role of neutrino oscillations in shaping the dynamics of Population III (Pop III) gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Using models of core-collapse in massive, metal-free progenitors, we analyze how flavor conversion in dense stellar environments affects energy deposition, baryon loading, and jet acceleration. Our results indicate that oscillation-induced modifications to neutrino heating can impose significant constraints on outflow energetics, influencing both prompt emission and afterglow properties. These findings suggest that neutrino flavor physics is a critical factor in understanding the extreme environments of Pop III GRBs.
introduction:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic phenomena in the universe, releasing vast amounts of energy over short timescales. Population III (Pop III) stars, the first generation of stars formed from pristine, metal-free gas, are prime candidates for progenitors of extremely energetic GRBs due to their large masses and short lifespans. The collapse of massive Pop III stars is expected to produce relativistic jets, intense neutrino emission, and high-energy photons, offering a unique laboratory to probe fundamental physics under extreme conditions. In particular, the role of neutrinos in the dynamics of these events has garnered increasing attention, as they are produced copiously in the core collapse and jet formation processes, and can propagate largely unimpeded from the source to the observer.

Neutrino oscillations—flavor conversions arising from non-zero neutrino masses and mixing—are now firmly established through solar, atmospheric, reactor, and accelerator experiments. In the environment of a Pop III GRB, these oscillations can be influenced by matter effects, magnetic fields, and potentially by neutrino–neutrino forward scattering in dense regions. Such processes can alter the flavor composition of the neutrino flux, thereby modifying the energy deposition rates in the jet and surrounding stellar envelope. Since neutrino interactions are a key driver of the baryon loading, jet breakout, and the amount of energy available for gamma-ray production, oscillation-induced modifications may act as constraints on the dynamics and observable properties of Pop III GRBs.

Investigating neutrino oscillations in this context not only deepens our understanding of the microphysics governing GRB engines, but also provides a potential indirect probe of Pop III star properties, which remain observationally elusive. By linking neutrino flavor evolution to macroscopic jet dynamics, we can explore how fundamental particle physics impacts the most luminous explosions in the early universe, offering insights into both high-redshift astrophysics and beyond-Standard-Model phenomena.
conclusion:
The analysis presented here highlights the potential role of neutrino oscillations as a non-trivial dynamical factor in the physics of Population III (Pop III) gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). By incorporating neutrino flavor conversion into models of the central engine and relativistic outflow, we find that oscillation-induced modifications to the neutrino energy spectra and flavor composition can, in principle, influence the thermal and lepton number balance in the dense regions surrounding the progenitor. This, in turn, may affect baryon loading, jet collimation, and the efficiency of energy transfer from the collapsing core to the emergent relativistic jet.

Given the extreme densities and temperatures expected in Pop III progenitors, matter-enhanced (MSW) oscillations and collective neutrino oscillation effects could operate in regimes markedly different from those in present-day stellar explosions. Our results suggest that, under certain conditions, flavor transformations may alter the neutrino heating rates and the neutrino–antineutrino annihilation efficiency, thereby imposing constraints on the achievable Lorentz factors and prompt emission characteristics of Pop III GRBs. These constraints may manifest as limits on the duration, spectral hardness, and total isotropic-equivalent energy output, potentially offering indirect observational diagnostics, even for events at very high redshift.

While the present study employs simplified assumptions regarding the progenitor’s rotation, magnetic field, and neutrino transport, the findings underscore the need to incorporate realistic neutrino flavor evolution into numerical simulations of Pop III GRBs. Future work should address the interplay between neutrino oscillations and magnetohydrodynamic processes in three-dimensional settings, as well as the impact of beyond–Standard Model neutrino properties on the explosion dynamics. Moreover, the detectability of high-energy neutrinos from Pop III GRBs with next-generation neutrino observatories could provide a unique probe of both the astrophysical environment and fundamental neutrino physics.

In summary, neutrino oscillations are not merely an ancillary effect but may serve as a meaningful constraint on the dynamics of Pop III GRBs, shaping both their physical evolution and their observable signatures. Incorporating these effects is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the earliest and most energetic stellar deaths in the Universe.

title: Distributed Representation of Subgraphs
abstract: We present a framework for learning distributed representations of subgraphs that captures both structural and semantic information in complex networks. Unlike existing approaches that focus primarily on node- or graph-level embeddings, our method explicitly models subgraph structures as first-class objects, enabling richer analysis of localized patterns. The proposed approach employs a hierarchical encoding scheme that aggregates node features within subgraphs while preserving their topological context through message passing and positional encodings. We introduce a contrastive learning objective that aligns subgraph embeddings based on structural similarity and discriminates against randomly sampled counterparts, improving generalization across tasks. Experiments on benchmark datasets for graph classification, link prediction, and motif detection demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance while producing embeddings that are robust to noise and scalable to large graphs. Furthermore, we show that the learned representations support transfer learning, enabling effective adaptation to unseen domains with minimal fine-tuning. This work advances subgraph-level representation learning as a distinct and powerful paradigm.
introduction:
Graphs are a fundamental data structure for representing complex relationships among entities, with applications spanning social networks, biological systems, transportation networks, and knowledge graphs. In many of these domains, the structural properties within subgraphs—connected subsets of nodes and edges—carry essential semantic and functional information. For example, a subgraph in a protein–protein interaction network may correspond to a functional module, while in a social network, it may represent a closely-knit community or interaction pattern. Effectively capturing and reasoning about the structure and attributes of subgraphs is therefore a key challenge in graph mining and representation learning.

Recent advances in graph representation learning have largely focused on generating vector embeddings for individual nodes or entire graphs. Node embeddings aim to capture the local topology and features surrounding each node, while whole-graph embeddings summarize the global structure of the entire network. However, many tasks in practice, such as motif detection, subgraph classification, and similarity search, inherently operate on subgraphs of varying sizes and shapes. Relying solely on node-level or graph-level representations can obscure the intermediate structural patterns that occur at the subgraph level, limiting the performance of downstream applications.

Distributed representations, or embeddings, of subgraphs provide a promising approach to bridge this gap. By mapping subgraphs into a continuous vector space, it becomes possible to leverage geometric proximity as a proxy for structural and semantic similarity. Such embeddings enable the deployment of standard machine learning methods for classification, clustering, and retrieval, while preserving key topological and attribute-based characteristics. The challenge lies in designing encoding schemes that are both expressive—capable of distinguishing between non-isomorphic subgraphs—and efficient, scaling to large graphs and diverse subgraph sizes.

Existing approaches to subgraph representation face several limitations. Methods based on handcrafted features, such as graph kernels or motif counts, often suffer from high computational complexity and may fail to capture nuanced structural information in large networks. Deep learning-based methods, including extensions of graph neural networks (GNNs), have shown promise, but many still focus on node or graph-level tasks, requiring non-trivial adaptations to handle subgraphs effectively. Moreover, ensuring permutation invariance, accommodating varying subgraph sizes, and integrating rich node and edge attributes remain open challenges.

In this work, we investigate the problem of learning distributed representations for subgraphs in a principled and scalable manner. We aim to develop a framework that generalizes beyond fixed-size patterns, captures both structural and attribute information, and supports a wide range of downstream tasks. By systematically exploring design choices in subgraph encoding and training objectives, we seek to advance the understanding of how subgraph-level embeddings can be learned effectively. Our contributions not only address theoretical considerations such as expressiveness and invariance, but also demonstrate practical advantages through empirical evaluation on diverse benchmark datasets. Through this study, we highlight the central role of subgraph representation in bridging local and global perspectives in graph learning.
conclusion: This work has explored the distributed representation of subgraphs, demonstrating how embedding techniques can capture both structural and semantic properties efficiently. By leveraging learned vector spaces, our approach enables scalable analysis and comparison of complex graph patterns. Experimental results confirm its effectiveness across diverse tasks, suggesting broad applicability in domains such as network science and bioinformatics. Future research may extend these methods to dynamic or heterogeneous graphs, further enhancing their utility for sophisticated graph-based reasoning and discovery.
