title: Robustness Certification of Visual Perception Models via Camera Motion Smoothing
abstract: We investigate the problem of certifying the robustness of visual perception models under physically plausible input perturbations induced by camera motion. While existing robustness certification methods primarily target additive pixel-level noise or bounded adversarial perturbations, they fail to capture geometric distortions arising from realistic camera trajectories. In this work, we formalize a threat model based on bounded, smooth camera motion, encompassing both translational and rotational components over a finite temporal window. We introduce a novel certification framework that leverages motion smoothing constraints to bound the induced transformation of each frame, enabling provable guarantees on model predictions. Our approach combines a continuous-time camera motion model with a differentiable image formation process, deriving tight bounds on the resulting pixel displacements. By integrating these bounds into an interval-based propagation method, we obtain certified robustness radii in the space of motion parameters. We evaluate our method on standard visual recognition and detection benchmarks using synthetic and real-world motion traces. Results show that our technique significantly outperforms baselines adapted from pixel-space certification, achieving larger certified regions while maintaining computational efficiency. Moreover, our analysis reveals that motion smoothing constraints naturally improve certification tightness, as high-frequency jitter is excluded from the threat model. This work establishes a principled pathway toward robustness certification of vision systems deployed in dynamic environments, bridging the gap between formal verification and physically grounded perturbations.
introduction:
The deployment of deep learning–based visual perception models in safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and surveillance has heightened the need for rigorous robustness guarantees. These models operate on sensor inputs that are often subject to various perturbations arising from real-world environmental factors. Among these, camera motion—whether due to platform dynamics, mechanical vibrations, or environmental disturbances—can significantly distort the captured images, thereby degrading perception accuracy. While recent years have seen substantial progress in certifying model robustness to additive noise, pixel-level perturbations, and geometric transformations, the specific challenge of robustness to camera motion remains underexplored. This gap is concerning, as camera motion constitutes a natural and frequently occurring source of input variation that can induce structured and temporally correlated distortions not well captured by conventional perturbation models.

Camera motion effects in visual data can be complex, involving combinations of translation, rotation, scaling, and motion blur that evolve over time. In perception pipelines, such perturbations may cause significant deviations in object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation outputs. Furthermore, in systems with closed-loop control, erroneous perception under motion-induced distortions can lead to unsafe actions. Addressing this issue requires both a principled understanding of how camera motion impacts the input space and methods to quantify and certify a model’s tolerance to such variations. However, existing certification frameworks are typically designed for static, per-image perturbation sets, such as \(\ell_p\)-bounded adversarial changes, and do not directly extend to temporally coherent and physically plausible transformations caused by camera motion.

A promising approach to mitigating the adverse effects of camera motion is to incorporate motion smoothing mechanisms at the input stage, effectively constraining the range of possible perturbations reaching the perception model. Camera motion smoothing refers to processing techniques—either in hardware, such as gimbal stabilization, or in software, such as video stabilization algorithms—that reduce high-frequency jitter and abrupt viewpoint changes. From a robustness certification perspective, such smoothing can be viewed as a pre-processing transformation that reduces the dimensionality and magnitude of the perturbation set. This reduction can, in turn, enable stronger and more efficient certification guarantees by limiting the adversary’s capacity to induce harmful input variations.

Despite its intuitive appeal, the integration of camera motion smoothing into formal certification pipelines raises several questions. How should the perturbation model be adapted to account for the stabilizing effect of smoothing? What are the trade-offs between smoothing strength, information loss, and certified robustness? How can certification frameworks be extended to handle temporal sequences and structured perturbations aligned with physical motion models? Addressing these challenges requires bridging concepts from computer vision, control theory, and robustness certification, and developing new analysis tools that couple the dynamics of camera motion with the stability properties of perception models.

In this work, we propose a framework for robustness certification of visual perception models under camera motion perturbations, leveraging motion smoothing as a key component. Our approach models camera motion as a bounded, temporally smooth trajectory in the space of geometric transformations, capturing realistic motion behaviors encountered in practice. We then incorporate a smoothing operator that attenuates high-frequency components of this trajectory, thereby restricting the adversarial perturbation space. By integrating this smoothed perturbation model into the certification process, we derive formal guarantees on the model’s output stability for all admissible camera motions within specified bounds. This formulation allows us to quantify the robustness benefits of different smoothing strategies and to identify optimal trade-offs between motion suppression and perception fidelity.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a physically grounded model of camera motion perturbations that accounts for temporal coherence and transformation constraints typical of real-world scenarios. Second, we formalize the effect of camera motion smoothing in reducing the adversarial perturbation space and develop a corresponding certification method that operates on video sequences. Third, we empirically evaluate our framework on standard visual perception benchmarks, demonstrating that motion smoothing can substantially improve certified robustness against realistic camera motion while preserving high task performance. Our results highlight the importance of considering physically motivated perturbations and pre-processing strategies in the design and certification of robust perception systems, paving the way toward safer deployment in dynamic, real-world environments.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced a framework for robustness certification of visual perception models against camera motion perturbations, leveraging camera motion smoothing as a principled defense mechanism. By modeling realistic motion trajectories and incorporating them into the certification process, we derived provable guarantees on model performance under bounded motion disturbances. Our empirical evaluation demonstrated that the proposed method achieves tighter certification bounds and higher certified accuracy compared to existing approaches, while maintaining competitive clean performance. The results highlight the importance of explicitly accounting for temporal and geometric consistency in certifying perception systems deployed in dynamic environments. Beyond static robustness, our approach extends certification to scenarios that more closely match real-world deployment conditions for autonomous systems and robotics. Future work will explore extending this framework to multi-modal perception and adaptive smoothing strategies, further enhancing certified reliability in the presence of complex, time-varying perturbations.

title: Dense Volume-to-Volume Vascular Boundary Detection
abstract: We present a dense volume-to-volume convolutional network for accurate vascular boundary detection in three-dimensional medical imaging. Unlike patch-based or slice-wise approaches that suffer from incomplete spatial context, our architecture processes entire volumetric inputs to directly produce dense boundary probability maps. The network leverages multi-scale feature extraction and deep supervision at intermediate layers to enhance boundary localization, while preserving fine anatomical details. A novel volumetric fusion scheme integrates hierarchical features to capture both global vessel topology and subtle local boundary cues. We evaluate our method on multiple 3D angiographic datasets, demonstrating superior performance over state-of-the-art approaches in terms of boundary accuracy, continuity, and robustness to noise. Quantitative results show substantial improvements in Dice coefficient and average symmetric surface distance, while qualitative analysis confirms precise delineation of complex vascular structures. Our framework enables efficient, end-to-end learning and inference, making it suitable for large-scale vascular analysis and potential integration into clinical workflows.
introduction: Accurate detection of vascular boundaries in volumetric medical imaging is critical for a wide range of diagnostic, interventional, and research applications. Precise delineation of vessel walls enables reliable quantification of vascular morphology, supports early detection of pathological changes, and facilitates planning of surgical or endovascular procedures. However, this task remains challenging due to the complex, branching topology of vascular networks, the presence of imaging noise, partial volume effects, and variability in vessel size and contrast across patients and modalities. Traditional vessel enhancement and segmentation approaches often rely on handcrafted features or local filtering, which may fail to capture fine structural details or global contextual cues. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated strong potential for medical image analysis, yet many existing methods process volumes in a patch-wise or slice-wise manner, limiting their ability to exploit full 3D spatial context. In this work, we propose a dense volume-to-volume convolutional architecture specifically designed for vascular boundary detection, enabling end-to-end learning from entire volumes and capturing both local detail and long-range dependencies for improved accuracy and robustness.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a dense volume-to-volume framework for vascular boundary detection that directly processes 3D medical image volumes to produce precise, high-resolution boundary predictions. By leveraging fully convolutional 3D architectures with dense connectivity, our method effectively captures multi-scale spatial context while preserving fine structural details critical for vascular analysis. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrated superior accuracy and robustness compared to existing approaches, particularly in challenging cases with low contrast or complex topology. These findings suggest the proposed framework is well-suited for integration into clinical workflows, enabling more consistent and efficient vascular assessment. Future work will explore domain adaptation and real-time processing for broader applicability.

title: Online Tree Caching
abstract: We investigate the online tree caching problem, a generalization of classic online caching in which items are organized as nodes of a rooted tree and caching decisions must respect the tree structure. Requests arrive sequentially for tree nodes, and the algorithm must decide, without knowledge of future requests, whether to store each node in cache, subject to capacity constraints. Fetching or evicting a node incurs a cost, and the goal is to minimize total cost over the request sequence. We present new competitive algorithms for this setting, analyze their performance, and establish lower bounds that match our upper bounds up to constant factors. Our results extend known bounds for standard caching to structured domains, demonstrating the impact of hierarchical relationships on online caching strategies.
introduction:
The proliferation of large-scale, hierarchical data structures in modern computing applications has brought renewed attention to the problem of efficient data retrieval and storage management in tree-structured environments. Many domains, such as file systems, XML databases, hierarchical key-value stores, and dynamic search trees, require repeated access to items organized in a tree topology. In such settings, the cost of retrieving data is often influenced not only by the identity of the requested item but also by its position within the tree and the path required to access it. This has motivated the study of *tree caching*, an abstraction that generalizes the classical paging problem to hierarchical structures, where decisions about which nodes to keep in fast-access memory must account for the inherent dependencies imposed by tree connectivity.

In the traditional paging model, the cache is conceived as a flat set of items, and the cost of accessing an item is uniform. In contrast, tree caching introduces structural constraints: caching a node without caching its ancestors may be either impossible or inefficient, depending on the access model. This naturally arises in systems where cached information is incrementally built from the root toward the leaves, as in web browsers storing parts of a DOM tree, or distributed systems maintaining partial views of a global hierarchy. In such contexts, the cache must often satisfy *prefix closure* or *connectedness* properties, meaning that if a node is cached, all nodes along the path from the root to that node must also be cached. This requirement significantly alters the complexity landscape and the design of efficient caching algorithms.

The *online* variant of the tree caching problem is of particular importance. In online algorithms, requests arrive sequentially and decisions must be made without knowledge of future requests. This is a natural model for real-world systems in which workloads are unpredictable or dynamically changing. The aim is to design eviction and admission policies that minimize the total cost of servicing requests, where costs may include the retrieval of uncached nodes from secondary storage or the recomputation of data. The performance of online algorithms is often evaluated through *competitive analysis*, comparing the cost incurred by the online algorithm to that of an optimal offline algorithm with complete knowledge of the request sequence.

Tree caching models have been studied in various guises, including *hierarchical caching*, *tree paging*, and *prefix caching*. These models capture scenarios where the caching decision space is constrained by a rooted tree structure and where evictions may need to remove entire subtrees to maintain feasibility. Such problems are more challenging than their flat counterparts because they require balancing local and global considerations: caching a deep node may necessitate caching a potentially large set of ancestors, while evicting a high-level node may remove many descendants at once, potentially leading to large future miss costs. Moreover, the structure of the request sequence—whether it exhibits locality within subtrees, moves frequently between branches, or follows a depth-first pattern—can have a profound impact on algorithm performance.

The study of online tree caching is not only of theoretical interest but also has practical implications. Hierarchical storage systems, content distribution networks, and in-memory representations of large datasets all face the challenge of managing limited cache space under structural constraints. Advances in this area can translate into more responsive user experiences, reduced latency, and lower bandwidth or computation costs. Furthermore, insights from competitive analysis can guide the design of robust caching strategies that perform well under a wide range of conditions, including worst-case scenarios.

In this work, we investigate the online tree caching problem in a formal setting, aiming to design and analyze algorithms that achieve strong competitive guarantees while respecting the connectivity constraints inherent in tree-structured data. We build on prior results in online caching theory, extending them to accommodate hierarchical dependencies, and we explore the trade-offs between competitiveness, implementation complexity, and adaptability to changing request patterns. By doing so, we contribute both to the theoretical foundations of online algorithm design and to the practical toolkit available for managing hierarchical data in real-world systems.
conclusion: This work has examined the online tree caching problem, extending classical caching models to hierarchical data structures. By formalizing the problem and analyzing its unique structural constraints, we developed competitive algorithms that exploit the underlying tree topology to make informed eviction and retrieval decisions. Our results demonstrate that leveraging hierarchical dependencies can significantly improve performance bounds compared to treating items as independent. We established both upper and lower bounds on the achievable competitive ratios, showing the inherent trade-offs between cache size, access patterns, and the complexity of maintaining consistency across tree nodes. Experimental evaluations confirmed that our algorithms perform robustly under diverse request sequences, reflecting realistic workloads. These findings suggest that tree-aware caching policies are particularly well suited for applications such as hierarchical databases, XML processing, and file system management. Future research may explore extensions to dynamic tree structures, probabilistic access models, and distributed environments, further broadening the applicability of online tree caching in modern computational systems.

title: Monotone false discovery rate
abstract: We investigate monotone false discovery rate (FDR) procedures, establishing conditions ensuring monotonicity in rejection thresholds. Analytical and simulation results demonstrate improved statistical power and interpretability while controlling FDR. Applications to high-dimensional data highlight advantages over existing methods in adaptive multiple testing.
introduction:
In large-scale multiple hypothesis testing, researchers are often confronted with the challenge of distinguishing true signals from noise while controlling for the rate of false discoveries. The false discovery rate (FDR), introduced by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), has emerged as a central error metric in this setting, balancing the competing goals of discovery and reliability. In a variety of scientific domains—such as genomics, neuroimaging, and signal processing—the number of simultaneous tests can reach into the tens or hundreds of thousands, intensifying the need for methods that both control the FDR and retain statistical power. As the scale and complexity of data increase, refinements to the classical FDR approach are necessary to address practical issues such as interpretability, robustness, and efficiency.

One refinement that has received growing attention is the concept of a monotone false discovery rate. In its general form, the local false discovery rate (local fdr) is defined as the posterior probability that a given observation is null, given its test statistic or corresponding p-value. This function, as a function of the test statistic, is not guaranteed to be monotonic in practice, particularly when the test statistics are estimated from finite samples or under model misspecification. Non-monotonicity can manifest as counterintuitive behavior: larger test statistics, which intuitively should correspond to stronger evidence against the null, may yield higher estimated local fdr values than smaller test statistics. Such irregularities complicate interpretation and may lead to suboptimal decision rules.

The appeal of enforcing monotonicity in the local fdr arises from both theoretical and practical considerations. From a decision-theoretic perspective, the optimal rejection region for maximizing power at a given FDR level is characterized by thresholding a monotone function of the test statistic, under certain regularity conditions. If the estimated local fdr is not monotone, the resulting rejection region may be fragmented or otherwise inefficient. Enforcing monotonicity can restore the desirable property that stronger evidence against the null leads to a uniformly lower probability of being null, yielding more coherent and interpretable rejection regions. From a practical standpoint, monotonic estimates are often smoother and less sensitive to sampling variability, which can improve stability in high-dimensional settings.

Several strands of literature have touched upon monotonicity in FDR-related quantities. Early work on monotone likelihood ratio properties in hypothesis testing established the connection between monotonicity and uniformly most powerful tests. More recently, Efron and colleagues have emphasized the empirical estimation of the local fdr from observed data, typically by modeling the distribution of test statistics as a mixture of null and alternative components. In these empirical Bayes frameworks, the estimated local fdr can be highly non-monotone if the mixture model is misspecified or if the estimation procedures are noisy. Adjustments that impose monotonicity—either through constrained optimization, isotonic regression, or post hoc smoothing—have been proposed in related contexts, but a comprehensive treatment within the FDR framework remains relatively underdeveloped.

The monotone false discovery rate can be viewed as a post-processed version of the traditional local fdr in which monotonicity with respect to the test statistic is enforced by construction. This adjustment aims to preserve the probabilistic interpretation of the local fdr while eliminating artifacts arising from estimation variability. The resulting monotone local fdr can then be used to derive rejection regions, estimate the overall FDR, and inform adaptive thresholding procedures. The monotone approach also aligns with the intuition underlying the original Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, in which smaller p-values are always treated as stronger evidence against the null; in the local fdr context, monotonicity ensures that this ordering principle is respected.

The motivation for studying monotone false discovery rates is particularly strong in modern high-throughput applications. In genomic studies, for example, test statistics such as z-scores derived from gene expression data may exhibit non-monotone estimated local fdrs due to heteroscedasticity, dependence, or deviations from assumed parametric forms. Neuroimaging analyses, which involve spatially correlated test statistics over thousands of voxels, likewise present estimation challenges that can produce irregular local fdr curves. In these settings, enforcing monotonicity has the potential to yield more reliable inference without sacrificing much power, and may reduce the risk of spurious patterns driven by estimation noise rather than genuine signal.

Despite these potential benefits, the properties of monotone false discovery rate estimators, and their implications for multiple testing procedures, remain incompletely understood. Important questions include how monotonicity enforcement interacts with bias and variance in local fdr estimation; how it affects the finite-sample and asymptotic control of the FDR; and how it performs relative to unconstrained estimators in terms of discovery power. Furthermore, the choice of methodology for imposing monotonicity—whether through isotonic regression, shape-constrained density estimation, or model-based approaches—can influence both theoretical guarantees and practical performance. A systematic investigation of these issues is essential for guiding the adoption of monotone FDR methods in applied research.

In this work, we develop a formal framework for the monotone false discovery rate, characterize its theoretical properties, and evaluate its performance through simulations and real-data applications. By situating monotonicity enforcement within the broader empirical Bayes and multiple testing literature, we aim to clarify its role in improving interpretability and efficiency of large-scale inference. Our results suggest that monotone FDR methods can offer a robust and principled enhancement to existing procedures, particularly in complex, high-dimensional settings where standard estimators may falter.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the concept of a monotone false discovery rate (FDR) and its implications for multiple hypothesis testing. By formalizing conditions under which the FDR exhibits monotonicity, we provide a framework that enhances interpretability and stability of inference procedures. Our results demonstrate that enforcing monotonicity can improve power while maintaining rigorous control over type I error rates, particularly in settings with structured hypotheses or dependence. The theoretical developments are supported by simulations illustrating practical benefits. These findings suggest that monotone FDR procedures offer a principled approach to balancing discovery and reliability, and merit further exploration in diverse applications such as genomics, neuroimaging, and large-scale screening studies.

title: The BACCO Simulation Project: A baryonification emulator with Neural Networks
abstract: We present the BACCO Simulation Project baryonification emulator, a novel tool that combines high-resolution cosmological simulations with neural network techniques to model the impact of baryonic physics on the matter distribution across cosmic time. Our approach builds on a suite of gravity-only simulations from the BACCO project, to which we apply a fast, physically motivated baryonification procedure calibrated against state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulations. We train deep neural networks to emulate the non-linear matter power spectrum and correlation functions over a wide range of cosmological parameters and baryonic feedback strengths. The emulator achieves sub-percent accuracy on scales relevant for current and forthcoming weak lensing and galaxy clustering surveys, while reducing computational costs by several orders of magnitude compared to full hydrodynamical runs. We demonstrate its performance through extensive validation against independent simulation sets, highlighting the flexibility of the framework to incorporate new feedback models. The BACCO baryonification emulator provides an efficient and accurate pathway to marginalize over baryonic uncertainties in large-scale structure analyses, enabling robust cosmological inference from next-generation survey data. The code and trained networks are publicly available to support community use and further development.
introduction:
The accelerated growth of cosmological surveys over the past decade has driven the need for increasingly accurate theoretical predictions of the large-scale structure of the Universe. Upcoming experiments such as *Euclid*, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will deliver unprecedented measurements of cosmic matter distribution, placing stringent constraints on the physics of dark matter, dark energy, and the laws of gravity. However, the interpretation of these data requires forward models that capture the impact of both dark matter and baryonic physics on cosmological observables across a wide range of scales.

While gravity-only \(N\)-body simulations have achieved remarkable precision in predicting the dark matter distribution, hydrodynamical simulations reveal that baryonic processes—such as gas cooling, star formation, and feedback from supernovae and active galactic nuclei—can significantly alter the matter power spectrum and correlation functions at quasi-linear and non-linear scales. Directly incorporating these effects into cosmological inference is computationally prohibitive, as high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations are expensive and cannot be run for the vast number of cosmological models required in parameter estimation. Consequently, efficient and accurate methods for “baryonifying” dark-matter-only simulations have emerged as a promising alternative.

The BACCO (Baryons and Cosmology with COsmological simulations) project aims to develop high-precision emulators for cosmological statistics, leveraging a suite of large-volume, high-resolution simulations. In this work, we introduce a baryonification emulator based on artificial neural networks (ANNs), trained on the BACCO simulation suite. Our approach applies a physically motivated baryonification algorithm to gravity-only simulations, producing fast and flexible predictions of the matter distribution that account for baryonic effects. The ANN is then trained to interpolate between baryonification parameters and cosmological models, enabling rapid generation of observables without rerunning expensive simulations.

By combining the speed of gravity-only simulations with the fidelity of physically motivated baryonic corrections, our emulator provides a powerful tool for the analysis of forthcoming survey data. We present the methodology, training process, and performance of the neural network emulator, and assess its accuracy against full hydrodynamical runs. This work represents a step toward bridging the gap between computational feasibility and the high-precision modeling required for next-generation cosmology.
conclusion:
In this work we have presented the BACCO simulation project’s baryonification emulator, a novel framework that combines state-of-the-art cosmological simulations with neural network emulation to model the impact of baryonic physics on the matter distribution. Our approach builds on the extensive suite of high-resolution dark-matter-only and hydrodynamical simulations within BACCO, and leverages a parametrized baryonification scheme to efficiently incorporate the effects of feedback processes on large-scale structure observables. By training neural networks to emulate the baryonification corrections across a wide parameter space, we have demonstrated that it is possible to produce fast, accurate predictions for power spectra and correlation functions that include realistic baryonic effects.

The emulator achieves high precision in reproducing the baryon-corrected results from full hydrodynamical simulations, with typical errors well below the observational requirements for current and forthcoming large-scale structure surveys. This level of accuracy is maintained across a broad range of redshifts, cosmological parameters, and baryonic feedback strengths, confirming the flexibility and robustness of the neural network approach. Compared to traditional interpolation or analytic fitting functions, the neural network emulator provides superior performance in capturing complex, nonlinear dependencies, particularly in the transition regime between linear and strongly nonlinear scales where baryonic effects become significant.

The computational efficiency of the emulator is a key advantage. Once trained, it can generate predictions orders of magnitude faster than running full hydrodynamical simulations, enabling its integration into parameter inference pipelines that require repeated model evaluations. This makes it particularly well suited for cosmological analyses of weak lensing, galaxy clustering, and other probes sensitive to the small-scale matter distribution. The ability to marginalize over baryonic uncertainties in a statistically rigorous way will be crucial for exploiting the full statistical power of surveys such as Euclid, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

An additional strength of our framework lies in its transparency and modularity. The baryonification model is physically interpretable, with explicit parameters controlling halo profiles, gas fractions, and feedback-induced redistribution of matter. This allows for direct physical interpretation of constraints on baryonic parameters and facilitates the incorporation of external astrophysical information. The neural network serves as an efficient mapping between these physically motivated parameters and the resulting matter statistics, without obscuring the underlying model assumptions.

We have also explored the extrapolation capabilities of the emulator. While the network is trained within a finite parameter volume, we find that it behaves reasonably in mildly extrapolated regimes, provided the underlying baryonification model remains valid. Nevertheless, we stress the importance of careful parameter space design and coverage in training datasets, as well as the need to quantify uncertainties in regions where training data are sparse. Future work will expand the training set to include additional cosmological models, feedback prescriptions, and alternative baryonification schemes, further increasing the generality and applicability of the emulator.

The methodology presented here opens several promising avenues for further research. First, the framework can be extended beyond two-point statistics to emulate higher-order measures such as the bispectrum, which are also sensitive to baryonic physics. Second, incorporating observational systematics into the emulator training could allow for end-to-end forward modeling of survey data, reducing potential biases in cosmological inference. Third, the combination of emulation techniques with simulation-based inference offers a natural path toward fully Bayesian constraints on cosmology and astrophysics from large-scale structure data.

More broadly, the BACCO baryonification emulator illustrates the potential of combining physically motivated models with machine learning to tackle complex problems in cosmology. By embedding neural networks within an interpretable theoretical framework, we can retain physical insight while exploiting the flexibility and computational speed of modern learning algorithms. This hybrid approach is likely to become increasingly important as cosmological data improve in precision and as the demand for accurate, efficient theoretical predictions continues to grow.

In summary, we have developed and validated a neural network emulator for baryonification within the BACCO simulation project that delivers fast, accurate, and physically interpretable predictions for the impact of baryons on the matter distribution. This tool will enable the cosmological community to incorporate baryonic effects into large-scale structure analyses with unprecedented efficiency, helping to ensure that the next generation of surveys can achieve their ambitious scientific goals without being limited by our understanding of small-scale astrophysics. The public release of the emulator, together with the underlying simulation data, will further enhance its utility and foster collaboration across the fields of cosmology, astrophysics, and machine learning.

title: Particular object retrieval with integral max-pooling of CNN activations
abstract: We address the problem of retrieving particular objects in images using compact and discriminative representations derived from convolutional neural network (CNN) activations. Building on regional maximum activations of convolutions (R-MAC), we introduce an integral max-pooling scheme that enables efficient aggregation of region-based CNN features over multiple scales. This approach eliminates the need for exhaustive region evaluation by leveraging integral images adapted to max-pooling, thus significantly reducing computational cost while preserving retrieval accuracy. The resulting descriptors remain compact and translation-invariant, making them well-suited for large-scale image retrieval. We further explore fine-tuning CNNs for the specific task of particular object retrieval, demonstrating that task-oriented training enhances feature discriminability. Comprehensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including Oxford5k, Paris6k, and Holidays, show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with competitive memory and runtime efficiency. The proposed framework combines effectiveness, efficiency, and scalability, offering a practical solution for instance-level image retrieval in real-world applications.
introduction:
In recent years, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have emerged as the dominant paradigm for a wide range of computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and retrieval. Their ability to learn hierarchical feature representations directly from raw image data has led to significant advances over traditional handcrafted descriptors. In the context of image retrieval, CNN-based descriptors have been shown to outperform conventional local features such as SIFT when applied to the problem of retrieving images containing a specific object instance. However, the design of effective aggregation and pooling strategies for CNN activations remains a critical component in achieving high retrieval performance, particularly when the goal is to localize and retrieve particular objects within complex scenes.

Particular object retrieval differs from category-level retrieval in that the focus is on finding images containing the same specific object, often under varying viewpoints, illuminations, scales, and partial occlusions. This task poses unique challenges: the object of interest may occupy only a small fraction of the image, may be surrounded by clutter, and may appear in different spatial contexts. Global image descriptors derived from CNN activations can capture rich semantic information, but without careful pooling or spatial analysis they may be dominated by background content, leading to reduced discriminative power for the target object. Therefore, accurate localization and the ability to focus representation on the most relevant regions are essential for robust particular object retrieval.

A common approach to derive compact image descriptors from CNN feature maps is to apply spatial pooling, such as max-pooling or average-pooling, over the activation maps of convolutional layers. Max-pooling preserves the most prominent activation within a region, thereby capturing the strongest evidence for a given feature, while average-pooling aggregates all responses, potentially offering robustness to noise. However, both fixed pooling strategies are limited when the object of interest occupies an arbitrary portion of the image, since the pooling region is fixed and often spans the entire feature map. In such cases, the descriptor may integrate irrelevant background activations, diluting the signature of the object.

To address this limitation, region-based search methods have been proposed, in which descriptors are computed for multiple subregions of the image and compared with query features. While these approaches can improve retrieval performance by better isolating the object, they are computationally expensive, especially when the number of candidate regions is large. The computational burden is further exacerbated when applied at scale, such as in large image databases, where efficient search is paramount. Consequently, there is a strong motivation to develop pooling and search techniques that both improve localization and maintain computational efficiency.

Integral images, originally introduced for rapid computation of Haar-like features, provide a mechanism to compute region sums or averages in constant time regardless of region size. This principle can be extended to CNN activation maps, enabling the efficient evaluation of pooled feature responses over arbitrary rectangular regions. By leveraging integral images for feature aggregation, it becomes possible to implement a form of integral max-pooling that approximates the maximum activation over a region without exhaustively scanning all contained features. Such an approach offers a promising trade-off between localization accuracy and computational cost.

In this work, we explore the use of integral max-pooling of CNN activations for the task of particular object retrieval. Our method builds on the observation that the most discriminative features for an object instance are often localized to specific spatial regions in the convolutional feature maps. By efficiently identifying and aggregating the strongest activations over candidate regions, we obtain descriptors that are more focused on the target object while avoiding the prohibitive cost of exhaustive region evaluation. We study how integral max-pooling can be integrated into a retrieval pipeline, analyze its approximation properties, and evaluate its impact on retrieval accuracy and efficiency.

Through extensive experiments on standard retrieval benchmarks, we demonstrate that our approach not only improves retrieval performance compared to global pooling baselines but also achieves competitive efficiency relative to existing region-based methods. The proposed technique thus offers a practical solution for large-scale particular object retrieval, combining the representational strength of CNN features with the computational advantages of integral image-based pooling.
conclusion: We have presented an approach for particular object retrieval that leverages integral max-pooling over convolutional neural network activations to efficiently localize and describe image content. By formulating max-pooling in an integral form, our method enables rapid computation of pooled features across multiple regions, significantly reducing the cost of evaluating many candidate boxes. Experiments demonstrate that this representation preserves strong discriminative power while enabling precise object localization, leading to improved retrieval performance on challenging benchmarks. The approach is compatible with off-the-shelf CNN models and does not require task-specific retraining, making it broadly applicable to diverse retrieval scenarios. Future work will explore integration with region proposal mechanisms and end-to-end learning to further enhance efficiency and accuracy in large-scale visual search systems.

title: The Octave (Birmingham - Sheffield Hallam) automated pipeline for extracting oscillation parameters of solar-like main-sequence stars
abstract: We present *The Octave* (Birmingham–Sheffield Hallam) automated analysis pipeline for the extraction of global asteroseismic parameters from solar-like oscillators on the main sequence. The pipeline is designed for high-throughput processing of photometric time-series data, delivering robust estimates of the frequency of maximum power (*ν*<sub>max</sub>) and the mean large frequency separation (Δν). It employs iterative background fitting, automated detection of the oscillation power excess, and Bayesian parameter estimation to ensure reliability across a wide range of signal-to-noise regimes. Performance is validated using synthetic datasets and benchmarked against Kepler observations, demonstrating accuracy and precision comparable to established methods. *The Octave* enables efficient, homogeneous analysis of large stellar samples, supporting current and future space missions such as *TESS* and *PLATO*, and facilitating population-level studies of stellar structure and evolution.
introduction:
Asteroseismology has emerged as a powerful tool for probing the internal structure and dynamics of stars by measuring and interpreting their oscillation modes. For solar-like main-sequence stars, these oscillations are stochastically excited and intrinsically damped by near-surface convection, producing characteristic patterns in their frequency spectra. The precise measurement of global oscillation parameters, such as the frequency of maximum oscillation power (\( \nu_{\mathrm{max}} \)) and the large frequency separation (\( \Delta\nu \)), enables robust estimates of stellar masses, radii, and ages via scaling relations and detailed modelling. With the advent of high-precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions such as *Kepler*, K2, and TESS, the volume of high-quality time-series data has increased dramatically, creating a pressing need for automated, reliable, and scalable analysis pipelines.

Manual or semi-automated analysis of oscillation spectra is no longer practical for large stellar samples, particularly in the context of ongoing and forthcoming surveys expected to deliver data for tens of thousands of solar-like oscillators. Automated pipelines must therefore be capable of detecting oscillations, extracting global seismic parameters, and providing associated uncertainties in a consistent and reproducible manner without extensive human intervention. Such tools are essential not only for population-level studies of stellar structure and evolution, but also for the rapid characterisation of stars hosting exoplanets, where accurate stellar parameters are critical for determining planetary properties.

The Octave (Birmingham–Sheffield Hallam) pipeline has been developed to address these challenges by delivering an end-to-end, automated solution for the extraction of global oscillation parameters from photometric time-series data. Building upon established methods in the asteroseismic community, Octave implements a sequence of processing steps – from initial time-series preparation and noise characterisation to the detection of oscillation power excess and the determination of \( \nu_{\mathrm{max}} \) and \( \Delta\nu \). The pipeline employs statistically robust detection algorithms and incorporates Monte Carlo simulations to assess parameter uncertainties.

In this paper, we present the design, implementation, and validation of the Octave pipeline. We describe its performance on both simulated datasets and real observations from the *Kepler* mission, and we compare its outputs with those from other widely used asteroseismic analysis tools. By providing a transparent and reproducible framework, Octave is intended to support large-scale stellar characterisation efforts and to facilitate the exploitation of current and upcoming space-based photometric datasets. Its modular design also allows adaptation to different missions and noise regimes, ensuring continued applicability in the era of high-volume asteroseismic data.
conclusion:
The development of the Octave (Birmingham – Sheffield Hallam) automated pipeline represents a significant step forward in the efficient and reliable extraction of oscillation parameters for solar-like main-sequence stars. By combining robust statistical techniques with automated quality control and validation procedures, the pipeline achieves consistent performance across a wide range of stellar signal-to-noise regimes. Its modular design allows for flexibility in adapting to different input datasets and observational constraints, while maintaining a standardised approach that is essential for large-scale, homogeneous analyses.  

Application of the pipeline to both simulated and real data has demonstrated its capability to recover key asteroseismic parameters, such as the frequency of maximum oscillation power and the large frequency separation, with precision comparable to or exceeding that of manual analyses. The integration of automated outlier rejection and parameter uncertainty estimation provides a rigorous framework for downstream stellar modelling, ensuring that the extracted parameters are both physically meaningful and statistically robust.  

One of the strengths of Octave lies in its scalability. The growing volume of asteroseismic observations from missions such as *Kepler*, *TESS*, and the forthcoming *PLATO* requires tools that can process thousands of light curves with minimal human intervention. The pipeline’s performance in benchmark tests indicates that it can meet these demands, making it a valuable asset for current and future large-scale stellar surveys.  

The results presented here also highlight the importance of cross-validation with independent pipelines to identify systematic differences and potential biases. Continued collaboration between research groups will further refine the methodology, improve accuracy, and expand applicability to a broader range of stellar types, including subgiants and red giants.  

In summary, Octave delivers a fast, reliable, and reproducible means of determining oscillation parameters for solar-like main-sequence stars. Its deployment will contribute to the efficient exploitation of high-quality photometric datasets, enabling more comprehensive population studies and more precise constraints on stellar evolution models. Future work will focus on extending its capabilities, incorporating additional diagnostics, and ensuring seamless integration into the global asteroseismic analysis framework in preparation for the data-rich era ahead.

title: Investigating an online social network using spatial interaction models
abstract: This study applies spatial interaction models to examine structural patterns within an online social network. By conceptualizing user connections as flows between spatially distributed entities, we investigate how interaction intensity relates to virtual distance, user activity, and network topology. Using anonymized data from a large-scale platform, model parameters reveal the extent to which proximity in digital space influences tie formation. Results highlight spatial analogies in online behavior, offering insights into network dynamics and informing the design of more effective digital communication environments.
introduction:
Online social networks (OSNs) have become integral to contemporary social, cultural, and economic life, facilitating interactions among individuals, groups, and organizations across diverse geographic and social boundaries. Platforms such as Facebook, Twitter, and LinkedIn enable the exchange of information, the maintenance of relationships, and the formation of new connections, often transcending physical distance. While these platforms operate in virtual environments, the patterns of interaction they host are often shaped by spatial, temporal, and socio-demographic factors. Understanding the determinants of such patterns is crucial for explaining the structure and dynamics of online networks, predicting information diffusion, and informing the design of more effective communication and engagement strategies.

Spatial interaction models, initially developed in geography and regional science, provide a powerful framework for studying flows between discrete locations, whether those flows represent the movement of people, goods, or information. Rooted in the analogy to Newtonian gravity, these models posit that the volume of interaction between two locations is positively associated with their size or importance and negatively associated with the distance or friction separating them. Over the past decades, spatial interaction models have been applied to contexts as varied as migration, commuting, trade, and tourism. More recently, scholars have begun to explore their applicability to digital environments, in which interactions occur online but may still be conditioned by underlying spatial and social structures.

In the context of OSNs, spatial interaction models offer a means of quantifying how geographic distance, population size, and other attributes influence the likelihood and intensity of online ties. Even in ostensibly placeless digital spaces, empirical evidence suggests that physical proximity continues to play a role: users are more likely to interact with others in similar or nearby locations, and regional clusters of activity are common. Additionally, social and cultural boundaries—often correlated with geography—can shape interaction patterns. By adapting spatial interaction models to online settings, it becomes possible to test hypotheses about the persistence of spatial effects in a digitally mediated world.

This study investigates the structure of an online social network through the lens of spatial interaction modelling. Using a dataset that captures connections and interactions among users, along with their geographic locations and relevant attributes, we assess the extent to which classical spatial determinants—such as distance decay and population size—explain observed patterns. We also consider extensions to the basic model that incorporate measures of social similarity and network topology, allowing for a richer understanding of the interplay between spatial and social factors.

Through this analysis, we aim to contribute to both the methodological literature on spatial interaction models and the substantive literature on online social networks. Methodologically, our work demonstrates how models traditionally applied to physical flows can be adapted for digital contexts. Substantively, our findings shed light on the enduring role of geography in shaping online social structures, offering implications for theories of social interaction, digital inequality, and the localization of online content. By bridging spatial analysis and network science, this research advances our understanding of how spatial processes manifest in virtual domains.
conclusion:
This study has examined the structure and dynamics of an online social network through the lens of spatial interaction models, adapting methodologies traditionally employed in the analysis of physical flows of people, goods, and information to the digital sphere. By conceptualising user interactions as spatial flows between nodes embedded in a virtual space, we have demonstrated that many of the principles governing offline spatial behaviour—such as distance decay, attraction based on size or influence, and the role of intervening opportunities—retain explanatory power in an online context. The empirical results indicate that the intensity of interaction between users is significantly shaped by both virtual proximity, as operationalised through network distance, and by attributes of the nodes themselves, including activity level and popularity.

Our findings suggest that spatial interaction models can effectively capture the patterned nature of online communications, revealing a nuanced interplay between structural constraints and individual agency. The adaptation of gravity-type formulations provided a robust framework for quantifying these relationships, while also allowing for the incorporation of online-specific variables such as topical similarity and temporal synchrony. The results support the proposition that even in ostensibly ‘borderless’ digital environments, spatial-like frictions persist, influencing the distribution and volume of interaction flows.

Beyond methodological contributions, the study underscores the value of integrating perspectives from geography, network science, and computational social science to enhance our understanding of digital social systems. The spatial interaction approach offers a parsimonious yet flexible toolset for modelling and predicting patterns of online engagement, with potential applications in areas such as information diffusion modelling, targeted communication strategies, and the detection of anomalies in interaction patterns.

Nevertheless, several limitations warrant acknowledgement. The operationalisation of ‘distance’ in virtual environments remains an evolving challenge, and future work should explore alternative metrics that more fully capture the multidimensional nature of online proximity. Additionally, the cross-sectional design of the present analysis constrains our ability to assess temporal dynamics; longitudinal studies could illuminate how spatial interaction parameters evolve as networks grow or undergo structural changes. Finally, expanding the scope of analysis to include multiple platforms and diverse user populations would enhance the generalisability of the findings.

In conclusion, this investigation demonstrates that spatial interaction models, when thoughtfully adapted, offer a powerful lens for analysing online social networks. By bridging conceptual frameworks from physical and digital domains, such models deepen our understanding of the patterned flows that underpin social connectivity in networked societies and open promising avenues for future interdisciplinary research.

title: CNNATT: Deep EEG & fNIRS Real-Time Decoding of bimanual forces
abstract: We propose **CNNATT**, a novel deep learning framework for real-time decoding of bimanual force generation from simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) signals. The method integrates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for hierarchical spatial–temporal feature extraction with an attention mechanism to adaptively weight modality-specific contributions. EEG and fNIRS data were recorded from healthy participants performing graded, independent force tasks with both hands. Preprocessing included artifact removal and temporal alignment to enable precise multimodal fusion. CNNATT was trained to predict continuous force trajectories for each hand, leveraging complementary neural and hemodynamic information. Results demonstrated superior decoding accuracy and robustness compared to unimodal and non-attention baselines, with statistically significant improvements in correlation and root mean square error metrics. The attention maps revealed dynamic shifts in modality relevance across time and force levels, highlighting neurovascular coupling variations. These findings indicate that CNNATT enables accurate, low-latency estimation of bimanual forces, supporting future applications in brain–computer interfaces, neurorehabilitation, and motor control research.
introduction:
Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a transformative technology for enabling direct communication between the human brain and external devices, with applications in neurorehabilitation, assistive robotics, and human–machine interaction. A key challenge in BCI research lies in accurately decoding complex motor intentions, particularly those involving bimanual coordination, from non-invasive neural signals in real time. Bimanual force generation, which underlies many daily activities, requires the simultaneous and coordinated activation of distributed cortical and subcortical networks. Capturing and interpreting these neural dynamics is essential for developing BCIs that can support naturalistic motor control in both healthy individuals and patients with motor impairments.

Electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) are two complementary neuroimaging modalities that offer distinct advantages for non-invasive BCI systems. EEG provides high temporal resolution, capturing rapid electrophysiological responses associated with motor preparation and execution, while fNIRS measures hemodynamic changes with higher spatial resolution and is less susceptible to electrical noise. Combining EEG and fNIRS has been shown to improve decoding accuracy by exploiting both the fast electrical and slower metabolic signatures of brain activity. However, most existing multimodal BCI studies have focused on discrete motor tasks such as simple limb movements or motor imagery, and relatively few have addressed the continuous and dynamic decoding of bimanual force generation.

Recent advances in deep learning have opened new possibilities for modeling the complex, nonlinear relationships in multimodal brain signals. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are particularly suited for learning spatial–temporal patterns in EEG and fNIRS data without the need for extensive handcrafted feature extraction. Furthermore, attention mechanisms have demonstrated the ability to adaptively focus on the most informative signal components, potentially enhancing decoding performance in noisy, high-dimensional datasets. Despite these developments, the integration of attention-based deep learning approaches for real-time decoding of continuous bimanual forces from combined EEG and fNIRS signals remains largely unexplored.

Real-time decoding imposes additional constraints on BCI design, including low-latency processing, robustness to inter-subject variability, and resilience to motion artifacts, particularly in naturalistic motor tasks. Achieving these goals requires architectures that can efficiently process multimodal data streams while maintaining high predictive accuracy. Additionally, the decoding of continuous force trajectories—rather than categorical movement states—presents greater demands on temporal modeling and regression performance.

In this study, we propose CNNATT, a novel deep learning framework that integrates convolutional neural networks with an attention mechanism to decode continuous bimanual force outputs from simultaneous EEG and fNIRS recordings in real time. The model leverages modality-specific feature extraction, cross-modal fusion, and adaptive weighting of salient temporal–spatial patterns to enhance decoding accuracy and responsiveness. We evaluate CNNATT in a controlled experimental setting involving graded bimanual force tasks, assessing its performance against conventional regression models and unimodal baselines. Our results demonstrate that CNNATT can achieve accurate, low-latency decoding of bimanual forces, underscoring its potential for next-generation neurorehabilitation and human–robot interaction applications.
conclusion: This study introduced CNNATT, a deep learning framework integrating convolutional neural networks with attention mechanisms for real-time decoding of bimanual force generation from simultaneous EEG and fNIRS recordings. By leveraging the complementary temporal resolution of EEG and hemodynamic sensitivity of fNIRS, CNNATT effectively captured multimodal neural signatures, enabling precise and robust estimation of continuous force trajectories. The proposed model outperformed conventional unimodal and multimodal baselines, demonstrating superior accuracy and temporal stability, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for online applications. Attention-based feature weighting further enhanced interpretability by highlighting modality- and region-specific contributions during force exertion. These findings underscore the potential of hybrid neuroimaging with deep attention architectures for advancing brain–computer interfaces in motor rehabilitation, neuroprosthetics, and human–machine interaction. Future work will explore generalization across participants, adaptation to dynamic movement contexts, and integration with closed-loop control systems to enhance functional restoration and assistive technologies reliant on accurate, real-time decoding of complex motor behaviors.

title: Modelling recombinations during cosmological reionization
abstract: We present a semi-analytic framework for modelling hydrogen recombinations during the epoch of cosmological reionization. Our approach incorporates inhomogeneous density fields, evolving ionization topologies, and temperature-dependent recombination coefficients to capture the spatial and temporal complexity of the process. We calibrate the model against high-resolution radiative transfer simulations, achieving good agreement in the evolution of the ionized fraction and recombination rate density. Application to large-scale reionization scenarios reveals the significant contribution of dense clumps and filaments to photon consumption, delaying reionization completion. This work provides a computationally efficient tool for interpreting observations of the high-redshift intergalactic medium and constraining the sources driving reionization.
introduction:
The epoch of reionization (EoR) marks a major phase transition in the history of the Universe, during which the initially neutral hydrogen in the intergalactic medium (IGM) became ionized by the first luminous sources. This process, occurring over redshifts approximately \( 6 \lesssim z \lesssim 15 \), was driven by ultraviolet (UV) photons emitted by early populations of stars, galaxies, and possibly accreting black holes. The interplay between ionizing radiation, gas density structure, and the evolving source population determines both the timing and morphology of reionization. Understanding the EoR is crucial for connecting cosmological initial conditions to the complex, nonlinear structures observed in the later Universe, as well as for interpreting forthcoming observational data from facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), and 21 cm intensity mapping experiments.

A key factor governing the progress and completion of reionization is the balance between ionizations and recombinations. While ionizing photons carve out expanding H II regions, recombination processes within these regions act to consume photons, increasing the overall photon budget required to reionize the Universe. The rate of recombinations depends sensitively on the density distribution of the ionized gas: overdense clumps can have recombination timescales much shorter than the Hubble time, repeatedly capturing free electrons and necessitating multiple ionizations. The so-called “clumping factor” is often used to parameterize the enhancement of recombination rates relative to a uniform medium, but its value and evolution are strongly influenced by small-scale structure, radiative feedback, and hydrodynamical processes.

Accurately modelling recombinations during the EoR is a challenging problem. On the one hand, large-scale cosmological simulations are required to capture the global topology of reionization and the statistics of ionized regions across hundreds of comoving megaparsecs. On the other hand, recombination rates are dominated by sub-kiloparsec scales, where gas becomes self-shielded and dynamically responds to photoheating. Bridging these scales demands hybrid approaches that combine large-scale radiative transfer and structure formation with high-resolution modelling of the IGM’s small-scale clumpiness. Simplified analytic prescriptions, semi-numerical models, and parameterized subgrid treatments have been widely adopted, but their accuracy remains uncertain without careful calibration against high-resolution simulations or observational constraints.

The impact of recombinations extends beyond the photon budget. Because recombination rates scale with the square of the electron density, they are sensitive to the thermal history of the IGM, which itself is shaped by the timing and intensity of reionization. Photoheating during reionization can smooth out small-scale baryonic structures, reducing the clumping factor and thus lowering subsequent recombination rates. Conversely, in regions where reionization is delayed, cold, dense structures may persist longer, sustaining high recombination rates once ionized. This feedback between the thermal and ionization state of the IGM introduces nontrivial spatial and temporal variations in recombination histories.

In this work, we develop and analyse models for recombinations during cosmological reionization that aim to capture both the global evolution and the influence of small-scale structure. By systematically comparing different treatments and incorporating recent high-resolution simulation results, we assess the limitations of common parametrizations and explore their implications for the timing, topology, and photon requirements of reionization. Our approach provides a framework for interpreting current and upcoming observational probes of the EoR in the context of the physical processes that regulate it.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the role of recombinations in shaping the progress and morphology of cosmological reionization, focusing in particular on their impact on the ionization history and the topology of the ionized regions. By developing and applying a physically motivated model for the inhomogeneous distribution of recombination rates, we have been able to capture the effects of small-scale gas clumping on large-scale reionization dynamics. Our approach bridges analytic theory and numerical simulation, allowing us to quantify departures from the simplifying assumptions of uniform recombination or constant clumping factors often adopted in earlier studies.

The results demonstrate that recombinations are not merely a uniform sink for ionizing photons, but a spatially and temporally varying process whose importance grows as reionization progresses. In the early stages, when ionized bubbles are small and concentrated around sources, recombinations are relatively inefficient due to the low mean density of ionized gas. However, as ionized regions expand into denser environments and begin to overlap, the enhanced clumping of the ionized medium significantly increases the recombination rate. This leads to a self-regulating effect: the growth of ionized regions slows, and the overlap phase is extended relative to models with simplified recombination treatments.

Our modelling further reveals that neglecting the inhomogeneity of recombinations can lead to systematic underestimates of the ionizing photon budget required to complete reionization. In particular, the tail end of the process is strongly affected, with inhomogeneous recombinations delaying the final percolation of ionized regions and increasing the overall photon consumption by factors of order unity. This has direct implications for interpreting high-redshift galaxy luminosity functions, the ionizing efficiency of sources, and constraints from the Thomson optical depth.

While the model captures key physical effects, further refinements are warranted. In particular, coupling the recombination treatment to detailed radiative transfer, incorporating feedback from photoheating on small-scale gas structure, and calibrating against high-resolution simulations will improve the robustness of predictions. Moreover, future observations, including upcoming 21 cm experiments and deep galaxy surveys, will offer critical tests of the predicted recombination-driven modulation of the reionization timeline.

Overall, our findings highlight the necessity of incorporating spatially resolved recombination physics into models of reionization. Doing so is essential for accurately connecting theoretical predictions to observational probes of the epoch when the first luminous sources transformed the intergalactic medium.

title: TrajeVAE: Controllable Human Motion Generation from Trajectories
abstract: We present **TrajeVAE**, a novel generative framework for controllable human motion synthesis driven by user-specified spatial trajectories. Unlike prior motion generation approaches that rely heavily on action labels or predefined motion templates, TrajeVAE learns a latent representation that jointly models trajectory patterns and corresponding full-body motions. Our method employs a conditional variational autoencoder architecture, where a trajectory encoder extracts spatial–temporal features, and a motion decoder produces realistic pose sequences consistent with both the trajectory and the underlying motion style. By disentangling trajectory control from motion dynamics, TrajeVAE enables flexible manipulation of path shape, speed, and stylistic attributes without requiring paired trajectory–motion datasets for every variation. We introduce a trajectory-conditioned latent fusion mechanism that preserves motion naturalness while adhering closely to the desired path. Extensive experiments on benchmark motion capture datasets demonstrate that TrajeVAE achieves state-of-the-art performance in trajectory following accuracy, motion realism, and style controllability. Our approach offers a versatile solution for animation, virtual reality, and robotics applications requiring precise yet expressive human motion generation.
introduction:
Human motion generation has emerged as a central research problem in computer graphics, computer vision, and robotics, with applications ranging from animation and virtual reality to human–robot interaction and autonomous agents. The challenge lies in producing realistic, diverse, and context-appropriate motion sequences conditioned on high-level controls while preserving both physical plausibility and stylistic coherence. Traditional motion synthesis pipelines have relied on motion capture databases combined with interpolation, blending, or procedural methods. While such approaches can produce plausible results in constrained scenarios, they often require extensive manual authoring, are limited in diversity, and struggle to generalize to unseen motion patterns or control signals.

In recent years, deep generative models have transformed the landscape of motion synthesis. Architectures such as recurrent neural networks, generative adversarial networks (GANs), and more recently variational autoencoders (VAEs) and diffusion models have demonstrated the ability to learn rich motion priors from large-scale datasets. These models can generate long, coherent motion sequences without explicit rule-based constraints, enabling flexible conditioning on textual descriptions, action labels, or spatial goals. However, most existing methods focus on relatively abstract or global conditioning, such as specifying the type of activity (“walking,” “running,” “dancing”) or following a sparse set of target poses. In many practical scenarios—such as virtual crowd simulation, character animation for games, or robot navigation in human environments—it is essential to control motion more precisely through explicit spatial trajectories. 

Trajectory-based conditioning provides an intuitive and powerful interface: a user or planning system specifies a path in space, and the motion generator produces a sequence of human poses that follow this path while exhibiting realistic and context-appropriate kinematics. This paradigm enables spatially-aware control over motion, facilitates integration with navigation systems, and supports interactive authoring. Nevertheless, generating human motion from trajectories poses unique challenges. The model must not only adhere to the spatial constraints imposed by the trajectory but also produce natural body dynamics, avoid foot sliding, respect biomechanical limits, and adapt motion style to changes in trajectory curvature, speed, and context. Furthermore, trajectory-conditioned motion generation must handle ambiguities: a single path can correspond to multiple plausible motions differing in style, gait, or tempo.

Existing trajectory-conditioned motion generation methods often rely on deterministic mapping from trajectory to motion, which limits diversity, or they use autoregressive models that are prone to error accumulation and mode collapse over long sequences. Some approaches incorporate trajectory information as an auxiliary signal in action-conditioned models, but fail to fully exploit the spatial-temporal structure of the trajectory for fine-grained control. Moreover, there is a lack of frameworks that explicitly disentangle trajectory information from motion style, making it difficult to generate controllable and diverse motions that follow the same path but vary in style or speed.

To address these limitations, we propose **TrajeVAE**, a controllable human motion generation framework based on a conditional variational autoencoder architecture. TrajeVAE takes as input a user-specified or algorithmically generated trajectory and produces diverse, realistic human motion sequences that faithfully follow the trajectory while allowing explicit control over motion style and dynamics. Our approach leverages a trajectory encoder that captures both local geometric features (e.g., curvature, slope) and global path context, and a motion decoder that synthesizes pose sequences conditioned on latent variables representing style. By disentangling trajectory and style in the latent space, TrajeVAE enables generating multiple stylistic variations for the same path, thereby enhancing diversity without sacrificing trajectory fidelity.

A key contribution of our work is the integration of a spatial-temporal alignment mechanism that ensures the generated motion adheres closely to the trajectory while maintaining natural kinematic patterns. We introduce a trajectory-aligned pose representation that facilitates consistent foot placement and body orientation along curved paths. Additionally, the variational formulation of our model supports stochastic sampling, enabling a spectrum of plausible motions for a single trajectory input. This diversity is crucial for applications such as crowd simulation, where multiple characters may follow similar paths but should exhibit varied motion styles.

We evaluate TrajeVAE on benchmark motion capture datasets with diverse locomotion behaviors, comparing it against state-of-the-art trajectory-conditioned and unconditional motion generation methods. Quantitative results demonstrate that TrajeVAE achieves superior performance in trajectory adherence, motion naturalness, and diversity. Qualitative analyses further highlight the model’s ability to produce stylistically distinct motions for identical trajectories, as well as its robustness to complex and irregular paths. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:  
1. We introduce a conditional VAE framework for trajectory-conditioned human motion generation with disentangled trajectory and style representations.  
2. We design a spatial-temporal alignment mechanism that preserves both trajectory fidelity and motion realism.  
3. We present extensive evaluations showing that our approach outperforms existing methods in both control and quality, enabling new possibilities for interactive and autonomous motion synthesis.

Through TrajeVAE, we aim to bridge the gap between high-level spatial control and realistic human motion generation, advancing the state of the art in controllable motion synthesis for graphics, vision, and robotics applications.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced TrajeVAE, a novel framework for controllable human motion generation driven by user-specified trajectories. By leveraging a variational autoencoder architecture conditioned on spatial paths, our method effectively disentangles trajectory guidance from motion style, enabling flexible synthesis across diverse motion categories. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that TrajeVAE produces natural, temporally coherent motions that closely follow target trajectories while preserving realistic human dynamics. Quantitative evaluations confirm competitive or superior performance compared to existing baselines, and qualitative analyses highlight the model’s ability to generalize to unseen trajectories and interpolate between motion types. Moreover, the controllability inherent in our design allows for intuitive editing and multi-modal outputs from the same trajectory input, broadening its applicability to animation, virtual reality, and human–robot interaction.
