While our approach focuses on 3D skeletal motion, future work will explore integration with full-body mesh models, richer environmental constraints, and interactive trajectory design. We believe TrajeVAE contributes a flexible and effective tool for trajectory-conditioned motion generation, paving the way for more accessible and creative motion synthesis systems that bridge the gap between user intent and high-quality animated human movement.

title: Quantifying the heart of darkness with GHALO - a multi-billion particle simulation of our galactic halo
abstract: We present **GHALO**, a high-resolution N-body simulation of a Milky Way–sized dark matter halo, resolved with over three billion particles. This unprecedented resolution enables us to probe the internal structure of the halo to sub-parsec scales, revealing the intricate density profile, shape, and substructure population of the Galactic dark matter distribution. The simulation was initialized within a ΛCDM cosmology using a multi-level zoom-in technique to capture both the large-scale environment and the fine-grained inner halo dynamics. We quantify the inner slope of the density profile, finding a gradual shallowing toward the center consistent with recent theoretical predictions, and characterize the abundance and radial distribution of subhalos down to masses of ~10⁵ M☉. The results provide robust constraints on the phase-space structure relevant for direct and indirect dark matter detection experiments. GHALO offers a benchmark for future simulations and an essential resource for connecting cosmological models with high-precision Galactic observations.
introduction:
The nature and structure of dark matter halos remain central questions in contemporary cosmology. In the prevailing Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) paradigm, galaxies form within extended halos of collisionless dark matter that dominate their mass budget. Numerical N-body simulations have been instrumental in elucidating the density profiles, substructure content, and dynamical evolution of such halos across cosmic time. Over the past decades, advances in computational algorithms and hardware have enabled simulations of ever-increasing resolution, revealing intricate features in the phase-space distribution of dark matter. These developments have refined our understanding of halo concentration, cusp slopes, and the abundance of bound subhalos, while also providing critical inputs for interpreting astrophysical observations and designing dark matter detection experiments.

Despite these advances, several aspects of halo structure remain insufficiently constrained, particularly in the innermost regions where the density profile and substructure distribution are most sensitive to both the nature of dark matter and the assembly history of the system. Observational probes at these scales are severely limited by baryonic physics and resolution, rendering high-fidelity simulations a crucial tool. However, resolving the inner kiloparsecs of a Milky Way–sized halo with sufficient particle numbers to robustly quantify density slopes, phase-space densities, and small-scale substructure requires simulation sizes well beyond the billion-particle scale. Achieving this resolution while maintaining accurate integration over cosmological timescales poses significant computational challenges, including the need for efficient parallelization, optimized force solvers, and careful treatment of numerical artifacts.

In this work, we present GHALO, a multi-billion particle N-body simulation of a galactic-scale dark matter halo, designed to probe the “heart of darkness” — the innermost structure of our Galaxy's halo — with unprecedented detail. GHALO follows the evolution of a Milky Way–mass halo from high redshift to the present day within a cosmological context, employing over four billion particles within the virial radius and achieving a force resolution sufficient to resolve sub-kiloparsec scales with high fidelity. This resolution allows for robust measurements of the inner density profile, the phase-space density distribution, and the subhalo population down to masses several orders of magnitude smaller than previous studies.

By quantifying the internal structure of the simulated halo at this level of detail, we aim to address key questions regarding the universality of density profiles, the survival and disruption of substructure in high-density environments, and the implications for both indirect and direct dark matter detection. The GHALO simulation represents a significant step forward in the numerical exploration of galactic halos, pushing the limits of current computational capabilities and providing a benchmark dataset for future theoretical and observational studies.
conclusion:
The GHALO simulation represents a significant step forward in our ability to model the structure and dynamics of a Milky Way–sized dark matter halo with unprecedented resolution. By employing over twenty billion particles in the initial conditions and retaining more than six billion high-resolution particles within the virial radius at \( z = 0 \), we have been able to probe the density profile, substructure population, and phase-space properties of the halo to a level of detail that previous cosmological simulations could not achieve. This extraordinary particle count, combined with a careful choice of initial conditions and refinement strategy, has allowed us to explore the innermost regions of the halo—down to scales of order 100 parsecs—while still maintaining statistical robustness in the outer regions.

Our analysis confirms that the spherically averaged density profile continues to deviate from simple analytic forms such as the Navarro–Frenk–White or Moore profiles when examined at sufficiently small radii. The inner slope appears to become progressively shallower toward the center, consistent with a non-universal, slowly varying logarithmic slope rather than a fixed power law. This result strengthens the emerging consensus from other high-resolution simulations that the central structure of cold dark matter halos is more complex than originally assumed, and that no single parametrization fully captures the radial dependence across all scales.

The extraordinary resolution of GHALO also offers new insight into the abundance and distribution of subhalos. We find that the subhalo mass function retains a near–scale-free form down to the smallest resolved masses, with no indication of a turnover. The spatial distribution of subhalos is markedly less centrally concentrated than the smooth dark matter halo, a property that persists to within a few kiloparsecs of the center. The high particle number permits the survival and identification of subhalos in regions of strong tidal fields, improving our understanding of the interplay between global halo potential and substructure resilience. These results have important implications for indirect detection experiments, as the clumpiness of dark matter can enhance annihilation signals and influence observational strategies.

Furthermore, the simulation provides a rich phase-space portrait of the halo, revealing coherent tidal streams, remnants of disrupted subhalos, and a wealth of fine-grained structure. The coarse-grained phase-space density profile follows a nearly universal power law over several decades in radius, suggesting that the processes governing the mixing and relaxation of collisionless matter operate similarly across scales. The tidal debris and streams identified in the simulation are a natural outcome of hierarchical assembly, and their properties can inform efforts to detect stellar counterparts in the Milky Way, offering a direct link between dark matter simulations and stellar halo surveys.

The GHALO dataset is not without limitations. Despite the high resolution, the simulation remains constrained by the assumptions inherent in collisionless cold dark matter and a ΛCDM cosmology. Baryonic physics, which can alter the central density profile and substructure survival rates, is absent from this calculation. Future work incorporating gas dynamics, star formation, and feedback processes will be necessary to fully capture the interplay between dark and luminous matter. Nonetheless, by isolating the dark matter component, GHALO provides a clean benchmark against which to compare more complex simulations and observational inferences.

In summary, the GHALO simulation has delivered an unprecedented view of the structure, substructure, and phase-space complexity of a Milky Way–sized dark matter halo. The results presented here refine our understanding of the inner density profile, confirm the scale-free nature of the subhalo mass function to new limits, and reveal the rich dynamical tapestry imprinted by hierarchical formation. These findings not only advance the theoretical characterization of dark matter halos but also offer concrete predictions and constraints relevant to ongoing and future observational campaigns. By pushing the limits of numerical resolution, GHALO underscores the value of extreme-scale simulations in bridging the gap between cosmological theory and the observable universe, and it sets the stage for the next generation of experiments aimed at uncovering the true nature of the dark matter that dominates our Galaxy.

title: Neutrino-Electron Scattering: General Constraints on Z' and Dark Photon Models
abstract: We investigate neutrino–electron scattering as a sensitive probe of physics beyond the Standard Model, focusing on constraints for hypothetical neutral gauge bosons, including generic \(Z'\) and dark photon scenarios. Using precision measurements from reactor, accelerator, and solar neutrino experiments, we derive model-independent bounds on the couplings and masses of such mediators. Our analysis incorporates both vector and axial-vector interactions, accounting for interference effects with Standard Model processes. The resulting limits significantly improve on existing constraints in certain parameter regions, demonstrating the utility of low-energy neutrino scattering data in testing light, weakly coupled gauge bosons across a broad mass range.
introduction:
The study of neutrino-electron scattering has long played a pivotal role in testing the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics and probing possible scenarios of new physics beyond it. Within the SM, neutrinos interact with electrons through charged-current (for electron neutrinos) and neutral-current processes mediated by the \( W \) and \( Z \) bosons. The precision of the theoretical predictions for these processes, combined with improvements in experimental techniques to measure low-energy recoil electrons, make neutrino-electron scattering an exceptionally clean probe of electroweak physics. Deviations from the SM expectations in such scattering rates or angular distributions could be indicative of new gauge interactions, exotic mediators, or non-standard neutrino properties.

In recent years, there has been significant interest in light neutral gauge bosons, generally referred to as \( Z' \) bosons, which appear in many well-motivated extensions of the SM. These bosons can arise naturally in theories with additional \( U(1) \) symmetries, such as those motivated by grand unified theories, string-inspired constructions, or anomaly-free extensions involving new fermion content. A particularly simple and frequently studied case is that of the so-called “dark photon,” a spin-1 boson associated with a hidden \( U(1)_D \) gauge group that kinetically mixes with the SM hypercharge. Depending on its couplings and mass, a \( Z' \) or dark photon could mediate new interactions between neutrinos and charged leptons, altering the cross section for neutrino-electron scattering in a manner potentially accessible to current or near-future experiments.

Neutrino-electron scattering offers several advantages for such searches. First, the purely leptonic nature of the interaction ensures that nuclear uncertainties—often a limiting factor in neutrino-nucleus scattering experiments—are absent. Second, the low momentum transfer in typical reactor, solar, or accelerator-based neutrino experiments enhances the sensitivity to light mediators, including those with masses in the sub-GeV range. Third, the kinematic distributions of the recoil electrons are calculable with high precision, allowing subtle modifications from new interactions to be identified. Consequently, a wide range of laboratory experiments, including CHARM-II, TEXONO, LSND, GEMMA, and Borexino, as well as ongoing coherent neutrino scattering programs, can be used to place constraints on \( Z' \) and dark photon scenarios.

The phenomenology of such new mediators in neutrino-electron scattering depends critically on their mass, couplings to SM fermions, and possible mixing with SM gauge bosons. For a generic \( Z' \), the relevant parameters include the gauge coupling \( g' \), the charge assignments of SM fields under the new \( U(1) \), and the mediator mass \( m_{Z'} \). In the case of the dark photon, the coupling to charged SM particles arises through kinetic mixing with the photon, parameterized by a dimensionless mixing angle \( \epsilon \), while neutrino couplings may be induced indirectly via mixing with the \( Z \) boson or through additional model-dependent interactions. These couplings modify the neutrino-electron scattering amplitude both through interference with the SM \( Z \)-mediated amplitude and through the exchange of the new mediator itself. The resulting changes to both the total cross section and the recoil spectrum can be substantial for sufficiently large couplings or for mediator masses comparable to the momentum transfer.

Existing studies have explored a variety of new physics scenarios in neutrino-electron scattering, from non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) to light scalar mediators and magnetic moment enhancements. However, the systematic treatment of general \( Z' \) and dark photon models within a unified framework remains an active area of investigation. Given the diversity of possible charge assignments and couplings, it is valuable to derive constraints that are as model-independent as possible, relying only on the basic features of the interaction and the kinematic reach of available data. Moreover, the interplay between laboratory bounds, astrophysical limits from stellar cooling or supernova neutrinos, and cosmological constraints from Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the cosmic microwave background makes it essential to delineate the parameter space accessible to neutrino-electron scattering experiments.

The present work aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of general constraints on \( Z' \) and dark photon models from neutrino-electron scattering. We begin by reviewing the SM prediction for the scattering cross section, paying particular attention to the dependence on neutrino flavor and energy, as well as the experimental conditions relevant for past and current measurements. We then introduce the general formalism for incorporating a new neutral vector mediator, detailing its contribution to the scattering amplitude and the resulting modifications to observables. Special cases of interest, including dark photons with purely kinetic mixing and \( Z' \) bosons associated with anomaly-free \( U(1)_{B-L} \) or \( U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau} \) symmetries, are considered within this framework.

Using data from a range of neutrino-electron scattering experiments, we derive bounds on the relevant coupling constants and mediator masses, highlighting the regions of parameter space excluded at high confidence level. We compare these laboratory limits with complementary constraints from other probes, emphasizing the unique role of neutrino scattering in covering otherwise unconstrained regions, especially for very light mediators. Finally, we discuss the prospects for future improvements, both from planned experimental upgrades and from novel approaches to measuring low-energy neutrino interactions.

By systematically analyzing neutrino-electron scattering in the presence of new neutral gauge bosons, this study contributes to the broader effort to map out the landscape of viable light mediator models and to sharpen the experimental tools needed to detect or exclude them. Our results underscore the continuing importance of precision neutrino physics as a window into potential new forces and hidden sectors.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the implications of precision measurements of neutrino–electron scattering for constraining extensions of the Standard Model featuring an additional neutral gauge boson, either in the form of a generic \(Z'\) or a kinetically mixed dark photon. By considering both model-independent parameterizations and specific benchmark scenarios, we have incorporated the most recent experimental data from reactor, accelerator, and solar neutrino experiments to derive updated bounds on the relevant couplings and mediator masses. Our analysis demonstrates that even in the absence of direct production, low-energy neutrino scattering provides a complementary and, in some mass ranges, leading probe of such new interactions.

For light mediators with masses below the GeV scale, the constraints obtained from neutrino–electron scattering are particularly stringent due to the enhancement of the cross section at low momentum transfer. In the case of a dark photon with purely vector couplings, we have shown that existing data significantly restrict the kinetic mixing parameter \(\epsilon\) over a broad range of mediator masses, in some regions surpassing collider and beam dump limits. For the \(Z'\) scenarios considered, which allow for non-universal couplings to leptons, our results highlight the sensitivity of neutrino–electron channels to flavor-dependent structures that are less accessible to other experimental approaches.

Beyond setting exclusion limits, our framework underscores the synergy between different neutrino sources and detection techniques. The combination of solar and reactor neutrino measurements constrains the low-mass region with high precision, while accelerator-based experiments extend the reach towards heavier mediators. This complementarity will become even more pronounced with upcoming facilities offering improved statistics and reduced systematic uncertainties.

Overall, our findings reaffirm the role of neutrino–electron scattering as a precision tool for exploring hidden sector physics. Future measurements, in particular those anticipated from next-generation coherent scattering and low-threshold detectors, have the potential to probe unexplored parameter space and further elucidate the possible existence of new light gauge bosons. Continued progress in both experimental sensitivity and theoretical modeling will be essential to fully exploit this avenue in the search for physics beyond the Standard Model.

title: Dynamic Implicit-Solvent Coarse-Grained Models of Lipid Bilayer Membranes : Fluctuating Hydrodynamics Thermostat
abstract: We present a dynamic implicit-solvent coarse-grained modeling framework for lipid bilayer membranes that incorporates a fluctuating hydrodynamics thermostat to capture the coupled dynamics of lipids and the surrounding solvent. Traditional implicit-solvent coarse-grained approaches often neglect hydrodynamic correlations and thermal fluctuations of the solvent, limiting their ability to reproduce mesoscale dynamical phenomena. Here, the membrane is represented by coarse-grained lipid particles interacting via effective potentials, while the solvent is modeled as a continuum fluid obeying the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations augmented with stochastic stress terms to satisfy the fluctuation–dissipation theorem. Lipid–solvent coupling is achieved through no-slip constraints enforced via distributed hydrodynamic coupling kernels, allowing momentum exchange between the discrete membrane particles and the fluctuating solvent field. The method enables efficient simulation of large membrane patches with realistic dynamical properties, including membrane undulations, lipid lateral diffusion, and collective flow patterns. We validate the approach by comparing equilibrium fluctuation spectra and diffusion coefficients with theoretical predictions and experimental measurements. The results demonstrate that the fluctuating hydrodynamics thermostat faithfully reproduces the correct temperature, hydrodynamic correlations, and thermal noise spectrum without the need for explicit solvent particles. This framework provides a computationally efficient and physically consistent tool for studying membrane dynamics over experimentally relevant length and time scales, and can be extended to investigate curvature-mediated interactions, protein–lipid coupling, and non-equilibrium processes in complex biomembrane systems.
introduction:
Lipid bilayer membranes are fundamental structural components of biological systems, providing the essential barrier and functional interface between cells and their environment. Their mechanical properties, dynamical behavior, and interactions with proteins are central to numerous biological processes, including signaling, trafficking, and membrane remodeling. Computational modeling has become an indispensable tool for exploring these phenomena at molecular and mesoscopic scales. However, fully atomistic simulations of membranes and their surrounding solvent remain computationally demanding, especially when large spatial domains and long timescales are required to capture collective fluctuations and hydrodynamic coupling.

Coarse-grained (CG) models offer a powerful framework for bridging the gap between atomistic detail and continuum descriptions. By reducing the number of degrees of freedom, they enable the study of large membrane patches over microsecond to millisecond timescales. In many CG approaches, the solvent is treated implicitly, which greatly reduces computational cost. Nevertheless, the absence of explicit solvent molecules poses challenges for accurately reproducing momentum transport and long-range hydrodynamic interactions, both of which are known to influence membrane dynamics and fluctuation spectra.

To address these challenges, implicit-solvent models can be augmented with fluctuating hydrodynamics thermostats, which couple the CG degrees of freedom to a continuum description of the solvent. Fluctuating hydrodynamics incorporates both deterministic fluid motion and stochastic thermal noise, consistent with the fluctuation–dissipation theorem, thereby enabling the recovery of correct hydrodynamic correlations. In the context of membrane simulations, such approaches can capture the interplay between membrane undulations, lateral viscosity, and solvent-mediated forces without the computational overhead of explicit solvent particles.

Recent developments in dynamic implicit-solvent CG models have demonstrated the feasibility of integrating fluctuating hydrodynamics with membrane representations that retain essential structural and mechanical features, such as bending rigidity, area compressibility, and lipid self-assembly. These hybrid models open the door to quantitatively accurate simulations of membrane fluctuations, protein–membrane coupling, and non-equilibrium processes such as flow-driven deformation.

In this work, we present a dynamic implicit-solvent coarse-grained model of lipid bilayer membranes that is coupled to a fluctuating hydrodynamics thermostat. Our approach systematically incorporates stochastic hydrodynamic fields into the membrane dynamics, preserving momentum conservation and thermal equilibrium while enabling the study of large-scale, time-resolved membrane processes. We validate the model against theoretical predictions and experimental data, and illustrate its ability to capture the coupled dynamics of membranes and surrounding solvent flows.
conclusion: We have developed and analyzed a dynamic implicit-solvent coarse-grained model for lipid bilayer membranes that incorporates a fluctuating hydrodynamics thermostat to capture solvent-mediated interactions and thermal fluctuations without explicit solvent particles. By coupling coarse-grained lipid dynamics to a continuum hydrodynamic field with stochastic forcing, the approach preserves momentum conservation, reproduces correct long-wavelength hydrodynamic correlations, and maintains computational efficiency. Simulations demonstrate that the model accurately reproduces key membrane properties, including bending rigidity, lateral diffusion, and fluctuation spectra, while allowing access to mesoscopic length and time scales inaccessible to fully atomistic or explicit-solvent coarse-grained simulations. The fluctuating hydrodynamics thermostat ensures consistent thermalization across coupled lipid–solvent modes, enabling physically realistic nonequilibrium and dynamic processes such as vesicle shape fluctuations and membrane remodeling. This framework provides a versatile foundation for investigating complex membrane phenomena where hydrodynamic coupling plays a critical role, including protein–membrane interactions, curvature generation, and collective lipid flows. Future work will extend the method to heterogeneous and multicomponent bilayers, as well as to active membranes, further broadening its applicability in biophysical modeling of cellular membranes and synthetic lipid assemblies.

title: Multi-Scale Feature Fusion: Learning Better Semantic Segmentation for Road Pothole Detection
abstract: Pothole detection is a critical task for road maintenance and traffic safety, yet challenges such as varying pothole sizes, lighting conditions, and complex backgrounds hinder accurate segmentation. This paper presents a multi-scale feature fusion framework for semantic segmentation tailored to road pothole detection. The proposed method integrates features from multiple receptive fields within a deep convolutional neural network, enhancing both global context understanding and fine-grained boundary localization. By combining high-level semantic cues with detailed spatial information through an adaptive fusion mechanism, the network effectively captures pothole structures of diverse scales. Experiments conducted on benchmark pothole datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, Intersection-over-Union, and robustness to environmental variations. The results indicate that multi-scale feature fusion significantly improves segmentation quality, offering a reliable solution for real-world automated road inspection systems and laying the groundwork for safer and more efficient transportation infrastructure maintenance.
introduction:
Road infrastructure plays a critical role in the safety, efficiency, and sustainability of transportation systems. Among the various forms of pavement distress, potholes are one of the most common and hazardous defects, posing serious risks to vehicle integrity, passenger safety, and traffic flow. Timely and accurate detection of potholes is essential for effective maintenance planning, cost reduction, and accident prevention. Traditional pothole detection methods, such as manual inspection or vehicle-mounted vibration sensors, are often labor-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to subjectivity or environmental constraints. In recent years, advances in computer vision and deep learning have enabled the development of automated detection systems based on visual data, offering a promising alternative for real-time and large-scale road surface monitoring.

Semantic segmentation, which assigns a class label to each pixel in an image, has emerged as a powerful approach for precise pothole localization. By leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and their variants, semantic segmentation models can learn hierarchical feature representations that distinguish between road surfaces and defects. However, pothole detection presents unique challenges that limit the performance of conventional segmentation networks. First, potholes vary greatly in size, shape, depth, and texture, and may appear under diverse lighting and weather conditions. Second, visual cues for potholes can be subtle and easily confused with shadows, stains, or other surface irregularities. Third, the high intra-class variability and low inter-class contrast require models to capture both global context and fine-grained details simultaneously.

Multi-scale feature representation is critical for addressing these challenges. Features extracted at different spatial resolutions provide complementary information: higher-level features capture semantic context, while lower-level features retain detailed boundary and texture information. Many modern segmentation architectures, such as U-Net, DeepLab, and Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN), incorporate multi-scale processing to improve accuracy. Nevertheless, naive aggregation of multi-scale features may lead to redundancy, noise amplification, or loss of discriminative information, particularly when dealing with small and irregular targets like potholes. This calls for more effective feature fusion strategies that can adaptively integrate information across scales, enhancing the model’s ability to distinguish potholes from complex backgrounds.

In this work, we investigate a multi-scale feature fusion framework tailored for semantic segmentation in road pothole detection. Our approach leverages the strengths of both high-resolution and low-resolution feature maps, combining them through a fusion mechanism designed to preserve spatial precision while enriching semantic understanding. By selectively emphasizing relevant features and suppressing irrelevant ones, the proposed method addresses the limitations of existing architectures that either overemphasize coarse context or overfit to local patterns. The fusion strategy is integrated into an end-to-end trainable network that can be efficiently deployed for real-time or near-real-time road inspection tasks.

The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we propose a novel multi-scale feature fusion module that adaptively weights and aggregates features from different resolutions, improving the representation of small and irregular potholes. Second, we integrate this module into a semantic segmentation network optimized for road surface analysis, achieving a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Third, we evaluate our method on benchmark pothole datasets as well as challenging real-world road imagery, demonstrating significant improvements over baseline and state-of-the-art models in terms of detection accuracy and robustness under varying environmental conditions.

Through this research, we aim to advance the development of intelligent road maintenance systems that can operate autonomously and at scale. By improving the accuracy and reliability of pothole segmentation, the proposed multi-scale feature fusion approach contributes to safer transportation networks, reduced maintenance costs, and enhanced quality of service for road users.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed a multi-scale feature fusion framework to enhance semantic segmentation performance for road pothole detection. By integrating features across multiple receptive fields, the model effectively captures both fine-grained boundary details and broader contextual information, leading to improved localization and classification of potholes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly under challenging illumination and occlusion conditions. The results confirm the importance of combining multi-scale information for complex road surface analysis. Future work will explore lightweight architectures and real-time deployment strategies to facilitate on-vehicle implementation. Overall, the proposed method presents a promising direction for reliable, automated road condition monitoring in intelligent transportation systems.

title: Scaling Factorial Hidden Markov Models: Stochastic Variational Inference without Messages
abstract: We present a scalable stochastic variational inference algorithm for factorial hidden Markov models (FHMMs) that eliminates the need for traditional forward–backward message passing. Our approach leverages a structured mean-field approximation combined with stochastic optimization to handle large datasets and high-dimensional latent structures efficiently. By avoiding message passing, we reduce memory and computational requirements, enabling inference in regimes previously inaccessible to FHMMs. We derive unbiased stochastic gradient estimators for the variational parameters and demonstrate competitive accuracy and substantial speedups on synthetic and real-world sequence data. This framework broadens the applicability of FHMMs to modern large-scale sequential modeling tasks.
introduction:
Probabilistic models with latent temporal structure have long been a cornerstone of statistical machine learning, enabling principled reasoning about sequential data across domains such as speech recognition, computational biology, and finance. The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is perhaps the most widely used of these models, coupling a discrete latent state sequence to observable data through emission distributions. While standard HMMs capture a single chain of latent dynamics, many real-world processes involve multiple interacting factors evolving in parallel. The factorial hidden Markov model (FHMM) extends the HMM by representing the latent structure as several independent Markov chains whose joint configuration influences the observations. This richer structure allows FHMMs to capture combinatorial state spaces with exponentially fewer parameters and to model complex dependencies in multivariate time series.

Despite their expressive power, FHMMs present significant computational challenges. The classical forward–backward algorithm for HMM inference requires dynamic programming messages whose complexity in the FHMM setting grows exponentially with the number of latent chains. Exact inference quickly becomes intractable, restricting the applicability of FHMMs to small-scale problems. Variational inference has provided a scalable alternative, replacing exact computations with optimization of a tractable lower bound on the marginal likelihood. Structured mean-field approximations, for example, decouple the chains in the variational distribution and use iterative message passing to update local posteriors. However, even these approximations can be computationally heavy for large datasets, long sequences, or high-dimensional latent spaces, and they often require storing and manipulating messages whose size scales with the sequence length.

Recent advances in stochastic variational inference (SVI) offer a promising route to scaling latent variable models to massive datasets by subsampling observations and updating global parameters using noisy gradient estimates. Yet, applying SVI to FHMMs remains challenging. Standard SVI approaches for time series still rely on message passing to compute expected sufficient statistics, which entails nontrivial bookkeeping and limits the achievable speed-ups. Moreover, message passing inherently ties together all time steps in a sequence, complicating mini-batch strategies and parallelization.

In this work, we propose a stochastic variational inference algorithm for FHMMs that entirely avoids message passing. Our approach leverages a reparameterization of the variational distribution over latent states that permits unbiased gradient estimates of the evidence lower bound (ELBO) from randomly sampled subsequences. By sidestepping the need for forward–backward recursions, we eliminate the principal computational bottleneck and enable direct application of SVI with constant-time updates per subsequence, irrespective of the number of latent chains. This formulation naturally accommodates long sequences and large datasets, facilitates distributed computation, and allows the use of modern automatic differentiation frameworks.

We demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance while drastically reducing computational cost compared to message-based variational inference. Through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we explore the trade-offs between approximation quality, convergence speed, and scalability. Our results indicate that message-free stochastic variational inference opens the door to applying FHMMs to domains previously beyond reach due to computational constraints, offering a new tool for flexible and scalable modeling of complex sequential phenomena.
conclusion: We have presented a scalable stochastic variational inference framework for factorial hidden Markov models that avoids the costly message-passing steps of traditional algorithms. By exploiting a structured mean-field approximation and mini-batch optimization, our method significantly reduces computational and memory demands while maintaining competitive accuracy. This approach enables efficient learning in high-dimensional sequential models previously intractable at scale. Empirical results demonstrate favorable trade-offs between speed and statistical performance across diverse datasets. The elimination of global message passing opens opportunities for parallelization and streaming applications. Future work will explore richer dependencies within the variational family and extensions to non-conjugate and deep generative sequential models.

title: Photon-neutrino interaction in theta-exact covariant noncommutative field theory
abstract: We investigate photon–neutrino interactions within the framework of θ-exact covariant noncommutative field theory, extending beyond the perturbative Seiberg–Witten expansion. Employing a fully covariant formulation, we derive interaction vertices and scattering amplitudes valid for arbitrary noncommutativity parameters. The analysis reveals novel momentum-dependent couplings absent in commutative settings, leading to potentially observable deviations in astrophysical and cosmological environments. Our results provide a consistent, gauge-invariant description of photon–neutrino processes at all orders in θ, offering new avenues to probe spacetime noncommutativity through high-energy neutrino and photon phenomenology.
introduction:
The study of particle interactions in the framework of noncommutative (NC) field theories has attracted considerable attention, motivated both by theoretical consistency requirements and potential phenomenological consequences. Noncommutative geometry naturally emerges in certain limits of string theory and quantum gravity scenarios, where the space–time coordinates satisfy nontrivial commutation relations parameterized by an antisymmetric tensor \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\). Such modifications lead to deformations of the standard gauge and matter field interactions, with possible observable effects at high energies.  

In particular, the photon–neutrino interaction, absent at tree level in the Standard Model, can be induced in NC gauge theories through novel couplings mediated by the noncommutative structure. These couplings persist even for electrically neutral fermions and can have implications for astrophysical processes, cosmology, and high-energy experiments. A theta-exact treatment of the NC action, as opposed to perturbative expansions in \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\), is essential in order to capture the full range of nonperturbative effects, especially when \(|\theta p q|\) is not necessarily small.  

Here we investigate the photon–neutrino interaction in a theta-exact covariant formulation of NC field theory. We derive the relevant interaction vertices, examine their symmetry properties, and discuss potential phenomenological signatures, thereby contributing to the ongoing effort to connect NC field theoretical predictions with experimentally accessible observables.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the photon–neutrino interaction within the framework of θ-exact covariant noncommutative field theory, focusing on the implications of space-time noncommutativity for neutral fermion–gauge boson couplings. By employing a θ-exact Seiberg–Witten map, we have derived interaction vertices without resorting to perturbative expansions in the noncommutative parameter, thereby capturing all orders of θ-effects. Our analysis demonstrates that noncommutativity induces novel couplings between photons and neutrinos absent in the commutative Standard Model, with strengths governed by both the noncommutative scale and the momentum transfer. These effects persist at high energies and exhibit characteristic angular dependencies linked to the underlying θ-tensor structure. We have also discussed phenomenological consequences, including potential modifications to astrophysical processes and high-energy scattering cross sections, which may serve as probes of noncommutative geometry. The θ-exact treatment ensures that our results remain valid beyond the small-θ regime, allowing for reliable predictions in scenarios where noncommutative effects could be sizable. Future work may extend this analysis to include loop corrections, finite temperature effects, and constraints from cosmology, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of photon–neutrino dynamics in noncommutative space-time. Our findings reinforce the potential of precision neutrino and photon measurements as sensitive tests of fundamental space-time structure.

title: Comparison between high-energy proton and charged pion induced damage in Lead Tungstate calorimeter crystals
abstract: Radiation damage in lead tungstate (PbWO₄) calorimeter crystals was systematically studied under high-energy proton and charged pion irradiation to assess their relative impact on optical and scintillation properties. Samples were exposed to 24 GeV/c protons and 290 MeV/c π⁺ beams to fluences representative of high-luminosity collider environments. Light transmission and scintillation yield were monitored before and after irradiation, with recovery trends assessed over extended periods. Results indicate that proton-induced damage is significantly more severe and less recoverable than that from pions at comparable fluences, suggesting distinct microscopic damage mechanisms. These findings have important implications for calorimeter performance and lifetime in future experiments.
introduction: Lead tungstate (PbWO₄) crystals are widely employed as scintillators in high-energy physics calorimeters due to their high density, short radiation length, and fast scintillation response. However, prolonged exposure to intense radiation fields in collider environments can degrade their optical and scintillation properties, impacting detector performance. While extensive studies have been conducted on photon- and electron-induced damage, less attention has been given to the comparative effects of different hadronic projectiles. In particular, high-energy protons and charged pions, both prevalent in hadronic showers, may produce distinct damage mechanisms due to differences in nuclear interaction cross sections and secondary particle production. Understanding these differences is essential for accurate lifetime predictions and for developing mitigation strategies in current and future experiments. This work presents a systematic comparison of proton- and charged pion-induced damage in PbWO₄ crystals, focusing on changes in light transmission and induced absorption.
conclusion: The comparative study of high-energy proton and charged pion irradiation on Lead Tungstate (PbWO₄) calorimeter crystals has demonstrated that, while both types of hadrons induce measurable degradation in optical and scintillation performance, the underlying damage mechanisms and their magnitudes differ. Protons, due to their higher probability of inducing nuclear interactions with high momentum transfer, generate a greater density of displacement damage and contribute more significantly to the formation of color centers, leading to stronger and more persistent transmission losses. Charged pions, though also capable of producing displacement damage, typically deposit energy through interactions with lower momentum transfer, resulting in comparatively less severe attenuation of light transmission for equivalent fluences. The experimental results indicate that, under similar irradiation conditions, proton-induced damage accumulates more rapidly and shows slower recovery at room temperature than damage from pions. These findings align with theoretical expectations based on hadronic interaction cross-sections and secondary particle production spectra. For calorimeter applications in high-luminosity collider environments, where the hadronic radiation field contains a significant fraction of high-energy protons, these results emphasize the need for careful lifetime predictions and possible mitigation strategies. Understanding the distinct damage profiles from different hadron species is essential for accurate performance modeling, informed material selection, and the development of annealing or operational protocols to maintain detector performance over extended periods of irradiation.

title: Local ePolitics Reputation Case Study
abstract: This case study examines the dynamics of online reputation management in local ePolitics, focusing on a municipal election campaign in a mid-sized city. Through qualitative content analysis of social media activity, local news coverage, and community forum discussions, the research explores how candidates construct, defend, and adapt their public image in digital spaces. Particular attention is given to the interplay between grassroots engagement and strategic communication, as well as the role of misinformation and rapid-response tactics. Findings reveal that reputation in local ePolitics is shaped by both controlled messaging and uncontrolled community narratives, with responsiveness, authenticity, and networked support emerging as critical factors in sustaining positive public perception in a competitive political environment.
introduction:
In the evolving landscape of digital communication, political engagement increasingly unfolds within online platforms that shape public perception and influence local governance. The rise of what can be termed “local ePolitics” reflects the intersection of community-level political activity and the pervasive use of digital media, where reputation management becomes a critical factor for political actors. Local politicians, advocacy groups, and civic participants now operate in an environment where information flows rapidly, narratives are contested in real time, and reputational gains or losses can result from a single viral post. This shift has amplified both opportunities for direct engagement with constituents and risks associated with misinformation, polarization, and strategic image manipulation.

The study of reputation in local ePolitics is essential because it reveals how trust, legitimacy, and authority are constructed and contested in the digital public sphere. Unlike national politics, local contexts often involve closer interpersonal networks, overlapping roles, and more immediate impacts on everyday life, making reputational dynamics especially potent. By examining a specific case study, this research aims to illuminate the mechanisms through which online discourse, social media interactions, and digital campaigning influence the standing of political actors within their communities. Through a qualitative analysis of digital traces, stakeholder interviews, and contextual factors, the paper seeks to contribute to the broader understanding of how reputation operates as both a resource and a vulnerability in contemporary local political arenas.
conclusion: The examination of this local ePolitics reputation case study demonstrates how digital platforms have reshaped the dynamics of political image-building and public perception. By analyzing interactions, content strategies, and audience engagement, the study reveals that online reputation is both more fragile and more rapidly influenced than in traditional political arenas. The findings suggest that strategic use of social media can amplify positive narratives, but also that missteps or negative framing can spread swiftly, potentially undermining credibility. In the local context, personal proximity between candidates and constituents intensifies the reputational stakes, as digital impressions often merge with offline relationships and community narratives. The case illustrates that authenticity, consistent messaging, and responsiveness are critical to sustaining trust, while the capacity to manage crises effectively can determine long-term viability. Moreover, the research underscores the role of local digital influencers and community networks in shaping reputational trajectories. Ultimately, the study affirms that ePolitics in localized settings demands a hybrid approach that integrates traditional grassroots engagement with nuanced, proactive online reputation management. As digital channels continue to evolve, political actors who adapt to these intersecting realms are more likely to maintain resilience and influence in the competitive landscape of contemporary local governance.

title: New Supersymmetric and Stable, Non-Supersymmetric Phases in Supergravity and Holographic Field Theory
abstract: We investigate new supersymmetric and non-supersymmetric, yet perturbatively stable, solutions in the context of gauged supergravity and their holographic duals in strongly coupled quantum field theories. Employing consistent truncations of higher-dimensional supergravity, we construct a family of AdS vacua exhibiting novel symmetry-breaking patterns. The supersymmetric phases preserve varying fractions of the original supersymmetry, while the non-supersymmetric configurations, though lacking supercharges, evade standard instability mechanisms and satisfy the Breitenlohner–Freedman bound. Using holographic techniques, we identify the dual conformal field theories and interpret the phases as distinct vacua or infrared fixed points, connected by renormalization group flows triggered by relevant operators. The stability of the non-supersymmetric solutions is analyzed via scalar fluctuation spectra and supported by the absence of tachyonic modes. Our results enrich the known landscape of holographic phases, highlight the role of consistent truncations in uncovering hidden sectors, and open avenues for exploring strongly coupled dynamics beyond supersymmetric constraints.
introduction:
The study of supersymmetric solutions in supergravity has long played a central role in elucidating the nonperturbative structure of string theory and its holographic duals. Supersymmetry not only simplifies the underlying equations of motion but also guarantees stability through the saturation of BPS bounds. However, in the broader landscape of string theory vacua, physically relevant phases need not preserve supersymmetry. Understanding the full spectrum of both supersymmetric and non-supersymmetric solutions is essential for connecting supergravity constructions to realistic quantum field theories and cosmological models.  

Recent advances have uncovered new classes of solutions in gauged supergravity theories that exhibit rich phase structures, including stable, non-supersymmetric vacua. These phases challenge the conventional expectation that supersymmetry breaking generically induces instabilities, such as tachyonic modes or runaway behavior. The existence of stable, non-supersymmetric states raises important questions about vacuum selection, moduli stabilization, and the possible holographic dual descriptions of strongly coupled field theories without supersymmetry.  

From the holographic perspective, the AdS/CFT correspondence provides a powerful framework to interpret these supergravity solutions in terms of renormalization group flows and phase transitions in lower-dimensional field theories. Supersymmetric fixed points correspond to conformal field theories with extended symmetry, while non-supersymmetric yet stable fixed points correspond to strongly coupled phases with reduced symmetry. The interplay between these phases, and the domain walls or flows connecting them, offers a controlled setting to study dynamical supersymmetry breaking and the emergence of mass gaps or confinement.  

In this work, we present new examples of both supersymmetric and stable non-supersymmetric phases arising in consistent truncations of higher-dimensional supergravity. We analyze their stability through fluctuation spectra, explore their embedding in string theory, and discuss the implications for holographic dual field theories. Our results broaden the catalogue of known solutions and provide further evidence for the richness of the supergravity and holographic landscape.
conclusion: We have identified and analyzed novel supersymmetric and stable, non-supersymmetric phases within the framework of supergravity, elucidating their holographic interpretation in the dual field theories. Our results demonstrate that stability in non-supersymmetric regimes can emerge from intricate scalar potential structures and nontrivial moduli dynamics, extending the known landscape of consistent solutions. The holographic perspective reveals distinctive signatures in the renormalization group flows, providing new insights into strongly coupled gauge dynamics. These findings broaden the understanding of phase structure in gauge/gravity duality and suggest promising directions for constructing phenomenologically relevant models. Future work will explore the interplay between these phases, their possible embeddings in string theory, and their implications for nonperturbative dynamics.

title: Probing small x(g) region with the LHeC based gamma-p colliders
abstract: The LHeC-based gamma–proton colliders offer unique opportunities to explore the small x(g) region with unprecedented precision. We discuss their potential to probe gluon distributions at low Bjorken‑x, enhancing understanding of QCD dynamics and parton evolution beyond current experimental reach.
introduction:
The study of the gluon distribution function at very small values of the Bjorken scaling variable \(x(g)\) is of paramount importance for advancing our understanding of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) in the high-energy limit. At small \(x\), gluon densities inside the proton rise steeply, and nonlinear QCD effects such as gluon recombination and parton saturation are expected to emerge. These phenomena are not only crucial for testing the fundamentals of perturbative QCD but also for providing accurate predictions for processes at current and future high-energy colliders. Precise knowledge of the gluon distribution in this regime will significantly impact the modeling of hadronic final states, backgrounds, and cross sections in a broad range of particle physics experiments.

Deep inelastic scattering (DIS) experiments, such as those conducted at HERA, have provided valuable insights into the parton structure of the proton, extending measurements down to \(x \sim 10^{-5}\). However, the kinematic reach of HERA has been limited by its center-of-mass energy, leaving a vast unexplored region at even smaller \(x\) values. The proposed Large Hadron–Electron Collider (LHeC) represents a major step forward, offering the possibility of colliding multi-hundred GeV electrons with multi-TeV protons from the LHC, thereby accessing unprecedented small-\(x\) and high-\(Q^2\) regions. In particular, the LHeC concept can be extended to operate in a \(\gamma p\) collision mode, where high-energy photons are produced via Compton backscattering of intense laser light off the electron beam. This configuration offers unique advantages for probing the gluon distribution at very small \(x\) through processes dominated by photon–gluon interactions.

In \(\gamma p\) collisions, heavy quark pair production (\(c\bar{c}\), \(b\bar{b}\)) proceeds predominantly via the boson–gluon fusion mechanism, \(\gamma g \rightarrow Q \bar{Q}\), providing a clean and direct sensitivity to the gluon content of the proton. By measuring the cross sections and kinematic distributions of such final states over a wide range of photon virtualities and rapidities, one can extract \(x(g)\) values far below the current experimental limit, potentially approaching \(x \sim 10^{-6}\) or smaller. The high luminosities achievable in the LHeC–based \(\gamma p\) mode, combined with the large photon flux from Compton backscattering, ensure statistically precise measurements even in these extreme kinematic domains.

Furthermore, the exploration of the small-\(x\) region at the LHeC in \(\gamma p\) mode will complement and extend the physics reach of both electron–proton DIS measurements and hadron–hadron collision studies at the LHC. It will enable stringent tests of QCD evolution equations, including the Dokshitzer–Gribov–Lipatov–Altarelli–Parisi (DGLAP) and Balitsky–Fadin–Kuraev–Lipatov (BFKL) formalisms, and will provide empirical input to theoretical approaches incorporating saturation effects, such as the Color Glass Condensate framework. The improved knowledge of parton distribution functions (PDFs) obtained from such measurements will also reduce theoretical uncertainties in Higgs boson, top quark, and potential new physics production cross sections at the energy frontier.

In this work, we investigate the potential of LHeC–based \(\gamma p\) colliders to probe the gluon distribution at very small \(x(g)\) values. We focus on heavy quark photoproduction as a sensitive channel, analyze the accessible kinematic regions, and estimate the expected reach in \(x(g)\) for different machine configurations. Our results demonstrate the significant impact such measurements can have on constraining the proton’s gluon content in a region that remains largely unexplored.
conclusion:
In this study, we have examined the potential of the LHeC-based γp colliders to probe the small‑\(x_g\) region of the gluon distribution in the proton. By exploiting the high-energy photon beams obtained via Compton backscattering of laser light off energetic electron beams, in combination with the high-energy proton beams from the LHC, such a facility offers unprecedented kinematic reach, extending deep into the low-\(x_g\) domain beyond the capabilities of existing and planned electron–proton colliders. Our analysis indicates that processes such as heavy quark pair production, particularly \(c\bar{c}\) and \(b\bar{b}\) final states, are highly sensitive to the gluon density at very small momentum fractions. The clean experimental environment of the γp mode, together with high luminosity, enables precise measurements with reduced background contamination, thereby improving constraints on parton distribution functions in an unexplored regime.

The results demonstrate that the LHeC-based γp collider could access \(x_g\) values down to the order of \(10^{-6}\) for heavy quark production at high \(Q^2\), significantly extending the kinematic coverage of HERA and complementing the LHeC electron–proton programme. Such measurements would directly test QCD evolution dynamics in the small‑\(x\) region, providing critical input for understanding gluon saturation phenomena and the onset of non-linear QCD effects. Moreover, the ability to probe heavy quark production with high precision will have a direct impact on global parton distribution function fits, reducing uncertainties in predictions for processes at the LHC and future hadron colliders.

In conclusion, the LHeC-based γp collider option represents a powerful tool for advancing our knowledge of proton structure. Its unique capability to investigate the small‑\(x_g\) frontier with high precision makes it an essential complement to other collider programmes, with the potential to address fundamental questions in QCD and to refine theoretical models applicable to high-energy particle physics.

title: Pulsational pair-instability supernovae: gravitational collapse, black-hole formation, and beyond
abstract: Pulsational pair-instability supernovae (PPISNe) represent a transitional endpoint in the evolution of very massive stars, occurring for helium-core masses in the range ∼30–64 M⊙. In these stars, the production of electron–positron pairs at high temperatures reduces radiation pressure support, triggering partial gravitational collapse and explosive thermonuclear outbursts. Unlike full pair-instability supernovae, PPISNe do not completely unbind the progenitor; instead, they expel successive shells of material over timescales from months to decades, with each pulse reducing the stellar mass and altering the subsequent collapse dynamics. We investigate the interplay between pulsational mass loss, core contraction, and the ultimate fate of the remnant, employing detailed stellar evolution models coupled to hydrodynamic simulations. Our results indicate that repeated pair-instability pulses can strip the hydrogen envelope and significantly reduce the final core mass, leading, in most cases, to direct collapse into a black hole with a mass below the pair-instability mass gap. We further explore the observational signatures of PPISNe, including transient light curves powered by shell–shell collisions and their potential connection to luminous red transients and some superluminous supernovae. The influence of rotation, metallicity, and binary interactions on the PPISN mass thresholds is also examined, highlighting the role of angular momentum transport and tidal stripping in shaping the pre-collapse configuration. Our findings have implications for interpreting gravitational-wave detections of massive black holes, constraining stellar evolution models at low metallicity, and understanding the chemical enrichment from the ejected shells. PPISNe thus serve as a crucial link between massive star evolution, transient astrophysics, and compact-object demographics.
introduction:
Massive stars with initial masses in the range of approximately 80–140 M⊙ encounter a unique evolutionary pathway in which the production of electron–positron pairs in their cores triggers a partial dynamical instability. This phenomenon, known as the pulsational pair-instability (PPI), occurs when the core temperature rises to values exceeding ~10^9 K, leading to copious pair production that reduces the adiabatic index below the critical value of 4/3. The resulting loss of pressure support initiates a rapid contraction of the stellar core, igniting runaway oxygen burning. In the PPI regime, the energy released is sufficient to reverse the collapse and eject substantial outer layers of the star, yet insufficient to completely unbind the stellar remnant. This cycle of collapse, thermonuclear pulse, and partial mass ejection may occur multiple times before the star’s final fate is sealed.

The cumulative mass loss through PPI episodes significantly alters the pre-supernova structure, reducing the final helium core mass and influencing whether the star ultimately undergoes core-collapse to form a black hole, or, in more extreme cases, proceeds to a full pair-instability supernova that leaves no remnant. The interplay between pulsational mass ejection, fallback accretion, and core contraction timescales introduces rich phenomenology relevant to both transient astrophysics and gravitational-wave astronomy. Observationally, PPI events have been proposed to explain certain luminous, multi-peaked supernova light curves, as well as the apparent upper mass gap in the stellar-mass black hole population inferred from gravitational-wave detections.

Recent advances in multi-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations and stellar evolution modeling have expanded our understanding of PPI dynamics, yet key uncertainties remain. The treatment of convection, rotation, metallicity-dependent mass loss, and nuclear reaction rates all critically affect predictions for the number, strength, and timing of pulsations. Moreover, the potential for circumstellar interaction between ejected shells and subsequent supernova ejecta offers a promising avenue to constrain PPI signatures observationally. In this work, we examine the conditions under which pulsational pair-instability leads to gravitational collapse and black-hole formation, and explore the broader implications for the mass spectrum of compact remnants, electromagnetic transients, and the role of PPI in shaping the high-mass stellar population.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the physical mechanisms and astrophysical consequences of pulsational pair‑instability supernovae (PPISNe), emphasizing their role in the late stages of massive stellar evolution. Our discussion has traced the onset of pair production, the resulting dynamical instabilities, and the sequence of mass‑ejection episodes that precede final gravitational collapse. We have highlighted how these pulsations can significantly alter the remnant mass, influencing whether the core ultimately forms a neutron star or collapses directly into a black hole. The interplay between repeated outbursts and the circumstellar environment shapes unique observational signatures, offering prospects for identifying PPISNe in both nearby and high‑redshift galaxies. Furthermore, we have considered the implications for the black‑hole mass spectrum, particularly in relation to the predicted upper mass gap arising from pair‑instability effects. Continued multi‑dimensional simulations, coupled with time‑domain surveys, are essential to constrain the progenitor properties and refine theoretical models. Beyond their intrinsic interest, PPISNe serve as a natural laboratory for exploring extreme stellar physics, gravitational collapse, and the pathways to black‑hole formation, thereby enriching our understanding of the life cycles of the most massive stars in the universe.

title: Conductivity of Graphene with Resonant Adsorbates: Beyond the Nearest Neighbor Hopping Model
abstract: We investigate the electronic transport properties of graphene with resonant adsorbates, extending beyond the conventional nearest-neighbor tight-binding approximation. Using a tight-binding framework that includes next-nearest-neighbor hopping and realistic impurity potentials, we analyze the influence of resonant scatterers on conductivity over a broad range of carrier densities. Numerical calculations based on the Kubo-Greenwood formalism reveal that next-nearest-neighbor coupling significantly modifies the low-energy electronic structure, shifting resonance energies and altering the symmetry of impurity-induced states. These effects lead to qualitative changes in the conductivity near the Dirac point, including enhanced particle–hole asymmetry and modified scaling of the minimum conductivity. Comparison with the nearest-neighbor model highlights the necessity of extended hopping terms for quantitative agreement with experimental measurements. Our results provide a more accurate description of graphene’s transport in the presence of resonant adsorbates and offer insights into tuning conductivity via controlled impurity engineering.
introduction: Graphene’s exceptional electronic properties arise from its two-dimensional honeycomb lattice and massless Dirac fermion excitations. However, the presence of impurities, particularly resonant adsorbates such as hydrogen or certain organic molecules, can strongly modify its transport behavior by introducing localized states near the Dirac point. Most theoretical studies address this problem within the nearest-neighbor tight-binding approximation, which neglects longer-range hopping and subtle band-structure effects. Here, we investigate the impact of resonant adsorbates on graphene’s conductivity using an extended tight-binding model, aiming to capture more accurately the interplay between impurity scattering, electronic structure, and quantum transport.
conclusion: In summary, we have investigated the conductivity of graphene with resonant adsorbates beyond the nearest-neighbor hopping approximation. Incorporating longer-range interactions reveals significant deviations from conventional models, particularly near the Dirac point, where impurity-induced states and modified scattering processes dominate. Our results demonstrate that extended hopping terms enhance localization effects and alter the scaling of conductivity with impurity concentration. These findings highlight the necessity of refined theoretical frameworks for accurately describing transport in functionalized graphene and related two-dimensional materials.

title: A PAC-Bayesian Tutorial with A Dropout Bound
abstract: We present a self-contained tutorial on the PAC-Bayesian framework for deriving generalization bounds, with a particular focus on its application to dropout regularization in machine learning. The tutorial introduces the foundational concepts of PAC-Bayesian theory, including stochastic classifiers, prior and posterior distributions over hypotheses, and the role of the Kullback–Leibler divergence in controlling generalization error. Building on these principles, we derive a novel PAC-Bayesian bound tailored to dropout, treating the dropout mechanism as a stochastic perturbation of network parameters. This approach yields an explicit relationship between dropout rates, empirical risk, and generalization guarantees, offering theoretical insight into the regularization effect of dropout. The bound is presented alongside intuitive explanations and step-by-step derivations, making the material accessible to readers with a basic background in statistical learning theory. We conclude by discussing implications for neural network training and suggesting directions for further refinement of PAC-Bayesian analyses in deep learning contexts.
introduction:
The PAC-Bayesian framework has emerged as a powerful and versatile set of tools for deriving generalization bounds in statistical learning theory. Rooted in the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) paradigm and infused with Bayesian perspectives, it provides a principled way to connect the complexity of a hypothesis class, the empirical performance of a learning algorithm, and the probabilistic guarantees on its expected risk. Unlike classical uniform convergence approaches, PAC-Bayesian bounds exploit a posterior distribution over hypotheses, often informed by the data, and a fixed prior distribution, typically chosen independently of the data, to yield bounds that can be both tight and interpretable. This blend of Bayesian and frequentist reasoning has made the framework attractive for analyzing modern learning algorithms, particularly those that are randomized or that can be expressed as stochastic predictors.

In recent years, the PAC-Bayesian methodology has found renewed interest in the context of contemporary machine learning practices such as ensemble methods, stochastic gradient descent, and regularization techniques that introduce randomness into the training process. Among these, dropout has become a widely used and empirically effective regularization method, especially in deep neural networks. Dropout operates by randomly omitting units or connections during training, thereby preventing co-adaptation of features and promoting robustness. While its empirical benefits are well documented, understanding dropout from a theoretical perspective remains an active area of research. Several intuitive explanations have been proposed, linking dropout to model averaging, adaptive regularization, and noise injection, but formal generalization guarantees grounded in statistical learning theory are less common.

The PAC-Bayesian framework is particularly well-suited to analyze dropout because dropout training can be viewed as learning a distribution over subnetworks or perturbed versions of the original model. In this view, the posterior distribution corresponds to the stochastic predictor induced by the dropout mechanism, while the prior can be chosen to reflect structural assumptions or uninformative beliefs about the hypothesis space. This perspective allows one to derive bounds that directly capture the effect of dropout-induced randomness on generalization performance, potentially yielding insights into why and when dropout improves learning outcomes.

This tutorial aims to provide a self-contained introduction to the PAC-Bayesian theory, emphasizing conceptual clarity and practical relevance. We begin by reviewing the foundational ideas behind PAC-Bayesian bounds, including the role of Kullback–Leibler divergence in relating the posterior to the prior, and how these bounds connect empirical performance to expected risk. We then discuss various forms of PAC-Bayesian inequalities, highlighting their assumptions and interpretations. The tutorial proceeds to apply these tools to the specific case of dropout, deriving a bound that explicitly incorporates the dropout rate and the structure of the hypothesis space. This “dropout bound” illustrates how PAC-Bayesian reasoning can be adapted to analyze a concrete and widely used learning algorithm.

Our treatment is intended for readers with some familiarity with basic probability and learning theory, but no prior exposure to PAC-Bayesian methods is assumed. By combining rigorous derivations with intuitive explanations, we seek to make the PAC-Bayesian approach accessible and to demonstrate its utility in bridging the gap between theory and practice. In doing so, we hope to contribute both to the broader understanding of PAC-Bayesian methods and to the theoretical foundations of dropout and related stochastic regularization techniques.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a PAC-Bayesian perspective on generalization, culminating in a dropout bound that unifies stochastic regularization with probabilistic guarantees. By framing dropout within the PAC-Bayesian framework, we highlighted its theoretical grounding and potential advantages for model robustness. Our analysis bridges practical deep learning techniques with rigorous statistical learning theory, offering insights for both researchers and practitioners. Future work may extend these results to adaptive dropout strategies and more complex, data-dependent prior constructions.

title: Combining complex and radial slave boson fields within the Kotliar-Ruckenstein representation of correlated impurities
abstract: We present a formulation of the Kotliar–Ruckenstein slave boson representation for correlated impurity models that combines complex and radial slave boson fields within a unified functional integral framework. The approach retains the gauge invariance of the original formalism while enabling a partial radial gauge fixing that simplifies the treatment of charge fluctuations without sacrificing the dynamical phase degrees of freedom. We demonstrate how this mixed representation facilitates analytical manipulations and numerical implementations by reducing the number of fluctuating phases. Applications to the single-impurity Anderson model illustrate the method’s accuracy in reproducing exact results for thermodynamic quantities and low-energy effective parameters.
introduction:
Strong electronic correlations remain at the forefront of condensed matter physics, as they give rise to a wide range of emergent phenomena, including the Mott metal–insulator transition, unconventional superconductivity, and intricate magnetic ordering. Theoretical descriptions of correlated systems often require both a faithful treatment of local interaction effects and an efficient representation of the low-energy quasiparticle degrees of freedom. Among the variety of approaches developed for this purpose, slave boson methods have proven particularly versatile. By introducing auxiliary bosonic and fermionic fields to represent the physical electron operators, these methods enable an explicit enforcement of local constraints while providing a transparent mean-field picture of quasiparticle renormalization.

The Kotliar–Ruckenstein (KR) slave boson representation constitutes a paradigmatic example of such an approach. Initially formulated for the Hubbard model, it introduces a set of auxiliary bosons corresponding to the different local occupancy states. The physical electron operator is replaced by a composite of a fermionic quasiparticle operator and bosonic amplitude operators, together with constraints that project onto the physical Hilbert space. At the saddle-point level, the KR formalism captures the Brinkman–Rice picture of the Mott transition, while fluctuations beyond mean field can be systematically included. For impurity problems, such as the Anderson impurity model, the KR approach reproduces the correct non-interacting and atomic limits, and provides a controlled way to interpolate between them.

In the standard KR formulation, the slave bosons are complex fields whose phases and amplitudes are both retained. While this representation is complete, it also contains gauge redundancies associated with the unphysical degrees of freedom, which in practical calculations must be handled carefully. An alternative is the radial slave boson representation, in which only the modulus (radial component) of the bosonic fields is kept, the phase variables being integrated out. This radial formulation eliminates explicit gauge degrees of freedom and is particularly advantageous in numerical evaluations of partition functions and correlation functions, especially in discretized path-integral treatments.

Despite their respective merits, the complex and radial slave boson formalisms have typically been employed separately. Complex fields are well suited for analytical developments, diagrammatics, and the study of dynamical fluctuations, whereas radial fields offer a more economical parametrization for static or thermodynamic quantities. A unified framework that combines both types of fields within the KR representation could exploit the complementary advantages of each, enabling more flexible and accurate treatments of correlated impurity systems. Such a formulation would allow one to keep complex bosonic variables where phase fluctuations are essential, while employing radial variables where gauge redundancy can be safely removed, potentially reducing computational cost without sacrificing physical fidelity.

In this work, we introduce and analyze a hybrid KR slave boson representation for correlated impurities, in which selected bosonic fields are retained in their complex form while others are expressed in radial coordinates. We discuss the general construction of this mixed representation, its implementation for the single-impurity Anderson model, and its consequences for both mean-field and fluctuation analyses. Our results demonstrate that this combined approach preserves the exact mapping to the physical Hilbert space and reproduces benchmark limits, while offering new possibilities for efficient analytical and numerical treatments.
conclusion: We have developed a unified framework that incorporates both complex and radial slave boson fields within the Kotliar–Ruckenstein representation for correlated impurity systems. By combining these complementary formulations, the method preserves the analytical transparency of the radial approach while retaining the flexibility of complex bosons to capture dynamical correlations.
