Our analysis demonstrates that this hybrid representation reproduces known limits exactly and provides a controlled treatment of fluctuations beyond mean-field. Benchmark calculations for single-impurity models confirm its accuracy in describing quasiparticle weights, local charge fluctuations, and spectral properties across interaction strengths. The formalism is readily extendable to multi-orbital and non-equilibrium situations, offering a versatile tool for studying strongly correlated nanostructures. This work thus establishes a consistent and efficient representation, bridging distinct slave boson schemes and enhancing their applicability to diverse correlated electron problems.

title: Generalized Bouncy Particle Sampler
abstract: We introduce the Generalized Bouncy Particle Sampler, a novel non-reversible Markov chain Monte Carlo method extending the classical Bouncy Particle Sampler to broader classes of target distributions and event dynamics. Our approach incorporates adaptive velocity updates and flexible switching rules, improving mixing and robustness in high dimensions. Theoretical analysis establishes ergodicity and convergence guarantees, while empirical results demonstrate substantial efficiency gains over existing samplers across diverse Bayesian inference and statistical physics applications.
introduction:
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are central to modern computational statistics, enabling sampling from complex, high-dimensional probability distributions that arise in Bayesian inference, statistical physics, and machine learning. Traditional MCMC schemes, such as the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), rely on proposals that are either purely stochastic or driven by Hamiltonian dynamics with occasional momentum resampling. While these approaches are widely applicable, they can suffer from random-walk behavior, poor scalability with dimension, or high computational cost due to the need for repeated gradient evaluations and accept–reject steps.

Piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to conventional MCMC algorithms. In contrast to discrete-time updates, PDMP-based samplers evolve deterministically between random event times, at which the process undergoes an instantaneous change in velocity or direction. This framework enables non-reversible dynamics, which can lead to improved mixing and reduced asymptotic variance in Monte Carlo estimates. The Bouncy Particle Sampler (BPS) is a prominent example of a PDMP-based method. It simulates the motion of a particle moving at constant velocity, punctuated by “bounces” off an energy landscape determined by the target distribution. At each bounce, the particle’s velocity is updated through a deterministic reflection with respect to the gradient of the log-target density, and occasional velocity refreshments are introduced to maintain ergodicity.

The original BPS offers several advantages: it avoids the need for a Metropolis–Hastings correction, can exploit gradient information efficiently, and exhibits non-reversible dynamics that help explore the state space more effectively. However, it is not without limitations. The deterministic reflection rule may lead to poor exploration in anisotropic or multimodal distributions if bounces are highly correlated, and the event rate can be sensitive to the choice of velocity distribution. Furthermore, the standard BPS formulation assumes a Euclidean geometry and a specific form of velocity update, which may not be optimal for all target distributions or computational settings.

These considerations motivate the development of generalized versions of BPS that retain its advantageous non-reversible, rejection-free properties while offering greater flexibility in the choice of dynamics, event rules, and velocity updates. A generalized Bouncy Particle Sampler (GBPS) framework can encompass a broader class of PDMPs by allowing alternative reflection mechanisms, velocity refreshment schemes, and event rate functions, potentially adapting to the geometry of the target distribution or incorporating problem-specific structure. Such generalizations may improve robustness, mixing efficiency, and scalability, while preserving the theoretical guarantees of ergodicity and correctness.

In this work, we introduce a Generalized Bouncy Particle Sampler that unifies and extends existing PDMP-based methods. Our formulation defines a class of continuous-time, non-reversible Markov processes characterized by flexible event dynamics and velocity transformations. We show how the proposed GBPS recovers the standard BPS as a special case, while also admitting novel variants that can better handle challenging target distributions. We provide theoretical results establishing invariance with respect to the target distribution under mild conditions, along with practical guidelines for designing event mechanisms. Through a series of experiments on synthetic and real-world problems, we demonstrate that our generalized framework can offer substantial performance gains over the standard BPS and related MCMC algorithms, particularly in high-dimensional or ill-conditioned settings.

By situating the GBPS within the broader landscape of MCMC and PDMP methods, this work aims to contribute both a unifying theoretical perspective and a practical tool for efficient sampling in complex statistical models.
conclusion: We have introduced the Generalized Bouncy Particle Sampler, extending existing piecewise-deterministic Markov process methods to broader target distributions and adaptive dynamics. Empirical results demonstrate improved mixing and robustness across diverse models. This framework offers a flexible foundation for future advances in non-reversible Monte Carlo, with potential applications in large-scale Bayesian inference and computational statistics.

title: Induced gravitational collapse at extreme cosmological distances: the case of GRB 090423
abstract: We investigate the phenomenon of induced gravitational collapse (IGC) in the context of GRB 090423, one of the most distant gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) observed to date, with a redshift of *z* ≈ 8.2. The IGC paradigm describes a process in which a Type Ib/c supernova in a close binary system triggers the collapse of a neutron star companion into a black hole, producing an associated long-duration GRB. This framework has been successfully applied to several nearby GRB–supernova associations, but its applicability at extreme cosmological distances remains largely unexplored. We analyze the prompt emission and afterglow data of GRB 090423 obtained from *Swift* and other facilities, and compare its spectral and temporal properties to those of lower-redshift IGC candidates. Despite the high redshift and corresponding time dilation, the prompt emission exhibits a rest-frame duration and isotropic energy release consistent with the IGC class. The late-time X-ray afterglow, when corrected to the source rest frame, follows the canonical luminosity evolution pattern identified in IGC sources, suggesting a common underlying mechanism. We discuss the implications for the progenitor’s binary parameters, the energetics of the collapse, and the detectability of the associated supernova component, which is rendered unobservable in the optical/NIR due to extreme distance and intergalactic medium absorption. Our findings support the hypothesis that the IGC process can operate essentially unchanged in the early Universe, implying the presence of massive binary systems capable of producing both a supernova and a GRB within the first 600 Myr after the Big Bang. This result provides new constraints on massive star formation, binary evolution, and compact object demographics at very high redshift.
introduction:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic phenomena in the Universe, capable of releasing in a few seconds an amount of energy comparable to that emitted by the Sun over its entire lifetime. Since their discovery in the late 1960s, GRBs have been divided into two broad classes—short and long—based on their observed duration and spectral hardness. Long GRBs (lasting more than 2 seconds) are generally associated with the core-collapse of massive stars, often accompanied by Type Ic supernovae, while short GRBs are linked to compact binary mergers. However, as observational capabilities have advanced, it has become clear that the diversity of GRB properties cannot be fully explained by this simple dichotomy. Among the proposed theoretical frameworks is the induced gravitational collapse (IGC) paradigm, which posits that some long-duration GRBs originate in tight binary systems comprising a massive star and a neutron star companion. In this scenario, the supernova explosion of the massive star triggers the accretion-induced collapse of the neutron star into a black hole, thereby producing the GRB.

The IGC model has been invoked to explain a class of events showing a characteristic temporal and spectral structure, including a supernova-like optical component emerging days after the prompt gamma-ray emission. Observational support for the IGC scenario has been obtained primarily for sources at relatively low to intermediate redshifts, where follow-up campaigns can reveal the associated supernova. At higher redshifts, the increasing faintness and cosmological time dilation make the detection of these counterparts challenging, and the direct confirmation of IGC events becomes more elusive. Nonetheless, identifying possible IGC events at extreme cosmological distances is of paramount importance for constraining their progenitor properties, exploring the evolution of massive binary systems over cosmic time, and understanding the role of such systems in the early Universe.

GRB 090423, detected by the Swift satellite on April 23, 2009, is a landmark in high-redshift astrophysics. With a measured redshift of \( z \approx 8.2 \), it is among the most distant GRBs ever observed, corresponding to a look-back time of over 13 billion years, when the Universe was less than 600 million years old. The prompt emission of GRB 090423 lasted about 10 seconds in the observer frame, placing it within the long-duration class, but its rest-frame duration is significantly shorter. The event’s isotropic-equivalent energy release and spectral characteristics suggest a powerful explosion in the early Universe, but the nature of its progenitor remains uncertain. The extreme redshift precludes direct optical detection of any associated supernova, and the sparse multiwavelength data make classification challenging.

In this work, we explore the possibility that GRB 090423 can be interpreted within the induced gravitational collapse framework. We examine the prompt emission properties in comparison with nearby confirmed IGC sources, investigate the afterglow behavior in the X-ray band, and assess whether the observed characteristics are consistent with the expectations of the IGC model at such an early cosmological epoch. This analysis is motivated not only by the aim to classify GRB 090423, but also by the broader goal of testing the viability of the IGC scenario under the extreme conditions of the high-redshift Universe, where metallicities, stellar initial mass functions, and binary evolution pathways may differ from those observed locally. Our results have implications for the detectability of IGC events in the reionization era and for the use of GRBs as probes of the first generations of massive stars.
conclusion:
The analysis presented in this work has extended the theoretical framework of the induced gravitational collapse (IGC) paradigm to one of the most extreme cosmological distances at which a gamma-ray burst (GRB) has been observed, namely GRB 090423 at a redshift of \( z \approx 8.2 \). By applying the IGC model to this event, we have sought to elucidate the physical processes that may underlie the prompt emission and afterglow properties in a regime where the Universe was less than 650 million years old. Our results support the viability of the IGC mechanism—originally developed to explain nearby, energetic long GRBs associated with Type Ib/c supernovae—as a candidate explanation for phenomena at the dawn of cosmic history.

Through the comparison of GRB 090423 with lower-redshift members of the IGC sample, we have found that, once corrected for cosmological effects, its light curve morphology, spectral evolution, and energetics are consistent with those expected from a binary progenitor system composed of an evolved massive star and a neutron star companion. In this context, the collapse of the massive star into a supernova triggers the rapid accretion of ejecta onto the neutron star, leading to its gravitational collapse into a black hole and the concomitant release of the GRB. The ability of the IGC scenario to reproduce the observed temporal and spectral features at such high redshift lends weight to the proposition that the fundamental astrophysical processes driving these bursts have remained largely unchanged over the majority of cosmic time.

A noteworthy implication of our findings is the potential universality of the IGC mechanism across a vast range of redshifts and progenitor metallicities. At \( z \sim 8.2 \), stellar populations were dominated by low-metallicity, possibly Population II stars, yet the binary evolutionary pathways required for the IGC appear attainable. This suggests that the progenitor configurations necessary for the IGC process were already established in the early Universe, enabling the occurrence of GRBs of comparable luminosity and duration to their lower-redshift counterparts. Furthermore, the detection of GRB 090423’s afterglow in multiple bands underscores the feasibility of using such events as probes of the intergalactic medium and star formation in the epoch of reionization.

The application of the IGC model to GRB 090423 also provides constraints on the physical parameters of the progenitor system, including the mass of the neutron star prior to collapse, the density profile of the supernova ejecta, and the efficiency of mass transfer. These constraints, in turn, offer insight into the nature of massive binary evolution at early times. The agreement between model predictions and observations reinforces the relevance of binary interactions in shaping the high-energy transient sky across cosmic epochs.

Looking ahead, the detection of additional high-redshift GRBs will be essential to further test the robustness and universality of the IGC paradigm. The forthcoming observational capabilities of facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope, the Extremely Large Telescope, and next-generation GRB-dedicated missions will significantly enhance our ability to characterise the afterglows and host environments of such bursts. High-resolution spectroscopy, in particular, will allow us to probe the chemical composition and ionisation state of the circumburst medium, offering deeper insight into the link between GRB progenitors and the early stages of galaxy evolution.

In conclusion, the successful application of the IGC scenario to GRB 090423 not only strengthens the case for induced gravitational collapse as a unifying mechanism for a subset of long GRBs with associated supernovae, but also demonstrates its relevance in the extreme conditions of the early Universe. This work highlights the enduring nature of certain astrophysical processes across more than 13 billion years of cosmic history, and points to the powerful role that high-redshift GRBs can play in bridging the fields of stellar evolution, relativistic astrophysics, and observational cosmology.

title: Constraints on the angular distribution of satellite galaxies about spiral hosts
abstract: We investigate the angular distribution of satellite galaxies around spiral host galaxies using a statistically significant sample drawn from wide-field survey data. By quantifying the relative orientations of satellites with respect to their hosts’ projected major axes, we test for deviations from isotropy that may reflect underlying dynamical or environmental processes. Our analysis incorporates constraints from projection effects, selection biases, and completeness limits to ensure robust measurements. We find that the satellite distribution is consistent with a mild anisotropy, with a tendency for satellites to align preferentially along the hosts’ disk planes. This signal is more pronounced for satellites at smaller projected separations and for hosts in lower-density environments. These results provide new constraints on models of satellite accretion and the role of large-scale structure in shaping satellite systems.
introduction:
The spatial distribution of satellite galaxies around their hosts provides an important observational constraint on models of galaxy formation and the evolution of structure in the Universe. In the standard cosmological framework, dark matter haloes grow hierarchically, accreting smaller subhaloes that may host satellite galaxies. The dynamics and present-day configuration of these satellites retain imprints of their accretion history, the shape and orientation of the host halo, and the interplay between baryonic and dark matter components. Consequently, characterizing the angular distribution of satellites relative to the central galaxy’s orientation offers a means to test theoretical predictions and to probe the processes shaping galaxy systems.

Early studies in the Local Group revealed that the Milky Way’s brightest satellites are not isotropically distributed, but instead populate a flattened structure inclined with respect to the Galactic disc. Similarly, M31 exhibits a coherent plane of satellites, suggesting that anisotropic satellite configurations may be common. On larger samples, statistical analyses of satellite systems in surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) have reported both isotropic and anisotropic trends, with some works finding an excess of satellites along the projected major axes of their hosts, and others indicating minor-axis alignments. These discrepancies may arise from differences in host morphology, selection criteria, or projection effects, underscoring the need for careful sample definition and robust statistical methods.

For spiral galaxies in particular, the alignment of satellite systems with respect to the host disc is of special interest. In cold dark matter simulations without baryonic physics, subhalo distributions often trace the triaxial shape of the host halo, which is typically aligned with the major axis of the stellar disc only imperfectly. Including baryonic effects can alter the halo shape and angular momentum, potentially leading to different alignment patterns. Observationally, the disc inclination offers a geometric handle on the three-dimensional orientation of the system, allowing for tests of whether satellites preferentially occupy the polar regions, the disc plane, or an intermediate configuration.

Constraining the angular distribution around spiral hosts also bears on the physics of satellite accretion. Anisotropic infall along cosmic filaments can imprint preferred directions in the satellite system, while dynamical friction and tidal interactions may subsequently reshape the distribution. The persistence or erosion of anisotropy over time is sensitive to satellite orbital parameters and the potential of the host, providing a connection between observed present-day configurations and the underlying assembly history.

In this work, we investigate the angular distribution of satellite galaxies around a well-defined sample of spiral hosts, selected to minimise contamination and projection biases. By quantifying the degree of anisotropy and its dependence on satellite and host properties, we aim to place new constraints on the interplay between halo shape, disc orientation, and accretion geometry. Our results are compared with predictions from cosmological simulations, enabling a critical assessment of current models of satellite system formation and evolution.
conclusion:
The analysis presented here has sought to quantify and interpret the angular distribution of satellite galaxies around spiral hosts, with a particular focus on identifying constraints that can be placed on anisotropies relative to the host disc plane. By combining a statistically significant sample of host–satellite systems with careful control of selection effects, projection biases, and contamination from interlopers, we have been able to assess the degree to which the observed distributions deviate from isotropy, and to compare these findings with theoretical expectations from current models of galaxy formation in a ΛCDM framework.

Our results indicate that, within the uncertainties, the satellite population of spiral galaxies exhibits only modest departures from isotropy when considered over the full range of projected radii examined. For the majority of hosts, the angular distribution is consistent with a random orientation relative to the disc, though there is tentative evidence for a mild excess of satellites located near the disc plane at small projected separations. This trend, while not strong enough to claim a definitive detection in the present dataset, is qualitatively consistent with predictions from hydrodynamical simulations in which anisotropic accretion along filaments and the dynamical influence of the host disc can imprint planar alignments on the inner satellite system.

In assessing possible sources of systematic error, we have demonstrated that the observed distribution is sensitive to the criteria used to define host and satellite samples, particularly the relative magnitude and redshift cuts. The contamination by background galaxies masquerading as satellites can artificially dilute any true anisotropy, underscoring the importance of spectroscopic confirmation and robust statistical background subtraction. Furthermore, the inclination angle of the host disc introduces projection effects that must be modelled explicitly to recover the intrinsic three-dimensional distribution from two-dimensional data.

Comparisons with cosmological simulations suggest that the level of anisotropy permitted by our constraints is compatible with scenarios in which the outer halo satellites retain a memory of their filamentary infall directions, while the inner satellites have been dynamically heated and redistributed over several gigayears. The weak planar alignment signal we find, if real, may point to a complex interplay between the accretion history, the gravitational potential of the disc and halo, and the effects of satellite–satellite interactions. The absence of a strong polar alignment, such as that seen in the Milky Way’s “Vast Polar Structure,” implies that such configurations are not a ubiquitous feature of spiral galaxy satellite systems at the mass scales probed here.

From an observational perspective, the constraints derived here underscore the need for larger, deeper, and more homogeneous samples to decisively detect or rule out subtle anisotropies. Upcoming wide-field spectroscopic surveys, combined with high-resolution imaging, will enable more precise measurements of host disc orientations, satellite positions, and velocity information, thereby reducing uncertainties and allowing for more stringent tests of theoretical models. In particular, three-dimensional kinematic data will be essential for disentangling bound satellites from chance projections and for probing the orbital coherence that may accompany planar structures.

Looking forward, the integration of observational constraints such as those presented here with cosmological simulations that include baryonic physics will be key to advancing our understanding of satellite system formation and evolution. By jointly analysing spatial distributions, kinematics, and satellite properties such as colour and morphology, we can begin to unravel the relative importance of environmental processes, accretion geometry, and internal dynamical evolution in shaping the present-day configurations of satellites around spiral hosts.

In summary, our study places quantitative limits on the degree of angular anisotropy in the satellite distributions of spiral galaxies, finding no compelling evidence for strong deviations from isotropy, but allowing for mild planar enhancements at small separations. These results are consistent with the view that while anisotropic accretion and disc–halo interactions can influence satellite orbits, the cumulative effects of dynamical evolution tend to erase strong initial alignments over time. As observational capabilities continue to expand, the framework developed here provides a basis for more definitive characterisations of satellite anisotropy, offering an important empirical benchmark for models of galaxy formation in the cosmological context.

title: Rethinking Deep Contrastive Learning with Embedding Memory
abstract: Deep contrastive learning has emerged as a powerful framework for unsupervised representation learning, yet its performance often depends on large batch sizes or auxiliary memory banks to provide sufficient negative samples. This paper rethinks the role of embedding memory in contrastive frameworks, proposing a novel architecture that integrates a dynamic embedding memory module directly into the learning process. Unlike conventional memory banks that store fixed representations, our approach maintains and updates embeddings in a momentum-driven manner, enabling the model to capture evolving semantic relations while mitigating representation staleness. We introduce a memory-regularized contrastive loss that adaptively balances contributions from mini-batch and memory-stored samples, improving both training stability and representation diversity. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and fine-grained datasets, demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under constrained batch sizes. Moreover, the proposed design reduces computational overhead compared to large-batch training and exhibits robustness to noise and domain shifts. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component, highlighting the synergy between dynamic memory updates and regularization. Our findings suggest that embedding memory, when reinterpreted as an active participant in representation learning rather than a passive repository, can significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of deep contrastive learning.
introduction:
Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in representation learning, particularly through the paradigm of contrastive learning. By encouraging representations of similar samples to be close in the embedding space while pushing apart those of dissimilar samples, contrastive methods have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition. Central to their success is the ability to mine informative positive and negative pairs from large datasets and to optimize feature encoders in a self-supervised or weakly supervised manner. Despite these advances, the design of effective contrastive objectives remains challenging, especially when balancing the need for diverse negative samples with the stability and efficiency of training.

A critical factor influencing the quality of contrastive representations is the size and diversity of the negative set. Many popular approaches, such as SimCLR, rely on large batch sizes to provide a sufficient number of negatives, but this requirement significantly increases memory consumption and computational cost, limiting applicability on resource-constrained hardware. Other methods, such as MoCo, circumvent this limitation by maintaining a large dynamic dictionary of embeddings via a momentum-updated encoder, enabling the reuse of negative samples across batches. While these approaches alleviate some constraints, they also introduce new complexities, including the staleness of stored embeddings and sensitivity to hyperparameters controlling the update dynamics.

The concept of embedding memory—persistently storing and reusing intermediate representations—offers a promising avenue for addressing these trade-offs. Embedding memory can be viewed as an external storage mechanism that decouples the availability of diverse negative samples from the instantaneous batch composition. By maintaining a repository of past embeddings, the learning process can leverage a broader and more varied context, potentially leading to richer feature spaces and improved generalization. However, naive implementations of embedding memory risk degrading performance due to outdated or inconsistent representations, particularly in rapidly evolving feature spaces during early training stages.

Incorporating memory into contrastive learning raises fundamental questions about the temporal consistency of embeddings, the mechanisms for updating and refreshing stored representations, and the interplay between memory size, retrieval strategies, and model convergence. While momentum encoders partially address the consistency problem, they do so at the cost of additional parameters and training complexity. Moreover, the optimal trade-off between embedding freshness and diversity remains poorly understood, and existing methods often rely on heuristics rather than principled design choices.

Another dimension of this problem concerns the role of embedding memory in facilitating long-range semantic relationships. Standard contrastive learning typically emphasizes instance discrimination—distinguishing among individual samples—which can lead to representations that are locally coherent but may not capture higher-level structure. By contrast, a well-designed embedding memory could enable the model to access and integrate information from semantically related but temporally distant samples, thus promoting more globally consistent representations. This capability is particularly valuable in scenarios with non-i.i.d. data streams, imbalanced class distributions, or evolving data distributions, where the immediate context provided by a minibatch may be insufficient for stable learning.

Recent work has begun to explore variants of memory-augmented contrastive learning, including queue-based systems, memory banks, and hybrid architectures that integrate clustering or prototype-based representations. These approaches suggest that embedding memory can serve not only as a reservoir of negatives but also as a scaffold for structuring the representation space. For example, prototypes derived from memory contents can act as anchor points for aligning semantically similar samples, thereby complementing the pairwise learning signal of traditional contrastive loss functions. Nonetheless, the full potential of embedding memory has yet to be realized, as current methods often treat it as a static or auxiliary component rather than a dynamic, learnable part of the model.

In this work, we revisit deep contrastive learning through the lens of embedding memory, seeking to systematically understand and enhance its role in representation learning. We propose a framework that treats memory not merely as a cache of past embeddings but as an active participant in the learning process, with mechanisms for adaptive refresh, relevance-based sampling, and integration with the loss function. Our approach aims to simultaneously improve the diversity and consistency of training signals, reduce the dependence on large batch sizes, and enable the capture of more global semantic structure. By rethinking the interaction between embedding memory and contrastive objectives, we aim to advance the scalability, efficiency, and robustness of self-supervised representation learning across diverse domains.

Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our memory-centric perspective leads to significant gains over existing contrastive baselines, particularly in settings with limited computational resources or complex, non-stationary data. Our findings not only validate the proposed framework but also shed light on broader principles for integrating memory into deep learning architectures, with implications beyond contrastive learning itself.
conclusion: In this work, we revisited deep contrastive learning through the lens of embedding memory, proposing a framework that explicitly retains and leverages historical representations. By integrating memory into the contrastive objective, our approach enhances representation stability, mitigates forgetting, and improves sample efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent gains across benchmarks, particularly in scenarios with limited batch sizes or long-tailed distributions. The memory mechanism also offers interpretability benefits by enabling analysis of embedding evolution. These findings suggest that embedding memory is a powerful and general tool for advancing contrastive learning. Future research may explore adaptive memory management and broader applications across self-supervised and multimodal domains, further unlocking the potential of memory-augmented representation learning.

title: Study of ageing in Al-Mg-Si alloys by positron annihilation spectroscopy
abstract: The ageing behaviour of Al-Mg-Si alloys has been investigated using positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) in order to elucidate the microstructural evolution associated with natural and artificial ageing. Samples of a commercial 6xxx-series alloy were solution heat-treated, quenched, and subjected to various ageing treatments at room temperature and elevated temperatures. Positron lifetime and Doppler broadening measurements were performed to monitor changes in the type and concentration of positron trapping sites during the ageing process. The results reveal a pronounced sensitivity of PAS parameters to the formation and transformation of solute clusters and precipitates. In the early stages of natural ageing, a rapid decrease in positron lifetime indicates the formation of coherent Mg-Si clusters, which act as shallow positron traps. Artificial ageing at intermediate temperatures leads to further evolution towards semi-coherent β'' precipitates, accompanied by characteristic shifts in Doppler broadening spectra. Prolonged over-ageing results in the coarsening of precipitates and a reduction in positron trapping efficiency. The combination of lifetime and momentum distribution data allows for discrimination between vacancy-solute complexes and coherent precipitates, providing a detailed picture of defect kinetics. These findings demonstrate that PAS is a powerful non-destructive technique for characterising the ageing state of Al-Mg-Si alloys, enabling correlation between microstructural changes and mechanical property development.
introduction:
Al-Mg-Si alloys, belonging to the 6xxx series of aluminium alloys, have attracted considerable attention due to their favourable combination of low density, good corrosion resistance, high specific strength, and excellent formability. These properties make them widely used in automotive, aerospace, and construction industries, where weight reduction and mechanical performance are critical design considerations. A key feature of Al-Mg-Si alloys is their age-hardening capability, which arises from the precipitation of metastable phases during controlled thermal treatments. Ageing processes in these alloys involve a sequence of microstructural transformations, from solute-rich clusters to coherent and semi-coherent precipitates, which strongly influence mechanical properties such as hardness, yield strength, and ductility.

Understanding the ageing behaviour of Al-Mg-Si alloys is essential for optimising their performance. In conventional precipitation sequences, supersaturated solid solutions obtained by solution heat treatment and quenching undergo natural ageing at ambient temperature or artificial ageing at elevated temperatures, leading to the formation of Guinier–Preston (GP) zones, βʺ, βʹ, and β phases. The early stages of ageing, dominated by solute clustering and vacancy-solute interactions, are particularly important, as they determine the nucleation of strengthening precipitates and strongly depend on the alloy composition, quench rate, and thermal history. However, these early stages are difficult to characterise by conventional microscopy techniques due to the small size and low contrast of the clusters.

Positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) has emerged as a sensitive tool for investigating defects and solute-vacancy complexes at the atomic scale in metallic systems. The technique exploits the sensitivity of positrons to open-volume defects such as vacancies, dislocations, and vacancy clusters. When positrons annihilate with electrons in these defects, changes in measurable parameters such as positron lifetime and Doppler broadening of the annihilation radiation provide direct information about the nature, size, and concentration of the defects. In age-hardenable aluminium alloys, PAS is particularly useful for studying the interaction between vacancies and solute atoms during the initial stages of ageing, offering insight into vacancy migration, trapping, and the formation of early clusters that are otherwise challenging to detect.

Previous studies have demonstrated the applicability of PAS to Al-based alloys, revealing that quenched-in vacancies play a pivotal role in solute clustering during natural and artificial ageing. In Al-Mg-Si alloys, vacancies interact strongly with Mg and Si atoms, facilitating their diffusion and accelerating the nucleation of GP zones and βʺ precipitates. Systematic PAS measurements enable the identification of distinct ageing stages and the correlation of positron annihilation parameters with mechanical property evolution. Despite these advances, there remain open questions concerning the precise kinetics of vacancy-solute complex formation, the effect of alloy composition on early clustering, and the influence of thermal treatments on defect evolution.

The present study aims to investigate the ageing behaviour of Al-Mg-Si alloys using positron annihilation spectroscopy, with a focus on the early stages that critically determine the final microstructure and mechanical properties. By combining positron lifetime measurements with complementary hardness tests, we seek to establish a detailed correlation between defect evolution and age-hardening response. The alloys are subjected to various isothermal and natural ageing conditions to capture the temporal evolution of vacancies, solute-vacancy complexes, and clusters. Particular attention is given to the influence of Mg:Si ratio and quenching conditions on the kinetics of defect transformation.

A deeper understanding of these processes will contribute to the optimisation of heat treatment schedules for Al-Mg-Si alloys, enabling the tailoring of microstructures for specific engineering applications. Moreover, this work underscores the utility of PAS as a powerful, non-destructive probe of atomic-scale processes governing the mechanical performance of precipitation-hardenable aluminium alloys. Through systematic experimentation and analysis, we aim to provide new insights into the interplay between defect dynamics and precipitation phenomena in these technologically important materials.
conclusion: The present investigation has demonstrated that positron annihilation spectroscopy is a sensitive and effective technique for studying the ageing behaviour of Al-Mg-Si alloys. Measurements of positron lifetime and Doppler broadening parameters have revealed distinct microstructural changes associated with natural and artificial ageing, including the formation, growth, and transformation of vacancy–solute complexes and coherent precipitates. The observed evolution in positron trapping characteristics correlates well with established ageing stages, providing insight into the kinetics of clustering and precipitation processes. Differences in annihilation parameters between various ageing treatments indicate that the technique can discriminate between subtle changes in defect structures and solute distributions. These findings underscore the value of positron annihilation methods in complementing conventional characterization techniques for aluminium alloys. The results contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between microscopic defect evolution and macroscopic property changes during ageing, offering guidance for the optimization of heat treatment schedules to achieve desired mechanical performance.

title: Relativistic tunneling picture of electron-positron pair creation
abstract: We present a relativistic tunneling framework for describing electron–positron pair creation in strong external fields. Building on the semiclassical picture of quantum tunneling, we extend the formalism to incorporate relativistic dynamics and spin effects within the context of quantum electrodynamics. The approach unifies intuitive space–time trajectories with gauge-invariant formulations, enabling a consistent interpretation of the pair creation process in both constant and inhomogeneous field configurations. We analyze the role of the effective potential barrier, the influence of field polarization, and the correspondence with exact solutions. This relativistic tunneling picture offers a transparent, physically motivated description, bridging nonperturbative theory and experimental observables in ultra-intense laser–matter interactions.
introduction:
Electron–positron pair creation in strong electromagnetic fields is one of the most striking nonperturbative predictions of quantum electrodynamics (QED). Originally formulated in seminal works by Sauter, Heisenberg and Euler, and Schwinger, the phenomenon embodies the instability of the quantum vacuum in the presence of sufficiently intense fields. In the simplest case of a static, spatially uniform electric field, the Schwinger mechanism predicts an exponentially suppressed rate of pair production, with the characteristic critical field strength \(E_{\mathrm{cr}} = m^2 c^3 / e\hbar \approx 1.3\times 10^{18} \,\mathrm{V/m}\). While such extreme conditions lie far beyond the reach of current laboratory technology, advances in high-intensity laser systems and the development of ultra-relativistic particle beams have fueled renewed interest in both theoretical and experimental aspects of vacuum pair creation.

A particularly fruitful framework for understanding nonperturbative pair production is the tunneling picture. In the nonrelativistic analogy of barrier penetration, an external electric field tilts the Dirac sea, enabling electrons from negative-energy states to tunnel into the positive-energy continuum, leaving behind positrons as holes in the sea. In the relativistic context, the tunneling process must be formulated covariantly, accounting for the full spacetime structure of the background field and the dynamics of both particles in the pair. This picture provides an intuitive bridge between semiclassical methods, such as the worldline instanton approach, and fully quantum field-theoretic treatments.

In realistic scenarios, fields are neither perfectly static nor homogeneous. Time-dependent electric fields, as generated by focused laser pulses, lead to rich dynamical phenomena, including the dynamically assisted Schwinger effect, in which the combination of a strong, slowly varying field with a weaker, rapidly varying field can dramatically enhance the production rate. Spatial inhomogeneities, on the other hand, influence the tunneling trajectories and can modify the momentum spectrum of the created particles. In these cases, the relativistic tunneling picture must be generalized beyond its simplest form to incorporate the effects of field gradients and temporal modulation.

The extension of the tunneling framework to relativistic regimes requires a careful treatment of the electron and positron trajectories in complexified spacetime. Within the semiclassical approximation, the tunneling amplitude is dominated by stationary-phase paths—so-called instantons—that connect classically allowed regions through classically forbidden ones. In the relativistic domain, these trajectories are determined by the Lorentz force in imaginary proper time, and their projection onto real spacetime encodes measurable quantities such as final momenta and angular distributions. This approach not only yields the exponential suppression factor in the pair creation rate but also provides insight into the sub-barrier dynamics.

Moreover, the tunneling picture offers a natural language for describing pair creation in combined electromagnetic fields, including those involving strong magnetic components or counterpropagating laser waves. In such configurations, the interplay between electric and magnetic forces can lead to novel features, such as momentum-dependent suppression or enhancement, as well as spin-dependent effects. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for interpreting signals in planned high-intensity laser experiments and for exploring connections to related processes in astrophysical environments, such as near magnetars or in pulsar magnetospheres.

In this work, we develop a fully relativistic tunneling description of electron–positron pair creation in general electromagnetic backgrounds. Building on semiclassical techniques, we derive the conditions under which the tunneling picture remains valid, elucidate the role of complex trajectories, and analyze how temporal and spatial field structures shape the production process. By comparing with exact QED results in solvable field configurations, we assess the accuracy and limitations of the approach. Our aim is to provide a unified and physically transparent framework that can be applied to both idealized model fields and realistic experimental setups, thereby advancing the theoretical foundation for probing the quantum vacuum under extreme conditions.
conclusion:
In this work, we have developed and analyzed a relativistic tunneling framework for describing the nonperturbative creation of electron–positron pairs in strong external fields. By extending the semiclassical tunneling picture to incorporate fully relativistic kinematics and field configurations, we have provided a unified description that connects the intuitive barrier-penetration concept with the formal solutions of the Dirac equation in external backgrounds. Our approach clarifies how the notion of a tunneling trajectory can remain meaningful in the presence of space–time–dependent electromagnetic fields, and how the key tunneling parameters emerge naturally from the relativistic invariants of the field.

We have shown that, in the constant crossed-field limit, our formulation reproduces the known Schwinger rate, while for more general field geometries it yields physically transparent predictions for the momentum spectra and angular distributions of the produced particles. The relativistic tunneling picture makes explicit the role of the canonical and kinetic momenta, and elucidates how the energy gap between negative- and positive-energy states is dynamically bridged during the sub-barrier motion. This perspective also allows a direct comparison between purely electric backgrounds and situations where strong magnetic components modify the tunneling dynamics.

Furthermore, we have highlighted the connection between the imaginary-time trajectories found in our approach and the worldline instanton formalism, demonstrating that both arise from the same underlying saddle-point structure of the quantum amplitude. The tunneling picture thus serves as a bridge between semiclassical intuition and fully covariant quantum field theoretical treatments, providing an efficient tool for interpreting numerical simulations and experimental observables.

Our results suggest several promising directions for future research. Extending the present analysis to include back-reaction effects and dynamically evolving fields will be essential for describing pair creation in realistic high-intensity laser–plasma interactions. Moreover, the relativistic tunneling framework may be adapted to explore strong-field processes in astrophysical contexts, such as magnetar magnetospheres or the early-universe electrodynamics. Finally, the conceptual clarity of the tunneling picture could be exploited in designing experimental configurations that optimize pair production rates or probe specific aspects of relativistic quantum dynamics.

In summary, the relativistic tunneling picture provides a coherent, physically intuitive, and quantitatively accurate description of strong-field electron–positron pair creation, complementing existing theoretical approaches and opening avenues for both fundamental studies and practical applications in high-field physics.

title: Pair localization in dipolar systems with tunable positional disorder
abstract: We investigate the localization of bound pairs in one-dimensional dipolar systems with tunable positional disorder. Using exact diagonalization and finite-size scaling, we analyze how long-range dipole–dipole interactions and correlated disorder influence the mobility of two-particle states. By varying the degree of positional randomness, we identify a crossover from extended to localized pair states, with localization lengths strongly dependent on dipolar anisotropy and interaction strength. Our results reveal that positional disorder can enhance or suppress pair localization compared to uncorrelated on-site disorder, and that dipolar coupling leads to nontrivial spatial correlations in the localized wavefunctions. These findings provide insight into controlling transport properties in dipolar quantum simulators, with potential applications to cold polar molecules, Rydberg arrays, and solid-state spin systems.
introduction:
Disorder-induced localization has long been recognized as a central theme in condensed matter physics, with profound implications for transport, coherence, and many-body dynamics. Since Anderson’s seminal work on single-particle localization in disordered lattices, the interplay between disorder and interactions has remained a topic of intense theoretical and experimental interest. In particular, while strong disorder can suppress transport by localizing particles, interactions can either facilitate delocalization through inelastic scattering, or, conversely, enhance localization via bound-state formation. Understanding the conditions under which localization persists or is destroyed in interacting systems is of fundamental importance, not only for elucidating non-equilibrium phases of matter, but also for controlling quantum information in engineered platforms.

Dipolar systems offer a unique arena in which to study these questions. Unlike short-range Hubbard-type interactions, dipole–dipole couplings are long-ranged and anisotropic, leading to qualitatively different transport and localization behavior. Advances in ultracold atomic and molecular physics, as well as in solid-state implementations such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, have enabled the realization of controllable dipolar lattices with high tunability of interaction strength, geometry, and dimensionality. Recent developments also allow for the controlled introduction of disorder into such systems, whether through random positioning of lattice sites, optical speckle potentials, or engineered defects. These capabilities open the door to systematic studies of localization phenomena in regimes inaccessible to traditional condensed matter systems.

A particularly intriguing phenomenon in disordered interacting systems is the emergence of *pair localization*. When two particles interact attractively in a disordered potential, they may form bound states whose effective mass differs substantially from that of single particles. In some cases, these bound pairs can be more strongly localized than individual particles, as their composite nature leads to a reduced kinetic energy relative to the disorder scale. Alternatively, in certain parameter regimes, pairing can enhance mobility by effectively averaging over the disorder landscape. The competition between these tendencies depends sensitively on the interaction range, disorder strength, and the underlying lattice structure.

In dipolar systems, the situation is further enriched by the spatially extended character of the interactions. For polar molecules, Rydberg atoms, or magnetic dipoles, the interaction can be tuned via external fields, enabling the exploration of both attractive and repulsive regimes, as well as anisotropy in the interaction profile. Moreover, positional disorder—arising from random displacements of particles from an ideal lattice configuration—directly modulates both the on-site energies and the coupling strengths between sites. Unlike purely on-site (diagonal) disorder, positional disorder in dipolar systems inherently generates correlated off-diagonal disorder, since the interaction amplitudes depend sensitively on interparticle distances and orientations. This interdependence leads to novel localization physics not captured by standard Anderson models.

The goal of this work is to investigate the localization properties of bound pairs in dipolar lattices with *tunable positional disorder*. By systematically varying the disorder amplitude and interaction strength, we aim to map out the regimes in which pair localization is enhanced or suppressed relative to single-particle localization. We focus on one- and two-dimensional geometries, where localization effects are particularly pronounced, but where long-range couplings can qualitatively alter the scaling behavior. Our analysis combines numerical simulations of finite-size systems with analytical insights into the effective Hamiltonians governing bound pairs. The results shed light on how long-range interactions and correlated disorder conspire to shape the transport properties of composite excitations.

Beyond their fundamental significance, these findings bear relevance for experimental platforms seeking to harness dipolar interactions for quantum simulation and information processing. Controlled pair localization could serve as a mechanism for storing quantum excitations, protecting them from decoherence, or mediating entanglement over short distances. By clarifying the microscopic mechanisms governing pair dynamics in disordered dipolar systems, this work contributes to the broader effort to understand and control many-body localization phenomena in regimes where both disorder and interactions are strongly tunable.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the emergence and stability of pair localization in one-dimensional dipolar systems subject to tunable positional disorder. By systematically varying the degree of spatial randomness in the arrangement of dipolar sites, we have elucidated the interplay between long-range interactions and disorder-induced localization phenomena, with particular emphasis on the formation and robustness of bound pairs. Our analysis, combining numerical simulations with analytical considerations, demonstrates that positional disorder can induce a rich localization landscape, in which single-particle and two-particle states respond differently to the same perturbations.

A central finding is that pair localization is not merely a trivial extension of single-particle Anderson localization, but instead arises from a delicate balance between interaction-driven binding and disorder-induced scattering. In the absence of disorder, long-range dipolar couplings support extended two-body states whose spatial structure reflects the algebraic decay of the interaction. Introducing positional disorder disrupts these extended modes, leading to a crossover into a regime where pairs become spatially confined. Notably, the critical disorder strength for the onset of strong pair localization is significantly lower than that for individual particles, indicating that bound states are more susceptible to disorder due to their composite nature and enhanced effective mass.

We have also shown that the degree of tunability in positional disorder offers a powerful control knob for engineering localization properties. Weak disorder selectively localizes higher-energy pairs while leaving low-energy bound states relatively delocalized, enabling energy-dependent transport control. At stronger disorder, localization lengths collapse across the spectrum, and both pair and single-particle excitations become immobile. The observed scaling of localization length with disorder strength and dipolar interaction range suggests that long-range couplings slow down the localization process compared to short-range interacting systems, but do not prevent it.

Our findings have implications for a variety of experimental platforms, including ultracold polar molecules, Rydberg atom arrays, and solid-state spin systems, where dipolar interactions and controlled disorder can be realized with high precision. The sensitivity of pair localization to disorder strength and interaction range points toward possible applications in the design of disorder-assisted quantum devices, where transport of bound excitations can be selectively suppressed or enhanced. Furthermore, the interplay between disorder and interaction range may be exploited to explore many-body localization phenomena in regimes inaccessible to short-range models.

Future work could extend these results to higher dimensions, time-dependent disorder, and the presence of external driving fields, in order to assess the robustness of pair localization under more complex, experimentally relevant conditions. The present study thus establishes a framework for understanding and controlling bound-state localization in dipolar systems, bridging the gap between fundamental localization theory and practical quantum engineering.

title: Parameter efficient dendritic-tree neurons outperform perceptrons
abstract: We investigate the representational power and efficiency of dendritic-tree neuron models compared to standard perceptrons. By leveraging nonlinear subunit processing within a hierarchical dendritic structure, these neurons achieve superior accuracy on classification tasks while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent performance gains relative to parameter-matched perceptrons, highlighting the benefits of localized nonlinear integration. Our findings suggest that biologically inspired dendritic computation offers a promising avenue for building compact, high-performing neural networks with improved efficiency and scalability.
introduction: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet the basic computational unit—the perceptron—remains a highly simplified abstraction of biological neurons. In contrast, real neurons exhibit complex dendritic trees that perform rich, nonlinear computations, enabling efficient integration of synaptic inputs. Recent neurophysiological evidence suggests that dendritic subunits act as independent computational compartments, dramatically increasing a neuron’s representational capacity without a proportional increase in parameters. Motivated by these findings, researchers have begun exploring dendritic-inspired models to enhance efficiency and expressivity in artificial systems. However, the parameter–performance trade-offs between dendritic-tree neurons and conventional perceptrons remain underexplored in machine learning contexts. In this work, we introduce a parameter-efficient dendritic-tree neuron model and systematically compare its performance against standard perceptrons across benchmark tasks. Our results demonstrate that dendritic-tree neurons can achieve superior accuracy with fewer parameters, highlighting their potential as powerful, biologically inspired building blocks for next-generation neural network architectures.
conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient dendritic-tree neurons consistently outperform standard perceptrons across diverse tasks while using fewer trainable parameters. By leveraging dendritic substructures, these models capture complex nonlinear interactions more effectively than conventional architectures. This efficiency suggests promising avenues for scaling neural networks without proportional parameter growth. Future work should explore integrating dendritic-tree neurons into deep architectures and examining their biological plausibility, potentially bridging neuroscientific insights with practical advances in machine learning efficiency and capability.

title: Exact 4-point Scattering Amplitude of the Superconformal Schrodinger Chern-Simons Theory
abstract: We compute the exact 4-point scattering amplitude in the superconformal Schrödinger Chern-Simons theory, employing nonrelativistic conformal symmetry and supersymmetric constraints to fully determine its functional form. The analysis incorporates all-loop resummation of planar diagrams and exploits integrability-inspired techniques to fix dynamical factors. We find a compact expression consistent with unitarity, crossing, and the full Schrödinger superalgebra. Our result provides a benchmark for nonrelativistic holography and a precise test for conjectured dualities involving supersymmetric Chern-Simons-matter models in three dimensions.
introduction:
Nonrelativistic conformal field theories have attracted considerable interest in recent years, motivated both by condensed matter applications and by their role in the broader landscape of gauge/gravity dualities. Among these, theories with Schrödinger symmetry — the nonrelativistic analog of conformal invariance — provide a particularly rich arena in which to explore exact results. The Schrödinger algebra extends the Galilean group by including scale transformations and special conformal transformations that act anisotropically on space and time, with dynamical exponent \( z=2 \). Such symmetries are realized in certain critical points of many-body systems, such as cold atoms at unitarity, and in specific gauge theories in 2+1 dimensions.

Chern–Simons gauge theories coupled to matter fields constitute an especially tractable class of models in three dimensions, as the gauge sector is topological and often allows for exact computations. When the matter content and interactions are tuned to preserve nonrelativistic superconformal symmetry, the resulting theories combine the constraints of supersymmetry with those of the Schrödinger algebra. This structure can lead to nontrivial, exactly computable observables, offering a rare opportunity to study strongly coupled dynamics in a controlled setting. Furthermore, supersymmetric Chern–Simons–matter theories have played a central role in the study of the AdS/CFT correspondence and its nonrelativistic generalizations, where the bulk dual geometries exhibit Schrödinger isometries. 

A central observable in any quantum field theory is the scattering amplitude, which encodes the dynamical content of the theory and serves as a bridge between abstract symmetry principles and measurable quantities. In relativistic conformal field theories, the constraints of conformal invariance severely restrict the form of scattering processes, often ruling out nontrivial amplitudes in flat space. In contrast, nonrelativistic conformal symmetry permits a richer scattering structure, though still under significant kinematic and dynamical constraints. The four-point scattering amplitude is of particular interest: it is the simplest process that probes both the spectrum and the interaction structure beyond trivial two-body kinematics, and it is the building block for understanding higher-point processes.

In the superconformal Schrödinger Chern–Simons theory, the interplay between the topological gauge dynamics, matter interactions, and symmetry constraints makes the exact computation of scattering amplitudes both challenging and illuminating. Previous work on nonrelativistic Chern–Simons–matter systems has established the existence of exact two-body S-matrices, often controlled by anyonic phases arising from the gauge interaction. Exact results for four-point functions have been obtained in certain supersymmetric relativistic theories, but the nonrelativistic superconformal case has not been fully explored. The combination of gauge invariance, supersymmetry, and Schrödinger symmetry suggests that the four-point amplitude may be determined exactly, potentially revealing hidden structures analogous to those found in integrable models.

From a methodological standpoint, exact computation in such theories often exploits a combination of symmetry constraints, Ward identities, and the simplifications afforded by the Chern–Simons gauge sector. Nonrelativistic supersymmetry further refines the space of allowed interactions, sometimes enforcing non-renormalization theorems that protect certain quantities from quantum corrections. As a result, it is plausible that the full energy and momentum dependence of the four-point amplitude can be determined analytically, without resorting to perturbation theory beyond the leading order. Moreover, the topological nature of the gauge field implies that scattering is dominated by statistical phases and contact interactions, simplifying the dynamical analysis.

The aim of this work is to compute the exact four-point scattering amplitude in the \( \mathcal{N} \)-extended superconformal Schrödinger Chern–Simons theory in 2+1 dimensions. We will derive the amplitude by combining the constraints of the super-Schrödinger symmetry algebra with explicit evaluation of the relevant Feynman diagrams, showing that the result is protected from higher-loop corrections. We will demonstrate that the amplitude factorizes into a universal anyonic phase, determined solely by the Chern–Simons level and the representation of the matter fields, and a rational function of the kinematic invariants fixed by symmetry. This exact result provides a rare example of a nontrivial, fully determined scattering amplitude in a nonrelativistic quantum field theory with both gauge and supersymmetry.

Beyond its intrinsic theoretical interest, the exact amplitude we obtain has potential applications in the study of nonrelativistic holography, where it may serve as a test of proposed gravity duals with Schrödinger asymptotics. It also offers insight into the dynamics of anyonic excitations in supersymmetric settings, with possible relevance to planar condensed matter systems. More broadly, our result exemplifies how the confluence of topology, symmetry, and supersymmetry can lead to exact solvability in a strongly coupled quantum field theory. In the following sections, we present the structure of the superconformal Schrödinger Chern–Simons theory, outline the symmetry constraints on scattering, and carry out the exact computation of the four-point amplitude.
conclusion: In this work we have presented the exact computation of the 4-point scattering amplitude in the superconformal Schrödinger Chern-Simons theory. Employing a combination of nonrelativistic supersymmetric Ward identities, unitarity constraints, and the analytic structure dictated by conformal symmetry, we have derived a closed-form expression valid for arbitrary values of the Chern-Simons level and matter content consistent with \(\mathcal{N}=2\) super-Schrödinger invariance. The amplitude exhibits the expected factorization properties and matches known perturbative results in the weak coupling expansion, while also capturing nonperturbative effects inherent to the topological gauge sector. Our analysis reveals that the interplay between gauge interactions and nonrelativistic kinematics leads to a remarkably simple functional dependence on the kinematic invariants, reflecting the underlying integrable structure of the theory. Furthermore, the exact result provides a testing ground for conjectured dualities between distinct superconformal Schrödinger theories, as it offers a precise observable on which such correspondences can be checked. The methods developed here are readily generalizable to higher-point functions and to theories with extended supersymmetry or different matter representations. Future work could explore the holographic interpretation of our result, particularly its implications for nonrelativistic AdS/CFT correspondence, as well as potential applications to condensed matter systems with emergent Schrödinger symmetry. Our findings thus not only complete the exact characterization of the simplest nontrivial scattering process in this theory, but also open new avenues for probing its rich mathematical and physical structure.

title: Optimal wavy surface to suppress vortex shedding using second-order sensitivity to shape changes
abstract: The suppression of vortex shedding in bluff body flows is a critical objective in reducing unsteady aerodynamic forces and flow-induced vibrations. This study investigates the optimal design of a wavy surface to attenuate vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder, employing a second-order sensitivity framework with respect to surface shape modifications. While first-order sensitivity analysis provides the leading-order effect of infinitesimal shape changes, it vanishes for base flows symmetric to the shedding mode, making it insufficient for predicting optimal configurations in this context. We therefore derive and implement an adjoint-based second-order sensitivity formulation, enabling the direct evaluation of the quadratic variation of the shedding growth rate with respect to surface perturbations. The wavy surface is parameterized by a spanwise sinusoidal modulation of the cylinder radius, and the optimal amplitude and wavelength are determined to minimize the linear instability growth rate. Direct numerical simulations confirm that the predicted optimal geometry achieves a substantial reduction in vortex shedding intensity and Strouhal number shift, with results consistent across a range of Reynolds numbers in the subcritical regime. The analysis reveals that the suppression mechanism arises from the spanwise modulation of the separating shear layers, which disrupts the coherence of Kármán vortices and promotes three-dimensional energy redistribution. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of second-order sensitivity analysis in cases where first-order effects vanish, and provides a systematic framework for passive flow control through targeted three-dimensional surface shaping. The methodology is applicable to a broad class of bluff bodies and can inform the design of drag- and noise-reducing structures.
introduction:
Vortex shedding is a fundamental unsteady flow phenomenon that occurs when a bluff body is immersed in a fluid stream, leading to the periodic formation and release of vortices in the wake. This process is commonly associated with the generation of fluctuating forces, increased drag, and structural vibrations, which can have detrimental effects on the performance, stability, and longevity of engineering systems. Examples range from flow-induced vibrations in offshore structures, bridges, and chimneys to tonal noise from wind turbine blades and heat exchanger tubes. Consequently, the suppression of vortex shedding has been a subject of sustained interest in fluid mechanics and engineering design, motivating the development of a wide range of passive and active control strategies.

Among the various control approaches, passive control via surface geometry modification offers an appealing compromise between effectiveness, robustness, and simplicity. By altering the shape of the body or its surface features, the near-wake dynamics can be modified to disrupt the coherent formation of vortices. Wavy surfaces, in particular, have attracted attention as a means of introducing spanwise variations in the shedding process, thereby weakening the spatial coherence of the wake. Such surfaces can be implemented as three-dimensional variations in the geometry along the span, for example in the form of sinusoidal waviness on a nominally cylindrical body. Previous studies have shown that appropriately designed wavy geometries can reduce vortex-induced vibrations and unsteady loading, although the optimal design parameters depend sensitively on the flow regime and the specific performance objectives.

The design of optimal wavy surfaces for vortex suppression is inherently a problem of shape optimization in fluid flows, which is complicated by the inherently nonlinear dependence of the flow field on geometric modifications. A straightforward approach based on trial-and-error or exhaustive parameter sweeps is computationally burdensome and rarely offers insight into the physical mechanisms underlying performance improvements. Adjoint-based sensitivity analysis provides a more efficient framework for shape optimization by enabling the computation of gradients of an objective function with respect to shape changes at a cost essentially independent of the number of design parameters. This methodology has been successfully applied to a variety of inverse design and flow control problems, particularly in aerodynamics and hydrodynamics.

However, when the base flow is linearly stable with respect to the perturbations of interest, first-order sensitivity to shape modifications may vanish, rendering conventional linear sensitivity analysis ineffective. In such cases, the leading effect of shape changes appears at second order, necessitating the use of second-order sensitivity analysis. This higher-order approach captures the quadratic dependence of the objective on infinitesimal geometry changes, allowing for the prediction of how subtle shape variations influence quantities such as growth rates of unstable modes, mean drag, or energy amplification. Recent methodological advances have extended the adjoint framework to compute second-order sensitivities efficiently, enabling the systematic design of passive control features that act through higher-order effects.

In the context of vortex shedding suppression, the global linear instability of the wake behind a bluff body is often the primary target for control. By modifying the surface in a way that alters the eigenvalues associated with the unstable modes, one can delay or entirely suppress the onset of periodic vortex shedding. For flows past nominally two-dimensional bluff bodies, introducing three-dimensional geometric variations—such as spanwise waviness—can couple modes of different spanwise wavenumbers and redistribute energy in the instability spectrum. The challenge lies in determining the optimal amplitude, wavelength, and phase of such variations to achieve maximum suppression with minimal penalty to other performance metrics.

The present work addresses this challenge by applying second-order sensitivity analysis to the problem of designing an optimal wavy surface for a canonical bluff body. Using a steady base flow as the reference state, we evaluate the second-order sensitivity of the unstable eigenvalues to infinitesimal shape changes parameterized along the body surface. This information is then used to construct an optimality condition that directly yields the wavy geometry most effective at reducing the growth rate of the primary shedding mode. The approach avoids the need for repeated direct numerical simulations for each candidate geometry, drastically reducing computational cost while providing physical insight into the mechanisms by which spanwise waviness influences the global instability.

By formulating the problem in this way, we bridge the gap between empirical observations of the benefits of wavy surfaces and a rigorous, optimization-based design methodology. Our results not only identify the specific geometric patterns that maximize suppression efficiency but also elucidate the role of mode coupling and three-dimensionality in stabilizing the wake. The methodology presented here is general and can be extended to other configurations and objectives, including drag reduction, noise mitigation, and enhancement of mixing. Moreover, it provides a foundation for integrating higher-order sensitivity-based design into practical engineering workflows, enabling the rapid development of passive control solutions tailored to specific applications.
conclusion: This study has examined the use of second-order sensitivity analysis to design an optimal wavy surface capable of suppressing vortex shedding. By systematically accounting for the influence of small-amplitude shape modifications on the global stability properties of the flow, we identified surface geometries that achieve a significant attenuation of the primary instability without requiring large deformations. The results demonstrate that the optimal waviness introduces spanwise modulations in the base flow that effectively disrupt the coherent formation of vortices, leading to a substantial reduction in growth rates. Comparisons with first-order approaches highlight that second-order effects are essential to capture the stabilizing mechanisms at play, particularly when the first-order sensitivity vanishes. This methodology provides a predictive and computationally efficient framework for passive flow control through targeted shape design. The approach is general and can be extended to other bluff body configurations and flow regimes, offering a robust tool for the development of energy-efficient, stability-optimized engineering surfaces.

title: The Cerenkov effect revisited: from swimming ducks to zero modes in gravitational analogs
abstract: We revisit the Cerenkov effect through a unifying perspective that spans classical and emergent analog systems, from wave patterns generated by swimming ducks to zero-mode excitations in gravitational analog spacetimes. By examining dispersive wave propagation in media with varying effective metrics, we highlight the role of phase–group velocity mismatch in generating radiation-like signatures. Using both hydrodynamic and condensed-matter analogs, we identify universal features of Cerenkov-type emission and connect them to horizon and ergoregion physics. Our analysis provides a framework for exploring radiation phenomena across disciplines, revealing deep correspondences between everyday fluid disturbances and exotic relativistic field configurations.
introduction: The Cerenkov effect, classically observed as the emission of light by charged particles exceeding the phase velocity of light in a medium, has long served as a paradigm for radiation from superluminal disturbances. Its manifestations extend far beyond high-energy physics, inspiring analogies in fluid dynamics, condensed matter, and astrophysical contexts. Recent studies have revealed strikingly similar phenomena in systems as disparate as swimming ducks generating V-shaped wakes on water surfaces, and quasiparticles in media with effective spacetime geometries. Such analog models provide fertile ground for exploring exotic regimes, including the emergence of zero modes in gravitational analogs, where horizons or effective metrics alter wave propagation.
