Revisiting the Cerenkov effect through this interdisciplinary lens not only unifies disparate observations under a common theoretical framework but also opens avenues for probing fundamental processes in controlled laboratory settings. This work aims to synthesize these perspectives, highlighting connections and uncovering novel implications for wave–medium interactions.
conclusion:
In revisiting the Cerenkov effect through the lens of both classical fluid analogies and emergent spacetime phenomena, we have sought to bridge a conceptual gap between familiar macroscopic manifestations and their more exotic counterparts in gravitational analog systems. Beginning with the intuitive imagery of swimming ducks generating surface waves when exceeding the phase velocity in water, we have traced the underlying kinematic condition for radiation emission—the matching of the source velocity with the phase velocity of excitations in the medium—across widely differing physical contexts. This approach underscores the unifying role of dispersion relations and medium-specific refractive properties in governing the onset and characteristics of Cerenkov-like processes.

By extending this framework to gravitational analogs, where effective metrics arise in condensed matter or optical systems, we have shown that the same emission criterion can give rise to phenomena such as zero modes and horizon-induced radiation. The analogy is not merely pedagogical: it offers predictive power in identifying regimes where dissipationless emission or mode amplification may occur, even in the absence of a traditional electromagnetic field. The emergence of zero modes, in particular, highlights a deep correspondence between kinematic thresholds for radiation and the topology of the effective spacetime experienced by excitations.

Our analysis suggests that the Cerenkov effect should be regarded less as a peculiarity of charged particles in dielectrics and more as a universal kinematic phenomenon manifesting wherever sources outrun the relevant signal speed in a structured medium. This perspective opens avenues for experimental exploration in laboratory analogs of curved spacetime, where parameters can be tuned to probe thresholds, dispersion, and nonlinear backreaction in regimes inaccessible to astrophysical observation. Ultimately, the reexamination from swimming ducks to gravitational zero modes reveals the Cerenkov condition as a versatile and unifying principle, linking everyday hydrodynamics with the frontiers of analogue gravity and quantum field theory in curved spacetime.

title: A Two-Phase Quasi-Newton Method for Optimization Problem
abstract: This paper presents a two-phase quasi-Newton method for solving unconstrained optimization problems. The first phase generates an improved search direction using modified Hessian approximations, while the second phase refines convergence through adaptive step adjustments. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves faster convergence and higher accuracy compared to standard quasi-Newton approaches across a range of benchmark problems.
introduction: Optimization plays a fundamental role in science and engineering, where efficient algorithms are essential for solving large-scale problems. Quasi-Newton methods are widely used due to their balance between computational efficiency and convergence speed. However, traditional approaches may suffer from slow convergence in early iterations or instability near the solution. This paper presents a two-phase quasi-Newton method that combines rapid initial progress with robust local refinement. The proposed approach aims to improve both convergence rate and numerical stability, making it suitable for a wide range of unconstrained optimization problems.
conclusion: The proposed two-phase quasi-Newton method demonstrates improved convergence and computational efficiency for a range of optimization problems. Numerical experiments confirm its robustness and accuracy compared to standard approaches. Future work will explore adaptive strategies and extensions to large-scale, constrained problems, further enhancing its applicability in complex real-world optimization scenarios across diverse scientific and engineering domains.

title: Evolution of nonclassicality of the quasi-Bell states for a strongly coupled qubit-oscillator system
abstract: We investigate the evolution of nonclassical properties of quasi-Bell states in a strongly coupled qubit–oscillator system. Employing the adiabatic approximation, we analyze the dynamics of quasi-probability distributions in phase space, including the Wigner, Husimi \(Q\), and Glauber–Sudarshan \(P\) functions. The study reveals how strong coupling and detuning influence the persistence and decay of nonclassical features such as negativity in the Wigner function. We further quantify nonclassicality through measures based on phase-space volume and entropic characteristics of the Husimi function. Our results provide insight into coherence preservation and quantum-to-classical transition mechanisms in hybrid quantum systems under strong interaction regimes.
introduction:
The study of hybrid quantum systems comprising discrete and continuous variables has attracted considerable attention in recent years, driven both by fundamental questions in quantum theory and by the prospects for novel quantum technologies. Among such systems, the coupling of a two-level system (qubit) to a harmonic oscillator provides a paradigmatic model, encompassing a wide range of physical implementations from cavity and circuit quantum electrodynamics to trapped ions and nanomechanical resonators. In particular, the regime of strong and ultrastrong coupling, wherein the interaction strength becomes comparable to or exceeds the characteristic frequencies of the subsystems, has emerged as a fertile ground for exploring nonperturbative dynamics, nonclassical state generation, and the breakdown of the rotating-wave approximation.

An important class of initial states in this context is provided by quasi-Bell states, which are coherent superpositions of product states involving the qubit and coherent states of the oscillator. These states exhibit quantum correlations and interference effects that are sensitive to the details of the system dynamics, rendering them useful probes of decoherence, entanglement evolution, and the emergence of classicality. The nonclassicality of such states can be characterized in multiple, complementary ways, including negativities of the Wigner function, sub-Poissonian photon statistics, and violations of classical inequalities. Tracking the time evolution of these indicators offers insight into the interplay between coherent dynamics and environmental influences, as well as into the redistribution of quantum correlations between subsystems.

In the strong coupling regime, the evolution of quasi-Bell states is markedly different from that predicted by simplified models. Counter-rotating terms and higher-order processes contribute significantly, leading to complex phase-space structures, collapse and revival phenomena, and persistent oscillations in nonclassicality measures. Understanding these features is not only of theoretical interest but also relevant for experimental platforms where such coupling strengths are routinely achieved. Moreover, the ability to control and sustain nonclassical states under strong coupling has implications for quantum information processing, precision measurements, and the simulation of complex quantum systems.

In this work, we investigate the dynamics of nonclassicality for quasi-Bell states in a strongly coupled qubit–oscillator system, employing phase-space methods to quantify and visualize the evolution. By systematically analyzing the role of coupling strength and initial parameters, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms governing the persistence or degradation of nonclassical features, thereby contributing to the broader understanding of hybrid quantum systems in the nonperturbative regime.
conclusion: In summary, we have analyzed the evolution of nonclassicality in quasi-Bell states for a strongly coupled qubit–oscillator system, focusing on the interplay between coupling strength and dynamical features of the state. By employing phase-space quasiprobability distributions, we identified clear signatures of nonclassical behavior, including negativities and interference patterns, whose persistence or decay is governed by the system parameters. Our results show that strong coupling can both enhance and sustain nonclassical correlations over extended timescales, while also inducing complex revival–collapse structures in the state’s evolution. These findings provide deeper insight into the dynamical generation and control of nonclassical states in hybrid quantum systems, with potential implications for quantum information processing and quantum control protocols. Future work may explore the impact of decoherence and engineered environments on the robustness of such nonclassical features.

title: How and When to Flatten Java Classes?
abstract: Flattening Java classes, the process of merging inherited fields and methods into a single, self-contained representation, is an important technique in software engineering for analysis, refactoring, and optimization. This paper examines the conceptual foundations, practical motivations, and appropriate contexts for flattening class hierarchies. We discuss how flattening impacts code maintainability, readability, performance, and tool support, with attention to object-oriented design principles and trade-offs between abstraction and explicitness. Guidelines are proposed for determining when flattening is beneficial, supported by empirical examples and case studies. The study aims to assist developers, researchers, and tool builders in making informed decisions about class flattening strategies.
introduction:
In object-oriented software development, the design of class hierarchies plays a pivotal role in determining the maintainability, extensibility, and comprehensibility of a system. Java, as one of the most widely adopted object-oriented programming languages, encourages developers to use inheritance and composition to model complex domains. While inheritance offers mechanisms for code reuse and polymorphism, overly deep or convoluted class hierarchies can lead to rigidity, increased coupling, and difficulties in understanding and modifying the codebase. In certain circumstances, it becomes advantageous to simplify such hierarchies by reducing the levels of inheritance, a process often referred to as “flattening” classes. Flattening involves merging inherited members into a single class, thereby eliminating intermediate superclasses and potentially decreasing structural complexity.

The decision to flatten a Java class is not trivial, as it directly impacts software quality attributes such as cohesion, coupling, and encapsulation. On one hand, flattening can improve readability by consolidating relevant functionality into a single, self-contained unit, making it easier for developers to trace behavior without navigating multiple layers of abstraction. On the other hand, it can also result in code duplication, loss of polymorphic flexibility, and a diminished capacity to reuse components in other contexts. Therefore, determining both how and when to flatten a class requires a nuanced understanding of the system’s design goals, evolution history, and anticipated maintenance needs.

Software engineering literature has long addressed the trade-offs inherent in inheritance-based designs. Metrics such as depth of inheritance tree (DIT) and number of children (NOC) have been used to assess complexity and guide refactoring decisions. However, empirical evidence on the practical thresholds for these metrics remains inconclusive, and the decision to restructure a hierarchy often relies on expert judgment. Flattening is one among several refactoring techniques—alongside extraction, inlining, and encapsulation—that can be employed to address design smells such as “refused bequest,” “lazy class,” or “god class.” It is particularly relevant in legacy systems where the original rationale for deep hierarchies may no longer be valid, or where evolving requirements have rendered parts of the hierarchy redundant.

In Java development practice, flattening can be achieved through automated refactoring tools integrated into modern integrated development environments (IDEs), as well as through manual restructuring. Automated approaches can ensure syntactic correctness and help preserve behavior, but they may overlook subtle semantic implications, such as changes in method overriding or interface contracts. Consequently, developers must carefully assess preconditions, dependencies, and potential side effects before initiating such transformations. Moreover, timing is crucial: flattening too early in the development lifecycle may preempt beneficial reuse opportunities, whereas postponing it too long may allow architectural debt to accumulate, thereby increasing the cost and risk of later modifications.

This paper seeks to explore both the methodological aspects of flattening Java classes and the contextual factors that influence when it should be applied. We aim to synthesize insights from existing design principles, empirical studies, and practical case analyses to offer a coherent framework for decision-making. By clarifying the benefits, risks, and implementation strategies of class flattening, we intend to provide Java developers, software architects, and maintainers with evidence-based guidance for managing inheritance hierarchies. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the broader discourse on sustainable software design by elucidating a practice that, while sometimes overlooked, can be instrumental in improving the long-term health and adaptability of Java systems.
conclusion: Flattening Java classes is a refactoring strategy that can improve code comprehensibility, reduce unnecessary inheritance, and simplify maintenance when applied judiciously. This paper has examined the conditions under which flattening is beneficial, such as when hierarchies are shallow yet fragmented, or when subclass responsibilities are minimal and cohesion is low. It has also highlighted scenarios where flattening may introduce redundancy, reduce flexibility, or hinder extensibility, underscoring the importance of rigorous analysis before restructuring. Effective flattening requires careful assessment of coupling, cohesion, and the intended evolution of the software system. By aligning refactoring decisions with project goals, development team skills, and software architecture constraints, practitioners can ensure that flattening supports long-term maintainability. Ultimately, flattening should be seen as one tool among many, to be applied with precision, context-awareness, and an understanding of its trade-offs.

title: Generalised Object Detection and Semantic Analysis: Casino Example using Matlab
abstract: This paper presents a generalised framework for object detection and semantic analysis, demonstrated through a casino-themed application implemented in MATLAB. The proposed approach integrates image preprocessing, feature extraction, and machine learning-based classification to detect and categorise objects such as playing cards, chips, and dice. A semantic analysis layer interprets detected elements within the context of casino gameplay, enabling higher-level understanding such as game state estimation and event recognition. The system employs adaptable algorithms to accommodate varying lighting conditions, occlusions, and object orientations, ensuring robustness across diverse scenarios. MATLAB’s image processing and computer vision toolboxes are utilised for rapid prototyping and evaluation. Experimental results on a curated dataset illustrate the framework’s accuracy, adaptability, and potential for deployment in surveillance, automated monitoring, and interactive entertainment systems. The methodology is extendable to other domains requiring real-time object detection coupled with contextual semantic interpretation.
introduction:
Object detection and semantic analysis have emerged as core components in the broader field of computer vision, enabling machines to identify, classify, and interpret objects within a visual scene. These capabilities underpin a wide range of applications, from autonomous navigation and industrial automation to surveillance and interactive entertainment. The generalisation of object detection methods, wherein algorithms can robustly recognise diverse object categories under varying conditions, remains a central research challenge. Traditional approaches often rely on domain-specific training, which can limit adaptability and scalability when confronted with novel environments or object types. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have significantly improved detection accuracy and semantic understanding, yet practical deployment demands careful consideration of computational efficiency, data availability, and context-specific requirements.

Casinos present a compelling domain for exploring these concepts due to their complex, dynamic, and visually rich environments. In such settings, object detection can be applied to identify gaming equipment, playing cards, chips, dealer actions, and player gestures, while semantic analysis can interpret higher-level activities such as game states, betting behaviour, or compliance with operational protocols. The high density of objects, frequent occlusions, and variation in lighting conditions pose additional challenges that make the casino context an ideal testbed for evaluating the robustness and generalisation capacity of detection algorithms. Moreover, the potential applications extend beyond security; automated monitoring can enhance fairness verification, operational analytics, and player experience.

MATLAB provides a versatile platform for implementing and testing object detection and semantic analysis frameworks, offering integrated toolboxes for image processing, machine learning, and deep learning. Its accessible environment facilitates rapid prototyping and performance evaluation, supporting both academic investigation and applied development. This work presents a generalised object detection and semantic analysis approach, illustrated through a casino-based example implemented in MATLAB. The aim is to demonstrate the adaptability of modern detection techniques to complex, real-world scenarios, and to highlight the methodological considerations necessary for achieving reliable performance across varying contexts.
conclusion:
The work presented has demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of implementing a generalised object detection and semantic analysis framework within the context of a casino environment using MATLAB. By employing robust image processing techniques, feature extraction methods, and machine learning-based classification, the system was able to identify and categorise a variety of objects relevant to casino operations, such as playing cards, chips, and table layouts. The integration of semantic analysis allowed for an additional interpretative layer, enabling the system not only to detect objects but also to infer contextual meaning, such as recognising winning hands or tracking chip movements over time.

The results highlight the adaptability of the proposed approach, which can be extended beyond the specific casino example to other domains requiring accurate object recognition and contextual interpretation. MATLAB’s comprehensive toolboxes and visualisation capabilities proved instrumental in rapid prototyping, algorithm refinement, and performance evaluation. Experimental validations indicated satisfactory detection accuracy and semantic reasoning under a range of lighting and occlusion conditions, although some performance degradation was observed in highly cluttered or low-contrast scenes.

Overall, the study underscores the potential of combining object detection with semantic analysis for enhanced situational awareness in visually rich environments. While the casino scenario provided a controlled and application-specific testbed, the generalised nature of the framework supports scalability and adaptation to diverse use cases, such as security surveillance, industrial inspection, and automated monitoring systems. Future work could focus on integrating deep learning models for improved feature generalisation, real-time processing capabilities, and multi-camera data fusion to overcome current limitations. Additionally, incorporating adaptive learning mechanisms would allow the system to update its knowledge base dynamically, further improving accuracy in evolving operational contexts. This research thus contributes a flexible and practical approach to intelligent visual recognition and interpretation, with significant implications for both academic study and real-world deployment.

title: Probing the Spacetime Around Supermassive Black Holes with Ejected Plasma Blobs
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of plasma blobs ejected near supermassive black holes to probe their surrounding spacetime geometry. Using relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations and ray-tracing, we model observable trajectories and emission signatures. Our results show that blob motion encodes strong-gravity effects, enabling constraints on black hole mass, spin, and deviations from the Kerr metric through high-resolution, time-resolved observations.
introduction:
Supermassive black holes (SMBHs), with masses ranging from millions to billions of solar masses, reside at the centers of most galaxies and play a fundamental role in galaxy evolution. The extreme gravitational fields in their vicinity provide an unparalleled laboratory for testing general relativity (GR) in the strong-field regime, far beyond the conditions accessible in the Solar System or with stellar-mass black holes. Probing the spacetime geometry near SMBHs is essential both for verifying the predictions of GR and for exploring possible deviations that may arise from alternative theories of gravity. However, direct observational access to the immediate vicinity of the event horizon remains challenging due to the extreme compactness and optical thickness of the surrounding accretion flows.

One promising avenue for investigating the strong gravity regime involves tracking the motion of discrete plasma condensations—often referred to as “blobs”—that are ejected from the innermost regions of the accretion flow or relativistic jets. Such ejecta can be produced by magnetic reconnection events, disk instabilities, or jet launching processes, and they serve as test particles whose dynamics are governed predominantly by the underlying spacetime geometry. High-resolution very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations, particularly with instruments such as the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and the Global mm-VLBI Array, are now capable of resolving structural changes near the gravitational radius on timescales comparable to the light-crossing time.

By carefully modeling the trajectories and apparent motions of ejected plasma blobs, it is possible to extract constraints on the black hole mass, spin, and quadrupole moment, as well as on the inclination and orientation of the system. These measurements can, in turn, be used to test the Kerr nature of astrophysical black holes and to search for signatures of non-GR effects. Moreover, the polarization and spectral evolution of such blobs carry information about the magnetic field configuration and particle acceleration processes in the vicinity of the event horizon.

In this work, we explore the feasibility of using high-precision astrometric and timing observations of plasma blobs ejected from the vicinity of SMBHs as probes of the surrounding spacetime. We present theoretical models for their motion, discuss observational strategies, and assess the potential for future facilities to enhance our understanding of strong-field gravity.
conclusion: Our analysis demonstrates that plasma blobs ejected from the vicinity of supermassive black holes offer a promising probe of the surrounding spacetime geometry. By tracking their trajectories and evolution, one can extract signatures of relativistic effects, including gravitational lensing, time dilation, and the influence of black hole spin. Numerical modeling indicates that deviations from purely ballistic motion carry imprints of the metric parameters, enabling constraints on mass, spin, and possible departures from the Kerr solution. High-resolution, multi-wavelength observations, particularly with very long baseline interferometry, will be crucial for disentangling plasma dynamics from gravitational signatures. Future coordinated campaigns targeting transient ejection events could therefore provide stringent tests of general relativity in the strong-field regime. This approach complements existing methods and expands the observational toolkit for exploring the physics of supermassive black holes.

title: Probing Vector Mesons in Deuteron Break-up Reactions
abstract: We investigate the production of light vector mesons in deuteron break-up reactions as a means to probe the short-range structure of the deuteron and the underlying dynamics of meson–nucleon interactions. Using a combination of theoretical modeling and phenomenological input, we analyze exclusive processes of the type \( \gamma d \rightarrow V p n \), where \(V\) denotes a vector meson (\(\rho\), \(\omega\), or \(\phi\)), with particular emphasis on kinematic regimes sensitive to high relative momenta between the outgoing nucleons. The framework incorporates relativistic kinematics, realistic deuteron wave functions, and production amplitudes constrained by existing meson–nucleon scattering and photoproduction data. By isolating configurations in which one nucleon acts as a spectator while the other participates in meson production, we examine final-state interaction effects and explore their role in shaping observables such as differential cross sections and polarization asymmetries. Special attention is given to the near-threshold region, where coherent and incoherent mechanisms may interfere, and to the sensitivity of the reaction to possible modifications of vector meson properties in the nuclear medium. Our results indicate that measurements of vector meson production in deuteron break-up at moderate to high momentum transfer can discriminate between competing descriptions of short-distance nucleon–nucleon dynamics and provide constraints on the meson–nucleon scattering amplitudes. We outline experimental conditions at existing and forthcoming photon and electron beam facilities that would allow for precise tests of our predictions. This study demonstrates that deuteron break-up reactions offer a versatile and sensitive probe of both the internal deuteron structure and the interactions of vector mesons with nuclear matter.
introduction:
The study of vector meson production in nuclear reactions provides a unique window into the strong interaction in the non-perturbative regime of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). Vector mesons, such as the ρ, ω, and φ, are bound states of a quark and an antiquark carrying spin-parity \( J^P = 1^- \). Their masses fall in a range where both hadronic and partonic degrees of freedom can play an important role, making them excellent probes of the transition region between these descriptions. In particular, the interaction of vector mesons with nucleons and nuclei is of fundamental interest for understanding the modification of hadron properties in a nuclear medium, the onset of color transparency, and the role of meson–nucleon final-state interactions.

Among the simplest and most informative nuclear systems for such studies is the deuteron, the bound state of a proton and a neutron. Its weak binding energy (\(\sim 2.2\) MeV) and well-known wave function make it an ideal effective neutron target and a testing ground for few-body reaction mechanisms. In reactions involving deuteron break-up, the final-state kinematics can be selected to emphasize quasi-free scattering from either nucleon, or to explore configurations in which both nucleons participate coherently. This flexibility allows one to disentangle competing reaction mechanisms and to probe short-range nucleon–nucleon correlations.

The production of vector mesons in deuteron break-up reactions, such as \( \gamma d \to V p n \) or \( p d \to V p p n \), offers several advantages. First, the photon- or hadron-induced production from a bound neutron can be accessed by detecting the spectator proton at low momentum, thereby approximating free neutron kinematics. Second, the detection of both outgoing nucleons in coincidence with the vector meson decay products enables full reconstruction of the final state, providing stringent constraints on theoretical models. Third, by varying the momentum transfer and the vector meson kinematics, one can investigate the onset of medium modifications, the role of re-scattering processes, and the space-time evolution of the produced meson.

From the theoretical perspective, vector meson production on the deuteron involves a rich interplay of mechanisms. The impulse approximation, in which the photon or projectile interacts with a single nucleon while the other nucleon acts as a spectator, provides the baseline description. However, for certain kinematic regimes, particularly near threshold or at large momentum transfer, additional processes become significant. These include meson–nucleon final-state interactions, nucleon–nucleon re-scattering, and contributions from meson exchange currents. The relative importance of these mechanisms depends sensitively on the binding and momentum distribution of the nucleons in the deuteron, as well as on the properties of the produced vector meson.

Experimentally, the study of vector meson production in deuteron break-up reactions has benefited from advances in photon and hadron beam facilities, high-resolution spectrometers, and large-acceptance detectors. Measurements at Jefferson Lab, ELSA, COSY, and other laboratories have provided data on cross sections, angular distributions, and polarization observables for \(\rho\), \(\omega\), and \(\phi\) production on the proton and neutron. In the deuteron case, tagging the spectator nucleon and performing kinematically complete measurements have allowed for the isolation of quasi-free production channels and the examination of re-scattering effects. These experimental capabilities open the door to systematic studies of the vector meson–nucleon interaction and the modification of meson properties in the nuclear environment.

One of the enduring questions in this field is the extent to which vector meson spectral functions are altered in nuclear matter. Models based on QCD sum rules and hadronic many-body theory predict mass shifts and broadening of vector mesons due to their coupling to nucleon–hole and resonance–hole excitations in the medium. Deuteron break-up reactions, while involving only two nucleons, can still provide insight into these effects by enabling precise control over the nuclear environment and by serving as a benchmark for heavier nuclei. Moreover, the small size of the deuteron reduces the complexity of many-body effects, allowing for more direct comparisons between theory and experiment.

In this work, we investigate vector meson production in deuteron break-up reactions with the aim of elucidating the underlying reaction mechanisms and extracting information on the vector meson–nucleon interaction. By combining theoretical modeling with available experimental data, and by proposing new measurements in carefully chosen kinematic regimes, we seek to advance the understanding of how vector mesons propagate and interact in few-body nuclear systems. The results obtained in the deuteron provide essential input for extending such studies to more complex nuclei, thereby contributing to the broader effort of mapping the behavior of hadrons in the nuclear medium.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the role of vector meson production in deuteron break-up reactions as a means of probing the short-range structure of the deuteron and the underlying dynamics of nucleon–nucleon interactions. By focusing on kinematic regions where final-state interactions and meson–nucleon rescattering effects are enhanced, we have demonstrated that such processes provide a sensitive testing ground for models of hadronic structure and reaction mechanisms. The analysis underscores the utility of vector mesons as selective probes: their coupling to nucleons and sensitivity to off-shell effects enable the disentanglement of competing contributions in the reaction amplitude, including those from isobar configurations and hidden-color components.

Our results indicate that measurements of differential cross sections and polarization observables in carefully chosen kinematic regimes can discriminate between competing theoretical descriptions, particularly those incorporating explicit meson-exchange currents versus quark–gluon degrees of freedom. The study also highlights the importance of incorporating realistic deuteron wave functions and consistent treatment of meson–nucleon scattering amplitudes in theoretical calculations.

Future experimental programs at facilities capable of high-luminosity photon and electron beams will be crucial to extend these investigations. In particular, coincidence measurements with full reconstruction of the final state can significantly reduce ambiguities associated with background processes. The combination of refined theoretical treatments and precise data will allow a deeper exploration of short-distance nucleon correlations and the onset of non-nucleonic degrees of freedom in nuclei.

In summary, vector meson production in deuteron break-up reactions emerges as a powerful tool for advancing our understanding of nuclear dynamics at the interface of hadronic and quark–gluon descriptions. The insights gained from such studies contribute not only to nuclear physics but also to the broader effort of mapping the transition from hadronic to partonic matter in quantum chromodynamics.

title: Bayes' theorem and early solar short-lived radionuclides: the case for an unexceptional origin for the solar system
abstract: We apply Bayes’ theorem to evaluate competing hypotheses for the origin of short-lived radionuclides (SLRs) in the early solar system, focusing on whether their abundances require an exceptional astrophysical event. Using updated meteoritic constraints and astrophysical priors, we compare models involving nearby supernova injection, stellar winds, and galactic chemical evolution. Our analysis shows that, under reasonable prior assumptions, the observed SLR inventory is consistent with typical star-forming environments. This supports an unexceptional origin for the solar system, with no need for rare or fine-tuned enrichment scenarios.
introduction:
The origin of short-lived radionuclides (SLRs) in the early solar system remains a central question in cosmochemistry and astrophysics. These isotopes, with half-lives of less than a few million years, are recorded in primitive meteoritic components such as calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions (CAIs) and chondrules, and provide chronometric constraints on events in the protoplanetary disk as well as clues to the astrophysical environment of solar system formation. The abundances of SLRs such as ^26Al, ^60Fe, ^41Ca, and ^36Cl in early solar system solids have often been interpreted as evidence for a nearby, unusual, or even singular stellar event—such as injection from a core-collapse supernova or a massive star’s winds—occurring shortly before or during the collapse of the solar nebula. This interpretation has motivated extensive modelling of triggered star formation and specific stellar encounters.

However, astrophysical surveys and models of Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) indicate that many SLRs are produced continuously over time by a variety of nucleosynthetic sources, and their abundances in star-forming regions can reflect steady-state processes rather than singular events. In this context, the apparent “anomalies” in early solar system SLR abundances may be reconcilable with an origin in typical molecular cloud environments, without invoking rare or highly specific conditions. The challenge lies in quantitatively evaluating the plausibility of different scenarios given the diverse observational and theoretical constraints.

Bayes’ theorem provides a rigorous statistical framework for such evaluations, allowing prior knowledge—in this case, the astrophysical frequency of different enrichment scenarios—to be combined with the likelihood of reproducing the measured isotopic abundances. This approach enables moving beyond qualitative arguments about rarity or typicality, toward explicit probabilistic assessments of competing hypotheses. In particular, Bayesian inference can formalise the question: given the measured SLR inventory of the early solar system, how strongly should we update our belief in an unusual nearby injection event versus an origin in a standard star-forming environment?

Here we apply a Bayesian framework to the case of early solar system SLRs, focusing on ^26Al and ^60Fe as key diagnostics of stellar nucleosynthesis and delivery. We combine data from meteoritic analyses, GCE models, and star formation statistics to estimate the posterior probabilities of distinct enrichment scenarios. Our results suggest that the early solar system’s SLR abundances are consistent with expectations for a typical molecular cloud, without requiring exceptional astrophysical circumstances. This outcome has important implications for understanding the Sun’s birth environment and for interpreting isotopic signatures in extrasolar planetary systems.
conclusion:
The application of Bayes’ theorem to the problem of early solar system short-lived radionuclides (SLRs) provides a quantitative framework for evaluating competing hypotheses for their origin. By explicitly incorporating prior knowledge about star formation environments and the statistical likelihood of enrichment processes, this approach allows us to reassess long-standing interpretations that invoke unusual or singular events to explain the solar system’s inventory of isotopes such as ^26Al, ^60Fe, and others. Our analysis shows that when realistic astrophysical priors are adopted—derived from observations of star-forming regions, stellar yields, and dynamical mixing—the probability that the early solar system’s SLR abundances arose from typical star-forming processes is high. Conversely, the posterior probabilities for scenarios requiring rare or fine-tuned events, such as a narrowly timed nearby supernova injection, are substantially lower unless one adopts strongly biased priors.

This finding carries significant implications for our understanding of the Sun’s birth environment. The presence of SLRs has often been taken as evidence that the solar system formed in an exceptional context, for example in immediate proximity to a massive star undergoing core collapse. However, the Bayesian framework underscores that similar SLR levels can be generated through more common mechanisms, including inheritance from the average interstellar medium enriched by multiple generations of stellar activity, supplemented by contributions from stellar winds in a clustered environment. The posterior estimates indicate that such scenarios are not only plausible but likely, given the observed distribution of abundances in young stellar objects and molecular clouds.

An important outcome of this work is the clarification of how interpretative biases can arise from neglecting the role of priors. If one implicitly assumes that the SLRs must be explained by a specific, singular astrophysical event, the likelihood analysis alone may appear to support that hypothesis. But when the full Bayesian treatment is applied, the weight of prior plausibility strongly moderates such conclusions. This aligns with a growing body of observational evidence that the physical and chemical conditions of the early solar system were broadly similar to those seen in typical star-forming regions in the Galaxy today.

The Bayesian perspective also integrates naturally with advances in astrophysical modelling. Simulations of giant molecular cloud evolution, stellar feedback, and isotope transport show that SLR enrichment is an ongoing, stochastic process across many parsecs and over millions of years. The solar system’s initial SLR levels fall within the envelope of variation produced in these models without invoking extreme coincidences. This further supports the conclusion that our planetary system did not require an extraordinary trigger for its isotopic inventory.

Beyond the specific case of SLRs, this study illustrates the value of a probabilistic approach to cosmochemical problems. Many debates in planetary science hinge on weighing multiple lines of evidence with varying degrees of uncertainty. Bayes’ theorem offers a formal mechanism for combining these, clarifying which conclusions are robust to changes in assumptions and which depend critically on particular choices of prior. In the present case, it has shifted the balance of evidence toward a more ordinary origin for the solar system, embedded in a moderately massive stellar cluster with ongoing enrichment from the surrounding stellar population.

Recognizing that the solar system is unlikely to have formed under exceptional conditions has broader consequences for comparative planetology and the search for habitable worlds. If the isotopic and chemical conditions that prevailed in our protoplanetary disk are commonplace, then the processes leading to the formation of rocky planets with volatile inventories similar to Earth’s may also be widespread. This perspective reduces the need to invoke rare astrophysical circumstances to explain our own existence and encourages the use of the solar system as a representative case study for planetary system evolution.

In summary, applying Bayes’ theorem to the origin of early solar system SLRs leads to a coherent and quantitatively supported conclusion: the most probable explanation for their observed abundances is that they arose from typical enrichment processes operating in a common star-forming environment. This conclusion reconciles cosmochemical data with astrophysical context, avoids reliance on low-probability events, and situates the solar system firmly within the mainstream of Galactic star formation history. By reframing the problem in probabilistic terms, we gain not only a more parsimonious explanation for the data but also a more generalizable understanding of planetary system formation.

title: Scaling Multidimensional Inference for Structured Gaussian Processes
abstract: Structured Gaussian Processes (SGPs) provide a flexible probabilistic framework for modeling complex, multidimensional dependencies in spatiotemporal and other structured domains. However, exact inference in high-dimensional SGPs is computationally prohibitive due to the cubic scaling in the number of observations and the need to exploit intricate covariance structures. We present a scalable inference methodology that leverages multidimensional Kronecker and Toeplitz algebra, combined with stochastic variational inference, to significantly reduce both time and memory complexity. Our approach generalizes existing structure-exploiting techniques to handle arbitrary tensor-product kernels and partially observed grids, enabling efficient learning in settings with millions of observations. We introduce a novel factorized variational posterior that preserves key structural properties, allowing for fast matrix-vector multiplications and efficient marginal likelihood estimation. Empirical evaluations on large-scale spatiotemporal datasets, including climate modeling and video data, demonstrate that our method achieves predictive accuracy comparable to exact inference while reducing runtime by orders of magnitude. This work broadens the applicability of SGPs to previously intractable problem domains and provides a unifying framework for scaling multidimensional Gaussian process inference without sacrificing statistical fidelity.
introduction:
Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a powerful, nonparametric Bayesian framework for modeling complex functions and quantifying uncertainty in predictions. Their flexibility and principled treatment of uncertainty have led to widespread adoption in regression, classification, spatial statistics, and spatio-temporal modeling. However, the computational cost of exact GP inference scales cubically with the number of observations, rendering naïve implementations impractical for large datasets. This challenge is further exacerbated in multidimensional settings, where the complexity of the underlying covariance structure increases substantially.

Structured Gaussian processes—those exploiting Kronecker, Toeplitz, or other algebraic structures in the covariance matrix—offer an avenue for efficient computation, particularly when the input domain exhibits a separable structure across dimensions. Such structure enables fast matrix-vector multiplications, reduced memory footprints, and scalable inference via iterative methods. Yet, extending these benefits to high-dimensional inference tasks remains nontrivial. The curse of dimensionality, anisotropic correlations, and the need to integrate over latent functions in multiple dimensions introduce both theoretical and practical difficulties.

Existing approaches often rely on strong simplifying assumptions, such as independence across dimensions or strict separability of the kernel, which can compromise modeling fidelity. Others resort to inducing point approximations or sparse variational methods, which, while effective, may not fully exploit the latent algebraic structure inherent in the covariance. Consequently, there is a pressing need for scalable inference methods that retain the expressive power of full multidimensional GPs while leveraging structural properties for computational gains.

In this work, we develop a framework for scaling multidimensional inference in structured Gaussian processes that unifies efficient algebraic exploitation with flexible kernel design. By integrating structure-aware numerical linear algebra techniques with advanced variational inference schemes, our method achieves significant reductions in time and memory complexity without sacrificing predictive performance. We demonstrate the approach on diverse synthetic and real-world datasets, highlighting its capacity to address large-scale, high-dimensional GP modeling challenges.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the problem of scaling multidimensional inference for structured Gaussian processes (GPs), focusing on the interplay between model expressiveness, computational tractability, and numerical stability. Our approach was motivated by the increasing need to deploy GP-based models in high-dimensional settings where the structure of the underlying domain—whether spatial, temporal, or more abstract—can be exploited to achieve substantial computational gains without sacrificing the fidelity of the posterior representation.

We began by identifying the fundamental computational bottlenecks in multidimensional GP inference, particularly the cubic complexity of naive covariance matrix manipulations and the memory demands of storing large dense matrices. By leveraging structure in the covariance—such as Kronecker and Toeplitz forms induced by separable kernels—we demonstrated how inference can be reformulated to exploit efficient linear algebra routines that scale linearly or near-linearly with respect to each individual dimension. This structural exploitation was complemented by careful consideration of approximation error, ensuring that the gains in scalability did not come at the expense of predictive accuracy.

Our contributions extend beyond the adoption of existing structured algebra techniques. We introduced a generalized framework for combining multiple forms of structure in a single model, allowing multidimensional dependencies to be captured with greater flexibility than in purely separable approaches. By formulating inference in terms of tensor algebra, we were able to unify a range of existing scalable GP methods and identify new opportunities for hybridization. This perspective also facilitated the design of novel preconditioning strategies tailored to the structured setting, improving the convergence rates of iterative solvers for the linear systems arising in posterior computation.

Through extensive empirical evaluation, we have shown that our structured multidimensional inference approach achieves competitive or superior predictive performance compared to both exact but unstructured inference and traditional sparse approximations, across a range of synthetic and real-world datasets. In particular, our method maintained high accuracy even in regimes where the number of inducing points or basis functions required by other scalable methods would become prohibitive. Furthermore, the structured approach exhibited remarkable stability in high-dimensional domains, a property we attribute to the preservation of the exact covariance relationships along each dimension.

The experiments also underscored the benefits of our framework for tasks involving multidimensional signal reconstruction, spatio-temporal forecasting, and multivariate sensor fusion. In these settings, the ability to incorporate domain-specific structural priors directly into the kernel—while retaining tractable computation—proved especially advantageous. Our results suggest that many application domains that have previously relied on heavily simplified GP models due to computational constraints can now revisit more expressive formulations without incurring prohibitive costs.

While the proposed framework addresses many of the scaling challenges in multidimensional GP inference, several avenues remain for future exploration. One promising direction is the integration of our structured inference methods with deep kernel learning, enabling automatic discovery of both low-level features and high-level structural patterns from raw data. Another is the extension to non-Gaussian likelihoods via scalable variational inference or expectation propagation within the structured setting, which would broaden the applicability of our approach to classification, count modeling, and other non-regression problems. Additionally, investigating adaptive structure learning—where the model infers the most beneficial decomposition of the domain based on data—could further enhance both efficiency and predictive performance.

From a theoretical standpoint, there is scope to develop tighter bounds on the approximation error introduced by combining multiple types of structure, as well as to better understand the trade-offs between expressiveness and scalability in different regimes of data sparsity and dimensionality. Such analyses would not only strengthen the mathematical foundations of structured GP inference but also provide practical guidance for practitioners in selecting appropriate model configurations.

In summary, we have presented a scalable and flexible framework for multidimensional inference in structured Gaussian processes that unifies and extends existing structured algebra techniques, introduces new preconditioning strategies, and demonstrates strong empirical performance across diverse tasks. By explicitly exploiting the rich structure inherent in many multidimensional domains, our approach makes it feasible to deploy expressive GP models at scales previously considered impractical. We believe that the ideas and tools developed here will contribute to a broader adoption of Gaussian processes in complex, high-dimensional applications, and will inspire further research into the intersection of probabilistic modeling, numerical linear algebra, and high-performance computation.

title: Towards the Development of a Rule-based Drought Early Warning Expert Systems using Indigenous Knowledge
abstract: This study presents the conceptual design of a rule-based drought early warning expert system integrating indigenous knowledge with computational reasoning. Indigenous communities possess rich experiential insights into environmental indicators, such as plant phenology, animal behavior, and atmospheric patterns, which have historically guided drought prediction. The proposed system formalizes these indicators into a structured rule base, enabling systematic inference and timely alerts. By combining qualitative indigenous observations with rule-based logic, the approach seeks to enhance prediction accuracy in data-scarce regions. The framework emphasizes knowledge elicitation, rule formulation, and validation through community engagement. This integration aims to support proactive decision-making, strengthen climate resilience, and preserve valuable cultural heritage while complementing scientific drought monitoring techniques in vulnerable rural contexts.
introduction: Drought remains one of the most devastating natural hazards, adversely affecting livelihoods, ecosystems, and economies worldwide. In many rural communities, particularly in developing countries, access to modern meteorological data and forecasting tools is limited, making timely drought prediction and preparedness challenging. Indigenous knowledge, accumulated through generations of close interaction with the environment, offers valuable insights into local climatic patterns through indicators such as plant phenology, animal behavior, and celestial observations. Integrating this knowledge into systematic frameworks can enhance early warning capabilities, especially where scientific data is scarce. Rule-based expert systems, which use explicit if–then rules to model expert reasoning, provide a suitable approach for formalizing and operationalizing indigenous drought indicators. This study explores the development of a rule-based drought early warning expert system that leverages indigenous knowledge to improve forecasting accuracy, foster community participation, and support proactive drought management. By bridging traditional wisdom and computational reasoning, the system aims to strengthen climate resilience and food security.
conclusion:
This study has explored the potential of developing a rule-based drought early warning expert system that integrates indigenous knowledge with modern computational approaches. By systematically documenting and formalizing local indicators—such as animal behavior, plant phenology, and atmospheric signs—into a structured rule base, the proposed framework demonstrates that indigenous knowledge can be translated into a functional decision-support tool. This integration addresses the limitations of conventional meteorological systems in rural and resource-constrained settings, where access to scientific forecasting may be limited or delayed.  

The findings underscore that indigenous knowledge is not only contextually relevant but also temporally sensitive, reflecting generations of environmental observation and adaptation. Encoding this knowledge in a rule-based system preserves its cultural value while enhancing its applicability for contemporary risk management. Moreover, the approach fosters community participation and ownership, which are critical for the acceptance and sustainability of early warning systems.  

While the conceptual framework presented holds promise, the study also recognizes the need for further validation through longitudinal testing under diverse climatic conditions. Incorporating hybrid approaches that combine indigenous indicators with meteorological data could further strengthen predictive accuracy. Additionally, issues such as the dynamic nature of environmental cues and the potential erosion of traditional knowledge warrant ongoing documentation and refinement of the rule set.  

In conclusion, the research affirms that leveraging indigenous knowledge within a rule-based expert system offers a viable, culturally grounded, and cost-effective pathway for drought early warning, particularly in vulnerable communities. Advancing this work will require interdisciplinary collaboration, sustained community engagement, and iterative system improvement to ensure robust, reliable, and locally meaningful drought preparedness.

title: AiR -- An Augmented Reality Application for Visualizing Air Pollution
abstract: Air pollution is a critical environmental and public health concern, yet its largely invisible nature makes it difficult for individuals to perceive and understand its immediate impact. This paper presents **AiR**, an augmented reality (AR) application designed to visualize real-time air pollution data within the user’s physical environment. Leveraging geolocated air quality measurements from open data sources and low-cost sensors, AiR overlays dynamic, context-aware visualizations—such as particulate matter clouds, color-coded haze, and pollutant-specific markers—onto the live camera view of a mobile device. The system architecture integrates data acquisition, spatial mapping, and rendering pipelines to deliver accurate, location-specific representations of pollutant concentrations, while maintaining interactive frame rates. A user-centered design approach informed the choice of visual metaphors to balance scientific accuracy with intuitive comprehension. We conducted a mixed-method evaluation involving 42 participants in urban outdoor settings. Quantitative results indicate significant improvements in participants’ ability to identify high-pollution zones and recall pollutant types compared to a baseline 2D map interface. Qualitative feedback highlights increased environmental awareness and perceived engagement, though concerns about potential visual clutter suggest the need for adaptive visualization strategies. AiR demonstrates the potential of augmented reality to make abstract environmental data tangible, fostering informed decision-making and promoting public engagement with air quality issues. The findings contribute to ongoing research in environmental informatics, AR-based data visualization, and persuasive technology for sustainability, and point toward future integration with wearable AR devices for continuous, personalized exposure awareness.
introduction:
Air pollution is one of the most pressing environmental and public health challenges of the 21st century. According to the World Health Organization, exposure to polluted air is responsible for millions of premature deaths annually, with significant impacts on respiratory and cardiovascular health, cognitive functioning, and overall quality of life. Beyond its health consequences, air pollution also exacerbates climate change, damages ecosystems, and imposes substantial economic costs on societies worldwide. Despite widespread recognition of the problem, public awareness and understanding of air pollution remain uneven, often hindered by the invisibility of many pollutants and the abstract nature of air quality metrics. While air quality indices and monitoring networks provide valuable quantitative data, these representations are often difficult for lay audiences to interpret, limiting their capacity to translate data into meaningful behavioral or policy responses.

Recent advances in digital technologies have opened new possibilities for making environmental data more tangible and comprehensible. In particular, augmented reality (AR) offers a compelling medium for embedding environmental information directly into the user’s perception of the surrounding world. AR overlays computer-generated content onto the physical environment in real time, enabling users to see and interact with otherwise invisible phenomena. This capacity to situate abstract data within the lived environment has been shown to enhance engagement, comprehension, and retention of complex information. In the context of air pollution, AR could bridge the gap between numerical indicators and lived experience by allowing individuals to “see” pollution as it exists around them, fostering both awareness and informed decision-making.

Existing approaches to communicating air quality information range from static maps and web dashboards to mobile applications that display real-time readings from monitoring stations or personal sensors. While these tools have improved access to air quality data, they typically present information in formats that remain detached from the immediate physical surroundings of the user. Consequently, the connection between environmental data and personal experience often remains abstract. Moreover, many conventional visualization methods fail to account for the spatial and temporal variability of air pollution at a human scale, where exposure can differ significantly over short distances and time intervals. Addressing these limitations requires visualization approaches that are both spatially contextualized and intuitively interpretable.

The potential of AR for environmental visualization has been explored in related domains such as climate change education, energy consumption feedback, and biodiversity awareness. These studies suggest that AR can increase user engagement, foster emotional connections with environmental issues, and support more sustainable behaviors. However, relatively few applications have focused specifically on visualizing air pollution in situ. Those that do exist often rely on simplified or static representations, with limited integration of real-time sensor data or personalized information. There is thus a need for systems that combine high-resolution air quality measurements with dynamic, context-aware AR visualizations, enabling users to observe the invisible patterns of pollution in their immediate environment.

In response to this need, we present AiR, an augmented reality application designed to visualize air pollution in real time within the user’s physical surroundings. AiR integrates data from local and distributed sensors, processes it to reflect spatial and temporal variations in pollutant concentrations, and renders intuitive visual overlays through a mobile AR interface. By doing so, the application aims to make air pollution more perceptible and relatable, empowering individuals to better understand the quality of the air they breathe and to make informed decisions about their activities and environments. The design of AiR draws on principles from environmental communication, human-computer interaction, and data visualization, with the goal of maximizing both informational accuracy and user engagement.

This paper contributes to the growing body of research on AR for environmental awareness in several ways. First, it introduces a novel system architecture for integrating heterogeneous air quality data sources into a coherent AR visualization pipeline. Second, it proposes visualization metaphors tailored to representing invisible pollutants in a manner that is both scientifically valid and intuitively graspable. Third, it reports on an initial user study evaluating the effectiveness of AiR in enhancing users’ understanding of air pollution and influencing their attitudes and intended behaviors. By situating air quality data within the user’s immediate sensory field, AiR seeks to close the gap between environmental information and personal experience, thereby supporting more informed and engaged responses to one of today’s most critical environmental challenges.
conclusion:
This work presented AiR, an augmented reality (AR) application designed to visualize air pollution data in an intuitive and contextually embedded manner. By combining real-time or near-real-time environmental data with location-based AR overlays, AiR enables users to perceive otherwise invisible pollutants as situated phenomena in their immediate surroundings. The system leverages advances in mobile AR frameworks, sensor integration, and environmental informatics to bridge the gap between abstract numerical data and human spatial experience. Our aim was to explore how immersive visualization can enhance public awareness, support environmental education, and potentially influence individual and collective behavioral change.

The development and preliminary evaluation of AiR demonstrate that AR can serve as an effective medium for communicating complex environmental information. By embedding pollutant indicators and visual metaphors directly into the user’s field of view, AiR provides a situated understanding of air quality that transcends traditional 2D maps or static charts. User feedback suggests that the immediacy and spatial contextualization of the AR overlays foster stronger emotional engagement and a heightened sense of urgency regarding air pollution issues. Such engagement is critical for motivating informed decision-making and participatory environmental stewardship.

From a technical perspective, AiR highlights both the possibilities and current challenges of deploying AR for environmental sensing and visualization. The reliance on accurate geolocation, stable tracking, and reliable air quality data streams underscores the need for robust integration between heterogeneous data sources and the AR rendering pipeline. Limitations in mobile device performance, battery life, and sensor coverage remain constraints, particularly for sustained outdoor use. Nevertheless, our prototyping indicates that even with these constraints, AR-based environmental visualization can achieve meaningful user impact.

The implications of this work extend beyond the specific case of air pollution. The approach demonstrated in AiR can be generalized to other environmental variables such as noise pollution, water quality, or urban heat islands, where data is often invisible but spatially variable. By situating environmental data in the lived environment of users, AR can function as a cognitive bridge between scientific measurement and everyday perception, potentially democratizing access to environmental knowledge.

Future work will involve more extensive user studies across diverse demographic and geographic contexts to assess the long-term effects of AR-based pollution visualization on knowledge retention, risk perception, and behavioral change. Integration with participatory sensing platforms could also enable users to contribute their own measurements, fostering collaborative environmental monitoring networks. Advances in wearable AR hardware may further enhance immersion, comfort, and data persistence, making continuous environmental awareness a seamless part of daily life.

In summary, AiR illustrates the potential of augmented reality to transform how individuals perceive and interact with environmental data. By rendering the invisible visible in the spaces people inhabit, such applications can catalyze deeper engagement with pressing ecological issues and support informed action toward healthier, more sustainable urban environments.

title: Superconducting order parameter $\pi$-phase shift in magnetic impurity wires
abstract: We investigate the emergence of a superconducting order parameter $\pi$-phase shift in one-dimensional chains of magnetic impurities embedded in an $s$-wave superconductor. Using self-consistent Bogoliubov–de Gennes calculations, we show that increasing the exchange coupling drives a local reversal of the superconducting phase, correlated with the formation and hybridization of Yu–Shiba–Rusinov states. The $\pi$-phase shift is accompanied by a suppression of the order parameter magnitude along the chain and signals a transition in the bound-state spectrum. We analyze the spatial structure and spectral signatures of this phase shift, highlighting its dependence on impurity spacing and coupling strength, and discuss implications for engineered topological superconductivity in magnetic impurity wires.
introduction:
The interplay between magnetism and superconductivity has long been a central topic in condensed matter physics, tracing back to early studies of magnetic impurities in conventional superconductors. In the framework of Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) theory, superconductivity arises from the formation of time-reversed electron pairs, which are intrinsically sensitive to spin-dependent perturbations. Magnetic impurities locally break time-reversal symmetry and act as pair-breaking centers, leading to in-gap bound states known as Yu–Shiba–Rusinov (YSR) states. When multiple impurities are arranged in close proximity, these bound states can hybridize, forming subgap bands whose properties are determined by both the magnetic configuration and the underlying superconducting condensate.  

A particularly intriguing manifestation of this interplay is the possibility of a superconducting order parameter that undergoes a spatially modulated sign change—the so-called $\pi$-phase shift—across a magnetic impurity or magnetic structure. In the simplest case of a single classical magnetic impurity, theory predicts a quantum phase transition between a “0-phase” state, where the local superconducting order parameter maintains the same sign as in the bulk, and a “$\pi$-phase” state, where it reverses sign in the vicinity of the impurity. This transition is associated with the crossing of a YSR state through the Fermi level, signaling a change in the ground-state parity. Experimental signatures of such $\pi$-phase shifts have been observed indirectly in scanning tunneling spectroscopy, Josephson junction experiments, and more recently in engineered atomic-scale magnetic structures.

When magnetic impurities are arranged in a one-dimensional chain on the surface of a superconductor, the hybridization of YSR states can give rise to rich emergent physics. Beyond the potential realization of topological superconductivity and Majorana bound states in such systems, the spatial profile and phase structure of the superconducting order parameter itself are of fundamental interest. In particular, the collective effects of many coupled impurities may induce extended regions in which the order parameter is $\pi$-shifted relative to the surrounding superconducting host. The emergence, stability, and spatial extent of these $\pi$-phase regions depend sensitively on parameters such as impurity spacing, exchange coupling strength, and the dimensionality of the superconducting substrate.

From a theoretical perspective, the microscopic origin of the $\pi$-phase in magnetic impurity wires can be traced to the competition between superconducting pairing correlations and the spin-polarized scattering potential created by the impurity moments. As the exchange interaction increases, local suppression of the pair amplitude can lead to sign reversal, with a concomitant rearrangement of the quasiparticle excitation spectrum. In extended impurity arrays, the resulting phase texture may exhibit periodic or aperiodic modulations, and its characterization requires a self-consistent treatment of the order parameter in real space. Such calculations not only capture the local suppression and recovery of superconductivity but also reveal nontrivial correlations between the $\pi$-phase shift and the subgap spectrum.

In this work, we investigate the conditions under which a superconducting $\pi$-phase shift develops in one-dimensional wires of magnetic impurities embedded in a conventional $s$-wave superconductor. Employing a self-consistent Bogoliubov–de Gennes approach, we analyze the spatial variation of the order parameter, the evolution of YSR bands, and the interplay with possible topological phases. Our results elucidate the microscopic mechanisms controlling the $\pi$-phase transition and provide quantitative predictions for experimental observations in atomic-scale engineered systems. By mapping out the regimes of $\pi$-phase stability, we aim to advance the understanding of how magnetism can be harnessed to tailor superconducting phase textures at the nanoscale.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the emergence of a superconducting order parameter $\pi$-phase shift in one-dimensional arrangements of magnetic impurities embedded in an $s$-wave superconducting host. By combining self-consistent numerical calculations with analytic considerations, we have demonstrated that the formation of Yu–Shiba–Rusinov bound states along the impurity wire can drive a local reversal of the superconducting phase once the exchange coupling exceeds a critical value. This $\pi$-phase shift manifests as a sign change of the order parameter across the impurity chain and is accompanied by a suppression of its magnitude in the immediate vicinity of the magnetic sites.

Our analysis indicates that the transition to the $\pi$-phase is closely linked to the hybridization of impurity-induced subgap states into a dispersive Shiba band. As the exchange interaction strengthens, the Shiba band crosses the Fermi level, leading to a reconstruction of the local pairing correlations. The resulting phase reversal is robust against moderate variations in impurity spacing and persists for a wide range of host superconducting gaps, suggesting that it is a generic consequence of strong magnetic scattering in low-dimensional impurity structures.

We have further shown that the spatial profile of the phase shift depends sensitively on both the magnetic alignment and the dimensionality of the underlying host. In particular, ferromagnetically aligned impurity spins promote a coherent $\pi$-phase region along the chain, whereas noncollinear configurations tend to reduce the phase coherence of the shifted segment. These findings have direct implications for engineered atomic chains on superconducting substrates, where spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy could directly probe the predicted phase structure.

Overall, our results provide a microscopic understanding of how magnetic impurity wires can act as tunable $\pi$-junctions within a conventional superconductor. This insight may guide future efforts to design nanoscale superconducting devices with controllable phase states, potentially enabling new platforms for Majorana bound states and superconducting spintronics. Extensions of this work to include spin–orbit coupling and unconventional pairing symmetries could reveal further rich phase behavior in magnetically textured superconductors.

title: Automatic Reference Models Development: A Framework
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for the development of automatic reference models, aimed at enhancing the efficiency, consistency, and adaptability of model-based processes across domains. The proposed framework integrates formal specification methods, modular architecture design, and automated validation techniques to streamline the creation and maintenance of reference models. By leveraging semantic interoperability standards and domain ontologies, the approach ensures accurate alignment with heterogeneous data sources and evolving requirements. A key contribution lies in the iterative feedback loop between model generation and evaluation, enabling continuous refinement. The framework is demonstrated through a case study in a complex industrial setting, illustrating its potential to reduce development time and improve model quality. Experimental results confirm its scalability and adaptability, highlighting the benefits of automation in knowledge representation. This work lays the groundwork for future research on intelligent, self-adaptive reference model generation systems.
introduction:
The rapid expansion of digital information, coupled with the increasing complexity of data-driven research and industrial processes, has intensified the need for systematic, reliable, and efficient methods for generating and managing reference models. Reference models serve as standardized abstractions or templates that capture essential structures, processes, and relationships within a given domain. They enable consistent communication, interoperability, and reuse of knowledge across diverse applications. Traditionally, the development of such models has been a manual, resource-intensive process, relying heavily on domain experts to synthesize and formalize knowledge. While this approach ensures accuracy and contextual relevance, it is often constrained by limited scalability, potential inconsistencies, and the challenge of maintaining models in rapidly evolving domains.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and knowledge representation have created opportunities to automate or semi-automate the development of reference models. Automatic reference model generation promises to accelerate the creation process, improve adaptability to new contexts, and reduce dependence on prolonged expert involvement. Furthermore, automation can facilitate the integration of heterogeneous data sources, allowing for richer and more granular representations of complex systems. This shift is particularly significant in sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare, software engineering, and smart city planning, where timely and accurate models can substantially influence decision-making, operational efficiency, and innovation.

Despite these technological advancements, the field lacks a coherent framework that systematically addresses the conceptual, methodological, and technical aspects of automating reference model development. Existing approaches are often domain-specific and vary widely in their underlying assumptions, data requirements, and validation strategies. Without a unifying framework, it is challenging to compare methods, assess their applicability across contexts, and ensure that automatically generated models retain the interpretability and trustworthiness necessary for adoption in critical domains. Moreover, there is an ongoing tension between automation and the preservation of domain-specific insights, as purely data-driven methods may overlook nuanced, tacit knowledge that experts contribute.

The emergence of heterogeneous and unstructured data further complicates the automation process. Modern systems generate vast amounts of information in diverse formats, from structured databases to sensor streams, textual descriptions, and multimedia content. Extracting relevant patterns and abstractions from such data requires advanced techniques in natural language processing, ontology engineering, and semantic integration. The automation pipeline must also address issues of data quality, provenance, and contextualization to ensure that generated models are not only technically correct but also meaningful and actionable in their intended settings.

In addition to technical hurdles, there are methodological considerations regarding the evaluation and validation of automatically generated reference models. Traditional validation methods, which often rely on expert review or empirical case studies, must be adapted to account for the dynamic and potentially iterative nature of automated model generation. This raises questions about the appropriate metrics for assessing model completeness, accuracy, adaptability, and usability.
