It also underscores the need for transparent processes that allow stakeholders to understand and, if necessary, refine the automated outputs.

This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for the automatic development of reference models, integrating conceptual design principles with methodological guidelines and enabling technologies. The framework aims to provide a structured approach that can be adapted to various domains while maintaining a focus on interoperability, scalability, and explainability. By articulating the components, processes, and evaluation criteria involved, the framework seeks to bridge the gap between domain-specific implementations and a generalized understanding of automatic reference model generation. Ultimately, this work aspires to facilitate more efficient knowledge formalization, foster cross-domain learning, and support the development of intelligent systems that can evolve in tandem with the environments they represent.
conclusion: This paper has presented a structured framework for the development of automatic reference models, integrating methodological rigor with practical adaptability. By formalizing model generation processes and emphasizing modularity, the framework supports consistency, scalability, and reusability across diverse application domains. The proposed approach addresses key challenges in automating reference model construction, including knowledge representation, validation, and domain alignment. Through its systematic stages, it enables both improved efficiency and enhanced quality in model outputs. The framework’s adaptability ensures relevance in rapidly evolving technological contexts, while its emphasis on standardization facilitates interoperability and knowledge sharing. Future work will focus on refining automated validation techniques and exploring integration with emerging AI-driven modeling tools. Ultimately, this framework provides a foundation for advancing the automation of reference model creation, contributing to more robust, transparent, and accessible modeling practices for research and industry alike.

title: An Efficient Multi-Indicator and Many-Objective Optimization Algorithm based on Two-Archive
abstract: Many-objective optimization problems (MaOPs) pose significant challenges due to the difficulty of simultaneously achieving convergence toward the Pareto front and maintaining diversity among solutions in high-dimensional objective spaces. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an efficient multi-indicator and many-objective optimization algorithm based on a two-archive framework. The proposed method maintains two co-evolving archives: a Convergence Archive (CA) that emphasizes proximity to the Pareto front, and a Diversity Archive (DA) that prioritizes the preservation of well-distributed solutions. A multi-indicator strategy, integrating convergence-oriented and diversity-preserving performance measures, guides the selection and update of both archives. Specifically, the CA employs convergence indicators such as the inverted generational distance, while the DA leverages diversity indicators including hypervolume contribution and shift-based density estimation. The complementary evolution of the two archives facilitates a balanced exploration–exploitation process, where the CA drives search toward optimality and the DA simultaneously broadens coverage of the objective space. An adaptive mating selection mechanism based on archive quality further enhances search efficiency. The proposed algorithm is tested on a range of benchmark MaOPs with varying complexity and dimensionality, and its performance is compared with several state-of-the-art many-objective evolutionary algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently achieves superior convergence and diversity performance, as reflected in multiple quality indicators, and exhibits strong robustness across different problem instances. This study contributes a flexible, indicator-driven, and computationally efficient framework for solving many-objective optimization problems, offering a promising direction for real-world applications involving numerous conflicting objectives.
introduction:
Many-objective optimization problems (MaOPs), characterized by more than three conflicting objectives, arise in a wide range of scientific and engineering domains, including energy management, transportation planning, and complex system design. Solving such problems effectively poses significant challenges to conventional multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs), which often suffer from performance degradation as the dimensionality of the objective space increases. In particular, traditional dominance-based selection mechanisms lose their discriminative capacity in high-dimensional spaces, leading to poor convergence and diversity maintenance. Furthermore, the computational cost of evaluating and comparing solutions escalates rapidly, necessitating more efficient and scalable optimization strategies.

To address these challenges, researchers have explored various extensions of MOEAs for MaOPs, including decomposition-based methods, indicator-based selection schemes, and hybrid frameworks. Among these, indicator-based approaches have shown promise due to their ability to directly guide the search toward convergence and diversity objectives using quantitative performance measures such as hypervolume, inverted generational distance, or R2 metrics. However, reliance on a single indicator may bias the search toward certain regions of the Pareto front, potentially overlooking other desirable trade-offs. Multi-indicator strategies, which integrate the strengths of different performance metrics, can mitigate such bias and improve solution quality. Yet, combining multiple indicators in a computationally efficient manner remains a nontrivial task, particularly in the many-objective context.

Another promising direction is the use of dual-archive frameworks, which maintain two co-evolving solution sets with complementary search roles. Typically, one archive emphasizes convergence toward the Pareto front, while the other focuses on preserving diversity across the objective space. This separation of concerns can balance exploration and exploitation, reduce the risk of premature convergence, and enhance the adaptability of the search process. Nevertheless, the integration of multi-indicator evaluation within a two-archive mechanism for many-objective optimization has not been fully investigated. Existing methods often employ a single indicator or rely on fixed selection strategies, limiting their ability to adapt to different problem landscapes and search stages.

In this work, we propose an efficient multi-indicator and many-objective optimization algorithm based on a two-archive architecture. The proposed method leverages complementary performance indicators to guide selection in each archive, enabling a more nuanced balance between convergence and diversity. By designing indicator-combination strategies tailored to the respective roles of the convergence-oriented and diversity-oriented archives, and by introducing efficient update mechanisms to control computational overhead, our approach aims to achieve superior performance on challenging MaOP benchmarks. Through extensive experimental evaluation, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm attains competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art many-objective optimizers, offering a robust and scalable solution framework for high-dimensional multi-objective optimization tasks.
conclusion:
In this work, we have proposed an efficient multi-indicator and many-objective optimization algorithm based on a two-archive framework, aiming to address the persistent challenges of balancing convergence and diversity in many-objective evolutionary optimization. By integrating multiple performance indicators into the selection process and employing a cooperative mechanism between two complementary archives, the proposed method effectively leverages the strengths of both convergence-oriented and diversity-oriented search strategies. The algorithm is designed to overcome the limitations of traditional single-archive approaches, which often struggle to maintain a good trade-off among multiple conflicting objectives when the dimensionality of the objective space increases.

The core innovation lies in the use of two distinct archives: one dedicated to guiding the search toward the Pareto front with high convergence pressure, and the other focused on preserving diversity across the objective space through indicator-based selection. This dual-archive structure enables the algorithm to explore and exploit the search space more effectively, mitigating the risk of premature convergence and the loss of diversity, which are common issues in many-objective scenarios. The integration of multiple indicators, including those measuring convergence, diversity, and distribution quality, provides a more comprehensive and reliable basis for selection decisions than relying on any single metric.

Extensive comparative experiments against a set of state-of-the-art many-objective optimization algorithms on widely used benchmark suites have demonstrated the superior performance and robustness of the proposed method. The results show that our algorithm consistently achieves better or competitive outcomes across a variety of problem types, including those with irregular Pareto fronts, deceptive landscapes, and high dimensionality. In particular, the two-archive mechanism has proven effective in maintaining a healthy balance between convergence and diversity throughout the evolutionary process, as evidenced by both quantitative performance metrics and visual inspection of the obtained solution sets.

Moreover, the proposed framework exhibits good scalability with respect to the number of objectives. While many conventional algorithms experience significant performance degradation as the number of objectives increases, our approach maintains stable and reliable behavior. This robustness can be attributed to the complementary roles of the two archives: the convergence-oriented archive prevents the search from stagnating away from the Pareto front, while the diversity-oriented archive ensures adequate coverage of the solution space. The multi-indicator fusion further enhances adaptability by dynamically adjusting the selection pressure in response to the evolving population distribution.

Another notable advantage of the proposed method is its flexibility. The framework allows for the incorporation of different types of indicators or alternative selection strategies within each archive, making it adaptable to a wide range of problem characteristics without substantial modifications to the overall structure. This extensibility suggests that the algorithm can serve as a general platform for future developments in many-objective optimization, where problem-specific knowledge or additional performance measures can be seamlessly integrated.

While the results are promising, it is important to recognize that there remain open challenges and opportunities for further research. For instance, the computational cost associated with calculating multiple indicators, especially for large populations and high-dimensional objectives, may become significant in certain applications. Although our implementation demonstrates acceptable efficiency for the tested benchmarks, further optimization of indicator computation or the design of surrogate-assisted variants could enhance applicability to real-world problems with expensive objective evaluations. Additionally, exploring adaptive mechanisms for dynamically allocating computational resources between the two archives based on problem feedback could further improve efficiency and performance.

In summary, this study contributes a novel two-archive, multi-indicator approach to many-objective optimization that effectively addresses the critical balance between convergence and diversity. Through careful integration of complementary search behaviors and multiple evaluation criteria, the proposed algorithm achieves superior performance across a range of challenging test problems, demonstrating both robustness and scalability. Beyond its immediate contributions, the framework offers a flexible foundation for continued exploration and enhancement in the field of evolutionary many-objective optimization. Future work will aim to extend this approach to constrained, dynamic, and large-scale multi-objective problems, as well as to investigate hybridization with other metaheuristic paradigms to further enrich its search capabilities and broaden its applicability to complex real-world optimization tasks.

title: Models of Bars I: Flattish Profiles for Early-Type Galaxies
abstract: We present dynamical models for stellar bars in early-type disk galaxies, focusing on systems with relatively flat luminosity profiles along the bar major axis. Using a family of three-dimensional Ferrers-type density distributions with modified radial fall-offs, we explore a parameter space that reproduces the surface brightness characteristics observed in S0 and early-type spiral galaxies. The models are constrained by near-infrared photometry, ensuring minimal dust effects, and are embedded in axisymmetric bulge–disk–halo potentials. We investigate orbital structures through numerical integration, identifying families of stable periodic orbits that support the bar morphology. Particular attention is given to the role of elongated x1 orbits and their contribution to the apparent flatness of the surface density profile. We also assess the influence of bar strength and pattern speed on the profile shape. Our results indicate that flattish bar profiles can be sustained over a wide range of dynamical parameters, providing a framework for interpreting observed bar morphologies in early-type disk systems.
introduction:
Bars are among the most striking morphological features observed in disk galaxies, representing elongated stellar structures that can dominate the central regions of their hosts. They are ubiquitous in the nearby Universe, with surveys indicating that a majority of disk galaxies exhibit some form of bar (e.g., Eskridge et al. 2000; Menéndez-Delmestre et al. 2007). Bars play a fundamental role in the dynamical and secular evolution of galaxies, redistributing angular momentum between stars, gas, and dark matter, and driving radial flows of interstellar material toward the central kiloparsec. These flows can fuel central star formation, contribute to the growth of bulges or pseudobulges, and potentially feed active galactic nuclei. Understanding the structural and dynamical properties of bars is thus essential for developing a coherent picture of galaxy evolution.

The global shape of a bar, its radial surface brightness (or mass density) profile, and its kinematic signatures are the outcome of complex dynamical processes, including resonances, orbital trapping, and interactions with other galactic components. Observationally, bars in early-type disk galaxies (S0–Sb) often exhibit relatively “flattish” surface brightness profiles along their major axes, in contrast to the more “exponential” profiles seen in many late-type systems (Elmegreen & Elmegreen 1985; Ohta et al. 1990). Flattish profiles are characterised by a roughly constant intensity over a substantial fraction of the bar length before steeply truncating at the ends, often near the location of the corotation radius. This morphology suggests that early-type bars are dynamically more evolved and possibly stronger in terms of the non-axisymmetric perturbations they induce.

From a theoretical perspective, such flat-topped profiles have been linked to long-lived orbital families, particularly the elongated x1 orbits aligned with the bar (Contopoulos & Papayannopoulos 1980; Athanassoula 1992). The distribution and population of these orbits, as well as the influence of vertical resonances leading to boxy or peanut-shaped bulges, can imprint distinctive radial light profiles along the bar. N-body simulations have shown that bars can evolve from initially exponential profiles toward flatter ones as they capture more stars into elongated orbits and grow in length and amplitude. The interplay between the stellar bar and the surrounding disk and halo—mediated by angular momentum exchange—is a key driver of this evolution.

Despite the progress in both observational characterisation and theoretical modeling, a systematic link between the observed flatness of bar profiles in early-type galaxies and the underlying dynamical models remains incomplete. Many analytic or semi-analytic models adopt simplified density laws for bars, often tuned to match late-type systems. Yet the early-type bar population may require distinct prescriptions that capture their characteristic flat brightness distributions, high axial ratios, and sharp truncations. A realistic model should reconcile photometric constraints with dynamical plausibility, allowing for applications in orbital analysis, gas flow studies, and interpretation of integral-field kinematics.

In this work, we present a family of bar models designed explicitly to reproduce the flattish major-axis profiles observed in early-type disk galaxies. By constructing density distributions that are both observationally motivated and dynamically consistent, we aim to provide a framework for studying the orbital structure and gravitational influence of such bars. Section 2 reviews the empirical properties of early-type bar profiles and outlines the constraints they impose. Section 3 introduces our modeling approach and parameterisation. Section 4 explores the resulting orbital families and compares them with observational trends, and Section 5 summarises our findings and discusses implications for bar evolution.
conclusion:
In this study we have examined a set of dynamical models for bars in early-type galaxies, focusing specifically on those capable of producing relatively flattish surface brightness profiles along the bar major axis. Our analysis was motivated both by the observed prevalence of such profiles in early-type systems and by the need for self-consistent dynamical interpretations that can reproduce them without invoking unrealistic structural parameters. By constructing models with varying degrees of central concentration, pattern speed, and orbital structure, we have explored the range of conditions under which flat or near-flat bar profiles arise naturally.

Our results demonstrate that flattish bar profiles can be reproduced within a family of models in which the bar is supported predominantly by elongated x1 orbits that are radially well-mixed over a broad range of semi-major axes. In these configurations the surface density does not decline steeply from the bar centre to its end, but instead remains comparatively uniform, in agreement with observations of early-type barred galaxies. This behaviour is enhanced in models with relatively slow pattern speeds, which allow for a more extended trapping of orbits and a smoother radial distribution of stellar mass along the bar. Conversely, models with higher pattern speeds or more centrally peaked mass distributions tend to produce steeper light profiles, inconsistent with the flattish profiles under consideration.

We have also found that the presence of a moderately strong bulge component does not preclude the existence of a flat bar profile, provided that the bar’s orbital structure is sufficiently extended. In fact, the combined contribution of bulge and bar can help to maintain a high surface brightness over much of the bar length, while still allowing for the observed sharp drop at the bar ends. This is consistent with the morphological classification of many early-type bars, which often display a luminous central region contiguous with a relatively uniform bar section.

An important outcome of our modelling is the recognition that flattish profiles are not necessarily transient or unstable features. In the context of our dynamical models, such profiles can persist over many bar rotation periods, indicating that they may represent a long-lived structural configuration for early-type barred galaxies. This stability arises from the underlying orbital support: the bar is maintained by a coherent family of orbits whose radial density distribution is inherently flat, and which is robust against moderate perturbations.

The comparison with available photometric data shows that our models can reproduce both the amplitude and radial extent of the flat profile segments observed in real galaxies. While our study has not attempted a detailed fit to individual systems, the general agreement between model predictions and the ensemble properties of early-type bars lends credence to the proposed dynamical interpretation.

Future work should aim to refine these models by incorporating additional observational constraints, such as stellar kinematics along the bar and detailed two-dimensional photometric decompositions. N-body simulations with realistic gas fractions and star formation prescriptions will also be valuable in assessing the impact of dissipative processes on the persistence of flattish profiles. Nevertheless, the present results suggest that the structural and dynamical characteristics of early-type bars are well captured by models that combine extended orbital support with moderate pattern speeds, offering a coherent explanation for one of their most distinctive photometric signatures.

title: The Art of Food: Meal Image Synthesis from Ingredients
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to meal image synthesis that generates realistic food images directly from a list of ingredients. Leveraging recent advances in conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) and multimodal embeddings, we design a model that learns a joint representation of textual ingredient descriptions and corresponding visual features. The system is trained on a large-scale dataset of recipes paired with high-quality food photographs, enabling it to capture fine-grained associations between ingredients, cooking styles, and visual presentation. To enhance fidelity and diversity, we incorporate an attention mechanism that focuses on ingredient-specific cues during image generation. Quantitative evaluation using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) demonstrates that our method produces images that are both perceptually convincing and semantically aligned with the input ingredients. Qualitative analysis confirms the ability to render diverse cuisines and complex dishes. This work not only advances the state of food image synthesis but also opens possibilities for applications in culinary creativity, dietary planning, and augmented reality-based gastronomy experiences.
introduction:
The visual presentation of food plays a critical role in culinary culture, influencing perception, appetite, and even nutritional choices. In the era of digital media and online recipe sharing, images of meals have become an essential complement to textual ingredient lists. However, capturing high-quality food images requires resources, equipment, and expertise that are not always accessible. Recent advances in generative modeling, particularly in image synthesis, present an opportunity to bridge this gap by creating realistic meal imagery directly from ingredient descriptions. Such capabilities could enhance recipe databases, assist in dietary planning, and support culinary creativity.

Generating convincing food images from ingredient lists poses unique challenges. Unlike generic image synthesis, the task demands an understanding of complex relationships between ingredients, cooking methods, and their visual outcomes. Variations in preparation style, portioning, and presentation further complicate prediction. Prior works have explored text-to-image synthesis, but these approaches often lack the domain-specific knowledge necessary for food realism. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for meal image synthesis conditioned on ingredient inputs. Our method leverages multimodal learning to capture semantic and visual correlations, enabling the generation of plausible and appetizing meal representations. We evaluate our approach both quantitatively and through perceptual studies to assess realism and relevance.
conclusion: This work has explored the synthesis of realistic meal images from ingredient lists, highlighting the potential of generative models to bridge textual and visual modalities in the culinary domain. By leveraging structured ingredient representations and advanced image generation techniques, we demonstrated that it is possible to produce visually coherent depictions that align closely with the specified components. Our evaluation, both quantitative and perceptual, suggests that such models can capture not only the presence of ingredients but also plausible arrangements and styles informed by culinary conventions. These findings open promising avenues for applications in recipe recommendation, dietary planning, and gastronomic creativity. Nonetheless, challenges remain, including improving fine-grained ingredient rendering, managing cultural and regional variability, and ensuring nutritional and visual accuracy. Future research may benefit from richer multimodal datasets, integration of cooking process descriptions, and user-centered evaluation metrics. Ultimately, meal image synthesis from ingredients offers a compelling intersection of food science, computer vision, and creative AI.

title: Deliberation Scheduling for Time-Critical Sequential Decision Making
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of deliberation scheduling in time-critical sequential decision-making environments, where computational resources are limited and actions must be selected under stringent deadlines. We present a framework that dynamically allocates computation across decision stages to balance the trade-off between immediate action quality and future decision improvement. Our approach integrates models of computation time, decision quality, and environmental dynamics to guide the scheduling process. We develop algorithms that adaptively prioritize deliberation tasks based on their expected impact on overall performance. Experimental results in simulated domains demonstrate that our methods outperform fixed or myopic scheduling strategies, yielding higher cumulative rewards under tight time constraints. The results highlight the importance of principled deliberation scheduling in real-time autonomous systems and other resource-bounded applications.
introduction:
In many real-world domains, intelligent agents must make a sequence of interdependent decisions under tight time constraints. Examples range from autonomous robots navigating dynamic environments, to real-time resource allocation in communication networks, to decision support systems in emergency response. In such scenarios, the agent’s ability to act effectively depends not only on the quality of its decision-making algorithms, but also on the timely allocation of computational resources to deliberation. This raises the central challenge of deliberation scheduling: determining how much time to allocate to thinking versus acting, and how to organize the sequence of deliberative steps so as to maximize overall performance in a time-critical setting.

Sequential decision-making problems are often modeled using frameworks such as Markov decision processes (MDPs) or partially observable MDPs (POMDPs), which provide a principled foundation for reasoning about uncertainty, action consequences, and long-term utility. While optimal policies can be computed in theory for such models, the computational demands of exact planning typically grow prohibitively with problem size. In practice, agents employ approximate methods—heuristic search, simulation-based planning, or policy refinement—that incrementally improve decision quality given more computation. In time-critical domains, deliberation must be interleaved with execution: the agent cannot afford to compute an optimal policy before acting, but must instead decide when to interrupt computation to take action, and which computational tasks to prioritize.

This problem is further complicated by the sequential nature of the environment. Decisions made at early stages influence the state in which future decisions are made, and thus the value of additional computation varies over time. Moreover, the opportunity cost of deliberation is context-dependent: spending more time to improve the current decision may reduce the time available for future planning, potentially degrading overall performance. Therefore, deliberation scheduling requires balancing immediate action quality against the preservation of computational resources for future decisions. The agent must reason not only about the external environment, but also about its own computational processes.

Existing research on metareasoning and anytime algorithms has addressed aspects of this challenge by modeling computation as a resource-bounded action with associated costs and benefits. Early work on bounded rationality emphasized the trade-off between decision quality and computational effort, while more recent approaches have framed deliberation scheduling as an optimization problem over possible computational actions. However, much of this work has focused on single-decision settings or assumes stationary environments, limiting applicability to complex sequential tasks where time constraints vary and the set of relevant computational tasks evolves dynamically.

In this paper, we investigate deliberation scheduling in the context of time-critical sequential decision making, where an agent must repeatedly decide both what to do in the environment and how to allocate limited time among competing deliberative tasks. We develop a formal model that integrates decision-theoretic planning with meta-level control of computation, enabling principled trade-offs between immediate execution and further deliberation. Our approach accommodates dynamically changing deadlines, varying task complexities, and evolving state information. Through analysis and empirical evaluation, we demonstrate how effective deliberation scheduling can significantly improve performance in challenging time-critical domains, offering both theoretical insights and practical algorithms for real-world applications.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the problem of deliberation scheduling for time-critical sequential decision making, focusing on how an agent can optimally allocate its limited computational resources across planning and execution activities. By framing the challenge as a trade-off between improving decision quality through further computation and acting in the environment to capture time-sensitive opportunities, we have formalized a set of strategies that balance these competing demands. Our analysis has shown that in domains where both environmental dynamics and computational processes evolve over time, naive scheduling approaches can lead to significant performance degradation, either through excessive deliberation that incurs opportunity costs or through premature action based on underdeveloped plans.  

We have proposed a framework that integrates models of computational performance with models of task dynamics, enabling the agent to predict the marginal value of additional deliberation and to schedule decision-making activities accordingly. Empirical evaluation in simulated environments demonstrates that our approach consistently outperforms fixed or myopic scheduling policies, particularly in scenarios where the value of information changes rapidly and task deadlines are tight. The results indicate that incorporating principled deliberation scheduling can yield substantial gains in both efficiency and task success rates.  

Beyond the specific algorithms presented, our findings underscore the broader importance of meta-level reasoning in autonomous systems operating under real-time constraints. Effective deliberation scheduling allows for adaptive control over the decision process itself, making it possible to respond flexibly to variations in both computational conditions and environmental urgency. This capability will be increasingly critical as decision-making agents are deployed in complex, high-stakes domains such as autonomous vehicles, robotic surgery, and real-time strategic planning.  

Future work can extend these results by incorporating richer models of computation, including learning-based predictors of planning improvement, and by exploring interactions between multiple concurrent decision processes. Additionally, investigating deliberation scheduling in multi-agent settings, where coordination and communication introduce new temporal trade-offs, remains a promising direction. Ultimately, the integration of deliberation scheduling into the broader architecture of intelligent agents represents a step toward systems that are not only capable of making good decisions, but of managing the decision-making process itself in a principled, time-aware manner.

title: DeFMO: Deblurring and Shape Recovery of Fast Moving Objects
abstract: We present DeFMO, a novel computational framework for simultaneous deblurring and shape recovery of fast moving objects (FMOs) in single images. FMOs, such as balls, projectiles, or thrown tools, undergo rapid motion during exposure, producing elongated motion blur and posing significant challenges for conventional image restoration techniques. DeFMO leverages a physics-inspired motion formation model coupled with a deep neural network to disentangle object appearance, shape, and trajectory from blurred observations. Our method estimates object boundaries and recoveries sharp textures while inferring motion parameters, enabling accurate reconstruction of both geometry and motion path. We train the network using synthetically generated blur from high-speed video datasets, and demonstrate strong generalization to real-world scenes without additional fine-tuning. Quantitative evaluations show that DeFMO outperforms state-of-the-art deblurring baselines in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and shape accuracy. The approach enables novel applications in sports analysis, robotics, and visual forensics, where understanding the precise shape and motion of FMOs is critical.
introduction:
Fast moving objects (FMOs) are prevalent in a wide range of real-world scenarios, from sports and industrial inspection to surveillance and robotics. When captured in video or still images, their high velocities relative to the camera’s exposure time cause them to appear as elongated, semi-transparent streaks, often accompanied by severe motion blur and loss of shape detail. This visual degradation poses significant challenges for both human interpretation and automated vision systems, as the resulting observations contain little direct information about the object’s true geometry, texture, and instantaneous position. Recovering the sharp appearance and precise shape of FMOs is thus a critical step toward enabling accurate object recognition, motion analysis, and interaction in dynamic environments.

The problem of FMO recovery differs substantially from conventional image deblurring. Traditional motion blur typically arises from camera shake or moderate object motion, where the blurred appearance can be modeled as a convolution with a relatively short and smooth motion kernel. In contrast, FMOs can traverse large portions of the image plane within a single exposure, leading to blur kernels that are long, spatially variant, and potentially curved due to changes in velocity or direction. Moreover, the object’s projected shape can change over time because of rotation, deformation, or perspective effects, making the blur not simply a translational smear of a static template. These factors conspire to make the blind deblurring of FMOs an ill-posed and highly underdetermined inverse problem.

Prior work has addressed aspects of this challenge by imposing simplifying assumptions, such as known object shapes, constant velocity, or availability of high-speed imaging. Some methods exploit temporal redundancy in video sequences, leveraging multiple frames to estimate motion trajectories and reconstruct appearance. Others rely on physical priors, such as symmetry or known dimensions, to constrain the solution space. While these approaches have demonstrated promising results in constrained settings, their applicability is often limited in practical scenarios where the object identity is unknown, motion is complex, and only standard frame-rate video or single images are available. Furthermore, many existing algorithms treat motion estimation and deblurring as separate stages, which can lead to suboptimal results when the two processes are tightly coupled.

In this work, we introduce DeFMO, a unified framework for the joint deblurring and shape recovery of fast moving objects. Our approach is motivated by the observation that the appearance of an FMO in an image is the result of an integration of its sharp, time-varying projection along a continuous motion path. By explicitly modeling both the object’s latent sharp texture and its motion trajectory within the exposure interval, we can formulate the recovery task as a joint optimization problem that enforces consistency between these latent variables and the observed blurry measurement. The proposed formulation naturally accommodates general, non-linear motion paths and allows for shape changes, enabling robust recovery in a wide variety of settings.

A key feature of DeFMO is its ability to operate under minimal assumptions about the object’s identity or motion. We leverage a physics-based image formation model that accounts for spatially varying blur induced by complex trajectories, while incorporating regularization terms that promote plausible shape and texture reconstructions. To solve the resulting inverse problem, we develop an iterative estimation algorithm that alternates between refining motion parameters and updating the sharp object estimate, with each step informed by the current reconstruction. This joint refinement loop helps mitigate the ambiguities inherent in separately estimating motion and deblurring, leading to more accurate and visually faithful results.

We evaluate DeFMO on a diverse dataset of synthetic and real-world FMO sequences, spanning sports footage, everyday objects in motion, and challenging low-light conditions. Quantitative comparisons against state-of-the-art baselines demonstrate that our method consistently achieves superior performance in terms of both reconstruction fidelity and motion estimation accuracy. Qualitative results further highlight DeFMO’s ability to recover fine structural details and sharp boundaries from severely blurred inputs, even when the motion path is curved or the object rotates significantly during exposure.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we present a general image formation model for FMOs that captures spatially varying blur from arbitrary trajectories and shape changes. Second, we propose a joint optimization framework for simultaneous motion estimation and shape recovery from a single blurred observation or standard frame-rate video. Third, we provide extensive experimental validation showing that our approach outperforms existing methods in both controlled and in-the-wild scenarios. By addressing the intertwined challenges of deblurring and motion estimation in a unified manner, DeFMO opens new possibilities for accurate analysis of fast moving objects in natural imaging conditions.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced DeFMO, a novel approach for deblurring and recovering the shape of fast moving objects from a single motion-blurred image. By leveraging a tailored motion-aware model, our method effectively disentangles object appearance from motion trajectories, enabling accurate reconstruction of both shape and texture. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeFMO outperforms existing techniques in terms of sharpness, fidelity, and robustness across diverse motion patterns. The proposed framework opens new opportunities for high-speed scene analysis in challenging imaging conditions. Future work will explore integration with temporal information and extension to multi-object scenarios for broader applicability in real-world vision systems.

title: Automatic Hyperparameter Tuning Method for Local Outlier Factor, with Applications to Anomaly Detection
abstract: The Local Outlier Factor (LOF) algorithm is widely used for unsupervised anomaly detection, yet its performance is highly sensitive to the choice of the neighborhood size parameter, *k*. Manual tuning is challenging in the absence of labeled data, limiting practical applicability. This paper proposes an automatic hyperparameter tuning method for LOF based on stability analysis of anomaly rankings across multiple *k* values. The approach identifies an optimal parameter by minimizing ranking variability while preserving sensitivity to local density deviations. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves near-optimal detection performance without supervision, outperforming conventional heuristic choices. Applications to network intrusion detection and industrial fault monitoring illustrate its robustness and adaptability, enabling reliable LOF-based anomaly detection in diverse domains without the need for manual parameter selection.
introduction:
Anomaly detection plays a critical role in a wide range of domains, including fraud detection in financial transactions, fault diagnosis in industrial systems, intrusion detection in cybersecurity, and identification of rare diseases in healthcare. The goal is to identify data instances that deviate significantly from the majority, often under conditions where anomalous patterns are rare and diverse. While numerous approaches have been proposed for anomaly detection, the Local Outlier Factor (LOF) remains one of the most widely used density-based methods due to its intuitive formulation and robustness in handling complex data distributions. LOF estimates the degree of abnormality of each data point by comparing its local density to that of its neighbors, making it particularly effective in datasets with varying densities.

Despite its popularity, the performance of LOF is highly sensitive to the choice of its hyperparameters, most notably the neighborhood size parameter \(k\). This parameter controls the scope of locality in density estimation: a small \(k\) may capture only very local structures and fail to detect broader anomalies, while a large \(k\) can oversmooth the local density estimates and obscure meaningful deviations. Selecting an appropriate \(k\) is challenging because the optimal value depends on the intrinsic structure of the data, which is typically unknown in unsupervised settings where no labeled anomalies are available. In practice, \(k\) is often chosen heuristically or through trial-and-error, leading to suboptimal detection performance and reduced reproducibility.

The problem of hyperparameter tuning in anomaly detection is further compounded by the lack of ground truth in most real-world scenarios. Unlike supervised learning, where cross-validation can be used to optimize parameters based on predictive accuracy, anomaly detection often operates without labeled data. As a result, researchers and practitioners must rely on indirect criteria, such as stability, density distribution characteristics, or assumptions about the proportion of anomalies, to guide parameter selection. Although some studies have explored adaptive or data-driven methods for tuning \(k\) in LOF, there is still no consensus on a robust, automatic approach that generalizes well across different types of datasets and anomaly structures.

Recent advances in automatic machine learning (AutoML) and meta-learning have highlighted the potential of systematic, algorithmic approaches to hyperparameter optimization in unsupervised settings. However, many of these frameworks are tailored to supervised tasks or require labeled validation data, limiting their direct applicability to anomaly detection. In the context of LOF, an effective automatic hyperparameter tuning method would need to operate entirely without labels, adapt to diverse data distributions, and maintain computational efficiency for large-scale applications.

The importance of addressing this challenge is underscored by the growing availability of high-dimensional and heterogeneous datasets in modern applications. In domains such as network intrusion detection, sensor networks, and biomedical data analysis, anomalies may manifest in subtle and context-dependent ways, making them sensitive to the scale at which neighborhood relationships are evaluated. An inappropriate choice of \(k\) can result in either excessive false alarms or missed detections, both of which have significant practical consequences. Therefore, a principled, automated method for selecting LOF hyperparameters has the potential to substantially improve anomaly detection performance and reliability.

In this work, we propose an automatic hyperparameter tuning method for the Local Outlier Factor that addresses these limitations. Our approach is fully unsupervised and leverages intrinsic properties of the data to determine the optimal neighborhood size without requiring labeled anomalies or extensive manual search. The method is designed to balance sensitivity to local density variations with robustness against noise, enabling it to adapt to datasets with complex, multi-scale structures. We evaluate the proposed approach on a diverse set of benchmark and real-world anomaly detection datasets, comparing its performance against standard LOF configurations and existing tuning strategies.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a novel, data-driven criterion for hyperparameter selection in LOF that operates without supervision and accounts for varying density structures. Second, we provide a systematic evaluation of the proposed method across multiple domains, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability. Third, we offer insights into the relationship between neighborhood size, data topology, and anomaly detectability, contributing to a deeper understanding of LOF parameterization in practice.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on LOF, hyperparameter tuning in unsupervised learning, and existing approaches to automatic anomaly detection. Section 3 details the proposed automatic tuning method, including its theoretical motivation and computational properties. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results, while Section 5 discusses the implications, limitations, and potential extensions of our work. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.
conclusion:
This work presented an automatic hyperparameter tuning method for the Local Outlier Factor (LOF) algorithm, aimed at improving its robustness and applicability in real-world anomaly detection tasks. By addressing one of the primary limitations of LOF—its sensitivity to the choice of neighborhood size—our approach removes the need for manual parameter selection, which is often ad hoc and dataset-dependent. The proposed method leverages data-driven criteria to identify an optimal configuration, thus enhancing both detection accuracy and stability across diverse scenarios.  

Extensive experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrated that the automatically tuned LOF consistently outperforms the default and manually selected configurations in terms of precision, recall, and overall detection performance. In particular, the method proved effective in balancing sensitivity to subtle anomalies with resilience against noise, a challenge common in high-dimensional and heterogeneous data. Furthermore, the results confirmed that the tuning procedure incurs only modest computational overhead, making it suitable for integration into automated anomaly detection pipelines.  

Applications to real-world datasets, including network intrusion detection and industrial fault monitoring, highlighted the practical value of the approach. In these domains, the automatic tuning not only improved detection rates but also reduced the risk of overfitting to specific operational conditions. This property is especially important in dynamic environments where data distributions evolve over time.  

Future work will extend the framework to accommodate streaming data, enabling continuous adaptation of LOF parameters in real time. Additionally, integrating the method with ensemble-based anomaly detection strategies may further enhance robustness. Overall, the proposed automatic hyperparameter tuning for LOF offers a principled, efficient, and effective solution for anomaly detection across a broad range of applications.

title: Causal Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Causal Bayesian Optimization (CBO) is an emerging framework that integrates causal inference with Bayesian optimization to improve decision-making in complex, uncertain environments. Traditional Bayesian optimization methods treat the black-box objective as a purely statistical surface, ignoring underlying causal structures that may govern the relationship between interventions and outcomes. In contrast, CBO exploits prior knowledge or learned causal graphs to guide the selection of queries, enabling more efficient exploration and more reliable extrapolation under interventions. We formalize the CBO problem, defining an acquisition function that incorporates causal constraints and counterfactual reasoning to focus search on causally relevant variables. Our approach accommodates uncertainty in both the objective function and the causal model, leveraging probabilistic representations to balance exploration and exploitation under intervention-specific constraints. Through synthetic benchmarks and a real-world application in experimental design, we demonstrate that CBO outperforms standard Bayesian optimization in both data efficiency and robustness to distributional shifts, highlighting its potential for domains where causal relationships are central to effective optimization.
introduction:
Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a powerful framework for the global optimization of black-box functions that are expensive to evaluate. By modeling the objective with a probabilistic surrogate, typically a Gaussian process, and selecting evaluation points through an acquisition function, BO achieves sample-efficient exploration and exploitation. This approach has been successfully applied in diverse domains, including hyperparameter tuning in machine learning, experimental design in the physical sciences, and engineering optimization. Despite its demonstrated effectiveness, standard BO formulations often treat the input–output relationship as an opaque mapping, without explicitly accounting for underlying structural dependencies or causal mechanisms.

In many real-world problems, however, the variables under consideration are not independent nor arbitrary; they are connected through causal relationships that constrain the feasible interventions and influence the outcome. For example, in clinical treatment planning, modifying a given intervention variable may indirectly affect other covariates through physiological pathways; in manufacturing process optimization, changing one control parameter may propagate through equipment dependencies before influencing final product quality. Ignoring such causal structure can lead to suboptimal or even infeasible recommendations, as BO may propose interventions that are theoretically optimal in the statistical sense but impractical or invalid in the real system.

Causal Bayesian optimization seeks to integrate causal modeling into the BO framework, leveraging knowledge of the underlying causal graph or its partial estimation to guide the optimization process. By incorporating structural constraints, one can restrict the search space to feasible interventions, better predict the effects of actions, and improve sample efficiency by avoiding evaluations in causally implausible regions. Furthermore, causal reasoning enables the distinction between correlation and causation in observational data, allowing the optimization to focus on actionable variables whose manipulation leads to genuine changes in the objective.

This paper investigates methods for embedding causal knowledge into Bayesian optimization, developing algorithms that exploit both probabilistic surrogate modeling and causal inference principles. We examine how causal graphs and do-calculus can inform acquisition strategies, and we analyze the theoretical and empirical benefits of causal-aware BO in settings where interventions are constrained or costly. Through synthetic benchmarks and real-world case studies, we demonstrate that causal Bayesian optimization can achieve superior performance, particularly in domains where respecting causal structure is essential for effective and reliable decision-making.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated the integration of causal reasoning into Bayesian optimization, introducing a framework that leverages causal structure to guide the search for optimal interventions. By explicitly modeling causal relationships among variables, our approach moves beyond purely associational methods, enabling more sample-efficient optimization in settings where interventions have structured, directional effects. We demonstrated that incorporating prior causal knowledge can reduce the exploration of irrelevant variables, focusing computational resources on actionable factors with the greatest potential impact on outcomes. Empirical results on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets showed consistent improvements in convergence speed and solution quality compared to standard Bayesian optimization. Furthermore, our framework offers interpretability benefits, as the learned causal models provide insight into the mechanisms underlying the observed improvements. These findings suggest that causal Bayesian optimization is a promising paradigm for domains where interventions are costly or limited, such as healthcare, manufacturing, and policy design. Future work will explore extensions to partially observed and dynamic causal graphs, as well as integration with active causal discovery methods to relax the assumption of fully known structures while maintaining optimization efficiency.

title: Breakdown of Bell's Theorem for incompatible measurements
abstract: Bell’s theorem demonstrates that no local hidden-variable theory can reproduce all predictions of quantum mechanics, assuming jointly measurable observables. However, in realistic quantum experiments, certain measurement settings are mutually incompatible, preventing their simultaneous realization. This paper examines the implications of such incompatibility for the logical structure of Bell’s argument. We analyze how counterfactual reasoning about unperformed measurements underpins the derivation of Bell inequalities and show that the non-commutativity of relevant operators challenges the assignment of predefined outcomes. By formalizing the role of measurement incompatibility, we identify conditions under which the standard derivation fails, without invoking experimental loopholes. Our results clarify the conceptual boundaries of Bell’s theorem, providing a refined understanding of locality, realism, and the operational constraints of quantum theory.
introduction:
Bell’s theorem occupies a central place in the foundations of quantum mechanics, providing a rigorous framework for testing the limits of local realism. Building on the pioneering work of John S. Bell in 1964, the theorem demonstrates that no physical theory based on local hidden variables can reproduce all of the predictions of quantum mechanics. The mathematical expression of this insight, typically in the form of Bell inequalities, allows for direct experimental confrontation between classical intuitions about separability and the nonlocal correlations predicted by quantum theory. Over the past decades, increasingly sophisticated experiments have confirmed violations of Bell inequalities under progressively stricter conditions, lending strong empirical support to the quantum mechanical description.

However, the standard derivations of Bell’s inequalities rely on assumptions that implicitly presuppose the joint definability of outcomes for distinct measurement settings. In particular, the inequalities are often derived by considering hypothetical results of measurements that, in the actual experimental arrangement, are mutually exclusive or incompatible. This counterfactual reasoning is formally unproblematic in a classical probabilistic framework, where all observables can, in principle, be assigned definite values simultaneously. In quantum theory, by contrast, incompatible observables are represented by noncommuting operators, and the formalism forbids their simultaneous precise specification. The tension between the classical assumption of joint probability distributions and the quantum mechanical structure of measurement thus becomes a focal point for understanding the applicability and interpretation of Bell’s theorem.

A careful breakdown of the theorem in the context of incompatible measurements is therefore essential for clarifying the scope of its conclusions. While the incompatibility of measurements is often acknowledged in discussions of the theorem, its precise role in the logical structure of the derivation is sometimes left implicit. This can lead to conceptual confusion, particularly in debates over whether violations of Bell inequalities necessarily imply some form of nonlocal influence, or whether they might instead indicate a failure of classical reasoning about measurement outcomes. By explicitly examining the interplay between measurement incompatibility and the derivation of Bell-type bounds, one can more sharply delineate what features of quantum theory are genuinely in conflict with local realism, and what features are artifacts of applying classical probability theory beyond its legitimate domain.

Moreover, the growing interest in generalized probabilistic theories and alternative frameworks for describing measurement outcomes further motivates a systematic analysis. Such frameworks often relax or modify the assumptions about joint distributions, sometimes allowing for probabilistic constraints that differ from those imposed by classical Kolmogorovian probability. In these settings, the notion of incompatibility can take on different formal expressions, and the connection between Bell-type inequalities and locality assumptions may require re-examination. A breakdown of Bell’s theorem tailored to incompatible measurements can thus inform not only foundational debates, but also the design of experiments that probe the boundaries between classical, quantum, and post-quantum theories.

In this work, we undertake a detailed analysis of Bell’s theorem with particular attention to the role of incompatible measurements in its derivation and interpretation. By tracing the logical dependencies of the theorem’s assumptions and isolating those that rest on counterfactual assignments to noncommuting observables, we aim to clarify the conceptual landscape. This approach not only sharpens the foundational understanding of Bell’s result, but also provides a framework for exploring generalized scenarios in which incompatibility plays a central role in shaping observable correlations.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the limitations of Bell’s theorem when applied to scenarios involving incompatible measurements, focusing on the conceptual and mathematical structures underlying its derivation. Our analysis highlights that the standard form of Bell inequalities presupposes the existence of joint probability distributions for all measurement settings, an assumption that is invalid in the presence of genuinely incompatible observables. When such incompatibility is taken into account, the counterfactual reasoning required to assign simultaneous values to non-commuting quantities becomes untenable, undermining the logical chain that leads to the inequalities themselves. This observation does not diminish the empirical significance of experimental violations of Bell inequalities, but rather clarifies the precise conditions under which those violations constitute evidence against local realism. By dissecting the interplay between measurement incompatibility and the formal requirements of Bell’s argument, we have shown that certain apparent contradictions arise from extending classical intuitions beyond their legitimate domain. Our findings suggest that a more nuanced formulation of nonlocality tests should explicitly incorporate the operational constraints imposed by quantum incompatibility. This perspective opens new avenues for refining the conceptual foundations of quantum theory and for designing experiments that more faithfully reflect its intrinsic measurement structure.

title: VLT Spectroscopic Analysis of HH 202. Implications on dust destruction and thermal inhomogeneities
abstract: We present a detailed spectroscopic study of the Herbig–Haro object HH 202 in the Orion Nebula, based on high–resolution, long–slit observations obtained with the Ultraviolet-Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES) at the Very Large Telescope (VLT). The spectral coverage from 3100 to 10400 Å allows the measurement of an unprecedented number of emission lines from a wide range of ionic species. The analysis of collisionally excited and recombination lines yields precise determinations of electron temperatures, densities, and ionic abundances. Significant discrepancies between abundances derived from different diagnostics are interpreted in the context of thermal inhomogeneities, parametrized by the temperature fluctuation parameter *t²*. We find evidence for enhanced gas-phase abundances of refractory elements such as Fe, Ni, and Cr in the shocked regions of HH 202, consistent with partial destruction of dust grains by shock waves. The spatial distribution of these enhancements, together with the derived physical conditions, supports a scenario where dust destruction is localized and efficient in high–velocity knots. Our results provide quantitative constraints on the interplay between shocks, dust processing, and temperature structure in ionized nebulae, and highlight the importance of high–dispersion spectroscopy for disentangling the complex physical and chemical processes in Herbig–Haro flows.
introduction: Herbig–Haro (HH) objects are small-scale shock regions formed when collimated outflows from young stellar objects interact with the surrounding interstellar medium. HH 202, located in the Orion Nebula, is one of the brightest and best-studied examples, offering a unique laboratory for probing shock physics, dust processing, and nebular conditions. High-resolution spectroscopy with the Very Large Telescope (VLT) enables precise measurements of emission-line ratios, ionic abundances, and kinematic structures. Such data are essential for investigating the efficiency of dust destruction in shocked gas and assessing the role of spatial and thermal inhomogeneities in abundance determinations. This study presents a detailed spectroscopic analysis of HH 202, aiming to constrain dust-related processes and improve our understanding of physical conditions in ionized nebulae.
conclusion:
The spectroscopic analysis of HH 202 using the Very Large Telescope has provided new insights into the physical conditions, chemical composition, and microphysical processes occurring within this Herbig–Haro object. By employing high-resolution, wide-wavelength coverage data, we have been able to disentangle emission from different kinematic components, thereby isolating the signatures of shocked gas from those of the surrounding photoionized nebula. This separation has proven essential in assessing the role of dust destruction and in quantifying thermal inhomogeneities within the ionized medium.

Our results indicate that the gas in the shock component exhibits enhanced abundances of refractory elements such as Fe, Ni, and Cr when compared to the ambient Orion Nebula gas. These enhancements are consistent with the partial destruction of dust grains in fast shocks, releasing metals into the gas phase. The magnitude of the observed enrichment suggests that dust destruction is an efficient mechanism in HH 202, though likely incomplete, with the efficiency depending on both the shock velocity and pre-shock grain composition. In particular, the elevated [Fe III] and [Ni III] line intensities provide direct evidence for grain processing in the interaction zone, supporting theoretical models of grain sputtering and shattering in radiative shocks.

We have also found that the shock and ambient components display different electron temperature structures, as inferred from multiple diagnostic line ratios. The presence of significant temperature variations within the shock component, alongside smaller but non-negligible inhomogeneities in the ambient gas, suggests that the assumption of a single, uniform temperature is inadequate for precise abundance determinations. The application of the \( t^2 \) formalism to our dataset yields values substantially larger in the shocked region than in the surrounding medium, reinforcing the view that shocks are a major driver of thermal inhomogeneities in ionized nebulae.

The discrepancy between abundances derived from collisionally excited lines (CELs) and recombination lines (RLs) is also more pronounced in the shocked gas. This pattern aligns with the expectation that temperature fluctuations, together with possible small-scale chemical inhomogeneities, can account for the CEL–RL abundance discrepancy. Our findings support scenarios in which both dust destruction and thermal inhomogeneities are interlinked: the energy dissipation and mixing induced by shocks can simultaneously increase metal abundances in the gas phase and create localized temperature enhancements.

These results have wider implications for the interpretation of emission-line spectra in other astrophysical contexts. In particular, the evidence from HH 202 underscores the necessity of considering shock-induced dust processing and temperature fluctuations when deriving chemical abundances in regions influenced by outflows and jets. This is especially relevant for studies of star-forming regions, supernova remnants, and extragalactic H II regions, where unresolved shock components may bias abundance measurements if not properly accounted for.

In summary, the VLT observations of HH 202 demonstrate that high spatial and spectral resolution spectroscopy is a powerful tool for probing the interplay between shocks, dust, and gas in nebular environments. By revealing the signatures of dust destruction and quantifying thermal inhomogeneities, our study contributes to a more accurate picture of the chemical and thermal state of ionized gas in dynamic star-forming regions. Future work combining spectroscopic diagnostics with detailed shock and dust evolution modelling will be essential to fully constrain the efficiency of dust destruction and the origin of temperature fluctuations in these complex systems.

title: Exact Langevin Dynamics with Stochastic Gradients
abstract: We present a framework for performing exact Langevin dynamics using stochastic gradients, enabling scalable Bayesian inference without introducing discretization bias. Our method combines stochastic gradient estimates with a correction mechanism that preserves the target posterior as the invariant distribution. Unlike conventional stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, our approach does not require diminishing step sizes and achieves asymptotically exact sampling. We derive theoretical guarantees for convergence and illustrate the method’s efficiency on large-scale models. Empirical results demonstrate accurate posterior estimates with substantially reduced computational cost, making the approach suitable for high-dimensional and data-intensive Bayesian learning tasks.
introduction:
Bayesian inference provides a principled framework for reasoning under uncertainty, enabling robust predictions and calibrated measures of confidence in modern machine learning systems. However, in many applications of interest, the posterior distribution over parameters is analytically intractable and computationally expensive to approximate, particularly in the regime of large datasets and high-dimensional parameter spaces. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods remain a standard tool for posterior sampling, offering asymptotic guarantees of correctness under mild conditions. Among these, Langevin dynamics–based algorithms, which combine stochastic differential equations with Monte Carlo integration, have emerged as an attractive class of methods due to their ability to exploit gradient information to accelerate convergence.  

Classical Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) discretizes the overdamped Langevin diffusion, whose stationary distribution coincides with the target posterior. In large-scale settings, however, computing the full-data gradient at each step becomes prohibitive. Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) addresses this challenge by replacing the exact gradient with an unbiased stochastic estimate obtained from a minibatch of data. This replacement dramatically reduces per-iteration cost and allows the method to scale to massive datasets. Yet, the use of stochastic gradients introduces additional noise into the dynamics, altering the stationary distribution and leading to biased samples unless the step size is annealed to zero. Annealing, in turn, slows exploration and can impair mixing, limiting the practical utility of SGLD in fixed-step-size regimes.

Recent work has sought to correct for the bias induced by stochastic gradients while retaining computational efficiency. Control variates, modified noise terms, and Metropolis–Hastings corrections have been proposed, but these approaches often require either additional passes over the dataset, nontrivial variance estimation, or acceptance–rejection steps that negate the benefits of mini-batching. Furthermore, many of these corrections are approximate, sacrificing either exactness or scalability. This tension between computational tractability and sampling fidelity motivates the search for methods that can achieve *exact* Langevin dynamics in the presence of stochastic gradients, without resorting to diminishing step sizes or full-data computations.

In this work, we develop a framework for performing exact Langevin dynamics using stochastic gradient information, preserving the target posterior as the invariant distribution for any constant step size. Our approach is grounded in a careful analysis of the discretized Langevin equation with noisy gradients, identifying the precise conditions under which additional, structured noise can compensate for gradient stochasticity. We derive an algorithm that injects a calibrated Gaussian perturbation whose covariance is matched to the variance of the stochastic gradient noise, ensuring that the resulting Markov chain is reversible with respect to the desired posterior. Crucially, our method only requires quantities that can be estimated on the fly from minibatches, and it avoids any global variance estimation or acceptance–rejection steps.

By reconciling exactness with scalability, the proposed method opens the door to practical MCMC sampling in large-data regimes where traditional approaches are either too costly or statistically biased. We provide theoretical guarantees of correctness, analyze the impact of variance estimation error, and demonstrate through empirical studies that our algorithm achieves accurate posterior sampling with computational efficiency comparable to SGLD. This work thus contributes a principled and implementable solution to a longstanding challenge at the intersection of stochastic optimization and Bayesian computation.
conclusion: In this work, we have developed and analyzed an exact formulation of Langevin dynamics that accommodates stochastic gradient estimates without sacrificing the correctness of the stationary distribution. By introducing a principled correction mechanism for gradient noise, our approach preserves the target posterior while retaining the computational advantages of minibatch-based learning. The resulting dynamics unify ideas from stochastic differential equations, Bayesian sampling, and variance control, offering a tractable alternative to approximate Langevin methods that incur bias. Empirical studies confirm that the proposed method achieves accurate posterior inference across a range of models, with convergence behavior consistent with theoretical predictions. Moreover, the framework is compatible with adaptive step-size schedules and scalable to large datasets, making it suitable for modern machine learning applications. Future work will explore extensions to non-Euclidean geometries, integration with advanced preconditioning techniques, and applications to high-dimensional Bayesian deep learning, further advancing the practicality and scope of exact Langevin dynamics with stochastic gradients.

title: Categories without structures
abstract: This paper investigates categories devoid of additional structure, focusing on their foundational role in category theory. We examine the extent to which meaningful mathematical results arise without enrichment, limits, or internal composition laws beyond the axioms. By analyzing examples and counterexamples, we clarify the conceptual boundaries of structure-free categories and illuminate their significance for abstraction, generality, and the architecture of categorical frameworks.
introduction:
In contemporary category theory, much of the literature focuses on categories equipped with additional structures—monoidal products, limits and colimits, enrichment, higher-dimensional analogues, and various internal logics. These structures are often indispensable for applications in algebra, topology, computer science, and logic. However, the foundational notion of a category, stripped of any supplementary adornments, remains a rich subject of investigation in its own right. The study of “bare” categories, considered solely in terms of their objects, morphisms, composition, and identities, prompts questions about which phenomena genuinely require extra structure and which are intrinsic to the categorical framework itself.

This perspective invites a re-examination of basic categorical concepts—such as functors, natural transformations, and equivalences—without presupposing structural enhancements. In doing so, we can better understand the minimal assumptions necessary for various constructions and theorems, and identify results that hold in the most general categorical context. Such an approach also clarifies the logical boundaries between pure category theory and its structured variants, shedding light on how much of the conceptual apparatus derives from the axioms of categories alone.

Moreover, categories without structures serve as a testing ground for abstraction. By avoiding reliance on specific enrichments or properties like completeness, one can explore the extent to which categorical reasoning depends only on the formal compositional framework. This can yield insights into the transferability of ideas across different mathematical domains and into the nature of categorical equivalence itself. The present work aims to articulate a systematic account of categories in their most general form, to chart the scope of structure-independent results, and to consider the methodological implications for the development of category theory as a whole. In doing so, it underscores the theoretical significance of the unadorned categorical landscape.
conclusion:
This study has examined the conceptual and formal landscape of categories without structures, aiming to clarify what is lost and what is gained when the usual apparatus of internal compositional or algebraic constraints is absent. By stripping away the structural enrichments that often accompany categorical frameworks—such as limits, colimits, monoidal products, or internal homs—we have sought to isolate the minimal conditions under which categorical reasoning can still proceed. This has required revisiting the foundational definitions of categories, morphisms, and identity, and considering them in their most austere form.

One central outcome of this investigation is the recognition that categories without additional structures are not merely impoverished versions of better-equipped categories, but rather occupy a distinct position in the conceptual hierarchy. They reveal the extent to which categorical thinking can survive without recourse to richer internal features, relying solely on the bare pattern of objects and arrows, and the composition law that binds them. In doing so, they foreground the role of composition itself as the primary structural element, while highlighting that many of the intuitions drawn from algebraic or topological contexts cannot be directly imported into this minimal setting.

The absence of structure has both limiting and liberating effects. On the one hand, many familiar constructions fail to be definable; universal properties often have no meaningful instantiation, and the absence of enrichment renders certain categorical equivalences or dualities void. On the other hand, the minimal framework forces us to confront the generality of the categorical language, making explicit which results depend essentially on additional assumptions and which are truly structural in the categorical sense. This, in turn, offers a clearer view of the boundary between category theory as a general theory of compositional systems and its specialised, structure-laden subclasses.

Moreover, the exploration of categories without structures opens up methodological possibilities. They can serve as a testing ground for the logical and philosophical analysis of categorical concepts, providing a null context against which richer frameworks can be compared. They also function as a reminder that categories, at their core, are not defined by the particular nature of their objects, but by the network of morphisms and the coherence of their compositions. In pedagogical terms, beginning with such minimal categories may help students appreciate the incremental role of added structures, rather than taking them as given.

In summary, categories without structures are not merely degenerate cases, but foundational exemplars that illuminate the essence of categorical reasoning. They sharpen our understanding of what category theory minimally requires, and thereby deepen our grasp of why, and how, additional structures matter. By attending to these bare frameworks, we not only refine our theoretical understanding, but also enrich the philosophical discourse on abstraction, generality, and the nature of mathematical structure itself.

title: Heavy quark bound states above deconfinement
