abstract: We investigate the survival of heavy quarkonium states in the quark–gluon plasma above the deconfinement temperature using potential models informed by lattice QCD data. Spectral functions are computed to assess binding and dissociation patterns for charmonium and bottomonium. Our results indicate that deeply bound states persist well above the critical temperature, while excited states dissolve rapidly, providing insight into quark–gluon plasma properties and heavy-ion collision observables.
introduction:
The study of heavy quark bound states, such as charmonium and bottomonium, has long been recognized as a powerful probe of the properties of strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions. In particular, the behavior of these states in a deconfined medium — the quark–gluon plasma (QGP) — provides valuable insight into color screening, in-medium modifications of the heavy quark potential, and the mechanisms governing hadronization in high-energy nuclear collisions. Since the seminal proposal by Matsui and Satz that suppression of the \( J/\psi \) yield could serve as a signature of QGP formation, a substantial body of theoretical and experimental work has been devoted to understanding the dissociation patterns of heavy quarkonia in hot and dense QCD matter.

From a theoretical perspective, the fate of quarkonium above the deconfinement temperature \( T_c \) is determined by the interplay between binding energy, medium-induced screening of the color force, and dynamical scattering with medium constituents. Potential models, informed by finite-temperature lattice QCD calculations of the static quark–antiquark free energy, suggest that the binding of the ground states may persist above \( T_c \), while excited states dissolve at lower temperatures. Spectral function analyses, both from lattice simulations and effective field theory approaches such as potential Non-Relativistic QCD (pNRQCD), have refined this picture, indicating a sequential melting pattern that depends on the quark mass, the principal quantum number, and the medium temperature.

Experimentally, measurements at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have revealed a rich phenomenology. Quarkonium suppression patterns vary with collision energy, centrality, and rapidity, and are further complicated by regeneration processes, in which deconfined heavy quarks recombine into bound states during the later stages of the medium evolution. The interplay between suppression and regeneration necessitates dynamical models that couple quarkonium transport to the hydrodynamic expansion of the QGP. In this context, distinguishing genuine deconfinement effects from cold nuclear matter modifications remains a central challenge.

Understanding heavy quark bound states above deconfinement is thus crucial for establishing quantitative connections between QCD theory and experimental observables. It requires a synthesis of nonperturbative calculations, effective theories, and realistic modeling of the space–time evolution of heavy-ion collisions. In this work, we investigate the in-medium properties of heavy quarkonia in the deconfined phase, combining lattice QCD inputs with potential model analyses to assess their survival probabilities and dissolution temperatures. Our goal is to elucidate the microscopic mechanisms driving quarkonium modification in the QGP and to provide theoretical constraints that can guide the interpretation of current and future experimental data.
conclusion: Our analysis indicates that heavy quark bound states can persist above the deconfinement temperature, though their stability is sensitive to screening effects and medium-induced modifications of the interquark potential. Spectral function studies and lattice QCD inputs suggest that ground-state quarkonia, particularly bottomonium, survive well into the quark–gluon plasma phase, while excited states dissolve rapidly. These findings have important implications for using quarkonium suppression as a probe of deconfinement. Future work combining improved lattice calculations with effective field theory approaches will further clarify the dynamics governing heavy quarkonia in extreme conditions.

title: Gradient Optics of subwavelength nanofilms
abstract: We investigate the optical properties of subwavelength nanofilms with continuously varying refractive index profiles, a regime described by gradient optics. Such nanofilms, whose thickness is well below the wavelength of incident light, exhibit unique interference, tunneling, and dispersion phenomena that cannot be captured by conventional thin-film theory. Using analytical modeling based on exact solutions of the wave equation in graded media, supported by numerical simulations, we explore how tailored index gradients enable broadband antireflection, enhanced transmission, and nontrivial phase modulation. The study reveals that smooth refractive index variations suppress Fresnel reflections, while specific gradient shapes induce controlled slow-light effects and asymmetric spectral responses. Experimental feasibility is discussed in terms of modern nanofabrication techniques, including atomic layer deposition and gradient doping. Our findings demonstrate that gradient-index nanofilms provide a versatile platform for compact, tunable, and low-loss photonic components, with potential applications in integrated optics, sensors, and metamaterial-inspired devices operating across visible and infrared spectral ranges.
introduction: Gradient optics in subwavelength nanofilms enables precise light control, offering novel opportunities for photonic device design and advanced optical functionalities.
conclusion: In summary, the study demonstrates that gradient optics provides an effective framework for understanding and engineering the optical response of subwavelength nanofilms. By tailoring refractive index profiles at the nanoscale, it is possible to achieve precise control over light propagation, reflection, and transmission, enabling functionalities beyond those of uniform films. The results highlight the significance of spatial dispersion and interference effects in shaping spectral characteristics. Such insights can inform the design of advanced photonic devices, including filters, sensors, and modulators. Future research may extend these concepts to nonlinear regimes and dynamic tunability, further expanding the scope of gradient nanophotonics.

title: A Mechanised Proof of G\"odel's Incompleteness Theorems using Nominal Isabelle
abstract: We present a fully mechanised proof of Gödel’s incompleteness theorems within the Nominal Isabelle framework. Our development formalises the syntax and semantics of first-order arithmetic using nominal techniques to handle binding and substitution rigorously. We construct Gödel numbering, arithmetise syntactic notions, and derive the fixed-point (diagonal) lemma. From this, we establish both the first and second incompleteness theorems for Peano Arithmetic, with all reasoning verified by Isabelle/HOL. This work demonstrates the feasibility of encoding intricate metamathematical arguments in a theorem prover, ensuring complete correctness and providing a reusable infrastructure for further formal logic developments.
introduction:
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems are among the most profound results in mathematical logic, showing inherent limitations of formal axiomatic systems capable of expressing elementary arithmetic. Their proofs rely on subtle syntactic encodings of semantic notions, such as provability, and on the careful construction of self-referential sentences. Formalising these results in a proof assistant both deepens our understanding and increases confidence in their correctness, but it also poses significant challenges. In particular, the reasoning involves intricate manipulations of binding structures, substitution, and variable renaming, all of which must be handled with precision to avoid errors.  

In this work we present a mechanised proof of Gödel’s first and second incompleteness theorems in the Nominal Isabelle framework. Nominal Isabelle provides robust support for reasoning about syntax with binders, enabling concise and faithful formalisation of the metatheory of first-order logic and primitive recursive arithmetic. Our development follows a textbook-style proof, but with explicit and rigorous treatment of all syntactic constructions and proofs within the logic of Isabelle/HOL. The resulting formalisation is self-contained, human-readable, and machine-verified, demonstrating that modern nominal techniques suffice to mechanise one of the most celebrated achievements of twentieth-century logic.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a fully mechanised proof of Gödel’s incompleteness theorems within the Nominal Isabelle framework. By leveraging the nominal approach to syntax with binding, we were able to represent the language of first-order arithmetic and reason about substitution, free variables, and α-equivalence in a manner closely aligned with traditional pen-and-paper proofs, yet with the additional assurance of formal verification. Our development formalises both the diagonalisation lemma and the fixed-point construction in a way that cleanly separates the syntactic and semantic components of the argument, thereby providing a modular structure amenable to reuse.

The mechanisation demonstrates that nominal techniques are well suited to capturing the intricate binding structures and substitution mechanisms inherent in Gödel’s proof. The formal proof not only mirrors the classical reasoning but also exposes and resolves subtleties that are often glossed over in informal treatments, such as issues of variable capture and the precise handling of meta-level assumptions. Moreover, the work serves as a case study in applying Nominal Isabelle to a landmark result in mathematical logic, illustrating how modern theorem proving environments can faithfully encode and verify sophisticated metamathematical arguments.

Our results contribute to the growing body of formally verified foundational mathematics and highlight the potential for interactive theorem provers to serve as trustworthy repositories of deep theoretical results. Future work could address the second incompleteness theorem in greater generality, explore alternative encodings of syntax within Isabelle/HOL, or investigate connections with other mechanisations of incompleteness in different proof assistants. Beyond Gödel’s theorems, the lessons learned here—particularly regarding the management of binding and substitution—are applicable to a wide range of formal developments in logic and computer science. By providing a machine-checked account of one of the most profound results in logic, this work underscores the value of mechanised reasoning in clarifying, preserving, and extending our understanding of fundamental mathematics.

title: Spin period evolution of the X-ray pulsar GX 1+4
abstract: We present a study of the long-term spin period evolution of the symbiotic X-ray pulsar GX 1+4, using archival timing measurements spanning more than four decades. GX 1+4 has exhibited one of the most dramatic torque reversals observed in accreting neutron stars, transitioning from rapid spin-up in the 1970s to sustained spin-down since the mid-1980s. By combining historical data from *CGRO*, *BeppoSAX*, *INTEGRAL*, and *Fermi*/GBM with recent observations, we trace the detailed changes in spin period and spin-down rate. Our analysis reveals persistent spin-down interspersed with episodes of torque variability, possibly linked to changes in the accretion flow from its M-giant companion. The measured long-term spin-down rate remains among the highest for known accretion-powered pulsars. We discuss the implications for models of quasi-spherical wind accretion and magnetospheric interaction, and suggest that variations in mass transfer rate and stellar wind structure play a dominant role in the observed torque behaviour of GX 1+4.
introduction: GX 1+4 is a symbiotic X-ray binary exhibiting remarkable long-term spin period evolution. Observations reveal alternating spin-up and spin-down episodes, offering crucial insights into accretion torque mechanisms and magnetic field interactions in neutron star systems.
conclusion: The spin period evolution of GX 1+4 reveals a complex interplay between accretion dynamics and torque mechanisms. Our analysis confirms the long-term transition from spin-up to spin-down, consistent with quasi-spherical accretion models in a symbiotic X-ray binary environment. Short-term fluctuations indicate variable mass-transfer rates, possibly linked to changes in the donor’s stellar wind. These results underscore the importance of continuous monitoring to disentangle transient behavior from secular trends, offering valuable constraints on accretion physics and neutron star magnetic field evolution in such systems.

title: Tomographic Study of Internal Erosion of Particle Flows in Porous Media
abstract: This study investigates the internal erosion mechanisms of particle-laden flows in porous media using high-resolution X-ray computed tomography. Experiments were conducted with controlled flow rates and particle size distributions to simulate sediment transport and clogging phenomena. Sequential tomographic scans captured the temporal evolution of pore structure and particle migration, enabling three-dimensional visualization and quantitative analysis of erosion patterns. Image processing techniques were applied to extract parameters such as porosity variation, preferential flow path development, and localized detachment zones. The results reveal that erosion initiates at constrictions with elevated shear stress and propagates along interconnected pore networks. These findings provide new insights into the dynamic interplay between hydrodynamics and granular transport, contributing to improved predictive models for filtration systems, soil stability, and subsurface fluid flow management.
introduction:
Internal erosion in porous media is a fundamental process with profound implications for natural and engineered systems. It refers to the migration and redistribution of fine particles within a solid matrix under the influence of fluid flow, often leading to structural degradation, permeability alteration, and in some cases catastrophic failure. This phenomenon is critical in geotechnical engineering, hydrology, petroleum engineering, and environmental science, where the stability and functionality of porous structures such as soils, aquifers, embankments, and filtration systems depend on the integrity of their internal architecture. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms governing internal erosion remain incompletely understood, particularly at the pore scale, where the interplay between fluid dynamics, particle transport, and the evolving geometry of the solid skeleton dictates the onset and progression of damage.

Classically, internal erosion has been studied through bulk measurements of hydraulic conductivity, pressure drop, or effluent particle concentration in laboratory column tests. While such macroscopic approaches have yielded valuable empirical relationships and failure criteria, they inherently obscure the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of erosion processes. The internal redistribution of particles is often non-uniform, proceeding through localized preferential pathways, clogging, or channel formation, which are challenging to infer from outlet measurements alone. Furthermore, the dynamic feedback between the evolving pore geometry and the local flow field can lead to complex, non-linear behavior that is not readily captured by continuum models without detailed experimental validation.

Recent advances in imaging technologies have opened new possibilities for probing the interior of opaque porous materials in situ and in real time. In particular, X-ray computed tomography (CT) has emerged as a powerful, non-destructive tool for three-dimensional visualization and quantification of internal structure at resolutions spanning from micrometers to millimeters. By acquiring sequential tomographic scans during flow experiments, it is possible to reconstruct the evolution of the pore network and solid phase distribution, thereby capturing the spatial patterns and kinetics of erosion as they unfold. This capability enables direct observation of processes such as particle detachment, migration, deposition, and the concomitant morphological changes in the porous framework, offering unprecedented insights into the micro-mechanisms of internal erosion.

Tomographic studies of particle-laden flows in porous media have been applied to a variety of systems, including granular filters, packed beds, and natural soils. These investigations have revealed that internal erosion is often highly localized, with preferential flow paths developing in response to subtle heterogeneities in pore size distribution or packing structure. They have also shown that clogging and erosion can coexist in different regions of the same specimen, and that the competition between these processes can strongly influence the bulk hydraulic response. Moreover, pore-scale visualization has facilitated the validation and refinement of numerical models, such as lattice-Boltzmann or discrete element simulations, which aim to predict erosion behavior based on fundamental physical principles.

Nevertheless, several challenges remain in leveraging tomography for erosion studies. Achieving adequate temporal resolution without sacrificing image quality is essential for capturing rapid events, yet scanning speed is limited by instrument capabilities and sample size. Image segmentation and quantitative analysis of evolving multiphase systems require robust algorithms to distinguish between solid matrix, mobile particles, and fluid-filled pores, especially when contrast between phases is low. Additionally, correlating structural changes with hydraulic measurements demands careful experimental design to synchronize imaging and flow data.

In this work, we present a tomographic investigation of internal erosion in particle flows through model porous media under controlled laboratory conditions. Our approach combines high-resolution X-ray computed tomography with simultaneous hydraulic monitoring, enabling us to directly link morphological evolution with changes in flow properties. By systematically varying flow rates, particle size distributions, and matrix configurations, we aim to elucidate the pore-scale mechanisms that govern the initiation, propagation, and stabilization of erosion channels. Particular emphasis is placed on quantifying spatial patterns of particle loss and deposition, assessing their impact on permeability evolution, and identifying key structural precursors to localized failure.

The insights gained from this study are expected to contribute to a more mechanistic understanding of internal erosion, thereby improving predictive capabilities for the performance and stability of porous systems in both natural and engineered contexts. Beyond geotechnical and hydrological applications, the methods and findings may also inform the design of filtration systems, enhanced oil recovery strategies, and remediation technologies where control over particle transport in porous media is critical. By integrating advanced tomographic imaging with quantitative analysis, this work seeks to bridge the gap between pore-scale processes and macroscopic behavior, offering a comprehensive framework for studying particle-fluid-solid interactions in complex porous structures.
conclusion: This study employed tomographic imaging to investigate the mechanisms and progression of internal erosion in particle-laden flows through porous media. The high-resolution datasets enabled the visualization and quantification of structural changes, particle migration, and pore connectivity loss over time. Results demonstrated that erosion onset is strongly influenced by local heterogeneities in pore geometry, leading to preferential flow paths and localized clogging. Progressive material removal altered the permeability distribution and, in some cases, triggered rapid channelization. The tomographic approach proved effective for capturing these dynamic processes in three dimensions, offering valuable insights beyond conventional measurement techniques. These findings contribute to a better understanding of erosion-driven permeability evolution and can inform predictive models for soil stability, filtration performance, and subsurface flow management. Future work will focus on coupling tomographic data with numerical simulations for improved forecasting of erosion onset and progression.

title: IFGAN: Missing Value Imputation using Feature-specific Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: We propose IFGAN, a novel framework for missing value imputation that employs feature-specific generative adversarial networks to model heterogeneous data distributions. Unlike conventional GAN-based methods that treat all features uniformly, IFGAN trains dedicated generators and discriminators for each feature, enabling fine-grained learning of conditional dependencies. This design enhances the accuracy and robustness of imputations, particularly in datasets with complex feature interactions and varied missingness patterns. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that IFGAN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art imputation methods in terms of predictive performance and imputation error, illustrating its effectiveness for improving downstream machine learning tasks in the presence of incomplete data.
introduction:
The presence of missing values is a pervasive challenge in real-world datasets, arising from diverse sources such as sensor malfunctions, data entry errors, privacy concerns, and incomplete surveys. Missing data can significantly degrade the performance of machine learning models, bias statistical estimates, and compromise the validity of downstream analyses. Consequently, effective handling of missing values is a critical prerequisite for reliable data-driven decision making. Traditional approaches to missing value imputation, such as mean or median substitution, k-nearest neighbors (KNN) imputation, and matrix factorization, often rely on strong assumptions about the underlying data distribution. While computationally inexpensive, these methods may fail to capture the complex, non-linear dependencies among features, resulting in suboptimal reconstructions, especially in high-dimensional or heterogeneous datasets.

In recent years, deep learning-based methods have emerged as powerful alternatives for missing value imputation, leveraging the representational capacity of neural networks to model intricate patterns in data. Among these, generative adversarial networks (GANs) have gained particular attention due to their ability to learn high-fidelity data distributions in an unsupervised or semi-supervised manner. GAN-based imputers, such as GAIN (Generative Adversarial Imputation Nets), frame the imputation problem as a data generation task, where a generator synthesizes plausible values for missing entries and a discriminator distinguishes between imputed and observed components. This adversarial training paradigm enables the imputer to produce realistic and coherent estimates that respect the joint distribution of the observed features.

However, existing GAN-based imputation frameworks often adopt a uniform generation strategy across all features, implicitly assuming that the same generative process is equally effective for every variable. In practice, features can differ widely in type, scale, distributional characteristics, and relationships with other variables. For example, continuous numerical variables may exhibit smooth correlations, while categorical variables may depend on discrete, domain-specific constraints. A single generator may struggle to capture such heterogeneity, particularly in datasets with mixed data types or strong feature-specific patterns. This limitation can lead to inaccurate imputations and reduced robustness, especially when the proportion of missing data is high.

To address these challenges, we propose IFGAN, a novel imputation framework based on Feature-specific Generative Adversarial Networks. IFGAN decomposes the imputation task into feature-level subproblems, assigning a dedicated generator–discriminator pair to each feature. This design enables each generator to focus on learning the conditional distribution of its target feature given all others, while the corresponding discriminator evaluates the fidelity of the imputed values for that specific feature. By tailoring the generative process to the statistical properties of individual features, IFGAN is able to more precisely model heterogeneous dependencies and better preserve the structural integrity of the dataset. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that IFGAN consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art imputation methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, highlighting the promise of feature-specific adversarial learning for missing data problems.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed IFGAN, a novel framework for missing value imputation that leverages feature-specific generative adversarial networks to model heterogeneous data distributions. By tailoring generators and discriminators to individual features, IFGAN captures complex inter-feature dependencies while preserving feature-specific statistical characteristics. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that IFGAN consistently outperforms conventional and recent deep learning-based imputation methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly under high missingness rates. Furthermore, the approach yields imputed datasets that maintain downstream predictive performance, underscoring its practical utility in real-world applications. The modular design of IFGAN also facilitates adaptability to diverse data types and missingness mechanisms. Future work will explore extensions to temporal and multi-modal datasets, as well as integration with uncertainty quantification to further enhance reliability in critical decision-making contexts.

title: Scalar field with the source in the form of the stress-energy tensor trace as a dark energy model
abstract: We investigate a scalar field model in which the source term is proportional to the trace of the stress-energy tensor, exploring its potential as a dark energy candidate. The field dynamics, coupled to matter via the trace, yield late-time cosmic acceleration without fine-tuning. We analyze cosmological solutions, stability conditions, and observational constraints, demonstrating consistency with current data and viability as an alternative to ΛCDM.
introduction:
The accelerated expansion of the Universe, inferred from Type Ia supernova observations and supported by cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies and large-scale structure surveys, remains one of the most profound challenges in modern cosmology. Within the standard ΛCDM model, this phenomenon is attributed to a cosmological constant, representing a uniform vacuum energy density. While remarkably successful in fitting observational data, the cosmological constant scenario faces conceptual difficulties, such as the fine-tuning and coincidence problems. These issues have motivated the exploration of alternative explanations, including modifications of gravity and dynamical dark energy models based on scalar fields.  

Scalar fields have been widely studied in cosmology, both as inflaton candidates in the early Universe and as possible drivers of late-time acceleration. In typical quintessence and k-essence models, the scalar field couples minimally to gravity and evolves under the influence of a potential. More generalized frameworks consider non-minimal couplings to curvature or to matter fields, leading to richer phenomenology and potentially alleviating fine-tuning constraints. One intriguing possibility is to consider a scalar field sourced by the trace of the stress-energy tensor of matter, \(T\), which vanishes for radiation but is nonzero for non-relativistic matter and vacuum energy.  

Such a coupling introduces a dynamical link between the scalar field evolution and the matter content of the Universe, allowing the field to respond to the changing equation of state of cosmic components. This mechanism may naturally trigger the onset of acceleration at late times, without requiring extremely small mass scales or finely tuned potentials. Moreover, the trace coupling can emerge in certain scalar-tensor theories or effective field theory descriptions of modified gravity.  

In this work, we investigate a cosmological model in which the source term for the scalar field is proportional to the stress-energy tensor trace. We derive the field equations, analyze the background dynamics, and assess the viability of the model in describing the observed cosmic acceleration.
conclusion: The proposed scalar field model, sourced by the stress-energy tensor trace, offers a viable framework for describing dark energy dynamics. Its coupling naturally links cosmic acceleration to matter content, potentially alleviating fine-tuning issues. Results indicate compatibility with observed expansion history, motivating further investigation into perturbative effects and constraints from large-scale structure and cosmological observations.

title: Chemical Case Studies in KeYmaera X
abstract: We present a set of chemical case studies developed and verified using the hybrid systems theorem prover KeYmaera X. These case studies model dynamic chemical processes, such as reaction kinetics, mixing, and transport phenomena, by combining continuous dynamics from differential equations with discrete control decisions. Our work demonstrates how formal verification can ensure safety, stability, and invariant properties of chemical systems subject to uncertainties and operational constraints. We illustrate the modeling methodology, formalization of chemical laws, and proof strategies tailored to hybrid dynamics. The case studies serve both as benchmarks for hybrid systems verification and as exemplars for applying formal methods in chemical engineering. Results highlight the potential of theorem proving to complement simulation-based analysis in guaranteeing correctness of safety-critical chemical processes.
introduction: Hybrid systems, which integrate discrete and continuous dynamics, are increasingly central to the modeling and analysis of chemical processes. Chemical systems often involve nonlinear reaction kinetics, safety-critical constraints, and interactions with control mechanisms, making their verification both challenging and essential. KeYmaera X, a theorem prover for differential dynamic logic (dL), provides a rigorous framework for the formal verification of hybrid systems by combining deductive reasoning with symbolic computation. While its applications have been demonstrated in domains such as automotive control and robotics, its potential for chemical case studies remains underexplored. This paper investigates the modeling and verification of representative chemical processes within KeYmaera X, focusing on both the correctness of dynamic behavior and the satisfaction of safety properties. We present detailed formalizations of chemical reaction models, including reaction rate equations and safety boundaries, and discuss proof strategies tailored to the nonlinear and coupled nature of chemical dynamics. Through these case studies, we aim to illustrate the feasibility and benefits of theorem-proving-based verification in chemical engineering contexts, highlighting both methodological insights and practical considerations for integrating formal verification into chemical process design and analysis.
conclusion: The presented chemical case studies demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of KeYmaera X in modeling, specifying, and verifying hybrid systems with chemical dynamics. By formally capturing both continuous reaction kinetics and discrete control interventions, the studies illustrate how differential dynamic logic can be used to ensure safety, stability, and performance properties of chemical processes. The ability to reason rigorously about nonlinear reaction rate laws, equilibrium conditions, and process constraints highlights the tool’s potential for advancing reliable design in chemical engineering. Moreover, the case studies reveal how formal verification can uncover subtle flaws in system assumptions and guide the refinement of process control strategies. While the examples considered are simplified, they establish a foundation for scaling to more complex, industrially relevant scenarios. Future work will extend these methods to larger reaction networks, integrate with experimental data, and explore automated proof strategies, further strengthening the role of formal verification in chemical process safety and optimization.

title: On Relations Between Tight Bounds for Symmetric $f$-Divergences and Binary Divergences
abstract: We investigate tight bounds for symmetric $f$-divergences in terms of binary divergences, establishing explicit relations that unify and extend known inequalities. By characterizing extremal distributions, we derive sharp constants and identify conditions for equality. Our approach reveals structural connections between general symmetric $f$-divergences and their binary counterparts, offering a framework for translating bounds and optimizing divergence measures in statistical inference and information theory.
introduction:
$f$-divergences$ constitute a broad and important class of discrepancy measures between probability distributions, encompassing many classical quantities such as the Kullback–Leibler divergence, total variation distance, Hellinger distance, and $\chi^2$-divergence. When the generating function is symmetric, the corresponding $f$-divergence inherits properties that facilitate both theoretical analysis and practical estimation. In various statistical and information-theoretic problems, it is of interest to determine tight bounds between different divergence measures, as such relationships can yield sharper inequalities, improved performance guarantees, and deeper structural insights.

A particularly fruitful approach to studying $f$-divergences exploits their reduction to binary experiments. In the binary case, divergence measures simplify to functions of a single parameter, enabling explicit computations and geometric interpretations. For symmetric $f$-divergences, this reduction can often be leveraged to derive bounds that are tight in the general setting. Such bounds, when expressed in terms of binary divergences, provide both conceptual clarity and computational tractability.

Recent work has explored extremal relationships between pairs of divergences, identifying the distributions that achieve the limits and characterizing the functional dependence between the measures. However, a systematic understanding of the precise connections between tight bounds for symmetric $f$-divergences and their binary counterparts remains incomplete. In this paper, we investigate these connections, establishing conditions under which the bound for arbitrary distributions is attained in the binary case, and showing how this equivalence can be used to derive and unify several known inequalities. Our results contribute to the broader program of relating information measures through sharp, interpretable, and computationally accessible bounds.
conclusion: In this work, we established explicit connections between tight bounds for symmetric \( f \)-divergences and their binary counterparts. By leveraging the structure of binary divergences, we derived sharper inequalities that hold uniformly over all probability distributions, thereby unifying and extending several known results. Our analysis revealed that optimal bounds in the binary setting naturally induce optimal bounds in the general case, highlighting the fundamental role of binary models in understanding divergence behavior. These findings not only clarify the interplay between different divergence measures but also provide a systematic approach for deriving new inequalities. Future research may explore analogous relationships for asymmetric divergences and higher-order generalizations.

title: Topological Disorder in Spin Models on Hierarchical Lattices
abstract: We investigate the effects of topological disorder on spin models defined over hierarchical lattices, focusing on variations in connectivity and scaling structure. Using real-space renormalization group techniques, we analyze thermodynamic properties and critical behavior under quenched randomness in lattice topology. Our results reveal shifts in critical points, modified universality classes, and nontrivial crossover phenomena driven by geometric fluctuations. Comparisons with regular hierarchical structures highlight the interplay between topology and spin correlations, offering insight into disordered systems with fractal-like geometries across statistical and condensed matter physics contexts.
introduction:
The study of spin models has long provided a fertile ground for exploring fundamental aspects of statistical mechanics, critical phenomena, and phase transitions. Among the many platforms for such investigations, hierarchical lattices occupy a special place due to their recursive structure, which allows for exact or quasi-exact renormalization group treatments. By replacing translational invariance with self-similarity, hierarchical lattices offer a controllable setting in which the interplay between geometry, disorder, and interactions can be systematically examined. In recent years, growing attention has been directed toward understanding how various forms of disorder—whether in couplings, external fields, or topology—affect the thermodynamic and critical properties of spin systems. While quenched randomness in bond strengths or site occupancies has been extensively studied, the role of topological disorder, i.e., randomness in the connectivity pattern of the lattice itself, remains less well understood, particularly in hierarchical geometries.

Topological disorder can arise naturally in physical systems where the underlying connectivity is neither perfectly periodic nor purely random, but instead exhibits fluctuations due to structural defects, growth processes, or intentional design. In network science, such structural variability is known to influence dynamical processes ranging from percolation to synchronization. In the context of spin models, changes in the coordination number distribution or in the arrangement of bonds can modify local environments, alter correlation pathways, and ultimately shift phase boundaries or universality classes. Hierarchical lattices, with their flexible construction rules, present an ideal framework for introducing and controlling such topological variability in a mathematically tractable manner.

Previous investigations into spin models on hierarchical lattices have largely focused on deterministic constructions, such as the Migdal–Kadanoff or diamond hierarchical lattices, where the exact recursion relations for thermodynamic quantities can be derived. These studies have yielded deep insights into critical exponents, scaling functions, and crossover phenomena. Extensions to include quenched bond randomness have revealed rich phase diagrams and novel fixed points. However, the incorporation of topological disorder into hierarchical models introduces new challenges. The recursive structure must now be generalized to accommodate stochastic rules for lattice generation, leading to ensembles of graphs rather than a single deterministic object. This in turn requires averaging procedures over both thermal fluctuations and structural realizations, complicating the renormalization group analysis.

A systematic study of topological disorder in such settings is motivated not only by theoretical curiosity but also by potential applications. Many real-world systems—such as disordered magnets, polymer networks, and certain classes of porous or granular materials—exhibit hierarchical organization combined with irregular connectivity. Understanding how such structural irregularities influence collective behavior is essential for developing predictive models. Furthermore, hierarchical lattices with topological disorder can serve as simplified analogues for more complex disordered networks, allowing for controlled exploration of how geometry and randomness interplay in determining macroscopic properties.

In this work, we investigate spin models defined on hierarchical lattices endowed with topological disorder. By introducing randomness into the recursive construction process, we generate ensembles of lattices characterized by distributions over local connectivities and bond arrangements. We develop renormalization group recursion relations that incorporate both thermal and topological averaging, enabling us to analyze how disorder strength and structural correlations affect critical points and scaling behavior. Our approach provides a bridge between deterministic hierarchical models and fully random networks, offering new insights into the role of connectivity fluctuations in cooperative phenomena. Through this framework, we aim to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms by which topological disorder modifies the phase structure and universality of spin systems.
conclusion: In summary, we have investigated the effects of topological disorder on spin models defined over hierarchical lattices, elucidating how the interplay between lattice geometry and randomness influences critical behavior. By employing exact and numerical renormalization techniques, we demonstrated that hierarchical structures amplify the impact of disorder, leading to nontrivial shifts in transition points and, in some regimes, to the emergence of novel scaling laws. The results highlight the sensitivity of universality classes to variations in connectivity patterns and fractal dimensionality, emphasizing that topological randomness cannot be treated as a mere perturbation. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of disordered systems, offering a framework for exploring analogous effects in other complex networks. Future work may extend this approach to quantum spin systems and non-equilibrium dynamics on similarly disordered hierarchical substrates.

title: Dialect-robust Evaluation of Generated Text
abstract: Evaluating the quality of generated text often assumes standard language norms, overlooking the variability introduced by dialectal differences. This bias can lead to systematic underestimation of quality for outputs in non-standard or underrepresented dialects, reinforcing inequities in language technologies. We propose a dialect-robust evaluation framework that explicitly accounts for dialectal variation in both human and automated assessments. Our approach combines dialect-aware reference construction, linguistic normalization, and bias-adjusted scoring to produce fairer evaluations across diverse language varieties. We curate benchmark datasets spanning multiple English dialects, including African American English, Caribbean English, and regional British variants, and conduct experiments with leading large language models. Results show that conventional metrics penalize dialectal features, while our framework yields more consistent correlations with human judgments across dialects. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dialect-robust evaluation can reveal genuine model capabilities obscured by standard metrics. This work highlights the importance of equitable evaluation methodologies and provides practical tools for researchers and practitioners to assess generated text in a linguistically inclusive manner.
introduction:
Natural language generation (NLG) systems are increasingly deployed across domains such as customer service, education, and healthcare, where they interact with users from diverse linguistic backgrounds. While recent evaluation benchmarks have driven impressive advances in fluency, coherence, and factuality, these benchmarks overwhelmingly focus on a narrow range of standardized language varieties. Consequently, the performance of NLG models in handling dialectal variation—differences in vocabulary, syntax, phonology, and discourse patterns tied to regional, ethnic, or social identities—remains underexplored. This gap poses both practical and ethical risks: systems that fail to accommodate or accurately represent dialects may alienate users, propagate bias, or contribute to linguistic marginalization.

Dialect-robust evaluation seeks to assess whether generated text maintains quality, accuracy, and appropriateness across dialectal forms. Such evaluation is challenging for several reasons. First, linguistic resources for many dialects are scarce, limiting the availability of representative corpora for training and testing. Second, dialectal variation can be subtle and context-dependent, complicating automated measurement. Third, quality dimensions such as grammaticality or naturalness may need to be redefined relative to the norms of each dialect, requiring evaluators with specific sociolinguistic expertise.

Existing work on robustness in NLG has primarily addressed topical shifts, domain adaptation, or noise tolerance, with only limited attention to dialectal variation. Studies in speech recognition and machine translation suggest that dialect-aware evaluation can reveal significant performance disparities masked by standard benchmarks. However, these findings have not been systematically extended to text generation tasks, leaving open questions about the magnitude and nature of dialect-related degradation in generated outputs.

In this paper, we introduce a framework for dialect-robust evaluation of generated text that integrates dialect-specific test sets, human and automatic metrics adapted to dialectal norms, and analysis methods for identifying systematic errors. We apply this framework to multiple NLG tasks and dialects, demonstrating its utility in uncovering biases and guiding model improvements. By foregrounding dialectal diversity in evaluation, our work aims to promote more inclusive NLG systems that respect and reflect the full spectrum of linguistic variation.
conclusion:
This work has examined the challenges and opportunities associated with evaluating generated text across dialectal variation, with a particular focus on ensuring that evaluation methods remain robust to linguistic diversity. Through a series of empirical analyses, we demonstrated that widely used automatic evaluation metrics, as well as human evaluation protocols, can exhibit systematic biases when confronted with text in non-standard dialects or regionally marked varieties. Such biases can distort performance estimates, unfairly penalizing systems that produce dialectally faithful outputs, and potentially reinforcing linguistic inequities.

Our investigation revealed that many current evaluation pipelines implicitly assume a standardized variety as the normative benchmark, leading to diminished metric scores for otherwise fluent, contextually appropriate, and semantically accurate outputs in other varieties. We showed that this effect is not merely a consequence of surface-level lexical differences, but often reflects deeper mismatches in syntactic, morphological, and idiomatic patterns. In human evaluations, we observed similar tendencies, with annotators’ judgments influenced by familiarity with the dialect in question, underscoring the importance of annotator training and demographic diversity.

To address these shortcomings, we proposed a framework for dialect-robust evaluation that integrates three complementary strategies: dialect-aware reference construction, metric adaptation via dialectal embeddings and normalization, and structured human evaluation guidelines that explicitly account for variation. Our experiments indicated that these strategies substantially reduce evaluation disparities, yielding performance estimates that more accurately reflect model capabilities across dialects. In doing so, they also facilitate the development of systems that can serve a broader range of language users without privileging a single standardized form.

The implications of this study extend beyond the immediate scope of text generation evaluation. As natural language processing systems are increasingly deployed in multilingual and multicultural contexts, the ability to fairly and accurately assess outputs in diverse linguistic settings is essential for equitable technology design. Dialect-robust evaluation is a necessary step toward mitigating the risk of marginalizing speakers of minority or non-standard varieties, and toward fostering inclusivity in language technologies. Moreover, our findings suggest that robust evaluation can drive model improvements: when metrics and human judgments faithfully reward high-quality dialectal output, system designers have clearer incentives to support linguistic diversity.

Future work should explore expanding the set of dialects and sociolects considered, incorporating low-resource varieties, and refining metric calibration techniques. Additionally, longitudinal studies could assess how dialect-robust evaluation protocols influence the evolution of model behavior over time. By continuing to refine and adopt dialect-robust practices, the research community can ensure that progress in text generation reflects genuine advances in communicative competence across the full spectrum of language use, rather than improvements narrowly tailored to a single dominant variety. In this way, evaluation itself can become a tool for promoting linguistic equity alongside technical performance.

title: Tevatron Combination and Higgs Boson Properties
abstract: We present the combined results of Higgs boson searches performed by the CDF and DØ collaborations at the Fermilab Tevatron collider, analyzing up to 10 fb⁻¹ of proton–antiproton collision data at √s = 1.96 TeV. The combination incorporates multiple production mechanisms and decay channels, with advanced multivariate techniques to enhance sensitivity. An excess of events is observed near a Higgs boson mass of 125 GeV, consistent with the Standard Model expectation. The local significance of the excess reaches approximately three standard deviations. Measurements of production rates and decay branching fractions are compatible with Standard Model predictions within uncertainties. These results provide independent confirmation of the Higgs boson discovery and contribute to the global determination of its properties, including couplings to fermions and bosons.
introduction:
The discovery of the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in 2012 marked a cornerstone in particle physics, confirming the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking as described by the Standard Model (SM). Prior to this breakthrough, extensive searches for the Higgs boson had been conducted at various facilities, including the Tevatron collider at Fermilab, which operated proton–antiproton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 1.96 TeV. The Tevatron’s two multi-purpose detectors, CDF and DØ, accumulated substantial datasets, enabling sensitive searches for Higgs boson production across a range of masses, particularly in the low-mass region where associated production with a vector boson followed by decay into bottom–antibottom quark pairs is dominant.

Combining results from multiple experiments and search channels is essential to maximize sensitivity and achieve robust constraints on Higgs boson properties. The Tevatron combination program brought together the full statistical power of CDF and DØ, employing advanced multivariate techniques, consistent signal and background modeling, and rigorous treatment of systematic uncertainties. These combined analyses provided some of the most stringent pre-LHC limits on the SM Higgs boson mass and, in certain mass ranges, offered evidence consistent with its production.

Beyond exclusion limits, the Tevatron data also enabled measurements of Higgs boson coupling strengths, production rates, and decay branching ratios, offering complementary information to that obtained at the LHC. In particular, the Tevatron’s sensitivity to fermionic decay modes provided an important cross-check of the boson’s properties and its consistency with SM predictions.

This paper presents the final Tevatron combination of Higgs boson searches, incorporating the complete Run II datasets from both experiments. We describe the datasets, analysis methods, and combination procedure, and we summarize the resulting constraints on the Higgs boson mass, signal strength, and couplings. The results are discussed in the context of SM expectations and compared with measurements from other facilities, highlighting the enduring scientific value of the Tevatron program.
conclusion: The combined results from the Tevatron experiments provide a coherent and consistent picture of Higgs boson production and decay in proton–antiproton collisions. By integrating data from multiple final states and employing advanced statistical techniques, the analyses achieve improved sensitivity across a broad mass range. The observed excesses and measured signal strengths align with Standard Model expectations within uncertainties, offering complementary constraints to those obtained at the LHC. Furthermore, the Tevatron measurements contribute unique information on fermionic couplings and production via associated channels. These results not only reinforce the discovery of the Higgs boson but also enhance our understanding of its properties, underscoring the enduring value of the Tevatron legacy in particle physics.

title: Unsupervised learning with sparse space-and-time autoencoders
abstract: We present an unsupervised learning framework using sparse space-and-time autoencoders for high-dimensional spatiotemporal data. Our model leverages sparsity to efficiently capture structure across both spatial and temporal domains, reducing computational cost while preserving representational power. By jointly encoding spatial and temporal dependencies, the approach learns compact latent embeddings, enabling effective reconstruction and downstream analysis without supervision, and demonstrating strong performance on complex real-world datasets.
introduction: Unsupervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extracting meaningful representations from high-dimensional data without reliance on extensive manual annotations. In spatiotemporal domains, such as video analysis and dynamic 3D scene understanding, learning compact and informative features remains challenging due to the large volume and sparsity of data across both space and time. Autoencoders provide a natural framework for this task, enabling the encoding of rich structures into low-dimensional latent spaces while preserving essential dynamics. However, conventional dense architectures are computationally inefficient and prone to overfitting in sparse settings. Sparse space-and-time autoencoders address these limitations by exploiting inherent structural sparsity, reducing complexity, and enhancing scalability. This work investigates unsupervised learning with such models, aiming to capture robust spatiotemporal representations that generalize effectively across diverse, sparsely sampled environments.
conclusion: We presented an unsupervised framework using sparse space-and-time autoencoders to learn compact, discriminative spatiotemporal representations. Experiments demonstrate robust performance across diverse datasets, highlighting efficiency and scalability. Future work will explore richer temporal dynamics, multimodal integration, and downstream transfer to further enhance representation quality and generalization in complex real-world scenarios.

title: Probabilistic Temporal Reasoning with Endogenous Change
abstract: We present a formal framework for probabilistic temporal reasoning in dynamic domains where change is driven by both exogenous events and endogenous processes. While much prior work in temporal probabilistic models has focused on externally triggered events, many real-world phenomena evolve through continuous or discrete endogenous mechanisms whose timing and effects are uncertain. Our approach integrates a representation of endogenous change into a probabilistic temporal reasoning architecture, enabling coherent inference about system states over time in the presence of interacting causal processes. We model endogenous change as arising from stochastic processes whose hazard rates depend on the current state, allowing the prediction of future events and the updating of beliefs when partial observations are obtained. The framework supports both projection—predicting likely future evolutions from incomplete initial information—and explanation—inferring the most probable histories consistent with observed evidence. We present algorithms for incremental belief updating that exploit structure in the temporal and causal dependencies to improve computational efficiency. The proposed methods are evaluated on scenarios involving multiple interacting processes, demonstrating their ability to capture complex temporal patterns such as competing risks, cascading effects, and delayed consequences. Our results indicate that explicitly modeling endogenous change yields more accurate and robust inferences than approaches that treat such processes as purely exogenous or ignore their temporal dynamics. This work contributes to bridging the gap between probabilistic reasoning and realistic temporal process modeling, with potential applications in domains such as medicine, industrial process monitoring, and environmental forecasting.
introduction:
Reasoning about how the world evolves over time is central to many areas of artificial intelligence, from robotics and autonomous systems to decision support and diagnosis. In realistic settings, an agent must contend not only with uncertainty about the initial state of the world and the effects of actions, but also with ongoing, endogenous processes that cause change independently of explicit interventions. For example, a patient’s medical condition may improve or deteriorate naturally, a mechanical system may wear down gradually, or environmental conditions may shift due to internal dynamics. Capturing such processes requires temporal models that can represent probabilistic change occurring continuously or at discrete intervals, even in the absence of external actions.

Classical approaches to temporal reasoning have often focused on exogenous change—state transitions triggered directly by modeled events or actions. While these models are well suited for planning or event recognition in controlled environments, they can be inadequate when endogenous processes play a significant role. Probabilistic temporal reasoning frameworks, such as dynamic Bayesian networks or continuous-time Markov processes, have the expressive capacity to represent such processes, but often require strong independence assumptions or discretizations that limit their applicability in complex domains.

The challenge lies in integrating endogenous change into a coherent probabilistic framework that supports reasoning over extended time horizons, accommodates uncertainty in both process dynamics and observations, and remains computationally tractable. This integration must allow inference about past and future states, evaluation of the likelihood of observed sequences, and prediction of potential evolutions under varying conditions.

In this work, we present a probabilistic temporal reasoning framework that explicitly models endogenous change alongside exogenous events, enabling richer and more accurate inferences about dynamic systems. Our approach combines structured representation of process dynamics with efficient inference algorithms, balancing expressiveness and scalability. We demonstrate its applicability across domains where endogenous change is intrinsic, and show that accounting for such processes leads to more robust predictions and decisions under uncertainty.
conclusion:
This work has examined the problem of probabilistic temporal reasoning in domains where change is driven endogenously by the system’s own dynamics, rather than solely by exogenous events. We have proposed a formal framework that integrates probabilistic models of uncertainty with temporal projection mechanisms capable of representing and reasoning about continuous and discrete changes initiated internally. By explicitly modeling endogenous causal processes, our approach captures the persistence, decay, and triggering of states over time in a way that purely event-driven or memoryless models cannot.  

Through this lens, we have shown how probabilistic temporal reasoning can accommodate incomplete or noisy observations, while still maintaining coherent predictions about the evolution of system states. Our framework supports the incremental incorporation of new evidence, updating beliefs about both the timing and likelihood of changes. This yields more accurate temporal inferences in domains such as autonomous systems, process monitoring, and dynamic situation assessment, where internal change mechanisms play a crucial role.  

The results suggest that coupling endogenous change models with probabilistic inference not only improves predictive performance but also enhances interpretability, as the temporal causal structure remains explicit. Moreover, the framework is compatible with a range of underlying probabilistic formalisms, enabling integration with existing reasoning systems.  

Future work will explore scaling these methods to large, richly interconnected domains, as well as extending the representation to handle more complex feedback loops and multi-scale temporal dynamics. Another promising direction lies in integrating learning mechanisms that can automatically induce endogenous process models from observational data. Overall, this research underscores the importance of explicitly representing endogenous change in probabilistic temporal reasoning, providing a principled basis for more robust and context-sensitive temporal inference.

title: An extremely peculiar hot subdwarf with a ten-thousand-fold excess of zirconium, yttrium, and strontium
abstract: We report the discovery and detailed spectroscopic analysis of an extraordinarily peculiar hot subdwarf star exhibiting extreme overabundances of certain heavy elements. High-resolution optical spectra obtained with the ESO Very Large Telescope reveal a photospheric composition dominated by helium, with hydrogen severely depleted. Most strikingly, the star’s spectrum is characterized by exceptionally strong absorption lines of singly ionized zirconium, yttrium, and strontium, with measured abundances exceeding solar values by factors of order 10⁴. These enhancements are unprecedented among hot subdwarfs and cannot be explained by standard diffusion or radiative levitation models alone. The effective temperature and surface gravity, derived from non-LTE model atmosphere fits, place the object among the helium-rich sdB/sdO transition stars. The absence of detectable carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen enrichment, combined with the extreme heavy-element anomalies, suggests a selective atmospheric process or external accretion scenario that has yet to be identified. Radial velocity measurements show no significant variability over a baseline of several months, arguing against a short-period binary companion as the source of the anomalies. The rarity of such chemical peculiarities in this class of stars raises important questions about nucleosynthesis, mass loss, and transport processes in post–red giant branch evolution. We discuss possible origins of the observed abundance pattern, including diffusion in a stable, radiatively supported atmosphere and the remnants of prior s-process enrichment, and highlight the need for further ultraviolet spectroscopy to constrain the full elemental inventory and physical mechanisms responsible.
introduction:
Hot subdwarfs are evolved, compact stars located at the blue end of the horizontal branch, generally understood to be core helium-burning objects with very thin hydrogen envelopes. Their atmospheres are typically dominated by hydrogen or helium and, in many cases, exhibit anomalous abundances of certain heavy elements. These peculiarities are often attributed to atomic diffusion processes, including radiative levitation and gravitational settling, which can strongly modify surface compositions compared to initial stellar abundances. While moderate overabundances of iron-group and some heavy elements have been documented, extreme enhancements remain rare and poorly understood.

In this work we present the discovery and analysis of an extraordinarily peculiar hot subdwarf whose optical spectrum reveals extraordinary overabundances—by factors approaching 10⁴—of zirconium, yttrium, and strontium. Such enhancements, far exceeding those observed in chemically peculiar main-sequence stars or other hot subdwarfs, challenge existing models of diffusion and radiative support. The star’s atmospheric parameters place it firmly within the hot subdwarf regime, yet its abundance pattern is unlike any known object in this class.

The identification of such an extreme chemical anomaly offers a unique laboratory for studying the interplay between diffusion, weak stellar winds, and possibly binary evolution in shaping surface compositions. It also raises questions about the nucleosynthetic history and prior evolutionary phases of the star. Here we describe the observational data, spectral analysis, and abundance determinations, and we discuss the implications for diffusion theory and the broader understanding of heavy-element anomalies in hot subdwarfs. This remarkable object extends the known limits of atmospheric chemical stratification in evolved stars.
conclusion:
The discovery and analysis of this hot subdwarf have revealed an extraordinarily unusual chemical composition, characterized by enhancements of zirconium, yttrium, and strontium by factors of approximately 10,000 relative to solar abundances. Such extreme overabundances are unprecedented among hot subdwarfs and challenge current models of diffusion and radiative levitation in stellar atmospheres. The absence of comparable anomalies in other heavy elements suggests a highly selective enrichment process, possibly linked to a delicate interplay between atomic diffusion, weak stellar winds, and the star’s specific temperature–gravity regime.  

Spectroscopic modelling has demonstrated that these enhancements are robust against reasonable variations in stellar parameters, reinforcing the conclusion that they are intrinsic to the star and not artefacts of measurement or modelling. The narrowness of the identified absorption lines supports the interpretation of a stable, slowly rotating atmosphere where diffusion processes can operate efficiently over long timescales.  

This object thus represents an extreme example of chemical stratification in hot subdwarfs, offering a unique test case for theoretical studies of atomic diffusion under unusual conditions. Further investigation, including time-series spectroscopy and ultraviolet observations, will be critical to probing the depth dependence of these anomalies and assessing their stability. Additionally, a systematic search for similar objects in large spectroscopic surveys could establish whether this star is a singular outlier or part of a rare but physically significant subpopulation. Ultimately, understanding the origin of these extraordinary abundances will advance our knowledge of stellar surface chemistry and the microphysical processes shaping the atmospheres of evolved stars.

title: Alleviating the $\bar B \to D \tau \nu$ and $\bar B \to D^* \tau \nu_\tau$ puzzle in the MSSM
abstract: We investigate the potential of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) to address the long-standing discrepancies in the semileptonic decays $\bar B \to D \tau \nu$ and $\bar B \to D^* \tau \nu_\tau$. Employing a comprehensive analysis of MSSM parameter space, we explore the impact of charged Higgs exchange and loop-induced corrections on the relevant Wilson coefficients. Our results show that, within experimentally allowed regions, supersymmetric contributions can significantly reduce the tension between Standard Model predictions and current measurements of $R(D)$ and $R(D^*)$. We further discuss constraints from flavor observables and direct searches, highlighting viable scenarios consistent with all data.
introduction:
In recent years, semileptonic decays of $B$ mesons involving tau leptons have attracted significant attention as sensitive probes of possible physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). In particular, the ratios  
\[
R(D) = \frac{\mathcal{B}(\bar{B} \to D \tau \bar{\nu}_\tau)}{\mathcal{B}(\bar{B} \to D \ell \bar{\nu}_\ell)}, \quad
R(D^*) = \frac{\mathcal{B}(\bar{B} \to D^* \tau \bar{\nu}_\tau)}{\mathcal{B}(\bar{B} \to D^* \ell \bar{\nu}_\ell)}, \quad \ell = e, \mu ,
\]
provide theoretically clean observables in which many hadronic uncertainties cancel. The SM predictions for these quantities are robust, relying on well–understood heavy quark effective theory (HQET) inputs, and are currently known with percent-level precision.  

Experimental measurements by the BaBar, Belle, and LHCb collaborations have persistently reported values of $R(D)$ and $R(D^*)$ in excess of their SM predictions. The combined averages, as compiled by the Heavy Flavor Averaging Group (HFLAV), indicate deviations at the level of roughly $3\sigma$ from the SM expectations. While the statistical significance of the discrepancy has fluctuated with new data, the trend of elevated central values for both ratios has remained stable. This so-called $R(D^{(*)})$ anomaly has motivated extensive theoretical work to understand whether it could be accommodated within extensions of the SM.  

From a theoretical standpoint, these decays are particularly sensitive to contributions from charged scalar or vector particles that couple preferentially to third-generation fermions. In the SM, the process proceeds dominantly via a tree-level $W$ boson exchange, yielding a purely left-handed charged current interaction. New physics (NP) can alter the decay rates either by introducing additional operators—scalar, pseudoscalar, tensor, or right-handed vector currents—or by modifying the SM operator coefficients. Consequently, a variety of NP frameworks, including leptoquark models, extended Higgs sectors, and scenarios with additional gauge bosons, have been examined as potential explanations.  

The Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) is a particularly well-motivated candidate to address such anomalies. As a minimal supersymmetric extension of the SM, it provides a rich particle spectrum, natural dark matter candidates, and gauge coupling unification, while also accommodating new sources of flavor and CP violation. In the MSSM, charged Higgs bosons arise naturally within the two-Higgs-doublet structure, and their couplings to fermions are enhanced for large values of $\tan\beta$. These charged Higgs contributions can significantly modify the $\bar{B} \to D^{(*)}\tau\nu$ decay rates at tree level, and additional loop-induced effects from supersymmetric particles can further alter the effective Wilson coefficients.  

However, explaining the $R(D^{(*)})$ anomalies within the MSSM is nontrivial. The parameter space is constrained by direct searches for supersymmetric particles, limits from flavor-changing neutral currents, precision electroweak data, and in particular, by $B\to X_s\gamma$ and $B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$ measurements. Moreover, the same charged Higgs coupling structure that can enhance $R(D)$ may produce tension with other observables unless carefully balanced.  

In this work, we re-examine the potential of the MSSM to alleviate the $\bar{B} \to D \tau \nu$ and $\bar{B} \to D^* \tau \nu_\tau$ anomalies. We explore both tree-level charged Higgs exchange and the impact of loop-induced corrections to the relevant effective operators, paying special attention to viable regions of parameter space consistent with all current experimental bounds. Our goal is to determine whether the MSSM can reconcile the measured values of $R(D)$ and $R(D^*)$ with other flavor and collider constraints, thereby providing a coherent supersymmetric explanation of the observed deviations.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the potential of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) to address the long-standing anomalies observed in the semileptonic decays $\bar B \to D \tau \nu$ and $\bar B \to D^* \tau \nu_\tau$. Motivated by persistent deviations from Standard Model (SM) predictions in the ratios $R(D)$ and $R(D^*)$, as reported by BaBar, Belle, and LHCb, we explored whether MSSM parameter space can accommodate these measurements while remaining consistent with other flavour, collider, and precision constraints. Our analysis incorporated both tree-level and loop-induced contributions, with special attention paid to charged Higgs exchange and possible enhancements from supersymmetric particle loops.

We have shown that, within the MSSM framework, it is possible to generate sizable modifications to the relevant effective operators governing $b \to c \tau \nu$ transitions. In particular, the charged Higgs boson can contribute at tree level to scalar-type operators, and its effects can be amplified in regions of parameter space with large $\tan\beta$ and relatively light charged Higgs masses. Furthermore, loop corrections involving sleptons, charginos, and neutralinos can non-trivially affect the Wilson coefficients, providing additional flexibility to reconcile the observed deviations. By performing a numerical scan over the MSSM parameters, we identified viable regions where the predicted $R(D)$ and $R(D^*)$ values are simultaneously brought into closer agreement with the experimental world averages, without violating bounds from $B \to X_s \gamma$, $B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$, and direct searches for supersymmetric particles.

Our findings indicate that the MSSM can indeed alleviate, though not completely eliminate, the tension between SM predictions and current experimental data for these decay modes. The allowed regions generally require a moderately light charged Higgs and non-negligible contributions from supersymmetric loops, pointing to a correlated pattern of deviations in other flavour observables that could be tested in upcoming measurements. In addition, the preferred parameter space often predicts distinctive collider signatures, such as enhanced production of sleptons or charginos, which could be probed at the High-Luminosity LHC or future lepton colliders.

In summary, the MSSM remains a viable candidate for explaining the $\bar B \to D \tau \nu$ and $\bar B \to D^* \tau \nu_\tau$ anomalies, offering a coherent framework that links flavour physics anomalies with potential signals at high-energy experiments. Future improvements in experimental precision, both in flavour and direct searches, will be crucial in further testing this scenario and clarifying the role of supersymmetry in resolving these intriguing deviations.

title: Non-Markovian Control with Gated End-to-End Memory Policy Networks
abstract: We propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for non-Markovian control tasks based on Gated End-to-End Memory Policy Networks (GEMPNs). Many real-world control problems exhibit partial observability and long-term temporal dependencies that challenge conventional Markovian assumptions. Our approach integrates recurrent gating mechanisms with a differentiable memory architecture to enable selective reading, writing, and forgetting of past observations over extended horizons. By coupling the memory with a policy network in an end-to-end trainable architecture, GEMPNs learn to encode task-relevant histories and exploit them for action selection without requiring explicit state estimation. We evaluate the method on a suite of synthetic and continuous-control benchmarks designed to capture non-Markovian dynamics, including tasks with delayed rewards, hidden goals, and temporally extended dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that GEMPNs consistently outperform recurrent baselines such as LSTMs and GRUs, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence. The proposed framework offers a principled and scalable approach for addressing memory-dependent decision-making, bridging the gap between model-free reinforcement learning and non-Markovian control, and enabling robust performance in environments where critical information is dispersed over time.
introduction:
Sequential decision-making in partially observable environments presents a fundamental challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents. In such settings, the agent does not have direct access to the complete state of the environment but instead receives noisy or incomplete observations over time. This partial observability induces *non-Markovian* dynamics from the agent’s perspective: the optimal action may depend on a history of prior observations and actions, rather than solely on the current observation. Classical RL algorithms, designed under the Markov decision process (MDP) assumption, often fail to capture these long-term dependencies, leading to suboptimal performance.

A natural approach to non-Markovian control is to equip agents with an internal memory mechanism that allows them to integrate information over extended time horizons. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units and gated recurrent units (GRUs), have been widely adopted for this purpose, as they can, in principle, store and retrieve relevant features from past observations. However, recurrent architectures often struggle to selectively focus on specific, task-relevant pieces of information in long sequences, especially when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. Moreover, backpropagation through long temporal spans can be computationally expensive and prone to vanishing or exploding gradients.

Memory-augmented neural networks offer a promising alternative by explicitly separating memory storage from control flow. End-to-end memory networks, initially proposed for question answering in natural language processing, incorporate an external memory component and a learned attention mechanism for retrieving relevant information based on a query. By allowing the policy to read from and write to such an external memory, the agent can maintain a structured representation of past experience, and dynamically attend to parts of the history most relevant to the current decision. This explicit addressing mechanism can mitigate some of the difficulties inherent in purely recurrent models.

In this work, we introduce *gated end-to-end memory policy networks* for non-Markovian control tasks. Our architecture combines the temporal integration capabilities of gated recurrent units with the selective recall afforded by external memory modules.
