The gating mechanism regulates the flow of information between the controller and the memory, enabling the policy to balance between retaining long-term context and incorporating new observations. The end-to-end differentiable design allows the entire policy, including memory operations, to be optimized jointly using policy gradient methods. This approach aims to address two key challenges: maintaining relevant information over long horizons, and retrieving it efficiently when needed.

We evaluate the proposed architecture on a suite of partially observable control problems, including synthetic benchmarks designed to stress long-term dependency handling, and more realistic domains that exhibit delayed rewards and sparse informative cues. Our results demonstrate that gated end-to-end memory policies consistently outperform standard recurrent baselines, particularly in environments with extended temporal dependencies and high observation noise. These findings suggest that combining gated control with explicit memory addressing is a viable and effective strategy for non-Markovian decision-making, opening avenues for more robust agents in complex, real-world settings.
conclusion: This work has presented a framework for addressing non-Markovian control problems through Gated End-to-End Memory Policy Networks, integrating gated recurrent architectures with differentiable memory mechanisms to capture long-term temporal dependencies. By explicitly modeling histories beyond the Markov assumption, the proposed approach enables policies to reason over extended sequences of observations, leading to improved performance in partially observable environments. Experimental results demonstrate that the architecture can effectively store, retrieve, and utilize relevant contextual information, outperforming baseline recurrent and feedforward policies across a range of benchmarks. The gating mechanisms were shown to be critical for mitigating memory overload and ensuring stability during training, while the end-to-end differentiable design facilitates joint optimization of perception, memory, and control. This study contributes to bridging the gap between deep memory-augmented models and reinforcement learning for complex decision-making tasks. Future work will explore scaling the method to multi-agent and hierarchical settings, as well as investigating its robustness under noisy or adversarial perturbations. Overall, Gated End-to-End Memory Policy Networks offer a promising direction for advancing control in domains where the Markov property does not hold, and where explicit temporal reasoning is essential for optimal decision-making.

title: Same-sign WW production in proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC as a signal for double parton scattering
abstract: We investigate same-sign \(W^\pm W^\pm\) production in proton–nucleus (\(pA\)) collisions at the LHC as a sensitive probe of double parton scattering (DPS). Owing to the enhanced parton flux in nuclei, the DPS contribution to this rare electroweak final state is expected to be significantly larger than in proton–proton interactions, while single parton scattering backgrounds remain suppressed. We present leading-order cross section estimates incorporating nuclear parton distribution functions and realistic kinematic cuts, and evaluate the expected event yields for current and future \(pA\) running conditions. The distinctive same-sign dilepton signature allows for efficient background rejection, enabling a clean extraction of the DPS signal. Our results demonstrate that \(pA\) collisions offer a promising environment to study multi-parton interactions and constrain the effective cross section parameter \(\sigma_{\text{eff}}\).
introduction:
The study of multiple parton interactions (MPI) in high-energy hadronic collisions has emerged as a crucial avenue for probing the partonic structure of nucleons and nuclei beyond the conventional single hard scattering picture. At the energies accessible at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the probability that more than one pair of partons undergoes a hard interaction in a single proton–proton or proton–nucleus collision is no longer negligible. In particular, double parton scattering (DPS), where two distinct hard parton–parton scatterings occur within the same collision, offers unique insights into the spatial and momentum correlations of partons inside hadrons. DPS is not only an important background to rare Standard Model processes and possible signals of new physics, but also a signal process in its own right, sensitive to multi-parton distributions and to the interplay between perturbative and non-perturbative QCD dynamics.

Proton–nucleus (pA) collisions provide a particularly advantageous environment to study DPS. The large effective parton density in the nuclear target enhances the DPS cross section relative to proton–proton (pp) collisions. In the simplest geometric picture, the DPS rate in pA collisions receives contributions from interactions in which both hard scatterings involve partons from the same nucleon, as well as from those in which the two scatterings occur with partons belonging to two different nucleons in the nucleus. The latter configuration grows linearly with the nuclear mass number \(A\) and can dominate the DPS yield in pA collisions at LHC energies. This enhancement, combined with the cleaner experimental environment of pA runs compared to nucleus–nucleus collisions, makes pA collisions an ideal laboratory for DPS studies and for extracting information about multi-parton correlations.

Among various possible final states, the production of same-sign W boson pairs (\(W^{\pm} W^{\pm}\)) stands out as a particularly promising channel for isolating DPS contributions. In the Standard Model, same-sign WW production via single parton scattering (SPS) is a rare electroweak process, occurring mainly through vector boson scattering or higher-order electroweak interactions, with small cross sections at the LHC energies. In contrast, in DPS the production of a same-sign WW final state can proceed via two independent quark–antiquark annihilations producing W bosons of the same charge, leading to significantly larger relative rates. Furthermore, the leptonic decays of the W bosons yield a clean experimental signature with two same-sign leptons, missing transverse energy, and minimal hadronic activity, which helps suppress backgrounds from other processes.

The study of same-sign WW production in pA collisions thus offers a dual benefit: it provides a sensitive probe of DPS dynamics and a channel in which the SPS background is naturally suppressed. Measuring this process can constrain the effective DPS cross section, \(\sigma_{\text{eff}}\), in a nuclear environment, and test the validity of factorisation assumptions relating \(\sigma_{\text{eff}}\) in pp and pA collisions. Moreover, it can shed light on the possible modifications of parton distribution functions (PDFs) in nuclei, such as shadowing or antishadowing effects, which may influence both DPS and SPS contributions.

In this work, we investigate the feasibility of using same-sign WW production in proton–nucleus collisions at the LHC as a signal for DPS. We present theoretical predictions for the DPS and SPS contributions to this process at \(\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}} = 8.8\) TeV, corresponding to the planned pPb run conditions, taking into account realistic detector acceptances and selection cuts. We evaluate the expected event rates for integrated luminosities achievable in pA operation, and discuss the potential for observing a statistically significant DPS signal. Our analysis demonstrates that this channel can provide a robust and experimentally accessible probe of double parton scattering in a novel kinematic regime, opening a new window on multi-parton dynamics in high-energy hadronic interactions.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the production of same-sign \( W^\pm W^\pm \) boson pairs in proton–nucleus collisions at the LHC as a novel probe of double parton scattering (DPS). The unique kinematic and topological features of same-sign \( WW \) final states, together with the enhanced DPS probability in asymmetric hadronic systems, render this channel a particularly clean and sensitive observable for studying multi-parton interactions in QCD. By combining state-of-the-art perturbative calculations for the single-parton scattering (SPS) background with realistic estimates of the DPS contributions, we have demonstrated that proton–nucleus collisions provide a significant amplification of the DPS signal relative to proton–proton collisions, owing to the larger effective parton flux in the nuclear target.

Our analysis shows that, for LHC energies and integrated luminosities achievable in current and future runs, the DPS contribution to same-sign \( WW \) production in p–Pb collisions can be comparable to, or even exceed, the SPS background in certain kinematic regions. This opens the possibility of extracting the effective cross section \(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}\) in a nuclear environment with unprecedented precision, offering new insight into the spatial and momentum correlations of partons inside the nucleon and nucleus. Furthermore, the reduced contamination from other electroweak and QCD processes in the same-sign channel enhances the robustness of such measurements.

These findings highlight the potential of proton–nucleus collisions as a complementary laboratory to proton–proton collisions for probing the multi-parton structure of hadrons. A dedicated experimental analysis exploiting the clean leptonic decay modes of the \( W \) bosons, combined with advanced event selection strategies, could provide a decisive test of the DPS mechanism and its nuclear dependence. Future high-luminosity LHC runs, possibly supplemented by improved detector capabilities, will be essential to fully exploit this opportunity and refine our understanding of multi-parton dynamics in QCD.

title: Dead Zones around Young Stellar Objects: FU Orionis Outbursts and Transition Discs
abstract: Dead zones—regions of suppressed turbulence due to low ionization—are expected to play a central role in the evolution of protoplanetary discs around young stellar objects (YSOs). Their presence can influence angular momentum transport, mass accretion rates, and the emergence of large-scale disc structures. In this work, we investigate the interplay between dead zones, FU Orionis-type accretion outbursts, and the formation of transition discs. Using a suite of time-dependent, viscous disc models incorporating layered accretion and thermally triggered instabilities, we show that mass accumulation within dead zones can drive episodic accretion events with amplitudes and durations consistent with FU Ori outbursts. The sudden increase in luminosity during such events can thermally ionize the disc, altering the extent of the dead zone and triggering structural changes. We further explore how repeated outbursts can promote the development of inner cavities and dust-depleted regions, potentially linking dead-zone dynamics to the observed properties of transition discs. These results suggest that dead zones act as both reservoirs and regulators of mass in YSO discs, with outburst cycles providing a natural pathway from continuous discs to the transitional morphologies observed in the later stages of disc evolution.
introduction:
Protoplanetary discs around young stellar objects (YSOs) are the birthplaces of planetary systems, evolving over timescales of a few million years through processes that redistribute mass and angular momentum. These discs are composed of gas and dust and are subject to a variety of physical mechanisms, including viscous accretion, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, photoevaporation, and planet–disc interactions. A crucial factor in disc evolution is the efficiency of angular momentum transport, which in many theoretical models is mediated by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). However, the ionization fraction in large regions of the disc midplane can be too low for the MRI to operate efficiently, leading to so-called “dead zones” of reduced turbulence and suppressed viscosity. The presence and extent of dead zones have profound implications for the dynamics of solids, the formation and migration of planets, and the long-term accretion history of the central star.

One of the most dramatic manifestations of non-steady disc evolution is the FU Orionis (FUor) outburst phenomenon, in which the accretion rate onto the central protostar increases by several orders of magnitude, producing a large brightening lasting decades to centuries. These events are widely interpreted as episodes of rapid mass transfer from the disc to the star, possibly triggered by instabilities in the disc structure. Models invoking dead zones suggest that mass can accumulate in the quiescent, low-viscosity region until a critical threshold is reached, at which point a thermal or gravitational instability can activate enhanced turbulence, allowing the stored mass to accrete rapidly. Such mechanisms naturally produce long quiescent intervals punctuated by short, intense accretion bursts, consistent with FUor phenomenology.

In parallel, observations with high-angular-resolution facilities over the past two decades have revealed a class of protoplanetary systems known as transition discs, characterized by large inner cavities or gaps in the dust distribution. These features are often interpreted as signatures of planet formation, photoevaporative clearing, or dust filtration at pressure maxima. However, some transition discs also exhibit ongoing gas accretion onto the central star, suggesting that the cavities are not entirely devoid of material. The interplay between dead zones and cavity formation provides a possible explanation: reduced turbulence in the inner disc can alter the radial distribution of pressure and magnetic stresses, potentially creating or sustaining regions of depleted dust density while still allowing gas flow through narrow channels.

Understanding the connections between dead zones, episodic accretion outbursts such as those seen in FUors, and the structural evolution of discs into transition-disc configurations is essential for building a coherent picture of early stellar and planetary evolution. In this work, we investigate the role of dead zones in shaping both the long-term accretion variability of YSOs and the emergence of large-scale disc substructures, with particular emphasis on linking theoretical models to recent observational constraints.
conclusion:
The results presented here highlight the critical role of dead zones in shaping the accretion history and observable characteristics of young stellar objects (YSOs), particularly in the context of FU Orionis-type outbursts and the emergence of transition discs. Our analysis suggests that the presence of magnetorotational instability (MRI)-inactive regions within protoplanetary discs can lead to a build-up of mass in the inner disc, which, when destabilized, may trigger the rapid, large-scale accretion events characteristic of FU Ori outbursts. This offers a coherent physical pathway linking disc microphysics with the episodic nature of early stellar mass assembly.

The connection between dead zones and transition discs is also reinforced by our findings. The reduced ionization and suppressed turbulence within dead zones can promote dust settling and grain growth, contributing to the development of radial opacity variations and inner disc cavities. When combined with the effects of outburst-driven disc evolution—such as enhanced photoevaporation, planet formation, or dynamical clearing—the dead zone framework provides a plausible explanation for the diverse observational signatures of transition discs. In particular, outburst episodes can significantly alter the thermal and chemical structure of the disc, potentially accelerating the dispersal of gas and dust in specific regions, thereby hastening the transition disc phase.

This work underscores the importance of coupling disc instability models with time-dependent chemical and radiative transfer calculations to capture the interplay between ionization physics, accretion dynamics, and observable disc morphology. The episodic nature of FU Ori events, if indeed rooted in dead zone physics, implies that disc evolution is highly non-linear and subject to feedback between heating events and ionization states. Such feedback may influence not only the mass accretion rates onto the central star but also the initial conditions for planet formation and migration.

Future progress will require multiwavelength monitoring of YSOs over decadal timescales, combined with high-resolution imaging and spectroscopic studies capable of probing both the gas and dust components of the inner disc. Numerical models that integrate magnetohydrodynamic turbulence, non-ideal MHD effects, and evolving dust populations will be essential for testing the scenarios proposed here. By bridging the gap between small-scale disc physics and long-term evolutionary outcomes, we can better understand how dead zones, FU Ori outbursts, and transition disc formation are intertwined in the early lives of planetary systems.

title: Brane Bounce from logarithmic entropic corrections in the bulk
abstract: We investigate a non-singular cosmological scenario in a braneworld framework, where the bounce arises from logarithmic entropic corrections to the bulk horizon entropy. Starting from a modified Friedmann equation induced by bulk thermodynamics, we incorporate quantum corrections to the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy, leading to additional terms in the effective brane dynamics. We show that the logarithmic contributions can generate a negative effective energy density at high curvature, naturally producing a bounce without introducing exotic matter on the brane. The resulting cosmological evolution smoothly connects a contracting to an expanding phase, avoiding the big bang singularity. We analyse the stability of the bounce and discuss constraints from observational data. Our findings highlight the role of bulk quantum gravitational effects in early-universe cosmology and their implications for braneworld scenarios.
introduction:
In recent years, the study of nonsingular cosmological scenarios has gained considerable attention as a possible resolution to the classical big bang singularity problem. Among the various proposals, bouncing cosmologies provide a compelling framework in which the Universe undergoes a contraction phase followed by a smooth transition to expansion. Such models avoid the initial singularity, address issues of geodesic incompleteness, and open new avenues for understanding the early Universe and its thermodynamical properties. Within the context of higher–dimensional theories and braneworld cosmology, bounces can emerge naturally from modifications in the bulk dynamics, especially when quantum gravity effects are taken into account.

Braneworld models, inspired by string theory and higher–dimensional gravity, posit that our observable Universe is a four–dimensional hypersurface (the brane) embedded in a higher–dimensional spacetime (the bulk). The gravitational dynamics on the brane are influenced not only by the standard matter content but also by the geometry and energy–momentum distribution in the bulk. In particular, thermodynamical interpretations of gravitational field equations have revealed intriguing connections between horizon entropy, temperature, and the effective Friedmann equations on the brane. These developments suggest that modifications to the entropy–area relation, motivated by quantum gravity or statistical considerations, can significantly alter cosmological evolution.

One class of such modifications arises from logarithmic corrections to the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy. These corrections appear in various approaches to quantum gravity, including loop quantum gravity, string theoretic calculations, and quantum field theory in curved spacetime, typically as subleading terms in the entropy formula. In the braneworld context, incorporating logarithmic entropy corrections in the bulk horizon thermodynamics modifies the effective Friedmann equations on the brane, potentially inducing novel dynamical features such as nonsingular bounces. The logarithmic term effectively encodes bulk quantum fluctuations and finite size effects, which, when projected onto the brane, can influence the high–energy regime of cosmological evolution.

Previous investigations have shown that entropy–corrected Friedmann equations can lead to early–time acceleration, avoidance of singularities, and modified matter–energy scaling. However, the specific role of bulk logarithmic corrections in generating a bounce on the brane remains less explored. A systematic treatment requires combining the thermodynamical derivation of brane dynamics with the corrected entropy–area relation, and analyzing the resulting cosmological solutions. In particular, it is important to determine under what conditions on the correction parameters and matter content a smooth bounce occurs, and how the effective equation of state evolves through the bounce.

In this work, we study a braneworld cosmology in which the bulk horizon entropy receives logarithmic quantum corrections. By applying the first law of thermodynamics to the apparent horizon in the bulk and projecting the resulting dynamics onto the brane, we derive the modified Friedmann equations. We then examine their solutions in the presence of standard matter fields, focusing on the conditions required for a nonsingular bounce. Our analysis highlights how the interplay between bulk quantum corrections and brane matter content can yield a consistent bouncing scenario, shedding light on possible quantum gravitational imprints in early–universe cosmology.
conclusion: In this work, we have shown that logarithmic entropic corrections in the bulk can naturally induce a nonsingular brane bounce, avoiding the conventional big bang singularity. By incorporating these corrections into the bulk-brane dynamics, the resulting modified Friedmann equations permit a smooth transition from contraction to expansion. Our analysis demonstrates that such quantum-inspired entropy modifications offer a viable mechanism for early-universe regularization, opening new avenues for exploring holographic and quantum gravity effects in braneworld cosmology.

title: Universal Approximation of Markov Kernels by Shallow Stochastic Feedforward Networks
abstract: We study the expressive power of shallow stochastic feedforward neural networks in approximating Markov kernels. We establish universal approximation results, showing that such networks can approximate arbitrary Markov kernels with finite discrete state spaces to any desired accuracy. Our analysis characterizes minimal hidden layer sizes, providing tight bounds and constructive proofs, thereby elucidating the representational capabilities of stochastic architectures for probabilistic mappings.
introduction:
The ability of artificial neural networks to approximate complex functions underlies much of their success in a wide range of applications. The universal approximation theorem, in its various forms, establishes that sufficiently wide feedforward networks with appropriate nonlinearities can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain to arbitrary precision. While these results have been extensively studied in the deterministic setting, many real-world systems are inherently stochastic, and their dynamics are often best described in probabilistic terms. In such cases, the objects of interest are not deterministic mappings but stochastic transformations, which can be formalized as Markov kernels: mappings from inputs to probability distributions over outputs.

Markov kernels arise naturally in numerous contexts, including stochastic control, probabilistic graphical models, reinforcement learning, and Bayesian inference. In these domains, learning or approximating a stochastic transition mechanism is a central task. For instance, in model-based reinforcement learning, the environment’s dynamics are often represented as a Markov kernel mapping states and actions to distributions over next states. Similarly, in generative modeling, one may aim to learn a stochastic mapping from latent variables to observable data. The question of whether neural architectures can approximate such stochastic operators with the same generality as they approximate deterministic functions is thus of both theoretical and practical significance.

Recent work has begun to extend universal approximation results beyond deterministic function spaces, showing that certain classes of stochastic neural networks can approximate arbitrary conditional distributions under mild regularity assumptions. A particularly appealing class of models for this purpose are stochastic feedforward networks, in which randomness is injected into the hidden or output layers, allowing the network to represent a variety of conditional distributions. Shallow architectures, consisting of a single hidden layer, are of special interest due to their analytical tractability and the insight they offer into the representational properties of stochastic networks.

In this work, we focus on shallow stochastic feedforward networks with finitely many hidden units, and investigate their capacity to approximate arbitrary Markov kernels between finite input and output sets. Our main contribution is to establish universal approximation theorems in this discrete setting, quantifying the minimal number of hidden units required to approximate any given stochastic mapping to within a specified tolerance. We show that even with a single hidden layer, such networks can represent any stochastic transformation between finite spaces, provided the number of hidden units meets certain bounds that we characterize explicitly.

These results bridge the gap between deterministic universal approximation theory and the stochastic domain, offering a rigorous foundation for the expressive power of simple stochastic neural architectures. Beyond their theoretical value, our findings have implications for the design of compact probabilistic models in areas where discrete states and stochastic transitions are fundamental, including planning, game theory, and statistical decision processes.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the capacity of shallow stochastic feedforward networks to approximate arbitrary Markov kernels between finite sets of input and output states. Building on the universal approximation paradigm well established for deterministic neural networks, we have extended the scope of such results to stochastic transformations, showing that even networks of minimal depth can, in principle, represent any desired probabilistic mapping to arbitrary accuracy, provided that sufficient width is allowed. Our analysis formalized the relationship between network architecture and the expressive power required to capture the full range of conditional distributions, thereby bridging a gap between the theory of stochastic processes and the design of probabilistic neural models.

The results demonstrate that a single hidden layer suffices for universality in the approximation of Markov kernels, under mild assumptions on the activation functions and parameterization of the stochastic units. This finding underscores the efficiency of shallow architectures for representing complex stochastic dependencies, complementing prior work that has largely focused on deep or recurrent structures. By quantifying the number of hidden units necessary for universality, we provide both a constructive proof of representational sufficiency and a set of bounds that can inform practical model design.

Beyond the theoretical contribution, our work has implications for applied settings in which one seeks to learn or implement stochastic policies, transition models, or generative mechanisms over discrete state spaces. In reinforcement learning, for example, the ability to approximate arbitrary transition kernels with a compact network could facilitate the design of policy models and simulators with controlled complexity. Similarly, in probabilistic modeling and Bayesian computation, shallow stochastic feedforward networks offer a flexible and interpretable parameterization for conditional distributions that might otherwise require more cumbersome representation schemes.

There remain several avenues for future research. Extending the universality results to continuous state spaces, or to hybrid discrete–continuous domains, would broaden the applicability of the framework. Investigating the trade-offs between network width, sample complexity, and generalization performance in finite-data regimes could yield insights into the practical limitations of the theoretical bounds. Moreover, exploring the interplay between stochasticity at the unit level and architectural constraints may uncover more efficient parameterizations for specific classes of Markov kernels.

In summary, we have established that shallow stochastic feedforward networks possess universal approximation capabilities for Markov kernels between finite sets, thereby enriching the theoretical foundations of probabilistic neural modeling and opening new directions for both theoretical inquiry and practical application.

title: Analysis of roles and groups in blogosphere
abstract: This study examines the roles and group structures within the blogosphere, focusing on patterns of interaction, influence, and content dissemination. By analyzing network connections and thematic clusters, the research identifies key contributors, peripheral participants, and emergent communities. Findings illuminate how social dynamics and role differentiation shape discourse, collaboration, and information flow in online blogging environments.
introduction: The blogosphere has emerged as a dynamic and influential sphere of online communication, fostering the creation, dissemination, and exchange of information across diverse communities. Blogs serve not only as personal publishing platforms but also as nodes within complex social networks, where individuals assume distinct roles and form overlapping groups. These roles—ranging from content creators and commentators to curators and amplifiers—shape the flow of information and the construction of collective narratives. Similarly, groups within the blogosphere may coalesce around shared interests, ideologies, or topical specializations, influencing both the structure and dynamics of discourse. Understanding how roles and groups interact is essential for comprehending the mechanisms of influence, agenda-setting, and knowledge production in digital contexts. Existing scholarship has examined aspects of online communities, yet a systematic analysis of role differentiation and group formation specific to the blogosphere remains underdeveloped. This paper aims to address this gap by exploring the interplay between roles and groups, offering insights into the patterns of interaction and the social structures that underpin the blogosphere.
conclusion: This analysis highlights the diverse roles and interconnected groups shaping the blogosphere. Bloggers function as content creators, curators, and community builders, while groups form around shared interests, values, or goals. Understanding these dynamics reveals the blogosphere’s complexity, its capacity for influence, and its evolving role in digital communication and public discourse.

title: Proca Q Tubes and their Coupling to Gravity
abstract: We investigate cylindrically symmetric, non-topological soliton solutions—Proca Q-tubes—arising in a self-interacting complex Proca field theory, and analyze their coupling to Einstein gravity. In the absence of gravity, we construct regular solutions characterized by a conserved Noether charge and finite energy per unit length, exploring their parameter space and stability conditions. Including gravitational backreaction, we solve the coupled Einstein–Proca equations numerically, revealing substantial modifications to the field profiles, energy distribution, and maximal charge. We identify regimes where gravity stabilizes configurations otherwise absent in the flat-space limit, and examine the transition to black string formation at strong coupling. Our results extend previous studies of Q-balls and boson stars to cylindrically symmetric Proca fields, providing new insights into solitonic structures in vector field theories and their relevance in astrophysical and cosmological contexts.
introduction: Proca Q tubes are cylindrically symmetric, non-topological solitonic configurations arising in theories with a massive complex vector (Proca) field endowed with a self-interaction potential. They generalize the concept of Q-balls to one-dimensional extended objects, where the conserved Noether charge is distributed along the tube’s length. Such structures are of interest both as theoretical laboratories for exploring nonlinear field dynamics and as potential candidates for exotic matter in astrophysical or cosmological contexts. Coupling these configurations to gravity is a natural extension, allowing investigation of their stability, backreaction effects, and possible role in self-gravitating systems. The interplay between the Proca field’s mass, self-interaction, and gravitational attraction can lead to novel equilibrium solutions. This work aims to analyze these coupled systems, elucidating their parameter space and highlighting physical regimes of relevance.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the properties of Proca Q tubes—non-topological solitonic configurations supported by a complex massive vector field—and their coupling to gravity. Extending previous analyses of Proca Q-balls and related scalar field structures, we have shown that the inclusion of cylindrical symmetry leads to qualitatively distinct solution branches, characterized by their energy per unit length, charge distribution, and stability profiles. The self-interactions of the Proca field, together with the harmonic time dependence, enable the existence of localized tubes in flat spacetime, while gravitational effects introduce further structure and constraints on their parameter space.  

Our analysis demonstrates that gravity can both stabilize and destabilize certain branches of Proca Q tubes, depending on the strength of the coupling and the central field amplitude. In particular, we observe that gravitational binding allows for configurations with higher central densities than their flat-spacetime counterparts, but also imposes an upper bound on the admissible frequency range. The transition between stable and unstable regimes is sensitive to the interplay between the Proca mass, self-coupling, and gravitational strength, echoing phenomena familiar from boson star studies yet revealing novel features due to the vector nature of the field.  

These findings contribute to the broader understanding of solitonic solutions in vector field theories and their astrophysical relevance. Proca Q tubes may serve as effective models for exotic matter distributions in cylindrical geometries, potentially relevant to cosmic string-like structures or as building blocks in more complex composite systems. Future work will extend the present study to rotating configurations, dynamical stability analyses, and interactions with external fields, thereby deepening the theoretical framework and exploring observational signatures of these intriguing gravitational solitons.

title: Efficient algorithms for maximum induced matching problem in permutation and trapezoid graphs
abstract: The maximum induced matching problem is a well-studied combinatorial optimization problem with applications in scheduling, resource allocation, and network design. While the problem is NP-hard in general graphs, specialized graph classes permit more efficient solutions. In this paper, we present improved algorithms for computing maximum induced matchings in permutation graphs and trapezoid graphs. For permutation graphs, we propose a novel dynamic programming approach that achieves optimal time complexity, outperforming previous methods. For trapezoid graphs, we introduce the first algorithm with polynomial running time, leveraging structural properties and geometric representations. We provide correctness proofs, complexity analysis, and implementation details. Our results extend the algorithmic frontier for these graph classes and open avenues for addressing the problem in broader intersection graph families.
introduction: The maximum induced matching problem is a well-studied combinatorial optimization problem with applications in network design, scheduling, and resource allocation. While the problem is NP-hard in general graphs, several graph classes admit efficient algorithms. This paper investigates permutation and trapezoid graphs, presenting new algorithms that significantly improve known results. Our methods exploit structural properties of these graphs to achieve optimal or near-optimal performance, advancing both theory and practice.
conclusion: We presented efficient algorithms for solving the maximum induced matching problem in permutation and trapezoid graphs, improving on previous complexity bounds. Our methods exploit structural properties of these graph classes, enabling faster computation. These results contribute to both theoretical understanding and practical applications, suggesting directions for further algorithmic optimization.

title: Electron positron pairs in blazar jets and gamma-ray loud radio-galaxies
abstract: We investigate the role of electron–positron (\(e^\pm\)) pairs in shaping the radiative properties of blazar jets and γ-ray loud radio galaxies. In relativistic jets, pair production can occur through photon–photon interactions between high-energy γ-rays and lower-energy synchrotron or external photons, potentially altering particle composition and energy distribution. Using multiwavelength spectral energy distributions and γ-ray variability constraints from *Fermi*-LAT and ground-based Cherenkov telescopes, we estimate the pair content required to reproduce observed luminosities without exceeding plausible jet powers. We explore scenarios in which pairs are created in situ along the jet or injected from the central engine, and quantify their impact on synchrotron and inverse Compton emission. Our analysis indicates that moderate pair enrichment can enhance radiative efficiency while remaining consistent with constraints from kinetic power estimates and jet dynamics. For γ-ray loud radio galaxies, where jets are viewed at larger angles, pair content may still influence high-energy emission through structured jet models. These results suggest that electron–positron pairs are a non-negligible component in many powerful active galactic nuclei, affecting both emission mechanisms and energetics, and should be incorporated in models aiming to unify blazars and misaligned radio-loud AGN.
introduction:
Relativistic jets launched by active galactic nuclei (AGN) are among the most powerful particle accelerators in the Universe, capable of emitting radiation across the entire electromagnetic spectrum. In blazars, where the jet is oriented close to our line of sight, relativistic beaming amplifies the observed emission, making them dominant contributors to the extragalactic gamma-ray sky. Radio galaxies, which are believed to be the misaligned counterparts of blazars, can also be strong gamma-ray emitters, particularly those classified as gamma-ray loud radio galaxies (GLRGs). Understanding the physical composition of these jets—specifically, whether they are dominated by electron–proton plasma or contain a significant fraction of electron–positron pairs—is essential for constraining their formation mechanisms, radiative processes, and impact on their surrounding environments.

The presence of electron–positron pairs in AGN jets has been a subject of debate for decades. Theoretically, pairs can be generated in a variety of environments, including the magnetosphere near the central supermassive black hole through electromagnetic cascades, in the inner jet via photon–photon annihilation, or in shocks and reconnection layers further downstream. The injection of pairs can strongly influence the jet’s dynamics, radiative efficiency, and particle acceleration efficiency, as well as modify the observed spectra. In particular, a high pair content can reduce the kinetic power required to produce the observed emission, while altering the polarization and variability properties in ways that can be probed observationally.

Observational constraints on the pair content of blazar jets have been challenging. Estimates of jet power derived from broadband spectral modeling often exceed those inferred from large-scale radio lobes if a pure electron–proton composition is assumed, suggesting that an additional light component, such as pairs, may be present. Spectral signatures in the X-ray to gamma-ray regime, including spectral breaks and high-energy cutoffs, can also hint at the presence of pairs. In radio galaxies, where the jet inclination reduces the effects of beaming, the detection of gamma-ray emission by instruments such as the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT) has provided an opportunity to examine jet composition under different geometrical and beaming conditions.

The study of electron–positron pairs is particularly relevant for understanding the unification of blazars and radio galaxies. In the unification scheme, flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) and BL Lac objects correspond to Fanaroff–Riley type II (FR II) and type I (FR I) radio galaxies viewed at small angles to the line of sight, respectively. If pairs are abundant in blazar jets, they should also be present in their misaligned counterparts, potentially affecting the gamma-ray loudness of certain radio galaxies. Comparing the spectral properties and inferred jet powers of aligned and misaligned sources can thus provide an indirect probe of pair content across the AGN population.

Recent advances in high-energy observations, combined with improved theoretical models of pair production and annihilation, have opened new avenues for constraining the role of pairs in relativistic jets. Time-dependent multiwavelength campaigns, very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) imaging, and polarimetric studies now allow for more precise estimates of jet parameters, including Doppler factors, magnetic field strengths, and particle densities. By examining the interplay between pair content, jet energetics, and observed gamma-ray emission, it is possible to place meaningful limits on the composition of blazar jets and GLRGs, thereby advancing our understanding of the physical processes that govern the most energetic phenomena in the Universe.
conclusion: Our analysis indicates that electron–positron pairs play a significant role in shaping the radiative output of blazar jets and gamma-ray loud radio galaxies. The inferred pair content affects both the spectral energy distribution and the efficiency of high-energy photon production, suggesting that pair-enriched jets can sustain intense gamma-ray emission without requiring extreme bulk kinetic powers. By comparing observational constraints with theoretical jet models, we find that the pair fraction is consistent with values that alleviate the energetic demands implied by purely electron–proton compositions. This has important implications for jet launching mechanisms, energy dissipation processes, and the unification of blazars with their misaligned counterparts. Future multiwavelength campaigns, combined with improved modeling of pair creation and annihilation, will be essential to refine these estimates and to clarify the interplay between composition, dynamics, and radiation in relativistic jets. Such advances will enhance our understanding of particle acceleration and high-energy astrophysical phenomena.

title: The correlations between the spin frequencies and kHz QPOs of Neutron Stars in LMXBs
abstract: We investigate the correlations between neutron star spin frequencies and the kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations (kHz QPOs) observed in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs). Using a compiled sample of published measurements, we examine relationships between spin frequencies, derived from X-ray pulsations or burst oscillations, and the frequency separation of twin kHz QPOs. Our analysis reveals that for many sources, the QPO frequency separation is close to either the spin frequency or half of it, although significant deviations occur. We find no universal scaling, but trends suggest that the spin may modulate the QPO mechanism in a source-dependent manner. These results provide constraints on models linking kHz QPOs to orbital motion and beat-frequency processes, and highlight the influence of neutron star rotation on accretion dynamics.
introduction:
Low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) containing neutron stars provide a unique laboratory for studying matter under extreme conditions of density, gravity, and magnetic field strength. In these systems, a neutron star accretes matter from a low-mass companion star via Roche-lobe overflow, forming an accretion disk that emits strongly in the X-ray band. A characteristic feature observed in many neutron star LMXBs is the presence of kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations (kHz QPOs) in their X-ray power spectra. These oscillations, typically appearing as twin peaks at frequencies of several hundred to over one thousand hertz, are believed to originate from processes occurring in the innermost regions of the accretion flow, close to the neutron star surface or the innermost stable circular orbit.

Another fundamental property of neutron stars in LMXBs is their spin frequency, which can be measured directly through X-ray pulsations in accreting millisecond pulsars or inferred indirectly via burst oscillations during thermonuclear X-ray bursts. Theoretical models have suggested that the frequencies of kHz QPOs may be linked to the neutron star spin, for instance through beat-frequency mechanisms or relativistic precession effects. In particular, the frequency separation between the twin kHz QPO peaks has been proposed to correspond to either the spin frequency or half of it, depending on the nature of the modulation process.

However, observational studies have revealed a more complex picture, with the QPO frequency separation varying with source state and accretion rate, and in some cases deviating significantly from simple integer relations with the spin. This has led to ongoing debates regarding the physical origin of kHz QPOs and their connection to neutron star rotation. In this work, we investigate the correlations between spin frequencies and kHz QPO properties across a sample of neutron star LMXBs, aiming to clarify the extent and nature of this relationship and to provide constraints on theoretical models of accretion and strong-field gravity.
conclusion: Our analysis reveals a significant correlation between neutron star spin frequencies and the properties of kHz QPOs in low-mass X-ray binaries, supporting models in which QPOs are linked to orbital motion in the inner accretion disk modulated by the stellar spin. The observed relations suggest that spin plays a key role in shaping the QPO frequency separation and variability patterns. These results provide important constraints on theoretical models of disk–magnetosphere interactions and the dense matter equation of state.

title: Perceived Social Loafing in Undergraduate Software Engineering Teams
abstract: This study investigates perceived social loafing in undergraduate software engineering teams, examining its prevalence, antecedents, and perceived impact on team performance. Data were collected through surveys from 142 students enrolled in a semester-long, project-based course. Results indicate that perceptions of unequal effort were common, often linked to poor communication, unclear role definitions, and uneven task distribution. Social loafing perceptions were associated with reduced satisfaction and lower self-reported team effectiveness. Findings highlight the need for structured collaboration practices to mitigate perceived inequities in team-based learning environments.
introduction:
Teamwork is a central component of undergraduate software engineering education, aiming to prepare students for the collaborative nature of professional software development. In many curricula, capstone projects, course-based team assignments, and agile-inspired classroom practices provide students with opportunities to develop not only technical competencies but also interpersonal and project management skills. These team-based activities are intended to mirror industry contexts, where software is rarely the product of an individual working in isolation. However, the benefits of collaborative learning are sometimes undermined by an imbalance in individual contributions, a phenomenon often described as social loafing. Social loafing refers to the tendency of individuals to exert less effort when working in a group compared to when working alone, a behaviour that can hinder both group performance and individual learning outcomes. In educational settings, particularly in project-based courses, the perception of social loafing among team members may have significant implications for motivation, satisfaction, and the development of professional skills.

The concept of social loafing has been studied extensively in social psychology since the seminal work of Ringelmann in the early twentieth century, which demonstrated a decline in individual effort as group size increased. In the context of software engineering education, social loafing may manifest through missed deadlines, incomplete or low-quality task contributions, avoidance of responsibilities, or a general lack of engagement with the team’s objectives. Perceptions of social loafing—whether or not such loafing is objectively occurring—can be equally detrimental, as they may erode trust, increase interpersonal conflict, and reduce overall team cohesion. In project-based learning environments, where assessment often combines group outputs with individual grading components, perceived inequities in workload distribution can lead to dissatisfaction and diminished commitment to collective goals.

Several factors may contribute to the occurrence and perception of social loafing in undergraduate software engineering teams. Task visibility is a key determinant; when individual contributions are difficult to monitor or measure, the likelihood of reduced effort can increase. Similarly, the perceived dispensability of one’s contribution, insufficient accountability mechanisms, and unclear role definitions can foster conditions in which social loafing is more probable. Personality traits, prior experience with teamwork, cultural background, and the level of interpersonal trust within the team can also influence how individuals perceive and respond to unequal effort distribution. In software engineering projects—often involving complex interdependent tasks, version control systems, and collaborative tools—technical skill disparities may exacerbate perceptions of loafing, as less experienced members might contribute less visibly even when they are making an effort to learn.

The consequences of perceived social loafing extend beyond the immediate project. Students who feel that their peers are not contributing equitably may experience frustration and reduced motivation, potentially leading to disengagement from the team or from future collaborative tasks. This, in turn, may limit opportunities for skill development in areas such as communication, conflict resolution, and collaborative problem solving—skills that are vital in professional software engineering practice. From an instructional perspective, unmanaged perceptions of loafing can undermine the intended pedagogical benefits of team-based assignments, leading to poorer learning outcomes and negative attitudes toward teamwork.

Existing research on social loafing in educational contexts has largely focused on general group work in higher education, with some attention to disciplines such as business, psychology, and engineering. However, software engineering projects are distinct in their reliance on distributed collaboration tools, iterative development processes, and often self-managed team structures. These features may shape both the dynamics of actual effort distribution and the ways in which students perceive the contributions of their peers. Yet, despite the prevalence of team-based work in software engineering curricula, there is relatively limited empirical investigation into how undergraduate students experience and interpret social loafing in this specific context. Understanding these perceptions is essential for designing instructional interventions, assessment strategies, and team management practices that mitigate negative effects and promote equitable participation.

This study seeks to explore perceived social loafing within undergraduate software engineering teams, with the aim of identifying the factors that influence such perceptions and the potential impacts on team functioning and student learning. By examining the interplay between individual experiences, team processes, and the educational environment, this research contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how social loafing is understood and managed in software engineering education. The findings may inform educators, curriculum designers, and institutional policy makers in developing strategies to foster effective, equitable, and engaging team-based learning experiences that better prepare students for the collaborative demands of the software industry.
conclusion:
The findings of this study highlight the multifaceted nature of perceived social loafing within undergraduate software engineering teams. While prior research has often treated social loafing as a uniform phenomenon, our results suggest that students’ perceptions are shaped by a combination of individual, interpersonal, and contextual factors. These include the clarity of task allocation, the transparency of individual contributions, and the extent to which team members feel accountable to one another. Importantly, the perception of unequal effort distribution was not always linked to measurable performance deficits, indicating that social loafing in this context may be as much a matter of perception and communication as of actual behavior.

The study also underscores the role of project management practices and instructional design in mediating these perceptions. Teams that employed structured planning, regular progress tracking, and explicit role assignments reported lower levels of perceived loafing. Conversely, those with ambiguous goals, inconsistent communication, or limited instructor oversight were more likely to report frustration with team members whom they perceived as underperforming. This suggests that interventions aimed at improving process transparency and accountability may be more effective in mitigating perceived loafing than punitive measures or increased assessment weight on individual work.

From an educational perspective, addressing perceived social loafing is not merely about ensuring equitable workload distribution, but about fostering trust, mutual respect, and shared responsibility within teams. Instructors can play a critical role by providing teams with tools for self-management, encouraging open dialogue about workload expectations, and offering timely feedback on both process and product. Additionally, integrating reflective components into team projects may help students become more aware of their own contributions and the challenges faced by their peers, potentially reducing misperceptions.

While this study offers valuable insights, it is constrained by its reliance on self-reported data and a single institutional context. Future research could benefit from triangulating perceptions with objective measures of contribution, exploring the longitudinal effects of team dynamics across multiple projects, and examining the influence of cultural factors on perceptions of fairness and effort. Ultimately, by better understanding the drivers of perceived social loafing, educators and students alike can work toward creating more cohesive, equitable, and effective software engineering teams.

title: The Application of Data Mining to Build Classification Model for Predicting Graduate Employment
abstract: This study investigates the application of data mining techniques to construct a classification model for predicting graduate employment outcomes. Using a dataset comprising academic performance, demographic factors, and extracurricular involvement, several classification algorithms were evaluated, including Decision Trees, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines. The dataset was preprocessed through normalization, feature selection, and handling of missing values to enhance model accuracy. Cross-validation was employed to assess performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score as evaluation metrics. Results indicate that the Random Forest model achieved the highest predictive performance, demonstrating robust generalization to unseen data. The findings highlight the potential of data mining in supporting educational institutions and policymakers by providing data-driven insights into employability factors. This approach can inform targeted interventions to improve graduate employment rates and better align academic programs with labor market needs.
introduction:
In recent years, the expansion of higher education and the rapid changes in the global labor market have intensified concerns over graduate employability. Universities are under increasing pressure from stakeholders—including students, employers, and policymakers—to ensure that graduates are adequately prepared for employment. However, despite significant investments in educational infrastructure and curriculum development, a gap often persists between the skills acquired by graduates and the requirements of the job market. This disparity has prompted researchers and practitioners to explore data-driven approaches to better understand and predict employment outcomes for graduates. Among these approaches, data mining techniques have emerged as powerful tools for extracting meaningful patterns from large and complex datasets, enabling the construction of predictive models that can inform educational policy and career guidance.

Data mining is a process that involves the extraction of hidden, previously unknown, and potentially useful information from large datasets. It encompasses a range of computational techniques from statistics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, which can be applied to discover patterns, relationships, and trends within data. In the context of higher education, vast amounts of data are generated from student academic records, demographic information, extracurricular activities, and post-graduation employment histories. Harnessing these data through mining techniques provides a valuable opportunity to develop predictive models that classify graduates according to their likelihood of securing employment within a given period after graduation.

Classification, one of the primary tasks in data mining, involves the development of models that can assign instances to predefined categories based on their attributes. In this study’s context, the classification model seeks to categorize graduates into employable or unemployed groups, or into finer-grained categories such as employed in a related field, employed in an unrelated field, or pursuing further studies. Such models can be instrumental for universities in identifying at-risk students early and implementing targeted interventions to improve their employability prospects. They can also assist career services in tailoring guidance and resources to specific student profiles, ultimately enhancing graduates’ success in the labor market.

The application of data mining to graduate employment prediction is supported by a growing body of literature that demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning algorithms—such as decision trees, support vector machines, random forests, and neural networks—in building accurate and interpretable classification models. These techniques have been applied successfully in various educational data mining contexts, including student performance prediction, dropout prevention, and course recommendation systems. In the specific domain of employment prediction, prior studies have highlighted the influence of academic performance indicators, internship experiences, participation in extracurricular activities, socio-demographic factors, and labor market conditions on graduate employment outcomes.

Nevertheless, challenges remain in developing robust and generalizable models. Data quality, feature selection, class imbalance, and the dynamic nature of the labor market can all affect the reliability of predictions. Additionally, ethical considerations around data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the potential consequences of classification outcomes must be addressed to ensure the responsible use of predictive analytics in education. These challenges underscore the need for rigorous model development, validation, and evaluation, as well as transparent communication of the models’ capabilities and limitations to end users.

This study aims to contribute to the field by applying data mining techniques to construct and evaluate a classification model for predicting graduate employment. By leveraging historical graduate data, the research seeks to identify the most significant predictors of employment outcomes and assess the performance of different classification algorithms. The findings are expected to provide actionable insights for higher education institutions, enabling them to make data-informed decisions that enhance graduate employability and align educational outputs with labor market demands. Through this approach, the study not only advances methodological knowledge in educational data mining but also addresses a pressing socio-economic challenge faced by graduates and institutions alike.
conclusion:
This study demonstrated the potential of data mining techniques in developing a classification model for predicting graduate employment outcomes. By applying systematic preprocessing, feature selection, and model training, the research identified key factors influencing employability, such as academic performance, field of study, internship experience, and participation in extracurricular activities. The comparative analysis of multiple classification algorithms revealed that models such as Random Forest and Support Vector Machine achieved high predictive accuracy, underscoring their suitability for this context.  

The findings highlight the importance of data-driven approaches in addressing the growing challenge of graduate unemployment and underemployment. The model developed in this study can serve as a decision-support tool for higher education institutions, enabling them to monitor employment trends, evaluate the effectiveness of academic programs, and provide targeted interventions to improve graduate readiness for the labor market. Additionally, policymakers may leverage such predictive models to design more effective workforce development strategies aligned with industry needs.  

While the results are promising, the study acknowledges certain limitations. The dataset, though comprehensive, was restricted to a specific geographical and institutional context, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Furthermore, employment outcomes are influenced by dynamic economic conditions and labor market fluctuations that may not be fully captured in the model. Future research should explore larger, more diverse datasets, incorporate longitudinal data, and integrate advanced methods such as ensemble learning or deep learning to enhance predictive performance.  

In conclusion, the application of data mining to build classification models offers a valuable framework for predicting graduate employment with practical benefits for universities, students, and policymakers. By identifying factors associated with employability, such models can inform targeted support and improve workforce preparedness, ultimately contributing to more efficient alignment between higher education outputs and labor market demands.

title: Scalar field cosmological models with finite scale factor singularities
abstract: We investigate scalar field cosmological models exhibiting finite scale factor singularities, where the scale factor remains finite while other physical quantities diverge. Employing analytical and numerical techniques, we classify singular behaviors and identify conditions on scalar field potentials leading to such scenarios. Our results demonstrate the role of potential shape in singularity formation and provide explicit examples, offering insights into late-time cosmic evolution beyond standard singularity classifications.
introduction:
In recent years, increasing attention has been devoted to cosmological models that admit non-standard singularities, extending the traditional classification beyond the Big Bang and Big Crunch scenarios. Among these, finite scale factor singularities (FSFS) constitute a particularly intriguing class, characterized by the divergence of certain physical quantities—such as the energy density or pressure—while the cosmological scale factor remains finite. Such singularities can emerge in both modified gravity frameworks and in models involving exotic matter components, including scalar fields with non-canonical potentials. Their study is motivated not only by theoretical curiosity, but also by the possibility that they may occur in the relatively near future of the Universe’s evolution, thereby offering potentially observable signatures.

Scalar fields play a central role in modern cosmology, providing a unified description of early- and late-time accelerated expansion through inflationary dynamics and dark energy models, respectively. The flexibility in constructing scalar field potentials allows for the realization of a wide range of cosmological behaviours, including the approach to FSFS. In these scenarios, the evolution towards the singularity is determined by the interplay between the field’s kinetic and potential energies, which can lead to divergences in the pressure or higher derivatives of the Hubble parameter while the scale factor remains well-defined.

Understanding the conditions under which FSFS arise, and their stability with respect to perturbations, is crucial for assessing their physical plausibility. Moreover, the classification of FSFS within the broader landscape of cosmological singularities provides insight into the ultimate fate of the Universe. This work investigates scalar field cosmological models that give rise to finite scale factor singularities, focusing on analytical and numerical solutions to the field equations and the associated dynamical behaviour. By systematically exploring the parameter space of the scalar field potential, we aim to identify the mechanisms that generate FSFS and to elucidate their possible observational consequences in the context of contemporary cosmology.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated scalar field cosmological models that admit finite scale factor singularities, focusing on their dynamical properties and physical implications. By considering a range of potentials and initial conditions, we have identified regimes in which the scale factor approaches a finite value at a finite cosmic time, while curvature invariants and dynamical variables such as the Hubble parameter and its derivatives diverge. These singularities, which differ qualitatively from the standard big bang or big rip scenarios, arise naturally within certain classes of scalar field dynamics without requiring exotic matter beyond the scalar sector.

Our analysis has shown that the occurrence and type of finite scale factor singularity depend sensitively on the shape of the scalar field potential and on the initial configuration of the field. In particular, potentials with specific asymptotic behaviors in the vicinity of critical field values can trigger the finite-time blow-up of curvature while keeping the metric scale factor finite. We have classified the singularities encountered according to their strength and possible geodesic completeness, thereby clarifying their potential role in cosmological evolution.

The results suggest that finite scale factor singularities may represent viable alternatives or complements to other exotic future or past singularities in scalar field cosmology. They also open up the possibility of connecting such singular behaviors with quantum gravity effects, which might regulate or resolve the divergences. Future work should extend the present analysis to include perturbative stability, coupling to other matter components, and confrontation with observational constraints, in order to assess the physical plausibility and detectability of these singularity scenarios.

title: Influence of the Earth on the background and the sensitivity of the GRM and ECLAIRs instruments aboard the Chinese-French mission SVOM
abstract: We investigate the impact of the Earth’s presence in the field of view on the background levels and sensitivity of the Gamma-Ray Monitor (GRM) and the ECLAIRs coded-mask telescope aboard the Sino-French SVOM mission. Using detailed Monte Carlo simulations, we model various Earth positions relative to the instruments in low-Earth orbit. Results show that atmospheric and albedo contributions significantly modify background spectra, influencing detection thresholds for transient events. These findings provide essential input for optimizing observation strategies and maximizing SVOM’s scientific return.
introduction: The Space-based multiband astronomical Variable Objects Monitor (SVOM) is a joint Chinese-French mission dedicated to the detection and study of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and other high-energy transients. Its payload includes the Gamma-Ray Monitor (GRM) and the ECLAIRs coded-mask camera, whose performance depends critically on background levels. The Earth’s presence in the instruments’ field of view can modify their background and sensitivity. Understanding this influence is essential for optimizing detection strategies and maximizing the scientific return of SVOM observations.
conclusion:
The present study has examined in detail the impact of the Earth’s presence in the field of view on the background levels and resulting sensitivity of the Gamma-Ray Monitor (GRM) and ECLAIRs instruments aboard the Chinese–French SVOM mission. By combining realistic geometric modelling of the spacecraft–Earth configuration with spectral simulations of the major high-energy background components, we have quantified how the Earth’s position relative to the detectors modulates the instrumental environment across the relevant energy ranges. The results demonstrate that, for both instruments, the Earth acts as both a shield and a source: it significantly attenuates the diffuse cosmic X- and gamma-ray backgrounds when partially or fully occulting the field of view, while simultaneously introducing an additional albedo contribution from atmospheric scattering and emission.

For GRM, whose sensitivity is optimised for higher energies, the dominant effect of the Earth’s presence is the reduction of the cosmic gamma-ray background in the 30 keV–5 MeV range, with the albedo component becoming increasingly relevant above several hundred keV. The net effect on sensitivity depends on the balance between shielding and the introduction of Earth-origin photons, which varies with orbital phase and pointing strategy. In particular, configurations with partial Earth occultation can yield an overall background reduction, thereby improving the minimum detectable flux for transient events. However, when the Earth subtends a large solid angle in the field of view, the albedo contribution can outweigh the shielding benefit at higher energies, leading to a modest sensitivity degradation.

For ECLAIRs, which covers the lower-energy band from 4 keV to 150 keV, the situation is more nuanced. The Earth’s atmosphere reflects and emits in this range less efficiently than at higher energies, so the predominant influence is a reduction in diffuse cosmic X-ray background. This shielding effect can produce a measurable improvement in sensitivity for faint soft transients when the Earth partially occultates the field. Nonetheless, the presence of atmospheric fluorescence lines and scattered solar X-rays introduces variability in the low-energy background that must be accounted for in sensitivity estimates and detection algorithms.

Our findings emphasise that the Earth’s modulation of the background is not a static effect but a dynamic one, driven by the spacecraft’s low-Earth orbit and survey strategy. The variation in background level over an orbit implies that the instantaneous sensitivity of both GRM and ECLAIRs is time-dependent, with potential implications for transient detection rates, false trigger probabilities, and the interpretation of flux limits. Incorporating this orbital modulation into real-time trigger algorithms and offline search pipelines will be essential to maximise the scientific return, particularly for short-lived and faint gamma-ray bursts.

In summary, the Earth’s influence on the instrumental background for SVOM is twofold: a shielding of the isotropic cosmic background and an addition of anisotropic albedo emission. The relative importance of these components varies with energy, geometry, and orbital position, leading to a complex dependence of sensitivity on observational conditions. By quantifying these effects, this work provides a framework for predicting and correcting sensitivity variations, ultimately enabling more accurate characterisation of the mission’s detection capabilities and optimising its contribution to time-domain high-energy astrophysics.

title: On the Capacity of the Multiuser Vector Adder Channel
abstract: We investigate the capacity of the multiuser vector adder channel, a communication model in which several users transmit binary vectors whose componentwise sum is observed at the receiver. Both synchronous and asynchronous transmission scenarios are considered. We derive asymptotic expressions for the sum capacity as the number of users grows, and provide bounds for finite settings. Our analysis employs combinatorial and probabilistic techniques to characterize achievable rates. The results offer insights into coding strategies and performance limits for multiuser systems with integer-valued superposition at the channel output.
introduction:
The multiuser vector adder channel is a communication model in which several users transmit binary or vector-valued signals simultaneously, and the channel output is given by the component-wise sum of all users’ inputs. This model serves as an abstraction for a variety of practical systems where signals from multiple sources superimpose without interference in other dimensions, such as certain optical, molecular, or wireless multiple-access scenarios. Unlike conventional multiple-access channels in which interference is mitigated or separated through coding, orthogonalization, or interference cancellation, the vector adder channel preserves the aggregate sum, and the receiver’s task is to decode the users’ messages from this summed observation.

Understanding the capacity of such a channel—the maximum achievable sum rate under given constraints—is of both theoretical and practical interest. The model exhibits nontrivial behavior because the output alphabet grows with the number of simultaneously active users, and the statistics of the sum depend on the distribution of user inputs. In particular, the interplay between the number of users, the vector dimension, and the constraints on input distributions leads to rich combinatorial and information-theoretic structures. Traditional results on multiple-access channels do not directly apply, as the vector adder channel imposes a deterministic and invertible mapping from the set of joint inputs to the output, but with potential ambiguity when multiple input configurations yield the same sum.

Previous studies have examined the scalar adder channel and certain special cases of the vector adder channel, deriving achievable rates and bounds under specific assumptions, such as synchronous transmission and uniform input distributions. Extensions to asynchronous or noisy settings have also been considered, though a complete characterization of the capacity region remains open in most general cases. Recent advances in coding theory, combinatorial design, and probabilistic methods suggest new approaches to analyze and approach capacity limits for these channels.

In this work, we investigate the capacity of the multiuser vector adder channel under a range of input constraints and asymptotic regimes. We aim to derive tight bounds and, where possible, exact expressions for the capacity in the limit of large vector lengths and many users. Our analysis leverages both information-theoretic inequalities and combinatorial enumeration techniques to capture the growth of the output alphabet and to quantify the degree of ambiguity in decoding. The results contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental limits of sum-based multiple access and provide insights that may inform the design of efficient coding and decoding strategies for practical systems.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated the capacity of the multiuser vector adder channel under various traffic and coding assumptions. By deriving analytical bounds and asymptotic expressions, we characterized how capacity scales with the number of users and the vector dimension. The results reveal fundamental trade-offs between user load, noise tolerance, and achievable rates, providing insight into optimal system design. Numerical evaluations confirmed the tightness of the proposed bounds in both sparse and dense regimes. These findings extend existing multiaccess channel theory to vector adder models, offering a foundation for future research on coding strategies and practical multiuser communication protocols.

title: COBRAS-TS: A new approach to Semi-Supervised Clustering of Time Series
abstract: We present COBRAS-TS, a novel method for semi-supervised clustering of time series data that extends the recently proposed COBRAS framework to handle temporal structures effectively. COBRAS-TS integrates pairwise constraints into a dynamic clustering process, iteratively refining partitions while exploiting both labeled and unlabeled data. To address the specific challenges of time series, such as temporal misalignment and varying sequence lengths, our approach incorporates elastic distance measures and local shape-based similarity within the COBRAS iterative refinement loop. This combination allows COBRAS-TS to capture meaningful temporal patterns while respecting supervision signals.
