abstract: We propose a novel approach to sentence relation modeling by incorporating auxiliary character-level embeddings alongside conventional word-level representations. While existing models predominantly rely on word embeddings, they often struggle with rare words, morphological variations, and noisy text. Our method augments a base sentence relation model with a parallel character-level encoder, whose output is fused with word-level features to enhance semantic representation. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets for natural language inference and semantic textual similarity demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines. Analysis reveals that the character-level component is particularly effective in handling out-of-vocabulary words and capturing subword information, leading to more robust and accurate modeling of sentence relations across diverse linguistic contexts.
introduction:
Understanding and modeling the relationships between sentences is a fundamental problem in natural language processing (NLP), underpinning a wide range of tasks such as natural language inference (NLI), paraphrase identification, question answering, and discourse analysis. These tasks require systems to capture both the semantic content of individual sentences and the nuanced relationships that arise between them. Recent advances in neural network architectures, particularly models based on recurrent networks, convolutional networks, and more recently Transformer-based architectures, have yielded significant improvements in sentence relation modeling. Central to these advances is the use of pre-trained word embeddings, which provide rich semantic representations learned from large corpora. However, word-level embeddings face inherent limitations when dealing with rare words, out-of-vocabulary (OOV) tokens, and morphologically complex languages.

In practical scenarios, sentences often contain words that were infrequent or unseen during model pre-training. Word-level representations struggle to encode such tokens effectively, leading to degraded performance in downstream sentence pair tasks, especially in domains with specialized vocabulary or noisy user-generated content. Moreover, many languages exhibit rich morphological structures, where the meaning of a word can be inferred from its subword or character composition. Purely word-based models are less capable of capturing such morphological and orthographic cues, which can be crucial for precise semantic interpretation.

Character-level modeling offers a compelling complement to word-based representations by enabling the model to encode subword information, handle misspellings, and generalize better to unseen words. Character-level embeddings can capture morphological patterns, affixes, and orthographic features that are lost when only word-level embeddings are used. Integrating character-level information into sentence relation modeling has the potential to enhance robustness and improve performance across diverse domains and languages. However, naively replacing word-level embeddings with character-level ones often results in higher computational cost and slower convergence due to longer input sequences. Furthermore, character-level models alone may struggle to capture higher-level semantic abstractions that are more easily learned from word-level distributions.

A promising direction is to incorporate character-level information as an auxiliary signal alongside standard word-level embeddings. In such a hybrid representation, word-level embeddings provide semantic priors derived from large-scale corpora, while character-level embeddings contribute morphological and orthographic detail, particularly for rare or OOV words. The auxiliary character-level embedding can be fused with word-level representations through concatenation, gating mechanisms, or attention-based integration, enabling the model to leverage both coarse-grained semantics and fine-grained form-based cues. This approach can be particularly beneficial in sentence relation modeling, where subtle morphological variations may change the entailment or contradiction relationship, or where orthographic similarity can hint at paraphrasing.

Despite the intuitive appeal of such hybrid models, there remain open questions about the most effective ways to integrate character-level and word-level information for sentence pair tasks. Prior work has explored character-aware encoders for single-sentence classification and sequence labeling, but relatively less attention has been given to their role in explicitly modeling inter-sentence relations. Moreover, the interaction between auxiliary character-level embeddings and modern pre-trained language models, which already incorporate subword tokenization schemes, is not yet fully understood. Investigating whether additional character-level signals can still offer performance gains in the presence of strong contextualized embeddings is thus an important research question.

In this work, we propose an enhanced sentence relation modeling framework that incorporates auxiliary character-level embeddings into a word-level encoder architecture. Our approach is designed to retain the semantic richness of pre-trained word embeddings while augmenting them with morphological and orthographic cues at the character level. We evaluate the proposed model on benchmark sentence pair datasets across different domains and languages, analyzing its ability to handle rare words, noisy text, and morphologically rich languages. The contributions of this paper are threefold: (1) we design an efficient integration mechanism for auxiliary character-level embeddings in sentence relation modeling; (2) we conduct comprehensive experiments to quantify the benefits of this hybrid representation; and (3) we provide an in-depth analysis of the interaction between character-level signals and contextualized word embeddings. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves performance over strong baselines, highlighting the enduring value of character-level modeling in modern NLP systems.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed an approach to enhance sentence relation modeling by incorporating auxiliary character-level embeddings alongside traditional word-level representations. By explicitly capturing subword information, our method improves the handling of rare, morphologically complex, and out-of-vocabulary words, thereby strengthening semantic representation. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent gains over strong baselines, highlighting the complementary nature of character-level features in relational reasoning tasks. Furthermore, the approach introduces minimal computational overhead, making it practical for large-scale applications. These findings suggest that integrating character-level signals can serve as a robust enhancement to existing sentence relation models. Future work will explore adaptive fusion mechanisms and cross-lingual extensions to further leverage fine-grained linguistic cues for improved performance.

title: Dynamo-driven plasmoid ejections above a spherical surface
abstract: We present numerical simulations of magnetohydrodynamic processes that generate recurrent plasmoid ejections above a spherical surface, driven self-consistently by a turbulent dynamo operating beneath it. The computational domain encompasses a lower layer, where helical forcing sustains large-scale magnetic field generation, and an overlying coronal layer, in which the plasma is nearly force-free. The transition between the layers allows magnetic structures to emerge and evolve dynamically. Our results show that the dynamo produces twisted magnetic field bundles that rise buoyantly and reconnect in the coronal region, leading to the intermittent release of plasmoids into the overlying atmosphere. These ejections are accompanied by current sheet formation and associated signatures of magnetic reconnection. The frequency and morphology of the events depend on the dynamo cycle and field topology, with stronger large-scale fields producing more energetic ejections. The study demonstrates a direct link between sub-surface dynamo action and coronal mass ejection-like phenomena, providing a physically consistent framework for understanding magnetic energy release above astrophysical bodies with convective interiors. Implications for solar and stellar coronae are discussed.
introduction:
Magnetized plasmas in astrophysical and laboratory contexts often exhibit the spontaneous formation and ejection of plasmoids—localized, magnetically confined structures carrying mass, momentum, and magnetic flux. In stellar environments, such as the solar corona, plasmoid ejections are observed as coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and are believed to play a central role in the transport of magnetic helicity and energy into the heliosphere. The physical mechanisms underlying their generation are commonly associated with magnetic reconnection, driven by large-scale field emergence and restructuring, often in the presence of dynamo-generated magnetic fields within the stellar interior.  

Numerical studies of dynamo action have demonstrated that large-scale magnetic fields can be maintained by turbulent flows in rotating, stratified spherical shells. When such fields interact with overlying plasma layers, dynamic processes can lead to episodic release of magnetic structures into the outer atmosphere. While Cartesian models have provided valuable insights into the physics of reconnection and plasmoid formation, the curvature and global topology of a spherical system can introduce qualitatively different behaviors. In particular, the coupling between a self-consistently operating dynamo and the open, stratified atmosphere above a spherical surface remains less explored.  

In this work, we investigate dynamo-driven plasmoid ejections in a global spherical geometry, using three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations that self-consistently generate large-scale magnetic fields beneath the surface. The simulations allow us to study the emergence of magnetic flux into the coronal layer and the subsequent formation, acceleration, and release of plasmoids into the outer domain. By focusing on the interplay between the deep-seated dynamo and the outer atmospheric dynamics, we aim to elucidate the role of global geometry in shaping the properties of ejection events and to provide a framework for interpreting observations of stellar and solar eruptive phenomena.
conclusion:
The numerical experiments presented in this study have demonstrated that dynamo action within a spherical domain can give rise to recurrent plasmoid ejections into an overlying coronal-like exterior. By coupling a self-consistent large-scale dynamo in the turbulent interior with a force-free or weakly magnetised outer atmosphere, we have been able to reproduce the emergence, rise, and subsequent propagation of magnetised structures that resemble coronal mass ejections in several key respects. The spherical geometry has proven essential for capturing the global connectivity of the magnetic field, the curvature of emerging flux systems, and the manner in which large-scale helicity is transported through the surface.

The simulations confirm that when the dynamo operates in a regime producing cyclic polarity reversals, the build-up of twisted magnetic structures above the surface is a natural consequence of the underlying field evolution. The interplay between differential rotation, turbulent convection, and the large-scale α-effect generates substantial magnetic helicity of opposite signs in the two hemispheres. This helicity is shed into the exterior via plasmoid-like ejections, which act as a conduit for regulating the dynamo’s operation and preventing the excessive accumulation of magnetic twist in the domain. The ejections are thus not merely incidental by-products of surface activity, but appear to play a dynamical role in the saturation of the dynamo.

We have further shown that the morphology and timescales of the simulated ejections depend sensitively on the dynamo period, the stratification across the surface, and the coronal Alfvén speed. In particular, stronger stratification and lower coronal densities tend to produce more rapid and elongated plasmoid structures, while higher coronal magnetisation can extend the time over which ejections remain coherent. The spherical configuration naturally allows for the study of latitudinal variations in ejection properties, revealing systematic hemispheric asymmetries linked to the sign of the helicity and the phase of the dynamo cycle.

From a methodological standpoint, this work extends previous Cartesian dynamo–corona coupling studies into a global context, bridging localised flux-emergence modelling with whole-sphere magnetohydrodynamic simulations. This approach enables the investigation of global transport processes, the interaction between open and closed field regions, and the role of curvature in shaping eruptive events. The results suggest that global dynamo simulations, when supplemented with an explicit coronal layer, can serve as a valuable tool for interpreting observational signatures of large-scale eruptions and their cyclic modulation.

Future work should aim to refine the representation of the coronal plasma, including more realistic thermodynamics, radiative losses, and solar-wind driving, in order to better match the observed kinematics and energetics of coronal mass ejections. Higher resolution will be necessary to capture the full spectrum of scales involved in the onset of eruption and in the turbulence that develops in their wake. Additionally, a systematic exploration of parameter space, including rotation rate, magnetic Reynolds number, and boundary conditions, will help to clarify the universality of the mechanisms identified here.

In summary, our findings support the view that large-scale dynamo action in spherical geometry can self-consistently produce recurrent plasmoid ejections whose properties are intrinsically tied to the global magnetic cycle. Such ejections provide a natural channel for helicity removal and may be a fundamental aspect of stellar magnetic activity across a range of spectral types and rotation rates.

title: Radiative corrections to $h^0\to WW^*/ZZ^*\to 4$\,leptons in the MSSM
abstract: We present a calculation of one-loop radiative corrections to the decay $h^0\to WW^*/ZZ^*\to 4$ leptons in the MSSM. Virtual supersymmetric particle effects and Higgs-sector mixing are included. Numerical results illustrate deviations from the Standard Model predictions, highlighting the sensitivity of four-lepton final states to supersymmetric parameter space.
introduction:
The discovery of a scalar resonance with a mass around 125 GeV at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations has marked a milestone in particle physics, confirming the existence of a Higgs boson as predicted by the Standard Model (SM). Subsequent measurements of its couplings and decay properties have so far shown remarkable agreement with SM expectations, within current experimental uncertainties. Nevertheless, the possibility remains that the observed state could be part of an extended Higgs sector, as predicted in many scenarios of physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). Among these, the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) offers a theoretically well-motivated framework that addresses the hierarchy problem, provides a candidate for dark matter, and predicts a richer Higgs spectrum consisting of two CP-even neutral bosons ($h^0$, $H^0$), one CP-odd neutral boson ($A^0$), and a pair of charged bosons ($H^\pm$).

In the MSSM, the lighter CP-even Higgs boson $h^0$ can naturally be identified with the state observed at the LHC, provided radiative corrections—particularly those from the top–stop sector—are taken into account. Once the mass is fixed to the measured value, precise predictions for the couplings and decay rates of $h^0$ become an essential tool for probing supersymmetric effects indirectly. Among the various decay channels, those involving electroweak gauge bosons, such as $h^0 \to WW^*$ and $h^0 \to ZZ^*$, followed by purely leptonic decays of the gauge bosons, play a central role in Higgs property measurements due to their clean experimental signatures and relatively low backgrounds.

At a Higgs mass of approximately 125 GeV, at least one of the vector bosons in these decays is off-shell, leading to the three- or four-body final states collectively denoted as $h^0 \to WW^*/ZZ^* \to 4\ell$ (with $\ell = e, \mu$ and including $\ell\nu$ channels for the $WW^*$ case). The kinematical complexity of such processes requires an accurate treatment of finite-width effects and spin correlations in the intermediate boson propagators. In the SM, radiative corrections to these modes have been computed with high precision, and are known to modify partial widths and kinematic distributions at the few-percent level. In the MSSM, additional loop contributions from supersymmetric particles and an altered Higgs coupling structure can introduce further deviations, which become particularly relevant in precision Higgs studies.

Radiative corrections in the MSSM to Higgs decays into gauge bosons have been investigated in various approximations, often focusing either on on-shell decays into $WW$ or $ZZ$ above threshold, or on effective coupling modifications extracted from loop-corrected Higgs mixing angles. However, for a light Higgs boson in the mass range realised in nature, a complete one-loop treatment of the off-shell processes $h^0 \to WW^*/ZZ^* \to 4$ leptons—including both SM-like and genuine MSSM contributions—remains necessary to match the precision of current and future experimental analyses. Such a computation must consistently incorporate the full set of virtual corrections, soft and hard bremsstrahlung, and the finite widths of the gauge bosons, while ensuring gauge invariance and the correct implementation of mass renormalisation in the supersymmetric Higgs sector.

The motivation for such a study is twofold. First, the four-lepton channels constitute “golden modes” for Higgs coupling measurements at the LHC and prospective colliders, with statistical and systematic uncertainties steadily decreasing. Second, in the MSSM parameter space where superpartners are heavy and direct production is suppressed, indirect effects in loop-induced observables may offer one of the few viable avenues for detecting supersymmetric physics. Precise theoretical predictions for $h^0 \to WW^*/ZZ^* \to 4\ell$ thus contribute directly to the programme of constraining or revealing new physics through high-precision Higgs measurements.

In this work we present a comprehensive calculation of the one-loop radiative corrections to the decays $h^0 \to WW^*/ZZ^* \to 4$ leptons in the MSSM. We include the full set of SM and MSSM diagrams, treat the gauge bosons with complex masses to account for their finite widths, and implement both virtual and real photon corrections to cancel infrared singularities. Our results are given for partial decay widths and selected differential distributions, and we discuss the dependence on MSSM parameters in representative benchmark scenarios. By comparing with the corresponding SM predictions, we quantify the size of possible supersymmetric effects and assess their visibility in current and future experimental datasets.
conclusion:
In this work we have presented a detailed analysis of the radiative corrections to the decay processes \( h^0 \to WW^*/ZZ^* \to 4\ell \) within the framework of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), with particular emphasis on the one-loop electroweak contributions and their interplay with supersymmetric particle effects. Our study has been carried out in the context of the decoupling regime, as well as in scenarios where the non–Standard Model degrees of freedom remain sufficiently light to leave an imprint in precision Higgs phenomenology. The motivation for this investigation stems from the fact that the four-lepton channels, especially the so-called “golden channel” \( h^0 \to ZZ^* \to 4\ell \), provide some of the cleanest probes of Higgs boson properties at the LHC and future colliders. In the MSSM, the lightest CP-even Higgs boson can closely mimic the Standard Model Higgs in its tree-level couplings, but radiative effects—both from the extended Higgs sector and from superpartners—can subtly modify these couplings and decay widths. Quantifying these deviations is essential for exploiting the precision frontier in Higgs physics.

Our calculation has incorporated the full set of MSSM one-loop diagrams contributing to the effective \( h^0 WW \) and \( h^0 ZZ \) vertices, including loops of fermions, sfermions, charginos, neutralinos, and the extended Higgs bosons. For the off-shell gauge boson decays into leptons, we have retained the complete gauge-invariant set of diagrams and accounted for finite-width effects in the intermediate vector boson propagators. The use of the complex mass scheme has ensured a consistent treatment of unstable particles, maintaining gauge invariance in the presence of off-shell kinematics. We have also examined the numerical impact of higher-order QED corrections in the final state, which, while typically subdominant for inclusive observables, can be relevant in precision differential distributions.

The results indicate that in the decoupling limit—where all SUSY particles and heavy Higgs states are much heavier than the electroweak scale—the radiative corrections to the partial widths \( \Gamma(h^0 \to WW^*, ZZ^*) \) are dominated by the Standard Model–like top-quark and gauge boson loops, with MSSM-specific effects suppressed by powers of \( M_Z^2/M_{\mathrm{SUSY}}^2 \). In this regime, the deviations from the SM predictions are typically below the percent level, well within current experimental uncertainties, but potentially resolvable at next-generation lepton colliders. However, for scenarios with relatively light superpartners—particularly light charginos, neutralinos, and third-generation sfermions—the corrections can be significantly enhanced. We have found that chargino loops can shift the effective \( h^0WW \) and \( h^0ZZ \) couplings by up to a few percent in magnitude, depending on the gaugino–Higgsino mixing parameters. Similarly, stop and sbottom loops, especially in the presence of large trilinear couplings \( A_t \) and \( A_b \), can induce noticeable modifications through both vertex and wave-function renormalization effects.

An important aspect of our study is the comparative behaviour of the \( WW^* \) and \( ZZ^* \) channels. While the underlying loop corrections to the \( h^0VV \) vertices are common to both, the different kinematic configurations and phase-space suppressions in the off-shell decays lead to slightly different sensitivities to new physics. In particular, we observe that the relative correction to \( h^0 \to ZZ^* \) is typically marginally larger than that to \( h^0 \to WW^* \) in scenarios with enhanced couplings to neutralinos, owing to the absence of charged-current constraints in the neutral channel. Nevertheless, the theoretical correlation between the two channels remains strong, and a combined analysis of both modes offers a powerful consistency check of the MSSM predictions.

Our numerical analysis, performed for a representative set of benchmark points consistent with current collider and flavour constraints, has demonstrated that the MSSM-induced deviations in the four-lepton final states can reach the level of several percent in the partial widths, and in certain corners of parameter space, can slightly distort the invariant mass and angular distributions of the leptons. Such effects, while challenging to detect at the LHC due to limited statistics and systematic uncertainties, could become accessible at high-luminosity runs or at future \( e^+e^- \) machines with dedicated Higgs programs. The clean experimental signature of the four-lepton final state, together with the precise theoretical control achievable on both the SM and MSSM predictions, makes these channels particularly valuable in the search for indirect signs of supersymmetry.

From a theoretical standpoint, our work underscores the necessity of a consistent treatment of radiative corrections when confronting precision Higgs measurements with MSSM predictions. The loop effects we have computed are gauge invariant, ultraviolet finite (after renormalization in an on-shell scheme), and incorporate the full dependence on the supersymmetric particle spectrum. This ensures that they can be readily implemented in phenomenological analyses and global fits aiming to constrain the MSSM parameter space. Furthermore, the methods employed here—particularly the handling of off-shell intermediate states and the inclusion of finite-width effects—are directly applicable to a broader class of Higgs decay processes and to other extensions of the SM.

Looking ahead, our results suggest several avenues for further research. Extending the present analysis to include two-loop contributions of leading MSSM corrections, especially those enhanced by large Yukawa couplings or strong interactions, would improve the theoretical precision to match the expected experimental accuracy at future colliders. Similarly, incorporating full NLO QED corrections to the four-lepton final state, including lepton–photon recombination procedures matched to realistic detector acceptances, would be essential for high-precision differential studies. Finally, exploring the correlation of \( h^0 \to 4\ell \) observables with other Higgs decay channels, such as \( h^0 \to \gamma\gamma \) and \( h^0 \to Z\gamma \), could provide complementary constraints on the electroweakino and sfermion sectors.

In conclusion, the decay channels \( h^0 \to WW^*/ZZ^* \to 4\ell \) remain a cornerstone of precision Higgs physics, offering a clean laboratory for testing the SM and probing virtual effects of new particles predicted by the MSSM. Our comprehensive one-loop calculation has clarified the size and structure of the radiative corrections in this framework, highlighted the conditions under which MSSM effects could be observable, and established a solid foundation for future phenomenological and experimental investigations. As experimental measurements of Higgs properties advance into the percent-level regime, the careful incorporation of such radiative effects will be indispensable for uncovering or constraining the subtle footprints of supersymmetry in the Higgs sector.

title: Optimizing polynomials for floating-point implementation
abstract: Polynomial evaluation is a fundamental operation in many scientific and engineering computations, yet its efficient and accurate implementation on floating-point hardware remains challenging. This work addresses the problem of optimizing polynomial forms to minimize numerical error and computational cost in floating-point arithmetic. We investigate transformation techniques, including coefficient scaling, variable substitution, and reordering based on Horner’s method and Estrin’s scheme, to reduce rounding error propagation and improve parallelism. The analysis combines theoretical bounds on floating-point error with empirical evaluation across a range of polynomial degrees and coefficient magnitudes. We also explore trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and memory usage, providing guidelines for selecting evaluation strategies under different hardware constraints. Experimental results on modern CPU and GPU architectures demonstrate that carefully optimized polynomial representations can achieve significant improvements in both performance and precision compared to naïve implementations. The proposed methodology offers a systematic approach to tailoring polynomial evaluation for high-performance, numerically robust floating-point computation.
introduction: Polynomial evaluation is a fundamental operation in numerous scientific and engineering applications, including numerical analysis, signal processing, and computer graphics. When implemented in floating-point arithmetic, the accuracy and efficiency of polynomial computations can be significantly affected by rounding errors and hardware constraints. Optimizing polynomials for floating-point implementation involves selecting appropriate formulations and evaluation strategies that minimize numerical error while maintaining computational efficiency. This process often includes reformulating polynomials, reordering terms, or employing specialized algorithms such as Horner’s method. This paper investigates techniques for optimizing polynomial representations to improve stability and performance in floating-point environments, providing both theoretical analysis and empirical validation.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined strategies for optimizing polynomial expressions for efficient and accurate implementation in floating-point arithmetic. By analyzing both the algebraic structure of polynomials and the computational characteristics of floating-point hardware, we developed methods that balance numerical stability, computational cost, and ease of implementation. Our approach combined classical techniques such as Horner’s method and factorization with more recent advancements in error analysis and automated term rearrangement, allowing us to minimize rounding errors while reducing the number of arithmetic operations.

We demonstrated that careful reformulation of polynomial evaluation sequences can significantly improve both performance and accuracy, particularly for high-degree polynomials or those with coefficients spanning a wide dynamic range. Experimental results showed measurable reductions in relative error when compared to naïve evaluation, as well as improvements in execution time on contemporary processor architectures. Moreover, we highlighted the trade-offs between aggressive optimization for speed and the preservation of numerical fidelity, underscoring that the optimal balance is application-dependent.

The presented methodology is not limited to a specific class of polynomials; it can be adapted to various domains, including approximation theory, signal processing, and numerical simulation, where polynomial evaluation is a core computational task. Furthermore, the techniques are compatible with automated code generation and compiler optimizations, suggesting a path toward integration into existing numerical software toolchains.

Future work may extend these results by exploring mixed-precision implementations, adaptive evaluation schemes that select the optimal form at runtime, and integration with symbolic pre-processing to handle special polynomial structures. Investigating the impact of hardware-specific features, such as fused multiply–add operations and vectorized execution, could yield further gains. Additionally, extending the analysis to polynomials evaluated over complex domains or in the context of interval arithmetic would broaden the applicability of the approach.

Overall, our findings reinforce the importance of algebraic reformulation and numerical analysis in achieving efficient and reliable floating-point computations. By bridging theoretical optimization techniques with practical implementation concerns, this work provides a foundation for more robust and performant polynomial evaluation strategies in a wide range of computational settings.

title: The Twelvefold Way of Non-Sequential Lossless Compression
abstract: We introduce the Twelvefold Way of Non-Sequential Lossless Compression, a unifying framework that categorizes compression strategies into twelve distinct, mathematically grounded classes. By decoupling symbol ordering from redundancy modeling, our approach generalizes existing algorithms and reveals new, efficient schemes. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation demonstrate competitive performance across diverse datasets, highlighting the framework’s potential to guide systematic design and optimization of non-sequential lossless compression methods.
introduction:
Lossless data compression is a foundational technique in information theory and computer science, enabling the reduction of data size without any loss of information. Classical compression algorithms, such as Huffman coding, Lempel–Ziv schemes, and arithmetic coding, typically operate on sequential data streams, exploiting redundancy through local symbol correlations and probabilistic modeling. While these paradigms have proven effective for a wide range of applications, they are inherently constrained by the sequential nature of their execution and by the structural assumptions embedded in their models. In contrast, non-sequential lossless compression seeks to dissociate the order of data processing from the original ordering of the input, thereby expanding the design space for compression strategies.

The study of non-sequential approaches opens the possibility of exploiting global structural patterns, combinatorial symmetries, and multidimensional data arrangements that are not readily accessible to sequential methods. Such approaches are particularly relevant in contexts where data has an inherently unordered or partially ordered structure, as in certain database records, graph representations, or multidimensional sensor arrays. However, the theoretical framework for systematically categorizing and analyzing non-sequential compression methods remains underdeveloped. Without such a framework, it is difficult to compare algorithms, reason about their optimality, or identify unifying principles that transcend specific implementations.

This work introduces the Twelvefold Way of Non-Sequential Lossless Compression, a formal classification scheme inspired by combinatorial enumeration theory. The proposed framework organizes non-sequential compression strategies into twelve distinct classes, defined by the interplay between data element distinguishability, storage location constraints, and permissible transformation operations. By drawing an analogy to the classical Twelvefold Way of combinatorics, we provide a rigorous, exhaustive categorization that captures the diversity of possible non-sequential compression designs. This classification not only serves as a conceptual map for existing algorithms but also highlights unexplored regions in the design space, suggesting novel compression paradigms.

Through this formalism, we aim to bridge the gap between abstract information-theoretic limits and concrete algorithmic realizations. The Twelvefold Way framework offers a structured lens for understanding the fundamental trade-offs and symmetries in non-sequential lossless compression, laying the groundwork for both theoretical advances and practical innovations in data representation.
conclusion: This work has outlined the Twelvefold Way of non-sequential lossless compression, unifying diverse strategies under a coherent theoretical framework. By decoupling compression from strict data ordering, we demonstrated pathways for improved adaptability, efficiency, and applicability across heterogeneous data domains. The taxonomy clarifies relationships among existing methods while revealing underexplored design spaces. Future research should refine these principles, extend formal proofs of optimality, and explore real-world implementations, enabling more resilient, domain-agnostic compression systems capable of leveraging the strengths of non-sequential processing.

title: Linear Response Theory for Nonlinear Stochastic Differential Equations with $\alpha$-stable L\'{e}vy Noises
abstract: We develop a linear response framework for nonlinear stochastic differential equations driven by $\alpha$-stable L\'{e}vy noises. Unlike Gaussian-driven systems, the heavy-tailed jumps induce nonlocal dynamics, requiring fractional operators in the response formulation. We derive explicit susceptibility functions via generalized Fokker–Planck equations and validate them through numerical simulations. The theory accurately predicts system responses to weak external perturbations, highlighting the interplay between nonlinearity and non-Gaussian noise in shaping statistical properties and dynamical sensitivity across a broad range of stability indices.
introduction:
Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) driven by non-Gaussian noise have attracted considerable attention in recent years due to their ability to model complex systems subject to abrupt, heavy-tailed fluctuations. Among the non-Gaussian processes, symmetric $\alpha$-stable Lévy motions play a central role. They generalize Brownian motion by allowing for discontinuous sample paths and probability distributions with infinite variance, thus capturing the statistics of impulsive, jump-like perturbations observed in a wide range of phenomena, from climate dynamics and geophysical processes to finance, neuroscience, and engineering systems. The parameter $\alpha \in (0,2]$ controls the tail heaviness and jump frequency, with the Gaussian case recovered as $\alpha \to 2$. For $\alpha<2$, the lack of finite second moments invalidates many classical tools of stochastic calculus and statistical mechanics, thereby requiring new analytical and numerical approaches.

Nonlinear SDEs with $\alpha$-stable Lévy noise present particular challenges when one is interested in their response to external perturbations. In the Gaussian framework, linear response theory — epitomized by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) — provides a powerful formalism to predict the change in statistical observables induced by small changes in system parameters or forcing, without solving the perturbed dynamics directly. The FDT relates the response function to correlation functions computed in the unperturbed steady state, thus enabling efficient sensitivity analysis and control. However, the derivation of FDT relies heavily on properties specific to Gaussian measures, such as finite variance and certain integration-by-parts identities, which break down in the presence of Lévy noise with $\alpha<2$. Consequently, the extension of linear response theory to systems driven by $\alpha$-stable Lévy processes is nontrivial and remains an active area of research.

Recent progress in stochastic analysis for jump processes has provided new tools to study the statistical and dynamical properties of Lévy-driven systems, including fractional Fokker–Planck equations, generalized Itô formulas, and spectral methods adapted to nonlocal operators. These developments create opportunities to revisit linear response theory in the non-Gaussian, heavy-tailed context. In particular, for nonlinear systems far from equilibrium, it is important to understand how the interplay between deterministic nonlinearities and nonlocal stochastic forcing shapes the sensitivity to external perturbations. This understanding is essential for both theoretical insights into nonequilibrium statistical mechanics and practical applications such as risk assessment, signal detection, and optimal control in environments dominated by rare but significant events.

In this work, we develop a linear response framework for nonlinear SDEs driven by symmetric $\alpha$-stable Lévy motions. Our approach accommodates dynamical systems with arbitrary nonlinear drift, allowing for both additive and multiplicative Lévy noise structures. We derive explicit expressions for the first-order variation of expectation values of observables with respect to small perturbations, in terms of unperturbed system statistics. The analysis accounts for the nonlocality introduced by the Lévy generator and the absence of finite second moments. Furthermore, we discuss the conditions under which the response formula is valid, including regularity assumptions on the drift and observables, as well as ergodicity of the underlying Lévy-driven dynamics. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and highlight qualitative differences between Gaussian and $\alpha$-stable Lévy responses, especially in regimes dominated by large jumps. Our findings contribute to the broader effort of extending response theory beyond the Gaussian paradigm, enabling predictive modeling of complex systems subject to heavy-tailed stochastic forcing.
conclusion: In this work, we have developed a linear response framework for nonlinear stochastic differential equations driven by symmetric $\alpha$-stable Lévy noises. By extending classical fluctuation–dissipation concepts to non-Gaussian, heavy-tailed settings, we derived explicit response formulas that account for the nonlocal jump structure of the underlying dynamics. The approach accommodates systems lacking finite variance, thereby broadening the applicability of linear response theory beyond the Gaussian paradigm. Analytical results were complemented by numerical experiments, which demonstrated the accuracy of the proposed formulas in predicting ensemble-averaged observables under small external perturbations. In particular, we observed that the interplay between nonlinearity and Lévy noise leads to distinctive response behaviors, such as enhanced sensitivity or suppressed responses, depending on the stability index and system parameters. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating the full nonlocal generator in response calculations for heavy-tailed systems. The methodology presented here provides a theoretical tool for investigating stability, control, and prediction in complex systems with impulsive fluctuations, such as in physics, finance, and climate science. Future work will focus on extending the framework to multiplicative Lévy noise, spatially extended systems, and data-driven estimation of response operators, further bridging stochastic theory with practical modeling needs in non-Gaussian environments.

title: Structure and Vertical Modes in Finite 2D Plasma Crystals
abstract: We investigate the structural properties and vertical oscillation modes of finite two-dimensional (2D) plasma crystals composed of charged microparticles confined in a parabolic potential well. Using molecular dynamics simulations with Yukawa-type interparticle interactions, we analyze equilibrium configurations for varying particle numbers and Debye screening lengths. The results reveal concentric shell structures in the horizontal plane, with a tendency toward hexagonal ordering in the central region and circular arrangements near the boundary. Vertical modes are characterized through normal mode analysis, showing a discrete spectrum whose features depend sensitively on particle number and screening strength. The highest-frequency vertical mode corresponds to rigid-plane oscillation of the entire cluster, while lower-frequency modes exhibit mixed radial and vertical displacements with complex spatial patterns. Comparisons with horizontal mode spectra highlight distinct scaling behaviors and mode degeneracies. These findings provide insight into the coupling between structural ordering and collective excitations in finite 2D plasma crystals, with implications for experimental diagnostics and control in laboratory dusty plasma systems.
introduction:
Complex (dusty) plasmas, consisting of micron-sized solid particles embedded in a weakly ionized gas, have emerged as versatile model systems for studying strongly coupled many-body phenomena. When the charged dust particles are confined in two dimensions by an external potential and interact via screened Coulomb (Yukawa) forces, they can self-organize into ordered lattice structures known as plasma crystals. These systems offer the unique advantage that individual particle positions and trajectories can be directly resolved in real time using optical imaging, enabling detailed investigations of structural properties, collective excitations, and dynamical processes at the particle level.

In laboratory experiments, two-dimensional (2D) plasma crystals are typically formed in the sheath region above a powered electrode in a radio-frequency (RF) discharge. The vertical electric field in the sheath counterbalances gravity, while horizontal confinement arises from the plasma potential profile. The interplay between the external confinement and the interparticle Yukawa repulsion determines the equilibrium arrangement of particles. For sufficiently strong coupling, particles arrange into hexagonal lattices, but finite system sizes and confinement anisotropies can introduce defects, distortions, and variations in symmetry. Understanding the structural properties of finite 2D plasma crystals is essential for interpreting experimental results and for developing accurate theoretical models.

Beyond static configurations, dusty plasmas support rich spectra of collective oscillations. In 2D plasma crystals, these include in-plane (longitudinal and transverse) modes as well as out-of-plane (vertical) modes. While in-plane modes have been extensively studied both experimentally and theoretically, vertical modes—arising from the finite vertical confinement and the restoring forces due to sheath electric fields—have received comparatively less attention, particularly in finite systems. Vertical oscillations are sensitive to the strength and anisotropy of the vertical confinement, as well as to the coupling between particles mediated by the plasma environment. The mode spectra encode detailed information about the interparticle interaction potential and the external confinement parameters, and can thus serve as diagnostic tools.

Recent advances in numerical simulations, such as molecular dynamics with Yukawa interactions under parabolic confinement, allow systematic exploration of both structural and dynamical properties of finite 2D plasma crystals. By varying particle number, screening length, and confinement strengths, it is possible to identify trends in lattice symmetry, defect formation, and collective mode characteristics. In particular, the analysis of vertical mode structures in finite systems can reveal discrete mode patterns, frequency ordering, and spatial localization effects not present in infinite or periodic crystals.

This work investigates the interplay between structure and vertical oscillation modes in finite 2D plasma crystals. We employ numerical simulations to determine equilibrium configurations and to compute the full spectrum of vertical modes. Our results elucidate how confinement, screening, and finite-size effects shape both the static lattice arrangement and the dynamic vertical response, providing new insights into the physics of strongly coupled, low-dimensional plasma systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the structural properties and collective vertical oscillation modes of finite two‑dimensional plasma crystals using numerical simulations and mode analysis. By systematically varying the number of particles and the confining potential parameters, we have characterized the transition from disordered to ordered states, as well as the dependence of equilibrium configurations on system size. The results confirm that for small particle numbers, concentric ring structures dominate, while for larger clusters a well‑defined hexagonal interior emerges, surrounded by circular outer shells. This structural evolution reflects the competition between interparticle Yukawa repulsion and the anisotropic confinement imposed by the external potential.

Our analysis of vertical modes provides new insight into the three‑dimensional dynamics of these nominally two‑dimensional systems. The calculated spectra show that the highest‑frequency vertical mode corresponds to a rigid, in‑phase oscillation of the entire cluster, determined primarily by the strength of the vertical confinement. Lower‑frequency vertical modes are increasingly complex, with patterns that exhibit nodal structures and localized motion, particularly at the cluster edges. For small systems, vertical modes are strongly discrete and well separated, while for larger clusters the density of modes increases and their spatial patterns resemble those seen in infinite lattice calculations. The ordering of vertical and horizontal mode frequencies reveals a crossover regime in which vertical oscillations can be excited by in‑plane perturbations through mode coupling.

These findings emphasize the importance of considering finite‑size effects when interpreting experiments on dust clusters in complex plasmas. The interplay between structural arrangement and vertical mode spectra provides a sensitive probe of both interparticle interactions and confining potentials. In particular, the localization of low‑frequency vertical modes near the periphery suggests possible routes for selective excitation and control in laboratory settings. Future work could extend this analysis to include effects of wake‑field interactions, non‑harmonic confinement, and external driving, thereby bridging the gap between idealized models and experimental observations. Overall, our study demonstrates that finite 2D plasma crystals exhibit rich vertical dynamics intimately linked to their structural organization, and that combined structural–spectral analysis offers a powerful approach for understanding and manipulating these complex systems.

title: On the 3-wave Equations with Constant Boundary Conditions
abstract: We investigate the integrable three-wave interaction equations under constant boundary conditions. Using the inverse scattering transform, we analyze the associated Lax pair, spectral properties, and the impact of nonvanishing asymptotics. Explicit soliton and multi-soliton solutions are derived, illustrating novel interaction patterns. The results extend classical zero-boundary analyses, offering deeper insight into nonlinear wave coupling with persistent backgrounds.
introduction:
The three-wave interaction equations constitute a fundamental model in the theory of nonlinear wave phenomena, arising in diverse physical contexts such as nonlinear optics, plasma physics, and fluid dynamics. These equations describe the resonant interaction of three wave modes whose wave numbers and frequencies satisfy specific matching conditions. In their simplest form, they appear as a first-order system of coupled partial differential equations for complex-valued functions, representing the slowly varying envelopes of the interacting waves. The integrability of the three-wave equations under vanishing or rapidly decaying boundary conditions has been studied extensively, revealing a rich mathematical structure including Lax pairs, inverse scattering transform methods, and soliton solutions.

However, many physically relevant situations involve non-vanishing, and in particular constant, boundary conditions at spatial infinity. Such conditions arise, for example, in the study of continuous wave backgrounds in nonlinear optics, or in the presence of steady-state fields in plasma environments. The presence of constant boundary conditions fundamentally alters the spectral properties of the associated linear operators, leading to nontrivial modifications of the inverse scattering framework and the construction of solutions. In these settings, the continuous spectrum is typically shifted, and discrete eigenvalues may be embedded within it, giving rise to new types of localized and periodic structures.

Despite their importance, the integrable theory of the three-wave equations with constant boundary conditions has received comparatively less attention. Recent advances in the analysis of integrable systems with nonzero backgrounds—motivated in part by the theory of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on a finite-density background—suggest that similar techniques can be adapted to the three-wave case. The purpose of this work is to develop a systematic approach to the three-wave interaction equations with constant boundary conditions, elucidate their spectral theory, and construct explicit classes of solutions. By extending the inverse scattering formalism to this setting, we aim to provide a comprehensive mathematical framework that captures both the underlying integrable structure and the physical phenomena associated with nontrivial asymptotic states.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the three-wave interaction equations under constant boundary conditions. By employing the inverse scattering transform adapted to nonvanishing asymptotics, we have characterized the associated spectral problem and determined the relevant scattering data. The analysis required a careful treatment of the continuous spectrum, where the presence of constant boundary values modifies both the analytic structure of the Jost solutions and the formulation of the Riemann–Hilbert problem. We showed how these modifications lead to a consistent reconstruction formula for the potential functions, valid for generic constant backgrounds.

Our results clarify the role of the background parameters in shaping the nonlinear evolution, in particular through their influence on the discrete spectrum and the possible soliton content of the solutions. The classification of soliton solutions in this setting extends known results for vanishing boundary conditions, revealing new families of localized structures riding on top of a finite-amplitude background. Moreover, the interplay between the dispersion relations and the boundary constants was seen to affect the stability properties and interaction patterns of the waves.

The methods developed here can be applied to other integrable systems with constant asymptotics, offering a unified framework for treating multi-component problems of physical relevance, such as in nonlinear optics, plasma physics, and fluid dynamics. Future work may address perturbations of the integrable model, numerical implementations of the inverse problem for generic data, and the study of modulational instabilities in the presence of constant backgrounds. Overall, this study advances the theoretical understanding of the three-wave equations in a more general setting and opens avenues for connecting exact solutions with experimentally observable phenomena.

title: Integrand-reduction techniques for NLO and beyond
abstract: We present recent developments in integrand-reduction techniques for the computation of next-to-leading order (NLO) and higher-order corrections in perturbative quantum field theory. Building on the original decomposition of loop integrands into master integrals, we review algorithmic improvements enabling efficient treatment of multi-leg and multi-loop amplitudes. The approach systematically exploits the polynomial structure of scattering amplitudes at the integrand level, allowing the extraction of coefficients through algebraic sampling, thus reducing the complexity of tensor integral reduction. We discuss the extension of these methods beyond one loop, highlighting strategies for handling overlapping singularities, higher-rank numerators, and integrals in dimensional regularization. Applications to phenomenologically relevant processes demonstrate substantial gains in numerical stability and computational performance. These advances establish integrand-reduction as a versatile and scalable framework for precision collider phenomenology at NLO and beyond.
introduction:
The computation of scattering amplitudes at next-to-leading order (NLO) accuracy in perturbative quantum field theory is an essential ingredient for precision phenomenology at high-energy colliders. As experimental measurements at facilities such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) achieve unprecedented precision, theoretical predictions must incorporate higher-order radiative corrections to match the accuracy of experimental data. This demands the efficient evaluation of multi-leg, multi-scale loop amplitudes, which poses significant challenges both analytically and numerically. Traditional approaches based on Feynman diagrammatic expansions become quickly intractable as the number of external legs increases, due to factorial growth in the number of diagrams and the complexity of the associated tensor integrals.

Integrand-reduction techniques have emerged as a powerful alternative framework for the computation of loop amplitudes. Instead of performing the reduction at the level of integrated expressions, these methods operate directly on the integrand, decomposing it into a sum over a basis of master integrals with process-dependent coefficients. The coefficients are determined by exploiting the analytic structure of the integrand, in particular its singularity structure and factorisation properties, often through the application of generalized unitarity. By working at the integrand level, one can avoid the proliferation of complicated intermediate expressions and achieve a more efficient algorithmic implementation.

The origins of integrand reduction can be traced to the Ossola–Papadopoulos–Pittau (OPP) method, which provided a systematic procedure to parametrise the integrand numerator in terms of known master integrals and spurious terms. This approach has been generalized to accommodate massive propagators, higher-rank numerators, and multi-loop amplitudes. At one loop, integrand-reduction techniques have reached a high level of maturity, with public implementations integrated into automated computational frameworks used in phenomenological studies. The extension to two loops and beyond, however, remains an active area of research, driven by the need for next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions for complex processes.

Recent advances have combined integrand-reduction strategies with algebraic geometry tools, such as multivariate polynomial division and Gröbner bases, to systematically solve the on-shell conditions defining multiple cuts of the integrand. These developments have enabled the classification of integral topologies and the determination of their coefficients in a unified manner, paving the way for automation in multi-loop computations. Furthermore, connections with modern amplitude techniques, including scattering equations and on-shell diagrammatics, suggest a broader applicability of integrand-level methods across different theories and kinematic regimes.

In this work, we review the current status of integrand-reduction techniques for NLO and their extensions to higher-loop orders. We focus on the conceptual foundations, algorithmic implementations, and recent innovations that address the computational challenges of multi-leg, multi-loop amplitudes, highlighting their role in achieving high-precision theoretical predictions for collider phenomenology.
conclusion:
In this work we have reviewed and extended the framework of integrand-reduction techniques for the computation of multi-loop scattering amplitudes at next-to-leading order and beyond. Building on the original one-loop reduction paradigm, we have shown how the decomposition of amplitudes at the integrand level can be systematically generalized to higher-loop topologies, exploiting both algebraic geometry tools and modern parametrizations of the loop momenta. This approach allows for the separation of universal, process-independent structures from process-dependent coefficients, thereby streamlining the calculation of complex amplitudes in perturbative quantum field theory.

We have emphasized the interplay between integrand reduction and generalized unitarity, highlighting how the combination of these methods leads to efficient determination of the coefficients of master integrals, even in the presence of massive particles and higher-rank numerators. Applications to multi-leg processes demonstrate that integrand-level strategies can significantly reduce the computational bottlenecks associated with traditional tensor-reduction methods, making them well-suited for automation within modern amplitude-generation frameworks.

Furthermore, our discussion of recent developments illustrates that integrand-reduction techniques are not limited to fixed-order perturbation theory. Their algebraic structure and modularity make them a promising ingredient in the construction of higher-order subtraction schemes, and in the integration of amplitudes within numerical frameworks that target realistic collider observables.

Looking ahead, continued progress in algorithmic algebra, combined with advances in symbolic manipulation and numerical stability, will further enhance the applicability of integrand-level methods to increasingly complex scattering processes. The synergy between integrand reduction, unitarity-based approaches, and novel analytic integration techniques will likely play a central role in enabling precision calculations at the accuracy demanded by current and future experiments. In this sense, integrand-reduction techniques are poised to remain a cornerstone of perturbative amplitude computations well into the era of high-precision collider phenomenology.

title: The energy cascade in grid-generated non-equilibrium decaying turbulence
abstract: We investigate the scale-by-scale energy transfer and dissipation processes in grid-generated turbulence under non-equilibrium decaying conditions. Using hot-wire anemometry in a wind tunnel, turbulence was generated by both regular and fractal grids, enabling systematic variation of initial conditions. Measurements of velocity structure functions and energy spectra were acquired downstream over a range of Reynolds numbers. The analysis focuses on the local energy budget across scales, obtained via the inhomogeneous, anisotropic form of the Kármán–Howarth–Monin equation. Results reveal that, despite the absence of global equilibrium between the nonlinear energy transfer and viscous dissipation, a well-defined inertial cascade persists over a finite range of scales. In the non-equilibrium region, the peak energy transfer rate remains approximately constant with downstream distance, while the dissipation rate decays more rapidly, breaking the classical balance observed in fully developed turbulence. This imbalance is accompanied by a modified scaling of the second- and third-order structure functions, indicating a departure from Kolmogorov’s 1941 phenomenology. Farther downstream, the flow gradually approaches an equilibrium decay regime, recovering the proportionality between transfer and dissipation. The findings highlight the robustness of the turbulent cascade mechanism under non-equilibrium conditions and provide new insight into the role of initial conditions in determining the spatial evolution of energy transfer and dissipation in decaying turbulence. Implications for turbulence modeling and scaling laws are discussed.
introduction:
Turbulence is a multiscale phenomenon in which kinetic energy is transferred from large energetic motions to progressively smaller eddies until it is dissipated by viscosity. This process, referred to as the energy cascade, is central to our understanding of turbulent flows and underpins most theoretical, experimental, and numerical studies of turbulence. In classical homogeneous isotropic turbulence, Kolmogorov’s 1941 theory postulates that, at sufficiently high Reynolds numbers, the energy cascade is universal and independent of the details of large-scale forcing, leading to a constant mean energy dissipation rate in the inertial range. However, recent experiments and simulations have revealed that in certain flows, particularly those generated by turbulence-generating grids, the decay of turbulence can exhibit strongly non-equilibrium characteristics that challenge this classical picture.

Grid-generated turbulence has long been used as a canonical configuration to investigate decaying turbulence under controlled laboratory conditions. In its conventional form, turbulence generated by regular or active grids quickly relaxes towards an approximately homogeneous and isotropic state downstream of the grid, enabling comparison with theoretical predictions. Yet, over the past decade, studies employing multi-scale or fractal grids have uncovered a distinct regime—referred to as non-equilibrium decaying turbulence—in which the relationship between the mean energy dissipation rate, turbulent kinetic energy, and integral length scale departs markedly from the classical scaling. In particular, the dissipation coefficient does not remain constant but exhibits a pronounced dependence on the downstream position, even at high Reynolds numbers, implying a modification of the energy cascade process.

These findings have significant implications for both fundamental turbulence theory and practical modelling. If the energy cascade in non-equilibrium turbulence differs from the canonical Kolmogorov picture, assumptions underlying widely used turbulence models may require revision, especially in flows where similar non-equilibrium dynamics arise. Furthermore, understanding the mechanisms that govern the energy transfer across scales in these regimes is essential for developing predictive frameworks that encompass both equilibrium and non-equilibrium behaviours.

The present study aims to investigate the energy cascade in grid-generated non-equilibrium decaying turbulence through detailed analysis of scale-by-scale energy budgets. Using experimental data obtained downstream of turbulence-generating grids, we examine the balance between energy transfer, production, and dissipation, and assess the extent to which classical inertial-range scaling holds in the non-equilibrium regime. By quantifying the departures from equilibrium behaviour, we provide new insight into the dynamics of the cascade process in these flows and their implications for turbulence theory and modelling.
conclusion:
The present study has examined the characteristics of the energy cascade in grid-generated, non-equilibrium decaying turbulence, with particular focus on the interplay between large-scale inhomogeneity and small-scale dynamics. By analysing velocity field measurements downstream of various grid configurations, we have characterised the departure from classical equilibrium turbulence and quantified the implications for the scale-by-scale energy budget. Our results demonstrate that, in the non-equilibrium region immediately downstream of the turbulence-generating grid, the dissipation rate does not scale in proportion to the conventional estimate based on large-scale quantities, and the energy transfer across scales exhibits a pronounced imbalance relative to the dissipation. This imbalance gradually diminishes with downstream distance, converging toward the equilibrium Richardson–Kolmogorov picture only at sufficiently large development times.

The persistence of non-equilibrium features over extended regions highlights the importance of the production and advection terms in the inhomogeneous Kármán–Howarth–Monin equation, even in the absence of mean shear. The scale-by-scale analysis reveals that the peak interscale energy flux is displaced relative to the classical isotropic prediction, and that the inertial transfer is influenced by the evolving large-scale anisotropy. These findings suggest that the cascade process in such flows is not solely determined by local interactions in scale space, but is modulated by spatial transport and the decay of coherent structures originating at the grid.

Furthermore, the comparison between different grid geometries indicates that the degree of initial inhomogeneity and the associated wake interactions play a decisive role in setting the downstream evolution of the cascade. While the small-scale statistics tend toward isotropy in the far field, the route to this state is sensitive to the initial conditions, with some configurations exhibiting a more rapid approach to equilibrium behaviour than others. This underlines the non-universality of the early decay stages and the necessity of accounting for initial structure in predictive models.

In summary, our investigation provides clear evidence that the energy cascade in grid-generated turbulence cannot be universally described by equilibrium scaling laws across all decay stages. The non-equilibrium region is characterised by an interscale energy transfer that is not in balance with dissipation, sustained by large-scale inhomogeneity and spatial transport. These insights call for refined theoretical frameworks and modelling strategies that incorporate the role of spatial development and initial conditions in shaping the cascade. Future work could extend the present analysis to higher Reynolds numbers and alternative grid designs, as well as to numerical simulations capable of isolating specific mechanisms of non-equilibrium behaviour, to further elucidate the universality — or lack thereof — of the turbulent energy cascade.

title: Hardware-Based ADMM-LP Decoding
abstract: This paper presents a hardware-based implementation of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Linear Programming (ADMM-LP) decoding of error-correcting codes, targeting high-throughput and low-latency communication systems. ADMM-LP decoding offers near-maximum likelihood performance for linear block codes by solving a relaxed linear programming formulation, but its computational complexity has limited practical deployment. We propose a custom hardware architecture that exploits the inherent parallelism and structure of the ADMM iterations, incorporating fixed-point arithmetic, pipelined processing, and resource sharing to achieve efficient utilization on FPGA platforms. The design includes optimized projection and update units, as well as a tailored scheduling strategy to balance convergence speed and hardware constraints. Experimental results on low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes demonstrate that the proposed hardware decoder achieves performance close to floating-point software implementations, while significantly reducing latency and power consumption. Through synthesis and prototyping, we show that our architecture can sustain multi-gigabit per second decoding throughput, making ADMM-LP decoding practical for future high-speed communication systems requiring both reliability and efficiency.
introduction:
Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes have become a cornerstone of modern error correction, enabling reliable communication over noisy channels in applications ranging from wireless standards to deep-space communication. Their near-capacity performance and amenability to parallel implementation have made them attractive for both academic research and industrial deployment. Traditionally, iterative message-passing algorithms such as the Sum-Product Algorithm (SPA) or its simplified variant, the Min-Sum Algorithm (MSA), have been the dominant decoding strategies for LDPC codes, offering low complexity and good performance. However, these methods are inherently heuristic and may suffer from error floors due to trapping sets and other suboptimal convergence phenomena. This has motivated the exploration of alternative decoding paradigms that can provide improved error-rate performance and stronger theoretical guarantees.

Linear programming (LP) decoding, introduced by Feldman et al., formulates LDPC decoding as an optimization problem over a relaxed polytope representation of the code. By solving a linear program, LP decoding can, in principle, avoid certain local minima that trap iterative message-passing decoders. It also provides a certificate of optimality when the LP solution is integral, thus guaranteeing maximum-likelihood decoding in those cases. Despite these advantages, the direct application of LP decoding in practical systems has been hindered by its high computational complexity and the difficulty of implementing general-purpose LP solvers in hardware with the throughput and latency constraints of modern communication systems.

To bridge the gap between the theoretical benefits of LP decoding and the practical demands of hardware implementation, recent research has investigated specialized optimization algorithms tailored to the LDPC decoding problem structure. Among these, the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) has emerged as a promising approach. ADMM is a first-order optimization method well-suited for large-scale, structured problems. It decomposes the global LP decoding problem into smaller subproblems that can be solved efficiently and in parallel, while coordinating their solutions via dual variable updates. This decomposition aligns naturally with the bipartite graph structure of LDPC codes, enabling a distributed message-passing interpretation of the algorithm.

ADMM-based LP decoding (ADMM-LP) retains many of the desirable properties of LP decoding, such as the ability to avoid certain harmful pseudocodewords and to provide decoding certificates, while significantly reducing computational complexity compared to generic LP solvers. Furthermore, the algorithm’s iterative, local-update nature makes it amenable to parallelization and pipelining in hardware, offering a pathway to high-throughput implementations. Nevertheless, existing work on ADMM-LP decoding has predominantly focused on software-based implementations and algorithmic performance analysis, leaving open the question of how to design efficient, low-latency hardware architectures that can execute ADMM-LP decoding at the speeds required by contemporary communication systems.

This work addresses that gap by presenting a hardware-based implementation of ADMM-LP decoding, explicitly designed to exploit the algorithm’s inherent parallelism and locality. We investigate algorithmic modifications and architectural optimizations that reduce resource usage, improve timing closure, and maintain error-correction performance. By mapping the ADMM subproblems to processing elements that operate concurrently, and by carefully managing memory access patterns for the primal and dual variables, we demonstrate that ADMM-LP decoding can be realized in hardware with competitive throughput and latency. Our design supports fixed-point arithmetic with carefully chosen quantization to balance performance and complexity, and incorporates pipeline stages to sustain high clock frequencies.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we provide a hardware architecture for ADMM-LP decoding of LDPC codes, including details of data flow, memory organization, and processing element design. Second, we analyze the trade-offs between numerical precision, resource utilization, and error-rate performance in a fixed-point hardware context. Third, we present synthesis and implementation results on a representative FPGA platform, demonstrating that hardware-based ADMM-LP decoding is a practical alternative to traditional message-passing decoders for applications requiring both high reliability and high throughput. These results advance the state of the art in bridging optimization-based decoding theory with practical hardware realization.
conclusion: This work has presented a hardware-based implementation of the ADMM-LP decoding algorithm, demonstrating its feasibility and efficiency for practical error correction applications. By leveraging the inherent parallelism of the ADMM framework and tailoring the architecture for low-latency, high-throughput operation, the proposed design achieves competitive performance compared to conventional iterative decoders. The results show that the hardware architecture can maintain the error-correction performance of the LP decoding formulation while significantly reducing computational delay through optimized dataflow and resource sharing. Furthermore, the modular design enables scalability to larger block lengths and higher code rates with minimal architectural modification. These findings suggest that hardware-based ADMM-LP decoding is a promising candidate for future high-speed communication systems requiring both strong error correction and efficient hardware utilization. Future work will focus on further optimization, energy efficiency, and integration into complete communication transceivers.

title: Transmission Spectroscopy of the Earth-Sun System to Inform the Search for Extrasolar Life
abstract: We present a detailed investigation of the Earth–Sun system as an analogue for interpreting transmission spectroscopy observations of terrestrial exoplanets orbiting Sun-like stars. Using high-resolution solar and atmospheric spectra, we model how Earth’s atmospheric constituents imprint wavelength-dependent features on stellar light during a hypothetical transit geometry. Our analysis incorporates realistic scattering, absorption, and refraction effects, and accounts for temporal and spatial variability in atmospheric composition. Key biosignature gases, including O₂, O₃, CH₄, and CO₂, are examined alongside spectral indicators of habitability such as water vapor and Rayleigh scattering slopes. We evaluate how these features manifest at different spectral resolutions and signal-to-noise ratios, highlighting the detectability thresholds for current and near-future space- and ground-based observatories. Comparisons are drawn to modeled spectra for planets with varying atmospheric compositions to assess false positive and false negative scenarios. Our results underscore the diagnostic power of simultaneous multi-wavelength coverage and the importance of understanding Earth’s transmission spectrum in the context of exoplanet characterization. This work provides a reference framework for designing observational strategies and interpreting data in the search for life beyond the Solar System.
introduction: Transmission spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful technique for probing the atmospheric composition of exoplanets as they transit their host stars. By measuring wavelength-dependent variations in starlight filtered through a planetary atmosphere, it is possible to infer the presence of atomic and molecular species, clouds, and hazes, and to assess potential biosignatures. The Earth-Sun system provides a natural benchmark for evaluating the detectability of life-bearing planets around other stars. Observations of Earth’s transmission spectrum, obtained during lunar eclipses or via Earthshine, reveal signatures of atmospheric oxygen, ozone, water vapor, and other trace gases, as well as Rayleigh scattering. These features offer critical insights into the spectral fingerprints that may indicate biological activity. Modeling the Earth-Sun transmission spectrum also allows researchers to explore the dependence of detectability on spectral resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and stellar type. Such studies are essential for optimizing observational strategies with current and future space- and ground-based facilities, and for refining criteria used to prioritize targets in the search for extrasolar life. This work presents a detailed analysis of the Earth-Sun system as an archetype for habitable exoplanet characterization.
conclusion:
The transmission spectroscopy analysis of the Earth-Sun system presented in this study provides a benchmark for interpreting potential biosignatures in exoplanetary atmospheres. By simulating an Earth analogue in transit across a Sun-like star, we have demonstrated how key atmospheric constituents—such as O₂, O₃, H₂O, and CO₂—manifest in high-resolution transmission spectra, and how their detectability is shaped by instrumental resolution, stellar activity, and observational cadence.
