The simultaneous presence of multiple species linked to biological and geochemical processes underscores the importance of searching for biosignature suites rather than isolated spectral lines, thereby reducing the likelihood of false positives arising from abiotic mechanisms.

Our results reinforce that Earth’s spectrum, when viewed as an exoplanet, reveals a rich interplay of absorption features that are both temporally and spectrally variable. Seasonal and diurnal changes in cloud cover and atmospheric composition introduce complexities that future missions must account for when designing observing strategies. These variations highlight the necessity of repeated, time-resolved observations to confidently distinguish between persistent biosignatures and transient spectral artifacts.

Moreover, the study illustrates the challenges posed by stellar heterogeneity. Simulated stellar contamination from faculae and spots can mimic or obscure atmospheric features, particularly in bands critical for biosignature detection. This finding emphasizes the need for robust stellar characterization alongside planetary spectroscopy, and suggests that joint modeling of stellar and planetary signals will be essential for accurate atmospheric retrievals.

In the broader context of the search for extrasolar life, the Earth-Sun transmission spectrum serves as both a proof of concept and a cautionary example. It demonstrates that, under favorable conditions, a complex, life-bearing atmosphere can be identified through transit observations, but also that such identifications are inherently probabilistic and require careful consideration of confounding factors. As upcoming facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope, the Extremely Large Telescope, and future dedicated exoplanet missions push the boundaries of spectral sensitivity and resolution, the lessons learned from our own planet’s transmission spectrum will be instrumental in guiding observational priorities and retrieval methodologies.

Ultimately, the Earth remains our only confirmed inhabited world, and its transmission signature is the most tangible reference for what life elsewhere might reveal. By rigorously characterizing this signal in the context of realistic astrophysical noise sources, we can refine the criteria by which we assess habitability and biosignatures, thereby enhancing the scientific return of future searches for life beyond our Solar System.

title: Ab initio simulation of attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy in two-dimensional materials
abstract: We present an *ab initio* framework for simulating attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (ATAS) in two-dimensional (2D) materials, enabling direct access to ultrafast electron dynamics with sub-femtosecond resolution. The approach combines time-dependent density functional theory with real-time propagation to capture many-body and excitonic effects beyond the independent-particle picture. We apply the method to prototypical 2D semiconductors, resolving the interplay between interband transitions and exciton formation on the attosecond timescale. The simulations reveal distinct spectral signatures of carrier relaxation and screening dynamics, in quantitative agreement with experimental trends. This work establishes a predictive tool for interpreting ATAS in low-dimensional systems and provides microscopic insight into light–matter interaction in the extreme time domain.
introduction:
Attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (ATAS) has emerged as a powerful technique for probing ultrafast electron dynamics in solids, enabling the direct observation of processes occurring on sub-femtosecond timescales. By coupling extreme ultraviolet (XUV) attosecond pulses with synchronized infrared or visible control fields, ATAS provides element-specific and state-resolved insight into the interplay between electronic excitations, many-body interactions, and lattice degrees of freedom. While the technique has been extensively applied to atoms, molecules, and bulk solids, its application to two-dimensional (2D) materials remains largely unexplored, despite their unique optoelectronic properties and strongly correlated electronic states.

Two-dimensional materials, such as graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), and their heterostructures, exhibit reduced screening, pronounced excitonic effects, and tunable band structures. These characteristics make them ideal platforms for studying light–matter interactions in the ultrafast regime, where coherent electron–hole dynamics and many-body correlations play a decisive role. Understanding these processes at the attosecond scale could open new avenues for manipulating quantum states in low-dimensional systems, with implications for next-generation electronics, photonics, and quantum technologies.

Ab initio simulations offer a predictive framework for interpreting ATAS measurements in 2D materials, enabling the resolution of microscopic mechanisms underlying experimental observables. First-principles approaches based on time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) or many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) can capture the non-equilibrium evolution of electronic states under intense, ultrashort fields, while accounting for material-specific structural and electronic properties. In this work, we present ab initio simulations of ATAS in prototypical 2D materials, elucidating the role of excitonic effects, interband coherences, and ultrafast screening dynamics. Our results provide theoretical benchmarks for future experiments and contribute to the fundamental understanding of attosecond-scale phenomena in low-dimensional condensed matter systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a comprehensive *ab initio* framework for simulating attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (ATAS) in two-dimensional (2D) materials, enabling a direct connection between ultrafast light–matter interactions and the underlying many-body electronic structure. By combining time-dependent density functional theory with a real-time propagation scheme that explicitly accounts for core-level excitations and many-body effects, we have demonstrated the capability to resolve sub-femtosecond electron dynamics with element-specific and orbital-specific sensitivity. Our approach captures both the coherent evolution of excited-state populations and the ultrafast dephasing processes arising from electron–electron and electron–hole interactions in reduced dimensionality.  

We applied the methodology to prototypical 2D semiconductors, where the interplay between reduced screening, strong excitonic effects, and anisotropic band dispersion gives rise to distinctive signatures in the transient absorption spectra. The simulations reproduce key spectral features observed in recent ATAS experiments, including time-dependent shifts and broadening of core-to-valence transitions, as well as modulations in oscillator strength driven by coherent exciton–plasmon coupling. The temporal resolution inherent in the attosecond probe allows us to disentangle these contributions, revealing the role of ultrafast charge transfer between inequivalent sublattices and the influence of local field effects on the core-level response.  

Our findings emphasize that ATAS, when combined with *ab initio* modeling, provides a powerful avenue for mapping the attosecond-scale evolution of carrier distributions and excitonic correlations in 2D materials. The ability to track these processes in real time opens opportunities for manipulating quantum states via tailored light fields and for engineering optoelectronic functionalities at their fundamental speed limits. Furthermore, the predictive nature of our simulations enables the exploration of regimes beyond current experimental reach, such as extreme doping levels, high-field excitation, and heterostructures with tailored interlayer coupling.  

Future extensions of this work could incorporate higher-order many-body corrections, non-adiabatic coupling to lattice vibrations, and spin–orbit interactions to address a broader class of layered materials, including topological and magnetic 2D systems. The methodologies developed here are not restricted to a specific material class and can be generalized to study ultrafast phenomena in other low-dimensional systems. Overall, this study establishes a robust theoretical foundation for interpreting and guiding attosecond spectroscopic experiments in 2D materials, advancing our understanding of light–matter interaction at the shortest timescales relevant to electronic motion.

title: Understanding Softmax Confidence and Uncertainty
abstract: Softmax outputs are widely interpreted as model confidence in classification tasks, yet their probabilistic meaning and relationship to uncertainty remain contested. This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of the softmax function, highlighting its role in mapping logits to a categorical probability distribution and the limitations of equating maximum softmax probability with true confidence. We analyze scenarios where softmax scores are miscalibrated, particularly under dataset shift and adversarial perturbations, and distinguish between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in this context. Through experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the pitfalls of relying solely on softmax confidence and discuss alternative uncertainty quantification methods, offering guidance for designing more reliable decision-making systems in safety-critical applications.
introduction:
In recent years, deep learning models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of tasks, including image classification, natural language processing, and speech recognition. Central to many of these architectures is the use of the softmax function in the output layer to produce a probability distribution over discrete classes. By mapping raw model outputs, or logits, to normalized values that sum to one, the softmax operation enables straightforward interpretation: the predicted class is assigned the highest probability, and the magnitude of this probability is often taken as a measure of the model’s confidence. This convention has been widely adopted in both academic research and industry practice, influencing decision-making in safety-critical applications such as medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, and financial forecasting.

Despite its appeal, the interpretation of softmax outputs as calibrated probabilities or reliable indicators of uncertainty is not guaranteed. Numerous studies have demonstrated that modern neural networks can be overconfident in their predictions, assigning high softmax scores even to inputs far removed from the training distribution or to misclassified examples. This overconfidence can have serious consequences in high-stakes settings, where an unwarranted sense of certainty may obscure the need for human intervention or additional verification. Consequently, a growing body of work has sought to disentangle the notions of softmax confidence, probability calibration, and epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty.

The core issue lies in the fact that the softmax transformation is a deterministic mapping from logits to a simplex, without explicit modeling of uncertainty. While it ensures that outputs are bounded between zero and one and sum to unity, it does not inherently account for the variability in the model’s parameters or the inherent ambiguity in the data. As a result, the softmax score for the predicted class reflects the relative differences among logits, rather than a well-calibrated belief about the correctness of the prediction. Factors such as the scale of the logits, the degree of overfitting, and the presence of adversarial perturbations can all distort the relationship between softmax confidence and true predictive accuracy.

Understanding this distinction is essential for the development of robust machine learning systems. Calibration techniques, such as temperature scaling, Platt scaling, and isotonic regression, have been proposed to align softmax outputs with empirical accuracies. At the same time, Bayesian approaches, ensemble methods, and stochastic regularization strategies aim to capture model uncertainty more directly, offering complementary perspectives to the information conveyed by softmax scores. The interplay between these approaches highlights the need for a principled framework to interpret and utilize softmax confidence in practice.

This paper aims to provide a rigorous examination of the relationship between softmax outputs, model confidence, and uncertainty estimation. We begin by reviewing the mathematical formulation of the softmax function and its statistical interpretation, followed by an analysis of empirical evidence illustrating its limitations as a proxy for uncertainty. We then survey methodological advances designed to improve calibration and uncertainty quantification, situating softmax confidence within a broader taxonomy of predictive uncertainty. By clarifying the conceptual and practical distinctions between these notions, we seek to inform the design of machine learning models that can make accurate predictions while expressing appropriate levels of uncertainty, thereby supporting safer and more transparent deployment in real-world scenarios.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the interpretation, limitations, and practical implications of softmax outputs in the context of model confidence and uncertainty estimation. While the softmax function is widely used to convert raw logits into normalized probability-like scores, our analysis highlights that these values should not be conflated with well-calibrated probabilities or reliable measures of epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty. The tendency of softmax to produce overconfident predictions, even in the presence of ambiguous or out-of-distribution inputs, underscores the importance of caution when relying on these scores for decision-making in critical applications.

We have discussed how the mathematical structure of the softmax function ensures that one class will always be assigned the highest probability, regardless of the model’s true certainty, and how this property can lead to misleading interpretations. Furthermore, we have reviewed calibration techniques, such as temperature scaling, and alternative uncertainty quantification approaches, including Bayesian neural networks, Monte Carlo dropout, and ensemble methods, which can complement or replace raw softmax scores when more faithful uncertainty estimates are required.

Our findings suggest that improving the interpretability of model outputs requires a dual strategy: first, by recognizing the inherent constraints of the softmax transformation, and second, by integrating post-hoc calibration or probabilistic modeling techniques into the predictive pipeline. This is particularly relevant for safety-critical domains such as medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, and legal decision support, where overconfidence can have severe consequences.

In addition, we have emphasized the need for more robust evaluation metrics that go beyond accuracy to explicitly measure calibration and uncertainty quality. Metrics such as expected calibration error, Brier score, and negative log-likelihood provide complementary perspectives on the reliability of probabilistic predictions. Incorporating these measures into model development and validation processes can foster more trustworthy AI systems.

Ultimately, understanding the nuanced relationship between softmax confidence and true predictive uncertainty is essential for responsible deployment of machine learning models. By combining theoretical insights, empirical analysis, and practical guidelines, this work contributes to a more informed use of softmax outputs and supports ongoing efforts to develop models whose predictions are not only accurate but also meaningfully interpretable in terms of uncertainty. Future research should further explore hybrid methods that leverage the computational simplicity of softmax while addressing its shortcomings through principled uncertainty estimation frameworks.

title: Magnetohydrodynamic waves in solar partially ionized plasmas: two-fluid approach
abstract: We investigate the propagation and damping of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves in solar partially ionized plasmas using a two-fluid theoretical framework in which the ion–electron and neutral components are treated as interpenetrating fluids coupled by collisions. This approach allows us to capture the effects of ion–neutral drift and collisional dissipation that are absent in single-fluid MHD. Linear perturbation analysis is applied to a uniform, magnetized plasma representative of solar chromospheric and prominence conditions. We derive the full dispersion relation for Alfvén, slow, and fast magnetoacoustic modes, and examine the influence of ionization fraction, collision frequency, and propagation angle on wave properties. Our results show that ion–neutral collisions lead to significant damping, particularly for high-frequency Alfvén and fast waves, and can produce cut-off wavenumbers beyond which certain modes cannot propagate. The slow mode is strongly affected in regimes of high neutral fraction, exhibiting reduced phase speeds and enhanced attenuation. Comparisons with the single-fluid approximation demonstrate that the two-fluid model predicts shorter damping times and reveals additional dispersive effects. These findings have implications for interpreting high-resolution observations of wave phenomena in the lower solar atmosphere and for understanding the role of MHD wave dissipation in chromospheric and prominence heating. Our analysis highlights the necessity of multi-fluid treatments for accurately modelling wave dynamics in partially ionized astrophysical plasmas.
introduction:
Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves play a fundamental role in the dynamics and energetics of the solar atmosphere, where they are regarded as key agents for energy transport, momentum transfer, and plasma structuring. Observations over the past decades have revealed the ubiquitous presence of a variety of wave modes, from the photosphere to the corona, in a broad range of spatial and temporal scales. Understanding their propagation, damping, and mode conversion is essential for explaining phenomena such as coronal heating and solar wind acceleration. While ideal MHD theory has provided a robust framework for describing many aspects of wave behaviour in fully ionized plasmas, much of the lower solar atmosphere, including the photosphere, chromosphere, and prominences, is only partially ionized. In such environments, the presence of a significant fraction of neutral atoms introduces additional physical processes that can profoundly modify wave dynamics.

Partial ionization leads to a decoupling between ions and neutrals on time scales shorter than the collisional coupling time, giving rise to multi-fluid effects not captured by the single-fluid MHD approximation. Ion–neutral collisions produce frictional damping of waves, modify dispersion relations, and can enable the propagation of modes that are absent in fully ionized plasmas. Furthermore, the differential motion between charged and neutral species can generate currents and heating through ambipolar diffusion, with implications for the energy balance of the plasma. These processes are especially relevant in the chromosphere, where the ionization degree can vary by orders of magnitude with height, and in prominences, where neutrals can constitute the majority species.

A two-fluid approach, in which ions (together with electrons) and neutrals are treated as separate but interacting fluids, provides a natural framework for studying these effects. This formalism retains the collisional coupling terms and allows for the emergence of phenomena such as ion–neutral drift and the associated damping of MHD waves. Compared with single-fluid models incorporating effective transport coefficients, the two-fluid description can capture high-frequency behaviour, dispersive effects, and mode conversion between ion-dominated and neutral-dominated waves.

In this work, we investigate the properties of magnetohydrodynamic waves in partially ionized solar plasmas within the two-fluid framework. We focus on the linear wave regime, deriving and analysing the dispersion relations for a homogeneous background, and exploring the dependence of wave characteristics on ionization degree, collisional frequency, and magnetic field strength. The results provide insight into the role of partial ionization in shaping wave propagation in the solar atmosphere, and establish a basis for interpreting high-resolution observations of wave phenomena in these complex, multi-component plasmas.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the properties of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves in solar partially ionized plasmas within the framework of a two-fluid model, treating the ion–electron and neutral components as interpenetrating but interacting fluids. By incorporating ion–neutral collisional coupling, we have analyzed the modifications to wave dispersion, damping rates, and mode conversion processes relative to the single-fluid approximation. Our results demonstrate that partial ionization introduces significant frequency-dependent damping, particularly for Alfvén and fast magnetoacoustic modes, with the strongest effects occurring when the wave frequency is comparable to the ion–neutral collision frequency. This leads to the attenuation of short-period waves and can contribute to localized heating in the solar chromosphere and prominences. In contrast, slow magnetoacoustic modes are less affected in the low-β regime, though their propagation characteristics can still be altered in regions of enhanced neutral fraction.

The two-fluid approach captures dispersive effects arising from ion–neutral drift, which are absent in single-fluid MHD, and allows for a more accurate description of wave behaviour in the weakly ionized layers of the solar atmosphere. The results presented here highlight the necessity of considering multi-fluid effects when interpreting high-resolution observations of wave phenomena, especially with current and upcoming solar facilities. Future work should extend this analysis to include non-linear regimes, realistic stratification, and the presence of multi-species ion populations, as well as coupling with radiative transfer effects. Such developments will further clarify the role of partially ionized plasma dynamics in energy transport and dissipation, thereby deepening our understanding of the complex interplay between waves and heating in the solar atmosphere.

title: A Comparative Study of Coarse to Dense 3D Indoor Scene Registration Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a comparative study of coarse-to-dense 3D indoor scene registration algorithms, evaluating their accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency across varied real-world datasets. We examine representative methods spanning global coarse alignment, local refinement, and dense reconstruction stages, including feature-based, learning-based, and hybrid approaches. Performance is assessed under challenges such as occlusion, clutter, and varying sensor noise. Quantitative results highlight trade-offs between alignment precision and runtime, while qualitative analyses reveal strengths in specific scene configurations. The findings provide practical guidelines for selecting suitable registration pipelines, and identify key areas for improvement in robust, scalable 3D indoor scene reconstruction.
introduction:
Three-dimensional (3D) indoor scene registration is a foundational task in computer vision, robotics, and spatial computing, enabling the accurate alignment of spatial data acquired from different viewpoints or sensors into a unified coordinate system. This process underpins a wide range of applications, including autonomous navigation, augmented and virtual reality, digital twin construction, and heritage preservation. In indoor environments, registration is particularly challenging due to factors such as clutter, occlusions, repetitive structural patterns, and varying illumination conditions. Furthermore, the need to integrate data from heterogeneous sensing modalities—such as LiDAR, RGB-D cameras, or photogrammetry—adds complexity to the alignment process.

A common approach to 3D registration follows a coarse-to-dense (or coarse-to-fine) paradigm. In the coarse stage, the goal is to estimate an initial transformation that brings the datasets into approximate alignment, often using global feature descriptors or keypoint matching. This step must be robust to large initial misalignments and partial overlaps. In the dense stage, fine-grained optimization techniques refine the alignment by minimizing geometric or photometric discrepancies over a large set of correspondences, typically leveraging iterative closest point (ICP) variants or probabilistic formulations. The coarse-to-dense strategy combines the robustness of global methods with the precision of local refinement, making it well suited to indoor scenarios where data quality and overlap can vary significantly.

Over the past decade, numerous algorithms have been proposed to address each stage of this pipeline. Coarse alignment methods range from feature-based approaches—employing descriptors such as FPFH (Fast Point Feature Histograms), SHOT (Signature of Histograms of Orientations), or learned descriptors from deep networks—to global optimization schemes leveraging RANSAC or branch-and-bound frameworks. Dense registration methods have similarly evolved, with classical ICP variants being enhanced by point-to-plane or generalized formulations, and more recent methods incorporating robust loss functions, multi-scale strategies, or learned correspondence weighting. While many studies have evaluated individual methods, comprehensive comparative analyses that bridge both coarse and dense stages, especially under the constraints of realistic indoor datasets, remain limited.

The purpose of this study is to provide a systematic comparison of representative coarse-to-dense 3D indoor scene registration algorithms, examining their performance across common evaluation metrics such as alignment accuracy, robustness to noise and occlusion, computational efficiency, and scalability. By conducting experiments on diverse benchmark datasets, we aim to identify the strengths and limitations of different algorithmic combinations, and to elucidate trade-offs relevant to practical deployment. The results of this comparative study will not only inform the selection of suitable registration techniques for specific indoor applications but also highlight open challenges and promising directions for future research in robust, efficient, and generalizable 3D registration.
conclusion:
This study presented a comparative evaluation of coarse-to-dense 3D indoor scene registration algorithms, examining their performance across varying levels of scene complexity, sensor noise, and initial alignment accuracy. By systematically benchmarking representative methods from feature-based, global optimization, and iterative refinement categories, we highlighted the strengths and limitations inherent to each approach. The results indicate that coarse global alignment methods relying on robust feature descriptors provide reliable initialization even in cluttered or partially overlapping environments, while dense refinement techniques such as ICP variants consistently improve alignment accuracy when initialized within a suitable convergence basin. Hybrid strategies that integrate learned feature extraction with geometric optimization demonstrated promising resilience to occlusion and textureless regions, though they remain sensitive to significant viewpoint changes.  

Our analysis further revealed that computational efficiency varies widely, with some high-accuracy methods incurring substantial runtime costs, which may limit applicability in real-time systems. The choice of algorithm should therefore be guided by the balance between accuracy, robustness, and computational constraints dictated by the application domain.  

Future work should explore adaptive frameworks that dynamically select or combine registration strategies based on scene characteristics and confidence measures. Incorporating semantic cues and leveraging multi-modal sensing could further enhance robustness in challenging indoor environments. Overall, the comparative insights provided here can inform the selection and design of coarse-to-dense registration pipelines, supporting more reliable 3D reconstruction, mapping, and localization in complex real-world indoor scenarios.

title: Summary of Tests of General Relativity with GWTC-3
abstract: We present an overview of tests of general relativity (GR) performed using gravitational-wave observations from the third Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC-3) of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration. GWTC-3 includes compact binary coalescences detected during the first three observing runs, enabling stringent constraints on deviations from GR. We summarize results from parametrized waveform analyses, inspiral–merger–ringdown consistency tests, and searches for residual signals beyond GR predictions. Across the catalog, no statistically significant evidence for departures from GR is found. The measurements improve bounds on possible dispersion of gravitational waves, deviations in post-Newtonian coefficients, and ringdown mode frequencies. These results extend and refine previous tests, demonstrating the increasing precision with which the strong-field, highly dynamical regime of gravity can be probed using gravitational waves, and reinforcing the consistency of current observations with GR.
introduction:
The direct detection of gravitational waves (GWs) from compact binary coalescences (CBCs) has opened a new observational window onto the strong-field, highly dynamical regime of gravity. Since the landmark observation of GW150914 by the Advanced LIGO detectors in 2015, the global network of ground-based interferometers—comprising the Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA observatories—has accumulated a steadily growing catalog of GW events. The third Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC-3) encompasses detections from the first half of the third observing run (O3a), in addition to events from previous runs, providing the most comprehensive dataset to date for probing the validity of general relativity (GR) in the radiative, strong-field regime.

General relativity, proposed by Einstein in 1915, has withstood more than a century of experimental scrutiny, from Solar System tests to binary pulsar timing. These tests have confirmed the theory’s predictions to remarkable precision in the weak-field or moderately relativistic regimes. However, the merger of stellar-mass black holes and neutron stars produces gravitational fields and spacetime curvatures far exceeding those accessible in previous experiments. In such regimes, the dynamics of gravity are fully nonlinear, and deviations from GR—if present—could be amplified. Gravitational waves encode the dynamics of the entire coalescence process, from the slow inspiral to the rapid merger and the ringdown of the remnant, offering a direct probe of the nature of gravity in these extreme conditions.

The GWTC-3 events enable a broad array of tests of GR. These include parameterized tests of the gravitational waveform, which search for generic deviations from the predictions of GR in the inspiral, merger, and ringdown phases; residual tests, which assess the consistency of the data with the best-fitting GR waveform; and null tests, which exploit internal consistency relations predicted by the theory, such as the agreement between parameters measured independently from different portions of the signal. Additional analyses target specific alternative theories or phenomenological modifications, such as constraints on the graviton mass, tests of Lorentz invariance, or the polarization content of gravitational waves.

The statistical power of these tests depends critically on the number, variety, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the observed events. The 90 confidently identified compact binary mergers in GWTC-3—comprising binary black holes (BBHs), binary neutron stars (BNSs), and neutron star–black hole (NSBH) systems—span a broad range of component masses, mass ratios, and spins. This diversity allows for tests across different physical regimes, including systems with high total mass, where the merger and ringdown dominate the detectable signal, and lower-mass systems, where the inspiral phase is well resolved. Combining results from multiple events enables more stringent constraints by reducing statistical uncertainties and mitigating the impact of individual-event outliers.

Performing these tests requires accurate waveform models that incorporate the full relativistic dynamics predicted by GR. For BBH systems, state-of-the-art models calibrated to numerical relativity simulations are used to describe the inspiral, merger, and ringdown phases. For BNS and NSBH systems, waveform models additionally incorporate tidal effects arising from the finite size and internal structure of neutron stars. Parameterized deviations can be introduced into these models to search for departures from GR predictions. The resulting posterior distributions on deviation parameters, when consistent with zero within uncertainties, support the validity of GR.

The O3a data also allow for targeted searches for phenomena beyond GR. For example, the dispersion relation of gravitational waves can be tested by allowing the propagation speed to depend on frequency, thereby constraining the mass of the graviton. The polarization content can be probed by comparing data from multiple detectors with different antenna patterns, testing whether only the two tensor polarizations predicted by GR are present. Furthermore, precise measurements of the ringdown frequencies and damping times from high-mass BBH mergers can be compared with the black hole perturbation theory predictions, providing a test of the no-hair theorem.

In this work, we present a comprehensive summary of the tests of GR performed with the GWTC-3 dataset. We describe the methods employed, the results obtained for individual events and their combined constraints, and the implications for the validity of GR and for alternative theories of gravity. By leveraging the most extensive set of gravitational-wave observations to date, we provide the most stringent and wide-ranging strong-field tests of general relativity yet achieved.
conclusion: The analysis of GWTC-3 events provides stringent tests of general relativity in the strong-field, highly dynamical regime. Across multiple independent methods, no statistically significant deviations from general relativistic predictions were observed. Constraints on parameterized deviations improve upon previous results, further limiting possible extensions to the theory. While current measurements remain consistent with general relativity, future detections with greater sensitivity and broader parameter coverage will enhance our ability to probe potential departures. These findings reinforce general relativity’s robustness while motivating continued precision gravitational-wave observations.

title: A highly efficient measure of mass segregation in star clusters
abstract: We present a novel and computationally efficient method for quantifying mass segregation in star clusters, suitable for both observational and simulated data. Traditional approaches, such as the minimum spanning tree technique, though robust, often require significant computational resources and can be sensitive to sample incompleteness. Our method instead employs a ranked radial distribution analysis, in which stellar masses are ordered and compared through a cumulative radial profile statistic, enabling rapid assessment of segregation levels across a wide mass range. By calibrating the measure against synthetic clusters with known segregation states, we demonstrate that it reliably distinguishes between unsegregated, partially segregated, and highly segregated configurations, even in the presence of realistic observational uncertainties. Application to N-body simulations of young and dynamically evolved clusters reveals clear correlations between segregation strength, cluster age, and dynamical relaxation times. The method’s simplicity, speed, and robustness make it a powerful tool for large surveys and simulation suites, providing new opportunities to investigate the role of mass segregation in cluster formation and evolution.
introduction:
Star clusters serve as fundamental laboratories for studying the processes that govern stellar formation, evolution, and dynamics. Within these systems, the spatial distribution of stars of different masses often reveals crucial information about their dynamical state and history. One key signature of dynamical evolution is *mass segregation*, the tendency for more massive stars to be preferentially located toward the cluster centre, while lower-mass stars are found at larger radii. This phenomenon can arise through two main channels: as a primordial imprint of the star formation process, or as a result of subsequent dynamical relaxation driven by energy equipartition. Distinguishing between these scenarios is important for constraining both the initial conditions of cluster formation and the timescales over which relaxation processes operate.

Quantifying mass segregation in observed and simulated clusters has been the subject of extensive study. Traditional approaches often rely on comparing the radial distributions of stellar subpopulations, for example by measuring the difference in half-mass radii between massive and low-mass stars, or by applying Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests to their cumulative radial profiles. While such methods are conceptually simple, they may be sensitive to projection effects, incompleteness in the data, and the somewhat arbitrary choice of radial bins or mass thresholds. Furthermore, these techniques can suffer from reduced statistical power when the number of massive stars is small, a common situation in both real and simulated clusters.

More sophisticated methods have been developed to address these limitations. One influential approach is the minimum spanning tree (MST) technique, which assesses mass segregation by comparing the spatial compactness of a subset of the most massive stars to that of randomly selected subsets of stars. This method has the advantage of being non-parametric and independent of the cluster centre definition, making it more robust for irregular or substructured systems. However, MST-based measures can be computationally expensive for large datasets and may still require careful interpretation when the cluster exhibits significant substructure or when observational uncertainties are large.

The continuing growth of high-resolution simulations and large-scale observational surveys demands efficient, statistically robust, and easily interpretable measures of mass segregation. An ideal diagnostic should be applicable to both smooth and substructured clusters, insensitive to projection effects, and computationally tractable for samples containing thousands to millions of stars. Moreover, it should provide a direct, quantitative comparison of the spatial distributions of different mass groups, without relying heavily on arbitrary parameter choices.

In this work, we present a highly efficient measure of mass segregation that meets these criteria. Our method combines the conceptual simplicity of radial distribution comparisons with the robustness of graph-based spatial statistics, yielding a tool that is both fast and reliable. We demonstrate its accuracy and efficiency using a suite of N-body simulations and discuss its applicability to observational datasets, including those from upcoming wide-field astrometric and photometric surveys. This new approach offers a practical framework for probing the dynamical state of star clusters across a wide range of ages, masses, and environments.
conclusion: We have presented a highly efficient method for quantifying mass segregation in star clusters, offering a robust and computationally inexpensive alternative to existing techniques. By leveraging spatial and mass information in a unified framework, our approach reliably captures segregation signatures across a wide range of cluster morphologies and evolutionary stages. Tests on simulated and observed datasets demonstrate its sensitivity to both strong and subtle segregation, while avoiding biases from substructure and sampling incompleteness. The method’s scalability makes it well-suited to the large stellar catalogs produced by modern surveys. Its efficiency enables systematic studies of segregation as a function of age, environment, and dynamical history, thereby providing new constraints on star formation and cluster evolution scenarios. Future work will extend the method to multi-mass dynamical models.

title: Memory Matching Networks for Genomic Sequence Classification
abstract: We propose Memory Matching Networks (MMNs), a novel architecture for genomic sequence classification that integrates deep embedding learning with a differentiable memory module. MMNs encode genomic sequences into latent representations and compare them against a learned memory bank of class prototypes, enabling efficient pattern matching and improved generalization to unseen variants. The memory component facilitates few-shot adaptability, addressing challenges in sparse or imbalanced genomic datasets. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that MMNs consistently outperform conventional convolutional and recurrent baselines, achieving superior accuracy and robustness. Our results highlight the potential of memory-augmented neural networks for scalable, interpretable genomic sequence analysis.
introduction:
The rapid growth of high-throughput sequencing technologies has led to an unprecedented accumulation of genomic data, offering new opportunities for biological discovery and clinical applications. Accurate classification of genomic sequences is a foundational task in bioinformatics, underpinning applications such as species identification, functional annotation, detection of pathogenic variants, and the characterization of regulatory elements. Traditional sequence analysis methods, including alignment-based approaches like BLAST and HMMER, have been widely adopted for these purposes. While effective, these methods often incur substantial computational cost and may struggle to generalize when confronted with highly divergent sequences or novel sequence patterns that are underrepresented in reference databases.

In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling biological sequences. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have demonstrated strong performance in various sequence classification tasks, capturing local motifs and long-range dependencies without the need for handcrafted features. More recently, attention-based architectures, such as Transformers, have further advanced the state of the art by modeling complex dependencies over arbitrary distances. Despite these advances, many deep learning models require large labeled training datasets, and their performance tends to degrade when applied to sequences from classes not represented during training—a significant limitation in genomic applications, where novel sequences are continually discovered.

Few-shot learning has been proposed as a means to address these challenges, enabling models to generalize to new classes from only a handful of labeled examples. Among the approaches in this area, memory-augmented neural networks provide an explicit mechanism for storing and retrieving information about reference examples, thereby supporting rapid adaptation to new tasks. Memory Matching Networks (MMNs) extend this idea by incorporating a learned embedding space in which query sequences can be compared directly to stored exemplars, using similarity metrics to guide classification without retraining the model for each new class. Such architectures are especially well-suited for genomic sequence classification, where it is often necessary to assign labels to sequences with minimal prior examples and where interpretability of similarity relationships can provide valuable biological insights.

In this work, we explore the application of Memory Matching Networks to genomic sequence classification. We hypothesize that combining deep sequence embeddings with a memory-based matching mechanism can achieve robust performance across both well-represented and rare classes, while reducing the computational burden associated with alignment-based methods. We evaluate our approach on multiple benchmark datasets spanning taxonomic classification, functional annotation, and regulatory element prediction, comparing against both traditional bioinformatics tools and contemporary deep learning models. Our contributions include the adaptation of the MMN framework to handle variable-length genomic sequences, the incorporation of biologically informed embedding architectures, and a systematic assessment of few-shot classification performance in realistic genomic scenarios. Through this study, we aim to demonstrate that memory-augmented models offer a promising direction for scalable, accurate, and adaptable genomic sequence analysis.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced Memory Matching Networks for genomic sequence classification, leveraging an external memory module to capture representative patterns and improve discrimination among complex sequence classes. By integrating memory-augmented neural architectures with attention-based matching, our approach demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional deep learning baselines across multiple genomic datasets. The ability to explicitly store and retrieve informative subsequences enables the model to generalize effectively to rare or ambiguous patterns, a critical requirement in genomic analysis. Our results suggest that memory mechanisms can bridge the gap between high-capacity sequence models and interpretable, biologically relevant representations. Future work will explore scaling to larger genomic corpora, incorporating domain-specific priors, and extending the framework to related tasks such as variant effect prediction and functional genomics annotation.

title: A massive momentum-subtraction scheme
abstract: We present a novel massive momentum-subtraction (MOM) renormalization scheme tailored for quantum field theories with massive degrees of freedom. Unlike conventional MOM approaches, our formulation consistently incorporates mass effects at all subtraction points, enabling improved precision in low- and intermediate-energy regimes. We define the scheme through explicit subtraction conditions on vertex functions with off-shell external momenta and finite particle masses. The resulting renormalization group functions are computed to one-loop order, and their mass dependence is analyzed. Applications to scalar and gauge theories demonstrate the scheme’s utility in bridging between massless high-energy limits and realistic massive phenomenology without introducing infrared ambiguities.
introduction: Renormalization is a central procedure in quantum field theory, allowing the removal of ultraviolet divergences and the definition of finite, physically meaningful quantities. Among the various renormalization schemes, momentum-subtraction (MOM) schemes are of particular interest due to their direct connection to Green’s functions evaluated at specific kinematic configurations. In this work, we investigate a variant we refer to as the massive momentum-subtraction (mMOM) scheme, in which subtraction points are chosen in the presence of a nonzero mass scale. This modification preserves the practical advantages of MOM schemes while accommodating theories where mass effects cannot be neglected, such as in low-energy QCD or effective field theories with heavy degrees of freedom. We outline the formal definition of the mMOM scheme, analyze its renormalization group properties, and compare it with conventional schemes like \(\overline{\mathrm{MS}}\). Our aim is to provide a consistent framework that improves the treatment of mass-dependent corrections while maintaining computational tractability and physical interpretability.
conclusion:
In this work, we have developed and analyzed a massive momentum-subtraction (MOM) scheme tailored to accommodate the presence of an explicit mass scale in the renormalization procedure. By extending the conventional MOM framework to incorporate massive propagators and vertices, we have provided a systematic approach for defining renormalized Green’s functions in theories where mass effects cannot be neglected, such as in low-energy QCD or in electroweak sectors with heavy fields. Our formulation preserves the central virtues of momentum-subtraction schemes—most notably, their direct physical interpretation and transparent connection to measurable amplitudes—while ensuring that mass-dependent terms are consistently treated.

Through explicit calculations at one- and two-loop order, we have demonstrated that the scheme yields finite, well-defined renormalization constants and maintains compatibility with known massless limits. The matching to the \(\overline{\mathrm{MS}}\) scheme was carried out, allowing for a clear translation between mass-dependent renormalization group functions and their mass-independent counterparts. This matching also provides a useful tool for lattice QCD applications, where massive MOM schemes can bridge the gap between nonperturbative computations and high-energy perturbative results.

Our analysis confirms that the massive MOM scheme leads to modified renormalization group equations in which the running of couplings and masses reflects both ultraviolet behavior and explicit mass thresholds. This feature can be exploited in phenomenological studies where threshold effects are significant. Moreover, the framework offers a consistent way to implement renormalization conditions at kinematic points relevant to the physical processes under consideration.

Future work may extend the present results to higher-loop orders, explore applications to gauge theories beyond the Standard Model, and investigate nonperturbative implementations. The massive momentum-subtraction scheme introduced here thus provides a versatile and robust tool for addressing the interplay of mass scales and renormalization in quantum field theory, with both theoretical and phenomenological relevance.

title: Integral population control of a quadratic dimerization process
abstract: We investigate the integral population control of a nonlinear quadratic dimerization process, where monomers reversibly bind to form dimers. Such processes arise in biochemical networks, synthetic biology, and molecular self-assembly, and are characterized by quadratic reaction terms in the governing mass-action kinetics. We formulate a control strategy based on integral feedback to achieve robust regulation of the total molecular population—monomers plus twice the dimer count—despite parametric uncertainty and disturbances. A reduced-order model is derived to capture the essential nonlinear dynamics, enabling analytical stability and performance analysis. Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed integral controller ensures asymptotic convergence of the total population to the desired setpoint, demonstrating resilience to reaction rate variations and measurement noise.
introduction:
Population control in chemical and biochemical processes is a central theme in systems and control theory, with applications ranging from synthetic biology to chemical engineering. Many natural and engineered systems exhibit nonlinear reaction dynamics, where the rate of change of a species depends nonlinearly on its concentration. Among these, quadratic dynamics are particularly prevalent in processes involving dimerization, in which two molecules of the same type bind to form a dimer. Dimerization is a fundamental reaction motif, influencing the behavior of protein–protein interactions, receptor binding, and polymer formation. Mathematical models of such processes often take the form of mass-action kinetics, leading to nonlinear ordinary differential equations where quadratic terms couple the dynamics of the monomer and dimer populations.

From a control perspective, quadratic dimerization processes pose unique challenges. The inherent nonlinearity can lead to rich dynamical phenomena such as multiple equilibria, bistability, and nonlinear sensitivity to input perturbations. In the context of synthetic biology, for example, the ability to precisely regulate the concentration of a monomeric species despite fluctuations in environmental conditions or parameter uncertainties is of paramount importance. Similarly, in chemical process control, maintaining desired concentrations of reactive species ensures product quality, process safety, and economic efficiency. This requires control strategies capable of robust performance in the face of nonlinearities and disturbances.

A widely adopted approach in control engineering for achieving robust setpoint regulation is the use of integral control. Integral action ensures that steady-state error is driven to zero by integrating the difference between the measured output and the desired setpoint, and feeding this accumulated error back into the control input. In linear systems, the benefits of integral control are well understood, supported by classical results such as the Internal Model Principle. However, the extension of integral control to nonlinear systems, and particularly to systems governed by quadratic kinetics, is nontrivial. Issues such as integrator windup, loss of stability margins, and the emergence of oscillatory or even chaotic behavior must be addressed through careful design and analysis.

In recent years, there has been increasing interest in applying feedback control theory to regulate biomolecular populations, with a particular emphasis on genetic circuits and enzymatic reactions. The notion of “population control” here refers to the regulation of the number—or more precisely, the concentration—of a target molecular species within a reaction network. For quadratic dimerization, the control objective might be to maintain the monomer population at a prescribed level, either by modulating synthesis rates or by influencing degradation pathways. Achieving such control in a biologically or chemically realistic setting often means dealing with constraints such as positivity of concentrations, bounded control inputs, and stochastic fluctuations at low copy numbers.

Theoretical studies of controlled reaction networks have highlighted the interplay between network topology, reaction order, and achievable control performance. Quadratic dimerization processes are particularly interesting because the monomer concentration enters the dimerization reaction rate quadratically, leading to a nonlinear sink term in the monomer dynamics. This means that the effect of disturbances and control actions is state-dependent in a nonlinear fashion, complicating the design of controllers with guaranteed performance. Moreover, in many practical cases, the dimer itself is not directly measured, so the controller must operate based on partial information about the system state.

Integral control for such systems can be implemented in various ways. In a purely engineering context, an external feedback loop can manipulate an actuator to influence the monomer synthesis rate. In a synthetic biology context, integral action might be embedded in the reaction network itself, via an auxiliary “controller species” whose dynamics integrate the output error and adjust the production of the target species. The latter approach leads to “integral population control” architectures that are physically realizable in wet-lab settings and have been demonstrated in proof-of-concept experiments. Nevertheless, a rigorous mathematical treatment of integral control applied to quadratic dimerization processes remains relatively scarce.

The present work addresses this gap by developing and analyzing an integral control strategy for regulating the monomer concentration in a quadratic dimerization process. We consider a canonical dimerization reaction where monomers are produced at a controllable rate, bind pairwise to form dimers, and are degraded via first-order mechanisms. The control objective is to ensure that the monomer concentration converges to a prescribed reference value despite constant disturbances or uncertainties in system parameters. Our approach embeds integral action in the feedback loop, guaranteeing zero steady-state error for constant disturbances, while ensuring closed-loop stability and positivity of concentrations.

We begin by formulating the mathematical model of the quadratic dimerization process, capturing the essential nonlinearities arising from the bimolecular binding reaction. We then introduce the integral control architecture and analyze the closed-loop dynamics, deriving conditions for stability and convergence. Particular attention is paid to the interplay between the quadratic reaction term and the integrator state, as this determines both the transient and steady-state behavior. We further discuss implementation considerations, including constraints on control inputs and the avoidance of integrator windup.

By combining nonlinear systems analysis with control design principles, our results offer a framework for integral population control in a class of reaction networks that are both theoretically rich and practically relevant. The findings have potential applications in synthetic biology, where dimerization is a common motif in transcription factor regulation, as well as in chemical process control, where robust regulation of reactive species is a key operational objective. Beyond the specific case of quadratic dimerization, the methods developed here may be extended to more general nonlinear reaction networks, contributing to the broader goal of systematic control of population dynamics in nonlinear systems.
conclusion: In this work, we have developed and analyzed an integral population control strategy for a quadratic dimerization process, capturing both the nonlinear reaction kinetics and the closed-loop regulatory dynamics. By embedding integral feedback within the control architecture, the proposed method ensures robust set-point tracking of the total molecular population despite parameter uncertainties and external disturbances. Numerical simulations confirm that the scheme stabilizes the desired equilibrium and attenuates transient deviations without inducing oscillatory instabilities. The results demonstrate the feasibility of implementing integral control principles in systems governed by quadratic reaction terms, offering a foundation for broader application to synthetic biochemical networks and highlighting the potential for systematic control design in nonlinear population processes.

title: Suzaku Observations of Metal Distributions in the Intracluster Medium of the Centaurus Cluster
abstract: We present results from deep Suzaku X-ray observations of the Centaurus cluster, focusing on the spatial distribution of metals in the intracluster medium (ICM). Owing to Suzaku’s low and stable instrumental background, we measure abundances of O, Mg, Si, S, Ar, Ca, and Fe out to large radii, extending to approximately 0.5 r₁₈₀. The radial profiles show a pronounced central enhancement in Fe, peaking within 0.05 r₁₈₀, and significant gradients for other elements, indicating efficient enrichment by the central brightest cluster galaxy. Beyond 0.1 r₁₈₀, abundance ratios remain roughly constant, suggesting a well-mixed ICM at larger scales. Comparison with supernova yield models implies contributions from both Type Ia and core-collapse supernovae, with the central region exhibiting a higher Type Ia fraction. The Fe mass-to-light ratio increases with radius, consistent with early enrichment and subsequent redistribution of metals. Our results support a scenario in which metals in the outer regions were largely produced at high redshift and dispersed throughout the ICM, while the core has been enriched more recently by ongoing stellar mass loss and supernova activity in the central galaxy. These findings provide important constraints on the chemical evolution of galaxy clusters.
introduction:
Galaxy clusters are the largest gravitationally bound systems in the Universe, containing hundreds to thousands of galaxies, a massive dark matter halo, and a pervasive hot plasma known as the intracluster medium (ICM). The ICM, with temperatures of several keV, emits strongly in X-rays via thermal bremsstrahlung and line emission from heavy elements. These metals—elements heavier than helium—are synthesized in stars and supernovae within cluster galaxies and subsequently transported into the ICM through processes such as galactic winds, ram-pressure stripping, and active galactic nucleus (AGN) outflows. As such, the spatial distribution and abundance patterns of metals in the ICM provide key insights into the chemical enrichment history, feedback processes, and dynamical evolution of clusters.

Detailed measurements of metal abundances in the ICM have been made possible through X-ray spectroscopy with satellites such as ASCA, XMM-Newton, Chandra, and Suzaku. Observations have revealed that many clusters exhibit centrally peaked metallicity profiles, particularly in cool-core systems where central dominant (cD) galaxies reside. In these systems, the excess of metals in the core is often attributed to enrichment from Type Ia supernovae in the cD galaxy, superimposed on a more spatially extended distribution of metals from earlier enrichment episodes dominated by core-collapse supernovae. The relative abundances of elements such as oxygen, magnesium, silicon, sulfur, and iron can be used to disentangle the contributions of different supernova types and to constrain the timescales of enrichment.

The Centaurus cluster (Abell 3526), at a redshift of *z* ≈ 0.0104, is a nearby, X-ray bright, cool-core cluster that has long been recognized for its unusually high central metallicity. Previous X-ray studies with ASCA, XMM-Newton, and Chandra have shown that the iron abundance in the central region can reach values exceeding solar, and that the metallicity declines with radius. The cluster’s proximity allows for high spatial resolution studies of its ICM, making it an ideal laboratory for investigating the processes that shape metal distributions. Moreover, the Centaurus cluster exhibits evidence of dynamical complexity, including possible sloshing of the ICM and interactions between the central galaxy NGC 4696 and the surrounding plasma, which may influence the redistribution of metals.

Suzaku, with its low and stable instrumental background and relatively large effective area for X-ray spectroscopy, is particularly well suited for measuring faint emission lines from the ICM at large radii. This capability enables the study of metal abundances beyond the bright cluster core, where the X-ray surface brightness drops significantly. By extending metallicity measurements to larger cluster-centric distances, it becomes possible to probe the integrated enrichment history of the cluster and to test models of early pre-enrichment versus ongoing enrichment.

In this work, we present Suzaku observations of the Centaurus cluster aimed at mapping the radial distributions of key elemental abundances, including O, Mg, Si, S, and Fe, from the central regions out to the cluster outskirts. We investigate the relative abundance ratios to infer the relative contributions of Type Ia and Type II supernovae, and we compare our findings with results for other nearby clusters. Our study provides new constraints on the mechanisms responsible for transporting metals into the ICM and on the chemical evolution of the Centaurus cluster. By combining Suzaku’s sensitivity to low surface brightness emission with the wealth of previous high-resolution observations of the core, we aim to construct a comprehensive picture of the metal enrichment and distribution in this archetypal cool-core system.
conclusion: We have analyzed Suzaku X-ray observations to investigate the spatial distribution of metals in the intracluster medium (ICM) of the Centaurus Cluster. Our measurements reveal centrally peaked abundances of Fe, Si, and S, which decline gradually with radius, consistent with enrichment dominated by Type Ia supernovae in the core. Beyond ~0.05 r\(_{200}\), the abundance ratios approach values indicative of a mixed contribution from both Type Ia and core-collapse supernovae, suggesting early, widespread enrichment of the ICM. The relatively flat abundance profiles at large radii imply efficient metal transport processes, potentially driven by AGN activity or sloshing motions. Comparisons with other nearby cool-core clusters indicate that Centaurus exhibits one of the highest central Fe concentrations, likely reflecting its long-lived, undisturbed core. These results support a scenario in which the bulk of the metals were produced at early epochs, with subsequent enrichment in the core from the brightest cluster galaxy. Future high-resolution spectroscopic observations will be essential to disentangle the detailed enrichment history and to constrain the physical mechanisms governing metal transport in cluster environments.

title: Large Deviations of the Finite-Time Magnetization of the Curie-Weiss Random Field Ising Model
abstract: We investigate the large-deviation properties of the finite-time magnetization in the Curie–Weiss random field Ising model, a paradigmatic mean-field system with quenched disorder. Focusing on stochastic single-spin-flip dynamics at finite temperature, we analyze the probability distribution of the time-averaged magnetization over trajectories of fixed duration. Using a path-integral formalism combined with a saddle-point evaluation, we derive the corresponding scaled cumulant generating function and obtain the associated rate function via Legendre–Fenchel transform. Our results reveal distinct dynamical regimes depending on temperature and disorder strength, including symmetry-breaking effects in the large-deviation function induced by the random field. We further identify dynamical phase transitions manifested as non-analyticities in the rate function, reflecting competing relaxation pathways in the magnetization dynamics. Numerical simulations based on importance-sampling Monte Carlo methods corroborate the analytical predictions and quantify finite-size corrections. This study extends the understanding of fluctuation phenomena in disordered mean-field systems and highlights the interplay between quenched randomness and dynamical large deviations.
introduction:
The study of fluctuations in macroscopic observables of interacting spin systems has long been a central theme in statistical mechanics. In particular, the Curie–Weiss model, as the paradigmatic example of a fully-connected ferromagnet, has provided deep insights into equilibrium phase transitions, collective behaviour, and the role of symmetry breaking. Its analytical tractability stems from the mean-field nature of the interactions, allowing for exact results for thermodynamic quantities and a detailed understanding of finite-size effects. When this model is subjected to external disorder, such as spatially varying or random magnetic fields, its behaviour becomes richer and more complex. The Curie–Weiss random field Ising model (CW-RFIM) has thus emerged as a valuable framework for examining the interplay between quenched randomness and cooperative phenomena.

While the equilibrium statistical mechanics of the CW-RFIM is by now well understood, much less is known about its non-equilibrium dynamics and the statistics of time-dependent fluctuations. In many physical contexts, the system is not observed at asymptotically large times but rather over finite time intervals, during which the magnetization undergoes stochastic evolution governed by the underlying microscopic dynamics. Understanding the distribution of the magnetization accumulated over such finite time windows is essential for describing transient phenomena, for quantifying rare events in dynamical trajectories, and for connecting theoretical predictions with experimental measurements that necessarily have finite temporal resolution.

Large deviation theory provides a natural framework for analysing the probabilities of atypical fluctuations in stochastic systems. In the context of spin models, large deviations of the time-averaged magnetization encode information about metastable states, switching events, and dynamical phase transitions. For mean-field systems, these large deviation functions can often be computed exactly or semi-analytically, offering a rare opportunity to characterise the fluctuation spectrum far beyond the Gaussian regime described by the central limit theorem. In the presence of random fields, however, the situation is more intricate: the quenched disorder couples to the magnetization in a way that modifies both typical and rare trajectories, and averaging over disorder configurations introduces an additional layer of complexity.

In this work, we investigate the large deviations of the finite-time magnetization in the CW-RFIM with Glauber-type dynamics. Specifically, we consider the empirical magnetization, defined as the time average of the instantaneous magnetization over a fixed observation time \( T \), and study the probability distribution of its fluctuations in the long but finite \( T \) regime. We focus on the regime where both the system size \( N \) and the observation time are large, allowing us to employ the joint large deviation principle in \( N \) and \( T \). The key object of interest is the rate function governing the exponential decay of the probability of observing a given time-averaged magnetization, which encapsulates the cost of sustaining atypical magnetization trajectories.

Our analysis combines techniques from dynamical large deviation theory, mean-field spin dynamics, and disorder averaging. We derive an explicit variational representation of the rate function that accounts for the coupling between the magnetization and the quenched random fields. The resulting expression reveals how the disorder distribution influences the shape of the rate function, in particular its convexity properties and the emergence of non-analyticities signalling dynamical phase transitions in trajectory space. We also address the distinction between quenched and annealed large deviations, highlighting the subtle differences in the fluctuation behaviour under these two types of disorder averaging.

By elucidating the large deviation structure of the finite-time magnetization in the CW-RFIM, our work contributes to the broader understanding of fluctuation phenomena in disordered mean-field systems. Beyond its intrinsic theoretical interest, our results may inform the analysis of rare events in a variety of complex systems where interactions and disorder coexist, such as neural networks, social dynamics, and disordered materials, and where only finite-time observations are available.
conclusion:
In this work we have analyzed the large deviation properties of the finite-time magnetization in the Curie–Weiss random field Ising model, focusing on the interplay between mean-field interactions and quenched disorder in determining the probability of atypical magnetization trajectories. By formulating the problem within a path-integral framework and employing saddle-point methods, we derived explicit expressions for the rate function governing the exponentially rare fluctuations of the time-averaged magnetization over a finite observation window. Our results demonstrate that the presence of the random field profoundly modifies the shape and symmetry of the rate function compared to the pure Curie–Weiss case, leading to nontrivial asymmetries and changes in curvature that reflect the breaking of the global spin-flip symmetry by the disorder.

We have shown that, depending on the disorder strength and temperature, the system exhibits qualitatively distinct regimes: in the weak-disorder limit, the rate function retains a near-quadratic form around its minimum but develops skewness in the tails, whereas in the strong-disorder regime, rare events are dominated by configurations in which the local random fields align cooperatively to produce large deviations. The analytical predictions were corroborated by numerical simulations using importance-sampling Monte Carlo methods, which confirmed both the location of the most probable magnetization and the scaling of deviations.

An important conceptual outcome of our study is the clarification of how quenched randomness modifies the finite-time fluctuation structure in mean-field spin systems. While equilibrium magnetization fluctuations in the thermodynamic limit are well understood, our analysis exposes the specific mechanisms by which disorder reshapes the exponential suppression of finite-time deviations, even in a fully connected geometry. These insights may have broader implications for understanding fluctuation phenomena in disordered mean-field models, including glassy systems and neural networks.

Future work could extend the present approach to non-Gaussian disorder distributions, time-dependent random fields, or dynamics beyond Glauber-type single-spin flips, as well as to finite-connectivity random graphs where spatial heterogeneity becomes relevant. Moreover, exploring connections between the rate function and dynamical phase transitions in trajectory space could provide a deeper unifying framework for rare-event statistics in disordered interacting systems. Overall, the present results contribute to a more complete characterization of fluctuation behavior in the Curie–Weiss random field Ising model, bridging the gap between equilibrium thermodynamics and finite-time nonequilibrium statistics.

title: On the Nature of Programming Exercises
abstract: Programming exercises are a central component of computer science education, serving both as a means of reinforcing theoretical concepts and as a gateway to practical problem-solving skills. This paper examines the nature of programming exercises from pedagogical, cognitive, and design perspectives. We investigate how variations in problem structure, domain context, and scaffolding influence learner engagement and conceptual retention. Drawing on empirical studies and educational theory, we propose a taxonomy that categorizes exercises according to complexity, openness, and required abstraction level. Special attention is given to the balance between challenge and achievability, as well as the role of automated feedback in supporting iterative learning. Our analysis highlights common pitfalls in exercise design, including over-reliance on syntactic drills and insufficient real-world relevance. The findings provide actionable guidelines for educators seeking to craft programming exercises that foster deeper understanding, transferable skills, and sustained motivation among diverse learner populations.
introduction:
Programming exercises have long been a central component of computer science education, serving both as a means of reinforcing theoretical concepts and as a vehicle for developing practical problem-solving skills. From the earliest stages of instruction, learners are introduced to small, well-defined tasks designed to foster familiarity with syntax, control structures, and basic algorithms. As students advance, exercises grow in complexity, integrating multiple concepts and requiring the application of higher-order thinking. The design and selection of such exercises, however, is far from trivial. They must balance clarity and challenge, guiding learners without overwhelming them, while also aligning with pedagogical goals and assessment criteria.

The nature of programming exercises has evolved alongside changes in technology, pedagogy, and the broader computing landscape. In the past, exercises often reflected the constraints of limited computational resources and emphasized manual tracing, efficiency, and algorithmic ingenuity. Today, the ubiquity of powerful computing devices, integrated development environments, and automated grading systems has broadened the scope of what exercises can entail. Modern exercises not only address traditional problem-solving skills but also incorporate elements such as debugging, code comprehension, and collaborative development. Furthermore, the rise of online learning platforms and competitive programming arenas has brought new formats and expectations, influencing how exercises are designed, delivered, and evaluated.

Despite their ubiquity, programming exercises remain underexplored as a distinct object of study. Instructors often rely on personal experience or existing repositories without explicit consideration of the cognitive and motivational factors that influence learner engagement and success. The diversity of learners—in terms of prior knowledge, learning styles, and cultural background—adds further complexity to the task of crafting exercises that are both accessible and stimulating. Additionally, there is an ongoing tension between exercises as practice tools for skill acquisition and as assessment instruments for measuring competence.

Understanding the nature of programming exercises requires examining their structural characteristics, pedagogical roles, and the contexts in which they are deployed. This includes investigating how problem statements are framed, the kinds of knowledge and skills they target, and the strategies learners employ in approaching them. By analyzing programming exercises through these lenses, we can gain insight into their educational affordances and limitations, and ultimately inform the development of more effective teaching and learning practices. This paper aims to contribute to such an understanding by exploring the defining features, functions, and implications of programming exercises within contemporary computing education.
conclusion: This discussion has examined the nature of programming exercises, highlighting their dual role as both pedagogical tools and vehicles for cultivating computational thinking. By analyzing their structure, intent, and cognitive demands, we have seen how exercises can scaffold learning from foundational syntax to complex problem-solving. Effective design balances challenge with accessibility, encouraging incremental mastery while fostering creativity and resilience. Moreover, the alignment between exercise objectives and assessment criteria is crucial for meaningful learning outcomes. As programming education evolves, incorporating authentic, context-rich tasks alongside traditional drills may better prepare learners for real-world applications. Future work should explore adaptive, personalized approaches that respond to diverse learner needs and backgrounds.
