Ultimately, well-crafted programming exercises not only develop technical competence but also nurture the habits of mind essential for success in an increasingly digital world.

title: Photometry and H$alpha$ studies of a Low Mass Ratio Overcontact binary ASAS J082243+1927.0
abstract: We present new photometric observations and H$\alpha$ line studies of the low mass ratio overcontact binary ASAS J082243+1927.0. Time-series CCD photometry was obtained in the Johnson $V$ band, and the resulting light curves were analyzed using the Wilson–Devinney (W–D) code to derive the system’s photometric elements. The light curves exhibit a total eclipse at the secondary minimum, enabling a reliable determination of the mass ratio and degree of overcontact. Our solutions indicate a low mass ratio of $q \approx 0.10$ and a high fill-out factor of $\sim$72\%, placing the system among the extreme low-$q$ overcontact binaries potentially approaching the merger stage. We detect an O’Connell effect in the light curves, which is modeled with a cool spot on the more massive component, suggesting significant magnetic activity. Medium-resolution spectroscopy covering the H$\alpha$ region was also obtained to investigate chromospheric activity. The H$\alpha$ absorption profile shows variable fill-in at different orbital phases, with the deepest fill-in near secondary eclipse, consistent with activity localized on the primary star. The correlation between the H$\alpha$ equivalent width and orbital phase supports the presence of active regions associated with the spotted surface. We discuss the system’s position in the period–color diagram and its evolutionary status in the context of angular momentum loss and thermal relaxation oscillation theories. Given its extreme mass ratio, high contact degree, and activity signatures, ASAS J082243+1927.0 emerges as an important target for monitoring orbital period changes and for probing the late evolutionary stages of overcontact binaries.
introduction:
Overcontact binary systems are among the most intriguing classes of eclipsing binaries, characterized by both stellar components filling their Roche lobes and sharing a common convective envelope. These systems are typically classified into A-type and W-type W UMa binaries based on the temperature of the components and the morphology of their light curves (Binnendijk 1970). They are of particular astrophysical interest because they represent an advanced evolutionary stage of close binary stars, where mass and energy exchange between the components leads to significant changes in their structure and orbital parameters. Studies of such systems provide critical insights into angular momentum loss, magnetic activity, and the processes that can lead to their eventual merger, potentially forming single, fast-rotating stars or more exotic objects.

The mass ratio \( q \) (secondary-to-primary mass) in overcontact binaries is a crucial parameter influencing their stability and evolutionary fate. Low mass ratio systems (\( q < 0.25 \)) are especially important, as they are thought to be near the theoretical limit of tidal stability (Rasio 1995). In these binaries, the less massive secondary is often highly evolved relative to its mass, and the system may be undergoing or approaching a merger phase. Observations of such binaries can thus provide empirical constraints on theoretical models of contact binary evolution and the role of mass loss and angular momentum evolution.

Photometric studies remain the principal tool for characterizing overcontact binaries, allowing determination of orbital periods, inclination angles, fill-out factors, and temperature differences between components. High-precision light curves, when modeled with appropriate techniques such as the Wilson-Devinney (WD) code, can yield robust physical and geometrical parameters. Complementary spectroscopic or spectrophotometric observations, particularly of emission features such as the H\(\alpha\) line, can provide valuable diagnostics of chromospheric activity, mass transfer, and magnetic phenomena within the common envelope. The H\(\alpha\) line, in particular, is a well-established tracer of stellar activity, and variations in its equivalent width over the orbital cycle can reveal the spatial and temporal distribution of active regions.

ASAS J082243+1927.0 (hereafter ASAS J0822+1927) is a relatively bright eclipsing binary system identified in the All Sky Automated Survey (ASAS) database. Preliminary classifications suggest it is an overcontact binary with a low mass ratio, making it a promising candidate for detailed photometric and spectroscopic study. Despite its apparent suitability for such analysis, the system has not been extensively investigated in the literature. A dedicated study combining high-quality multi-band photometry with H\(\alpha\) spectroscopy can therefore yield new insights into its physical parameters, activity level, and evolutionary status.

In this work, we present new CCD photometric observations and H\(\alpha\) spectroscopic measurements of ASAS J0822+1927. Using simultaneous light and radial profile modeling, we determine the system’s fundamental parameters and examine its chromospheric activity. We discuss the implications of our findings for the evolutionary status of low mass ratio overcontact binaries and compare ASAS J0822+1927 with other systems near the tidal stability limit.
conclusion:
New photometric observations of the low mass ratio overcontact binary ASAS J082243+1927.0 have been presented and analyzed in conjunction with H$\alpha$ line studies. The light curves were modeled using the Wilson–Devinney code, yielding a mass ratio $q \approx 0.106$ and a high degree of overcontact ($f \approx 72\%$), confirming the system as an extreme low mass ratio overcontact binary. The morphology of the $V$-band light curve displays a total eclipse at the secondary minimum, allowing reliable determination of system parameters. The derived absolute parameters suggest that the binary is composed of a more massive, hotter primary and a significantly less massive secondary that is nevertheless close to Roche lobe filling.  

The H$\alpha$ equivalent width measurements indicate chromospheric activity, with a tendency for decreased absorption at certain orbital phases, possibly linked to magnetic activity or mass transfer phenomena. The combined photometric and spectroscopic evidence supports the classification of ASAS J082243+1927.0 as a candidate for the merger pathway of contact binaries, consistent with theoretical instability limits for systems with $q < 0.1$.

The position of the components in the mass–radius and mass–luminosity diagrams suggests evolutionary advancement toward coalescence, possibly forming a rapidly rotating single star. Continued monitoring of the orbital period via minima timing could reveal secular period changes indicative of angular momentum loss or mass transfer. High-resolution spectroscopy would further constrain radial velocity curves and activity indicators, providing more precise physical parameters.

In summary, ASAS J082243+1927.0 is an important addition to the small sample of well-studied extreme low mass ratio overcontact binaries, offering valuable constraints on evolutionary models and the end states of close binary systems.

title: Eigenvalue Formulation of Quantum Mechanics Near Closed Timelike Curves
abstract: We present an eigenvalue-based framework for analyzing quantum mechanical systems interacting with regions containing closed timelike curves (CTCs). By reformulating the Deutsch consistency condition as a nonlinear eigenvalue problem, we explore the spectral structure of admissible quantum states and their evolution. This approach reveals constraints on unitarity, causality, and state self-consistency, offering new insights into time-loop-induced correlations. Our formulation provides a systematic method for examining quantum dynamics near CTCs and assessing their implications for fundamental physics.
introduction:
The study of quantum mechanics in the presence of closed timelike curves (CTCs) lies at the intersection of fundamental physics, quantum information theory, and the foundations of spacetime. CTCs, predicted as possible solutions to Einstein’s field equations in general relativity, represent worldlines in spacetime that loop back onto themselves, theoretically permitting travel to the past. While their physical existence remains speculative, their theoretical implications for causality, determinism, and consistency are profound. In particular, embedding quantum systems within spacetimes containing CTCs challenges our conventional understanding of quantum evolution, measurement, and information flow.

Classical treatments of CTCs have long grappled with consistency conditions, such as those proposed by Novikov, to avoid paradoxes like the “grandfather paradox.” Quantum mechanically, these issues manifest in questions about the unitarity of evolution and the preservation of probability. Deutsch’s influential model of quantum mechanics with CTCs introduces a self-consistency condition on the density matrix of the system traversing the curve, leading to nonlinear and non-unitary evolution for the chronology-respecting part of the system. Subsequent frameworks, including the post-selected teleportation model, have sought to capture alternative dynamics while maintaining logical consistency. However, the mathematical structure underlying these approaches is often framed operationally, leaving open avenues for more formal spectral and operator-theoretic formulations.

An eigenvalue-based formulation offers a promising route to recast the CTC problem in a form that is both mathematically rigorous and physically transparent. In conventional quantum mechanics without CTCs, time evolution is represented by unitary operators whose spectral properties directly encode dynamical behavior. In the presence of CTCs, the effective dynamics can be represented by nonlinear maps or fixed-point equations; recasting these as eigenvalue problems allows the use of powerful mathematical tools from functional analysis and linear algebra to characterize possible solutions. Such a formulation can also clarify the role of consistency conditions, as fixed points of evolution maps correspond to eigenvectors with unit eigenvalue in an appropriately defined operator space.

Moreover, an eigenvalue perspective may shed light on key physical questions: the multiplicity and stability of self-consistent solutions, the emergence of nonlinearity in effective dynamics, and the relationship between the spectral properties of the associated operators and the information-processing capabilities of CTC-assisted quantum systems. By bridging the gap between operational models and spectral theory, one can explore whether constraints analogous to quantum no-go theorems arise naturally from the eigenvalue structure, and how these constraints might generalize in more complex spacetime topologies.

In this work, we develop an eigenvalue formulation of quantum mechanics in the vicinity of closed timelike curves. We systematically construct the relevant operator equations, analyze their spectral properties, and discuss the physical interpretation of the resulting eigenstates and eigenvalues. This approach not only offers a new mathematical perspective on quantum-CTC interactions but also contributes to the broader program of unifying quantum theory with the causal structure of spacetime.
conclusion: The eigenvalue formulation developed here offers a consistent framework for analyzing quantum systems in the vicinity of closed timelike curves. By recasting the problem in spectral terms, we have clarified constraints on allowable states and identified conditions for self-consistency. This approach illuminates the interplay between causality and quantum evolution, providing a foundation for further exploration of nontrivial spacetime topologies and their implications for quantum information, unitarity, and the structure of physical law.

title: Challenges on Probabilistic Modeling for Evolving Networks
abstract: Probabilistic modeling of evolving networks has emerged as a critical tool for understanding the dynamics of complex systems such as social, biological, and technological networks. However, capturing temporal evolution while preserving structural dependencies poses significant challenges. Models must balance expressiveness with scalability, as real-world networks often involve high-dimensional, sparse, and noisy data. Temporal correlations, non-stationary dynamics, and heterogeneous node and edge attributes further complicate inference and prediction. Moreover, evaluation is hindered by limited availability of longitudinal datasets and the difficulty of defining appropriate performance metrics for dynamic settings. Approximate inference methods can mitigate computational costs but may sacrifice accuracy or interpretability. This paper reviews key obstacles in probabilistic modeling for evolving networks, highlighting methodological trade-offs and open problems, and discusses potential directions, including scalable Bayesian methods, temporal representation learning, and principled uncertainty quantification for robust and interpretable dynamic network analysis.
introduction: Probabilistic modeling has emerged as a powerful framework for understanding the dynamic behavior of evolving networks, which arise in domains such as social media, biological systems, and communication infrastructures. Unlike static networks, evolving networks exhibit temporal changes in structure and interaction patterns, posing unique challenges for model design and inference. Capturing both topological evolution and stochastic variability requires balancing model complexity with computational tractability. Furthermore, the scarcity of longitudinal data and the presence of noise complicate parameter estimation and validation. These challenges are amplified by the need to account for heterogeneity, non-stationarity, and potential latent factors. Addressing these issues is essential for developing robust probabilistic models capable of accurately representing and predicting the behavior of real-world evolving networks.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the principal challenges associated with probabilistic modeling for evolving networks, emphasizing both theoretical and practical considerations. As networks in many domains—such as social interaction, communication infrastructures, and biological systems—are inherently dynamic, capturing their temporal evolution within a probabilistic framework is critical for accurate inference and prediction. However, our analysis reveals that several interconnected difficulties persist. Chief among these are the high dimensionality and sparsity of temporal data, the non-stationary nature of evolving structures, and the need to balance model expressiveness with computational tractability. In particular, probabilistic models must contend with structural changes that occur at multiple time scales, often driven by latent processes that are only partially observable. This complicates parameter estimation, model selection, and the assessment of uncertainty.

Moreover, the integration of heterogeneous data sources—combining structural, temporal, and node-level attributes—remains a non-trivial task that challenges existing statistical formulations. Scalability is another recurring concern, as many state-of-the-art methods struggle to operate efficiently on large-scale, rapidly changing networks. These limitations highlight the necessity for novel inference algorithms, adaptive modeling strategies, and principled approaches to regularization that can accommodate both the complexity and volatility of real-world systems.

Looking forward, advances in probabilistic representation learning, streaming inference, and hybrid modeling that couples mechanistic and data-driven approaches may offer promising avenues to address these issues. Furthermore, the development of standardized benchmarks and evaluation protocols for dynamic network models would facilitate more rigorous comparisons and accelerate methodological progress. Ultimately, tackling the outlined challenges will not only enhance our capacity to model evolving networks with greater fidelity but also deepen our understanding of the underlying processes that govern their formation and transformation over time.

title: A systematic review of Python packages for time series analysis
abstract: Time series analysis is a fundamental component of data science, enabling the modeling, forecasting, and interpretation of temporal data across diverse domains such as finance, healthcare, and environmental science. Python has emerged as a leading language for time series research and applications, supported by a growing ecosystem of specialized packages. This systematic review examines the landscape of Python libraries for time series analysis, with a focus on functionality, usability, interoperability, and performance. We conducted a structured search of peer-reviewed literature, official documentation, and community resources to identify and evaluate relevant packages. The review covers core libraries such as pandas, statsmodels, and scikit-learn, as well as domain-specific and advanced toolkits including Prophet, tsfresh, darts, and Kats. Each package is assessed according to criteria including preprocessing capabilities, statistical modeling options, machine learning integration, visualization tools, and support for irregular or multivariate data. Strengths, limitations, and unique contributions are discussed to guide practitioners in selecting appropriate tools for specific analytical tasks. The findings reveal substantial diversity in scope and maturity, with a trend toward hybrid solutions that combine statistical and deep learning approaches. This synthesis provides a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners seeking effective Python-based solutions for time series analysis.
introduction:
Time series analysis is a fundamental component of data science, supporting tasks such as forecasting, anomaly detection, and signal processing across diverse domains including finance, healthcare, climate science, and engineering. The growing availability of large-scale temporal datasets has heightened the need for accessible, efficient, and versatile analytical tools. Python, as one of the most widely used programming languages in data science, offers a rich ecosystem of open-source packages that facilitate various stages of time series analysis, from preprocessing and visualization to modeling and evaluation. However, the breadth and diversity of these packages present challenges for practitioners in selecting the most appropriate tools for specific analytical goals.

Over the past decade, the Python scientific computing stack—anchored by libraries such as NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn—has been complemented by specialized time series packages, including those focused on statistical modeling (e.g., statsmodels), machine learning approaches (e.g., tslearn), and deep learning frameworks (e.g., GluonTS). These packages vary considerably in their functionality, methodological scope, computational efficiency, and ease of integration with other tools. While numerous tutorials and blog posts provide informal comparisons, a systematic, academically rigorous review that synthesizes the capabilities, strengths, and limitations of Python-based time series packages remains lacking.

This paper addresses this gap by systematically reviewing Python packages designed explicitly for time series analysis. We examine the scope of supported methods, interoperability with the broader Python ecosystem, ease of use, extensibility, and performance considerations. By organizing and critically evaluating these tools, we aim to provide researchers, data scientists, and practitioners with a structured reference to guide package selection, identify areas of overlap or complementarity, and highlight opportunities for future development in Python-based time series analytics.
conclusion: This systematic review examined a range of Python packages for time series analysis, evaluating their functionality, usability, documentation quality, and suitability for diverse analytical tasks. Our findings indicate that while mature libraries such as *statsmodels*, *pandas*, and *scikit-learn* provide robust foundational tools, specialized packages like *tsfresh*, *prophet*, and *Kats* offer domain-specific capabilities that address more complex forecasting, feature extraction, and anomaly detection needs. The ecosystem demonstrates a high degree of interoperability, though inconsistencies in API design and documentation remain barriers for seamless adoption. Emerging libraries integrating deep learning frameworks show promise but often lack stability and long-term maintenance commitment. Overall, Python’s time series analysis landscape is rich and evolving, enabling both rapid prototyping and advanced modeling. However, future development would benefit from standardized interfaces, improved cross-library compatibility, and more comprehensive benchmarking. Researchers and practitioners should select packages based on project requirements, balancing feature richness with sustainability and ease of integration.

title: Audio-Visual Segmentation
abstract: Audio-visual segmentation aims to identify and delineate objects in a visual scene that correspond to specific audio signals. This task has gained increasing attention due to its potential in applications such as video understanding, human–computer interaction, and assistive technologies. We present a novel framework that jointly leverages spatial, temporal, and cross-modal cues to achieve fine-grained segmentation of sounding objects. Our approach integrates a transformer-based audio encoder with a vision backbone, enabling robust feature alignment across modalities. A cross-attention mechanism explicitly models the correspondence between audio events and visual regions, while a temporal consistency module enforces stable predictions across frames. We evaluate our method on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art techniques in both segmentation accuracy and temporal stability. Qualitative results further highlight the framework’s ability to handle challenging scenarios involving occlusion, background noise, and multiple simultaneous sound sources. This work advances the integration of auditory and visual information for more comprehensive scene understanding.
introduction: Audio-visual segmentation is an emerging research area that aims to jointly exploit auditory and visual cues to partition scenes into semantically meaningful regions. By integrating information from both modalities, it enables more robust and context-aware understanding of dynamic environments. Recent advances in deep learning have significantly enhanced the ability to model complex cross-modal relationships. This capability is essential for applications such as video understanding, human-computer interaction, and autonomous systems, where accurate segmentation under diverse conditions is critical for reliable performance.
conclusion: This work presented an approach to audio-visual segmentation that effectively integrates multimodal cues for precise object boundary detection. Experimental results demonstrate improved accuracy over unimodal baselines. Future research will explore more robust temporal alignment and cross-modal attention mechanisms, aiming to enhance generalization across diverse audio-visual contexts and challenging real-world scenarios.

title: Uncertainty and Surprisal Jointly Deliver the Punchline: Exploiting Incongruity-Based Features for Humor Recognition
abstract: Humor often arises from the tension between uncertainty and surprise, yet computational models rarely exploit their joint effects. This work investigates incongruity-based features derived from probabilistic language models to predict humorous text. We operationalize uncertainty as the entropy of word predictions and surprisal as the negative log-probability of observed words, capturing both anticipation and violation in language processing. Using a large corpus of jokes and non-jokes, we extract these features at multiple linguistic levels and integrate them into supervised classifiers. Experimental results demonstrate that combining uncertainty and surprisal yields significant improvements over baseline lexical and semantic features, highlighting their complementary roles. Our findings suggest that modeling humor as the interplay of expectation and deviation offers a principled framework for computational humor recognition and broader affective language understanding.
introduction: Humor is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon, often arising from the interplay between expectation and surprise. Cognitive theories, such as the incongruity-resolution model, propose that amusement emerges when an anticipated mental pattern is violated in an unexpected yet coherent way. In computational humor recognition, capturing such mechanisms remains challenging, as it requires modeling both the likelihood of linguistic events and the degree of deviation from expectation. Recent advances in probabilistic language modeling enable quantification of these aspects through measures such as uncertainty and surprisal. By jointly considering these features, it becomes possible to approximate the cognitive processes underlying joke comprehension. This work investigates how uncertainty and surprisal can be exploited as incongruity-based cues, providing a principled approach to detecting humorous content in natural language.
conclusion: This study demonstrated that integrating uncertainty and surprisal as complementary indicators of incongruity provides a robust basis for automatic humor recognition. By operationalizing these cognitive-linguistic constructs through language model predictions, we captured nuanced patterns that traditional surface-level features often miss. Our experiments showed that combining uncertainty-driven variability with surprisal-based unexpectedness yields consistent performance gains across diverse datasets. These findings support theoretical accounts of humor as arising from the resolution of incongruous expectations and highlight the potential of cognitively inspired features in computational humor research. Future work may extend this framework to multimodal contexts and adaptive, real-time settings, further refining the interplay between linguistic unpredictability and perceived humor in naturalistic human–machine interactions.

title: Damage-sensitive and domain-invariant feature extraction for vehicle-vibration-based bridge health monitoring
abstract: Vehicle-vibration-based bridge health monitoring offers a cost-effective and scalable alternative to traditional structural inspection methods, but its performance is hindered by variability in vehicle and environmental conditions. This study proposes a novel framework for extracting damage-sensitive and domain-invariant features from vehicle vibration data to improve the robustness of damage detection. The method employs a deep learning architecture that integrates domain-adversarial training with feature regularization to separate structural damage information from nuisance factors such as vehicle speed, mass, and road surface roughness. Simulated vehicle–bridge interaction models and field measurements are used to evaluate the approach under varying operational conditions. Results demonstrate that the proposed features maintain high sensitivity to structural damage while significantly reducing domain-induced variability, enabling consistent detection performance across diverse operating scenarios. This work advances the practicality of drive-by bridge health monitoring by addressing a key limitation of existing approaches and enhancing generalization to unseen environmental and vehicular conditions.
introduction: Bridge health monitoring is essential for ensuring structural safety and serviceability. Traditional structural health monitoring (SHM) methods often rely on fixed sensors, which can be costly to install and maintain. Recently, vehicle-vibration-based techniques have emerged as a promising alternative, exploiting responses from ordinary traffic to assess bridge conditions. However, extracting features that are both sensitive to structural damage and robust to variations in vehicle properties, speeds, and environmental conditions remains a significant challenge. Domain variability between different vehicles or operational scenarios can obscure damage-related patterns, leading to reduced diagnostic accuracy. To address this, domain-invariant feature extraction methods aim to suppress irrelevant variations while retaining sensitivity to damage-induced changes. This study proposes a novel approach for simultaneously achieving damage sensitivity and domain invariance, enabling more reliable and scalable bridge health assessments from vehicle-induced vibrations without reliance on controlled experiments or specialized instrumentation.
conclusion: This study presented a method for extracting damage-sensitive yet domain-invariant features from vehicle-induced bridge vibrations, enabling robust structural health monitoring under varying operational and environmental conditions. By integrating domain adaptation with damage-sensitive representation learning, the approach mitigates domain shift while preserving critical damage information. Experimental results demonstrated improved damage detection accuracy across diverse vehicle types and speeds. The findings highlight the potential of vehicle-vibration-based monitoring as a scalable, non-intrusive solution for bridge assessment, supporting timely maintenance decisions and enhancing the resilience of transportation infrastructure.

title: Fine-tuning Image Transformers using Learnable Memory
abstract: We propose a novel fine-tuning strategy for Vision Transformers (ViTs) that augments the model with a set of learnable memory tokens, enabling efficient adaptation to downstream tasks while preserving pre-trained representations. Unlike conventional full-parameter fine-tuning, our method introduces a small, fixed number of memory tokens that interact with image patch embeddings through self-attention layers. These tokens act as task-specific context vectors, capturing discriminative features without modifying the bulk of the model’s weights. Experiments on multiple image classification benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to full fine-tuning and adapter-based methods, while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters. Furthermore, we show that the learned memory tokens can be transferred across related tasks, facilitating rapid adaptation. Our results highlight learnable memory as a lightweight yet powerful mechanism for parameter-efficient transformer fine-tuning in vision applications.
introduction: Transformers have recently emerged as a powerful architecture for visual recognition tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks. Their ability to model long-range dependencies through self-attention enables rich contextual reasoning, yet this comes at the cost of substantial data and computational requirements during training. Fine-tuning pre-trained vision transformers has become a practical strategy to adapt them to downstream tasks; however, conventional approaches often involve updating all model parameters, which can be inefficient and prone to overfitting, especially with limited data. Parameter-efficient tuning methods attempt to mitigate these issues, but may struggle to preserve the representational capacity of the original model. In this work, we propose augmenting vision transformers with learnable memory tokens during fine-tuning. These tokens act as external, task-specific context vectors, interacting with image patches through attention, enabling adaptation without extensive parameter updates. Our approach demonstrates improved efficiency and generalization, providing a flexible mechanism for tailoring pre-trained transformers to diverse vision tasks.
conclusion:
In this work, we introduced a fine-tuning strategy for image transformers that augments the model with a set of learnable memory tokens. These tokens serve as an external, trainable reservoir of task-specific information, enabling the model to adapt to new domains and tasks without extensive modification of its original parameters. Through experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, we demonstrated that our approach consistently improves performance over standard fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods, particularly in low-data regimes. The learnable memory mechanism facilitates the integration of new visual concepts while preserving the general representational power acquired during pre-training, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting.  

Our analysis further revealed that the memory tokens act as complementary feature carriers, enriching the attention patterns in the transformer layers and enhancing the model’s ability to capture fine-grained details. This effect was especially pronounced in tasks requiring nuanced spatial reasoning and semantic alignment. Additionally, our method offers a favorable trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, since it requires updating only a small fraction of parameters.  

The proposed framework is broadly applicable and can be readily combined with other adaptation techniques, suggesting promising directions for future research. Potential extensions include dynamic memory allocation, cross-modal memory sharing, and integration with continual learning pipelines. Overall, learnable memory tokens provide a flexible, efficient, and effective means of fine-tuning image transformers, advancing their adaptability to diverse visual tasks while maintaining the efficiency advantages critical for large-scale deployment.

title: Stochastic Approximation on Riemannian manifolds
abstract: We investigate stochastic approximation algorithms on Riemannian manifolds, extending classical Euclidean results to curved spaces. By leveraging tools from differential geometry, we establish convergence properties under geodesic convexity and bounded curvature conditions. Our analysis accommodates manifold-valued data and noise, yielding asymptotic normality results. Applications to optimization on matrix manifolds and statistical estimation illustrate the framework’s versatility, demonstrating improved performance in scenarios where intrinsic geometry plays a critical role.
introduction: Stochastic approximation methods are fundamental tools for solving root-finding and optimization problems when only noisy observations are available. While extensively studied in Euclidean spaces, many modern applications involve data and parameters residing on nonlinear geometric structures such as Riemannian manifolds. Examples include optimization over the space of positive definite matrices, Grassmann manifolds, and rotation groups, arising in signal processing, computer vision, and machine learning. Extending stochastic approximation to these settings requires incorporating the manifold’s geometry into algorithm design and analysis. This work develops a framework for stochastic approximation on Riemannian manifolds, establishing convergence properties under general conditions and illustrating its applicability through examples that highlight both theoretical and practical benefits of the proposed approach.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated stochastic approximation algorithms formulated on Riemannian manifolds, extending classical Euclidean schemes to settings with nontrivial geometric structure. By leveraging tools from differential geometry, such as exponential maps, parallel transport, and geodesic convexity, we established convergence properties under appropriate smoothness and noise conditions. Our analysis demonstrates that curvature plays a critical role in both the rate and stability of convergence, influencing the choice of step-size sequences and the design of retraction mappings.  

The proposed framework accommodates a broad class of manifolds, including symmetric spaces and Lie groups, thereby broadening the applicability of stochastic approximation to problems in signal processing, machine learning, and statistical inference where constraints naturally define a manifold. In particular, the results presented here provide a rigorous foundation for iterative procedures in non-Euclidean parameter spaces, supporting both theoretical understanding and practical algorithm design.  

Future work may address high-probability bounds and finite-time performance guarantees, as well as extensions to manifolds with less regular structure or with metric connections differing from the Levi-Civita connection. Moreover, incorporating variance reduction techniques and adaptive step-size rules in the Riemannian setting offers promising avenues for improving practical performance. Overall, this study contributes to unifying stochastic approximation theory with modern geometric optimization.

title: The (1+1) Elitist Black-Box Complexity of LeadingOnes
abstract: We analyze the (1+1) elitist black-box complexity of the classical **LeadingOnes** problem, a well-studied benchmark in the theory of randomized search heuristics. In the black-box model, algorithms have access only to objective function evaluations, and the elitist restriction requires that the algorithm retains the best-so-far search point in each iteration. While the unrestricted black-box complexity of LeadingOnes is known to be Θ(n log n), the impact of elitist constraints on its complexity has not been fully understood. We provide tight bounds showing that the (1+1) elitist black-box complexity of LeadingOnes is exactly Θ(n²). Our analysis reveals that the elitist condition fundamentally limits the algorithm’s ability to explore the search space efficiently, forcing a sequential discovery of the optimal bit string. We prove a matching lower bound by constructing adversarial function instances within the LeadingOnes class and exploiting information-theoretic arguments. The upper bound is established by analyzing a simple randomized search heuristic that modifies one bit at a time while preserving elitism. These results demonstrate a clear separation between elitist and non-elitist settings and highlight the significant performance gap induced by elitist selection. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how selection mechanisms affect the black-box complexity of structured optimization problems.
introduction:
The analysis of randomized search heuristics, such as evolutionary algorithms (EAs), has developed into a mature research field that combines tools from probability theory, combinatorics, and the theory of algorithms. A central aim of this line of work is to quantify the resources required by such algorithms to solve optimization problems, in order to better understand their strengths and limitations and to guide their design. One prominent approach to this goal is black-box complexity analysis, which studies the minimal number of fitness evaluations that any algorithm from a given class needs to solve a problem. In the *elitist black-box complexity* model, algorithms are restricted to retaining only the best-so-far search points, reflecting the behavior of many practically relevant elitist EAs.

Among the benchmark problems used to benchmark and analyze the behavior of EAs, the **LeadingOnes** function occupies a special place. Defined on bit strings of length \(n\), it returns the length of the longest prefix of consecutive one-bits, starting from the first position. Despite its apparent simplicity, LeadingOnes has been instrumental for understanding algorithmic behavior on problems where progress must be made in a specific order, and where local improvements can be misleading with respect to global progress. The function’s structure introduces strong dependencies between bit positions, making it a useful test case for investigating the interplay between variation operators, selection mechanisms, and search dynamics.

The \((1+1)\) elitist setting constitutes one of the most fundamental algorithmic frameworks in evolutionary computation. In this setting, the algorithm maintains a single current search point and in each iteration generates one offspring by applying a variation operator, typically mutation, to the parent. The better of the two individuals is then retained for the next iteration. This minimalistic design allows for rigorous runtime analysis and serves as a baseline for more complex algorithms. Understanding the black-box complexity of LeadingOnes in the \((1+1)\) elitist model therefore provides both a theoretical benchmark and a foundation for analyzing more sophisticated search heuristics.

Previous work has determined the unrestricted black-box complexity of LeadingOnes as well as its complexity under various restricted models, such as unbiased variation operators of bounded arity. However, the precise complexity in the \((1+1)\) elitist model has not been fully characterized. While upper bounds can be derived from the performance of specific algorithms, matching lower bounds require careful adversarial arguments that account for the limited information available to the algorithm under elitist constraints. In particular, the inability to store or revisit worse solutions imposes a strong restriction on the learning process about the target bit string, potentially increasing the required number of evaluations.

In this work, we close this gap by determining the \((1+1)\) elitist black-box complexity of LeadingOnes. We present both upper and lower bounds that match up to constant factors, thereby establishing the exact asymptotic complexity in this model. Our results not only contribute to a more complete understanding of the complexity landscape of LeadingOnes but also shed light on the fundamental impact of elitism in randomized search heuristics.
conclusion: In this work, we have analyzed the \((1+1)\) elitist black-box complexity of the **LeadingOnes** problem, contributing to a deeper understanding of the performance limits of simple evolutionary strategies under restrictive selection mechanisms. By focusing on the elitist model, where only strictly improving solutions are accepted, we isolated the effects of such selection pressure from other algorithmic components. Our results establish tight bounds that close existing gaps in the literature and confirm that elitism can significantly influence the attainable runtime compared to more general black-box settings. In particular, we have shown that the \((1+1)\) elitist black-box complexity of **LeadingOnes** matches the typical performance of standard mutation-based \((1+1)\) evolutionary algorithms, thus formalizing the intuition that elitist selection does not permit substantial speedups for this class of functions. Beyond the specific bounds proved, our analysis introduced methodological tools that may be applicable to a broader range of problems in elitist black-box models. Future research could extend these techniques to higher-arity variation operators, alternative selection rules, or dynamic objective functions. We believe our findings provide both a precise characterization of the elitist case for **LeadingOnes** and a foundation for further exploration of the inherent limitations and potential of elitist search in black-box optimization.

title: On the effects of rotation on acoustic stellar pulsations: validity domains of perturbative methods and close frequency pairs
abstract: We investigate the influence of uniform rotation on acoustic pulsations in stellar models, with particular emphasis on the applicability limits of perturbative methods and the occurrence of close frequency pairs. Two-dimensional calculations of oscillation spectra are performed for polytropic models across a range of rotation rates, and the resulting frequencies are compared with those obtained from perturbative expansions up to third order in the rotation rate. We identify the rotation domains in which perturbative approaches remain accurate within typical observational uncertainties, distinguishing between low-order and high-order p-modes. Our results indicate that perturbative methods are reliable only for relatively slow rotators, with the validity limit depending sensitively on mode frequency and degree. Beyond these limits, full two-dimensional computations are required to capture the effects of rotational coupling and structural distortion. We also examine the emergence of near-degenerate frequency pairs in rapidly rotating models, assessing their potential to explain the close frequency spacings reported in δ Scuti stars. Our analysis suggests that while some close pairs can result from rotational effects, their distribution and incidence rate do not fully account for the observational statistics. These findings provide quantitative guidance for mode identification and asteroseismic modelling in rotating stars.
introduction:
The study of stellar oscillations provides a powerful tool for probing the internal structure and dynamics of stars. In recent decades, the development of asteroseismology, supported by high-precision space missions such as *CoRoT* and *Kepler*, has yielded unprecedented measurements of oscillation frequencies in a wide variety of stars. Among the factors influencing these frequencies, stellar rotation plays a central role, introducing shifts, splittings, and couplings between modes. Understanding and accurately modelling the effects of rotation is therefore essential for interpreting observed pulsation spectra.

In many cases, rotation is treated as a small perturbation to the non-rotating stellar structure, with first- or second-order perturbative methods providing analytical corrections to the oscillation frequencies. These methods are computationally efficient and have been widely used in the interpretation of observed modes. However, their validity is intrinsically limited: for stars with moderate to rapid rotation, the centrifugal distortion of the equilibrium structure and the Coriolis force can no longer be treated as small corrections. In such regimes, fully two-dimensional computations that incorporate rotation non-perturbatively become necessary.

An additional complication arises from the occurrence of close frequency pairs in the oscillation spectra of rotating stars. These near-degeneracies, which may be either intrinsic or rotation-induced, can lead to strong mode coupling, challenging the assumptions underlying perturbative treatments. The proper identification and interpretation of such pairs in observational data require a careful assessment of the domains where perturbative approaches remain reliable.

In this work, we investigate the effects of rotation on acoustic modes in intermediate- and high-mass stars, focusing on the accuracy and limitations of perturbative methods. By comparing perturbative frequency calculations with fully two-dimensional models, we delineate the parameter space in which perturbative approaches yield acceptable results. We also examine the formation and properties of close frequency pairs, discussing their implications for mode identification and seismic diagnostics in rotating stars. Our results aim to provide practical guidelines for the seismic analysis of rotating pulsators in the light of current and future asteroseismic observations.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined in detail the influence of rotation on acoustic pulsations in stellar models, with particular emphasis on assessing the validity domains of perturbative approaches and on characterizing the occurrence of close frequency pairs. By comparing perturbative results of various orders with complete two–dimensional calculations for a range of stellar rotation rates, we have quantified the regimes in which the simpler methods yield results of sufficient accuracy for asteroseismic applications.  

Our analysis shows that, for low to moderate rotation rates, first- and second-order perturbative methods reproduce the frequency spectra of acoustic modes with good fidelity. The precise threshold in rotation rate beyond which perturbative treatments become unreliable depends on the mode frequency and angular degree, but in general the breakdown occurs earlier for higher-order modes and for stars with more rapid rotation. We have delineated these thresholds by examining the relative differences between perturbative and full computations, thereby providing practical criteria for selecting the appropriate modelling approach in observational analyses.  

Beyond these limits, the full two–dimensional calculations reveal significant departures from perturbative predictions, reflecting the increasing influence of centrifugal distortion and the coupling between modes of different spherical degrees. In such regimes, perturbative expansions fail to capture both the global frequency shifts and the detailed local structure of the spectrum. Our results thus underscore the necessity of using non-perturbative methods for stars with rotation rates exceeding these identified limits, particularly in the context of high-precision space-based photometry, where even small frequency mismatches can lead to erroneous mode identifications.  

We have also investigated the distribution of close frequency pairs, which have been reported in several rapidly rotating δ Scuti stars. Our synthetic spectra indicate that rotation can induce near-degeneracies between modes of different degrees and radial orders, leading to frequency separations on the order of observational resolution. However, the occurrence rate and distribution of such pairs in our models do not fully reproduce the patterns observed in all stars, suggesting that additional physical effects—such as differential rotation, magnetic fields, or nonlinear mode interactions—may play a role in generating the observed frequency clustering.  

The combination of a clearly defined perturbative validity domain and a detailed characterization of rotation-induced frequency proximity offers a framework for interpreting complex oscillation spectra in rotating stars. These findings are directly applicable to the analysis of asteroseismic data from current and future missions, enabling more reliable mode identification and more accurate inference of stellar properties. Future work should extend this approach to include more realistic structural models, varying internal rotation profiles, and the coupling between acoustic and gravity modes, in order to further refine our understanding of stellar oscillations in the presence of rotation.

title: Localization of $q-$form fields on $AdS_{p+1}$ branes
abstract: We investigate the localization mechanism for bulk $q$‑form fields on $AdS_{p+1}$ branes embedded in higher‑dimensional spacetimes. Employing a warped geometry framework, we derive the effective field equations and analyze the normalizability of zero modes under various bulk mass and coupling configurations. The dependence of localization conditions on the form rank $q$, the brane dimension $p$, and the curvature scale is systematically examined. Our results reveal distinct regimes where localization is possible without additional interactions, and we discuss implications for gauge invariance, mass spectra, and phenomenological constraints in braneworld models with anti‑de Sitter geometry.
introduction:
The study of field localization on branes embedded in higher-dimensional spacetimes has become a central topic in the exploration of braneworld scenarios. In these frameworks, our observable universe is modeled as a lower-dimensional hypersurface (the brane) embedded in a higher-dimensional bulk, with the extra dimensions potentially playing a significant role in particle physics and cosmology. The idea, first popularized by the seminal works of Randall and Sundrum, provides an elegant geometrical approach to the hierarchy problem and has inspired numerous investigations into the behavior of various fields in warped geometries. In particular, understanding the localization mechanism for different types of bulk fields is essential for determining the phenomenological viability of such models.

While the localization of scalar, spinor, and vector fields has been extensively studied, the case of higher-rank antisymmetric tensor fields, or $q$‑form fields, has received comparatively less attention. These fields appear naturally in the low-energy limits of string theory and supergravity, where they play crucial roles in the description of fundamental interactions, flux compactifications, and topological charges. In string theory, for instance, $q$‑form gauge fields couple naturally to extended objects such as $p$‑branes, and their dynamics can influence moduli stabilization, cosmological evolution, and the realization of gauge symmetries in effective four-dimensional theories. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of their localization properties is important for connecting higher-dimensional theories to observable physics.

Most of the existing literature on $q$‑form localization has focused on flat or de Sitter branes embedded in either flat or anti-de Sitter (AdS) bulks. However, there are compelling motivations to consider branes that themselves possess constant curvature, in particular $AdS_{p+1}$ branes. Such configurations arise naturally in certain supergravity solutions and can be relevant for holographic setups in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, where the brane geometry encodes information about a dual field theory with a nontrivial infrared structure. Moreover, $AdS_{p+1}$ branes can appear as near-horizon geometries of intersecting brane systems, and they offer a richer structure for the study of localization phenomena due to their intrinsic curvature.

In warped braneworld scenarios, the possibility of localizing a field on the brane depends on the interplay between the bulk geometry, the form of the field’s action, and possible couplings to background fields. For $q$‑form fields, the localization problem is technically more intricate than for scalar or vector fields because of their gauge symmetry, the antisymmetric structure of their field strengths, and the fact that their effective degrees of freedom depend sensitively on the spacetime dimension. Furthermore, the duality between $q$‑form and $(D-q-2)$‑form fields in $D$ dimensions implies that localization results must be consistent with the dual description, adding an additional layer of theoretical constraint.

In the context of $AdS_{p+1}$ branes embedded in higher-dimensional AdS bulks, the localization of $q$‑form fields requires careful analysis of the bulk wave equations in the warped background, as well as the boundary conditions dictated by the brane. The warp factor and the curvature of the brane both influence the effective Schrödinger-like potential governing the extra-dimensional profile of the field modes. Normalizability of the zero mode — which corresponds to the massless mode from the brane observer’s point of view — is the key criterion for localization. In addition, the continuum spectrum of massive Kaluza–Klein modes can have important phenomenological implications, including corrections to long-range interactions and potential resonant states.

The purpose of this work is to systematically investigate the localization properties of $q$‑form fields on $AdS_{p+1}$ branes within warped geometries. We aim to determine the conditions under which the zero mode can be localized, to analyze the influence of the brane’s curvature on the localization mechanism, and to explore the mass spectrum of excitations. Our analysis will be carried out in a general $(D)$‑dimensional setting, allowing for arbitrary values of $p$ and $q$, and will account for the possible presence of bulk mass terms or couplings to background scalar fields. By extending previous studies to the case of curved branes, our results provide a broader understanding of field localization in braneworld models and contribute to the theoretical foundation necessary for embedding such constructions into realistic high-energy frameworks.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the localization properties of bulk \(q\)-form fields in the background of an \(AdS_{p+1}\) brane embedded in a higher-dimensional spacetime. By analyzing the corresponding field equations and their effective Schrödinger-like form, we determined the conditions under which normalizable zero modes can be trapped on the brane. Our results show that the interplay between the bulk mass of the form field, the curvature scale of the \(AdS_{p+1}\) geometry, and the rank \(q\) decisively affects localization. In particular, we have found that for certain ranges of \(q\) and bulk mass parameters, the effective potential supports bound states corresponding to localized massless modes, while outside these ranges the modes are delocalized into the bulk. This behavior generalizes known results for scalar, vector, and antisymmetric tensor fields in warped geometries, highlighting distinctive features of localization in \(AdS\) brane scenarios. The analysis also indicates that the brane curvature can enhance localization compared to flat brane models. These findings contribute to a more complete understanding of field localization mechanisms in braneworld models and may have implications for the low-energy spectrum of effective field theories arising from higher-dimensional theories.

title: Detecting causality in Plant electrical signal by a hybrid causal analysis approach
abstract: Plant electrical signals (PES) are crucial indicators of physiological responses to environmental stimuli, yet identifying causal relationships within these complex, noisy signals remains challenging. This study proposes a hybrid causal analysis approach integrating Granger causality and convergent cross mapping to detect directional interactions in PES. The method combines the statistical rigor of time-series modeling with the nonlinear dynamics sensitivity of state-space reconstruction, enabling robust detection under varying noise levels and nonlinearity. Experimental data from controlled plant stimulation demonstrate improved accuracy and resilience compared to single-method analyses. The results highlight the potential of hybrid causal inference to enhance understanding of plant signaling networks, offering new opportunities for monitoring plant health and environmental adaptation mechanisms.
introduction:
Plants, as sessile organisms, have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to perceive, process, and respond to environmental stimuli. Among these mechanisms, plant electrical signals (PES) play a pivotal role in mediating rapid long-distance communication within plant tissues. These electrical signals, which encompass action potentials, variation potentials, and system potentials, are triggered by a variety of biotic and abiotic stimuli, including mechanical wounding, changes in light intensity, temperature fluctuations, and pathogen attack. The propagation of PES is thought to orchestrate downstream physiological and biochemical responses such as stomatal regulation, photosynthetic adjustments, and activation of defense pathways. Understanding the causal relationships embedded in plant electrophysiological dynamics is thus essential for elucidating the fundamental principles of plant signaling networks and for enhancing applications in precision agriculture and environmental monitoring.

Despite the growing body of research on PES, a significant challenge remains: the reliable detection of causal interactions within complex plant electrical networks. Unlike in animal electrophysiology, where the spatial and temporal organization of neural circuits is relatively well mapped, plant electrical signaling is less understood, and its dynamics can be strongly nonlinear, time-varying, and influenced by multiple interacting factors. Moreover, PES data are often noisy and of limited duration, making causal inference a non-trivial task. Traditional statistical approaches, such as correlation analysis, can identify associations but fail to distinguish cause from effect, especially in the presence of confounding influences and feedback loops. This limitation hinders the development of robust models for predicting plant responses to environmental changes.

To address these challenges, researchers have turned to causal analysis frameworks, particularly those based on time series data. Granger causality, for instance, has been widely applied in neuroscience and econometrics to detect directional influences between signals by assessing whether past values of one time series improve the prediction of another. However, Granger causality assumes linearity and stationarity, conditions that are rarely met in the context of plant electrophysiology. Extensions to nonlinear Granger causality and transfer entropy have been proposed to capture more complex dependencies, but each approach has its own trade-offs in terms of computational complexity, sensitivity to noise, and interpretability. In addition, the intrinsic variability of plant responses across species, developmental stages, and environmental conditions requires methods that are both flexible and robust.

Recent advances in hybrid causal analysis approaches offer a promising avenue for overcoming these limitations. By integrating complementary techniques—such as combining model-based methods with information-theoretic measures—it is possible to leverage the strengths of each while mitigating their individual weaknesses. For example, a hybrid framework might employ nonlinear state-space reconstruction to model system dynamics, followed by transfer entropy estimation to quantify directed information flow. Such integrative strategies can improve detection accuracy, enhance robustness to noise, and provide richer insights into the temporal structure of causal relationships. Furthermore, hybrid methods can be tailored to incorporate domain-specific knowledge about plant physiology, such as known conduction velocities or the spatial arrangement of vascular tissues, thereby improving biological interpretability.

In the context of plant electrical signaling, a hybrid causal analysis approach could enable researchers to disentangle the complex web of interactions between different parts of the plant and between the plant and its environment. This capability has practical implications for developing biosensors that monitor plant health in real time, optimizing irrigation and fertilization strategies based on plant feedback, and advancing our understanding of how plants integrate multiple signals to coordinate growth and defense. By providing a more nuanced picture of causality in PES, hybrid methodologies can bridge the gap between raw electrophysiological data and actionable biological insights.

This study aims to develop and apply a hybrid causal analysis framework for detecting causality in plant electrical signals. We focus on integrating complementary analytical tools to address the nonlinear, nonstationary, and noisy nature of PES data. Through experimental validation and comparative evaluation against existing methods, we seek to demonstrate the enhanced accuracy, robustness, and biological relevance of this approach. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the methodological toolkit available for plant signal analysis and to deepen our understanding of plant information processing in dynamic environments.
conclusion:
This study proposed and evaluated a hybrid causal analysis approach for detecting causality in plant electrical signals, integrating both model-based and data-driven methodologies to enhance robustness and sensitivity. By combining Granger causality with transfer entropy, the method leverages the strengths of linear parametric inference and non-linear, model-free detection, enabling it to capture a broader spectrum of causal interactions inherent in plant electrophysiological dynamics. Experimental results demonstrated that the hybrid approach outperformed individual methods in identifying directional information flow under varying environmental stimuli, reducing false positives while maintaining high detection accuracy. This suggests that complex plant signaling processes, which often exhibit both linear and nonlinear dependencies, benefit from multi-perspective causal analysis.

The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of plant signal transduction mechanisms, offering a framework that can be extended to other bioelectrical systems. Importantly, the approach accommodates the inherent variability and noise in plant electrical recordings, making it suitable for real-world experimental conditions. Future research could explore adaptive weighting between the constituent methods, as well as real-time implementation for continuous monitoring of plant responses to environmental changes. Additionally, integrating physiological context and multimodal sensing may further improve interpretability and biological relevance. Overall, this work demonstrates that hybrid causal analysis offers a powerful and versatile tool for advancing plant electrophysiology, paving the way for novel applications in precision agriculture, plant health monitoring, and the broader field of plant neurobiology.

title: The pear-shaped fate of an ice melting front
abstract: We investigate the evolution of a melting front in ice subjected to localized heating, revealing a robust tendency toward pear-shaped geometries. Using a combination of controlled laboratory experiments and numerical simulations based on phase-change heat transfer, we track interface dynamics from initial perturbations to fully developed shapes. The results demonstrate that asymmetric heat fluxes, amplified by curvature-dependent melting rates, drive a spontaneous elongation along the heat source axis. This morphological instability emerges even under nominally symmetric conditions, suggesting that small imperfections seed persistent anisotropy. Quantitative comparison between experimental profiles and model predictions shows strong agreement, with shape metrics converging to a characteristic aspect ratio. Our findings provide insight into natural and industrial melting processes, where pear-shaped fronts may influence transport, mixing, and structural integrity. The study highlights the interplay of geometry, thermodynamics, and instability in phase-transition interfaces.
introduction:
Phase change phenomena involving the melting of ice in contact with a warmer fluid are of central importance in both natural environments and engineered systems. The dynamics of melting fronts govern the evolution of sea ice in polar oceans, the retreat of glaciers, the stability of permafrost, and the performance of thermal energy storage units relying on solid–liquid phase change materials. In each of these contexts, the interplay between heat transfer, fluid flow, and interface motion produces a rich variety of geometries and temporal behaviours. Understanding the shape evolution of melting interfaces is therefore essential for predicting system performance, assessing environmental change, and designing efficient thermal processes.

When ice is immersed in a liquid at a temperature above the melting point, heat is conducted across the solid–liquid boundary and, simultaneously, convected by the motion of the surrounding fluid. For quiescent fluids, melting fronts tend to maintain symmetry dictated by the initial geometry, with deformation arising primarily from non-uniform thermal conduction. However, in the presence of buoyancy-driven or externally forced flows, the heat flux becomes strongly non-uniform along the interface. This non-uniformity can lead to accelerated melting in some regions and retardation in others, producing complex shapes that deviate significantly from the initial configuration. The emergence of pear-shaped melting fronts is a striking example of such morphology, often observed when ice bodies are exposed to upward buoyant flows or asymmetric shear.

Pear-shaped geometries have been reported in laboratory experiments in which initially spherical or cylindrical ice samples melt in water under the influence of natural convection. The shape asymmetry typically manifests as a gradual tapering toward one end of the specimen, accompanied by a bulging or widening in the opposite direction. This morphological transition arises from the coupling between the evolving geometry and the surrounding flow field: as the ice melts, density differences in the fluid generate convective currents, which in turn alter the local heat transfer rates and reinforce the asymmetric melting. Such feedback mechanisms are of particular interest because they can lead to self-sustaining shape evolution, even in the absence of externally imposed flow.

Despite a number of experimental observations and computational studies, the precise mechanisms controlling the onset and persistence of pear-shaped melting fronts remain incompletely understood. Many existing models assume simplified geometries, neglect variations in curvature, or treat the interface motion quasi-statically. While such approaches can capture the gross melting rate, they often fail to predict the detailed shape evolution observed in practice. A more complete description requires coupling the transient heat equation in both phases with the Navier–Stokes equations for the fluid, subject to appropriate interface conditions for temperature, heat flux, and mass conservation.

The motivation for the present work is to investigate the formation and development of pear-shaped interfaces during the melting of ice in a convecting fluid. By combining controlled experiments with high-resolution numerical simulations, we aim to examine how buoyancy-driven flow structures interact with the evolving solid–liquid boundary and to identify the governing dimensionless parameters that dictate the morphological transition. In doing so, we seek to bridge the gap between idealised theoretical treatments and the complex behaviours observed in real systems, thereby contributing to a more general understanding of phase change phenomena in convective environments.
conclusion: The present study has examined the evolution of an ice–water interface under asymmetric thermal forcing, revealing a characteristic pear-shaped melting front. High-resolution measurements and numerical simulations consistently demonstrated that the curvature of the interface is governed by the interplay between heat conduction through the melt layer and convective transport in the surrounding fluid. The observed shape emerges from a subtle balance between lateral and axial heat fluxes, with geometric amplification of melting rates near the tip region. Our analysis suggests that even small departures from uniform heating can lead to pronounced morphological asymmetries, which persist throughout the melting process. These findings not only clarify the physical mechanisms underpinning the pear-shaped front, but also provide a quantitative framework for predicting interface evolution under a range of boundary conditions. Such insights have potential relevance for cryospheric processes, phase-change material design, and controlled melting in manufacturing contexts. Future work could extend this approach to three-dimensional geometries, transient heat sources, and the coupling between melting and fluid instabilities, thereby deepening understanding of the complex, nonlinear dynamics that shape melting fronts in natural and engineered systems.

title: Electron doping evolution of the neutron spin resonance in NaFe$_{1-x}$Co$_{x}$As
abstract: We report a systematic inelastic neutron scattering study of the evolution of the neutron spin resonance in NaFe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$As across a wide range of electron doping. In the underdoped regime, where superconductivity coexists with static antiferromagnetic order, we observe a sharp resonance mode whose energy increases gradually with Co substitution. Near optimal doping, the resonance becomes more intense and shifts to higher energy, tracking the superconducting transition temperature. In the overdoped region, where static magnetism is absent, the resonance broadens in energy and momentum, accompanied by a reduction in spectral weight. Our results reveal that the resonance energy does not scale simply with the superconducting gap, but is strongly influenced by changes in the low-energy spin excitation spectrum and Fermi surface topology induced by electron doping. These findings demonstrate a continuous evolution of the spin resonance across the phase diagram of NaFe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$As, highlighting the intimate connection between spin dynamics and superconductivity in iron-based superconductors.
introduction:
The interplay between magnetism and superconductivity in unconventional superconductors has been a central topic in condensed matter physics over the past decades. In the iron-based superconductors, parent compounds typically exhibit long-range antiferromagnetic (AF) order, which is suppressed upon carrier doping or application of pressure, giving rise to superconductivity. This proximity between antiferromagnetism and superconductivity has led to the proposal that spin fluctuations may play an important role in the formation of Cooper pairs. A key experimental signature of such a connection is the neutron spin resonance—a collective magnetic excitation that appears below the superconducting transition temperature \(T_c\) at the antiferromagnetic wave vector. The resonance mode has been observed in various families of unconventional superconductors, including the copper oxides, heavy fermion systems, and iron pnictides, and is often interpreted as a spin exciton arising from sign-reversing superconducting gap symmetry.

In the iron pnictides, the resonance has been extensively studied in the so-called 122 family, such as BaFe\(_{2-x}\)Co\(_x\)As\(_2\), where systematic doping-dependent neutron scattering measurements have revealed that the resonance energy scales approximately with \(T_c\) and is sensitive to the evolution of the superconducting gap structure with doping. In contrast, the 111 family, exemplified by NaFeAs and its electron-doped derivatives NaFe\(_{1-x}\)Co\(_x\)As, has received comparatively less attention. NaFeAs exhibits a lower Néel temperature and a smaller ordered moment compared to the 122 compounds, and its superconductivity emerges upon modest electron doping through Co substitution at the Fe site. These features provide an opportunity to explore the evolution of spin excitations in a regime where magnetism is relatively weak and more easily perturbed by doping.

Recent inelastic neutron scattering studies have confirmed the presence of a neutron spin resonance in optimally doped NaFe\(_{1-x}\)Co\(_x\)As, with an energy below twice the superconducting gap magnitude, consistent with the spin exciton scenario. However, a comprehensive understanding of how the resonance evolves across the superconducting dome, from underdoped compositions with coexisting AF order to overdoped compositions where superconductivity is weakened, remains incomplete. In particular, it is of interest to determine whether the resonance in NaFe\(_{1-x}\)Co\(_x\)As exhibits similar doping dependencies to those observed in the 122 family, and how its energy, linewidth, and spectral weight correlate with changes in \(T_c\), the superconducting gap, and the normal-state spin fluctuations.

From a theoretical perspective, the doping evolution of the resonance is sensitive to changes in the Fermi surface nesting conditions, the magnitude and anisotropy of the superconducting gaps on different bands, and the degree of quasiparticle damping. In electron-doped iron pnictides, Co substitution reduces the size of the hole pockets and enlarges the electron pockets, thereby weakening nesting and modifying the interband scattering processes that are thought to generate the resonance. Additionally, impurity scattering introduced by Co dopants can broaden the resonance and shift its energy. Therefore, systematic neutron scattering measurements across a wide doping range can provide valuable constraints on microscopic pairing theories and on the interplay between electronic structure, magnetism, and superconductivity.

In this work, we present a detailed inelastic neutron scattering investigation of NaFe\(_{1-x}\)Co\(_x\)As single crystals with electron doping spanning from the underdoped AF-superconducting coexistence regime through optimal doping to the overdoped side of the phase diagram. We track the evolution of the neutron spin resonance mode and its relationship to changes in \(T_c\) and low-energy spin dynamics, thereby offering new insights into the nature of magnetism and its connection to superconductivity in the 111 family of iron-based superconductors.
conclusion:
In summary, we have systematically investigated the evolution of the neutron spin resonance in NaFe$_{1-x}$Co$_{x}$As single crystals as a function of electron doping across the underdoped, optimally doped, and overdoped superconducting regimes. By combining inelastic neutron scattering measurements with careful characterisation of the superconducting and magnetic properties, we have elucidated how the energy, spectral weight, and momentum structure of the resonance evolve in parallel with the suppression of antiferromagnetic order and the modification of the superconducting gap structure.

Our results demonstrate that in the underdoped regime, where long-range antiferromagnetic order coexists microscopically with superconductivity, the resonance appears as a relatively sharp mode at an energy well below twice the superconducting gap, consistent with a spin exciton arising from sign-reversed quasiparticle scattering between hole and electron Fermi surface pockets. The resonance in this regime is accompanied by residual low-energy spin-wave–like excitations associated with the static magnetic order, and its intensity is enhanced below $T_c$ without a significant shift in energy. This behaviour suggests that the resonance is strongly influenced by the reconstructed Fermi surface and the interplay between magnetism and superconductivity.

At optimal doping, where static antiferromagnetic order is fully suppressed and $T_c$ reaches its maximum, the resonance sharpens further in both energy and momentum space, and its spectral weight is maximised. The resonance energy scales approximately with $T_c$ in a manner similar to that observed in other iron-based superconductors, reinforcing the universality of the spin resonance as a signature of unconventional superconductivity with a sign-changing order parameter. The momentum profile at optimal doping reflects the nesting geometry between the hole and electron pockets, and the temperature dependence of the mode is consistent with the opening of the superconducting gap.

Upon further electron doping into the overdoped regime, we observe a marked reduction in the resonance intensity and a broadening of the mode in energy, accompanied by a shift of the peak to higher energies relative to $T_c$.
