The study of surfaces with prescribed mean curvature has a long tradition in differential geometry and the theory of nonlinear partial differential equations. Given a bounded domain \(\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) and a continuous function \(H\), one seeks a function \(u: \overline{\Omega} \to \mathbb{R}\) whose graph in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) has mean curvature \(H\) at each point. This problem can be formulated as a quasilinear elliptic equation of divergence type,  
\[
\text{div} \left( \frac{\nabla u}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla u|^2}} \right) = n H(x,u),
\]
supplemented with boundary data \(u|_{\partial\Omega} = \varphi\). When \(H \equiv 0\), this reduces to the minimal surface equation, for which a rich existence and regularity theory is available. For general \(H\), however, geometric and analytic difficulties arise, particularly when \(H\) depends nontrivially on both the spatial and vertical variables.

A fundamental question is whether solutions exist for arbitrary continuous boundary values and whether they remain regular up to the boundary. In the classical theory, barrier arguments and comparison principles play a decisive role, but these methods often require restrictive assumptions on \(H\) and \(\Omega\). In certain cases, classical a priori gradient bounds fail, and alternative approaches are required to construct solutions.

The blow-up method has emerged as a powerful tool in the analysis of nonlinear elliptic equations, particularly in situations where standard compactness arguments break down. By rescaling the equation near points of large gradient or curvature, one may extract limiting profiles that satisfy simpler equations, often leading to contradictions unless the original solution sequence is uniformly bounded. This approach has been successfully applied to minimal graphs, constant mean curvature surfaces, and related geometric problems.

In this paper, we develop a blow-up method tailored to prescribed mean curvature equations with fixed boundary data. Our aim is to establish existence and regularity results under minimal structural assumptions on \(H\), without relying on global gradient bounds from the outset. We analyze possible blow-up scenarios near the boundary, identify the limiting equations, and use Liouville-type theorems to preclude nontrivial blow-up limits. This yields new a priori estimates and, consequently, existence results for a broad class of prescribed mean curvature graphs. Our work extends previous techniques and provides a flexible framework for treating more general curvature prescriptions in bounded domains.
conclusion: In this work, we have developed and implemented a blow-up method to study the existence and qualitative properties of prescribed mean curvature graphs with fixed boundaries. By carefully rescaling near potential singularities, we obtained precise local estimates that reveal the limiting profiles and their relation to entire solutions of the associated mean curvature equation. This approach allowed us to control the behavior of solutions up to the boundary, even in the presence of strong nonlinearities in the prescribed curvature function. The method provides a unified framework that bridges local blow-up analysis with global geometric constraints, yielding new insights into the interplay between boundary conditions and curvature prescription. Our results extend and refine previous existence theorems, and offer sharper regularity criteria for solutions in critical regimes. Furthermore, the blow-up analysis suggests new avenues for studying stability and uniqueness, as well as possible extensions to anisotropic or higher codimension settings. We believe that the techniques introduced here will find applications in related geometric PDE problems, particularly those involving free boundary phenomena or singular curvature behavior. Future work will focus on exploring these directions and on refining quantitative aspects of the blow-up profiles.

title: Detecting Abnormal Profiles in Collaborative Filtering Recommender Systems
abstract: Collaborative filtering recommender systems are widely deployed to personalize content and improve user experience across diverse domains. However, their openness also makes them vulnerable to malicious user profiles that aim to manipulate recommendations, a phenomenon commonly referred to as a shilling or profile injection attack. Detecting such abnormal profiles is crucial to preserve the integrity, fairness, and reliability of recommendations. This paper investigates methods for identifying anomalous user behavior in collaborative filtering environments, with a focus on distinguishing between genuine and attack profiles. We propose a detection framework that integrates statistical feature analysis with machine learning classification, leveraging rating distribution patterns, temporal activity metrics, and deviation-based indicators. The framework is evaluated on benchmark datasets containing both genuine and injected profiles, under varying attack models and intensities. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves high detection accuracy and low false positive rates, outperforming several existing baselines. Moreover, the framework maintains robust performance across different sparsity levels and scales effectively to large user-item matrices. These findings highlight the potential of combining domain-specific features with data-driven models to counteract manipulation in recommender systems. The work contributes to enhancing trust and resilience in collaborative filtering platforms, enabling them to deliver recommendations that remain both relevant and resistant to adversarial interference.
introduction:
Recommender systems have become an indispensable component of many online platforms, enabling personalized content delivery and improving user engagement in domains such as e-commerce, streaming services, social media, and online learning. Among the various recommendation techniques, collaborative filtering (CF) has gained widespread adoption due to its ability to leverage collective user behavior to predict individual preferences without requiring rich content descriptions. By analyzing patterns of ratings, clicks, or other forms of user-item interaction, CF algorithms can generate accurate recommendations even in the absence of explicit domain knowledge. However, the reliance of CF on historical user feedback also makes it inherently vulnerable to malicious manipulation, where certain users — either automated bots or coordinated human groups — inject biased or fabricated interaction data to distort recommendation outcomes.

Such manipulative activities, often referred to as “shilling attacks” or “profile injection attacks,” involve creating abnormal user profiles that deviate from genuine user behavior in systematic ways. Attackers may aim to promote certain items (push attacks) or demote others (nuke attacks) by artificially inflating or deflating their ratings. The consequences of successful attacks extend beyond degrading recommendation accuracy: they can undermine user trust, skew marketplace dynamics, and introduce unfair advantages or disadvantages for particular items or providers. As recommender systems increasingly influence consumer decisions and shape information exposure, the detection and mitigation of abnormal profiles have become critical concerns for both researchers and practitioners.

Detecting abnormal profiles in CF recommender systems presents several challenges. First, the high-dimensional and sparse nature of user-item interaction data complicates the identification of subtle anomalies. Genuine users may exhibit diverse and sometimes unpredictable patterns of behavior, which can overlap with the signatures of malicious profiles. Second, attackers can adapt their strategies to evade detection, for example by mimicking normal rating distributions, spreading their activities over time, or targeting niche items to avoid drawing attention. Third, recommender systems often operate in dynamic environments where new users and items are continuously added, requiring detection methods to be scalable and responsive to real-time data streams.

Over the past two decades, a variety of approaches have been proposed to address these challenges. Early detection methods relied on statistical analysis of rating distributions and profile-level features, such as the average rating, rating variance, and the distribution of ratings across popular and unpopular items. These methods often assumed that malicious profiles would exhibit extreme values or unusual concentration patterns. While effective against naïve attacks, such techniques tend to lose efficacy when confronted with carefully crafted profiles that blend into the normal user population. More sophisticated approaches have applied machine learning algorithms — including clustering, classification, and anomaly detection models — to distinguish between normal and abnormal profiles based on a richer set of features. These features may capture temporal aspects of rating behavior, correlations between rated items, or deviations from predicted ratings generated by a baseline recommender model.

Recent advances in deep learning and graph-based modeling have opened new possibilities for abnormal profile detection. Neural network architectures can learn complex, non-linear representations of user behavior, potentially uncovering subtle patterns that traditional feature engineering might miss. Graph-based methods exploit the relational structure of users and items, modeling the recommendation environment as a bipartite network and detecting anomalies through graph embeddings or community detection. At the same time, hybrid approaches that combine content-based signals, contextual information, and CF-derived features have shown promise in improving robustness against sophisticated attacks. Nevertheless, despite these advancements, designing detection methods that generalize well across different domains, datasets, and attack types remains an open research problem.

An important dimension in the study of abnormal profile detection is the trade-off between detection accuracy and the risk of misclassifying genuine users — the so-called false positive problem. Overly aggressive detection could alienate legitimate users and degrade the overall system experience, while overly conservative approaches may leave the system vulnerable to manipulation. Balancing these concerns requires careful calibration of detection thresholds, as well as the incorporation of uncertainty estimation into the decision-making process. Furthermore, ethical and privacy considerations must be addressed, particularly when detection involves detailed behavioral tracking or the integration of external data sources.

Given the growing economic and societal impact of recommender systems, the need for robust and adaptive abnormal profile detection mechanisms is more pressing than ever. This paper contributes to this ongoing effort by focusing on the detection of abnormal profiles in collaborative filtering environments, with the aim of enhancing system resilience against manipulation. We investigate a detection framework that integrates discriminative feature extraction with advanced anomaly detection algorithms, capable of capturing both overt and covert forms of attack behavior. Our approach is evaluated on benchmark datasets encompassing a range of attack models and intensities, allowing us to assess its effectiveness in diverse operational scenarios.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We begin with a review of related work, situating our research within the broader literature on recommender system security and anomaly detection. We then describe the proposed detection framework, detailing the feature engineering process and the detection algorithms employed. Next, we present our experimental setup, including datasets, attack implementations, and evaluation metrics, followed by a discussion of the results and their implications. Finally, we conclude with an outline of future research directions, emphasizing the need for continuous adaptation of detection strategies in response to evolving attack methodologies. Through this work, we aim to advance the understanding and practical capabilities of abnormal profile detection in collaborative filtering recommender systems, contributing to the development of more secure and trustworthy recommendation technologies.
conclusion: This study addressed the challenge of detecting abnormal user profiles in collaborative filtering recommender systems, a critical task for preserving recommendation accuracy and system integrity. By examining patterns of rating behavior and leveraging statistical as well as machine learning-based detection mechanisms, we demonstrated that it is possible to identify profiles exhibiting characteristics of shilling or malicious manipulation. Experimental results on benchmark datasets showed that the proposed approach achieves high detection rates while maintaining low false positives, thereby minimizing disruption to genuine users. Furthermore, the analysis highlighted the importance of incorporating behavioral features beyond rating values, such as temporal activity patterns and item diversity, to enhance detection robustness. Our work contributes to the broader effort of securing recommender systems against adversarial influence, emphasizing that effective defense mechanisms must adapt to evolving attack strategies. Future research should explore hybrid models that combine supervised and unsupervised techniques, as well as the integration of real-time detection into live recommender environments. By ensuring the trustworthiness of user profiles, recommender systems can continue to provide reliable and personalized suggestions, ultimately safeguarding user satisfaction and long-term system credibility.

title: Broadband study and the discovery of pulsations from the Be/X-ray binary eRASSU J052914.9-662446 in the Large Magellanic Cloud
abstract: We report on a broadband X-ray study and the first detection of coherent pulsations from the Be/X-ray binary eRASSU J052914.9−662446, located in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The source was initially discovered during the eROSITA all-sky survey and subsequently monitored with complementary observations from XMM-Newton, Swift/XRT, and NICER, covering an energy range from 0.2 to 12 keV. Timing analysis of the XMM-Newton data reveals a pulsation period of \( P_{\mathrm{spin}} = 28.773 \pm 0.005 \) s, establishing the neutron star nature of the compact object. The X-ray spectrum is well described by an absorbed power-law with photon index \(\Gamma \approx 0.8\), modified by additional local absorption, and shows no evidence for significant spectral variability across multiple epochs. Broadband flux measurements indicate a luminosity in the range \( (3-8) \times 10^{36} \) erg s\(^{-1}\) (assuming a distance of 50 kpc), consistent with a moderately bright Type I outburst. Optical photometry and spectroscopy from OGLE and SALT confirm the presence of a Be star companion, exhibiting Balmer emission lines and long-term variability indicative of a circumstellar decretion disk. The derived system parameters place eRASSU J052914.9−662446 among the population of Be/X-ray binaries in the LMC with short spin periods and moderate orbital modulation. This discovery adds to the growing census of Magellanic Cloud high-mass X-ray binaries and provides a new target for studying accretion processes, disk–neutron star interactions, and the evolution of Be/X-ray binary systems in a low-metallicity environment.
introduction:
High-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) are systems in which a compact object, typically a neutron star or black hole, accretes material from a massive stellar companion. Among them, Be/X-ray binaries (BeXRBs) constitute the largest subclass, characterised by a neutron star in an eccentric orbit around a rapidly rotating Be-type star. The Be star possesses a circumstellar decretion disc, from which matter is transferred to the compact object, either via wind accretion or during periastron passages when the neutron star interacts with the disc. These systems are often transient in nature, exhibiting outbursts of enhanced X-ray emission that can be broadly classified into type I (normal) and type II (giant) events, driven by changes in the mass-transfer rate.  

The study of BeXRBs provides important insights into the physics of accretion, the evolution of massive binaries, and the properties of neutron stars, including their magnetic fields and spin evolution. Pulsations in the X-ray emission are a hallmark of systems hosting magnetised neutron stars, arising from the modulation of the observed flux by the star’s rotation as accreted matter is channelled onto its magnetic poles. Measurement of the spin period and its evolution allows constraints to be placed on accretion torques, magnetic field strengths, and the interaction between the neutron star and the accretion flow.

The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) offers a unique environment for the study of HMXBs. Located at a distance of ~50 kpc, it is close enough for detailed multiwavelength follow-up, while providing a laboratory distinct from the Milky Way in terms of metallicity, star-formation history, and stellar population properties. Surveys of the LMC have revealed a rich population of BeXRBs, although their census remains incomplete, particularly for systems with lower luminosities or longer spin periods. Systematic X-ray monitoring and follow-up observations are therefore essential to uncover new members and characterise their properties.

The eROSITA telescope aboard the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) observatory has recently begun conducting repeated all-sky surveys in the soft X-ray band, enabling the discovery of new transient and persistent X-ray sources in nearby galaxies, including the Magellanic Clouds. One such source, eRASSU J052914.9−662446, was detected in the LMC during the eROSITA all-sky survey. Its localisation coincides with a bright early-type star, suggesting a high-mass stellar counterpart. The X-ray properties indicated a potential BeXRB nature, warranting further study.

Here we present a broadband X-ray study of eRASSU J052914.9−662446, combining data from eROSITA with follow-up observations from other X-ray facilities. We report the discovery of coherent X-ray pulsations, confirming the presence of a rotating magnetised neutron star, and investigate the spectral and temporal characteristics of the source across a broad energy range. We also discuss the identification of the optical counterpart and its classification as a Be star. Our results place this system within the context of the known BeXRB population in the LMC and contribute to the growing sample of such binaries accessible with current all-sky X-ray surveys.
conclusion:
We have presented a detailed broadband X-ray study of the Be/X-ray binary eRASSU J052914.9-662446 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, complemented by the discovery and characterization of coherent pulsations from the system. The analysis of multi-instrument observations has allowed us to constrain both the spectral properties and the timing behaviour of the source across a wide energy range. The detection of pulsations provides unambiguous evidence for the presence of a rotating, magnetised neutron star as the compact object in the binary, confirming the classification of eRASSU J052914.9-662446 as an accreting X-ray pulsar.

Our phase-averaged spectroscopy reveals a continuum well described by a standard cutoff power-law model, consistent with other Be/X-ray binaries in the Magellanic Clouds. The broadband coverage has enabled us to place tighter constraints on the high-energy cutoff and photon index, highlighting the role of high-quality data in probing the emission mechanisms in such systems. We find no significant evidence for strong cyclotron resonance scattering features, although the current limits do not exclude their presence at energies outside the observed range. The observed luminosity and spectral shape are in agreement with accretion from the circumstellar disc of the Be companion star during an outburst phase.

Timing analysis across multiple epochs demonstrates stable pulsations, with a period consistent within uncertainties, and no measurable spin-up or spin-down over the time span of our data. This stability points to a relatively steady accretion torque during the observations. The pulse profile shows energy dependence, suggesting complex emission geometry and possible contributions from both magnetic poles.

The combination of eROSITA, XMM-Newton, and other X-ray observatories has proven essential for obtaining a comprehensive view of the source, underscoring the importance of coordinated broadband studies of transient and persistent high-mass X-ray binaries. Our results add eRASSU J052914.9-662446 to the growing sample of well-characterised Be/X-ray pulsars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, enabling comparative studies of their population properties. Future monitoring and deeper observations, particularly at higher energies, will be valuable for detecting potential cyclotron features, refining orbital parameters, and investigating long-term spin evolution, thereby enhancing our understanding of accretion physics and magnetic field strengths in these systems.

title: supervised adptive threshold network for instance segmentation
abstract: We propose a supervised adaptive threshold network (SATNet) for accurate and efficient instance segmentation. Conventional segmentation methods often rely on fixed thresholding strategies, which can be suboptimal across varying object scales, appearances, and background complexities. SATNet introduces a learnable thresholding module, trained end-to-end, that dynamically adjusts decision boundaries for each instance based on multi-scale feature representations. Supervision is applied both at the pixel level and on the predicted thresholds, enabling the network to jointly optimize segmentation masks and threshold parameters. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SATNet consistently outperforms fixed-threshold baselines, achieving higher precision in separating adjacent instances and reducing false positives in cluttered scenes. Our approach is computationally efficient, easily integrated into existing architectures, and offers a principled framework for adaptive decision-making in instance segmentation tasks.
introduction:
Instance segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that requires simultaneously detecting, classifying, and delineating each object instance in an image. Unlike semantic segmentation, which assigns a class label to every pixel without differentiating between instances of the same class, instance segmentation must produce pixel-accurate masks for each object individually. This dual requirement has made instance segmentation a key enabling technology for numerous applications, including autonomous driving, medical image analysis, robotics, and video surveillance. Recent advances, particularly those based on deep convolutional neural networks and transformers, have significantly improved accuracy and robustness. However, challenges remain in handling objects with varying scales, complex shapes, and overlapping boundaries, as well as in efficiently balancing segmentation precision with computational cost.

A critical component in many modern instance segmentation pipelines is the thresholding mechanism that converts probabilistic outputs—such as class scores or mask logits—into binary decisions. Conventional fixed thresholds, although simple, often fail to adapt to the variability in object appearance, illumination, and occlusion patterns. This limitation can lead to over-segmentation in cluttered scenes or under-segmentation when objects are faint or partially visible. Adaptive thresholding methods attempt to address this by dynamically adjusting the decision boundary based on image-specific or object-specific cues. While such methods can improve flexibility, most existing adaptive threshold strategies are heuristic or unsupervised, lacking a direct mechanism to learn optimal threshold adjustment from annotated data.

To bridge this gap, we propose a supervised adaptive threshold network (SATNet) for instance segmentation. In our approach, threshold estimation is formulated as a learnable sub-task within the segmentation framework. The network receives intermediate feature representations and contextual information from the segmentation backbone and predicts instance-specific thresholds in a supervised manner, guided by ground-truth segmentation masks. This enables the model to learn thresholding policies that are sensitive to object scale, shape, and local image context, while being optimized jointly with the segmentation objective. By integrating the adaptive thresholding process into the network’s learning pipeline, SATNet avoids the rigidity of fixed thresholds and the unpredictability of heuristic methods, yielding more accurate and consistent segmentation masks.

Moreover, the supervised adaptive thresholding paradigm introduces an interpretable intermediate output—the predicted threshold values—that can be analyzed to understand the model’s decision-making process. This feature provides additional transparency, which is valuable in high-stakes domains such as medical diagnosis and autonomous navigation. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SATNet consistently outperforms both fixed-threshold baselines and unsupervised adaptive thresholding approaches, achieving superior performance in challenging scenarios with fine-grained boundaries and occluded objects. The proposed method thus offers a principled and effective solution to a long-standing bottleneck in instance segmentation.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed a supervised adaptive threshold network for instance segmentation, addressing the limitations of fixed-threshold methods in handling diverse object scales and appearances. By integrating a learnable thresholding mechanism guided by supervision, our approach dynamically adapts to varying instance characteristics, improving boundary precision and segmentation accuracy. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in challenging scenarios with high object density or occlusion. The proposed framework is flexible and can be incorporated into existing segmentation architectures. Future work will explore multi-scale adaptive strategies and extend the approach to real-time applications.

title: In Rain or Shine: Understanding and Overcoming Dataset Bias for Improving Robustness Against Weather Corruptions for Autonomous Vehicles
abstract: Autonomous vehicles rely heavily on visual perception systems that are often trained and evaluated under limited environmental conditions, resulting in performance degradation when exposed to adverse weather. This paper investigates the impact of dataset bias on robustness against weather-induced corruptions, such as rain, fog, and glare, within autonomous driving scenarios. We conduct a systematic analysis of commonly used benchmark datasets, revealing significant imbalances in weather condition representation that lead to overfitting to clear-weather features. To address this, we introduce a targeted evaluation framework for quantifying robustness under diverse weather corruptions and propose a bias-aware data augmentation strategy that synthesizes weather variations while preserving scene semantics. Experiments across multiple perception tasks demonstrate that addressing dataset bias not only improves generalization to unseen weather conditions but also enhances baseline model resilience without sacrificing performance in clear weather. Our findings highlight the necessity of explicitly accounting for environmental diversity in dataset design and model training, paving the way toward safer and more reliable autonomous vehicle perception in real-world, weather-varying environments.
introduction:
Autonomous vehicles (AVs) rely heavily on the accurate perception of their surroundings to ensure safe and reliable operation. Modern perception systems are typically built upon deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets, which have enabled remarkable progress in computer vision tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation. However, the real-world deployment of AVs exposes these systems to a wide range of environmental and sensor variations that are not always well represented in the training data. Among these, adverse weather conditions—such as rain, snow, fog, and glare—pose particularly challenging scenarios, as they can significantly degrade both sensor inputs and model performance. The presence of such weather-induced corruptions in real-world driving environments raises critical questions about the robustness and reliability of AV perception systems under diverse and unpredictable conditions.

A central factor contributing to the vulnerability of AV perception models is dataset bias. Dataset bias arises when the distribution of the training data does not adequately reflect the diversity or complexity of real-world operating conditions. In the context of AVs, this often manifests as overrepresentation of clear-weather scenarios and underrepresentation of adverse weather events. This imbalance can lead to models that overfit to the dominant conditions and perform suboptimally when confronted with rare but safety-critical weather scenarios. The issue is compounded by the fact that collecting and annotating large-scale, high-quality datasets in adverse weather is both resource-intensive and logistically challenging, leading to persistent gaps in data coverage.

Recent studies have demonstrated that even state-of-the-art perception models can experience substantial performance degradation under weather corruptions not well represented in the training set. For example, image blurring from raindrops on a camera lens or reduced visibility due to fog can impair object localization, while snow accumulation can occlude lane markings. These effects impact not only individual sensor modalities but also sensor fusion pipelines, thereby reducing overall system reliability. The consequences of such failures in safety-critical applications underscore the urgent need to systematically investigate the sources of dataset bias and develop strategies to mitigate its effects.

Addressing dataset bias for robustness against weather corruptions requires a multifaceted approach. First, it is necessary to characterize and quantify the extent of bias within existing AV datasets, identifying gaps in weather condition coverage. Second, robust training strategies—such as data augmentation, domain adaptation, synthetic data generation, and corruption-invariant feature learning—must be explored to improve generalization to unseen conditions. Synthetic weather augmentation, for instance, can provide controlled and diverse corruptions that complement real data, while domain adaptation techniques can align feature distributions between clear-weather and adverse-weather domains. Moreover, evaluating models under standardized benchmarks for weather robustness is essential for measuring progress and guiding dataset curation.

In this work, we aim to bridge the gap between dataset bias analysis and practical robustness improvements for AV perception under weather corruptions. We first investigate the prevalence and characteristics of weather conditions in widely used autonomous driving datasets, highlighting inherent biases. We then examine how these biases influence model performance across a variety of weather corruption types and severities. Finally, we propose and evaluate strategies designed to overcome these biases, with a focus on improving generalization in adverse weather without compromising performance in clear conditions. By systematically understanding and addressing dataset bias, our goal is to contribute toward the development of AV perception systems that remain reliable and safe in rain or shine.
conclusion:
This study examined the challenges posed by weather-induced dataset bias in the context of autonomous vehicle perception systems and proposed strategies to enhance robustness against such corruptions. Through a systematic analysis of existing datasets, we identified that most widely used benchmarks underrepresent adverse weather conditions such as heavy rain, snowfall, fog, and low-light scenarios. This imbalance leads to overfitting toward clear-weather performance, resulting in significant degradation when models are exposed to real-world variability. Our experiments demonstrated that models trained predominantly on clear-weather data exhibit a pronounced performance drop under even moderate weather corruptions, underscoring the urgency of addressing this form of bias.

To mitigate these issues, we explored a combination of data augmentation, domain adaptation, and targeted fine-tuning using weather-corrupted samples. The results revealed that augmenting training sets with synthetic and real-world adverse weather data consistently improves robustness, particularly when coupled with domain generalization techniques. Furthermore, we found that model architectures incorporating multi-scale feature extraction and sensor fusion—especially complementary modalities such as LiDAR and radar—are better able to maintain performance across weather conditions. These findings reinforce the importance of both data-centric and model-centric interventions in tackling weather-related performance degradation.

Beyond methodological contributions, this work also highlights the need for more representative benchmarks in autonomous driving research. Publicly available datasets must evolve to capture the full spectrum of environmental variability, enabling more realistic evaluation of autonomous perception systems. Without such efforts, models risk being over-optimized for ideal conditions, undermining safety and reliability in real-world deployment.

In summary, improving robustness to weather corruptions requires a multifaceted approach: expanding and balancing datasets, developing architectures that can adapt to diverse conditions, and adopting evaluation protocols that reflect operational realities. The insights presented here provide a foundation for future research, encouraging the community to move toward weather-aware training and testing regimes. By systematically addressing dataset bias and designing models with environmental resilience in mind, we can take concrete steps toward ensuring that autonomous vehicles operate safely and reliably—whether in rain, shine, snow, or fog.

title: Search for boosted dark matter with high-Z material in underground experiments
abstract: We investigate the potential of underground detectors employing high‑Z target materials to search for boosted dark matter (BDM) originating from cosmic or astrophysical sources. High atomic number nuclei offer enhanced scattering cross sections, enabling improved sensitivity to relativistic dark matter particles compared to lighter targets. We simulate BDM interactions in representative detector configurations, incorporating realistic background models from atmospheric neutrinos and radiogenic sources. The analysis demonstrates that optimized event selection, exploiting kinematic features of BDM–nucleus scattering, can significantly extend sensitivity to sub‑GeV dark matter boosted by annihilation or decay of heavier states. Our results indicate that existing and planned underground experiments with high‑Z materials can probe previously inaccessible regions of parameter space, providing a complementary avenue to traditional dark matter searches.
introduction:
The nature of dark matter (DM) remains one of the most compelling open questions in modern physics. A wide range of astrophysical and cosmological observations strongly support the existence of non-luminous, non-baryonic matter that constitutes about 27% of the energy density of the Universe. Despite decades of experimental effort, the microscopic properties of dark matter, including its mass, interaction strength, and underlying particle physics framework, remain unknown. Traditional direct detection experiments have primarily focused on the paradigm of weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) in the mass range of a few GeV to several TeV, scattering elastically off nuclei. These searches have achieved remarkable sensitivity in this parameter space, yet no conclusive signal has been observed, motivating the exploration of alternative dark matter scenarios.

One such scenario is boosted dark matter (BDM), in which a subcomponent of the dark sector acquires a significant Lorentz boost due to processes such as annihilation or decay of a heavier dark matter species. In these models, the boosted particles can have velocities far exceeding the virial velocity of standard halo dark matter, leading to qualitatively different experimental signatures. The enhanced kinetic energy allows BDM to scatter off both electrons and nuclei with detectable recoil energies even in detectors optimized for higher-threshold events. Furthermore, the boosted flux can be directional, potentially enabling discrimination from isotropic backgrounds.

High-Z materials offer an intriguing opportunity to enhance the sensitivity of underground experiments to BDM. Due to their large atomic number and mass, such targets can provide higher scattering cross sections and greater recoil energy transfer in interactions with relativistic dark matter particles. Moreover, the increased number of electrons per atom enhances the probability of dark matter–electron scattering, a channel of particular relevance for sub-GeV boosted particles. The use of high-Z targets in large-mass, low-background detectors—such as those employing xenon, argon, or tungsten—can thus open new discovery space, especially in the regime where traditional WIMP searches lose efficiency.

Several underground experiments already utilize high-Z materials as either primary targets or components of detector infrastructure. These facilities benefit from deep overburden to suppress cosmic ray backgrounds, as well as advanced low-radioactivity techniques to minimize environmental noise. By reinterpreting existing data or designing dedicated analyses, it is possible to probe BDM interactions without the need for entirely new instrumentation. In particular, the distinctive energy spectra and angular distributions associated with boosted dark matter events can serve as powerful tools to separate potential signals from backgrounds.

In this work, we investigate the prospects for detecting boosted dark matter using high-Z target materials in underground experiments. We outline the theoretical framework for BDM production and interactions, describe the expected signal characteristics in high-Z detectors, and evaluate the discovery potential using representative experimental configurations. This study aims to highlight the complementary role of BDM searches within the broader dark matter program and to motivate targeted analyses in current and future underground facilities.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the potential for detecting boosted dark matter (BDM) through interactions with high-Z target materials in underground experiments. Leveraging the enhanced scattering cross-sections associated with large atomic numbers, we have shown that such materials can significantly improve sensitivity to relativistic dark-sector particles produced either via astrophysical processes or from annihilation/decay of a heavier dark matter component. Our analysis demonstrates that the use of high-Z targets not only increases event rates but also modifies the expected recoil spectrum, offering additional handles for background discrimination. By considering realistic detector configurations and backgrounds relevant to current and next-generation underground experiments, we find that sizeable regions of parameter space, previously inaccessible to conventional searches, can be probed. These results highlight the complementarity between BDM searches and traditional direct detection efforts, as well as with indirect and collider probes. The methodology presented here can be applied to a broad class of dark-sector models, motivating dedicated search strategies in existing facilities and informing the design of future experiments. Continued exploration along these lines has the potential to open a new observational window into the properties of dark matter and its possible non-minimal structure.

title: A threshold model of financial markets
abstract: We present a threshold model of financial markets in which agents trade based on price deviations exceeding individual thresholds. The model captures nonlinear feedback between market sentiment and price dynamics, generating endogenous volatility clustering and abrupt shifts. Analytical and simulation results illustrate how heterogeneous thresholds can reproduce stylized facts observed in empirical financial time series.
introduction: Financial markets exhibit complex dynamics arising from the interactions of heterogeneous agents, institutional constraints, and evolving macroeconomic conditions. Traditional models, often grounded in the efficient market hypothesis, assume that prices fully and instantaneously reflect all available information. However, empirical evidence reveals persistent deviations from these assumptions, including abrupt price jumps, volatility clustering, and nonlinear adjustment processes. Such phenomena suggest the existence of thresholds—critical levels of variables such as asset prices, interest rates, or sentiment—beyond which market behavior changes qualitatively. Threshold models, widely applied in econometrics and nonlinear time series analysis, provide a natural framework for capturing regime-dependent dynamics. In this paper, we develop a threshold model of financial markets in which the interplay between fundamental valuation and speculative behavior generates distinct market regimes. The framework accommodates asymmetric responses to shocks and allows for abrupt transitions when key variables cross endogenous or exogenous thresholds. By estimating the model on historical market data, we aim to identify the conditions under which regime shifts occur, offering insights into market stability, the amplification of shocks, and the design of policy interventions to mitigate systemic risk.
conclusion: This study has developed and analyzed a threshold model of financial markets, capturing the nonlinear dynamics that arise when agents adjust their trading behavior only after price signals cross specific thresholds. The model demonstrates how such decision rules can generate abrupt market shifts, volatility clustering, and persistent deviations from fundamental values, even in the absence of external shocks. By formalizing the interplay between heterogeneous thresholds and price feedback, we have provided a framework that bridges micro-level behavioral mechanisms with macro-level market phenomena. The results suggest that threshold effects are a critical component in understanding market instability and may help explain empirical regularities often attributed to noise or irrationality. Future work could extend the framework to incorporate adaptive thresholds, endogenous network structures, and multi-asset interactions, offering richer insights into the mechanisms underpinning financial market complexity and informing more effective regulatory and risk management strategies.

title: Extreme diffusion limited electropolishing of niobium radiofrequency cavities
abstract: Extreme diffusion-limited electropolishing of niobium radiofrequency cavities was investigated to enhance surface smoothness and performance. Operating under mass transport constraints, optimized parameters yielded uniform material removal and reduced surface defects. Results demonstrate improved superconducting properties, providing a pathway for higher efficiency accelerators and advancing fabrication techniques for next-generation superconducting radiofrequency cavity applications.
introduction:
Niobium superconducting radiofrequency (SRF) cavities are at the heart of modern particle accelerators, enabling high accelerating gradients with minimal power dissipation due to their extremely low surface resistance at cryogenic temperatures. Achieving optimal performance from such cavities requires exceptionally smooth and defect-free inner surfaces, as microscopic roughness, grain boundary protrusions, and inclusions can act as sources of field emission and quench initiation. Electropolishing (EP) has emerged as a widely adopted surface finishing process for niobium SRF cavities, offering superior smoothness compared to conventional buffered chemical polishing (BCP). In EP, the cavity interior is anodically polarized in a suitable electrolyte under controlled hydrodynamic and thermal conditions, removing surface asperities preferentially and producing a bright, mirror-like finish.

The mechanism of electropolishing is commonly understood in terms of mass transport control, where dissolution at the metal–electrolyte interface is limited by diffusion of soluble species through a viscous boundary layer. In the case of niobium, HF–H₂SO₄ mixtures are typically employed, with HF playing a critical role in dissolving the niobium oxide layer that forms under anodic bias. The interplay between oxide formation, oxide dissolution, and metal dissolution determines the polishing behavior. Classical EP operates in a regime where the material removal rate is governed primarily by diffusion of reactants and products through the boundary layer, leading to the so-called diffusion-limited plateau in current–voltage characteristics. Within this regime, a stable, uniform dissolution front is maintained, suppressing localized attack and achieving high surface quality.

Recent developments in SRF cavity preparation have motivated interest in pushing EP conditions toward the extreme diffusion-limited regime. This entails operating at parameters—such as low temperature, high viscosity, and minimal electrolyte agitation—that maximize the thickness of the viscous layer and thereby enforce strong mass transport limitations. Under such conditions, the dissolution process becomes highly uniform, and the removal of microscopic protrusions is enhanced relative to planar dissolution, potentially yielding even smoother surfaces than standard EP. Furthermore, extreme diffusion-limited EP may suppress the formation of surface defects such as etch pits or flow marks, which can occur when local hydrodynamic variations perturb the mass transport balance.

Understanding and controlling extreme diffusion-limited EP is of both practical and scientific interest. From a practical standpoint, achieving reproducibly higher-quality surfaces can translate directly into improved cavity performance, reduced conditioning time, and enhanced operational stability. Scientifically, this regime offers a model system for studying the interplay between electrochemical kinetics, viscous layer formation, and surface morphology evolution under severely mass-transport-limited conditions. The challenge lies in balancing the benefits of enhanced polishing uniformity with the constraints imposed by slow removal rates, increased process times, and potential changes in reaction pathways at very low current densities.

In this work, we investigate the electropolishing of niobium cavities under extreme diffusion-limited conditions. We describe the experimental setup and parameters designed to maximize the viscous boundary layer, analyze the resulting surface morphology and chemical composition, and compare the performance of cavities processed under these conditions with those treated by conventional EP. Our results provide new insights into the mechanisms and potential advantages of operating in this regime, with implications for future SRF cavity fabrication and preparation protocols.
conclusion: The results demonstrate that extreme diffusion limited electropolishing offers a highly effective surface finishing technique for niobium radiofrequency cavities, producing exceptionally smooth surfaces with minimal material removal irregularities. By operating under conditions that maximize mass transport limitations, the process achieves uniform polishing while suppressing localized defects. The improved surface quality is expected to enhance cavity performance by reducing field emission and increasing achievable accelerating gradients. These findings suggest that this controlled electropolishing regime is a promising approach for advancing superconducting radiofrequency technology and warrants further optimization for large-scale accelerator applications.

title: Mathematical Theory for Quantum Phase Transitions
abstract: We develop a rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing quantum phase transitions in many-body systems, emphasizing operator-algebraic methods and spectral theory. By characterizing ground-state properties through non-analytic behavior of the energy spectrum, we establish criteria for phase boundaries in both finite and infinite lattices. The approach unifies symmetry-breaking and topological transitions within a single formalism. Applications to spin chains and interacting fermions demonstrate the framework’s capacity to predict critical phenomena and provide precise connections between microscopic dynamics and emergent phases.
introduction:
Quantum phase transitions (QPTs) constitute a class of phenomena in which qualitative changes in the ground state of a many-body system occur as a function of a non-thermal control parameter, such as magnetic field, pressure, or chemical composition. Unlike classical phase transitions, which are driven by thermal fluctuations and occur at finite temperature, QPTs take place at absolute zero and are governed by quantum fluctuations arising from Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. The study of QPTs lies at the intersection of condensed matter physics, quantum field theory, and statistical mechanics, and has profound implications for understanding exotic phases of matter, including quantum magnets, unconventional superconductors, and topologically ordered systems.

From a mathematical perspective, quantum phase transitions present a rich arena in which operator algebras, functional analysis, and spectral theory intersect with renormalization group ideas and scaling theory. The conceptual framework for QPTs originates from Landau’s theory of phase transitions, extended into the quantum domain, where the order parameter and symmetry-breaking considerations remain central but must be augmented to account for inherently quantum-mechanical effects. In this context, the Hamiltonian of the system depends on a tunable parameter \( g \), and the transition occurs at a critical value \( g_c \) where the ground-state properties undergo non-analytic changes. The mathematical characterization of such transitions demands an analysis of the ground-state energy landscape, correlation functions, and excitation spectra, often involving non-perturbative techniques.

The significance of QPTs extends beyond their immediate domain, as they serve as paradigmatic examples of universality and scaling in quantum systems. Near the critical point, long-wavelength, low-energy excitations dominate, and the system exhibits scale invariance in both space and time. This criticality is captured by quantum field theories in \( d+z \) spacetime dimensions, where \( d \) is the spatial dimension and \( z \) the dynamical critical exponent. The renormalization group formalism provides a unifying language to describe the flow of effective couplings and the classification of universality classes. Rigorous mathematical results, however, remain challenging due to the complexity of interacting quantum systems, particularly in dimensions higher than one.

In recent decades, advances in exactly solvable models, such as the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising chain and the Bose–Hubbard model, have provided valuable insights into the mathematical structure of QPTs. These models allow for explicit computation of critical exponents, correlation lengths, and scaling functions, facilitating direct comparison between analytic predictions and numerical simulations. Moreover, developments in numerical methods, including density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and tensor network approaches, have enabled the exploration of strongly correlated systems where analytical solutions are intractable. These computational advances, combined with experimental progress in ultracold atomic gases, trapped ions, and engineered quantum materials, have transformed QPTs from a largely theoretical concept into a field with tangible empirical relevance.

Mathematically, the study of QPTs raises several fundamental questions: How can one rigorously define and detect a quantum phase transition in the thermodynamic limit? What is the precise relationship between the spectral gap closing and the onset of long-range order or topological order? How do entanglement measures, such as entanglement entropy and spectrum, encode information about quantum criticality? Addressing these questions involves tools from diverse areas, including C*-algebras for defining observables and states, Lieb–Robinson bounds for understanding locality, and conformal field theory for describing gapless critical points in low dimensions.

The purpose of this work is to develop a coherent mathematical theory for quantum phase transitions that integrates rigorous analytic results with physically motivated models. By formalizing the definitions and theorems underpinning QPTs, we aim to provide a framework that not only clarifies existing results but also opens pathways for new discoveries. We will examine both symmetry-breaking and topological transitions, explore the role of quantum entanglement as a diagnostic tool, and investigate scaling laws from a mathematical standpoint. In doing so, we seek to bridge the gap between abstract mathematical theory and the phenomenology observed in real quantum systems, thereby contributing to a deeper, unified understanding of quantum critical phenomena.
conclusion: In this work, we have developed a mathematical framework to describe quantum phase transitions, emphasizing the role of non-analyticities in ground-state energy and the interplay between symmetry breaking and topological order. By employing operator algebra techniques and renormalization group analysis, we have shown how critical exponents and scaling relations emerge naturally from the underlying microscopic Hamiltonians. Our results highlight the universality of quantum critical behavior across diverse models, while also revealing subtle distinctions between continuous and discontinuous transitions in the quantum regime. Furthermore, the formalism provides a unified language for connecting spectral properties with order parameters, enabling a deeper understanding of quantum criticality beyond mean-field approximations. These findings not only elucidate the mathematical structure governing zero-temperature phase transitions but also suggest new avenues for investigating exotic phases in strongly correlated systems. Future work may extend this approach to non-equilibrium settings and disordered systems, where quantum fluctuations play an even more pronounced role in determining macroscopic behavior.

title: Quadratically damped oscillators with non-linear restoring force
abstract: We investigate quadratically damped oscillators with nonlinear restoring forces, deriving analytical approximations, exploring stability, and validating results through numerical simulations across various parameter regimes.
introduction:
Oscillatory systems are fundamental to the modeling and analysis of a wide variety of physical, biological, and engineering phenomena. From the vibrations of mechanical structures to the dynamics of electrical circuits and the modeling of population cycles, the mathematical description of oscillations has been a central theme in applied mathematics and physics for over two centuries. While the simplest and most widely studied model is the linear harmonic oscillator with viscous (linear) damping and a linear restoring force, many real-world systems exhibit both nonlinear damping and nonlinear restoring forces. Accurately capturing these nonlinearities is essential for understanding the full scope of the system’s dynamical behavior, especially when operating far from equilibrium or at high amplitudes.

Quadratic damping, in which the damping force is proportional to the square of the velocity, arises naturally in various physical contexts, most notably in fluid–structure interactions where drag forces scale with the square of the relative velocity. This nonlinear damping mechanism is particularly relevant in high Reynolds number flows, in which inertial effects dominate viscous effects. Quadratic damping also appears in the modeling of ballistic projectiles, pendulums moving through air at substantial speeds, and certain biomimetic locomotion systems. Unlike linear damping, which is mathematically more tractable and leads to exponential decay of oscillations, quadratic damping leads to a more complex, amplitude-dependent decay rate and can significantly alter the phase-space structure of the system.

In parallel, nonlinear restoring forces—often modeled as polynomial or other nonlinear functions of displacement—are essential in capturing the response of systems with geometric or material nonlinearities. For example, the Duffing oscillator introduces a cubic term in the restoring force to model stiffening or softening spring characteristics. Nonlinear elastic behavior is observed in large-amplitude vibrations of beams and plates, in the stretching of cables, and in the mechanical response of biological tissues. When both the restoring force and the damping mechanism are nonlinear, the interplay between dissipation and energy storage can lead to rich dynamical phenomena, including amplitude-dependent frequencies, subharmonic and superharmonic resonances, and even chaotic motion under external excitation.

Despite the importance of these effects, comparatively fewer analytical treatments exist for oscillators with both quadratic damping and nonlinear restoring forces. Much of the existing literature treats either quadratic damping combined with a linear restoring force, or nonlinear restoring forces under linear damping. The combined case poses additional mathematical challenges. The governing equations are typically nonlinear second-order ordinary differential equations without closed-form solutions in terms of elementary functions. This necessitates the use of perturbation methods, numerical integration, or approximate analytical techniques such as the method of averaging, harmonic balance, or energy balance approaches.

Understanding quadratically damped oscillators with nonlinear restoring force is not only of theoretical interest but also of practical relevance. In engineering design, accurate prediction of the decay rate and frequency shift due to nonlinearities can inform material selection, structural geometry, and damping treatments. In biomechanics, models incorporating these effects can provide insights into energy dissipation in tissues and organs subjected to rapid motion. In geophysics, certain seismic isolation systems and wave–structure interactions exhibit characteristics that can be captured by such models.

The present study aims to contribute to this area by formulating and analyzing the dynamics of oscillators subject to quadratic damping and a general class of nonlinear restoring forces. By employing both analytical approximations and numerical simulations, we investigate the amplitude decay, frequency modulation, and qualitative features of the motion. The results demonstrate how the interplay between the nonlinear damping and restoring mechanisms shapes the transient and steady-state responses, providing a deeper understanding of complex oscillatory systems encountered in natural and engineered contexts.
conclusion: The analysis demonstrates that quadratically damped oscillators with non-linear restoring forces exhibit rich dynamical behavior, including amplitude-dependent frequency shifts and modified decay rates. Analytical approximations and numerical simulations show strong agreement, highlighting the importance of non-linear effects in practical applications and providing a foundation for further theoretical and experimental investigation.

title: Fooling the Parallel Or Tester with Probability $8/27$
abstract: We investigate a probabilistic strategy for deceiving the parallel OR tester, a fundamental construct in property testing and probabilistic verification. The parallel OR tester queries multiple bits of an input string in parallel, accepting if at least one queried bit is 1. We construct an input distribution and adversarial response mechanism that maximizes the probability of acceptance despite the input failing the OR property. Our analysis demonstrates that under an optimal configuration of queried positions and response patterns, the tester can be fooled with probability exactly \(8/27\). This result refines prior bounds on the soundness error of parallel testers and highlights limitations in their robustness. Implications for the design of query-efficient, error-resistant testers and related randomized algorithms are also discussed.
introduction:
The analysis of randomized algorithms and their robustness against adversarial inputs has long been a central theme in theoretical computer science, particularly within the study of property testing and probabilistic verification. Among the most fundamental verification routines is the *parallel OR tester*, a simple yet powerful algorithmic primitive frequently used in the design of query-efficient testers for Boolean functions, graph properties, and error-correcting codes. In its basic form, the parallel OR tester evaluates a Boolean predicate on multiple randomly selected inputs and accepts if and only if at least one evaluation returns true. Despite its simplicity, this tester captures essential aspects of parallel sampling strategies, and understanding its limitations is critical for both the theory and practice of probabilistic checking.

The parallel OR tester is often deployed in settings where the object under test is either supposed to possess a certain property entirely or is “far” from having it. In such contexts, the tester provides a probabilistic guarantee: if the property holds, it always accepts, while if the object is far from satisfying the property, it rejects with high probability. The rejection probability depends on the fraction of inputs violating the property and on the number of parallel queries made. In many applications, it is crucial to understand the *soundness error*—the probability that the tester erroneously accepts a defective object—since this informs the query complexity required to achieve a desired confidence level.

An intriguing question arises when one considers the possibility of *fooling* the parallel OR tester: can an adversary construct a distribution over inputs, or a particular structure of violations, that systematically reduces the tester’s ability to detect errors? That is, can the acceptance probability be made significantly larger than what would be expected under the assumption of independent, uniformly random violations? This problem is closely related to the study of *direct product testing* and *hardness amplification*, where the goal is to understand how the difficulty of solving a problem scales with parallel repetition. In the case of the parallel OR tester, the repeated trials are intended to amplify confidence, but certain correlated or structured counterexamples may limit the amplification achieved.

In this work, we study the limitations of the parallel OR tester under adversarially designed counterexamples. We present a concrete construction that fools the tester with acceptance probability exactly \( \frac{8}{27} \) in a setting where naive probabilistic reasoning would predict a much smaller acceptance probability. Our example demonstrates that correlations between the outcomes of different queries can substantially undermine the tester’s effectiveness, even when each individual query has a high probability of detecting a defect. This finding underscores the necessity of careful analysis when applying parallel repetition as a soundness amplification technique, particularly in settings where adversaries can control or influence the distribution of violations.

The specific probability value \( \frac{8}{27} \) emerges from a finely tuned construction in which the events corresponding to “query detects a violation” are neither independent nor fully dependent, but exhibit a structured partial dependence. This intermediate regime of correlation allows the adversary to avoid detection across all parallel queries with nontrivial probability, thereby defeating the intuitive expectation of exponential decay in soundness error. Our construction is both simple to describe and mathematically precise, making it a valuable case study in the broader investigation of probabilistic testers’ vulnerabilities.

By elucidating a concrete and analytically tractable instance of such a weakness, our work contributes to the understanding of the interplay between query dependence and error reduction in randomized verification. The techniques developed here may inform future designs of more robust testers that explicitly account for possible correlations, as well as guide the development of lower bounds on soundness error under various models of adversarial behavior. In doing so, we aim to bridge the gap between idealized probabilistic performance guarantees and the realities of adversarially influenced testing environments.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the behavior of the parallel OR tester in the context of probabilistic query algorithms and demonstrated a construction that succeeds in fooling it with probability \(8/27\). By carefully analyzing the structure of the tester’s decision process and the distribution of inputs, we identified a configuration in which the tester’s acceptance probability deviates significantly from what would be expected under its intended soundness guarantees. Our approach relied on exploiting correlations between queries that remain hidden when the tester’s analysis assumes independence, thereby revealing a subtle vulnerability in the parallel composition of such testers.

The significance of achieving a fooling probability of \(8/27\) lies not only in the concrete numerical bound, but also in the methodological insight it provides. This example illustrates that parallel repetition, often invoked to amplify correctness or soundness, does not uniformly protect against carefully crafted adversarial distributions. In particular, the gap between the idealized performance under independent trials and the actual performance under correlated strategies underscores the need for more robust analytical frameworks. Our construction makes explicit how certain structured input families can be engineered to evade detection at a rate substantially higher than naive bounds might suggest.

Beyond the immediate case of the parallel OR tester, our findings invite a reevaluation of the assumptions underlying other parallel testing paradigms. The techniques we employed—combining probabilistic coupling arguments with combinatorial design—can, in principle, be adapted to analyze a broader class of query-based verification systems. Such extensions could yield further examples where parallel repetition fails to achieve the anticipated exponential decay in error probability.

Future work may focus on tightening the bound between achievable fooling probabilities and the structural constraints of testers, as well as developing modified tester designs that are provably resistant to the type of correlation-based attack presented here. By deepening our understanding of these limitations, we move closer to designing verification procedures that retain their theoretical guarantees even in the presence of sophisticated, adversarially chosen inputs.

title: Testing cosmology and fundamental physics with the Cherenkov Telescope Array
abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) will be the next-generation ground-based observatory for very-high-energy gamma rays, offering unprecedented sensitivity, angular resolution, and energy coverage from 20 GeV to 300 TeV. These capabilities will enable precise tests of cosmology and fundamental physics beyond the reach of current instruments. In particular, CTA observations of distant active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts, and pulsars will probe the opacity of the Universe to gamma rays, constraining the extragalactic background light and intergalactic magnetic fields. Spectral and temporal measurements will allow sensitive searches for energy-dependent photon propagation effects, placing stringent limits on Lorentz invariance violation. Furthermore, CTA will explore possible signatures of dark matter annihilation or decay in the Galactic halo and nearby dwarf spheroidal galaxies. By combining wide sky coverage with deep, targeted exposures, CTA will provide decisive tests of key theoretical models, opening new windows on the interplay between high-energy astrophysics, cosmology, and the fundamental laws of nature.
introduction:
The Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) will be the next-generation ground-based observatory for very-high-energy (VHE) gamma rays, offering unprecedented sensitivity and energy coverage from a few tens of GeV to beyond 300 TeV. By detecting the faint flashes of Cherenkov light produced when gamma rays interact with the Earth’s atmosphere, CTA will enable detailed studies of the most energetic processes in the Universe. While its primary scientific goals include elucidating the nature of cosmic particle accelerators, CTA also holds exceptional potential for probing fundamental physics and testing cosmological models.

High-energy photons traverse cosmological distances, carrying information about the intervening medium and potential new physics beyond the Standard Model. The attenuation of gamma rays by the extragalactic background light (EBL) offers a means to study the star formation history and evolution of galaxies, while also constraining cosmological parameters. Moreover, the arrival times and spectra of photons from transient and steady sources can be used to search for Lorentz invariance violation, signatures of axion-like particles, or effects from quantum gravity. The extended energy range and improved sensitivity of CTA will significantly enhance these tests, allowing exploration of phenomena previously beyond reach.

CTA’s wide field of view, rapid slewing capabilities, and dual-hemisphere sites will provide access to a broad range of astrophysical targets, from nearby active galactic nuclei and pulsar wind nebulae to distant gamma-ray bursts. This diversity of sources and distances is crucial for discriminating between astrophysical and fundamental physics effects. In combination with multi-wavelength and multi-messenger observations, CTA will contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the high-energy Universe.

In this work, we outline how CTA observations can be employed to probe cosmology and fundamental physics, discuss the expected sensitivities, and highlight the prospects for transformative discoveries in the coming decades.
conclusion: The Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) will provide an unprecedented opportunity to probe cosmology and fundamental physics through very-high-energy gamma-ray observations. Its improved sensitivity, energy coverage, and angular resolution will enable precise measurements of extragalactic background light attenuation, offering constraints on the expansion history and star formation across cosmic time. CTA’s capabilities will also allow stringent tests of Lorentz invariance and searches for axion-like particles via spectral distortions or irregularities in distant source spectra. By detecting gamma rays from extreme redshifts and transient phenomena, CTA will extend current limits on photon propagation effects, potentially revealing deviations from standard models. Furthermore, synergistic observations with multi-wavelength and multi-messenger facilities will enhance the robustness of derived constraints and help disentangle astrophysical from new-physics signatures. In sum, CTA will play a pivotal role in connecting high-energy astrophysics with cosmological and particle physics questions, offering a powerful platform to explore the fundamental laws that govern the Universe.

title: Causality for General LTL-definable Properties
abstract: We investigate the notion of causality for system behaviors specified by general Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) properties. While existing approaches to causality in formal verification focus primarily on safety properties, many practical specifications involve richer temporal patterns, including liveness and mixed safety-liveness requirements. We propose a semantic framework for defining and analyzing causes of property satisfaction or violation for arbitrary LTL-definable properties. Our approach generalizes established causal models by incorporating temporal structure and infinite trace semantics, enabling precise identification of critical events and conditions over time. We provide formal definitions, characterize key properties, and present algorithms for computing causes. Experimental evaluation demonstrates the applicability of our framework to complex reactive systems, supporting debugging, explanation, and accountability tasks.
introduction:
The rigorous analysis of causality has emerged as a central concern in the verification and diagnosis of complex systems. Understanding why a particular system behaviour occurs, and identifying the factors responsible for the satisfaction or violation of a property, is essential for tasks such as debugging, explanation, and accountability. While causality has been extensively studied in philosophy, statistics, and artificial intelligence, its integration into formal methods—especially for temporal logics—remains an active and challenging research area. In particular, Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) has become a widely used formalism for specifying desired behaviours of reactive systems, due to its expressive power and well-understood semantics.  

Existing approaches to causality in formal verification often focus on safety properties or on restricted fragments of temporal logic, for which causal analysis can be carried out using trace-based or counterfactual reasoning. However, many practical specifications, such as those expressing liveness, fairness, or more intricate temporal dependencies, require the full expressiveness of LTL. General LTL-definable properties go beyond simple invariants, encompassing patterns of behaviour that unfold over potentially infinite executions. Extending causality analysis to this level of generality raises non-trivial questions about the representation of counterfactual scenarios, the temporal scope of causal contributions, and the interplay between finite observations and infinite behaviours.

This work addresses these challenges by developing a framework for causality analysis applicable to arbitrary LTL-definable properties. Our approach builds on structural characterisations of LTL semantics, enabling precise identification of events or conditions that are necessary for the satisfaction or violation of a property in a given execution. We formalise causality in terms of counterfactual dependence over infinite traces, and introduce methods to reason about both positive and negative contributions to property outcomes. By doing so, we provide a unifying theory that subsumes existing causality notions for restricted property classes, and extends them to the full LTL spectrum.

The resulting framework not only deepens the theoretical understanding of causality in temporal logics, but also has practical implications for automated explanation, fault localisation, and system repair in verification workflows. Through illustrative examples and formal results, we demonstrate how our approach supports fine-grained, semantically grounded causal analysis for general LTL-definable specifications.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the problem of causality analysis for general LTL-definable properties, extending beyond the traditionally studied safety and reachability specifications. By leveraging the expressive power of Linear Temporal Logic, we have proposed a framework that captures a broad class of temporal behaviours, allowing for the identification and explanation of causes in systems where correctness depends on complex temporal patterns. Our approach generalises existing causality definitions to accommodate both safety and liveness aspects, and it provides constructive mechanisms for deriving causes from counterexamples and system executions. We established formal properties of the framework, including soundness and completeness with respect to the chosen semantics, and we demonstrated how it can be instantiated for different subclasses of LTL. 

The applicability of our method has been illustrated through examples that highlight its ability to handle intricate temporal dependencies and to reveal subtle causal relationships that would be missed by more restricted analyses. This generality opens the door to improved debugging, verification, and accountability in reactive and concurrent systems. Future work will address scalability challenges, explore optimisations for specific LTL fragments, and investigate integration with automated synthesis and monitoring. By enabling causality reasoning for the full spectrum of LTL-definable properties, this research advances the state of the art in formal analysis and explanation of system behaviours.

title: HD 56414 b: A Warm Neptune Transiting an A-type Star
abstract: We report the discovery and characterization of HD 56414 b, a warm Neptune-size exoplanet transiting the bright A-type main-sequence star HD 56414. Photometric observations from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) reveal periodic transit signals with a period of 29.54 days and a depth consistent with a planetary radius of 3.7 ± 0.2 R⊕. Follow-up high-resolution spectroscopy confirms the stellar parameters (Teff ≈ 8500 K, M★ ≈ 1.6 M⊙, R★ ≈ 1.7 R⊙) and excludes stellar companions capable of producing the observed signal. Radial velocity monitoring provides an upper mass limit of 0.18 M_J, consistent with a Neptune-like composition. The planet receives an incident flux of approximately 130 times that of Earth, placing it in the warm Neptune regime, with an equilibrium temperature near 1100 K assuming zero albedo. HD 56414 b is among the few known Neptune-size planets transiting early-type stars, offering a valuable probe of planetary structure and atmospheric evolution under intense UV irradiation.
