N-body simulations directly integrate the trajectories of a large number of collisionless particles, providing a high-fidelity representation of the nonlinear regime, but at the cost of substantial computational resources and with limited analytical transparency. This has motivated the exploration of alternative formulations that can bridge the gap between the simplicity of fluid models and the completeness of N-body methods.

One such approach is the Schrödinger formalism for cosmological fluid dynamics, in which the evolution of a cold, self-gravitating medium is recast in terms of a complex scalar “wavefunction” obeying a Schrödinger equation coupled to Poisson’s equation. Originating in the work of Widrow and Kaiser and others, this representation exploits the Madelung transformation, in which the wavefunction’s amplitude and phase encode the density and velocity potential of the fluid, respectively. In the classical limit, and in the absence of a “quantum pressure” term, the Schrödinger–Poisson system reproduces the equations of motion for a pressureless, irrotational fluid. The quantum pressure term, proportional to the effective Planck constant squared, acts as a regularising mechanism, smoothing the density field below a characteristic scale and thereby preventing the formal singularities that arise at shell crossing.

The Schrödinger formalism offers several conceptual and practical advantages. It provides a phase-space-like description in terms of a single complex field, allowing interference and dispersion phenomena to mimic some aspects of multistream behaviour. The method admits efficient numerical implementations based on spectral techniques and fast Fourier transforms, and naturally incorporates a smoothing scale that can be tuned to balance resolution and regularity. Moreover, the formalism has deep connections with other areas of physics, including Bose–Einstein condensates and wave mechanics, which can be exploited to import analytical tools and intuition.

Recent years have seen renewed interest in wave-mechanical representations of cosmic structure formation, driven in part by the study of ultralight axion or fuzzy dark matter models, in which the Schrödinger–Poisson system arises as a fundamental description rather than an effective one. In the CDM context, however, the Schrödinger approach remains primarily a calculational device, whose efficacy and limitations in modelling nonlinear evolution merit careful assessment. Questions remain regarding the optimal choice of the effective Planck constant, the interpretation of interference patterns in the density field, and the extension of the method to include vorticity, velocity dispersion, or baryonic physics.

In this work we investigate the dynamics of a cosmological fluid within the Schrödinger formalism, focusing on the connection between the wave-mechanical variables and the underlying classical fluid quantities. We examine the behaviour of the system in the quasi-linear and nonlinear regimes, assess the role of the quantum pressure term, and explore the extent to which the formalism can capture phenomena beyond shell crossing. By comparing with analytical fluid solutions and numerical N-body results, we aim to clarify the strengths and shortcomings of this approach, and to identify the circumstances under which it provides an accurate and efficient description of cosmological structure formation. Through this analysis, we seek to advance the understanding of wave-mechanical methods as tools for cosmological dynamics, and to lay the groundwork for their broader application in astrophysical and cosmological modelling.
conclusion: In this work we have explored the description of cosmological fluid dynamics within the Schr\"odinger formalism, highlighting its capacity to recast nonlinear gravitational evolution into a wave-mechanical framework. By mapping the fluid density and velocity fields onto a complex scalar wavefunction, we have shown how the coupled Schr\"odinger–Poisson system encapsulates both continuity and Euler equations while offering advantages for analytical insight and numerical implementation. This approach naturally accommodates multi-streaming phenomena and avoids certain limitations of standard perturbative methods. Our analysis demonstrates that the formalism can recover known solutions in the linear regime and extend smoothly into the nonlinear domain. These results suggest that the Schr\"odinger representation provides a unifying language for studying large-scale structure formation, with potential for further development in relativistic contexts and in connection with quantum-inspired computational techniques.

title: Magic composite pulses
abstract: We introduce the concept of magic composite pulses, designed to enhance control fidelity in quantum systems subject to systematic errors and unwanted couplings. Building upon the theory of composite pulse sequences, we define “magic” conditions under which higher-order error terms are simultaneously suppressed while preserving desired spin dynamics. Analytical derivations, supported by numerical simulations, demonstrate that these sequences achieve robust performance against detuning and amplitude inhomogeneities. The magic composite pulses are constructed to satisfy specific geometrical constraints in the Bloch sphere representation, ensuring minimal cross-talk and improved coherence times in nuclear magnetic resonance and quantum information processing. Our results generalize existing composite pulse families and provide a systematic framework for designing high-fidelity control protocols in noisy environments, with potential applications across quantum sensing, spectroscopy, and scalable quantum computation.
introduction:
Quantum control techniques play a central role in the manipulation of physical systems ranging from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to quantum information processing. In many such contexts, precise control over the state of a quantum system is achieved through the application of sequences of electromagnetic pulses. These pulses are designed to drive specific transitions, implement unitary operations, or refocus unwanted interactions. However, the performance of any pulse sequence is inevitably degraded by experimental imperfections, including inhomogeneities in the control fields, detuning errors, and decoherence. Overcoming these limitations is essential for achieving high-fidelity operations in both fundamental studies and technological applications.

Composite pulses, which consist of a series of rotations with carefully chosen phases and durations, have long been recognized as a powerful strategy to mitigate systematic errors. By distributing a target rotation across multiple segments, composite pulses can be engineered to cancel the effects of certain imperfections to first or even higher orders in perturbation theory. Originally developed in the context of NMR to improve the accuracy of spin manipulations in the presence of radiofrequency field inhomogeneity, the concept has since been extended to a variety of physical settings, including trapped ions, superconducting qubits, and cold atoms. The underlying principle is to exploit interference between different pulse segments so as to render the net operation robust against a specified class of errors.

Within this broad family of techniques, *magic composite pulses* occupy a special place. The term “magic” refers to sequences designed not only to implement a desired rotation robustly, but also to preserve or engineer specific features of the system’s effective Hamiltonian. In solid-state NMR, for example, magic angle spinning and magic echo sequences are used to average out anisotropic interactions, such as dipole–dipole couplings, while retaining desired components of the spin dynamics. By analogy, magic composite pulses can be constructed to suppress unwanted terms in the average Hamiltonian while maintaining or enhancing others, thus enabling selective control over complex many-body interactions.

The design of magic composite pulses draws upon average Hamiltonian theory and symmetry considerations, enabling the systematic cancellation of undesirable terms to a given order in a Magnus expansion. This offers a flexible framework for crafting pulse sequences tailored to specific experimental constraints, such as limited bandwidth, finite pulse durations, or the presence of multiple error sources. The ability to manipulate effective interactions with such precision opens pathways to improved spectroscopy, enhanced decoupling in quantum memories, and the implementation of high-fidelity quantum gates under realistic conditions.

Despite their promise, the systematic exploration and classification of magic composite pulses remains incomplete. Previous studies have addressed particular designs for specialized purposes, but a general methodology for their construction across different platforms is still lacking. In this work, we extend the theoretical foundation of magic composite pulses, presenting new design principles and performance analyses that unify disparate approaches. By combining analytical derivations with numerical simulations, we demonstrate how these sequences can be optimized for robustness and selectivity, paving the way for their broader adoption in quantum control applications.
conclusion:
In this work, we have introduced and analyzed the concept of magic composite pulses, a class of tailored pulse sequences designed to achieve robust control of spin systems while preserving, cancelling, or selectively engineering specific interaction terms in the effective Hamiltonian. Building on the theoretical framework of average Hamiltonian theory and exploiting symmetry properties in both the internal and control Hamiltonians, we have demonstrated that these composite pulses can be systematically constructed to satisfy “magic” conditions of arbitrary order. Such conditions enable the suppression of undesired couplings while maintaining the desired evolution, thereby enhancing the fidelity of quantum operations in the presence of experimental imperfections.

Our analysis confirms that the magic composite pulse approach is versatile, applicable to a range of interaction types, including dipolar and scalar couplings, and is not limited to a specific experimental platform. By deriving explicit sequences and verifying their properties through both analytical calculations and numerical simulations, we have shown that these pulses retain their performance even in the presence of realistic amplitude and phase errors. Furthermore, the geometric interpretation of the magic conditions offers a clear and intuitive means of designing new sequences, complementing the more algebraic methods traditionally used in composite pulse theory.

The results presented here have direct implications for nuclear magnetic resonance, electron spin resonance, and quantum information processing, where precise control over coupled spin dynamics is essential. In particular, the ability to engineer the average Hamiltonian with high selectivity opens avenues for improving coherence times, implementing high-fidelity quantum gates, and performing precise spectroscopic measurements under conditions where conventional pulses would fail. Importantly, the methodology is compatible with existing hardware constraints and can be adapted to finite pulse widths and non-instantaneous control, making it relevant for a wide range of experimental implementations.

Looking forward, the framework developed here can be extended in several directions. One promising avenue is the incorporation of optimal control techniques to automate the search for magic composite pulses with tailored robustness profiles for specific experimental goals. Another is the exploration of higher-order magic conditions to further suppress residual interactions in strongly coupled systems. Finally, experimental validation across different platforms will be crucial to assess the full potential and limitations of this approach in practice.

In conclusion, magic composite pulses represent a powerful and flexible tool for quantum control, offering a systematic route to high-fidelity operations in complex spin systems. By uniting symmetry-based design principles with the rigor of average Hamiltonian theory, they provide a foundation for both fundamental studies and practical applications in coherent spin manipulation.

title: Edit wars in Wikipedia
abstract: This paper examines the phenomenon of edit wars in Wikipedia, where contributors repeatedly override each other’s changes. Drawing on case studies and revision history analysis, it explores the social, technical, and policy factors fueling such conflicts. The study highlights implications for collaborative knowledge production, conflict resolution mechanisms, and community governance, offering insights into sustaining constructive participation in large-scale, open-editing environments.
introduction:
Since its inception in 2001, Wikipedia has become one of the most widely used repositories of collaboratively produced knowledge, hosting millions of articles in multiple languages and attracting contributions from a vast and diverse community of volunteer editors. Its open editing model, which allows virtually anyone to create, modify, or delete content, has been celebrated as a democratization of knowledge production. However, this same openness also gives rise to tensions and disputes among contributors, particularly when editors hold differing interpretations of facts, diverging perspectives on controversial topics, or conflicting editorial priorities. One of the most visible manifestations of these conflicts is the phenomenon known as “edit wars.”

Edit wars occur when two or more editors repeatedly override each other’s contributions to a page, engaging in cycles of reversion rather than reaching consensus through discussion. Such disputes may stem from deep ideological disagreements—such as those surrounding political events, historical narratives, or social issues—or from more procedural concerns, including adherence to Wikipedia’s style guidelines, sourcing policies, and neutrality requirements. While occasional disagreement is a natural aspect of collaborative content creation, edit wars signify a breakdown in the intended consensus-building processes that Wikipedia’s governance structure promotes. They can lead not only to strained interpersonal relationships within the community but also to compromised content quality, as articles become unstable and subject to rapid, often contradictory changes.

The study of edit wars is significant for several reasons. First, they offer a lens into the dynamics of online collaboration, particularly in large-scale, decentralized environments. Understanding the triggers, escalation patterns, and resolution mechanisms of edit wars can contribute to broader theories of conflict in digital communities. Second, they have implications for information reliability: articles embroiled in persistent disputes may present inconsistent narratives or fail to meet Wikipedia’s standards of verifiability and neutrality, thereby impacting readers’ trust. Third, they raise questions about governance and moderation in open platforms, shedding light on the effectiveness of policies, such as the “three-revert rule,” dispute resolution processes, and administrator interventions.

Previous research has approached edit wars from multiple angles, including computational detection of conflict behavior, qualitative analysis of discussion pages, and network analysis of editor interactions. While these studies have advanced our understanding, there remains a need for integrative perspectives that bridge technical detection methods with the social and cultural contexts in which disputes unfold. This paper seeks to contribute to that conversation by examining the nature, causes, and consequences of edit wars in Wikipedia, situating them within the broader landscape of online collaborative knowledge production. By doing so, it aims to illuminate not only the specific challenges faced by Wikipedia but also the general dynamics of cooperation and conflict in open, participatory systems.
conclusion:
The phenomenon of edit wars on Wikipedia underscores the complex interplay between collaborative knowledge production and the contestation of meaning in open, networked environments. As this study has shown, edit wars are not merely trivial disputes over wording or formatting; rather, they often reveal deeper ideological, cultural, and epistemological disagreements among contributors. These conflicts highlight the tension between Wikipedia’s guiding principles—such as neutrality, verifiability, and consensus—and the diverse perspectives and motivations of its global editor base. While Wikipedia’s policies and governance mechanisms, including discussion pages, administrator intervention, and the “three-revert rule,” are designed to mitigate such disputes, they cannot entirely eliminate the underlying social dynamics that drive them.

The persistence of edit wars points to the need for a more nuanced understanding of how consensus is negotiated in decentralized communities. The findings suggest that edit wars can both hinder and enrich the encyclopedia’s quality: on one hand, prolonged disputes may discourage participation, reduce article stability, and delay the resolution of factual inaccuracies; on the other, the process of contestation can lead to more rigorous sourcing, broader perspectives, and heightened editorial vigilance. This dual nature challenges simplistic evaluations of conflict as purely detrimental and instead positions it as a potential driver of epistemic robustness—albeit at a cost.

From a broader perspective, the study of edit wars offers valuable insights into the dynamics of collaborative digital platforms more generally. As similar patterns of conflict emerge in other user-generated content environments, the lessons from Wikipedia—particularly regarding the importance of transparent rules, community norms, and accessible dispute resolution—can inform the design of more resilient and inclusive systems. Additionally, the role of power, expertise, and persistence in shaping outcomes within Wikipedia raises important questions about equity and representation in open knowledge projects.

Ultimately, edit wars exemplify the challenges inherent in building a collectively authored, constantly evolving repository of human knowledge. They remind us that knowledge production is not a neutral or purely technical process but a social one, shaped by negotiation, disagreement, and compromise. Future research could further explore the long-term effects of edit wars on editor retention, article quality, and community cohesion, as well as investigate interventions that balance the benefits of open participation with the need for stability and accuracy. In doing so, scholars and practitioners alike can better understand—and perhaps more effectively navigate—the productive tensions at the heart of collaborative knowledge creation.

title: Cost-Sensitive Support Vector Machines
abstract: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are widely used for classification tasks due to their solid theoretical foundation and strong empirical performance. However, standard SVM formulations assume equal misclassification costs for all classes, which can lead to suboptimal performance in domains where the costs of different types of errors are imbalanced, such as fraud detection, medical diagnosis, or fault prediction. This paper investigates cost-sensitive extensions to SVMs that explicitly incorporate asymmetric misclassification penalties into the optimization framework. We present a systematic analysis of cost-sensitive SVM formulations, including modifications to the hinge loss function and the use of class-dependent regularization parameters, and discuss their theoretical implications on the decision boundary. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets with varying imbalance ratios demonstrate that cost-sensitive SVMs significantly improve the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity compared to their cost-insensitive counterparts. We further examine the impact of cost parameter selection on model performance and propose a data-driven approach for tuning these parameters to reflect real-world cost structures. The results highlight the importance of incorporating domain-specific misclassification costs in SVM training to achieve more practically relevant classification outcomes in imbalanced and high-stakes decision-making scenarios.
introduction:
Support Vector Machines (SVMs) have long been recognized as one of the most powerful and versatile supervised learning algorithms for classification tasks. Rooted in statistical learning theory, SVMs aim to find an optimal separating hyperplane that maximizes the margin between classes, thereby enhancing generalization to unseen data. Their theoretical elegance, combined with strong empirical performance across diverse domains such as text categorization, image recognition, and bioinformatics, has established SVMs as a standard tool in the machine learning practitioner’s repertoire. However, the canonical formulation of SVMs implicitly assumes that all classification errors incur the same penalty, an assumption that does not hold in many real-world applications where the costs of misclassifications are asymmetric.

In numerous practical scenarios, the consequences of different types of misclassification errors can vary dramatically. For example, in medical diagnosis, failing to detect a malignant tumor (false negative) may have far more severe repercussions than incorrectly diagnosing a benign tumor as malignant (false positive). Similarly, in fraud detection, overlooking a fraudulent transaction could result in substantial financial losses, whereas incorrectly flagging a legitimate transaction may cause inconvenience but less critical damage. Standard SVMs, by treating all errors equally, may yield models that perform well in terms of overall accuracy but fail to adequately address the more costly error type. This mismatch between the learning objective and the application’s true cost structure motivates the development of cost-sensitive learning methods.

Cost-sensitive learning explicitly incorporates misclassification costs into the model training process, guiding the learning algorithm to prioritize the reduction of more expensive errors. In the context of SVMs, this entails modifying the objective function or constraints so that the penalty for misclassifying examples from certain classes is proportionally increased relative to others. This approach can be implemented by assigning different regularization parameters, or slack penalties, to different classes, thereby biasing the decision boundary in a way that reflects the underlying cost asymmetry. By aligning the optimization criterion more closely with the application-specific loss, cost-sensitive SVMs can achieve better performance in terms of cost-weighted metrics, even if this comes at the expense of traditional performance measures such as overall accuracy.

Research into cost-sensitive SVMs has explored various strategies for incorporating cost information. One common approach is to introduce class-dependent penalty parameters into the soft-margin SVM formulation, effectively scaling the slack variable penalties according to the misclassification costs. Alternative formulations include modifying the kernel function to reflect cost considerations, or re-sampling and re-weighting the training data in proportion to the associated costs. These methods differ in complexity, computational overhead, and their ability to handle diverse cost structures, but they share the central goal of producing classifiers that are better aligned with the decision-making needs of the target domain.

The importance of cost-sensitive SVMs is underscored by the prevalence of imbalanced datasets in real-world problems. Class imbalance, where one class is significantly underrepresented relative to others, often correlates with cost asymmetry: the minority class is frequently the one associated with higher misclassification costs. Traditional SVMs, when trained on highly imbalanced data without cost adjustment, tend to favor the majority class, leading to poor detection of minority class instances. Cost-sensitive modifications counteract this bias by effectively amplifying the influence of minority class examples during training, thereby improving recall for the costly class without excessively sacrificing precision.

Despite their practical utility, cost-sensitive SVMs introduce new challenges. Selecting appropriate cost parameters requires domain expertise and may involve trial-and-error or systematic search methods. Over-penalizing certain errors can lead to overfitting, while under-penalizing them fails to address the original problem. Furthermore, in some applications, misclassification costs may be uncertain, context-dependent, or subject to change over time, complicating the design of a fixed cost-sensitive model. These considerations highlight the need for robust methods that can adapt to varying cost structures and for principled strategies to estimate or learn cost parameters from data.

This paper focuses on the formulation, analysis, and empirical evaluation of cost-sensitive SVMs. We review the theoretical underpinnings of integrating cost information into the SVM framework, survey existing approaches, and discuss their relative strengths and limitations. We then present an experimental study on benchmark datasets with varying degrees of class imbalance and cost asymmetry, comparing cost-sensitive SVMs to standard SVMs and other cost-sensitive classifiers. Our results demonstrate the potential benefits of incorporating cost information directly into the SVM training process, particularly in domains where the cost of errors is highly skewed. By aligning model training with the true objectives of decision-making, cost-sensitive SVMs offer a principled and effective approach to tackling classification problems in cost-critical environments.
conclusion: This study has examined the formulation and application of cost-sensitive support vector machines for imbalanced classification problems. By incorporating asymmetric misclassification costs into the SVM framework, the proposed approach effectively addresses the bias toward majority classes, improving performance on minority class detection without severely degrading overall accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that appropriate cost parameter tuning can yield significant gains in precision-recall trade-offs and reduce the impact of class imbalance. Future work may explore adaptive cost-setting strategies and integration with ensemble methods. Overall, cost-sensitive SVMs provide a practical and robust extension to traditional SVMs for domains with unequal classification costs.

title: MMSE precoder for massive MIMO using 1-bit quantization
abstract: This paper investigates the design of a minimum mean-squared error (MMSE) precoder for downlink massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems employing 1-bit digital-to-analog converters (DACs) at the base station. The extreme quantization significantly reduces hardware cost and power consumption but introduces severe nonlinear distortion, complicating precoder optimization. We propose an efficient MMSE-based precoding scheme that incorporates the 1-bit quantization constraint directly into the design, leveraging Bussgang’s theorem to model the quantization effect and derive closed-form expressions for the precoding matrix. The method mitigates multiuser interference while accounting for quantization noise. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves substantial performance gains over conventional linear precoders under identical hardware constraints, approaching the performance of systems with higher-resolution DACs, thereby enabling energy-efficient massive MIMO deployment with minimal performance degradation.
introduction:
Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) has emerged as a key enabling technology for next-generation wireless communication systems, promising substantial improvements in spectral efficiency, energy efficiency, and reliability. By equipping the base station (BS) with a very large number of antennas, massive MIMO can simultaneously serve many user terminals in the same time-frequency resource, exploiting favorable propagation and channel hardening effects. These gains, however, come at the cost of increased hardware complexity, power consumption, and signal processing requirements. In particular, the radio frequency (RF) chains and high-resolution digital-to-analog converters (DACs) at the transmitter pose significant challenges in terms of cost and energy efficiency, especially when scaling to hundreds of antennas.

One promising approach to mitigate these hardware constraints is the use of low-resolution DACs, and in the extreme case, 1-bit DACs. With 1-bit quantization, each real and imaginary component of the baseband signal is represented by only one bit, reducing the DAC complexity and power consumption dramatically. Furthermore, the analog front-end can be simplified, and the resulting constant-envelope transmit signals are compatible with highly efficient nonlinear power amplifiers. Despite these advantages, 1-bit quantization introduces strong nonlinear distortion, which significantly complicates the design of transmit precoders and the analysis of system performance. The severe quantization noise can cause substantial degradation in achievable rates and error performance if not properly addressed.

Linear precoding schemes, such as matched filtering (MF), zero-forcing (ZF), and minimum mean-square error (MMSE) precoding, have been widely studied for conventional massive MIMO systems with high-resolution DACs. Among these, MMSE precoding offers a favorable balance between interference suppression and noise enhancement, providing robustness in scenarios with imperfect channel state information (CSI) and finite signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). However, in the presence of 1-bit quantization, conventional linear precoders designed for unquantized systems are no longer optimal, as they do not take into account the nonlinear distortion introduced by the coarse quantization. This mismatch leads to performance losses, motivating the need for precoding strategies that explicitly consider the quantization effects.

Recent research on massive MIMO with 1-bit quantization has explored both nonlinear and linearized approaches to precoder design. Nonlinear methods, such as symbol-level precoding or iterative optimization techniques, can achieve high performance but often entail high computational complexity, which may be prohibitive in practical large-scale systems. Linearized approaches, on the other hand, aim to retain computational efficiency while incorporating the quantization characteristics into the precoder design. Bussgang’s theorem has been widely applied in this context to model the quantizer as a linear gain plus uncorrelated distortion, enabling tractable analysis and design of linear precoders adapted to the quantized setting.

Within this framework, MMSE-based precoders for 1-bit massive MIMO systems have attracted significant attention. By exploiting the statistical properties of the quantization distortion and the channel, MMSE design can be adapted to minimize the mean-square error between the transmitted and received signals, accounting for the quantization nonlinearity. Such designs aim to balance the mitigation of multiuser interference and the suppression of quantization noise, thereby improving overall system performance. Moreover, MMSE precoders can be implemented with relatively low complexity compared to nonlinear alternatives, making them appealing for real-time deployment in massive MIMO base stations.

Nevertheless, several challenges remain. Accurate characterization of the quantization distortion in the multiuser, multi-antenna scenario is nontrivial, especially under realistic channel models and imperfect CSI. Furthermore, practical constraints such as per-antenna power limits, channel estimation errors, and hardware impairments must be considered to fully assess the viability of MMSE precoding with 1-bit DACs. Addressing these challenges requires careful modeling, algorithmic innovation, and performance evaluation under a variety of operational conditions.

In this work, we investigate the design and performance of MMSE precoders for massive MIMO downlink systems employing 1-bit DACs at the base station. Building on the Bussgang decomposition, we derive an MMSE precoder formulation that explicitly accounts for the quantization effects, and we analyze its performance in terms of achievable sum rate and error probability. Our contributions include a low-complexity implementation approach suitable for large antenna arrays and an evaluation under realistic propagation scenarios. The results demonstrate that, with proper design, MMSE precoding can significantly mitigate the adverse effects of 1-bit quantization, offering an attractive trade-off between performance and hardware efficiency in massive MIMO systems.
conclusion: This work investigated an MMSE precoding scheme for the downlink of massive MIMO systems employing 1-bit DACs. By explicitly accounting for the severe nonlinearity introduced by coarse quantization, the proposed approach effectively mitigates distortion and inter-user interference, achieving significant performance gains over conventional linear precoders. Simulation results demonstrated that the method approaches the performance of systems with higher-resolution DACs while maintaining the hardware simplicity and energy efficiency inherent to 1-bit architectures. The findings confirm that MMSE-based design remains a powerful tool in quantized massive MIMO, enabling a favorable trade-off between complexity, spectral efficiency, and power consumption. Future work will explore extensions to frequency-selective channels, adaptive algorithms, and robust designs under imperfect channel state information.

title: Non-equilibrium steady states in the quantum XXZ spin chain
abstract: We investigate non-equilibrium steady states (NESS) in the anisotropic spin-1/2 Heisenberg (XXZ) chain driven at its boundaries by Markovian reservoirs. Using a combination of exact diagonalization and matrix product operator techniques, we analyze steady-state transport properties across a range of anisotropy parameters and driving strengths. Our results reveal distinct transport regimes, from ballistic to diffusive, depending on the interplay between anisotropy and dissipation. In particular, for the gapless regime, we observe robust ballistic spin currents, while in the gapped phase the steady state exhibits signatures of diffusive transport with enhanced boundary-induced correlations. We further characterize the NESS via spin profiles, correlation functions, and entanglement entropy, identifying universal scaling behaviors in the weak-driving limit. The study highlights the role of integrability-breaking perturbations and reservoir coupling asymmetry in shaping non-equilibrium features. Our findings contribute to the understanding of quantum transport in low-dimensional systems, with implications for engineered quantum devices where dissipation can be harnessed to stabilize and control strongly correlated steady states.
introduction:
The study of non-equilibrium phenomena in low-dimensional quantum systems has emerged as a central theme in contemporary condensed matter physics. While the equilibrium properties of integrable models are by now well understood through the combined use of the Bethe ansatz, conformal field theory, and numerical simulations, the theoretical description of their non-equilibrium dynamics remains far less complete. In particular, the characterization of non-equilibrium steady states (NESS) that emerge when quantum systems are driven out of equilibrium has attracted considerable attention, both for its fundamental importance and for its relevance to quantum transport in nanoscale devices. Unlike equilibrium ensembles, which are dictated by the principles of statistical mechanics, NESS are determined by the interplay of coherent quantum dynamics, external driving, and dissipation, leading to rich and often unexpected behaviour.

One of the most widely studied paradigms for exploring quantum transport and relaxation is the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This model is described by the Hamiltonian  
\[
H_{\mathrm{XXZ}} = J \sum_{j=1}^{L-1} \left( S_j^x S_{j+1}^x + S_j^y S_{j+1}^y + \Delta S_j^z S_{j+1}^z \right),
\]
where \(S_j^\alpha\) are spin-\(\frac12\) operators, \(J\) is the exchange coupling, and \(\Delta\) controls the anisotropy between the \(z\)- and \(xy\)-components. The XXZ chain interpolates between the isotropic Heisenberg model (\(\Delta = 1\)), the easy-plane regime (\(|\Delta|<1\)), and the Ising-like regime (\(|\Delta|>1\)), each exhibiting distinct transport and relaxation characteristics. Its integrability, solvable via the Bethe ansatz, makes it an invaluable testing ground for theoretical ideas, allowing for exact results in certain regimes and providing a benchmark for numerical and approximate analytical methods.

In the context of non-equilibrium physics, the XXZ chain has been investigated under a variety of driving protocols. A particularly fruitful approach is the boundary-driven setting, in which the system is coupled at its ends to external reservoirs imposing different magnetisations or chemical potentials. In the long-time limit, the competition between coherent bulk dynamics and incoherent boundary driving can lead to the formation of a unique NESS supporting steady transport of spin and energy. The properties of such NESS depend sensitively on the anisotropy, the strength and nature of the driving, and the presence or absence of integrability-breaking perturbations. While certain exact solutions for boundary-driven NESS have been obtained for specific values of the anisotropy parameter and particular forms of dissipators, a general understanding of the full parameter space remains elusive.

The XXZ chain also serves as a platform for exploring fundamental questions about the nature of transport in interacting quantum systems. In the gapless easy-plane regime, ballistic transport is supported by the existence of quasi-local conserved quantities, while in the gapped easy-axis regime transport can be diffusive or subdiffusive, depending on temperature and driving conditions. The study of NESS in these regimes provides direct insight into the mechanisms of current-carrying states, the role of integrability in sustaining ballistic channels, and the onset of diffusive behaviour when integrability is perturbed. Moreover, recent advances in numerical techniques, such as matrix product state (MPS) and matrix product operator (MPO) methods, have enabled the simulation of large systems in the steady-state regime, allowing for quantitative comparison with analytical predictions.

Beyond their theoretical appeal, NESS in the XXZ chain are relevant to experimental realisations in cold atomic gases, trapped ions, and solid-state spin chains, where controlled driving and measurement of transport properties are now feasible. These developments provide a timely motivation to deepen our understanding of non-equilibrium phenomena in integrable quantum spin systems, bridging the gap between idealised models and realistic many-body dynamics. In this work, we investigate the formation, structure, and transport properties of NESS in the boundary-driven XXZ spin chain, elucidating how integrability, anisotropy, and driving protocols conspire to produce rich steady-state behaviour. Our results shed light on universal aspects of quantum transport far from equilibrium and contribute to the broader effort to formulate a coherent theory of steady states in interacting quantum systems.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the emergence, structure, and properties of non-equilibrium steady states (NESS) in the quantum XXZ spin chain under boundary driving. By combining analytical insights with numerical simulations, we have elucidated how the interplay between coherent bulk dynamics and dissipative boundary processes gives rise to steady states that exhibit rich transport behaviour and nontrivial correlations. Our analysis has focused on a range of anisotropy parameters, thereby covering regimes from the gapless, critical phase to the gapped, Ising-like phase, and has highlighted the distinct mechanisms that govern relaxation and current-carrying capabilities in these different domains.

We have shown that the NESS in the XXZ chain is highly sensitive to both the anisotropy and the driving protocol. In the gapless regime, our results are consistent with ballistic spin transport, as evidenced by the scaling of the spin current with system size and the persistence of long-range correlations. In contrast, in the gapped regime transport is suppressed, and the steady state exhibits exponentially decaying correlations, indicative of insulating behaviour. The crossover between these regimes is marked by qualitative changes in the spectral properties of the Liouvillian superoperator, which determines the approach to stationarity.

A key outcome of our study is the identification of signatures of integrability in the steady-state properties, even in the presence of dissipation. The XXZ chain, being integrable in the bulk, retains certain conservation laws that strongly constrain the form of the NESS. This manifests in anomalous transport coefficients and in the emergence of quasi-local conserved quantities that influence relaxation dynamics. Our numerical data suggest that the breaking of integrability through sufficiently strong boundary driving leads to a gradual restoration of diffusive behaviour, though remnants of ballistic transport persist over intermediate length scales.

We have also examined spatially resolved observables, such as local magnetisation profiles and two-point correlation functions, which reveal nontrivial structures in the steady state. In particular, we observe boundary-induced correlations extending deep into the bulk in the critical regime, a phenomenon that can be interpreted in terms of the interplay between coherent quasiparticle propagation and the continual injection and removal of excitations at the system’s edges. These findings underscore the fact that NESS in quantum many-body systems are not merely local thermal states, but can display complex, long-range structures determined by both microscopic dynamics and external constraints.

Our work opens several avenues for future research. Extending the analysis to time-dependent or stochastic boundary driving could shed light on the stability of NESS and the possibility of dynamical phase transitions. Furthermore, the methods developed here can be applied to other integrable and non-integrable spin models, as well as to higher-dimensional systems, where the nature of steady states remains largely unexplored. From an experimental perspective, recent advances in cold-atom and solid-state platforms provide promising opportunities to probe the predicted transport regimes and correlation patterns in controlled settings.

Overall, this study contributes to the growing understanding of how quantum coherence, many-body interactions, and dissipation conspire to produce non-equilibrium steady states with distinctive and sometimes surprising features, enriching the broader theory of quantum transport and open quantum systems.

title: Assembly history of subhalo populations in galactic and cluster sized dark haloes
abstract: We investigate the assembly history of subhalo populations within galactic- and cluster-sized dark matter haloes using high-resolution cosmological N-body simulations. By tracing the merger trees of host haloes across cosmic time, we quantify the accretion rates, mass loss, and survival probabilities of subhaloes as a function of redshift and host halo mass. Our analysis reveals that the majority of present-day subhaloes were accreted relatively late, with median infall redshifts of \(z \sim 1\) for galactic hosts (\(M_{\mathrm{vir}} \sim 10^{12} M_\odot\)) and \(z \sim 0.6\) for cluster hosts (\(M_{\mathrm{vir}} \sim 10^{15} M_\odot\)). However, the most massive surviving subhaloes tend to be early arrivals, reflecting their resilience against tidal disruption. We find that subhalo mass functions are remarkably self-similar across host masses when expressed in terms of the ratio of subhalo-to-host virial mass at infall, although the detailed shape is mildly affected by the dynamical age of the host. Subhaloes in clusters experience more rapid mass loss and orbital decay due to stronger tidal forces and more frequent interactions, leading to a higher disruption rate compared to galactic environments. The cumulative effect of these processes imprints distinct radial distributions, with galactic subhaloes exhibiting a less concentrated profile than cluster subhaloes. Our results provide a coherent picture of subhalo assembly that links the statistical properties of substructure to the growth history of their hosts, offering key constraints for semi-analytic models of galaxy formation and for interpreting strong lensing and dynamical studies targeting substructure in different mass regimes.
introduction:
In the current paradigm of structure formation, dark matter haloes grow hierarchically through the successive accretion and merging of smaller systems. Within this framework, massive haloes, whether on galactic or cluster scales, are expected to host a population of bound substructures—subhaloes—that are the remnants of earlier accretion events. These subhaloes are of central importance to a wide range of astrophysical phenomena: they are the sites in which galaxies may reside, they influence the dynamical and lensing properties of their host haloes, and they provide an important testing ground for predictions of the cold dark matter (CDM) model. Understanding the assembly history of subhalo populations is therefore crucial for linking the growth of dark matter structures to observable properties of galaxies and clusters.

While the overall abundance and spatial distribution of subhaloes have been studied extensively in high-resolution cosmological simulations, their detailed assembly histories—how and when they were accreted, how they evolve dynamically, and how these processes depend on host halo mass—remain active topics of investigation. In particular, the relative importance of early versus late accretion events, the survivability of subhaloes over cosmic time, and the role of tidal stripping and dynamical friction in shaping their mass and velocity functions are subjects of continuing debate. On galactic scales, subhaloes are thought to be the progenitors of satellite galaxies, and their orbital decay and disruption histories are directly connected to the morphology and star formation histories of these satellites. In clusters, subhaloes trace the infall of galaxy groups and provide insight into the environmental transformation of galaxies in dense regions.

Previous work has demonstrated that the subhalo mass function is approximately self-similar across a wide range of host halo masses, but there is evidence that the assembly histories of subhalo populations may differ between galactic and cluster haloes. For example, the deeper potential wells and higher velocity dispersions of clusters may inhibit subhalo disruption, leading to higher survival rates, whereas in galactic haloes, subhaloes may be more strongly affected by baryonic processes such as disk shocking. Moreover, the cosmological growth rate of haloes depends on their mass, which could imprint systematic differences in the timing and frequency of subhalo accretion.

In this work, we investigate the assembly history of subhalo populations in both galactic and cluster-sized dark matter haloes, using high-resolution N-body simulations to track individual subhaloes from the time of infall to the present epoch. By comparing the accretion histories, survival times, and mass evolution of subhaloes in these two regimes, we aim to elucidate the physical processes governing subhalo demographics and to assess their implications for galaxy formation and evolution.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the assembly histories of subhalo populations residing within galactic- and cluster-sized dark matter haloes, using high-resolution cosmological simulations to trace their evolution from early times to the present epoch. By following the formation, accretion, and subsequent dynamical evolution of subhaloes, we have quantified the similarities and differences in the substructure growth histories across a wide range of host halo masses, and explored the implications for their present-day abundance, mass spectrum, and spatial distribution.

Our analysis shows that the overall qualitative picture of subhalo assembly is remarkably similar for haloes of galactic and cluster scale: in both regimes, the majority of surviving subhaloes were accreted relatively late, typically after redshift \( z \sim 1 \), and the internal substructure hierarchy is continuously replenished through ongoing infall from the surrounding large-scale structure. However, we find clear and systematic trends with host halo mass. Cluster-sized haloes, forming later in hierarchical structure formation, tend to have a higher fraction of recently accreted subhaloes, leading to a larger proportion of massive and relatively unstripped systems at \( z=0 \). In contrast, galactic-sized haloes, with earlier assembly times, host subhalo populations that have, on average, been subject to longer periods of tidal evolution, orbital decay, and mass loss, resulting in steeper present-day subhalo mass functions and more centrally depleted radial distributions.

We have demonstrated that the accretion rate histories of subhaloes are closely tied to the mass accretion histories of their hosts, but also modulated by the dynamical environment. For massive clusters, the higher recent accretion rates reflect the continuing growth of the host through mergers with group-sized systems, which themselves bring in rich substructure. For galaxy-sized haloes, the accretion of sizeable subhaloes is rarer at late times, and the surviving population is dominated by long-lived satellites accreted at intermediate redshifts. These differing histories lead to distinct survivability patterns: recently accreted subhaloes in clusters are more likely to retain a large fraction of their infall mass, whereas older subhaloes in galaxies are more heavily stripped or disrupted.

By tracking individual subhaloes from infall to the present, we have also characterised the timescales for tidal mass loss and orbital evolution. Our results indicate that the median mass-loss rate after accretion is substantial in both environments, but the efficiency of stripping depends strongly on the depth of the potential well and the typical orbital parameters. In smaller hosts, closer pericentric passages and shorter dynamical times contribute to more rapid depletion of subhalo mass. This has important implications for interpreting observed satellite galaxy populations, as the underlying dark matter subhaloes may be significantly reduced in mass relative to their initial values, affecting abundance matching and halo occupation models.

The comparison between galactic and cluster haloes further reveals that the shape of the cumulative subhalo mass function is established early and preserved in a self-similar form, but its normalisation evolves differently. Clusters maintain higher normalisations at late times due to recent infall, while galaxies experience a gradual decline as older subhaloes are disrupted. The spatial distributions of subhaloes likewise retain a broadly universal form when scaled by the host virial radius, yet exhibit subtle mass-dependent variations linked to the assembly history.

Taken together, these findings reinforce the hierarchical nature of structure formation and the robustness of certain statistical properties of subhalo populations, while highlighting the sensitivity of detailed subhalo demographics to the growth history of the host. The differences we measure between galactic- and cluster-sized haloes are not merely a consequence of present-day mass, but emerge naturally from the interplay between cosmological accretion patterns, dynamical evolution, and environmental effects over cosmic time.

Future work will benefit from extending these analyses to even higher resolution, enabling the study of lower-mass subhaloes and their associated luminous components, as well as from incorporating baryonic physics to assess how processes such as gas cooling, star formation, and feedback modify the assembly and survival of substructure. Observational probes, including gravitational lensing in clusters and deep surveys of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way and other nearby systems, will provide critical tests of the predictions outlined here. By combining numerical, theoretical, and observational approaches, a more complete picture of subhalo assembly can be achieved, offering deeper insights into the small-scale structure of the Universe and the nature of dark matter itself.

title: Sparsity Aware Normalized Least Mean p-power Algorithms with Correntropy Induced Metric Penalty
abstract: This paper proposes sparsity-aware normalized least mean p-power (NLMP) algorithms incorporating a correntropy induced metric (CIM) penalty to enhance performance in impulsive noise environments. By integrating the CIM penalty into the NLMP framework, the proposed approach promotes coefficient sparsity while maintaining robustness against heavy-tailed noise. The p-power error criterion offers improved resilience to outliers, and the CIM term adaptively exploits sparsity without prior knowledge of system structure. Analytical stability conditions are derived, and computational complexity is discussed. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms achieve faster convergence and lower steady-state error compared to conventional NLMP and other sparsity-aware adaptive filters.
introduction:
Adaptive filtering has been widely employed in diverse signal processing applications such as system identification, echo cancellation, channel equalization, and noise suppression. Among various adaptive algorithms, the least mean square (LMS) algorithm and its variants have been extensively studied due to their simplicity and robustness. However, in scenarios where the system is subject to non-Gaussian impulsive noise, traditional LMS-based methods often suffer from performance degradation because their update rules rely on minimizing the mean square error, which is highly sensitive to large outliers. To address this limitation, the least mean p-power (LMP) family of algorithms has been proposed, where the squared error is replaced by the p-th power of the absolute error, providing improved robustness against heavy-tailed noise distributions.

In parallel, the normalized least mean p-power (NLMP) algorithms introduce a normalization factor to mitigate the effects of input signal variations, enhancing stability and convergence performance. While NLMP algorithms offer better resilience in impulsive noise environments, they often do not exploit potential structural properties of the unknown system, such as sparsity. In many practical applications—such as sparse channel estimation in broadband communications, network echo path modeling, and acoustic impulse response identification—the system to be identified is sparse, meaning that a large proportion of its coefficients are zero or negligibly small. Leveraging this prior knowledge can lead to significant improvements in convergence speed and steady-state accuracy.

To incorporate sparsity into adaptive filtering, various sparse regularization techniques have been developed, including ℓ₁-norm penalties, reweighted norms, and other sparsity-inducing constraints. Nevertheless, these approaches may still be vulnerable to performance degradation in the presence of impulsive noise, as they do not explicitly consider robustness in the error domain. Recently, the Correntropy Induced Metric (CIM) has emerged as a powerful similarity measure capable of capturing both second-order and higher-order statistical information. By effectively down-weighting large deviations, CIM provides robustness against outliers, making it attractive for non-Gaussian environments.

This work proposes a novel sparsity-aware normalized least mean p-power algorithm with a Correntropy Induced Metric penalty. The proposed method integrates three key elements: (i) the robustness of the NLMP framework in impulsive noise environments; (ii) sparsity promotion via an explicitly designed CIM-based penalty term that enhances the identification of sparse systems; and (iii) an adaptive structure that balances convergence speed, steady-state error, and robustness. The CIM penalty not only encourages sparsity in the coefficient vector but also inherently mitigates the influence of heavy-tailed noise, leading to improved estimation performance under challenging conditions.

Extensive simulations will be presented to evaluate the proposed algorithm in sparse system identification scenarios contaminated by impulsive noise. Results will demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms conventional NLMP and sparsity-aware algorithms in terms of convergence rate, steady-state error, and robustness, thereby providing an effective solution for real-world sparse adaptive filtering problems.
conclusion: In this work, sparsity aware normalized least mean p‑power algorithms incorporating a correntropy induced metric penalty were proposed to enhance performance in impulsive noise environments. By integrating sparsity constraints with robust similarity measures, the proposed approach achieves improved convergence speed, steady‑state accuracy, and resilience to outliers. Simulation results demonstrated superior performance over conventional methods in both sparse system identification and noise‑corrupted scenarios. These findings suggest the method’s potential for broad application in adaptive filtering tasks requiring robustness and sparsity exploitation.

title: Bound states in the continuum in strong-coupling and weak-coupling regimes under the cylinder-ring transition
abstract: We investigate the emergence and evolution of bound states in the continuum (BICs) during the geometrical transition from a cylindrical waveguide to a ring-shaped resonator, focusing on both strong- and weak-coupling regimes. Using a full-wave theoretical model supported by numerical simulations, we analyze how the interplay between geometry-induced symmetry and mode hybridization governs the formation, stability, and spectral position of BICs. In the strong-coupling regime, where mode splitting is pronounced, BICs arise from destructive interference between hybridized modes, exhibiting high quality factors and robustness to small perturbations in geometry. In the weak-coupling regime, BIC formation is driven primarily by symmetry protection, with reduced sensitivity to coupling strength but increased dependence on precise structural parameters. The cylinder-to-ring transition reveals a continuous transformation of modal profiles, with critical points where quasi-BICs evolve into true BICs. We identify parameter domains where BICs persist across the transition and regions where they vanish due to symmetry breaking. These findings provide a unified framework for controlling BICs via geometry and coupling strength, offering potential applications in sensing, filtering, and lasing devices that leverage high-Q resonances in photonic and acoustic platforms.
introduction:
Bound states in the continuum (BICs) constitute a class of localized modes that, despite their spectral overlap with the radiation continuum, remain perfectly confined due to destructive interference or symmetry protection. Since their original theoretical prediction, BICs have attracted considerable attention for their fundamental implications and potential applications in high‑Q resonators, sensing, and wave control. In photonic and electronic systems, BICs emerge under a variety of structural and symmetry conditions, and their realization has been reported in both weak‑ and strong‑coupling regimes. The coupling regime, determined by the interaction strength between discrete states and the continuum, profoundly influences the formation, stability, and tunability of BICs.

Among the diverse platforms supporting BICs, cylindrical and ring‑like geometries offer a compelling setting due to their rich modal structure and inherent rotational symmetry. Cylindrical cavities support well‑defined angular momentum channels, while ring geometries introduce an inner boundary, modifying confinement and coupling pathways. The transition from a solid cylinder to a narrow ring alters the spatial overlap between discrete modes and the continuum, thereby enabling controlled exploration of the conditions under which BICs can be sustained or suppressed. Such a geometrical transformation also facilitates the study of symmetry‑protected versus accidental BICs, as well as the interplay between geometry‑induced spectral shifts and coupling strengths.

In the strong‑coupling regime, mode hybridization can lead to avoided crossings and the stabilization of new BIC configurations, whereas in the weak‑coupling limit, BIC formation is often governed by fine‑tuned destructive interference. Understanding how the cylinder‑to‑ring transition mediates these effects is crucial for developing design rules for devices with tailored confinement properties. This work systematically investigates BIC behavior across coupling regimes during the continuous transformation from cylindrical to ring geometries, elucidating the role of geometry in shaping the conditions for bound‑state formation in open systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the emergence and evolution of bound states in the continuum (BICs) during the transition from a cylindrical geometry to a ring-like configuration, considering both strong- and weak-coupling regimes. By systematically varying the inner radius and tracking the spectral and spatial characteristics of the modes, we have elucidated how geometric deformation influences the conditions for destructive interference and symmetry protection that give rise to BICs. Our analysis reveals that the cylinder–ring transition provides a continuous pathway for tuning the modal coupling to the radiative continuum, enabling the controlled creation, annihilation, or transformation of BICs across distinct coupling regimes.

In the strong-coupling regime, the interplay between multiple discrete states and the continuum is highly sensitive to the geometry, leading to pronounced avoided crossings and hybridization effects. Under these conditions, BICs emerge primarily through interference between coupled resonances, and their existence is tied to fine-tuned phase relationships that can be manipulated by the ring opening. This regime supports robust, high-Q states that can persist over a range of geometries but exhibit abrupt changes when the coupling balance is perturbed.

Conversely, in the weak-coupling regime, the interaction with the continuum is minimal, and BIC formation is dominated by symmetry constraints inherent to the structure. As the cylinder transitions into a ring, these symmetry-protected BICs can either remain unaffected or undergo gradual leakage depending on whether the symmetry is preserved or broken. The weak-coupling limit thus offers a more predictable and less geometry-sensitive environment for sustaining BICs, albeit with reduced capacity for dynamic control compared to the strong-coupling case.

A key outcome of this study is the identification of parameter domains where the cylinder–ring transition enables a crossover between strong- and weak-coupling dominated BICs. This crossover is accompanied by qualitative changes in mode profiles, Q-factor scaling, and radiation patterns, pointing to possible strategies for engineering resonances with tailored confinement and radiation properties. The ability to steer the system through these regimes suggests opportunities for designing devices with switchable or tunable BIC-based functionalities.

In summary, the cylinder–ring transition serves as a versatile platform for exploring the fundamental mechanisms of BIC formation and transformation under varying coupling conditions. Our results not only deepen the understanding of geometry-driven BIC phenomena but also provide practical guidelines for exploiting these states in photonic, acoustic, and other wave-based systems. Future work may extend these concepts to more complex topologies and dynamic modulation schemes, further broadening the scope of BIC applications in integrated and reconfigurable devices.

title: Effective Capacity of Delay Constrained Cognitive Radio Links Exploiting Primary Feedback
abstract: This paper investigates the effective capacity of a cognitive radio link under statistical delay constraints, exploiting primary user (PU) feedback to enhance performance. We model a secondary user (SU) that adapts its transmission strategy based on both spectrum sensing outcomes and overheard acknowledgments or negative acknowledgments from the PU. The system is represented by a finite-state Markov chain capturing channel sensing errors, feedback reliability, and interference constraints. Closed-form expressions for the effective capacity are derived, and the impact of feedback exploitation is analytically and numerically assessed. Results show that incorporating PU feedback significantly improves the SU’s effective capacity compared to conventional sensing-only schemes, particularly under stringent delay requirements. The analysis also quantifies the trade-off between sensing accuracy, feedback utility, and achievable throughput. These findings provide useful guidelines for designing delay-aware cognitive radio protocols that leverage primary feedback for enhanced spectrum utilization.
introduction:
The rapid growth of wireless communication services has led to an unprecedented demand for radio spectrum resources. Traditional static spectrum allocation policies have resulted in large portions of the licensed spectrum remaining underutilized in time, frequency, or space, despite the increasing scarcity perceived by network operators and regulators. Cognitive radio (CR) technology has emerged as a promising paradigm to address this apparent spectrum shortage by enabling unlicensed secondary users (SUs) to opportunistically access licensed frequency bands without causing harmful interference to the primary users (PUs) who hold the spectrum rights. By allowing dynamic spectrum access, cognitive radios can significantly improve spectrum utilization efficiency while maintaining the quality of service (QoS) of incumbent systems.

In the underlay, overlay, and interweave models of cognitive radio operation, the interweave approach—where the SU transmits only when the PU is inactive—has attracted considerable attention due to its simplicity and reduced interference footprint. A key enabler of interweave CR systems is spectrum sensing, whereby the SU detects the PU’s activity before initiating transmission. However, practical spectrum sensing is subject to imperfections, including missed detections and false alarms, which can degrade system performance and lead to interference with the PU or missed transmission opportunities for the SU. Consequently, efficient exploitation of any available side information about PU activity can enhance the reliability of sensing decisions and the overall throughput of the SU.

One important but often underexploited form of side information is the primary feedback, such as automatic repeat request (ARQ) acknowledgments (ACKs) or negative acknowledgments (NACKs) transmitted from the PU receiver to the PU transmitter. In many wireless standards, such feedback is broadcast and thus potentially overheard by nearby SUs. Since the feedback reflects the outcome of the PU’s recent transmission attempt, it contains valuable information about the PU’s channel conditions and activity state. For example, a NACK implies that the PU will likely retransmit the same packet in the next slot, indicating a high probability of PU activity. If the SU can overhear and interpret this feedback, it can adjust its access strategy accordingly, avoiding collisions and reducing interference. Conversely, an ACK suggests that the PU may proceed with new data or remain idle, depending on the traffic arrival process, which can be exploited to refine the SU’s sensing and transmission decisions.

While the throughput performance of CR systems has been extensively studied, real-time applications impose additional constraints that must be addressed. Many emerging wireless services, including voice over IP, video conferencing, and industrial control, are characterized by stringent delay requirements. In such scenarios, it is not sufficient to evaluate performance solely in terms of average throughput; instead, delay-sensitive metrics become critical. The effective capacity (EC) framework has been introduced as a powerful tool to quantify the maximum constant arrival rate a wireless channel can support under given statistical QoS constraints, such as delay violation probabilities. EC extends the concept of Shannon capacity by incorporating the stochastic nature of wireless fading and queueing dynamics, providing a comprehensive measure of performance for delay-sensitive communications.

In the context of cognitive radio, incorporating delay constraints into the performance analysis is essential for designing protocols that can meet the QoS requirements of secondary applications while respecting the PU’s priority. Despite the potential benefits of exploiting primary feedback, its impact on the effective capacity of delay-constrained CR links has not been fully explored. Most prior works have focused on throughput or outage probability, often neglecting the interplay between feedback exploitation, sensing errors, and statistical delay constraints.

This paper addresses this gap by investigating the effective capacity of a delay-constrained interweave cognitive radio link that leverages primary feedback to enhance spectrum access decisions. We consider a realistic system model where the SU performs spectrum sensing with possible errors and can overhear PU feedback messages. Based on the overheard feedback, the SU adapts its transmission strategy to reduce interference with the PU and improve its own delay performance. We analyze the system using a Markov chain framework that captures the joint dynamics of PU activity, SU sensing decisions, feedback exploitation, and channel fading. The effective capacity is derived under statistical QoS constraints, enabling us to quantify the delay performance gains attributable to feedback exploitation.

The main contributions of this work are threefold. First, we propose a cognitive radio transmission strategy that integrates spectrum sensing outcomes with overheard primary feedback to make more informed access decisions. Second, we develop an analytical model for the effective capacity of the proposed scheme under realistic sensing imperfections and fading channel conditions. Third, we present numerical results demonstrating that exploiting primary feedback can significantly enhance the effective capacity of delay-constrained CR links, especially in scenarios with high PU activity or stringent delay requirements. These results provide valuable insights for the design of future cognitive radio systems that aim to support delay-sensitive secondary applications while efficiently coexisting with primary networks.
conclusion: This work analyzed the effective capacity of delay-constrained cognitive radio links utilizing primary feedback. Results showed that exploiting feedback improves performance under QoS constraints, outperforming no-feedback schemes. The proposed approach enhances spectrum utilization and reliability, offering promising potential for future cognitive radio network designs.

title: Learning Agile Locomotion Skills with a Mentor
abstract: We present a framework for learning agile locomotion skills in legged robots through a mentor-guided approach that combines reinforcement learning with demonstration-based initialization. In our method, a pre-trained mentor policy—either learned in simulation or derived from expert demonstrations—provides guidance to a student policy during early training, shaping exploration and accelerating convergence toward high-performance behaviors. The student progressively reduces dependence on the mentor, enabling autonomous adaptation to novel terrains and dynamic environments. We evaluate our approach on a range of challenging locomotion tasks, including high-speed running, obstacle traversal, and abrupt directional changes, in both simulated and real-world settings. Experimental results show that mentor-guided learning significantly improves sample efficiency, stability, and final performance compared to baseline reinforcement learning and imitation learning techniques. Furthermore, the mentor framework facilitates transfer of complex skills across morphologies and domains, highlighting its potential for scalable, general-purpose locomotion training. This work advances the integration of mentorship into autonomous skill acquisition for agile robotic mobility.
introduction:
Agile locomotion is a fundamental capability for autonomous agents operating in complex and dynamic environments. From legged robots traversing rough terrain to virtual characters navigating interactive simulations, the ability to adapt movement strategies to changing conditions is crucial for both performance and safety. Traditional control approaches often rely on carefully engineered controllers tailored to specific tasks or environments, which can be brittle when faced with unmodeled disturbances or novel situations. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have shown promise in enabling agents to acquire locomotion skills directly from experience; however, these methods typically require extensive trial-and-error learning, which can be sample-inefficient and pose risks for physical systems.

One promising direction to address these challenges is to incorporate guidance from a mentor—an expert agent, either human or artificial—that can provide demonstrations, corrective feedback, or high-level strategies during training. Mentor-assisted learning leverages prior knowledge to accelerate skill acquisition, improve robustness, and reduce the search space for effective policies. In the context of agile locomotion, a mentor could demonstrate complex maneuvers, suggest corrective actions when the learner deviates from optimal trajectories, or shape the reward signal to encourage desirable behaviors. By integrating such guidance into modern RL frameworks, it becomes possible to achieve faster convergence and higher-quality solutions than learning in isolation.

While imitation learning and apprenticeship learning have explored aspects of mentor-based training, the domain of agile locomotion poses unique challenges, including high-dimensional continuous control, delayed rewards, and the need for rapid adaptation to perturbations. This work investigates a framework for learning agile locomotion skills with the assistance of a mentor, combining model-free reinforcement learning with targeted mentor interventions. We examine how different forms of mentor input influence learning efficiency and final policy performance, and evaluate the approach across a variety of simulated locomotion tasks. Our results demonstrate that mentor-assisted training can significantly enhance both learning speed and agility, suggesting a practical path toward more capable and resilient autonomous agents.
conclusion: This work presented a mentor-guided framework for acquiring agile locomotion skills, enabling an agent to leverage expert demonstrations and adaptive feedback to accelerate learning. By combining model-free reinforcement learning with mentor-derived guidance, the approach effectively reduced exploration complexity and improved policy robustness across diverse terrains and dynamic conditions. Experimental results demonstrated that mentor involvement not only improved convergence speed but also enhanced skill generalization to previously unseen environments. The proposed method offers a structured pathway for transferring high-level strategies and motion patterns from an experienced mentor to a novice learner, bridging the gap between purely autonomous training and fully supervised control. These findings suggest that mentor-assisted learning can play a critical role in developing agile, adaptable locomotion in artificial agents, particularly where safety, efficiency, and versatility are paramount. Future work will explore scaling to more complex morphologies, incorporating multiple mentors with complementary expertise, and extending the framework to cooperative multi-agent locomotion tasks.

title: Small-scale structure of the interstellar medium towards rho Oph stars: diffuse band observations
abstract: We present high–resolution spectroscopic observations of diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) towards a selection of early–type stars in the ρ Ophiuchi cloud complex, aimed at probing small–scale structure in the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM). Using spectra obtained with resolving powers exceeding 60,000, we measured the equivalent widths and profiles of several prominent DIBs, including features at 5780, 5797, 6196, and 6614 Å, along closely spaced sightlines separated by less than 0.5 pc projected distance. Significant variations in DIB strengths were detected between adjacent lines of sight, with fractional changes up to 15% over sub-parsec scales. These differences are compared with variations in interstellar atomic (Na I, K I) and molecular (CH, CN) absorption, revealing that DIB carriers do not always trace the same structures as the small–scale atomic and molecular gas. Correlations between specific DIB ratios, such as 5780/5797, and known tracers of UV radiation field strength suggest that local environmental conditions modulate DIB carrier abundance and/or excitation. Our results demonstrate that the diffuse ISM towards ρ Oph exhibits measurable heterogeneity on scales comparable to or smaller than the separation between binary and multiple stellar systems, underscoring the need for high spatial resolution in studies of interstellar structure and DIB carrier properties.
introduction:
The interstellar medium (ISM) is not a uniform entity, but instead exhibits structure and variability over a wide range of spatial scales, from parsec-sized molecular clouds down to sub-AU density fluctuations. Understanding the small-scale structure of the ISM is essential for constraining the physical processes that govern its evolution, including turbulence, magnetic fields, and the interaction between diffuse and dense phases.
