Observations over the past decades have revealed significant variations in interstellar absorption features along closely spaced sight-lines, indicating that the ISM contains fine-scale inhomogeneities in density, temperature, and chemical composition. Such variations have been detected in atomic and molecular absorption lines, as well as in the strengths and profiles of diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs).

DIBs are broad, weak absorption features seen in the optical and near-infrared spectra of reddened stars, arising from the diffuse ISM. First discovered by Heger (1922), more than 500 DIBs are now catalogued, yet their carriers remain largely unidentified, although complex carbonaceous molecules are favoured candidates. The sensitivity of DIB strengths to physical and chemical conditions makes them valuable tracers of interstellar environment. Variations in DIB equivalent widths (EWs) across small angular separations can therefore be used to probe the fine-scale distribution of the diffuse ISM. Previous studies have reported such variations in several regions, including the Orion Trapezium, Sco–Oph, and Cygnus OB2, suggesting that DIB carriers are not uniformly distributed even within relatively homogeneous-looking diffuse clouds.

The ρ Ophiuchi cloud complex is one of the nearest and best-studied sites of low- and intermediate-mass star formation, located at a distance of approximately 120–140 pc. It contains a rich mixture of dense molecular regions, translucent clouds, and diffuse material, making it an ideal laboratory for studying the interplay between different ISM phases. Several bright, early-type stars lie in close angular proximity to the main cloud cores, providing multiple sight-lines through the same general region but sampling slightly different paths through the intervening medium. This geometry offers the opportunity to investigate small-scale variations in interstellar absorption with high spatial resolution, potentially down to scales of 10^3–10^4 AU.

Earlier work on the Sco–Oph region has shown measurable differences in atomic lines such as Na I and K I, and in molecular features such as CH and CN, between sight-lines separated by only a few arcminutes. However, the behaviour of DIBs on such scales remains less well characterised, particularly for the more weakly reddened, diffuse sight-lines around ρ Oph. By comparing high signal-to-noise optical spectra of several closely spaced stars in this region, it is possible to quantify the degree to which DIB strengths vary, and to compare these variations with those seen in atomic and molecular tracers.

In this paper, we present new observations of a selection of strong and well-studied DIBs towards a small group of bright ρ Oph stars. We investigate the amplitude of DIB EW variations over projected separations of less than 0.5 pc, and explore correlations between DIB behaviour and the properties of atomic and molecular lines in the same spectra. Our aim is to assess whether the carriers of the observed DIBs trace the same fine-scale structure as other interstellar species, or whether they show distinct distribution patterns that may reflect differences in physical or chemical sensitivity. These results provide new constraints on the spatial distribution of DIB carriers and the nature of small-scale structure in the diffuse ISM.
conclusion:
The observations presented in this work provide new insights into the small-scale structure of the interstellar medium (ISM) in the direction of the ρ Ophiuchi star-forming region, as traced by diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) and related absorption features. By exploiting high-resolution spectroscopy of multiple, closely spaced sightlines towards members of the ρ Oph system, we have been able to probe spatial variations in DIB strengths and profiles on scales of order hundreds to thousands of astronomical units. These variations, when compared with those of well-known atomic and molecular tracers, reveal that the carriers of certain DIBs are not uniformly distributed, but instead exhibit measurable inhomogeneities within the intervening diffuse and translucent clouds.

Our analysis shows that some DIBs, particularly those in the 5780 and 5797 Å range, display significant equivalent width differences between sightlines separated by less than 0.1 pc. This behaviour suggests that the carriers of these features respond sensitively to local changes in physical conditions such as UV radiation field strength, density, and possibly the local ionisation balance. In contrast, other bands appear more spatially uniform, implying that their carriers are either more resilient to environmental variations or more broadly mixed with the general ISM material. The comparison with CH, CH⁺, and CN line strengths further indicates that the small-scale structure traced by DIBs may not always coincide with that traced by small molecules, pointing to a complex relationship between different ISM constituents.

The results therefore support a picture in which the ISM, even in relatively simple diffuse cloud environments, is highly structured on small scales, with variations in composition and excitation state occurring over sub-parsec distances. The ρ Oph sightlines provide a particularly clear demonstration of this phenomenon, due to the combination of proximity, well-characterised stellar targets, and intervening material of intermediate density. The observed diversity in DIB behaviour also adds to the growing body of evidence that different DIBs have different carriers and formation pathways, each with their own sensitivity to local conditions.

From a methodological standpoint, this study reinforces the value of using closely spaced stellar pairs or clusters as probes of ISM structure. By comparing multiple sightlines through essentially the same large-scale cloud, we can isolate the effects of small-scale variations and disentangle them from the broader environmental influences. This approach is complementary to large-scale DIB surveys, offering a higher-resolution view of the ISM’s complexity.

Future work should extend this type of analysis to other regions with similar stellar configurations, and to a wider range of DIBs, including those in the near-infrared. Combining DIB measurements with high-resolution mapping of atomic and molecular species, polarisation data, and dust extinction will provide a more complete picture of how small-scale ISM structure influences, and is influenced by, the carriers of these enigmatic features. Ultimately, such studies will help constrain the nature of DIB carriers and their role in the physics and chemistry of the interstellar medium.

title: Observation of Higgs boson production in association with a top quark pair at the LHC with the ATLAS detector
abstract: We report the observation of Higgs boson production in association with a top quark–antiquark pair (tt̄H) using proton–proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis uses the full Run 2 dataset, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 139 fb⁻¹. Multiple Higgs boson decay channels, including H → bb̄, H → WW*, H → τ⁺τ⁻, and H → ZZ*, are combined to maximize sensitivity. The measured tt̄H production rate is consistent with the Standard Model prediction, with a significance of 6.3 standard deviations above the background-only hypothesis, constituting the first observation of this process by ATLAS. This measurement provides a direct probe of the top quark Yukawa coupling, an essential parameter of the Standard Model, and strengthens constraints on possible contributions from physics beyond the Standard Model. Implications for Higgs sector phenomenology are discussed.
introduction:
The discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) marked a milestone in particle physics, confirming the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking as formulated in the Standard Model (SM). Subsequent measurements of its properties, including mass, spin, and couplings to gauge bosons and fermions, have been broadly consistent with SM predictions. However, precise determinations of these couplings remain a central objective, as any deviation could signal the presence of new physics beyond the Standard Model.

In the SM, the interaction strength between the Higgs boson and fermions is proportional to the fermion mass, making the coupling to the top quark—the heaviest known elementary particle—particularly significant. The top quark Yukawa coupling, \( y_t \), plays a crucial role in electroweak symmetry breaking and has a value close to unity. Direct measurements of \( y_t \) provide a stringent test of the SM and are sensitive to modifications arising from physics at higher energy scales. While loop-induced processes such as gluon–gluon fusion and Higgs decay to two photons offer indirect sensitivity to \( y_t \), an unambiguous determination requires observation of Higgs boson production in association with a top–antitop quark pair (\( t\bar{t}H \)).

The \( t\bar{t}H \) production process has a relatively small cross section at LHC energies, approximately an order of magnitude smaller than that of gluon–gluon fusion, and presents substantial experimental challenges due to complex final states and significant backgrounds. Depending on the Higgs boson decay mode, the experimental signatures can involve multiple leptons, photons, and jets, including those originating from bottom quarks. Accurate reconstruction and identification of these objects, along with sophisticated analysis techniques, are essential to separate the signal from processes such as \( t\bar{t} \) production with additional jets or vector bosons.

Prior searches for \( t\bar{t}H \) production using Run 1 data provided evidence consistent with the SM expectation but were limited by statistical precision. The increased centre-of-mass energy and integrated luminosity of the LHC Run 2 dataset offer substantially greater sensitivity, enabling a definitive observation of the process. This paper reports the observation of Higgs boson production in association with a top quark pair, using proton–proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS detector at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The measurement combines multiple Higgs boson decay channels to maximise sensitivity, and the results are interpreted in terms of the top quark Yukawa coupling within the framework of the Standard Model.
conclusion:
The observation of Higgs boson production in association with a top quark pair (\(t\bar{t}H\)) presented in this work constitutes a significant milestone in the exploration of the Standard Model (SM) and in the precise understanding of the Higgs sector. Using the full Run 2 dataset collected with the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 139 fb\(^{-1}\) at a centre-of-mass energy of \(\sqrt{s} = 13\) TeV, we have measured the production rate of \(t\bar{t}H\) events in multiple Higgs boson decay channels, achieving an observed significance above the threshold for discovery. This result provides direct evidence of the Yukawa coupling between the Higgs boson and the top quark, the heaviest known elementary particle, thereby confirming a key prediction of the SM.

The analysis combines final states with different Higgs decay modes, including \(H \to b\bar{b}\), \(H \to \gamma\gamma\), \(H \to ZZ^* \to 4\ell\), and \(H \to WW^* \to \ell\nu\ell\nu\), exploiting their complementary sensitivities and systematic uncertainties. Advanced reconstruction techniques and multivariate analysis methods were employed to enhance the separation between signal and background, with particular emphasis on the suppression of irreducible backgrounds such as \(t\bar{t}\) production with additional jets. The consistent observation of the signal across all channels, and the compatibility of the measured production rate and kinematic distributions with SM expectations, reinforce the robustness of the result.

The measured signal strength, defined as the ratio of the observed production rate to the SM prediction, is compatible within uncertainties with unity, indicating no significant deviation from the SM in the \(t\bar{t}H\) sector. This agreement places stringent constraints on scenarios of physics beyond the Standard Model that predict modifications to the top–Higgs coupling, including certain classes of composite Higgs models, two-Higgs-doublet models, and models with vector-like quarks. The direct nature of this measurement, independent of loop-induced processes, provides an essential complement to indirect determinations from gluon–gluon fusion and Higgs boson decay channels.

The observation of \(t\bar{t}H\) production opens the way to a new era of precision measurements of the top–Higgs interaction. Future analyses with larger datasets from the upcoming LHC runs, as well as refined theoretical predictions, will enable more precise determinations of the coupling strength and its possible CP structure, and will improve sensitivity to rare Higgs decay modes in association with top quarks. In this way, the work reported here not only confirms a cornerstone of the SM but also establishes a foundation for further exploration of the electroweak symmetry-breaking mechanism and the search for new phenomena in the Higgs sector.

title: Bat Algorithm is Better Than Intermittent Search Strategy
abstract: This paper investigates the comparative performance of the Bat Algorithm (BA) and the Intermittent Search Strategy (ISS) in solving complex optimization problems. While ISS alternates between local intensive search and global exploration, its efficiency diminishes in high-dimensional or multimodal landscapes. BA, inspired by the echolocation behavior of microbats, adaptively balances exploration and exploitation through frequency tuning, loudness adjustment, and pulse emission rate. Experimental results on benchmark optimization functions demonstrate that BA consistently achieves faster convergence, higher solution accuracy, and greater robustness than ISS. The findings highlight BA’s superior adaptability and scalability, suggesting its broader applicability for real-world optimization challenges across diverse domains.
introduction:
Nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithms have gained significant attention in recent years due to their ability to solve complex optimization problems efficiently. Among these, the Bat Algorithm (BA), inspired by the echolocation behavior of microbats, has demonstrated notable success across a wide range of applications, including engineering design, image processing, and scheduling. BA combines frequency tuning, velocity updates, and adaptive pulse emission to balance exploration and exploitation effectively. In contrast, the Intermittent Search Strategy (ISS), rooted in theoretical models of foraging behavior, alternates between slow, intensive local searches and fast, extensive global searches. While ISS provides an analytically tractable framework for search processes, its performance in high-dimensional and multimodal optimization tasks is often limited by its simplistic switching mechanism and lack of adaptive parameter control. 

Recent comparative studies indicate that BA consistently outperforms ISS in terms of convergence speed, solution accuracy, and robustness to local optima. This advantage is attributed to BA’s dynamic control of search parameters and its inherent capability to adjust the balance between diversification and intensification as the search progresses. This paper investigates, through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, the reasons behind the superior performance of BA over ISS, offering insights into algorithmic design principles that can enhance search efficiency in complex problem domains.
conclusion: The comparative analysis between the Bat Algorithm (BA) and the Intermittent Search Strategy (ISS) demonstrates that BA offers superior performance in solving complex optimization problems. Through its adaptive frequency tuning, loudness control, and balanced exploration–exploitation mechanisms, the Bat Algorithm consistently achieves faster convergence rates and higher-quality solutions across a variety of benchmark functions. While ISS provides a structured approach to alternating between exploration and exploitation phases, its fixed switching rules limit flexibility in dynamic search landscapes. In contrast, BA’s parameter adaptation enables it to respond effectively to problem-specific characteristics, reducing the likelihood of premature convergence. Experimental results confirm that BA not only improves solution accuracy but also enhances computational efficiency. These findings suggest that the Bat Algorithm’s bio-inspired search dynamics make it a more versatile and robust choice for tackling diverse optimization tasks, reinforcing its advantage over the Intermittent Search Strategy in both theoretical and practical contexts.

title: Sharp Threshold for the Frechet Mean (or Median) of Inhomogeneous Erdos-Renyi Random Graphs
abstract: We investigate the existence of a sharp threshold for the Fréchet mean and median of inhomogeneous Erdős–Rényi random graphs under the graph distance induced by the edit (Hamming) metric. In this setting, edges appear independently with heterogeneous probabilities, and the Fréchet minimizers are defined over the finite space of simple graphs. We show that, as the number of vertices grows, there is a critical scaling of the edge-probability profile at which the structure of the Fréchet mean (or median) changes abruptly from sparse to dense. This threshold phenomenon is characterized in terms of the aggregate edge probability, and our results extend classical homogeneous Erdős–Rényi threshold behavior to the inhomogeneous regime. The proofs combine concentration inequalities with combinatorial enumeration to control fluctuations of the empirical distance function. Applications to graph-based consensus and network data analysis are discussed.
introduction:
The study of metric and probabilistic properties of random graphs has become a central theme in modern probability theory, combinatorics, and network science. Among the various models of random graphs, the classical homogeneous Erdős–Rényi model \( G(n,p) \), where each edge between \(n\) vertices is present independently with probability \(p\), has served as a canonical testing ground for probabilistic methods and limit theorems. A rich theory of phase transitions and threshold phenomena has emerged in this context, with critical points identified for properties such as connectivity, the emergence of a giant component, and Hamiltonicity. Beyond these structural features, interest has grown in understanding geometric and statistical descriptors of random graphs viewed as points in a suitable metric space. In this geometric viewpoint, one may equip the space of graphs with a distance—such as the Hamming distance on adjacency matrices or graph edit distance—and study random samples of graphs via notions from metric geometry and statistics.

One such notion is the Fréchet mean (or more generally, the Fréchet median), defined as the minimizer of the expected squared (or absolute) distance to the sample or distribution. In Euclidean spaces, this coincides with the classical mean (or median) and serves as a fundamental measure of central tendency. In metric spaces, and in particular in the discrete and high-dimensional space of graphs, the Fréchet mean encapsulates a “central” graph that best represents a given distribution. This concept has found applications in shape analysis, computational biology, and network data analysis, where the data points are graphs rather than vectors. Theoretical properties of Fréchet means in non-Euclidean spaces have been studied in probability theory and statistics, but relatively little is known in the context of large random graphs, especially when the underlying distribution is itself a random graph model.

In this paper, we investigate the Fréchet mean (and median) of inhomogeneous Erdős–Rényi random graphs. The inhomogeneous model generalizes \( G(n,p) \) by allowing the probability of an edge between vertices \(i\) and \(j\) to be \(p_{ij}\), possibly varying across pairs. This framework encompasses a wide class of random graph models, including stochastic block models and graphs with prescribed expected degrees, and is both mathematically tractable and relevant for modeling real-world networks with heterogeneous connectivity patterns. Our interest lies in the emergence of sharp thresholds: abrupt changes in the structure of the Fréchet mean graph as the underlying edge probabilities cross certain critical values.

Threshold phenomena are well understood for many monotone graph properties in homogeneous models. In our setting, the property of interest is the presence or absence of a given edge in the Fréchet mean graph. As the parameters \(p_{ij}\) vary, there may exist a critical probability at which the optimality of including that edge in the mean changes suddenly. We show that such thresholds are sharp in the limit \(n \to \infty\), and we identify their locations in terms of the underlying distribution. The analysis combines probabilistic concentration for empirical edge frequencies, combinatorial properties of the metric space of graphs, and stability of optimization problems under small perturbations.

Our results contribute to both the theory of random graphs and the statistical analysis of network-valued data. They reveal that even in highly heterogeneous settings, the “central” graph determined by the Fréchet mean exhibits phase transitions analogous to those in classical percolation and connectivity problems, but at the level of individual edges. This fine-grained threshold behavior underscores the sensitivity of central tendency estimators in discrete structures and provides a rigorous foundation for understanding their large-sample limits. In addition, the sharp threshold phenomenon has implications for algorithms that estimate representative graphs from data, suggesting that small changes in observed edge frequencies may lead to abrupt changes in the estimated mean or median graph. These insights open the door to further exploration of geometric statistics in random graph models, including higher-order structures, alternative metrics, and robustness considerations in the presence of noise or model misspecification.
conclusion:
In this work we investigated the emergence of a sharp threshold for the existence and stability of the Fréchet mean (or median) in the setting of inhomogeneous Erdős–Rényi random graphs. By extending classical threshold phenomena from homogeneous random graph models to the inhomogeneous regime, we identified precise asymptotic conditions under which the Fréchet mean transitions from being ill-defined or highly unstable to being well-defined and robust with high probability. Our analysis incorporated heterogeneous edge probabilities and leveraged concentration inequalities for dependent Bernoulli structures, allowing us to capture the interplay between graph sparsity, degree heterogeneity, and the geometry of the metric space in which the mean is computed.

We showed that the threshold is governed by a critical scaling of the minimal and average connection probabilities, and that the transition is sharp: small perturbations around the critical regime lead to a qualitative change in the behaviour of the empirical Fréchet functional. Above the threshold, the empirical mean converges to its population counterpart with high probability, and the variance shrinks rapidly with graph size. Below the threshold, the functional landscape becomes fragmented, leading to multiple nearly optimal but mutually distant minimizers, and the notion of a central tendency loses statistical meaning.

The results apply equally to both the Fréchet mean and the Fréchet median, with differences manifesting only in constant factors and in the sensitivity to extreme configurations. In particular, the median exhibits slightly greater robustness in the vicinity of the threshold, consistent with its resistance to outliers in deterministic settings.

Beyond their theoretical interest, these findings have implications for practical applications in network analysis, where the Fréchet mean is used to aggregate or summarise graph-valued data. In settings with heterogeneous connectivity, our results offer guidance on the sampling regimes and connectivity levels necessary to ensure meaningful aggregation. Future work could extend these ideas to dynamic or weighted networks, or to other intrinsic metrics on graph spaces, and explore whether similar sharp thresholds arise for higher-order Fréchet-type descriptors. Our analysis underscores that the phenomenon of threshold behaviour is not confined to purely combinatorial properties, but extends to statistical and geometric summaries of random structures.

title: Ultra Diffuse Galaxies in the IC1459 Group from the VEGAS Survey
abstract: We present a study of ultra diffuse galaxies (UDGs) identified in the IC 1459 group using deep imaging from the VST Early-type GAlaxy Survey (VEGAS). Through careful surface photometry and structural analysis, we detect and characterize 12 UDG candidates, defined by their large effective radii (Re > 1.5 kpc) and low central surface brightness (μ0,g > 24 mag arcsec⁻²). We investigate their spatial distribution, colors, and scaling relations, comparing them with UDGs in clusters and other group environments. Our results suggest that group UDGs share structural properties with cluster counterparts, but may follow distinct evolutionary paths shaped by weaker environmental effects in low-density regions.
introduction:
Ultra diffuse galaxies (UDGs) are a class of low surface brightness systems that have attracted significant attention in recent years due to their unusual structural properties and uncertain formation pathways. Defined broadly by their large effective radii (typically \(R_e \gtrsim 1.5\) kpc) and low central surface brightnesses (\(\mu_{0,g} \gtrsim 24\) mag arcsec\(^{-2}\)), UDGs possess stellar masses comparable to those of dwarf galaxies but exhibit spatial extents similar to those of much more massive systems. First identified in large numbers in the Coma cluster (van Dokkum et al. 2015), UDGs have since been detected in a variety of environments, from dense clusters to loose groups and even the field. Their ubiquity suggests that they constitute a significant population whose origins and evolutionary histories remain open questions.

The nature of UDGs is still debated. Competing scenarios propose that they are either “failed” massive galaxies that lost their gas early and ceased star formation, or diffuse dwarfs whose extended sizes result from internal processes such as stellar feedback–driven gas outflows, tidal heating, or high angular momentum. Environmental effects are also likely to play a role: in high-density regions, ram-pressure stripping, tidal harassment, and galaxy–galaxy interactions may contribute to their present-day structure, while in low-density environments, secular processes may dominate. Observationally, the structural parameters, colors, stellar populations, and spatial distributions of UDGs in different environments provide important constraints on these models.

Most systematic UDG studies have focused on massive clusters, where they can be identified in large numbers against a well-defined background. However, investigations in lower-density environments, such as galaxy groups, are crucial for disentangling the roles of environment and intrinsic formation mechanisms. Groups are particularly interesting laboratories as they represent intermediate-density regions where both internal and external processes can shape galaxy evolution. The IC 1459 group is a nearby (\(D \approx 29\) Mpc) loose group dominated by the massive elliptical galaxy IC 1459, with a diverse population of early- and late-type members. Its relative proximity and modest distance modulus make it an excellent target for studying faint, extended galaxies down to low surface brightness limits.

The VST Early-type GAlaxy Survey (VEGAS) provides deep, high-quality imaging well suited to the detection and characterization of LSB systems, including UDGs. Conducted with the VLT Survey Telescope (VST) using OmegaCAM, VEGAS offers multi-band optical data with wide field coverage and exquisite depth, enabling the exploration of galaxy outskirts and the detection of faint companions. In the context of the IC 1459 group, VEGAS data allow us to systematically search for UDG candidates, measure their structural parameters, and compare their properties to those in other environments.

In this work, we present the identification and analysis of UDG candidates in the IC 1459 group based on deep VEGAS imaging. We describe the data and methods used for detection and photometric characterization, assess the robustness of our candidate selection, and discuss the implications of our findings for the formation and survival of UDGs in group environments. By extending the census of UDGs beyond rich clusters, our study contributes to a more complete understanding of the diversity and evolutionary pathways of these intriguing galaxies.
conclusion: We have presented an analysis of ultra diffuse galaxy (UDG) candidates in the IC1459 group based on deep imaging from the VEGAS survey. The unprecedented depth and resolution of the data have enabled the detection and structural characterization of a statistically significant sample of low surface brightness systems in this nearby group environment. Our sample exhibits a range of effective radii, surface brightnesses, and Sérsic indices consistent with UDG populations identified in other group and cluster environments, though with some diversity in morphology and luminosity. The spatial distribution of the candidates suggests a possible association with the group’s large-scale structure, hinting at environmental influences on their formation and survival. Comparisons with UDGs in denser clusters indicate that the IC1459 group hosts objects of comparable size but potentially lower central surface brightness, which may reflect differences in tidal processing or quenching histories. These findings contribute to the growing evidence that UDGs are not exclusive to rich clusters but are also prevalent in lower-density group environments. Future spectroscopic follow-up will be essential to confirm group membership, probe stellar populations, and constrain dynamical masses. Such studies will shed further light on the origins of UDGs and their role in the broader context of galaxy evolution across diverse environments.

title: A new method of CCD dark current correction via extracting the dark information from scientific images
abstract: Dark current, an inherent noise source in charge-coupled device (CCD) imaging, degrades image quality and limits the accuracy of quantitative measurements, particularly in long-exposure or low-light scientific observations. Conventional dark current correction relies on separate dark frames acquired under the same exposure and temperature conditions as the target images. However, obtaining adequate dark frames can be impractical in field observations, and mismatch in environmental conditions often leads to residual noise. This paper presents a novel method for CCD dark current correction that extracts dark information directly from the scientific images themselves, without the need for dedicated dark frames. The proposed approach leverages statistical analysis of image pixel distributions and temporal variability to isolate the dark signal component from scene-dependent features. By modeling the spatial structure of dark current and its temperature dependence, the method reconstructs an accurate dark frame surrogate, which is then subtracted from the original image. Validation on astronomical CCD datasets demonstrates that the technique effectively suppresses dark current noise while preserving fine image details, achieving comparable or superior performance to traditional dark frame subtraction. This approach offers a practical and reliable solution for dark current correction in situations where dark frames are unavailable, enabling improved precision in scientific imaging applications across astronomy, remote sensing, and low-light microscopy.
introduction:
Charge-coupled devices (CCDs) have been widely employed as imaging sensors in a broad range of scientific applications, including astronomy, microscopy, remote sensing, and spectroscopy, due to their high quantum efficiency, linearity, and dynamic range. In such contexts, the accuracy and reliability of the recorded image data are of paramount importance, as quantitative analyses often depend on the precise measurement of faint signals. However, raw CCD images are inevitably affected by various instrumental and environmental noise sources, among which dark current is one of the most significant. Dark current arises from thermally generated electrons within the sensor material, which are accumulated during the exposure time, even in the absence of incident photons. The presence of dark current introduces an additive signal component that can obscure faint features, degrade image contrast, and bias quantitative measurements.

The characteristics of dark current are influenced by multiple factors, including the CCD’s operating temperature, the exposure time, and intrinsic pixel-to-pixel variations due to manufacturing imperfections. In many scientific imaging systems, dark current is reduced by cooling the detector, often to cryogenic temperatures. Nevertheless, even at low temperatures, residual dark current can remain non-negligible, particularly in long exposures. Moreover, the spatial non-uniformity of dark current across the sensor gives rise to fixed-pattern noise, which can be especially problematic in the analysis of weak signals. Accurate correction of dark current is therefore a critical step in CCD image calibration pipelines.

The conventional approach to dark current correction involves acquiring a set of “dark frames,” which are exposures taken with the shutter closed, under the same operating conditions—temperature, exposure time, and readout mode—as the target scientific images. By averaging these dark frames, a master dark frame can be constructed, which represents the spatial distribution and magnitude of the dark current. This master dark is then subtracted from the corresponding science images to remove the dark signal. While effective in principle, this method has several limitations. First, it requires dedicated calibration time to obtain dark frames, which may be impractical in certain observational campaigns or experimental setups where instrument time is limited. Second, mismatches between the conditions under which the dark frames and science frames are acquired—due to temperature drifts, temporal variations in the detector, or changes in readout electronics—can lead to imperfect subtraction and residual artifacts. Third, in some scenarios, such as space-based observations or autonomous remote sensing platforms, acquiring contemporaneous dark frames may be infeasible.

To address these challenges, alternative approaches have been explored. Some methods model the dark current behavior as a function of temperature and exposure time, allowing for synthetic dark frame generation based on housekeeping telemetry. Others employ statistical techniques to separate the dark signal from the true scene content in image series, for example by exploiting temporal redundancy or using regions of the detector that are shielded from illumination. However, these methods often rely on assumptions that may not hold in all cases, such as the availability of multiple exposures, stable scene content, or the existence of masked pixels.

In this work, we present a new method for CCD dark current correction that extracts the dark information directly from the scientific images themselves, without the need for separate dark frame acquisition. The proposed technique leverages the intrinsic properties of the image data and noise characteristics of the detector to estimate both the spatial distribution and magnitude of the dark current. By carefully isolating regions or components of the image that are dominated by dark signal rather than scene signal, and employing robust statistical estimation procedures, our method can reconstruct an accurate dark map under the same conditions as the science acquisition. This approach offers several advantages: it eliminates the overhead associated with dedicated dark frame acquisition, mitigates the risks of mismatch due to temporal or thermal variations, and can be applied retrospectively to archival data lacking accompanying calibration frames.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the theoretical background of CCD dark current generation and its statistical properties. Section 3 describes the methodology of the proposed dark current extraction technique, including the underlying assumptions, algorithmic steps, and implementation details. Section 4 presents experimental results obtained from both simulated data and real scientific imagery, demonstrating the performance of the method in comparison with conventional dark frame subtraction. Section 5 discusses the implications, potential limitations, and possible extensions of the approach. Finally, Section 6 summarizes our conclusions and outlines directions for future research.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a novel method for correcting CCD dark current by extracting dark signal information directly from scientific images, without the need for dedicated dark frames. This approach was motivated by the limitations of traditional calibration procedures, which require separate dark exposures under matched temperature and exposure conditions, often resulting in increased observational overhead and reduced efficiency. By leveraging the statistical characteristics of image data and isolating the dark current contribution from the underlying signal, our method enables effective correction even when conventional calibration data are unavailable or incomplete.

The proposed technique is based on a systematic extraction of dark current components through pixel-level analysis, incorporating both temporal and spatial features of the sensor response. By modeling the dark signal as a stable, repeatable component independent of scene content, and applying robust separation algorithms, we demonstrated that it is possible to reconstruct an accurate dark frame from the scientific exposures themselves. This reconstructed dark frame can then be subtracted from the raw data to mitigate the bias introduced by thermally generated electrons, leading to a significant improvement in photometric precision and image quality.

Experimental validation on datasets from multiple CCD systems under varying observational conditions confirmed the robustness and versatility of the method. Comparisons with traditional dark frame subtraction showed that our approach achieves comparable, and in some cases superior, performance in reducing dark current–related noise. Importantly, the method proved effective across a range of temperatures and exposure times, highlighting its adaptability to diverse observing environments. In addition, tests on archival data sets demonstrated that the technique can recover valuable information from images lacking proper calibration files, thus extending the scientific utility of such data.

One of the key advantages of this approach is its ability to reduce calibration overheads in observational campaigns, particularly in situations where observing time is limited, or environmental conditions change rapidly. By removing the reliance on dedicated dark frames, observers can maximize the proportion of time spent on target acquisition, while still preserving high-quality data correction. Furthermore, the algorithm’s independence from specific hardware configurations suggests that it can be readily adapted to different CCD architectures and potentially to other detector types with analogous dark current characteristics.

While the method shows strong promise, certain limitations remain. The accuracy of dark current extraction depends on the statistical diversity of the image content and may be reduced in cases where the scene is dominated by extended uniform emission. Future work will focus on refining the separation algorithms to address such cases, exploring machine learning–based enhancements, and extending the approach to multi-channel detectors and time-series imaging. Additionally, integrating this method into automated data reduction pipelines could further streamline its application in large-scale surveys.

In summary, the presented dark current correction technique offers a practical, efficient, and versatile alternative to traditional calibration methods. By enabling the recovery of dark information directly from scientific images, it enhances data quality, expands the usability of archival observations, and optimizes the use of valuable observation time. This innovation has the potential to become a standard tool in CCD data processing, contributing to improved accuracy and efficiency in a wide range of scientific imaging applications.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning amidst Lifelong Non-Stationarity
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved remarkable success in complex decision-making domains, yet its robustness is challenged by lifelong non-stationarity, where the environment’s dynamics, reward structures, and state distributions evolve over extended time horizons. Conventional DRL methods, often trained under stationary assumptions, tend to suffer from catastrophic forgetting, brittle adaptation, and unstable performance when faced with such continual change. This paper investigates algorithmic principles and architectures that enable DRL agents to learn, adapt, and retain knowledge in perpetually shifting environments. We formalize lifelong non-stationarity as a spectrum of distributional shifts, encompassing gradual drifts, abrupt transitions, and recurring contexts. Building upon meta-learning, continual learning, and uncertainty-aware exploration, we propose a unified framework that integrates adaptive policy modulation with memory-based consolidation. Empirical evaluations across diverse non-stationary benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance gains, improved sample efficiency, and resilience to forgetting compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Our findings highlight the importance of explicitly modeling temporal evolution and suggest pathways toward truly lifelong autonomous agents capable of thriving in dynamic, real-world settings.
introduction:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved remarkable success across a range of domains, from mastering complex games to controlling high-dimensional robotic systems. These achievements have largely relied on the assumption that the environment’s dynamics and reward structures remain stationary or change only within narrow, well-defined bounds. In real-world applications, however, this assumption rarely holds. Agents deployed in open-ended, evolving environments must contend with continual shifts in dynamics, objectives, and constraints—a setting often referred to as lifelong non-stationarity. Such non-stationarity may arise from external factors, such as seasonal patterns, market fluctuations, or changing user preferences, as well as from internal factors, such as the agent’s own influence on the environment.

Lifelong non-stationarity poses fundamental challenges for DRL. Standard training procedures, which aim to converge to a fixed optimal policy, are ill-suited for environments in which the optimal policy itself changes over time. The agent must not only learn effective strategies for the present but also detect and adapt to shifts in the environment without catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge. Moreover, the temporal structure of non-stationarity can vary widely: changes may be abrupt or gradual, periodic or irregular, predictable or adversarial. This variability complicates the agent’s task of balancing exploitation of current knowledge with exploration to detect and respond to emerging conditions.

Existing approaches to non-stationary reinforcement learning have addressed aspects of this problem through mechanisms such as meta-learning, continual learning, and adaptive policy ensembles. Meta-learning seeks to endow agents with rapid adaptation capabilities, while continual learning aims to preserve performance across a sequence of tasks without destructive interference. Other lines of work introduce explicit change-point detection, context inference, or hierarchical control to manage adaptation. While these methods have demonstrated promise, they often target specific types of non-stationarity or assume access to privileged signals about task boundaries, limiting their applicability in truly lifelong, open-ended settings.

A deeper integration of these strategies, informed by the unique constraints of lifelong operation, is needed to advance DRL in non-stationary worlds. This entails developing representations that are both flexible enough to accommodate novel conditions and stable enough to preserve core competencies, devising learning algorithms that can calibrate their plasticity in response to the rate and magnitude of change, and incorporating mechanisms to anticipate and prepare for possible future shifts. Furthermore, evaluation protocols must reflect the longitudinal nature of the problem, assessing agents over extended sequences of evolving conditions rather than isolated episodes.

In this work, we investigate the challenges and opportunities of deep reinforcement learning in the presence of lifelong non-stationarity. We aim to formalize the problem, analyze existing approaches through this lens, and propose algorithmic innovations that enable robust, adaptive, and memory-efficient learning over an unbounded sequence of changing tasks. Our contributions seek to bridge the gap between the success of DRL in controlled benchmarks and the demands of persistent, real-world deployment.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the challenges and opportunities of applying deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in environments characterized by lifelong non-stationarity. Unlike stationary or episodically shifting domains, lifelong non-stationary settings present agents with a continual stream of evolving dynamics, reward structures, and task distributions. This requires not only robust function approximation but also mechanisms for continual adaptation without catastrophic forgetting. By surveying recent algorithmic developments and proposing a conceptual framework that integrates meta-learning, representation stability, and uncertainty-aware exploration, we have articulated a path toward more resilient lifelong learning agents.

Our analysis underscores that traditional DRL assumptions—such as ergodicity, fixed transition dynamics, and stable value targets—are fundamentally violated in lifelong non-stationary contexts. Consequently, methodological innovations must explicitly account for temporal drift in both environment statistics and optimal policies. Techniques such as modular architectures, dynamic memory systems, and regularization-based consolidation offer partial solutions but remain insufficient in isolation. We argue that a unified approach combining rapid context inference with long-term knowledge retention is essential for scalable adaptability.

Furthermore, we have emphasized the importance of evaluation protocols that reflect the open-ended nature of lifelong learning. Benchmarks should incorporate gradual and abrupt shifts, recurring tasks, and unforeseen variations, enabling a more rigorous assessment of an agent’s capacity to generalize and recover. The interplay between sample efficiency, stability, and adaptability emerges as a key axis along which future research must optimize.

In conclusion, deep reinforcement learning amidst lifelong non-stationarity demands a paradigm shift from static-policy optimization toward continual, context-aware decision-making. Progress will hinge on bridging insights from continual learning, meta-reinforcement learning, and robust control, guided by benchmarks that faithfully capture the complexity of real-world change. By advancing algorithms that can learn, remember, and adapt indefinitely, we move closer to the vision of autonomous agents capable of thriving in perpetually evolving environments.

title: Headline Diagnosis: Manipulation of Content Farm Headlines
abstract: This paper examines the rhetorical strategies and linguistic manipulations employed in content farm headlines to maximize click-through rates. By analyzing a corpus of headlines from prominent content farm platforms, the study identifies patterns of lexical ambiguity, emotional priming, and curiosity gaps. The findings reveal deliberate use of incomplete information, hyperbolic phrasing, and personalization cues to exploit cognitive biases and drive engagement. The paper situates these practices within broader discussions of digital media economics and audience manipulation, highlighting their implications for information quality, reader autonomy, and the ethics of online publishing in an algorithmically-driven attention economy.
introduction:
In the contemporary digital information ecosystem, headlines function as critical gateways between content producers and audiences, shaping the decision to engage with an article. Content farms—websites that produce large volumes of low-cost, search-engine-optimized material—have become adept at exploiting headline construction to maximize clicks and ad revenue. These platforms frequently prioritize attention-grabbing phrasing over informational accuracy, employing techniques such as sensationalism, ambiguity, and emotional triggers. While such strategies are not unique to content farms, their industrialized scale and algorithm-driven optimization amplify their influence on news consumption and public discourse.  

The manipulation of headlines by content farms raises significant concerns regarding information quality, trust in media, and the cultivation of informed citizenry. Prior research has examined clickbait and other persuasive headline structures, but less attention has been devoted to understanding the specific linguistic and cognitive mechanisms deployed by content farms. This gap is particularly relevant given the role of algorithmic curation and social media sharing in accelerating the reach of misleading or manipulative headlines.  

By systematically analyzing the rhetorical patterns, semantic framing, and psychological appeals embedded in content farm headlines, this study seeks to illuminate how such manipulations operate and to what extent they distort reader expectations. Understanding these dynamics is essential for developing literacy tools, policy responses, and platform interventions aimed at mitigating the societal impact of low-quality, high-visibility digital content.
conclusion:
This study has examined the ways in which content farm headlines deploy linguistic, structural, and affective strategies to manipulate reader attention and drive engagement, often at the expense of informational clarity and journalistic integrity. By analyzing a corpus of such headlines, we have shown that their rhetorical design is not merely incidental but foundational to their economic and operational model. Techniques such as forward referencing, strategic vagueness, emotional intensification, and the exploitation of curiosity gaps work synergistically to encourage clicks, prolong dwell time, and facilitate algorithmic amplification. These strategies align with broader patterns in attention economy media, yet their concentration and formulaic recurrence within content farm output reveal a deliberate and optimized system of manipulation.

The implications of these findings are twofold. First, the prevalence of such headlines contributes to the erosion of trust in digital news ecosystems, as audiences become increasingly aware of sensationalistic and misleading framing. Second, the measurable success of these strategies in capturing attention suggests that similar manipulative practices may diffuse into more reputable outlets pressured by the same economic incentives. This blurring of boundaries between content farm material and mainstream digital journalism presents a challenge for media literacy, regulatory frameworks, and automated content moderation systems.

While our analysis has focused on headline-level manipulation, the broader discursive and cognitive consequences warrant further investigation. Future research should explore how repeated exposure to such attention-optimizing framings affects readers’ critical engagement, recall accuracy, and susceptibility to misinformation. Additionally, cross-linguistic comparisons could illuminate whether these manipulative strategies are culturally specific or globally transferable.

Ultimately, the manipulation of headlines by content farms is symptomatic of a media environment in which the monetization of attention supersedes the ethical imperatives of accurate, transparent communication. Addressing this phenomenon requires not only technical interventions—such as platform-level demotion of clickbait—but also educational efforts to strengthen audience resilience against manipulative cues. By situating content farm headlines within the broader dynamics of the attention economy, this study underscores the urgency of developing sustainable models for digital content that prioritize informational value over exploitative engagement tactics. The challenge ahead lies in balancing the commercial realities of online publishing with the societal need for trustworthy and meaningful communication.

title: Expressive Stream Reasoning with Laser
abstract: We present LASER, a novel framework for expressive stream reasoning that unifies complex event processing with rich temporal logic capabilities. LASER enables the continuous evaluation of high-level, declarative rules over rapidly evolving data streams, supporting both short- and long-term temporal dependencies. Unlike traditional stream reasoning systems that are limited to fixed temporal windows or simple patterns, LASER employs an incremental evaluation algorithm grounded in first-order temporal logic, allowing it to capture intricate relationships across events with varying time granularities. The system supports dynamic rule updates, efficient memory management, and scalable execution over high-throughput streams. We formally define LASER’s semantics, prove correctness of its evaluation strategy, and analyze its computational complexity. An extensive empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that LASER achieves low-latency reasoning while maintaining expressiveness, outperforming existing approaches in both flexibility and performance. This work advances the state of the art in real-time reasoning over complex, heterogeneous data streams.
introduction:
The proliferation of dynamic, heterogeneous, and continuously evolving data sources has stimulated a growing interest in stream reasoning, a research area at the intersection of Semantic Web, Knowledge Representation, and Stream Processing. Modern applications in domains such as the Internet of Things (IoT), smart cities, real-time monitoring, and financial analytics demand the ability to process and reason over high-velocity data streams in a timely and semantically rich manner. These applications require not only the efficient handling of transient, time-stamped information but also the capacity to integrate such information with background knowledge and to derive conclusions that may evolve as new data arrives. The challenge is to reconcile the expressiveness of logical formalisms with the computational constraints imposed by streaming environments.

Stream reasoning extends traditional reasoning paradigms by explicitly incorporating the temporal dimension and by operating incrementally over data that is potentially unbounded. While classical reasoning approaches over static datasets can leverage global availability of all relevant facts, stream reasoning must cope with partial, transient windows of data, where information may expire and conclusions must be revised accordingly. This shift in setting introduces new challenges for knowledge representation, such as defining suitable temporal models, managing evolving contexts, and ensuring that reasoning tasks remain tractable in the face of continuous updates.

Over the past decade, a variety of frameworks for stream reasoning have been proposed, including extensions of Description Logics, rule-based systems, and temporal query languages. Most existing approaches, however, strike a compromise between expressiveness and efficiency, often limiting the reasoning capabilities to ensure real-time performance. For example, some systems support only conjunctive queries over sliding windows of RDF streams, thereby restricting the temporal and logical constructs available to the user. While such restrictions facilitate efficient evaluation, they limit the range of applications that can be supported, particularly in settings where complex temporal patterns, rich ontological constraints, or non-monotonic reasoning are required.

The Laser system (Logical sAfe Stream rEasoning) has emerged as a promising platform that aims to balance expressive power with scalability in stream reasoning. Designed to operate over RDF streams enriched with ontological knowledge, Laser supports reasoning with window operators, temporal modalities, and safe rule-based inference. Its architecture is grounded in an incremental evaluation strategy that avoids recomputation from scratch, thereby enabling low-latency responses while maintaining a high level of expressiveness. Laser’s rule language allows users to define complex patterns over streaming data, combining temporal and logical constructs in a unified framework. This capability makes it suitable for advanced applications such as real-time anomaly detection, context-aware decision making, and monitoring of compliance with temporal policies.

Nevertheless, the pursuit of expressive stream reasoning raises several open research questions. How can we ensure that the reasoning process remains decidable and efficient in the presence of rich temporal constructs and ontological axioms? What are the trade-offs between the size of the reasoning window, the complexity of the rule language, and the achievable throughput? How can incremental reasoning be optimized to minimize memory usage and computational overhead without sacrificing expressiveness? These questions are particularly pertinent as the scale and heterogeneity of streaming data continue to grow.

In this paper, we investigate expressive stream reasoning with Laser, focusing on its ability to support complex reasoning tasks over high-velocity RDF streams. We present the underlying formalism, discuss the mechanisms for incremental evaluation, and analyze the system’s performance under various configurations. Our contributions are threefold: (i) we extend the theoretical foundations of Laser’s rule language to capture a broader class of temporal reasoning patterns; (ii) we provide an empirical evaluation demonstrating the system’s scalability and responsiveness in realistic streaming scenarios; and (iii) we identify key design considerations for balancing expressiveness and efficiency, offering guidelines for the development of future stream reasoning systems. Through this work, we aim to advance the state of the art in stream reasoning and to show that high expressiveness and practical performance need not be mutually exclusive in real-time semantic applications.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented an investigation into expressive stream reasoning with Laser, a system designed to combine the efficiency of stream processing with the expressive power of complex reasoning over dynamic data. Our study has demonstrated that it is possible to reconcile the competing demands of high-throughput, low-latency processing and the need for rich, temporally aware logical inference. By extending the underlying reasoning formalism to accommodate both temporal operators and non-monotonic constructs, Laser enables applications to operate effectively in environments where data is both time-sensitive and semantically complex.

Through formalisation, we have shown how Laser’s reasoning model supports a broad range of use cases, from real-time monitoring and anomaly detection to decision support in rapidly evolving scenarios. The adoption of well-defined semantics ensures that reasoning outcomes remain predictable and verifiable, even in the presence of incomplete or evolving information. This is particularly relevant for domains such as IoT, financial analytics, and autonomous systems, where the interplay between continuous data streams and sophisticated decision rules is critical.

Our evaluation, using both synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets, indicates that Laser achieves competitive performance while preserving expressive capabilities that surpass those of many existing stream reasoning systems. The results highlight that careful design of incremental evaluation mechanisms, combined with optimisations such as windowed materialisation and selective recomputation, can significantly mitigate the computational costs traditionally associated with expressive logical reasoning. Moreover, the modular architecture of Laser allows for flexible integration with diverse data sources and stream processing infrastructures, broadening its applicability.

Several important insights emerge from this study. First, expressiveness in stream reasoning need not be sacrificed for scalability; instead, a principled balance can be achieved through targeted optimisation and incremental reasoning strategies. Second, the explicit treatment of temporal dynamics within the logical framework not only enhances expressiveness but also provides a natural means to manage the inherent uncertainty and volatility of streaming data. Finally, our findings suggest that further advances in expressive stream reasoning will benefit from deeper integration with learning-based methods, enabling adaptive reasoning that can evolve with the data.

Looking forward, we see multiple avenues for continuing this research. Extending Laser to harness distributed and heterogeneous compute environments could further enhance scalability. Investigating hybrid reasoning paradigms that combine symbolic and statistical techniques may open up new opportunities for robust, context-aware decision-making in complex, dynamic domains. Additionally, exploring richer forms of user interaction, such as declarative query reformulation and explanation facilities, could make expressive stream reasoning more accessible to non-expert users.

In summary, this work confirms the feasibility and value of expressive reasoning in high-velocity data contexts, and positions Laser as a step toward a new generation of reasoning systems capable of operating effectively in the fast-moving, information-rich environments of the future.

title: First muon anti-neutrino disappearance oscillation results from T2K
abstract: We present the first muon anti-neutrino disappearance oscillation results from the T2K experiment. A beam of muon anti-neutrinos was produced at J-PARC and observed at Super-Kamiokande, 295 km away. Data correspond to an exposure of \(4.01\times10^{20}\) protons on target. The observed deficit is consistent with oscillations, yielding parameters compatible with previous neutrino-mode measurements and providing new constraints on anti-neutrino oscillation phenomena.
introduction:
Neutrino oscillations, a quantum mechanical phenomenon in which neutrinos change flavour as they propagate, provide compelling evidence for non-zero neutrino masses and mixing. Over the past two decades, a series of solar, atmospheric, reactor, and accelerator-based experiments have established a consistent three-flavour oscillation framework, characterised by the Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata (PMNS) matrix. Precision measurements of the oscillation parameters, including the mixing angles, mass-squared differences, and the CP-violating phase, remain central goals in contemporary neutrino physics. In particular, the study of muon neutrino (νμ) and muon anti-neutrino (\(\bar{\nu}_\mu\)) disappearance has played a crucial role in constraining the atmospheric mass-squared splitting \(|\Delta m_{32}^2|\) and the mixing angle \(\theta_{23}\).

While νμ disappearance has been measured with high precision by multiple experiments, corresponding measurements with \(\bar{\nu}_\mu\) beams are comparatively less precise. Such measurements are of particular interest because they provide an independent test of the three-flavour oscillation framework and enable direct searches for potential differences between neutrino and anti-neutrino oscillation parameters, which could indicate new physics beyond the Standard Model, such as CPT violation or non-standard interactions. In the standard framework, oscillations of neutrinos and anti-neutrinos are expected to be identical in vacuum, apart from matter effects that can introduce small differences over long baselines. Therefore, a precise comparison between νμ and \(\bar{\nu}_\mu\) disappearance is a sensitive probe of these effects.

The Tokai to Kamioka (T2K) experiment is a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment in Japan, designed to measure both appearance and disappearance channels for neutrinos and anti-neutrinos. A high-intensity beam of predominantly muon neutrinos or muon anti-neutrinos is produced at the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex (J-PARC) in Tokai, directed 2.5° off-axis towards the Super-Kamiokande (SK) water Cherenkov detector, located 295 km away in Kamioka. The off-axis configuration results in a narrow-band beam peaked near the first oscillation maximum, optimising sensitivity to oscillation parameters. Near detectors located 280 m from the production target are used to characterise the unoscillated beam and constrain flux and cross-section systematics.

In this work, we present the first \(\bar{\nu}_\mu\) disappearance oscillation results from T2K, using data collected in anti-neutrino mode. The analysis yields measurements of \(\sin^2(\bar{\theta}_{23})\) and \(|\Delta \bar{m}_{32}^2|\), which are compared to the corresponding νμ results to test the consistency of neutrino and anti-neutrino oscillations within the three-flavour paradigm.
conclusion: The first muon anti-neutrino disappearance oscillation results from the T2K experiment have been presented, providing a significant step toward precise measurements of oscillation parameters in the anti-neutrino sector. Using the anti-neutrino beam configuration and data collected over the analyzed run periods, the observed deficit of muon anti-neutrinos at the far detector is consistent with the hypothesis of neutrino oscillations. The extracted values of the oscillation parameters, |Δm²₃₂| and sin²θ₂₃, agree within uncertainties with those obtained from corresponding muon neutrino disappearance measurements, supporting the CPT invariance of neutrino oscillations. The precision achieved is currently limited by statistical uncertainties, but systematic effects have been carefully evaluated and found to be subdominant. These results complement previous measurements from other experiments and contribute to a global picture of neutrino and anti-neutrino oscillations. Future data-taking with increased beam power and exposure will allow T2K to improve the statistical precision and to probe possible differences between neutrino and anti-neutrino oscillations with greater sensitivity. In combination with appearance measurements, these studies will enhance constraints on the PMNS mixing framework and potential CP violation in the lepton sector, addressing fundamental questions about the origin of matter-antimatter asymmetry in the Universe.

title: Non-LTE time-dependent spectroscopic modelling of type II-plateau supernovae from the photospheric to the nebular phase: case study for 15 and 25Msun progenitor stars
abstract: We present time-dependent, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer simulations of Type II-Plateau (II-P) supernovae, following the spectral evolution from the early photospheric phase through to the nebular stage. Using progenitor models with initial masses of 15 and 25 M⊙ evolved to core collapse, we compute post-explosion ejecta structures with detailed hydrodynamics and subsequently model the radiation transport with full non-LTE treatment of ionization and excitation, including time-dependent terms in the statistical and radiative equilibrium equations. Our calculations cover the first ∼500 days after explosion, enabling a continuous description of the transition from optically thick to optically thin conditions. We investigate the influence of progenitor mass, ejecta density structure, and composition on the emergent spectral energy distribution and on the evolution of key spectroscopic features such as the Balmer series, Fe II multiplets, and forbidden emission lines of O, Ca, and Fe in the nebular phase. In the high-mass (25 M⊙) model, enhanced metal line blanketing and stronger nebular [O I] λ6300,6364 emission are found, reflecting the larger oxygen core and metal yields, while the lower-mass (15 M⊙) model exhibits narrower lines and reduced forbidden-line luminosity. We demonstrate that time-dependent ionization, particularly of hydrogen and metals, is essential to reproduce the observed delayed recombination and line strengths during the plateau and early nebular phases, and that steady-state assumptions lead to systematic discrepancies in both continuum shape and line profiles. Our results highlight the diagnostic potential of late-time spectra for constraining progenitor mass and explosion properties, and they underscore the necessity of a unified, time-dependent non-LTE approach to accurately model the spectroscopic evolution of Type II-P supernovae from early times to the nebular regime.
introduction:
Type II-plateau (II-P) supernovae are the most common explosions of massive stars, arising from red supergiant progenitors that retain substantial hydrogen envelopes at the time of collapse. Their characteristic plateau in the optical light curve, lasting roughly 100 days, reflects the recombination of hydrogen in the expanding ejecta. The interpretation of their spectra during the photospheric and nebular phases provides critical constraints on progenitor properties, explosion physics, and nucleosynthesis yields. However, accurate modelling of these spectra requires a detailed treatment of the complex non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) conditions that prevail in the low-density, rapidly expanding environment.  

While steady-state spectral models have been widely employed, the time-dependent evolution of level populations and ionisation states can significantly affect line strengths, ionisation balances, and continuum formation, particularly during the transition from the photospheric to the nebular phase. Incorporating time dependence within a non-LTE framework is therefore essential for a consistent interpretation of observed spectra over the entire evolution of the supernova.  

In this work, we present non-LTE, time-dependent radiative-transfer simulations for Type II-P supernovae originating from 15 M⊙ and 25 M⊙ progenitors. These progenitors span a representative range of masses for red supergiant explosions and allow us to study how initial stellar mass influences the spectroscopic evolution. We follow the ejecta from early photospheric epochs, through the plateau phase, into the nebular regime, where the inner metal-rich layers become visible. By comparing synthetic spectra with observed trends, we aim to elucidate the interplay between progenitor structure, ejecta dynamics, and radiative processes that shape the spectral signatures of Type II-P supernovae.
conclusion:
We have presented a comprehensive set of non-LTE, time-dependent radiative transfer simulations for Type II-plateau supernovae, following the evolution from the photospheric to the nebular phase for progenitors of 15 and 25 M⊙. By coupling detailed non-LTE physics with time-dependent terms in the statistical and radiative equilibrium equations, our models capture the progressive transition from optically thick, continuum-dominated spectra to optically thin, line-dominated emission. The inclusion of time dependence proves essential for reproducing the persistence of ionisation at late times, the delayed recombination in the hydrogen envelope, and the accurate modelling of Balmer line strengths during the plateau.  

The comparison between the two progenitor masses reveals systematic differences in luminosity evolution, colour temperature, and spectral line profiles, arising from distinct ejecta masses, kinetic energies, and chemical yields. In particular, the more massive progenitor maintains higher ionisation in the nebular phase, leading to stronger metal lines and slower decline rates in key diagnostics. Our results highlight the sensitivity of late-time spectra to both progenitor structure and explosion energy, offering a pathway to constraining progenitor properties from spectroscopic monitoring.  

This study demonstrates that non-LTE time-dependent modelling is indispensable for interpreting Type II-P spectra across all phases, avoiding systematic biases inherent in steady-state assumptions. Future work will extend these simulations to a broader grid of progenitor masses, metallicities, and explosion energies, and will incorporate 3D effects to assess asymmetry signatures. Such advances will strengthen the diagnostic power of supernova spectroscopy, enabling more precise connections between observed transients and their massive star progenitors.

title: Variational Autoencoders for Generative Modelling of Water Cherenkov Detectors
abstract: We present a variational autoencoder (VAE) framework for generative modelling of water Cherenkov detector responses to particle interactions. The model learns a low-dimensional latent representation from simulated detector data, enabling realistic event generation and efficient data augmentation. Our approach captures spatial and temporal hit distributions, preserving key physics features. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate high fidelity to Monte Carlo simulations, indicating the potential of VAEs to accelerate simulation pipelines and support analysis in large-scale neutrino and astroparticle experiments.
introduction:
Water Cherenkov detectors (WCDs) are among the most widely used instruments in experimental astroparticle physics for the detection of high-energy particles such as cosmic rays and neutrinos. By capturing the Cherenkov radiation emitted when relativistic charged particles traverse water, these detectors enable precise reconstruction of particle properties, including energy, arrival direction, and identity. Large-scale facilities such as Super-Kamiokande and the Pierre Auger Observatory rely on WCDs to probe fundamental questions in astrophysics, particle physics, and cosmology. However, the accurate reconstruction and interpretation of detector signals require extensive modelling of the detector response, which is typically achieved through detailed Monte Carlo (MC) simulations. While MC techniques offer high fidelity, they are computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially when simulating large datasets for rare-event searches or parameter scans.

Recent advances in machine learning, particularly in deep generative models, offer promising alternatives for accelerating detector simulations without sacrificing accuracy. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have emerged as a powerful framework for learning complex, high-dimensional data distributions. By encoding input data into a compact latent space and decoding it back to the original domain, VAEs can capture underlying statistical structures and generate new, realistic samples. Their probabilistic formulation allows for both reconstruction and sampling, making them well-suited for tasks that require generating synthetic data consistent with physical measurements.

In the context of water Cherenkov detectors, VAEs can be trained on simulated or experimental data to learn the mapping between particle-level inputs and detector-level observables. Once trained, they can rapidly generate realistic detector responses for arbitrary input conditions, significantly reducing computational requirements compared to traditional MC simulations. Furthermore, the latent space learned by the VAE may provide insights into the underlying physics by revealing low-dimensional representations of complex detector signals.

Despite the potential, the application of VAEs to WCD generative modelling remains relatively unexplored. Challenges include ensuring physical fidelity in generated samples, handling the stochastic nature of particle interactions, and incorporating domain-specific constraints into the learning process. Addressing these issues is essential for deploying VAEs as reliable surrogates for full detector simulations in physics analyses.

This work investigates the feasibility of using variational autoencoders for generative modelling of water Cherenkov detector responses. We present an architecture tailored to the spatial and temporal characteristics of WCD data, assess its performance against high-fidelity MC simulations, and evaluate its ability to generalise across different particle types and energies. Our results demonstrate that VAEs can achieve substantial computational speedups while maintaining accuracy, opening the door to their integration into large-scale astroparticle physics workflows.
conclusion: In this study, we investigated the application of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) for generative modelling of data from Water Cherenkov Detectors. By learning a compact latent representation of simulated detector responses, the VAE framework was able to reproduce key spatial and temporal features of Cherenkov light patterns with high fidelity. Our results demonstrate that VAEs can capture both the underlying physics and the statistical fluctuations inherent in detector signals, offering a promising approach for fast simulation and data augmentation. Compared to traditional Monte Carlo methods, the trained models provide significant reductions in computational cost while maintaining physically meaningful outputs. Furthermore, the latent space structure enables potential applications in event classification, anomaly detection, and detector calibration. While this work focused on simulated datasets, future research will address training with experimental data, incorporating domain adaptation techniques, and exploring more advanced generative architectures.
