introduction: Numerical integration in high dimensions is a central task in scientific computing, with applications ranging from uncertainty quantification to computational finance. Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) methods, and in particular lattice rules, are widely used for their ability to achieve higher convergence rates than standard Monte Carlo methods when the integrand possesses sufficient smoothness. Classical lattice rules are naturally suited to periodic functions, as their construction exploits Fourier analysis on the unit cube with periodic boundary conditions. However, in many practical problems the integrands are non-periodic, and the direct application of lattice rules may lead to a significant loss of accuracy. Vertex modified lattice rules provide a remedy by adjusting the weights associated with points near the boundary of the integration domain, thereby improving performance for non-periodic functions. In this paper, we analyse such vertex modifications in the setting of a non-periodic Sobolev space of smoothness one. We derive error bounds, investigate the dependence on the generating vector, and compare the performance with unmodified lattice rules through both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the performance and theoretical properties of vertex modified lattice rules for numerical integration in a non-periodic Sobolev space of functions with square-integrable mixed first derivatives. Building on the classical framework of lattice rules, the vertex modification was introduced to improve the treatment of boundary behaviour and to extend the applicability of these rules beyond periodic settings. Our analysis has provided explicit error bounds in terms of the generating vector and the smoothness parameters, highlighting the role of the vertex corrections in reducing the dominant boundary contributions to the worst-case error.

We have shown that, under appropriate choices of the generating vector, vertex modified lattice rules achieve the same asymptotic convergence rate as standard lattice rules in periodic spaces, while maintaining robustness in the non-periodic case. The theoretical results were supported by a decomposition of the error into periodic and non-periodic components, allowing a precise quantification of the improvement due to the modification. In particular, we identified conditions under which the error constants remain bounded independently of the dimension, thereby demonstrating the potential of these rules for high-dimensional integration.

Furthermore, the analysis revealed a close connection between the vertex modification and certain symmetrization techniques, suggesting that the modification can be interpreted as a means of restoring, in part, the structural advantages enjoyed in the periodic setting. This perspective may be useful for guiding future developments and for constructing further generalisations tailored to specific function spaces.

Overall, the present study establishes vertex modified lattice rules as an effective and theoretically sound approach for non-periodic Sobolev spaces, bridging the gap between the periodic theory and practical non-periodic applications. Future work will include the optimisation of generating vectors with respect to the derived bounds, the extension of the present analysis to higher-order smoothness spaces, and the exploration of hybrid methods that combine vertex modification with other boundary correction strategies.

title: New lower bounds for the Estrada and Signless Laplacian Estrada Index of a Graph
abstract: In this paper, we establish novel lower bounds for the Estrada index and the signless Laplacian Estrada index of a simple graph, expressed in terms of basic structural parameters. Our results improve upon previously known bounds and offer sharper estimates for various classes of graphs. Several examples are provided to illustrate the tightness of the proposed bounds. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of spectral graph invariants and their relationships with graph topology.
introduction:
The study of spectral graph invariants has been a central theme in algebraic graph theory due to their deep connections to structural properties of graphs and their wide range of applications in chemistry, physics, and network science. Among these invariants, the Estrada index has attracted considerable attention over the past two decades. For a simple graph \( G \) with \( n \) vertices and adjacency matrix \( A \), the Estrada index is defined as  
\[
EE(G) = \sum_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda_i},
\]  
where \( \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n \) are the eigenvalues of \( A \). This index was originally introduced by Ernesto Estrada in the context of molecular chemistry as a measure related to the degree of folding of polymeric molecules, and it has since found applications in quantifying subgraph centrality in complex networks, characterizing graph robustness, and modelling communicability in social and biological systems.

Closely related to the Estrada index is the *signless Laplacian Estrada index* (SLEE), defined for the signless Laplacian matrix \( Q = D + A \), where \( D \) is the diagonal degree matrix of \( G \). If \( q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n \) are the eigenvalues of \( Q \), then  
\[
SLEE(G) = \sum_{i=1}^n e^{q_i}.
\]  
The signless Laplacian and its spectrum have been extensively studied, as they encode important information about graph connectivity, bipartiteness, and structural balance. The SLEE extends the utility of the Estrada-type measures to spectral parameters that arise naturally in extremal and combinatorial problems.

One recurring theme in the study of these indices is the derivation of bounds—both upper and lower—that relate them to other fundamental graph parameters such as order, size, degree sequence, spectral radius, or energy. Upper bounds are often motivated by extremal structure identification, while lower bounds serve as guarantees of a minimal communicability or structural “cohesion” inherent to the graph. Lower bounds for the Estrada index have been obtained in various forms, for instance, in terms of the largest eigenvalue or the number of edges, often via inequalities such as Jensen’s or by exploiting convexity of the exponential function. Similar approaches have been applied to the SLEE, though its distinct spectral nature requires tailored arguments.

Despite the progress, there remains room for improvement in the known lower bounds, both in sharpness and in generality. Tighter bounds not only refine our theoretical understanding but also enhance the applicability of these indices in practical settings where exact computation is infeasible for large networks. In particular, bounds that are expressible directly in terms of accessible graph invariants are of high interest for computational efficiency and interpretability.

In this work, we present new lower bounds for both the Estrada index and the signless Laplacian Estrada index of a graph. Our results improve upon existing estimates by leveraging refined spectral inequalities and structural insights. We compare our bounds with known results through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples, demonstrating cases where our approach yields strictly better estimates. These contributions advance the quantitative theory of Estrada-type indices and offer new tools for their application in the analysis of complex networks.
conclusion:
In this work, we have established novel lower bounds for both the Estrada index and the signless Laplacian Estrada index of a graph, expressed in terms of easily computable graph parameters. By refining existing techniques and introducing new analytical inequalities for the exponential of eigenvalues, we have derived bounds that improve upon several previously known results. The proposed bounds are applicable to a wide class of graphs and can be evaluated without requiring full spectral information, which enhances their practical usefulness for large-scale networks.

Our results contribute to the growing body of research connecting spectral graph invariants with structural characteristics, offering sharper estimates that may serve as tools for further theoretical investigations. In particular, the bounds derived here may be applied in the study of network robustness, chemical graph theory, and complex systems analysis, where Estrada-type indices have found significant applications.

Future work could focus on extending these techniques to other graph matrices such as the normalized Laplacian, or to directed and weighted graphs, where analogous spectral measures are of interest. Additionally, exploring potential upper bounds complementary to the results obtained here would provide a more complete picture of the extremal behavior of these indices. The advancements presented here thus open new avenues for both theoretical development and applied spectral analysis in graph theory.

title: Rectangular Full Packed Format for Cholesky's Algorithm: Factorization, Solution and Inversion
abstract:
The Rectangular Full Packed Format (RFPF) is a compact storage scheme designed to efficiently represent symmetric or triangular matrices while preserving compatibility with Level 3 BLAS operations. This work investigates the application of RFPF to Cholesky’s algorithm, encompassing factorization, solution of linear systems, and matrix inversion. Traditional full and packed storage formats present trade-offs between memory use and computational performance: full storage facilitates high-performance computation at the cost of redundant storage, while packed storage minimizes memory requirements but hinders the use of optimized BLAS kernels. RFPF offers an attractive compromise, reducing storage by nearly half compared to full format, while enabling the use of high-performance routines without the complexity of specialized packed kernels.  

We present a detailed formulation of Cholesky factorization in RFPF, outlining the mapping of matrix elements to the format and the adaptation of computational steps to leverage existing BLAS and LAPACK functionalities. The proposed approach maintains numerical stability and accuracy equivalent to the full-storage implementation. Furthermore, we extend the methodology to the forward and backward substitution phases for solving symmetric positive definite systems, and to the computation of matrix inverses via the Cholesky factors in RFPF.  

Performance experiments on modern architectures demonstrate that RFPF-based implementations achieve execution times comparable to, or better than, their full-storage counterparts while reducing memory footprint by approximately 50%. The results confirm that RFPF provides both storage efficiency and computational effectiveness without requiring extensive reimplementation of existing high-performance kernels.  

This study highlights the practical advantages of adopting RFPF in numerical linear algebra software, particularly for large-scale problems where memory bandwidth and capacity are critical constraints. The findings suggest that RFPF is a viable and efficient alternative to traditional storage schemes for Cholesky’s algorithm and its associated operations.
introduction: Efficient storage and computation are critical in large-scale numerical linear algebra, where memory constraints and computational cost often dominate algorithmic design. The Rectangular Full Packed Format (RFPF) has emerged as a compact storage scheme for symmetric and triangular matrices, offering a balance between reduced memory footprint and computational efficiency. In particular, when applied to Cholesky’s algorithm, which decomposes a symmetric positive definite matrix into a triangular factor and its transpose, RFPF enables significant savings in storage while maintaining compatibility with high-performance BLAS and LAPACK routines. This format stores the relevant matrix elements in a rectangular two-dimensional array, avoiding the redundancy of full storage and the indexing complexity of conventional packed formats. Consequently, it facilitates vectorization and cache-friendly access patterns, improving runtime performance. This paper investigates the application of RFPF to three core computational tasks: Cholesky factorization, solution of linear systems, and matrix inversion. We present algorithmic adaptations, analyze their performance, and compare them with standard storage schemes. The results demonstrate that RFPF can achieve substantial efficiency gains without sacrificing numerical stability, making it a compelling choice for modern large-scale scientific and engineering computations.
conclusion: The Rectangular Full Packed format offers an efficient and storage-saving representation for symmetric matrices, enabling optimized implementation of Cholesky’s algorithm for factorization, solution, and inversion. By reducing memory requirements and improving computational performance, it enhances applicability in large-scale problems. The presented methods demonstrate both theoretical soundness and practical benefits, making RFP a valuable tool for high-performance numerical linear algebra in scientific and engineering applications.

title: Improving BDD Based Symbolic Model Checking with Isomorphism Exploiting Transition Relations
abstract: Symbolic model checking with Binary Decision Diagrams (BDDs) often suffers from state space explosion, where transition relation size becomes a major bottleneck. This paper presents a novel approach to improve BDD-based model checking by exploiting structural isomorphisms within transition relations. Many systems exhibit repeated substructures or symmetries in their transition systems, yet conventional methods fail to capitalize on these redundancies. Our method identifies isomorphic components in the transition relation and represents them using shared BDD fragments, thereby reducing memory usage and computational cost. We introduce efficient algorithms for detecting and mapping these isomorphisms, as well as techniques for integrating them into image computation. Experimental results on benchmark verification problems demonstrate significant reductions in BDD size and execution time, without loss of verification accuracy. This work shows that isomorphism exploitation can be a practical and scalable enhancement for BDD-based symbolic model checking.
introduction:
Symbolic model checking has emerged as a powerful technique for the formal verification of hardware and software systems, enabling the exhaustive exploration of state spaces that are often prohibitively large for explicit enumeration. A central representation in symbolic model checking is the Binary Decision Diagram (BDD), which compactly encodes Boolean functions such as sets of states and transition relations. Despite the efficiency gains offered by BDDs, the scalability of symbolic model checking remains a challenge, particularly for systems with vast and structurally complex state spaces. The size of the BDDs representing the transition relation can grow rapidly, leading to prohibitive memory and runtime requirements.

A well-established strategy for improving performance is to exploit structural properties of the system under verification. Many systems exhibit regularity, symmetry, or repeated subcomponents, particularly in domains such as replicated processors, network protocols, and parameterized hardware designs. In such cases, the transition relation often contains isomorphic substructures—parts of the system whose behavior is identical up to renaming of variables. Existing approaches to symmetry reduction have demonstrated that exploiting such isomorphisms can lead to significant reductions in the effective state space. However, these methods are typically applied at the state space level, requiring additional preprocessing or symmetry detection algorithms, and may not fully leverage the potential for compact BDD representation of the transition relation itself.

This work investigates an alternative and complementary approach: improving BDD-based symbolic model checking by directly exploiting isomorphisms in the transition relation. By identifying and reusing isomorphic BDD subgraphs, we can avoid redundant computations during image and preimage calculations, reduce the size of intermediate BDDs, and improve overall verification performance. The proposed method integrates isomorphism exploitation into the construction and manipulation of the transition relation, enabling transparent performance benefits without altering the high-level verification workflow. We evaluate the approach on benchmark systems with known structural regularities, demonstrating substantial reductions in memory usage and execution time. This work contributes to bridging the gap between symmetry-based reductions and BDD-level optimizations, providing a practical enhancement to symbolic model checking for systems with inherent structural isomorphism.
conclusion:
This work has presented an approach to improving BDD-based symbolic model checking by exploiting isomorphisms present in transition relations. By identifying structural similarities between subcomponents of the system model, we demonstrated how these symmetries can be leveraged to reduce the size of intermediate BDD representations and the cost of fixpoint computations. The proposed method systematically detects and reuses isomorphic transition relation fragments, avoiding redundant construction and manipulation of equivalent structures. Experimental results on a range of benchmarks indicate that this technique can significantly reduce memory consumption and, in many cases, improve verification time without compromising correctness.  

Our findings suggest that isomorphism exploitation is a promising complement to existing optimizations such as dynamic variable reordering and partitioned transition relations. The approach is particularly effective for systems with replicated components, parameterized architectures, or regular topologies, where isomorphic subrelations are abundant. While the present implementation focuses on exact structural matches, future work may extend the method to approximate isomorphisms or symmetry reductions at higher abstraction levels.  

Overall, the integration of isomorphism detection into symbolic model checking workflows enriches the toolbox of efficiency-enhancing techniques, enabling the verification of larger and more complex systems within practical resource limits. The results encourage further exploration of structural regularities in models as a means to push the scalability boundaries of formal verification tools.

title: Automatic Segmentation of Broadcast News Audio using Self Similarity Matrix
abstract: This paper presents an automatic segmentation approach for broadcast news audio based on the analysis of a self-similarity matrix (SSM). The proposed method exploits acoustic feature vectors extracted from the audio stream to construct the SSM, which captures temporal patterns and repetitions characteristic of news program structure. Change points are detected by identifying boundaries where similarity patterns shift significantly, corresponding to transitions between news stories, commercials, and other program segments. To enhance robustness, the method incorporates smoothing and adaptive thresholding to mitigate the effects of background noise and speaker variability. Experiments were conducted on a diverse broadcast news dataset, and segmentation performance was evaluated against manually annotated boundaries. Results demonstrate that the SSM-based approach achieves high accuracy, outperforming baseline segmentation methods in terms of precision and recall. The proposed framework is computationally efficient and can be integrated into real-time indexing and retrieval systems for broadcast media archives.
introduction:
The ever-growing availability of multimedia content has created an urgent demand for efficient tools that can process, analyze, and index large volumes of audio-visual data. Broadcast news, in particular, represents a significant portion of publicly accessible multimedia archives, offering a rich source of information for diverse applications, including media monitoring, content summarization, information retrieval, and automatic transcription. However, the continuous nature of broadcast news audio, often containing multiple stories, interviews, commercials, and musical interludes, poses a challenge for automated processing. Without reliable segmentation, subsequent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR), topic detection, and summarization risk decreased accuracy and efficiency. As a result, automatic segmentation of broadcast news audio into coherent, homogeneous segments has emerged as a critical preprocessing step in multimedia content analysis pipelines.

Segmentation in the context of broadcast news refers to the process of dividing a continuous audio stream into meaningful units, each corresponding to a distinct story, speaker, or program element. This segmentation enables more precise indexing and retrieval, improves the performance of downstream natural language processing (NLP) systems, and supports fine-grained content browsing. Traditional approaches to audio segmentation have relied on supervised learning methods or rule-based heuristics, making use of acoustic features such as energy, pitch, and spectral characteristics, as well as linguistic cues obtained from transcripts. While these methods have achieved moderate success, they often require extensive labeled data, language-specific resources, or prior knowledge of the broadcast structure, limiting their generalizability across domains and languages.

An increasingly promising direction for unsupervised segmentation lies in the use of self-similarity matrices (SSMs), a concept that has been widely applied in music structure analysis and speaker diarization. An SSM represents the pairwise similarity between every pair of frames or segments in an audio signal, often computed using feature vectors derived from short-time spectral analysis. By visualizing the SSM, one can observe block structures along the diagonal corresponding to homogeneous regions, with transitions between blocks indicating potential segment boundaries. This approach is attractive because it does not rely on labeled training data and can adapt to varying broadcast content styles, speaker identities, and background conditions.

In the context of broadcast news, the self-similarity matrix offers a means to capture the inherent repetition and homogeneity within stories, as well as to detect abrupt or gradual changes between different stories or program elements. For example, a news anchor’s voice and background studio noise may form a consistent acoustic pattern, while a switch to a field reporter or a commercial break would produce a noticeable change in the similarity structure. By systematically analyzing these patterns, it becomes possible to detect segment boundaries with high precision.

The use of SSM for broadcast news segmentation, however, is not without its challenges. Broadcast audio often contains overlapping speech, background music, and noise, which can obscure the acoustic cues necessary for boundary detection. Furthermore, the variability in story length and production style across different channels and regions introduces additional complexity. To address these challenges, robust feature extraction techniques, noise-resilient similarity measures, and effective post-processing strategies are required. Common features such as Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), perceptual linear prediction (PLP) coefficients, or more recently, embeddings derived from neural networks, can be employed to represent the audio signal in a way that highlights relevant similarities and differences. Similarity measures such as cosine similarity or correlation coefficients can then be applied to construct the SSM.

Once the SSM is computed, various techniques can be used to detect segment boundaries, including novelty detection functions based on convolution with checkerboard kernels, clustering approaches, or graph-based partitioning. The novelty score, which quantifies the degree of change between adjacent regions in the SSM, is particularly effective for locating boundaries in continuous audio streams. By smoothing and thresholding the novelty curve, one can identify points of significant change corresponding to story or speaker transitions.

This paper presents an unsupervised method for automatic segmentation of broadcast news audio using the self-similarity matrix as the central analytical tool. The proposed approach leverages robust acoustic features, an efficient similarity computation strategy, and a novelty-based boundary detection mechanism to achieve accurate segmentation without the need for labeled data. We evaluate the method on a diverse set of broadcast news recordings, demonstrating its effectiveness across different languages, production styles, and acoustic conditions. The results show that SSM-based segmentation provides a flexible and scalable solution for structuring broadcast news audio, paving the way for improved multimedia indexing, retrieval, and analysis.
conclusion: This work presented an approach for automatic segmentation of broadcast news audio based on the analysis of a self-similarity matrix. By exploiting acoustic feature correlations over time, the method effectively identified change points corresponding to topic or speaker transitions. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed technique achieves reliable segmentation without requiring prior transcription or manual intervention, making it suitable for large-scale audio indexing and retrieval. The approach proved robust to variations in speaker characteristics, background noise, and production styles typical of broadcast content. Future work will explore integrating semantic information and deep learning-based feature extraction to further enhance segmentation accuracy. Overall, the findings indicate that self-similarity analysis is a promising framework for structuring and organizing broadcast news archives efficiently.

title: Exact equation for classical many-particle systems in closed form: from mechanics to statistical thermodynamics
abstract: An exact, closed-form equation governing the evolution of classical many-particle systems is derived directly from Newtonian mechanics without statistical or probabilistic assumptions. The formulation incorporates inter-particle interactions and external fields, yielding a deterministic description valid for systems with arbitrary particle number and interaction range. By suitable transformations, the equation serves as a bridge from microscopic dynamics to macroscopic thermodynamic behavior, enabling a rigorous derivation of equilibrium and nonequilibrium statistical properties. This approach unifies mechanical and thermodynamic perspectives, offering a foundational framework for analyzing transport processes, relaxation phenomena, and collective effects in classical systems across diverse physical contexts.
introduction: The fundamental challenge of statistical thermodynamics lies in establishing a rigorous connection between the microscopic laws of classical mechanics and the macroscopic properties of many-particle systems. While the equations of motion for individual particles are well defined within Newtonian mechanics, the direct integration of these equations for systems with a large number of interacting particles is generally intractable. Traditional approaches, such as the Liouville equation, the BBGKY hierarchy, and kinetic theories, introduce approximations or statistical assumptions to bridge this gap. However, obtaining an exact, closed-form description that remains faithful to the underlying mechanics has remained elusive. In this work, we present an exact equation for classical many-particle systems that is derived directly from the principles of mechanics and expressed in a form suitable for statistical thermodynamic analysis. This formulation avoids uncontrolled approximations and provides a transparent link between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic observables. The resulting framework offers a unified perspective for understanding equilibrium and nonequilibrium phenomena, enabling the systematic derivation of thermodynamic relations from first principles and opening new avenues for analytical and computational studies of complex systems.
conclusion: In this work, an exact, closed-form equation for the evolution of classical many-particle systems has been derived directly from the fundamental laws of mechanics, without recourse to statistical hypotheses. The obtained relation unifies microscopic dynamics and macroscopic statistical descriptions by expressing the time evolution of the system in terms of measurable physical quantities. This approach provides a rigorous bridge from deterministic particle motion to the statistical thermodynamic framework, offering a transparent foundation for equilibrium and nonequilibrium phenomena. The result encompasses both conservative and dissipative interactions, thereby extending its applicability to a broad class of realistic systems. In the limit of large particle numbers, the formalism naturally reproduces established results of classical statistical mechanics while retaining exactness for finite systems. This framework not only clarifies the underlying assumptions of traditional approaches but also opens new avenues for analytical and computational studies of complex many-body dynamics. Future work will explore specific applications to transport processes and relaxation in interacting particle ensembles.

title: Tensors over Semirings for Latent-Variable Weighted Logic Programs
abstract: We extend weighted logic programming to support latent variables by introducing tensors over arbitrary commutative semirings as a unifying algebraic framework. In our approach, proof structures are annotated with multidimensional arrays whose entries encode semiring-valued weights, enabling joint reasoning about observed and hidden components. This generalization subsumes existing sum-product and max-product inference schemes, while accommodating richer algebraic operations for tasks such as parameter estimation, probabilistic inference, and optimization. We formalize tensor-semiring composition rules, provide semantics for latent-variable programs, and illustrate the expressiveness of the framework through examples from probabilistic grammars and graphical models. The approach supports modular, efficient implementation via semiring-based program transformations.
introduction:
Weighted logic programming (WLP) extends the classical logic programming paradigm by associating weights with facts and rules, enabling the modeling of quantitative information alongside symbolic inference. By parameterizing inference with an algebraic structure known as a semiring, WLP unifies a broad range of computational tasks under a single declarative framework. Different choices of semirings recover well-known algorithms: the Boolean semiring yields standard logical inference; the tropical (min-plus) semiring corresponds to shortest-path computations; and the probability semiring enables probabilistic inference. This algebraic abstraction has proven valuable in fields as diverse as natural language processing, probabilistic reasoning, and constraint satisfaction.

A fundamental advantage of the semiring-based perspective is its modularity: the logic program specifies the structure of the computation, while the semiring determines the nature of the weights and the operations used to combine them. This separation allows researchers and practitioners to repurpose the same program for different kinds of inference simply by changing the underlying semiring. However, many real-world applications involve uncertainty about hidden or latent structures, such as unobserved variables in probabilistic models or intermediate derivations in parsing. In these cases, the weights of interest are not directly observable; instead, they are aggregated over latent configurations. Capturing this process within the semiring framework requires more sophisticated algebraic machinery.

Tensors over semirings offer a natural and expressive means to address latent-variable inference in WLP. A tensor can be viewed as a multidimensional array whose entries are drawn from a semiring, supporting generalized notions of addition and multiplication. When the semiring encodes probabilities, a tensor can represent a joint distribution over multiple variables; with other semirings, it can capture analogous weighted relationships. The tensor formalism permits the compact representation of high-dimensional dependencies and the efficient computation of marginalizations and combinations, which are essential when summing over latent variables during inference.

Incorporating tensors into the semiring-weighted logic programming framework enables a uniform treatment of both structure and parameters. The rules of a logic program can be annotated with tensor-valued weights, where each tensor dimension corresponds to a logical variable or latent factor. Unification in the logic program induces index matching in the tensors, and the semiring operations dictate how tensor entries are combined. This perspective generalizes traditional WLP by allowing weights to carry rich, multidimensional information while preserving the declarative semantics of logic programming.

Latent-variable weighted logic programs arise naturally in many domains. In probabilistic grammars, nonterminal symbols may expand into sequences of symbols whose probabilities depend on hidden syntactic categories. In finite-state transducers for speech recognition, paths through the automaton may include unobserved states representing acoustic or linguistic features. In knowledge graph completion, reasoning paths may traverse unobserved relations or entities. In each case, the core computational task involves summing or otherwise aggregating over latent structures to produce observable predictions or likelihoods. The tensor-over-semirings approach provides a principled and compositional way to model these situations, capturing both the combinatorial structure of the derivations and the algebraic structure of the weights.

From a computational standpoint, adopting tensors over semirings raises questions about efficiency and scalability. Naïvely representing and manipulating high-order tensors may be infeasible for large-scale problems. Fortunately, the logic programming setting offers opportunities for implicit tensor representations, where tensor operations are carried out symbolically through program execution without materializing the full arrays. Moreover, advances in tensor factorization, low-rank approximation, and sparse representation can be adapted to the semiring setting, yielding practical algorithms for large models with latent variables. By aligning these techniques with the declarative semantics of WLP, it becomes possible to express complex models succinctly and execute them efficiently.

The integration of tensors into semiring-weighted logic programming also opens avenues for theoretical analysis. It connects the semantics of logic programs with multilinear algebra over abstract algebraic structures, suggesting new forms of algebraic reasoning about program behavior. For example, properties such as distributivity and associativity in the semiring translate into predictable transformations of tensor-valued weights, enabling correctness proofs for optimized inference strategies. Furthermore, this perspective facilitates the transfer of results between seemingly disparate areas, such as probabilistic graphical models, constraint satisfaction, and algebraic dynamic programming.

This paper develops a formal framework for tensors over semirings in the context of latent-variable weighted logic programs. We begin by reviewing the necessary background on semirings, tensors, and weighted logic programming. We then present a generalized semantics in which program clauses carry tensor-valued weights and unification triggers semiring-based tensor contractions. We show how common latent-variable models can be expressed in this framework, and we analyze the computational implications of various tensor representations. Finally, we demonstrate the approach on illustrative examples from probabilistic parsing and structured prediction, highlighting both the expressiveness and the efficiency benefits of the method. In doing so, we aim to provide both a unifying theory and practical tools for algebraic reasoning about latent-variable inference in declarative languages.
conclusion: We have presented a framework for interpreting latent-variable weighted logic programs through tensors over semirings, unifying algebraic and probabilistic perspectives. This approach generalizes existing inference methods, enabling systematic handling of hidden structure while preserving compositionality. By exploiting semiring polymorphism, our method accommodates diverse scoring schemes and supports efficient computation. The tensor formulation clarifies the interaction between logical structure and numerical evaluation, offering a principled basis for future extensions to richer models, scalable algorithms, and integration with modern machine learning architectures.

title: Temperature Dependent Reverse Recovery Characterization of SiC MOSFETs Body Diode forSwitching Loss Estimation In a Half-Bridge
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive experimental investigation of the temperature-dependent reverse recovery characteristics of the body diode in Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFETs, with the aim of improving switching loss estimation in half-bridge configurations. Measurements were conducted over a wide junction temperature range to capture variations in reverse recovery charge, peak reverse recovery current, and recovery time. A double-pulse test setup was employed to isolate diode behavior and quantify its contribution to total switching losses under realistic operating conditions. The influence of temperature on dynamic parameters was analyzed, revealing significant variations in reverse recovery energy that directly impact overall converter efficiency. The experimental results were incorporated into a refined loss estimation model, enabling more accurate prediction of switching losses across temperature ranges. This work highlights the importance of accounting for temperature effects in high-frequency, high-efficiency power converter design, and provides practical insights for optimizing SiC-based half-bridge operation in applications demanding robust performance over a wide thermal envelope.
introduction:
Silicon carbide (SiC) power MOSFETs are increasingly being adopted in high-performance power electronics due to their superior material properties compared to conventional silicon devices. Wide bandgap (WBG) characteristics, such as a wide energy bandgap (~3.26 eV for 4H-SiC), high critical electric field strength, and high thermal conductivity, enable SiC MOSFETs to operate at higher blocking voltages, higher switching frequencies, and elevated junction temperatures while maintaining lower conduction and switching losses. These advantages make them highly attractive for applications in electric vehicle traction inverters, renewable energy conversion systems, solid-state transformers, and aerospace power electronics, where efficiency, power density, and thermal robustness are critical.

In half-bridge converter topologies, which are widely used in these applications, each MOSFET incorporates an intrinsic body diode formed by the p–n junction between the p-body and the n-drift region. Although this body diode is not typically the primary conduction path in normal operation, it inevitably conducts during dead times between the switching of the two devices in a leg. In such scenarios, the reverse recovery behavior of the body diode becomes an important factor influencing switching losses, electromagnetic interference (EMI), and overall converter efficiency. When the diode transitions from forward conduction to reverse blocking, stored charge in the depletion and diffusion regions must be removed, causing a reverse recovery current. This current interacts with the voltage transition during the turn-on of the complementary switch, leading to additional energy dissipation and potential voltage overshoot.

SiC MOSFET body diodes exhibit reverse recovery characteristics that are fundamentally different from those of silicon devices. Due to the strong intrinsic properties of SiC, the stored charge is significantly lower, and the reverse recovery time is shorter. Nonetheless, the reverse recovery process is not negligible, particularly at elevated temperatures and under high current conditions. Moreover, unlike external SiC Schottky barrier diodes (SBDs), the body diode of a SiC MOSFET is a bipolar p–n junction device, which can suffer from bipolar degradation and shows temperature-dependent behavior due to minority carrier injection. Understanding its reverse recovery performance across a wide temperature range is therefore essential for accurate switching loss estimation and reliable converter design.

Temperature exerts a profound influence on the carrier dynamics within the body diode. As junction temperature increases, carrier lifetime and mobility change, impacting both the magnitude and duration of the reverse recovery current. This, in turn, affects the energy dissipated during the turn-on of the complementary MOSFET in a half-bridge configuration. Without accurate knowledge of these dependencies, designers may underestimate switching losses, leading to thermal management challenges, reduced efficiency, or even device overstress. While datasheets often provide typical values for reverse recovery charge (Q_rr) and time (t_rr) at a single reference temperature, they rarely capture the full temperature dependence under realistic operating conditions.

Existing literature has addressed various aspects of SiC MOSFET performance, including static and dynamic characteristics, gate drive optimization, and reliability concerns such as threshold voltage stability and body diode degradation. However, comprehensive experimental studies focusing on the temperature-dependent reverse recovery behavior of the intrinsic body diode in realistic half-bridge switching scenarios remain relatively scarce. In particular, there is limited work that directly links measured reverse recovery parameters over a broad temperature range to quantitative switching loss estimation in converter-relevant conditions.

Accurate switching loss estimation is critical for optimizing converter efficiency, selecting appropriate cooling solutions, and ensuring long-term device reliability. In the case of half-bridge circuits, the turn-on loss of the high-side or low-side device is strongly influenced by the reverse recovery of the complementary device’s body diode. This coupling means that the body diode’s temperature-dependent behavior must be characterized and incorporated into loss models to predict performance under varying load profiles and thermal states.

This work aims to fill this gap by experimentally characterizing the reverse recovery behavior of the body diode in commercially available SiC MOSFETs over a wide junction temperature range. Measurements are conducted under controlled double-pulse test conditions that replicate the commutation events in a half-bridge. Key reverse recovery parameters, including reverse recovery charge, peak reverse recovery current, and reverse recovery time, are extracted as functions of temperature and forward current. These results are then used to estimate the corresponding switching losses in a half-bridge configuration, providing designers with practical insights for thermal and efficiency optimization.

By systematically investigating the temperature dependence of the SiC MOSFET body diode’s reverse recovery, this study contributes to a more accurate and application-oriented understanding of WBG device performance. The findings enable more precise converter loss modeling, support informed device selection, and help in developing design strategies that fully exploit the advantages of SiC technology while mitigating potential drawbacks associated with intrinsic diode conduction.
conclusion: The experimental investigation presented has demonstrated the temperature-dependent reverse recovery characteristics of the SiC MOSFET body diode and their impact on switching loss estimation in a half-bridge configuration. Measurements across a wide temperature range revealed that while SiC devices exhibit significantly lower reverse recovery charge compared to their silicon counterparts, both the magnitude and dynamics of recovery are influenced by junction temperature. The results indicate that higher temperatures generally lead to reduced peak reverse recovery current but increased tail duration, affecting energy dissipation during turn-on. The proposed characterization approach enables accurate extraction of reverse recovery parameters, which can be directly employed in loss modeling for converter design and optimization. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating temperature variation into predictive models to ensure reliable efficiency estimation under real operating conditions. The work provides a foundation for refining thermal-aware switching loss calculations and highlights the advantages of SiC MOSFETs for high-frequency, high-efficiency power conversion applications, particularly where wide temperature excursions are expected.

title: The Magic of Logical Inference in Probabilistic Programming
abstract: Probabilistic programming integrates statistical modeling with the expressive power of general-purpose programming languages, enabling concise representation of complex uncertainty. At its core, logical inference provides a principled mechanism for deriving conclusions from probabilistic models, bridging symbolic reasoning and statistical computation. This paper explores the “magic” of logical inference within probabilistic programming, emphasizing its role in automating model construction, guiding efficient sampling, and enhancing interpretability. We examine how probabilistic logic frameworks unify discrete and continuous domains, allowing rich, compositional model specification. Furthermore, we analyze recent advances in inference algorithms that combine deductive reasoning with Bayesian updating, yielding scalable solutions for high-dimensional problems. Through theoretical discussion and illustrative case studies, we demonstrate that embedding logical inference into probabilistic programming significantly expands its applicability across artificial intelligence, scientific discovery, and decision-making under uncertainty.
introduction: Probabilistic programming has emerged as a powerful paradigm for expressing and solving complex statistical models, enabling practitioners to encode uncertainty directly into computational frameworks. By integrating probabilistic models with general-purpose programming languages, it allows concise specification of stochastic processes while leveraging automated inference algorithms to reason about latent variables. Within this context, logical inference plays a crucial role, bridging the gap between declarative model specification and efficient computation of posterior distributions. Logical inference mechanisms—rooted in formal reasoning and constraint satisfaction—enhance the expressiveness and interpretability of probabilistic programs, allowing domain knowledge to be incorporated in structured, rule-based forms. This synergy enables the construction of hybrid systems where symbolic constraints guide probabilistic reasoning, improving both efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, the integration of logical inference into probabilistic programming supports explainable AI, as inference steps can be traced and justified through formal logic. Recent advances in probabilistic inference algorithms, such as variational methods and Monte Carlo techniques, have further expanded the scope of such systems, making them applicable to domains ranging from natural language understanding to robotics. This paper explores the theoretical foundations, computational strategies, and practical implications of combining logical inference with probabilistic programming, highlighting its potential to transform the way we model and reason about uncertainty in complex systems.
conclusion:
This exploration of logical inference within the context of probabilistic programming has sought to illuminate both the theoretical elegance and the practical efficacy of integrating formal reasoning with uncertainty modeling. By bridging the gap between symbolic logic and probabilistic computation, we have demonstrated that the expressive power of probabilistic programming languages can be significantly enhanced, enabling them to address a broader class of problems that require nuanced representation of both structured knowledge and stochastic processes.

A central insight emerging from our discussion is that logical inference serves not merely as a computational tool, but as an organizing principle that shapes the design of probabilistic models. The disciplined structure of logical formalisms offers a means of encoding domain knowledge with clarity and precision, while probabilistic semantics allow for robust reasoning in the face of incomplete, noisy, or contradictory information. This synthesis mitigates the limitations inherent in purely logical or purely probabilistic approaches, producing systems that can both reason deductively and adapt inductively.

The examples and arguments presented suggest that this integration is not only theoretically compelling but also pragmatically advantageous. Applications ranging from natural language understanding to robotics, from decision-making under uncertainty to scientific discovery, can benefit from the combined strengths of symbolic representation and probabilistic inference. Furthermore, recent advances in inference algorithms, particularly those leveraging modern computational resources and approximate methods, have rendered the deployment of such hybrid models increasingly feasible at scale.

Nevertheless, the path forward entails several challenges. The computational complexity of probabilistic logical inference remains a barrier, especially as models grow in richness and scope. Balancing expressivity with tractability will require continued innovation in algorithm design, possibly drawing on techniques from constraint satisfaction, variational inference, and neural-symbolic integration. Moreover, careful attention must be paid to the interpretability of such models, ensuring that the transparency afforded by logical structure is preserved even as probabilistic components introduce layers of abstraction.

The “magic” of logical inference in probabilistic programming resides in its capacity to unify disparate modes of reasoning into a coherent framework that is both mathematically rigorous and practically useful. This magic is not mystical; it emerges from the deliberate and thoughtful integration of complementary paradigms. In recognizing the symbiotic relationship between logic and probability, we open the door to richer modeling idioms, more adaptive systems, and deeper insights into the nature of reasoning itself.

Future work should continue to investigate formal properties of these integrated systems, develop scalable inference techniques, and explore diverse application domains. As we refine the theory and practice of probabilistic programming infused with logical inference, we move closer to a vision of intelligent systems capable of reasoning with the depth, flexibility, and subtlety that complex real-world environments demand. In this convergence lies both the intellectual beauty and the transformative potential of the field.

title: Real-time Joint Tracking of a Hand Manipulating an Object from RGB-D Input
abstract: We present a real-time method for jointly tracking a human hand and a manipulated object from RGB-D input. Accurate tracking in such scenarios is challenging due to severe occlusions, complex hand–object interactions, and the high dimensionality of articulated motion. Our approach integrates a parametric hand model with a rigid object representation in a unified optimization framework, leveraging depth and color cues to robustly estimate their poses. We employ a discriminative–generative strategy: a convolutional network provides initial correspondences and segmentation, while an energy minimization step refines the full 3D configuration by enforcing temporal coherence, physical plausibility, and contact constraints. The system runs in real time on commodity hardware, enabling interactive applications. We evaluate our method on public benchmarks and newly captured sequences featuring diverse objects and manipulation tasks. Results demonstrate improved accuracy and stability compared to state-of-the-art single-entity trackers, particularly under severe occlusion. Our framework supports natural interaction in augmented reality and robotics, and can facilitate data acquisition for learning-based manipulation models.
introduction: Accurate real-time tracking of hand-object interactions is essential for applications in augmented reality, human-computer interaction, and robotic manipulation. While significant progress has been made in hand pose estimation and object tracking separately, jointly tracking both remains challenging due to severe mutual occlusions, complex hand articulation, and the dynamic interaction between hand and object. RGB-D sensors provide complementary color and depth information, enabling richer geometric and appearance cues for pose estimation. However, existing methods often suffer from reduced accuracy or high computational cost when handling fast motions or continuous contact. Recent advances in deep learning and model-based optimization offer promising avenues for robust, real-time performance. In this work, we present a method for simultaneous estimation of hand and object poses from a single RGB-D stream, leveraging a unified representation that fuses depth geometry with learned appearance features. Our approach achieves accurate joint tracking at interactive frame rates, even in the presence of significant occlusions and complex manipulations.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a method for real-time joint tracking of a hand manipulating an object using RGB-D input. By simultaneously estimating the articulated hand pose and the 6-DoF object pose, our approach captures detailed interaction dynamics without requiring markers or intrusive instrumentation. The combination of depth-based geometric constraints with appearance cues enables robust performance under occlusions and complex contact configurations. Experiments on challenging sequences demonstrate that our method achieves accurate joint and object pose estimates at interactive frame rates, outperforming baseline approaches in both precision and stability. These results highlight the potential of our framework for applications in augmented reality, human–computer interaction, and robotics. Future work will address learning-based priors for improved generalization, as well as the extension to multi-object and multi-hand interactions in unconstrained environments, further broadening the applicability of real-time manipulation tracking systems.

title: Problem of Time: Temporal Relationalism Compatibility of Other Local Classical Facets Completed
abstract: We investigate the problem of time in classical and semiclassical contexts, focusing on the temporal relationalism approach and its compatibility with other local classical facets of background-independent theories. Temporal relationalism posits that time is not a fundamental external parameter but emerges from change, encoded via parametrization-irrelevant actions and Machian principles. This framework has been extensively studied in isolation; here, we complete the analysis of its interplay with complementary local classical features such as configurational relationalism, the constraint closure property, beables, and spacetime reconstruction. We systematically examine how temporal relationalism integrates with these facets within finite models and local field-theoretic settings, ensuring consistency with the Dirac constraint analysis and the avoidance of hidden temporal structures. Special attention is paid to the compatibility of emergent time functions with the algebra of constraints, showing that temporal relationalism can be maintained without violating closure or introducing anomalies. We also discuss the implications for classical canonical general relativity, where the Hamiltonian constraint plays the dual role of generator of refoliations and enforcer of temporal relationalism. Our results indicate that, once properly formulated, temporal relationalism is not only consistent with but in certain cases clarifies the structure of other local classical aspects of background independence. This completion of the compatibility program establishes a coherent foundation for extending temporal relationalism into semiclassical and quantum gravitational regimes, providing a unified local classical underpinning for further investigations into the problem of time.
introduction:
The “Problem of Time” remains one of the most persistent conceptual challenges in the pursuit of a coherent theory uniting general relativity with quantum mechanics. At its core, it reflects a deep tension between the temporal structure inherent to general relativity, in which time is an emergent and relational concept tied to spacetime geometry, and the fixed, external time parameter presupposed in canonical formulations of quantum theory. Among the various proposed resolutions, Temporal Relationalism has emerged as a particularly promising classical-level principle. Rooted in Machian philosophy, Temporal Relationalism posits that time is not a fundamental backdrop but a construct abstracted from change in the configurations of the universe. This approach seeks to eliminate any notion of an external or absolute time variable from the outset, replacing it with a fully relational description in which dynamics is encoded in correlations between physical degrees of freedom.

A central question arises when one attempts to apply Temporal Relationalism to realistic models of physics: is it compatible with the other local classical structures that are well-established in the field? Classical mechanics and field theory possess a variety of “facets” — such as locality in space, the existence of constraints, canonical formulations, and gauge symmetries — that must be respected if any reformulation is to be viable. In particular, local classical field theories, including general relativity itself, are built on the interplay between constraint algebras, spatial diffeomorphism invariance, and the preservation of local degrees of freedom. Temporal Relationalism, by altering the role of time and the form of dynamical evolution, may interact nontrivially with these features.

Previous work has demonstrated that Temporal Relationalism can be consistently implemented in certain finite-dimensional mechanical models, such as relational particle mechanics, by replacing an explicit time parameter with an emergent time functional constructed from the system’s change. Extending this compatibility to the local field-theoretic setting, however, is a non-trivial undertaking. In this context, the elimination of time from the primary formulation must be reconciled with the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints, the structure of the Dirac–Bergmann constraint analysis, and the preservation of constraint closure. Furthermore, spatial locality imposes additional demands: the theory must remain well-defined on a manifold with local fields, respecting covariance and the propagation of constraints without recourse to an external clock.

The present work completes the analysis of Temporal Relationalism’s compatibility with a full set of local classical facets relevant to general relativity and related theories. Building on prior partial results, we systematically examine the incorporation of Temporal Relationalism into the canonical formalism of local classical field theories, ensuring that each structural ingredient — from the form of the constraints to the invariance under spatial symmetries — remains intact. This completion establishes a coherent framework in which Temporal Relationalism is not merely a philosophical reinterpretation of time, but a concrete principle compatible with the technical machinery of local classical physics. By securing this compatibility, we pave the way for subsequent investigations into the quantum-level Problem of Time, where the relational perspective on temporality may offer significant conceptual and mathematical advantages.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the Problem of Time from the perspective of Temporal Relationalism, focusing on the extent to which other local classical facets can be rendered compatible with it. Our analysis has proceeded by first isolating the underlying principles of Temporal Relationalism—most centrally, the absence of any external or absolute time parameter and the consequent requirement that temporal structure be abstracted from change itself—and then systematically testing these principles against the remaining local facets of the Problem of Time in a classical setting. By doing so, we have aimed to clarify whether Temporal Relationalism can serve not only as a coherent philosophical stance but also as a structurally robust foundation for the consistent treatment of dynamics in background-independent theories.

The central finding is that the implementation of Temporal Relationalism at the local classical level can indeed be harmonized with other key facets, provided the appropriate reformulations are made. Constraints arising from configurational relationalism, the need for consistent local beables, and the requirements of refoliation invariance can each be accommodated without violating the underlying temporal-relational principles. This requires a careful reformulation of the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints in purely relational terms, ensuring that the emergent temporal parameter is constructed from the system’s own degrees of freedom rather than imposed from outside. In this way, the evolution of the system can be described consistently and locally, without appeal to any hidden absolute clock.

An important outcome of this investigation is the recognition that certain apparent tensions between Temporal Relationalism and other facets are, in fact, artefacts of retaining residual absolutist structures in the mathematical formalism. By eliminating these residuals—whether in the form of surplus variables, gauge choices that presuppose an external time, or unphysical coordinate artifacts—one finds that the relational approach naturally dovetails with the principles of general covariance and constraint closure. This, in turn, reinforces the idea that the classical Problem of Time is not an insurmountable obstruction but rather a guide to the necessary structural adjustments for a fully relational formulation.

At a methodological level, this study demonstrates the utility of working through the Problem of Time facet by facet, using Temporal Relationalism as a unifying filter. This approach allows for the identification of both genuine incompatibilities and superficial conflicts. In the present case, all examined local classical facets could be brought into line with Temporal Relationalism, suggesting that any remaining difficulties at the local level are likely to arise in the quantum or global extensions of the theory rather than in its classical, local structure.

From a broader perspective, these results lend further support to the program of constructing background-independent theories from first principles that reject absolute temporal structure. They also suggest a coherent pathway for integrating Temporal Relationalism into canonical and covariant frameworks without sacrificing mathematical consistency or physical interpretability. While the present analysis has been confined to local classical considerations, the strategies developed here—particularly the systematic elimination of external temporal parameters and the relational reformulation of constraints—provide a template for tackling the corresponding issues in semiclassical and quantum regimes.

Future work will need to address the challenges that arise when these local classical compatibilities are extended to the global and quantum domains, where issues such as the global problem of time, the implementation of the semiclassical time approximation, and the consistent histories approach may present new obstacles. Nonetheless, the present findings establish a solid classical foundation: Temporal Relationalism is not only philosophically defensible but also practically compatible with the other local classical facets of the Problem of Time, thereby reinforcing its role as a viable cornerstone for the ongoing search for a coherent, relationally founded theory of spacetime and dynamics.

title: Holographic Weyl anomaly for GJMS operators: one Laplacian to rule them all
abstract: We revisit the computation of holographic Weyl anomalies associated with conformally covariant GJMS operators on even-dimensional manifolds, focusing on a unifying approach based on a single, higher-dimensional Laplacian. GJMS operators, defined as a hierarchy of conformally invariant differential operators of increasing order, play a central role in conformal geometry and quantum field theory in curved space. Their holographic realisation arises naturally in the AdS/CFT correspondence, where the bulk dual encodes boundary conformal data, including the Weyl anomaly. In this work, we demonstrate that the full series of holographic anomalies for the GJMS family can be extracted from the spectral analysis of one appropriately chosen Laplacian in the bulk, rather than by treating each operator separately. This “one Laplacian to rule them all” framework exploits the factorisation of higher-order operators in Einstein spaces and the universality of the associated bulk-to-boundary propagators. By evaluating the heat kernel coefficients of the bulk Laplacian in a suitably regularised asymptotically hyperbolic geometry, we obtain closed expressions for both type‑A and type‑B contributions to the anomaly in arbitrary even dimensions. Our method clarifies the geometric origin of the anomaly coefficients, making explicit their dependence on curvature invariants such as the Euler density and Weyl invariants, and yields results consistent with known special cases, including the conformal Laplacian and the Paneitz operator. Beyond its computational efficiency, the approach highlights deep structural connections between conformal geometry, holography, and spectral theory, suggesting possible extensions to other conformally invariant operators and to non‑Einstein backgrounds. This unified Laplacian framework thus provides a powerful and conceptually transparent tool for analysing holographic Weyl anomalies across the entire GJMS hierarchy.
introduction: The study of GJMS operators reveals deep connections between conformal geometry and holography. In the AdS/CFT correspondence, their determinants encode Weyl anomalies of boundary conformal field theories. We show that these anomalies can be computed from a single bulk Laplacian, unifying all orders. This approach clarifies structural patterns and provides an efficient route to exact holographic Weyl anomaly coefficients.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the holographic computation of the Weyl anomaly associated with GJMS operators on conformally curved manifolds, placing particular emphasis on the unifying role played by a single bulk Laplacian in the dual AdS geometry. By systematically analysing the bulk-to-boundary correspondence for higher-derivative conformally covariant operators, we have shown that the entire family of GJMS operators—characterised on the boundary by their order and conformal weight—can be generated holographically from the spectral data of a single, well-chosen Laplacian operator in the bulk. This observation provides a streamlined framework for the computation of conformal anomalies, bypassing the need for operator-specific bulk constructions.

Our results demonstrate that the holographic Weyl anomaly for a GJMS operator of arbitrary order can be extracted from the heat kernel expansion of the bulk Laplacian, with the relevant Seeley–DeWitt coefficients encoding the local curvature invariants that appear in the anomaly. In particular, we have confirmed that the type-A and type-B contributions are captured universally by the bulk Laplacian spectrum, and that their dependence on the order of the GJMS operator enters only through simple multiplicative factors determined by the operator’s conformal weight. This universality extends to all even-dimensional boundaries for which the GJMS operators are defined, and it is consistent with previously known special cases such as the Yamabe and Paneitz operators.

From the holographic perspective, the “one Laplacian to rule them all” principle is a manifestation of the deeper geometric fact that higher-derivative conformal operators can be understood as residues of meromorphic families generated by powers of the Laplacian on the ambient space. The AdS bulk provides a natural ambient extension, and the holographic dictionary translates the bulk spectral data directly into boundary conformal invariants. This insight not only simplifies anomaly calculations but also clarifies the structural relationship between different members of the GJMS hierarchy.

Beyond its computational advantages, our approach sheds light on the interplay between conformal geometry and holography. The ability to encode the anomalies of all GJMS operators into a single bulk object suggests that there may be an underlying unifying principle—perhaps linked to the representation theory of the conformal group or to the geometry of the ambient construction—that governs the structure of conformal anomalies in general. Moreover, the method is adaptable to situations involving nontrivial topology, boundaries with additional structure, or coupling to background fields, opening avenues for further exploration.

Future work could aim to extend this framework to odd-dimensional boundaries, where local conformal anomalies vanish but global terms may survive, or to supersymmetric settings, where higher-derivative operators appear naturally in protected sectors. Another promising direction is to investigate whether similar unifying bulk operators exist for other classes of conformally covariant differential operators beyond the GJMS family. We expect that such developments will continue to illuminate the geometric and physical significance of the holographic approach to conformal anomalies.

title: Weak asymptotics of wave function for N-particle system and asymptotic filtering
abstract: We investigate the weak asymptotic behavior of wave functions for an \(N\)-particle quantum system in the limit of large times. Using asymptotic analysis in the sense of distributions, we construct explicit weak asymptotic expansions that capture the long-range structure of multi-particle scattering states. The approach allows for a systematic separation of singular and regular components of the wave function, providing a rigorous basis for asymptotic filtering of physically relevant states. We demonstrate how the method yields effective reduced descriptions of the system by isolating dominant asymptotic contributions. Applications to model systems illustrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed framework.
introduction:
The study of asymptotic behavior of quantum systems with a large number of particles remains one of the central themes in mathematical physics, with implications ranging from many-body quantum mechanics to statistical mechanics and quantum field theory. In the context of the Schrödinger equation for an \(N\)-particle system, the complexity of the configuration space grows rapidly with \(N\), rendering direct analysis of exact solutions intractable. Consequently, asymptotic methods, both in the semiclassical and large-\(N\) regimes, provide indispensable tools for understanding the qualitative and quantitative features of the wave function. Among these, weak asymptotic techniques have emerged as a particularly flexible framework, allowing one to extract leading-order behavior in situations where traditional pointwise asymptotics are inaccessible or ill-defined.

Weak asymptotics refer to the description of the limiting behavior of a family of functions, such as wave functions or correlation functions, in the sense of distributions rather than in the strict pointwise sense. This approach is well suited to problems where oscillatory structures, singularities, or interference effects dominate, and where the natural observables are integrated quantities. In the setting of multi-particle quantum mechanics, the wave function often exhibits highly oscillatory dependence on both spatial coordinates and time, particularly in high-energy or semiclassical limits. Weak asymptotic analysis captures the averaged or smeared-out structure of such functions, providing insight into physical quantities such as scattering amplitudes, density profiles, and transition probabilities.

For an \(N\)-particle system, the relevant asymptotic regimes may involve large interparticle separations, high total energy, or limits in which some subset of particles become bound while others are scattered. The complexity of the asymptotic expansion arises from the combinatorial proliferation of possible cluster decompositions of the system. In scattering theory, for example, the configuration space is stratified according to the partitioning of particles into clusters, and each stratum supports its own type of asymptotic behavior. The generalization of well-known two-body asymptotics to the many-body case is highly nontrivial, requiring careful treatment of long-range interactions, threshold phenomena, and the interplay of different scattering channels.

One of the central challenges in this context is the separation of physically relevant asymptotic modes from the full solution. In the presence of multiple scales and overlapping asymptotic regions, direct extraction of a single asymptotic component can be ambiguous. This motivates the concept of asymptotic filtering, by which we mean the systematic isolation of a desired asymptotic contribution—such as the outgoing component corresponding to a particular scattering channel—while suppressing or eliminating other contributions. Asymptotic filtering can be formulated in both physical and Fourier space, and often involves the use of projection operators, convolution with test functions, or integration against phase factors designed to select a given asymptotic regime.

In the weak asymptotic framework, filtering can be interpreted as the application of a functional to the wave function that annihilates all but a specified asymptotic term. This is closely related to the use of stationary phase and microlocal analysis, where one isolates contributions from specified regions of phase space. For \(N\)-particle systems, the filtering procedure must account for the geometry of the configuration space and the structure of singularities in the spectral representation of the solution. Asymptotic filtering thus serves as both a conceptual and computational tool, clarifying the meaning of the asymptotic expansion and enabling the derivation of reduced equations for the dominant components.

The present work is motivated by the need for a systematic and rigorous description of weak asymptotics for multi-particle wave functions, together with a concrete implementation of asymptotic filtering in this setting. Our aim is twofold. First, we develop a general formalism for representing the weak asymptotics of solutions to the \(N\)-particle Schrödinger equation in scattering-type regimes. This involves an explicit characterization of the leading-order terms associated with each partition of the particle set, and the derivation of corresponding distributional limits. Second, we introduce and analyze a filtering mechanism that isolates a chosen asymptotic term, thereby enabling focused analysis of specific scattering channels or bound-state configurations.

The approach presented here builds on and extends earlier work on two-body scattering, cluster decomposition, and time-dependent scattering theory. We draw upon techniques from distribution theory, oscillatory integral analysis, and the theory of generalized eigenfunctions, adapting them to the high-dimensional, multi-scale setting of the \(N\)-body problem. Our formalism accommodates both short-range and suitably decaying long-range potentials, and it is compatible with the standard Hamiltonian framework of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics.

Beyond its intrinsic mathematical interest, the study of weak asymptotics and asymptotic filtering has practical implications. In computational quantum mechanics, for example, numerical methods for large systems often rely on approximations that implicitly involve weak limits or filtered asymptotics—such as in time-dependent surface flux methods or in the extraction of scattering observables from finite-time simulations. A rigorous framework for these concepts can therefore inform algorithm design and error analysis. Similarly, in theoretical physics, the ability to isolate and characterize specific asymptotic contributions is essential for interpreting experimental data in terms of underlying microscopic processes.

In what follows, we first review the general structure of the \(N\)-particle Schrödinger equation and the associated scattering theory, emphasizing the role of weak limits. We then formulate the weak asymptotic representation of the wave function, organize the asymptotic terms according to cluster decompositions, and define a class of filtering operators that isolate individual terms. Finally, we analyze the properties of these filtered components, including their stability under time evolution and their relation to physical observables. This program yields a coherent picture of the asymptotic landscape of multi-particle quantum systems, and provides a set of tools for both theoretical analysis and practical computation.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the weak asymptotic behavior of the wave function for an \(N\)-particle quantum system in the limit where interparticle distances and characteristic scales permit a systematic asymptotic analysis. By employing the framework of weak asymptotics, we have been able to capture leading-order contributions to the many-body wave function in a distributional sense, thus avoiding the restrictive assumptions inherent in pointwise asymptotics. This approach has proven especially effective in dealing with singularities arising from short-range interactions and in isolating the physically relevant components of the asymptotic expansion.
