A central aspect of our analysis has been the introduction of an asymptotic filtering procedure, designed to separate the dominant scattering and bound-state contributions from rapidly oscillating or negligible terms. This filtering not only clarifies the structure of the asymptotic wave function but also establishes a robust link between the microscopic interaction parameters and the emergent macroscopic behavior of the system. In particular, we have shown that the filtered asymptotics retain the essential dynamical information required for the formulation of effective reduced models.

The results obtained here suggest that weak asymptotic techniques, combined with carefully designed filtering, offer a powerful tool for studying the large-distance or large-time behavior of complex quantum systems without resorting to uncontrolled approximations. The methodology is readily adaptable to various interaction types and boundary conditions, and can be extended to incorporate external fields or relativistic corrections. Future work will focus on refining the filtering criteria to optimize numerical implementations and on exploring the interplay between weak asymptotics and semiclassical approximations in high-dimensional systems. The present study thus lays a foundation for both theoretical advancements and practical applications in the asymptotic analysis of many-particle quantum dynamics.

title: Sensitivity of LHC experiments to exotic highly ionising particles
abstract: We investigate the sensitivity of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) to exotic, highly ionising particles (HIPs) predicted in various extensions of the Standard Model. Such particles, including magnetic monopoles and stable multi-charged states, would produce distinctive experimental signatures characterised by anomalously high energy loss in tracking detectors and prolonged time-of-flight. Using detailed simulations of detector response and realistic reconstruction algorithms, we evaluate detection efficiencies across a broad range of masses, charges, and lifetimes. We assess the impact of trigger thresholds, background rejection strategies, and systematic uncertainties on the achievable sensitivity. Our results indicate that LHC experiments can probe previously unexplored parameter space, providing robust constraints on HIP production and guiding future searches in Run 3 and beyond.
introduction:
The search for new physics phenomena beyond the Standard Model (SM) constitutes one of the primary objectives of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) physics programme. Among the wide variety of possible signatures, the existence of exotic, highly ionising particles (HIPs) offers a distinctive experimental opportunity. HIPs are characterised by unusually large electric charges, magnetic charges, or other non-standard couplings to the electromagnetic field, resulting in significantly enhanced ionisation energy loss as they traverse detector material. Their extreme ionisation properties distinguish them from SM particles and provide a relatively background-free signature, making them a compelling target for discovery-oriented searches.

Several theoretical scenarios predict the existence of HIPs. Magnetic monopoles, first postulated by Dirac to explain the quantisation of electric charge, are a well-known example. Other possibilities include dyons (particles carrying both electric and magnetic charge), stable heavy charged particles arising in supersymmetric or other beyond-the-SM frameworks, and stable or long-lived states from hidden-sector models with large effective charges. In many of these scenarios, HIP masses can lie well above the electroweak scale, potentially within the kinematic reach of the LHC. Their high masses would typically imply low production rates, but their striking signatures could enable detection even with limited datasets.

The experimental detection of HIPs at the LHC faces unique challenges. Their high ionisation can saturate readout electronics, cause track reconstruction inefficiencies, or lead to non-standard energy deposition patterns in calorimeters. Moreover, HIPs are expected to have low velocities (β ≪ 1) for a wide range of masses, which affects time-of-flight measurements and complicates triggering strategies. Dedicated analyses must therefore account for unconventional detector responses, non-standard reconstruction efficiencies, and potential acceptance losses in various sub-detectors. Robust simulation of HIP interactions with matter is essential, yet difficult, due to limited experimental data on particles with such extreme charges or velocities.

Previous searches at the LHC, conducted by both ATLAS and CMS, have set limits on HIP production across a range of charges, masses, and magnetic charges. These studies have exploited diverse sub-detector systems, including inner trackers, calorimeters, and dedicated timing detectors, as well as specialised triggers designed to capture slow or anomalous particles. Nonetheless, the sensitivity of these experiments depends critically on the interplay between production kinematics, detector acceptance, and the specific ionisation response.

This work aims to provide a detailed assessment of the sensitivity of LHC experiments to exotic HIPs, integrating realistic modelling of detector performance with theoretical production scenarios. By quantifying detection efficiencies and exploring the parameter space of HIP properties, we seek to clarify current experimental reach and identify strategies to enhance future searches in Run 3 and beyond.
conclusion:
The study presented has explored in detail the potential of the LHC experiments to detect exotic highly ionising particles (HIPs), with an emphasis on scenarios motivated by theories beyond the Standard Model, including magnetic monopoles, dyons, and other stable or long-lived states with large electric and/or magnetic charge. By combining a review of the underlying theoretical motivations with a quantitative assessment of detector response, trigger capabilities, and background rejection strategies, it has been possible to estimate the reach of ATLAS, CMS, and dedicated subdetectors such as MoEDAL in a broad range of mass and charge hypotheses.

The analysis shows that HIPs, owing to their distinctive energy loss and track signatures, can be efficiently discriminated from Standard Model backgrounds, provided that dedicated triggers and reconstruction algorithms are implemented. The extreme ionisation produced in tracking detectors, along with the possibility of saturation effects in calorimeters, underscores the importance of accurate modelling of detector material and response over the full kinematic range. The complementarity between the general-purpose experiments and specialised detectors emerges as a key factor: while ATLAS and CMS benefit from high luminosity and large coverage, MoEDAL’s passive trapping and high-Z material arrays provide unmatched sensitivity to slowly moving and multiply charged particles.

Projected sensitivities indicate that, with the dataset already accumulated and that expected from the High-Luminosity LHC phase, the accessible parameter space extends well beyond previous collider limits, probing monopole masses in excess of several TeV for charges up to the Dirac value and substantially higher for multiply charged states. For electrically charged HIPs, the reach in mass and charge is similarly extended, constrained primarily by trigger thresholds and detector saturation effects. Systematic uncertainties related to modelling non-perturbative production mechanisms, such as the photon–photon fusion process for monopoles, remain a limiting factor in translating detector reach into model-independent cross-section limits.

The findings highlight the necessity of continuing to refine both experimental techniques and theoretical predictions. On the experimental side, improvements in trigger algorithms capable of handling extreme ionisation, enhanced calibration of detector response to HIP-like signals, and the integration of machine learning tools for offline selection can all contribute to maximising discovery potential. On the theoretical side, better understanding of HIP production cross-sections and kinematics will sharpen the interpretation of any observed excesses or null results.

In conclusion, the LHC experiments possess significant and growing sensitivity to a wide class of exotic highly ionising particles. The combination of diverse detection strategies, large datasets, and targeted analysis approaches places the LHC in a unique position to either discover such particles or set the most stringent constraints to date, thereby providing valuable guidance for models of new physics at the TeV scale.

title: Bayesian Dropout
abstract: We investigate Bayesian Dropout, a probabilistic interpretation of dropout regularization that enables principled uncertainty estimation in deep neural networks. Traditional dropout randomly deactivates units during training to prevent overfitting, but its stochasticity can also be viewed as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes. Building on this perspective, we formalize dropout as a variational approximation to the posterior distribution over network weights and extend it to support adaptive dropout rates informed by model uncertainty. Our approach integrates variational Bayesian principles with standard training procedures, requiring minimal changes to existing architectures and computational overhead. We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets for image classification and regression, demonstrating that Bayesian Dropout retains the regularization benefits of standard dropout while yielding calibrated predictive uncertainties. The method improves robustness to overfitting, enhances generalization, and provides reliable confidence measures useful for decision-making under uncertainty. These results highlight Bayesian Dropout as a practical, scalable tool for uncertainty-aware deep learning.
introduction: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of tasks, yet their tendency to overfit and their lack of calibrated uncertainty estimates remain persistent challenges. Dropout, a simple and effective regularization technique, mitigates overfitting by randomly deactivating units during training, thereby preventing co-adaptation of features. While initially motivated as a heuristic, recent theoretical advances have revealed a compelling interpretation of dropout as an approximate Bayesian inference method in deep Gaussian processes. This Bayesian perspective offers a principled framework for quantifying model uncertainty, which is crucial in safety-critical applications such as medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, and scientific discovery. By interpreting dropout as variational inference, one can obtain predictive distributions without significant modifications to the training procedure, enabling practical uncertainty estimation at scale. This work builds on and extends the Bayesian interpretation of dropout, exploring its theoretical foundations and empirical performance. We aim to bridge the gap between probabilistic modeling and deep learning practice, demonstrating how Bayesian dropout can enhance both model robustness and decision-making under uncertainty.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the interpretation of dropout as a Bayesian approximation, exploring both its theoretical underpinnings and practical implications for deep learning models. By framing dropout within a probabilistic perspective, we showed that it can be understood as performing approximate variational inference in deep Gaussian processes. This perspective not only offers an explanation for its regularization properties but also provides a principled foundation for uncertainty estimation in neural networks. Our analysis reinforces the view that dropout is more than a heuristic to prevent overfitting; it is a computationally efficient means of integrating Bayesian reasoning into large-scale models.

Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrated that Bayesian dropout yields well-calibrated predictive uncertainties across a range of tasks, including image classification and regression. These uncertainties can guide decision-making in risk-sensitive applications, where confidence estimates are as critical as point predictions. Furthermore, we highlighted that the Bayesian interpretation enables natural extensions, such as adaptive dropout rates informed by posterior variance, and facilitates integration with other approximate inference techniques.

One of the key insights from our study is that the stochasticity introduced by dropout, when interpreted through the Bayesian lens, corresponds to sampling from an implicit distribution over model weights. This allows practitioners to capture epistemic uncertainty without substantially increasing computational cost compared to standard dropout training. Additionally, we discussed the trade-offs between accuracy, calibration, and efficiency, noting that while Bayesian dropout incurs some overhead at inference time due to multiple stochastic forward passes, the cost remains manageable in many practical scenarios.

Limitations of the current approach include its reliance on specific assumptions in the variational approximation and the potential mismatch between the induced prior and the true data-generating process. Future research could address these limitations by exploring richer prior formulations, structured variational distributions, and hybrid inference strategies that combine dropout with other Monte Carlo or deterministic approximation methods. Moreover, investigating the interplay between Bayesian dropout and modern architectures, such as transformers and graph neural networks, remains a promising avenue.

Overall, our findings substantiate the value of interpreting dropout through a Bayesian framework. This perspective deepens our theoretical understanding, enhances the practical utility of the method, and opens new directions for developing reliable, uncertainty-aware deep learning systems. By bridging the gap between Bayesian inference and scalable neural network training, Bayesian dropout represents a compelling step toward more principled and trustworthy machine learning models.

title: Identifying Player\'s Strategies in No Limit Texas Hold\'em Poker through the Analysis of Individual Moves
abstract: This study investigates the identification of player strategies in No Limit Texas Hold’em Poker through the analysis of individual moves. While previous research often focuses on aggregated game outcomes or broad strategic profiles, this work emphasizes the granularity of decision-making at each stage of play. Using a dataset of recorded hands from online poker environments, we extract features representing betting actions, positional context, stack sizes, and board texture. We apply statistical and machine learning techniques to classify moves and infer underlying strategic patterns, distinguishing between aggressive, passive, tight, and loose tendencies. The approach allows for dynamic tracking of strategy shifts within a single session, offering deeper insight into adaptive behavior. Results demonstrate that move-level analysis enhances predictive accuracy compared to aggregate metrics, revealing nuanced play styles that may be obscured in coarser models. These findings have implications for opponent modeling, artificial intelligence in games, and the broader study of decision-making under uncertainty.
introduction:
Poker, and in particular No Limit Texas Hold’em, has been the subject of extensive research in fields such as artificial intelligence, game theory, and behavioral science due to its complex interplay of skill, strategy, and uncertainty. Unlike games of perfect information such as chess, poker requires players to make decisions based on incomplete information, incorporating probabilistic reasoning, risk assessment, and psychological inference. This combination of stochastic elements and strategic depth makes it an ideal domain for studying human decision-making and the dynamics of competitive interaction. Among the various formats, No Limit Texas Hold’em is especially challenging because players are free to wager any amount of their remaining chips at any time, leading to a highly variable range of possible actions and strategies.

Traditional approaches to analyzing poker strategy often focus on aggregate statistics, such as win rates, positional advantage, or hand selection frequencies. While these measures are useful for evaluating overall performance, they tend to obscure the nuanced decision-making processes that occur on a move-by-move basis. Each betting action—whether a check, call, bet, raise, or fold—encapsulates a moment in which the player integrates multiple sources of information: private cards, community cards, opponent tendencies, stack sizes, and the history of prior actions. By examining these individual moves in detail, it is possible to gain deeper insight into the strategic reasoning of players, revealing patterns that may not be apparent from summary statistics alone.

Recent advances in data collection and computational analysis have made it feasible to record and examine large datasets of poker hands at the level of individual decisions. This enables the application of machine learning, statistical modeling, and sequential analysis to decode player tendencies, identify strategic archetypes, and track how strategies evolve over time or in response to specific contexts. Such granular analysis can illuminate the distinction between optimal, theory-driven play—such as that derived from game-theoretic equilibrium solutions—and the adaptive, exploitative strategies that human players often employ in practice.

Understanding strategy at the move level has implications beyond academic curiosity. In the realm of artificial intelligence, such insights can inform the development of more human-like or more exploitative poker agents. In behavioral economics and cognitive psychology, they can shed light on how individuals make high-stakes decisions under uncertainty, manage risk, and adapt to opponents. Moreover, in practical poker education, identifying the strategic signatures of skilled play can guide training methodologies and help players recognize and correct suboptimal tendencies.

This paper aims to investigate the strategies employed by players in No Limit Texas Hold’em by analyzing their individual moves within the context of complete hands. By integrating detailed decision-level data with robust analytical techniques, the study seeks to identify and characterize strategic patterns, providing a richer understanding of how players navigate the complex decision space of this iconic game.
conclusion: This study examined individual decision-making patterns in No Limit Texas Hold’em to identify underlying strategic approaches adopted by players. By analyzing discrete moves in various game contexts, we demonstrated that betting behaviors, positional awareness, and adaptation to opponents reveal consistent strategic profiles. The findings suggest that micro-level actions, when viewed in sequence, provide a reliable basis for distinguishing between aggressive, conservative, and balanced styles. Such insights have implications for both competitive play and the development of automated opponent modeling systems. While the analysis focused on a limited dataset, the methodology can be extended to larger samples and integrated with machine learning techniques for more precise classification. Future research may explore temporal dynamics and bluffing patterns to further refine the understanding of strategic diversity in poker.

title: Versatile Auxiliary Classifier with Generative Adversarial Network (VAC+GAN), Multi Class Scenarios
abstract: We propose the Versatile Auxiliary Classifier with Generative Adversarial Network (VAC+GAN) framework for multi-class scenarios, extending the applicability of GAN-based models to diverse classification tasks. VAC+GAN integrates an auxiliary classifier parallel to the discriminator, enabling simultaneous data generation and class discrimination without altering the underlying GAN architecture. The classifier’s loss is backpropagated through the generator, guiding it to produce class-specific samples. This architecture supports various GAN variants and loss functions, offering flexibility across domains. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate improved class-conditional sample quality and classification performance, confirming VAC+GAN’s effectiveness as a general and adaptable approach for multi-class generative modeling.
introduction:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as a powerful class of generative models capable of producing high-fidelity samples across various domains, including image synthesis, speech generation, and data augmentation. The core idea of GANs involves a game-theoretic framework in which a generator network learns to produce realistic samples while a discriminator network attempts to distinguish between real and generated data. While this adversarial training paradigm has demonstrated remarkable success, controlling the modes of generation, particularly in multi-class scenarios, remains a challenging problem. Standard GAN frameworks do not inherently provide a mechanism to guide the generator toward producing samples belonging to a specific class, which limits their applicability in tasks requiring fine-grained conditional generation.

Several extensions have been proposed to address this limitation, such as Conditional GANs (CGANs) and Auxiliary Classifier GANs (ACGANs). These models incorporate class information into the training process either by conditioning both the generator and discriminator on class labels or by augmenting the discriminator with an auxiliary classification objective. While these approaches have shown promise, they often require architectural modifications to the discriminator and can struggle to maintain high generation quality when scaling to multiple classes. Furthermore, coupling the classifier directly to the discriminator may restrict flexibility, as improvements or replacements to the classifier may necessitate redesigning the discriminator network.

In this context, the Versatile Auxiliary Classifier with Generative Adversarial Network (VAC+GAN) framework offers a flexible and modular alternative. Instead of embedding the classification task within the discriminator, VAC+GAN introduces an independent auxiliary classifier trained in parallel with the GAN. This design allows the generator to be guided by class-specific feedback from the classifier without altering the discriminator’s architecture or purpose. The decoupling of classification from discrimination enables seamless adaptation to different GAN variants and facilitates the use of specialized classifier architectures optimized for the target domain. Moreover, this separation allows the framework to scale more effectively to multi-class scenarios, as the classifier can be tailored to handle large label spaces without compromising the stability of adversarial training.

By leveraging the independent auxiliary classifier, VAC+GAN enhances control over the generative process, enabling the production of diverse, high-quality samples across multiple categories. This work investigates the effectiveness of VAC+GAN in multi-class image generation tasks, evaluates its performance against established conditional generation approaches, and demonstrates its versatility across various GAN backbones.
conclusion: In this work, we presented the Versatile Auxiliary Classifier with Generative Adversarial Network (VAC+GAN) framework, designed to address multi-class scenarios effectively. By integrating an auxiliary classifier in parallel with the discriminator, the proposed approach enables the generator to produce class-specific samples with improved fidelity and diversity. The architecture maintains the adversarial training benefits of conventional GANs while introducing a flexible classification component that can be adapted to various datasets and class configurations without significant architectural modifications. Experimental results demonstrated that VAC+GAN achieves competitive or superior performance compared to existing conditional generative models, particularly in terms of classification accuracy, intra-class diversity, and visual quality of generated samples. The framework’s versatility was evident in its ability to generalize across different multi-class datasets, highlighting its potential for broader generative modeling applications. Furthermore, the decoupled nature of the classifier allows for independent optimization, offering greater stability during training and reducing mode collapse tendencies. These findings suggest that VAC+GAN can serve as a robust solution for tasks requiring both high-quality sample generation and accurate class conditioning. Future work will explore extending this approach to more complex domains, such as high-resolution image synthesis and multi-modal generation, as well as investigating its integration with advanced GAN variants to further enhance stability and scalability. Overall, VAC+GAN contributes a flexible and effective tool to the generative modeling landscape.

title: PointHop++: A Lightweight Learning Model on Point Sets for 3D Classification
abstract: PointHop++ is a lightweight and effective learning framework for 3D object classification on point cloud data. It builds upon the original PointHop by introducing improved feature extraction and aggregation strategies, enabling higher accuracy with reduced computational complexity. The method leverages a hierarchical, hop-by-hop feature learning process without the need for extensive parameter tuning or heavy training, making it suitable for resource-constrained environments. By exploiting local-to-global geometric relationships, PointHop++ achieves robust representation of irregular and unordered point sets. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PointHop++ attains competitive or superior classification performance compared to state-of-the-art deep learning models, while requiring significantly fewer parameters and training data. This work offers an interpretable, efficient, and high-performing alternative for 3D point cloud analysis.
introduction:
Understanding and processing 3D point cloud data has become increasingly important with the rapid development of 3D sensing technologies such as LiDAR, depth cameras, and multi-view stereo systems. Point clouds, which represent objects or scenes as unordered sets of points in 3D space, offer rich geometric information but pose significant challenges for machine learning algorithms due to their irregular and unstructured nature. Unlike 2D images that reside on regular grids, point sets lack explicit spatial ordering and neighborhood structures, making the direct application of conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) nontrivial. This has led to a surge of research efforts aiming to design effective and efficient learning models tailored for point cloud analysis.

Early approaches for 3D object recognition often relied on transforming point clouds into regular representations, such as voxel grids or multi-view projections, so that standard deep learning architectures could be applied. While effective to some extent, these methods suffer from high memory consumption, quantization artifacts, and loss of geometric details. More recently, point-based neural networks, such as PointNet and PointNet++, have been proposed to directly operate on raw point sets. These models achieve impressive accuracy by learning permutation-invariant features and capturing local geometric structures through hierarchical processing. However, their reliance on extensive training data, large model sizes, and computationally expensive operations limits their deployment in resource-constrained environments such as embedded systems, mobile devices, and real-time applications.

To address these challenges, lightweight and interpretable learning frameworks have emerged, offering competitive performance with reduced computational burden. Among them, the PointHop method introduces a novel, non-iterative learning paradigm based on the successive extraction and aggregation of local-to-global features using a point set representation and subspace approximation. By avoiding end-to-end backpropagation, PointHop significantly reduces model complexity and training cost while maintaining competitive classification accuracy. Nevertheless, there remain opportunities to further enhance its discriminative power, robustness, and efficiency for large-scale 3D classification tasks.

In this work, we propose PointHop++, an improved lightweight learning model for point cloud classification that builds upon the PointHop framework. PointHop++ introduces refined feature extraction strategies, optimized neighborhood construction, and enhanced dimensionality reduction techniques to better capture both fine-grained local details and global shape characteristics. It maintains the feedforward, non-iterative nature of its predecessor while achieving higher accuracy and lower computational cost. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that PointHop++ achieves a favorable trade-off between performance and efficiency, making it an appealing choice for practical 3D recognition scenarios where resources are limited but accuracy remains critical.
conclusion: PointHop++ presents an efficient, lightweight framework for 3D point cloud classification, achieving competitive accuracy with reduced computational cost. By leveraging hierarchical feature extraction and optimized representation learning, it addresses scalability and resource constraints. Future work will explore broader tasks, larger datasets, and integration with real-time 3D perception systems.

title: Using Automated Theorem Provers to Teach Knowledge Representation in First-Order Logic
abstract: This paper investigates the pedagogical benefits of integrating automated theorem provers (ATPs) into the teaching of knowledge representation in first-order logic (FOL). While FOL is a foundational component of computer science and artificial intelligence curricula, students often struggle to bridge the gap between theoretical syntax–semantics concepts and practical problem-solving skills. We propose a teaching framework in which ATPs are used both as verification tools and as interactive learning environments. In our approach, students encode domain knowledge as FOL axioms and queries, submit them to an ATP, and iteratively refine their representations based on the prover’s feedback. This process encourages deeper engagement with formal semantics, promotes precision in modeling, and provides immediate, automated assessment of correctness. We conducted a classroom study with undergraduate AI students, integrating the ATP-based exercises into a semester-long module on FOL knowledge representation. Data collection included pre- and post-tests, analysis of submitted formalizations, and surveys on student perceptions. Results indicate significant improvement in students’ ability to construct and evaluate formal representations, with many reporting increased confidence in their understanding of FOL concepts. Furthermore, the ATP’s counterexamples and proof traces were found to be particularly effective in revealing misconceptions and fostering self-correction. We discuss design considerations, common pitfalls, and strategies for aligning ATP feedback with pedagogical objectives. Our findings suggest that ATPs, when used as instructional scaffolding, can enhance both conceptual understanding and practical competence in knowledge representation, offering a scalable and robust approach for FOL education in computer science programs.
introduction:
Knowledge representation is a central topic in artificial intelligence, concerned with encoding information about the world in a form that enables effective reasoning. First-Order Logic (FOL) provides a formal, expressive framework for representing complex relationships and supporting automated inference. However, teaching FOL poses pedagogical challenges: students must simultaneously acquire syntactic precision, semantic understanding, and the ability to apply formal reasoning methods. Traditional instruction often separates formalization exercises from the experience of automated reasoning, potentially limiting deeper comprehension.

Automated Theorem Provers (ATPs) offer a compelling pedagogical tool for bridging this gap. By allowing students to translate natural language statements into FOL and immediately test their formulations through automated reasoning, ATPs provide rapid feedback and concrete demonstrations of logical entailment. This interactive loop supports active learning, encourages experimentation, and can make abstract concepts more tangible. Moreover, ATPs expose students to the computational aspects of logic, illustrating both the power and limitations of automated reasoning systems.

This paper explores the use of ATPs as a teaching aid for knowledge representation in FOL. We discuss instructional strategies, present illustrative classroom activities, and evaluate their effectiveness in fostering both representational accuracy and reasoning skills, thereby enhancing student engagement and mastery of formal logic.
conclusion:
This work has explored the pedagogical potential of integrating automated theorem provers (ATPs) into the teaching of knowledge representation in first-order logic. By situating ATPs within the learning process, students can engage directly with the formal structures, inference rules, and representational choices that underlie logical reasoning. The immediate feedback provided by such systems fosters iterative refinement of formalizations, encouraging learners to critically examine the correspondence between natural language statements and their logical counterparts. Furthermore, automated reasoning tools help to demystify the abstract nature of first-order logic, making it more accessible through concrete verification of proofs and counterexamples.

Our observations suggest that ATPs can serve as both a diagnostic and formative assessment tool, revealing misconceptions about syntax, semantics, and proof strategies that might otherwise remain hidden. They also promote active experimentation, enabling students to explore alternative encodings and observe their consequences in a controlled environment. While the approach requires careful scaffolding to prevent over-reliance on automation, it can significantly enhance conceptual understanding when integrated with traditional instruction.

Future work should investigate the long-term effects of ATP-enhanced learning on students’ ability to transfer logical skills to novel domains, as well as the potential for adaptive tutoring systems that personalize challenges based on performance. Additionally, empirical studies comparing cohorts with and without ATP exposure would strengthen the evidence base for their pedagogical value. In sum, automated theorem provers, when thoughtfully embedded into the curriculum, offer a powerful means to deepen comprehension of knowledge representation in first-order logic and to cultivate more confident, capable reasoners.

title: On the geometrical hypotheses underlying wave functions and their emerging dynamics
abstract: We investigate the role of underlying geometrical hypotheses in shaping the formulation and interpretation of wave functions, with particular emphasis on the emergence of their dynamical properties. By examining configuration spaces endowed with specific metric and topological structures, we analyze how geometric constraints influence the admissible form of wave functions and the operators governing their evolution. The study draws connections between differential geometric frameworks and conventional quantum mechanical postulates, highlighting how curvature, connectivity, and dimensionality impact probability densities and phase evolution. We further explore how these geometrical features give rise to effective dynamical laws, bridging microscopic symmetries with macroscopic observables. Our approach unifies aspects of Riemannian geometry, symplectic structures, and gauge connections, revealing that the dynamical content of wave functions may be viewed as emergent from deeper spatial and configurational properties. This perspective opens pathways toward a reformulation of quantum dynamics in purely geometrical terms, with potential implications for quantum gravity, condensed matter systems, and foundational interpretations.
introduction:
The mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics rests upon the notion of the wave function as an abstract object, typically represented as a complex-valued function on configuration space or, more generally, as a vector in a Hilbert space. While the predictive success of this formalism is undeniable, the geometrical and conceptual foundations underlying the wave function remain a subject of ongoing investigation. The standard textbook presentation often treats the wave function as a purely mathematical device, whose physical meaning derives indirectly from the Born rule and the postulates of measurement. However, there is a growing body of work suggesting that the wave function may admit a more direct geometrical interpretation, potentially tied to the structure of the physical space or to generalized configuration spaces. The present work aims to examine the geometrical hypotheses implicit in the formalism and to explore how such hypotheses give rise to the dynamical laws that govern wave function evolution.

The Schrödinger equation, as the canonical dynamical law for non-relativistic quantum systems, is usually derived from postulates that include linearity, unitarity, and Galilean invariance. Yet, these postulates themselves can be traced to deeper geometrical assumptions about the nature of space, time, and the configuration manifold on which the wave function is defined. In particular, the choice of configuration space geometry—whether Euclidean, Riemannian, or of a more general fiber bundle structure—imposes constraints on the form of admissible Hamiltonians and thus on the dynamics of the system. For example, the Laplacian operator, which appears in the free-particle Hamiltonian, is defined in terms of the metric structure of configuration space. This suggests that the very form of quantum dynamics encodes specific geometrical hypotheses, whether or not they are explicitly acknowledged.

A related line of inquiry concerns the interpretation of the wave function as a section of a complex line bundle over configuration space, with the phase of the wave function corresponding to a connection on this bundle. This fiber bundle viewpoint naturally incorporates gauge structures and can be extended to accommodate spin degrees of freedom, internal symmetries, and topological phases. In such a framework, the geometry is not merely a background stage but an active participant in shaping the dynamics. The wave function’s transformation properties under symmetry groups, its global topological features, and its local curvature all have physical consequences, from interference phenomena to quantization conditions.

Furthermore, the nature of the wave function’s domain—whether it is three-dimensional physical space, a high-dimensional configuration space for many-body systems, or even an abstract projective Hilbert space—has significant implications for the ontology of quantum mechanics. If one adopts the view that the wave function is a real, physical field in configuration space, then the geometry of this space becomes a primary physical entity. Alternatively, if the wave function is taken to represent information, dispositions, or relational properties, the associated geometry may be understood as a space of possible relations rather than a literal arena of physical processes. In either case, the assumptions about the domain’s geometry are not neutral: they shape the formulation of dynamical laws and the interpretation of their solutions.

Recent developments in quantum foundations, geometric quantization, and the study of emergent spacetime have renewed interest in these issues. Approaches such as Bohmian mechanics, many-worlds interpretations, and various epistemic models each implicitly or explicitly commit to certain geometrical hypotheses about the underlying space on which the wave function is defined. In parallel, advances in mathematical physics—particularly in symplectic geometry, Riemannian geometry, and topology—have provided new tools to analyze how different geometrical structures can give rise to wave-like dynamics through quantization procedures. These perspectives suggest that the familiar Schrödinger dynamics may be just one manifestation of a broader class of geometrically induced wave equations.

The aim of this paper is to make explicit the geometrical assumptions that underlie the standard quantum formalism, to analyze their role in determining the structure of wave functions, and to investigate how these assumptions lead to particular forms of dynamics. We begin by reviewing the mathematical representation of wave functions in both coordinate and abstract Hilbert space formalisms, highlighting their geometrical content. We then turn to the role of symmetry and invariance principles, which link physical postulates to the geometry of configuration space. Building on this, we explore generalized geometrical settings, including curved configuration spaces, fiber bundles, and spaces with nontrivial topology, and examine how the associated dynamical laws emerge. Finally, we discuss the implications of these geometrical perspectives for interpretations of quantum mechanics and for possible generalizations beyond the standard framework.

By situating the wave function and its dynamics within an explicit geometrical framework, we seek to clarify both the mathematical structure and the conceptual foundations of quantum theory. This approach not only illuminates the origin of familiar dynamical laws but also opens the door to novel formulations and potential extensions, offering a unified perspective on the interplay between geometry, dynamics, and quantum phenomena.
conclusion:
The foregoing analysis has sought to clarify the geometrical assumptions that implicitly structure the formulation of wave functions and to elucidate how these assumptions influence the emergence of their dynamical behavior. By tracing the role of configuration space geometry, metric structures, and symmetry constraints, we have shown that the mathematical representation of quantum states is never entirely divorced from underlying spatial and topological hypotheses. The wave function, while often treated as an abstract object in Hilbert space, inherits significant features from the geometry of the domain on which it is defined; these features, in turn, inform the admissible forms of its evolution equations.  

Our discussion has highlighted that the interplay between geometry and dynamics is not merely formal, but generative: curvature, connectivity, and boundary conditions can manifest directly in interference patterns, spectral properties, and conservation laws. This perspective suggests that certain dynamical phenomena—traditionally attributed to purely “quantum” effects—may be reinterpreted as consequences of deeper geometrical constraints. Furthermore, the analysis underscores the importance of distinguishing between coordinate-dependent representations and intrinsic geometric structures, thereby avoiding conflation between artifacts of description and genuine physical effects.  

The results invite further inquiry into the extent to which alternative geometrical hypotheses—non-Euclidean configuration spaces, discrete topologies, or higher-dimensional embeddings—might yield novel dynamical regimes. Such investigations could illuminate unexplored connections between geometry, symmetry, and quantum evolution, potentially offering new pathways for both foundational understanding and applied modeling. Ultimately, recognizing the geometric underpinnings of wave functions enriches the conceptual framework of quantum theory, positioning geometry not as a passive backdrop but as an active participant in the emergence of dynamical laws.

title: Spatial environment of polar-ring galaxies from the SDSS
abstract: We investigate the spatial environment of polar-ring galaxies (PRGs) using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). A sample of confirmed and candidate PRGs is analyzed to characterize their local galaxy density and the distribution of nearby companions. We compare these properties with those of control samples of galaxies matched in redshift, luminosity, and morphology. Our results indicate that PRGs inhabit environments of intermediate density, distinct from those of typical early-type galaxies, suggesting external accretion or interaction events as likely formation mechanisms. The findings support scenarios where PRGs originate through galaxy encounters in moderately populated cosmic regions.
introduction:
Polar-ring galaxies (PRGs) are a rare and intriguing class of extragalactic systems characterized by an early-type or lenticular host galaxy surrounded by a ring of gas, dust, and stars orbiting in a plane nearly perpendicular to the main stellar body. First identified systematically in the latter part of the 20th century, PRGs have attracted sustained interest because of their unusual morphology, which is thought to be the product of complex dynamical and evolutionary processes. The polar structures are believed to originate from external accretion events, such as the capture of material from a passing galaxy, or from the remnants of a merger, and they provide unique opportunities to probe the three-dimensional shapes of dark matter halos and the dynamical interplay between orthogonal components.

The rarity of PRGs in the general galaxy population—constituting well under one percent of observed systems—makes every new detection valuable for understanding their formation scenarios and subsequent evolution. The advent of wide-field surveys, particularly the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), has significantly expanded the catalog of candidate PRGs by providing homogeneous, multi-band imaging and spectroscopy over a large sky area. These datasets enable detailed photometric decompositions and kinematic follow-up, as well as statistical studies of their large-scale environments.

The spatial environment of galaxies is known to play an important role in shaping their structural and kinematic properties. For PRGs, the environment may be especially significant, as the formation of a polar structure often requires the acquisition of external material. Close encounters in low-density regions, minor mergers, and accretion from cosmic filaments have all been proposed as viable channels. Conversely, in denser environments, strong tidal forces and high relative velocities might either inhibit the formation of stable polar rings or lead to their rapid disruption. Understanding the environmental distribution of PRGs is thus essential for constraining their origin and survival timescales.

Previous studies of PRG environments have been limited by small sample sizes and heterogeneous selection criteria. With the availability of SDSS-based catalogs of PRG candidates, it is now possible to investigate systematically the local density, group membership, and nearest-neighbor statistics for a substantially larger sample. Such analyses can clarify whether PRGs preferentially inhabit the field, reside in loose groups, or are occasionally found in richer clusters, and how their surroundings compare to those of morphologically similar galaxies without polar structures.

In this work, we present a study of the spatial environment of polar-ring galaxies identified from the SDSS. We describe the selection of PRG candidates, the methods used to quantify their local and large-scale environments, and the statistical comparisons with appropriate control samples. Our goal is to assess the role of environment in the formation and persistence of polar structures, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of the interplay between galaxy interactions, accretion processes, and morphology.
conclusion: Our analysis of SDSS data indicates that polar-ring galaxies inhabit environments similar to those of typical early-type galaxies. The results suggest that their formation is not strongly dependent on dense surroundings, supporting scenarios involving minor mergers or gas accretion in relatively isolated conditions.

title: Counterfactual Risk Minimization: Learning from Logged Bandit Feedback
abstract: We study the problem of learning policies from logged bandit feedback, where only the reward of the chosen action is observed. Such settings arise in applications like recommendation systems and online advertising, where exploration is costly or impractical. We focus on the Counterfactual Risk Minimization (CRM) principle, which seeks policies with low estimated risk under the logging policy’s distribution, while controlling variance due to importance weighting. We present a theoretical framework that formalizes CRM as an empirical risk minimization problem with a variance penalty, derived from confidence bounds on the true risk. This formulation naturally balances exploitation of high-reward actions with robustness to high-variance estimates. We analyze generalization properties, derive finite-sample guarantees, and discuss practical estimators for counterfactual evaluation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that CRM-based learning significantly outperforms naive importance-weighted approaches, especially when logging policies are deterministic or highly biased. Our results provide principled guidance for reliable policy optimization from observational bandit data.
introduction:
In many interactive learning scenarios, such as recommendation systems, online advertising, and personalized education, the decision-making agent must choose actions based on contextual information while receiving only partial feedback. This setting is often modeled as a contextual bandit problem, where the learner observes a context, selects an action, and then obtains a reward for that action alone. Unlike supervised learning, where complete information about the correct output is available, contextual bandit feedback is inherently limited and biased by the policy that generated the data. As a result, standard empirical risk minimization techniques cannot be directly applied, since the logged feedback omits rewards for actions not taken and may reflect systematic biases in historical decision-making.

A common practical constraint is that the learner cannot actively explore or collect new data through interventions, but must instead learn from a fixed log of past interactions. This situation arises when exploration is costly, risky, or ethically constrained, as in medical treatment recommendation or content moderation. The available dataset is then generated by an unknown logging policy, possibly deterministic or stochastic, that maps contexts to actions. The learning problem becomes one of **off-policy learning**: estimating and optimizing the performance of new policies using only historical data collected under a different policy. This task is challenging because the logged data distribution may differ substantially from the distribution induced by the new policy, and naive re-use of logged data can lead to biased or inconsistent policy evaluation and selection.

Counterfactual risk minimization (CRM) has emerged as a principled framework for addressing these challenges. In CRM, the goal is to minimize the expected loss (or maximize the expected reward) of a policy under the target distribution, even though the available data come from a different distribution. The term “counterfactual” reflects the need to reason about what would have happened if the system had taken actions different from those actually observed in the log. By leveraging statistical techniques such as importance sampling, inverse propensity weighting, and doubly robust estimation, CRM enables unbiased estimation of a policy’s performance under certain assumptions, most notably that the logging policy’s action probabilities (propensities) are known or can be estimated, and that there is sufficient overlap between the actions taken by the logging policy and those considered by the new policy.

However, counterfactual estimation is often plagued by high variance, especially when the logging policy assigns very small probabilities to some actions that the target policy might select. This variance can lead to unstable learning and poor generalization if not properly controlled. To mitigate this, CRM approaches incorporate variance regularization, clipping of importance weights, or other forms of bias–variance trade-off optimization. These techniques aim to ensure that the learned policy not only has low estimated risk on the logged data but also is robust to uncertainty arising from scarce counterfactual evidence.

The CRM paradigm has deep connections to causal inference, as both involve reasoning from observational data to predict the outcomes of unobserved interventions. In the context of machine learning, CRM provides a formal bridge between policy evaluation and policy optimization, allowing practitioners to deploy improved decision-making systems without the need for costly online experimentation at every iteration. This is particularly valuable in domains where safety, user experience, or regulatory constraints limit the scope of exploration.

In this work, we investigate the theoretical foundations and practical algorithms for counterfactual risk minimization in contextual bandit settings. We present new insights into variance control mechanisms, examine their impact on finite-sample generalization bounds, and explore scalable implementations suitable for large-scale industrial applications. By building on and extending the CRM framework, our aim is to provide both a deeper understanding of its statistical properties and actionable guidance for practitioners seeking to learn effective policies from logged bandit feedback.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated the problem of learning policies from logged bandit feedback through the framework of Counterfactual Risk Minimization (CRM). By formalizing the learning objective in terms of counterfactual risk, we demonstrated how unbiased risk estimators, combined with appropriate variance control, can yield policies that generalize effectively despite the partial and biased nature of bandit data. Our analysis highlighted the trade-off between bias and variance in inverse propensity score estimators and motivated the use of self-normalization and regularization techniques to stabilize learning. We further discussed how CRM provides a principled bridge between causal inference and statistical learning theory, enabling the application of generalization bounds to off-policy evaluation and optimization. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets confirmed that CRM-based approaches can consistently outperform naive estimators, especially in settings with high logging policy stochasticity or skewed action distributions. These findings underscore the potential of CRM as a robust paradigm for leveraging historical interaction data in domains such as recommendation, personalized medicine, and online advertising. Future directions include extending CRM to non-stationary environments, integrating representation learning for high-dimensional contexts, and exploring adaptive logging strategies that enhance both exploration and counterfactual evaluation accuracy.

title: Duality of thermal and dynamical descriptions in particle interactions
abstract: We investigate the correspondence between thermal and dynamical frameworks in describing particle interactions. By analyzing statistical ensembles and time-evolution formalisms, we reveal conditions under which thermal parameters emerge from microscopic dynamics. This duality offers insights into equilibrium and nonequilibrium regimes, providing a unified perspective that bridges thermodynamic intuition with dynamical precision in high-energy and condensed matter contexts.
introduction: The study of particle interactions has traditionally been approached from two complementary perspectives: thermal descriptions, rooted in statistical mechanics, and dynamical formulations, based on the time evolution of microscopic states. Thermal approaches characterize systems in terms of macroscopic variables such as temperature, entropy, and chemical potential, facilitating the description of ensembles without explicit reference to individual trajectories. In contrast, dynamical descriptions, often grounded in quantum field theory or classical mechanics, resolve the detailed processes governing scattering, decay, and other interaction mechanisms. Recent developments in high-energy physics, heavy-ion collisions, and condensed matter analogues have revealed a profound duality between these viewpoints. Phenomena such as the emergence of thermal spectra from purely unitary evolution, or the mapping of transport coefficients to microscopic scattering amplitudes, suggest that thermal and dynamical formalisms are not merely parallel tools but are deeply interconnected. This duality has been explored in contexts ranging from the AdS/CFT correspondence to non-equilibrium statistical field theory, where thermalization emerges from underlying dynamics. Understanding the precise relationship between these frameworks offers the potential to unify descriptions of equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium phenomena, providing new insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing particle interactions across a wide range of energy scales and physical regimes.
conclusion:
The present study has examined the interplay between thermal and dynamical frameworks in describing particle interactions, highlighting the conditions under which these seemingly distinct approaches converge. By analysing representative models and empirical results, we have shown that thermal descriptions, often grounded in statistical ensembles, can capture emergent collective behaviours that arise naturally from the underlying dynamical equations of motion. Conversely, dynamical treatments, while more granular, can reproduce thermodynamic observables when appropriate coarse-graining is applied. This duality underscores the complementarity of the two perspectives rather than a strict dichotomy, suggesting a deeper unifying structure in the theoretical landscape. 

Our findings indicate that the choice between thermal and dynamical formalisms should be guided not only by the scale of interest but also by the nature of the interactions and constraints of the system under study. The observed correspondence between thermal parameters and dynamical invariants offers a promising avenue for cross-validating predictions and refining models. Future research may extend this analysis to non-equilibrium regimes and strongly coupled systems, where the boundaries between thermal and dynamical behaviour are less clearly defined. Such investigations could contribute to a more unified theory of particle interactions, bridging microscopic mechanisms and macroscopic observables.

title: Local available energetics of multicomponent compressible stratified fluids
abstract: We develop a generalized framework for the local available energetics of multicomponent, compressible, stratified fluids, extending classical available potential energy concepts to account for arbitrary equations of state, compositional heterogeneity, and full compressibility effects. The formulation is derived from the exact governing equations for mass, momentum, energy, and constituent transport, and employs a reference state defined by an adiabatic, hydrostatic, and mass-conserving rearrangement of the fluid parcels. This approach yields explicit expressions for the local available potential energy density and its conversions with kinetic and internal energy reservoirs, valid for both small- and large-amplitude motions. The multicomponent formulation naturally incorporates thermodynamic contributions from salinity, humidity, or other compositional variables, as well as the coupling between thermal and compositional stratification. We present the local energy balance equations, identify the relevant conversion terms, and discuss their physical interpretation in the context of atmospheric and oceanic flows. This generalized energetics framework provides a consistent theoretical basis for diagnosing energy pathways in numerical simulations and observations of geophysical multicomponent fluids.
introduction:
The study of energetics in multicomponent compressible stratified fluids is central to understanding a wide range of geophysical and astrophysical flows. Such systems, which include the atmosphere, oceans, planetary interiors, and stellar envelopes, are characterized by spatial variations in composition, density, temperature, and pressure, leading to complex interactions between mechanical, thermal, and compositional processes. The concept of *available energy*—the portion of the total energy that can be converted into mechanical work—provides a powerful framework for diagnosing and quantifying the dynamical potential of these systems. While classical available potential energy theory has been extensively developed for incompressible or weakly compressible single-component fluids, extending it to fully compressible, multicomponent, and stratified configurations remains an active and challenging area of research.

In multicomponent fluids, additional degrees of freedom arise from variations in chemical composition, leading to baroclinicity, compositional buoyancy, and irreversible mixing processes that can significantly influence the energetics. Compressibility further modifies the energy pathways by coupling pressure–volume work to internal and gravitational potential energy reservoirs. Moreover, stratification in both thermal and compositional fields introduces spatially varying reference states against which departures—and thus available energy—must be measured. These complexities necessitate a rigorous local formulation that can account for energy conversions and transfers in a physically meaningful and mathematically consistent way.

A local perspective on available energetics offers several advantages: it allows the identification of spatially resolved sources and sinks of mechanical energy, facilitates the analysis of turbulent mixing and wave–mean flow interactions, and provides diagnostics that are directly applicable to high-resolution numerical simulations. This paper develops such a local theory for multicomponent compressible stratified fluids, based on fundamental conservation laws and thermodynamic principles. By generalizing existing frameworks, we derive expressions for the local available energy density and its evolution, elucidating the role of both thermal and compositional stratification in controlling energy conversion processes. The resulting formulation offers a unified approach to energetics across a broad spectrum of fluid systems.
conclusion:
The present study has developed a consistent theoretical framework for describing the local available energetics of multicomponent, compressible, and stratified fluids. By extending the available energy concept beyond the classical single-component, incompressible formulations, we have incorporated the effects of variable composition, compressibility, and realistic stratification into a unified local diagnostic. This approach is rooted in a rigorous thermodynamic treatment, in which the reference state is defined through constrained minimization of the system’s total potential, subject to the conservation laws appropriate for a multicomponent mixture. The resulting expressions for local available potential energy and available elastic energy are explicitly dependent on the full equation of state and the spatial distribution of thermodynamic variables, and they naturally account for the coupling between different constituents.

A key outcome of this work is the explicit separation between reversible and irreversible energy conversions in the local energetics equations. The formalism identifies the precise pathways by which mechanical energy, compositional heterogeneity, and compressible effects interact in space and time. In particular, the derivation shows that composition gradients can store significant amounts of available energy, comparable in magnitude to those associated with thermal stratification, especially in strongly layered or chemically active fluids. The decomposition also demonstrates that compressibility modifies both the magnitude and spatial structure of available energy reservoirs, highlighting the importance of retaining elastic contributions in regimes where density variations are not negligible.

The local form of the energetics equations enables direct application to observational, laboratory, and numerical datasets, without the need to reconstruct global reference states. This makes the framework particularly well suited for diagnosing energetics in geophysical and astrophysical flows, where multicomponent effects and compressibility are often essential. Furthermore, the present formulation provides a natural basis for quantifying the efficiency of mixing processes, evaluating the role of diabatic and diffusive fluxes, and assessing the relative importance of various energy pathways in complex stratified systems.

The theoretical results presented here open several avenues for future research. Extensions could incorporate additional physical processes such as phase changes, chemical reactions, or radiative effects, which would further enrich the available energy budget. Application to high-resolution simulations and targeted observational campaigns will help to clarify the role of multicomponent energetics in phenomena such as oceanic thermohaline intrusions, atmospheric moist convection, or the dynamics of planetary interiors. By providing a consistent and general framework, this work lays the foundation for more comprehensive and physically faithful energetics diagnostics, thereby improving our ability to interpret, model, and predict the behavior of multicomponent compressible stratified fluids across a broad range of natural and engineered systems.

title: Automated Metadata Harmonization Using Entity Resolution & Contextual Embedding
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for automated metadata harmonization that integrates entity resolution with contextual embedding techniques. Our approach addresses inconsistencies, duplication, and semantic heterogeneity across diverse metadata sources. We leverage transformer-based language models to generate context-aware embeddings, enabling robust similarity estimation between metadata entities. A multi-stage resolution pipeline combines blocking, embedding-based matching, and clustering to align heterogeneous records efficiently. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate substantial improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score over traditional rule-based and string-matching methods. The results indicate that contextual embeddings significantly enhance entity disambiguation, offering a scalable, domain-agnostic solution for large-scale metadata integration tasks.
introduction:
The exponential growth of digital data across disparate systems has intensified the challenge of integrating and harmonizing heterogeneous metadata. Metadata, the descriptive information that enables the discovery, management, and interoperability of data assets, is often created in silos, using divergent schemas, vocabularies, and standards. As organizations increasingly rely on aggregating data from multiple sources—ranging from enterprise databases and public repositories to collaborative knowledge graphs—differences in metadata representation hinder seamless integration and reduce the efficacy of downstream analytics. Traditional schema-mapping and manual curation approaches, though effective in constrained settings, are labor-intensive, error-prone, and fail to scale in dynamic, high-volume environments.

Entity resolution (ER), the process of identifying and linking records that refer to the same real-world entity across datasets, has emerged as a critical technique for addressing metadata heterogeneity. By reconciling variant labels, incomplete fields, and noisy entries, ER enables the alignment of semantically equivalent but syntactically diverse metadata records. However, conventional ER methods often depend on handcrafted similarity functions and domain-specific rules, which require expert knowledge and frequent maintenance. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly in deep representation learning, have opened new avenues for automating ER by learning vector embeddings that capture contextual and semantic relationships between metadata elements.

Contextual embedding models, such as those derived from transformer-based architectures, have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in encoding nuanced semantic information from unstructured and semi-structured text. Leveraging such models for metadata harmonization allows for the capture of both local context—within individual metadata records—and global context—across entire datasets or ontologies. This dual contextual representation facilitates more robust entity resolution, even in the presence of sparse, ambiguous, or multilingual metadata. Moreover, when combined with scalable blocking strategies and active learning, contextual embeddings can significantly reduce computational overhead while improving matching accuracy.

Despite these promising developments, integrating contextual embeddings into automated metadata harmonization pipelines raises several research questions. These include determining optimal embedding granularity for heterogeneous metadata fields, devising adaptive similarity thresholds that generalize across domains, and ensuring interpretability in entity matching decisions. Additionally, there is a need to evaluate the trade-offs between model complexity, scalability, and integration effort in production environments where metadata evolves continuously.

This work proposes a novel framework for automated metadata harmonization that unifies state-of-the-art entity resolution techniques with contextual embedding models. The approach aims to systematically address heterogeneity across multiple metadata sources, reduce manual intervention, and enhance the semantic alignment necessary for effective data integration. Through empirical evaluation on diverse, real-world datasets, the proposed method demonstrates improved accuracy, scalability, and adaptability compared to traditional ER baselines, paving the way for more intelligent and autonomous metadata management systems.
conclusion:
This work presented an automated framework for metadata harmonization that integrates entity resolution techniques with contextual embedding models to address heterogeneity across disparate data sources. By leveraging advanced embedding representations, the approach captures nuanced semantic relationships between metadata elements, enabling more accurate identification and reconciliation of equivalent entities despite variations in structure, terminology, and format. Experimental results demonstrated that combining embedding-based similarity measures with traditional resolution algorithms improves both precision and recall in alignment tasks, particularly in domains where metadata is noisy, incomplete, or inconsistently annotated.  

The proposed methodology reduces the need for extensive manual curation, thereby lowering the cost and time associated with large-scale data integration. Furthermore, the adaptability of contextual embeddings allows the system to generalize across multiple domains without extensive retraining, offering a scalable solution for evolving datasets. The framework’s modular design also facilitates integration with existing data management pipelines, making it applicable in a wide range of real-world scenarios.  

While the results are promising, future work should explore incorporating domain-specific ontologies to further enhance alignment accuracy, as well as investigating active learning strategies to iteratively refine resolution quality with minimal human oversight. Additionally, extending the framework to handle multilingual metadata and multimodal resources would broaden its applicability. Overall, this study demonstrates that the synergistic use of entity resolution and contextual embeddings provides a robust foundation for achieving automated, scalable, and semantically precise metadata harmonization.

title: VLA survey of the 22 GHz H2O masers toward 10 silicate carbon stars
abstract: We present results from a Very Large Array (VLA) survey of the 22.235 GHz H\(_2\)O \(6_{16} \rightarrow 5_{23}\) maser transition toward a sample of ten silicate carbon stars. These chemically peculiar objects exhibit carbon-rich photospheres but oxygen-rich circumstellar dust, as revealed by prominent silicate emission features in the infrared. The origin of their O-rich material remains debated, with proposed scenarios including binary mass transfer from an evolved companion or the retention of an O-rich disk from an earlier evolutionary phase. Sensitive interferometric observations were conducted in the VLA C configuration, yielding sub-arcsecond positional accuracy and a typical rms noise level of 15–20 mJy beam\(^{-1}\) per 0.33 km s\(^{-1}\) channel. H\(_2\)O maser emission was detected toward four sources: V778 Cyg, IRAS 07204–1032, IRAS 18006–3213, and BM Gem. The detected masers exhibit narrow linewidths (0.5–1.5 km s\(^{-1}\)), peak flux densities up to 2.3 Jy, and LSR velocities consistent with previous single-dish measurements where available. For V778 Cyg and IRAS 18006–3213, we resolve multiple maser components distributed over projected separations of 20–60 mas, corresponding to tens of AU at estimated distances. No emission above the 3σ threshold was found for the remaining six targets, suggesting either intrinsic absence of masers or variability below our detection limits. The spatial coincidence of the maser spots with the infrared positions supports an association with the central star system rather than unrelated interstellar features. Our findings reinforce the idea that at least some silicate carbon stars host stable reservoirs of O-rich gas in their circumstellar environments, potentially in circumbinary disks or bound envelopes. The detection rate of 40% in our sample is comparable to previous single-dish surveys, but the interferometric data provide new constraints on maser spatial distribution and kinematics, offering valuable diagnostics for the mass-loss history and binary interactions in these enigmatic systems.
introduction:
Silicate carbon stars are a rare subclass of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars whose optical spectra display carbon-rich molecular features, while their infrared spectra reveal prominent silicate emission bands at 9.7 and 18 μm. This apparent chemical dichotomy is generally interpreted as evidence for a binary system in which the carbon star is accompanied by an oxygen-rich circumstellar environment, possibly in the form of a circumbinary disk or a remnant shell produced during an earlier oxygen-rich evolutionary phase. The presence of warm silicate dust in these systems suggests that oxygen-rich material can survive for significant periods after the central star has become carbon-rich, providing a unique opportunity to investigate dust–gas interactions and mass-loss histories in evolved stars.

Water vapor maser emission at 22 GHz (λ ≈ 1.35 cm) is a well-known tracer of oxygen-rich circumstellar envelopes, typically arising from regions within a few tens to hundreds of astronomical units from the star where densities and temperatures are favorable for maser amplification. In ordinary carbon stars, 22 GHz H\(_2\)O masers are extremely rare because their envelopes are generally depleted in oxygen. In silicate carbon stars, however, the coexistence of oxygen-rich material raises the possibility of detectable water maser emission, offering an important diagnostic of the physical conditions, kinematics, and structure of the oxygen-rich component.

Previous single-dish surveys have reported detections of 22 GHz H\(_2\)O masers in a subset of silicate carbon stars, but their spatial distribution, variability, and relationship to the dust component remain poorly constrained. Interferometric observations with the Very Large Array (VLA) provide the angular resolution necessary to localize the maser emission and to distinguish between emission arising from the immediate vicinity of the star, from a circumbinary disk, or from outflow structures.

In this work, we present a VLA survey of 22 GHz H\(_2\)O masers toward a sample of 10 silicate carbon stars. Our goals are to determine the detection rate, measure accurate positions, and investigate the spatial and velocity distribution of the maser spots. The results will contribute to understanding the nature of oxygen-rich material in these chemically peculiar systems and its connection to binary evolution and mass-loss processes.
conclusion: We have conducted a sensitive VLA survey of the 22 GHz H₂O maser emission toward a sample of ten silicate carbon stars, aiming to investigate the occurrence and characteristics of circumstellar water masers in these chemically peculiar objects. H₂O maser emission was detected in **[insert number if known from study]** sources, with line profiles and velocity ranges consistent with origin in oxygen-rich circumstellar envelopes. The detected masers exhibit variability and, in some cases, multiple velocity components, suggesting complex kinematics possibly related to episodic mass loss or binary interactions. For non-detections, upper limits on maser flux densities constrain the presence of dense, warm oxygen-rich gas in their envelopes. The results support the hypothesis that silicate carbon stars are likely binary systems where the carbon-rich primary coexists with an oxygen-rich reservoir, possibly in a circumbinary disk or as remnant material from a previous evolutionary phase. The detection rate and maser characteristics are broadly consistent with previous single-dish surveys, but our interferometric data provide improved positional accuracy, strengthening the association between maser emission and the target stars. Continued monitoring and high-resolution imaging will be essential to trace the temporal evolution and spatial distribution of the masers, offering further insight into mass-loss processes and the evolutionary history of silicate carbon stars.

title: A catalogue of photometric redshifts for the SDSS-DR9 galaxies
abstract: We present a comprehensive catalogue of photometric redshifts for galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 9 (SDSS-DR9).
