Using a supervised machine learning approach based on the Multi Layer Perceptron with Quasi Newton Algorithm (MLPQNA), we derive redshift estimates for over 140 million galaxies with measured photometry in the *ugriz* bands. The training set is constructed from spectroscopic redshifts available in SDSS, carefully matched to photometric counterparts to optimise coverage in colour–magnitude space. We assess performance through a blind test sample, achieving a normalized median absolute deviation of 0.023 and a low fraction (<5%) of catastrophic outliers. The catalogue is designed to facilitate large-scale structure studies, galaxy evolution analyses, and cosmological applications where spectroscopic coverage is incomplete. All photometric redshifts, along with associated quality flags and estimated uncertainties, are publicly released. This work significantly expands the available redshift information for SDSS-DR9, enabling robust statistical analyses over unprecedented volumes in the low- to intermediate-redshift Universe.
introduction:
The determination of galaxy redshifts is a fundamental step in the study of the large-scale structure of the Universe, galaxy evolution, and cosmology. While spectroscopic redshifts provide highly accurate measurements, they require substantial observational time and resources, limiting their availability to a fraction of the observed galaxy population. Photometric redshift techniques, which estimate redshifts using broad-band photometry, offer a complementary approach that enables the analysis of much larger samples, albeit with lower precision. These methods have become increasingly important with the advent of large photometric surveys, where spectroscopic follow-up is impractical for the majority of detected sources.  

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has been one of the most influential astronomical surveys, providing both imaging and spectroscopy for millions of celestial objects. The ninth data release (SDSS-DR9) offers extensive photometric data in five optical bands, along with a substantial spectroscopic sample that can be used for training and validation of photometric redshift estimators. Leveraging these resources, it is possible to construct reliable and homogeneous photometric redshift catalogues that significantly expand the available redshift information for galaxies beyond the spectroscopic subset.  

In this work, we present a comprehensive catalogue of photometric redshifts for SDSS-DR9 galaxies, derived using robust machine learning techniques trained on the available spectroscopic data. We describe the data selection, the redshift estimation methodology, and the validation procedures employed. The resulting catalogue is intended as a valuable resource for a wide range of astrophysical applications, including statistical studies of galaxies and cosmological analyses requiring large-volume redshift information.
conclusion:
We have presented a comprehensive catalogue of photometric redshifts for galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 9 (SDSS-DR9), derived using a robust and well-calibrated methodology. By combining high-quality photometric data with a carefully constructed training set, we achieved redshift estimates with competitive accuracy and low bias across a wide range of magnitudes and redshifts. The catalogue provides photometric redshifts for several million galaxies, significantly extending the utility of the SDSS dataset for studies where spectroscopic measurements are unavailable or impractical.  

Quality assessments based on independent validation samples demonstrate that the scatter and outlier fractions are consistent with or surpass those of previous large-scale photometric redshift compilations from earlier SDSS releases. This improvement is particularly notable for faint and high-redshift galaxies, where photometric uncertainties are larger. The catalogue thus offers a valuable resource for statistical analyses of large galaxy populations, enabling investigations into galaxy evolution, large-scale structure, and cosmology.  

The full dataset and accompanying documentation are publicly available, facilitating its integration into a wide range of scientific projects. Future refinements may incorporate additional photometric bands, improved machine-learning techniques, and cross-matches with next-generation surveys to further enhance redshift precision. We anticipate that this catalogue will serve as a foundational tool for the astronomical community, supporting both targeted studies and broad statistical explorations in the era of increasingly large and deep photometric surveys.

title: Space-time Schr\"odinger symmetries of a post-Galilean particle
abstract: We investigate the space-time symmetries of a nonrelativistic particle governed by a post-Galilean deformation of the Schrödinger equation. By extending the conventional Galilei algebra, we identify modified generators and their commutation relations, revealing novel dynamical scaling properties. The resulting symmetry structure interpolates between Galilean and relativistic regimes, offering insights into intermediate kinematical frameworks. Potential applications to effective field theories and condensed matter systems with emergent nonstandard dispersion relations are discussed, highlighting the physical relevance of the symmetry deformation.
introduction:
The study of nonrelativistic symmetries and their deformations has played a central role in understanding both fundamental and effective descriptions of physical systems. The Galilei group, embodying the invariances of Newtonian mechanics, provides the starting point for the formulation of the Schrödinger equation and its well-known enlargement to the Schrödinger group, which incorporates scale and conformal transformations in space-time. These symmetries have far-reaching implications in areas ranging from cold atom physics to nonrelativistic holography. In recent years, interest has grown in exploring generalized kinematics that interpolate between Galilean and relativistic regimes, often referred to as post-Galilean frameworks. Such models arise naturally in effective field theories with higher-order corrections, in noncommutative geometry, and in certain condensed matter contexts where deviations from exact Galilean invariance become relevant.

A post-Galilean particle may be defined as a dynamical system whose kinematics are governed by a deformation of the Galilei algebra, incorporating subleading terms in an expansion in inverse powers of the speed of light or other characteristic scales. These modifications alter the structure of the conserved quantities and require a reassessment of the associated space-time symmetries. The central question addressed here is how the familiar Schrödinger invariance, with its rich algebraic and dynamical content, is modified in the presence of such post-Galilean corrections.

In this work we investigate the space-time Schrödinger symmetries of a free post-Galilean particle. We begin by formulating the effective dynamics from a deformed Lagrangian or Hamiltonian framework, identifying the modified generators of space-time transformations. We then determine the algebraic closure of these generators and compare it with the standard Schrödinger algebra. Particular attention is given to the fate of scale invariance, special conformal transformations, and the role of central extensions. Our analysis reveals both preserved and broken symmetry structures, shedding light on the interplay between deformation parameters and conformal-type invariances. These results provide a systematic foundation for extending nonrelativistic conformal methods to broader classes of kinematical algebras, with potential applications to quantum mechanical models beyond the strictly Galilean regime.
conclusion:
In this work, we have undertaken a systematic analysis of the space–time Schrödinger symmetries associated with a post-Galilean particle, elucidating both their algebraic structure and their physical implications. Starting from a nonrelativistic framework augmented by post-Galilean corrections, we have shown how the conventional Schrödinger group, well known as the maximal kinematical invariance group of the free Schrödinger equation, is modified when higher-order terms in \( 1/c \) are retained. These corrections, while preserving the essential features of nonrelativistic quantum kinematics, introduce nontrivial deformations in the generators and their commutation relations, leading to a generalized symmetry algebra.

Our investigation demonstrates that the post-Galilean regime interpolates smoothly between the Galilean and relativistic domains, with the symmetry transformations acquiring additional structure that reflects the finite but large value of the speed of light. In particular, we have identified the modified forms of boosts, dilations, and expansions, and determined how these affect the conserved quantities via Noether’s theorem. The persistence of certain subalgebras, even in the presence of post-Galilean terms, suggests a robustness of the underlying dynamical symmetries, while the deformation of other generators encodes the first relativistic corrections to nonrelativistic dynamics.

By constructing explicit realizations of the deformed Schrödinger algebra in space–time, we have clarified how the wavefunction transforms under the extended group and how invariant equations of motion can be formulated. This provides a concrete bridge between abstract algebraic considerations and physically relevant dynamical models. Moreover, we have discussed the role of mass as a central charge in the extended algebra, noting how its interpretation is subtly altered in the post-Galilean context.

The results presented here open several avenues for further research. One natural direction is the exploration of interacting systems within the same symmetry framework, examining whether and how potentials can be incorporated while retaining a generalized Schrödinger invariance. Another promising extension involves the study of field-theoretic models, where the interplay between post-Galilean corrections and many-body effects could yield novel emergent symmetries. From a mathematical perspective, the deformation patterns uncovered in this analysis invite a deeper classification effort, possibly linking to broader structures in nonrelativistic conformal algebras and their contractions from relativistic counterparts.

In summary, we have provided a coherent description of space–time Schrödinger symmetries for a post-Galilean particle, capturing the leading corrections to the Galilean limit and revealing the modified algebraic landscape that results. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to understand the symmetry principles governing quantum systems beyond the strict nonrelativistic approximation, thereby enriching both the conceptual and the technical toolkit available for future investigations at the interface of quantum mechanics and relativity.

title: Sparse representation of solutions of Kronecker product systems
abstract: We investigate sparse representations of solutions to linear systems whose coefficient matrices are Kronecker products. Exploiting tensor product structures, we develop algorithms that recover solutions with few nonzero coefficients in suitable bases. Theoretical bounds and numerical experiments demonstrate improved efficiency and accuracy over standard methods, particularly for high-dimensional problems arising in scientific computing and data analysis.
introduction:
Linear systems involving Kronecker products arise naturally in a wide range of scientific and engineering applications, including the numerical solution of partial differential equations, signal and image processing, control theory, and machine learning. A Kronecker product structure often appears when discretizing multidimensional problems using separable bases, leading to coefficient matrices that can be expressed as tensor products of smaller factors. This structure offers significant opportunities for computational savings, as operations with Kronecker products can be reformulated to reduce both storage requirements and arithmetic complexity.  

In many applications, the underlying solutions to Kronecker product systems exhibit additional structure beyond the separability of the coefficient matrix. In particular, the solution vectors or matrices may be sparse, either exactly or approximately, in a suitable basis. Exploiting sparsity can bring further gains in efficiency, enabling the treatment of large-scale problems that would otherwise be intractable. Sparse representations also enhance interpretability, as they identify the most relevant components of the solution in the chosen representation space.  

Despite the clear potential benefits, the theory and practice of combining Kronecker product structures with sparse representations remain underdeveloped. Existing approaches often treat these properties in isolation: algorithms for Kronecker systems focus on exploiting tensor-product factorizations, while sparse recovery methods address generic linear systems without leveraging Kronecker structure. The interaction between these two forms of structure raises new questions in approximation theory, numerical linear algebra, and optimization. For example, one may ask how sparsity patterns transform under Kronecker operations, or how to design solvers that jointly exploit separability and sparsity for optimal complexity.  

This work aims to address these questions by developing a framework for the sparse representation of solutions to Kronecker product systems. We investigate theoretical conditions under which sparse solutions exist, propose algorithms that exploit both forms of structure, and illustrate their performance on representative problems from computational science and engineering. Our results demonstrate that a careful integration of Kronecker and sparsity concepts yields substantial advantages in both accuracy and efficiency.
conclusion: We have presented a framework for sparse representation of solutions to Kronecker product systems, exploiting structural properties to reduce computational complexity. The proposed approach achieves efficient storage and reconstruction while preserving accuracy. Future work will address extensions to nonlinear settings and explore adaptive methods for improved sparsity and scalability.

title: Properties for the Frechet Mean in Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann Treespace
abstract: We investigate theoretical properties of the Fréchet mean in the Billera–Holmes–Vogtmann (BHV) treespace, a non-positively curved space of phylogenetic trees. The BHV framework enables rigorous statistical analysis of tree-structured data, yet the geometry complicates both computation and interpretation of the mean. We examine conditions for uniqueness and stability of the Fréchet mean under perturbations of input data, characterize its location in relation to orthants defined by tree topologies, and analyze its behavior in degenerate cases with varying edge lengths. Our results clarify the influence of geodesic structure and combinatorial constraints on the mean, and extend known convexity arguments in CAT(0) spaces. These findings provide a foundation for robust statistical inference in phylogenetics, with implications for algorithmic efficiency and the interpretation of consensus trees in evolutionary biology.
introduction:
The Billera–Holmes–Vogtmann (BHV) treespace, introduced by Billera, Holmes, and Vogtmann (2001), provides a rigorous geometric framework for studying phylogenetic trees. In this space, each point represents a fully resolved phylogenetic tree with a fixed set of leaves, and distances are computed via geodesics that traverse a complex of Euclidean orthants, each corresponding to a distinct tree topology. The BHV treespace is a globally non-positively curved (CAT(0)) metric space, which endows it with a unique geodesic between any two points and guarantees the existence and uniqueness of certain statistical summaries, notably the Fréchet mean. The Fréchet mean, defined as the minimizer of the sum of squared distances to a given set of points, serves as a natural notion of central tendency in non-Euclidean spaces. In the context of phylogenetic trees, it yields a consensus tree that incorporates both topological and branch length information.

The statistical analysis of data in BHV treespace has garnered significant attention in recent years, driven by the need to summarize and compare large collections of phylogenetic trees arising from Bayesian posterior samples, bootstrap replicates, or heterogeneous datasets. Traditional consensus methods, such as majority-rule consensus, focus only on topological frequencies and ignore branch length variation, potentially discarding valuable evolutionary information. The Fréchet mean, by contrast, operates directly within the metric structure of BHV treespace, thereby integrating both topology and geometry. Moreover, the CAT(0) property ensures that the Fréchet function is strictly convex, which eliminates the issue of multiple local minima and simplifies the theoretical analysis.

Despite these appealing properties, the computation and theoretical characterization of the Fréchet mean in treespace present substantial challenges. The piecewise Euclidean structure of BHV treespace, combined with its high-dimensional and stratified nature, leads to nontrivial behavior of geodesics and distance functions, especially when data points lie in different orthants. The mean may occur in a lower-dimensional orthant, corresponding to a less resolved tree, reflecting the presence of topological variability in the data. Understanding how the geometry of the space and the distribution of sample points influence the location, topology, and branch lengths of the Fréchet mean is therefore a key problem in statistical phylogenetics.

Prior work has established foundational properties of BHV treespace and the behavior of geodesics, as well as algorithms for computing geodesic distances and Fréchet means. Billera, Holmes, and Vogtmann (2001) proved the CAT(0) property and described the basic combinatorial structure of the space. Subsequent contributions have refined algorithms for geodesic computation (Owen & Provan, 2011) and developed iterative procedures for mean estimation. Statistical properties such as consistency of the sample Fréchet mean in BHV treespace follow from general results for CAT(0) spaces (Sturm, 2003), but many finer aspects—such as the influence of tree topology variability on the dimensionality of the mean, its stability under perturbations, and its asymptotic distribution—remain incompletely understood.

This work investigates the properties of the Fréchet mean in BHV treespace, with an emphasis on both geometric and statistical characterizations relevant to phylogenetic applications. We examine conditions under which the mean lies in a top-dimensional orthant versus a lower-dimensional stratum, and explore how the arrangement of data points across orthants determines the combinatorial type of the mean. We further analyze the sensitivity of the mean to small changes in the input trees, linking these behaviors to the structure of the geodesic network and the convexity of the Fréchet function. By integrating geometric analysis with statistical reasoning, we aim to clarify the relationship between tree-space geometry and the interpretability of the Fréchet mean as a consensus object.

The results presented here contribute to a deeper understanding of statistical summaries in non-Euclidean spaces, and in particular to the practical interpretation of Fréchet means in evolutionary biology. Beyond phylogenetics, these findings illustrate principles that may apply to other data types represented in stratified CAT(0) spaces, such as certain shape spaces or spaces of networks. Ultimately, a more complete characterization of the Fréchet mean in BHV treespace enhances both the methodological toolkit available to evolutionary biologists and the theoretical foundations of non-Euclidean statistics.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined fundamental properties of the Fréchet mean within the Billera–Holmes–Vogtmann (BHV) treespace, emphasizing its geometric and statistical characteristics. By leveraging the non-positively curved structure of BHV space, we established conditions for uniqueness and continuity of the Fréchet mean, and clarified how its location reflects both topological and metric variation among input trees. Our analysis highlighted the interplay between combinatorial changes in tree topology and the piecewise-Euclidean geometry of the space, showing how these features influence convergence and stability under perturbations of the data. Furthermore, we discussed implications for practical computation, including the role of geodesic convexity in algorithmic approaches. These findings provide a rigorous foundation for interpreting average structures in phylogenetic analysis, and suggest avenues for extending statistical methodology to higher-dimensional and more complex tree spaces. Future work may focus on robust variants, inferential frameworks, and applications to empirical datasets.

title: The SLUGGS survey: a new mask design to reconstruct the stellar populations and kinematics of both inner and outer galaxy regions
abstract: We present a new spectroscopic mask design developed for the SLUGGS (SAGES Legacy Unifying Globulars and GalaxieS) survey, optimised to recover the stellar populations and kinematics of both the inner and outer regions of early-type galaxies in a single observation. Traditional multi-slit masks are typically constrained to either the central, high surface-brightness regions or the sparse outer halo, limiting the ability to construct continuous radial profiles. Our new design combines densely packed slits in the galaxy core with strategically placed slits along the major and minor axes extending to several effective radii. This configuration maximises spatial coverage while maintaining sufficient signal-to-noise for absorption line spectroscopy using the Keck/DEIMOS instrument. We describe the mask optimisation process, including target prioritisation, slit placement algorithms, and strategies to minimise spectral overlap. Simulations and test observations demonstrate that the design yields high-quality stellar kinematics and line-strength measurements across the full radial extent, enabling robust constraints on galaxy mass distributions, orbital anisotropies, and stellar population gradients. This approach improves observational efficiency, reducing the need for multiple masks and telescope pointings. The new mask design significantly enhances the scientific return of the SLUGGS survey and can be applied to other wide-field spectroscopic studies of nearby galaxies, providing a powerful tool for connecting inner galaxy dynamics to their extended halos.
introduction: Understanding the formation and evolution of galaxies requires detailed knowledge of their stellar populations and kinematics across a wide range of radii. While integral-field spectroscopy has revolutionised studies of galaxy centres, the low surface brightness of outer regions remains a significant observational challenge. The SLUGGS (SAGES Legacy Unifying Globulars and GalaxieS) survey has been designed to address this limitation by combining deep imaging with multi-object spectroscopy to probe both the dense inner regions and the diffuse outskirts of early-type galaxies. Traditional spectroscopic mask designs often optimise either for central coverage or for sampling of discrete tracers, such as globular clusters, in the halo. This compromises the ability to obtain spatially continuous stellar kinematic and population measurements across the full radial extent. Here we present a new spectroscopic mask design that overcomes these constraints by strategically placing slits to sample both the central galaxy light and the surrounding halo simultaneously. This approach enables a unified reconstruction of stellar population gradients and kinematic profiles from the innermost regions to several effective radii. We describe the design methodology, its implementation within SLUGGS, and demonstrate its effectiveness through early observational results.
conclusion:
We have presented a new spectroscopic mask design developed for the SLUGGS survey, optimised to simultaneously probe the stellar populations and kinematics of both the inner and outer regions of nearby early-type galaxies. This design, which strategically places slits to sample a wide radial extent while maximising multiplexing efficiency, addresses the long-standing limitation of traditional slitmask layouts that favour either central or halo regions, but rarely both in a single configuration. By combining a dense sampling of the central regions with extended coverage to several effective radii, the new approach enables a more complete and spatially continuous reconstruction of galaxy properties.  

Application of the mask design to commissioning observations has demonstrated its effectiveness in delivering high-quality spectra across the full radial range. The central regions yield data of sufficient signal-to-noise to perform detailed stellar population modelling, while the outer halo spectra, though fainter, retain adequate quality for robust velocity and metallicity measurements. The resulting datasets bridge the gap between the well-studied inner structures of early-type galaxies and their less understood halos, allowing for coherent dynamical modelling and chemodynamical analysis over unprecedented scales.  

This capability is particularly important for testing galaxy formation scenarios. The outer halo regions retain signatures of accretion events and mergers, while the central regions reflect early, rapid star formation episodes. By unifying these regimes within a single, internally consistent spectroscopic dataset, the SLUGGS mask design facilitates direct comparisons between core and halo properties, providing stringent constraints on models of two-phase galaxy assembly. The improved efficiency also reduces telescope time requirements, enabling the survey of larger samples and thus improving the statistical robustness of results.  

The methodology outlined here is readily adaptable to other multi-object spectrographs and could be applied to a range of galaxy types and environments. Future work will extend the application of the mask design to the full SLUGGS sample, incorporating a wider diversity of galaxy masses and morphologies, and will explore its utility in combination with integral field spectroscopy for the innermost regions. As the dataset grows, we anticipate transformative insights into the structural and chemical evolution of galaxies, from their cores to their extreme outskirts.  

In summary, the new SLUGGS mask design overcomes a critical observational challenge, enabling unified, high-fidelity spectroscopic mapping across the full extent of early-type galaxies. This advance opens a powerful window on the interplay of stellar populations and kinematics, offering a more complete view of galaxy formation and evolution.

title: Interferometric and single-dish observations of 44, 84 and 95 GHz Class I methanol masers
abstract: We present a study of Class I methanol masers at 44, 84, and 95 GHz using a combination of interferometric and single-dish observations. Our sample comprises a diverse set of star-forming regions, enabling a comparative analysis of maser properties across transitions and spatial scales. Single-dish spectra were used to identify maser candidates and measure integrated flux densities, while interferometric imaging provided precise positions, angular extents, and brightness distributions. We investigate correlations in intensity and spatial association among the three transitions, assessing their occurrence in relation to known outflows and dense gas tracers. The results reveal that 84 GHz masers are frequently co-located with 44 and 95 GHz counterparts, though notable exceptions suggest differing excitation conditions. Our findings highlight the complementary nature of multi-transition, multi-scale observations in constraining the physical environments and pumping mechanisms of Class I methanol masers in massive star-forming regions.
introduction: Class I methanol masers are collisionally pumped molecular transitions that trace shocked gas in regions of star formation. They are frequently associated with molecular outflows and expanding H II regions, and their study provides key insights into the physical conditions and kinematics of dense gas. Among the most prominent transitions are those at 44, 84, and 95 GHz, which probe similar environments but may arise under differing excitation conditions. Interferometric observations offer high spatial resolution, enabling precise localization of maser spots, while single-dish measurements provide sensitivity to extended or diffuse emission that may be resolved out by arrays. Combining both techniques allows a more complete characterization of maser distributions and intensities. In this work, we present coordinated interferometric and single-dish observations of 44, 84, and 95 GHz Class I methanol masers toward a sample of star-forming regions, aiming to compare their spatial and spectral properties.
conclusion: Our combined interferometric and single-dish observations of the 44, 84, and 95 GHz Class I methanol maser transitions reveal consistent spatial associations with regions of active star formation and outflow activity. The data confirm that these maser lines often coexist, though with notable variations in intensity ratios and spatial distributions. Interferometric imaging resolves complex morphologies, while single-dish measurements provide complementary flux recovery. These results strengthen the use of multi-transition Class I methanol maser studies as probes of the physical conditions and kinematics in shocked molecular gas.

title: Photon rockets in (anti-)de Sitter universe
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of photon rockets—idealized bodies propelled by anisotropic emission of radiation—in spacetimes with a nonzero cosmological constant. Exact solutions of Einstein’s equations in both de Sitter and anti-de Sitter backgrounds are presented, generalizing the Kinnersley rocket to curved cosmological settings. The influence of spacetime curvature on acceleration, radiation patterns, and trajectories is analyzed. We discuss physical implications for propulsion limits, energy requirements, and asymptotic structure. These results extend photon rocket models to expanding and contracting universes, offering insights into accelerated motion in curved backgrounds.
introduction:
The concept of a photon rocket, a hypothetical spacecraft propelled by the emission of directed electromagnetic radiation, has long served as a useful theoretical model in both relativistic mechanics and general relativity. In the simplest form, a photon rocket converts energy directly into photons and emits them anisotropically to produce thrust. While technologically speculative, the photon rocket represents an idealized limit of propulsion efficiency, since photons travel at the speed of light and carry momentum without rest mass. From a theoretical standpoint, the photon rocket constitutes an exact solution of Einstein’s equations when the energy–momentum tensor is chosen to describe a pure radiation field aligned with the rocket’s direction of motion. Such solutions have been studied in the context of Minkowski spacetime for decades, yielding insights into relativistic kinematics, mass–energy conversion, and the self-consistent coupling between the emission of radiation and the motion of the source.

In cosmology, however, the background spacetime is not flat but curved, reflecting the large-scale matter–energy content of the universe. The discovery of cosmic acceleration and the interpretation of this effect in terms of a nonzero cosmological constant Λ, or more generally dark energy, have motivated renewed interest in exact solutions of Einstein’s equations in de Sitter (Λ > 0) and anti–de Sitter (Λ < 0) spacetimes. The de Sitter universe, maximally symmetric and characterized by constant positive curvature, serves as the standard model for an empty universe dominated by a cosmological constant. Conversely, the anti–de Sitter universe has constant negative curvature and appears naturally in contexts such as the AdS/CFT correspondence in high-energy physics. Understanding the motion and dynamics of accelerated bodies in these curved backgrounds is of both conceptual and practical interest, as it sheds light on fundamental aspects of general relativity, including radiation reaction, energy conservation, and the global structure of spacetime.

The study of accelerated motion in (anti-)de Sitter spacetimes presents unique challenges. The presence of a cosmological horizon in de Sitter space modifies the causal structure and the propagation of radiation, while the timelike conformal boundary of anti–de Sitter space imposes different global constraints. For photon rockets, which emit null radiation in a preferred direction, these features influence not only the trajectory but also the back-reaction of the emitted radiation on the spacetime geometry. In the presence of Λ, exact solutions describing such systems are relatively rare, and their analysis provides valuable benchmarks for testing theoretical ideas about energy–momentum exchange and the role of the cosmological constant in dynamical processes.

Previous work has examined photon rocket solutions in flat spacetime, notably the Kinnersley rocket, which describes a pointlike mass undergoing arbitrary acceleration due to anisotropic photon emission. Extensions of this framework to include a cosmological constant have been less extensively explored, though related classes of solutions—such as the generalized Robinson–Trautman spacetimes with pure radiation—are known. These metrics allow for a clear description of radiation fields aligned with a principal null direction and can incorporate both mass loss and acceleration in a curved background.

In this paper we investigate photon rockets in both de Sitter and anti–de Sitter universes, constructing explicit solutions of Einstein’s equations with Λ ≠ 0 that generalize the Kinnersley class. We analyze their geometrical and physical properties, including the influence of the cosmological constant on the motion, the characteristics of the emitted radiation, and the structure of horizons. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of accelerated systems in cosmological spacetimes and provide exact models that may be relevant for both classical relativity and theoretical considerations in high-energy and gravitational physics.
conclusion: In this work we have investigated the dynamics of photon rockets within the context of de Sitter and anti–de Sitter spacetimes, extending the classical analysis from asymptotically flat backgrounds to cosmological settings with nonzero curvature. By employing exact solutions of the Einstein field equations with null dust sources, we have shown how the presence of a cosmological constant modifies both the global structure of the spacetime and the efficiency of photon propulsion. In de Sitter space, accelerated motion is influenced by the cosmological horizon, placing limits on observable trajectories and energy transfer, whereas in anti–de Sitter space the confining geometry alters the radiation pattern and momentum exchange. Our results highlight the interplay between local acceleration mechanisms and the large–scale geometry of the universe, suggesting that cosmological curvature can have significant implications for relativistic propulsion concepts. These findings may also serve as a stepping stone toward further studies of accelerated sources, radiation back–reaction, and potential observational signatures in curved cosmological backgrounds.

title: Low-dimensionality energy landscapes: Magnetic switching mechanisms and rates
abstract: We investigate magnetic switching mechanisms and rates in systems whose energy landscapes can be described by a small number of collective coordinates. By projecting the high-dimensional micromagnetic dynamics onto these low-dimensional manifolds, we obtain intuitive representations of the switching process in terms of reaction coordinates that capture the essential physics. This reduction enables the application of transition state theory and related methods to compute thermally activated switching rates with high accuracy and reduced computational cost. We analyze model systems with uniaxial and biaxial anisotropies, identifying saddle points and minimum-energy paths that govern reversal. The interplay between applied fields, anisotropy, and temperature is explored, revealing how the topology of the energy landscape dictates the dominant switching pathways. Comparisons between full micromagnetic simulations and the reduced-coordinate approach demonstrate quantitative agreement over a broad range of parameters, validating the method. Our results clarify the role of low-dimensional projections in understanding magnetization dynamics and provide a practical framework for predicting switching rates in nanoscale magnetic elements. This approach can be extended to more complex systems, offering a general route to link detailed micromagnetic models with simplified, physically transparent descriptions of thermally activated processes.
introduction:
Magnetic switching, the process by which the magnetization of a system reverses its orientation under the influence of external stimuli, is a central phenomenon in modern magnetic materials physics. It underpins the operation of a wide range of technologies, from magnetic data storage devices to spintronic components and magnetic sensors. The efficiency, stability, and speed of these devices are determined not only by the intrinsic properties of the magnetic materials but also by the dynamical pathways through which magnetization reversal occurs. Understanding the mechanisms and rates of magnetic switching is therefore of both fundamental and technological importance.

At the microscopic level, magnetic switching is governed by the interplay between magnetic anisotropy, exchange interactions, applied fields, and thermal fluctuations. Theoretical descriptions often employ the concept of an energy landscape, in which the magnetization configuration is represented as a point in a high-dimensional space, and the energy of the system defines a surface over this space. The local minima correspond to stable or metastable magnetic states, while the saddle points and connecting valleys represent possible transition pathways. In the absence of thermal agitation, switching occurs when external fields or spin torques drive the system over the energy barrier separating the minima. At finite temperatures, thermal activation can assist this process, enabling switching at lower fields or currents.

While the full energy landscape of a magnetic system is generally high-dimensional, in many cases the relevant switching dynamics can be captured by a small number of collective coordinates. This low-dimensionality arises because magnetization reversal often proceeds along well-defined pathways determined by the symmetry and effective anisotropy of the system. By projecting the dynamics onto these few degrees of freedom, one obtains a reduced description that retains the essential physics while enabling tractable analysis. Such reduced models have proved invaluable for interpreting experimental measurements, guiding materials design, and developing predictive theories for switching rates.

Classical approaches to magnetic switching rates, such as the Néel–Brown theory, treat the problem as thermally activated escape over a single energy barrier in a one-dimensional potential. Extensions to multidimensional systems, as formulated by Langer and others, account for the role of saddle points and the curvature of the energy surface in determining the prefactor of the Arrhenius law. Recent advances in computational micromagnetics and atomistic spin dynamics have made it possible to compute minimum energy paths and attempt frequencies for realistic nanostructures, revealing complex reversal modes including domain wall nucleation and propagation, curling, and localized nonuniform excitations. These studies highlight the importance of correctly identifying the relevant collective coordinates and the topology of the low-dimensional energy landscape.

The notion of low-dimensionality energy landscapes provides a unifying framework for understanding diverse switching mechanisms. For uniformly magnetized single-domain particles, the landscape is often well described by the Stoner–Wohlfarth model, with a simple dependence on the direction of magnetization. In contrast, for patterned nanomagnets, thin films, or systems with competing anisotropies, the landscape can exhibit multiple minima and saddle points associated with different reversal modes. Mapping these landscapes and the transition paths between minima allows one to predict how switching rates depend on temperature, applied field, and material parameters. Moreover, this approach facilitates the incorporation of stochastic effects, such as thermal noise, into the description of magnetization dynamics via the Fokker–Planck or Langevin formalisms.

In this work, we investigate magnetic switching mechanisms and rates within the framework of low-dimensional energy landscapes. We focus on how the reduction to a small set of collective coordinates enables a detailed analysis of the relevant saddle points, energy barriers, and dynamical prefactors. By combining analytical theory with numerical simulations, we aim to elucidate the connection between the geometry of the energy landscape and the statistical properties of switching events. This perspective not only advances the fundamental understanding of magnetization reversal but also provides practical insights for optimizing the performance and reliability of nanoscale magnetic devices.
conclusion: We have examined magnetic switching in low-dimensionality energy landscapes, highlighting how reduced configurational complexity shapes transition pathways and rates. By combining theoretical analysis with computational modeling, we identified distinct switching mechanisms governed by energy barrier topology and anisotropy effects. Our results demonstrate that switching rates are strongly influenced by the interplay between thermal activation and landscape geometry. These findings provide a framework for predicting and controlling magnetization reversal in nanoscale systems, with implications for the design of energy-efficient magnetic memory and spintronic devices.

title: Enhancing spatial resolution of soft x-ray CCD detectors by single-photon centroid determination
abstract: We present a method to enhance the spatial resolution of soft x-ray charge-coupled device (CCD) detectors through single-photon centroid determination. In conventional CCD imaging, the intrinsic pixel size and charge cloud diffusion limit the achievable resolution, even when the detector is coupled to high-quality x-ray optics. By accurately estimating the impact position of individual photons, subpixel resolution can be attained. Our approach involves identifying isolated photon events in raw CCD frames, fitting the corresponding charge distributions with a two-dimensional Gaussian model, and calculating the centroid coordinates with precision significantly finer than the pixel pitch. We evaluate the method using soft x-ray illumination in the energy range 200–1000 eV, where charge spreading is substantial. Experimental results show that the effective spatial resolution improves by up to a factor of three compared to standard pixel-based reconstructions, yielding a point-spread function width below 10 μm for a pixel size of 24 μm. The trade-offs between spatial resolution, photon flux, and processing time are discussed, along with the influence of readout noise and event overlap on centroid accuracy. This centroiding technique offers a straightforward, software-based enhancement to existing CCD systems, enabling higher-resolution imaging in soft x-ray microscopy, spectroscopy, and scattering experiments without hardware modification.
introduction:
Soft x-ray detection plays a central role in a wide range of scientific and technological applications, spanning synchrotron radiation experiments, plasma diagnostics, materials characterization, and biological imaging. In many of these fields, charge-coupled devices (CCDs) have become the detectors of choice due to their high quantum efficiency, large dynamic range, and ability to provide two-dimensional spatial information. However, despite these advantages, the finite size of CCD pixels imposes a limit on the achievable spatial resolution. For soft x-ray photons, whose energies typically range from a few tens to a few thousand electronvolts, the interaction with the detector material leads to the generation of electron clouds that are subsequently collected and read out as discrete events. The spatial resolution is then determined not only by the pixel pitch but also by the physics of charge generation, diffusion, and collection within the CCD.

When a single soft x-ray photon is absorbed in the CCD’s sensitive layer, its energy is converted into a cloud of electron–hole pairs. This cloud undergoes lateral diffusion as it drifts under the influence of the internal electric field toward the potential wells of the pixels. As a result, the charge generated by a single photon is often distributed over multiple adjacent pixels, forming a so-called “charge spot” or “event.” The standard approach in CCD imaging integrates the signal over each pixel, effectively assigning the photon’s position to the center of the pixel containing the largest fraction of the charge. While straightforward, this method discards sub-pixel spatial information contained within the distribution of charge among neighboring pixels.

The concept of centroid determination, originally developed in visible-light photon-counting applications, offers a route to surpass the nominal pixel-limited spatial resolution. By calculating the center-of-mass of the charge distribution for each photon event, it is possible to estimate the photon’s impact position with a precision significantly finer than the pixel pitch. This single-photon centroiding technique exploits the statistical nature of charge sharing between pixels to retrieve positional information on a sub-pixel scale. The achievable improvement depends on factors such as the initial size of the generated charge cloud, the pixel geometry, the readout noise, and the algorithm used for centroid estimation.

In the soft x-ray regime, where photon energies produce relatively large charge clouds, centroiding can be particularly effective. The charge clouds often extend over several pixels, inherently providing the spatial diversity needed for accurate center-of-mass calculations. Moreover, many experiments in this spectral range are photon-limited, operating in conditions where photon arrival rates are low enough to resolve individual events without significant overlap. Under such circumstances, centroiding becomes a practical means of enhancing spatial resolution without hardware modification. This is especially relevant for synchrotron beamlines and free-electron laser facilities, where maximizing the resolving power of available detectors directly benefits the quality of spectroscopic and imaging data.

Despite its promise, the application of centroiding to soft x-ray CCD detection presents several challenges. Accurate centroid estimation requires precise mapping of the charge distribution, which can be compromised by readout noise, dark current, and imperfections in the detector response. The presence of split events, in which the photon-generated charge is divided among several non-contiguous pixels due to the geometry of the cloud and pixel boundaries, complicates the identification and analysis of valid photon events. Furthermore, the centroid algorithm must be robust against variations in event shape arising from changes in photon energy, incidence angle, and local electric field conditions within the device. In addition, the computational demands of real-time centroid processing may be non-trivial, particularly when dealing with large-format CCDs and high frame rates.

Recent advances in low-noise readout electronics, deep-depletion CCD architectures, and on-chip charge handling have stimulated renewed interest in centroiding techniques for x-ray detection. At the same time, the development of efficient algorithms for event recognition and centroid calculation has made it feasible to implement sub-pixel resolution enhancement in both offline data analysis and, in some cases, near real-time operation. Experimental studies have demonstrated resolution gains of a factor of two or more compared to the native pixel-limited performance, opening new possibilities for high-resolution soft x-ray imaging and spectroscopy.

The present work builds upon this foundation to investigate the enhancement of spatial resolution in soft x-ray CCD detectors through single-photon centroid determination. We focus on quantifying the degree of improvement achievable under realistic experimental conditions, taking into account the interplay between charge cloud size, pixel pitch, and detector noise. Using controlled laboratory measurements and simulations, we explore how centroiding performance depends on photon energy and detector operating parameters, and we assess the trade-offs between spatial resolution, detection efficiency, and processing complexity. Our aim is to provide a comprehensive evaluation of this technique in the context of soft x-ray applications, offering guidelines for its practical implementation and identifying the regimes in which it yields the most significant benefits.

By systematically analyzing the capabilities and limitations of single-photon centroid determination, this study contributes to the broader effort of pushing the spatial resolution of soft x-ray detectors beyond conventional limits. The results have implications for a variety of experimental scenarios where fine spatial detail is critical, including resonant inelastic x-ray scattering, coherent diffraction imaging, and high-resolution x-ray microscopy. In these and related fields, the ability to resolve features on a scale smaller than the pixel pitch of the detector can translate directly into enhanced scientific insight, enabling the observation of subtle structural and spectroscopic phenomena that would otherwise remain inaccessible.
conclusion:
In this work, we have demonstrated that the spatial resolution of soft X-ray CCD detectors can be significantly improved through the application of single-photon centroid determination techniques. By carefully analyzing the charge cloud distribution generated by individual photon events and accurately estimating their impact positions, we were able to surpass the intrinsic pixel-size limitation of conventional CCD readout. Our experimental results, supported by simulations, confirm that this approach yields a marked reduction in the point spread function, enabling resolution gains without hardware modifications to the detector itself.

The implementation of centroiding was shown to be robust across a range of photon energies within the soft X-ray regime, with the magnitude of improvement dependent on both the charge cloud size and the signal-to-noise ratio. We have also addressed the influence of readout noise and event pile-up, identifying optimal operating conditions where the benefits of centroid determination are maximized. The observed enhancement in spatial resolution opens the possibility for improved imaging performance in applications such as resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, coherent diffraction imaging, and X-ray microscopy, where fine spatial detail is critical.

Importantly, our findings indicate that the centroiding method can be integrated into existing data processing pipelines with modest computational overhead, making it a practical solution for both laboratory-based experiments and large-scale synchrotron or free-electron laser facilities. Future work will focus on refining event-detection algorithms to further suppress systematic biases, extending the technique to higher count rates, and exploring its applicability to other detector architectures. Overall, single-photon centroid determination represents a cost-effective and versatile strategy for enhancing the resolving power of soft X-ray CCD detectors, thereby advancing the capabilities of high-resolution X-ray science.

title: On-Shell Physics of Black Holes
abstract: We investigate the on-shell formulation of black hole physics, emphasizing its role in connecting classical geometry with quantum field theoretic descriptions. By restricting to solutions satisfying the gravitational field equations, we explore horizon thermodynamics, conserved charges, and scattering amplitudes in asymptotically flat and AdS backgrounds. Our analysis highlights how on-shell methods clarify the interplay between symmetries, soft modes, and entropy. These results offer a unified framework for probing quantum aspects of black holes without resorting to off-shell extensions.
introduction:
Black holes occupy a central role in our understanding of gravitational physics, providing a unique setting where general relativity, quantum field theory, and thermodynamics converge. Traditionally, much of black hole theory has been developed in an off-shell framework, where the geometry and matter content are treated as variables in a variational principle, and physical laws emerge from extremizing an action. However, an on-shell perspective—focusing on solutions that already satisfy the field equations—offers a complementary and often more physically transparent approach. In this setting, the emphasis shifts from arbitrary configurations to the intrinsic properties and constraints of physical black hole spacetimes.

The on-shell formalism has proven particularly fruitful in elucidating conserved charges, symmetries, and boundary terms that govern black hole behavior. By restricting attention to exact solutions, one can identify quantities that are invariant under allowed deformations, revealing deep connections between horizon geometry, asymptotic structure, and global conservation laws. This perspective also facilitates the derivation of thermodynamic identities directly from the equations of motion, circumventing ambiguities associated with off-shell extensions. In particular, the on-shell approach naturally encodes the first law of black hole mechanics, the Smarr relation, and other integral identities as exact statements about the space of solutions.

Recent developments in gravitational scattering amplitudes, holographic dualities, and near-horizon symmetries have further underscored the utility of on-shell methods. These tools allow for a unified treatment of classical and quantum aspects of black holes, linking their macroscopic thermodynamic properties to microscopic degrees of freedom in candidate quantum gravity theories. Moreover, by working directly with physical configurations, on-shell analyses can sidestep gauge redundancies and clarify the role of boundary conditions at infinity and at the horizon.

This work aims to explore the on-shell physics of black holes in a systematic manner, emphasizing the interplay between geometry, conserved quantities, and thermodynamic relations. We will develop a framework that captures essential physical features with minimal reliance on auxiliary structures, enabling a clearer understanding of black holes as exact, self-consistent solutions of the underlying gravitational theory.
conclusion: Our analysis demonstrates that on-shell methods yield deep insights into black hole dynamics, unifying classical and quantum perspectives while offering predictive frameworks for future gravitational and high-energy theoretical explorations.

title: Rotating Scalar Field and Formation of Bose Stars
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of a rotating self-gravitating scalar field and its role in the formation of gravitationally bound condensates, commonly referred to as Bose stars. Using a relativistic framework based on the Einstein–Klein–Gordon equations, we analyze the impact of angular momentum on the collapse and condensation processes of an ultralight bosonic field. Numerical simulations are performed for a range of initial rotation profiles and field self-interaction strengths, revealing that rotation significantly alters the collapse timescale, central density evolution, and final equilibrium configuration. We find that moderate rotation can delay gravitational collapse, leading to more extended and less dense condensates, while high angular momentum may inhibit star formation altogether. In cases where Bose stars do form, rotation induces anisotropic density distributions and modifies the stability properties compared to nonrotating configurations. Our results suggest that angular momentum is a key parameter governing the astrophysical formation channels of bosonic compact objects, with implications for dark matter structure formation and potential observational signatures in gravitational wave and lensing phenomena.
introduction:
The study of self-gravitating configurations of bosonic fields has attracted considerable attention in recent decades, driven both by fundamental theoretical questions and by their potential relevance to astrophysical phenomena. Ultralight bosonic particles, such as axions and axion-like particles, are well-motivated candidates for dark matter in extensions of the Standard Model. In cosmological scenarios, such particles can form macroscopic quantum states bound by gravity, often referred to as Bose stars or boson stars. These objects arise as solutions to the coupled Einstein–Klein–Gordon or Schrödinger–Poisson equations, depending on the relativistic or nonrelativistic regime considered. Their properties—mass, radius, stability, and dynamical evolution—are determined by the interplay between quantum pressure, self-interaction of the scalar field, and gravitational attraction.

Most studies to date have focused on configurations with zero net angular momentum, corresponding to spherically symmetric ground-state solutions. Such configurations are comparatively simple to analyze and are relevant for systems formed through gravitational relaxation or condensation without significant angular momentum. However, astrophysical environments are rarely devoid of rotation. Primordial density fluctuations, tidal torques, and mergers can impart angular momentum to dark matter condensates. The presence of rotation in a bosonic self-gravitating system changes its structure, stability properties, and formation pathways. Rotating boson stars are therefore of both theoretical and observational significance, potentially leading to distinctive signatures in gravitational wave emission, lensing, and dynamical interactions with baryonic matter.

The introduction of rotation in scalar field configurations has been approached in various ways. In the relativistic regime, stationary axisymmetric solutions of the Einstein–Klein–Gordon system have been constructed, often by assuming an azimuthal dependence of the scalar field phase proportional to \( e^{i m \phi} \), where \( m \) is the azimuthal quantum number. This ansatz leads to quantized angular momentum and toroidal or multi-lobed density profiles for higher \( m \). In the Newtonian limit, rotation manifests in the solutions of the Gross–Pitaevskii–Poisson equations, where vortices and other quantized flow structures may arise. The interplay between gravitational binding and centrifugal support in such systems determines whether stable equilibrium configurations can exist and how they evolve dynamically.

The formation of rotating Bose stars from realistic initial conditions remains an open problem. Numerical simulations of scalar field dark matter suggest that gravitational condensation can occur from initially incoherent wave-like fields, producing compact solitonic cores embedded in larger halos. When the initial conditions contain net angular momentum, either from large-scale tidal torques or from merging substructures, the condensation process may yield rotating configurations. The efficiency of angular momentum transport, the role of wave interference, and the possibility of vortex formation are key questions in determining the final equilibrium state. Furthermore, rotation may alter the critical mass above which configurations become unstable to collapse or fission, influencing the expected mass distribution of such objects in the Universe.

From a phenomenological standpoint, rotating Bose stars could exhibit observable differences from their nonrotating counterparts. Their density profiles are generally less centrally concentrated, potentially affecting gravitational lensing patterns and dynamical interactions with stars and gas. In the case of axion-like particles, self-interactions could couple with rotation to produce distinctive oscillatory or precessional dynamics. The detection of such signatures would provide insight into both the particle nature of dark matter and the role of angular momentum in cosmic structure formation.

In this work, we investigate the structure and formation of rotating Bose stars in the framework of a self-gravitating complex scalar field. We consider both the equilibrium configurations supported by a balance of gravity, quantum pressure, and centrifugal effects, and the dynamical processes leading to their formation from generic rotating initial states. Our approach combines analytical considerations of the stationary field equations with numerical simulations of the time-dependent dynamics. By systematically varying the amount of angular momentum and examining the resulting equilibrium and stability properties, we aim to clarify the conditions under which rotating Bose stars can form and persist. This study contributes to a more complete understanding of the landscape of possible bosonic compact objects and their astrophysical implications.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the dynamics of a rotating self-gravitating scalar field and its role in the formation of Bose stars. Our analysis shows that rotation modifies the collapse process, introducing centrifugal effects that can delay or reshape the onset of gravitational condensation. Numerical simulations indicate that angular momentum redistributes within the condensate, leading to equilibrium configurations that differ from their non-rotating counterparts in density profile and stability. We find that moderate rotation can still permit the formation of compact, self-bound objects, while excessive rotation may prevent collapse altogether. These results highlight the importance of including rotational degrees of freedom in models of bosonic dark matter structure formation. The study provides a foundation for future investigations into the astrophysical signatures of rotating Bose stars and their potential relevance to galactic dynamics, suggesting that rotation could serve as both a diagnostic and a constraint in identifying such exotic compact objects.

title: Nonequilibrium dynamical renormalization group: Dynamical crossover from weak to infinite randomness in the transverse-field Ising chain
abstract: We investigate the real-time dynamics of the disordered transverse-field Ising chain following a quantum quench, employing a nonequilibrium dynamical renormalization group (ndRG) approach. This framework systematically integrates out high-energy degrees of freedom in the time domain, enabling access to long-time, large-distance behavior beyond perturbative regimes. We demonstrate that the ndRG captures a dynamical crossover from weak disorder, characterized by ballistic quasiparticle propagation, to the infinite-randomness regime, where dynamics are dominated by rare-region effects and ultraslow entanglement growth. The method provides analytic insight into the emergent scaling laws governing spin autocorrelations and entanglement entropy, and reveals the role of Griffiths effects in the crossover. Comparison with numerical simulations based on exact diagonalization and time-evolving block decimation confirms the validity of the approach. Our results establish the ndRG as a powerful tool for exploring universal features of nonequilibrium quantum criticality in strongly disordered systems.
introduction:
Disordered quantum many-body systems exhibit a rich variety of dynamical phenomena far from equilibrium, often governed by rare events and emergent collective degrees of freedom. In particular, quenches across quantum phase transitions in the presence of quenched randomness can lead to unconventional dynamical scaling, including ultraslow relaxation and broad distributions of local observables. A paradigmatic example is the random transverse-field Ising chain (RTFIC), whose equilibrium critical properties are controlled by an infinite-randomness fixed point (IRFP) described by the strong-disorder renormalization group (SDRG). At such a fixed point, dynamical scaling is activated rather than algebraic, with the logarithm of the characteristic time scale growing as a power of the correlation length. While the static properties of the IRFP are well understood, much less is known about how nonequilibrium dynamics approach this regime following a quantum quench, and whether there exists a crossover from weak- to strong-disorder dynamical behavior.

Recent advances in both analytical and numerical techniques have made it possible to probe the real-time evolution of disordered integrable and nonintegrable chains after sudden parameter changes. For clean systems, the unitary dynamics after a quench are often captured by quasiparticle pictures or generalized hydrodynamics, leading to ballistic or diffusive spreading of correlations. In contrast, in disordered systems, interference effects and the broad distribution of local energies and couplings can result in subdiffusive transport, Griffiths effects, and in the extreme case, many-body localization (MBL). In the vicinity of an IRFP, the interplay of disorder and quantum fluctuations gives rise to exponentially broad distributions of relaxation times, which manifest as logarithmically slow growth of entanglement and other observables in time.

Despite these developments, the problem of quantitatively describing the real-time crossover from weak to infinite randomness remains largely open. Conventional SDRG methods are formulated in imaginary time or in terms of ground-state wavefunctions, and thus do not directly address real-time unitary dynamics. Exact diagonalization can capture the latter but is severely limited by system size, especially in the presence of strong disorder where large length scales become important. Time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (tDMRG) methods allow simulations of larger systems, but still face challenges due to entanglement growth and the need for disorder averaging. This motivates the development of a nonequilibrium dynamical renormalization group (ndRG) approach, capable of capturing the essential physics of the crossover while remaining computationally tractable.

In this work, we develop and apply such a ndRG scheme to the transverse-field Ising chain with quenched randomness in both couplings and transverse fields. Starting from microscopic dynamics after a global quench, the method iteratively eliminates high-energy degrees of freedom in real time, renormalizing the remaining couplings and fields in a manner analogous to SDRG, but formulated directly in the time domain. This enables us to follow the evolution of the system from short times, where the disorder is effectively weak and perturbative treatments apply, to long times, where the dynamics are dominated by rare regions and the flow approaches the IRFP.

We show that the ndRG captures a dynamical crossover characterized by a gradual slowing down of relaxation and the emergence of activated scaling in correlation and response functions. By comparing with exact numerical simulations for small systems and with known equilibrium results, we establish the validity of the approach and extract the crossover scales as a function of disorder strength and quench protocol. Our results provide a unified framework for understanding nonequilibrium dynamics in disordered quantum chains across the entire range from weak to infinite randomness, and open the door to studying related phenomena in higher dimensions and in systems with interactions beyond the Ising universality class.
conclusion:
We have developed and applied a nonequilibrium dynamical renormalization group (ndRG) framework to study the real-time evolution of the random transverse-field Ising chain following a quantum quench. By tracking the flow of couplings and fields under successive elimination of the fastest local degrees of freedom, the method captures both the short-time dynamics governed by weak randomness and the long-time crossover to an infinite-randomness regime. This approach extends the conceptual foundation of strong-disorder renormalization into the time domain, yielding analytical control over dynamical scaling in a system far from equilibrium.

Our analysis reveals that the post-quench dynamics exhibit a pronounced crossover scale, set by the initial disorder strength and quench parameters, separating a perturbative regime with nearly ballistic quasiparticle propagation from a late-time regime characterized by ultraslow, activated dynamics. In the latter regime, the RG flow approaches the infinite-randomness fixed point, and observables such as spin autocorrelations display stretched-exponential decay consistent with strong-disorder predictions. The ndRG thus provides a unified description of the entire evolution, from microscopic times to asymptotically large scales.

The results demonstrate that the dynamical crossover is not a sharp transition but an extended scaling regime in which the distribution of effective couplings broadens without bound. This broadening governs the suppression of coherent oscillations and the emergence of glassy relaxation. The framework can be generalized to other disordered quantum spin chains and higher-dimensional networks, offering a systematic route to explore nonequilibrium universality classes in strongly disordered systems.

In summary, the nonequilibrium dynamical renormalization group captures the essential physics of the disorder-driven dynamical crossover in the transverse-field Ising chain, bridging weak- and infinite-randomness descriptions within a single formalism. These findings open the door to controlled analytical studies of many-body localization precursors, quantum Griffiths effects, and long-time memory in a broad class of disordered quantum matter.

title: The prediction of rotation curves in gas-dominated dwarf galaxies with modified dynamics
abstract: We investigate the rotation curves of gas-dominated dwarf galaxies within the framework of modified dynamics, focusing on systems where the baryonic mass is primarily in the form of neutral gas rather than stars. Using high-resolution observational data for a representative sample of such galaxies, we compare predictions from modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) with those from standard dark matter halo models. In the gas-dominated regime, the stellar mass-to-light ratio plays a negligible role, enabling nearly parameter-free MOND predictions directly from the observed gas distribution. We find that MOND accurately reproduces both the amplitude and detailed shape of the observed rotation curves without invoking dark matter, while standard halo models require additional tuning. These results highlight the predictive power of modified dynamics in low-acceleration systems and emphasize the value of gas-rich dwarfs as critical laboratories for testing alternative theories of galactic dynamics.
introduction:
The study of galactic rotation curves has played a pivotal role in shaping our understanding of mass distribution in galaxies and the nature of gravity on galactic scales. Observations beginning in the latter half of the twentieth century revealed that the rotational velocities of stars and gas in disk galaxies often remain approximately constant, or "flat," at large radii, contrary to the expectation from Newtonian dynamics applied to the visible matter alone. This discrepancy has traditionally been interpreted as evidence for an unseen mass component—dark matter—distributed in extended halos around galaxies. While the dark matter paradigm has been successful in explaining a wide variety of cosmological and astrophysical phenomena, it remains challenged by certain empirical regularities in galaxy dynamics that appear to be tightly coupled to the distribution of baryonic matter.

One of the most striking of these regularities is the empirical relation between the observed baryonic mass distribution and the corresponding rotation curve, encapsulated in scaling laws such as the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation and the radial acceleration relation. Such correlations suggest a more direct link between baryons and dynamics than would be expected if the dominant gravitational influence arose from an independent dark matter halo. These observations have motivated consideration of alternative theories of gravity that modify the laws of motion at low accelerations, of which Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) is the most prominent example. MOND posits a modification to Newton’s second law or to the law of gravity below a characteristic acceleration scale, thereby accounting for flat rotation curves without invoking non-baryonic dark matter.

Gas-dominated dwarf galaxies offer a particularly valuable laboratory for testing predictions of modified dynamics. In these low-mass systems, the contribution of stars to the total baryonic mass is small, and the distribution of neutral hydrogen gas can be mapped in detail through 21-cm observations. This reduces uncertainties associated with stellar mass-to-light ratios, which can complicate dynamical analyses in more massive, star-dominated galaxies. Moreover, dwarf galaxies often exhibit low characteristic accelerations, placing them squarely in the regime where modified dynamics effects are expected to be most pronounced.

In this work, we focus on the prediction of rotation curves in a sample of gas-rich dwarf galaxies under the framework of modified dynamics. The central aim is to assess the degree to which the observed kinematic profiles can be anticipated solely from the measured distribution of baryonic matter, without recourse to dark matter halo modeling. By comparing the predicted curves directly to high-resolution observational data, we evaluate both the strengths and limitations of the modified dynamics approach in this regime. The results bear on the broader question of whether the observed coupling between baryonic mass and galactic dynamics is a natural consequence of gravitational law or an emergent property of galaxy formation within the dark matter paradigm.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the predictive capacity of modified dynamics for the rotation curves of gas-dominated dwarf galaxies, focusing on systems in which the contribution of stellar mass to the total baryonic mass is minimal. Such galaxies provide an especially stringent test of any theory purporting to link the observed distribution of baryons directly to the gravitational field, since uncertainties in stellar mass-to-light ratios, which complicate analyses in more massive spirals, are negligible here. The gas distribution can be mapped with high precision using 21 cm observations, and the gravitational potential inferred from such a map can, in principle, be compared directly to the observed kinematic profile.

Applying the framework of modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND) to this sample, we derived rotation curves from the observed baryonic mass distributions without recourse to free halo parameters. The only adjustable quantity was the galaxy distance within its observational uncertainty, and in some cases the inclination, as constrained by imaging and kinematic data. The resulting predicted curves were found to align closely with the observed velocity fields over a wide range of radii, reproducing not only the general amplitude of the rotation but also subtle features such as local rises and declines corresponding to structure in the gas surface density. This spatially resolved agreement is notable because, under MOND, the shape of the rotation curve emerges directly from the baryonic matter distribution, rather than from a tunable dark matter halo profile.

The success of the predictions across the sample reinforces the empirical link between baryonic mass distribution and kinematic response in low-acceleration systems. In the conventional dark matter paradigm, such a tight coupling is not generically expected without invoking correlations between baryons and halo properties that lack a fundamental explanation. In contrast, the modified dynamics framework naturally encodes this correlation through its governing relation between acceleration and enclosed baryonic mass. The fact that the predictions hold in gas-dominated dwarfs, where observational uncertainties in mass modelling are minimised, strengthens the case that this relation captures a genuine aspect of galactic dynamics rather than being an artefact of parameter fitting.

Nevertheless, several caveats warrant mention. While the agreement is generally good, there are individual cases where discrepancies persist, particularly in the outermost regions where observational uncertainties in inclination and beam smearing are largest. In some galaxies, asymmetric drift corrections or non-circular motions may also play a role in shaping the observed velocity field, potentially obscuring the underlying circular velocity profile. Moreover, our analysis has been confined to relatively isolated systems; environmental effects such as tidal interactions or ram-pressure stripping, which can alter both the gas distribution and kinematics, remain to be systematically explored in this context.

Our findings contribute to the broader debate on the origin of the mass–discrepancy–acceleration relation and the viability of alternatives to dark matter. The ability of a simple modified dynamics prescription to reproduce detailed kinematic features from the baryonic mass alone, without tuning halo parameters, is a striking result that any comprehensive theory of galaxy formation and dynamics must account for. Future work could expand the sample to include lower surface brightness systems, extend the analysis to three-dimensional kinematic data from upcoming interferometric surveys, and investigate the interplay between gas dynamics, star formation, and modified gravity in shaping the rotation curves.

In conclusion, the analysis presented here demonstrates that in gas-dominated dwarf galaxies, the rotation curves can be accurately predicted from the observed gas distribution when a modified dynamics framework is adopted.
