This predictive success, achieved with minimal freedom in the modelling, underscores the empirical robustness of the baryon–kinematics connection in the low-acceleration regime. Whether interpreted as evidence for a fundamental modification of gravity or as an emergent consequence of complex baryon–dark matter interactions, this tight coupling remains a key observational fact. The challenge for future theoretical and observational efforts lies in elucidating the physical origin of this relation and determining its domain of applicability across the full diversity of galactic systems.

title: Universal Successor Features for Transfer Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We propose **Universal Successor Features (USF)**, a framework for transfer in reinforcement learning that unifies generalization across both reward functions and environment dynamics. Successor features have been shown to enable efficient transfer between tasks with shared dynamics but varying rewards; however, their applicability is limited when dynamics differ. USF extends the successor feature representation by conditioning on explicit descriptions of both the reward and transition structure, enabling a single learned model to predict value functions for arbitrary task specifications. We introduce a scalable architecture that integrates universal value function approximators with successor feature learning, and we derive an objective that encourages compositional generalization across tasks. Empirical results on a suite of continuous-control and grid-world benchmarks demonstrate that USF achieves faster adaptation and higher asymptotic performance than conventional successor features and model-free baselines when transferring across both reward and dynamics changes, highlighting its potential as a general-purpose representation for multi-task and lifelong reinforcement learning.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in a variety of domains, from playing complex games at superhuman levels to controlling high-dimensional robotic systems. However, these achievements often come at the cost of extensive task-specific training, limiting the applicability of RL agents in scenarios where environments or objectives change. A key challenge in scaling RL to more general settings is the ability to transfer knowledge acquired in one task to accelerate learning in related tasks. Transfer reinforcement learning seeks to address this challenge by leveraging shared structure across tasks, enabling agents to adapt efficiently to new objectives without learning from scratch.

One promising approach to transfer in RL is to decompose the value function into separable components that capture environment dynamics independently from task-specific rewards. Successor Features (SFs) offer such a decomposition by representing the value function as the inner product of a feature representation of states and actions with a task-specific weight vector derived from the reward function. This factorization allows the dynamics-dependent component—the successor features—to be reused across tasks with different reward functions, facilitating rapid policy adaptation. Empirical studies have demonstrated that SFs can substantially accelerate learning when the reward function changes but the environment dynamics remain fixed.

Despite their promise, traditional successor features suffer from important limitations. Most notably, SFs are typically learned with respect to a single policy and a specific task, restricting their generality. When transitioning to a new task, the learned SFs may not generalize well, especially if the optimal policy changes significantly. Moreover, the dependency of SFs on the policy under which they are learned implies that transferring to new tasks often requires re-learning large parts of the representation, thereby diminishing the potential efficiency gains. This has motivated the search for representations that can generalize across a broader set of policies and tasks.

Universal Successor Features (USFs) extend the SF framework by conditioning the SF representation not only on states and actions but also on a goal or task descriptor. Inspired by universal value function approximators, USFs aim to learn a single function that predicts successor features for any task within a given distribution. By jointly training across multiple tasks, USFs can capture a richer, policy-independent representation of environment dynamics, enabling more effective transfer to unseen tasks. In principle, USFs allow an agent to rapidly compute value functions for novel reward functions by simply specifying the corresponding task descriptor, without requiring additional environment interaction.

Recent work has begun to explore the potential of USFs for transfer reinforcement learning, but several open questions remain. It is not yet fully understood how best to parameterize the task descriptors, how to balance generalization with representation fidelity, or how to ensure robustness when the target task lies outside the training distribution. Furthermore, while USFs offer theoretical advantages, empirical evaluations have often been limited to relatively simple environments, leaving their scalability to more complex domains an open challenge.

In this work, we investigate the use of Universal Successor Features for transfer reinforcement learning across a variety of environments and task distributions. We formalize the USF framework, analyze its theoretical properties, and propose practical algorithms for efficient learning and transfer. Our contributions include a detailed examination of how USFs can be trained to maximize generalization across tasks, an empirical evaluation demonstrating their advantages over traditional SFs in both sample efficiency and final performance, and an exploration of their limitations when task variation is substantial. By advancing the understanding and capabilities of USFs, we aim to bring RL agents closer to the goal of rapid, robust adaptation in dynamic, multi-task settings.
conclusion: We have presented an approach based on Universal Successor Features to facilitate transfer in reinforcement learning across varying tasks. By generalizing over both states and goals, our method enables efficient reuse of learned knowledge, reducing sample complexity and improving adaptability. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance compared to baseline transfer methods, particularly in environments with significant variation. These findings highlight the potential of universal successor representations as a scalable framework for multi-task and continual learning in complex, dynamic domains.

title: Planck 2015 results. II. Low Frequency Instrument data processing
abstract: We present the processing of data from the Low Frequency Instrument (LFI) aboard the *Planck* satellite for the 2015 cosmological release. This work describes the calibration, noise estimation, systematic error mitigation, and mapmaking procedures applied to time-ordered data from the 30, 44, and 70 GHz channels. Improvements over the 2013 release include refined beam models, enhanced gain calibration using the orbital dipole, and more accurate removal of instrumental systematics. We assess the noise properties and residual uncertainties, providing full-sky maps with increased fidelity for cosmological analysis. The resulting data products form a key component of the *Planck* 2015 release, enabling robust measurements of the cosmic microwave background.
introduction:
The Planck mission, launched by the European Space Agency (ESA) in May 2009, was designed to map the anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) with unprecedented precision over the full sky. It carried two instruments: the Low Frequency Instrument (LFI), operating in the 30–70 GHz range, and the High Frequency Instrument (HFI), covering 100–857 GHz. Together, these instruments provided complementary measurements that enabled detailed studies of the early Universe, the large-scale structure of the cosmos, and the astrophysical foregrounds that contaminate the CMB signal. The 2015 release of Planck results represents the second major public dissemination of data and scientific products from the mission, incorporating the full mission dataset for LFI and an improved calibration and analysis pipeline.

The LFI was specifically designed to measure the CMB temperature and polarization anisotropies at low frequencies, where Galactic synchrotron emission and other diffuse foregrounds are prominent. Its radiometer array, operating at 30, 44, and 70 GHz, employed pseudo-correlation receivers cooled to cryogenic temperatures to minimize instrumental noise. The instrument’s observing strategy, combined with the spacecraft’s scanning motion, provided multiple, redundant observations of every point on the sky over the mission lifetime. These characteristics made LFI data crucial both for astrophysical studies and for cross-calibration with HFI, particularly in polarization measurements where systematic effects are challenging to control.

Processing the raw telemetry from LFI into calibrated sky maps of the Stokes parameters (I, Q, U) requires a complex sequence of steps to address instrumental effects and systematic errors. The data must be cleaned of spikes from cosmic ray hits, corrected for gain variations, and calibrated against a well-understood celestial signal—primarily the CMB dipole induced by the spacecraft’s motion with respect to the CMB rest frame. Noise properties, including 1/f noise in the radiometers, must be characterized and mitigated through optimal mapmaking algorithms. Furthermore, the polarization sensitivity of LFI demands precise knowledge of the instrument’s bandpasses, beam patterns, and polarization angles, all of which require careful measurement and modelling.

The 2015 LFI data processing represents a significant advance over the previous 2013 release, incorporating the full 48 months of observations and implementing improved calibration procedures. The calibration pipeline now exploits the orbital component of the CMB dipole, enabling an absolute calibration accuracy at the sub-percent level. Beam reconstructions have been refined using observations of bright planets, leading to improved angular resolution and reduced uncertainties in beam window functions. Noise modelling has been enhanced to better capture the temporal correlations in the data, improving the fidelity of the resulting maps. Systematic effects, such as thermal fluctuations in the instrument and bandpass mismatches between radiometers, have been more thoroughly characterized and corrected.

This paper, the second in the series of Planck 2015 results, describes in detail the LFI data processing from raw telemetry to calibrated frequency maps. Section 2 provides an overview of the LFI instrument and its operation during the mission. Section 3 summarizes the main improvements to the calibration and beam characterization procedures. Section 4 describes the noise estimation and mapmaking algorithms, while Section 5 discusses the assessment and mitigation of systematic effects. In Section 6 we present the final LFI frequency maps and their main characteristics. The conclusions in Section 7 summarize the impact of these advances on the scientific exploitation of Planck data. Together, these developments ensure that the LFI data products meet the stringent requirements needed for high-precision cosmology and astrophysics.
conclusion: The Planck 2015 Low Frequency Instrument data processing has achieved significant improvements in calibration accuracy, noise characterization, and systematics removal compared to previous releases. Enhanced algorithms and refined processing pipelines have yielded maps of unprecedented quality at low frequencies, enabling more precise cosmological and astrophysical analyses. Cross-validation with independent datasets confirms the robustness of the results. These advances strengthen the scientific legacy of Planck, providing a reliable foundation for studies of the cosmic microwave background and Galactic foregrounds, and informing future missions targeting similar frequency ranges.

title: A Simulation Study of Electric Field Engineering with Multi-Level Pinned Photodiodes for Fast and Complete Charge Transfer
abstract: We present a simulation-based investigation of electric field engineering in multi-level pinned photodiodes (ML-PPDs) aimed at achieving fast and complete charge transfer. Using two-dimensional device simulations, we analyze the impact of potential profile modulation on carrier transport dynamics. By tailoring doping gradients and geometrical parameters, a stepwise potential drop is established from the photodiode’s collection region to the transfer gate, enhancing drift-driven charge motion while suppressing residual charge. The results show that optimized multi-level structures enable higher transfer speeds and near-complete charge evacuation compared with conventional single-level designs. This approach provides design guidelines for next-generation high-speed image sensors, where improved temporal resolution and low image lag are critical for performance in scientific, industrial, and consumer imaging applications.
introduction:
Pinned photodiodes (PPDs) have become the dominant pixel architecture in modern complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) image sensors due to their low dark current, high charge transfer efficiency, and suppressed image lag. The key feature of a PPD is the fully depleted photodiode region with a pinned surface potential, enabling near-complete transfer of photo-generated charge to the floating diffusion during readout. However, as pixel sizes continue to shrink and operating speeds increase, achieving both fast and complete charge transfer becomes increasingly challenging. Incomplete transfer can lead to residual image lag, while slow transfer limits frame rates and temporal resolution, degrading image quality in high-speed or low-light applications.

One promising approach to address these challenges is electric field engineering within the photodiode. By tailoring the potential profile, it is possible to create a strong and uniform electric field that drives carriers efficiently toward the transfer gate. Multi-level pinned photodiode structures, in which the doping profile and geometry are modified to introduce distinct potential steps, have been proposed to enhance carrier transport. These engineered potential gradients can reduce transfer time, minimize charge trapping, and improve overall pixel performance without significantly increasing noise or dark current.

Previous studies have investigated variations in doping concentration, junction depth, and transfer gate design to optimize charge transfer. However, systematic simulation-based evaluations of multi-level PPD configurations, particularly under varying operating conditions, remain limited. Device-level simulations offer a powerful means to explore the influence of structural parameters on the internal electric field distribution, enabling predictive optimization before fabrication.

In this work, we present a comprehensive simulation study of electric field engineering in multi-level pinned photodiodes aimed at achieving both fast and complete charge transfer. Using two-dimensional device simulations, we analyze the effects of multi-step potential profiles on carrier dynamics, quantify transfer times, and assess the degree of charge completeness under different biasing schemes. The results provide design guidelines for next-generation high-speed, high-performance CMOS image sensors, highlighting the trade-offs and benefits of multi-level electric field profiles in advanced PPD architectures.
conclusion: This study presented a comprehensive simulation of electric field engineering in multi-level pinned photodiodes to achieve fast and complete charge transfer. By tailoring doping profiles and potential distributions, the proposed structure enhanced the lateral and vertical electric fields, thereby reducing transfer time and minimizing residual charge. Simulation results demonstrated that the multi-level design effectively mitigates charge trapping and improves transfer efficiency compared to conventional pinned photodiodes. The approach provides a viable pathway for optimizing high-speed, low-noise image sensors, particularly in applications demanding rapid readout and high dynamic range. Future work will extend the analysis to include fabrication tolerances, temperature effects, and experimental validation, further bridging the gap between device simulation and practical implementation for next-generation imaging systems.

title: Simulating Bell inequalities violation with classical optics encoded qbits
abstract: We present a classical-optics framework for simulating the violation of Bell inequalities by encoding qubits into distinct degrees of freedom of coherent light beams. Using polarization and spatial modes as a tensor-product Hilbert space, we implement analogues of entangled states through mode coupling and phase control. Measurement settings are realized via cascaded wave plates and mode converters, enabling projections onto arbitrary qubit bases. Correlation functions are obtained from intensity measurements, and the resulting CHSH parameter exceeds the classical bound of 2, reaching values consistent with the quantum mechanical limit for maximally entangled states within experimental uncertainties. While no genuine quantum nonlocality is present, the scheme reproduces the algebraic structure of qubit state space and measurement statistics, providing an accessible platform for exploring quantum-like correlations. This approach offers pedagogical advantages, enabling demonstration of foundational quantum concepts using inexpensive, readily available optical components, and it may serve as a testbed for developing and validating protocols in quantum information processing within a fully classical context.
introduction:
Quantum mechanics challenges classical intuitions about the nature of physical reality, with one of its most striking predictions being the existence of correlations between spatially separated systems that cannot be explained by any local hidden variable theory. These correlations, formalized through Bell inequalities, have played a central role in deepening our understanding of entanglement and nonlocality. The experimental violation of Bell inequalities has been repeatedly demonstrated in systems of photons, ions, and other quantum platforms, providing compelling evidence against local realism. However, reproducing these quantum correlations using classical systems has emerged as an intriguing line of inquiry, both for educational purposes and for probing the boundary between classical and quantum descriptions of physical phenomena.

Classical optics offers a rich and versatile framework to simulate quantum-mechanical concepts, owing to the formal mathematical analogies between the polarization states of light and the state vectors of two-level quantum systems—qubits. In particular, the Jones calculus and the Poincaré sphere representation provide a direct mapping between the polarization of classical light and the Bloch sphere representation of qubit states. This correspondence enables the encoding of “qubit-like” information into the polarization degrees of freedom of coherent light beams, and the manipulation of these states using standard optical elements such as waveplates and polarizers. As a result, various quantum protocols—state preparation, unitary transformations, projective measurements—can be emulated with high fidelity in a purely classical setting.

The simulation of Bell inequality violations using classical optical systems does not constitute a genuine demonstration of quantum nonlocality, since the underlying degrees of freedom remain entirely classical and no true entanglement exists between spatially separated particles. Instead, such simulations recreate the statistical structure of quantum correlations by exploiting the mathematical isomorphism between classical field modes and quantum states. In this way, the exercise serves both as a didactic tool to explore the subtleties of quantum theory and as a platform to test experimental techniques relevant to quantum information processing, without requiring access to nonclassical light sources or single-photon detectors.

Previous works have demonstrated that by encoding two qubits into different degrees of freedom of a classical beam—such as polarization and transverse spatial modes—it is possible to construct states that are formally analogous to maximally entangled Bell states. By preparing such states and performing polarization and mode projections analogous to quantum measurements, one can obtain correlation functions that mimic those predicted by quantum mechanics for entangled qubits. When these correlation functions are used to evaluate a Bell–CHSH parameter, the resulting value can exceed the local hidden variable bound of 2, approaching the quantum limit of \( 2\sqrt{2} \). The violation observed in these classical simulations is a manifestation of the underlying vector space structure rather than any nonlocal causal influence, yet it reproduces the mathematical form of the quantum violation.

The present work builds on these ideas to implement and analyze a classical optical simulation of Bell inequality violation using polarization-encoded qubits. We describe a systematic procedure for encoding qubit states into the polarization of a laser beam, applying unitary transformations using waveplates, and performing measurement projections with polarizers. The experiment is designed to emulate the preparation of a maximally entangled state and the subsequent local measurements on each qubit, with measurement settings chosen to optimize the CHSH violation. By carefully controlling the polarization transformations and measurement angles, and by recording the resulting intensity distributions, we reconstruct the correlation functions necessary to evaluate the Bell parameter.

Beyond demonstrating the feasibility of such simulations, we aim to examine the limitations and interpretational nuances of reproducing quantum-like correlations in a classical framework. We discuss the role of coherence, mode structure, and measurement crosstalk in determining the fidelity of the simulated violation, and address the conceptual distinction between genuine quantum entanglement and classical analogues. In doing so, we highlight the pedagogical value of classical optics experiments in conveying the counterintuitive predictions of quantum mechanics, and their utility as a low-cost, accessible platform for exploring foundational ideas in quantum information science.

By situating our work at the intersection of quantum foundations and classical wave optics, we contribute to an ongoing discourse on the meaning of Bell inequality violations, the scope of classical analogies to quantum phenomena, and the practical use of such simulations in research and education. The approach presented here offers an experimentally straightforward yet conceptually rich means of engaging with one of the most profound results of quantum theory, using only the tools of classical optics.
conclusion:
In this work, we have demonstrated that it is possible to simulate the violation of Bell inequalities using classical optical fields in which qubits are encoded in well-controlled degrees of freedom, such as polarization and spatial modes. By carefully designing the optical setup and modulation schemes, we reproduced the statistical correlations predicted by quantum mechanics for entangled two-qubit states, despite the fact that our platform is entirely classical in nature. The experimental and numerical results confirm that the measured correlation functions can exceed the classical Bell bound, reaching values in close agreement with the quantum mechanical maximum for the chosen states and measurement settings.

This approach does not imply that classical fields possess quantum entanglement in the physical sense; rather, it highlights that Bell-type correlations can be mimicked in systems that share the same mathematical formalism as quantum two-level systems. The encoding of qubits into different classical degrees of freedom allows us to exploit the tensor-product structure of the Hilbert space and to implement projective measurements through standard optical components. In this sense, our work emphasizes the distinction between the mathematical simulation of quantum correlations and the physical realization of nonlocal quantum entanglement.

The results contribute to the ongoing discussion about the scope and limitations of classical analogues to quantum phenomena. While such simulations cannot violate locality in the quantum sense, they provide a versatile and accessible platform for exploring the structure of quantum theory, testing signal processing algorithms, and prototyping quantum information protocols in a controlled and low-cost environment. The implementation using classical optics benefits from high stability, ease of manipulation, and the ability to work at room temperature without the challenges associated with fragile quantum systems.

Furthermore, the methodology developed here can be extended beyond the two-qubit case. By encoding higher-dimensional quantum states or multi-qubit systems in additional optical degrees of freedom, one could explore generalized Bell inequalities, contextuality tests, and other fundamental aspects of quantum theory. The flexibility of the classical optical domain allows for rapid reconfiguration of measurement bases and state preparation, making it a powerful educational and research tool.

From a pedagogical perspective, our simulation offers an intuitive and tangible way to introduce concepts such as state superposition, entanglement analogues, and measurement-induced correlations without requiring access to advanced quantum hardware. The visual and measurable nature of optical fields can help bridge the gap between abstract quantum formalism and experimental realization, fostering a deeper understanding of the principles underlying quantum information science.

In conclusion, we have shown that classical optics can be employed to simulate the violation of Bell inequalities with encoded qubits, faithfully reproducing the correlation patterns expected from quantum mechanics. While these simulations do not challenge the fundamental distinction between classical and quantum realms, they underscore the utility of classical analogues as platforms for exploring, teaching, and developing quantum concepts. Future work will aim to expand the complexity and scope of such simulations, investigate their potential for hybrid classical–quantum information processing, and further clarify the conceptual boundaries between genuine quantum nonlocality and its classical imitations.

title: Homogenization of Bell inequalities
abstract: We investigate the homogenization procedure for Bell inequalities, transforming inhomogeneous forms into homogeneous ones by introducing additional measurement settings. This method enables a direct comparison between inequalities of different algebraic structures and clarifies their geometric interpretation within the correlation polytope. We present a systematic approach to homogenization, preserving the set of local realistic correlations while revealing new quantum violations. The relationship between the original and homogenized inequalities is analyzed, highlighting conditions under which homogenization amplifies or diminishes quantum advantage. Our results provide a unifying framework for studying Bell inequalities, offering insights into their symmetries, facet structure, and experimental implementability.
introduction:
Bell inequalities play a central role in the foundations of quantum mechanics, providing a quantitative framework to distinguish between the predictions of local realistic theories and those of quantum theory. Since Bell’s original work in 1964, numerous variants and generalizations have been proposed, each tailored to specific experimental scenarios or theoretical considerations. These inequalities are typically formulated in terms of correlations between measurement outcomes obtained by spatially separated parties, and their violation by quantum states reveals the presence of nonlocal correlations that cannot be explained by any local hidden variable model.

In their standard form, many Bell inequalities are expressed as non-homogeneous linear constraints on correlation functions or probabilities. Non-homogeneity here refers to the fact that the terms in the inequality may involve correlations of different orders or include constant terms, leading to expressions that are not invariant under uniform scaling of the correlators. While such formulations are often convenient for experimental tests, they can obscure certain structural and geometric properties of the set of correlations allowed by local realism. In particular, non-homogeneous inequalities may be less amenable to certain analytical techniques, such as polytope analysis, convex geometry, or algebraic reformulations that benefit from homogeneity.

The process of homogenization addresses this issue by transforming a given Bell inequality into an equivalent or closely related form in which all terms are of the same degree with respect to the relevant variables, typically the correlators. Homogeneous inequalities exhibit scale invariance and often possess a clearer geometric interpretation, as they define boundaries of cones rather than general polytopes in the space of correlations. This can simplify their classification, comparison, and optimization, and can also facilitate derivations of new inequalities from known ones. Furthermore, homogenization can reveal hidden symmetries and may lead to more elegant or compact formulations, potentially improving both theoretical understanding and practical applicability.

Beyond purely mathematical advantages, homogenized Bell inequalities can have implications for quantum information protocols. For instance, in device-independent quantum cryptography or randomness certification, the strength and robustness of nonlocal correlations play a critical role. Homogeneous forms may provide tighter or more transparent bounds for such applications, or enable more efficient numerical optimization when searching for quantum violations. They may also offer insights into the relationship between different families of inequalities, helping to unify various strands of research on nonlocality.

In this work, we investigate the homogenization of Bell inequalities from both theoretical and practical perspectives. We examine systematic methods for obtaining homogeneous forms, analyse the preservation of tightness and optimality under homogenization, and explore the consequences for quantum violations. By doing so, we aim to clarify the role of homogeneity in the structure of Bell inequalities and to provide tools that facilitate their study in foundational and applied contexts. Our approach bridges geometric, algebraic, and physical viewpoints, contributing to a deeper understanding of nonlocal correlations in quantum theory.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the process of homogenization of Bell inequalities, focusing on its structural, mathematical, and physical implications. By systematically reformulating existing inequalities into homogeneous forms, we have demonstrated how such a transformation can reveal hidden symmetries, clarify the role of measurement settings, and enhance the comparability between different inequalities. The homogenization procedure not only preserves the essential nonlocal features encoded in the original expressions but also facilitates the application of analytical tools from convex geometry and linear algebra, which often assume or benefit from homogeneity in the underlying constraints.

Our analysis has shown that homogenization can, in certain cases, increase the tightness of the resulting inequalities, thereby yielding stronger separations between classical and quantum correlations. Conversely, we have also identified scenarios where homogenization leaves the violation threshold unchanged, yet improves the interpretability of the inequality in terms of physical observables. This dual character underscores that the utility of homogenization extends beyond numerical performance; it serves as a methodological bridge between the abstract polytope description of local models and experimentally accessible correlation functions.

We have further explored how the homogenized forms fit within the broader classification schemes of Bell inequalities, particularly in relation to facet-defining inequalities and their geometric representations. The results suggest that homogenization can act as a unifying step, enabling a more systematic mapping between inequalities derived from distinct physical assumptions or optimization criteria.

Looking ahead, the homogenization framework opens several promising directions for further research. These include the automated generation of homogeneous inequalities from large datasets of candidate constraints, the extension of the method to multipartite and high-dimensional systems, and the investigation of its impact on device-independent protocols. By providing a clearer and often more symmetric mathematical structure, homogenization can play a key role in both theoretical developments and experimental implementations of nonlocality tests. We anticipate that the principles outlined here will be instrumental in refining our understanding of the boundary between classical and quantum correlations, and in guiding the design of future experiments probing the foundations of quantum theory.

title: Outlier detection from ETL Execution trace
abstract: Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) processes play a critical role in data warehousing by integrating heterogeneous data sources into a unified analytical repository. Ensuring the reliable and efficient execution of ETL workflows is essential for maintaining data quality and timely availability. However, anomalies in ETL execution, such as unexpected delays, failures, or deviations in resource usage, can significantly impact downstream analytics and decision-making. This paper investigates outlier detection techniques applied to ETL execution traces, which contain detailed logs of task runtimes, dependencies, and system metrics. We present a comprehensive methodology for preprocessing execution traces, extracting meaningful features, and applying statistical and machine learning approaches to identify abnormal executions. Our approach is evaluated using real-world ETL trace data, demonstrating its ability to detect both performance degradations and structural anomalies with high precision. We also discuss the interpretability of detected outliers, enabling root cause analysis and proactive maintenance. The proposed framework provides a foundation for automated ETL monitoring, reducing manual inspection efforts and minimizing the risk of unnoticed execution issues. This research contributes to improved operational reliability in data warehousing environments and opens avenues for adaptive ETL optimization strategies.
introduction:
Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) processes constitute a critical component of contemporary data warehousing and business intelligence systems. These processes are responsible for integrating heterogeneous data from multiple sources, transforming it into a consistent format, and loading it into target repositories for subsequent analysis and reporting. As organizations increasingly rely on data-driven decision-making, the reliability, efficiency, and performance of ETL workflows have become pivotal to maintaining data quality and ensuring timely availability of information. Any disruptions, anomalies, or inefficiencies in ETL execution can have cascading effects, leading to delayed analyses, incorrect insights, and potentially costly business decisions.

ETL execution traces, which record detailed logs of process activities, timings, resource usage, and intermediate outcomes, offer a valuable source of information for monitoring and diagnosing ETL operations. These traces capture both normal execution behavior and deviations that may arise due to system faults, configuration errors, data inconsistencies, or unexpected workload variations. Detecting outliers within ETL execution traces is thus an essential task for identifying unusual behaviors that may signal performance degradation, operational failures, or opportunities for optimization.

Outlier detection in this context presents several challenges. First, ETL processes are often complex, involving multiple interdependent tasks executed across distributed computing environments. This complexity leads to high-dimensional and heterogeneous trace data, encompassing diverse metrics such as execution time, CPU and memory utilization, I/O throughput, and data volume processed. Second, the definition of what constitutes an “outlier” may vary depending on operational contexts, historical baselines, and evolving workloads. Third, the dynamic nature of ETL pipelines—subject to changes in source data characteristics, transformation logic, and target schema—can make static detection rules inadequate. Consequently, robust and adaptive analytical approaches are required to discern truly anomalous behaviors from benign variations.

Recent advances in data mining and machine learning offer promising techniques for automated outlier detection in large-scale operational data. Methods ranging from statistical process control to clustering-based and density-based algorithms can be applied to ETL execution traces to uncover patterns that deviate significantly from expected behavior. However, many existing studies in outlier detection focus on domains such as network intrusion, sensor data, or financial fraud, where the data characteristics and anomaly types differ from those in ETL environments. There remains a need for domain-specific approaches that account for the structural and temporal properties of ETL workflows and their execution patterns.

This research addresses the problem of outlier detection in ETL execution traces by systematically analyzing process-level metrics and applying tailored detection algorithms to identify anomalies indicative of inefficiencies or failures. By leveraging historical execution data, the proposed approach aims to establish adaptive baselines, accommodate evolving process behavior, and reduce false positives. The findings are expected to contribute both to the operational resilience of ETL systems and to the broader understanding of anomaly detection in complex, process-oriented data environments.
conclusion:
This study investigated the problem of outlier detection in ETL execution traces, aiming to identify anomalous runs that may indicate inefficiencies, errors, or potential process failures. By analyzing execution logs and applying statistical and machine learning–based approaches, we demonstrated that it is possible to systematically detect deviations from normal operational behavior, even in complex and heterogeneous ETL environments. The proposed methodology combined data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model-based detection techniques to achieve a balance between detection accuracy and interpretability. Experimental results on real-world ETL trace datasets showed that the approach could reliably flag unusual executions, enabling earlier diagnosis and corrective actions.  

The findings highlight the importance of incorporating outlier detection mechanisms into ETL monitoring workflows, as they can significantly reduce manual inspection efforts and improve data pipeline reliability. Furthermore, the study underscores the value of leveraging both temporal and operational metrics from execution traces, as this multi-faceted perspective enhances the robustness of anomaly identification. While the results are promising, the work also revealed certain limitations, such as sensitivity to parameter tuning and potential performance degradation in the presence of evolving process patterns.  

Future work should explore adaptive and online learning methods to handle concept drift, as well as the integration of domain knowledge to reduce false positives. Additionally, extending the approach to support root cause analysis will further increase its practical utility. Overall, this research demonstrates that systematic outlier detection in ETL execution traces is both feasible and beneficial, contributing to more resilient, efficient, and trustworthy data integration processes.

title: NP Datalog: a Logic Language for Expressing NP Search and Optimization Problems
abstract: We present NP Datalog, a logic-based language designed for the declarative specification of NP search and optimization problems. The language extends stratified Datalog with intuitive constructs for expressing nondeterministic choices and constraints, enabling concise and natural problem formulations. NP Datalog’s semantics are grounded in stable model theory, ensuring a clear correspondence between solutions of a program and solutions to the encoded problem. We demonstrate how common NP-complete and NP-hard problems can be represented in a modular and readable form, facilitating both specification and reasoning. An execution mechanism based on translation into constraint programming and SAT is outlined, enabling efficient computation. Experimental results indicate that NP Datalog offers competitive performance while maintaining high-level expressiveness, making it a promising tool for both teaching and practical problem solving.
introduction: Declarative languages based on logic have proven effective for representing and solving complex computational problems. However, many real-world applications require expressing search and optimization tasks that belong to the NP complexity class. NP Datalog is introduced as a logic programming language specifically designed to naturally and concisely express such problems. By extending traditional Datalog with constructs for controlled nondeterminism and optimization, NP Datalog enables the specification of NP search problems in a purely declarative manner, separating problem description from solution strategy. This approach facilitates reasoning about problem properties, supports efficient evaluation through translation into constraint or SAT formulations, and broadens the applicability of logic-based methods. We present the language design, formal semantics, and illustrate its use in modeling representative NP search and optimization problems.
conclusion: We have presented NP Datalog, a logic-based language specifically designed for the declarative specification of NP search and optimization problems. By extending the expressive power of traditional Datalog with constructs for non-determinism and optimization, NP Datalog enables concise, high-level formulations of complex computational tasks that naturally fall within NP. The language integrates guess-and-check programming patterns in a way that preserves a clear semantic foundation, facilitating both formal reasoning about programs and practical implementation. We have shown how NP Datalog can capture a wide range of problems, from classic decision tasks to sophisticated optimization scenarios, while maintaining a syntax familiar to those experienced with logic programming. Moreover, its design allows direct translation into efficient solver-based execution frameworks, bridging the gap between high-level specification and performant computation. This combination of expressiveness, clarity, and implementability positions NP Datalog as a valuable tool for both theoretical investigations and real-world applications requiring NP-level problem solving. Future work will explore extensions to broader complexity classes, richer optimization capabilities, and integration with modern constraint-solving technologies.

title: Characterization of Kepler early-type targets
abstract: We present a spectroscopic and photometric characterization of a sample of early-type stellar targets observed by the *Kepler* mission. The sample comprises 116 stars originally classified as B- and A-type candidates based on broadband photometry and *Kepler* Input Catalog parameters. Medium-resolution spectra were obtained using facilities at several observatories, enabling accurate determinations of spectral types, effective temperatures, surface gravities, and projected rotational velocities. We complemented these data with *Kepler* long-cadence light curves to investigate variability properties and refine stellar classifications. Our analysis reveals that the sample spans a range of spectral types from late B through early F, with a significant fraction of objects misclassified in the initial catalog. We identify numerous chemically peculiar stars, including Ap and Am stars, as well as several Be stars exhibiting emission features. Rotational velocities vary widely, with some stars rotating near their breakup limits, while others are slow rotators, likely due to magnetic braking or binarity. Photometric variability is detected in over 60% of the sample, encompassing pulsations consistent with δ Scuti, γ Doradus, and slowly pulsating B-type stars, as well as eclipsing binaries and rotational modulation. The combination of precise *Kepler* photometry with our spectroscopic constraints allows for improved placement of these stars in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and better identification of pulsational instability domains. Our results provide a refined set of stellar parameters for early-type *Kepler* targets, enabling more accurate asteroseismic modeling and contributing to the study of variability in intermediate- and high-mass stars. This work highlights the necessity of spectroscopic follow-up to validate photometric classifications and demonstrates the diversity of stellar phenomena captured within the *Kepler* field. The compiled dataset serves as a valuable resource for further investigations into stellar structure, evolution, and the interplay between rotation, pulsation, and chemical peculiarity in early-type stars.
introduction:
The Kepler space telescope has provided an unprecedented dataset for the study of stellar variability, enabling the detection and characterization of a wide range of stellar phenomena across diverse spectral types. While much of the initial focus of the Kepler mission was directed toward the detection of exoplanets via transit photometry, the precision and continuity of its observations have also opened new avenues for stellar astrophysics. Among the various stellar classes observed, early-type stars—those of spectral types O, B, and early A—represent a particularly intriguing group. These stars, typically characterized by high masses, elevated surface temperatures, and relatively short lifespans, play a crucial role in the chemical and dynamical evolution of galaxies. Their strong stellar winds, high luminosities, and propensity for pulsations make them valuable laboratories for testing models of stellar structure and evolution.

Despite their astrophysical importance, early-type stars have historically been more challenging to study photometrically compared to cooler stars. Their intrinsic variability often occurs on short timescales and with amplitudes that require high-precision, continuous data to resolve. Moreover, their relatively low occurrence in the solar neighborhood, combined with the optical design and field selection of many photometric surveys, has meant that they are often underrepresented in variability studies. The Kepler mission, with its long time baseline and high photometric precision, has offered a unique opportunity to overcome these limitations, enabling the detection of subtle variability patterns and the characterization of pulsational and rotational signatures in early-type targets.

In the context of stellar variability, early-type stars encompass a range of phenomena including β Cephei and slowly pulsating B (SPB) stars, δ Scuti variables, and hybrid pulsators exhibiting both p- and g-mode oscillations. In addition, rotational modulation due to surface inhomogeneities, binarity effects such as eclipses and ellipsoidal variations, and stochastic variability related to stellar winds and magnetic activity contribute to the observed light curves. Disentangling these contributions requires a combination of precise photometry, robust variability classification, and, where possible, complementary spectroscopic data to constrain fundamental stellar parameters.

The Kepler Input Catalog (KIC) provides basic photometric and astrometric information for stars in the Kepler field, including estimated effective temperatures, surface gravities, and metallicities derived from broadband photometry. However, for early-type stars, these parameters are often subject to significant uncertainties due to the degeneracy of photometric colors at high temperatures and the effects of interstellar reddening. Consequently, careful validation and refinement of stellar parameters are essential for reliable classification and interpretation of variability.

In this work, we present a comprehensive characterization of early-type targets observed by Kepler, focusing on a curated sample selected for spectral types earlier than mid-A. We describe the selection criteria, the methods used to refine their stellar parameters, and the analysis techniques applied to their light curves to identify and classify variability. Our aim is to provide an updated census of early-type stars in the Kepler field, to quantify the occurrence rates of different variability classes, and to explore correlations between variability properties and fundamental stellar parameters. This study contributes to the broader effort to exploit the Kepler dataset for advancing our understanding of massive and intermediate-mass stars, offering new constraints for stellar pulsation models and evolutionary theory.
conclusion:
In this work, we have conducted a detailed characterization of a sample of early-type stars observed by the *Kepler* mission, focusing on their fundamental parameters, variability properties, and potential for asteroseismic studies. By combining high-precision *Kepler* photometry with complementary spectroscopic data, we have derived effective temperatures, surface gravities, projected rotational velocities, and luminosity estimates for the majority of the 274 objects in our primary sample, together with an extended set of 503 early-type *Kepler* targets identified from mission archives. This integrated approach has allowed us to refine classifications, identify peculiar objects, and provide a coherent framework for subsequent astrophysical interpretation.

Our analysis confirms that the early-type population within the *Kepler* field is diverse, spanning the full range from late-B to early-A spectral types, and exhibiting a broad distribution of rotational velocities. We detect a significant fraction of targets showing periodic variability consistent with pulsations, rotational modulation, or binarity. Several stars display hybrid variability patterns, suggesting the coexistence of different excitation mechanisms, and highlighting the potential complexity of their internal structure. In particular, we identify numerous candidates for slowly pulsating B-type (SPB) stars and δ Scuti variables, as well as a subset showing signatures of γ Doradus pulsations. The detection of such objects within a uniform photometric dataset offers valuable opportunities for comparative asteroseismic modelling.

The derived stellar parameters place most of the sample on or near the main sequence, with a smaller fraction occupying more evolved evolutionary stages. The combination of *Kepler* light curves and spectroscopic constraints has proved effective in resolving ambiguities in photometric classifications, reducing contamination from cooler interlopers, and revealing chemically peculiar stars. Our results underline the importance of accurate atmospheric parameters when interpreting variability, particularly for distinguishing between pulsational and rotational origins.

From an asteroseismic perspective, the characterization provided here establishes a robust starting point for detailed modelling of individual stars and for statistical studies of early-type stellar interiors. The identification of rapid rotators and chemically peculiar stars within the sample opens pathways for investigating the interplay between rotation, magnetic fields, and pulsation. Moreover, the presence of eclipsing and ellipsoidal binaries among the early-type population offers independent constraints on stellar masses and radii, complementing seismic inferences.

Looking ahead, the dataset and classifications presented in this work can be exploited in conjunction with *Gaia* astrometry, high-resolution spectroscopy, and upcoming time-domain surveys to further refine the evolutionary status and internal properties of these stars. In particular, the synergy between precise parallaxes, long-baseline photometry, and spectropolarimetric measurements will enable a deeper understanding of angular momentum transport, chemical mixing, and the excitation of pulsations in the upper main sequence.

In summary, we have provided the most comprehensive homogeneous characterization to date of *Kepler* early-type targets, delivering fundamental parameters, variability classifications, and candidate lists for follow-up. This work lays the groundwork for exploiting the full potential of the *Kepler* dataset for advancing our knowledge of massive star structure and evolution, and serves as a benchmark for interpreting observations from current and future space missions.

title: HiRID-ICU-Benchmark -- A Comprehensive Machine Learning Benchmark on High-resolution ICU Data
abstract: We present **HiRID-ICU-Benchmark**, a comprehensive machine learning benchmark built on the High Resolution ICU Dataset (HiRID), which contains rich, minute-by-minute clinical data from intensive care unit stays. This benchmark is designed to facilitate reproducible research in time-series modeling for critical care by providing standardized preprocessing, clearly defined prediction tasks, and unified evaluation protocols. HiRID-ICU-Benchmark encompasses diverse clinically relevant challenges, including mortality prediction, length-of-stay estimation, and early warning for physiological deterioration, enabling systematic comparison of algorithms across tasks and settings. The high temporal resolution and breadth of variables in HiRID allow for nuanced modeling of patient trajectories, while our benchmark framework ensures accessibility for both clinical and machine learning researchers. By releasing open-source code, curated datasets, and baseline models, we aim to accelerate progress in high-resolution ICU data analysis, foster transparency in model development, and support the translation of machine learning advances into improved critical care decision-making.
introduction:
Intensive Care Units (ICUs) provide life-sustaining treatment for critically ill patients, continuously monitoring vital signs, laboratory measurements, and therapeutic interventions at high temporal resolution. The dynamic and complex nature of critical illness, coupled with the heterogeneity of patient trajectories, makes ICU care one of the most data-rich and information-intensive settings in modern medicine. Over the past decade, the increased availability of electronic health record (EHR) data from ICUs has opened new opportunities for applying machine learning (ML) methods to improve patient monitoring, risk stratification, and clinical decision support. By leveraging continuous streams of physiological signals and clinical observations, ML models can potentially detect deteriorations earlier, predict complications, and assist in optimizing treatment strategies.

Several publicly available ICU datasets, such as MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD, have catalyzed research progress in this domain, enabling the development and evaluation of advanced algorithms. However, these datasets typically contain measurements at relatively coarse temporal resolutions, often aggregated to hourly or irregular intervals. This limits their ability to fully capture the fast-changing dynamics of critically ill patients, where clinically relevant changes can occur within minutes. In contrast, high-resolution datasets, which record observations at the granularity of minutes or even seconds, can reflect the rapid physiological variability inherent to ICU patients and allow for more precise temporal modeling. Such data, however, have been less accessible due to privacy, storage, and processing challenges, and publicly available benchmarks for high-resolution ICU prediction tasks remain scarce.

The High Time Resolution ICU Dataset (HiRID) was introduced to address these limitations. Collected at the University Hospital of Bern, Switzerland, HiRID contains minute-by-minute recordings of over 33,000 ICU admissions, including vital signs, laboratory results, medication administrations, and device settings. The dataset is de-identified and freely available for research under a data use agreement. By providing high-frequency, multivariate time series data alongside rich metadata, HiRID offers a unique opportunity to investigate ML methods for modeling rapid physiological changes, handling irregular sampling patterns, and integrating heterogeneous clinical information.

Despite its potential, the uptake of HiRID in the ML and clinical informatics communities has been comparatively modest. One contributing factor is the absence of a standardized benchmark that defines clinically meaningful prediction tasks, provides reproducible data processing pipelines, and establishes baseline performance metrics. Benchmarks play a critical role in accelerating research: they enable fair comparisons across methods, encourage the development of robust and generalizable models, and facilitate cumulative progress. In the broader ML field, benchmark datasets such as ImageNet in computer vision or GLUE in natural language processing have been instrumental in driving innovation. In the healthcare domain, well-defined benchmarks such as PhysioNet Challenges have similarly advanced the state of the art. For high-resolution ICU data, however, there is a notable gap.

To fill this gap, we present HiRID-ICU-Benchmark, a comprehensive machine learning benchmark built upon the HiRID dataset. The benchmark defines a suite of clinically relevant predictive tasks, including short-term and long-term mortality prediction, prediction of physiological decompensation, forecasting of laboratory values, and detection of specific interventions. Each task is accompanied by standardized preprocessing steps that handle missingness, irregular sampling, and variable-length episodes, as well as fixed train/validation/test splits to ensure reproducibility. We further provide strong baseline models spanning classical statistical methods, deep learning architectures for time series, and state-of-the-art sequence models, enabling researchers to gauge the difficulty of each task and to compare their approaches against established baselines.

By focusing on high-resolution ICU data, HiRID-ICU-Benchmark poses unique challenges for ML algorithms. These include effectively modeling long sequences with fine temporal granularity, capturing both short-term fluctuations and long-term trends, dealing with substantial missingness and noise, and integrating diverse data modalities. At the same time, the benchmark’s design emphasizes clinical interpretability and relevance, ensuring that improvements in predictive performance translate into potential utility in real-world ICU settings. In addition, by releasing the benchmark as open-source code with thorough documentation, we aim to lower the barrier to entry for researchers from both the ML and clinical communities.

In summary, the contributions of this work are threefold: (1) we introduce a standardized, reproducible benchmark for high-resolution ICU prediction tasks based on the publicly available HiRID dataset; (2) we define a diverse set of clinically meaningful tasks and provide robust preprocessing pipelines and data splits; and (3) we establish baseline results using a range of modeling approaches, offering reference points for future research. We believe HiRID-ICU-Benchmark will serve as a catalyst for developing and evaluating novel methods capable of leveraging the richness of high-frequency ICU data, ultimately contributing to advances in patient monitoring and decision support in critical care.
conclusion: HiRID-ICU-Benchmark provides a comprehensive, high-resolution benchmark for advancing machine learning research in intensive care. By integrating rich temporal signals with standardized tasks, it enables rigorous evaluation of models across clinically relevant scenarios. Our framework supports reproducibility, comparability, and transparency, fostering progress in predictive modelling for critical care. We anticipate that HiRID-ICU-Benchmark will serve as a valuable resource for the research community, catalyzing innovations that translate into improved patient outcomes and more effective, data-driven decision support in the ICU setting.

title: The super-correlator/super-amplitude duality: Part I
abstract: We investigate the duality between super-correlators and super-amplitudes in planar \(\mathcal{N}=4\) supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory, focusing on its precise formulation and initial consequences. Building on the correspondence between scattering amplitudes and light-like polygonal Wilson loops, we extend the framework to correlation functions of stress-tensor multiplets in superspace. We present a systematic derivation of the duality for the four- and five-point cases, demonstrating the exact matching between appropriately defined limits of super-correlators and super-amplitudes at tree level and beyond. Our analysis incorporates the full supersymmetric structure, including Grassmann coordinates, and clarifies the role of dual superconformal symmetry in ensuring the equivalence. We also discuss the constraints imposed by operator product expansions in the light-like limit, and outline how loop corrections preserve the duality. This work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the unified description of scattering processes and local operator dynamics, providing a foundation for the more intricate multi-point analysis developed in the sequel.
introduction:
The study of scattering amplitudes in maximally supersymmetric gauge theories has revealed a wealth of hidden structures and remarkable simplifications, far beyond what might be anticipated from traditional perturbative quantum field theory. Among the most striking discoveries is the existence of dualities linking seemingly different physical observables. One such correspondence — the duality between scattering super-amplitudes and certain supersymmetric correlation functions, often referred to as the super-correlator/super-amplitude duality — has emerged as a unifying framework for understanding the interplay between local operators and on-shell processes in \(\mathcal{N}=4\) supersymmetric Yang–Mills (SYM) theory.

This duality relates planar scattering amplitudes of on-shell states to correlation functions of protected operators, evaluated in specific light-like limits. In particular, it suggests that the generating function of stress-energy multiplet correlators, when restricted to configurations in which adjacent operator insertion points become null-separated, reproduces the full super-amplitude, including its intricate supersymmetric and helicity structure. The conjecture builds upon earlier, more restricted correspondences: the well-established duality between maximally helicity violating (MHV) amplitudes and light-like polygonal Wilson loops, and the identification of Wilson loops with certain light-like limits of operator correlators. By embedding both amplitudes and correlators into a common superspace formalism, the super-correlator/super-amplitude duality extends these ideas to the complete set of non-MHV processes.

From a conceptual standpoint, the duality is deeply tied to the hidden dual (super)conformal symmetry of planar \(\mathcal{N}=4\) SYM, a symmetry not manifest in the Lagrangian formulation but revealed in scattering amplitudes when expressed in terms of dual momentum variables. In this picture, the external on-shell momenta of the amplitude are reinterpreted as differences of coordinates in a dual space, naturally identified with the positions of local operators in the correlator. The light-like separation condition in the correlator then reflects the masslessness of the external particles, making the correspondence between the two observables precise.

On the technical side, the duality provides a powerful computational tool. While multi-loop scattering amplitudes are notoriously difficult to evaluate directly, correlation functions of half-BPS operators benefit from strong constraints of superconformal symmetry and can be computed using position-space techniques, harmonic superspace, and integrability-based methods. The duality thus opens the possibility of determining amplitudes indirectly, by computing correlators and taking appropriate null limits. Moreover, it offers a natural framework for understanding the analytic structure of amplitudes, including their singularities and factorisation properties, from the perspective of local operator dynamics.

The aim of the present work, the first in a two-part series, is to provide a systematic study of the super-correlator/super-amplitude duality, laying out its foundations, clarifying its precise formulation, and illustrating its validity through explicit examples. We will develop the superspace setup necessary to describe both correlators and amplitudes in a unified language, review the relevant aspects of \(\mathcal{N}=4\) SYM that underlie the correspondence, and present detailed computations at tree level and beyond. Special attention will be given to the role of R-symmetry, Grassmann expansions, and the matching of component structures across the duality. In doing so, we aim to not only substantiate the conjectured correspondence but also to highlight the deeper geometric and algebraic principles it reflects.

By the end of Part I, we will have established the groundwork for a more comprehensive analysis to be undertaken in Part II, where loop corrections, integrability implications, and potential generalisations beyond the planar limit will be addressed. Through this two-part exploration, we hope to contribute to the broader effort of charting the rich landscape of correspondences that connect different sectors of gauge theory dynamics and to further unravel the mathematical structures underlying scattering processes in supersymmetric quantum field theories.
conclusion: In this work we have examined the structure and implications of the proposed super-correlator/super-amplitude duality, focusing on its formulation and consistency in the planar limit. By analyzing explicit examples and symmetry constraints, we have shown how the correspondence emerges naturally from the underlying supersymmetric and conformal properties of the theory. Our results provide evidence that the duality extends beyond previously known cases, offering a unified framework for correlators and scattering amplitudes in maximally supersymmetric gauge theory. This study lays the groundwork for a deeper exploration of loop corrections, non-planar contributions, and potential generalizations to less supersymmetric or higher-dimensional settings.

title: The size of ABDorA from VLTI/AMBER interferometry
abstract: We present high angular resolution observations of the young, active star AB Doradus A (ABDorA) obtained with the VLTI/AMBER instrument in the near-infrared. Our aim is to directly measure the stellar angular diameter and compare it with predictions from evolutionary models for pre-main-sequence stars. Interferometric fringes were recorded in the H and K bands using multiple baseline configurations, providing spatial frequency coverage sufficient to resolve the stellar disk. The calibrated visibilities were fitted with uniform and limb-darkened disk models, yielding an angular diameter of \( \theta_{\mathrm{LD}} = 0.62 \pm 0.04 \) mas. Adopting the most recent parallax measurement from Gaia, this corresponds to a linear radius of \( 0.96 \pm 0.06\,R_\odot \). Our result is consistent with, but more precise than, previous indirect estimates based on photometry and rotational modulation. The measured radius is marginally larger than predicted by standard evolutionary tracks for the estimated age of the AB Doradus moving group (\(\sim 120\) Myr), suggesting a possible influence of magnetic activity and starspots on the stellar structure. These findings demonstrate the capability of long-baseline interferometry to directly constrain fundamental parameters of nearby young stars, providing critical benchmarks for stellar evolution models.
introduction:
The direct measurement of stellar diameters provides a fundamental constraint on stellar models, offering an essential link between theoretical predictions and observed stellar properties. In particular, accurate determinations of angular diameters, when combined with reliable distances, yield precise linear radii, which are critical for testing stellar evolution calculations, calibrating effective temperature scales, and refining empirical relations for different stellar populations. Long-baseline optical interferometry has emerged as one of the most powerful techniques for resolving the disks of nearby stars, achieving angular resolutions at the milliarcsecond level and enabling detailed characterization of stellar photospheres.

AB Doradus A (hereafter AB Dor A) is a nearby, young, and magnetically active K-type pre-main-sequence star, and the primary component of the AB Doradus moving group. Its proximity (distance ∼15 pc), youth (age ∼50–150 Myr), and rapid rotation (P_rot ≈ 0.5 d) make it an important benchmark for studies of stellar structure and evolution in the low-mass regime. The star’s high level of magnetic activity, manifested in strong chromospheric and coronal emission, as well as large starspots, offers a valuable opportunity to investigate the interplay between rotation, magnetic fields, and stellar radius inflation in young stars. Accurate radius measurements for AB Dor A are therefore particularly relevant for testing stellar models that incorporate magnetic effects and spot coverage.

Previous radius estimates for AB Dor A have relied primarily on spectrophotometric methods, rotational broadening measurements, and indirect constraints from evolutionary tracks. While these approaches have yielded broadly consistent results, they remain subject to systematic uncertainties related to stellar atmosphere models, inclination angles, and the treatment of surface inhomogeneities. Direct interferometric measurements can overcome many of these limitations by resolving the stellar disk and providing a model-independent angular diameter. However, such measurements for rapidly rotating, active stars are challenging due to their small angular sizes, the need for high spatial resolution, and potential complications from non-uniform surface brightness distributions.

The Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), equipped with the Astronomical Multi-BEam combineR (AMBER), offers an ideal facility for this task. Operating in the near-infrared with baselines up to several hundred meters, VLTI/AMBER can achieve the angular resolution and sensitivity required to resolve AB Dor A’s photosphere. In addition, the instrument’s capability to combine three telescopes simultaneously allows for the measurement of closure phases, which are sensitive to asymmetries in the stellar surface brightness and can help assess the role of spots or other surface structures.

In this work, we present new VLTI/AMBER interferometric observations of AB Dor A, aimed at directly measuring its angular diameter with unprecedented precision. We describe the observational strategy, data reduction, and visibility modeling procedures, and discuss the resulting linear radius in the context of current stellar evolution models for young, magnetically active stars. Our results provide an important empirical reference point for the calibration of theoretical models and contribute to a deeper understanding of the physical processes shaping the structure of young, low-mass stars.
conclusion:
The interferometric observations of AB Dor A obtained with the VLTI/AMBER instrument have provided a direct and precise measurement of the star’s angular diameter, enabling a robust determination of its linear radius when combined with the well-established parallax. The resulting value, consistent across different fitting approaches and wavelength ranges, offers a significant improvement over previous estimates based on indirect methods. Our analysis demonstrates the capability of long-baseline near-infrared interferometry to resolve young, nearby, fast-rotating stars despite the challenges posed by their complex photospheric structures.

The measured radius of AB Dor A agrees within uncertainties with the predictions of evolutionary models for pre-main-sequence stars of similar mass and age, though the slight excess relative to some theoretical tracks may reflect the influence of magnetic activity, rapid rotation, or starspot coverage—phenomena known to be significant in active young stars. The inclusion of these effects in future modeling will be essential to fully reconcile theory and observation. Our results also provide an independent check on parameters derived from photometry, spectroscopy, and surface brightness relations, strengthening the overall characterization of this benchmark object.

The consistency of our interferometric diameter with previous indirect estimates supports the reliability of multi-technique determinations of stellar properties. However, the direct nature of the VLTI/AMBER measurement reduces dependence on assumptions about limb darkening and model atmospheres, particularly in the near-infrared regime where such uncertainties are minimized. This underscores the importance of interferometry as a complementary tool to traditional spectroscopic and photometric methods, especially for active and rapidly rotating stars where standard approaches may be biased.

In addition to the radius determination, our study illustrates the potential of AMBER’s high spectral resolution to probe surface inhomogeneities and differential rotation. Although the present dataset does not allow a definitive detection of such effects, the achieved precision opens the way for time-resolved interferometric monitoring that could directly map stellar surface structures in the future. Such observations would provide critical constraints on dynamo processes and angular momentum evolution in young stars.

In summary, we have presented the first direct interferometric measurement of AB Dor A’s angular diameter, yielding a precise stellar radius that serves as a stringent test for pre-main-sequence evolutionary models. The results highlight both the scientific return and the technical feasibility of resolving nearby active stars with current VLTI instrumentation. Future observations with improved uv-coverage, higher sensitivity, and complementary imaging techniques will not only refine these measurements but also expand the sample of young stars with directly measured fundamental parameters. Such efforts will be key to advancing our understanding of stellar structure, activity, and evolution in the early stages of a star’s lifetime.

title: Classification of two and three dimensional Lie super-bialgebras
abstract: We present a complete classification of two- and three-dimensional Lie super-bialgebras. Using graded commutation relations and compatibility conditions, all non-isomorphic structures are determined. The results extend earlier classifications of Lie bialgebras to the supersymmetric case, providing a foundation for applications in integrable systems and quantum supergroup theory.
introduction:
The theory of Lie superalgebras has emerged as a natural generalization of Lie algebras, incorporating a \( \mathbb{Z}_2 \)-grading structure that allows for the unified treatment of bosonic and fermionic symmetries. This framework plays a central role in the mathematical formulation of supersymmetry, supergeometry, and various aspects of theoretical and mathematical physics. In particular, Lie super-bialgebras, as the super-analogue of Lie bialgebras introduced by Drinfel’d, provide the appropriate algebraic setting for the study of Poisson–Lie supergroups and quantum supergroups. The classification of such structures in low dimensions constitutes a crucial step toward understanding their general properties and applications.

A Lie super-bialgebra consists of a Lie superalgebra together with a compatible cobracket structure satisfying the super-co-Jacobi identity and a 1-cocycle condition. This compatibility ensures that the dual space inherits a natural Lie superalgebra structure, leading to the notion of dual pairs and, in turn, to the construction of the associated Drinfel’d superdoubles. The classification problem for Lie super-bialgebras thus involves determining all possible cobracket structures, up to isomorphism, for a given underlying Lie superalgebra. Low-dimensional cases are of particular interest as they often serve as building blocks for more complicated structures and provide concrete examples for testing conjectures and developing computational techniques.

In recent decades, the classification of low-dimensional Lie bialgebras has been extensively studied, yielding complete results for dimensions up to three in the purely bosonic case. Parallel progress for Lie super-bialgebras has been comparatively slower due to the richer algebraic structure arising from the graded commutation relations, sign conventions, and the interplay between even and odd generators. Nevertheless, classifications have been successfully obtained for certain families of two- and three-dimensional Lie superalgebras, though a systematic and comprehensive treatment for all such cases remains desirable.

The motivation for focusing on two- and three-dimensional Lie super-bialgebras is twofold. Firstly, these dimensions are sufficiently small to allow for explicit computation and direct verification of the super-Jacobi and cocycle conditions, enabling a complete enumeration of inequivalent structures. Secondly, they capture many of the essential features of the theory, including the emergence of nontrivial duals and the possibility of constructing non-abelian Drinfel’d superdoubles. Furthermore, low-dimensional examples frequently appear in physical models, such as supersymmetric extensions of two-dimensional sigma models, where Poisson–Lie T-duality plays a significant role.

In this work, we undertake a detailed classification of all two- and three-dimensional Lie super-bialgebras, building on existing knowledge of the underlying Lie superalgebra structures.
