Our approach is based on solving the super cocycle equations in a fixed basis, using known automorphism supergroups to identify isomorphic cases, and systematically determining the associated dual superalgebras. The results are presented in a form that facilitates their use in applications, including the explicit construction of Drinfel’d superdoubles and the study of quantum deformations. Through this classification, we aim to provide a complete reference for the smallest nontrivial examples of Lie super-bialgebras, thereby contributing to the broader understanding of graded extensions of quantum group theory.
conclusion: In this work we have presented a systematic classification of two- and three-dimensional Lie super-bialgebras by employing the standard definition based on the compatibility between the super-Lie bracket and the cocommutator structure. Using the explicit form of low-dimensional Lie superalgebras and their automorphism supergroups, we determined all inequivalent Lie super-bialgebra structures up to isomorphism. Our analysis includes both the even and odd generators, taking into account the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-grading and the super-Jacobi identities, thus ensuring the completeness and consistency of the classification. The results provide explicit lists of dual structures, highlighting the correspondence between a given Lie superalgebra and its dual, and revealing the role of the underlying symmetry in reducing equivalent cases. This classification enlarges the available catalogue of low-dimensional Lie super-bialgebras, serving as a basis for the construction of associated quantum deformations and Poisson–Lie supergroup structures. Furthermore, the explicit examples obtained here may be used to investigate integrable systems, supersymmetric sigma models, and Drinfel’d superdoubles in low dimensions. Future work may extend the present approach to higher-dimensional cases, explore their cohomological properties, and study the physical implications of the corresponding quantum supergroups. The present results thus form a concrete step toward a deeper understanding of the algebraic and geometric structures underlying supersymmetric extensions of Lie bialgebras.

title: Bayesian Optical Flow with Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: We propose a Bayesian framework for optical flow estimation that jointly predicts motion fields and quantifies the associated uncertainty. Unlike conventional deterministic approaches, our method models optical flow as a posterior distribution over pixel-wise motion vectors, enabling principled reasoning about confidence in the estimates. We formulate the problem within a probabilistic generative model that incorporates brightness constancy and spatial smoothness priors, and employ variational inference to approximate the intractable posterior. This yields both a mean flow field and per-pixel variance maps, capturing aleatoric uncertainty due to noise, occlusions, and textureless regions. To improve scalability, we integrate the inference procedure into a deep neural architecture, allowing efficient end-to-end training on large-scale datasets. Experimental results on standard optical flow benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive accuracy while providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. We further show that these uncertainty maps can guide downstream tasks, such as motion segmentation and robust tracking, by identifying unreliable regions. The proposed Bayesian optical flow model facilitates more reliable motion analysis in safety-critical applications, where understanding the confidence in predictions is as important as the predictions themselves.
introduction:
Optical flow estimation, the task of determining pixel-wise motion between consecutive frames in an image sequence, is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications ranging from video compression and visual odometry to activity recognition and autonomous navigation. Classical approaches to optical flow, such as those based on the variational framework of Horn and Schunck or the feature-based Lucas–Kanade method, have achieved significant success by exploiting assumptions of brightness constancy and spatial smoothness. However, these methods are often sensitive to violations of such assumptions, including illumination changes, occlusions, and motion discontinuities. More recent advances, particularly deep learning–based models, have demonstrated remarkable improvements in accuracy and robustness, leveraging large datasets and powerful network architectures to learn complex motion patterns. Despite these advances, most existing methods provide point estimates of motion fields without a principled characterization of the associated uncertainty.

The absence of uncertainty quantification in optical flow estimation is a critical limitation in safety-critical and decision-making applications. In domains such as autonomous driving, medical imaging, and robotics, it is not only important to predict motion accurately, but also to know when predictions may be unreliable. Uncertainty estimates can guide downstream modules to adaptively fuse information, trigger additional sensing, or defer decisions to human operators. They can also serve as a diagnostic tool for detecting out-of-distribution inputs and model failures, thereby improving the interpretability and trustworthiness of vision systems.

Bayesian methods provide a natural framework for uncertainty quantification by treating model parameters or outputs as random variables and inferring their posterior distributions given observed data. In the context of optical flow, a Bayesian formulation allows us to represent the motion field as a probabilistic entity, capturing both aleatoric uncertainty, stemming from inherent ambiguities in the data (e.g., textureless regions or motion blur), and epistemic uncertainty, arising from limited training data or model capacity. Such a formulation can be realized through variational inference, Monte Carlo sampling, or other approximate Bayesian techniques, and can be embedded into both classical and deep learning–based optical flow pipelines.

In this work, we propose a Bayesian optical flow framework that jointly estimates dense motion fields and quantifies associated uncertainties. Our approach builds upon recent probabilistic modeling advances to produce not only the most probable flow vectors but also spatially resolved uncertainty maps. By integrating Bayesian inference into the optical flow estimation process, our method can better handle ambiguous regions, improve robustness to noise, and provide actionable confidence measures for downstream tasks. We evaluate our approach on standard benchmarks, demonstrating competitive accuracy alongside calibrated uncertainty estimates. The proposed framework contributes toward making optical flow estimation not only more accurate but also more reliable, paving the way for its adoption in applications where understanding the limits of model predictions is as important as the predictions themselves.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a Bayesian framework for optical flow estimation that jointly infers motion fields and their associated uncertainty. Departing from purely deterministic formulations, our approach models optical flow as a posterior distribution over motion vectors given observed image sequences, enabling principled reasoning about the confidence in each estimate. By embedding optical flow inference within a probabilistic generative model, we have integrated prior knowledge about motion smoothness, spatial continuity, and photometric consistency with the data likelihood, leading to improved robustness in challenging conditions. The resulting formulation provides not only point estimates of motion but also credible intervals that reflect epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in the predictions.

Our experimental results have demonstrated the benefits of uncertainty quantification in multiple respects. First, the predictive mean flow fields achieved accuracy competitive with, and in some cases surpassing, state-of-the-art deterministic optical flow methods, particularly in regions with ambiguous motion cues or degraded image quality. Second, the uncertainty maps derived from the posterior distributions reliably indicated regions of potential error, allowing downstream processes to adaptively weight or discard unreliable motion estimates. This property is especially valuable in safety-critical applications such as autonomous navigation and medical imaging, where awareness of uncertainty can guide decision-making and prevent overconfident errors.

The Bayesian perspective also offers a unifying framework for incorporating diverse sources of prior information and for extending the model to more complex motion scenarios. Our formulation accommodates hierarchical priors, spatially varying smoothness constraints, and motion models that account for scene geometry or object segmentation. Furthermore, the probabilistic nature of the model makes it straightforward to integrate additional modalities, such as depth or semantic labels, by appropriately modifying the likelihood function. This flexibility suggests that the Bayesian approach can serve as a foundation for a new generation of multi-modal motion estimation systems.

From a computational standpoint, we have shown that variational inference and Monte Carlo sampling provide practical means of approximating the posterior over motion fields at scale. While exact inference remains intractable for high-resolution imagery, our experiments indicate that structured variational approximations and efficient sampling schemes can deliver accurate results within reasonable computational budgets. Nonetheless, there is room for improvement in inference efficiency, particularly for real-time applications; future work could explore amortized inference networks, sparse representations, or multi-resolution strategies to further accelerate convergence.

Our analysis of the uncertainty estimates suggests that they capture both measurement noise and model misspecification effects. In textured regions with consistent motion, uncertainties are low, reflecting high confidence in the estimates; conversely, in occluded or low-contrast areas, uncertainties rise, signaling the need for caution. This correlation between uncertainty and true error validates the informativeness of the proposed Bayesian approach. Importantly, we have also illustrated how uncertainty maps can be exploited for adaptive regularization, selective refinement, and active data acquisition, thus turning uncertainty from a byproduct into a functional asset.

Looking ahead, the integration of Bayesian optical flow estimation with deep learning architectures represents a promising avenue. Deep generative models can serve as flexible priors, while Bayesian inference can temper the tendency of overconfident predictions in neural networks. Moreover, the probabilistic formalism aligns naturally with active vision paradigms, where uncertainty guides the selection of viewpoints or sensing strategies to reduce ambiguity.

In summary, this work advances the state of the art in optical flow estimation by embedding motion inference within a Bayesian framework that delivers both accurate flow fields and meaningful uncertainty quantification. By enabling principled reasoning about confidence, our approach enhances the robustness, interpretability, and adaptability of motion estimation systems. We believe that the ideas and methods introduced here will stimulate further research into probabilistic vision models and foster safer, more reliable deployment of optical flow in real-world applications.

title: Sequential and Parallel Algorithms for the Addition of Big-Integer Numbers
abstract: This paper investigates sequential and parallel algorithms for adding big-integer numbers, focusing on computational efficiency and scalability. Traditional addition methods face performance limitations when operands exceed native machine word sizes, requiring special handling through digit-wise operations. We present a sequential algorithm optimized for minimal carry propagation and a parallel algorithm that partitions operands into independent segments, enabling concurrent processing and carry resolution. The parallel method leverages multi-core architectures to significantly reduce execution time for large inputs. Experimental evaluations compare runtime performance and speedup across varying operand sizes and processor counts. Results demonstrate that the proposed parallel approach achieves near-linear scalability for sufficiently large numbers, offering a practical solution for high-performance big-integer arithmetic in cryptography, scientific computing, and large-scale data processing.
introduction:
The rapid growth of data-intensive applications, such as cryptography, scientific computing, and large-scale numerical simulations, has intensified the demand for efficient arithmetic operations on big-integer numbers—integers whose size exceeds the standard word length supported by conventional processors. Big-integer arithmetic is fundamental to a variety of computational domains, including public-key encryption schemes like RSA, blockchain technologies, and arbitrary-precision computations in mathematical software. Among the core arithmetic operations, addition serves as a foundational procedure upon which multiplication, exponentiation, and modular reduction are built. Consequently, optimizing big-integer addition is a critical step toward improving the performance of higher-level algorithms.

In conventional computing systems, integers are typically represented using fixed-size data types, such as 32-bit or 64-bit words. When operands exceed these limits, they must be stored as arrays of smaller units, requiring algorithms that can process multiple words sequentially or in parallel. Sequential addition algorithms perform this task by iterating through the operand arrays from the least significant to the most significant word, propagating carries as needed. While conceptually simple, this approach may become a performance bottleneck when processing extremely large numbers, due to its inherently serial carry propagation. Furthermore, in high-throughput or real-time applications, the latency introduced by purely sequential addition becomes nontrivial.

Parallel computing architectures, ranging from multi-core CPUs to massively parallel GPUs and distributed systems, offer opportunities to accelerate big-integer operations by partitioning the computation across multiple processing units. Parallel algorithms for addition aim to reduce the carry propagation delay by employing techniques such as carry-lookahead, divide-and-conquer strategies, and parallel prefix computations. These methods exploit concurrency to achieve significant speedups, particularly for operands with millions of digits. However, designing efficient parallel algorithms for big-integer addition presents challenges in load balancing, memory access patterns, and synchronization overhead, all of which influence performance and scalability.

This paper investigates the design, implementation, and comparative performance of sequential and parallel algorithms for big-integer addition. We present a detailed analysis of algorithmic complexity, memory utilization, and execution time across varying operand sizes and hardware configurations. By systematically evaluating both paradigms, we aim to identify the circumstances under which parallelization yields substantial performance benefits and to quantify the trade-offs in terms of computational resources. The results of this study are relevant not only to the optimization of arithmetic libraries but also to the broader field of high-performance computing, where efficient big-integer arithmetic underpins a wide range of critical applications.
conclusion:
In this study, we examined the design, implementation, and performance characteristics of sequential and parallel algorithms for the addition of big-integer numbers. By analyzing the inherent computational structure of big-integer addition, we identified the potential for parallelization through decomposition of the operands into fixed-size segments and concurrent processing of partial sums. The sequential algorithm served as a baseline, demonstrating predictable performance but limited scalability due to its inherently serial carry-propagation process. In contrast, the parallel approach exploited multi-core architectures to reduce overall execution time, particularly for extremely large operands, by overlapping computation of independent segments and employing efficient carry-resolution strategies.

Experimental results confirmed that the parallel algorithm offers significant speedup over the sequential method as operand size increases, with the degree of improvement dependent on the number of available processing units and the efficiency of inter-thread communication. However, parallel performance gains were moderated by synchronization overhead and the non-trivial cost of carry propagation across segment boundaries. These findings suggest that while parallelization can substantially improve big-integer addition performance, careful algorithmic design is required to balance workload distribution with communication costs.

This work highlights the trade-offs between simplicity, scalability, and implementation complexity in big-integer arithmetic. Future research could explore hybrid approaches that combine parallel carry-lookahead techniques with adaptive load balancing, as well as the extension of these methods to distributed-memory systems and heterogeneous computing environments. Such advancements have the potential to further enhance the efficiency of big-integer operations in cryptography, scientific computing, and large-scale numerical applications.

title: Learning to Learn Variational Semantic Memory
abstract: We introduce *Learning to Learn Variational Semantic Memory* (L2VSM), a novel framework for meta-learning that integrates a variational memory architecture with a semantic embedding space. L2VSM enables rapid adaptation to new tasks by storing and retrieving distributed, probabilistic representations of task-relevant concepts. Unlike conventional memory-augmented neural networks, our approach explicitly models uncertainty in memory retrieval through a variational inference mechanism, allowing the system to generalize effectively from sparse and noisy data. The semantic memory is jointly optimized with the base learner in a meta-training phase, aligning latent memory representations with task-specific semantics. During meta-testing, the model can infer and update memory states on-the-fly, supporting efficient few-shot learning across diverse domains. We evaluate L2VSM on benchmark datasets for classification, regression, and reinforcement learning, demonstrating consistent improvements over strong meta-learning baselines. Our results suggest that combining semantic structure with probabilistic memory mechanisms provides a powerful inductive bias for learning-to-learn, enabling models to acquire and reuse abstract knowledge more effectively.
introduction:
Human cognition is characterized not only by the ability to acquire knowledge, but also by the capacity to learn how to learn. This meta-learning capability enables humans to generalize from prior experiences, adapt to novel tasks with minimal data, and build flexible internal models of the world. In recent years, the machine learning community has increasingly sought to endow artificial agents with similar meta-learning abilities, with the aim of creating systems that can rapidly adapt to new domains, tasks, and modalities. Despite notable advances, a central challenge remains: how to effectively model, store, and retrieve high-level semantic structure across diverse tasks in a manner that supports efficient learning-to-learn.

Meta-learning approaches typically rely on either optimization-based strategies, which adjust model parameters to enable fast adaptation, or memory-based strategies, which store and retrieve task-relevant information to support rapid inference. Optimization-based methods, such as Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), learn initialization points conducive to quick adaptation via gradient updates, while memory-based methods—exemplified by Matching Networks, Neural Turing Machines, and Memory-Augmented Neural Networks—explicitly encode and recall task-specific representations. However, these frameworks often face limitations when it comes to capturing abstract, compositional semantic relationships that transcend individual tasks, or when attempting to maintain coherent, generalizable knowledge over long time horizons.

Human memory is widely recognized to be structured in multiple interacting systems, including episodic memory for specific experiences and semantic memory for general knowledge and concepts. While episodic memory has been modeled in machine learning via explicit storage of task-specific examples, semantic memory—the repository of structured, abstract concepts—has received comparatively less computational attention, especially in the context of meta-learning. Semantic memory is essential for transfer and generalization: it enables humans to recognize patterns, infer rules, and apply learned concepts to unfamiliar problems. An artificial analogue of semantic memory could therefore serve as a crucial substrate for learning-to-learn, providing a compact, structured representation space from which new task solutions can be composed.

Variational methods offer a principled framework for learning such structured latent representations. By framing representation learning as probabilistic inference in latent variable models, variational approaches such as the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) can learn disentangled and semantically meaningful latent spaces. These spaces can capture high-level factors of variation in the data, which in turn can serve as a basis for generalization across tasks. Recent work has shown that variational inference can be integrated into memory systems to produce probabilistic embeddings that model uncertainty and structure. However, the integration of variational semantic memory within a meta-learning framework remains underexplored. In particular, there is a need for a mechanism that can accumulate, update, and retrieve abstract knowledge representations in a probabilistically coherent way, while supporting fast adaptation to novel tasks.

We propose to address this gap by introducing a model of variational semantic memory designed specifically for meta-learning. Our approach draws inspiration from cognitive theories of semantic memory as a network of conceptual relationships, and from probabilistic machine learning methods that learn latent structures capturing these relationships. The key idea is to maintain a global latent semantic space that is updated across tasks via variational inference, enabling the system to distill common structure and abstract knowledge from diverse experiences. When confronted with a new task, the model can query this semantic memory to retrieve relevant latent representations, which can then be combined with limited task-specific data to generate accurate predictions or policies. This design allows the system to leverage accumulated knowledge for zero- or few-shot learning, while continuously refining its semantic representations as more tasks are encountered.

Such a variational semantic memory has several advantages for learning-to-learn. First, by representing semantic knowledge probabilistically, the system can explicitly model uncertainty, allowing it to balance reliance on prior knowledge with adaptation to novel evidence. Second, the latent semantic space provides a compact, structured representation that facilitates compositional generalization, enabling the model to reconfigure known concepts in new ways. Third, the variational framework naturally supports continual learning: as new tasks are processed, the semantic memory can be updated in a Bayesian manner, reducing catastrophic forgetting while integrating new information. Finally, the explicit separation between semantic memory and task-specific adaptation encourages the emergence of more general, transferable knowledge.

In this work, we develop the theoretical foundations of variational semantic memory for meta-learning, present an architecture that implements these principles, and evaluate its performance on a range of few-shot classification and reinforcement learning benchmarks. We investigate how the learned semantic space evolves over time, how it supports rapid adaptation, and how it compares to existing meta-learning and memory-augmented approaches. Our results demonstrate that incorporating a variational semantic memory significantly improves generalization to novel tasks, reduces sample complexity, and yields interpretable latent representations that align with semantic concepts in the data. We further analyze the trade-offs between expressiveness, uncertainty modeling, and computational efficiency in the proposed framework.

By uniting the strengths of probabilistic latent variable modeling and meta-learning, our approach offers a step toward artificial agents that can learn to learn in a manner more akin to human cognition. In doing so, it opens new avenues for constructing systems that not only perform well on current tasks, but also build a structured, probabilistic understanding of the world that supports lifelong learning and flexible adaptation.
conclusion:
This work has introduced a framework for learning to learn within the context of variational semantic memory, integrating meta-learning principles with probabilistic generative modeling to support adaptive, structured, and generalizable memory representations. By unifying variational inference with a semantic memory architecture, the proposed approach enables both the rapid acquisition of new concepts from limited data and the retention of structured knowledge over extended timescales. Our results demonstrate that this integration not only improves performance on few-shot and continual learning tasks but also yields interpretable latent representations aligned with semantic structure.

The central contribution lies in formalizing semantic memory as a variational latent space whose parameters are themselves learned through meta-learning. This double adaptation mechanism allows the system to rapidly reshape its inference process in response to novel information, while maintaining coherence with prior knowledge. Experiments indicate that such a mechanism mitigates catastrophic forgetting, supports transfer to related domains, and facilitates compositional generalization. Moreover, the probabilistic formulation provides a principled means to quantify uncertainty, which in turn guides memory updating and retrieval.

Beyond empirical performance, the framework offers theoretical insights into the relationship between episodic experience and semantic abstraction. By modeling memory as a probabilistic generative process, we connect cognitive theories of memory consolidation with modern meta-learning algorithms, suggesting a computational pathway through which systems can autonomously refine their representational priors. This connection opens opportunities for cross-disciplinary research, linking machine learning with cognitive neuroscience and psychology.

While promising, the present work also highlights limitations and open questions. Scalability to large-scale knowledge bases, the integration of multimodal sensory streams, and the development of more efficient inference algorithms remain important challenges. Furthermore, the balance between stability and plasticity in the learned semantic space warrants deeper investigation, particularly in settings with non-stationary task distributions.

In summary, learning to learn variational semantic memory provides a flexible, principled, and cognitively inspired approach to building adaptive knowledge systems. By combining meta-learning’s adaptability with the structured uncertainty of variational models, this work takes a step toward artificial agents capable of continual, semantic-rich learning, bridging the gap between rapid adaptation and long-term knowledge organization.

title: Effects of simulated cosmological magnetic fields on the galaxy population
abstract: We investigate the impact of primordial magnetic fields on galaxy formation using a suite of cosmological magnetohydrodynamical simulations. Initial comoving field strengths ranging from 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁸ G are implemented to explore their influence on the statistical properties of the galaxy population at redshifts z = 0–6. We find that stronger seed fields lead to enhanced magnetic amplification in dense environments, modifying gas cooling rates and star formation histories. For seed fields ≥ 10⁻⁹ G, the galaxy stellar mass function shows a suppression at low masses, driven by increased magnetic pressure and reduced baryonic accretion. Morphological analysis reveals a trend toward thicker, more dispersion-supported disks in high-field runs. The cosmic star formation rate density is systematically lower for larger seed fields, particularly at early epochs. Our results suggest that cosmological magnetic fields of sufficient strength can leave detectable imprints on galaxy demographics, providing a potential observational avenue for constraining primordial magnetogenesis scenarios.
introduction:
Magnetic fields are a ubiquitous yet often overlooked component of the Universe, permeating environments from the interstellar medium of galaxies to the vast intergalactic space. Observations have revealed their presence across a wide range of scales, with microgauss-level fields in galaxies and galaxy clusters, and weaker but persistent fields in cosmic voids. Despite their apparent importance, the origin and evolution of large-scale magnetic fields remain an open question in astrophysics. Proposed scenarios include primordial seeding during inflation or phase transitions in the early Universe, as well as astrophysical processes such as outflows from galaxies and active galactic nuclei. Regardless of their origin, magnetic fields are expected to influence the dynamics and thermodynamics of baryonic matter, potentially altering the formation and evolution of galaxies.  

While the amplification of magnetic fields by small-scale dynamo processes during galaxy formation is relatively well studied, the impact of cosmological-scale magnetic fields seeded at early times on the galaxy population is less well constrained. Such fields can modify the pressure balance of the intergalactic medium, alter the collapse of matter into halos, and change the efficiency of gas cooling and star formation. In addition, magnetic fields can affect the transport of cosmic rays, the structure of galactic outflows, and the morphology of the circumgalactic medium, thereby influencing feedback processes that regulate galaxy growth.  

Numerical simulations of structure formation that include magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) have become increasingly sophisticated, enabling the study of magnetic field evolution in a cosmological context. Modern simulations can follow the amplification of seed fields through gravitational collapse, turbulence, and shear flows, while simultaneously modelling the complex baryonic physics of star formation, stellar feedback, and black hole growth. However, the initial conditions for magnetic fields in these simulations remain uncertain, and different assumed seed strengths and configurations can lead to diverse outcomes for the simulated galaxy population.  

Previous studies have begun to explore the consequences of varying seed field strengths, finding that strong primordial fields can suppress the formation of low-mass galaxies by providing additional non-thermal pressure support, while weaker fields have more subtle effects. Yet, a systematic quantification of these effects across a broad range of magnetic field strengths and their implications for observable galaxy properties, such as stellar mass functions, star formation rates, and gas content, is still lacking. Moreover, the interplay between magnetic fields and feedback processes in cosmological simulations has yet to be fully disentangled.  

In this work, we investigate the influence of different initial cosmological magnetic field strengths on the galaxy population using high-resolution cosmological MHD simulations. By varying the seed field amplitude while keeping other physical prescriptions fixed, we aim to isolate the effect of magnetisation on galaxy formation and evolution. We analyse the resulting galaxy properties and compare them to observational constraints, with the goal of assessing the viability of different primordial magnetisation scenarios and their role in shaping the galaxy population across cosmic time.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the influence of large-scale magnetic fields of cosmological origin on the statistical properties of the galaxy population, using a suite of high-resolution magnetohydrodynamical simulations. By systematically varying the initial magnetic field strengths and configurations, we have assessed their role in shaping galaxy formation and evolution within a ΛCDM framework. Our results demonstrate that even relatively weak seed fields, when amplified by structure formation processes such as compression, turbulent dynamo action, and mergers, can reach dynamically relevant strengths in galactic environments. This amplification in turn modifies the thermodynamical and kinematical state of the interstellar medium, with downstream consequences for star formation rates, gas accretion, and feedback efficiency.

We find that strong primordial magnetic fields tend to suppress the baryonic collapse in low-mass haloes, leading to a measurable reduction in the abundance of dwarf galaxies at low redshift. This suppression arises primarily from magnetic pressure support and enhanced coupling between the gas and feedback-driven outflows, which together inhibit the retention of cold gas. In more massive haloes, the effects are subtler but still significant: magnetically-influenced gas dynamics alter the morphology of galactic discs, promote thicker and more turbulent gas layers, and can delay the peak of star formation activity. These modifications lead to a galaxy population that is, on average, less gas-rich and has lower specific star formation rates compared to simulations without primordial fields.

Our analysis of large-scale statistical measures, including the stellar mass function, star formation rate density history, and galaxy size–mass relation, indicates that the imprint of cosmological magnetic fields is most pronounced at high redshift and in low-mass systems, but leaves detectable signatures even at z = 0. The comparison between different seed field strengths suggests a non-linear response of the galaxy population, with a threshold regime above which magnetic effects become comparable to other baryonic feedback processes.

These findings have important implications for the interpretation of current and future observations. The suppression of low-mass galaxies by magnetic fields could contribute to reconciling discrepancies between observed and simulated faint-end slopes of the stellar mass function. Furthermore, the predicted morphological and kinematic changes in gas-rich galaxies may be testable with high-resolution surveys of the interstellar medium in both the local Universe and at cosmic noon. Our results also highlight the necessity of including magnetohydrodynamical effects in cosmological simulations aiming for precision galaxy formation modelling, especially when probing the early Universe.

In summary, cosmological magnetic fields, even when seeded at levels consistent with current observational constraints, can exert a measurable influence on galaxy evolution across a broad range of masses and epochs. Their role is complementary to, but distinct from, other feedback processes, and their impact grows with decreasing galaxy mass and increasing redshift. Future work combining improved simulations with targeted observational campaigns will be essential to refine these conclusions and to constrain the origin and evolution of cosmic magnetism.

title: Inclusive Search for Squarks and Gluinos Production at CDF
abstract: We present an inclusive search for the production of squarks and gluinos in proton–antiproton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 1.96 TeV, using data collected with the CDF detector at the Fermilab Tevatron. The analysis is based on an integrated luminosity of 2 fb⁻¹ and targets final states with multiple jets and significant missing transverse energy, consistent with supersymmetric particle production. No significant excess over the Standard Model background expectation is observed, and we set 95% confidence level limits on squark and gluino masses within the mSUGRA framework.
introduction:
Supersymmetry (SUSY) is one of the most extensively studied extensions of the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics, offering elegant solutions to several theoretical challenges. By postulating a symmetry between fermions and bosons, SUSY stabilizes the Higgs boson mass against large radiative corrections and provides a natural candidate for dark matter through the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP), typically assumed to be stable under R-parity conservation. In many SUSY scenarios, the strongly interacting superpartners—the squarks (supersymmetric partners of quarks) and gluinos (partners of gluons)—are expected to have masses in the range accessible to current hadron colliders. Their production cross sections at the Tevatron energies are predicted to be significant, making them promising targets for discovery.

The Collider Detector at Fermilab (CDF) has collected a substantial dataset from proton-antiproton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of \(\sqrt{s} = 1.96\) TeV during Run II of the Tevatron. This dataset enables comprehensive searches for new phenomena in final states characterized by high transverse energy (E\(_T\)) jets and large missing transverse energy (\(/\!\!\!E_T\)), the latter arising from undetected LSPs escaping the detector. An *inclusive* search strategy, which does not restrict the analysis to specific decay chains, enhances sensitivity to a broad class of SUSY models and reduces dependence on particular mass hierarchies.

This work presents an inclusive search for squark and gluino production using the CDF Run II data, emphasizing final states with multiple energetic jets and significant \(/\!\!\!E_T\). Standard Model backgrounds, primarily from QCD multijet production, \(W/Z\) + jets, and top-quark processes, are estimated using a combination of Monte Carlo simulation and data-driven techniques. The results are interpreted within the framework of minimal supergravity (mSUGRA) and in terms of simplified models, allowing direct constraints on squark and gluino masses. This analysis extends the sensitivity of previous searches and provides stringent limits on strongly-produced supersymmetric particles at the Tevatron.
conclusion: A search for squark and gluino production has been performed using data collected with the CDF detector, employing an inclusive analysis strategy sensitive to a broad range of final states. No statistically significant excess over the Standard Model background prediction was observed. The results have been interpreted within the framework of supersymmetric models, yielding improved limits on squark and gluino masses. These findings constrain the parameter space of minimal supergravity scenarios and related supersymmetric extensions. Continued analysis with larger datasets and refined techniques will further enhance sensitivity to possible new strongly interacting particles.

title: Chat-crowd: A Dialog-based Platform for Visual Layout Composition
abstract: We present Chat-crowd, a dialog-based platform for collaborative visual layout composition. The system enables two participants—a director and a designer—to iteratively create structured visual arrangements through natural language interaction. The director conveys spatial requirements and object properties, while the designer modifies the layout accordingly, enabling refinement through multi-turn conversation. Chat-crowd supports both synchronous and asynchronous modes, allowing flexible task completion and scalability for data collection. We demonstrate its utility for generating diverse, high-quality visual layouts paired with rich linguistic descriptions, facilitating research in grounded language understanding, human-computer interaction, and multimodal reasoning, while offering a framework for studying collaborative visual problem solving.
introduction: Designing effective visual layouts is a complex task that often requires iterative refinement, domain expertise, and seamless communication between stakeholders. Traditional layout composition tools primarily focus on direct manipulation interfaces, which may limit accessibility for users without design experience. Recent advances in natural language processing and multimodal interaction suggest the potential for dialog-based systems to facilitate collaborative design. In this work, we present **Chat-crowd**, a dialog-driven platform enabling users to create and refine visual layouts through natural language conversation. By leveraging structured dialog acts and contextual understanding, Chat-crowd supports incremental modifications, clarifications, and feedback loops between users and the system. The platform is designed to accommodate both individual and crowd-sourced participation, enabling diverse perspectives in the composition process. Through this approach, we aim to lower barriers to entry for design tasks while preserving creative flexibility, ultimately contributing to more inclusive and efficient visual communication workflows.
conclusion: This work introduced Chat-crowd, a dialog-based platform enabling collaborative visual layout composition through interactive communication. By integrating natural language exchange with spatial reasoning, the system supports efficient, iterative design. Experimental results demonstrate its potential for enhancing creativity and coordination. Future work will extend capabilities to richer modalities and explore broader applications in human-computer collaborative design tasks.

title: Fully Automatic Page Turning on Real Scores
abstract: This paper presents a fully automatic system for page turning on real musical scores, designed to assist live performers by eliminating manual intervention. The proposed method combines computer vision techniques with optical music recognition to track score progression in real time, even under varying lighting and performance conditions. A robust alignment algorithm synchronizes live audio features with the corresponding score positions, enabling timely and accurate digital page transitions. Experiments on diverse repertoires and performance settings demonstrate high reliability and responsiveness, with minimal latency. The system supports seamless integration into digital music stands, offering practical benefits for both rehearsal and concert performance.
introduction: Page turning is a practical challenge for musicians performing from printed scores, as it can interrupt musical flow and demand physical actions that detract from performance focus. While digital devices have partly addressed this issue through touch or pedal-based navigation, these solutions require additional equipment and may not align with traditional performance contexts or the tactile preferences of many musicians. Fully automatic page turning offers an appealing alternative by enabling seamless score progression without manual intervention, thus preserving concentration and interpretive continuity. Previous research has explored score following and optical music recognition, but most approaches rely on symbolic representations or preprocessed digital scores, limiting their applicability to real-world printed materials. This work investigates a system capable of tracking live performances directly on real, physical scores, using computer vision and audio alignment to determine the precise moment for page turning. The proposed method aims to operate robustly under varying lighting conditions and performer styles, advancing the integration of automation into conventional music performance practices.
conclusion:
The work presented has demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of a fully automatic page turning system operating directly on real, printed musical scores. By integrating robust score following with reliable page detection and turning mechanisms, the proposed approach addresses a long-standing challenge for live performance and practice, where uninterrupted musical flow is essential. Unlike previous methods that rely on preprocessed or synthetically generated score images, this system was designed and evaluated on real-world materials, encompassing variations in print quality, lighting, and performer interpretation.

Experimental results confirmed that the combination of optical recognition, temporal alignment, and anticipatory page turning yields high accuracy across diverse repertoires and performance conditions. The system’s capacity to adapt in real time to expressive tempo changes and interpretative nuances ensures that page turns occur seamlessly, without distracting the performer. Moreover, the reliance on standard video input and consumer-grade hardware underscores the practicality and accessibility of the approach for a wide range of users.

While the current implementation achieves reliable performance, several avenues for improvement remain. Enhancing the robustness of image processing under extreme lighting or occlusion, extending compatibility to handwritten annotations, and refining predictive models for complex page layouts could further broaden applicability. Integration with digital score libraries and networked performance environments also presents promising directions for future development.

In summary, this research advances the state of the art in automatic page turning by delivering a complete, real-time solution tested on authentic printed scores in realistic conditions. The system not only alleviates a practical difficulty for musicians but also illustrates how computer vision and music information retrieval can be combined to augment live performance. Continued refinement and adaptation of such technologies have the potential to enrich musical practice, enabling performers to focus entirely on artistic expression without the physical constraint of manual page turning.

title: Simple Parallel Algorithms for Single-Site Dynamics
abstract: We present efficient parallel algorithms for simulating single-site dynamics in discrete-state spin systems, with a focus on models governed by local update rules such as Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. Single-site update schemes are inherently sequential, as each site’s state depends on the current configuration of its neighborhood. This apparent sequentiality limits the scalability of traditional simulation methods on modern parallel architectures. We address this challenge by developing simple yet provably correct parallel algorithms that preserve the statistical properties of the original dynamics while exploiting spatial independence to enable concurrent updates. Our approach partitions the lattice into subsets of sites that can be updated simultaneously without introducing bias, using graph coloring techniques to identify non-interacting neighborhoods. We analyze the correctness of these algorithms by showing that the stationary distribution remains unchanged relative to the sequential process. Performance evaluations on both synthetic and physical spin configurations demonstrate substantial speedups on multi-core and distributed systems, with only minimal overhead from synchronization and partitioning. Furthermore, we discuss extensions to irregular graphs and higher-dimensional lattices, as well as the trade-offs between granularity of parallelism and update frequency. The simplicity of the proposed algorithms facilitates their integration into existing simulation frameworks, making them broadly applicable to problems in statistical physics, combinatorial optimization, and Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Our results indicate that significant parallel efficiency can be achieved without sacrificing accuracy, providing a practical pathway for large-scale simulations of systems driven by single-site dynamics.
introduction:
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are a cornerstone of modern computational statistical physics, Bayesian inference, and combinatorial sampling. Among these, single-site dynamics—where configurations are updated by modifying one site or variable at a time—are especially prevalent due to their simplicity, locality, and ease of implementation. Examples include the well-known Glauber dynamics for the Ising model, the heat-bath and Metropolis updates for spin systems, and Gibbs sampling in probabilistic graphical models. Despite their conceptual simplicity, single-site dynamics are inherently sequential: each update depends on the current configuration, making parallelization nontrivial. As large-scale simulations and data analysis tasks increasingly demand high-performance computing, there is a pressing need for principled approaches to parallelize such dynamics without compromising their convergence properties.

The sequential nature of single-site updates presents both algorithmic and theoretical challenges. Naïve parallel schemes, such as updating many sites at once without regard for dependency structure, can introduce bias, alter the stationary distribution, or even prevent convergence. For systems with strong correlations or complex interaction graphs, careless parallelization can lead to systematic errors that are difficult to detect. Existing approaches, such as checkerboard updates for lattice models or coloring-based updates for general graphs, exploit specific structural properties to enable safe concurrent updates. However, these methods can be limited in scope, require problem-specific adaptations, or incur substantial coordination overhead.

Recent advances in parallel computing architectures, including multi-core CPUs, GPUs, and distributed-memory systems, have renewed interest in developing general-purpose parallel algorithms for MCMC. In particular, there is growing attention on designing *simple* parallel algorithms—those that retain the conceptual clarity and ease of implementation of traditional single-site methods—while achieving meaningful speedups in practice. Simplicity is not merely an aesthetic preference: simple algorithms are easier to analyze, adapt, and deploy across a wide range of models, and they facilitate rigorous understanding of convergence and mixing times in the parallel setting.

In this work, we investigate parallelization strategies for single-site dynamics that are both theoretically sound and practically effective. Our focus is on algorithms that require minimal structural assumptions about the underlying system, yet can be analyzed within established frameworks for Markov chains. We explore update schedules, dependency management, and randomization techniques that enable multiple updates to proceed concurrently without distorting the stationary distribution. Our approach seeks to balance parallel efficiency with the preservation of the probabilistic guarantees that make MCMC a reliable computational tool.

We present a family of simple parallel algorithms for single-site dynamics, analyze their convergence behavior, and evaluate their empirical performance on representative models. By making minimal assumptions and emphasizing clarity, we aim to provide a set of methods that practitioners can readily adopt, adapt, and extend. This work contributes to bridging the gap between the sequential foundations of MCMC and the realities of modern high-performance computation, enabling broader and more efficient application of single-site dynamics in scientific and statistical computing.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the design, analysis, and implementation of simple parallel algorithms for single-site dynamics, with a particular focus on systems that evolve according to local update rules such as those found in statistical physics models, probabilistic cellular automata, and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Our primary objective was to demonstrate that efficient parallelization is achievable without sacrificing the correctness of the underlying stochastic process, and that the resulting algorithms remain straightforward to implement and reason about.

We began by outlining the fundamental constraints imposed by single-site dynamics, namely the sequential dependence of updates in traditional formulations and the potential correlations introduced when updates are performed in parallel. By leveraging techniques such as graph colorings, domain decomposition, and careful scheduling, we showed that it is possible to partition the computational domain into subsets of sites that can be updated simultaneously without introducing spurious dependencies. The resulting algorithms preserve the intended stationary distribution and convergence properties of the original sequential process.

Our study provided both theoretical and empirical evidence for the scalability and robustness of these approaches. Theoretically, we established bounds on the parallel execution time and quantified the degree of independence attainable in various graph topologies. We demonstrated that for sparse and locally connected interaction graphs, the chromatic number—and hence the number of colors needed for safe parallel updates—remains small, enabling a high degree of concurrency. For denser or more irregular graphs, we discussed adaptive strategies that dynamically adjust the update schedule to maintain correctness while exploiting available parallelism.

Empirically, we implemented the proposed algorithms on representative models, including the Ising model and related spin systems, and measured performance across a range of problem sizes and processor counts. Our results indicated substantial speedups over naive sequential implementations and compared favorably with more complex parallelization schemes. Importantly, the simplicity of our methods facilitated straightforward implementation on both shared-memory and distributed-memory architectures, making them accessible to practitioners without deep expertise in parallel algorithm design.

An additional contribution of our work lies in clarifying the trade-offs between algorithmic simplicity, parallel efficiency, and statistical fidelity. While more intricate asynchronous or speculative update schemes may offer higher raw concurrency, they often require elaborate rollback mechanisms or bias corrections. In contrast, our focus on structured synchronous updates ensured exact preservation of the target dynamics, with minimal overhead for coordination. This balance is particularly beneficial in scientific simulations where reproducibility and theoretical guarantees are paramount.

Looking ahead, several avenues remain open for further investigation. One promising direction is the integration of our simple parallel update schemes with advanced variance reduction techniques or multi-level Monte Carlo frameworks, potentially amplifying the gains in efficiency. Another is the exploration of hybrid schedules that combine deterministic color-based updates with limited, controlled asynchrony to better utilize heterogeneous computing resources. Finally, extending the analysis to dynamics on time-evolving graphs or systems with long-range interactions will broaden the applicability of these methods.

In summary, we have shown that simple, structured parallel algorithms can effectively accelerate single-site dynamics while retaining their essential statistical properties. By grounding the design in well-understood combinatorial structures and maintaining a focus on implementation clarity, we have produced a set of techniques that are both theoretically sound and practically useful. We hope these results will encourage wider adoption of parallel strategies in the simulation of complex systems and stimulate further research into balancing simplicity, correctness, and performance.

title: Single supply of electrical energy in the supply distribution model: using GAMS to model the effects of network parameters on the level of consumer demand
abstract: This study investigates the influence of network parameters on consumer demand within a single-supply electrical energy distribution framework. A mathematical model was developed using the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS) to simulate how variations in parameters such as line impedance, transformer capacity, and load distribution affect demand levels. The model incorporates technical constraints and consumer demand elasticity, enabling the analysis of system performance under diverse operating conditions. Simulation results reveal that small changes in network characteristics can significantly alter demand patterns, highlighting the interdependence between supply quality and consumption behavior. The findings provide insights for optimizing system design and operation, with implications for improving reliability, minimizing losses, and enhancing demand management strategies in single-supply networks. This work contributes to more efficient planning and operation of electrical distribution systems.
introduction:
The reliable supply of electrical energy is a cornerstone of modern socio-economic development, with demand patterns and supply capabilities intricately linked through the operational characteristics of the distribution network. In many contexts, particularly in urban and semi-urban areas, the distribution model is designed to ensure that a single, uninterrupted supply source can meet the aggregate demands of a diverse consumer base. However, variations in network parameters—such as line impedance, transformer capacity, distribution losses, and voltage stability—can significantly influence the actual level of demand that can be satisfied at the consumer end. Understanding these relationships is critical for both planning and operational decision-making, especially in environments where infrastructure constraints and growing demand exert pressure on the existing network.

The complexity of electrical energy supply systems lies not only in the technical design but also in their dynamic interaction with consumer behaviour. As demand fluctuates throughout the day and across seasons, the network’s ability to deliver energy efficiently is affected by physical limitations and operational strategies. Factors such as network topology, feeder length, and load distribution patterns can create bottlenecks or inefficiencies that impact the quality and quantity of power delivered. These effects, in turn, influence consumer demand levels, as voltage drops, outages, or reduced service reliability often lead to changes in consumption behaviour.

Mathematical modelling offers a powerful means to analyse and predict such interactions, enabling system planners to simulate various scenarios and evaluate potential interventions. The General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS) provides an effective platform for formulating and solving complex optimisation problems in power systems. Its flexibility allows for the integration of technical constraints, economic considerations, and policy objectives into a unified analytical framework. By applying GAMS to the study of a single supply source within a distribution network, it becomes possible to quantify how changes in network parameters affect the balance between supply capability and consumer demand.

This study aims to model the effects of key distribution network parameters on the level of consumer demand in a single-supply configuration, using GAMS as the primary analytical tool. The results are expected to provide insights that can guide network design, operational adjustments, and policy measures aimed at improving supply reliability and meeting growing energy needs.
conclusion: The study demonstrated that GAMS-based modelling effectively captures how network parameters influence consumer demand under a single supply of electrical energy. Results indicate that variations in supply capacity, transmission efficiency, and distribution losses significantly impact demand levels. These insights can guide optimization strategies for enhancing reliability, efficiency, and sustainability in electricity supply systems.

title: Constraining some Horndeski gravity theories
abstract: We investigate observational constraints on a subset of Horndeski gravity theories, focusing on models that deviate minimally from General Relativity while allowing for modified gravitational wave propagation and cosmological dynamics. Employing recent gravitational wave standard siren measurements, cosmic microwave background data, and large-scale structure observations, we place joint bounds on key Horndeski parameters governing the scalar–tensor coupling and the speed of tensor modes. Our analysis reveals that the parameter space is tightly restricted, with deviations from luminal gravitational wave speed strongly disfavored. These results significantly limit viable extensions within this sector of Horndeski gravity and inform future theoretical developments.
introduction:
The quest to understand the fundamental nature of gravity remains one of the most compelling challenges in modern physics. General Relativity (GR), formulated by Einstein over a century ago, has withstood a wide range of experimental and observational tests, from Solar System scales to the recent detection of gravitational waves. Nonetheless, there exist both theoretical and observational motivations for considering modifications or extensions to GR. On the theoretical side, GR is a classical theory that is expected to break down in the ultraviolet regime, and it is not straightforward to reconcile with the principles of quantum mechanics. Observationally, the phenomena of cosmic acceleration and the inferred presence of dark energy and dark matter pose questions that GR, when combined with the Standard Model of particle physics, addresses only by introducing new, unobserved forms of matter or energy. These considerations have inspired the exploration of alternative theories of gravity that may offer new insights into high-energy physics and cosmology.

Among the most general and well-studied classes of such alternatives are the Horndeski theories. Originally formulated in the 1970s by Gregory Horndeski, this family of scalar-tensor theories represents the most general four-dimensional theories with a single scalar field coupled to the metric that yield second-order equations of motion. The avoidance of higher-order derivatives ensures the absence of Ostrogradsky instabilities, making Horndeski gravity a theoretically consistent and rich framework for phenomenology. The theory encompasses a broad spectrum of models, including quintessence, k-essence, and covariant Galileons, as well as many others obtained as specific parameter choices within the general Horndeski Lagrangian.

In the past decade, Horndeski theories have attracted significant attention, in part because they naturally accommodate self-accelerating cosmological solutions without the need for a cosmological constant. This has made them an appealing candidate framework for explaining the observed late-time acceleration of the Universe. Moreover, they can give rise to distinctive signatures in cosmological observables, such as modifications to the growth rate of large-scale structure, alterations in gravitational lensing potentials, and possible deviations in the propagation speed of gravitational waves from the speed of light. These features have motivated both theoretical developments and increasingly precise observational tests.

A watershed moment in constraining modified gravity theories came with the observation of the binary neutron star merger GW170817 and its electromagnetic counterpart GRB 170817A. The near-simultaneous arrival of gravitational and gamma-ray signals imposed an extremely tight bound on the difference between the speed of gravitational waves and the speed of light, at the level of one part in \(10^{15}\). In the context of Horndeski gravity, this observation rules out large portions of the parameter space, particularly those in which the scalar field induces a deviation in the tensor propagation speed at late times. The surviving subclasses are therefore considerably more restricted, but still allow for nontrivial modifications to GR that can be probed with current and future observations.

Beyond gravitational wave constraints, a variety of cosmological and astrophysical data sets provide complementary ways to test viable Horndeski models. Measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies, baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), redshift-space distortions (RSD), weak gravitational lensing, and the abundance of galaxy clusters all offer sensitivity to the effects of modified gravity on the expansion history and growth of structure. On smaller scales, astrophysical systems such as stellar structure, black hole environments, and strong lensing time delays can, in principle, yield additional constraints, although screening mechanisms present in many Horndeski theories can suppress deviations from GR in high-density regions, complicating such analyses.

In this work, we focus on constraining a subset of Horndeski theories that remain consistent with the GW170817 bound on the speed of gravitational waves and do not introduce pathologies at the level of linear perturbations. We parameterize the modifications to the gravitational sector in terms of a reduced set of functions that capture the relevant departures from GR in the scalar and metric sectors. This approach allows us to bring together several contemporary data sets to obtain joint constraints on the allowed parameter space. Our analysis aims not only to place bounds on specific models but also to assess the constraining power of different observational probes and their complementarity.

The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, we review the essential aspects of Horndeski gravity and the reduced parameterization adopted in light of the gravitational wave speed constraint. Section 3 describes the cosmological and astrophysical data sets used in our analysis and the methodology for combining them. In Section 4, we present our results, including marginalized constraints on the model parameters and their physical interpretation. Section 5 discusses the implications of our findings for the viability of the considered theories and outlines the prospects for future observational tests. Finally, Section 6 summarizes our conclusions.

By systematically applying a broad range of observational constraints to a theoretically consistent subset of Horndeski gravity, we aim to clarify the extent to which such modifications to GR remain viable and to identify the most promising pathways for further narrowing down the space of alternative gravitational theories.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated observational constraints on a subset of Horndeski gravity models, focusing on those sectors that remain viable in light of recent theoretical consistency requirements and astrophysical measurements. By restricting attention to models that respect the speed of gravitational waves inferred from GW170817 and its electromagnetic counterpart, we have considered the reduced parameter space in which higher-order derivative interactions are limited and certain non-minimal couplings are suppressed. Within this framework, we have confronted the models with cosmological and astrophysical data, including background expansion histories, large-scale structure growth, and Solar System bounds.  

Our analysis has shown that the combination of gravitational wave constraints, cosmic microwave background measurements, baryon acoustic oscillations, and redshift-space distortion data significantly narrows the range of admissible model parameters. In particular, we find that the allowed deviations from general relativity in the effective gravitational coupling are typically small and, in several cases, confined to the percent level at cosmological scales. This result underscores the increasing precision with which modified gravity scenarios can be tested, even in the absence of direct laboratory-scale measurements.

Moreover, we have highlighted that the surviving Horndeski models tend to exhibit screening mechanisms that are efficient in high-density environments, thereby satisfying local gravity constraints. However, the same mechanisms also limit the magnitude of cosmological deviations, making them challenging to distinguish from a cosmological constant within the precision of current surveys. Future improvements in large-scale structure probes, weak lensing measurements, and multi-messenger astrophysics will be essential in breaking residual degeneracies between modified gravity and standard dark energy models.

An important outcome of this study is that the subset of Horndeski theories consistent with present data is markedly smaller than the space originally envisaged when these models were introduced. The theoretical requirement of avoiding ghost and gradient instabilities, combined with the empirical determination of the gravitational wave propagation speed, has eliminated entire classes of couplings, leaving only a restricted set of scalar-tensor interactions that remain phenomenologically interesting. This has practical implications for model building, as it directs attention to a narrower family of theories where meaningful departures from general relativity can still occur while respecting all known constraints.

In summary, our results demonstrate that current observational data already place tight bounds on many viable Horndeski models, pushing them toward regions of parameter space that closely mimic ΛCDM at both background and perturbative levels. While this convergence toward general relativity is significant, it does not entirely rule out modified gravity effects, and forthcoming high-precision cosmological and gravitational wave observations hold promise for either detecting subtle deviations or further constraining these theories.

title: Asymptotic Delsarte cliques in distance-regular graphs
abstract: We investigate the asymptotic structure of cliques in distance-regular graphs whose size approaches the Delsarte bound. The Delsarte bound, derived from eigenvalue techniques, gives an upper limit on the size of a clique in a distance-regular graph in terms of its valency and least eigenvalue. While equality yields the classical notion of a Delsarte clique, much less is known about cliques that nearly attain this bound. We introduce the concept of an *asymptotic Delsarte clique*, defined for sequences of distance-regular graphs in which the clique size is within a vanishing fraction of the bound. Using spectral and combinatorial arguments, we derive constraints on the intersection numbers and local structure imposed by the presence of such cliques. In particular, we show that asymptotic Delsarte cliques force strong regularity in the local graphs and imply restrictions on feasible parameter arrays. We also provide examples and non-existence results, illustrating the interplay between spectral extremality and geometric substructures in large distance-regular graphs.
introduction:
Distance-regular graphs form a central class of highly symmetric structures in algebraic combinatorics, characterized by the regularity of their intersection numbers. Their rich interplay between combinatorial, geometric, and spectral properties has led to deep connections with coding theory, finite geometry, and the theory of association schemes. Among the most studied substructures in this context are *Delsarte cliques*: maximal cliques whose size meets the Delsarte bound, which is derived from the Hoffman bound via the spectrum of the graph. These cliques play a key role in understanding extremal configurations, often arising in distance-regular graphs with strong regularity constraints.

The existence, size, and distribution of Delsarte cliques impose significant restrictions on the global structure of a distance-regular graph, and, conversely, the presence of many such cliques can indicate proximity to well-understood families such as Johnson graphs, Hamming graphs, or Grassmann graphs. While classification results are known in several finite cases, much less is understood about the asymptotic regime, where the diameter or valency tends to infinity. In particular, it is natural to ask whether large distance-regular graphs with parameters approaching certain limits must contain Delsarte cliques whose structure mirrors that of known examples.

In this paper, we investigate the asymptotic behaviour of Delsarte cliques in distance-regular graphs, focusing on parameter ranges where spectral bounds are nearly tight. We develop general inequalities relating graph parameters to clique sizes, and identify conditions under which asymptotically large Delsarte cliques must exist. Our results contribute to a broader understanding of the extremal geometry of distance-regular graphs and suggest new avenues for classification in high-valency and large-diameter limits.
conclusion: In this work we investigated the occurrence and structure of Delsarte cliques in large distance-regular graphs, focusing on their asymptotic properties. We established bounds on their size and frequency, and identified conditions under which such cliques approach extremal configurations. Our results suggest a deep interplay between spectral parameters and combinatorial substructures in the asymptotic regime. Future research may explore analogous phenomena in broader classes of association schemes, potentially revealing new links between algebraic and extremal graph theory.

title: On the Hausdorff Continuity of Free L\`evy Processes and Free Convolution Semigroups
abstract: We investigate the Hausdorff continuity of supports for free Lévy processes and free convolution semigroups. Employing analytic subordination and potential-theoretic techniques, we establish continuity results under natural moment and regularity conditions. Our findings extend previous work on free additive convolution, yielding new insights into the fine structure and stability of spectral distributions in free probability.
introduction: Free Lévy processes and free convolution semigroups play a central role in free probability, providing a framework for studying noncommutative analogues of classical stochastic processes. An important aspect of their analysis is the regularity of their spectral distributions with respect to time. In this work, we investigate the Hausdorff continuity of the supports of these distributions, establishing conditions under which the support varies continuously in the Hausdorff metric. Our results extend previous continuity theorems for classical Lévy processes to the free setting, offering new insights into the interplay between free convolution, measure regularity, and geometric properties of spectral supports.
conclusion: We have established Hausdorff continuity for the supports of measures arising from free Lévy processes and, more generally, from free convolution semigroups. Our analysis clarifies the interplay between analytic subordination, regularity of Cauchy transforms, and topological stability of supports. These results extend existing continuity theorems in free probability and suggest further investigations into finer geometric properties of evolving spectra in noncommutative stochastic processes.

title: The Automorphism Group of an Extremal [72,36,16] Code does not contain elements of order 6
abstract: We investigate the structure of the automorphism group of a putative extremal binary self-dual \([72,36,16]\) code. In particular, we focus on the possible existence of automorphisms of order \(6\). Using a detailed analysis of the fixed-point and cycle structure of such permutations, combined with constraints from the weight enumerator and known classification results for smaller codes, we show that no automorphism of order \(6\) can occur. This eliminates another case in the ongoing classification program and further restricts the possible automorphism groups of an extremal \([72,36,16]\) code, should such a code exist.
introduction:
Binary linear codes of length \(n\), dimension \(k\), and minimum distance \(d\) are denoted by \([n,k,d]\). Among these, *extremal* self-dual codes are those achieving the highest possible minimum distance allowed by the Mallows–Sloane bound. For a binary self-dual code of length \(n\), the bound states that  
\[
d \leq 4\lfloor n/24\rfloor + 4,
\]
with an additional \(+2\) in certain congruence cases. When equality holds, the code is called extremal. These codes occupy a central place in coding theory due to their optimal distance properties, rich algebraic structure, and connections to lattices, modular forms, and finite group theory.

The case \(n=72\) has attracted particular attention. For length \(72\), a binary self-dual code has dimension \(36\), and the bound gives \(d \leq 16\). A hypothetical extremal \([72,36,16]\) code would be a remarkable object, yet no example has been found despite extensive computational and theoretical efforts. Understanding the possible structure of such a code, if it exists, is therefore of significant interest. One important approach is to study its *automorphism group*: the group of coordinate permutations that leave the code invariant. Constraints on the automorphism group can substantially limit the search space and, in some cases, exclude certain configurations altogether.

Over the past decades, various authors have investigated the possible orders of elements in the automorphism group of an extremal \([72,36,16]\) code. It has been shown that automorphisms of prime orders such as \(5,7,11,13\) and certain composite orders cannot occur. The elimination of specific element orders relies on a combination of fixed-point analysis, orbit structure under the automorphism, and properties of the fixed subcode and its dual. In this paper, we extend these investigations to automorphisms of order \(6\).

Our main result establishes that the automorphism group of an extremal \([72,36,16]\) code cannot contain an element of order \(6\). The proof combines structural analysis of order \(6\) permutations, decomposition of the code into eigenspaces over extension fields, and bounds on the minimum distance of projected and shortened codes. This further narrows the possibilities for the automorphism group and contributes to the broader program of classifying, or ruling out, extremal codes of length \(72\).
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the possible structure of the automorphism group of a putative extremal binary self-dual \([72,36,16]\) code.
