By analyzing the fixed code under an automorphism of order 6 and studying its decomposition into eigenspaces over suitable extension fields, we have shown that such an element cannot occur. Our arguments relied on the interplay between the cycle structure of the automorphism, constraints on weight enumerators, and bounds arising from known classification results for shorter self-dual codes. This eliminates order 6 from the list of possible orders of automorphisms, further narrowing the search for the full automorphism group of such a code, should it exist. The methods developed here may be applicable to excluding other automorphism orders, thereby contributing to the broader program of determining the symmetry properties and possible existence of the extremal \([72,36,16]\) code.

title: Testing the minimum variance method for estimating large-scale velocity moments
abstract: We investigate the performance of the minimum variance (MV) method for estimating large-scale velocity moments from peculiar velocity surveys. Using mock catalogues constructed from N-body simulations, we test the ability of the MV formalism to recover bulk flow, shear, and octupole moments under realistic observational conditions, including sparse sampling, measurement errors, and survey geometry. The MV method aims to minimize aliasing from small-scale power while preserving sensitivity to large-scale flows, offering an improvement over traditional maximum likelihood estimators. We quantify biases, variances, and correlations of the recovered moments, and compare results to theoretical expectations from the ΛCDM model. Our tests show that MV estimators provide unbiased measurements with reduced sensitivity to nonlinear scales, even for surveys with limited depth and irregular sky coverage. These results support the MV method as a robust tool for extracting cosmological information from current and upcoming peculiar velocity data sets, enabling improved constraints on large-scale structure and growth rate.
introduction:
The study of large-scale motions of galaxies provides a direct probe of the growth of structure in the Universe and offers an important test of cosmological models. Peculiar velocities—deviations of galaxy motions from the pure Hubble flow—arise from gravitational interactions with surrounding matter and thus trace the underlying mass distribution. Measurements of these velocities can be used to estimate bulk flows, shear, and higher-order moments that quantify the coherent motion of matter on large scales. Such measurements complement constraints from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure surveys, providing an independent test of the standard cosmological paradigm and possible deviations from it.

Estimating large-scale velocity moments from observational data is challenging. Peculiar velocity surveys are subject to significant measurement errors, sparse and uneven sky coverage, and complex selection functions. Furthermore, peculiar velocities are generally inferred from distance indicators, which introduce substantial uncertainties, particularly for objects at large distances. These limitations can bias estimates of velocity moments if not properly accounted for. Traditional methods, such as simple averaging over survey volumes or maximum likelihood estimators, may yield results that are sensitive to small-scale velocity noise and survey geometry, thereby obscuring the large-scale signal of interest.

The minimum variance (MV) method has been proposed as a way to mitigate these issues. In this approach, velocity moments are estimated using optimally weighted combinations of individual galaxy velocity measurements, designed to minimise the variance of the estimator given the survey’s characteristics and observational uncertainties. By appropriately down-weighting contributions from poorly constrained or noisy regions of the survey and taking into account the expected statistical properties of the velocity field, the MV method aims to produce unbiased and low-variance estimates of bulk flow and other moments. This technique has the potential to extract the maximum amount of cosmological information from existing and forthcoming peculiar velocity data sets.

Despite its theoretical appeal, the performance of the MV method in realistic conditions requires careful testing. Surveys differ in depth, sky coverage, and measurement accuracy, and the method’s ability to recover the true large-scale moments under such circumstances must be quantified. Numerical simulations, incorporating realistic survey geometries and error models, provide a valuable means of assessing the accuracy, bias, and robustness of the MV estimators. Such tests are essential to establish confidence in the method before applying it to interpret observational data and draw cosmological conclusions.

In this work, we carry out a systematic evaluation of the minimum variance method for estimating large-scale velocity moments. Using mock catalogues derived from cosmological simulations, we investigate the method’s performance across a range of survey configurations and compare it to alternative estimation techniques. Our goal is to determine the reliability and limitations of the MV approach and to identify the conditions under which it can deliver accurate and precise constraints on the large-scale velocity field.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined the performance of the minimum variance (MV) method for estimating large-scale velocity moments from peculiar velocity surveys. By applying the MV formalism to both mock catalogues and observationally motivated datasets, we have assessed its ability to recover bulk flows, shear, and octupole moments under realistic survey geometries and noise conditions. Our analysis shows that the MV estimators are capable of producing unbiased measurements of the underlying flow field, provided that the survey sampling adequately reflects the scales of interest and that measurement errors are properly modelled. In particular, the method reduces the variance relative to conventional maximum likelihood estimators, especially for sparse or irregularly distributed data, while retaining robustness against small-scale velocity noise.

Tests on synthetic datasets demonstrate that the MV approach effectively suppresses contributions from poorly constrained modes, yielding improved accuracy for the largest-scale moments. Comparisons with input model flows confirm that systematic biases are minimal, even for surveys with complex selection functions. Application to realistic mock surveys further indicates that the MV method delivers consistent results across different realisations, suggesting that it can be reliably employed in the analysis of current and forthcoming peculiar velocity compilations.

These findings support the use of MV estimators as a powerful tool for probing the cosmic velocity field on large scales. Incorporating this methodology into analyses of next-generation surveys will enhance our ability to constrain models of structure formation and test cosmological parameters. Future work will extend the framework to include non-linear corrections and explore its performance in the presence of correlated measurement uncertainties.

title: Compressive Sensing Approaches for Autonomous Object Detection in Video Sequences
abstract: This paper investigates compressive sensing methodologies for enhancing autonomous object detection in video sequences, aiming to reduce computational load while maintaining detection accuracy. We propose a framework that integrates compressed domain feature extraction with sparse representation-based classification, allowing object detection directly from undersampled video measurements. By exploiting spatial-temporal correlations, the approach minimizes data acquisition requirements and accelerates processing, making it suitable for real-time applications in resource-constrained environments. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive performance compared to conventional full-frame detection pipelines, while significantly lowering bandwidth and storage demands. The results highlight the potential of compressive sensing as an enabling technology for efficient, scalable, and adaptive autonomous vision systems, particularly in scenarios where energy efficiency and rapid response are critical.
introduction:
The rapid growth of autonomous systems has intensified the demand for efficient and reliable object detection in video sequences. Applications ranging from self-driving vehicles and unmanned aerial systems to intelligent surveillance networks rely critically on the ability to extract salient visual information in real time, often under stringent computational and bandwidth constraints. Traditional video acquisition pipelines employ the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem, which dictates high sampling rates to accurately reconstruct signals. However, in many practical settings, these high rates result in excessive data volumes that strain storage, transmission, and processing resources. This challenge motivates the exploration of alternative acquisition and processing paradigms that can maintain or even enhance detection performance while reducing data requirements.

Compressive sensing (CS) has emerged as a promising framework for acquiring and reconstructing signals from far fewer samples than conventional methods, provided the signal exhibits sparsity in some domain. By exploiting sparsity priors and incoherent sampling strategies, CS enables the recovery of high-dimensional data from low-dimensional measurements. In the context of video analysis, this property implies the possibility of capturing essential scene information using significantly fewer measurements, thereby reducing resource consumption without sacrificing critical visual content.

Recent research has extended CS principles to dynamic scenes, where temporal redundancy can be leveraged alongside spatial sparsity to improve reconstruction fidelity. For object detection tasks, this means that moving or salient objects can be identified directly from compressive measurements or from partially reconstructed frames, avoiding the need for full-resolution video recovery. Such approaches can be particularly advantageous in scenarios with limited communication bandwidth, such as remote sensing or mobile robotics, where transmitting compressed measurements rather than full video streams can substantially decrease latency and energy usage.

Despite these advantages, integrating CS into autonomous object detection pipelines presents several challenges. Measurement noise, complex backgrounds, and varying illumination can degrade reconstruction quality and impede detection accuracy. Furthermore, real-time operation requires efficient algorithms capable of jointly handling measurement acquisition, reconstruction, and object detection within strict latency budgets. Advances in optimization techniques, deep learning-based reconstruction, and measurement matrix design have shown promise in addressing these issues, yet further research is needed to balance accuracy, speed, and resource constraints.

This paper investigates compressive sensing approaches tailored for autonomous object detection in video sequences, with an emphasis on exploiting spatial-temporal sparsity and task-driven measurement strategies. We examine methods for direct detection from compressive measurements, as well as hybrid schemes that combine partial reconstruction with modern detection architectures. The goal is to establish a framework that enables robust, real-time object detection in resource-limited environments, paving the way for more efficient and capable autonomous vision systems.
conclusion:
This work has explored the integration of compressive sensing techniques into autonomous object detection for video sequences, highlighting their potential to reduce computational loads while maintaining detection accuracy. By leveraging the sparsity inherent in visual data, the proposed approaches enable efficient acquisition and reconstruction of salient information, thereby minimizing the need for full-frame processing. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that these methods can achieve competitive detection performance compared to conventional algorithms, even under constrained bandwidth and storage conditions, which are common in embedded and mobile robotic platforms.

The study further examined the balance between compression ratios and detection fidelity, showing that appropriately tuned sensing matrices and reconstruction algorithms preserve critical object features while discarding redundant background information. This balance is crucial in real-time applications where latency and resource usage are critical constraints. Furthermore, the integration of compressive sensing with modern deep learning-based detectors suggests a promising pathway toward hybrid systems that exploit both the statistical structure of data and the representational power of neural networks.

While the results are encouraging, several challenges remain. The robustness of compressive sensing-based detection under varying illumination, occlusion, and motion blur conditions warrants deeper investigation. Additionally, adaptive sensing strategies that dynamically adjust measurement rates based on scene complexity could further enhance performance. Future research should also address the scalability of these approaches to multi-object tracking and scene understanding tasks in complex, cluttered environments.

In summary, compressive sensing offers a compelling framework for efficient, autonomous object detection in video sequences, especially in scenarios with stringent resource limitations. By continuing to refine sensing strategies, reconstruction methods, and their integration with advanced detection models, it is feasible to develop systems that are both computationally efficient and capable of high detection accuracy in demanding real-world conditions.

title: Demystifying the Performance of HPC Scientific Applications on NVM-based Memory Systems
abstract: The emergence of non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies offers new opportunities for high-performance computing (HPC) systems by combining the persistence of storage with the byte-addressability and low latency of main memory. However, the distinct performance characteristics of NVM, such as higher access latency and lower bandwidth compared to DRAM, introduce new challenges for scientific applications that demand extreme throughput and scalability. This work investigates the performance behavior of representative HPC scientific applications on NVM-based memory systems through detailed experimental evaluation and microbenchmark analysis. We characterize the sensitivity of key computational kernels to memory access patterns, bandwidth limitations, and latency overheads, and identify application classes that are more amenable to NVM integration. Our study reveals that while certain memory-bound applications experience notable slowdowns, others exhibit minimal degradation due to computation-to-memory access balance or inherent locality. Furthermore, we explore hybrid memory configurations that combine DRAM and NVM, demonstrating that intelligent data placement can mitigate performance penalties. These findings provide valuable insights for application developers, system architects, and runtime designers seeking to effectively leverage NVM in next-generation HPC platforms.
introduction:
The growing demand for computational power in scientific research has driven high-performance computing (HPC) systems to the forefront of discovery in domains such as climate modeling, molecular dynamics, astrophysics, and large-scale data analytics. These applications are characterized by their massive data requirements, high degrees of parallelism, and stringent performance constraints. Traditionally, HPC architectures have relied on a hierarchical memory system composed of fast but volatile dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) at the node level, coupled with slower but persistent storage devices such as hard disk drives (HDDs) or solid-state drives (SSDs). While DRAM offers low latency and high bandwidth, its limited capacity and volatility impose significant bottlenecks for data-intensive scientific workloads. As datasets continue to grow in size and complexity, the limitations of conventional memory and storage hierarchies become increasingly pronounced, motivating the exploration of alternative memory technologies.

Non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies, such as Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory, Phase Change Memory (PCM), and Resistive RAM (ReRAM), have emerged as promising candidates to augment or partially replace DRAM in HPC systems. NVM devices combine attributes traditionally associated with both memory and storage: they offer persistence and higher capacity than DRAM, yet support byte-addressability and latencies significantly lower than NAND flash storage. These properties make them attractive for bridging the performance gap between volatile main memory and persistent storage, potentially enabling new memory hierarchy designs that improve application performance, system efficiency, and resilience. In particular, NVM can be deployed in different modes—such as memory mode, where it extends main memory capacity, or app-direct mode, where software manages its persistent space—each with distinct implications for performance and programmability.

Despite their potential, the integration of NVM into HPC environments is accompanied by challenges that must be carefully addressed. NVM technologies typically exhibit higher access latencies and lower bandwidth than DRAM, and their asymmetric read/write performance characteristics can impact application behavior in subtle ways. Moreover, the endurance limits of certain NVM technologies necessitate careful consideration of write intensity. The interplay between scientific application memory access patterns and the architectural characteristics of NVM-based systems is complex, and understanding it requires detailed empirical evaluation. Furthermore, the suitability of NVM for diverse HPC workloads may vary depending on factors such as computational intensity, data locality, communication patterns, and input/output (I/O) demands.

Recent studies have begun to investigate the performance implications of NVM in HPC contexts, but there remains a lack of comprehensive, application-driven analysis that bridges the gap between device-level benchmarks and end-to-end scientific workloads. Many existing evaluations rely on synthetic benchmarks or microarchitectural simulations, which, while useful for isolating specific behaviors, may not capture the full range of interactions that occur in production-scale applications. For HPC practitioners and system architects, actionable insights require analyses grounded in realistic execution environments, considering both hardware and software factors, including operating system support, runtime systems, and parallel programming models.

This work aims to demystify the performance of HPC scientific applications on NVM-based memory systems by conducting a systematic, empirical study across a representative set of workloads. We focus on identifying the key factors that influence performance when NVM is used in different configurations, quantifying the trade-offs in comparison to DRAM-only systems, and exploring the impact on application scalability and efficiency. By correlating observed performance trends with application characteristics and memory access patterns, we seek to provide guidance for both application developers and system designers on how to effectively exploit NVM in HPC environments. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how emerging NVM technologies can be integrated into next-generation HPC architectures to meet the growing demands of scientific computing.
conclusion: This study has examined the performance characteristics of HPC scientific applications on NVM-based memory systems, providing insights into the opportunities and challenges posed by emerging non-volatile technologies. Through detailed benchmarking and analysis, we have shown that while NVM offers clear benefits in terms of persistence, scalability, and potential energy savings, its distinct latency and bandwidth profiles can significantly influence application behavior. Our results indicate that memory-bound workloads are particularly sensitive to these differences, and that careful consideration of access patterns and data placement strategies is critical for achieving performance parity with DRAM-based systems. Moreover, we have demonstrated that hybrid memory configurations, when managed effectively, can mitigate some of the inherent performance penalties of NVM while leveraging its capacity advantages. These findings highlight the need for both application-level optimizations and system-level innovations, such as intelligent runtime management and compiler-guided data allocation, to fully exploit NVM’s potential in HPC contexts. Future work should explore adaptive memory hierarchies, deeper co-design between hardware and software, and broader application domains to generalize these observations. Ultimately, our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how NVM can be integrated into next-generation HPC architectures to support demanding scientific workloads efficiently.

title: Mandelstam-Leibbrandt prescription
abstract: We investigate the Mandelstam–Leibbrandt prescription, a causal method for regulating light-cone gauge singularities in gauge field theory. By systematically analyzing its derivation and implementation, we clarify its role in preserving gauge invariance and Lorentz consistency. Comparisons with alternative prescriptions highlight its advantages in avoiding spurious divergences and ensuring well-defined propagators. Applications to perturbative calculations in quantum chromodynamics demonstrate its efficacy, confirming its relevance for both analytical computations and numerical simulations in high-energy theoretical physics contexts.
introduction:
The Mandelstam–Leibbrandt (ML) prescription plays a central role in the consistent quantization of gauge theories formulated in light-cone gauge. In this gauge choice, the elimination of redundant degrees of freedom simplifies the physical interpretation of the theory, but it also introduces spurious singularities in the gauge field propagator, typically of the form \(1/(n \cdot k)\), where \(n^\mu\) is a light-like vector. These singularities complicate perturbative calculations and demand a well-defined prescription to ensure both mathematical consistency and the preservation of fundamental symmetries, such as causality and Lorentz invariance. Early approaches, including the principal value prescription, were found to violate these requirements in certain contexts, leading to ambiguities and inconsistencies in loop integrals. 

The ML prescription, independently proposed by Mandelstam and Leibbrandt, offers a causal and symmetry-preserving method to handle these poles by introducing an auxiliary light-like vector \(\tilde{n}^\mu\) and defining the singular factor in a way that ensures correct analytic continuation. This approach has been widely adopted in perturbative quantum field theory, particularly in QCD calculations in light-cone gauge, and has proven effective in maintaining gauge invariance at the quantum level. In this work, we revisit the derivation, properties, and applications of the Mandelstam–Leibbrandt prescription, emphasizing its role in regularizing light-cone singularities and exploring its implications for modern gauge theory computations.
conclusion: The Mandelstam–Leibbrandt prescription provides a consistent and well-defined method for handling the singularities arising in light-cone gauge propagators, ensuring the preservation of causality and gauge invariance in perturbative calculations. By offering a precise treatment of the ill-defined poles, it avoids ambiguities inherent in other prescriptions and facilitates the application of dimensional regularization. Its compatibility with fundamental symmetries makes it a crucial tool in both gauge theory computations and the study of high-energy scattering processes. The analysis presented here reaffirms its mathematical rigor and practical utility, highlighting its role in enabling systematic and unambiguous results. Future work may explore its extensions to non-perturbative frameworks and its interplay with modern amplitude-based approaches.

title: On the Independent Crossing Approximation in Three Flavor Neutrino Oscillations
abstract: We investigate the validity of the Independent Crossing Approximation (ICA) in the context of three-flavor neutrino oscillations in matter with varying density profiles. The ICA assumes that multiple non-adiabatic level crossings can be treated as independent two-level transitions, enabling a factorized description of flavor evolution. We analyze its applicability for realistic supernova and solar density profiles by comparing exact numerical solutions of the three-flavor evolution equations with ICA-based predictions. Particular attention is given to regimes where resonances overlap or are closely spaced, potentially inducing interference effects beyond ICA. Our results quantify deviations in survival probabilities and identify parameter regions where ICA remains accurate. These findings provide guidance for modeling neutrino flavor transformation in astrophysical environments with complex matter effects.
introduction:
Neutrino oscillations provide a sensitive probe of fundamental particle properties and the structure of matter through which they propagate. In the framework of three active flavors, oscillations arise from the misalignment between flavor and mass eigenstates, characterized by the Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata (PMNS) mixing matrix and the squared mass differences. When neutrinos traverse a medium, the forward scattering off background particles modifies the effective Hamiltonian via the Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein (MSW) effect, leading, in certain regimes, to resonant flavor conversion. In realistic astrophysical and cosmological environments, such as the solar interior, core-collapse supernovae, and the early universe, the matter density can vary significantly along the neutrino path, making the understanding of flavor evolution in non-uniform media a central problem in neutrino physics.

In the two-flavor case, matter effects can be described analytically in several limiting regimes. The Landau–Zener formalism offers a powerful approximation for non-adiabatic transitions at level crossings, allowing a simple expression for the transition probability in terms of an exponential of an adiabaticity parameter. For three flavors, however, the structure of the Hamiltonian is more complex: there are, in general, two distinct MSW resonances associated with the two independent mass-squared differences. The simultaneous presence of these resonances, and the possible interference between transitions occurring at different density scales, makes an exact analytic treatment challenging. Numerical integration of the Schrödinger equation in matter is always possible, but often obscures the simple physical interpretation afforded by analytical methods.

The independent crossing approximation (ICA) is a widely used scheme to simplify the analysis of three-flavor neutrino propagation in matter. The central assumption of the ICA is that the two resonances can be treated as independent two-level systems, each described by its own Landau–Zener probability, and that the net transition probability can be obtained by combining the two in a factorized form. This approximation is expected to hold when the resonances are well separated in space (or, equivalently, in matter density), so that the non-adiabatic transitions occur in distinct regions and the evolution between them is adiabatic. Under such circumstances, interference between the two transitions is negligible, and the flavor evolution can be understood as a sequence of independent level crossings.

The appeal of the ICA lies in its simplicity: it reduces the full three-level problem to two decoupled two-level problems, making it possible to obtain semi-analytic expressions for flavor transition probabilities in varying matter profiles. This has proven especially useful in interpreting solar neutrino data, where the hierarchy of mass-squared differences and the smooth density profile of the Sun ensure that the solar (1–2) and atmospheric (1–3) resonances are well separated. The approximation has also been employed in studies of supernova neutrinos, where the density profile features both large-scale gradients and sharp discontinuities due to shock waves. In such environments, the ICA can provide a first estimate of survival probabilities and flavor conversion patterns without resorting to full numerical simulations.

Nevertheless, the validity of the ICA is not guaranteed in all situations. When the two resonances are close in density, or when the adiabaticity parameters are such that non-adiabatic transitions have significant overlap, interference effects can become important. These effects manifest as deviations from the factorized probability formulas, potentially leading to observable consequences in the energy spectra and flavor composition of neutrinos arriving at a detector. Particularly in supernovae, where turbulent density fluctuations and collective neutrino–neutrino interactions can further modify the effective potential, the assumptions underlying the ICA may break down. Assessing the range of validity of this approximation, and quantifying the corrections when it fails, is essential for reliable modeling of neutrino signals.

Previous works have examined the ICA in various contexts, employing both analytic estimates and numerical simulations. Some studies have derived criteria based on the separation of resonance densities relative to the width of the non-adiabatic regions, while others have explored the role of CP-violating phases and non-standard neutrino interactions in modifying the crossing probabilities. There has also been interest in generalizing the ICA to cases with more than three flavors, or to scenarios with sterile neutrinos, where additional resonances may occur. Despite these efforts, a systematic and broadly applicable understanding of the ICA’s limitations remains incomplete, particularly for arbitrary matter profiles and for the full range of mixing parameters allowed by current oscillation data.

In this work, we revisit the independent crossing approximation in the context of three-flavor neutrino oscillations in matter. We aim to clarify the physical assumptions underlying the approximation, to derive precise conditions for its validity, and to identify regimes in which it fails. By combining analytic methods with controlled numerical studies, we will explore how the separation of resonances, the adiabaticity parameters, and the interference terms depend on the mixing angles, mass hierarchy, and matter density profile. Our goal is to provide a unified framework for assessing the ICA in both terrestrial and astrophysical settings, thereby improving the interpretation of current and future neutrino experiments.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined the validity and implications of the Independent Crossing Approximation (ICA) in the context of three–flavor neutrino oscillations in matter. By formulating the problem in terms of the full three–level Schrödinger equation and comparing with the product of two–level Landau–Zener transition probabilities, we have quantified the conditions under which the ICA provides an accurate description of flavor evolution. Our analysis has emphasized the interplay between the two nonadiabatic level crossings, associated with the solar and atmospheric mass-squared differences, and the role of the matter density profile in regulating their separation and interference.

We have shown that the ICA is well justified when the resonances are sufficiently separated in coordinate or energy space so that the evolution through each crossing can be treated independently. In this regime, the total transition probability can be approximated by the sequential application of two–level formulas, with corrections that are parametrically small. This separation is enhanced for monotonic density profiles and for energies away from the region where the effective resonances overlap. Conversely, in situations where the resonance widths become comparable to their separation — for example in dense astrophysical environments such as supernova cores or in certain regions of the early Universe — interference effects between the crossings can become significant, leading to deviations from the ICA description.

Numerical simulations of the full three–flavor evolution, incorporating realistic density profiles, have confirmed these expectations. The ICA reproduces the exact results to within a few percent in the separated-resonance regime, but can fail qualitatively when the adiabaticity parameters at the two crossings are both small and the level ordering allows for coherent coupling between all three states. In such cases, the use of exact numerical integration or improved analytic schemes that account for interference terms becomes necessary.

Our findings clarify the domain of applicability of the ICA and provide a framework for its systematic assessment in phenomenological studies. This is of practical importance for modeling neutrino flavor conversion in astrophysical settings, where computational simplicity is often desired but accuracy remains essential for interpreting observational signatures. Future work could extend this analysis to include additional effects such as neutrino–neutrino forward scattering, turbulence in the matter profile, or nonstandard interactions, all of which can modify the structure of the level crossings and hence the validity of the ICA.

Overall, the Independent Crossing Approximation remains a valuable and efficient tool in three–flavor neutrino physics when applied within its regime of validity. Recognizing its limitations and the conditions under which it breaks down ensures that it can be used with confidence in both theoretical and observational studies of neutrino flavor transformation.

title: Particle dynamics near extreme Kerr throat and supersymmetry
abstract: We examine particle dynamics in the near-horizon geometry of an extreme Kerr black hole, focusing on integrability, hidden symmetries, and supersymmetric extensions. Employing the near-horizon extreme Kerr metric, we construct conserved quantities and analyze classical trajectories. A supersymmetric particle model is formulated, revealing enhanced symmetry structures. Our results clarify the interplay between black hole geometry, particle motion, and supersymmetry, offering insights into extremal rotating black hole microphysics.
introduction:
The study of particle dynamics in the vicinity of black holes offers a fertile testing ground for both classical and quantum aspects of gravity. In particular, the near-horizon geometry of extremal Kerr black holes – rapidly rotating solutions of the vacuum Einstein equations saturating the Kerr bound – has attracted sustained attention due to its enhanced symmetry structure and its role in holographic correspondences. The so-called near-horizon extremal Kerr (NHEK) geometry exhibits an \(SL(2,\mathbb{R}) \times U(1)\) isometry group, reflecting an emergent conformal symmetry that has been exploited in the Kerr/CFT correspondence. The associated "extreme Kerr throat" provides an analytically tractable background in which to investigate the behavior of test particles, both massive and massless, as well as fields of various spins.

From a classical mechanics standpoint, the dynamics of geodesics in the Kerr spacetime is integrable, thanks to the presence of the Carter constant in addition to the conserved energy and angular momenta. In the extremal limit, the near-horizon scaling isolates a region with its own causal and geometrical properties, leading to novel dynamical regimes. Studies of trajectories in the extreme Kerr throat have revealed particular features such as critical orbits, enhanced stability properties for certain bound states, and universal scaling behaviors near the horizon. These phenomena are not only of theoretical interest but also bear relevance for astrophysical processes, such as the motion of matter in the innermost regions of accretion disks and the generation of high-energy emissions.

Beyond the purely gravitational setting, the NHEK geometry serves as a natural stage for exploring the interplay between black hole physics and supersymmetry. While the extremal Kerr solution itself is not supersymmetric in standard four-dimensional supergravity, its near-horizon geometry shares structural similarities with backgrounds that do admit supersymmetric extensions. Supersymmetric mechanics – the supersymmetric generalization of classical particle dynamics – provides a framework in which bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom are treated on equal footing, and conserved supercharges arise alongside the usual constants of motion. Constructing supersymmetric models for particle motion in curved spacetimes can illuminate hidden symmetry structures, clarify the role of spin degrees of freedom, and offer insights into possible embeddings of the geometry into higher-dimensional or string-theoretic contexts.

The motivation for examining supersymmetric particle dynamics in the extreme Kerr throat is twofold. First, supersymmetric extensions often reveal integrability properties and algebraic structures that are obscured in the purely bosonic theory, potentially leading to exact quantization in certain sectors. Second, such models can serve as toy systems for understanding how near-horizon geometries might arise in supersymmetric black hole microstate counting, even when the parent spacetime is not itself supersymmetric. In this regard, the NHEK background may act as a bridge between the well-studied BPS black hole throats, such as \(AdS_2 \times S^2\), and more general rotating geometries.

In this work, we undertake a detailed analysis of test particle motion in the near-horizon region of an extremal Kerr black hole, with a particular focus on constructing and examining its \(\mathcal{N}=2\) supersymmetric extension. We begin by revisiting the classical bosonic dynamics, identifying the conserved quantities and effective potentials in the throat geometry. We then formulate the corresponding supersymmetric mechanics model, elucidating the structure of the supercharges and their algebra. Our goal is to clarify how the enhanced symmetries of the extreme Kerr throat manifest in the supersymmetric setting, and to explore the implications for integrability and possible quantization. By doing so, we aim to contribute to the broader understanding of particle dynamics in highly symmetric near-horizon backgrounds, and to shed light on the connections between extreme rotation, conformal symmetry, and supersymmetry.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the dynamics of test particles in the near-horizon geometry of an extreme Kerr black hole, with particular emphasis on the interplay between the enhanced symmetry structure of the so-called extreme Kerr throat and possible supersymmetric extensions of the particle model. By exploiting the isometry group \( SL(2,\mathbb{R}) \times U(1) \) inherent to the near-horizon region, we have constructed the conserved quantities governing geodesic motion and clarified the role of hidden symmetries in ensuring complete integrability. The analysis has shown that the separation of variables in the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism persists in the throat limit, and that the surviving Carter-like constant is directly related to the residual Killing tensor structure.

We have further examined the motion of both massive and massless particles, identifying the characteristic trajectories dictated by the warped \(AdS_2 \times S^2\) geometry and the frame-dragging effects that remain significant even in the near-horizon limit. For massive particles, the energy and angular momentum constraints were shown to admit stable bound orbits within the throat under specific parameter ranges, while null geodesics exhibit critical behavior near the photon orbit. These results underline the distinctive nature of the extreme Kerr throat as a dynamical arena, in which the enhanced symmetry not only simplifies the equations of motion but also supports qualitative features absent in generic Kerr geometries.

On the supersymmetric side, we have argued that the near-horizon limit provides a natural setting for \(\mathcal{N}=2\) supersymmetric mechanical models. By coupling the bosonic particle dynamics to worldline fermions and exploiting the \(SL(2,\mathbb{R})\) conformal structure, we constructed the supersymmetry generators and verified the closure of the corresponding superalgebra, up to terms vanishing on-shell. This suggests that the extreme Kerr throat can be interpreted as a supersymmetric background for certain point-particle probes, a fact that may have implications for the embedding of such systems into supergravity or string theory frameworks.

Overall, our findings highlight the rich structure of particle dynamics in the vicinity of extremal rotating horizons. The combination of enhanced spacetime symmetries and the possibility of consistent supersymmetric extensions opens new avenues for exploring holographic correspondences, stability analyses, and quantum aspects of near-horizon geometries. Future work may build on these results by incorporating interactions, backreaction effects, and higher-spin probes, thereby deepening the connection between extremal black hole physics, integrable systems, and supersymmetric theories.

title: Content Based Image Retrieval System using Feature Classification with Modified KNN Algorithm
abstract: Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) systems aim to retrieve relevant images from large databases based on visual content rather than textual annotations. This paper presents a CBIR framework that integrates feature classification with a modified k-nearest neighbor (KNN) algorithm to improve retrieval accuracy and efficiency. The proposed system extracts low-level image features, including color, texture, and shape descriptors, which are then normalized and combined to form robust feature vectors. A feature classification stage is employed to group images into relevant categories, reducing the search space during retrieval. The modified KNN algorithm incorporates adaptive distance weighting and dynamic neighborhood selection to enhance discrimination between similar and dissimilar images while mitigating the effects of noisy or redundant features. Experimental evaluations on benchmark image datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves higher precision and recall compared to conventional CBIR methods using standard KNN. The results indicate that the integration of feature classification with the modified KNN significantly improves retrieval performance, making the system suitable for large-scale image databases in diverse application domains such as medical imaging, digital libraries, and surveillance.
introduction:
Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) has emerged as a critical area of research in the field of computer vision and multimedia information retrieval, driven by the exponential growth of digital image repositories across diverse domains such as medical imaging, remote sensing, digital libraries, and social media platforms. Unlike traditional text-based image retrieval systems that rely on manually annotated metadata, CBIR systems utilize the actual visual content of images—such as color, texture, and shape—to identify and retrieve similar images from large databases. This approach offers improved scalability, reduces the dependency on manual labeling, and enables more accurate retrieval, particularly in scenarios where semantic content is difficult to describe with keywords.

A central challenge in CBIR lies in the effective extraction, representation, and classification of image features to ensure high retrieval accuracy and efficiency. Feature classification techniques play a pivotal role in bridging the gap between low-level image descriptors and high-level semantic understanding. Among various classification algorithms, the k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) method has been widely adopted due to its simplicity, robustness, and effectiveness in handling multi-class problems. However, the traditional KNN algorithm suffers from limitations such as sensitivity to noisy data, high computational cost for large datasets, and equal weighting of neighbors, which may not optimally reflect the underlying feature distribution.

To address these challenges, this research proposes a Content-Based Image Retrieval system that incorporates feature classification with a modified KNN algorithm. The proposed modification aims to enhance retrieval performance by introducing adaptive neighbor weighting and optimized distance metrics, thereby improving classification accuracy and reducing computational overhead. By integrating advanced feature extraction techniques with this enhanced classification strategy, the system is designed to deliver more precise retrieval results while maintaining scalability for large image collections.

The remainder of this paper details the methodology of the proposed system, evaluates its performance against existing approaches, and discusses its potential applications in real-world retrieval tasks where accuracy and efficiency are paramount.
conclusion: The proposed Content Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) system employing feature classification with a modified K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) algorithm has demonstrated improved retrieval accuracy and efficiency compared to conventional approaches. By integrating optimized feature extraction and classification techniques, the system effectively reduces semantic gaps and enhances the relevance of retrieved images. The modification to the KNN algorithm addresses limitations related to distance weighting and noisy data, resulting in more robust performance across diverse image datasets. Experimental results indicate notable gains in precision and recall, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed method. This work contributes to advancing CBIR research by offering a scalable and adaptable retrieval framework. Future investigations may explore deep learning-based feature integration and real-time implementation to further improve system responsiveness and applicability in large-scale multimedia databases.

title: Reionization process dependence of the ratio of CMB polarization power spectra at low-$\ell$
abstract: We investigate the sensitivity of the ratio of large–scale E–mode and B–mode polarization power spectra of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) to variations in the reionization history. Using a set of parametrized ionization fraction models spanning a range of onset redshifts, durations, and ionization morphologies, we compute the low–$\ell$ polarization spectra with a Boltzmann code. We find that the ratio of E– to B–mode power at $\ell \lesssim 10$ is influenced not only by the total Thomson optical depth, but also by the detailed temporal profile of reionization. In particular, extended or multi–step reionization scenarios can modify this ratio by several percent relative to instantaneous models, with implications for the interpretation of large–scale polarization measurements from current and upcoming CMB experiments. Our results highlight the potential of low–$\ell$ polarization ratios as complementary probes of the reionization process, offering a model–dependent but potentially robust diagnostic alongside absolute power spectrum measurements.
introduction: The reionization history of the Universe leaves a distinct imprint on the large–scale polarization anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). In particular, the low–$\ell$ $E$–mode power spectrum is sensitive to both the timing and duration of reionization. Ratios of polarization spectra at different multipoles provide a complementary probe, reducing certain cosmological parameter degeneracies. Understanding the dependence of these ratios on the reionization process enables more precise constraints from current and upcoming CMB observations. Here we investigate how variations in reionization models affect the low–$\ell$ polarization power spectrum ratios.
conclusion: We have examined how variations in the reionization history affect the ratio of large-scale CMB polarization power spectra. Our analysis shows that the low-$\ell$ ratio is sensitive to both the timing and duration of reionization, offering a complementary probe to optical depth measurements. These results highlight the potential of polarization ratios as diagnostics for distinguishing among reionization scenarios in future CMB observations.

title: First case of strong gravitational lensing by a QSO : SDSS J0013+1523 at z = 0.120
abstract: We report the discovery and analysis of the first confirmed case of strong gravitational lensing produced by a quasi-stellar object (QSO), SDSS J0013+1523, at a redshift of \( z = 0.120 \). Using spectroscopic and imaging data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) complemented by high-resolution follow-up observations, we identify multiple images of a background galaxy lensed by the foreground QSO host galaxy. The background source is spectroscopically confirmed to lie at \( z \approx 0.640 \), with emission lines clearly separated from the QSO’s own spectral features. Deep imaging reveals two distinct lensed images situated symmetrically about the QSO, with angular separations consistent with strong lensing by a massive galaxy-scale halo. Lens modeling, assuming a singular isothermal ellipsoid (SIE) profile, yields an Einstein radius of \( \theta_E \approx 0.72'' \), corresponding to a projected mass within the Einstein radius of \( M_E \approx 1.6 \times 10^{11} M_\odot \). The inferred dynamical mass is consistent with expectations for a massive early-type galaxy hosting an active nucleus. The presence of luminous QSO emission poses unique challenges for lens detection, as it can obscure the lensed features; careful spectral decomposition and subtraction were required to isolate the background galaxy’s signal. This discovery demonstrates that active galactic nuclei (AGN) can serve as effective gravitational lenses, offering rare opportunities to probe both the mass distribution of QSO host galaxies and the interplay between AGN activity and galaxy structure. The system SDSS J0013+1523 thus represents a new class of gravitational lensing configuration and provides a benchmark for future systematic searches for QSO-lens systems in large spectroscopic and imaging surveys. Our findings open a novel window on the co-evolution of supermassive black holes and their galactic environments, and highlight the importance of combining spectroscopic identification with high-resolution imaging for uncovering such rare astrophysical laboratories.
introduction:
Quasi-stellar objects (QSOs), or quasars, are among the most luminous and distant active galactic nuclei (AGN) known, powered by the accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes. Their extreme luminosities make them detectable across vast cosmological distances, allowing them to serve as powerful probes of the high-redshift Universe. In most cases, QSOs are studied either as background sources whose light may be gravitationally lensed by intervening mass concentrations, or as intrinsically bright beacons for studying the intergalactic medium. However, QSOs themselves can also act as foreground gravitational lenses if they reside at sufficiently low redshift and possess a massive host galaxy. Such configurations are expected to be rare due to the relatively small cross-section for strong lensing and the scarcity of low-redshift QSOs with favourable alignments to background galaxies.

Gravitational lensing by galaxies is now a well-established phenomenon, with hundreds of strong lens systems identified in large-scale surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the Cosmic Lens All-Sky Survey (CLASS), and others. These discoveries have been instrumental in constraining the mass profiles of galaxies, studying the interplay between luminous and dark matter, and measuring cosmological parameters. In most strong lens systems, the deflector is a quiescent early-type galaxy or, less commonly, a late-type galaxy. Lensing by galaxies hosting bright AGN presents additional observational challenges: the bright point-source emission from the AGN can outshine the lensed background features, complicating their detection and confirmation. Nevertheless, such systems are of particular interest because they provide the opportunity to study the mass distribution of active galaxies, the connection between black hole growth and galaxy mass, and the co-evolution of AGN and their host galaxies.

Prior to this work, a few candidate systems had been proposed in which the lensing galaxy also hosted an active nucleus, but clear-cut cases of confirmed strong lensing by a QSO remained elusive. Theoretical expectations suggest that if the host galaxy is sufficiently massive, the presence of a central AGN should not inhibit strong lensing, although the observational identification requires high-quality imaging and spectroscopic separation of the lens and source components. The identification of such systems can also benefit from spectroscopic surveys where composite spectra reveal both low-redshift QSO emission lines and higher-redshift emission features from a background galaxy.

In this paper, we report the discovery of the first confirmed case of strong gravitational lensing by a QSO, SDSS J0013+1523, at a redshift of \( z = 0.120 \). This system was identified through careful examination of SDSS spectroscopic data, which revealed emission lines inconsistent with the QSO redshift, indicating the presence of a more distant background galaxy. Follow-up observations with high-resolution imaging confirmed the lensing nature of the system, revealing multiple images of the background source. This discovery opens a new observational window for studying the mass distribution of QSO host galaxies and provides a rare laboratory for investigating the interplay between AGN activity and gravitational lensing phenomena. In the following sections, we describe the discovery process, follow-up observations, lens modelling, and implications for future searches for similar systems.
conclusion: We have presented the discovery of SDSS J0013+1523, the first known case of strong gravitational lensing by a low-redshift QSO. This finding demonstrates that active galactic nuclei can act as efficient gravitational lenses, offering a novel probe of both QSO host galaxy mass distributions and background source properties, and opening avenues for future observational studies.

title: Online Behavioral Analysis with Application to Emotion State Identification
abstract: This paper presents a framework for online behavioral analysis aimed at real-time emotion state identification. Leveraging multimodal data streams, the approach integrates behavioral cues with machine learning models to detect emotional states dynamically. Experimental results demonstrate high accuracy and responsiveness, highlighting the framework’s potential for applications in human-computer interaction, adaptive learning, and mental health monitoring.
introduction:
In recent years, the rapid proliferation of digital communication platforms and the increasing integration of online interactions into daily life have generated vast amounts of behavioral data. These data, derived from social media activity, instant messaging, online forums, and other virtual environments, offer unprecedented opportunities for understanding human behavior in a non-intrusive and scalable manner. Among the many dimensions of human behavior that can be inferred from online activity, the identification of emotional states has emerged as a particularly compelling research direction, with applications in mental health monitoring, user experience optimization, targeted content delivery, and human–computer interaction.

Emotions play a central role in human cognition, decision-making, and interpersonal relationships. They influence not only face-to-face communication but also the way individuals express themselves in digital spaces. Textual content, visual media, interaction patterns, and even temporal activity rhythms can reflect underlying affective states. The ability to automatically detect and analyze these states in online contexts opens possibilities for real-time interventions, adaptive systems, and enhanced understanding of collective mood dynamics. However, the online environment presents unique challenges for emotion recognition, including the absence of physical cues such as facial expressions and vocal tone, the prevalence of ambiguous or exaggerated expressions, and the influence of platform-specific norms on communication style.

Traditional approaches to emotion recognition have relied heavily on laboratory-controlled settings, where participants’ affective states can be assessed through self-reports, physiological measurements, and multimodal sensor data. While these methods provide high-quality ground truth labels, they are often limited in ecological validity and scalability. In contrast, online behavioral analysis leverages naturally occurring data, enabling the study of emotions in real-life contexts and across large populations. This shift from controlled experiments to in-the-wild observations necessitates new methodological frameworks that combine computational techniques from natural language processing (NLP), computer vision, and network science with psychological theories of emotion.

Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep learning architectures, have significantly improved the capacity to model complex patterns in high-dimensional behavioral data. NLP techniques such as transformer-based language models can capture nuanced semantic and syntactic information from textual content, while computer vision algorithms can extract affective cues from user-generated images and videos. Additionally, temporal modeling approaches enable the detection of emotional trajectories over time, potentially revealing patterns associated with mood disorders, stress, or well-being. However, the interpretability of these models and their alignment with established psychological constructs remain active areas of research.

Ethical considerations are integral to the development and deployment of online emotion recognition systems. Privacy concerns are paramount, as emotional states are deeply personal and sensitive. Informed consent, data anonymization, and secure data handling must be ensured to protect individuals from potential misuse. Furthermore, algorithmic biases stemming from unbalanced or culturally homogeneous training datasets can lead to inaccurate or discriminatory outcomes, underscoring the need for fairness-aware design and cross-cultural validation.

This paper investigates the methodological foundations and practical implications of online behavioral analysis for emotion state identification. We focus on integrating multimodal behavioral signals with computational models to achieve robust emotion inference in real-world digital environments. Our approach emphasizes the interplay between data-driven algorithms and theory-driven psychological frameworks, seeking to bridge the gap between computational efficiency and conceptual validity. By systematically examining feature extraction techniques, model architectures, and evaluation strategies, we aim to contribute to the development of reliable, interpretable, and ethically responsible emotion recognition systems.

The remainder of this work is organized as follows. We first review existing literature on online behavioral analysis and emotion detection, highlighting key advances and persistent challenges. We then present our proposed framework for multimodal emotion identification, detailing the data sources, preprocessing methods, and model components. Experimental results on benchmark and real-world datasets are discussed, followed by an analysis of limitations and potential avenues for future research. Finally, we conclude with reflections on the broader implications of emotion-aware systems in online contexts.
conclusion: This study presented an approach to online behavioral analysis with a specific focus on emotion state identification. By integrating real-time data acquisition, feature extraction, and machine learning-based classification, the proposed framework demonstrated the potential to infer emotional states from observed online interactions. Experimental results indicated that behavioral patterns, when modeled appropriately, can provide meaningful indicators of affective states, enabling more adaptive and personalized digital experiences. Furthermore, the methodology supports continuous monitoring, allowing for dynamic adjustment to evolving user behaviors. While promising, the findings highlight the importance of addressing privacy, ethical considerations, and data representativeness to ensure responsible deployment. Future work will aim to enhance classification robustness, incorporate multimodal data sources, and explore broader applications in mental health, education, and human-computer interaction. Overall, this research underscores the value of behavioral analytics as a viable pathway for emotion-aware online systems.

title: Singular curves and cusp points in the joint space of 3-RPR parallel manipulators
abstract: This paper investigates the singular curves and cusp points arising in the joint space of planar 3-RPR parallel manipulators. Such configurations are critical for understanding motion capabilities and avoiding control instabilities. By formulating the singularity conditions directly in the joint space, we characterize the loci where the manipulator loses instantaneous mobility. Special attention is given to cusp points, which permit non-singular assembly mode changes and thus extend the usable workspace. Analytical derivations, supported by numerical examples, reveal the structure and multiplicity of these singular features. The results provide deeper insight into the topology of the joint space and offer practical guidelines for trajectory planning, enabling safer and more efficient operation of 3-RPR manipulators in complex tasks.
introduction:
Parallel manipulators have attracted significant attention in the field of robotics due to their high stiffness, compact structure, and potential for high-precision tasks. Among these architectures, the planar 3-RPR parallel manipulator—comprising three extensible prismatic actuators (P) connected to the base and the moving platform by revolute (R) joints—has been extensively studied for both theoretical and practical applications. The analysis of singularities in such mechanisms is of paramount importance, as singular configurations are associated with a loss of control, unbounded internal forces, and reduced stiffness, which may compromise operational accuracy and safety. In particular, the study of singular curves in the joint space provides valuable insight into the workspace characteristics, motion capabilities, and safe trajectory planning for these devices.

In the case of the 3-RPR manipulator, singularities arise when the three leg axes become either concurrent or parallel, resulting in the loss of constraint along certain motion directions. These singularities can be represented as curves in the joint space, which is defined by the actuated prismatic joint variables. Mapping and characterizing these curves is crucial for avoiding problematic configurations during operation. Beyond ordinary singularities, special points known as cusp points appear along these curves. Cusp points hold particular significance because they are associated with the ability of the manipulator to change assembly modes without crossing a singularity, a property that can be exploited to enlarge the usable workspace and improve maneuverability.

The concept of cusp points originates in the broader context of kinematic mapping and singularity theory, where they represent higher-order degeneracies of the constraint equations. In the joint space of a 3-RPR manipulator, a cusp point corresponds to a configuration where three direct kinematic solutions coincide. The existence and location of such points have important implications for both the design and control of the mechanism. From a design perspective, the distribution of cusp points influences the topology of the reachable workspace and the feasible motion strategies. From a control perspective, knowledge of cusp point locations can facilitate assembly mode changing strategies that avoid dangerous singular passages.

Previous studies have addressed the identification of singularities in 3-RPR manipulators using geometric, algebraic, or numerical approaches. While considerable progress has been made in understanding the singular curves, the explicit characterization and computation of cusp points in the joint space remains challenging due to the nonlinear nature of the governing equations. Recent advances in computational algebra and symbolic manipulation offer promising tools to systematically locate such points and to study their influence on the manipulator’s kinematic behavior.

This work aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of singular curves and cusp points in the joint space of planar 3-RPR parallel manipulators. By combining analytical derivations with computational techniques, we identify and classify cusp points, elucidate their geometric meaning, and explore their implications for assembly mode changes. The results contribute to a deeper understanding of the kinematic structure of these manipulators, offering guidelines for safer and more efficient motion planning.
conclusion: This work has investigated the singular curves and cusp points arising in the joint space of planar 3-RPR parallel manipulators. By formulating the singularity conditions in the joint variable domain, we have characterized the loci where the manipulator loses control of certain motion directions. The analysis has shown that these singular curves partition the joint space into distinct regions corresponding to different assembly modes. Particular attention was given to cusp points, which correspond to higher-order singularities where three assembly modes coincide. The identification of these points is of practical importance, as their presence allows non-singular transitions between assembly modes, thereby expanding the usable workspace without crossing singular configurations. Through both analytical derivation and numerical examples, we have demonstrated how the geometry of the manipulator influences the number, location, and structure of cusp points. The results provide insights into the design parameters that control the complexity of the singularity set and the feasibility of non-singular mode changing motions. This deeper understanding of the joint space topology contributes to improved manipulator design and trajectory planning strategies. Future work will focus on extending the methodology to more general architectures, incorporating joint limits, and exploring real-time algorithms for singularity avoidance and mode transition, thereby enhancing the operational flexibility and safety of parallel manipulators in practical applications.

title: A Tutorial on Deep Latent Variable Models of Natural Language
abstract: Deep latent variable models have emerged as powerful tools for capturing complex, structured dependencies in natural language. By introducing latent representations, these models enable flexible modeling of semantics, syntax, and discourse while supporting uncertainty quantification. This tutorial provides a comprehensive overview of key architectures, including variational autoencoders, generative adversarial approaches, and hierarchical latent structures. We discuss training objectives, inference techniques, and challenges such as posterior collapse. Applications in text generation, machine translation, and dialogue modeling are highlighted. The tutorial aims to equip researchers with both theoretical foundations and practical insights for leveraging deep latent variable models in natural language processing.
introduction:
Deep latent variable models (DLVMs) have emerged as a powerful class of generative models for natural language, combining the representational capacity of deep neural networks with the probabilistic semantics of latent variable models. By introducing latent structures that capture global or contextual properties of text, DLVMs enable richer modeling of linguistic phenomena than purely deterministic architectures. They offer a principled framework for addressing challenges such as capturing long-range dependencies, handling variability and ambiguity, and learning interpretable representations. In recent years, advances in variational inference, amortized learning, and scalable optimization have made it feasible to train such models on large-scale text corpora, leading to their adoption in tasks ranging from language modeling and machine translation to dialogue generation and text summarization.

Natural language exhibits complex structure at multiple levels: syntax, semantics, discourse, and pragmatics. Traditional recurrent neural networks (RNNs), convolutional architectures, and more recently transformers have demonstrated impressive performance in sequence modeling, but their deterministic hidden states often conflate multiple sources of variation, making it difficult to disentangle underlying factors. Latent variable models, in contrast, explicitly posit unobserved random variables to capture these factors, allowing for a separation between observed linguistic data and the abstract variables governing its generation. This explicit probabilistic formulation enables reasoning under uncertainty, marginalization over latent factors, and principled incorporation of prior knowledge.

The integration of deep learning with latent variable modeling bridges complementary strengths. Deep networks excel at learning flexible, high-dimensional mappings from data to latent spaces and back, while probabilistic models provide a coherent generative interpretation and tools for handling incomplete or noisy data. In the context of natural language, this synergy allows DLVMs to model both local sequential dependencies and global attributes such as topic, style, sentiment, or speaker identity. For example, a variational autoencoder (VAE) with a recurrent or transformer-based decoder can generate diverse sentences conditioned on latent codes, while a hierarchical latent structure can capture discourse-level coherence across multiple utterances.

Despite their promise, deep latent variable models pose significant challenges in natural language processing (NLP). One difficulty lies in the intractability of exact posterior inference: computing the distribution of latent variables given observed text is typically impossible analytically. Variational inference, especially in its amortized form using inference networks, has become the de facto approach to this problem. However, issues such as posterior collapse—where the latent variables become ignored by a powerful decoder—can hinder learning. Moreover, discrete latent variables, which are often natural for representing symbolic linguistic structures, require specialized gradient estimators or continuous relaxations to be trained effectively with gradient-based methods. These challenges necessitate careful model design, regularization, and training strategies to ensure that latent variables capture meaningful aspects of language.

The study of DLVMs for natural language is motivated not only by performance considerations but also by scientific and cognitive interests. Latent variables can serve as proxies for hidden cognitive states in human language processing, offering a computational lens on how people represent and generate language. Furthermore, interpretable latent factors can support controllable text generation, where users specify desired attributes and the model produces corresponding outputs. This controllability is valuable in applications such as personalized dialogue systems, style transfer, and bias mitigation.

Over the past decade, a variety of DLVM architectures have been proposed and explored. Variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks (GANs) with latent codes, normalizing flows, and energy-based latent models have each been adapted to textual data, often in combination with sequence models such as LSTMs or transformers. Hierarchical models introduce multiple layers of latent variables to capture structure at different granularities, while conditional models incorporate side information such as images, knowledge graphs, or structured annotations. Parallel to modeling advances, inference techniques have evolved, including reparameterization tricks for continuous variables, Gumbel-softmax relaxations for discrete variables, and importance-weighted bounds for tighter likelihood estimation.

This tutorial aims to provide a comprehensive and accessible overview of deep latent variable models of natural language. We will begin by reviewing the probabilistic foundations of latent variable modeling, then introduce the key deep learning architectures used for parameterizing components of these models. We will discuss variational inference in depth, including both continuous and discrete latent variables, and examine practical issues such as posterior collapse, KL annealing, and inference network design. The tutorial will survey prominent DLVMs applied to NLP tasks, highlighting architectural choices, training methods, and empirical performance. We will also address open challenges and recent research directions, such as incorporating structured priors, leveraging pre-trained language models, and scaling to multimodal settings. By the end, readers should have both a conceptual understanding and practical guidance for applying deep latent variable models to natural language, as well as an appreciation of their potential and limitations in advancing both engineering and scientific goals.
conclusion: In this tutorial, we have reviewed the foundations, motivations, and methodological advances underlying deep latent variable models for natural language. By integrating probabilistic graphical modeling with deep neural architectures, these approaches enable richer representations of linguistic structure, capturing complex dependencies and uncertainty that purely deterministic models may overlook. We have discussed key model classes, including variational autoencoders, generative adversarial frameworks, and structured latent variable models, along with inference techniques such as variational inference and amortized learning. Practical considerations, such as regularization, posterior collapse, and evaluation, were highlighted to bridge theoretical insights with empirical performance. Applications spanning text generation, dialogue systems, and semantic representation illustrate the versatility of these methods. While notable progress has been made, challenges remain in scaling inference, ensuring interpretability, and aligning latent representations with human-interpretable semantics. Future directions include leveraging advances in self-supervised learning, integrating symbolic priors, and developing more robust training objectives. We hope this tutorial provides a coherent entry point for researchers and practitioners, fostering further exploration of deep latent variable models as a powerful paradigm for modeling the richness and variability inherent in natural language.

title: A Categorical Compositional Distributional Modelling for the Language of Life
abstract: We propose a novel framework for modelling the “language of life” by integrating categorical compositional distributional semantics with biological sequence analysis. Inspired by advances in computational linguistics, our approach treats biological sequences—such as proteins and nucleic acids—as structured linguistic objects, where grammatical composition reflects functional and structural constraints. Using category theory as the unifying formalism, we model the compositional rules governing biological syntax, while distributional semantics captures contextual meaning derived from large-scale biological corpora. This dual representation enables the encoding of both local sequence patterns and higher-order organisational principles, bridging the gap between symbolic structure and statistical representation. We demonstrate the applicability of our model by mapping protein domains to grammatical types and representing their functional contexts in high-dimensional semantic spaces, enabling compositional reasoning over biological functions. Preliminary experiments on protein–protein interaction prediction and function classification show that our method outperforms standard sequence-based embeddings, highlighting the value of explicitly modelling compositional structure. This work lays the theoretical and computational foundation for a linguistically informed, category-theoretic approach to biological sequence understanding, opening new avenues for interpretable, structured predictions in systems biology and bioinformatics.
introduction:
The study of natural language has long benefited from the interplay between formal compositional semantics and statistical models of lexical meaning. In recent years, categorical compositional distributional models (DisCoCat) have emerged as a promising framework for unifying these two approaches, leveraging the mathematical structure of category theory to integrate grammatical composition with distributional representations of word meaning. In parallel, the biological sciences have increasingly adopted the language metaphor to describe and analyse the complex information-processing systems underlying life, from the genetic code to cellular signalling and metabolic regulation. This convergence invites the question: can the tools developed for modelling human language be adapted to the “language of life” — the structured, symbolic, and context-dependent systems through which living processes encode, transform, and interpret information?

The “language of life” encompasses multiple levels of biological organisation, including the sequence structure of nucleic acids and proteins, the syntactic rules of molecular interaction, and the semantics of functional outcomes in cellular contexts. At the molecular level, the genetic code can be seen as a lexicon mapping nucleotide triplets to amino acids, while higher-order structures and pathways enact compositional rules akin to grammar. Distributional regularities arise from evolutionary and functional constraints, suggesting that statistical models can capture meaningful patterns in sequence usage and molecular interactions.
