However, as in human language, meaning in biology is not merely a property of isolated units but emerges from their composition within structured contexts.

Categorical compositional distributional semantics offers a principled method for modelling such compositionality. By representing grammatical types as objects in a compact closed category and lexical meanings as vectors or tensors in a corresponding semantic space, this framework enables systematic composition of meanings in a way that respects the underlying syntactic structure. When applied to biology, this approach can model how functional meaning emerges from the combination of biological “words” — such as codons, motifs, or domains — according to “grammatical” constraints enforced by biochemical and biophysical rules. The categorical formalism also naturally captures higher-order interactions and contextual dependencies, which are pervasive in biological systems.

There is growing recognition that purely symbolic or purely statistical models are insufficient to capture the complexity of biological information systems. Symbolic approaches, such as formal grammars for RNA secondary structures or protein domains, excel at expressing constraints and hierarchical organisation but struggle to incorporate graded, probabilistic, or context-dependent aspects of meaning. Conversely, statistical models, including deep learning architectures applied to sequence data, can capture rich distributional patterns but often lack interpretability and compositional structure. The categorical compositional distributional model offers a synthesis: it retains the interpretability and structural rigour of symbolic models while incorporating the empirical grounding and flexibility of statistical representations.

In this work, we explore how the DisCoCat framework can be adapted to model the language of life, focusing on the integration of biological syntax and semantics through category-theoretic structures. We investigate how the grammar of molecular sequences and interactions can be formalised in compact closed categories, and how empirical biological data can be embedded into semantic spaces suitable for compositional reasoning. By doing so, we aim to provide a mathematically rigorous, data-driven approach to understanding biological meaning-making processes, with potential applications ranging from functional annotation and pathway reconstruction to synthetic biology and bioinformatics.

Our proposal bridges disciplines — theoretical computer science, computational linguistics, and systems biology — to suggest a unified perspective on biological information. Just as compositional distributional semantics has advanced our understanding of human language, we anticipate that its categorical formulation can yield new insights into the structured complexity of life’s information systems, offering both explanatory frameworks and practical tools for analysing and engineering biological processes.
conclusion:
In this work, we have proposed a categorical compositional distributional framework for modelling the “language of life,” integrating insights from category theory, compositional semantics, and distributional representations. By treating biological sequences and their functional contexts analogously to linguistic structures, our approach allows the systematic composition of local meaning—encoded in distributional vector spaces—into higher-order functional interpretations via categorical morphisms. This unifies structural and statistical perspectives, enabling the incorporation of syntactic-like constraints with empirical co-occurrence data derived from biological corpora.

Our results suggest that categorical compositional models can capture non-trivial dependencies in biological data, facilitating interpretability and potentially improving predictive performance in tasks such as protein function inference or genetic regulatory analysis. The explicit compositional structure offers a principled means of modelling hierarchical organisation, while the distributional layer leverages large-scale sequence data to ground the representations in observed patterns.

Future work will involve scaling the framework to larger datasets, refining the categorical structures to better reflect domain-specific constraints, and exploring hybrid architectures that combine categorical compositionality with deep learning. More broadly, this study demonstrates the promise of importing rigorous semantic formalisms from computational linguistics into computational biology, thereby advancing a mathematically coherent, data-driven “grammar” for the language of life.

title: Training Heterogeneous Features in Sequence to Sequence Tasks: Latent Enhanced Multi-filter Seq2Seq Model
abstract: Sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models have achieved remarkable success in tasks such as machine translation, summarization, and speech recognition. However, effectively integrating heterogeneous feature representations—such as lexical, syntactic, and semantic cues—remains challenging due to differences in their statistical properties and temporal dynamics. This paper presents the Latent Enhanced Multi-filter Seq2Seq (LEM-Seq2Seq) model, which introduces a multi-filter encoder mechanism to process heterogeneous features in parallel, followed by a latent enhancement module that adaptively fuses their representations. The multi-filter encoder employs diverse convolutional and recurrent filters to capture complementary local and global dependencies, while the latent enhancement module leverages attention-based gating to emphasize salient information across feature spaces. We evaluate LEM-Seq2Seq on multiple benchmark datasets for text and speech tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements over strong baselines in BLEU, ROUGE, and WER metrics. Analysis shows that the proposed architecture enhances feature complementarity and robustness to noise. The results indicate that latent-enhanced multi-filter processing offers a promising direction for heterogeneous feature integration in Seq2Seq learning.
introduction: Sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models have demonstrated remarkable success across diverse domains, including machine translation, speech recognition, and text summarization. However, real-world tasks often involve heterogeneous features originating from multiple modalities or varying temporal dynamics, posing challenges for conventional architectures. Existing approaches typically process such features uniformly, potentially overlooking complementary relationships and latent structures. To address this limitation, we propose the Latent Enhanced Multi-filter Seq2Seq (LEM-Seq2Seq) model, which integrates heterogeneous features through multi-scale filtering and latent representation enhancement. This design enables more effective feature fusion, improved sequence modeling, and robust performance across tasks with complex, intertwined input characteristics.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed the Latent Enhanced Multi-filter Seq2Seq model to effectively integrate heterogeneous features in sequence-to-sequence tasks. By leveraging multi-filter mechanisms and latent space enhancement, the model captures diverse temporal and contextual dependencies, improving representation richness and translation accuracy. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrated consistent performance gains over strong baselines. These results highlight the importance of jointly modeling heterogeneous inputs with flexible filtering strategies. Future research may explore adaptive filter selection and broader application domains to further enhance generalization and scalability.

title: Quasi-dynamic Load and Battery Sizing and Scheduling for Stand-Alone Solar System Using Mixed-integer Linear Programming
abstract: This paper presents a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) approach for the optimal sizing and scheduling of quasi-dynamic electrical loads and battery storage in a stand-alone solar photovoltaic (PV) system. The proposed model simultaneously determines the capacities of PV generation and battery storage, as well as the operational schedule of flexible and fixed loads, to minimize the total system cost while ensuring energy autonomy. Quasi-dynamic loads are modeled to capture partial flexibility in operation, allowing for limited shifting within pre-defined time windows without violating service constraints. The MILP formulation incorporates hourly solar resource profiles, load demand patterns, battery charging and discharging dynamics, and technical limits, enabling a realistic representation of system performance. Case studies based on measured irradiance and demand data demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in balancing investment and operational costs, reducing battery oversizing, and improving solar utilization. Results show that coordinated load scheduling and correctly sized storage significantly enhance system reliability while lowering lifecycle costs compared to conventional static load assumptions. The proposed framework provides a systematic decision-support tool for designing cost-effective, reliable stand-alone PV systems, particularly suited for remote or off-grid applications where resource variability and demand flexibility must be jointly considered.
introduction:
The increasing global demand for electricity, coupled with the urgent need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, has accelerated the adoption of renewable energy sources. Among these, solar photovoltaic (PV) systems have emerged as one of the most promising solutions due to their scalability, low operational costs, and environmental benefits. In regions where access to the centralized power grid is limited or nonexistent, stand-alone solar PV systems offer a sustainable alternative for electrification. However, the intermittent and variable nature of solar energy presents significant challenges for meeting demand reliably, especially when the load profiles are dynamic and energy storage systems are required to ensure continuous power supply.

Effective design and operation of stand-alone solar systems require accurate modeling of both supply and demand components, as well as the optimal sizing of storage devices such as batteries. Load modeling is particularly important because demand in many off-grid applications is not constant, but varies over time due to user behavior, environmental conditions, and operational constraints of connected devices. Traditional static load models, which assume fixed or averaged demand, can result in suboptimal system designs that either fail to meet peak demands or lead to over-investment in generation and storage capacity. Quasi-dynamic load models, which capture the time-dependent variation in demand while maintaining computational tractability, offer a more realistic and effective framework for system design.

Battery storage plays a critical role in mitigating the mismatch between solar generation and electricity consumption. In stand-alone systems, batteries store excess energy generated during periods of high irradiance and discharge it during periods of low or no solar production. The sizing of the battery system directly affects both the reliability of supply and the overall cost of the system. Oversized batteries increase capital costs and may lead to underutilization, whereas undersized batteries can result in frequent energy shortages and reduced service quality. Furthermore, battery scheduling, which refers to the operational strategy for charging and discharging, is essential to maximize the lifetime of the storage system and ensure efficient utilization of available resources.

Optimizing the design and operation of stand-alone PV-battery systems is inherently a complex problem due to the interdependencies between load variation, solar generation profiles, battery characteristics, and cost considerations. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) has emerged as a powerful optimization tool for such applications because it can handle both discrete decisions—such as the number of battery units or specific operational states—and continuous variables, such as power flows and energy levels, within a unified mathematical framework. MILP formulations enable the incorporation of technical constraints, operational limits, and economic objectives, allowing for the derivation of optimal solutions that balance cost, performance, and reliability.

Recent research has explored various aspects of PV-battery system optimization, including generation forecasting, battery degradation modeling, and hybrid system integration. However, there remains a gap in the literature in terms of integrating quasi-dynamic load modeling with simultaneous battery sizing and scheduling in a single MILP framework for stand-alone systems. Addressing this gap is particularly relevant for remote communities, off-grid industrial operations, and emergency response scenarios, where load variability is pronounced and reliability is critical.

This study proposes a comprehensive MILP-based approach for the optimal sizing and scheduling of batteries in stand-alone solar PV systems, incorporating quasi-dynamic load representations. The proposed method aims to improve the accuracy of system design by accounting for realistic demand patterns, while optimizing operational strategies to ensure reliable and cost-effective energy supply. Through detailed modeling and case studies, the approach is demonstrated to provide practical insights into the trade-offs between system cost, reliability, and operational efficiency, offering a valuable decision-making tool for engineers and planners in the renewable energy sector.
conclusion:
This study presented a quasi-dynamic approach for load and battery sizing and scheduling in a stand-alone solar photovoltaic system using a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) framework. By integrating time-varying solar generation profiles, discrete load operation constraints, and battery state-of-charge dynamics into a unified optimization model, the proposed method effectively captured the operational interplay between generation, storage, and demand. The quasi-dynamic formulation enabled a balance between computational tractability and temporal accuracy, offering a practical alternative to fully dynamic models while retaining the ability to represent key system behaviors.

The results demonstrated that the MILP-based methodology can determine optimal battery capacities and load schedules that minimize cost and improve system reliability under varying solar resource conditions. Compared to conventional static sizing approaches, the quasi-dynamic model yielded more efficient battery utilization and reduced instances of unmet load, while also avoiding excessive oversizing of components. The scheduling decisions inherently reflected the intermittency of solar generation, aligning load operation with periods of high availability and leveraging storage to bridge deficits, thereby enhancing the self-sufficiency of the stand-alone system.

Sensitivity analyses indicated that the model is adaptable to different demand patterns, solar irradiation scenarios, and cost parameters, making it broadly applicable to diverse off-grid contexts. The flexibility in incorporating technical constraints—such as battery depth-of-discharge limits and load operation windows—demonstrates the suitability of the approach for real-world implementation, particularly in rural electrification projects and remote energy systems where resource variability and cost efficiency are critical.

Future work may extend the framework to include stochastic elements to account for solar forecast uncertainty, integrate multiple storage technologies, or consider hybrid renewable energy sources. Additionally, scaling the model to address multi-node microgrids with network constraints could further enhance its applicability. Overall, the quasi-dynamic MILP approach provides a robust and adaptable tool for the optimal design and operation of stand-alone solar systems, contributing to sustainable and cost-effective off-grid energy solutions.

title: Radio Polarimetry of 3C119, 3C318, and 3C343 at milliarcsecond resolution
abstract: We present milliarcsecond-resolution radio polarimetric observations of the compact steep-spectrum (CSS) radio sources 3C119, 3C318, and 3C343, obtained with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) at multiple frequencies between 1.4 and 5 GHz. These observations provide new insights into the sub-parsec scale polarization structure, Faraday rotation, and magnetic field geometry of these powerful radio galaxies and quasars. Total intensity images reveal complex, multi-component morphologies consistent with core–jet or lobe–hotspot structures embedded within dense interstellar media. Linear polarization is detected in multiple components of each source, with fractional polarizations typically below 10%, indicative of significant depolarization. Rotation measure (RM) maps show strong spatial variations, with peak rest-frame values exceeding several thousand rad m⁻². In 3C119, the highest RMs are associated with the brightest jet components, suggesting interaction with a magnetized circumnuclear medium. In 3C318, the polarization is concentrated in the outer jet regions, and the RM distribution is patchy, possibly due to inhomogeneous Faraday screens. For 3C343, the polarization is confined to compact hotspots with extremely high RMs, implying dense, magnetized plasma along the line of sight. The observed RM gradients across individual components suggest ordered magnetic fields on scales of tens of parsecs, while the magnitude of the RMs points to substantial thermal electron densities in the immediate environments of the radio sources. These results support a scenario in which CSS sources are young radio galaxies whose expansion is influenced by dense, asymmetric gaseous environments within their host galaxies. Our milliarcsecond-resolution polarimetry demonstrates the diagnostic power of VLBI techniques for probing the interplay between relativistic jets and their surrounding media, and highlights the importance of high-frequency, multi-epoch observations to disentangle intrinsic magnetic field structures from Faraday rotation effects.
introduction:
Active galactic nuclei (AGN) exhibiting powerful radio emission provide unique laboratories for investigating the physics of relativistic jets, magnetic field configurations, and the interaction of radio plasma with the surrounding medium. High-resolution imaging of their polarized emission offers direct insight into the structure and orientation of magnetic fields on parsec scales, as well as the properties of the magneto-ionic environment through which the radiation propagates. Compact steep-spectrum (CSS) sources, in particular, are of interest because they are thought to represent an early stage in the evolution of powerful radio galaxies and quasars, with projected linear sizes typically less than 20 kpc and steep radio spectra indicative of synchrotron emission from relatively small, confined jets and lobes.

Polarimetric observations at milliarcsecond resolution using very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) techniques enable the measurement of fractional polarization, electric vector position angles (EVPAs), and Faraday rotation measures (RMs) across the source structure. The RM distribution, in turn, provides constraints on the density, composition, and magnetic field strength of the ionized gas along the line of sight. For CSS sources, large and spatially variable RMs are commonly observed, suggesting significant interaction between the radio-emitting plasma and a dense circumnuclear medium. Such conditions may play a crucial role in shaping the morphology, dynamics, and evolution of the jets.

The radio sources 3C119, 3C318, and 3C343 are luminous CSS quasars and radio galaxies that exhibit compact structures resolvable with VLBI. Previous studies have reported complex total intensity morphologies and depolarization behavior in these objects, but polarimetric imaging at the highest available angular resolution remains limited. Detailed, multi-frequency, milliarcsecond-scale polarimetry of these sources is essential for disentangling the intrinsic magnetic field geometries from the effects of Faraday rotation and depolarization, and for assessing the role of environmental asymmetries in producing the observed structures.

In this work, we present new VLBI polarimetric observations of 3C119, 3C318, and 3C343 at multiple frequencies, achieving milliarcsecond angular resolution. Our goals are to map the distribution of polarized emission across each source, determine the Faraday rotation measures with high spatial fidelity, and investigate correlations between polarization properties, spectral structure, and total intensity morphology. By comparing the polarization characteristics of these three CSS sources, we aim to advance the understanding of magnetic field configurations and the influence of dense environments on the parsec-scale structures of young radio-loud AGN. This study thus contributes to the broader effort to connect small-scale jet physics with the evolutionary pathways of powerful extragalactic radio sources.
conclusion:
The milliarcsecond-resolution polarimetric observations presented here provide new insights into the sub-parsec scale structures and magnetoionic environments of the compact steep spectrum (CSS) quasars 3C119, 3C318, and 3C343. By combining high spatial resolution with full polarization analysis, we have been able to disentangle the fine-scale morphology of polarized emission, measure Faraday rotation with unprecedented precision for these sources, and assess the physical conditions in their immediate environments. The results demonstrate the diversity of polarization properties within this class of radio sources and underscore the importance of parsec-scale studies for understanding their evolution and interaction with the surrounding medium.

For 3C119, our data reveal a core–jet structure in which polarized emission is concentrated in distinct jet components separated by tens of parsecs in projection. The measured rotation measures (RMs) reach several thousand rad m⁻² in the innermost features, indicative of dense, magnetized plasma along the line of sight. The spatial gradients in RM suggest that the Faraday rotating medium is inhomogeneous on parsec scales, possibly associated with circumnuclear material or the inner narrow-line region. The electric vector position angles (EVPAs), corrected for Faraday rotation, align closely with the local jet axis, consistent with magnetic fields predominantly transverse to the flow. This geometry may be the result of shocks compressing a tangled magnetic field or of shear interactions with the surrounding medium.

In the case of 3C318, the polarized emission is more diffuse and distributed along a bent jet structure. The RMs are moderate, typically a few hundred rad m⁻², but exhibit ordered variations along the jet, pointing to a less extreme but still significant magnetoionic environment. The observed EVPA orientations, after correction, are consistent with a mix of transverse and longitudinal field components, suggesting variations in jet dynamics and possibly episodes of interaction with clumpy interstellar gas. The jet curvature and changes in polarization structure may reflect either precession of the central engine or deflection by dense clouds in the host galaxy’s interstellar medium.

3C343 presents the most complex polarimetric structure of the three sources. The polarized emission is detected in multiple compact knots embedded within a broader, weakly polarized halo. Extremely high RMs, in excess of 10³ rad m⁻², are found in the most compact regions, again implying a dense, magnetized screen close to the central engine. The RM distribution appears patchy, and the EVPA orientations show abrupt changes on sub-milliarcsecond scales, suggestive of a turbulent magnetoionic medium. This turbulence may be driven by strong jet–ISM interactions, potentially linked to the early evolutionary stage of the source.

Across all three objects, the detection of high and variable RMs on milliarcsecond scales supports the picture that CSS quasars are embedded in rich, dense environments within their host galaxies. The differences in RM magnitude, spatial distribution, and EVPA orientation between the sources highlight that the immediate surroundings of these AGN are not uniform, but shaped by local conditions, jet geometry, and evolutionary state. The presence of both ordered and disordered field structures inferred from the polarization data indicates that while large-scale magnetic configurations can be maintained within the jets, these are often modified by shocks, bends, and interactions with ambient gas.

Our results emphasize the diagnostic power of VLBI polarimetry for probing the physical conditions close to the central engines of young, powerful radio sources. By resolving individual polarized jet components, we can directly measure the Faraday rotation imparted by circumnuclear material, constrain the magnetic field geometry, and infer aspects of the jet–environment interaction. These measurements complement lower-resolution studies by revealing the small-scale structure that is otherwise averaged out, and they provide key constraints for models of jet propagation and confinement in dense galactic environments.

Future work should extend these observations to a larger sample of CSS and gigahertz peaked spectrum (GPS) sources, enabling statistical comparisons of RM distributions, magnetic field orientations, and their relation to source size and morphology. Multi-frequency monitoring on parsec scales would allow us to trace temporal changes in the polarization structure, potentially linking them to variability in the central engine or to evolving interactions with the surrounding medium. In addition, combining VLBI polarimetry with optical and X-ray diagnostics of the host galaxy environment would provide a more complete picture of the conditions that shape the early stages of radio source evolution. The observations reported here demonstrate that such integrated studies are both feasible and essential for advancing our understanding of the interplay between relativistic jets and their environments in the formative phases of radio-loud AGN.

title: High Efficiency Power Side-Channel Attack Immunity using Noise Injection in Attenuated Signature Domain
abstract: This work presents a novel countermeasure technique for enhancing the immunity of cryptographic implementations against power side-channel attacks (PSCAs) through noise injection in the attenuated signature domain. Traditional noise-based defenses often incur significant power and performance overheads due to the large amplitude of injected noise required to mask sensitive leakage. In contrast, the proposed method first attenuates the exploitable power signature through lightweight circuit-level modifications, thereby reducing the signal magnitude available to an attacker. Subsequently, controlled noise is injected at a reduced amplitude sufficient to obscure the residual leakage, enabling substantial improvements in security-to-overhead efficiency. The dual-stage approach leverages the synergistic effect of signature suppression and targeted noise addition, minimizing energy consumption while maintaining compatibility with existing hardware architectures. Experimental evaluation on an AES hardware core demonstrates that the proposed technique achieves a marked increase in the number of traces required for successful correlation power analysis, with up to 68% reduction in noise power compared to conventional noise injection strategies. These results highlight the potential of attenuated signature domain noise injection as a practical, low-overhead, and high-efficiency approach for securing cryptographic hardware against advanced side-channel threats.
introduction:
The proliferation of embedded systems in security-sensitive applications has heightened the importance of protecting cryptographic implementations against physical attacks, particularly side-channel attacks (SCAs). Among these, power analysis attacks exploit the correlation between processed data and instantaneous power consumption to extract secret keys with high efficiency and low cost. Differential Power Analysis (DPA) and Correlation Power Analysis (CPA) have been shown to compromise widely deployed algorithms such as AES and RSA, even when implemented on constrained hardware. Consequently, the development of countermeasures capable of mitigating power side-channel leakage without incurring prohibitive performance or area overhead has become a critical research priority.

Noise injection is a widely studied class of countermeasures that seeks to decorrelate the measured power traces from sensitive intermediate values by introducing controlled randomness into the power consumption profile. Traditional implementations often add switching activity, dummy operations, or random delays, thereby increasing the difficulty for an adversary to align and average traces effectively. However, conventional noise injection approaches can be costly in terms of power, area, and performance, and they may still be vulnerable to advanced statistical attacks that can filter out or average the injected noise. Thus, there is a demand for noise injection techniques that achieve superior immunity while maintaining high efficiency.

This work investigates a novel noise injection strategy applied in the attenuated signature domain, wherein the amplitude of the exploitable power signature is first reduced through architectural or circuit-level techniques before noise is superimposed. By attenuating the original leakage prior to noise addition, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at the attacker’s measurement point can be drastically reduced with less injected noise energy, thereby improving the power and performance efficiency of the countermeasure. This dual approach leverages the fact that noise injection effectiveness is proportional to the relative magnitude of noise to the residual leakage, rather than to the original unattenuated signature.

The proposed method is evaluated using representative cryptographic workloads on a hardware prototype, with detailed analysis of both security and implementation metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that the attenuated signature domain noise injection significantly increases the number of traces required for successful key recovery, while incurring minimal overhead compared to conventional noise injection. This research contributes to the design of practical, high-efficiency countermeasures capable of withstanding modern power SCA techniques in resource-constrained secure systems.
conclusion: The proposed noise injection technique in the attenuated signature domain demonstrates a high degree of immunity against power side-channel attacks while maintaining system efficiency. Experimental results confirm significant reduction in exploitable leakage without incurring substantial performance or energy penalties. By targeting the signature domain, the approach effectively masks sensitive operations, increasing the effort required for successful attacks. This method offers a practical balance between security and implementation overhead, making it suitable for resource-constrained devices. Future work will explore adaptive noise control to further optimize security-performance trade-offs in diverse cryptographic applications.

title: On the factorization of composite polymer knots into separated prime components
abstract: We investigate the factorization properties of composite knots formed within flexible polymer chains, focusing on the spatial separation of their prime components. Using extensive Monte Carlo simulations of self-avoiding polygons on a cubic lattice, we generate ensembles of polymer configurations containing prescribed composite topologies and analyze the distribution and interaction of their constituent prime knots. By employing a localized knot detection algorithm based on minimally interfering closure schemes, we quantify the extent of physical separation between prime components as a function of chain length and component complexity. Our results reveal that, for sufficiently long chains, prime knots within a composite polymer tend to localize and segregate along the contour, leading to an effective factorization into weakly interacting domains. This separation becomes sharper with increasing chain length, although residual entanglements may persist for shorter polymers or more complex components. We discuss the implications of these findings for the statistical mechanics of knotted polymers, propose scaling arguments for the separation length scale, and outline potential connections to biological systems, such as DNA under confinement, where composite knots may influence functional and mechanical properties.
introduction:
Knots in closed curves have long been a subject of mathematical and physical interest, with their classification forming a cornerstone of knot theory. In recent decades, the study of knots has transcended pure mathematics and found fertile ground in the physical sciences, particularly in polymer physics, molecular biology, and soft matter research. Circular polymers, such as closed DNA molecules, often exhibit nontrivial topologies that can be understood in terms of knot types. The topology of such polymers is not merely a mathematical curiosity; it can influence their physical properties, biological function, and interactions with other molecules. Consequently, the detailed investigation of the structure and dynamics of polymer knots has become a vibrant interdisciplinary field.

A central concept in knot theory is the decomposition of a knot into prime components. Analogous to the unique factorization of integers into prime numbers, a composite knot can be represented as a connected sum of prime knots, and this decomposition is unique up to ordering. In the context of polymer knots, the question arises as to whether and how such a factorization manifests physically in the spatial configuration of the polymer. Specifically, one may ask whether the prime components of a composite polymer knot are localized in distinct, well-separated regions along the polymer contour, or whether their structures are delocalized and intertwined. This issue is fundamental for understanding the statistical mechanics of knotted polymers, as it touches upon the interplay between topological constraints and configurational entropy.

Experimental and numerical studies have shown that polymers under certain conditions tend to localize their knotting into compact regions, a phenomenon referred to as knot localization. For prime knots, localization has been observed in both equilibrium and driven settings, and is often attributed to the entropic advantage of confining the topological constraint to a small segment of the chain. For composite knots, one might expect an analogous scenario in which each prime component occupies a separate, localized domain, resulting in a physical realization of the mathematical factorization. However, the extent to which such separation occurs, and the factors governing it, remain incompletely understood. Factors such as polymer stiffness, confinement, solvent quality, and applied tension can all influence the spatial arrangement of prime components.

From a theoretical perspective, understanding the factorization of composite polymer knots into separated prime components requires bridging rigorous topological results with statistical-mechanical models of polymer chains. This includes developing quantitative criteria for identifying prime components along fluctuating polymer conformations, and characterizing the probability distributions of their separations. Computational approaches, such as Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations, have proven indispensable for probing these questions in regimes difficult to access experimentally. Moreover, advances in single-molecule manipulation techniques, including optical and magnetic tweezers, provide opportunities to test predictions and explore the dynamic aspects of knot separation.

In this work, we investigate the factorization of composite polymer knots within a statistical-mechanical framework, focusing on the conditions under which prime components become spatially separated. By combining numerical simulations with topological analysis, we aim to quantify the degree of separation as a function of polymer length, topology, and physical parameters. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between knot theory and polymer physics, and shed light on the physical realizability of knot factorization in fluctuating, flexible chains.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the factorization of composite polymer knots into spatially separated prime components, with particular emphasis on the structural and statistical properties that govern this process. By combining topological analysis with statistical-mechanical modelling, we have demonstrated that the decomposition of a composite knot into its constituent prime factors can, under appropriate conditions, be realized in an extended polymer configuration, allowing for a clear spatial distinction between the components. Our findings confirm that the factorization is not merely a formal topological operation, but can correspond to physically observable arrangements in which individual prime knots occupy distinct, non-overlapping regions along the polymer contour.

The results highlight the interplay between polymer length, excluded volume effects, and thermal fluctuations in determining whether such separations occur spontaneously. For sufficiently long chains, the entropic cost of localizing each prime component is offset by the gain in configurational freedom for the remainder of the chain, leading to an effective repulsion between knotted regions and promoting their spatial segregation. This behavior was quantified through simulations and analytic arguments, both of which support the scaling predictions for the average separation distance and the degree of localization of each factor.

An important implication of this study is that the statistical independence of separated prime components is enhanced in regimes where their mutual interaction is minimized, suggesting that the overall configurational statistics of a composite knot can, to a good approximation, be derived from those of its factors. This provides a framework for predicting the properties of complex knotted polymers from knowledge of the simplest nontrivial knots, with potential applications in the interpretation of experiments on circular DNA, synthetic molecular rings, and knotted proteins.

Moreover, our analysis indicates that the factorization picture begins to break down for shorter chains or in conditions where confinement or crowding restricts the available configurational space, leading to partial overlap and coupling between components. This delineates the boundaries of applicability for the separated-factor model, and suggests directions for more refined treatments that incorporate interaction effects.

Future work may extend these results to dynamical scenarios, such as the kinetics of knot diffusion and recombination, or to polymers under external forces and torques, where the stability and separability of prime components could be altered. Overall, this study provides both conceptual clarity and quantitative tools for understanding the organization of composite knots in polymers, bridging the gap between abstract knot theory and the physical behavior of knotted macromolecular systems.

title: Gender Classification from Iris Texture Images Using a New Set of Binary Statistical Image Features
abstract: This study presents a novel approach for gender classification based on iris texture images, introducing a new set of Binary Statistical Image Features (BSIF) specifically optimized for this task. While prior research has demonstrated the discriminative potential of iris patterns for biometric identification, gender classification remains less explored. In the proposed method, iris images are preprocessed to isolate the normalized texture region, from which customized BSIF filters are learned to capture statistically significant local texture variations. The extracted feature vectors are then classified using a support vector machine with optimized parameters. Experimental evaluations were conducted on publicly available iris image datasets containing balanced male and female samples. Results indicate that the proposed BSIF configuration achieves higher classification accuracy and robustness compared to standard BSIF and other texture descriptors. These findings suggest that the tailored binary statistical representation of iris textures can serve as an effective and computationally efficient tool for soft biometric gender classification.
introduction:
Biometric technologies have gained significant attention in recent years due to their reliability and robustness in personal identification and verification. Among the various biometric traits, the human iris has emerged as one of the most distinctive and stable modalities, exhibiting unique texture patterns that remain consistent over a person’s lifetime and are minimally affected by environmental conditions. While iris recognition has been extensively studied for identity authentication, the potential of iris texture analysis for predicting soft biometric attributes, such as gender, has attracted growing interest in the research community. Soft biometrics, though not sufficient for identification on their own, can enhance recognition systems by narrowing search spaces, improving matching speed, and supporting forensic investigations.

Gender classification from iris images offers several advantages over traditional approaches based on facial features, voice, or gait, as the iris is less influenced by external factors such as makeup, hairstyle, or aging. However, the subtle textural differences between male and female irises present a significant challenge, demanding the development of highly discriminative feature extraction techniques. Conventional feature descriptors, such as Gabor filters, Local Binary Patterns (LBP), and wavelet transforms, have been employed in prior works, yet they may not fully capture the nuanced statistical variations embedded in iris textures for accurate gender prediction.

In this study, we propose a novel set of Binary Statistical Image Features (BSIF) specifically designed to characterize the fine-grained statistical properties of iris texture images for gender classification. The proposed method leverages the binary representation of local image patches, learned through independent component analysis, to construct robust feature vectors that encode the distribution of texture patterns. By integrating these features with a suitable classifier, the approach aims to improve the discriminative capability for gender differentiation while maintaining computational efficiency.

Extensive experiments are conducted on publicly available iris image datasets to evaluate the proposed method’s performance against existing techniques. The results demonstrate that the newly developed BSIF-based features significantly enhance classification accuracy, underscoring their effectiveness and potential for integration into multimodal biometric systems. This work contributes to advancing soft biometric research and opens avenues for more refined attribute prediction from iris textures.
conclusion:
This study presented a novel approach for gender classification from iris texture images by introducing a new set of Binary Statistical Image Features (BSIF). The proposed method aimed to exploit the rich textural information in the iris region, which has been shown to exhibit subtle yet discriminative patterns linked to biological sex. By leveraging BSIF, we were able to encode local spatial structures into binary codes derived from learned filters, producing a compact yet highly descriptive representation of iris texture. The experimental results demonstrated that the proposed feature set, when coupled with a robust classifier, achieved superior performance compared to conventional texture descriptors such as Local Binary Patterns (LBP) and Gabor filters, across multiple benchmark iris datasets.

The effectiveness of the method can be attributed to the ability of BSIF to capture fine-scale statistical regularities in the iris stroma, which are less affected by illumination changes and sensor variations. Furthermore, the learned filter responses emphasized discriminative micro-patterns that may be overlooked by handcrafted descriptors. The comparative analysis showed consistent gains in classification accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, indicating the robustness of the proposed approach. This improvement was particularly evident in cross-sensor and cross-database scenarios, underscoring the potential of the method for real-world biometric applications where data heterogeneity is common.

In addition to performance gains, the computational efficiency of BSIF-based feature extraction makes the approach suitable for integration into practical biometric systems, where speed and scalability are critical. The compactness of the feature representation also reduces storage requirements without compromising accuracy, which is advantageous for large-scale deployments.

While the proposed method achieved promising results, there remain avenues for further research. Future work could explore the integration of BSIF with deep learning frameworks to exploit both handcrafted and learned feature representations. Investigating the impact of demographic and environmental factors on iris texture-based gender classification, as well as extending the approach to multimodal biometric systems, may further enhance performance and generalizability. Moreover, ethical considerations surrounding gender classification in biometrics should be addressed to ensure responsible use.

Overall, the study contributes a new, effective feature representation for iris texture analysis and demonstrates its utility in the challenging task of gender classification, paving the way for more accurate and efficient biometric recognition systems.

title: Non-thermal Higgsino Dark Matter: Cosmological Motivations and Implications for a 125 GeV Higgs
abstract: We investigate the viability of Higgsino-like neutralinos as non-thermal dark matter candidates in light of cosmological constraints and the measured Higgs boson mass near 125 GeV. In minimal supersymmetric scenarios, thermal Higgsinos typically underproduce the observed relic density, motivating mechanisms for non-thermal production, such as late decays of heavy moduli or gravitinos. We analyze the parameter space in which such scenarios are consistent with Big Bang nucleosynthesis, cosmic microwave background limits on energy injection, and current collider bounds. The requirement of a 125 GeV Higgs mass favors heavy scalar superpartners, which naturally suppress unwanted thermal relic production while enhancing compatibility with non-thermal generation. We explore the resulting implications for indirect detection signals, direct detection cross sections, and collider signatures, highlighting the complementarity of astrophysical and laboratory probes. Our results demonstrate that non-thermal Higgsino dark matter remains a compelling possibility in supersymmetric models, linking the Higgs mass measurement to the early-Universe history and motivating targeted searches in upcoming dark matter and collider experiments.
introduction:
The discovery of a Higgs-like boson with a mass near 125 GeV at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has profound implications for theories beyond the Standard Model (SM), particularly supersymmetric (SUSY) extensions. In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), accommodating a Higgs boson of this mass typically requires either heavy scalar top quarks and/or significant left–right stop mixing. These requirements, in turn, suggest a SUSY spectrum that may be heavier than traditionally anticipated in naturalness-driven scenarios. Such a spectrum can have important consequences for the nature and cosmological history of dark matter, especially in frameworks where the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) is a neutralino.

In many SUSY models consistent with a 125 GeV Higgs, the lightest neutralino tends to acquire a substantial Higgsino component. A pure or nearly pure Higgsino LSP with a mass near the electroweak scale is a well-motivated dark matter candidate, possessing gauge interactions that render it thermally under-abundant in the standard cosmological scenario. For Higgsino masses in the range of a few hundred GeV to about 1 TeV, thermal freeze-out typically yields a relic density significantly below the observed dark matter abundance measured by cosmic microwave background experiments such as *Planck*. This under-abundance opens the door for alternative, non-thermal production mechanisms that can replenish the Higgsino population in the early Universe.

Non-thermal dark matter production mechanisms naturally arise in a variety of well-motivated extensions of the standard cosmological history. For instance, in many string-inspired or high-scale supersymmetry-breaking scenarios, scalar fields such as moduli or the gravitino can dominate the energy density of the Universe at late times and decay after the era of Higgsino freeze-out. The decay of such fields can inject both entropy and LSPs, thereby modifying the relic density calculation. Similar effects can occur if the Universe underwent a period of late-time reheating at temperatures below the Higgsino freeze-out temperature. In these cases, the final Higgsino abundance is determined by a competition between production from late decays and annihilation processes that may still be active after reheating.

The cosmological motivations for non-thermal Higgsino dark matter are thus intertwined with the particle physics requirements imposed by the Higgs mass measurement. Accommodating a heavy Higgs within the MSSM often points toward a “split” or “mini-split” SUSY spectrum, in which scalar masses are large while gauginos and Higgsinos can remain relatively light. In such spectra, anomaly-mediated contributions to gaugino masses can place the Higgsino as the lightest electroweakino, with wino and bino states significantly heavier. This mass hierarchy naturally leads to suppressed thermal relic densities for the Higgsino, enhancing the relevance of non-thermal cosmological histories.

The interplay between the Higgs mass, SUSY spectrum, and cosmological evolution has important phenomenological consequences. Non-thermal production can raise the Higgsino relic abundance to the observed value without requiring multi-TeV Higgsino masses, thereby maintaining prospects for detection in upcoming direct and indirect dark matter searches. Moreover, the same late-decaying fields responsible for non-thermal production can generate distinctive imprints on the cosmic microwave background or alter the light element abundances from Big Bang nucleosynthesis, providing complementary constraints. Understanding these connections is critical for interpreting both collider data and cosmological observations in the context of supersymmetric dark matter.

In this work, we explore the cosmological motivations for non-thermal Higgsino dark matter in light of a 125 GeV Higgs, examine the conditions under which late-time production can yield the correct relic density, and discuss the resulting implications for dark matter detection and SUSY phenomenology. Our analysis highlights the importance of embedding Higgsino dark matter scenarios within a complete cosmological framework that consistently links particle physics and early Universe dynamics.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the cosmological viability of non-thermal Higgsino dark matter in light of a Standard Model-like Higgs boson with a mass near 125 GeV. We have argued that in scenarios where thermal relic Higgsinos underproduce the observed dark matter density, late-time decays of heavy fields such as moduli can naturally replenish the Higgsino abundance to the measured value. This mechanism is well-motivated in UV-complete frameworks, including string-inspired models, and is consistent with constraints from big bang nucleosynthesis and cosmic microwave background observations. The resulting dark matter candidates are typically in the TeV or sub-TeV mass range, with annihilation cross sections that can be probed by indirect detection experiments. 

A Higgs mass near 125 GeV points toward heavy scalar superpartners, which in turn favor a Higgsino-like lightest supersymmetric particle through radiative electroweak symmetry breaking. The non-thermal production mechanism reconciles this spectrum with dark matter phenomenology, while preserving gauge coupling unification and accommodating current collider bounds. Future astrophysical observations, together with precision measurements at colliders, will further test this picture. Non-thermal Higgsino dark matter thus emerges as a theoretically motivated and observationally accessible scenario linking early-universe cosmology with the properties of the Higgs sector.

title: Propagation of Highly Efficient Star Formation in NGC 7000
abstract: We present a multiwavelength study of star formation activity in the North America Nebula (NGC 7000) focusing on the spatial and temporal propagation of highly efficient star formation. Using deep near-infrared photometry, mid-infrared archival data, and molecular line observations, we identify a sequence of young stellar objects (YSOs) distributed along dense molecular filaments. Analysis of their evolutionary classes and spatial distribution indicates a clear age gradient, consistent with triggered star formation progressing from the southeast to the northwest. The highest star formation efficiency, exceeding 10%, is found in compact clumps coincident with recent molecular gas compression traced by CO and HCO⁺. The observed morphology and kinematics suggest that an expanding H II region, driven by massive OB stars, is compressing adjacent gas and inducing collapse in pre-existing clumps. Our results support a scenario in which feedback from massive stars initiates sequential star formation, leading to a propagating wave of high-efficiency star formation across NGC 7000.
introduction:
Star formation is a fundamental process shaping the structure and evolution of galaxies, yet its triggering mechanisms and propagation patterns remain subjects of active investigation. In particular, regions of highly efficient star formation provide key laboratories for testing theoretical models, as they offer insight into the interplay between gas dynamics, feedback from young stars, and the large-scale environment of molecular clouds. The North America Nebula (NGC 7000), a prominent emission nebula in the Cygnus region, constitutes a nearby example of an active star-forming complex. Its relative proximity, extended morphology, and association with dense molecular material make it an ideal target to study the spatial and temporal development of star formation activity.

Previous studies have revealed that NGC 7000 is part of a larger complex of ionized and molecular gas, interacting with the adjacent Pelican Nebula (IC 5070). The region hosts a rich population of young stellar objects (YSOs) spanning a broad range of evolutionary stages, from deeply embedded protostars to pre-main-sequence stars with dissipating circumstellar disks. Observations in optical, infrared, and radio wavelengths indicate that the star formation efficiency (SFE) in certain subregions of NGC 7000 is significantly higher than the Galactic average, suggesting that local environmental factors may be promoting rapid gas-to-star conversion. Possible drivers of this enhancement include external triggering by expanding H II regions, sequential star formation along molecular filaments, and compression by large-scale shocks.

The concept of triggered and propagating star formation, in which stellar feedback initiates new episodes of collapse in adjacent gas, has been widely explored in both observational and theoretical contexts. In the case of NGC 7000, the detailed spatial distribution of YSOs and dense gas clumps provides an opportunity to test whether the observed stellar populations are consistent with a scenario of sequential triggering. The elongated arrangement of active star-forming sites, together with age gradients inferred from YSO classifications, hints at a wave of star formation progressing through the cloud. However, a quantitative assessment of the propagation timescales, efficiency, and physical mechanisms requires combining multiwavelength datasets with robust statistical analyses.

Understanding the propagation of highly efficient star formation in NGC 7000 has broader implications for star formation theory. If external feedback is indeed capable of sustaining high SFE over extended regions, this may help explain the origin of stellar clusters and associations in similar Galactic environments. Conversely, if the observed patterns arise primarily from internal cloud dynamics, this would support models in which turbulence and gravitational instability dominate over feedback in regulating star formation. In this work, we present a comprehensive study of NGC 7000, integrating infrared observations, molecular line maps, and YSO population analyses to investigate the spatial and temporal progression of star formation and to evaluate the mechanisms responsible for its apparent efficiency.
conclusion:
Our investigation of the star-forming region in NGC 7000 reveals a coherent picture of sequential, highly efficient star formation propagating through the molecular cloud complex. By combining high-resolution molecular line data with infrared photometry, we have identified spatially distinct subregions at different evolutionary stages, consistent with a progression of triggered star formation from the southeast to the northwest. The observed age gradient among the embedded clusters, together with the morphology of the associated gas, supports a scenario in which feedback from earlier generations of massive stars compresses adjacent dense gas, initiating the collapse of new stellar systems.

The star formation efficiency derived for the most active subregions exceeds typical values for Galactic molecular clouds, indicating that feedback has not only initiated star formation but also enhanced its conversion rate. The correlation between dense gas fraction and young stellar object surface density further underscores the importance of local gas conditions in determining the pace of star formation. The alignment of ionization fronts, shock tracers, and young stellar concentrations points to a causal connection between expanding H II regions and the onset of gravitational collapse.

These findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that large-scale feedback processes can promote, rather than solely inhibit, star formation under favorable conditions. In the case of NGC 7000, the interplay between feedback-driven compression and the pre-existing cloud structure appears to have orchestrated an efficient, wave-like propagation of star formation. Future high-resolution spectroscopic mapping will be essential for constraining the kinematics of the gas and quantifying the timescales involved, thereby refining our understanding of triggered star formation in massive Galactic complexes.

title: Improved surface quality of anisotropically etched silicon {111} planes for mm-scale integrated optics
abstract: We present an improved anisotropic etching process yielding high-quality silicon {111} planes for millimeter-scale integrated optics. Optimized KOH-based etching with controlled temperature and additive chemistry significantly reduces surface roughness. Resulting planes exhibit enhanced optical performance, enabling low-loss waveguide integration. This method supports scalable fabrication of precision silicon photonic and micro-optical components.
introduction:
Silicon micromachining by anisotropic wet etching has become a key enabling technology for the fabrication of high-precision structures in microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and integrated photonic devices. The {111} crystallographic planes of silicon, which emerge naturally during anisotropic etching in alkaline solutions such as potassium hydroxide (KOH) or tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH), are of particular interest due to their low etch rate, high smoothness, and well-defined angular relationship to the wafer surface. These properties make {111} planes especially attractive for applications requiring optically flat surfaces, such as mirrors, waveguide facets, and beam-steering elements in millimeter-scale integrated optics. However, when device dimensions extend to the millimeter range, the stringent surface quality requirements imposed by optical performance metrics become more challenging to meet. Surface roughness, residual etch hillocks, and contamination can lead to scattering losses, degraded reflectivity, and reduced device efficiency.

Although the intrinsic etch anisotropy of silicon in alkaline solutions tends to produce smooth {111} planes, the final surface quality is influenced by numerous factors, including etchant composition, temperature, agitation, mask design, and the presence of impurities. Previous studies have demonstrated that optimizing etching parameters can reduce microroughness, but the literature often focuses on microscale structures, where tolerances are less demanding for optical applications. For millimeter-scale optical components, even sub-nanometer deviations in surface height can have measurable effects on performance, necessitating further refinement of processing techniques.

Recent advances in process control, wafer cleaning protocols, and post-etch treatments offer the potential to significantly improve the optical quality of etched {111} silicon surfaces. For example, the addition of surfactants to the etchant has been shown to suppress hydrogen bubble adhesion, thereby minimizing local etch rate variations. Similarly, post-etch chemical polishing or thermal oxidation followed by oxide removal can reduce residual roughness. Nonetheless, systematic investigations that directly link process parameters to the optical-grade surface quality of large-area {111} planes remain limited.

In this work, we address the challenge of producing millimeter-scale {111} silicon surfaces with improved smoothness suitable for integrated optics. We present a detailed study of anisotropic etching conditions, combined with optimized pre- and post-etch treatments, to achieve surfaces with reduced microroughness and minimal defect density. The resulting improvements in surface quality are quantified using high-resolution profilometry and atomic force microscopy, and the implications for optical device integration are discussed.
conclusion: The present study demonstrates that careful optimization of anisotropic etching parameters can significantly enhance the surface quality of silicon {111} planes, enabling their use in millimeter-scale integrated optics applications. By controlling etchant composition, temperature, and agitation, we achieved reduced roughness and improved planarity, which are critical for minimizing optical scattering and maximizing device performance. The results indicate that the refined etching process yields surfaces with reproducibility suitable for large-scale fabrication, without compromising structural integrity. These advances facilitate more precise alignment and integration of optical components on silicon substrates, expanding the potential for compact, high-performance photonic systems. Future work will focus on further reducing etch-induced defects and integrating this approach with advanced lithographic patterning for complex optical architectures.

title: Fractional Zaslavsky and Henon Discrete Maps
abstract: We investigate fractional generalizations of the Zaslavsky and Hénon discrete maps, introducing memory effects via fractional difference operators. By extending classical discrete dynamical systems to non-integer orders, we capture long-term correlations and nonlocal interactions absent in the standard formulations. Analytical derivations connect the proposed maps to corresponding fractional differential equations, ensuring consistency in the continuous-time limit. Numerical simulations reveal that the fractional order parameter significantly alters stability domains, bifurcation structures, and the onset of chaos. In particular, memory-induced modifications lead to novel attractor geometries and extended transient dynamics. These results provide new insights into the role of memory in nonlinear discrete systems, offering a framework for modeling real-world processes where hereditary effects and complex temporal dependencies are essential.
introduction:
Discrete maps play a central role in the study of nonlinear dynamical systems, providing simplified yet powerful frameworks for understanding complex temporal evolution. By representing time in discrete steps rather than as a continuous variable, such maps are capable of capturing essential features of chaotic motion, bifurcation structures, and transport phenomena while remaining analytically and numerically tractable. Among the most prominent examples are the Zaslavsky map, which emerges in the context of dissipative chaotic systems, and the Hénon map, a paradigmatic two-dimensional area-contracting map originally introduced as a simplified model of the Poincaré section of the Lorenz system. These discrete dynamical systems have been extensively investigated in their classical integer-order forms, revealing a wealth of behaviors that have informed theory and found applications across physics, engineering, and applied mathematics.

In recent decades, the framework of fractional calculus has been increasingly applied to the modeling of dynamical systems. Fractional derivatives and integrals, which generalize the notion of integer-order differentiation and integration to arbitrary non-integer orders, provide a natural means of describing systems with memory and hereditary properties. The inclusion of fractional-order operators in differential equations has led to the development of fractional continuous-time dynamical models capable of capturing long-range temporal correlations and anomalous transport phenomena observed in a variety of complex systems. Extending this perspective to discrete-time systems has resulted in the formulation of fractional discrete maps, in which the state at a given time step depends not only on the immediately preceding state but on a weighted history of past states. This memory effect profoundly alters the dynamics, enriching the structure of attractors and modifying stability and bifurcation properties.

The Zaslavsky map, originally derived from a periodically kicked, weakly dissipative oscillator, serves as an important model for studying chaotic transport in Hamiltonian systems with dissipation, as well as mixing in nonlinear systems. Its fractional generalization has been considered in order to incorporate memory effects into the dynamics of chaotic transport, thereby providing a more realistic representation of physical systems such as plasmas, turbulent fluids, and viscoelastic media. Similarly, the Hénon map, well known for its simple quadratic form and rich chaotic behavior, has also been generalized to fractional orders. The resulting fractional Hénon map exhibits novel dynamical features, including modified route-to-chaos scenarios, altered attractor geometries, and history-dependent stability regimes.

The study of fractional Zaslavsky and fractional Hénon maps is motivated by both theoretical and applied considerations. From a theoretical standpoint, these systems provide an accessible setting to explore the interplay between nonlinearity, dissipation, and memory in discrete-time dynamics. They serve as testbeds for analytical techniques and numerical algorithms tailored to fractional difference equations, and they raise fundamental questions concerning the nature of chaos, ergodicity, and invariant measures in systems with long-range temporal dependencies. From an applied perspective, fractional discrete maps can model processes in which the evolution is inherently discrete but retains a persistent influence from the past, such as in population dynamics with generational memory, iterative learning control in engineering systems, and signal propagation in complex networks with delay and feedback.

Despite growing interest, the literature on fractional versions of well-known discrete maps remains relatively sparse compared to their integer-order counterparts. In particular, a systematic comparison of the fractional Zaslavsky and fractional Hénon maps, including their derivations, numerical implementations, and dynamical properties, is still lacking. Such a comparative analysis can elucidate the role of memory in shaping chaotic transport, attractor formation, and stability boundaries, and can contribute to a deeper understanding of fractional discrete-time systems as a whole.

This work aims to address this gap by presenting a detailed study of the fractional Zaslavsky and Hénon maps, with emphasis on their construction, mathematical properties, and dynamical behaviors. By examining these two archetypal models within a unified fractional framework, we seek to uncover common patterns, distinct features, and potential applications arising from the incorporation of memory into discrete nonlinear dynamics.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the formulation and dynamical properties of fractional generalizations of the Zaslavsky and Hénon discrete maps. By introducing fractional-order memory terms into the classical map equations, we extended their applicability to systems exhibiting long-range temporal correlations and nonlocal interactions. The analysis demonstrates that the inclusion of fractional derivatives alters the phase space structure, leading to qualitatively new behaviors, including modified routes to chaos and the emergence of complex, history-dependent attractors. Numerical simulations confirm that the fractional order acts as a control parameter, influencing stability regions, bifurcation scenarios, and the degree of chaos. Comparisons with the integer-order counterparts highlight the richer dynamical repertoire available in the fractional setting. These results contribute to the growing understanding of discrete-time systems with memory and suggest potential applications in modeling physical, biological, and engineered systems where hereditary effects are significant. Future work may explore analytical stability criteria, higher-dimensional extensions, and experimental validation, further advancing the role of fractional discrete maps as a versatile framework for complex dynamical phenomena.

title: Gaia Data Release 2. Cross-match with external catalogues - Algorithms and results
abstract: We present the algorithms and results of the cross-match between the Gaia Data Release 2 (DR2) catalogue and a selection of major external astronomical surveys. The aim of the cross-match is to provide the scientific community with reliable associations between Gaia sources and their counterparts in other catalogues, enabling multi-wavelength studies and enhancing the scientific exploitation of Gaia data. The adopted methodology combines positional matching with a probabilistic framework that accounts for positional uncertainties, proper motions, source densities, and, when available, photometric information. Dedicated strategies were developed to handle the specific characteristics of each external catalogue, including differences in epoch, astrometric precision, and depth. We describe the validation procedures, which include statistical checks, analysis of sky distributions, and examination of crowded regions. The resulting cross-match tables contain, for each Gaia source, the most probable counterpart(s), associated probabilities, and relevant quality indicators. We present a summary of the achieved completeness and contamination rates, and discuss limitations and caveats. These results provide a robust basis for exploiting Gaia DR2 in combination with complementary surveys across the electromagnetic spectrum.
introduction:
The second data release (DR2) of the European Space Agency’s Gaia mission represents a major milestone in astrometry, photometry, and spectroscopy, providing unprecedented positional and kinematic information for more than 1.6 billion sources across the sky. This wealth of data offers transformative opportunities for a broad range of astrophysical investigations, from studies of stellar populations and Galactic structure to the identification of rare objects. However, to fully exploit Gaia DR2, it is essential to relate its content to existing astronomical knowledge accumulated in external catalogues. Cross-matching Gaia sources with other large surveys enables the combination of complementary measurements, such as multi-wavelength photometry, spectroscopic parameters, and time-domain information, thereby enriching the scientific return.

The cross-identification of sources between Gaia and external catalogues is a challenging task, primarily due to differences in astrometric accuracy, photometric systems, spatial resolution, and survey depth. While Gaia DR2 provides positions with sub-milliarcsecond precision for many sources, external catalogues often have larger positional uncertainties, potentially compounded by epoch differences and the effects of proper motion. Additionally, source confusion in crowded regions, blended detections, and varying selection functions must be carefully addressed to avoid spurious matches and to ensure completeness. The design of robust, efficient, and reproducible cross-match algorithms is therefore critical to producing reliable associations between datasets.

In this context, the Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium (DPAC) has undertaken a systematic effort to cross-match Gaia DR2 with a range of major all-sky and large-area surveys spanning different wavelength domains. The adopted methodology builds upon the experience gained from Gaia DR1, but incorporates significant improvements in the treatment of positional uncertainties, the handling of high proper-motion objects, and the probabilistic assessment of candidate counterparts. The algorithms aim to account for the specific characteristics of each external catalogue, including astrometric reference frames, observational epochs, and magnitude limits, while maintaining a consistent framework that ensures comparability of results across surveys.

The present work describes the algorithms developed for the Gaia DR2 cross-match with external catalogues, as well as the main characteristics of the resulting association tables. We summarise the selection of external datasets, the criteria and statistical models used to identify the most probable counterparts, and the performance metrics that assess the quality of the matches. The resulting cross-match products provide an essential resource for the astronomical community, enabling multi-faceted exploitation of Gaia DR2 and fostering new discoveries through the integration of complementary datasets.
conclusion:
The cross-match results between Gaia Data Release 2 (DR2) and a wide range of external catalogues presented in this work provide an essential resource for the astronomical community, enabling the exploitation of Gaia’s high-precision astrometry, photometry, and, for a subset of sources, radial velocities in conjunction with complementary data. By developing and implementing dedicated algorithms tailored to the characteristics of both Gaia and the various external catalogues, we have aimed to maximise completeness while preserving reliability, taking into account differences in source density, positional uncertainties, magnitude limits, and epoch discrepancies. The methodology adopted, based on a probabilistic approach and incorporating local astrometric error models, has proven effective in mitigating false associations while retaining true counterparts, even in crowded regions and for catalogues with heterogeneous quality.

The resulting cross-match tables are designed to be both robust and flexible, providing users with best-match associations, along with quality indicators and alternative matches where relevant. This enables researchers to adapt their selection to the specific scientific problem at hand, whether the focus is on statistical samples with minimal contamination or on completeness for rare-object searches. The inclusion of detailed documentation and the provision of full match statistics are intended to promote transparency and reproducibility, allowing users to understand the trade-offs inherent in the matching process.

The comparison of Gaia DR2 with multiple surveys spanning different wavelength regimes and scientific domains highlights the broad applicability of the cross-match products. From optical, infrared, and ultraviolet catalogues to spectroscopic and variability surveys, the matched datasets unlock new avenues for multi-wavelength studies, population analyses, and the calibration of astrophysical parameters. The consistent framework applied across all external catalogues ensures that the results can be used in combination, facilitating large-scale, homogeneous investigations.

Nevertheless, limitations remain, rooted in the intrinsic differences between Gaia and the external catalogues, and in the challenges posed by crowded fields, high proper-motion sources, and variable or extended objects. Users are encouraged to consider these factors when interpreting the results, particularly for sources near the detection limits or in complex environments. Future Gaia releases, with improved astrometry, photometry, and extended time baselines, will enable more accurate and complete cross-matches, and the algorithms described here can be refined accordingly.

In summary, the Gaia DR2 cross-match programme delivers a comprehensive, well-characterised set of associations with major astronomical catalogues, grounded in a rigorous and transparent methodology. These products will serve as a cornerstone for a wide range of astrophysical investigations, maximising the scientific return from Gaia by linking its unprecedented dataset to the rich legacy of past and ongoing surveys.

title: ShuffleDet: Real-Time Vehicle Detection Network in On-board Embedded UAV Imagery
abstract: We present ShuffleDet, a lightweight convolutional neural network designed for real-time vehicle detection in on-board embedded UAV imagery. Leveraging the efficiency of ShuffleNet units and modified inception modules, ShuffleDet achieves a favorable balance between detection accuracy and computational cost. The architecture is optimized for deployment on resource-constrained embedded platforms, enabling high frame-rate inference without sacrificing detection performance.
