Extensive experiments on the CARPK and PUCPR+ datasets demonstrate that ShuffleDet attains competitive accuracy while significantly reducing model size and inference time compared to state-of-the-art methods. On an NVIDIA Jetson TX2, the network processes aerial video at over 14 frames per second. These results highlight ShuffleDet’s suitability for real-time traffic monitoring, surveillance, and other UAV-based applications requiring efficient on-board object detection under stringent hardware limitations.
introduction: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have emerged as a cost-effective and flexible platform for traffic monitoring, surveillance, and disaster management. Real-time vehicle detection from UAV imagery is crucial for these applications, yet remains challenging due to factors such as platform motion, varying altitudes, complex backgrounds, and limited computational resources on embedded systems. Traditional object detection models often suffer from high latency or excessive memory demands, making them unsuitable for on-board processing. Recent advances in lightweight convolutional neural networks offer promising solutions, but achieving a balance between detection accuracy and inference speed is non-trivial. In this work, we propose ShuffleDet, a real-time vehicle detection network tailored for embedded UAV platforms, leveraging efficient feature extraction and optimized architecture design to deliver accurate detection under stringent resource constraints.
conclusion: This work presented ShuffleDet, a lightweight and efficient convolutional neural network tailored for real-time vehicle detection in on-board embedded UAV imagery. By leveraging channel shuffle operations and depthwise separable convolutions, the proposed architecture achieves a favorable balance between detection accuracy and computational cost, making it suitable for deployment on resource-constrained aerial platforms. Experimental results on benchmark UAV datasets demonstrate that ShuffleDet delivers competitive detection performance while maintaining high inference speed, enabling reliable operation in dynamic aerial surveillance scenarios. The network’s design facilitates low-latency processing, crucial for time-sensitive applications such as traffic monitoring, disaster response, and security patrols. Additionally, the reduced memory footprint and energy efficiency contribute to prolonged UAV flight times and operational flexibility. Future work will explore further architectural optimizations, domain adaptation techniques for varying environmental conditions, and integration with multi-object tracking frameworks to enhance situational awareness. Overall, ShuffleDet offers a practical and scalable solution for real-time vehicle detection in embedded UAV systems.

title: Step-Indexed Logical Relations for Probability (long version)
abstract: We develop step-indexed logical relations for a higher-order probabilistic programming language with impredicative polymorphism and recursive types. Our construction combines step-indexing with a measure-theoretic treatment of probabilistic choice, enabling reasoning about contextual equivalence in the presence of both recursion and continuous probability distributions. We establish fundamental properties of the relation, including soundness and completeness with respect to contextual equivalence, and demonstrate its applicability through illustrative examples. The step-indexed approach simplifies reasoning about potentially non-terminating computations while accommodating the subtleties of probabilistic behavior, providing a robust semantic framework for verifying program equivalences in expressive probabilistic languages.
introduction:
Probabilistic programming languages have emerged as a powerful paradigm for describing and reasoning about computations that involve uncertainty. By integrating probabilistic choice into the core computational model, these languages enable concise expression of randomized algorithms, statistical inference procedures, and stochastic simulations. The semantic foundations of probabilistic computation have been studied extensively, drawing on ideas from measure theory, domain theory, and operational semantics. Yet, as with their deterministic counterparts, a central challenge remains: how can we reason about program equivalence in a probabilistic setting, especially when higher-order functions, recursion, and rich type structures are present?

Logical relations have long been a robust and compositional method for establishing program equivalence. Originating in the study of parametric polymorphism and type theory, logical relations have been extended to a variety of computational effects, including nontermination, mutable state, and concurrency. For deterministic higher-order languages, step-indexed logical relations have proven particularly effective in handling features such as general recursion, where traditional inductive definitions fail due to circularity. By indexing the relation by a natural number representing a bound on the computation steps, one obtains a well-founded structure that supports inductive reasoning even in the presence of potentially nonterminating computations.

The probabilistic setting introduces new subtleties. First, program equivalence is no longer a simple binary property: the semantics of a probabilistic program is typically given by a distribution over outcomes, and observational equivalence must account for the fact that two programs may produce the same results with different probabilities. Second, when combining probabilistic choice with higher-order functions and recursion, one must reconcile the quantitative nature of probability with the qualitative reasoning patterns of higher-order semantics. Finally, standard relational reasoning techniques must be adapted to capture convergence in distribution and to respect the measure-theoretic structure underlying probabilistic semantics.

Recent work has explored various approaches to logical relations for probabilistic languages. Some approaches adopt metric-space models, interpreting types as metric spaces and programs as non-expansive maps, thereby enabling the use of probabilistic bisimulations and quantitative reasoning. Others develop measure-theoretic logical relations, often requiring sophisticated machinery to handle higher-order functions. However, the combination of step-indexing and probabilistic semantics remains underdeveloped. Step-indexing offers a modular and operationally grounded way of defining relations, which is particularly attractive for languages with both recursion and probabilistic effects. The challenge lies in designing the step-indexed structure so that it faithfully captures probabilistic behavior while retaining the inductive strength needed for proofs.

In this work, we present a framework for step-indexed logical relations tailored to a higher-order probabilistic language with countable probabilistic choice and recursion. Our approach builds on the operational semantics of the language, defining a family of relations indexed by natural numbers that approximate contextual equivalence. The step index bounds the number of probabilistic computation steps under consideration, and the relation is defined so as to respect the probabilistic distribution of results at each step. By carefully structuring the relation, we ensure that increasing the index yields finer approximations, and that the limit coincides with full contextual equivalence.

A key technical contribution is the integration of probability into the step-indexing discipline without collapsing the index to triviality. Naively combining step-indexing with probability can lead to definitions that either fail to be well-founded or fail to be extensional. We address this by defining the relation in terms of probabilistic observations obtained within the step bound, using a form of bounded probabilistic coupling. This allows us to reason inductively on the step index while preserving the necessary measure-theoretic properties. We also show that our relation is compatible with standard type formers, including function types, product types, and recursive types, providing a compositional proof principle for probabilistic program equivalence.

We validate our framework by proving several fundamental properties. First, we establish soundness: if two programs are related at every step index, then they are contextually equivalent. Second, we demonstrate adequacy: the step-indexed relation captures all observable probabilistic behavior as the index tends to infinity. Third, we show that the relation is closed under the standard program constructs, enabling modular reasoning about components. These results are obtained within a syntactic operational framework, avoiding the need for heavy category-theoretic or measure-theoretic machinery in the exposition, though the underlying semantics is consistent with established probabilistic models.

Beyond the theoretical development, our step-indexed logical relations have practical implications. They provide a structured method for reasoning about the equivalence of probabilistic programs, which is essential for compiler correctness, program optimization, and secure information flow in probabilistic settings. The step-indexed approach offers a clear operational intuition, making it accessible to language designers and practitioners who may not be familiar with advanced semantic models.

In summary, this paper develops a step-indexed logical relation for a higher-order probabilistic language with recursion, demonstrating that step-indexing can be successfully adapted to the probabilistic domain. Our results bridge a gap between operational reasoning and probabilistic semantics, offering a compositional and inductive proof method that is both sound and adequate. We believe that this approach opens the door to further extensions, including richer probabilistic effects, continuous distributions, and integration with other computational effects, paving the way for a comprehensive relational theory of probabilistic programming.
conclusion: We have presented a step-indexed logical relations framework for reasoning about probabilistic programming languages, extending traditional step-indexing techniques to accommodate quantitative aspects of computation. By integrating probability measures into the relational structure, our approach supports compositional reasoning about both termination behavior and probabilistic choice. The resulting relations are shown to be sound with respect to contextual equivalence, and we demonstrated their applicability through representative examples involving higher-order functions and recursion. This development bridges a gap between operational semantics for probabilistic languages and denotational or measure-theoretic models, enabling fine-grained, syntax-directed proofs of program equivalence. Future work includes extending the framework to richer probabilistic effects, such as continuous distributions and conditioning, as well as exploring mechanization within proof assistants. Overall, our results illustrate that step-indexed methods can be adapted naturally to reason about complex quantitative properties in higher-order probabilistic computation.

title: A fair comparison of many max-tree computation algorithms (Extended version of the paper submitted to ISMM 2013
abstract: This paper presents an extensive experimental comparison of several state-of-the-art algorithms for computing the max-tree, a hierarchical representation widely used in mathematical morphology for image processing. We review and implement multiple approaches, including flooding-based, union-find, and hybrid strategies, under a unified framework to ensure fairness in evaluation. The study considers both theoretical complexity and practical performance on a diverse set of images, varying in size, dimension, and content. Detailed benchmarks analyse execution time, memory consumption, and scalability. Results highlight the strengths and weaknesses of each method, providing guidance for practitioners and insight into algorithmic behaviour in different application contexts.
introduction:
The max-tree is a hierarchical representation of connected components of thresholded images, widely used in mathematical morphology for tasks such as filtering, segmentation, and shape analysis. By encoding the inclusion relationships between connected components at various gray-level thresholds, the max-tree provides an efficient and compact structure for implementing connected operators that preserve the essential shapes in an image while removing irrelevant details. Over the years, numerous algorithms have been proposed for computing the max-tree, each with different design choices, computational complexities, and memory requirements. These algorithms are often based on concepts such as union-find, flooding simulations, or recursive region growing, and their relative performance can vary significantly depending on the nature of the input data and the implementation details.

Despite the proliferation of approaches, a fair and systematic comparison between existing max-tree construction algorithms has been lacking. Many published performance evaluations are carried out under differing experimental settings, using different datasets, hardware platforms, or stopping criteria, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. In addition, some algorithms have been introduced with a focus on theoretical complexity without an in-depth analysis of their practical behavior, while others are optimized for specific image types or hardware architectures.

This work aims to provide a comprehensive and unbiased comparison of a broad selection of max-tree computation algorithms. We review the theoretical foundations of each method, implement them within a common framework, and evaluate them on a shared set of test images under controlled conditions. By doing so, we seek to clarify the trade-offs between speed, memory consumption, and implementation complexity, and to offer practical guidance for researchers and practitioners selecting a max-tree algorithm for their applications. The extended version presented here includes additional algorithms, experiments, and discussions beyond those reported in the original ISMM 2013 submission.
conclusion: In this work, we presented an extensive and fair comparison of several max-tree computation algorithms, considering both theoretical complexity and practical performance. By evaluating diverse strategies on a wide range of images and sizes, we highlighted the conditions under which each method excels or becomes inefficient. Our results show that no single algorithm dominates in all scenarios; instead, performance depends strongly on image characteristics, implementation details, and available computational resources. This underscores the importance of selecting algorithms according to application-specific constraints rather than relying on general assumptions. Furthermore, the experimental framework and datasets we used can serve as a benchmark for future developments. We hope this comparative study will guide practitioners in making informed choices and motivate further research on more adaptive and scalable max-tree construction techniques.

title: Average balance equations, scale dependence, and energy cascade for granular materials
abstract: We investigate the scale-dependent balance equations governing dense granular materials, focusing on the interplay between translational and rotational degrees of freedom. Using a coarse-graining framework, we derive averaged mass, momentum, and energy balance equations that explicitly account for particle-scale fluctuations and their dependence on the averaging scale. Particular attention is given to the decomposition of the energy budget into translational kinetic, rotational kinetic, and elastic contributions, as well as the fluxes and dissipation terms that mediate energy transfer between scales. Numerical simulations of three-dimensional granular flows under steady shear are employed to evaluate the scale dependence of the balance terms and to quantify the role of collisional and frictional dissipation. The results reveal a clear cascade-like transfer of energy from large-scale mean motion to small-scale fluctuations, where it is ultimately dissipated. The analysis further demonstrates that the scale at which dissipation dominates depends on particle properties and flow regime. These findings provide a unified framework for interpreting granular flow energetics and offer guidance for multiscale modeling strategies.
introduction:
Granular materials, composed of discrete macroscopic particles, are ubiquitous in natural and industrial processes, ranging from geophysical flows such as landslides and sediment transport, to the handling and processing of powders and grains in manufacturing. Despite their apparent simplicity, granular systems exhibit complex behaviors that challenge conventional theoretical frameworks. Depending on the flow regime and the level of agitation, granular assemblies can behave like solids, fluids, or gases, with transitions between these states mediated by particle-scale interactions, dissipation through inelastic collisions or friction, and the emergence of collective structures. Understanding the governing principles of granular dynamics is essential not only for predicting and controlling such systems in engineering contexts, but also for advancing fundamental knowledge of non-equilibrium matter.

A central difficulty in describing granular flows lies in bridging the gap between particle-scale dynamics and continuum-level descriptions. At the microscopic scale, the motion of each grain is governed by Newton’s laws, with forces arising from contact interactions, friction, and possibly cohesive effects. At the macroscopic scale, continuum models based on conservation laws for mass, momentum, and energy are often employed. These models require closure relations—constitutive laws—that encapsulate the effects of unresolved microscopic processes. The development of such closures, and the validation of continuum models, depend critically on understanding how averaged balance equations emerge from the discrete dynamics, and how the form of these equations depends on the spatial and temporal scales over which averaging is performed.

Scale dependence plays a particularly important role in granular materials because of the absence of clear scale separation in many regimes. In inertial granular flows, for example, velocity fluctuations, force chains, and mesoscale structures can coexist over a wide range of scales, complicating the definition of representative volume elements (RVEs) and the interpretation of averaged fields. In addition, granular materials are intrinsically dissipative: kinetic energy is continually converted into heat or other internal modes via inelastic collisions and frictional sliding. This dissipation has profound consequences for the energy budget and for the possibility of energy cascades analogous to those in turbulent fluids. Whereas in classical turbulence kinetic energy injected at large scales cascades to smaller scales before being dissipated by viscosity, granular systems may exhibit more complex pathways, with dissipation occurring at multiple scales and with possible inverse cascades mediated by clustering or coherent structures.

Recent advances in experimental diagnostics, discrete element method (DEM) simulations, and coarse-graining techniques have opened new possibilities for systematically deriving balance equations from particle data and for quantifying scale-dependent effects. The coarse-graining approach, in particular, provides a mathematically consistent framework for transitioning from discrete to continuum descriptions by convolving particle properties with a smoothing kernel of characteristic size. Varying the coarse-graining scale allows one to probe how averaged quantities and their associated fluxes change with resolution, yielding insight into the spatial distribution of sources, sinks, and transfer processes. Such analyses have revealed, for example, that the form of the stress tensor, the partition between translational and rotational modes, and the relative importance of collisional versus kinetic contributions can depend sensitively on the chosen scale.

Within this context, the study of energy cascades in granular media remains at a relatively early stage compared with its counterpart in fluid turbulence. While several works have examined velocity fluctuation spectra and correlations, the precise mechanisms by which energy is transferred across scales—and the interplay between transfer and dissipation—are far from fully understood. The lack of scale invariance in most granular flows, combined with strong anisotropy and inhomogeneity, suggests that the classical picture of a universal inertial range may not apply directly. Instead, one may expect a richer variety of scale-dependent behaviors, potentially requiring generalized cascade concepts that account for the distinctive features of granular interactions.

The present work aims to contribute to this effort by formulating average balance equations for mass, momentum, and energy in granular systems, explicitly incorporating the dependence on coarse-graining scale, and by analyzing the implications for energy transfer and dissipation. By systematically varying the averaging scale in DEM simulations of model granular flows, we investigate how the different terms in the balance equations evolve, identify regimes in which scale-independent behavior emerges, and characterize the pathways of energy cascade and loss. This approach allows us to connect microscale interaction physics with mesoscale and macroscale transport, providing a coherent picture of the multi-scale dynamics of granular materials. Ultimately, such understanding is essential for developing predictive continuum models that faithfully capture the essential physics across scales, and for informing the design and control of granular processes in both natural and engineered systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the average balance equations for granular materials with explicit attention to their dependence on the spatial scale of averaging, and we have discussed the implications of this scale dependence for the description of energy transfer and cascade processes. By systematically applying coarse-graining techniques over a range of averaging volumes, we have shown that the macroscopic fields emerging from microscopic dynamics are not invariant to the choice of scale, but instead exhibit systematic trends that reflect the underlying heterogeneity of granular flows. This behaviour contrasts with that of simple fluids and underscores the importance of selecting, or at least characterising, an appropriate averaging scale in both experimental analyses and numerical simulations.

Our analysis of the energy balance equation reveals that the granular temperature, fluctuation energy fluxes, and collisional dissipation rates are all sensitive to the coarse-graining length. This sensitivity is rooted in the inherently discrete and dissipative nature of grain–grain interactions, which produce strong spatial correlations and intermittent structures. The non-trivial scale dependence of the production and dissipation terms suggests that the energy cascade in granular systems cannot be interpreted as a straightforward analogue of the inertial cascade in classical turbulence. Instead, the cascade is interrupted by dissipation at multiple scales, and the redistribution of fluctuation energy between scales is mediated by both enduring contacts and rapid collisions.

We have further demonstrated that, over an intermediate range of scales, it is possible to define effective transport coefficients and energy fluxes that exhibit approximate scale invariance. This regime provides a useful bridge between the grain-scale physics and the continuum description, offering a foundation for constitutive modelling that incorporates fluctuating energy transport. However, outside this range, either discrete effects at small scales or bulk inhomogeneities at large scales dominate, leading to significant deviations from scale-independent behaviour.

The results presented here emphasise that a full understanding of granular flows requires not only the correct form of the averaged balance equations, but also a careful consideration of the averaging scale itself. The coupling between scale-dependent energy pathways and macroscopic flow properties implies that predictive models must either resolve the relevant range of scales or incorporate explicit scale dependence into their closures.

Future work should seek to generalise these findings to more complex flow geometries, polydisperse systems, and non-spherical particles, as well as to explore the role of external driving and confinement. Such extensions will be essential for constructing a unified framework that links microscopic dynamics, mesoscopic energy transfer, and macroscopic transport in granular materials.

title: Disk Polarization From Both Emission and Scattering of Magnetically Aligned Grains: The Case of NGC 1333 IRAS4A1
abstract: We present high–angular resolution polarimetric observations of the Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS4A1 that reveal polarization signatures arising from both direct thermal emission and dust self–scattering by magnetically aligned grains. Using ALMA Band 6 data at 1.3 mm, we detect a complex polarization morphology within the inner few hundred astronomical units of the disk–envelope system. The polarization pattern shows an azimuthal component consistent with scattering in an inclined, optically thick disk, superposed on a more ordered configuration aligned with the large–scale magnetic field traced in the envelope. We model the observations with radiative transfer calculations incorporating both magnetically aligned, non–spherical grains and scattering by large dust particles. The results indicate that grain alignment with the magnetic field dominates the polarization at lower optical depths and larger radii, while dust self–scattering becomes significant in the dense, inner disk where grain growth to millimeter sizes is likely. The coexistence of these mechanisms within a single system produces a wavelength–dependent and spatially varying polarization morphology, which can account for apparent deviations from simple magnetic field tracing in young disks. Our analysis constrains the maximum grain size to be on the order of a few hundred microns in the scattering regions, and suggests a magnetic field geometry that remains largely poloidal in the envelope but may be modified by rotation and infall within the disk. These findings demonstrate the importance of including both emission from aligned grains and scattering in interpreting protostellar polarization, and they provide new insights into dust evolution and magnetic field structure in the earliest stages of star formation.
introduction:
Polarized thermal dust emission has emerged as a powerful probe of magnetic fields in star-forming regions. In particular, high-resolution polarimetric observations with facilities such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) have revealed complex polarization morphologies in protostellar disks and envelopes. Traditionally, such polarization has been attributed to thermal emission from non-spherical dust grains aligned with respect to the local magnetic field via radiative alignment torques (RATs). Under this paradigm, the polarization orientation traces the projected magnetic field structure, offering insight into the role of magnetism in disk formation and evolution. However, recent studies have demonstrated that additional mechanisms, notably dust self-scattering, can also produce significant polarized emission, especially in optically thick regions with large grains. This recognition has prompted a re-evaluation of polarization interpretations, as scattering-induced polarization depends on the anisotropy of the radiation field rather than directly on the magnetic field geometry.

The Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS4A1, located in the Perseus molecular cloud, presents a particularly interesting case. Previous interferometric observations at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths have revealed a compact disk-like structure embedded within a dense envelope, with polarization patterns that cannot be explained by a single mechanism alone. The coexistence of conditions favorable to both magnetic grain alignment and scattering—such as strong magnetic fields, high optical depths, and evidence for significant grain growth—makes IRAS4A1 an ideal laboratory to study the interplay of these processes.

In this work, we investigate the polarization properties of IRAS4A1 by modeling contributions from both direct emission of magnetically aligned grains and scattering by large, potentially aligned grains. By comparing synthetic polarization maps with existing high-resolution observations, we aim to disentangle the relative importance of each mechanism and assess their implications for the interpretation of disk polarization in young stellar objects. This approach advances our understanding of dust physics and magnetic field diagnostics in the earliest stages of star formation.
conclusion: We have investigated the polarization properties of the Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS4A1, considering the combined contributions from thermal emission and dust self-scattering by magnetically aligned grains. Our analysis demonstrates that both mechanisms can operate simultaneously in the inner disk, with their relative strengths depending sensitively on grain size distribution, magnetic field geometry, and viewing inclination. The observed polarization morphology and fraction are best reproduced when elongated grains, aligned with a poloidal or toroidal magnetic field, emit thermally while also producing a significant scattering signal at submillimeter wavelengths. This hybrid scenario naturally explains polarization vectors that deviate from purely azimuthal or radial patterns, as well as modest polarization fractions that would be difficult to obtain from either mechanism alone. The results imply that magnetic alignment remains effective in high-density, optically thick regions, and that scattering can be a non-negligible contributor to the polarized flux even in the presence of aligned grains. This has important consequences for interpreting polarization as a magnetic field tracer in young disks, highlighting the need for multi-wavelength, high-resolution observations to disentangle the two mechanisms. Future modeling incorporating realistic grain alignment physics and disk structure will be essential to fully constrain the magnetic field topology and dust properties in deeply embedded protostellar systems.

title: Schwarzschild solution of the modified Einstein field equations
abstract: We investigate the Schwarzschild solution within the framework of modified Einstein field equations incorporating additional curvature-dependent terms. Starting from a generalized action, we derive the corresponding field equations and examine static, spherically symmetric vacuum configurations. Analytical integration yields a metric that reduces to the standard Schwarzschild form in the appropriate limit, while deviations emerge at small or large radial scales, depending on the modification parameters. We analyze the resulting horizon structure, singularity properties, and asymptotic behavior. Potential implications for astrophysical observations and constraints from classical tests of general relativity are briefly discussed, highlighting avenues for further theoretical refinement.
introduction:
The Schwarzschild solution occupies a central position in the study of general relativity, representing the simplest exact solution to Einstein’s field equations that describes the spacetime geometry outside a static, spherically symmetric, non-rotating mass. Since its original derivation in 1916, this solution has provided the theoretical foundation for the description of astrophysical objects such as planets, stars, and black holes, and has served as a benchmark for understanding gravitational phenomena in the absence of matter outside a central source. The classical Schwarzschild metric arises from the Einstein field equations in vacuum, \(R_{\mu\nu} - \frac{1}{2} R g_{\mu\nu} = 0\), and its predictions, including the existence of an event horizon and the gravitational redshift of light, have been extensively confirmed by experimental and observational evidence.

In recent decades, there has been increasing interest in modifications to the Einstein field equations, motivated by both theoretical and observational considerations. On the theoretical side, general relativity, though remarkably successful, is widely regarded as an effective theory that must be reconciled with quantum mechanics at high energies. Various approaches to quantum gravity, including string theory, loop quantum gravity, and semiclassical corrections, suggest the possibility of higher-order curvature terms, nonlocal modifications, or additional fields coupled to gravity. On the observational side, phenomena such as the accelerated expansion of the universe, galactic rotation curves, and the inferred presence of dark matter and dark energy have prompted the exploration of alternative or extended gravitational theories that might explain these effects without invoking exotic forms of matter.

Modified Einstein field equations can emerge from a variety of frameworks, such as \(f(R)\) gravity, scalar–tensor theories, Gauss–Bonnet corrections, and nonminimal matter–geometry couplings. In many of these theories, the vacuum equations differ from their general relativity counterparts, leading to different spacetime geometries even in the presence of the same symmetry assumptions. Understanding how the Schwarzschild solution is altered in such contexts is essential for assessing the viability of these modifications, since solar system tests and astrophysical observations impose stringent constraints on deviations from the general relativistic predictions.

The study of spherically symmetric solutions in modified gravity serves multiple purposes. First, it provides insight into the structural stability of the Schwarzschild geometry under theoretical deformations of the underlying field equations. Second, it enables the derivation of phenomenological consequences—such as corrections to perihelion precession, light deflection, and gravitational time delay—that can be compared with precision measurements. Third, it offers a pathway to investigate the nature of black holes and compact objects in alternative gravitational frameworks, potentially revealing differences in horizon structure, singularity formation, and thermodynamic properties.

In the present work, we examine the Schwarzschild-like solutions arising from a specific class of modified Einstein field equations. Our approach preserves the assumptions of staticity and spherical symmetry, enabling a direct comparison with the classical Schwarzschild metric. We will derive the modified field equations from the chosen gravitational action, identify the resulting metric functions, and analyze their dependence on the parameters characterizing the modification. Special attention will be given to the conditions under which the solution reduces exactly to the Schwarzschild metric, thereby recovering general relativity as a limiting case.

The motivation for this analysis is twofold. From a theoretical standpoint, exact solutions play a crucial role in revealing the internal consistency and mathematical structure of gravitational theories. They also serve as starting points for perturbative studies and for embedding local solutions into cosmological backgrounds. From a phenomenological standpoint, the compatibility of modified gravity with well-tested regimes—such as the solar system—requires that deviations from the Schwarzschild geometry be either absent or sufficiently small, making the analysis of these solutions a decisive step in testing the theory.

This investigation thus contributes to the broader effort of mapping the landscape of possible spacetime geometries permitted by modified gravity theories. By systematically deriving and interpreting the Schwarzschild solution within a modified framework, we aim to clarify the extent to which general relativity’s predictions are robust, and to identify potential signatures that could be probed by current or future experiments. The results obtained may have implications for both fundamental theory and observational astrophysics, reinforcing the pivotal role of exact solutions in gravitational physics.
conclusion: In this work, we have derived and discussed the Schwarzschild solution within the framework of the modified Einstein field equations, highlighting the deviations from the classical general relativity case. Our analysis shows how the introduced modifications alter the spacetime geometry, particularly in the vicinity of the event horizon, and may lead to measurable effects in strong-field regimes. The limiting case recovers the standard Schwarzschild metric, ensuring consistency with well-tested predictions in the weak-field domain. These results provide a basis for further theoretical and observational studies aimed at probing gravitational phenomena beyond general relativity, and demonstrate the utility of exact solutions in assessing the physical implications of alternative gravitational theories.

title: Global solutions to general polynomial benchmark optimization problems
abstract: We present a unified framework for obtaining global solutions to general polynomial benchmark optimization problems. Leveraging advances in polynomial optimization and semidefinite programming, our approach efficiently handles nonconvexity and scalability challenges. Extensive computational experiments on established benchmark instances demonstrate superior performance, delivering globally optimal solutions with improved accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.
introduction: Polynomial optimization problems (POPs) arise in diverse scientific and engineering contexts, encompassing control, signal processing, and operations research. Solving general POPs to global optimality is challenging due to their nonconvex nature and potential high dimensionality. Benchmark instances play a crucial role in evaluating and comparing solution algorithms. This work addresses global solutions to general polynomial benchmark optimization problems, presenting methods that exploit algebraic structure, convex relaxations, and computational advances. Our study aims to provide insights into performance, scalability, and practical applicability of modern global optimization techniques.
conclusion: This study has explored global solution strategies for general polynomial benchmark optimization problems, integrating theoretical advances with empirical evaluation. By leveraging structured polynomial properties and advanced global optimization algorithms, we demonstrated improved accuracy, robustness, and scalability across diverse benchmark sets. The proposed framework effectively balances computational efficiency with solution quality, offering a reliable approach for complex, high-dimensional problems. Our results highlight the potential for extending these methods to broader classes of nonconvex optimization tasks. Future work will focus on enhancing algorithmic efficiency, incorporating parallelization, and addressing uncertainty in real-world polynomial optimization applications.

title: Quantum transport in graphene Hall bars: Effects of vacancy disorder
abstract: We investigate quantum transport in graphene Hall bar structures in the presence of vacancy-induced disorder using a tight-binding framework combined with the Landauer–Büttiker formalism. Vacancies are introduced with controlled concentrations and spatial distributions to model realistic defect scenarios, and their impact on electronic transport properties is systematically analyzed. Numerical calculations reveal that even low vacancy densities lead to pronounced modifications of the conductance quantization, with the suppression or broadening of Hall plateaus and the emergence of localized states near the Dirac point. The breaking of sublattice symmetry by vacancies induces intervalley scattering, which enhances backscattering and reduces carrier mobility. We further examine the interplay between magnetic field strength and disorder, finding that stronger fields partially mitigate the disorder effects by reinforcing Landau level formation, though significant deviations from the ideal quantum Hall regime persist at higher defect densities. Our results provide quantitative insight into the mechanisms by which atomic-scale disorder degrades topological transport signatures in graphene, offering guidance for interpreting experimental measurements and for engineering devices with improved robustness against structural imperfections.
introduction:
Graphene, a two-dimensional allotrope of carbon with a honeycomb lattice structure, has attracted immense interest since its experimental isolation due to its exceptional electronic, mechanical, and thermal properties. Its low-energy quasiparticles are described by a massless Dirac equation, leading to a linear energy dispersion near the charge neutrality point and unconventional charge transport phenomena. Among these, the quantum Hall effect (QHE) in graphene exhibits an anomalous sequence of Hall plateaus, reflecting the chiral nature and Berry phase of its carriers. Such properties make graphene a promising platform for both fundamental studies of relativistic-like quasiparticles in condensed matter systems and potential applications in nanoelectronics, spintronics, and quantum metrology.

Electronic transport in realistic graphene devices is inevitably influenced by disorder originating from various sources, including charged impurities, substrate-induced potential fluctuations, ripples, adatoms, and lattice defects. Among the latter, atomic vacancies—missing carbon atoms in the lattice—are of particular interest because they act as strong short-range scatterers. Such defects can be introduced during fabrication, irradiation, or chemical processing, and they profoundly affect the local electronic structure by generating resonant states near the Dirac point. Vacancy-induced disorder not only modifies the density of states but also impacts both semiclassical and quantum transport regimes. Understanding these effects is crucial for interpreting experimental measurements and for engineering graphene’s electronic response in practical devices.

The Hall bar geometry, widely employed in transport studies, offers a controlled framework for probing the interplay between disorder and quantum transport under magnetic fields. In clean graphene Hall bars, the QHE manifests through well-defined Landau levels and robust edge state transport, leading to quantized Hall conductance plateaus and vanishing longitudinal resistance at low temperatures. Introducing vacancy disorder into such systems can disrupt edge states, induce backscattering, and facilitate localization phenomena, thereby modifying the quantization sequence and the width of Hall plateaus. Moreover, at high defect concentrations, the Landau level spectrum itself may be significantly broadened or even suppressed, altering the overall magnetotransport behavior.

Previous theoretical and experimental efforts have examined the influence of various disorder types on graphene’s QHE, including long-range potential fluctuations and adatom-induced scattering. However, a systematic investigation of vacancy disorder effects in graphene Hall bars—particularly in the quantum transport regime—remains incomplete. Tight-binding simulations, combined with Landauer–Büttiker formalism and Green’s function techniques, offer a powerful route to explore these effects at the atomic scale, capturing both the microscopic scattering processes and the macroscopic conductance response.

In this work, we investigate quantum transport in graphene Hall bar devices in the presence of vacancy disorder under perpendicular magnetic fields. By employing large-scale numerical calculations within a nearest-neighbor tight-binding framework, we analyze how varying vacancy concentration influences the formation of Landau levels, the stability of edge states, and the quantization of Hall conductance. Our results reveal distinct regimes of disorder-induced degradation of the QHE and provide insights into the mechanisms by which atomic-scale defects control magnetotransport in graphene. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of disorder effects in two-dimensional Dirac materials and has implications for the design and optimization of graphene-based quantum devices.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the influence of vacancy-induced disorder on quantum transport in graphene Hall bar devices, with a particular focus on the interplay between disorder strength, spatial distribution of vacancies, and the resulting modifications to the Hall conductance and longitudinal resistance. By employing a tight-binding framework combined with Green’s function techniques, we have systematically analyzed how mono- and di-vacancies alter the characteristic signatures of the quantum Hall regime in both low- and high-field limits.

Our results demonstrate that even relatively low concentrations of vacancies can lead to significant broadening and distortion of Landau levels, accompanied by the emergence of localized states within the spectral gaps. These localized states mediate backscattering processes that weaken the robustness of the quantized Hall plateaus. For monovacancies, which break sublattice symmetry locally, the alterations to the density of states are more pronounced near the Dirac point, leading to an accelerated decay of the zero-energy Hall plateau. In contrast, divacancies, being more symmetric defects, induce less severe sublattice imbalance but still contribute to scattering and plateau suppression at higher energies.

We have also shown that the spatial distribution of vacancies plays a critical role in determining the transport response. Uniformly distributed vacancies tend to produce homogeneous broadening of transport features, while clustering of defects can induce percolation-like pathways for backscattering, leading to abrupt deviations from quantized conductance. This sensitivity to vacancy arrangement suggests that microscopic disorder configurations must be considered when interpreting experimental deviations from ideal quantum Hall behavior in real graphene samples.

At high magnetic fields, the disorder-induced mixing of edge and bulk states becomes particularly relevant. Our simulations reveal that vacancies located near the sample edges are especially effective at coupling counter-propagating channels, thereby enhancing longitudinal dissipation without completely destroying the Hall quantization. This finding underscores the intricate balance between edge-state protection and disorder-mediated scattering in topologically nontrivial transport regimes.

From a broader perspective, our study highlights that vacancy disorder, an almost unavoidable feature in realistic graphene devices due to fabrication and processing steps, can exert a nontrivial and tunable influence on quantum Hall transport. The dependence of the transport signatures on defect type, concentration, and spatial arrangement opens potential avenues for engineering graphene’s electronic response through controlled defect introduction. Conversely, understanding these effects is crucial for mitigating disorder in applications where precise quantization is required, such as resistance standards.

Future work could extend the present analysis by including electron–electron interactions, finite-temperature effects, and more complex forms of disorder, such as ripples or adatoms, to build a more comprehensive picture of transport in realistic graphene Hall bars. Furthermore, experimental correlation between controlled irradiation-induced vacancies and transport measurements would be invaluable for validating and refining the theoretical predictions presented here.

title: Bianchi type-I model with cosmic string in the presence of a magnetic field: spinor description
abstract: We investigate a Bianchi type-I cosmological model containing a cloud of cosmic strings in the presence of a magnetic field, employing a spinor field description. The Einstein field equations are formulated with an appropriate energy–momentum tensor incorporating both string and electromagnetic contributions. Exact solutions are derived under specific assumptions for the spinor field nonlinearity. The influence of the magnetic field and spinor dynamics on the anisotropic evolution is analyzed, revealing conditions for isotropization and the impact on the universe’s expansion rate.
introduction:
Anisotropic cosmological models have attracted considerable attention in recent decades as they provide a framework for exploring deviations from the high degree of isotropy observed in the present-day Universe. Among such models, the Bianchi type-I spacetime represents the simplest generalization of the flat Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric, allowing for anisotropic expansion along mutually orthogonal spatial directions while retaining homogeneity. This class of models serves as an effective theoretical laboratory for studying the influence of various physical fields and topological defects in the early Universe, where anisotropies may have played a significant role in cosmic evolution.

Topological defects, such as cosmic strings, are predicted to arise during symmetry-breaking phase transitions in the early Universe, as suggested by grand unified theories. These one-dimensional objects can have significant gravitational effects, potentially leaving imprints on the large-scale structure and cosmic microwave background. While observational constraints indicate that a cosmic string network, if it exists, must contribute only a small fraction to the present energy density, their role in the early Universe remains an open question. Modeling cosmic strings within anisotropic cosmologies provides an avenue to study their dynamical influence under general relativistic conditions.

In addition to cosmic strings, the presence of large-scale magnetic fields in the Universe is well established through astrophysical observations. Although their origin is still debated, primordial magnetic fields could have been generated during early phase transitions or inflationary processes. Such fields, if present in the early Universe, might have interacted with matter and topological defects, potentially affecting the expansion dynamics and anisotropy dissipation. The combined consideration of cosmic strings and magnetic fields in anisotropic spacetimes thus offers an enriched model for probing early-Universe physics.

Spinor fields present another compelling ingredient in cosmological modeling. Originally introduced in particle physics to describe fermionic matter, spinor fields have been successfully applied in cosmology to represent matter sources with intrinsic degrees of freedom not captured by scalar or vector fields. A spinor description allows for a unified and self-consistent treatment of matter that can incorporate elastic properties of strings and possible couplings to electromagnetic fields.

The present work focuses on a Bianchi type-I cosmological model containing a cloud of cosmic strings in the presence of a magnetic field, with the matter content described by a nonlinear spinor field. By analyzing the coupled Einstein–Maxwell–Dirac system, we aim to investigate the interplay between anisotropy, topological defects, magnetic effects, and spinor dynamics in shaping the evolution of the early Universe.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated a Bianchi type-I cosmological model with a cloud of cosmic strings in the presence of a magnetic field, employing a spinor field description. The formalism allowed us to express the dynamical effects of strings and magnetism in terms of spinor bilinear invariants, providing a unified treatment. The influence of the magnetic field was shown to affect the anisotropic expansion, while the spinor representation offered an efficient description of the string energy–momentum tensor. Our results suggest that such models can yield viable anisotropic cosmologies and may shed light on early-universe dynamics involving topological defects and fields.

title: Phase diagram of the dissipative quantum particle in a box
abstract: We investigate the phase diagram of a quantum particle confined in a one-dimensional box and linearly coupled to a dissipative environment. Using path-integral Monte Carlo simulations complemented by analytical scaling arguments, we characterize the interplay between confinement, quantum fluctuations, and Ohmic dissipation. Our results reveal a sharp crossover between delocalized and localized regimes, controlled by the dissipation strength and the box size. We identify critical parameters governing the suppression of quantum coherence and the emergence of classical-like behavior. The findings provide a unified framework for understanding dissipative confinement in mesoscopic systems, with implications for quantum control and decoherence engineering.
introduction:
The study of quantum particles subject to dissipation has attracted considerable attention over the past several decades, as it lies at the intersection of fundamental quantum mechanics, statistical physics, and condensed matter theory. In particular, the interplay between coherent quantum dynamics and coupling to an external environment gives rise to rich physical behaviour, including decoherence, localization, and nontrivial phase transitions. A paradigmatic framework for such investigations is provided by the Caldeira–Leggett model, in which a quantum particle interacts linearly with a bath of harmonic oscillators representing environmental degrees of freedom. This approach has proven successful in describing a variety of physical systems, ranging from Josephson junctions and nanomechanical resonators to quantum dots and cold-atom setups.

While much of the early work on dissipative quantum systems focused on free particles or particles in periodic potentials, relatively less attention has been devoted to confined geometries, such as the quantum particle in a box. The particle-in-a-box problem is one of the simplest and most instructive models in quantum mechanics, illustrating the role of boundary conditions in quantizing energy levels and shaping wave functions. Introducing dissipation into this otherwise textbook problem raises fundamental questions about how environmental coupling modifies confinement-induced quantization, energy spectra, and the nature of eigenstates. Moreover, it provides a controlled setting for exploring the competition between quantum fluctuations, boundary effects, and dissipative suppression of motion.

From a theoretical perspective, the dissipative particle in a box offers a novel arena for studying quantum phase diagrams in a finite geometry. Dissipation can be characterized by a spectral density, with ohmic, sub-ohmic, and super-ohmic baths leading to qualitatively different dynamics. In the ohmic case, for instance, the system can exhibit a quantum phase transition from a delocalized phase, where the particle explores the entire box, to a localized phase, where it becomes trapped near a given position due to strong coupling to the environment. Such transitions have analogies with the localization transition in the spin–boson model and the pinning of a particle in a periodic potential, but the presence of hard-wall boundaries introduces distinctive features absent in translationally invariant systems.

Recent developments in numerical renormalization group techniques, path-integral Monte Carlo simulations, and variational methods have made it possible to explore the full phase diagram of dissipative quantum systems with increasing accuracy. These tools allow for the systematic investigation of how the coupling strength, bath exponent, and temperature influence the ground-state properties and dynamical response of the particle in a box. They also enable the characterization of crossover phenomena, finite-size scaling behaviour, and the emergence of new phases or regimes in parameter space.

Beyond their intrinsic theoretical interest, studies of the dissipative particle in a box may find relevance in experimental contexts where quantum degrees of freedom are confined and coupled to complex environments. Examples include electrons in quantum dots connected to resistive leads, atoms trapped in optical boxes with engineered dissipation, and superconducting qubits in tailored electromagnetic environments. Understanding the phase structure of such systems is crucial for controlling decoherence, optimizing quantum control protocols, and engineering desired quantum states.

In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of the phase diagram of a dissipative quantum particle confined in a box. We focus on the dependence of the system’s phases on the dissipation strength and spectral properties of the bath, elucidating the mechanisms driving localization–delocalization transitions and the role of finite-size effects. Our results provide insight into the fundamental physics of dissipation in confined geometries and contribute to the broader effort to map and understand quantum phase diagrams in open systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the phase diagram of a quantum particle confined in a one-dimensional box and subject to dissipative coupling to an external environment. By combining analytical arguments with numerical analysis, we have elucidated how the interplay between quantum confinement, dissipation strength, and temperature gives rise to distinct dynamical regimes. Our study extends previous treatments of dissipative quantum systems by explicitly incorporating the hard-wall boundary conditions of the box, allowing us to resolve features in the phase diagram that are absent in translationally invariant models such as the dissipative free particle.

We have shown that dissipation induces a crossover from a delocalized quantum regime, in which coherent motion is preserved over the scale of the box, to a localized regime characterized by strong suppression of tunnelling between spatial regions. At zero temperature, this crossover sharpens into a quantum phase transition as the dissipation strength exceeds a critical value, consistent with the known localization transition in related Caldeira–Leggett-type models. However, the finite spatial extent of the box modifies the critical behaviour, introducing size-dependent scaling that we have quantified. At finite temperatures, thermal fluctuations compete with dissipation, leading to a smoothening of the transition and the emergence of a rich structure in the phase diagram, where quantum coherent, thermally activated, and overdamped regimes can be clearly distinguished.

Our results highlight the crucial role of confinement in modifying dissipative quantum dynamics, with implications for mesoscopic and cold-atom systems where environmental coupling and boundary effects are both significant. The finite-size scaling analysis we have presented provides a framework for interpreting experimental data in such systems and for predicting how coherence properties degrade with increasing dissipation. Moreover, our findings suggest that controlled variation of the box size and bath coupling offers a route to engineer specific quantum-to-classical crossovers.

Future work could extend the present approach to higher-dimensional geometries, more structured environments, or time-dependent confining potentials, which may reveal further nontrivial features in the phase diagram. The methodology developed here is also amenable to inclusion of particle–particle interactions, potentially opening a path toward understanding dissipative many-body confinement. In summary, the phase diagram we have obtained provides a comprehensive map of the regimes accessible to a dissipative quantum particle in a box, bridging theoretical predictions and experimentally relevant parameter ranges.

title: GWU NLP Lab at SemEval-2019 Task 3: EmoContext: Effective Contextual Information in Models for Emotion Detection in Sentence-level in a Multigenre Corpus
abstract: We describe the GWU NLP Lab submission to SemEval-2019 Task 3: EmoContext, which focuses on detecting emotions in textual conversations by leveraging contextual information. Our approach integrates sentence-level representations with context from preceding utterances to improve classification across multiple genres. We explore recurrent neural networks and transformer-based encoders, incorporating attention mechanisms to model dependencies between conversational turns. Experimental results demonstrate that including contextual cues significantly enhances performance over utterance-only baselines. Our best system achieves competitive results on the official benchmark, highlighting the benefit of explicit context modeling for emotion detection. We also provide an analysis of errors and genre-specific challenges encountered.
introduction: Understanding emotions expressed in text is a critical component of natural language understanding, with applications ranging from sentiment analysis and dialogue systems to mental health monitoring and social media analysis. However, emotion detection presents unique challenges, as emotions are often conveyed implicitly and depend heavily on contextual cues beyond the sentence level. In particular, short, informal, and conversational texts—common in social media and chat platforms—frequently require consideration of surrounding utterances to accurately interpret emotional content. The SemEval-2019 Task 3: EmoContext competition focuses on this challenge by providing a multigenre corpus of short dialogues annotated for emotions such as happy, sad, angry, and others, requiring systems to classify the emotion of the last utterance given its conversational context. This task emphasizes the importance of modeling contextual information effectively to capture nuanced shifts in meaning and sentiment. In this work, we present the GWU NLP Lab’s approach to the EmoContext task, exploring multiple neural architectures and strategies for integrating contextual signals, and demonstrating that context-aware models substantially improve emotion classification performance in conversational settings.
conclusion: In this work, we presented the GWU NLP Lab system for SemEval-2019 Task 3, focusing on emotion detection in textual conversations. Our approach emphasized leveraging contextual information within multi-turn dialogues, combining deep learning architectures and pretrained embeddings to capture nuanced emotional cues. Experimental results demonstrated that incorporating surrounding utterances significantly improves classification performance across multiple genres. The findings highlight the importance of modeling conversational context for robust emotion recognition. Future work will explore richer dialogue representations, domain adaptation techniques, and integration of external knowledge sources to further enhance generalization and performance in diverse conversational and affective computing applications.

title: New results on Mesonic Weak Decay of $p$-shell $\Lambda$-Hypernuclei
abstract: We report new measurements of the mesonic weak decay of $p$-shell $\Lambda$-hypernuclei, obtained with high-resolution detection techniques at an electron beam facility. The $\pi^{-}$ momentum spectra were reconstructed for several hypernuclear species, allowing precise determination of partial decay widths. Our results improve the accuracy of previous measurements and extend the available data to higher mass members of the $p$-shell. Comparison with shell-model calculations including $\Lambda$–nucleon and pion–nucleus final-state interactions shows good overall agreement, while indicating the need for refined treatment of nuclear medium effects. These findings provide stringent constraints on theoretical models of the $\Lambda$ weak decay process, contributing to a deeper understanding of hypernuclear structure and the interplay between mesonic and non-mesonic decay channels.
introduction: The study of mesonic weak decay (MWD) of $\Lambda$-hypernuclei provides essential insights into the weak interaction in the nuclear medium and the modification of hadronic properties in bound systems. In $p$-shell hypernuclei, where the $\Lambda$ hyperon is bound to light and medium-mass nuclear cores, MWD competes with non-mesonic decay channels, with its rate strongly influenced by the Pauli suppression of low-momentum decay nucleons. Precise measurements of MWD spectra and branching ratios offer stringent tests for theoretical models incorporating nuclear structure effects, $\Lambda N$ interactions, and pion final-state interactions. Recent experimental advances, particularly in high-resolution spectroscopy and large-acceptance detection systems, have enabled more accurate determinations of pion momenta and decay widths. These developments motivate a re-examination of MWD in $p$-shell $\Lambda$-hypernuclei, aiming to clarify the role of nuclear medium modifications on decay dynamics. In this work, we present new experimental results and compare them with state-of-the-art theoretical predictions.
conclusion: The present study has provided new measurements of mesonic weak decay rates in $p$-shell $\Lambda$-hypernuclei, improving the precision of existing data and extending the range of investigated isotopes. The results confirm the strong suppression of the $\pi^{-}$ decay mode with increasing nuclear mass and support theoretical predictions based on the Pauli blocking mechanism and nuclear structure effects. Comparison with shell-model calculations shows overall agreement, while small deviations point to the need for refined treatments of nuclear medium effects. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of hypernuclear weak decay dynamics and their role in baryon–baryon interaction studies.

title: Quantum metrology with generalized cat states
abstract: We investigate the potential of generalized Schrödinger cat states for quantum metrology, focusing on their phase estimation capabilities beyond the standard quantum limit. By extending the notion of optical cat states to superpositions of coherent states with arbitrary relative phases and amplitudes, we derive analytical expressions for the quantum Fisher information and identify regimes where these states achieve near-Heisenberg scaling. Our analysis reveals that appropriately engineered generalized cat states can outperform both classical coherent states and standard even/odd cat states under realistic photon loss, retaining enhanced sensitivity in the presence of decoherence. We further explore optimal parameter choices, showing how the interplay between coherent amplitude and superposition phase determines robustness and metrological gain. Numerical simulations of interferometric phase estimation confirm our theoretical predictions and highlight the feasibility of practical implementations with current or near-term photonic platforms. These results broaden the applicability of nonclassical superposition states in precision measurement and open new avenues for tailoring quantum resources to specific sensing tasks.
introduction:
Quantum metrology exploits uniquely quantum mechanical features, such as superposition and entanglement, to enhance the precision of parameter estimation beyond the limits achievable with classical resources. By harnessing nonclassical states of light or matter, it is possible to reach the so‑called Heisenberg limit, where the estimation error scales inversely with the total number of particles or resources employed, surpassing the standard quantum limit (SQL) that governs classical interferometry. Among the various nonclassical states proposed for quantum metrology, Schrödinger cat states—superpositions of macroscopically distinguishable coherent states—have attracted considerable attention due to their potential to achieve Heisenberg‑limited sensitivity while being relatively accessible in certain experimental platforms.

The canonical optical cat state is a coherent superposition of two coherent states with opposite phases, often written as \(|\alpha\rangle + |-\alpha\rangle\). These states exhibit interference fringes in phase space and possess quantum coherence between macroscopically distinct components, features that can be exploited for precise phase estimation in interferometric schemes. However, the idealized cat state is only one member of a broader family of superpositions that can be engineered by altering the relative amplitudes, phases, or the number and arrangement of the constituent coherent states. Generalized cat states, which may include multi‑component superpositions, asymmetric amplitudes, or displaced and rotated variants, offer a richer parameter space for tailoring quantum resources to specific metrological tasks.

Recent theoretical and experimental progress has demonstrated the feasibility of generating generalized cat states in various physical systems, including optical cavities, superconducting microwave circuits, and trapped ions. In parallel, there has been growing interest in understanding how these generalized states perform under realistic conditions, such as photon loss, dephasing, and other decoherence mechanisms that inevitably degrade quantum advantages. While the metrological power of ideal cat states is well established, the extent to which generalized cat states can improve robustness to noise, extend the dynamic range, or simplify state preparation remains an open question.

The study of generalized cat states in quantum metrology is motivated by several factors. First, by tuning the structure of the superposition, one can in principle optimize the Fisher information for a given noise model or experimental constraint, thereby achieving better performance than conventional two‑component cat states. Second, the ability to interpolate continuously between classical‑like and highly nonclassical regimes allows for flexible trade‑offs between sensitivity and resource requirements. Third, certain generalized configurations may be more amenable to generation with current technology, lowering the barrier to practical quantum‑enhanced sensing.

In this work, we systematically investigate the quantum Fisher information and phase estimation performance of a class of generalized cat states, encompassing both symmetric and asymmetric multi‑component superpositions. We analyze their scaling behavior in the ideal, noiseless limit, and quantify the degradation of precision under typical decoherence channels. Our approach highlights the interplay between the geometric arrangement of coherent components in phase space and the achievable metrological gain. Furthermore, we identify parameter regimes in which generalized cat states not only approach Heisenberg‑limited scaling but also exhibit enhanced resilience to loss compared to traditional cat states.

By elucidating the metrological potential of generalized cat states, our results contribute to the broader effort of designing quantum states tailored for realistic sensing scenarios. The insights gained here may inform the development of next‑generation interferometric sensors, ranging from optical phase trackers to frequency standards and field detectors, where quantum resources are judiciously engineered to maximize precision within the constraints of experimental implementation.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the role of generalized cat states in quantum metrology, focusing on their potential to enhance phase estimation beyond the standard quantum limit. By extending the concept of Schrödinger cat states to superpositions of multiple coherent components, we demonstrated that such generalized states can exhibit increased robustness to certain noise channels while retaining high quantum Fisher information. Our analysis revealed that the metrological advantage depends sensitively on the structure of the superposition and the degree of coherence between its components. In particular, appropriately engineered generalized cat states can approach the Heisenberg scaling in ideal conditions and maintain a significant advantage under moderate loss. These findings suggest that generalized cat states offer a versatile resource for precision measurements, bridging the gap between highly fragile nonclassical states and experimentally accessible coherent states. Future work may focus on experimental realizations in platforms such as superconducting circuits or trapped ions, as well as optimization strategies tailored to specific sensing tasks. Overall, our results highlight the promise of generalized cat states as practical, noise-resilient probes for next-generation quantum metrology.

title: Modelling the Extreme X-ray Spectrum of IRAS 13224-3809
abstract: We present a detailed spectral analysis of the extreme narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy IRAS 13224-3809, utilising deep X-ray observations from *XMM-Newton* and *NuSTAR*. This source is renowned for its extraordinary X-ray variability and pronounced relativistic reflection features, providing a valuable laboratory for probing the innermost regions of active galactic nuclei. We model the broadband spectrum, spanning 0.3–50 keV, with physically motivated reflection models that incorporate relativistic blurring and ionised disc emission. Our fits reveal a steep primary continuum (photon index Γ ≈ 2.7) and strong reflection from a highly ionised accretion disc, consistent with a rapidly spinning black hole (spin parameter a* > 0.9). Prominent broad Fe K and Fe L emission features, as well as a pronounced soft excess, are well described by reflection from material within a few gravitational radii. The extreme light-bending inferred suggests a compact corona located very close to the event horizon. These results reinforce the role of relativistic reflection as the dominant process shaping the X-ray spectrum of IRAS 13224-3809 and highlight its potential for constraining the geometry and physics of the corona–disc system in active galaxies.
introduction:
Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are among the most luminous persistent sources of electromagnetic radiation in the Universe, powered by accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs). In the X-ray regime, the innermost regions of the accretion flow can be probed, providing critical insights into the physics of the corona, the geometry of the accretion disc, and the relativistic effects in the vicinity of the event horizon. Narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies (NLS1s) are a subclass of AGN characterised by their narrow optical permitted emission lines, relatively low black hole masses, and high accretion rates relative to the Eddington limit. They often display extreme variability and steep soft X-ray spectra, making them valuable laboratories for studying accretion physics under extreme conditions.

IRAS 13224–3809 is a prototypical example of an extreme NLS1 galaxy. Located at a redshift of \( z \approx 0.066 \), it is renowned for its rapid and large-amplitude X-ray variability, with flux changes by factors of several occurring on timescales of hours or less. Observations with *XMM-Newton* and *NuSTAR* have revealed a rich phenomenology in its X-ray spectrum, including a pronounced soft excess below ~2 keV, strong relativistically broadened iron K and L emission lines, and deep flux-dependent absorption features. The combination of these features suggests that relativistic reflection from the inner accretion disc, gravitational light bending, and complex ionised absorption all play important roles in shaping its X-ray spectrum.

The extreme and rapidly variable nature of IRAS 13224–3809 has made it an important target for detailed spectral–timing studies. Reverberation mapping analyses, measuring time delays between the primary coronal emission and the reflected response from the accretion disc, have provided constraints on the size and location of the X-ray emitting corona. In addition, the detection of ultrafast outflows (UFOs) in the source, with velocities up to ~0.24c, has linked the X-ray spectral variability to powerful disc winds that may contribute to AGN feedback processes.

Despite substantial progress, modelling the full complexity of IRAS 13224–3809’s X-ray spectrum remains challenging. The observed spectral shape changes dramatically with flux state, suggesting that the geometry and physical conditions of the corona, disc, and outflowing material are highly dynamic. Self-consistent modelling must therefore account for relativistic reflection, variable absorption, and the effects of strong gravitational fields near the SMBH. Moreover, disentangling the contributions of these components is complicated by the significant spectral degeneracies that arise in fitting the data.

In this work, we present a detailed spectral modelling analysis of IRAS 13224–3809, focusing on its extreme high- and low-flux states. Using recent deep X-ray observations, we apply state-of-the-art relativistic reflection and photoionisation models to characterise the physical conditions in the corona, the ionisation structure of the disc, and the properties of the outflowing absorbers. By comparing models across different flux regimes, we aim to elucidate the interplay between coronal variability, relativistic effects, and disc winds in shaping the observed X-ray spectra. Our results provide new constraints on the accretion geometry and outflow dynamics in this remarkable AGN, and contribute to a broader understanding of the high-energy behaviour of extreme NLS1 galaxies.
conclusion:
In this study, we have presented a detailed spectral analysis of the extreme X-ray emission from the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy IRAS 13224‑3809, employing high-quality data to explore the physical processes shaping its remarkable variability and spectral complexity. Using advanced relativistic reflection models in combination with variable absorption components, we have demonstrated that the observed spectral features — including the pronounced soft excess, broad iron K emission, and rapid flux-dependent spectral changes — can be self-consistently explained within the framework of a compact corona irradiating an ionised accretion disc in the strong gravity regime close to a rapidly spinning black hole.

Our modelling indicates that extreme relativistic blurring is required to reproduce the breadth and shape of the reflection features, implying an inner disc radius consistent with the innermost stable circular orbit of a near-maximally rotating Kerr black hole. The inferred high reflection fraction supports the interpretation of a compact X-ray emitting region located within a few gravitational radii of the black hole, where strong light bending enhances the reflected component.
