We also find that the ionisation state of the disc responds to changes in illumination on short timescales, consistent with rapid coronal variability driving the observed flux-dependent spectral evolution.

The detection of subtle absorption signatures suggests the presence of an outflowing, ionised wind whose properties vary with source luminosity, potentially linking the inner disc and large-scale outflows. However, the dominant spectral variability can be explained without invoking large column density changes, reinforcing the picture of intrinsic coronal and disc ionisation changes as the primary drivers.

Our results place IRAS 13224‑3809 among the most extreme examples of relativistic reflection in active galactic nuclei and provide stringent constraints on the geometry and dynamics of the innermost accretion flow. Future high-throughput, high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy will be essential to disentangle the interplay between reflection, absorption, and coronal physics, offering the prospect of mapping the strong-gravity environment of supermassive black holes with unprecedented precision.

title: Exchangeable exogenous shock models
abstract: We propose a novel class of exchangeable exogenous shock models that capture dependence structures driven by common but unobserved external events. By formalizing shocks as latent variables with exchangeable distributions, our framework accommodates heterogeneous responses across components while preserving tractable probabilistic properties. We derive conditions for identifiability, characterize the resulting joint laws, and explore connections with de Finetti-type representations. Applications to risk aggregation and systemic event modeling demonstrate the approach’s flexibility in handling heavy-tailed and asymmetric dependence. Simulation studies illustrate efficiency gains over traditional copula-based methods. Our results provide theoretical foundations and practical tools for modeling systems subject to shared, unpredictable shocks.
introduction:
In many domains, systems are subject to sudden and unpredictable changes driven by factors external to their internal dynamics. These *exogenous shocks*—whether arising from macroeconomic events, policy interventions, environmental disturbances, or technological breakthroughs—can have profound and persistent effects. Modeling such shocks is essential for understanding system resilience, forecasting outcomes, and designing appropriate responses. A central challenge lies in representing collections of shocks whose order of occurrence is irrelevant, while still accounting for their statistical dependencies. The concept of *exchangeability*, originating in probability theory, provides a natural framework for this purpose. An exchangeable sequence treats the joint distribution of shocks as invariant under permutations, thereby capturing symmetry in their probabilistic structure without assuming independence. This property is particularly appealing when the analyst lacks detailed temporal or causal ordering information, yet must infer from aggregate or unordered data.

Exchangeable exogenous shock models offer a unifying approach that bridges stochastic process theory, Bayesian inference, and applied modeling in economics, finance, environmental science, and engineering. By leveraging de Finetti–type representation theorems, such models enable the decomposition of complex shock patterns into latent structural components and observable realizations. This facilitates both theoretical analysis and empirical estimation, while accommodating heterogeneity and uncertainty. In this work, we develop a general framework for exchangeable exogenous shock models, examine their probabilistic foundations, and illustrate their applicability through analytical results and simulation-based examples.
conclusion:
This study has examined the formulation, properties, and implications of exchangeable exogenous shock models, with the aim of clarifying both their theoretical underpinnings and their practical relevance in empirical applications. By situating these models within the broader literature on stochastic processes and dependence structures, we have identified the key role of exchangeability as a simplifying yet powerful assumption, enabling tractable representations of complex systems subject to common shocks. Our analysis has highlighted how the exchangeable framework facilitates both analytical derivations and statistical inference, while also outlining the boundaries of its applicability.

The central contribution of this work lies in demonstrating that exchangeable exogenous shock models provide a unifying structure for a wide class of phenomena in which multiple units or agents are jointly influenced by latent, randomly occurring events. Through the lens of de Finetti-type representations, we have shown that such models can be decomposed into mixtures of independent processes, conditional on a latent shock sequence. This decomposition offers both interpretative clarity and computational convenience, allowing researchers to separate the stochastic structure of the shocks from the conditional independence of the responses. Moreover, the exchangeable setting naturally accommodates heterogeneity in the timing and magnitude of shocks, without sacrificing tractability.

From a methodological standpoint, we have explored identification issues, estimation strategies, and the implications of model misspecification. In particular, the assumption of exchangeability imposes symmetry that may not fully capture directional or network-based dependencies in certain empirical contexts. Nevertheless, where symmetry is a reasonable approximation, the resulting models offer parsimonious yet flexible descriptions of joint dynamics. Simulation studies and illustrative examples confirm that even in moderately sized systems, the exchangeable specification can yield reliable inference on shock distributions and their impact patterns.

The theoretical results established here also underscore the connections between exchangeable exogenous shock models and other statistical frameworks, including hierarchical Bayesian models, frailty models in survival analysis, and contagion models in finance and epidemiology. The common thread across these applications is the need to model dependence induced by unobserved, externally driven events, where direct measurement of the shock process is infeasible. By recasting these situations within the exchangeable exogenous shock paradigm, it becomes possible to leverage a coherent set of tools for estimation, prediction, and uncertainty quantification.

At the same time, our findings point to several avenues for further research. Relaxing the strict exchangeability assumption to allow for partial exchangeability or structured heterogeneity could expand the applicability of the models to settings with identifiable subgroups or network structures. Incorporating temporal dependence in the shock process, beyond the i.i.d. or renewal-type assumptions considered here, would increase realism in contexts where shocks are clustered or persistent. Methodologically, the integration of nonparametric Bayesian techniques could enable richer modeling of the shock distribution, especially in high-dimensional or sparse-data regimes.

In conclusion, exchangeable exogenous shock models occupy a valuable niche in the repertoire of stochastic modeling tools. They balance interpretability, tractability, and flexibility, making them suitable for a range of disciplines concerned with the joint impact of unobserved external events. By formalizing their structure and elucidating their connections to established statistical paradigms, this work lays the foundation for both theoretical advances and applied innovations. The results suggest that, when the underlying assumptions are met, these models can yield insights into the mechanisms by which common shocks propagate through systems, influence collective behavior, and generate observable patterns of dependence. Future developments that extend and adapt the exchangeable framework will further enhance its utility, ensuring its continued relevance in the analysis of complex, shock-driven phenomena.

title: Graph-based Retrieval for Claim Verification over Cross-Document Evidence
abstract: Claim verification often requires aggregating and reasoning over evidence dispersed across multiple documents. Existing retrieval approaches typically rank documents or sentences independently, overlooking the structural relationships between evidence fragments. We propose a graph-based retrieval framework that explicitly models inter-evidence connections for improved claim verification. Our method constructs a heterogeneous evidence graph where nodes represent candidate sentences and edges encode semantic, entity, and discourse-level links across documents. A graph neural network propagates contextual signals over this structure to produce relevance scores that jointly reflect local content and global evidence coherence. Retrieved evidence sets are then passed to a verification model to determine claim veracity. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach substantially outperforms strong baselines in both retrieval precision and end-to-end verification accuracy, particularly for claims requiring multi-hop reasoning. Further analysis shows that the learned graph structure effectively captures cross-document dependencies, enabling more faithful and complete evidence aggregation. This work highlights the benefits of graph-based retrieval in complex, multi-document fact-checking scenarios.
introduction: The rapid proliferation of misinformation across online platforms has intensified the need for automated fact-checking systems capable of verifying claims against reliable evidence. A key challenge in this domain lies in retrieving and integrating information that is dispersed across multiple documents. Conventional retrieval methods typically treat documents as independent units, often overlooking the rich inter-document relationships that can be crucial for accurate verification. Recent advances in graph-based representations offer a promising direction, enabling the modeling of entities, events, and semantic links across sources. By structuring evidence as interconnected nodes and edges, graph-based retrieval can capture contextual dependencies, reconcile conflicting information, and support reasoning over multiple evidence fragments. This approach is particularly valuable for complex claims that require synthesizing corroborating or contradictory details from diverse texts. In this work, we investigate a graph-based retrieval framework for claim verification over cross-document evidence, aiming to enhance retrieval precision, improve evidence coverage, and facilitate more reliable automated fact-checking in scenarios where critical information is distributed and context-dependent.
conclusion: This work explored a graph-based retrieval framework for claim verification that leverages cross-document evidence. By modeling documents, sentences, and entities as interconnected nodes, our approach enables effective propagation of contextual signals and facilitates the discovery of multi-hop evidence scattered across disparate sources. Experimental results demonstrated that graph-structured representations can outperform traditional retrieval baselines, particularly on claims requiring the integration of complementary information from multiple documents. Furthermore, the framework’s ability to capture relational dependencies offers a principled way to bridge semantic gaps and mitigate information fragmentation. Our analysis highlights that incorporating graph connectivity not only improves retrieval precision but also enhances the interpretability of evidence selection, as supporting paths can be explicitly traced. Future work will investigate scaling the graph construction to larger corpora, incorporating temporal and causal relations, and integrating retrieval with end-to-end claim verification pipelines. Overall, this study underscores the promise of graph-based methods for robust, explainable, and context-aware fact-checking in complex information environments.

title: Dimerization in ultracold spinor gases with Zeeman splitting
abstract: We investigate dimer formation in ultracold spinor gases under Zeeman splitting, analyzing how spin-dependent interactions and magnetic fields influence bound-state energies. Using a multi-channel scattering framework, we identify regimes of enhanced pairing and magnetic-field-tunable resonances, revealing controllable dimerization pathways relevant for quantum simulation and spinor condensate engineering.
introduction:
The study of ultracold atomic gases has provided an exceptionally versatile platform for exploring quantum many-body physics under highly controllable conditions. In particular, spinor Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs), composed of atoms with internal spin degrees of freedom, have enabled the investigation of a wide range of spin-related phenomena, including spin-mixing dynamics, magnetic ordering, and spin–orbit coupling. The interplay between spin and motional degrees of freedom in such systems leads to a rich variety of quantum phases, with tunability afforded by optical, magnetic, and microwave fields. Among the many avenues of research in spinor gases, the formation of bound states—dimers—has emerged as a key element in understanding both equilibrium properties and dynamical processes.

Dimerization in ultracold gases typically arises from resonant interactions, as in the case of Feshbach resonances, or from effective low-energy scattering processes mediated by the spin structure of the system. In spinor condensates, the spin-dependent contact interactions can couple different spin channels, enabling the formation of spin-singlet or spin-polarized molecular states. The presence of an external magnetic field introduces Zeeman splitting between spin sublevels, thereby modifying the scattering channels and the energetics of possible bound states. This Zeeman effect can be used as a tuning knob to selectively enhance or suppress dimerization processes, and to control the internal spin composition of the resulting bound pairs.

From a theoretical standpoint, the competition between spinor interaction energies, kinetic energy, and Zeeman splitting yields a complex landscape for few-body bound states embedded in a many-body medium. The quadratic Zeeman effect, in particular, can shift the relative energies of spin manifolds in a way that qualitatively changes the stability and symmetry of dimers. Understanding how these shifts influence dimer binding energies, wave functions, and dynamical formation rates is essential for constructing accurate models of spinor gas behavior in realistic experimental settings.

Recent advances in high-resolution spectroscopy and control of external fields have made it possible to directly probe dimer states in ultracold gases, including their internal spin correlations. This opens the way to experimentally test predictions about the field dependence of dimer formation and to explore regimes where dimers coexist with unpaired atoms in novel quantum phases. Moreover, such studies have relevance beyond atomic physics, offering analogies to pairing phenomena in condensed matter systems with spin-dependent interactions.

In this work, we investigate the mechanisms of dimerization in ultracold spinor gases subject to Zeeman splitting, focusing on the interplay between spin-dependent scattering, magnetic field control, and the structure of bound states. Our analysis aims to clarify the conditions under which magnetic fields can be used to manipulate dimer properties, and to provide theoretical predictions relevant to current and future experiments.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the mechanisms and consequences of dimer formation in ultracold spinor gases subject to Zeeman splitting, with particular emphasis on the interplay between spin-dependent interactions, external magnetic fields, and quantum statistical effects. By combining analytical modeling with numerical simulations, we have elucidated how the competition between spin-exchange processes and Zeeman energy shifts governs the stability and binding energies of dimers across a range of experimentally relevant parameters. Our analysis demonstrates that the presence of a Zeeman field not only modifies the energy landscape of the spinor manifold but also induces nontrivial coupling between spin and motional degrees of freedom, thereby shaping the dimerization dynamics in a qualitatively distinct manner from that in scalar gases.

A key finding is that the Zeeman splitting introduces tunable asymmetries in the spin-channel interactions, effectively selecting preferred spin configurations for bound pairs. This selection mechanism manifests as sharp resonances in the two-body scattering amplitudes, which can be exploited to control the dimer binding energy and wavefunction composition. In regimes of weak field strength, spinor symmetry is largely preserved and dimerization reflects the underlying SU(2) or higher symmetries of the spin sector. As the field strength increases, symmetry breaking leads to spin-selective binding, with corresponding suppression or enhancement of particular spin channels. Our results indicate that this tunability can be harnessed to engineer dimers with tailored spin correlations, potentially useful for quantum information protocols or as building blocks for exotic many-body states.

Furthermore, we have shown that the interplay between Zeeman splitting and spin-dependent collisions can lead to nonmonotonic behavior in the dimer binding energy as a function of field strength, arising from the competition between energy shifts and interaction-induced mixing. This behavior suggests the possibility of field-tuned avoided crossings between bound states of different spin character, opening avenues for coherent state manipulation via magnetic field ramps. The sensitivity of these features to the scattering length ratios in different spin channels underscores the importance of precise interaction control, achievable through optical or microwave Feshbach resonances.

From an experimental perspective, our predictions are accessible with current ultracold atom platforms, particularly in alkali and alkaline-earth-like species with rich hyperfine structure. Observable signatures include shifts in radio-frequency association spectra, changes in spin-resolved momentum distributions, and modifications to the dynamics of quenched spinor clouds. We anticipate that the phenomena described here will inspire targeted experiments probing the crossover from weak to strong Zeeman regimes, as well as the role of dimers in the collective behavior of spinor condensates and degenerate Fermi gases.

In summary, the study reveals that Zeeman splitting provides a powerful and versatile knob for controlling dimerization in ultracold spinor gases. By dictating the spin composition and energetics of bound states, it enables the exploration of novel pairing mechanisms and spin-entangled composite particles in a highly controllable setting. These findings not only deepen our understanding of few-body physics in spinor systems but also lay groundwork for engineering complex quantum phases where spin and pairing degrees of freedom are intricately intertwined.

title: The influence of photo-induced processes and charge transfer on carbon and oxygen in the lower solar atmosphere
abstract: The interaction between radiation fields and atomic species in the lower solar atmosphere plays a critical role in determining the ionization balance and chemical state of key elements such as carbon and oxygen. In this study, we investigate the influence of photo-induced processes, including photoionization and photodissociation, together with charge transfer reactions, on the populations of neutral and ionized carbon and oxygen under conditions representative of the photosphere and low chromosphere. Using a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer framework, we incorporate detailed atomic models with cross sections and rate coefficients from recent laboratory measurements and quantum calculations. The results reveal that photoionization from excited levels, driven by the ultraviolet continuum, significantly alters the ionization fractions, particularly in regions of reduced electron density. Charge transfer with hydrogen and protons emerges as a dominant coupling mechanism, efficiently redistributing charge between carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen species, thereby moderating the effects of direct photoionization. The combined action of these processes leads to departures from Saha–Boltzmann equilibrium that are strongly height-dependent and wavelength-sensitive. We find that the balance between photo-induced ionization and charge exchange is essential for reproducing observed line profiles in both C I and O I transitions. Our findings underscore the necessity of including both mechanisms in realistic solar atmosphere models, with implications for elemental abundance determinations and diagnostics of solar atmospheric dynamics. This work provides refined constraints on atomic processes that shape the emergent spectrum and energy balance in the lower solar atmosphere.
introduction:
The lower solar atmosphere, comprising the photosphere and chromosphere, is a dynamic region where radiative, thermal, and magnetic processes interact to shape the physical and chemical state of the plasma. Among the many constituents of this environment, carbon and oxygen are of particular astrophysical interest. These elements are not only among the most abundant in the Sun after hydrogen and helium, but also play a crucial role in the formation of molecules, the regulation of radiative cooling, and the interpretation of spectroscopic diagnostics. Understanding their ionization balance, excitation states, and chemical interactions is essential for accurate modeling of the solar atmosphere and for deriving elemental abundances that inform solar and stellar evolution theories.

In the lower atmosphere, the prevailing temperatures and densities lead to conditions where photo-induced processes and charge transfer reactions become central to the behavior of carbon and oxygen species. Photoionization, driven by the intense solar radiation field, competes with recombination processes to determine the ionization fractions of C I/II and O I/II. Photodissociation of CO and other molecules releases atomic species, altering the local chemical equilibrium. These processes are strongly wavelength-dependent, being influenced by the spectral distribution of the radiation field, which itself varies with height and is modulated by opacity sources such as H− and metal lines.

Charge transfer reactions, particularly between carbon or oxygen ions and abundant neutral species such as hydrogen, can proceed at rates comparable to or exceeding those of radiative processes. For example, the near-resonant charge exchange between O II and H, or between C II and H, can efficiently couple the ionization states of these elements to that of hydrogen, thereby linking their spatial and temporal variations to the hydrogen ionization balance. Such coupling is especially significant in non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) conditions, which prevail throughout much of the lower solar atmosphere.

The interplay of photo-induced and charge transfer processes has important implications for interpreting solar spectra. Non-LTE radiative transfer models that neglect these mechanisms may misestimate level populations, leading to systematic errors in abundance determinations or inferences about temperature and density structures. Furthermore, the relative importance of these processes can vary substantially with height, local radiation field characteristics, and magnetic activity, suggesting that their effects may be diagnostic of specific atmospheric conditions.

This study aims to quantify the influence of photo-induced ionization, recombination, and photodissociation processes, together with charge transfer reactions, on the populations of carbon and oxygen species in the lower solar atmosphere. By incorporating recent atomic and molecular data into detailed non-LTE models, we seek to improve the physical realism of solar atmospheric simulations and to refine the interpretation of spectroscopic observations in this fundamental region of the Sun.
conclusion:
The present investigation has examined in detail the role of photo-induced processes and charge transfer in governing the ionization balance, excitation states, and overall abundance diagnostics of carbon and oxygen in the lower solar atmosphere. By integrating advanced radiative transfer modelling with updated atomic cross-sections and rate coefficients, we have been able to quantify the extent to which these processes alter the population densities of relevant atomic and ionic species under realistic solar conditions. Our analysis confirms that the interplay between photoionization from the ground and excited states, resonant charge exchange with abundant protons and other ions, and subsequent recombination pathways exerts a significant influence on the thermodynamic and spectroscopic properties of the photosphere and low chromosphere.

A central finding of this work is that photoionization, particularly from low-lying metastable levels, is far from negligible for both carbon and oxygen at depths where the continuum optical depth is still appreciable. The inclusion of such channels leads to a measurable shift in the neutral-to-ionized ratio, with consequences for the line formation of key diagnostic transitions in the visible and near-ultraviolet. These effects are amplified when coupled with charge transfer reactions, which act as an efficient mechanism for redistributing charge between carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen. The bidirectional nature of these reactions, and their relatively large cross-sections at the prevailing temperatures of the lower atmosphere, introduces a feedback loop that mitigates or enhances the impact of photoionization depending on the local radiation field and electron density.

Our computations show that neglecting charge transfer with hydrogen tends to overestimate the ionization fraction of carbon and oxygen in the lower layers, leading to systematic biases in abundance determinations derived under the assumption of statistical equilibrium without such processes. Conversely, including these interactions tends to stabilize the ionization balance against fluctuations in the radiation field, particularly in the case of oxygen, whose ionization potential is close to that of hydrogen. This stabilizing effect is less pronounced for carbon but remains non-negligible, especially when considering the fine balance between neutral and singly ionized stages in line-forming regions.

The implications of these findings are manifold. From a diagnostic standpoint, the accurate modelling of photo-induced and charge transfer processes is essential for interpreting high-resolution solar spectra, particularly in the context of disentangling subtle abundance anomalies or temporal variations associated with magnetic activity. Given that carbon and oxygen are key tracers of solar and stellar chemical evolution, even modest systematic errors in their inferred photospheric abundances can propagate into broader astrophysical conclusions, such as the calibration of stellar evolution models or the benchmarking of solar interior opacities.

Furthermore, our results highlight the necessity of moving beyond simplified treatments that either omit or parametrise these processes without reference to detailed atomic data. The sensitivity of the ionization balance to the interplay between radiation field anisotropy, level-specific photoionization cross-sections, and the temperature dependence of charge exchange rates suggests that future modelling efforts must maintain a high degree of self-consistency between radiative and collisional processes. This is particularly pertinent as observational capabilities continue to improve, offering spectral diagnostics of unprecedented precision and spatial resolution.

Looking ahead, the incorporation of time-dependent effects, three-dimensional radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations, and non-equilibrium ionization calculations will be essential to fully capture the dynamic nature of the lower solar atmosphere. In such a framework, the role of transient radiation enhancements, shock-induced heating, and magnetic reconnection events on photo-induced and charge transfer processes can be systematically evaluated. In addition, improved laboratory measurements and quantum mechanical calculations of cross-sections for specific transitions—especially for excited states that are significantly populated under solar conditions—will further constrain model predictions.

In summary, this study underscores that photo-induced ionization and resonant charge transfer are not merely peripheral processes but are integral to the accurate description of carbon and oxygen in the lower solar atmosphere. Their combined effects shape the ionization equilibrium, influence emergent spectral line profiles, and ultimately affect our ability to derive reliable elemental abundances. By rigorously incorporating these processes into our modelling, we take a significant step toward resolving long-standing discrepancies in solar abundance determinations and towards a more comprehensive understanding of the microphysical processes that underpin the observable properties of the Sun’s lower atmosphere.

title: Generic Optical Singularities in Brewster-reflected Post-paraxial Beam-fields
abstract: We investigate the formation and evolution of generic optical singularities in Brewster-reflected, post-paraxial beam-fields. By extending beyond the paraxial approximation, we reveal how polarization-dependent phase shifts at the Brewster angle generate structurally stable singularity morphologies, including vortices and polarization C-points. Analytical modelling, supported by numerical simulations, captures the interplay between beam geometry, angular spectrum, and reflection-induced spatial dispersion. The results elucidate universal features of singularity topology in non-paraxial regimes, offering new insight into vectorial light–matter interactions and potential applications in singular optics-based metrology.
introduction:
Optical singularities, defined as loci of phase dislocations or polarization degeneracies in an electromagnetic field, have emerged as a central theme in modern singular optics. These structural features of light—whether phase vortices, C-points, L-lines, or more exotic entities—are not merely mathematical curiosities but are associated with measurable physical consequences, including the spatial organization of polarization and intensity in optical beams. The study of such singularities has expanded considerably beyond the paraxial regime, propelled by advances in beam shaping, high numerical aperture focusing, and the exploration of nontrivial reflection and refraction geometries. In these contexts, the interplay between beam structure and boundary interactions gives rise to novel topologies of singularities whose properties cannot be captured by conventional scalar or paraxial approximations.

Among the simplest and most instructive boundary interactions is reflection at a dielectric interface. In the special case of incidence at the Brewster angle, the reflectivity for p-polarized plane waves vanishes in the framework of geometric optics. For real, finite-width beams, however, the situation is more intricate. The angular spectrum of such beams inevitably contains components away from the exact Brewster condition, producing nonzero reflected fields and giving rise to spatially varying polarization patterns. The Brewster geometry thus constitutes a fertile setting for the generation and control of optical singularities, especially polarization singularities such as C-points (points of circular polarization) and V-points (vector field phase singularities). The precise arrangement and evolution of these singularities depend sensitively on the beam’s angular spread, polarization state, and focusing conditions.

Much of the foundational work in this area has been conducted under the paraxial approximation, where the angular spectrum is narrowly concentrated and longitudinal field components are negligible. In this regime, analytic treatments are often tractable, and the resulting singularity structures exhibit symmetries inherited from the underlying Gaussian or Laguerre–Gaussian beam models. However, as beam divergence increases—either intentionally via tight focusing or unavoidably due to finite aperture effects—paraxial assumptions break down. The inclusion of post-paraxial corrections, incorporating higher-order terms in the angular spectrum expansion and fully vectorial field components, leads to qualitative modifications in the singularity landscape. These corrections can shift singularity positions, alter their topological charges, and even create or annihilate singularity pairs, reflecting the richer structure of the underlying Maxwell fields.

Recent theoretical and experimental studies have demonstrated that post-paraxial effects are especially pronounced in Brewster-reflected beams, where the vanishing of certain polarization components near the central incidence angle amplifies the role of off-axis angular components. The resulting reflected field is a superposition of spatially varying polarization states, in which generic optical singularities naturally emerge. Here, “generic” refers to structurally stable singularities—those robust against small perturbations of system parameters—that are classified by singularity theory and catastrophe optics. Examples include isolated C-points with lemon, star, or monstar morphologies, and networks of L-lines organizing the surrounding polarization ellipse fields. Understanding the formation and arrangement of these generic singularities in the post-paraxial Brewster reflection regime is not only of fundamental interest but also relevant to applications in optical metrology, beam diagnostics, and the design of singular optics-based devices.

In this work, we undertake a systematic analysis of generic optical singularities arising in the Brewster-reflected fields of tightly focused beams, treated within a post-paraxial formalism. By employing a full vectorial angular spectrum representation, we capture the essential physics beyond the paraxial approximation, enabling quantitative predictions of singularity locations, morphologies, and stability. We identify the characteristic parameter regimes in which singularity patterns exhibit universal features, and we elucidate the mechanisms by which post-paraxial corrections generate deviations from the paraxial predictions. Our results bridge the gap between idealized paraxial models and realistic high-aperture beam scenarios, providing a deeper theoretical framework for interpreting and exploiting singularity phenomena in optical reflection.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the emergence and structural characteristics of generic optical singularities in Brewster-reflected post-paraxial beam-fields, with particular emphasis on the interplay between non-paraxial corrections and polarization-selective reflection. By extending the theoretical framework beyond the conventional paraxial approximation, we have demonstrated that higher-order spatial phase and amplitude variations significantly influence the creation, annihilation, and morphology of singularity networks in the reflected field. The Brewster geometry, imposing a strong polarization constraint at the interface, was shown to act as a selective filter that not only modifies the amplitude distribution but also reshapes the phase topology, thereby giving rise to singularity patterns that cannot be captured within simpler models.

Our analysis reveals that the post-paraxial terms introduce asymmetries in the reflected beam’s spatial structure, leading to the unfolding of degenerate singularities into generic configurations such as isolated vortices, vortex pairs, and nodal lines with well-defined topological charges. These features are robust against small perturbations in incidence angle and beam waist, indicating that they are intrinsic to the combined effect of Brewster reflection and finite-aperture beam propagation. The mapping of these singularity landscapes confirms that their spatial arrangement follows predictable bifurcation scenarios as the system parameters are varied, in agreement with singular optics theory.

The results further suggest that the Brewster-reflected post-paraxial field serves as a natural platform for studying the controlled generation of polarization-dependent singularities, with potential applications in precision metrology, optical trapping, and beam-shaping techniques. The sensitivity of the singularity structure to the relative orientation of the polarization vector and the incidence plane offers a route to dynamically modulate the topology of the reflected field without altering the optical components.

Overall, this study underscores the necessity of incorporating post-paraxial corrections in the analysis of optical fields near polarization-selective angles, and highlights the rich phenomenology that emerges when vectorial and non-paraxial effects are treated on equal footing. Future work could address the experimental realisation of these predictions, explore the role of material dispersion and surface structuring, and extend the framework to other polarization-selective configurations, thereby broadening our understanding of singularity formation in realistic optical systems.

title: Conditional Super Learner
abstract: We propose the Conditional Super Learner, an extension of the Super Learner ensemble method that adapts model weighting to covariate-specific contexts. By conditioning the ensemble weights on observed predictors, the method captures heterogeneity in predictive performance across subpopulations. We present a general framework for estimating conditional weights via cross-validation and demonstrate its theoretical oracle properties. Simulation studies and real-world applications illustrate substantial improvements over traditional global-weight ensembles, particularly in settings with strong effect modification, highlighting the utility of conditional ensembling for flexible and robust predictive modeling.
introduction:
Modern statistical and machine learning methods increasingly aim to leverage data-adaptive algorithms to achieve optimal prediction and estimation performance across a wide range of domains. Ensemble learning, in particular, has emerged as a powerful paradigm for combining the strengths of multiple candidate learners to produce predictions that are, in theory and practice, at least as good as the best-performing constituent algorithm. Among such approaches, the Super Learner framework has gained considerable attention for its theoretically grounded performance guarantees, flexible integration of diverse model classes, and applicability to both prediction and causal inference. The classical Super Learner constructs a weighted convex combination of candidate estimators, with weights chosen to minimize cross-validated risk, thereby asymptotically achieving the performance of the best convex combination in the library.

Despite these strengths, the traditional Super Learner assumes a single set of optimal weights for all observations in the target population. This global weighting may be suboptimal in settings where the relative performance of candidate algorithms varies systematically with observed covariates. For example, in precision medicine, certain predictive models may perform better for specific subgroups defined by clinical or demographic characteristics. Similarly, in environmental science, models may differ in accuracy across geographical regions or temporal periods. In such contexts, a global ensemble weight vector can obscure important heterogeneity in predictive accuracy, leading to suboptimal performance for particular subpopulations.

To address this limitation, we propose the Conditional Super Learner, an extension of the Super Learner framework that allows ensemble weights to vary as functions of observed covariates. The Conditional Super Learner estimates a mapping from covariates to optimal weights using flexible regression or classification methods, thereby enabling the ensemble to adapt locally to the structure of the data. This approach preserves the generality of the Super Learner—any set of candidate algorithms can be included in the library—while introducing an additional layer of adaptivity that targets improved conditional performance. By tailoring the weighting scheme to subgroups or regions of the covariate space, the Conditional Super Learner aims to achieve prediction accuracy gains over the global-weight alternative, particularly in heterogeneous data-generating environments.

The methodological development of the Conditional Super Learner raises important questions regarding estimation, regularization, and theoretical guarantees. Extending the cross-validation framework to accommodate covariate-dependent weights requires careful consideration to avoid overfitting and to ensure robustness. Furthermore, the asymptotic optimality properties of the classical Super Learner must be revisited in this more general setting, with attention to conditions under which similar oracle inequalities hold. In this work, we present the formal definition of the Conditional Super Learner, propose estimation strategies, and investigate its theoretical and empirical properties. Through simulation studies and real-data applications, we demonstrate that allowing ensemble weights to depend on covariates can yield substantial predictive improvements in settings with meaningful heterogeneity, thereby extending the applicability and effectiveness of the Super Learner paradigm.
conclusion: This work introduced the Conditional Super Learner, a flexible ensemble framework that extends the traditional Super Learner by incorporating context-specific model weighting. By conditioning the ensemble on relevant covariates, the approach adapts to heterogeneous data structures and improves predictive performance in settings where the optimal algorithm may vary across subpopulations. Simulation studies and empirical applications demonstrated that the Conditional Super Learner consistently matched or outperformed standard aggregation methods, especially in complex, non-stationary environments. These results highlight the value of conditional weighting in enhancing model adaptivity and robustness. Future research may explore theoretical guarantees, computational efficiency, and broader applications, positioning the Conditional Super Learner as a powerful tool for precision prediction in diverse domains.

title: The dependence of gamma-ray burst X-ray column densities on the model for Galactic hydrogen
abstract: We investigate the impact of different models for the Galactic hydrogen distribution on the inferred X-ray absorbing column densities of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Accurate determination of the intrinsic absorption in GRB afterglows requires a reliable estimate of the Galactic contribution, yet various surveys and modelling approaches yield systematically different column densities. We analyse a sample of 198 Swift X-ray afterglows with well-constrained spectra, comparing results obtained using three widely adopted Galactic hydrogen maps: the Leiden/Argentine/Bonn (LAB) 21 cm survey, the HI4PI survey, and a model including molecular hydrogen inferred from dust extinction. For each model, we fit the afterglow spectra with an absorbed power-law, holding the Galactic column fixed and allowing the intrinsic host-frame absorption to vary. We find that the choice of Galactic model introduces systematic shifts in the derived host column densities, with typical median differences of 10–25%, and up to a factor of two for sightlines through high-density regions. The inclusion of molecular hydrogen generally reduces the inferred host absorption, particularly for low-redshift bursts. We further explore correlations between host absorption estimates and Galactic latitude, finding that discrepancies among models are most pronounced at low latitudes. Our results demonstrate that uncertainties in the Galactic hydrogen model can contribute significantly to the dispersion in GRB absorption measurements, and must be accounted for in population studies and when interpreting correlations between host absorption and other GRB properties. We provide recalculated host absorption values for the sample under each Galactic model to facilitate future work.
introduction:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic phenomena in the universe, releasing vast amounts of energy over timescales of milliseconds to minutes. Following their prompt γ-ray emission, GRBs exhibit afterglows across the electromagnetic spectrum, from X-rays to radio waves. X-ray afterglows, in particular, provide a powerful probe of the physical conditions in the immediate environment of the burst and along the line of sight. The X-ray spectra of GRB afterglows are generally well described by a power-law continuum modified by photoelectric absorption. This absorption is due to intervening material both within the Milky Way and in the host galaxy of the GRB, as well as potentially from the intergalactic medium. The observed attenuation is typically parameterised by an equivalent hydrogen column density, \( N_{\mathrm{H}} \), derived from spectral fits.

In order to estimate the intrinsic absorption associated with the GRB’s host galaxy, it is necessary to disentangle the contribution from the Milky Way. This foreground component is usually characterised using maps of Galactic neutral hydrogen. The most widely adopted approach has been to use 21 cm surveys to determine the column density of atomic hydrogen, \( N_{\mathrm{HI}} \), along the line of sight. These values are then fixed in the spectral modelling of the X-ray afterglow, with any excess absorption attributed to material at the redshift of the GRB. However, this procedure is subject to systematic uncertainties arising from the choice of Galactic hydrogen model. Several all-sky surveys and compilations exist, each differing in angular resolution, survey methodology, and treatment of molecular gas, leading to differences in the derived \( N_{\mathrm{HI}} \) values.

The Leiden–Argentine–Bonn (LAB) survey, for example, has long served as a reference for Galactic atomic hydrogen column densities, offering improved baseline stability and full-sky coverage at moderate angular resolution. More recently, the HI4PI survey has provided higher resolution and sensitivity, incorporating data from the Effelsberg–Bonn HI Survey (EBHIS) and the Galactic All-Sky Survey (GASS). In addition to these 21 cm–based maps, some models combine atomic hydrogen measurements with estimates of molecular hydrogen based on CO line emission or dust extinction, providing a more complete view of the total hydrogen column. The choice among these models can systematically affect the derived intrinsic \( N_{\mathrm{H}} \) for GRB afterglows, especially for lines of sight through the Galactic plane or regions of high molecular fraction.

The sensitivity of intrinsic column density estimates to the assumed Galactic foreground model has important implications. Intrinsic \( N_{\mathrm{H}} \) values are widely used to investigate the circumburst environment, the interstellar medium (ISM) of GRB host galaxies, and their redshift evolution. For example, studies have reported a correlation between intrinsic \( N_{\mathrm{H}} \) and redshift, suggesting either an increasing gas content in high-redshift hosts or cumulative absorption by the intergalactic medium. However, if the Galactic foreground is systematically under- or overestimated, such trends may be biased. Similarly, attempts to relate intrinsic absorption to other host galaxy properties—such as star-formation rate, metallicity, or dust extinction—depend on accurate separation of the Galactic and extragalactic contributions.

Furthermore, X-ray absorption measurements complement optical and near-infrared studies of dust extinction, enabling constraints on dust-to-gas ratios and the chemical enrichment of GRB hosts. Discrepancies between dust- and gas-derived column densities have been interpreted in terms of dust destruction by the GRB, unusual dust properties, or variations in metallicity. Yet such interpretations require confidence in the foreground correction, particularly for bursts located behind complex Galactic structures.

In this work, we investigate how the derived X-ray column densities of GRB afterglows depend on the choice of Galactic hydrogen model. Using a homogeneous sample of Swift X-Ray Telescope (XRT) afterglow spectra, we perform spectral fits adopting different foreground \( N_{\mathrm{H}} \) estimates from widely used surveys and composite models. By comparing the resulting intrinsic column densities, we quantify the systematic uncertainties introduced by the Galactic model choice and assess their impact on statistical studies of GRB environments. Through this analysis, we aim to provide guidance for future GRB afterglow studies in selecting and applying Galactic hydrogen models, and to clarify the extent to which foreground uncertainties can influence astrophysical conclusions.
conclusion:
We have examined the influence of different models for Galactic hydrogen on the determination of X-ray column densities in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), focusing on how the assumed foreground absorption impacts the inferred intrinsic properties of the bursts’ host environments. By systematically comparing results obtained using several widely adopted Galactic hydrogen maps and prescriptions, we find that the choice of model can lead to measurable differences in the derived excess column densities. Although these differences are often modest for individual events, they become significant when considering statistical trends across large GRB samples.

Our analysis shows that models incorporating both atomic and molecular hydrogen components, and accounting for small-scale structure in the interstellar medium, tend to yield systematically lower excess column densities than those relying solely on atomic hydrogen maps. This shift has implications for interpreting the physical conditions within GRB host galaxies, particularly in relation to dust content, metallicity, and the role of circumburst material. The dependence on the Galactic foreground model is most pronounced for low-redshift bursts and for sightlines through regions of higher Galactic extinction, where the foreground contribution is substantial.

These results underscore the importance of a consistent and physically motivated choice of Galactic absorption model in GRB afterglow studies. Discrepancies in the adopted foreground correction can introduce biases in correlations between column density and other observables, such as redshift, host galaxy properties, and afterglow luminosity, potentially leading to erroneous inferences about GRB progenitors and environments. Future population studies should therefore explicitly state the Galactic model used and, where possible, assess the robustness of their conclusions against alternative foreground prescriptions.

Looking ahead, improvements in all-sky hydrogen mapping, particularly with higher resolution and better constraints on the molecular fraction, will reduce systematic uncertainties in derived GRB column densities. Combining multiwavelength Galactic surveys with refined X-ray absorption modelling will allow for more accurate separation of foreground and host contributions. By adopting such approaches, the community can ensure that interpretations of GRB X-ray spectra rest on a more secure foundation, enabling more reliable use of GRBs as probes of the interstellar medium in the distant Universe.

title: Novel DNNs for Stiff ODEs with Applications to Chemically Reacting Flows
abstract: We present novel deep neural network (DNN) architectures tailored for the efficient and accurate solution of stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs) arising in chemically reacting flows. Our approach integrates stiffness-aware training objectives with implicit time-stepping schemes embedded within the network structure, enabling stable learning across disparate temporal scales. By leveraging domain-specific regularization and adaptive sampling, the proposed models capture rapid transients and slow dynamics without resorting to prohibitively small time steps. We validate the methodology on benchmark reacting flow problems, including detailed combustion mechanisms, demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy and computational efficiency over conventional solvers and standard physics-informed neural networks. The results highlight the potential of stiffness-informed DNNs as a robust surrogate modeling framework for multiscale reactive systems in science and engineering applications.
introduction:
The numerical integration of stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs) remains a central challenge in the simulation of multiscale physical systems. Stiffness typically arises when disparate temporal scales coexist, necessitating prohibitively small time steps for explicit schemes to maintain stability. Implicit solvers alleviate this restriction but incur significant computational cost due to the repeated solution of large, often nonlinear, algebraic systems. In chemically reacting flows, the governing equations couple fluid dynamics with detailed chemical kinetics, leading to stiffness ratios that can span many orders of magnitude. As a result, efficient and accurate time integration methods are essential for predictive simulations in combustion, atmospheric chemistry, and related fields.

Recent years have witnessed increasing interest in leveraging machine learning, and in particular deep neural networks (DNNs), to accelerate or augment numerical solvers. DNN-based surrogate models can learn reduced representations of complex dynamics, bypassing some of the computational bottlenecks of traditional schemes. However, the application of DNNs to stiff ODEs presents unique difficulties: learned models must capture both the fast and slow dynamics without compromising stability or physical fidelity. Conventional architectures often struggle to generalize across stiffness regimes or to respect invariants such as mass conservation.

In this work, we propose novel DNN architectures tailored to the integration of stiff ODEs, with a focus on chemically reacting flows. Our approach incorporates stiffness-aware network designs and training strategies that embed physical constraints directly into the learning process. By coupling these networks with established operator-splitting frameworks, we achieve stable and accurate integration over a wide range of stiffness parameters. Numerical experiments on representative reacting flow problems demonstrate that the proposed methods can significantly reduce computational cost while maintaining high fidelity to reference solutions. The results indicate that carefully designed DNNs can provide a viable path toward efficient simulation of stiff multiscale systems, opening new possibilities for real-time prediction and control in chemically reactive environments.
conclusion:
In this work, we have developed and evaluated novel deep neural network architectures tailored to the efficient and accurate solution of stiff ordinary differential equations, with a particular focus on applications arising in chemically reacting flows. By incorporating stiffness-aware features into the network design, including implicit-inspired layers and adaptive time-stepping mechanisms, the proposed models demonstrate superior stability and generalization properties compared to conventional data-driven approaches. Numerical experiments on representative reaction mechanisms illustrate that the networks can capture fast and slow dynamics simultaneously, reducing the computational cost typically associated with traditional implicit solvers while maintaining high fidelity in the predicted solutions. 

Furthermore, we have shown that the framework is flexible, enabling direct integration into multi-physics simulation pipelines where stiff kinetics play a critical role. Analysis of error behavior and computational performance confirms that the approach offers a promising balance between accuracy and efficiency, particularly for large-scale or real-time applications. Future work will explore extension to partial differential equation systems with coupled stiff source terms, as well as strategies for embedding physical invariants directly into the learning process. Overall, the proposed DNN methodology provides a viable and scalable alternative for the simulation of complex reacting flow phenomena.

title: The radius and mass of the close solar twin 18 Sco derived from asteroseismology and interferometry
abstract: We present precise determinations of the radius and mass of the nearby solar twin 18 Sco using combined asteroseismic and interferometric observations. Oscillation frequencies from high-precision photometry yield a mean large frequency separation, from which the stellar mean density is derived. Interferometric angular diameter measurements, together with the Hipparcos parallax, provide a direct radius estimate. Combining these independent constraints allows us to determine the stellar mass with high accuracy. We find that 18 Sco closely matches the Sun in both radius and mass, reinforcing its status as a near-identical solar analogue and providing a benchmark for stellar modeling and calibration.
introduction:
Solar twins are stars that closely resemble the Sun in their fundamental properties, such as effective temperature, luminosity, and chemical composition. Among the known solar twins, 18 Scorpii (18 Sco, HD 146233) has attracted considerable attention because it is one of the closest and brightest examples, making it an ideal target for detailed observational studies. Located at a distance of approximately 14 parsecs, 18 Sco shares near-identical atmospheric parameters with the Sun, yet it provides an opportunity to examine subtle differences that may yield insights into solar evolution and the broader context of stellar astrophysics.

A precise determination of stellar radius and mass is essential for characterizing solar twins and for anchoring stellar models. Traditionally, such parameters have been inferred from photometric and spectroscopic analyses in combination with stellar evolutionary models. However, these indirect methods are often limited by systematic uncertainties. Recent advances in observational techniques now allow for direct and model-independent measurements. In particular, asteroseismology — the study of stellar oscillations — provides powerful constraints on a star’s mean density and internal structure, while long-baseline optical interferometry enables direct angular diameter measurements, which, when combined with accurate parallaxes, yield precise linear radii.

In the case of 18 Sco, the combination of high-precision asteroseismic data and interferometric observations offers a unique opportunity to determine its fundamental properties with unprecedented accuracy. Asteroseismic observations from ground-based campaigns have revealed clear solar-like oscillations, enabling the extraction of the large frequency separation and other seismic parameters that are directly related to the star’s mean density. Interferometric measurements with modern facilities can resolve 18 Sco’s disk and measure its angular diameter to better than a percent, providing a direct radius estimate when coupled with precise distance determinations from astrometric missions such as *Hipparcos* and *Gaia*.

By combining these complementary techniques, it is possible to derive the radius and mass of 18 Sco with minimal reliance on stellar models, thereby providing a robust benchmark for solar twin studies. Such measurements not only refine our understanding of this particular star but also contribute to the calibration of stellar scaling relations and evolutionary tracks. In this work, we present new determinations of the radius and mass of 18 Sco derived from the synthesis of asteroseismic and interferometric data, and we discuss their implications for the characterization of solar twins and the validation of stellar models.
conclusion:
We have presented a determination of the fundamental parameters of the nearby solar twin 18 Sco by combining asteroseismic measurements with long-baseline interferometry. The analysis of high-precision oscillation frequencies yielded a robust estimate of the mean stellar density, while interferometric angular diameter measurements, together with the precise parallax, provided a direct determination of the stellar radius. From these complementary constraints, we derived a mass estimate that is largely model-independent and benefits from the synergy between seismic and interferometric techniques.  

Our results indicate that 18 Sco has a radius and mass very close to those of the Sun, reinforcing its classification as the closest solar twin known to date. The agreement between our measurements and previous spectroscopic and photometric analyses confirms the reliability of the adopted methods and highlights the power of combining independent observational diagnostics. The precision achieved here represents a significant improvement over earlier determinations, underscoring the potential of similar approaches for characterizing other bright solar-type stars.  

The methodology applied to 18 Sco demonstrates the importance of integrating asteroseismology with interferometry in the era of high-precision stellar astrophysics. Such combined analyses are crucial for testing stellar evolution models, calibrating scaling relations, and refining our understanding of the Sun’s place among nearby stars. Future observations with improved seismic coverage and higher angular resolution will further reduce the uncertainties and may reveal subtle differences between the Sun and its closest analogues, offering deeper insight into solar and stellar physics.

title: Overdensity of X-ray Sources in the Field of Nearby Clusters of Galaxies
abstract: We present an analysis of the spatial distribution of X-ray point sources in the fields of a sample of nearby galaxy clusters, based on archival observations from the *Chandra X-ray Observatory*. Our study investigates potential overdensities of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and other compact X-ray emitters associated with the cluster environment. We selected clusters with redshifts \( z < 0.1 \) and high-quality imaging data, enabling uniform source detection down to flux limits of \(\sim 10^{-15}\) erg cm\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\) in the 0.5–8 keV band. The X-ray source catalogs were constructed using wavelet-based detection algorithms, and field contamination was quantified through comparison with blank-field surveys. We find a statistically significant (\(>3\sigma\)) excess of X-ray sources within projected radii of \(\sim 1\) Mpc from the cluster centers, relative to expectations from the cosmic X-ray background. The radial distribution of the excess population declines toward the cluster periphery, suggesting a physical association with the cluster potential. Spectral hardness ratios indicate a mixture of absorbed and unabsorbed AGN, along with a smaller population of X-ray luminous star-forming galaxies. The observed overdensity is consistent with enhanced AGN triggering through galaxy–galaxy interactions and ram-pressure effects in the dense intracluster medium. Our results support the notion that the cluster environment plays a significant role in shaping the nuclear activity of member galaxies, and they provide constraints for models of AGN fueling in dense cosmic structures.
introduction:
Galaxy clusters are the largest gravitationally bound systems in the Universe and serve as crucial laboratories for studying the interplay between large-scale structure formation, galaxy evolution, and the intracluster medium (ICM). X-ray observations have long played a central role in characterizing the physical conditions within clusters, revealing both the thermal emission from the hot ICM and the presence of compact, high-energy sources associated with active galactic nuclei (AGN), X-ray binaries, and other energetic phenomena. While the diffuse ICM emission dominates the X-ray luminosity of massive clusters, point-like X-ray sources distributed within and around the cluster environment provide valuable information about the population of AGN and their relation to the dense large-scale environment.

Several studies over the past decades have reported an apparent overdensity of X-ray point sources in the vicinities of galaxy clusters compared to blank fields. Such overdensities have been detected both in the central regions of clusters and at larger projected radii, sometimes extending beyond the virial radius. The origin of these excess sources is still under debate. Possible explanations include enhanced AGN activity triggered by galaxy interactions and mergers in the dense cluster environment, infalling galaxies hosting AGN in the cluster outskirts, gravitational lensing amplification of background sources, or contributions from cluster member galaxies with elevated X-ray emission. Distinguishing between these scenarios is challenging, requiring careful statistical analysis and multiwavelength identification of X-ray sources.

The study of X-ray source overdensities in cluster fields has implications for several areas of astrophysics. It can shed light on the environmental dependence of AGN triggering and fueling, offering clues to the co-evolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes. It may also help refine models of galaxy transformation in dense environments, where processes such as ram-pressure stripping, harassment, and tidal interactions can affect both star formation and nuclear activity. Furthermore, understanding the nature of excess X-ray sources is important for cosmological studies that rely on cluster surveys, since contamination from unrelated background or foreground sources can bias cluster property measurements.

With the advent of sensitive X-ray observatories such as *Chandra* and *XMM-Newton*, it has become possible to detect faint X-ray sources in and around clusters with high angular resolution and sensitivity, enabling robust statistical comparisons with field populations. In this work, we investigate the overdensity of X-ray sources in the fields of nearby galaxy clusters, drawing on archival observations to quantify the significance and spatial distribution of the excess. We aim to disentangle the contributions from cluster member AGN, lensed background sources, and unrelated field objects, thereby providing new constraints on the relationship between AGN activity and the cluster environment.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the distribution of X-ray sources in the projected fields of several nearby clusters of galaxies, with the aim of assessing the presence and significance of any overdensities relative to blank-field expectations. By combining archival X-ray observations with robust source detection algorithms and careful statistical analyses, we have quantified the surface density of sources as a function of cluster-centric radius and compared these measurements to well-established log N–log S relations derived from deep extragalactic surveys. Our results reveal a statistically significant excess of X-ray sources within projected distances of a few hundred kiloparsecs from the cluster centers. This overdensity is most pronounced at intermediate flux levels, where the contribution from background AGN is well understood, and diminishes toward the faintest fluxes, where sensitivity limitations play a more significant role.

The spatial distribution of the excess sources suggests that a substantial fraction are likely associated with the clusters themselves. Possible contributors include active galactic nuclei hosted by cluster member galaxies, luminous X-ray binaries, and hot gaseous structures linked to ongoing galaxy interactions and mergers within the dense cluster environment. The observed radial decline in overdensity is consistent with the decreasing galaxy density profile and with expectations from models of AGN triggering by environmental processes such as tidal interactions and ram-pressure effects. Nonetheless, some contribution from gravitational lensing magnification of background sources cannot be excluded, particularly in the innermost regions, and future work incorporating multiwavelength identifications will be essential to disentangle these effects.

Comparisons across our cluster sample indicate that the amplitude of the overdensity correlates, albeit weakly, with global cluster properties such as richness and X-ray luminosity, hinting at a connection between the large-scale potential well and the fueling of accretion-powered sources. However, the scatter in this relation underscores the complexity of environmental influences on X-ray source populations and points to the importance of cluster dynamical state and recent merger history. Our findings are broadly consistent with earlier reports of excess X-ray sources in cluster environments but benefit from improved statistical robustness owing to the larger sample size and uniform analysis methods employed here.

In summary, the detection of a measurable overdensity of X-ray sources in the vicinity of nearby galaxy clusters strengthens the case for the cluster environment playing a significant role in shaping the population of luminous X-ray emitters. This work highlights the need for coordinated X-ray and optical spectroscopic follow-up to confirm source memberships and to characterize their nature. Such studies will provide deeper insight into the interplay between large-scale structure, galaxy evolution, and the growth of supermassive black holes in dense environments.

title: Coherent states and the classical-quantum limit considered from the point of view of entanglement
abstract: We investigate the role of coherent states in elucidating the classical–quantum correspondence, focusing on their behaviour from the perspective of entanglement. Coherent states, often regarded as the most classical of quantum states, provide a natural framework for analysing the transition between quantum superposition and classical dynamics. We explore how entanglement generation is suppressed for initially separable systems prepared in coherent states, and how this suppression depends on system parameters and interactions. By comparing coherent states with other nonclassical states, we identify signatures of classicality in the reduced entanglement growth and phase-space localization. Our analysis reveals that the classical limit emerges not solely from large quantum numbers, but also from structural features of the states that minimise quantum correlations. These findings deepen the understanding of the interplay between coherence, entanglement, and classical behaviour in composite quantum systems.
introduction:
The interplay between classical and quantum descriptions of physical systems has long been a central theme in the foundations of quantum mechanics. Coherent states, originally introduced in the context of the quantum harmonic oscillator, occupy a distinguished position in this dialogue. They are often regarded as the “most classical” pure states of a quantum system, minimising the Heisenberg uncertainty relation and exhibiting dynamics that closely parallel classical trajectories. As such, they provide a natural framework for examining the correspondence principle and the transition from quantum to classical behaviour.

Recent advances in quantum information theory have opened new perspectives on this transition by framing it in terms of quantum correlations, particularly entanglement. Entanglement, as a hallmark of nonclassicality, offers a quantitative measure of the departure from classical physics. In composite systems, the generation or suppression of entanglement can signal the degree to which quantum effects manifest in dynamical evolution. Consequently, coherent states serve as a useful testing ground for exploring how entanglement behaves in regimes approaching the classical limit.

Investigations along these lines address both conceptual and practical questions. Conceptually, they clarify whether the classical limit should be characterised merely by the suppression of interference phenomena or more broadly by the vanishing of entanglement in relevant partitions of the system. Practically, they inform the design of quantum technologies, where controlling the onset of classicality is essential for preserving quantum coherence. The study of coherent states in interacting systems, or in the presence of decoherence, thus bridges foundational issues with applied concerns in quantum optics, quantum control, and semiclassical dynamics.

In this work, we analyse the properties of coherent states from the perspective of entanglement generation and decay, aiming to elucidate the structural features of the classical–quantum boundary. By doing so, we contribute to a unified understanding of coherence, correlations, and the emergence of classical behaviour in quantum systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the role of coherent states in elucidating the transition from quantum to classical behaviour, with particular emphasis on the perspective afforded by entanglement. Coherent states, by virtue of their minimal uncertainty and dynamics that closely follow classical trajectories, provide a natural framework in which to analyse how quantum correlations evolve and diminish in regimes approaching the classical limit. By treating entanglement not merely as a hallmark of quantumness but as a quantitative probe of the departure from classicality, we have highlighted how the structure and persistence of entanglement in composite systems can serve as an indicator of the degree to which coherent-state descriptions remain valid.

Our analysis underscores that, while coherent states often display reduced entanglement compared to generic quantum states, they are not entirely devoid of quantum correlations, especially in interacting systems. The residual entanglement reflects subtle quantum effects that persist even in states with quasi-classical dynamics. This observation suggests that the classical limit cannot be identified solely with vanishing entanglement; rather, it emerges through a balance between the suppression of nonclassical correlations and the stability of phase-space localisation.

Furthermore, the entanglement-based viewpoint reveals that decoherence processes, which tend to drive systems towards mixtures of coherent states, play a dual role: they suppress interference and reduce certain forms of entanglement, yet may leave behind classical correlations that shape the emergent classical behaviour. The coherent-state formalism thus offers both a conceptual bridge and a calculational tool for tracking the interplay between quantum coherence, entanglement, and the onset of classicality.

Overall, by situating coherent states within the broader context of entanglement theory, we have provided a framework for reinterpreting the classical–quantum boundary. This approach invites further exploration of more complex systems, where coherent-state approximations and entanglement measures together may yield deeper insight into the mechanisms underlying the emergence of classical physics from its quantum foundations.

title: Lyapunov and Sylvester equations: A quadrature framework
abstract: We present a unified quadrature-based framework for the numerical solution of continuous-time Lyapunov and Sylvester matrix equations. The approach exploits integral representations of the solutions, enabling the use of efficient numerical quadrature rules to approximate the required matrix function evaluations. By leveraging structural properties of the coefficient matrices, the method accommodates large-scale and sparse problems, while maintaining accuracy and stability. We analyze convergence behavior in relation to quadrature node selection and spectral characteristics, and discuss computational complexity. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of the framework compared to established iterative schemes, demonstrating its potential for scalable and robust computation in control and systems theory applications.
introduction: The Lyapunov and Sylvester equations play a central role in control theory, signal processing, and numerical linear algebra. Their efficient solution is critical in large-scale applications, where direct methods become computationally prohibitive. Recent advances exploit low-rank structures and Krylov subspace techniques, yet challenges remain in balancing accuracy and cost. In this work, we develop a unified quadrature-based framework for solving these matrix equations. Our approach leverages integral representations and numerical quadrature to achieve high efficiency, offering new insights into algorithmic design and performance for large-scale problems.
conclusion: In this work, we have presented a unified quadrature-based framework for the numerical treatment of continuous-time Lyapunov and Sylvester equations. By exploiting integral representations of the solutions, we have shown how appropriate quadrature rules can be systematically derived and adapted to the spectral properties of the coefficient matrices. This perspective not only recovers several existing methods as particular cases, but also provides a coherent basis for designing new algorithms with predictable accuracy and stability. The analysis highlights the interplay between quadrature error, conditioning of the underlying operators, and computational cost, offering clear guidelines for parameter selection. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in large-scale settings where low-rank structures can be exploited. Moreover, the framework naturally accommodates extensions to related operator equations, suggesting a broad applicability in control, model reduction, and signal processing. Future work will focus on adaptive quadrature strategies, integration with Krylov subspace methods, and the treatment of time-varying or stochastic variants of the equations. The proposed methodology thus provides both theoretical insight and practical tools for the efficient solution of a fundamental class of matrix equations, bridging classical analysis with modern computational demands.

title: Distributed Stabilization by Probability Control for Deterministic-Stochastic Large Scale Systems : Dissipativity Approach
abstract: This paper investigates distributed stabilization for deterministic–stochastic large-scale systems via probability control within a dissipativity framework.
