Our analysis shows that the undulant universe can mimic the concordance ΛCDM model over the redshift range directly probed by current observations, provided the oscillation amplitude and frequency are sufficiently small. In such cases, the effective equation of state remains close to −1 on average, preserving consistency with distance–redshift relations from supernovae and the angular scale of the CMB acoustic peaks. However, larger oscillations or shorter periods lead to tension with the data, particularly in the high-redshift regime where integrated effects on the sound horizon and growth factor become significant. The BAO scale, acting as a standard ruler, proves especially sensitive to deviations from smooth expansion, while the linear growth rate of structure provides an additional and complementary constraint.

An attractive feature of the undulant scenario is its potential to address the “cosmic coincidence” problem by making the current acceleration a phase within a recurring cycle, rather than a unique epoch. This quasi-periodic behavior could, in principle, reduce the need for fine-tuning the onset of acceleration. Nevertheless, our results indicate that any such oscillations must be heavily suppressed to remain compatible with observations, limiting the extent to which this mechanism can offer a compelling dynamical alternative to ΛCDM. The oscillatory nature of the model also implies modifications to the growth history of perturbations, which, if detectable, could serve as a distinguishing signature in future surveys.

We have also explored the implications of allowing for correlated parameter variations, particularly between the oscillation frequency and the mean equation of state. Marginalization over these degeneracies reveals that while certain parameter combinations can evade current bounds, they predict features in the late-time expansion or growth history that may be within reach of next-generation experiments. In particular, high-precision measurements of the Hubble parameter at intermediate redshifts and improved determinations of the growth index could either detect or strongly rule out the mild oscillations permitted by present data.

In summary, the undulant universe remains an intriguing phenomenological framework that embeds the observed acceleration within a richer dynamical context. While it can be made consistent with present cosmological observations for a narrow range of parameters, the model’s distinctive predictions are constrained to be small in amplitude, reducing their explanatory power for the coincidence problem. Future observational advances—including deeper supernova samples, enhanced BAO mapping from galaxy and 21 cm surveys, and refined weak lensing and redshift-space distortion measurements—will be decisive in testing the remaining viable parameter space. If the predicted oscillatory imprints are absent at the improved sensitivity levels, the undulant universe will be effectively indistinguishable from ΛCDM in its observational consequences. Conversely, the detection of even subtle periodic departures from a constant equation of state would provide compelling evidence for a more complex cosmic acceleration history, with profound implications for the nature of dark energy.

title: Towards the Usage of MBT at ETSI
abstract: Model-Based Testing (MBT) has emerged as a promising approach to improve the efficiency, effectiveness, and maintainability of testing processes. This paper explores the ongoing initiatives and considerations for adopting MBT within the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI). We first review the current testing methodologies in ETSI standardization activities and identify limitations that MBT could address, including issues of scalability, traceability, and consistency across test specifications. We then outline the strategic and technical challenges associated with integrating MBT into ETSI’s established workflows, such as tooling interoperability, model quality assurance, and the need for specialized expertise. A preliminary framework for MBT adoption at ETSI is proposed, focusing on harmonizing modeling languages, enhancing test generation capabilities, and fostering collaboration among stakeholders. The study concludes that a gradual, well-supported integration of MBT can significantly enhance the quality and agility of ETSI’s test development, ultimately contributing to more robust and interoperable telecommunications standards.
introduction:
Model-Based Testing (MBT) has emerged as a systematic approach to designing and executing software tests based on abstract models of system behavior. By deriving test cases from formal or semi-formal models, MBT aims to improve test coverage, efficiency, and maintainability compared to traditional, manually crafted test suites. In recent years, the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) has increasingly recognized the potential of MBT to enhance the quality and consistency of conformance and interoperability testing for standardized technologies. ETSI’s work involves complex, evolving protocols and systems, where traditional testing methodologies may struggle to keep pace with specification changes and the breadth of required verification.  

The adoption of MBT within ETSI offers opportunities to automate significant parts of the test development process, ensuring that tests remain closely aligned with normative specifications. MBT can facilitate traceability from requirements to test cases, enabling early detection of ambiguities or inconsistencies in standards. Furthermore, it can support the generation of executable test suites for multiple platforms from a single model, thus reducing duplication of effort and increasing reusability across different test campaigns.  

However, integrating MBT into ETSI’s established testing processes presents both technical and organizational challenges. These include selecting appropriate modeling notations and tools, ensuring stakeholder acceptance, training experts in MBT methodologies, and establishing robust processes for model validation and maintenance. There is also the question of balancing the initial investment in modeling with the anticipated long-term gains in productivity and quality.  

This paper explores the motivations, potential benefits, and practical considerations for adopting MBT at ETSI. It discusses the current state of MBT in standards-based testing, reviews ETSI’s prior experiences, and outlines a framework for integrating MBT into its conformance and interoperability testing activities. The aim is to provide a foundation for informed decision-making on the sustained usage of MBT within ETSI’s technical environment.
conclusion: This work has examined the potential and challenges of adopting Model-Based Testing (MBT) within ETSI’s standardization processes. By aligning MBT methodologies with ETSI’s existing practices, it is possible to improve test development efficiency, consistency, and traceability, while supporting higher quality and maintainability of test suites. The analysis highlights that successful integration requires not only suitable tooling and modelling approaches, but also organizational commitment, skill development, and adaptation of workflows. Furthermore, the standardization of modelling languages and the definition of clear guidelines are essential to ensure interoperability and repeatability across different domains. While initial experiences demonstrate promising results, further case studies and iterative refinements will be necessary to fully realize MBT’s benefits. Ultimately, the adoption of MBT at ETSI has the potential to enhance the robustness of conformance testing and strengthen the overall quality of telecommunications standards.

title: A Graph-Based Inference Method for Conditional Independence
abstract: We present a novel graph-based inference method for determining conditional independence among random variables. Our approach leverages structural properties of probabilistic graphical models to efficiently identify separations using graph traversal and edge-removal techniques. By integrating algorithmic optimizations, the method reduces computational complexity while maintaining accuracy. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate superior performance compared to traditional statistical tests, particularly in high-dimensional settings. This work advances scalable, interpretable tools for dependency analysis in complex multivariate systems.
introduction:
Conditional independence is a central concept in probabilistic reasoning, underpinning the structure and interpretation of graphical models such as Bayesian networks and Markov random fields. It allows for the decomposition of complex joint probability distributions into simpler, tractable components, thereby enabling efficient inference and learning. Determining whether two variables are conditionally independent given a set of conditioning variables is a fundamental operation in tasks ranging from causal discovery to probabilistic inference and structure learning. However, identifying conditional independencies directly from data can be computationally demanding, especially in high-dimensional domains where the number of potential variable subsets grows combinatorially.

Graph-based methods provide a natural framework for representing and reasoning about conditional independencies. In such models, vertices correspond to random variables and edges encode direct probabilistic interactions, while the absence of an edge often implies a conditional independence relation. Criteria such as d-separation in directed acyclic graphs or separation in undirected graphs offer elegant, graph-theoretic characterizations of independence relations that hold in the underlying distribution, given certain assumptions. These graphical criteria enable the transformation of statistical independence testing into a graph traversal problem, potentially reducing computational complexity.

Despite their appeal, existing graph-based approaches face challenges when applied to incomplete or noisy data, when the true independence structure is only partially known, or when the graph representation itself must be inferred. In these contexts, robust and scalable inference methods are needed to reliably detect conditional independencies and support downstream reasoning tasks.

In this work, we propose a novel graph-based inference method for conditional independence that leverages structural properties of graphical representations in conjunction with efficient computational techniques. Our approach aims to improve the accuracy and scalability of independence detection, accommodate uncertainty in graph structure, and integrate seamlessly with probabilistic modeling frameworks. We evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in diverse application scenarios.
conclusion:
This work has presented a novel graph-based inference method for determining conditional independence relationships in probabilistic models. By leveraging structural properties of graphical representations, the proposed approach systematically identifies conditional independencies without requiring exhaustive enumeration of joint distributions. The method integrates principles from graph theory with probabilistic reasoning to yield an efficient and interpretable framework, capable of handling both directed and undirected graphical models. Experimental evaluations demonstrated that the approach achieves competitive accuracy while significantly reducing computational complexity compared to traditional statistical tests, particularly in high-dimensional settings.  

Beyond efficiency, the method enhances transparency in inference by providing a clear correspondence between graph topology and inferred independence statements. This interpretability is valuable for model validation, causal analysis, and knowledge discovery. While the current formulation assumes known graph structures, future extensions could incorporate structure learning, enabling broader applicability in data-driven scenarios. Additionally, integrating robustness measures to account for noisy or uncertain graph information would further improve practical performance.  

In summary, the proposed graph-based inference approach offers a principled, efficient, and interpretable tool for conditional independence analysis. It bridges theoretical foundations with practical utility, providing a basis for scalable reasoning in complex probabilistic systems. The findings suggest promising directions for extending graphical methodologies in both statistical inference and machine learning applications.

title: A sequential reduction method for inference in generalized linear mixed models
abstract: We propose a sequential reduction method for efficient inference in generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs). The approach systematically reduces the dimensionality of the random effects space through a series of conditional decompositions, enabling accurate likelihood evaluation with substantially reduced computational cost. By exploiting model structure, the method accommodates non-Gaussian responses and complex correlation patterns while maintaining numerical stability. Simulation studies demonstrate that the sequential reduction yields parameter estimates comparable to standard techniques but with significant gains in speed. Applications to real datasets illustrate its practical utility for large-scale and high-dimensional GLMM analysis.
introduction:
Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) provide a flexible framework for analyzing non-Gaussian data with complex correlation structures, arising commonly in clustered, longitudinal, and hierarchical settings. By incorporating random effects into the linear predictor of generalized linear models, GLMMs account for unobserved heterogeneity and enable valid inference in the presence of dependence among observations. Despite their broad applicability, statistical inference in GLMMs remains computationally challenging, particularly when the dimension of the random effects is large or when the link function induces severe nonlinearity in the likelihood. The integrals defining the marginal likelihood are generally intractable and require approximation or simulation-based techniques for practical estimation.

A substantial body of research has addressed these challenges through methods such as Laplace approximation, adaptive Gaussian quadrature, variational inference, and Markov chain Monte Carlo. While these approaches have advanced the feasibility of GLMM analysis, they may suffer from accuracy loss, high computational cost, or convergence difficulties, especially in high-dimensional settings. Sequential or stepwise reduction methods, which aim to decompose or simplify the likelihood in a structured manner, offer a promising alternative by exploiting conditional independencies and lower-dimensional representations of the model.

In this work, we propose a sequential reduction method for inference in GLMMs that systematically reduces the dimension of the integration problem while preserving the essential statistical structure. The approach is applicable to a wide class of link functions and random effect distributions, and it is designed to balance computational efficiency with estimation accuracy. We derive the methodological framework, investigate its theoretical properties, and evaluate performance through simulation studies and real data applications. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method yields reliable inference in settings where conventional approximations are computationally burdensome or insufficiently accurate.
conclusion: This work has presented a sequential reduction method for efficient inference in generalized linear mixed models, addressing the computational challenges inherent in high-dimensional random effects structures. By systematically reducing the dimensionality of the integration problem through a sequence of lower-dimensional approximations, the proposed approach achieves substantial gains in computational efficiency while maintaining high accuracy in parameter estimation and inference. Simulation studies demonstrated that the method provides estimates comparable to those obtained via more computationally intensive techniques, with significant reductions in runtime. Applications to real data further illustrated the practicality and adaptability of the approach across a range of model specifications. The sequential nature of the algorithm also facilitates incremental model refinement and offers a transparent framework for balancing precision and computational cost. These findings suggest that the sequential reduction method is a promising alternative for large-scale or complex generalized linear mixed models, particularly in settings where traditional methods become computationally prohibitive. Future research may extend the framework to accommodate more complex correlation structures and explore its integration with modern parallel computing architectures.

title: Measuring Alignment Bias in Neural Seq2Seq Semantic Parsers
abstract: We investigate alignment bias in neural sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) semantic parsers, focusing on how model architectures and training regimes influence systematic deviations in token-to-token alignments between natural language inputs and meaning representations. While recent neural parsers achieve high overall accuracy, they may rely on spurious or unbalanced alignments that reduce generalization, especially in low-resource or compositional settings. We introduce a quantitative framework for measuring alignment bias by comparing model attention patterns and gold-standard alignments across multiple benchmark datasets. Experiments reveal consistent biases toward frequent lexical patterns and syntactic proximity, regardless of semantic relevance. Furthermore, we show that alignment bias correlates with specific error types in compositional generalization tests. Our findings highlight the need for bias-aware training objectives and evaluation protocols to improve the robustness and interpretability of neural semantic parsers.
introduction:
Neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have become a dominant paradigm for semantic parsing, enabling the direct mapping from natural language utterances to executable meaning representations. By jointly learning to encode input sequences and decode structured outputs, these models have achieved state-of-the-art results across a variety of semantic parsing benchmarks. However, their success often masks subtle systematic errors, including biases in how the models align input tokens with output symbols. Such *alignment biases* can cause the model to over-rely on superficial correlations in the training data, leading to brittle generalization, reduced interpretability, and systematic errors in downstream applications.

Alignment bias refers to the tendency of a model’s internal attention or alignment mechanisms to consistently favor certain spurious or overly simplistic correspondences between natural language spans and elements of the target formal representation. For example, a model might repeatedly align a particular keyword with a specific logical predicate, even in contexts where the correct mapping differs. While alignment mechanisms, such as attention, are often assumed to provide interpretable insights into model behavior, existing work has shown that they can be misleading and may reflect learned biases rather than true semantic grounding.

Despite the potential impact of alignment bias on semantic parsing accuracy and robustness, there is a lack of systematic methods for quantifying and comparing such biases across models, datasets, and training regimes. Most prior research has focused on measuring overall performance metrics, leaving open the question of how to detect and characterize biases in the learned alignment patterns themselves. A principled measure of alignment bias would enable a deeper understanding of the inductive biases of neural parsers, reveal vulnerabilities to distribution shifts, and guide the development of more robust architectures and training strategies.

In this work, we propose a methodology for measuring alignment bias in neural seq2seq semantic parsers. We formalize alignment bias as a deviation from an idealized alignment distribution informed by gold-standard semantic correspondences, and introduce quantitative metrics to capture its magnitude and direction. Through controlled experiments and empirical analysis, we investigate how alignment bias correlates with model performance, generalization, and error patterns.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated alignment bias in neural seq2seq semantic parsers, proposing quantitative metrics to assess the extent to which models rely on spurious lexical correspondences rather than underlying meaning. Through controlled experiments across multiple datasets, we demonstrated that common architectures exhibit measurable bias, particularly when training data contains systematic lexical overlaps. Our findings highlight the limitations of current evaluation practices, as high accuracy can mask overreliance on surface form alignments. By diagnosing alignment bias, we provide a foundation for developing mitigation strategies, including data augmentation and model regularization. Future research should explore bias-aware training objectives to improve robustness and generalization in semantic parsing systems across diverse domains and linguistic variations.

title: The Masterclass of particle physics and scientific careers from the point of view of male and female students
abstract: This study examines male and female students’ experiences in a particle physics masterclass, focusing on perceptions of scientific content and career aspirations. Survey and interview data reveal gendered differences in confidence, engagement, and interest in pursuing physics-related careers. Findings highlight the importance of inclusive pedagogical approaches to foster equitable participation and long-term representation in science.
introduction:
Particle physics, as one of the most fundamental branches of science, seeks to uncover the basic constituents of matter and the forces governing their interactions. Beyond its technical and theoretical depth, the field has also become a platform for inspiring the next generation of scientists through outreach and educational programs. Among these, the “International Masterclasses – Hands on Particle Physics” initiative engages high school students worldwide in real data analysis from experiments such as those at CERN, offering an authentic glimpse into the work of particle physicists. These experiences not only enhance scientific literacy but also influence perceptions about careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).  

Despite considerable progress in promoting gender equality in STEM, persistent disparities remain in participation, self-confidence, and career aspirations between male and female students. The factors shaping these differences are complex, including sociocultural expectations, role models, and prior exposure to scientific content. Outreach activities like the Masterclasses offer an opportunity to investigate whether immersive, collaborative experiences in high-level physics can contribute to narrowing gender gaps in interest and self-perception.  

This study examines the impact of particle physics Masterclasses on students’ understanding of the scientific process, their attitudes toward physics, and their interest in pursuing scientific careers, with particular attention to male–female differences. We analyze students’ reflections, self-assessed learning gains, and reported career intentions to explore how such interventions may differentially shape experiences across genders. By focusing on both cognitive and affective outcomes, we aim to identify potential mechanisms through which outreach programs can foster inclusivity and broaden participation in physics. The findings may inform the design of future educational strategies that not only communicate cutting-edge science but also address the subtle factors influencing students’ long-term engagement with STEM careers.
conclusion: The present study has explored the experiences and perceptions of male and female students participating in the Masterclass of particle physics, with particular attention to their views on scientific careers. The findings indicate that while both groups expressed high levels of enthusiasm for the subject matter and valued the opportunity to engage directly with authentic research practices, subtle differences emerged in the ways they envisioned their potential career paths. Male students tended to report greater confidence in pursuing long-term careers in physics, often citing role models and prior exposure to scientific environments. Female students, while equally capable and engaged, more frequently mentioned concerns about work–life balance, representation, and the accessibility of career opportunities. These observations underscore the importance of fostering inclusive learning environments and providing diverse role models to help bridge confidence and aspiration gaps. The Masterclass format proved effective in stimulating interest and deepening understanding, suggesting its potential as a tool for encouraging broader participation in science. Future initiatives should build on these strengths, integrating mentorship and career guidance elements that address gender-specific challenges. By doing so, such programs can not only inspire the next generation of physicists but also contribute to a more equitable and diverse scientific community.

title: An updated analysis on the rise of the hadronic total cross-section at the LHC energy region
abstract: We present an updated analysis of the rise of the hadronic total cross-section in the high-energy regime, with particular emphasis on recent measurements from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Using the latest proton–proton scattering data at center-of-mass energies up to 13 TeV, we examine the energy dependence of the total cross-section within the framework of analyticity, unitarity, and dispersion relations. The results are interpreted in the context of phenomenological parameterizations inspired by Regge theory, including contributions from the Pomeron and subleading Reggeon exchanges. Special attention is paid to the verification of the Froissart–Martin bound and to the determination of the rate at which the asymptotic regime is approached. Statistical fits incorporating both pre-LHC and LHC data confirm a continued logarithmic-squared growth of the cross-section, consistent with theoretical expectations, but also reveal subtle deviations at the highest energies that may signal the onset of new dynamical effects. We assess the impact of systematic uncertainties and correlations among different experimental datasets, and discuss the compatibility of the updated trends with models based on QCD-inspired approaches, including mini-jet and saturation frameworks. The findings reinforce the view that the proton–proton total cross-section is still far from its ultimate asymptotic limit, while providing tighter constraints on phenomenological models relevant for both collider and cosmic-ray physics. This work thus contributes to refining our understanding of strong interaction dynamics in the high-energy frontier explored by the LHC.
introduction: The study of the hadronic total cross-section at high energies remains central to understanding strong interaction dynamics. Recent measurements at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have confirmed a continued rise in the total cross-section, extending trends observed at lower energies. This behavior, anticipated by general principles such as the Froissart bound, challenges theoretical models to provide accurate quantitative descriptions. Advances in experimental precision and the availability of data at unprecedented energies offer a unique opportunity to refine phenomenological fits and test QCD-inspired frameworks. Here, we present an updated analysis of the rise of the hadronic total cross-section in the LHC energy region, incorporating the latest experimental results.
conclusion:
In this work, we have revisited the problem of the rising behavior of the hadronic total cross-section in the high-energy domain, with particular emphasis on the most recent experimental results from the LHC. By incorporating the updated measurements of \( \sigma_{\text{tot}} \) at \(\sqrt{s} = 7, 8, 13\) TeV, together with earlier accelerator and cosmic-ray data, we have performed a comprehensive phenomenological analysis aimed at constraining the energy dependence of the hadronic interaction profile. Our approach has included both model-dependent fits inspired by Regge theory and analytic bounds, as well as model-independent parameterizations capable of capturing the essential asymptotic trends.

The updated dataset confirms the steady rise of \(\sigma_{\text{tot}}\) with increasing center-of-mass energy, a feature that has been firmly established since the ISR era and now extends into the multi-TeV range with unprecedented precision. The new LHC measurements not only reinforce this trend but also narrow the range of acceptable theoretical descriptions. In particular, fits incorporating a leading logarithmic-squared term in energy, as expected from the Froissart–Martin bound in the context of unitarity and analyticity, remain consistent with the data, although the precise value of the coefficient governing the asymptotic growth remains subject to statistical and systematic uncertainties.

Our analysis shows that purely power-law rises, while able to mimic the data over limited energy intervals, tend to overestimate \(\sigma_{\text{tot}}\) when extrapolated to cosmic-ray energies above \(\sqrt{s} \sim 100\) TeV. Conversely, logarithmic-squared fits maintain stability under extrapolation and appear to offer a more theoretically grounded description in line with axiomatic field theory. The inclusion of subleading logarithmic and constant terms is essential to account for the gentle curvature observed in the intermediate energy range, bridging the gap between ISR/SPS collider energies and the LHC regime.

From a phenomenological standpoint, the updated fits suggest that the hadronic interaction radius continues to grow with energy, reflecting an increasing dominance of peripheral collisions and a saturation of central opacity. This observation is consistent with recent analyses of the elastic slope parameter \(B(s)\) and the ratio \(\rho(s)\) of the real to imaginary forward scattering amplitude, both of which exhibit trends compatible with an expanding interaction region. The interplay between the total, elastic, and inelastic cross-sections at the LHC further supports the picture of a smooth asymptotic approach toward the black-disk limit, although the current energies remain far from any definitive saturation.

The results presented here have important implications for high-energy phenomenology, cosmic-ray air-shower modeling, and the ongoing effort to reconcile QCD-based approaches with rigorous S-matrix constraints. In particular, the confirmation of a logarithmic-squared rise at current energies lends support to models that incorporate gluon saturation or multiple-Pomeron exchange dynamics, while challenging those that predict significantly faster growth rates. The improved precision of the LHC data also opens the possibility of discriminating between competing theoretical frameworks on the basis of their subleading structure, a task that will benefit from forthcoming measurements at \(\sqrt{s} = 14\) TeV and beyond.

Looking forward, the continued monitoring of \(\sigma_{\text{tot}}\) in the high-energy region will remain a key probe of the nonperturbative regime of QCD. Future collider experiments, together with indirect determinations from ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, will extend the energy reach and help to clarify whether the observed rise persists indefinitely in accordance with the Froissart bound, or whether new dynamical mechanisms emerge at scales yet unexplored. In this regard, the synergy between accelerator-based measurements and cosmic-ray observations will be essential, requiring careful cross-calibration and a consistent treatment of systematic effects.

In summary, the updated analysis presented here consolidates the empirical evidence for a gradual, theoretically consistent rise of the hadronic total cross-section in the LHC energy region. The present data favor parameterizations rooted in fundamental principles of scattering theory, while leaving room for refinement as higher-energy measurements become available. This reinforces the role of \(\sigma_{\text{tot}}\) as a fundamental observable in strong-interaction physics, one that continues to illuminate the interplay between theory and experiment in our quest to understand the asymptotic behavior of hadronic matter.

title: Geodesic motion in the five-dimensional Myers-Perry-AdS spacetime
abstract: We investigate the geodesic structure of the five-dimensional Myers-Perry black hole with a negative cosmological constant. Employing the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism, we derive the equations of motion for massive and massless test particles in the general two-rotation-parameter case. The resulting system is shown to be separable, allowing for the identification of conserved quantities and effective potentials. We analyze the radial and polar motion, classify possible orbit types, and discuss the influence of rotation and AdS curvature on particle dynamics. Our results provide a foundation for studying astrophysical processes and holographic applications in higher-dimensional rotating AdS spacetimes.
introduction:
The study of geodesic motion in higher-dimensional spacetimes has become an important topic in both classical and quantum gravity, motivated by developments in string theory, brane-world scenarios, and the gauge/gravity correspondence. In particular, rotating black hole solutions in more than four dimensions play a central role in understanding the rich structure of general relativity beyond the familiar four-dimensional Kerr family. Among the most significant of these solutions is the Myers–Perry (MP) metric, which generalises the Kerr solution to arbitrary dimensions and accommodates multiple independent rotation parameters corresponding to the higher-dimensional rotation group. When a cosmological constant is included, one arrives at the Myers–Perry–anti-de Sitter (MP–AdS) solutions, which describe asymptotically AdS rotating black holes and serve as important backgrounds for the AdS/CFT correspondence.

The five-dimensional case holds a special place in this context. Five-dimensional Myers–Perry–AdS black holes admit two independent angular momenta associated with rotations in two orthogonal planes, leading to a richer parameter space than their four-dimensional counterparts. Such spacetimes appear naturally in the context of type IIB string theory compactifications and in studies of holographic duals of strongly coupled field theories on rotating backgrounds. The additional degrees of freedom in rotation not only alter the global structure of the spacetime but also affect the dynamics of test particles and light, leading to novel geodesic behaviour not present in lower dimensions.

Geodesic motion encodes fundamental information about the geometry of spacetime. In the absence of backreaction, the trajectories of test particles and photons are determined by the spacetime’s symmetries and curvature, and their analysis provides insight into causal structure, stability properties, and potential observational signatures. In the MP–AdS context, the study of geodesics is also relevant for understanding holographic probes, quasinormal modes, and potential astrophysical implications in scenarios where extra dimensions might have observable consequences. Furthermore, the integrability of the geodesic equations is intimately related to the existence of hidden symmetries, such as Killing–Yano tensors, which extend the manifest isometries and allow complete separation of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation.

Previous work on geodesic motion in higher-dimensional black holes has shown that in the asymptotically flat Myers–Perry spacetimes, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation is separable in all dimensions, leading to analytically tractable solutions for particle orbits. In the presence of a cosmological constant, separability persists in certain cases, though the structure of the radial and angular equations becomes more intricate. For the five-dimensional MP–AdS spacetime, the interplay between the two rotation parameters and the AdS curvature radius leads to a variety of qualitatively distinct regimes of motion, including bound and unbound trajectories, stable and unstable circular orbits, and intricate precession effects. These features are of both theoretical and phenomenological interest, as they influence the behaviour of accretion flows, gravitational lensing patterns, and the propagation of fields in such backgrounds.

The investigation of geodesics in the five-dimensional MP–AdS spacetime also provides a testing ground for methods in mathematical relativity. The separation of variables in the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism, the analysis of effective potentials, and the classification of orbit types all contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamical structure of these spacetimes. In addition, explicit solutions for the motion of particles and light can be expressed in terms of elliptic or hyperelliptic functions, linking the problem to well-developed areas of mathematical physics. Such exact solutions are valuable not only for theoretical completeness but also for benchmarking numerical relativity codes and for exploring limits such as the Kerr–AdS or Schwarzschild–AdS cases.

From the holographic perspective, geodesics in AdS spacetimes are connected to boundary correlation functions and entanglement entropy via geometric prescriptions. In rotating AdS backgrounds, the presence of angular momenta complicates the minimal surface problem and the causal structure, making the analysis of geodesic motion a useful preliminary step in more elaborate holographic calculations. Moreover, the existence or absence of certain classes of geodesics can have implications for bulk reconstruction and the interpretation of boundary observables.

In this work, we undertake a detailed study of test particle motion in the five-dimensional Myers–Perry–AdS spacetime with two independent rotation parameters. Starting from the metric in Boyer–Lindquist-type coordinates, we derive the geodesic equations via the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism and demonstrate the separability of the equations of motion. We analyse the resulting radial and angular effective potentials to classify the possible types of motion for both massive and massless particles. Special attention is given to circular orbits, their stability properties, and the influence of the cosmological constant and rotation parameters. Where possible, we present exact analytic solutions in terms of appropriate special functions, and we discuss limiting cases that connect our results to known four-dimensional and asymptotically flat scenarios.

By systematically exploring the parameter space of the five-dimensional MP–AdS black hole and the corresponding geodesic dynamics, we aim to provide a comprehensive picture that will be useful for future studies in both the classical and holographic contexts. The results presented here contribute to the broader effort to understand the interplay between rotation, curvature, and dimensionality in general relativity and its extensions.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the geodesic motion in the five-dimensional Myers–Perry–AdS spacetime, focusing on the dynamical features arising from the presence of two independent rotation parameters and a negative cosmological constant. By employing the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism, we demonstrated that the geodesic equations remain separable in this background, confirming the persistence of hidden symmetries encoded in a rank-two Killing tensor, even in the presence of the AdS curvature. The explicit separation allowed us to derive the radial and polar equations in terms of effective potentials, enabling a detailed classification of possible orbit types for both massless and massive particles.

Our analysis revealed that the inclusion of the AdS term modifies significantly the structure of the effective potentials, introducing confining features that can permit stable bound orbits at finite radii, in contrast with their asymptotically flat counterparts. The interplay between the two rotation parameters leads to a rich variety of trajectory configurations, including equatorial and off-equatorial motion, as well as more intricate three-dimensional orbital shapes in the five-dimensional spatial hypersurfaces. We have identified the conditions under which circular and spherical orbits occur, and examined their stability properties. In particular, the cosmological constant was shown to affect both the existence and location of such orbits, shifting the innermost stable circular orbit and altering the energy–angular momentum relations.

For null geodesics, we found that the photon regions exhibit a nontrivial dependence on the ratio of the rotation parameters, with possible implications for shadow formation in higher-dimensional contexts. The confining nature of AdS spacetime also results in distinctive global properties of null trajectories, which may be relevant for studies of holographic dualities and quasinormal mode spectra.

Overall, our results extend the understanding of geodesic structure in higher-dimensional rotating AdS spacetimes, providing a framework applicable to related geometries such as charged or deformed Myers–Perry–AdS solutions. The explicit characterization of effective potentials and orbit types offers a basis for future investigations into particle dynamics, field propagation, and observational signatures in higher-dimensional gravity theories. Further work will address the inclusion of perturbative effects, such as spin–curvature coupling, and explore the implications for gauge/gravity correspondence and higher-dimensional black hole phenomenology.

title: Monopoles, instantons and the Helmholtz equation
abstract: We investigate the interplay between monopole configurations, instanton solutions, and the spectral properties of the Helmholtz equation on curved manifolds. By employing gauge-theoretic methods, we construct explicit monopole and instanton backgrounds and analyze their influence on eigenfunction localization and spectral asymptotics. The study reveals novel correspondences between topological charges and spectral shifts, offering insights into geometric scattering phenomena. Our results extend the analytical framework for understanding field-theoretic solitons in relation to fundamental solutions of the Helmholtz equation in nontrivial geometries.
introduction:
Magnetic monopoles and instantons occupy a central place in modern theoretical physics, serving as paradigmatic examples of topologically nontrivial configurations in gauge theories. Since Dirac’s pioneering work on the quantization of magnetic charge, monopoles have been regarded not merely as hypothetical particles but as manifestations of deep geometric and topological structures in field theory. In non-Abelian gauge theories, the seminal constructions of ’t Hooft and Polyakov revealed that monopole solutions can arise as finite-energy, static field configurations in spontaneously broken gauge symmetries. Instantons, by contrast, are finite-action solutions of Euclidean field equations, representing tunnelling events between distinct vacua in the quantum theory. Both classes of objects illustrate the interplay between topology, gauge symmetry, and the dynamics of classical field equations.

A recurring theme in the analysis of monopoles and instantons is the reduction of the governing field equations to more tractable mathematical forms. In many cases, symmetry assumptions or ansätze transform the problem into a set of equations resembling familiar partial differential equations from mathematical physics. The Helmholtz equation, which describes time-harmonic scalar fields in Euclidean or Minkowski space, emerges naturally in various contexts as a simplified model capturing essential features of gauge field configurations. Its solutions are well understood in both Cartesian and curvilinear coordinates, and its spectral properties have profound connections to the stability and quantization of field configurations.

The connection between monopole and instanton solutions and the Helmholtz equation arises in several ways. For example, in certain gauge choices and under spherical symmetry, the radial profile of a monopole field can satisfy a form of the Helmholtz equation, with effective mass parameters determined by the Higgs field vacuum expectation value. Similarly, instanton moduli spaces can be probed by studying scalar Green’s functions governed by the Helmholtz operator on curved manifolds, particularly when investigating fluctuations around classical backgrounds. This correspondence allows the exploitation of the rich mathematical theory of the Helmholtz equation to gain insight into the qualitative and quantitative features of non-perturbative gauge configurations.

From a broader perspective, the study of these relationships contributes to several active areas of research. In mathematical physics, the interplay between gauge theory and integrable systems has revealed that many non-linear field equations admit reductions to linear equations such as the Helmholtz or Laplace equations under special conditions. In quantum field theory, understanding monopoles and instantons is crucial for elucidating phenomena such as charge quantization, confinement, and chiral symmetry breaking. In addition, these topological solitons play a role in cosmology, condensed matter analogues, and string theory, where generalizations of the Helmholtz equation appear in the description of brane configurations and compactification geometries.

The purpose of this work is to explore systematically the connections between monopole and instanton solutions in gauge theories and the Helmholtz equation, highlighting both the mathematical structures and the physical implications. We aim to show that, by casting certain aspects of the monopole and instanton equations into the form of the Helmholtz equation, one can leverage its well-developed analytical and numerical techniques to extract new results and clarify existing ones. In particular, we examine how boundary conditions, symmetry reductions, and spectral properties of the Helmholtz operator correspond to the topological charges and moduli of monopole and instanton configurations. This approach not only unifies disparate examples under a common mathematical framework but also suggests new avenues for constructing explicit solutions and for understanding their role in the non-perturbative dynamics of gauge fields.

In the following sections, we review the essential background on monopoles, instantons, and the Helmholtz equation, before presenting explicit mappings between these objects. We then analyse specific examples illustrating the utility of this correspondence, and conclude with a discussion of open problems and possible extensions to more general gauge groups and space-time geometries.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined the interplay between monopole and instanton configurations and the analytic structure of solutions to the Helmholtz equation, with particular emphasis on the geometric and topological frameworks that underlie their correspondence. By considering monopoles within the context of gauge theory and relating them to instanton solutions through dimensional reduction and symmetry constraints, we have highlighted the ways in which the Helmholtz equation emerges naturally in the description of certain field profiles. This connection is not merely formal: it provides a concrete analytic bridge between problems in classical field theory, spectral theory, and differential geometry.

Our analysis has shown that the Helmholtz equation, despite its apparent simplicity, encapsulates nontrivial information about the underlying gauge fields when interpreted in curved or nontrivial topological backgrounds. In particular, the separation of variables in appropriate coordinate systems reflects the hidden symmetries of monopole and instanton moduli spaces. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that specific classes of solutions to the Helmholtz equation can be mapped to field strengths satisfying the Bogomolny or self-duality conditions, thus offering a unified language for describing these solitonic objects.

The study also underlines the importance of boundary conditions and asymptotic behavior in connecting Helmholtz solutions to physically meaningful monopole and instanton configurations. The spectral properties of the associated differential operators, influenced by the topology of the background space, contribute directly to the quantization conditions and stability of these solutions. This insight opens the possibility of employing spectral and scattering theory techniques to classify and analyze monopole–instanton systems more broadly.

Looking ahead, the framework developed here suggests several avenues for further research. Extending the analysis to non-Euclidean signature metrics or to nontrivial fibrations could yield new classes of exact solutions, while numerical exploration of the Helmholtz equation in complex geometries may uncover novel correspondences. Moreover, the potential application of these ideas to condensed matter systems, where effective monopole or instanton-like excitations arise, remains an enticing direction. Ultimately, the confluence of analytic methods from partial differential equations and the geometric intuition from gauge theory enriches our understanding of both disciplines, and underscores the enduring role of equations like Helmholtz’s in bridging physical and mathematical insights.

title: Security Concerns in Minimum Storage Cooperative Regenerating Codes
abstract: Minimum Storage Cooperative Regenerating (MSCR) codes have emerged as a promising solution for distributed storage systems, enabling efficient repair of multiple node failures while maintaining storage optimality. Despite their advantages in reducing repair bandwidth and storage overhead, the cooperative repair process introduces unique security vulnerabilities that have not been comprehensively addressed. In particular, the simultaneous involvement of multiple helper nodes during repair can expose sensitive data to eavesdropping and collusion attacks, potentially compromising confidentiality and integrity. This paper investigates the security implications inherent to MSCR codes, focusing on scenarios where an adversary can access repair data, stored content, or both. We analyze the information leakage pathways in cooperative repair, characterizing the conditions under which an eavesdropper can reconstruct original file fragments. Furthermore, we propose a security framework incorporating encryption and coding-theoretic countermeasures tailored to the cooperative setting, balancing performance and protection. Our analysis quantifies the trade-offs between repair efficiency, storage overhead, and security guarantees, providing guidance for practical deployment in hostile or semi-trusted environments. Simulation results demonstrate that security-enhanced MSCR constructions can significantly mitigate leakage without severely impacting system efficiency. The findings highlight the necessity of integrating security considerations into the design of cooperative regenerating codes to ensure robust, efficient, and confidential distributed storage.
introduction: Distributed storage systems (DSS) have emerged as a crucial infrastructure for reliably storing massive data across multiple nodes. To enhance data reliability and repair efficiency, regenerating codes, particularly Minimum Storage Cooperative Regenerating (MSCR) codes, have been proposed. MSCR codes minimize storage overhead while enabling simultaneous repair of multiple node failures through cooperative mechanisms. However, their distributed nature and cooperative repair process introduce unique security vulnerabilities. Eavesdroppers or malicious nodes can exploit repair data exchanges to compromise confidentiality or integrity. Understanding these threats is essential for designing secure coding schemes. This work investigates security concerns in MSCR codes, analyzes potential attack models, and discusses strategies to mitigate risks without significantly degrading storage or repair performance.
conclusion: This work has examined the security challenges inherent in minimum storage cooperative regenerating (MSCR) codes, a class of erasure codes designed to minimize storage overhead while enabling efficient node repair in distributed storage systems. While MSCR codes achieve optimal bandwidth and storage trade-offs under cooperative repair settings, our analysis reveals that their structure may expose vulnerabilities to eavesdropping and collusion attacks, particularly when adversaries can observe repair traffic or compromise multiple nodes. We have discussed key threat models, highlighted the limitations of conventional security measures, and emphasized the need for coding schemes that integrate secrecy constraints without significantly degrading repair efficiency. Potential approaches include secure cooperative regenerating code constructions, information-theoretic secrecy mechanisms, and hybrid cryptographic-coding techniques tailored to the cooperative repair paradigm. Future research should investigate the trade-offs between secrecy capacity, repair bandwidth, and computational complexity, as well as the impact of dynamic adversary behavior. By addressing these open problems, it will be possible to design MSCR-based distributed storage systems that not only maintain optimal performance but also provide robust protection against realistic security threats.

title: Detection of subthreshold pulses in neurons with channel noise
abstract: The detection of weak, subthreshold stimuli by neurons is fundamentally influenced by intrinsic channel noise arising from the stochastic gating of ion channels. While such noise is often regarded as a detrimental source of variability, theoretical and experimental studies have shown that it can enhance signal detection through stochastic resonance–like mechanisms. In this work, we investigate the role of channel noise in the detection of single, subthreshold current pulses in a Hodgkin–Huxley–type neuron model with a finite number of sodium and potassium channels. Using numerical simulations, we systematically vary channel cluster sizes to modulate noise intensity and quantify detection performance via the probability of spike generation and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Our results demonstrate an optimal noise regime in which the probability of correctly detecting subthreshold pulses is maximized, with detection performance deteriorating for both lower and higher noise levels. Furthermore, we find that the optimal noise level depends on pulse amplitude and duration, indicating an interaction between stimulus parameters and intrinsic fluctuations. These findings highlight the constructive role of channel noise in neural signal processing and suggest potential functional benefits of variability in ion channel populations.
introduction:
The ability of neurons to reliably detect and respond to weak, time-varying stimuli is a fundamental aspect of sensory processing and neural computation. In many cases, biologically relevant signals are small in amplitude, fluctuating near or even below the threshold required to generate an action potential. These so-called subthreshold pulses are particularly challenging to detect because their amplitudes are insufficient to elicit a spike in the absence of additional inputs or intrinsic fluctuations. Nevertheless, neurons in vivo often operate in noisy environments where both external synaptic inputs and intrinsic sources of variability continuously perturb the membrane potential. Understanding how such noise influences the detection of weak signals is an important problem in computational neuroscience, with implications for sensory coding, neuronal reliability, and the design of bio-inspired signal processing systems.

In the classical view, noise is considered detrimental to information transmission, as it can obscure or distort small signals. However, a growing body of theoretical and experimental work has demonstrated that noise can, under certain conditions, enhance the detectability of weak inputs. This counterintuitive phenomenon, known as stochastic resonance (SR), has been observed in a variety of physical and biological systems, including sensory neurons, where an optimal level of noise can maximize the signal-to-noise ratio or detection probability. In neuronal membranes, noise can originate from multiple sources, including random synaptic release, fluctuations in ion concentrations, and stochastic gating of ion channels. While synaptic and network-induced noise have received substantial attention, intrinsic channel noise — arising from the probabilistic opening and closing of voltage-gated ion channels — is an inevitable feature of neuronal membranes, especially in small structures such as dendritic spines and thin axons.

Channel noise has several distinctive properties compared to externally applied noise. It is generated locally at the membrane, its statistics are shaped by the kinetics and densities of specific ion channel types, and it is often state-dependent, varying with membrane potential and channel gating variables. Theoretical studies based on stochastic versions of the Hodgkin–Huxley model have shown that channel noise can influence excitability, spike timing precision, and responsiveness to weak periodic signals. In small neurons or neuronal compartments with limited channel numbers, channel noise can even dominate over synaptic noise. Despite this, the role of channel noise in the detection of transient, subthreshold pulses has not been fully characterized, particularly for isolated pulses as opposed to periodic or continuous signals.

Detection of transient pulses is relevant for many real neural computations. For example, sensory neurons may encode brief environmental cues, and central neurons may be required to respond to sparse, temporally precise synaptic inputs embedded in ongoing activity. The success of such detection depends on both the intrinsic noise properties of the neuron and the temporal structure of the stimulus. Previous work has shown that for Gaussian white noise inputs, the reliability of detecting subthreshold pulses can exhibit resonance-like dependence on the noise intensity. However, intrinsic channel noise is neither white nor Gaussian, and its interaction with neuronal dynamics can produce qualitatively different effects. In particular, the gating kinetics of ion channels introduce correlations and a voltage dependence that could modulate the probability of a pulse triggering an action potential in complex ways.

In this work, we investigate the detection of isolated subthreshold pulses in a stochastic Hodgkin–Huxley neuron model subject solely to intrinsic channel noise. We focus on how the detection probability varies with the number of sodium and potassium channels, which controls the noise intensity, and on the temporal properties of the input pulses. By systematically varying channel numbers, we are able to explore regimes from low-noise, near-deterministic behavior to high-noise conditions representative of small membrane patches. We quantify detection performance using measures such as hit rate and false alarm rate, and examine whether an optimal noise level emerges, analogous to stochastic resonance, in the purely intrinsic noise setting.

Our motivation is twofold. First, from a biophysical perspective, understanding how channel noise influences pulse detection can shed light on the functional consequences of ion channel densities and distributions in neurons. Neurons may tune their channel complements not only for metabolic efficiency and excitability, but also for optimal signal detection in noisy environments. Second, from a computational perspective, insights into noise-assisted detection mechanisms could inform the design of neuromorphic devices or neural network models that exploit intrinsic stochasticity to enhance performance. By focusing on transient, subthreshold inputs and intrinsic noise sources, our study complements existing work on periodic signal detection and extrinsic noise, and contributes to a more complete picture of noise–signal interactions in neuronal systems.

The results we present demonstrate that intrinsic channel noise can facilitate the detection of weak, transient inputs, and that there exists a noise level — determined by the finite number of ion channels — at which detection performance is maximized. These findings highlight the dual role of noise in neural systems: while excessive fluctuations can degrade signal fidelity, appropriately tuned intrinsic stochasticity can enhance sensitivity to behaviorally relevant stimuli.
conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that channel noise can enhance the detection of subthreshold pulses in neurons, revealing a stochastic facilitation effect. This suggests intrinsic noise plays a functional role in neural signal processing. Such insights may inform models of sensory coding and guide the design of bio-inspired signal detection systems.

title: A Cloud-based Approach for Context Information Provisioning
abstract: The rapid proliferation of context-aware applications in domains such as smart cities, healthcare, and intelligent transportation systems has increased the demand for efficient and scalable mechanisms to provision context information. Traditional approaches often rely on resource-constrained devices or localized middleware, limiting their ability to handle large-scale, heterogeneous, and dynamic context data. This paper presents a cloud-based approach for context information provisioning that leverages the elasticity, ubiquitous accessibility, and computational power of cloud infrastructures. The proposed architecture integrates context acquisition, modeling, storage, and dissemination within a service-oriented framework, enabling on-demand access to context information by diverse applications and services. A layered design separates context sensing from processing and delivery, facilitating interoperability and adaptability to varying application requirements. Context data is aggregated from distributed sources, semantically enriched, and stored in scalable cloud repositories, while context reasoning services enable the derivation of higher-level information. The approach addresses key challenges such as latency reduction, quality-of-context assurance, and security through adaptive resource allocation, context validation mechanisms, and secure communication protocols. A prototype implementation on a public cloud platform is evaluated with simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating the system’s ability to support high request volumes with minimal performance degradation. Results indicate improved scalability, reduced provisioning time, and enhanced flexibility compared to conventional decentralized solutions. This work contributes a practical and extensible framework for delivering reliable and timely context information to support the next generation of pervasive and adaptive applications.
introduction:
The rapid proliferation of mobile devices, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, and ubiquitous computing has led to an unprecedented growth in the generation and consumption of context information. Context-aware systems, which adapt their behavior based on situational parameters such as user location, activity, preferences, and environmental conditions, have emerged as a key paradigm in enhancing user experience and enabling intelligent applications. These systems rely on accurate, timely, and relevant context information to deliver personalized and adaptive services. However, the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of context data, coupled with the increasing scale and diversity of context-aware applications, poses significant challenges in efficient provisioning, management, and dissemination of such information.

Traditional context provisioning approaches often assume localized data acquisition and processing, where context is gathered and interpreted within a limited scope, such as a single device or a small-scale network. While this model simplifies certain aspects of implementation, it suffers from scalability limitations, restricted context sharing, and difficulties in integrating diverse sources of information. As the number of context producers and consumers grows, these limitations become increasingly pronounced, leading to inefficiencies in resource usage, delays in context delivery, and inconsistencies in context interpretation.

Cloud computing offers a promising platform for addressing these challenges by providing elastic resources, ubiquitous accessibility, and powerful data management capabilities. The cloud’s ability to store, process, and distribute large volumes of data in a scalable manner makes it an ideal candidate for hosting context provisioning services. By leveraging cloud infrastructure, context-aware systems can benefit from on-demand scalability, high availability, and seamless integration of heterogeneous data sources. Moreover, cloud-based solutions can support advanced analytics and machine learning techniques to enhance context inference and prediction, thus improving the quality and relevance of the provided context information.

Despite these advantages, adopting a cloud-based approach for context provisioning is not without challenges. Issues such as latency, privacy, security, and the need for real-time responsiveness must be carefully addressed to ensure that cloud-hosted context services meet the stringent requirements of modern applications. Furthermore, designing efficient architectures and protocols for context acquisition, aggregation, and dissemination in the cloud environment is crucial for maximizing performance and minimizing operational costs.

In this paper, we propose a cloud-based approach for context information provisioning that aims to harness the scalability and computational power of cloud platforms, while addressing the specific demands of context-aware systems. Our approach integrates distributed context sources, employs flexible context modeling techniques, and exploits cloud-native capabilities for efficient context processing and delivery. The proposed framework is designed to support a wide range of applications, from smart cities and healthcare to industrial automation and personalized mobile services, thereby enabling a new generation of adaptive, intelligent, and responsive systems.
conclusion: This paper has presented a cloud-based approach for context information provisioning that leverages the scalability, flexibility, and ubiquitous accessibility of cloud computing infrastructures. By integrating distributed context sources with cloud-hosted processing and storage services, the proposed approach enables efficient acquisition, aggregation, and dissemination of context data to diverse applications and services. The architecture supports dynamic adaptation to varying workloads and heterogeneous data formats, while ensuring that context information remains accessible in real time to authorized consumers. Experimental evaluation and analysis indicate that the approach can reduce latency in context delivery, enhance reliability through redundancy, and support elastic scaling in response to demand fluctuations. Furthermore, the use of cloud-based resources facilitates easier maintenance and evolution of the context provisioning system, lowering operational complexity for developers and service providers. Future work will address advanced security and privacy mechanisms to protect sensitive context information, as well as the incorporation of intelligent data analytics for proactive and predictive context generation. Overall, the proposed solution offers a viable and effective foundation for next-generation context-aware systems, enabling richer user experiences and more adaptive services in pervasive and ubiquitous computing environments.

title: Progressive residual learning for single image dehazing
abstract: Single image dehazing is a challenging ill-posed problem due to the complex scattering of light in hazy environments and the absence of paired clean images in many real-world scenarios. We propose a progressive residual learning framework that restores haze-free images through a multi-stage refinement process. The network predicts residual haze components at successive scales, enabling gradual recovery of scene details and improved color fidelity. Each stage leverages features from both the input image and the intermediate dehazed outputs, facilitating effective error correction and structural enhancement. To better guide learning, we incorporate a multi-level supervision strategy and a perceptual loss term that preserves natural textures. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality, producing clearer, more natural images while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for practical applications.
introduction:
Haze is a common atmospheric phenomenon caused by the presence of fine particles such as dust, smoke, and water droplets suspended in the air, which absorb and scatter light. This degradation leads to reduced visibility, low contrast, and color distortion in captured images, severely impairing both visual quality and the performance of high-level computer vision tasks such as object detection, tracking, and scene understanding. Single image dehazing seeks to restore a clear scene from a single degraded observation without access to additional information, such as multiple views or depth maps. This problem is inherently ill-posed, as the information lost due to scattering and attenuation cannot be directly recovered without strong prior knowledge or effective learning-based models.

Traditional dehazing techniques often rely on the widely used atmospheric scattering model, which describes the formation of a hazy image as a combination of attenuated scene radiance and additive airlight. Early approaches exploited handcrafted priors to estimate the transmission map and atmospheric light, such as the dark channel prior (DCP), color-lines, or contrast maximization. While these methods achieved notable success in certain scenarios, their performance degrades under conditions that violate the assumed priors, such as bright objects, dense haze, or non-uniform illumination. Moreover, errors in intermediate estimations often propagate to the final restored image, resulting in artifacts or over-saturation.

With the advent of deep learning, data-driven methods have demonstrated significant improvements over traditional approaches by learning complex mappings from hazy to clear images directly from large-scale datasets. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and their variants have been employed to either estimate the transmission map and atmospheric light jointly or to learn an end-to-end dehazing transformation. These methods bypass explicit prior assumptions, allowing models to capture richer statistical and structural information. Nonetheless, deep dehazing models face their own challenges. Training very deep architectures often suffers from vanishing gradients, making optimization difficult, while overly complex models can lead to high computational cost and risk of overfitting. Furthermore, directly mapping a severely degraded input to a clean image in a single step can be suboptimal, as the restoration process is highly non-linear and requires careful handling of spatially varying degradation.

Recent research trends suggest that progressive restoration strategies—where the dehazing process is decomposed into multiple stages—can improve both accuracy and stability. Instead of attempting full restoration in one pass, progressive methods produce intermediate outputs that are iteratively refined, allowing the network to gradually recover lost details and correct estimation errors. This paradigm aligns with the concept of residual learning, where the network is trained to predict the difference between the degraded input and the desired output. Residual learning facilitates faster convergence, mitigates gradient degradation, and focuses model capacity on learning high-frequency details that are critical for perceptual quality.

In this work, we propose a progressive residual learning framework for single image dehazing that leverages the strengths of both progressive restoration and residual prediction. Our method decomposes the dehazing task into a sequence of residual estimation stages, where each stage is responsible for reducing the haze level of its input and producing a refined output for the next stage. This design enables the network to tackle the challenging restoration task in a coarse-to-fine manner, improving robustness to varying haze densities and scene complexities. Additionally, by structuring the learning problem around residuals, the network can more effectively focus on reconstructing structural and color details while avoiding over-correction and artifacts.

Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The progressive residual learning strategy not only enhances restoration accuracy but also yields visually pleasing results with natural colors and sharp edges. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we introduce a novel progressive residual learning architecture tailored to single image dehazing; (2) we design an effective multi-stage training scheme that facilitates stable optimization and efficient parameter usage; and (3) we provide comprehensive evaluations to validate the advantages of our method in diverse conditions. This study highlights the potential of progressive residual learning as a powerful framework for tackling complex image restoration problems beyond dehazing.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a progressive residual learning framework for single image dehazing, aimed at effectively restoring visibility and contrast in hazy images while preserving fine structural details. Motivated by the limitations of conventional end-to-end dehazing approaches, which often struggle with varying haze densities and complex atmospheric conditions, our method introduces a multi-stage residual refinement process. By progressively estimating and removing the haze components through successive residual learning blocks, the network is able to focus on different levels of detail at each stage, enhancing both global color fidelity and local texture reconstruction.

The proposed architecture leverages a coarse-to-fine strategy, where an initial estimate of the clean image is iteratively improved via intermediate residual predictions. This design not only facilitates the learning of haze-relevant features at multiple scales but also reduces the difficulty of directly mapping highly degraded inputs to clean outputs in a single step. The incorporation of skip connections and shared feature propagation between stages ensures that essential structural information is preserved throughout the reconstruction process. Our loss formulation, combining pixel-wise reconstruction loss with perceptual and structural similarity terms, further encourages the network to produce outputs that are both quantitatively accurate and visually pleasing.

Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world haze datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework over state-of-the-art single image dehazing methods. Quantitative evaluations show consistent improvements in PSNR and SSIM scores across diverse haze conditions, while qualitative comparisons reveal that our method produces clearer skies, more natural color tones, and sharper edges, with fewer artifacts and reduced over-saturation. In particular, the progressive residual learning paradigm proves effective in handling heavy haze scenarios, where single-pass approaches often fail to fully recover scene visibility.

A noteworthy advantage of our approach lies in its adaptability: the progressive design can be extended to incorporate additional stages or tailored to different degradation models, making it a promising candidate for broader image restoration tasks beyond dehazing. Furthermore, the modular architecture facilitates integration with other deep enhancement modules, such as attention mechanisms or domain adaptation strategies, to address real-world challenges such as non-uniform haze distribution, nighttime haze, or haze combined with other degradations.

While our method achieves strong performance, there remain avenues for future work. One limitation is the reliance on supervised training with paired data, which may not always be available or representative of real-world conditions. Exploring unsupervised or semi-supervised extensions, as well as domain adaptation techniques, could further enhance generalization. Additionally, optimizing the computational efficiency of the progressive stages would make the method more suitable for real-time applications, such as autonomous driving or aerial imaging.

In summary, the proposed progressive residual learning framework offers an effective and flexible solution for single image dehazing, capable of delivering high-quality reconstructions across a wide range of haze conditions. By combining multi-stage refinement, residual learning, and perceptually guided loss functions, our approach advances the state of the art and opens new directions for robust, detail-preserving image restoration in challenging atmospheric environments.

title: Badly approximable systems of affine forms, fractals, and Schmidt games
abstract: We investigate the set of badly approximable systems of affine forms and establish its strong winning properties in the sense of Schmidt games. Our results apply to intersections with certain fractal subsets of Euclidean space, including supports of measures satisfying power law conditions. This approach unifies and extends earlier work on Diophantine approximation and dynamical systems, revealing robustness under countable intersections and smooth mappings, and providing new insights into the interplay between metric number theory and fractal geometry.
introduction:
The study of Diophantine approximation occupies a central place in number theory, with a rich interplay between geometry, dynamics, and fractal analysis.
