A classical theme in the subject concerns the approximation properties of systems of linear or affine forms, and in particular the structure of the set of badly approximable systems. For a given system of affine forms, being badly approximable means that there exists a uniform bound away from zero for the error of approximation by integer vectors, scaled appropriately by the size of the integer inputs. While Dirichlet’s theorem guarantees good approximations for all systems, badly approximable ones represent the extremal opposite, exhibiting a certain rigidity in their metric behaviour.

These sets, although small in terms of Lebesgue measure, are large in other senses: they typically have full Hausdorff dimension, and their distribution is highly regular. Schmidt’s game, introduced by W. M. Schmidt, provides a powerful framework for quantifying such largeness. Winning sets in Schmidt’s game have remarkable stability properties: they are dense, of full Hausdorff dimension, and their winning property is preserved under countable intersections and certain smooth transformations. This technique has been instrumental in advancing our understanding of badly approximable systems and related exceptional sets.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in the interaction between Diophantine approximation and fractal geometry. One natural question is to determine the prevalence of badly approximable systems within sets of fractal structure, such as limit sets of iterated function systems or dynamically defined Cantor-like sets. The intersection of metric number theory with fractal geometry raises subtle challenges, as the standard tools often rely on translation invariance or uniform distribution, features not typically present in fractals.

The present work investigates badly approximable systems of affine forms in the context of fractal subsets of Euclidean space, employing Schmidt games and their variants as the principal tool. We aim to extend existing results by establishing winning properties for these sets in fractal settings, thereby demonstrating their robustness beyond homogeneous ambient spaces. Our approach combines techniques from homogeneous dynamics, geometric measure theory, and the theory of games, contributing to the broader understanding of extremal Diophantine phenomena in irregular environments.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the interplay between badly approximable systems of affine forms, the geometry of fractal subsets of Euclidean space, and the dynamical and game-theoretic framework provided by Schmidt games. Building upon earlier developments in Diophantine approximation and homogeneous dynamics, we have extended the scope of existing results to encompass a broad class of fractal sets that arise as supports of measures satisfying natural regularity and decay properties. Our analysis shows that the set of badly approximable systems retains a strong form of largeness—winning in the sense of Schmidt—when intersected with these fractal sets. This conclusion reinforces the robustness of winning properties under significant geometric and measure-theoretic constraints.

One of the central contributions of our study is the demonstration that the winning property for badly approximable affine forms is preserved under restrictions to supports of absolutely decaying and Federer measures. This general framework accommodates many self-similar and self-conformal fractals, including those with overlaps, thereby illustrating that the phenomena we describe are not confined to the smooth or uniformly distributed settings often considered in the literature. The invariance of winning sets under bi-Lipschitz transformations plays a crucial role in extending the results to these irregular contexts, enabling us to anchor the problem in a flexible geometric environment.

Furthermore, the methods developed here suggest deeper connections between the arithmetic complexity of affine systems and the fine-scale structure of the ambient set. The Schmidt game framework not only supplies a robust notion of largeness that is stable under countable intersections but also provides a constructive mechanism to exhibit points with prescribed Diophantine properties inside intricate geometric sets. This dual perspective—combining number-theoretic rigidity with fractal geometry—highlights the versatility of game-theoretic tools in modern metric Diophantine approximation.

Looking ahead, several avenues of inquiry remain open. It would be natural to investigate analogous winning properties for other classes of Diophantine sets, such as those defined by multiplicative approximation conditions or by constraints arising in inhomogeneous dynamics, within fractal subsets of both Euclidean and non-Euclidean spaces. Another promising direction is to refine the measure-theoretic hypotheses, potentially relaxing decay conditions while retaining sufficient control to apply game-theoretic arguments. We anticipate that further exploration along these lines will continue to illuminate the rich interconnections between Diophantine approximation, fractal geometry, and dynamical systems, and will expand the catalogue of settings in which badly approximable structures manifest their remarkable ubiquity.

title: Stream Containers for Resource-oriented RDF Stream Processing
abstract: We introduce *Stream Containers*, a novel abstraction for resource-oriented RDF stream processing that unifies heterogeneous data flows while preserving semantic context. Existing RDF stream processing approaches often focus on tuple-oriented models, limiting their ability to address resource-centric queries and dynamic link traversal at scale. Stream Containers encapsulate RDF triples by subject resource, maintaining coherent entity-level state across temporal windows. This design enables efficient filtering, aggregation, and enrichment based on resource identity, supporting both continuous and event-driven query patterns. We present a formal model for Stream Containers, along with an execution framework that integrates with existing RDF stream processors. Evaluation on real-world streaming datasets demonstrates reduced processing overhead and improved query expressiveness compared to conventional triple-at-a-time approaches. Our results suggest that Stream Containers provide a flexible and performant foundation for resource-oriented, semantically rich RDF stream processing in dynamic, data-intensive environments.
introduction: The proliferation of streaming data from sensors, social media, and IoT devices has intensified the demand for efficient, real-time processing of heterogeneous information. Resource Description Framework (RDF) has emerged as a standard for representing and interlinking data on the Web; however, traditional RDF processing systems are primarily designed for static datasets and lack mechanisms to handle continuous, high-velocity streams. RDF Stream Processing (RSP) extends RDF to support temporal and streaming semantics, yet existing approaches often struggle to balance expressiveness, scalability, and resource efficiency. In particular, fine-grained control over computational and network resources is crucial for deploying RSP in constrained or distributed environments. This paper introduces *stream containers*, a resource-oriented abstraction for RDF stream processing that encapsulates data flows together with their associated computational context. Stream containers enable modularity, isolation, and adaptive resource management, paving the way for more efficient and flexible RSP architectures. We present the conceptual model, implementation strategies, and evaluation results demonstrating their effectiveness.
conclusion: This work has introduced the concept of stream containers as a principled abstraction for resource-oriented RDF stream processing. By encapsulating streams within well-defined container boundaries, the approach enables uniform treatment of heterogeneous data sources while preserving the semantics of RDF resources over time. The proposed model supports fine-grained control over stream lifecycles, metadata management, and query execution, facilitating scalable and maintainable stream processing architectures. Experimental considerations suggest that stream containers can improve modularity and interoperability, particularly in distributed and dynamic environments where streams must be composed, transformed, and consumed by multiple stakeholders. Furthermore, the resource-oriented perspective aligns naturally with Linked Data principles, allowing seamless integration of streaming and static datasets. This opens opportunities for richer web-scale applications that require real-time reasoning and adaptive data flows. Future work will focus on optimizing container orchestration, exploring declarative query extensions, and evaluating performance in large-scale deployments. Overall, stream containers provide a solid foundation for advancing RDF stream processing towards more robust, reusable, and interoperable solutions.

title: Empirical Coordination with Two-Sided State Information and Correlated Source and State
abstract: We investigate empirical coordination in a point-to-point communication system where both encoder and decoder have access to correlated state information, and the source and states may be statistically dependent. The objective is to characterize the set of achievable joint distributions between source, states, and channel inputs/outputs under empirical coordination constraints. We derive single-letter necessary and sufficient conditions for achievability, highlighting the role of auxiliary random variables that capture correlation between source and states. Our results unify and extend existing coordination frameworks by accommodating two-sided state information and arbitrary source–state correlation. Several examples illustrate the impact of correlation structure on coordination capacity and optimal coding strategies.
introduction:
In modern communication systems, coordination between distributed agents often requires more than the reliable transmission of information. In many scenarios, the goal is to generate sequences of actions at different terminals whose joint empirical distribution approximates a target distribution, a problem known as empirical coordination. This framework extends beyond classical notions of source or channel coding by focusing on the joint statistical behavior of actions and states, rather than the recovery of exact information sequences.  

When the communication process is influenced by random states, the design problem becomes more intricate. State information may be available at the encoder, the decoder, or both, and it can be exploited to improve coordination performance. In a two-sided state information setting, both terminals observe side information sequences, possibly correlated with each other and with the source. This setup models a variety of practical systems, such as sensor networks with environmental side information, distributed control systems with local measurements, or multi-terminal communication with context awareness.

An additional layer of complexity arises when the source and the channel states are statistically dependent. In many real-world systems, the underlying phenomena affecting the source data and the communication medium are not independent. For instance, in wireless sensor networks, environmental conditions may simultaneously influence the sensed measurements and the channel characteristics. This correlation can be leveraged to improve coordination, but it also requires a careful reformulation of coding strategies and performance bounds.

Prior work on empirical coordination has largely focused on cases without state information, with one-sided state information, or with independent source and state variables. The presence of two-sided state information and correlated source-state pairs has received less attention, despite its relevance to realistic networked systems. Theoretical insights into this setting can illuminate fundamental trade-offs between communication rates, coordination accuracy, and the exploitation of side information.

In this paper, we study the problem of empirical coordination over a memoryless channel with two-sided state information and correlated source and channel state. We characterize the achievable coordination region under a general joint distribution of source and states, and we identify single-letter expressions for the optimal performance. Our results generalize existing coordination frameworks and unify several special cases in the literature. Furthermore, we provide examples illustrating how correlation between source and state can be harnessed to improve coordination efficiency. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of coordination under realistic state-dependent conditions and offers guidelines for the design of coordinated communication protocols in complex environments.
conclusion:
This work has investigated the problem of empirical coordination in a setting where both the encoder and the decoder have access to state information, and where the source and the channel state may be statistically correlated. By extending the classical framework of empirical coordination to this richer model, we have characterized achievable coordination regions under two-sided state information, highlighting the role of correlation between the source and the state in shaping optimal strategies. Our analysis builds upon information-theoretic tools and joint typicality arguments, adapting them to accommodate the dual presence of state knowledge and source–state dependence.

The results demonstrate that two-sided state information enables more efficient coordination than one-sided or no state information scenarios, particularly when the source and state are strongly correlated. In these cases, the encoder and decoder can exploit their respective state knowledge not only to mitigate uncertainty introduced by the channel but also to align their actions more closely with the desired empirical distribution. The achievable coordination region reflects a balance between the fidelity of reproducing the target joint distribution and the constraints imposed by the channel and state statistics. In particular, the correlation structure allows for partial inference of one terminal’s state from the other’s, which can be strategically leveraged to reduce the communication burden.

We have also delineated the impact of correlation: in the independent case, the coordination problem reduces to a form resembling previously studied models, whereas in the correlated case, new coding schemes emerge that combine binning, state-dependent encoding, and joint decoding. These schemes effectively synthesize the desired joint behavior while respecting the channel constraints. The inner and outer bounds derived here coincide in certain regimes, providing exact characterizations, and remain close in others, suggesting that the proposed strategies are near-optimal more generally.

Beyond the theoretical characterizations, our findings have implications for practical distributed systems in which agents operate with partial but complementary state information. Examples include sensor networks, distributed control systems, and cooperative communication scenarios, where exploiting correlation between observed phenomena and channel conditions can yield significant performance gains in coordinated behavior.

Future research directions include extending the analysis to multi-terminal configurations, incorporating causal or strictly causal state information constraints, and exploring coordination under additional operational constraints such as delay or complexity limits. Another promising avenue is the study of robustness to model mismatch in the source–state correlation, as real-world systems may only have approximate knowledge of the joint statistics. Overall, the results of this work contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between state information, correlation, and coordination, and open the way to more sophisticated designs for coordinated networks under realistic information structures.

title: Non-perturbative improvement of stout-smeared three flavour clover fermions
abstract: We present a non-perturbative determination of the clover coefficient for three-flavour lattice QCD with stout-smeared Wilson fermions. Using the Schrödinger functional framework, we tune the improvement coefficient to eliminate leading-order discretisation effects, enabling accurate continuum extrapolations. Stout smearing reduces ultraviolet fluctuations, improving signal quality and suppressing exceptional configurations. Our results cover a range of gauge couplings relevant for large-scale simulations, providing a parametrisation suitable for practical applications. We compare with perturbative estimates and find significant deviations at coarse lattice spacings, highlighting the necessity of non-perturbative improvement for precision QCD studies with smeared clover fermions.
introduction:
Lattice Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) provides a first-principles framework for the numerical study of the strong interaction, enabling quantitative predictions for a wide range of hadronic observables. In practice, these calculations require the discretization of the QCD action on a finite grid of spacetime points, which introduces discretization errors that must be controlled to reliably connect lattice results to the continuum limit. For Wilson-type fermion formulations, these errors are generically of order \(a\), the lattice spacing, and can be systematically reduced by the addition of appropriate improvement terms to the action and operators. The Sheikholeslami–Wohlert (“clover”) term is the most widely used \(O(a)\) improvement for Wilson fermions, with the associated coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{SW}}\) tuned to remove leading discretization artefacts.  

In recent years, link-smearing techniques have been employed to suppress ultraviolet fluctuations in the gauge fields entering the fermion action. Among these, stout smearing has proven particularly attractive due to its analytic nature, gauge covariance, and preservation of unitarity. Stout smearing reduces additive mass renormalization, improves chiral behaviour, and can lead to better scaling of physical observables. When combined with the clover term, stout-smeared Wilson fermions offer the potential for improved numerical stability and reduced discretization errors compared to their unsmeared counterparts. However, the interplay between smearing and non-perturbative improvement has not yet been fully explored for QCD with three dynamical flavours.

The determination of the clover coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{SW}}\) can be carried out perturbatively, but such estimates typically suffer from large uncertainties at the lattice spacings relevant for current simulations. Non-perturbative determination, for example through the Schrödinger functional method, has become the standard approach to ensure controlled improvement over a wide range of gauge couplings. For smeared actions, perturbative predictions for \(c_{\mathrm{SW}}\) can differ significantly from the true non-perturbative value, making a dedicated determination essential. Furthermore, the presence of stout smearing modifies the short-distance structure of the theory, and thus the renormalization pattern, in ways that may not be captured by unsmeared improvement studies.

In this work, we present a non-perturbative determination of the clover coefficient for three-flavour lattice QCD with stout-smeared Wilson fermions. We employ a single iteration of isotropic stout smearing in the fermion action, combined with a tree-level Symanzik-improved gauge action, and determine \(c_{\mathrm{SW}}\) using the Schrödinger functional framework. Our study spans a range of bare couplings corresponding to lattice spacings used in large-scale simulations, thereby providing directly applicable improvement coefficients for phenomenological applications. The improvement condition is imposed by requiring the restoration of the partially conserved axial current (PCAC) relation up to \(O(a^2)\) effects, ensuring that discretization errors are removed to first order in the lattice spacing.

By establishing the non-perturbative improvement for this smeared fermion action in the full three-flavour theory, our results enable more precise calculations of hadronic observables with reduced cutoff effects. This work thus provides a crucial ingredient for high-precision lattice QCD studies employing stout-smeared clover fermions, and contributes to the broader effort to optimize lattice actions for both accuracy and computational efficiency.
conclusion: We have demonstrated a non-perturbative improvement of stout-smeared three-flavour clover fermions, achieving reduced discretisation errors and improved scaling, thereby enabling more precise lattice QCD calculations for hadronic observables in future large-scale simulations.

title: Airy Function and 4d Quantum Gravity
abstract: We investigate the emergence of the Airy function in the nonperturbative formulation of four-dimensional quantum gravity, focusing on its role as a universal object encoding the partition function in certain regimes. Building on insights from lower-dimensional models and matrix model techniques, we explore how the Airy structure arises from the resummation of perturbative contributions around semiclassical geometries. In particular, we analyze the interplay between the gravitational path integral in the continuum and discrete approaches such as causal dynamical triangulations, where a finite-size scaling limit can lead to Airy-type behavior. We demonstrate that, under appropriate conditions on the coupling constants and boundary data, the wavefunction of the universe reduces to an Airy function, whose argument and scaling exponents encode key features of the underlying quantum geometry. This correspondence provides a bridge between continuum quantum cosmology and lattice-inspired models, offering a tractable analytic handle on nonperturbative effects. Our results suggest that the Airy function may serve as a universal signature of critical behavior in 4d quantum gravity, with potential implications for the semiclassical limit and holographic dual descriptions.
introduction:
The study of quantum gravity aims to reconcile the principles of quantum mechanics with those of general relativity, providing a consistent description of spacetime at the smallest scales. While significant progress has been made in various approaches—ranging from string theory to loop quantum gravity, causal dynamical triangulations, and holographic dualities—many fundamental questions remain open. One of the ongoing challenges is to identify universal structures or mathematical functions that capture essential features of quantum gravitational dynamics across seemingly disparate formulations. In recent years, a surprising connection has emerged between certain special functions, in particular the Airy function, and the nonperturbative partition functions of quantum gravity in diverse dimensions. This connection has been most thoroughly explored in three-dimensional quantum gravity and in matrix model formulations of two-dimensional gravity, but indications suggest that analogous structures may also arise in four-dimensional settings.

The Airy function, originally introduced in the context of differential equations describing diffraction and quantum mechanical tunneling, has long been recognized as a canonical special function with rich asymptotic properties. Its appearance in gravitational contexts is often tied to the exact summation of perturbative expansions or to the resummation of topological contributions in matrix models. In the context of three-dimensional gravity, particularly within the AdS\(_3\)/CFT\(_2\) correspondence, partition functions of certain supersymmetric gauge theories have been shown to reduce to expressions involving the Airy function, encoding both perturbative and nonperturbative effects. This has provided a powerful computational tool, allowing for exact predictions that interpolate between semiclassical geometries and fully quantum regimes.

In four dimensions, the situation is considerably more intricate. The local degrees of freedom of the gravitational field, absent in three dimensions, lead to a richer dynamical structure and more complex path integrals. Nevertheless, there are hints from supersymmetric localization, topological string theory, and holographic dualities that Airy-type structures may persist. For example, in certain \(\mathcal{N}=2\) supersymmetric gauge theories with holographic duals in AdS\(_4\), partition functions on three-spheres have been computed exactly and display a functional form strikingly reminiscent of the Airy function, suggesting a deep organizing principle at work. This observation raises the possibility that in some regimes of four-dimensional quantum gravity, particularly those accessible via supersymmetric or topological sectors, the Airy function may emerge as a universal descriptor of the nonperturbative path integral.

The emergence of the Airy function in quantum gravity contexts is not merely a calculational curiosity. It often signals that the underlying theory admits a matrix model or topological string description whose spectral curve has a cubic turning point, a structure known to produce Airy behavior in the associated wavefunctions. This, in turn, connects to the notion of quantum geometry and the quantization of moduli spaces, linking gravitational dynamics to well-studied areas of mathematical physics. In the four-dimensional case, identifying such structures could provide a new bridge between continuum formulations of quantum gravity and discrete or algebraic approaches, such as spin foams, tensor models, and refined topological strings.

From a physical perspective, the appearance of the Airy function in a gravitational partition function encodes a specific pattern of fluctuations around a saddle point, with subleading corrections determined by universal asymptotics. If such behavior is indeed present in four-dimensional quantum gravity, it would imply that certain observables—possibly including black hole microstate counts, cosmological wavefunctions, or holographic free energies—are governed by the same universal scaling laws found in lower-dimensional analogues. This universality would be a powerful guide in constructing and testing candidate theories of quantum gravity, as it would constrain the form of nonperturbative effects and provide benchmarks for numerical and analytical computations.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the role of the Airy function in four-dimensional quantum gravity, focusing on settings where exact or semi-exact computations are possible. We aim to clarify the mathematical origin of Airy behavior in these contexts, explore its physical implications, and assess its potential universality. By drawing on insights from supersymmetric localization, holography, and matrix model techniques, we seek to demonstrate that the Airy function is not an isolated artifact of lower-dimensional theories, but rather a manifestation of deeper structural features of gravitational path integrals. In doing so, we hope to contribute to the broader effort of uncovering universal patterns in quantum gravity, and to suggest new avenues for connecting discrete, continuum, and holographic approaches in four dimensions.
conclusion: In this work we have examined the emergence of the Airy function structure in the nonperturbative description of four-dimensional quantum gravity. By analyzing the relevant path integrals and their semiclassical expansions, we have shown how the universal features of the Airy function appear in the context of gravitational partition functions, echoing similar phenomena in lower-dimensional models. This correspondence suggests that certain aspects of the 4d theory retain a remarkable degree of analytic control, despite the complexity of the underlying dynamics. The interplay between continuum methods and discrete approaches, such as those inspired by matrix models and causal dynamical triangulations, reinforces the robustness of this connection. Furthermore, the Airy function behaviour provides valuable insight into the scaling properties near critical points and the role of quantum geometry fluctuations. Our analysis indicates that this structure is not merely a mathematical curiosity but a reflection of deep symmetries and universality in quantum gravity. Future work should explore the extent to which this framework can be extended to include matter couplings and higher-curvature corrections, potentially revealing a broader class of solvable structures within the full theory of four-dimensional quantum gravity.

title: Securing Smartphones: A Micro-TCB Approach
abstract: Smartphones increasingly handle sensitive personal and enterprise data, yet their complex software stacks enlarge the trusted computing base (TCB) and attack surface. This paper presents a micro-TCB architecture that isolates security-critical functions from the commodity operating system, thereby reducing vulnerability exposure. The proposed design leverages hardware-assisted virtualization and minimal trusted code to protect authentication, encryption, and policy enforcement mechanisms. We describe a prototype implementation on a modern smartphone platform and evaluate its security and performance. Results demonstrate that our micro-TCB can withstand common privilege-escalation and code-injection attacks while incurring negligible overhead for typical user workloads. By minimizing trusted components and enforcing strict isolation, this approach offers a practical path toward strengthening smartphone security without sacrificing usability or application ecosystem compatibility.
introduction:
Smartphones have evolved into ubiquitous personal computing platforms, integrating powerful processors, high-resolution displays, advanced sensors, and constant network connectivity. They now serve as primary devices for communication, financial transactions, personal data storage, and access to cloud-based services. As a result, they have become attractive targets for a wide range of security threats, from malware and spyware to sophisticated exploitation of system vulnerabilities. The increasing complexity of smartphone operating systems and application ecosystems, while enabling rich user experiences, has also expanded the attack surface, making it more challenging to ensure robust security guarantees.

Traditional approaches to securing smartphones often rely on monolithic operating system kernels and large trusted computing bases (TCBs). In such architectures, the TCB encompasses the entire kernel, device drivers, system services, and sometimes third-party components, all of which must be fully trusted to preserve system integrity. The sheer size of these TCBs—often millions of lines of code—makes comprehensive verification and bug-free assurance practically infeasible. A single vulnerability in any component within the TCB can potentially compromise the entire system, undermining the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of user data and services.

To address these concerns, the security community has increasingly turned attention toward architectural approaches that minimize the TCB, thereby reducing the trusted code footprint and the likelihood of exploitable vulnerabilities. The concept of a micro-TCB, or minimal trusted computing base, has emerged as a promising direction. A micro-TCB isolates only the most security-critical functions into a small, verifiable, and highly protected execution environment, while relegating non-critical functions to less trusted domains. By minimizing the amount of code that must be trusted, the micro-TCB approach facilitates formal verification, rigorous testing, and efficient vulnerability assessment, ultimately leading to stronger and more reliable security guarantees.

In the context of smartphones, a micro-TCB can be realized by leveraging hardware-based isolation mechanisms such as ARM TrustZone or secure enclaves, coupled with a carefully designed software architecture that separates sensitive operations from the general-purpose operating system. For example, cryptographic key management, biometric authentication, and secure storage can be implemented within the micro-TCB, ensuring that even if the main operating system is compromised, critical assets remain protected. This architectural separation aligns with the principle of least privilege, limiting the potential damage from any single component’s failure and enabling fine-grained control over security-critical resources.

However, adopting a micro-TCB approach in smartphones presents several challenges. These include ensuring efficient communication between trusted and untrusted components, maintaining usability and performance, integrating with existing application ecosystems, and addressing the evolving nature of mobile threats. Furthermore, designing a micro-TCB requires careful consideration of which functionalities must reside within the trusted domain and how to enforce strong isolation boundaries without impeding legitimate functionality.

This paper explores the design, implementation, and evaluation of a micro-TCB architecture tailored for modern smartphones. We examine the trade-offs between security, performance, and usability, and present a prototype system that demonstrates the feasibility of strong isolation for critical smartphone services. Our contributions include a detailed threat model for smartphone environments, a design methodology for identifying and isolating micro-TCB components, and a performance analysis of the resulting system. Through this work, we aim to advance the state of smartphone security by providing a practical pathway toward minimal, verifiable, and resilient trusted computing bases.
conclusion: This work has examined the potential of a micro-TCB architecture to address the growing security challenges associated with modern smartphones. By isolating a minimal trusted computing base from the complex and often vulnerable mobile operating system, we can significantly reduce the attack surface while providing a trustworthy foundation for sensitive operations. Our analysis demonstrates that even with stringent resource constraints, a carefully designed micro-TCB can enforce strong security properties, support critical applications, and facilitate user trust without imposing prohibitive performance overheads. Moreover, the modularity of the approach allows for incremental deployment, enabling integration into existing smartphone platforms with minimal disruption. While a micro-TCB is not a complete solution to all mobile security threats, it represents a pragmatic step toward more resilient architectures, particularly in an era of increasingly sophisticated mobile malware and pervasive connectivity. Future work will focus on refining the interface between the micro-TCB and the host OS, as well as extending its capabilities to protect emerging use cases such as mobile payments, health monitoring, and secure IoT integration. Through such efforts, micro-TCBs can play a central role in safeguarding the next generation of mobile computing.

title: Extremal dependence analysis of network sessions
abstract: We investigate extremal dependence structures in network session data to better understand the joint behavior of unusually large traffic events. Network sessions, defined by sustained communication between endpoints, often exhibit heavy-tailed characteristics in key metrics such as duration, volume, and peak rate. These heavy tails imply that extreme values are more probable than under light-tailed models, and that dependencies between such extremes can have significant implications for network reliability, capacity planning, and anomaly detection. Using a multivariate peaks-over-threshold framework, we extract session-level exceedances and apply tools from multivariate extreme value theory, including tail dependence coefficients and spectral measures, to quantify the strength and form of extremal dependence. We compare empirical findings across different session attributes and investigate asymptotic dependence versus independence regimes. The analysis reveals distinct dependence patterns: some pairs of metrics exhibit strong co-occurrence of extremes, while others tend toward asymptotic independence despite moderate correlation in the bulk of the distribution. These results highlight the limitations of conventional correlation-based analyses for risk assessment in network traffic. Our methodological approach and findings provide a rigorous basis for modeling joint tail risks in network environments, with potential applications in capacity management, intrusion detection, and resilience analysis.
introduction:
The characterization of dependence structures in extreme events has become an important topic in statistical modeling, with applications spanning finance, environmental science, and engineering. In the context of network traffic analysis, understanding the extremal dependence between session attributes is critical for identifying and mitigating rare but potentially disruptive events, such as sudden surges in traffic volume, anomalously long connection durations, or simultaneous high loads across multiple network links. Traditional correlation measures are inadequate for such settings, as they primarily capture average co-movements and fail to account for the joint behavior in the tails of the distribution. Extremal dependence analysis offers a principled framework to quantify the propensity of variables to exhibit extreme values simultaneously, thereby providing more relevant insights for risk assessment and anomaly detection in network systems.

Network sessions—defined as continuous interactions between endpoints over a network—are characterized by multiple features, including packet counts, byte volumes, throughput, and duration. While the marginal distributions of these features have been extensively studied, the dependence structure, particularly in the extremes, remains less well understood. This gap limits our ability to model and predict rare joint occurrences, such as sustained high-throughput, long-duration sessions that may signal malicious activity or stress on network infrastructure. Moreover, the increasing complexity and heterogeneity of modern networks, driven by diverse applications and communication patterns, necessitate robust statistical tools capable of capturing non-linear and asymmetric dependence in the tails.

Recent advances in multivariate extreme value theory (EVT) provide a suite of models and diagnostics for quantifying extremal dependence, including tail dependence coefficients, spectral measures, and copula-based approaches. These methods allow for distinguishing between asymptotic dependence—where extremes tend to occur together—and asymptotic independence—where co-occurrence of extremes is rare but still possible at finite thresholds. Applying such techniques to network session data can reveal structural relationships in extreme behaviors, inform the design of detection algorithms, and enhance resilience planning.

In this work, we conduct an extremal dependence analysis of network sessions using high-resolution traffic measurements. We investigate the joint tail behavior of key session metrics, assess the degree and nature of extremal dependence, and explore implications for network monitoring and security. By integrating statistical theory with empirical network observations, our study aims to advance the methodological toolkit for analyzing extremes in complex digital infrastructures, ultimately contributing to more effective anomaly detection and risk management in network operations.
conclusion:
This study has examined the extremal dependence structure of network sessions, with a particular focus on the statistical characterisation of joint tail behaviour in session-level metrics. By applying extreme value theory and tail dependence measures to high-resolution network traffic data, we have been able to identify patterns of co-occurrence between large values of key variables such as session duration, throughput, and packet counts. Our results indicate that extreme events in one metric are not always accompanied by extremes in others; rather, the dependence structure is heterogeneous, and in some cases, asymptotically independent. This finding challenges the assumption of uniform dependence across traffic characteristics and highlights the importance of modelling extremal dependence explicitly.

Through the utilisation of both parametric and non-parametric approaches—including the estimation of tail dependence coefficients and the application of copula models—we have demonstrated the nuanced nature of dependence in the extremes. The observed asymmetries suggest that network phenomena such as congestion episodes, high-throughput bursts, or unusually long sessions may have distinct generating mechanisms, which are only partially overlapping. This has important implications for network monitoring, as risk assessment based solely on marginal behaviours may underestimate the probability of joint extremes.

The analysis has also shown that temporal aggregation and filtering decisions can materially affect the estimation of extremal dependence. Short-term aggregation may preserve burst-level correlations, while longer aggregation intervals tend to dilute such dependencies, especially in the upper tails. This sensitivity underscores the need for methodological care when applying extreme value techniques to operational network data, where measurement granularity and collection policies vary.

From a practical standpoint, the recognition of heterogeneous extremal dependence can inform more robust anomaly detection frameworks. Models that incorporate tail dependence structures are better positioned to detect coordinated extreme behaviours, such as distributed denial-of-service patterns, which may not be evident from marginal analyses alone. Additionally, our findings suggest that capacity planning and resilience analysis should account for the possibility of simultaneous extremes in multiple session attributes, albeit with varying likelihoods.

While this work has provided a detailed empirical characterisation of extremal dependence in network sessions, it also opens several avenues for future research. Extending the analysis to include additional covariates, such as application type or geographic origin, could reveal further structure in the dependence patterns. Moreover, exploring the dynamics of extremal dependence over time may shed light on evolving usage patterns and emerging threats. Finally, integrating these statistical insights into real-time monitoring systems represents a promising step towards proactive network management.

In summary, the study underscores the complexity of extremal dependence in network traffic and demonstrates that careful statistical modelling is essential for accurate risk assessment and anomaly detection. By moving beyond marginal analyses, we can achieve a more comprehensive understanding of extreme behaviours in networked systems, ultimately contributing to their stability and resilience.

title: Tree Decomposition based Steiner Tree Computation over Large Graphs
abstract: We propose an efficient method for computing Steiner trees in large graphs using tree decomposition. Our approach exploits bounded treewidth structures to reduce computational complexity, enabling scalable solutions and improved performance on diverse benchmarks, while maintaining optimality guarantees for practical graph instances.
introduction:
The Steiner Tree problem is a well-known combinatorial optimization problem with numerous applications in network design, VLSI routing, phylogenetic tree construction, and computational biology. Given a graph and a subset of its vertices designated as terminals, the goal is to find a minimum-weight tree that spans all terminals, possibly including additional non-terminal vertices, referred to as Steiner vertices. Although the problem is NP-hard in general, its practical importance has motivated the development of a broad spectrum of exact, approximation, and heuristic algorithms. However, the rapid growth of real-world networks, both in size and complexity, poses significant challenges to existing approaches, particularly when dealing with large-scale graphs that cannot be processed efficiently using conventional methods.

One promising line of research exploits structural decompositions of graphs to enable more efficient algorithms for otherwise intractable problems. Tree decomposition, introduced by Robertson and Seymour in the context of graph minors theory, captures the notion of tree-likeness in a graph via the parameter of treewidth. Many NP-hard problems, including the Steiner Tree problem, can be solved in polynomial time when restricted to graphs of bounded treewidth, by leveraging dynamic programming over the decomposition. This has led to the successful application of tree decomposition techniques in domains such as constraint satisfaction, probabilistic inference, and database query optimization.

Despite these advances, applying tree decomposition-based methods to large, general graphs remains challenging. Real-world graphs often have large treewidth, and computing optimal or near-optimal tree decompositions is itself computationally hard. Furthermore, the size of dynamic programming tables grows exponentially with treewidth, leading to scalability bottlenecks. Recent work has begun to explore hybrid approaches, parallelization, and decomposition heuristics to address these limitations, yet their application to Steiner Tree computation over massive graphs is still in its early stages.

In this work, we investigate the use of tree decomposition-based techniques for computing Steiner Trees in large graphs, with a focus on practical scalability. We explore decomposition strategies suited for massive datasets, develop optimized dynamic programming formulations tailored to the Steiner Tree problem, and analyze their performance both theoretically and empirically. Our results demonstrate that, with careful algorithmic design and decomposition heuristics, it is possible to significantly extend the applicability of tree decomposition methods to large-scale Steiner Tree instances, bridging the gap between theoretical tractability and practical efficiency.
conclusion: In this work, we presented an approach for computing Steiner trees over large graphs by leveraging tree decomposition techniques. By exploiting the structural sparsity captured through low-width decompositions, our method decomposes the original problem into smaller, tractable subproblems that can be solved efficiently and combined to obtain globally optimal or near-optimal solutions. We demonstrated that this framework scales to graphs significantly larger than those addressable by conventional exact algorithms, while maintaining solution quality superior to that of common heuristics. The experimental evaluation across diverse datasets confirmed both the computational advantages and the robustness of the approach, particularly in scenarios with moderate treewidth. Furthermore, our method provides a principled way to incorporate additional constraints or optimization objectives without fundamentally altering the underlying algorithmic structure, making it flexible for various application domains. While the performance depends on the quality of the tree decomposition, advances in decomposition algorithms and heuristics can be directly integrated to further enhance scalability. Future work will explore dynamic and incremental settings, where graphs evolve over time, as well as parallelization strategies to exploit modern hardware. Overall, the proposed tree decomposition–based framework offers a promising and extensible direction for efficient Steiner tree computation in large-scale graphs.

title: Faster FAST(Feedback Arc Set in Tournaments)
abstract: We present Faster FAST, an improved algorithm for the Feedback Arc Set in Tournaments problem, achieving reduced complexity through refined combinatorial insights, enabling faster exact solutions and enhanced scalability across diverse tournament graph instances.
introduction:
The Feedback Arc Set problem is a well-studied combinatorial optimization problem that arises in diverse contexts such as ranking, circuit design, and computational social choice. Given a directed graph, the task is to find the smallest set of arcs whose removal makes the graph acyclic. In the special case of tournaments—complete asymmetric directed graphs—the problem is known as the Feedback Arc Set in Tournaments (FAST). This variant is particularly important due to its natural occurrence in ranking scenarios, where vertices represent items and directed edges encode pairwise preferences or comparisons. Despite its conceptual simplicity, FAST is NP-hard, and moreover, it is APX-hard, ruling out the possibility of a polynomial-time approximation scheme unless P = NP.

The combination of theoretical difficulty and practical relevance has spurred extensive research into both exact and approximate algorithms for FAST. From the perspective of exact computation, algorithms based on dynamic programming, branch-and-bound, and integer programming have been developed, with recent advances yielding improved fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms parameterized by the size of the optimal feedback arc set. On the approximation side, the best known polynomial-time algorithms achieve constant-factor approximations, with the current approximation ratio standing slightly above 1.36. In addition, heuristic and local-search-based methods have been explored for large-scale instances where exact computation is infeasible.

Motivated by applications in large ranking datasets, there is a growing demand for faster algorithms that can handle large tournaments while retaining strong guarantees on optimality or approximation quality. This demand is further amplified by the prevalence of noisy data, where the underlying preference structure is close to but not exactly acyclic, making robust and scalable algorithms crucial. Existing exact algorithms often suffer from high polynomial or even exponential time complexity, limiting their applicability in practice. Similarly, while approximation algorithms offer speed, their constants and overhead may not be competitive for truly large inputs.

In this work, we present a new algorithmic framework for FAST that significantly accelerates computation while maintaining competitive solution quality. Our approach leverages structural properties of near-optimal solutions in tournaments, coupled with refined combinatorial bounds and efficient search-space pruning. We provide both theoretical analysis and extensive experimental evaluation, demonstrating that our method offers substantial speedups over the state of the art, thereby expanding the range of FAST instances that can be solved or approximated effectively.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented Faster FAST, a novel algorithmic approach to the Feedback Arc Set problem in tournaments that improves upon the best-known running times while maintaining exactness. By combining refined combinatorial bounds with a carefully optimized dynamic programming scheme, we achieve a substantial reduction in both theoretical complexity and practical runtime. Our analysis demonstrates that exploiting structural properties of tournament instances—particularly degree imbalances and local ordering constraints—can be leveraged to prune the search space more aggressively than in previous methods. Experimental evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirms that Faster FAST consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art algorithms, often by significant margins, while producing identical optimal solutions.

Beyond the immediate performance gains, this work underscores the value of integrating fine-grained combinatorial insights into algorithm engineering for NP-hard problems. The techniques introduced here may be adaptable to other ranking and ordering problems with similar structural characteristics, potentially broadening their impact. Moreover, our findings suggest promising directions for future research, including further tightening of the recurrence relations, hybridization with approximation schemes for very large inputs, and the exploration of parallelization strategies to exploit modern computing architectures. 

In summary, Faster FAST advances both the theoretical and practical frontiers for solving the Feedback Arc Set problem in tournaments. It offers a more efficient tool for applications in ranking, preference aggregation, and competitive analysis, and lays the groundwork for continued improvements in exact algorithms for complex ordering problems.

title: Identifying Better Effective Higgsless Theories via W_L W_L Scattering
abstract: We investigate the identification of more effective Higgsless theories through a detailed analysis of longitudinal electroweak gauge boson scattering, focusing on \( W_L W_L \) processes at high energies. In the absence of a light Higgs boson, perturbative unitarity in these channels is endangered, providing a sensitive probe of the underlying dynamics responsible for electroweak symmetry breaking. We explore a range of effective field theory parameterizations, constrained by precision electroweak data, and evaluate their predictions for scattering amplitudes within experimentally relevant kinematic regimes. By comparing analytic unitarization schemes and incorporating next-to-leading order corrections, we delineate the parameter space consistent with both unitarity and current collider bounds. Our results highlight characteristic signatures—such as resonance enhancements and angular distributions—that distinguish viable Higgsless scenarios. These findings offer guidance for future collider measurements aimed at revealing or constraining alternatives to the Standard Model Higgs mechanism.
introduction:
The mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking (EWSB) remains a central question in particle physics. While the discovery of a Higgs-like scalar at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has provided strong evidence for the Standard Model (SM) Higgs mechanism, it remains of theoretical interest to explore scenarios in which EWSB occurs without a fundamental scalar field. Such “Higgsless” models, often realized in extra-dimensional or strongly coupled frameworks, achieve unitarization of longitudinally polarized weak boson scattering through the exchange of new vector resonances rather than a Higgs boson. These constructions provide an instructive testing ground for the limits of effective field theory (EFT) descriptions of electroweak interactions and for the search of new physics in vector boson scattering processes.

Longitudinal \( W_L W_L \) scattering is especially sensitive to the dynamics of EWSB, as in the absence of a Higgs boson the scattering amplitude grows with energy, eventually violating perturbative unitarity at the TeV scale. Effective Higgsless theories employ higher-dimensional operators or additional degrees of freedom to delay this unitarity breakdown, but the range of validity and predictive power of such theories depend sensitively on their parameterization and the spectrum of new states. Precision electroweak constraints, together with collider measurements of vector boson scattering, can therefore be used to discriminate between different Higgsless scenarios.

In this work, we investigate criteria for identifying more effective Higgsless EFTs by analyzing \( W_L W_L \) scattering amplitudes within a general parameter space. We emphasize the interplay between unitarity, causality, and experimental bounds, and identify regions where the EFT remains valid up to the highest accessible energies. Our results aim to guide the formulation of Higgsless models that are both theoretically consistent and phenomenologically viable in the era of high-energy collider experiments.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the potential of \(W_L W_L\) scattering as a probe for distinguishing among effective Higgsless theories. By systematically comparing scattering amplitudes across a range of representative models, we identified the key kinematic regions and observables most sensitive to deviations from the Standard Model expectations. Our analysis underscores the importance of incorporating both unitarity constraints and precision electroweak bounds in narrowing the viable parameter space. We find that certain classes of Higgsless scenarios can remain consistent with current data while predicting distinctive signatures in longitudinal gauge boson scattering at future colliders. These signatures, particularly in angular distributions and high-energy tails, offer promising avenues for experimental discrimination. Ultimately, refining measurements in these channels will be crucial for assessing the viability of Higgsless frameworks and for guiding the search for a more complete understanding of electroweak symmetry breaking.

title: Extragalactic Sources and Propagation of UHECRs
abstract: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), with energies exceeding \(10^{18}\) eV, provide a unique probe of the most extreme astrophysical environments. Their origin, acceleration mechanisms, and propagation through intergalactic space remain central questions in astroparticle physics. This work reviews and analyzes current evidence for extragalactic sources of UHECRs, including active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts, and starburst galaxies, emphasizing their potential to accelerate particles to the observed energies. We examine the role of large-scale magnetic fields and cosmic microwave background photons in shaping UHECR propagation, particularly through energy losses from photopion production and Bethe–Heitler pair production, leading to the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) suppression. Recent measurements of the UHECR spectrum, composition, and anisotropy from the Pierre Auger Observatory and Telescope Array are discussed in the context of source distribution and propagation models. We highlight the interplay between the observed transition from a light to heavier composition at the highest energies and the constraints it imposes on candidate sources. Numerical simulations incorporating magnetic deflections and energy loss processes are compared with observations to assess the viability of different source scenarios. The results underscore the importance of multi-messenger approaches, combining UHECR, gamma-ray, and neutrino data, to identify the astrophysical accelerators responsible for the highest-energy particles in the Universe.
introduction:
Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), defined as cosmic ray particles with energies exceeding \(10^{18}\) eV, represent one of the most intriguing frontiers in astroparticle physics. Their extreme energies, far beyond those achievable in terrestrial accelerators, imply origins in some of the most powerful astrophysical environments in the Universe. Despite decades of observations and theoretical work, the identification of their sources and the understanding of their propagation through cosmic space remain open challenges. Progress in these areas has profound implications not only for high-energy astrophysics but also for fundamental physics, including particle interactions at energies unattainable by human-made experiments.

A central question in UHECR research concerns the nature and location of their sources. Various classes of extragalactic astrophysical objects have been proposed as potential accelerators, including active galactic nuclei (AGNs), gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), radio galaxies, and clusters of galaxies. These environments are capable, in principle, of accelerating charged particles to ultra-high energies via mechanisms such as diffusive shock acceleration or unipolar induction. The distribution of such sources in the local Universe, their evolutionary histories, and their intrinsic luminosities directly influence the observable spectrum, composition, and anisotropy of UHECRs at Earth. Observational hints, such as correlations between the arrival directions of the highest-energy events and the large-scale structure of matter, suggest an extragalactic origin, though the degree of anisotropy and its interpretation remain topics of active debate.

The propagation of UHECRs from their sources to Earth is shaped by interactions with photon backgrounds and by deflections in cosmic magnetic fields. At energies above approximately \(5 \times 10^{19}\) eV, the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) effect limits the distance from which protons can arrive without significant energy loss, due to photopion production on the cosmic microwave background (CMB). For heavier nuclei, photodisintegration processes in interactions with the CMB and the extragalactic background light (EBL) further attenuate the flux over cosmological distances. Consequently, the observed UHECR spectrum encodes a convolution of source properties and propagation effects, with a horizon for the highest-energy events of order \(\sim 100\) Mpc. Magnetic deflections—both in the intergalactic medium and within the Milky Way—complicate the reconstruction of source directions, particularly for nuclei with higher charges.

Recent advances in UHECR observations, driven by large-scale experiments such as the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array, have yielded precise measurements of the energy spectrum, indications of a mixed mass composition at the highest energies, and increasingly stringent constraints on anisotropies. These data demand theoretical models that consistently link source acceleration physics, the distribution of potential sources in the nearby Universe, and the complex propagation phenomena en route to Earth. Multi-messenger approaches, correlating UHECR data with high-energy neutrinos and gamma rays, offer additional leverage in constraining source models, since these neutral messengers are unaffected by magnetic fields and provide more direct information on hadronic processes at the sources.

In this work, we review and analyze the current understanding of extragalactic sources and the propagation of UHECRs, emphasizing the interplay between astrophysical source modeling, cosmic magnetic field structure, and energy loss processes. By confronting theoretical predictions with the latest observational results, we aim to clarify the viable scenarios for the origin of UHECRs and to identify key observational tests for the next generation of cosmic-ray and multi-messenger observatories.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the role of extragalactic sources in the production and propagation of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), with particular attention to the interplay between source characteristics, cosmic magnetic fields, and energy loss mechanisms. By synthesizing observational constraints with theoretical models, we find that active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts, and other powerful astrophysical accelerators remain the most plausible candidates for generating particles above 10¹⁸ eV. The propagation of these particles through the intergalactic medium is strongly influenced by both large-scale magnetic structures and the cosmic microwave and infrared backgrounds, leading to characteristic energy attenuation features such as the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) cutoff. Our discussion highlights the sensitivity of arrival direction distributions and spectrum shapes to assumptions about source density, composition, and magnetic field strength.

The comparison of model predictions with current data suggests that a mixed composition scenario, coupled with a non-uniform distribution of nearby sources, can explain several observed spectral and anisotropy features. However, uncertainties in extragalactic magnetic field strengths and coherence lengths remain a significant limitation in reconstructing source positions and inferring acceleration conditions. Future high-statistics measurements from next-generation UHECR observatories, combined with multi-messenger observations in neutrinos and gamma rays, will be essential for breaking degeneracies between competing models.

Overall, our findings reinforce the view that UHECR studies occupy a critical intersection between astrophysics, particle physics, and cosmology. Continued progress will depend on both improved observational capabilities and refined theoretical treatments of source physics and propagation effects, ultimately bringing us closer to resolving the century-old question of the origin of the most energetic particles in the Universe.

title: Edge effect and significant increase of the superconducting transition onset temperature of 2D superconductors in flat and curved geometries
abstract: We investigate the influence of sample geometry and edge effects on the superconducting transition onset temperature \(T_{c}^{\mathrm{onset}}\) in two-dimensional superconductors. Using both flat and cylindrically curved geometries fabricated from atomically thin superconducting films, we systematically measure transport properties under identical environmental and measurement conditions. Our results reveal a significant enhancement of \(T_{c}^{\mathrm{onset}}\) in curved samples compared to their flat counterparts, with increases up to several percent depending on curvature radius. Detailed analysis suggests that this enhancement originates from edge-induced modifications of the local electronic density of states and strain distribution, which alter the pairing interaction. The effect is most pronounced in samples with high edge-to-area ratios, indicating a strong interplay between finite-size confinement, curvature-induced strain, and superconducting coherence length. These findings demonstrate that geometric design and edge engineering can serve as effective tools for tuning superconductivity in two-dimensional materials, offering a new pathway for optimizing performance in nanoscale superconducting devices.
introduction:
Two-dimensional (2D) superconductors have attracted considerable attention due to their unique electronic properties, tunability, and potential for applications in quantum technologies. In reduced dimensions, superconductivity is strongly influenced by finite-size effects, disorder, and electronic inhomogeneities, leading to deviations from the behavior observed in bulk materials. Among these influences, the role of sample geometry has emerged as a critical factor in determining superconducting characteristics. In particular, edges in 2D superconductors can host electronic states distinct from the bulk, potentially modifying the local pairing interaction and altering the superconducting transition temperature \( T_c \). Recent experimental and theoretical studies suggest that edge-induced modifications of the density of states, screening, and order parameter profile can give rise to measurable enhancements of the superconducting onset temperature.

While much of the existing literature has focused on planar geometries, recent advances in material fabrication allow the realization of 2D superconductors on curved substrates or in intrinsically non-planar configurations. Curvature introduces additional effects, such as strain-induced changes in electronic band structure, local variations in carrier density, and modified phonon spectra, all of which can influence superconductivity. The interplay between edge effects and curvature remains largely unexplored, despite its relevance for nanoscale devices, where both features may be prominent simultaneously. Understanding these geometric influences is essential for controlling superconductivity in low-dimensional systems and for designing devices with tailored superconducting properties.

In this work, we investigate the combined impact of edge effects and curvature on the superconducting transition onset temperature of 2D superconductors. Using a combination of experimental measurements and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that both flat and curved geometries can exhibit significant \( T_c \) enhancement near the edges, with curvature further amplifying this effect. Our results highlight geometry as a powerful tuning parameter for superconductivity in two dimensions, opening pathways to engineered superconducting states through nanoscale structural design.
conclusion: In summary, our study demonstrates that geometric factors, particularly edge effects and curvature, can substantially influence the superconducting transition onset temperature in two-dimensional superconductors. Through systematic comparison between flat and curved geometries, we have shown that confinement and boundary-induced modifications to the local electronic environment lead to a significant enhancement of \(T_c^{\text{onset}}\). The observed increase is consistent with theoretical models predicting amplified pairing interactions near edges and in regions of finite curvature. These findings highlight geometry as a powerful and tunable parameter in engineering superconducting properties at the nanoscale. Beyond fundamental interest, such control over \(T_c\) via structural design may open new avenues for optimizing performance in superconducting devices, including sensors and quantum circuits. Future work should explore the interplay between curvature, disorder, and dimensionality to fully map the design space for next-generation two-dimensional superconductors.

title: Hooks in the Headline: Learning to Generate Headlines with Controlled Styles
abstract: We present a method for generating news headlines with controllable stylistic attributes, enabling models to produce outputs that balance informativeness and reader engagement. Our approach extends sequence-to-sequence architectures with style control codes, allowing explicit specification of stylistic dimensions such as curiosity, urgency, or neutrality. We introduce a curated dataset of headline–article pairs annotated for style, and propose a multi-task training objective that jointly optimizes for factual alignment and stylistic fidelity. Automatic evaluations demonstrate that our model achieves higher style accuracy than strong baselines while maintaining semantic consistency with source articles. Human judgments confirm that generated headlines reflect intended styles without sacrificing clarity or relevance. Our findings highlight the feasibility of fine-grained style control in headline generation and suggest broader applications for style-aware text generation in journalism, marketing, and creative writing.
introduction: Headlines play a crucial role in attracting readers’ attention and framing their expectations for the accompanying content. Beyond summarizing, effective headlines often employ stylistic devices—such as curiosity gaps, emotional triggers, or rhetorical questions—to engage audiences. Recent advances in natural language generation have enabled automated headline creation, yet controlling the style of generated headlines remains a challenging task. Existing approaches typically focus on optimizing for relevance or click-through rates, with limited attention to fine-grained stylistic control. This paper addresses the problem of generating headlines with explicitly controlled styles, aiming to balance informativeness and engagement. We present a framework that learns to produce stylistically diverse headlines while preserving semantic fidelity, enabling more adaptable and targeted content generation for diverse editorial goals.
conclusion: This work presented a framework for generating headlines with controllable stylistic attributes, enabling models to balance informativeness with engagement. By incorporating style conditioning into headline generation, we demonstrated that it is possible to produce outputs aligned with specific tones, such as neutral, sensational, or humorous, without sacrificing semantic relevance. Experimental results on diverse datasets confirmed that our approach improves both stylistic fidelity and content preservation compared to baseline methods. These findings suggest promising applications in journalism, content recommendation, and automated media creation, while also raising considerations for ethical deployment. Future work will explore finer-grained style control, user-in-the-loop generation, and robustness across languages and domains to further refine headline generation capabilities.

title: Sliding without slipping under Coulomb friction: opening waves and inversion of frictional force
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of sliding without slipping under Coulomb friction, focusing on the emergence of opening waves and the associated inversion of the frictional force. Using numerical simulations and analytical modelling, we show that local separation at the contact interface can propagate as self-sustained opening waves, significantly altering the macroscopic frictional response. These waves induce transient reversal of the net frictional force, enabling motion opposite to the applied load. The results reveal a novel interplay between contact mechanics and frictional dissipation, with implications for the control of friction in engineering systems and for understanding rupture propagation in geophysical contexts.
introduction:
Sliding of elastic bodies in contact is a classical problem in mechanics, with applications ranging from earthquake dynamics and brake systems to the performance of seals, bearings, and robotic grippers. When two solids are pressed together and one is driven tangentially relative to the other, the interface experiences frictional tractions that resist motion. In the simplest Coulomb description, the tangential traction is proportional to the local normal pressure with a constant coefficient of friction, and sliding occurs when the shear traction reaches this limit. This idealized law, despite its simplicity, captures many essential aspects of frictional behavior and serves as a cornerstone for more elaborate constitutive models.

An important distinction in frictional contact mechanics is between gross sliding and partial slip. In the latter, regions of the interface alternate between sticking and slipping, producing complex stress distributions and energy dissipation patterns. The onset of gross sliding is often preceded by the nucleation and propagation of slip fronts at the interface, analogous in some respects to rupture fronts on geological faults. Under certain conditions, however, an even more unusual mode of interfacial motion can arise: opening waves, in which a local separation accompanies the slip front, momentarily lifting the surfaces apart. Such detachment waves have been observed in soft materials, layered systems, and more recently in hard elastic bodies, and they can profoundly alter the frictional response.

The mechanics of opening waves under Coulomb friction is particularly intriguing because they challenge the intuitive picture of friction always opposing motion. When a portion of the interface lifts off, the local normal pressure decreases sharply, reducing the available frictional resistance. Moreover, the transient kinematics of the wave can generate local relative velocities and tractions that lead to a reversal of the net frictional force, so that it assists rather than resists the macroscopic sliding. This inversion is counterintuitive from the standpoint of steady-state friction, yet it emerges naturally from the dynamic interplay of elastic waves, contact mechanics, and frictional constraints.

Despite the potential significance of such phenomena, systematic studies of opening waves in the context of Coulomb friction remain scarce. Most prior work has addressed steady sliding or conventional stick–slip under constant normal load, often neglecting the possibility of separation. The conditions under which opening waves appear, their propagation characteristics, and their impact on the global force–velocity relation are not fully understood. Furthermore, the role of material properties, geometry, and loading history in promoting or suppressing frictional force inversion has yet to be clarified.

This work investigates the dynamic sliding of elastic bodies under Coulomb friction with particular emphasis on the nucleation and propagation of opening waves and the associated inversion of the macroscopic frictional force. Through a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulation, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms that enable such counterintuitive behavior and to map the parameter regimes in which it arises. The results contribute to a deeper understanding of nontrivial frictional dynamics and may inform the design of engineering systems where control of frictional forces is critical.
conclusion: We have investigated the dynamics of sliding without slipping under Coulomb friction, with particular emphasis on the emergence of opening waves and the associated inversion of the frictional force. Through a combined analytical and numerical approach, we demonstrated that localized detachment fronts can propagate along the interface, transiently reducing the real area of contact. This process alters the local stress distribution in a way that can reverse the sign of the net tangential force, leading to a momentary acceleration of the slider in the direction opposite to the applied load. Our results show that such inversion arises from a subtle interplay between normal stress redistribution, finite compliance of the contacting bodies, and the nonlinearity inherent in Coulomb friction. The opening waves act as carriers of stored elastic energy, releasing it in a manner that can transiently counteract the macroscopic driving force. These findings extend the understanding of frictional sliding beyond the classical steady-state paradigm, highlighting that even in nominally stable configurations, complex spatio-temporal patterns can emerge. The implications are relevant for interpreting frictional instabilities in engineering systems and natural faults, suggesting that apparent violations of Amontons’ law may occur in dynamic regimes. Future work will explore parameter ranges and material combinations where such effects are most pronounced, and their potential for controlled friction modulation.

title: Comparing SVM and Naive Bayes classifiers for text categorization with Wikitology as knowledge enrichment
abstract: This study investigates the comparative performance of Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Naive Bayes (NB) classifiers for text categorization, enhanced through the integration of Wikitology as an external knowledge source. Wikitology, a hybrid knowledge base combining Wikipedia with structured ontologies, is employed to enrich document representations with semantic and conceptual features beyond the traditional bag-of-words model. We evaluate the classifiers on benchmark text datasets, both with and without Wikitology-based enrichment, to assess the impact of external knowledge on classification accuracy. Experimental results indicate that semantic enrichment improves performance for both approaches, with SVM generally outperforming NB in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score.
