The findings highlight the benefits of augmenting statistical text classification methods with structured external knowledge, particularly for handling semantic ambiguity and sparse features. This work contributes empirical evidence supporting hybrid approaches that combine machine learning techniques with knowledge-based feature augmentation for improved text categorization.
introduction:
Text categorization, the task of assigning predefined categories to textual documents, has become a fundamental component in various natural language processing (NLP) applications such as information retrieval, sentiment analysis, spam filtering, and topic detection. With the exponential growth of digital textual content, the need for accurate and efficient classification methods has intensified. Traditional machine learning algorithms, notably Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Naive Bayes (NB), have been widely employed for text categorization due to their robustness, computational efficiency, and proven performance across diverse domains. However, their effectiveness is often constrained by the representation of text data, which typically relies on bag-of-words or term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF–IDF) models that disregard semantic relationships between terms.

Recent research has explored the integration of external knowledge sources to enrich document representation, thereby potentially improving classification performance. One such approach involves leveraging structured and semi-structured knowledge bases to provide semantic context beyond the surface lexical features. Wikitology, a hybrid knowledge base derived from Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and other structured resources, offers a rich repository of concepts, categories, and relations. It integrates both encyclopedic and lexical knowledge, enabling the mapping of textual tokens to semantically related concepts and entities. By incorporating such enriched features, classifiers can benefit from a deeper understanding of the text, potentially overcoming issues related to synonymy, polysemy, and sparse data.

SVMs are well-regarded for their ability to find optimal separating hyperplanes in high-dimensional feature spaces and have demonstrated strong performance in text categorization tasks, particularly with sparse data. In contrast, the Naive Bayes classifier, grounded in probabilistic modeling and the assumption of conditional independence between features, offers simplicity, fast training, and competitive performance in many text classification scenarios. While SVMs are often considered more accurate, Naive Bayes classifiers remain attractive for large-scale or real-time applications due to their low computational cost. The comparative performance of these two methods, especially when supplemented with semantically enriched features, warrants systematic investigation.

This study aims to compare the performance of SVM and Naive Bayes classifiers in text categorization tasks when document representation is enhanced using Wikitology-based knowledge enrichment. By mapping terms to concepts, categories, and linked entities in Wikitology, we generate augmented feature sets that incorporate semantic relations absent in conventional bag-of-words models. We hypothesize that such enrichment will improve classification accuracy for both algorithms, but the degree of improvement may vary due to their differing learning paradigms.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive experimental evaluation using benchmark text datasets, comparing baseline models with their Wikitology-enhanced counterparts. We analyze classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F-measure, and discuss the implications of semantic enrichment for each classifier. The findings contribute to a better understanding of how external knowledge integration can influence the effectiveness of widely used text categorization algorithms, offering insights for designing more semantically aware NLP systems.
conclusion: This study compared the performance of Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Naive Bayes classifiers for text categorization, incorporating Wikitology as a source of knowledge enrichment. Experimental results demonstrated that leveraging Wikitology’s structured and unstructured semantic information improved classification accuracy for both models, with SVM generally outperforming Naive Bayes in most scenarios due to its robustness in handling high-dimensional feature spaces. Nevertheless, Naive Bayes remained competitive, particularly in settings with limited training data, benefiting from its probabilistic simplicity and efficiency. The integration of Wikitology features enhanced semantic representation, contributing to better discrimination between categories. These findings highlight the value of external knowledge bases in augmenting machine learning approaches for text classification. Future work may explore hybrid models, deeper semantic integration, and domain-specific adaptations to further exploit knowledge-enriched features for improved performance across diverse text categorization tasks.

title: SurfaceNet: An End-to-end 3D Neural Network for Multiview Stereopsis
abstract: We present SurfaceNet, an end-to-end 3D convolutional neural network for multiview stereopsis that directly infers surface occupancy from multiple calibrated images. Unlike traditional pipelines that rely on intermediate depth maps or handcrafted features, SurfaceNet operates entirely in 3D voxel space, jointly reasoning over geometry and appearance. The network encodes image evidence into a unified volumetric representation and predicts surface likelihoods, enabling accurate, consistent reconstructions. Trained on large-scale datasets, SurfaceNet achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging benchmarks, demonstrating robustness to wide baselines and occlusions. Our approach simplifies multiview stereo, reduces error accumulation, and provides a flexible framework for 3D scene understanding.
introduction:
Reconstructing accurate three-dimensional geometry from multiple two-dimensional images has long been a central problem in computer vision. Multiview stereopsis (MVS) seeks to recover dense surface representations by exploiting the geometric relationships among images captured from different viewpoints. This problem is of fundamental importance for a wide range of applications, including robotics, autonomous navigation, augmented and virtual reality, cultural heritage preservation, and film production. Despite considerable progress over the past decades, existing MVS methods still face significant challenges in terms of scalability, robustness to varying illumination and textureless regions, and the ability to produce high-fidelity reconstructions without extensive post-processing.

Traditional MVS pipelines typically decompose the reconstruction task into several sequential stages: feature detection and matching, camera pose estimation, depth map computation for each view, and fusion of depth maps into a consistent 3D model. While this modular approach allows for the use of specialized algorithms at each stage, it also introduces fragility, as errors in earlier steps propagate to subsequent stages. Moreover, hand-crafted components and heuristic fusion strategies may struggle to capture complex photometric and geometric variations present in real-world scenes.

Recent advances in deep learning have shown the potential to learn robust representations directly from data, leading to improved matching, depth estimation, and surface reconstruction. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and their 3D extensions have been applied to various subproblems of MVS, such as stereo matching and volumetric reconstruction. However, most existing deep learning approaches for MVS still retain the modular structure of traditional pipelines, training separate networks for depth estimation and for volumetric fusion. This separation limits the ability to jointly optimize all components toward the final reconstruction quality.

In this work, we present **SurfaceNet**, an end-to-end 3D neural network architecture that directly infers volumetric surface representations from multiple posed images. Our method takes as input a set of calibrated images and produces a discretized 3D occupancy grid representing the scene surface, without requiring intermediate depth maps or explicit fusion steps. By formulating MVS as a single, unified learning problem, SurfaceNet can exploit global context across views and spatial locations, and learn consistency constraints directly in 3D space. The network is trained to predict surface occupancy probabilities, enabling it to gracefully handle uncertainty and noise in the input images.

We evaluate SurfaceNet on benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it achieves competitive or superior reconstruction accuracy compared to both traditional and deep learning-based baselines. Furthermore, the end-to-end design simplifies the reconstruction pipeline, reduces cumulative error, and offers a flexible framework for incorporating additional cues such as semantics or temporal consistency. Our results highlight the promise of fully 3D, end-to-end neural architectures for advancing the state of the art in multiview stereopsis.
conclusion: In this work, we presented SurfaceNet, an end-to-end 3D convolutional neural network designed for multiview stereopsis. Unlike traditional pipelines that decompose the problem into sequential stages, SurfaceNet directly infers surface occupancy from multiple calibrated images, learning both photometric and geometric cues in a unified framework. By operating in a voxelized 3D space, our approach effectively aggregates information across views while preserving spatial consistency. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SurfaceNet achieves competitive or superior reconstruction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining robustness to varying viewpoints and lighting conditions. Furthermore, the learned model generalizes well to unseen scenes without the need for handcrafted similarity measures or post-processing heuristics. These results highlight the potential of fully trainable 3D architectures for dense multiview reconstruction. Future work will explore adaptive resolution strategies, memory-efficient network designs, and integration with learned depth priors to further improve scalability and detail recovery. SurfaceNet thus represents a promising step toward practical, data-driven 3D reconstruction from multiple images.

title: Proposition and validation of an original MAC layer with simultaneous medium accesses for low latency wireless control/command applications
abstract: This paper proposes and validates a novel Medium Access Control (MAC) layer enabling simultaneous medium accesses to reduce latency in wireless control and command applications. Unlike conventional contention- or schedule-based protocols, the proposed scheme exploits controlled concurrent transmissions with interference-aware signal processing to maximize channel utilization while preserving reliability. A formal model of the protocol is developed to predict performance under varying network densities and traffic patterns. The design is implemented and evaluated through simulation and hardware-in-the-loop experiments in industrial-like scenarios. Results demonstrate significant latency reduction, improved throughput, and deterministic timing guarantees compared to standard MAC approaches, confirming the suitability of the proposed method for time-critical wireless control systems.
introduction:
The increasing prevalence of wireless communication in industrial control and command systems has created a growing demand for ultra-reliable and low-latency transmission solutions. Applications such as factory automation, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and critical infrastructure monitoring require stringent timing guarantees and deterministic performance, often with end-to-end latencies in the order of a few milliseconds or less. Traditional wireless communication protocols, while effective for general data exchange, are often unable to meet these requirements due to medium access delays, contention-based mechanisms, and retransmission overheads. In such contexts, the design of the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer becomes a key determinant of overall system performance.

Conventional MAC protocols, such as those based on CSMA/CA or TDMA, exhibit inherent limitations in scenarios demanding both low latency and high reliability. CSMA/CA, as implemented in IEEE 802.11 or IEEE 802.15.4, suffers from unpredictable access delays caused by contention and backoff mechanisms, particularly under high traffic loads. TDMA-based approaches, while offering deterministic access, require precise synchronization and often result in underutilization of the channel when traffic patterns are variable. These constraints are exacerbated in industrial wireless control/command applications where multiple devices must frequently exchange short, time-critical messages.

To address these challenges, recent research has explored various enhancements, including hybrid MAC schemes, priority-based scheduling, and resource reservation techniques. However, most existing solutions still follow a sequential access paradigm, where only one node transmits at a time, limiting the achievable latency improvements. Emerging physical layer technologies, such as non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) and multi-packet reception (MPR), have opened new opportunities for MAC layer innovations by enabling simultaneous transmissions from multiple nodes. These capabilities can potentially transform medium access from a sequential to a concurrent process, thereby significantly reducing access delays.

This work proposes and validates an original MAC layer design that exploits the possibility of simultaneous medium accesses to meet the stringent requirements of low-latency wireless control/command applications. The proposed scheme leverages advanced interference management and decoding techniques to allow multiple devices to transmit concurrently without compromising reliability. By doing so, it aims to combine the predictability of deterministic access with the efficiency of high channel utilization. The paper details the design principles of the new MAC protocol, presents its theoretical performance analysis, and validates its effectiveness through simulation and experimental evaluation. The results demonstrate substantial latency reductions compared to conventional approaches, highlighting its potential for next-generation industrial wireless systems.
conclusion: This work has proposed and validated an original MAC layer enabling simultaneous medium accesses, specifically designed to meet the stringent requirements of low-latency wireless control and command applications. The proposed approach departs from conventional contention-based or strictly scheduled schemes by allowing controlled concurrent transmissions, thereby reducing access delays while maintaining reliable communication. Through analytical modeling, simulation, and experimental validation, we have demonstrated that the method achieves significant latency improvements without compromising packet delivery performance, even under high network load. The integration of interference management and precise synchronization mechanisms proved essential to ensuring robustness in realistic conditions. Comparative evaluations with existing MAC protocols confirmed the efficiency and scalability of the solution for various network sizes and traffic patterns. These results suggest that simultaneous medium access can be a viable paradigm for next-generation industrial and mission-critical wireless systems. Future work will focus on extending the protocol to heterogeneous traffic scenarios, investigating adaptive access control strategies, and exploring its integration with emerging physical layer technologies to further enhance performance and reliability in dynamic environments.

title: Real-time Sign Language Fingerspelling Recognition using Convolutional Neural Networks from Depth map
abstract: This paper presents a real-time system for recognizing sign language fingerspelling using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) applied to depth map data. Unlike approaches relying solely on RGB images, depth information provides robust hand shape representation under varying lighting and complex backgrounds, enhancing recognition accuracy. The proposed method captures depth maps of hand gestures, preprocesses them to isolate the region of interest, and inputs them into a CNN architecture optimized for spatial feature extraction. The system is trained on a dataset of isolated fingerspelling gestures and evaluated in real-time scenarios, demonstrating high accuracy and low latency suitable for interactive applications. Experimental results show that depth-based CNN recognition achieves reliable performance across different users and environmental conditions. This work contributes to assistive technologies for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community by enabling efficient, non-intrusive sign language interpretation, and highlights the potential of depth sensing combined with deep learning for robust gesture recognition systems.
introduction:
Sign language serves as a primary means of communication for the Deaf and hard-of-hearing community, enabling the expression of complex ideas through manual gestures, facial expressions, and body movements. Fingerspelling, a component of sign language, involves spelling out words letter by letter through distinct hand shapes, and is particularly useful for proper nouns, technical terms, or words without a specific sign. Automatic recognition of fingerspelling has the potential to bridge communication gaps between sign language users and non-signers, facilitating inclusion in both social and professional contexts.

Recent advances in computer vision and machine learning have enabled the development of automated sign language recognition systems. However, most existing approaches rely heavily on RGB images or video, which can be sensitive to lighting conditions, background clutter, and skin tone variations. Depth sensing technology offers a promising alternative, providing three-dimensional structural information of the hand independent of color or illumination. Depth maps can capture the fine-grained spatial details of hand shapes and positions, which are critical for accurate fingerspelling recognition.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance in image-based classification tasks due to their ability to learn hierarchical feature representations directly from raw data. In the context of depth map analysis, CNNs can effectively extract discriminative spatial features for hand shape recognition without the need for handcrafted descriptors. Moreover, the availability of affordable depth sensors has made it feasible to explore real-time applications.

This study presents a real-time fingerspelling recognition system based on CNNs using depth map inputs. The proposed approach aims to achieve high recognition accuracy while maintaining low latency, making it suitable for interactive communication scenarios. We evaluate the system on a dataset of depth images representing fingerspelled letters and assess its performance under real-time constraints. By leveraging depth information and deep learning, our method addresses limitations of traditional RGB-based systems and contributes toward more robust, accessible, and inclusive human-computer interaction for sign language users.
conclusion: This work presented a real-time sign language fingerspelling recognition system using convolutional neural networks applied to depth maps. By leveraging depth information, the approach demonstrated robustness to variations in lighting and background, enabling accurate recognition across diverse conditions. The proposed model achieved high accuracy while maintaining low latency, making it suitable for interactive applications. Experimental results confirmed its effectiveness in real-world scenarios, highlighting its potential to enhance communication accessibility for the Deaf and hard-of-hearing communities. Future work will explore integrating temporal modeling and expanding the vocabulary for more comprehensive sign language recognition.

title: Improving Speaker-Independent Lipreading with Domain-Adversarial Training
abstract: We propose a domain-adversarial training framework to improve speaker-independent lipreading, addressing the performance degradation caused by speaker variability. Our approach integrates a gradient reversal layer into a deep lipreading architecture, encouraging the learned visual features to be invariant to speaker identity while preserving discriminative power for speech recognition. Experiments are conducted on benchmark lipreading datasets with multiple speakers, evaluating both seen and unseen speaker scenarios. Results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms conventional training and other domain adaptation techniques in speaker-independent settings, achieving higher word accuracy and robustness. The findings highlight the effectiveness of adversarial domain-invariant feature learning for bridging the gap between training and testing speakers in visual speech recognition.
introduction:
Automatic lipreading, the task of inferring spoken content from visual cues of a speaker’s mouth region, has drawn increasing interest due to its potential applications in noisy environments, silent speech interfaces, and accessibility technologies for the hearing-impaired. Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved lipreading accuracy by leveraging spatiotemporal features extracted from video frames. However, most models are trained and evaluated on fixed sets of speakers, and their performance deteriorates substantially when tested on previously unseen individuals. This degradation stems from the fact that visual speech patterns vary across speakers due to differences in appearance, articulation style, and coarticulation effects, leading to a mismatch between training and testing distributions.

Speaker-independent lipreading seeks to generalize across such variations, enabling robust performance regardless of the identity of the speaker. Achieving this goal is challenging because conventional supervised learning tends to capture speaker-specific cues alongside linguistic content, inadvertently binding the learned features to the training speakers. As a result, models overfit to idiosyncratic characteristics rather than learning speaker-invariant representations of speech movements.

Domain-adversarial training has emerged as a promising approach to address domain shift problems in other modalities, such as speech recognition and text classification. By incorporating an adversarial objective that encourages the learned features to be indistinguishable across domains—in this case, different speakers—models can be guided toward encoding information that is maximally informative for the primary task while invariant to speaker identity. This framework offers a principled way to disentangle linguistic content from speaker-specific attributes.

In this work, we investigate the use of domain-adversarial training to improve speaker-independent lipreading. We explore architectures and training strategies that integrate adversarial speaker classification with visual speech recognition, and we evaluate their effectiveness on benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that adversarially learned representations can substantially reduce speaker dependency, leading to improved generalization to unseen speakers.
conclusion: This work demonstrated that domain-adversarial training can significantly enhance speaker-independent lipreading by reducing domain shift between training and unseen speakers. Experimental results showed consistent improvements over baseline models, highlighting the method’s ability to learn speaker-invariant visual features. The approach requires no additional labeled data from target speakers, making it practical for real-world deployment. Future work will explore integrating temporal attention mechanisms and multimodal cues to further improve robustness and accuracy across diverse speaking styles and conditions.

title: Delineating Intra-Urban Spatial Connectivity Patterns by Travel-Activities: A Case Study of Beijing, China
abstract: Understanding intra-urban spatial connectivity is essential for interpreting urban dynamics and guiding sustainable planning. This study investigates spatial connectivity patterns in Beijing by examining residents’ travel-activity behaviors derived from large-scale mobility data. Using origin–destination flows and activity-based classification, we construct a multi-layer network capturing work, leisure, and shopping trips. Network analysis reveals distinct spatial structures across activity types: work trips exhibit strong monocentric patterns centered on the urban core, while leisure and shopping trips show more polycentric and dispersed connectivity. We further identify spatial heterogeneity in interaction intensity, reflecting socio-economic and functional differences between districts. The findings highlight the value of activity-specific mobility analysis for understanding urban form and informing targeted transport and land-use policies in rapidly evolving megacities.
introduction:
Understanding the spatial connectivity patterns within cities is fundamental to urban planning, transportation management, and the promotion of sustainable mobility. As cities expand and diversify, the daily travel-activities of residents form complex interaction networks that shape the functionality and livability of urban spaces. Intra-urban spatial connectivity—defined as the degree and structure of linkages among different urban zones—reflects both the physical infrastructure and the socio-economic dynamics that influence how people move and interact. Examining these patterns can reveal underlying urban structures, highlight disparities in accessibility, and inform policies aimed at improving urban efficiency and equity.

In recent years, the proliferation of location-based data, such as GPS trajectories, mobile phone records, and smart card transactions, has provided unprecedented opportunities to study mobility at fine spatial and temporal scales. This data-driven approach enables researchers to capture not only the origins and destinations of trips but also the sequences of activities that constitute daily urban life. Travel-activity analysis goes beyond traditional trip-based models by incorporating the purpose, timing, and interdependence of movements, offering deeper insights into how individuals use and connect different parts of the city.

Beijing, the capital of China, presents a compelling case for investigating intra-urban connectivity through travel-activities. As a megacity with a population exceeding 20 million, Beijing exhibits a complex urban form shaped by rapid economic growth, extensive transportation investments, and evolving land-use patterns. The coexistence of historic cores, sprawling suburbs, and emerging business districts generates diverse travel demands and intricate spatial linkages. Understanding these linkages is critical for addressing challenges such as traffic congestion, spatial inequality, and environmental sustainability.

This study aims to delineate the intra-urban spatial connectivity patterns of Beijing by analyzing travel-activity data. By applying network-based methods to capture the structural characteristics of spatial interactions, we seek to identify dominant flows, functional clusters, and variations across time periods. The findings will contribute to a nuanced understanding of Beijing’s urban dynamics and provide empirical evidence to support integrated transportation and land-use planning in large metropolitan contexts.
conclusion:
This study examined intra-urban spatial connectivity patterns in Beijing through the lens of travel-activity behaviors, offering nuanced insights into the interplay between human mobility and urban structure. By integrating activity-based travel data with spatial network analysis, we identified heterogeneous connectivity patterns that reflect both the polycentric nature of Beijing’s urban form and the spatial clustering of specific activity types. The results reveal that work-related trips dominate long-distance connectivity, reinforcing the importance of major employment centers, while leisure and shopping trips tend to strengthen local linkages within sub-centers. Temporal variations further highlight peak-hour polarization around core business districts and off-peak dispersion toward peripheral zones.  

These findings emphasize that urban connectivity is not uniform but is shaped by the spatial distribution of activities, transport infrastructure, and temporal rhythms of the city. This suggests that planning interventions should account for the differentiated role of various activity types in shaping mobility flows, particularly in balancing centrality and accessibility across districts. Moreover, identifying high-connectivity corridors and under-connected zones can inform targeted transport improvements and land-use strategies aimed at enhancing urban efficiency and equity. Future research could extend this approach by incorporating emerging travel modes, dynamic land-use changes, and comparative analyses across cities to further advance the understanding of intra-urban connectivity in rapidly evolving metropolitan contexts.

title: Reduced-order 4D-Var: a preconditioner for the Incremental 4D-Var data assimilation method
abstract: We propose a reduced-order formulation of the Incremental 4D-Var data assimilation method, designed as a preconditioner to accelerate convergence while preserving accuracy. The approach projects the control space onto a low-dimensional subspace spanned by dominant modes, thereby reducing computational cost in the inner minimization. This reduced-order step is embedded within the full 4D-Var framework, serving as an efficient preconditioned iteration. Numerical experiments with a geophysical model demonstrate that the method achieves comparable analysis quality to standard Incremental 4D-Var, while significantly decreasing iteration counts and execution time, offering a practical strategy for large-scale assimilation problems.
introduction: Four-dimensional variational data assimilation (4D-Var) is a powerful technique for estimating the state of dynamical systems by optimally combining model forecasts with observational data over a time window. However, the high computational cost associated with large-scale applications limits its operational use, particularly in numerical weather prediction. The incremental formulation of 4D-Var addresses some of these challenges, yet the solution of the associated large linear systems remains demanding. Reduced-order approaches, which approximate the control space using a low-dimensional subspace, offer a promising means to accelerate convergence. In this work, we investigate a reduced-order 4D-Var formulation as a preconditioner for the incremental method, aiming to improve efficiency while retaining the accuracy of full-space assimilation.
conclusion: This study has demonstrated that the reduced-order 4D-Var approach can be effectively used as a preconditioner for the incremental 4D-Var data assimilation method. By projecting the control space onto a reduced subspace spanned by dominant modes, the method accelerates convergence while preserving the essential dynamical information. Numerical experiments indicate that this strategy improves computational efficiency and can reduce the number of iterations required to reach an optimal solution, without significant loss of accuracy in the analysis fields. The approach is particularly advantageous when the reduced basis is constructed to capture the main sources of variability in the system. Furthermore, the reduced-order preconditioning framework is flexible and can be adapted to different model configurations and observational scenarios. These findings suggest that integrating reduced-order techniques into variational assimilation schemes offers a promising pathway toward more efficient high-dimensional data assimilation, especially for operational applications where computational resources are limited and timeliness is critical.

title: A low-resolution, GSa/s streaming digitizer for a correlation-based trigger system
abstract: We present the design and implementation of a low‑resolution, gigasample‑per‑second (GSa/s) streaming digitizer developed to support a correlation‑based trigger system for high‑rate, wide‑bandwidth signal environments. The system targets applications in which continuous, real‑time digitization and processing of radio‑frequency signals are required, such as in high‑energy physics experiments and radio astronomy. The digitizer employs an 8‑bit analog‑to‑digital converter operating at 2 GSa/s, optimized for sustained data streaming rather than deep local buffering. A high‑throughput FPGA performs on‑board formatting and preliminary correlation operations, enabling low‑latency trigger decisions based on multi‑channel signal similarity. The hardware architecture emphasizes reduced resolution to balance sampling speed, power consumption, and manageable data rates for downstream processing. Streaming data are transmitted via high‑speed serial links to a back‑end processing cluster, where more sophisticated correlation algorithms refine the trigger decision. Laboratory characterization demonstrates effective bandwidth exceeding 800 MHz, stable timing performance, and linearity adequate for correlation‑based detection despite the reduced bit depth. A prototype deployment in a testbed trigger system validated continuous operation over extended periods with negligible data loss. This work shows that low‑resolution, high‑rate streaming digitizers can be an effective, resource‑efficient solution for correlation‑based triggering, particularly in scenarios where rapid identification of transient events outweighs the need for high‑precision waveform reconstruction. Future developments will explore scaling to larger channel counts and integration with advanced real‑time signal processing frameworks.
introduction:
High-energy physics experiments, radio astronomy arrays, and cosmic-ray detection systems increasingly rely on fast, flexible trigger architectures to identify rare events in large backgrounds. In many such applications, the trigger decision is based on the correlation of signals from multiple spatially separated sensors, enabling suppression of uncorrelated noise and improved sensitivity to transient phenomena. Implementing these correlation-based triggers requires digitization of wideband analog waveforms at gigasample-per-second (GSa/s) rates, combined with continuous, low-latency data streaming to downstream processing units.  

Conventional high-speed digitizers are typically designed for precision waveform capture, offering high resolution and deep buffering. While such devices are well-suited to detailed offline analysis, they are often over-specified for real-time trigger generation, where the emphasis lies on sustained throughput, manageable data volumes, and minimal dead time. In correlation-based systems, the amplitude resolution requirements can be relaxed, as the trigger algorithms primarily exploit timing and phase information rather than fine-grained amplitude measurements. This relaxation opens the possibility of designing low-resolution digitizers that operate at high sampling rates, with architectures optimized for continuous streaming rather than large local storage.

A streaming digitizer tailored for correlation-based triggering must address several technical challenges. These include maintaining signal integrity at multi-GSa/s rates, ensuring synchronization across multiple channels or boards, and providing an efficient interface to real-time processing hardware such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) or graphics processing units (GPUs). Additionally, it must achieve a balance between resolution, sampling rate, power consumption, and cost, to allow scalable deployment across large sensor arrays.

In this work, we present the design and implementation of a low-resolution, GSa/s streaming digitizer developed specifically for a correlation-based trigger system. The digitizer sustains continuous high-rate data transfer to processing units, enabling real-time computation of cross-correlations between channels. We describe the system requirements derived from the target application, the hardware architecture and data path, and the performance achieved in laboratory tests. Our approach demonstrates that by tailoring resolution and buffering to the needs of correlation triggering, it is possible to realize a compact, efficient digitizer suited to large-scale, high-speed sensor networks.
conclusion: The developed low-resolution, GSa/s streaming digitizer demonstrates effective performance for a correlation-based trigger system, achieving continuous high-speed data acquisition with manageable resource requirements. Its design balances sampling rate, resolution, and data throughput to meet the needs of real-time triggering while preserving flexibility for diverse experimental conditions. Results confirm robust operation and reliable correlation performance, validating the architecture for large-scale detector applications. Future work will focus on integration with full trigger and readout chains, and on optimizing firmware for enhanced efficiency and scalability.

title: Phenomenology of $\alpha_s$ at intermediate energy: the quark-hadron duality approach
abstract: We investigate the behaviour of the strong coupling $\alpha_s$ in the intermediate energy regime using a quark–hadron duality framework. By combining inclusive electron–nucleon scattering data with perturbative QCD evolution, we extract effective values of $\alpha_s$ bridging the perturbative and nonperturbative domains. The analysis emphasizes the role of resonance–continuum averaging in extending the applicability of QCD scaling concepts. Our results indicate a smooth transition between quark and hadron descriptions, supporting the notion of duality as a viable phenomenological tool for probing $\alpha_s$ beyond the purely asymptotic regime.
introduction:
The study of the strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$ across different energy scales remains a central task in quantum chromodynamics (QCD). While perturbative QCD provides a reliable description of high-energy processes, at intermediate energies—where the transition between perturbative quark-gluon dynamics and nonperturbative hadronic degrees of freedom occurs—the behavior of $\alpha_s$ is less well constrained. In this regime, the coupling grows, and purely perturbative expansions become inadequate, necessitating approaches that can bridge quark-level and hadron-level descriptions.

Quark-hadron duality offers a powerful phenomenological framework to address this problem. Originally observed in inclusive electron–nucleon scattering, it relates averaged hadronic observables to partonic calculations, suggesting that suitably averaged resonance-region data can be described by the same underlying quark-gluon dynamics that govern deep inelastic scattering. This duality provides an opportunity to extract information on $\alpha_s$ in a kinematic domain where nonperturbative effects are significant but not dominant enough to obscure quark-level behavior.

In recent years, refined experimental measurements and theoretical analyses have extended the applicability of quark-hadron duality to a variety of observables, including structure functions, sum rules, and moments of inclusive cross sections. By exploiting these connections, one can infer the running of $\alpha_s$ down to momentum transfers of a few GeV$^2$, probing the onset of confinement and the transition from asymptotic freedom to strong coupling. Such studies also offer a testing ground for models of the infrared behavior of $\alpha_s$, including scenarios with an effective coupling that freezes at low scales.

The present work aims to investigate the phenomenology of $\alpha_s$ in the intermediate-energy regime using the quark-hadron duality approach, combining experimental data and theoretical constraints. By systematically analyzing duality in inclusive processes, we seek to improve the extraction of $\alpha_s$ in this challenging kinematic region, providing insights into the interplay between perturbative and nonperturbative QCD dynamics.
conclusion: In this work we have examined the phenomenology of the strong coupling $\alpha_s$ in the intermediate–energy regime through the lens of quark–hadron duality. By confronting inclusive observables with perturbative QCD predictions supplemented by appropriate nonperturbative corrections, we have explored the extent to which duality holds and the implications for the running of $\alpha_s$ in the transition region between perturbative and hadronic descriptions. Our analysis indicates that, when averaged over suitable kinematic domains, quark–hadron duality provides a consistent framework for extracting an effective coupling that smoothly interpolates between high–energy and low–energy behaviors. The results suggest that duality–based approaches can reduce model dependence and offer complementary constraints to traditional determinations of $\alpha_s$. This reinforces the view that the intermediate–energy domain is not merely a boundary between regimes, but a region where perturbative and nonperturbative dynamics are intertwined in a quantifiable way, opening opportunities for refined studies of QCD’s strong interaction dynamics.

title: GeneSyst: a Tool to Reason about Behavioral Aspects of B Event Specifications. Application to Security Properties.
abstract: GeneSyst is a tool supporting the analysis of behavioral aspects of B event specifications by generating symbolic labelled transition systems from B models. This approach enables systematic reasoning about dynamic properties, including security requirements such as confidentiality or integrity. By deriving behavioral views directly from specifications, GeneSyst facilitates the verification of event sequences against desired properties. We illustrate its application to the formal validation of security properties, demonstrating how the tool aids in detecting potential violations early in the development process.
introduction:
Formal methods provide a rigorous framework for the specification, design, and verification of complex software and hardware systems. Among these methods, the B Method has gained wide acceptance for the formal development of safety- and security-critical systems, due to its mathematically precise notation and its support for stepwise refinement. Specifications in the B framework are expressed in terms of abstract machines, which encapsulate state variables, invariants, and operations that modify the state. The Event B style further emphasizes modeling systems as a collection of events, each describing a guarded state transition. While the B Method is well suited for expressing functional requirements and proving invariant preservation, reasoning about behavioral properties, such as the sequencing of events or the possibility of certain execution traces, remains a challenging task.

Behavioral aspects are particularly important when addressing security properties, where the correctness of a system not only depends on the validity of individual states but also on the admissible sequences of actions over time. Properties such as confidentiality, integrity, availability, and non-interference often require reasoning about all possible event traces that can arise from the specification. Traditional proof obligations generated in the B Method focus on ensuring consistency and refinement correctness but do not directly capture these temporal or trace-based concerns. As a result, designers must resort to additional modeling or verification techniques to ensure that the specified system meets its intended behavioral requirements.

GeneSyst has been developed to address this gap by providing automated support for reasoning about the behavioral semantics of B event specifications. The tool generates a symbolic labelled transition system (SLTS) directly from a B specification, preserving the abstraction of state variables through symbolic predicates rather than concrete valuations. This approach allows the exhaustive exploration of possible event sequences without requiring full instantiation of the state space, which is often infeasible for realistic systems. By working at the symbolic level, GeneSyst can efficiently capture the control-flow structure embedded in a B specification and expose it to formal analysis.

The SLTS produced by GeneSyst serves as an explicit behavioral model that can be used to verify a variety of properties, including those expressed in temporal logics or as trace-based constraints. In the context of security, this enables the formal validation of properties such as access control policies, information flow restrictions, and protocol invariants, by checking that no execution path violates the desired constraints. Because the transition system is derived automatically from the B model, the approach ensures consistency between the state-based functional specification and its behavioral interpretation, reducing the risk of divergence between design artifacts.

This paper presents the principles underlying GeneSyst, describes its architecture and algorithms for generating symbolic transition systems from B event specifications, and illustrates its application to the verification of security properties. We discuss how the tool integrates with existing B development environments, and how it can be employed to complement the standard proof-based verification process with behavior-oriented analysis. A running example drawn from the security domain is used to demonstrate the practical benefits of the approach, highlighting how GeneSyst facilitates the detection of behavioral flaws early in the development cycle. By bridging the gap between state-based specification and behavioral reasoning, GeneSyst offers a valuable addition to the formal methods toolkit for the development of dependable and secure systems.
conclusion:
The work presented in this paper has introduced **GeneSyst**, a tool designed to support the systematic reasoning about the behavioural aspects of *B* event-based specifications, with a particular emphasis on the verification of security properties. Our motivation stemmed from the observation that while the *B* method provides a solid mathematical framework for the development of correct systems, there is frequently a gap between the abstract specification level and the analysis of dynamic properties, especially those related to system behaviour over time. This gap can hinder the formal validation of requirements such as information flow control, confidentiality, integrity, or availability, which are inherently behavioural in nature.

GeneSyst addresses this issue by generating, from a given *B* event system, a *Symbolic Labelled Transition System* (SLTS) that preserves the formal semantics of the original specification. The SLTS form enables the explicit examination of event sequencing, state reachability, and condition satisfaction, while retaining symbolic representations that avoid unnecessary state explosion. By making the behavioural structure explicit, GeneSyst bridges the distance between the abstract state-based model and the operational reasoning needed for security analysis.

Through a combination of symbolic computation and constraint solving, GeneSyst can operate directly on the abstract state space defined in the *B* specification, without requiring premature refinement or concrete instantiation. This capability is particularly important for security properties, which are often best verified as early as possible in the development process. The tool’s output provides a behavioural model that is amenable to both manual inspection and automated property checking. For example, temporal constraints, sequences of events, or the absence of certain behaviours can be directly validated on the SLTS. This makes it possible to detect potential vulnerabilities or specification defects before implementation decisions have been made.

The application of GeneSyst to a set of representative case studies has demonstrated its effectiveness. In particular, we have shown how non-interference and other information flow properties can be expressed and verified within this framework. The tool’s symbolic approach allowed us to reason about large or infinite state spaces that would otherwise be intractable, and to focus verification efforts on those parts of the system behaviour that are relevant to the property under consideration. In doing so, we have illustrated that behavioural reasoning complements the proof obligations generated by the *B* method, which primarily address safety invariants and consistency but not necessarily richer temporal or security-oriented requirements.

From a methodological perspective, GeneSyst encourages a more integrated approach to formal specification and security analysis. By aligning the generation of a behavioural model with the existing *B* development workflow, it avoids introducing a separate, potentially inconsistent model solely for behavioural reasoning. This reduces the risk of divergence between models and ensures that any property proven on the SLTS is indeed valid for the original specification. Furthermore, since the SLTS generation is automated, the process is repeatable and can be applied at multiple stages of refinement, providing ongoing assurance as the specification evolves.

The contributions of this work are thus threefold. First, we have defined a formal and effective method for deriving symbolic behavioural models from *B* event specifications. Second, we have implemented this method in a practical tool that integrates with the *B* method’s formalism. Third, we have applied the tool to security property verification, demonstrating its utility in detecting and reasoning about behavioural aspects that are otherwise difficult to address within the standard *B* proof framework.

Future work will focus on extending GeneSyst in several directions. We plan to improve the efficiency of symbolic analysis, incorporate richer temporal logics for property specification, and explore integration with model checking back-ends to provide automated counterexample generation. We are also interested in applying the approach to larger industrial-scale systems, to further assess scalability and usability in complex development contexts. Finally, we aim to investigate its applicability beyond security, for example in the analysis of fault tolerance, performance constraints, and compliance with domain-specific regulations.

In summary, GeneSyst offers a valuable addition to the *B* method’s toolbox: it enables explicit, symbolic reasoning about behaviour while preserving the rigour of the underlying formal specification. By making dynamic properties visible and checkable within the same formal framework, it advances the goal of developing systems that are not only correct by construction, but also demonstrably secure in their behaviour.

title: Co-nonsolvency of PNiPAM at the transition between solvation mechanisms
abstract: Poly(N‑isopropylacrylamide) (PNiPAM) exhibits the well‑known phenomenon of co‑nonsolvency, in which it collapses in certain mixtures of two good solvents, typically water and a short-chain alcohol. Despite extensive study, the molecular origin of this behavior remains under debate, with proposed mechanisms ranging from preferential binding to changes in solvent structure. Here, we investigate PNiPAM in aqueous methanol solutions across the full composition range, focusing on the transition between solvation mechanisms. Using a combination of static and dynamic light scattering, differential scanning calorimetry, and molecular dynamics simulations, we identify a crossover from hydrophobic hydration–dominated solvation in water-rich mixtures to alcohol-mediated polymer–solvent interactions in methanol-rich environments. The co‑nonsolvency window emerges where these mechanisms compete, leading to a destabilization of the expanded coil state. Analysis of local solvent composition around the polymer reveals a non‑monotonic variation in preferential coordination, correlating with the collapse–reexpansion transition. Our results provide a unified description of PNiPAM co‑nonsolvency, reconciling hydration and preferential adsorption models within a single mechanistic framework.
introduction:
Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNiPAM) is one of the most extensively studied thermo-responsive polymers due to its lower critical solution temperature (LCST) behavior in aqueous environments, which has enabled applications ranging from drug delivery to smart coatings. Its conformational transitions in solution are highly sensitive to temperature, solvent quality, and composition. An intriguing manifestation of this sensitivity is the phenomenon of *co-nonsolvency*, in which a polymer that is soluble in two individual solvents becomes insoluble upon mixing them in certain proportions. For PNiPAM, co-nonsolvency is most prominently observed in mixed water–alcohol systems, where the polymer collapses at intermediate alcohol fractions despite being soluble in both pure water and pure alcohol.

The physical origin of co-nonsolvency in PNiPAM has been the subject of considerable debate. Early interpretations emphasized enthalpic effects, suggesting that competitive hydrogen bonding between solvent components and the polymer backbone leads to reduced solvation. More recent studies have highlighted the possible role of preferential adsorption of the cosolvent onto the polymer, altering the local solvent composition around the chain and triggering collapse. Simultaneously, entropic contributions arising from changes in the structure of water and the disruption of hydration shells have been recognized as important. This complexity reflects the fact that PNiPAM exhibits different solvation mechanisms depending on solvent composition: in water-rich environments, hydrophobic hydration dominates, whereas in alcohol-rich mixtures, solvation is governed by dispersion interactions and less structured solvent shells.

At the transition between these solvation regimes, the interplay between enthalpic and entropic driving forces becomes particularly subtle. Experiments using calorimetry, spectroscopy, and scattering techniques have revealed that the coil-to-globule transition can be induced not only by temperature changes but also by small adjustments in solvent composition near this crossover. Molecular simulation studies have provided complementary microscopic insight, showing that the structural organization of the solvent mixture around PNiPAM chains changes abruptly as the composition passes through the co-nonsolvency region. However, a unified description that connects these local structural rearrangements with macroscopic phase behavior remains elusive.

Understanding the co-nonsolvency of PNiPAM at the boundary between solvation mechanisms is not only of fundamental interest, but also of practical significance. In applications, controlling the polymer's responsive behavior requires precise tuning of solvent conditions. Knowledge of how specific interactions and solvent structures contribute to the transition can inform rational design strategies for stimuli-responsive materials. Furthermore, because co-nonsolvency involves subtle balance between competing solvation modes, it serves as a sensitive probe for testing theories of polymer solution thermodynamics in mixed solvents.

In this work, we investigate PNiPAM in mixed water–alcohol solvents with compositions spanning the transition from hydrophilic to less polar solvation. By combining experimental measurements of phase behavior and thermodynamic parameters with molecular-level structural characterization, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms underlying co-nonsolvency at this critical boundary. We focus on identifying how changes in solvent composition alter the hydration structure, polymer–solvent interactions, and the balance of enthalpic and entropic contributions to the free energy of solvation. Our results provide new insight into the cooperative nature of solvent–polymer interactions in mixed solvents, and clarify the molecular origin of co-nonsolvency in PNiPAM at the transition between distinct solvation regimes.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the co-nonsolvency behavior of poly(N‑isopropylacrylamide) (PNiPAM) in mixed aqueous and alcoholic solvents, focusing on the transition between distinct solvation mechanisms. By systematically varying solvent composition and temperature, and combining spectroscopic, calorimetric, and scattering techniques, we have identified a crossover from hydration-dominated solvation in water-rich environments to classical polymer–solvent interactions in alcohol-rich mixtures. Our results demonstrate that the pronounced collapse of PNiPAM at intermediate solvent compositions—despite both pure solvents being good—originates from a subtle interplay between enthalpic and entropic contributions that is sensitive to the molecular organization of the solvent mixture.

In water-rich mixtures, PNiPAM solvation is governed primarily by hydrophobic hydration and the structuring of water around the isopropyl groups, leading to temperature-dependent coil–globule transitions characteristic of lower critical solution temperature (LCST) behavior. The addition of small amounts of alcohol disrupts this hydration shell, reducing the enthalpic stabilization provided by structured water. As the alcohol fraction increases, the solvent environment gradually shifts toward one in which polymer–solvent contacts are described more accurately by Flory–Huggins-type interactions, with reduced sensitivity to the fine structure of the hydrogen-bond network. This transition region corresponds to the co-nonsolvency window, where the competing solvation mechanisms produce a net unfavorable free energy of mixing, inducing polymer collapse.

Our thermodynamic analysis indicates that the co-nonsolvency minimum coincides with the point at which neither hydration-induced enthalpic gains nor classical dispersion interactions dominate, resulting in a cooperative destabilization of the solvated coil state. The complementary scattering results reveal concomitant changes in polymer dimensions and solvent structuring, providing direct evidence for the molecular reorganization accompanying the collapse–reswelling sequence. Importantly, the observed crossover is not abrupt but rather manifests as a continuous shift in the balance of solvation forces, with a well-defined composition range over which co-nonsolvency is maximized.

These findings contribute to a more unified understanding of co-nonsolvency by explicitly linking the phenomenon to a transition between qualitatively different solvation regimes. Recognizing that PNiPAM experiences hydration-driven solvation in water-rich mixtures and conventional polymer–solvent interactions in alcohol-rich mixtures clarifies the molecular origins of the collapse behavior and rationalizes its sensitivity to solvent type, composition, and temperature. Beyond their relevance to fundamental polymer physics, these insights may inform the design of responsive polymer systems, where precise control over solvation mechanisms enables tunable switching between conformational states. Future work may extend this framework to other thermoresponsive polymers and mixed solvent systems, further elucidating the interplay between solvent structure, polymer chemistry, and macromolecular conformation.

title: Auxiliary Learning for Deep Multi-task Learning
abstract: Deep multi-task learning (MTL) aims to improve generalization by jointly learning multiple related tasks, enabling shared representations and leveraging inter-task synergies. However, the presence of tasks with varying levels of difficulty and data quality can lead to negative transfer, where the performance on primary tasks degrades due to interference from less relevant or noisy auxiliary signals. In this work, we investigate *auxiliary learning*, a strategy in which additional tasks—often not directly related to the primary target—are introduced to guide representation learning and regularize the shared parameters. We propose a principled framework that adaptively selects and weights auxiliary tasks during training, based on their estimated utility to the primary objectives. Our approach combines gradient similarity analysis with task uncertainty modeling to dynamically adjust the influence of each auxiliary task, mitigating harmful interference while amplifying beneficial contributions. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets spanning computer vision and natural language processing, we demonstrate that auxiliary tasks, when appropriately managed, can substantially improve the performance of primary tasks in both low-data and full-data regimes. Compared to conventional MTL baselines, our method achieves consistent gains in accuracy and robustness, and exhibits faster convergence. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal the importance of adaptive weighting and the selection of semantically complementary auxiliary tasks. These findings highlight the potential of auxiliary learning as a flexible and effective enhancement to deep multi-task learning, offering a pathway to more resilient and generalizable multi-task models in diverse application domains.
introduction:
Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in machine learning, enabling models to learn multiple related tasks simultaneously by sharing representations. By leveraging inductive transfer between tasks, MTL can improve generalization performance, reduce overfitting, and lower the need for large task-specific datasets. In the deep learning era, MTL has been successfully applied in diverse domains such as computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, where related tasks often share underlying structures. Despite its promise, the design of effective MTL systems remains challenging, particularly in settings where tasks vary in complexity, data availability, or label quality. One of the most persistent challenges is negative transfer — the phenomenon where learning multiple tasks together degrades performance on some or all tasks compared to learning them independently.

A critical factor influencing the success of MTL is the degree of task relatedness. When tasks are closely aligned, shared representations can facilitate mutual improvement. However, in practice, tasks may differ significantly in their data distributions or label semantics, leading to interference during joint training. This interference can manifest as gradient conflict, where the optimization directions favored by different tasks are inconsistent. Various strategies have been proposed to mitigate negative transfer, including dynamic loss weighting, task grouping, and the design of task-specific network components. While these approaches address certain aspects of task interference, they often require careful tuning and prior knowledge about task relationships, limiting their scalability.

Auxiliary learning has recently gained attention as a complementary strategy to enhance MTL. In auxiliary learning, in addition to the main tasks of interest, the model is trained on one or more auxiliary tasks that are not the ultimate evaluation objectives but are designed to facilitate the learning of better representations. Auxiliary tasks can be derived from self-supervised objectives, synthetically generated labels, or related datasets, and are typically chosen to be easier to learn or to provide inductive biases beneficial to the main tasks. By incorporating auxiliary tasks, the model can acquire more robust features, improve optimization stability, and accelerate convergence.

The appeal of auxiliary learning in the MTL context lies in its potential to bridge gaps between heterogeneous tasks. When primary tasks are loosely related or suffer from sparse supervision, auxiliary tasks can act as intermediate learning signals that guide the shared representation towards more generalizable features. For example, in computer vision, auxiliary edge detection or depth estimation tasks can enhance performance on semantic segmentation; in natural language processing, language modeling or syntactic parsing can serve as beneficial auxiliaries for downstream classification tasks. Moreover, auxiliary learning can be naturally integrated into deep architectures, leveraging multi-branch designs or multi-head outputs to accommodate diverse objectives.

Nevertheless, the integration of auxiliary learning into deep MTL frameworks raises several open questions. One challenge is the selection and design of auxiliary tasks: poorly chosen auxiliaries may lead to distraction or even exacerbate negative transfer. Another is balancing the contributions of auxiliary and primary tasks during training, as naïvely weighting them may cause the model to overfit to the auxiliaries or underutilize their signal. Additionally, understanding the conditions under which auxiliary learning provides the greatest benefit, such as specific task relationships or data regimes, remains an active area of research.

In this work, we investigate auxiliary learning as a means to enhance deep multi-task learning. We aim to systematically study how auxiliary tasks can be leveraged to improve performance on primary tasks, particularly in scenarios where task relatedness is weak or supervision is limited. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we propose a principled framework for integrating auxiliary tasks into deep MTL models, with mechanisms for dynamically balancing their influence; (2) we provide empirical evidence across multiple domains demonstrating that well-designed auxiliaries can mitigate negative transfer and improve overall performance; and (3) we offer insights into the interplay between auxiliary and primary tasks, highlighting factors that govern the effectiveness of auxiliary learning. Through this exploration, we seek to advance the understanding of how auxiliary learning can be systematically applied to realize the full potential of deep multi-task learning.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated auxiliary learning as a strategy to enhance deep multi-task learning. By introducing carefully designed auxiliary tasks, we demonstrated that shared representations can be regularized, leading to improved generalization and robustness across diverse primary tasks. Our experiments showed consistent performance gains, particularly in scenarios with limited training data or imbalanced task difficulty, highlighting the value of auxiliary supervision in mitigating negative transfer. Furthermore, we analyzed task relationships, providing insights into effective auxiliary task selection. These findings suggest that auxiliary learning can serve as a principled approach to optimize multi-task architectures. Future work will explore dynamic auxiliary task adaptation and automated task discovery to further advance the scalability and applicability of this paradigm.

title: Stochastic equivalence for performance analysis of concurrent systems in dtsiPBC
abstract: We introduce a notion of stochastic equivalence tailored for performance analysis of concurrent systems specified in discrete-time stochastic and immediate Petri box calculus (dtsiPBC). The proposed equivalence preserves both functional behaviour and quantitative performance characteristics, enabling model simplification without loss of analytical accuracy. By exploiting the compositional semantics of dtsiPBC, we formalise an equivalence relation that aggregates states exhibiting indistinguishable stochastic behaviour under all possible execution contexts. This reduction technique is shown to be congruent with respect to the operators of the calculus, ensuring that equivalent components can be substituted within larger systems. The approach facilitates efficient performance evaluation by reducing the size of underlying discrete-time Markov chains while retaining measures such as throughput and response time. Case studies illustrate the applicability of the equivalence to complex concurrent models, demonstrating significant computational savings and providing a rigorous foundation for scalable quantitative analysis in the dtsiPBC framework.
introduction: The design and analysis of concurrent systems require formal methods capable of capturing both functional and performance aspects. Discrete Time Stochastic and Immediate Petri Box Calculus (dtsiPBC) is a process algebra that integrates compositional modeling with discrete time stochastic semantics, enabling precise representation of concurrent, communicating components. While functional equivalences in process algebras have been extensively studied, performance evaluation often demands coarser relations that preserve quantitative measures without retaining full behavioral detail. Stochastic equivalence serves this purpose by identifying processes that, although possibly differing in internal structure, exhibit identical performance characteristics under specified conditions. This paper investigates a notion of stochastic equivalence tailored to dtsiPBC, providing a formal foundation for performance comparison of concurrent systems modeled in this framework. We define the equivalence, explore its properties, and demonstrate its applicability to state space reduction, which is crucial for mitigating the complexity of performance analysis. The proposed approach enables the systematic abstraction of models while guaranteeing preservation of relevant performance indices, thereby facilitating efficient analysis of large-scale, discrete time stochastic systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the notion of stochastic equivalence within the framework of discrete-time stochastic and immediate Petri Box Calculus (dtsiPBC) for the performance analysis of concurrent systems. Our primary objective was to provide a rigorous formal foundation enabling the replacement of a system component or subsystem by an equivalent one without altering the overall stochastic behaviour relevant to performance measures. By extending the theoretical underpinnings of equivalence to account for both probabilistic and immediate activities, we have established a sound basis for compositional reasoning in dtsiPBC models.

We have defined an equivalence relation that preserves the steady-state performance characteristics of systems, particularly throughput, utilization, and response time distributions, while also respecting the structural and temporal semantics of dtsiPBC. This relation enables a systematic aggregation of states and transitions in the underlying discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) representations, thereby reducing the size of the state space to be analysed without loss of accuracy in the measures of interest. The proposed equivalence is shown to be a congruence with respect to all operators of dtsiPBC, ensuring that equivalent components remain interchangeable in any modelling context.

The methodological contribution is twofold. First, we have provided a formal definition of stochastic equivalence tailored to the hybrid nature of dtsiPBC, which incorporates both stochastic and immediate multiactions. Second, we have developed a procedure for verifying equivalence between process terms, supported by the correspondence between the operational semantics of dtsiPBC and its DTMC-based interpretation. This procedure can be applied modularly, enabling model simplification at the component level before full system composition.

Through illustrative examples, we have demonstrated how stochastic equivalence can significantly reduce the complexity of performance evaluation while maintaining the fidelity of the results. In particular, the case studies reveal that substantial state space reductions are achievable in practical systems exhibiting concurrency, synchronisation, and choice, where structural symmetries or behavioural redundancies exist. This reinforces the value of equivalence-based methods in the analysis of large-scale discrete-time stochastic models.

The results presented here open several avenues for future research. One promising direction is the automation of the equivalence checking process, integrating it into software tools for dtsiPBC modelling and analysis. Another is the extension of the equivalence framework to encompass more general performance indices, such as reward-based measures or transient behaviours. Furthermore, exploring the relationship between the proposed equivalence and other forms of behavioural equivalence, such as probabilistic bisimulation or testing equivalence in discrete time, may yield deeper insights into the interplay between functional and performance modelling.

Overall, the stochastic equivalence introduced and characterised in this study provides a robust and compositional mechanism for simplifying and accelerating the performance analysis of concurrent systems in dtsiPBC. By enabling safe component substitution and model reduction while preserving key stochastic properties, it contributes to more efficient and scalable evaluation techniques for complex discrete-time systems.

title: The Unified Hydrodynamics and the Pseudorapidity Distributions in Heavy Ion Collisions at BNL-RHIC and CERN-LHC Energies
abstract: We investigate pseudorapidity distributions of charged particles produced in heavy ion collisions at BNL-RHIC and CERN-LHC energies within the framework of unified hydrodynamics. This approach integrates features of Landau and Bjorken hydrodynamic models to describe the longitudinal expansion of the produced matter. By deriving analytic expressions for the rapidity distribution and incorporating leading particle contributions, we compare theoretical predictions with experimental data from Au–Au and Pb–Pb collisions over a wide range of energies. The model successfully reproduces the central plateau and the fall-off in the fragmentation regions, demonstrating its applicability across different collision energies. Our results suggest that unified hydrodynamics provides a consistent description of the bulk particle production mechanism and offers insights into the longitudinal dynamics in high-energy heavy ion collisions.
introduction:
In relativistic heavy ion collisions, the study of particle production and collective motion provides crucial insights into the properties of strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions. At sufficiently high energies, such as those achieved at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, the colliding nuclei can create a hot and dense medium, commonly described as the quark–gluon plasma (QGP). Understanding the space–time evolution of this medium and the mechanisms governing particle emission is a central objective in contemporary high-energy nuclear physics.

Hydrodynamic models have proven to be effective tools for describing the collective behavior of the QGP. In particular, ideal and viscous hydrodynamics have been successfully applied to reproduce various experimental observables, including transverse momentum spectra, elliptic flow coefficients, and pseudorapidity distributions of produced charged particles. However, different hydrodynamic approaches, such as the Landau and Bjorken models, make distinct assumptions about the initial conditions and longitudinal expansion dynamics. A unified hydrodynamic framework, incorporating elements from both limits, can potentially provide a more comprehensive description of the longitudinal structure of the system.

The pseudorapidity distribution of charged particles is a key observable that encodes information about the energy deposition, entropy production, and longitudinal expansion in heavy ion collisions. Measurements at RHIC and LHC have revealed characteristic features, such as broad central plateaus and smooth fall-offs toward forward rapidities, which challenge simple extrapolations from lower-energy data. A successful theoretical description of these distributions must account for both the boost-invariant features at midrapidity and the deviations observed at larger pseudorapidities.

In this work, we employ a unified hydrodynamic model to analyze the pseudorapidity distributions of charged hadrons produced in central and peripheral heavy ion collisions at RHIC and LHC energies. This approach allows for a consistent treatment of the initial conditions and longitudinal dynamics across different collision energies. By comparing our model calculations with experimental data from the PHOBOS, BRAHMS, ALICE, and other relevant collaborations, we aim to assess the validity and predictive power of the unified hydrodynamic description, and to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing particle production in ultra-relativistic nuclear collisions.
conclusion: In this study, the unified hydrodynamics framework has been applied to describe the pseudorapidity distributions of charged particles produced in heavy ion collisions at BNL-RHIC and CERN-LHC energies. By incorporating both the Landau and Bjorken hydrodynamic limits within a single formalism, the model successfully captures the essential features of the longitudinal dynamics over a broad range of collision energies and centralities. Comparisons with experimental data demonstrate that the theoretical predictions reproduce the shape and magnitude of the measured pseudorapidity spectra with good accuracy, indicating the relevance of the unified approach in bridging different hydrodynamic regimes. The results suggest that the interplay between longitudinal expansion and finite rapidity particle production is crucial for understanding the evolution of the system created in such collisions. Furthermore, the extracted parameters provide insight into the initial conditions and the degree of thermalization achieved. The agreement across RHIC and LHC energies supports the robustness of the model and its potential applicability to future measurements, offering a consistent tool for exploring the longitudinal structure of the quark-gluon plasma in high-energy nuclear collisions.

title: MuFuRU: The Multi-Function Recurrent Unit
abstract: We introduce the Multi-Function Recurrent Unit (MuFuRU), a novel recurrent neural network architecture that generalizes existing gated recurrent units by enabling dynamic selection among multiple composition functions. Instead of committing to a fixed operation such as addition or reset-update gating, MuFuRU employs a controller to combine candidate functions—such as element-wise max, min, multiplication, and gating—based on the current input and hidden state. This design allows the network to adaptively tailor its state-update mechanism to diverse tasks.
