We evaluate MuFuRU on synthetic memory problems and real-world sequence modeling benchmarks, demonstrating improved performance and stability over standard GRU and LSTM baselines. The results suggest that flexible composition operations can enhance representational capacity in recurrent architectures.
introduction:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have become a cornerstone in modeling sequential data across a wide variety of domains, including natural language processing, speech recognition, and time-series forecasting. Over the past decade, gated architectures such as the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network and the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) have been proposed to address the vanishing and exploding gradient problems inherent in vanilla RNNs, enabling the capture of long-range dependencies and improving training stability. These gated mechanisms regulate the flow of information through internal memory states, thereby allowing the network to retain and update relevant contextual information over extended sequences. While such architectures have achieved substantial empirical success, they often employ fixed gating functions that may limit their flexibility in adapting to diverse task requirements or complex compositional structures in the data.

Recent research has explored variations of gating mechanisms, parameterizations, and state update functions to enhance the modeling capacity of recurrent architectures. Nevertheless, most existing variants remain constrained to a single, predetermined state update function, which may not be optimal for all types of sequential transformations. In many real-world applications, different parts of a sequence may require distinct computational behaviors—for instance, additive integration in some contexts and multiplicative interactions in others. A more general recurrent unit that can dynamically select from a set of compositional functions could better accommodate heterogeneous sequence patterns and improve overall performance.

In this work, we introduce the Multi-Function Recurrent Unit (MuFuRU), a novel recurrent architecture that unifies multiple composition operations within a single framework. The MuFuRU allows the network to learn, at each time step, how to combine the previous hidden state and the current input using a learned mixture over a set of predefined functions. This flexibility enables the model to adapt its internal state transitions to the varying structural requirements of the sequence, potentially leading to more efficient representation learning. We present the formulation of the MuFuRU, analyze its computational properties, and evaluate it on a range of synthetic and real-world tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that the MuFuRU not only matches or exceeds the performance of established recurrent architectures but also provides improved interpretability by revealing the dynamic selection of composition functions over time.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced the Multi-Function Recurrent Unit (MuFuRU), a novel recurrent architecture that extends conventional gating mechanisms by enabling dynamic selection among a set of compositional functions. This flexibility allows MuFuRU to adapt its state-update strategy to the characteristics of the input and context, leading to improved representational capacity without incurring substantial computational overhead. Empirical results across synthetic and real-world sequence modeling tasks demonstrated that MuFuRU consistently matches or outperforms established architectures such as LSTM and GRU, particularly in scenarios requiring heterogeneous temporal dynamics. Furthermore, the interpretability of its learned function-selection patterns offers additional insights into the temporal structure of the data. These findings suggest that incorporating multiple parameterized composition functions into recurrent units provides a promising direction for advancing sequence modeling. Future work will explore scaling MuFuRU to large-scale datasets, integrating it with attention mechanisms, and investigating its applicability in multimodal and reinforcement learning settings.

title: Change point detection for graphical models in the presence of missing values
abstract: We study the problem of change point detection in high-dimensional graphical models when observations contain missing values. Traditional methods often degrade under incomplete data, limiting their applicability in practical scenarios. We propose a novel framework that integrates imputation within a penalized likelihood approach, enabling consistent estimation of both change points and network structure. The method accommodates arbitrary missingness patterns and scales to large graphs. Theoretical guarantees are established under mild conditions, and simulations and real data experiments demonstrate superior accuracy and robustness compared to existing techniques.
introduction:
Graphical models provide a powerful and flexible framework for representing complex dependence structures among multivariate random variables. They have been widely applied in diverse domains such as computational biology, finance, neuroscience, and social network analysis, where understanding the underlying conditional independence relations is of central interest. In many real-world applications, however, the generating process of the data may undergo structural changes over time due to evolving system dynamics, interventions, or external shocks. Detecting such change points—time instants at which the underlying graphical model changes—has thus emerged as an important problem with significant practical implications. Accurate change point detection can enable timely interventions, improve predictive performance, and yield deeper scientific insights into the mechanisms driving the observed processes.

The literature on change point detection in high-dimensional graphical models has grown rapidly in recent years, with advances in both methodological development and theoretical understanding. Existing approaches typically rely on penalized likelihood or regularized covariance estimation techniques to infer the graph structure within segments of data, combined with statistical tests or optimization-based procedures to locate changes. While these methods have demonstrated effectiveness under idealized conditions, they often implicitly assume that the observed data are fully available. In practice, however, missing values are pervasive. They arise, for example, from sensor malfunctions in monitoring systems, patient dropout in longitudinal studies, reporting delays in economic series, or incomplete questionnaire responses in social research. Missingness can occur in arbitrary patterns and may be substantial in high-dimensional settings, posing serious challenges for both estimation and inference.

The presence of missing data complicates change point detection in graphical models in several ways. First, standard estimators of covariance or precision matrices can be severely biased or unstable when applied to incomplete data, leading to inaccurate graph recovery. Second, the missingness mechanism itself may vary over time, potentially obscuring or mimicking structural changes. Third, naive imputation prior to change point analysis may propagate errors and inflate false discovery rates. These challenges call for principled methods that can simultaneously accommodate missing values and reliably detect changes in the underlying graphical structure.

In this work, we address the problem of change point detection for graphical models in the presence of missing data. We develop a methodology that integrates robust estimation techniques for incomplete observations with efficient procedures for identifying structural changes. Our contributions include the formulation of a statistically sound framework, theoretical guarantees for detection accuracy under general missingness conditions, and empirical demonstrations on synthetic and real datasets that highlight the practical advantages of the proposed approach.
conclusion:
In this work, we investigated the problem of change point detection in graphical models when the data are subject to missingness, a setting that frequently arises in high-dimensional applications such as genomics, finance, and sensor networks. We developed a methodology that integrates statistical techniques for handling incomplete data with principled procedures for detecting structural changes in the underlying dependency graph. By leveraging both likelihood-based formulations and regularization strategies, our approach accommodates a wide range of missing data mechanisms, including those not missing completely at random, and remains computationally feasible in high-dimensional regimes.

The proposed framework extends existing change point detection methods by explicitly modeling the uncertainty introduced by missing values, rather than relying on ad hoc imputation or discarding incomplete observations. Through theoretical analysis, we established consistency guarantees for both change point localization and graphical structure estimation, under mild assumptions on the sparsity of the precision matrices and the distribution of missing entries. This contributes to bridging the gap between robust statistical inference and practical applicability in imperfect data settings.

Extensive simulation studies demonstrated that our method achieves accurate detection of both the number and location of change points, even when a substantial fraction of the data is missing. In comparison with benchmark procedures that ignore missingness or apply simplistic preprocessing, our approach showed superior performance in terms of detection accuracy, false positive control, and recovery of the graph structure before and after each change. Furthermore, the application to a real-world dataset illustrated the interpretability and domain relevance of the detected changes, highlighting the method’s potential for scientific discovery.

While our results are encouraging, several directions remain for future exploration. One natural extension is to relax the assumption of piecewise-constant graphical structures and allow for gradual, continuous changes. Another is to develop scalable online algorithms to enable real-time monitoring in streaming data environments with missing values. Additionally, exploring robust inference under more complex missingness mechanisms, such as those influenced by unobserved latent processes, would further enhance the applicability of the framework.

Overall, this study underscores the importance of explicitly accounting for missing data in change point analysis of graphical models. By integrating principled missing data handling with change detection, we provide a statistically sound and practically useful tool that advances the state of the art in high-dimensional time series and network data analysis. We anticipate that the proposed methodology will serve as a foundation for future research at the intersection of graphical modeling, change point theory, and incomplete data analysis.

title: Self-Supervised Bulk Motion Artifact Removal in Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography
abstract: Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) enables high-resolution, depth-resolved visualization of retinal and choroidal microvasculature without dye injection, but is highly susceptible to bulk motion artifacts arising from involuntary eye movements and blinking. These artifacts can obscure fine vascular details, degrade quantitative metrics, and confound clinical interpretation. Existing motion correction approaches often require repeated acquisitions, external eye tracking, or paired training data, limiting their robustness and clinical applicability. We propose a self-supervised deep learning framework for bulk motion artifact removal that leverages only single, corrupted OCTA volumes during training. Our method exploits the redundancy between orthogonal B-scan orientations to learn artifact-invariant vascular representations without explicit artifact-free labels. A dual-branch network architecture with shared weights processes orthogonal inputs, and a consistency loss enforces alignment of predicted angiograms, effectively disentangling motion-induced distortions. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of volumetric OCTA scans from healthy and diseased eyes, demonstrating substantial improvements in vessel continuity, contrast-to-noise ratio, and quantitative vascular metrics compared to conventional registration and filtering methods. Qualitative assessments by expert graders confirm enhanced visualization of capillary networks and lesion boundaries. The proposed self-supervised strategy enables efficient, label-free artifact removal, potentially improving the reliability of OCTA-based diagnostics in routine clinical workflows.
introduction:
Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA) is a non-invasive imaging modality that enables high-resolution, depth-resolved visualization of the microvasculature in biological tissue. By leveraging motion contrast from repeated B-scans at the same location, OCTA can reveal perfusion without the need for exogenous contrast agents, making it particularly attractive for ophthalmology, neurology, dermatology, and other biomedical applications. In ophthalmic practice, OCTA has become a critical tool for diagnosing and monitoring retinal diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and glaucoma, owing to its ability to delineate fine vascular detail and quantify microvascular changes over time. However, despite its clinical potential, OCTA image quality is frequently degraded by motion artifacts, which can obscure or distort vascular structures and impede both qualitative assessment and quantitative analysis.

Motion artifacts in OCTA arise primarily from involuntary eye movements, blinking, and patient motion during image acquisition. These artifacts manifest as discontinuities, vessel duplication, stretching, or displacement, often referred to collectively as bulk motion artifacts. Even with the use of high-speed swept-source or spectral-domain OCT systems, acquisition speeds are not sufficient to completely eliminate motion effects, especially in patients with poor fixation. Hardware-based motion correction approaches, such as eye-tracking systems or orthogonal scan patterns, can mitigate artifacts to some extent but require specialized instrumentation, increase acquisition complexity, and may not be available in all clinical settings. Software-based post-processing methods thus remain essential for improving the reliability and interpretability of OCTA images.

Traditional software-based motion correction methods often rely on explicit registration between repeated scans or adjacent B-scans, using structural OCT data to estimate and compensate for motion. While these approaches can be effective, they typically require careful tuning of registration parameters, may fail in regions with low signal-to-noise ratio, and can introduce interpolation artifacts. More recently, data-driven methods, including supervised deep learning, have been proposed for OCTA artifact removal, leveraging large amounts of paired data to learn a mapping from corrupted to clean images. However, supervised learning for artifact removal in OCTA faces significant challenges: acquiring perfectly paired motion-free and motion-corrupted images from the same subject is practically infeasible, and synthetic artifact generation may fail to capture the complexity and variability of real-world motion patterns. As a result, supervised models may not generalize well to unseen data or diverse patient populations.

Self-supervised learning offers a promising alternative for OCTA motion artifact removal by eliminating the need for paired training data. In self-supervised paradigms, models can learn directly from corrupted data by exploiting inherent structural redundancies, leveraging multiple repeated scans, or using internal image statistics. This approach is particularly well-suited to OCTA, where the rich spatial organization of vascular networks and the availability of multiple B-scans across time or space provide opportunities for learning artifact-robust representations. Several recent advances in self-supervised image restoration—such as noise2void, noise2self, and blind-spot networks—have demonstrated that it is possible to recover high-quality images from only corrupted observations, given appropriate assumptions about the corruption process. Extending these ideas to OCTA requires accounting for the unique characteristics of bulk motion artifacts, which are structured, spatially correlated, and often exhibit directionality tied to acquisition order.

A self-supervised framework for bulk motion artifact removal in OCTA would not only address the scarcity of clean ground-truth data but also offer adaptability to different imaging systems, scanning protocols, and patient populations. By integrating domain-specific priors, such as the continuity of vascular structures and the layered anatomy of the retina, self-supervised models can learn to disentangle motion-related distortions from true anatomical features. Furthermore, the ability to train directly on in vivo patient data without manual annotation or synthetic artifact simulation opens the door to continual learning and deployment in real-world clinical workflows. This is particularly important in longitudinal studies, where consistent image quality is critical for tracking disease progression or treatment response.

Despite these advantages, self-supervised motion artifact removal in OCTA remains relatively unexplored. Existing work in OCTA artifact correction has primarily focused on structural registration or supervised deep learning approaches. There is a need for systematic investigation into how self-supervised strategies can be adapted to the OCTA domain, how well they can handle diverse artifact patterns, and how their performance compares to established correction techniques. Moreover, evaluation of artifact removal methods in OCTA must consider both visual quality and preservation of quantitative vascular metrics, as excessive smoothing or distortion of fine vessels can adversely impact diagnostic utility.

In this work, we present a novel self-supervised learning approach for bulk motion artifact removal in OCTA. Our method leverages repeated B-scans and intrinsic redundancy in the vascular signal to train a deep neural network without requiring paired clean images. We design a learning objective that encourages the network to suppress motion-induced distortions while preserving fine vascular detail, guided by anatomical priors and the statistical properties of OCTA data. We evaluate our method on a diverse dataset acquired with a commercial OCTA system, comparing against both conventional registration-based correction and supervised deep learning baselines. Quantitative assessments and expert grading demonstrate that our approach effectively reduces bulk motion artifacts, enhances vessel continuity, and maintains the fidelity of clinically relevant vascular metrics. Through this work, we aim to advance the development of practical, data-efficient, and generalizable artifact removal techniques for OCTA, enabling improved diagnostic performance and broader clinical adoption of this powerful imaging technology.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a self-supervised framework for bulk motion artifact removal in optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), eliminating the need for paired training data or manual annotations. By leveraging intrinsic redundancies within repeated B-scans and incorporating motion-consistent constraints, the proposed method effectively suppressed motion-induced distortions while preserving fine vascular detail. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrated improved vessel continuity, enhanced image quality metrics, and robustness across different scanning protocols. Compared to conventional registration and filtering approaches, our approach reduced residual artifacts without compromising structural fidelity, enabling more reliable quantitative vascular analysis. The self-supervised design facilitates adaptation to diverse imaging settings and subjects, making it suitable for large-scale clinical deployment. Future work will investigate integration with real-time acquisition pipelines and extension to volumetric motion correction. Overall, this study establishes self-supervised motion artifact removal as a promising direction for improving the diagnostic utility of OCTA in both research and clinical practice.

title: Error corrected quantum annealing with hundreds of qubits
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate error-corrected quantum annealing using an array of several hundred physical qubits, implementing scalable strategies for suppressing control errors and mitigating thermal and decoherence effects. By encoding logical qubits into repetition codes and employing tailored penalty terms, we enhance robustness against bit-flip errors while preserving the native connectivity of the hardware graph. Our experiments span problem instances of varying size and complexity, showing consistent improvement in ground-state success probability compared to unencoded runs. We characterize the trade-offs between code distance, resource overhead, and performance gain, and benchmark results against both classical simulations and uncorrected quantum annealing. The observed scaling behaviour supports the feasibility of integrating quantum error correction into near-term annealers at significant qubit counts. These findings establish a practical pathway toward fault-tolerant quantum optimization, bridging the gap between noisy intermediate-scale devices and fully error-corrected quantum computation.
introduction:
Quantum annealing (QA) has emerged as a promising paradigm for solving combinatorial optimization problems by exploiting quantum fluctuations to explore complex energy landscapes. In recent years, commercially available QA processors have scaled to hundreds or even thousands of physical qubits, enabling investigations of problem instances beyond the reach of classical heuristics. However, the performance of such devices is fundamentally limited by decoherence, control errors, and thermal excitations, which can cause deviations from the intended quantum dynamics and reduce solution quality. These imperfections become increasingly significant as system size grows, motivating the development of error suppression and correction techniques tailored to the QA framework.

While quantum error correction is well established in the context of gate-based quantum computing, its application to QA presents unique challenges. The continuous-time evolution, analog control, and limited qubit connectivity of current annealers require strategies that can mitigate errors within these constraints. Recent studies have explored approaches such as energy gap protection, repetition encoding, and tailored penalty terms to suppress errors without prohibitive resource overheads. Among these, quantum annealing correction (QAC) schemes, which combine encoding with energy penalties, have demonstrated notable improvements in logical qubit performance on small- to medium-scale systems.

In this work, we investigate the implementation of error-corrected QA on devices with hundreds of physical qubits, focusing on scalable encoding and decoding strategies compatible with existing hardware architectures. We present experimental results demonstrating enhanced robustness against noise and control imperfections, and we assess the trade-offs between error suppression, resource overhead, and solution probability. By extending QAC to larger problem sizes, our study provides insights into the feasibility of error correction in near-term QA devices and its potential role in enabling practical quantum advantage. Our results contribute to the growing body of evidence that carefully designed error correction can substantially improve the computational reliability of quantum annealers at scale.
conclusion: We have demonstrated that error-corrected quantum annealing can be implemented at a scale involving hundreds of physical qubits, achieving robust performance in the presence of realistic noise. By integrating tailored error suppression and correction protocols with problem-encoding strategies, we were able to preserve solution quality and maintain high success probabilities across a range of benchmark instances. Our results indicate that both the logical qubit fidelity and the resilience to control errors improve markedly with the proposed scheme, confirming the viability of scaling error correction in near-term annealing devices. The experimental data and simulations suggest that the overhead introduced by error correction is offset by the performance gains, particularly for harder optimization problems. These findings provide a concrete foundation for exploring larger, more complex problem instances and for developing hybrid strategies that integrate error-corrected annealing with classical post-processing. Ultimately, this work represents a significant step toward practical, large-scale quantum annealing capable of addressing computationally challenging tasks under realistic experimental conditions.

title: Composition of ordinary generating functions
abstract: We investigate the composition of ordinary generating functions, focusing on conditions ensuring well-definedness and analytic properties. Techniques include formal power series manipulations, combinatorial interpretations, and convergence analysis. Applications to counting problems and recursive structures are presented, illustrating how composition encodes complex combinatorial constructions and facilitates the derivation of explicit formulas for sequence enumeration.
introduction: Ordinary generating functions (OGFs) constitute a cornerstone in enumerative combinatorics, providing a powerful algebraic framework for encoding and manipulating sequences. By representing a sequence \((a_n)_{n \geq 0}\) as a formal power series \(A(x) = \sum_{n \geq 0} a_n x^n\), one can translate combinatorial problems into problems of algebraic or analytic manipulation. Among the fundamental operations on generating functions, composition plays a particularly significant role. The composition \(F(G(x))\) of two OGFs often arises naturally in the study of structured combinatorial classes, where one type of combinatorial object is built from another in a nested or hierarchical fashion. This operation captures the substitution of combinatorial structures and is closely related to the symbolic method in combinatorics. Despite its apparent simplicity, the composition of OGFs raises delicate issues concerning convergence, formal validity, and the interpretation of coefficients. Moreover, explicit coefficient extraction from composed generating functions is a nontrivial problem that is addressed by classical results such as the Lagrange inversion theorem. This paper aims to provide a systematic treatment of OGF composition, exploring both its algebraic foundations and its combinatorial interpretations, and to develop effective methods for the computation of coefficients in a variety of applied contexts.
conclusion: The analysis demonstrates that composing ordinary generating functions provides a powerful framework for enumerative problems, enabling concise derivations and deeper structural insights, thereby enriching combinatorial theory and facilitating further advances in both theoretical and applied contexts.

title: Internal resonance in non-linear disk oscillations and the amplitude evolution of neutron star kilohertz QPOs
abstract: We investigate the role of internal resonance in shaping the non-linear oscillatory dynamics of accretion disks around neutron stars, with emphasis on the amplitude evolution of kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations (kHz QPOs). Using a reduced model based on coupled non-linear oscillators representing disk modes, we examine conditions under which near-commensurate eigenfrequencies enable efficient energy exchange through parametric coupling. Analytical perturbation techniques and numerical integrations reveal that 3:2 and related resonance ratios can lead to amplitude modulation, saturation, and intermittent dominance of specific modes. The model naturally accounts for observed correlations between QPO amplitudes and frequency ratios, as well as the appearance of amplitude anti-correlations between twin peaks. Our results suggest that internal resonance can provide a unifying framework linking frequency stability with variable amplitudes, without invoking large-scale changes in accretion flow structure. This mechanism offers a physically consistent explanation for several puzzling features of neutron star kHz QPO phenomenology and guides interpretation of future high-time-resolution X-ray observations.
introduction:
Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) observed in the X-ray flux of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries provide a powerful probe of the dynamics of matter in the strong-gravity regime. Among these, kilohertz (kHz) QPOs—appearing as twin peaks in the power density spectrum at frequencies of a few hundred to over a thousand hertz—are widely interpreted as signatures of orbital motion and oscillations in the innermost regions of the accretion disk. Their frequencies vary in correlation with X-ray luminosity and other spectral parameters, suggesting a close link between the oscillation mechanism and the accretion flow. Despite decades of observational and theoretical effort, the physical origin of kHz QPOs and the processes governing their amplitude evolution remain incompletely understood.

One promising framework invokes non-linear disk oscillations, in which the accretion flow supports a set of global modes that interact through non-linear couplings. In this picture, the observed QPOs correspond to specific oscillatory modes—such as vertical and radial epicyclic motions—whose eigenfrequencies are set primarily by the spacetime geometry and pressure forces in the disk. When two modes have commensurate frequencies, internal resonances can occur, facilitating an efficient exchange of energy between them. Such resonances are a natural consequence of the non-linear terms in the fluid equations governing the disk, and have been shown in other astrophysical contexts to produce amplitude modulation, frequency locking, and mode saturation.

Internal resonance models for kHz QPOs have attracted particular attention because they can account for the relatively stable frequency separations observed in many sources, as well as for the occurrence of frequency ratios close to small integers, notably 3:2. In the neutron star case, additional complexity arises from the stellar surface, magnetic field, and boundary layer, all of which can participate in or modify the oscillation spectrum. The presence of a solid surface introduces dissipative and driving mechanisms absent in black hole systems, potentially influencing both the excitation of modes and the persistence of resonant conditions.

A crucial yet less explored aspect of the internal resonance scenario is its prediction for the temporal evolution of QPO amplitudes. Observationally, kHz QPO amplitudes are not constant: they can vary on timescales from seconds to days, and often show systematic trends with frequency. In some cases, the amplitude of one peak appears to grow while the other diminishes, suggestive of energy transfer between modes. Such behaviour is qualitatively consistent with non-linear resonance theory, in which coupled oscillators exchange energy periodically or reach a steady-state distribution determined by the balance between driving and damping. However, quantitative comparisons between theoretical amplitude evolution and observational data have been limited.

The study of amplitude evolution in the context of internal resonance is important for several reasons. First, the amplitude response encodes information about the strength of the non-linear coupling coefficients, which depend on the disk’s physical conditions. Second, it can help discriminate between competing models for QPO origin, some of which predict very different amplitude–frequency correlations. Third, tracking the amplitude evolution provides an indirect probe of the mechanisms driving and damping the modes, including turbulence, magnetic stresses, and radiative processes. By confronting detailed resonance models with amplitude measurements, one can constrain both the microphysics of the accretion flow and the macroscopic spacetime parameters of the neutron star.

In this work, we investigate the amplitude evolution of neutron star kHz QPOs within the framework of internal resonance between non-linear disk oscillations. We develop a set of coupled amplitude equations describing two interacting modes near a low-order commensurability, incorporating generic driving and damping terms. We then explore the resulting dynamical behaviour, including steady states, limit cycles, and transient energy exchange, and compare the predictions to representative observational data. Our goal is to assess whether the observed amplitude variations can be naturally explained by internal resonance, and to identify the physical parameters most critical in shaping the QPO amplitude evolution.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the role of internal resonance in shaping the non-linear oscillatory dynamics of accretion disks around neutron stars, with particular emphasis on its implications for the amplitude evolution of kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations (kHz QPOs). By modelling the disk as a system of coupled, weakly non-linear modes subject to relativistic corrections, we have demonstrated that near-commensurate frequency ratios can naturally give rise to internal resonance phenomena. These resonances facilitate an efficient exchange of energy between modes, leading to amplitude modulation patterns consistent with those observed in several neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries.  

Our analysis shows that when two disk oscillation modes approach a low-order rational frequency ratio—most notably the 3:2 case—non-linear coupling terms become dynamically significant. The resulting internal resonance not only alters the instantaneous amplitudes but can also shift the effective oscillation frequencies through non-linear detuning. This behaviour provides a natural explanation for the observed correlation between QPO amplitudes and their centroid frequencies, a feature that has been challenging to reconcile within purely linear models. Importantly, the amplitude evolution predicted by our framework is not monotonic: energy periodically flows between modes, producing episodes of amplitude growth and decay on timescales much longer than the oscillation periods themselves.  

We have further shown that the strength and persistence of the resonance are sensitive to both the disk’s physical parameters—such as sound speed, scale height, and viscosity—and to the relativistic epicyclic frequency structure dictated by the neutron star’s mass and spin. This sensitivity offers a potential diagnostic tool: careful measurement of amplitude–frequency tracks in kHz QPOs could, in principle, constrain the underlying mode structure and the degree of non-linear coupling. The formalism developed here can also accommodate the inclusion of dissipative effects and stochastic driving, both of which are expected to play a role in realistic accretion flows and may account for the finite coherence times observed.  

Our results support the view that kHz QPOs are not purely linear probes of strong gravity, but rather manifestations of a complex, non-linear dynamical system in which internal resonance is a key organising principle. Future work should extend the present analysis to global magnetohydrodynamic disk models and explore the interaction between disk oscillations and neutron star surface or magnetospheric modes. High-time-resolution observations from upcoming X-ray missions will be crucial in testing the predicted amplitude modulation patterns and in refining the constraints on the non-linear coupling coefficients. Ultimately, understanding the detailed amplitude evolution of kHz QPOs will enhance their utility as probes of both accretion physics and the fundamental properties of neutron stars.

title: On the quantum f-relative entropy and generalized data processing inequalities
abstract: We investigate the properties of the quantum \( f \)-relative entropy for strictly positive operators, focusing on monotonicity under quantum operations. By extending classical \( f \)-divergences to the quantum regime, we derive generalized data processing inequalities applicable to a broad class of operator convex functions. Necessary and sufficient conditions for equality are established, revealing structural constraints on the underlying states and channels. Special attention is given to the quantum \( \alpha \)-relative entropy and related measures, illustrating the tightness of our bounds. Our results unify and extend existing inequalities in quantum information theory, providing a versatile framework for analyzing state distinguishability and information flow in quantum systems.
introduction:
Quantum information theory extends classical information concepts into the quantum domain, where states are described by density operators and physical processes by completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps. A central notion in this framework is that of quantum divergences, which measure the distinguishability between quantum states and play a pivotal role in characterizing information-theoretic tasks. Among these, the quantum relative entropy has emerged as a fundamental quantity, underpinning results such as the data processing inequality and strong converse theorems for quantum channel capacities.  

A natural generalization of the relative entropy is obtained by replacing the logarithmic function with a convex function \( f \), giving rise to the *quantum f-relative entropy*. This broader family encapsulates a range of divergences, including Rényi-type measures, and allows for a unified treatment of various operational and mathematical properties. The flexibility in choosing \( f \) enables the tailoring of distinguishability measures to specific physical or informational contexts, and facilitates the derivation of generalized inequalities.  

A cornerstone property of divergences is monotonicity under CPTP maps, expressed by the data processing inequality (DPI). For the quantum f-relative entropy, establishing conditions under which the DPI holds—along with characterizing the equality cases—is crucial for both theoretical insights and practical applications. Such results yield bounds on achievable rates in communication scenarios, constraints in thermodynamic transformations, and criteria for reversibility of quantum processes.  

In this work, we investigate the quantum f-relative entropy in detail, focusing on generalized data processing inequalities and their equality conditions. We explore the mathematical structure induced by operator convex functions \( f \), derive sufficient and necessary conditions for monotonicity, and highlight implications for quantum hypothesis testing and channel discrimination. Our approach unifies existing results for specific divergences and extends them to a broader operational framework, providing a deeper understanding of information flow in quantum systems.
conclusion: In this work, we have analyzed the quantum \( f \)-relative entropy and its fundamental properties, extending the framework of quantum information measures beyond the conventional Umegaki relative entropy. By employing operator convex functions, we established generalized data processing inequalities, highlighting conditions for equality and their operational significance. These results unify and broaden existing monotonicity theorems, offering a versatile tool for studying quantum statistical inference and resource-theoretic constraints. Our approach provides a systematic method to derive bounds and characterize transformations under completely positive trace-preserving maps. Future research may explore applications in quantum thermodynamics, hypothesis testing, and channel discrimination, where generalized entropic quantities can capture subtler aspects of quantum correlations and irreversibility.

title: Graph Neighborhood Attentive Pooling
abstract: Graph representation learning has achieved significant progress through the development of graph neural networks (GNNs), yet effectively summarizing local neighborhood information while preserving critical structural cues remains challenging. Existing pooling methods often rely on coarse node selection or global attention mechanisms, which may overlook fine-grained dependencies within local neighborhoods. In this work, we propose Graph Neighborhood Attentive Pooling (GNAP), a novel hierarchical pooling framework that adaptively aggregates node features by modeling attention within each node’s k-hop neighborhood. GNAP computes neighborhood-level attention scores that reflect the relative importance of nodes with respect to their local structural and feature contexts, enabling the pooling process to retain salient substructures and minimize information loss. Our approach integrates seamlessly with diverse GNN backbones and supports end-to-end training. Extensive experiments on benchmark graph classification datasets demonstrate that GNAP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art pooling baselines in terms of classification accuracy, while offering improved interpretability through attention heatmaps over neighborhoods. Further analysis reveals that GNAP is particularly effective in graphs with heterogeneous degree distributions, where preserving relevant local patterns is critical. The proposed method provides a principled and flexible mechanism for neighborhood-aware graph pooling, advancing the capability of GNNs to capture both local and global structural representations.
introduction:
Graph-structured data is ubiquitous across diverse domains, ranging from social and citation networks to molecular chemistry and recommendation systems. In such settings, nodes represent entities, and edges capture the relationships or interactions between them. The irregular and non-Euclidean nature of graphs poses unique challenges for machine learning algorithms, which have traditionally been designed for data residing in regular grids, such as images or sequences. In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for representation learning on graphs, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of tasks including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. Central to the success of GNNs is the message-passing paradigm, in which each node aggregates information from its neighbors to iteratively refine its representation.

While standard message-passing approaches effectively capture local structure, they often face limitations in modeling higher-order dependencies and in handling graphs with large or noisy neighborhoods. In many real-world graphs, neighborhood sizes vary widely, and not all neighbors contribute equally to the task at hand. As a result, uniform or degree-normalized aggregation schemes may dilute important signals with irrelevant or noisy information. Attention mechanisms have been introduced into GNNs to address this issue, allowing models to learn the relative importance of different neighbors when aggregating information. Graph Attention Networks (GATs) exemplify this strategy by computing attention coefficients over edges, enabling more expressive and adaptive neighborhood aggregation.

Despite their advantages, existing attention-based GNN architectures typically operate at the level of individual edges during message passing and aggregation. This edge-wise attention, while flexible, can be computationally expensive for large graphs and may struggle to capture more global or context-aware neighborhood patterns. Moreover, when the downstream task involves graph-level prediction—such as molecular property prediction or document classification—there is often a need to pool node representations into a single graph embedding. Standard pooling methods, including global mean or sum pooling, as well as hierarchical approaches like DiffPool, tend to treat node embeddings in isolation or rely on learned cluster assignments without explicitly modeling the structural context of neighborhoods in the pooling process.

Graph pooling is a crucial component in hierarchical graph representation learning, serving to reduce graph size while preserving task-relevant structural and semantic information. Effective pooling mechanisms should be able to identify informative substructures, discard redundant or noisy nodes, and maintain the integrity of important relationships. Recent works have explored various pooling strategies, such as top-k pooling based on node scores, structure-aware pooling guided by spectral properties, and attention-based pooling mechanisms. However, many of these methods either ignore the rich relational patterns within each node’s neighborhood during pooling or compute importance scores without explicitly accounting for the multi-hop structural context.

To address these gaps, we propose **Graph Neighborhood Attentive Pooling (GNAP)**, a novel pooling framework that integrates neighborhood-level attention into the pooling operation. Instead of assigning importance solely at the node level, GNAP evaluates the contribution of each node in the context of its local neighborhood, capturing both immediate and higher-order structural cues. By attending to neighborhoods rather than individual nodes in isolation, our approach can better identify structurally and semantically significant regions of the graph, leading to more informative coarsened representations.

The core idea of GNAP is to compute attention scores that reflect the relevance of a node’s neighborhood to the overall task, leveraging both node features and structural descriptors derived from the neighborhood topology. These attention scores guide the selection of nodes for pooling, ensuring that the retained subset preserves key patterns and relationships. The attention mechanism operates hierarchically, allowing the model to incorporate multi-scale neighborhood information and adaptively focus on different structural contexts depending on the input graph and task objective. This design bridges the gap between fine-grained, edge-level attention and coarse graph-level pooling, offering a more balanced and context-aware reduction of graph complexity.

From a computational perspective, GNAP is designed to be scalable to large graphs by restricting attention computation to local neighborhoods and by employing efficient sampling strategies. This makes it applicable to real-world scenarios where graphs can have millions of nodes and edges. Moreover, the framework is flexible and can be integrated with various backbone GNN architectures, such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), GATs, or Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs), thereby enhancing their graph-level prediction performance without extensive architectural modifications.

We evaluate GNAP on multiple benchmark datasets for graph classification, including social network graphs and molecular datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that GNAP consistently outperforms baseline pooling methods in terms of classification accuracy, while also producing more interpretable pooled graphs. We further analyze the attention distributions learned by GNAP, showing that the model effectively highlights neighborhoods corresponding to functionally important substructures, such as aromatic rings in molecules or densely connected communities in social networks.

In summary, the contributions of this work are threefold: (1) we introduce a neighborhood-attentive pooling mechanism that captures the structural and semantic context of nodes during pooling; (2) we develop an efficient and scalable implementation suitable for large-scale graphs; and (3) we provide extensive empirical evidence of the effectiveness of GNAP across diverse graph learning tasks. By explicitly modeling neighborhood context in the pooling process, GNAP advances the state of the art in hierarchical graph representation learning and opens new avenues for interpretable and efficient graph-level modeling.

conclusion: In this work, we introduced Graph Neighborhood Attentive Pooling, a novel framework that adaptively aggregates local neighborhood information through learned attention mechanisms. By explicitly modeling the relative importance of nodes within their structural context, our method enhances the representational capacity of pooled graph embeddings while preserving critical topological patterns. Experimental results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over existing pooling approaches, particularly in tasks requiring fine-grained structural discrimination. Furthermore, the proposed design offers flexibility to integrate with diverse graph neural network architectures, enabling broader applicability. Future research will explore extensions to dynamic and heterogeneous graphs, as well as theoretical analyses of attention weight distributions. Overall, our approach contributes an effective and interpretable pooling strategy for advancing graph representation learning.

title: Analysis of four-band WISE observations of asteroids
abstract: We present an analysis of four-band observations of asteroids obtained by the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) during its fully cryogenic mission phase. The dataset includes simultaneous measurements in the W1 (3.4 μm), W2 (4.6 μm), W3 (12 μm), and W4 (22 μm) bands, enabling comprehensive characterization of both reflected sunlight and thermal emission from asteroid surfaces. Our sample comprises several thousand objects spanning a broad range of sizes, albedos, and orbital classes, including near-Earth, main-belt, and Trojan asteroids. We applied thermophysical modeling to derive diameters and geometric albedos, incorporating color corrections specific to each bandpass and accounting for phase angle effects. The inclusion of short-wavelength W1 and W2 data allowed improved constraints on reflected-light contributions, while the longer-wavelength W3 and W4 channels provided robust measurements of thermal flux. We compare our results with previous single- and two-band thermal analyses, demonstrating that four-band coverage reduces degeneracies between size and albedo estimates and improves uncertainties by up to 30%. Additionally, spectral slope measurements from the W1–W2 color offer insights into compositional diversity. Our findings highlight the value of multi-band infrared photometry for asteroid characterization and provide an expanded, internally consistent catalog of physical properties that will support studies of asteroid populations, surface compositions, and thermal behavior across the solar system.
introduction:
Asteroids are remnants of the early Solar System, preserving information about the processes that governed planetary formation and evolution. Their physical and compositional properties, such as size, albedo, and surface thermal characteristics, provide important constraints on models of Solar System history. Observations in the thermal infrared are particularly effective for determining these properties, as they allow the separation of reflected sunlight from thermal emission and enable accurate radiometric modeling. The Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), launched by NASA in December 2009, carried out an all-sky survey in four broad infrared bands centered at 3.4, 4.6, 12, and 22 μm (designated W1–W4). This dataset represents an unprecedented resource for asteroid science, offering simultaneous multi-wavelength coverage over a wide range of phase angles and heliocentric distances.  

The four-band WISE measurements enable the derivation of diameters, albedos, and in some cases thermal properties, with improved precision compared to single-band or dual-band observations. By combining the reflected-light dominated W1 and W2 bands with the thermal-emission dominated W3 and W4 bands, it is possible to disentangle the contributions of surface reflectivity and emissivity. Previous analyses of WISE data have already produced catalogs encompassing hundreds of thousands of asteroids, but further work is needed to refine physical parameter estimates, assess systematic uncertainties, and explore correlations with dynamical and taxonomic classes.  

In this study, we present a detailed analysis of four-band WISE observations of a representative sample of asteroids, focusing on the consistency of derived parameters across the dataset and the potential for detecting variations in thermal properties among different populations. We describe the data processing, modeling techniques, and validation methods employed, and discuss the implications of our findings for asteroid characterization and Solar System evolution studies. Our results aim to enhance the utility of the WISE archive for ongoing and future investigations of small bodies.
conclusion: The analysis of four-band WISE observations has provided valuable constraints on the physical properties of asteroids, including diameters, albedos, and thermal characteristics. By exploiting the full spectral coverage, we improved the accuracy of thermal modeling and reduced uncertainties compared to single- or dual-band approaches. The results demonstrate the importance of multi-band infrared data for characterizing diverse asteroid populations and refining size–albedo distributions. These findings contribute to a more complete understanding of asteroid composition, evolution, and potential hazards, and emphasize the continued need for comprehensive multi-wavelength surveys.

title: The Central Star of NGC 2346 as a Clue to Binary Evolution through the Common Envelope Phase
abstract: We present new spectroscopic and photometric observations of the central star of the bipolar planetary nebula NGC 2346, aimed at constraining its binary parameters and shedding light on post–common envelope (CE) evolution. NGC 2346 is known to host an unusually wide binary for a post-CE system, with a separation inconsistent with simple CE ejection models. Our high-resolution spectra obtained over multiple orbital cycles yield refined orbital elements, confirming a period of 15.99 days and revealing evidence for irradiation effects on the secondary. Photometric monitoring shows variability consistent with ellipsoidal modulation and heating, enabling improved constraints on component masses and inclination. By comparing the derived parameters with population synthesis and hydrodynamical CE models, we discuss possible evolutionary pathways that can produce such systems, including partial envelope ejection and interaction with a circumbinary disk. The central star of NGC 2346 thus provides a key benchmark for testing CE theory and highlights the need for revised models capable of explaining intermediate-period post-CE binaries.
introduction:
Planetary nebulae (PNe) represent a brief but critical phase in the late evolution of low- to intermediate-mass stars, during which the progenitor sheds its outer layers and exposes its hot core. While traditionally modeled as the outcome of single-star evolution, an increasing body of evidence indicates that binary interactions play a decisive role in shaping many PNe. In particular, the common envelope (CE) phase—where a companion becomes engulfed in the extended envelope of the primary—has emerged as a key evolutionary channel capable of explaining the diverse morphologies and kinematic properties observed in these objects. The CE interaction leads to dramatic orbital shrinkage, envelope ejection, and potentially strong departures from spherical symmetry in the resulting nebula.

NGC 2346 is a striking example of a bipolar planetary nebula whose morphology and central binary system offer valuable insights into CE evolution. Its central star is known to be a close binary, with a period of roughly 16 days, placing it among the longer-period post-CE systems. This relatively wide separation suggests either a partial ejection of the envelope or a CE event that departed from the canonical prescriptions in population synthesis models. Furthermore, the nebular structure of NGC 2346, characterized by prominent bipolar lobes and an equatorial waist, is consistent with dynamical shaping by binary interactions and possibly by a circumbinary disk formed during or after the CE phase.

Studying the central star of NGC 2346, including its orbital parameters, stellar properties, and evolutionary history, can therefore provide critical constraints on the physical processes governing CE evolution. By combining spectroscopic, photometric, and morphological data, we can address key open questions: how do initial binary parameters influence post-CE periods, what mechanisms control envelope ejection efficiency, and how do these factors manifest in nebular morphology? NGC 2346 thus serves as a natural laboratory for testing and refining models of binary interaction in late stellar evolution.
conclusion:
The study of the central star of NGC 2346 offers important insights into the physical processes governing binary evolution through the common envelope (CE) phase. Our analysis of the system’s orbital parameters, stellar properties, and nebular morphology reinforces the interpretation that the progenitor binary underwent a CE interaction that dramatically altered its evolutionary pathway. The presence of a relatively close binary nucleus within an extended bipolar planetary nebula is consistent with models in which orbital energy and angular momentum are transferred to the envelope, leading to its ejection and the shaping of the circumstellar environment.

The derived orbital period and mass estimates support the scenario in which the precursor of the current hot central star expanded during the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase, filling its Roche lobe and initiating unstable mass transfer. The subsequent CE phase likely terminated the giant phase abruptly, leaving behind the compact remnant and a companion in a significantly reduced orbit. The observed nebular structure of NGC 2346, with its well-defined bipolar lobes and equatorial waist, aligns well with theoretical predictions that CE ejection is preferentially directed along the orbital plane, producing axisymmetric morphologies.

Importantly, the relatively long orbital period compared to other post-CE planetary nebulae suggests that the envelope ejection in NGC 2346 was unusually efficient or that the initial orbital separation was larger than in many comparable systems. This places valuable constraints on the efficiency parameter α in CE evolution models, indicating that high ejection efficiencies may occur under certain initial mass ratios and evolutionary states. The survival of a luminous companion further implies that mass accretion during or after the CE phase may have been non-negligible, potentially affecting both stellar evolution and the energetics of the ejection process.

By combining spectroscopic monitoring, photometric constraints, and nebular kinematics, this work strengthens the empirical foundation for CE theory, which remains one of the least well-understood phases in close binary evolution. NGC 2346 serves as a benchmark object against which hydrodynamic simulations and population synthesis models can be tested. Future observations, particularly high-resolution spectroscopy and spatially resolved imaging of the nebular gas, will refine the dynamical history of the system and better quantify the mass-loss mechanisms at play.

In summary, the central star of NGC 2346 exemplifies the transformative impact of the CE phase on binary evolution, linking stellar interior processes to large-scale nebular morphology. Its properties provide a critical data point for calibrating CE efficiency and for understanding the diversity of post-CE planetary nebulae, thereby contributing to a more complete picture of binary stellar evolution.

title: Static-static-light-light tetraquarks in lattice QCD
abstract: We present a lattice QCD study of static-static-light-light tetraquark systems, focusing on configurations with two static quarks and two dynamical light quarks. Using gauge field ensembles with \(N_f=2+1\) flavors of sea quarks, we extract potentials from correlation functions of suitable tetraquark operators. The dependence of the binding energy on quark separation and light-quark mass is examined. Our results indicate the presence of attractive channels that may support bound states or resonances, providing insight into the structure and stability of heavy-light tetraquarks.
introduction: Tetraquarks, bound states consisting of four quarks, provide a valuable testing ground for understanding the strong interaction beyond conventional mesons and baryons. In particular, systems containing two static heavy quarks and two light quarks, often referred to as static-static-light-light tetraquarks, allow for a clean theoretical investigation within lattice QCD. The static approximation simplifies the heavy-quark dynamics, enabling precise studies of interquark potentials and binding mechanisms. Such configurations are also relevant for interpreting exotic hadron candidates observed experimentally. By systematically varying the light-quark content and the separation between static quarks, lattice simulations can probe the role of color interactions and light-quark exchange. This work presents a lattice QCD study of these tetraquark systems, focusing on their energy spectra and the conditions under which bound states may form.
conclusion: In this work we have investigated the properties of static-static-light-light tetraquark systems using lattice QCD techniques. By employing static quarks as heavy constituents and varying the light quark content, we have extracted the interquark potentials and examined their dependence on spatial separation and flavour structure. Our results indicate that for certain quantum number combinations, the interaction between two static–light mesons exhibits attraction strong enough to support bound or near-threshold states. The flavour dependence observed is consistent with expectations from heavy quark symmetry and phenomenological models, while the spatial profiles of the potentials reveal the role of light-quark exchange mechanisms. Finite-volume and discretisation effects were carefully analysed to assess systematic uncertainties, and the extracted binding energies show stability within errors. These findings provide further evidence for the possible existence of tightly bound heavy–light tetraquark configurations in nature. Future studies with dynamical heavy quarks and finer lattice spacings will help to refine these conclusions and connect more directly with experimental searches.

title: On the Computation of Neumann Series
abstract: The Neumann series provides a fundamental tool for representing the inverse of operators close to the identity, with applications spanning numerical analysis, functional analysis, and applied mathematics. This paper investigates efficient computational strategies for evaluating Neumann series in both finite- and infinite-dimensional settings. We analyze convergence criteria in terms of operator norms, spectral properties, and perturbation bounds, thereby extending classical results to broader classes of bounded linear operators. A comparative study of truncation schemes and error estimates is presented, highlighting trade-offs between computational cost and accuracy. Furthermore, we propose adaptive algorithms that optimize truncation length based on residual norms. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, demonstrating robust performance in scenarios with slow spectral decay and near-critical convergence conditions.
introduction:
The Neumann series, named after the German mathematician Carl Neumann, occupies a central role in functional analysis, operator theory, and the numerical solution of linear and nonlinear equations. It arises as the formal analogue of a geometric series within the framework of Banach spaces, providing a powerful tool for representing and approximating the inverses of bounded linear operators. Specifically, given a Banach space \(X\) and a bounded linear operator \(T: X \to X\) with \(\|T\| < 1\), the Neumann series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty T^n\) converges in the operator norm, and its sum equals \((I - T)^{-1}\). This representation forms the theoretical foundation for a variety of computational techniques, including iterative methods for solving linear systems, perturbation expansions in spectral theory, and the analysis of stability for numerical schemes.

The historical emergence of the Neumann series was motivated by problems in potential theory and integral equations, where the inversion of operators of the form \(I - T\) was of fundamental importance. Since then, the scope of applications has expanded significantly, encompassing domains such as quantum mechanics, signal processing, control theory, and numerical analysis. In particular, the ability to express and approximate operator inverses via partial sums of a Neumann series enables both theoretical insights and practical algorithms, especially when direct inversion is computationally expensive or analytically intractable.

Despite its conceptual simplicity, the computation of Neumann series in practice raises important questions concerning convergence rates, numerical stability, and truncation error bounds. The basic convergence criterion \(\|T\| < 1\) ensures absolute convergence in the operator norm, but in applications one often encounters operators that do not satisfy this strict bound, or for which only weaker, problem-specific norms are available. In such cases, alternative convergence conditions, rescaling strategies, preconditioning techniques, or spectral radius considerations become relevant. Furthermore, the truncation of the series to a finite number of terms—inevitable in computational settings—introduces an approximation error whose behavior must be carefully understood in order to guarantee the reliability of numerical results.

The computational implementation of Neumann series is also influenced by the structure and properties of the operator \(T\). For example, when \(T\) is sparse, low-rank, or exhibits special symmetries, the cost of computing successive powers \(T^n\) can be greatly reduced. Conversely, in high-dimensional settings or when \(T\) lacks exploitable structure, naive computation of the series terms may be prohibitively expensive. These considerations have motivated the development of specialized algorithms that exploit matrix factorizations, fast transform techniques, or iterative refinement to accelerate convergence or reduce computational complexity. The interplay between theoretical convergence criteria and algorithmic design is a recurring theme in contemporary numerical linear algebra.

Another important dimension of the problem lies in its generalizations. The Neumann series framework extends naturally to unbounded operators under suitable domain restrictions, to nonlinear operators via formal power series expansions, and to stochastic operator models arising in uncertainty quantification. In each of these contexts, the computation of the series becomes more intricate, demanding adapted analytical tools and numerical strategies. Moreover, truncation and rounding errors can interact in nontrivial ways, especially in finite-precision arithmetic, leading to subtle stability issues that must be addressed for robust computation.

The study of Neumann series thus sits at the intersection of pure and applied mathematics. On the one hand, it draws upon the rich theoretical apparatus of functional analysis, spectral theory, and operator algebras. On the other, it engages with the concrete realities of algorithm design, computational cost, and numerical error analysis. The present work aims to bridge these perspectives by examining both the theoretical underpinnings and the practical aspects of computing Neumann series. We review classical results on convergence and error estimation, explore modern algorithmic approaches tailored to different operator classes, and investigate the influence of problem structure on computational efficiency. Particular attention is given to the derivation of rigorous truncation error bounds, the design of stable iterative schemes, and the extension of the Neumann series method to broader classes of problems beyond the strictly contractive case.

By systematically addressing these issues, we seek to provide a coherent framework for the computation of Neumann series that is both theoretically sound and practically effective. Such a framework is essential for leveraging the full potential of this classical tool in contemporary applications, where high-dimensional operators, complex problem structures, and stringent accuracy requirements are the norm rather than the exception.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the computation of Neumann series from both a theoretical and a practical perspective, with particular attention to the conditions under which such series converge and the implications for numerical implementation. By revisiting the classical convergence criterion based on the spectral radius of the underlying operator, we have clarified the relationship between operator norms, spectral properties, and the rate of convergence. This analysis has allowed us to identify scenarios in which the Neumann series provides an efficient computational tool, as well as those in which alternative formulations may be preferable.

Our numerical experiments have demonstrated that, when the convergence conditions are satisfied, truncations of the Neumann series yield accurate approximations with relatively low computational cost. We have also addressed the influence of rounding errors and finite-precision arithmetic, showing that stability is maintained provided the norm of the perturbation remains sufficiently small. In particular, the interplay between truncation error and floating-point error suggests that optimal stopping criteria can be formulated to minimize the total error.

Furthermore, the techniques discussed here are not limited to the inversion of bounded linear operators, but extend naturally to the solution of certain classes of integral equations and to iterative refinement schemes in numerical linear algebra. The flexibility of the Neumann series approach, combined with its interpretability in terms of geometric series in operator form, makes it a valuable component in the computational toolkit for applied mathematics and engineering.

Future work may focus on adaptive truncation strategies, extensions to non-stationary operators, and the integration of Neumann series computation into large-scale parallel algorithms. Overall, the results presented confirm that, under the appropriate theoretical framework, the Neumann series remains a robust and effective method for solving a wide range of operator equations.

title: Classifier-agnostic saliency map extraction
abstract: We propose a novel framework for generating classifier-agnostic saliency maps that highlight image regions most relevant to general visual recognition tasks, independent of any particular trained classifier. Unlike existing approaches that rely on gradients or activation maps from a specific network, our method optimizes saliency masks through a model-agnostic objective that measures the impact of selectively revealing image regions on a generic recognition performance metric. By iteratively perturbing input images and evaluating responses from an ensemble of surrogate models, we produce saliency maps that are robust to architectural biases and training idiosyncrasies. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our approach yields more interpretable and consistent explanations across diverse classifiers, while preserving high fidelity to the underlying semantic content. This classifier-agnostic capability facilitates fairer model comparisons, improves trust in visual explanations, and extends the applicability of saliency analysis to scenarios where the target classifier is unknown or inaccessible.
introduction:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. Despite their impressive performance, these models are often criticized for their lack of interpretability: the complex, high-dimensional transformations they perform make it difficult to ascertain the specific image regions and features that drive their predictions. As a result, interpretability methods have emerged as an important area of research, not only to promote transparency and trust in machine learning systems, but also to aid in debugging models, diagnosing dataset biases, and fulfilling regulatory requirements in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and autonomous driving.

One common approach to interpretability in vision systems is the use of saliency maps—visualizations that highlight the most influential regions of an input image with respect to a particular model’s output. Early methods for saliency extraction, such as gradient-based techniques, compute the derivative of the class score with respect to the input pixels, producing a heatmap that indicates sensitivity. While computationally efficient, these methods often suffer from noisy or diffuse attributions, and can be highly sensitive to model architecture, parameter initialization, and even imperceptible input perturbations. More recent approaches have sought to address these shortcomings through integrated gradients, guided backpropagation, and perturbation-based methods, each introducing its own trade-offs in terms of fidelity, robustness, and computational cost.

A key limitation of most existing saliency extraction methods is their dependence on a specific classifier. The majority of techniques are model-dependent: they require access to the internal gradients, activations, or decision scores of a trained network. This classifier-centric design constrains their applicability, especially in scenarios where the model is proprietary, inaccessible, or subject to change. Furthermore, model-dependent saliency maps may entangle the intrinsic visual cues present in an image with the idiosyncratic biases of the classifier, making it difficult to disentangle genuinely informative regions from artefacts of model training.

These limitations motivate the pursuit of classifier-agnostic saliency map extraction methods, which aim to identify salient image regions without relying on the details of a specific classifier’s architecture or parameters. Such methods promise several advantages: they can serve as a general-purpose tool for dataset analysis, support model-agnostic interpretability in black-box settings, and offer a more intrinsic characterization of the visual evidence available in the image itself. In addition, classifier-agnostic saliency maps can be used to probe the information content of image regions independently of any particular classification objective, potentially informing model design and feature selection.

The central challenge in classifier-agnostic saliency extraction lies in defining and operationalizing “saliency” without reference to a particular decision function. One promising strategy is to formulate saliency as the set of image regions that are necessary and sufficient for preserving the semantic content of the original image under a broad class of possible classifiers. This can be approached through optimization frameworks that search for minimal subsets of pixels or superpixels whose removal or masking significantly alters the predictions of many different classifiers or a classifier ensemble. Alternatively, generative models can be employed to inpaint or reconstruct occluded regions, enabling the estimation of their contribution to potential classification outcomes.

In this work, we propose a novel framework for classifier-agnostic saliency map extraction that leverages perturbation analysis across a diverse family of surrogate models. By aggregating the effects of region perturbations over multiple architectures and training regimes, our method produces saliency maps that are robust to the peculiarities of any single classifier. We demonstrate that our approach yields interpretable, high-fidelity saliency maps across a variety of datasets and tasks, and that these maps align with human perception more consistently than those produced by classifier-specific techniques. Our contributions advance the goal of developing interpretable vision systems whose explanations are grounded in the inherent visual evidence of the data, rather than the opaque internal representations of a single model.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a classifier-agnostic approach to saliency map extraction that decouples the explanation process from any specific predictive model. By formulating saliency estimation as an optimization problem independent of classifier architecture or parameters, our method enables the generation of interpretable visual explanations that are robust across diverse models. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework produces saliency maps with high fidelity to image content and strong alignment with human-perceived relevant regions, while avoiding biases introduced by any single classifier’s decision boundaries. This flexibility facilitates broader applicability in settings where model transparency is critical but classifier details are inaccessible. Future research may extend this approach to other modalities and explore its integration with model-agnostic interpretability pipelines, further advancing the development of reliable, general-purpose explanation tools for complex machine learning systems.

title: Electronic structure investigation of the cubic inverse perovskite Sc3AlN
abstract: The electronic structure of the cubic inverse perovskite Sc₃AlN has been investigated using a combination of soft X-ray emission spectroscopy, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. High-resolution spectra at the Sc L₂,₃, N K, and Al L₂,₃ edges provide element-specific insight into the occupied and unoccupied electronic states, enabling a detailed assessment of the chemical bonding. The experimental spectra are compared with calculated partial densities of states, revealing strong hybridization between Sc 3d and N 2p orbitals, as well as weaker interactions involving Al states. The results confirm that Sc–N bonding dominates the electronic structure near the Fermi level, while Al contributes primarily to states at higher binding energies. The agreement between experiment and theory demonstrates the reliability of DFT in describing this material’s electronic properties, providing a foundation for understanding its mechanical and electrical characteristics in the context of inverse perovskite nitrides.
introduction:
