The presence of a luminous active galactic nucleus and powerful radio jets in the lensing galaxy has implications for understanding the interplay between nuclear activity, host galaxy structure, and mass distribution. Our findings suggest that radio galaxies, though less frequently identified as lenses compared to radio-quiet systems, can serve as effective probes of both AGN-host coevolution and the statistical properties of the lensing population.  

Future high-resolution interferometric imaging, particularly with ALMA and next-generation radio facilities, will refine both the lens model and the resolved structure of the SMG. Deep optical and near-infrared spectroscopy of the lens and any associated group members will further constrain the lens environment and potential external shear contributions. Expanding the search for similar systems will improve constraints on the mass profiles of massive early-type galaxies hosting powerful radio sources and will enhance our ability to study star formation in the high-redshift universe through gravitational lensing.  

Thus, 3C 220.3 serves as a compelling demonstration of the scientific potential of combining radio, submillimeter, and optical datasets to investigate both the lenses and lensed, bridging studies of AGN physics, galaxy evolution, and cosmology.

title: Partially blind domain adaptation for age prediction from DNA methylation data
abstract: DNA methylation-based age prediction models often suffer performance degradation when applied to data from unseen cohorts due to distributional shifts between training (source) and deployment (target) domains. Conventional domain adaptation methods typically require access to target domain data during training, which is not always feasible in biomedical contexts owing to privacy and data-sharing restrictions. We propose a partially blind domain adaptation framework for age prediction from DNA methylation data, where only limited, aggregate-level information about the target domain is available. Our method leverages a small set of target summary statistics to guide feature reweighting and distribution alignment, enabling robust model adaptation without direct access to individual-level target samples. We evaluate the approach on multiple publicly available methylation datasets spanning diverse tissues and array platforms, simulating realistic inter-cohort shifts. Results demonstrate that our method consistently reduces prediction error compared to standard models trained solely on source data, and achieves performance competitive with fully supervised domain adaptation techniques that have access to complete target data. This work highlights the potential of partially blind adaptation to enhance model generalization in genomics, where privacy constraints limit data sharing, and provides a pathway toward more reliable epigenetic biomarkers across heterogeneous populations.
introduction:
DNA methylation is a key epigenetic modification that plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and maintaining cellular identity. Over the past decade, methylation patterns have been increasingly recognized as valuable biomarkers for biological age estimation, enabling the development of so‑called “epigenetic clocks.” These clocks leverage machine learning models trained on high‑dimensional methylation data to predict chronological age with remarkable accuracy, and in some cases, to infer biological age, which may better reflect an individual’s health status and aging trajectory. Accurate age prediction from DNA methylation has applications in epidemiology, forensic science, and biomedical research, including early disease detection and the study of age‑related pathologies.

However, predictive models for age estimation are often trained on methylation data collected from specific cohorts, laboratories, or array platforms. When applied to data from different distributions—due to variations in preprocessing pipelines, population demographics, tissue types, or measurement technologies—model performance can degrade substantially. This phenomenon, known as domain shift, poses a major challenge for the generalizability and robustness of epigenetic age predictors. In many real‑world scenarios, especially in biomedical contexts, the target domain may be only partially characterized: while some covariates or metadata are available, direct access to labeled target data (i.e., methylation profiles with known ages) may be restricted due to privacy, cost, or logistical constraints. This limitation motivates the development of domain adaptation approaches that can bridge distribution gaps without requiring extensive labeled data from the target domain.

Domain adaptation techniques aim to transfer knowledge from a well‑labeled source domain to a target domain with different data characteristics, thereby mitigating the impact of distributional discrepancies. Traditional supervised learning assumes that training and test data are drawn from the same distribution, but this assumption rarely holds in cross‑cohort DNA methylation studies. Fully supervised adaptation approaches require labels in the target domain, whereas unsupervised domain adaptation methods leverage only unlabeled target data alongside labeled source data. In many practical applications, an intermediate setting arises: limited information about the target distribution is available, but it is incomplete or “partially blind.” For example, researchers may have access to aggregated statistics, partial feature measurements, or a small subset of samples without corresponding labels. This partially blind scenario is particularly relevant in epigenetic research, where data sharing restrictions and cohort heterogeneity are prevalent.

Despite the growing interest in domain adaptation for biomedical applications, relatively little work has addressed partially blind domain adaptation in the context of DNA methylation‑based age prediction. Most existing epigenetic clock models assume homogeneous data sources or rely on extensive harmonization procedures, which can be labor‑intensive and may not fully correct for domain shift. Furthermore, the high dimensionality and complex correlation structure of methylation data exacerbate the challenge of aligning distributions across domains. Effective adaptation methods must account for both global shifts in feature distributions and local, feature‑specific patterns that are predictive of age.

In this study, we investigate a partially blind domain adaptation framework tailored for DNA methylation age prediction. Our approach seeks to exploit the structure of available target domain information—such as unlabeled methylation profiles or summary statistics—while constraining model adaptation to prevent overfitting to the source domain. We hypothesize that by integrating domain‑invariant feature learning with regularization informed by the limited target data, it is possible to improve age prediction accuracy in the target domain without compromising performance in the source domain. This framework is designed to accommodate the realities of biomedical research, where full access to target labels is often unattainable, but partial data can still inform adaptation.

We evaluate our method on multiple publicly available DNA methylation datasets spanning different tissues, array platforms, and demographic groups. Comparative experiments against baseline models and existing adaptation techniques provide insights into the effectiveness of partially blind adaptation in mitigating domain shift. Beyond demonstrating improved predictive performance, our results highlight the potential of this strategy to enhance the generalizability of epigenetic clocks, facilitating their broader application across diverse populations and experimental settings.

By addressing the challenge of domain shift under partial information constraints, this work contributes to the methodological foundation necessary for robust, cross‑domain epigenetic age prediction. The proposed framework opens avenues for more equitable and reproducible aging research, where predictive models can be reliably deployed across heterogeneous datasets without the prohibitive requirement of fully labeled target cohorts.
conclusion:
In this study, we introduced a partially blind domain adaptation framework for age prediction from DNA methylation data, addressing the challenges posed by distributional shifts between training and target domains with incomplete or missing covariate information. By leveraging domain-invariant feature learning while selectively incorporating available domain-specific signals, our approach bridges the gap between fully supervised domain adaptation and completely unsupervised transfer. Experimental results across multiple publicly available methylation datasets demonstrated that the proposed method consistently outperforms baseline models, including standard regression approaches, naïve domain adaptation, and fully blind transfer, in terms of prediction accuracy and robustness.  

The partially blind setting reflects realistic scenarios in biomedical research, where metadata or covariates from the target domain may be incomplete due to privacy constraints, missing annotations, or technical limitations. Our findings indicate that even partial domain information can be effectively exploited to improve generalization without overfitting to spurious domain-specific patterns. Moreover, the framework preserves biological interpretability, as the learned latent representations retained known age-associated methylation signatures.  

This work highlights the importance of developing flexible adaptation strategies tailored to the constraints of real-world epigenomic studies. Future research could extend this framework to incorporate multi-modal omics data, non-linear temporal dynamics of methylation changes, and uncertainty quantification for individual-level predictions. Additionally, exploring its applicability to other phenotypic traits or disease risk prediction tasks could further validate its utility.  

Overall, our results demonstrate that partially blind domain adaptation offers a practical and effective solution for improving age prediction models in heterogeneous DNA methylation datasets, contributing to more reliable and generalizable epigenetic biomarkers of aging.

title: Higher symplectic structure on torsionless Lie-Rinehart pairs
abstract: We develop a framework for higher symplectic structures within the setting of torsionless Lie–Rinehart pairs, extending the classical notion of symplectic geometry to encompass graded and higher-degree generalizations. Exploiting the torsionless condition, we construct a well-behaved Schouten–Nijenhuis bracket and establish compatibility with a closed, nondegenerate higher form. This yields a coherent theory of higher Poisson brackets on the associated graded algebra of multiderivations. Applications include a natural extension of Hamiltonian dynamics to the Lie–Rinehart context and structural results on cohomology. Our approach unifies geometric and algebraic perspectives, paving the way for further developments in higher Poisson geometry.
introduction:
The study of symplectic geometry has long provided a unifying language for diverse areas of mathematics and theoretical physics, from classical mechanics to deformation quantization. In recent decades, higher and derived generalisations of symplectic structures have emerged as essential tools in the formulation of field theories, the theory of shifted Poisson structures, and the study of moduli spaces in algebraic geometry. Parallel to these developments, Lie–Rinehart pairs have served as a powerful algebraic framework for encoding the interplay between a commutative algebra and a compatible Lie algebra of derivations, thereby generalising the relation between smooth functions and vector fields on a manifold.

In this article we investigate higher symplectic structures in the setting of torsionless Lie–Rinehart pairs. Torsionlessness, a condition ensuring the faithful action of the module of derivations on the underlying algebra, plays a crucial role in extending geometric intuition to this broader algebraic context. While symplectic and Poisson structures on Lie–Rinehart pairs have been studied, the systematic development of *higher* symplectic geometry in this setting remains largely unexplored. Our approach draws on the homotopy-theoretic viewpoint, where higher-degree closed, non-degenerate forms encode multi-bracket structures satisfying appropriate generalised Jacobi identities.

We aim to provide a coherent definition of higher symplectic structures adapted to torsionless Lie–Rinehart pairs, establish their basic properties, and relate them to known constructions in both differential and algebraic geometry. This framework not only encompasses the classical situation of smooth manifolds but also applies to settings of algebraic and noncommutative geometry where derivations replace vector fields. By extending the scope of higher symplectic geometry to this algebraic arena, we open the way to applications in deformation theory, representation theory, and the study of algebroid-like objects arising in derived geometry. Our results thus contribute both to the foundational understanding of higher symplectic structures and to their applicability in diverse mathematical contexts.
conclusion:
In this work we have developed a coherent framework for the study of higher symplectic structures in the setting of torsionless Lie–Rinehart pairs, unifying and extending several existing approaches to generalized Poisson and multisymplectic geometry. Beginning from the algebraic formulation of Lie–Rinehart pairs as a natural generalization of the Lie algebroid concept to the category of commutative algebras, we identified torsionlessness as the crucial regularity condition ensuring the existence of a well-behaved calculus of differential forms and multivector fields. This allowed us to extend familiar constructions from differential geometry—such as the Schouten–Nijenhuis bracket and exterior derivative—to a broad algebraic context without loss of key geometric identities.

Our main contribution has been the introduction of a precise notion of higher symplectic structure within this framework, understood as a closed, nondegenerate form of degree greater than two, together with the induced higher Poisson brackets on the underlying algebra. We have shown that the torsionless condition guarantees the nondegeneracy of the interior product pairing between forms and multivectors, which in turn enables us to invert the higher symplectic form and to define a hierarchy of multilinear operations satisfying generalized Jacobi-type identities. These operations naturally extend the binary Poisson bracket to an \(L_\infty\)-algebra structure on the space of smooth functions (or more generally, on the module of sections), in line with the principles of higher Poisson geometry.

By working entirely in the torsionless Lie–Rinehart setting, we have ensured that our results specialize to classical differential geometry when the base algebra is the algebra of smooth functions on a manifold, while also encompassing purely algebraic situations that arise, for example, in algebraic geometry or deformation theory. The formalism accommodates both finite- and infinite-dimensional examples, making it a flexible tool for applications in mathematical physics where higher symplectic structures play a role, such as in multisymplectic field theory or the BV–BRST formalism.

We have also established compatibility results between the higher symplectic form and the Lie–Rinehart differential, showing that closedness of the form is equivalent to the homotopy Poisson identities for the induced operations. This provides a clear algebraic criterion for recognizing higher symplectic structures and for constructing them in practice. In particular, we have outlined methods for generating examples from existing Lie–Rinehart pairs via extensions, reductions, and tensor products, illustrating the robustness of the theory.

Looking ahead, several directions emerge naturally from our findings. One is the exploration of cohomological obstructions to the existence of higher symplectic forms in a given torsionless Lie–Rinehart pair, potentially linking our framework to deformation quantization in the higher setting. Another is the examination of morphisms and reduction procedures that preserve higher symplectic structures, which could yield new insights into the symplectic geometry of moduli spaces. Finally, the interplay between our algebraic construction and the analytic or categorical aspects of field theory remains a fertile ground for further research.

In summary, the present work lays a solid algebraic foundation for higher symplectic geometry on torsionless Lie–Rinehart pairs, opening the way to both deeper theoretical developments and concrete applications across geometry, topology, and physics.

title: Transmission spectroscopy of the inflated exoplanet WASP-52b, and evidence for a bright region on the stellar surface
abstract: We present optical transmission spectroscopy of the inflated hot Jupiter WASP-52b, obtained with high-precision ground-based observations. The measured transmission spectrum spans 400–900 nm and reveals a generally flat continuum with a modest increase in transit depth toward the blue, suggestive of scattering in the planetary atmosphere. A pronounced feature near the Na I doublet is detected at high significance, consistent with narrow-line absorption from the planetary atmosphere. However, the overall spectral shape cannot be fully explained by a simple atmospheric model. We find evidence for temporal variability in the measured transit depths, correlated with stellar activity indicators. Modelling of the light curves indicates that an anomalously bright region on the stellar surface, occulted during transit, can reproduce the observed deviations. This interpretation implies that unocculted active regions and faculae may bias inferred planetary atmospheric properties. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for stellar surface heterogeneities when interpreting transmission spectroscopy of active host stars.
introduction:
The study of exoplanetary atmospheres through transmission spectroscopy has become a powerful tool for probing the physical and chemical properties of planets beyond our Solar System. When a planet transits its host star, a fraction of the starlight filters through the planet’s atmosphere, imprinting wavelength-dependent absorption features in the observed spectrum. These features can reveal the presence of atomic and molecular species, cloud and haze properties, and atmospheric dynamics. Such measurements are particularly effective for close-in gas giants, whose large radii and high temperatures produce extended atmospheres with prominent spectral signatures.

WASP-52b is a highly inflated hot Jupiter orbiting a relatively active K2V star with a period of 1.75 days. Its low surface gravity and large scale height make it an attractive target for transmission spectroscopy, while the stellar activity presents both challenges and opportunities. Starspots and faculae can alter the apparent transit depth in a wavelength-dependent manner, potentially mimicking or masking planetary atmospheric features. If properly modelled, these stellar heterogeneities can also provide insights into the host star’s magnetic activity and surface structure.

Previous studies of WASP-52b have reported evidence for atmospheric sodium absorption and possible cloud coverage, as well as variability in transit depths that could be linked to stellar activity. However, disentangling planetary and stellar contributions remains a key challenge. In particular, the role of bright regions—faculae or plages—on the stellar surface has been less explored in this system, despite their potential to bias transmission spectra.

In this work, we present new transmission spectroscopy observations of WASP-52b, obtained across the optical regime. We analyse the data to extract the planet’s transmission spectrum, investigate the impact of stellar surface features, and assess the evidence for a bright region on the host star. By combining atmospheric modelling with stellar heterogeneity analysis, we aim to improve constraints on the planet’s atmospheric properties while characterising the active stellar surface, thereby advancing understanding of both components of this closely coupled system.
conclusion:
We have presented an optical transmission spectrum of the highly inflated hot Jupiter WASP‑52b, obtained from time‑series spectrophotometry during a primary transit. The measured spectrum exhibits a generally flat continuum with a modest increase in transit depth toward shorter wavelengths, consistent with scattering by aerosols or hazes in the planetary atmosphere. Superimposed on this baseline, we detect features compatible with the presence of sodium absorption, although the line cores appear shallower than predicted by clear‑atmosphere models, further supporting the interpretation of high‑altitude opacity sources muting spectral features.

During our analysis, we identified an anomalous feature in the transit light curve, manifested as a localized increase in flux. This is best explained by the planet occulting a region on the stellar surface that is brighter than the surrounding photosphere, such as a facular or plage region associated with stellar magnetic activity. Modelling of this occultation event indicates that neglecting such stellar surface heterogeneities can bias the inferred planetary radius and spectral features, particularly in the blue optical range. Our findings therefore reinforce the necessity of accounting for stellar activity when interpreting transmission spectra, especially for active K‑type host stars like WASP‑52.

The combination of a muted spectral slope, possible sodium absorption, and evidence for a bright stellar inhomogeneity provides a coherent picture in which WASP‑52b’s atmosphere contains aerosols at high altitudes, while the host star exhibits active regions that can imprint wavelength‑dependent signals on the transit data. Future observations at higher spectral resolution and over a wider wavelength range, including the near‑infrared, will help disentangle the relative contributions of planetary atmospheric features and stellar heterogeneities. Simultaneous photometric monitoring of the host star will further constrain its activity level and surface structure.

In summary, WASP‑52b remains a valuable target for comparative exoplanetology, offering insights into the interplay between atmospheric processes in inflated hot Jupiters and the influence of stellar activity on transmission spectroscopy measurements. Our results highlight both the opportunities and the challenges inherent in characterising exoplanet atmospheres around active stars.

title: Towards a Computed Collateral Circulation Score in Ischemic Stroke
abstract: Collateral circulation plays a critical role in determining tissue viability and clinical outcomes in acute ischemic stroke. Current assessment methods rely on qualitative or semi-quantitative visual grading of imaging studies, which are subject to inter-observer variability and limited reproducibility. This study proposes a framework for deriving a computed collateral circulation score (CCCS) from multimodal computed tomography (CT) data, integrating CT angiography and perfusion imaging. We developed an image-processing pipeline that segments vascular structures, quantifies collateral vessel density, and incorporates perfusion delay metrics into a composite score. The CCCS was retrospectively applied to a cohort of 112 patients with anterior circulation large vessel occlusion. Correlation with established visual grading systems and functional outcomes at 90 days demonstrated strong agreement and superior predictive value for favorable recovery. The computed approach reduced evaluation time and minimized subjective bias. These findings support the potential of automated, quantitative collateral scoring as a robust biomarker for patient stratification and therapeutic decision-making in acute stroke care.
introduction:
Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, with an estimated 12.2 million incident cases and 6.6 million deaths annually. The outcome of an ischemic stroke is determined not only by the site and size of the arterial occlusion but also by the adequacy of collateral circulation—alternative vascular pathways that maintain perfusion to ischemic brain tissue. Robust collateral networks can sustain penumbral tissue for longer periods, extend therapeutic windows, and are associated with improved functional recovery. Conversely, poor collateral status is linked to rapid infarct progression and worse prognosis. As such, collateral circulation assessment has emerged as a crucial component of acute stroke evaluation, with significant implications for patient selection in endovascular therapy and other reperfusion strategies.

Collateral status is currently assessed using imaging modalities such as computed tomography angiography (CTA), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), or digital subtraction angiography (DSA). Several qualitative and semi-quantitative scoring systems have been developed for CTA, including the modified Tan score, the Maas score, and the American Society of Interventional and Therapeutic Neuroradiology/Society of Interventional Radiology (ASITN/SIR) scale. While these visual rating systems are widely used in both clinical and research settings, they are inherently subjective, rely heavily on reader expertise, and are susceptible to inter- and intra-observer variability. Furthermore, the scales themselves differ in grading criteria, limiting comparability across studies and institutions. Such variability hinders the integration of collateral assessment into standardized stroke workflows and clinical decision-making algorithms.

Recent advances in image processing, artificial intelligence, and quantitative neuroimaging offer opportunities to address these limitations by developing objective, reproducible, and automated measures of collateral circulation. Computed or quantitative collateral scoring seeks to extract relevant vascular features directly from imaging data, such as vessel density, branching patterns, and perfusion metrics, and to integrate them into a standardized numerical score. Automated algorithms could process raw imaging data rapidly, minimizing delays in acute management. Moreover, quantitative scores may capture subtle variations in collateral patterns that are not readily discernible to the human eye, potentially enhancing prognostic accuracy.

The development of a computed collateral circulation score entails several challenges. First, collateral circulation is anatomically and physiologically complex, involving dynamic flow redistribution that can vary over time and under different hemodynamic conditions. Second, imaging data quality and protocols vary across scanners and institutions, necessitating robust algorithms capable of handling heterogeneous inputs. Third, validation requires large, well-annotated datasets linking imaging-derived collateral metrics to clinical outcomes, such as infarct growth, reperfusion success, and functional status at follow-up. Addressing these challenges will require multidisciplinary collaboration between neurologists, neuroradiologists, biomedical engineers, and computer scientists.

A standardized, computed collateral score has the potential to transform acute stroke care. By providing an objective and reproducible measure, it could improve patient stratification for reperfusion therapies, guide individualized treatment decisions, and serve as a reliable endpoint in clinical trials. Furthermore, such a score could facilitate multicenter research by enabling consistent collateral assessment across diverse populations and imaging platforms. Ultimately, the integration of computed collateral scoring into stroke workflows aligns with the broader trend toward precision medicine, where treatment strategies are tailored based on quantitative patient-specific data.

In this context, the present work aims to explore the feasibility, methodology, and validation of a computed collateral circulation score in ischemic stroke. We review current collateral assessment methods, outline the principles of quantitative collateral measurement, and present a framework for developing and validating an automated scoring system. By bridging the gap between qualitative visual ratings and fully quantitative metrics, our goal is to advance toward a robust, clinically applicable tool that enhances decision-making and improves outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke.
conclusion: This work outlines a framework for developing a computed collateral circulation score to improve the assessment of ischemic stroke patients. By integrating quantitative imaging biomarkers with advanced computational methods, the proposed approach aims to overcome the limitations of current subjective and semi-quantitative collateral grading systems. The envisioned score could offer a reproducible, objective, and scalable tool for rapid evaluation across diverse healthcare settings, facilitating timely therapeutic decision-making and potentially improving patient outcomes. Our analysis suggests that multimodal imaging, coupled with machine learning algorithms, can capture the complexity of collateral physiology more comprehensively than conventional visual assessment alone. However, substantial work remains to validate such a score across large, heterogeneous cohorts and to ensure generalizability across imaging platforms and acquisition protocols. Future studies should emphasize standardized data collection, rigorous external validation, and exploration of the score’s predictive value for functional recovery. Ultimately, a robust computed collateral circulation score has the potential to become an integral component of precision stroke care, guiding both acute intervention and prognostication. By advancing towards objective, automated collateral assessment, the field moves closer to optimizing individualized treatment strategies and improving the overall quality of stroke management.

title: Noncommutative-geometry inspired charged wormholes with low tidal forces
abstract: We investigate a class of static, spherically symmetric charged wormhole solutions inspired by noncommutative geometry, focusing on configurations that satisfy low tidal force conditions suitable for hypothetical human traversal. The matter distribution is modeled using a Gaussian-smeared energy density, eliminating curvature singularities and incorporating the effects of spacetime noncommutativity. The electromagnetic field is included via a minimally coupled Maxwell term, and the resulting Einstein–Maxwell field equations are solved analytically for specific shape and redshift functions. We examine the energy conditions, throat geometry, and tidal accelerations, demonstrating that appropriate parameter choices yield traversable wormholes supported by small violations of the null energy condition. Our analysis shows that noncommutative geometry can naturally suppress tidal forces while sustaining charged wormhole geometries in a physically consistent framework.
introduction:
Wormholes are hypothetical topological features of spacetime that act as “shortcuts” connecting distant regions of the universe. Since the seminal work of Morris and Thorne, traversable wormholes have been a subject of sustained interest in general relativity and alternative theories of gravity, both for their theoretical implications and for their potential, albeit speculative, applications in interstellar travel. A key challenge in constructing physically reasonable wormhole solutions lies in satisfying the flare–out condition at the throat, which typically requires the violation of the null energy condition (NEC). This requirement has motivated the exploration of exotic matter sources and modified gravitational frameworks that can effectively model such exoticity.

In recent years, noncommutative geometry has emerged as a promising avenue for generating regular, singularity–free spacetimes. Inspired by developments in string theory, noncommutative geometry replaces point–like structures with smeared distributions characterized by a minimal length scale, thereby modifying the short–distance behavior of gravitational fields. In the context of wormhole physics, such smearing effects can alleviate the severity of NEC violations and lead to smoother energy–momentum profiles at the throat. Furthermore, the incorporation of electric charge into wormhole models has been shown to influence the geometry in ways that can, in some cases, reduce the amount of exotic matter required and alter stability properties.

Another important consideration for traversable wormholes is the magnitude of tidal forces experienced by travelers. Morris and Thorne emphasized that for humanly traversable wormholes, tidal accelerations must remain within tolerable limits, which imposes constraints on the spacetime curvature and thus on the wormhole metric functions. Achieving low tidal forces while maintaining a physically viable geometry is nontrivial, especially when additional fields such as electromagnetic charge are present.

In this work, we investigate charged wormhole geometries inspired by noncommutative–geometry corrections, with particular emphasis on configurations that exhibit low tidal forces. By employing a smeared mass–energy distribution to model the gravitational source, we derive exact solutions to the Einstein–Maxwell field equations that satisfy traversability criteria without introducing singular behavior. The interplay between electric charge and noncommutative smearing is analyzed to determine its effect on the throat structure, energy conditions, and tidal accelerations. Our results contribute to the ongoing effort to reconcile the theoretical possibility of traversable wormholes with physically plausible matter sources and traveler–friendly spacetime conditions.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated a class of charged wormhole geometries inspired by noncommutative geometry, focusing on configurations that exhibit low tidal forces, thereby allowing safe traversal by humanoid observers. By incorporating the smeared, Lorentzian-distributed matter profiles characteristic of noncommutative geometry into the Einstein–Maxwell field equations, we have obtained exact solutions describing static, spherically symmetric wormholes. The inclusion of electric charge modifies the shape and redshift functions, while the noncommutative parameter effectively regularizes the geometry, avoiding curvature singularities. Our analysis shows that appropriate choices of the charge, throat radius, and noncommutative scale yield tidal accelerations within tolerable limits, without violating the necessary flare-out condition. The matter content was found to minimally violate the averaged null energy condition, consistent with the noncommutative smearing interpretation. These results suggest that noncommutative geometry and electromagnetic fields can cooperate to support traversable wormholes with physically reasonable properties. Future work may extend this framework to dynamic scenarios, rotating solutions, or alternative gravity theories to further explore stability and observational signatures.

title: An update of the on-sky performance of the Layer-Oriented wave-front sensor for MAD
abstract: We present updated on-sky performance results of the Layer-Oriented wave-front sensor for the Multi-conjugate Adaptive optics Demonstrator (MAD). Recent observations confirm improved correction stability, sensitivity, and sky coverage. Performance metrics under varying seeing conditions are discussed, demonstrating enhanced image quality and validating the sensor’s potential for future adaptive optics applications.
introduction:
The Multi-conjugate Adaptive optics Demonstrator (MAD) was developed by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) as a test bench to demonstrate the feasibility of Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (MCAO) techniques on the sky. Unlike classical adaptive optics systems, which correct atmospheric turbulence over a narrow field of view using a single guide star and deformable mirror conjugated to the telescope pupil, MCAO employs multiple deformable mirrors conjugated to different atmospheric layers and multiple guide stars to achieve a more uniform correction across a wider field. MAD was designed to implement and compare two distinct wave-front sensing approaches: the Star-Oriented (SO) and the Layer-Oriented (LO) techniques. The LO wave-front sensor (WFS) is based on the optical co-addition of light from several guide stars on a set of detectors, each corresponding to a specific conjugation altitude, allowing a direct measurement of the turbulence at different atmospheric layers.

The LO approach offers several advantages, including improved sensitivity to faint guide stars and efficient use of the available photon flux, which is particularly important for observations in crowded stellar fields or in regions with limited bright reference stars. The MAD experiment represents the first on-sky implementation of the LO WFS in a full MCAO configuration, enabling the evaluation of its real-world performance under varying atmospheric conditions.

This paper presents an updated analysis of the on-sky performance of the LO WFS for MAD, based on recent observing runs. We describe the operational setup, calibration procedures, and observing strategies adopted, and we assess the quality of the correction achieved in terms of point spread function uniformity, Strehl ratio, and limiting magnitude. The results provide valuable insight into the capabilities and limitations of the LO approach, and they contribute to the design and optimization of future MCAO systems for large telescopes, including the next generation of Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs).
conclusion: The on-sky tests of the Layer-Oriented wave-front sensor for MAD have demonstrated the capability of this approach to achieve effective adaptive optics correction under realistic observing conditions. The results confirm that simultaneous sensing of multiple guide stars and the optical co-addition of their light onto multiple conjugate detectors can deliver stable and accurate wave-front measurements. Performance metrics show that the system meets the design expectations, with improvements in image quality and resolution across a range of atmospheric conditions. The flexibility of the Layer-Oriented technique in handling faint guide stars and extended asterisms has been validated, widening the range of accessible targets. Operational experience during these campaigns has also provided valuable insights into calibration procedures, alignment tolerances, and control strategies, informing future implementations. Overall, the on-sky performance confirms the maturity of the Layer-Oriented wave-front sensor concept, paving the way for its application in next-generation adaptive optics systems on large telescopes.

title: 1D CNN Architectures for Music Genre Classification
abstract: This paper investigates the application of one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN) architectures for automatic music genre classification. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on two-dimensional spectrogram representations, our method directly processes raw audio waveforms, preserving temporal resolution while reducing preprocessing requirements. We design and evaluate several 1D CNN configurations with varying kernel sizes, depths, and pooling strategies to capture both local rhythmic patterns and broader temporal dependencies. Experiments are conducted on benchmark datasets, including GTZAN, using stratified cross-validation to ensure robust performance assessment. Results demonstrate that optimized 1D CNN models achieve competitive accuracy compared to spectrogram-based CNNs, while requiring fewer computational resources. Analysis of learned filters reveals that early layers effectively model percussive and harmonic features directly from waveform data. These findings highlight the potential of 1D CNNs as efficient, end-to-end solutions for music genre classification, offering a promising alternative for real-time and embedded audio classification systems.
introduction:
Music genre classification has emerged as a prominent research topic within the broader fields of music information retrieval (MIR) and computational music analysis. The ability to automatically categorize music tracks into genres has wide-ranging applications, including music recommendation systems, playlist generation, music cataloging, and content-based retrieval. Traditionally, genre classification has relied on hand-crafted features such as Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), spectral contrast, chroma features, and rhythmic descriptors. While these approaches have achieved a certain level of success, their performance is often limited by the representational capacity of manually engineered features and by their inability to fully capture complex temporal and spectral patterns inherent in musical signals.

In recent years, the advent of deep learning has transformed the landscape of audio classification tasks. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), in particular, have demonstrated remarkable success in learning hierarchical feature representations directly from raw or minimally processed data. While early applications of CNNs to music genre classification often employed two-dimensional convolutional architectures on spectrogram representations—leveraging similarities between audio spectrograms and image data—there has been growing interest in one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNNs) that operate directly on time-domain signals or on one-dimensional feature sequences such as MFCC vectors. By focusing on the temporal structure and exploiting convolutional filters along a single dimension, 1D CNNs can reduce computational complexity, mitigate the need for extensive pre-processing, and potentially preserve fine-grained temporal information that might be smoothed or distorted in spectrogram-based approaches.

1D CNN architectures offer several advantages that make them well-suited for music genre classification. First, they are capable of capturing local temporal dependencies in audio signals through the use of convolutional kernels that slide along the time axis. This is particularly relevant for music, where rhythmic patterns, note sequences, and dynamic changes often occur over short time spans. Second, the reduced dimensionality of the input in a 1D framework generally leads to fewer parameters compared to equivalent 2D CNNs, which can be beneficial in terms of training efficiency, memory footprint, and overfitting prevention, especially when working with limited datasets. Third, when combined with pooling operations and deeper network structures, 1D CNNs can learn increasingly abstract representations that integrate information across longer temporal contexts, enabling the model to capture genre-defining characteristics such as instrumentation, harmonic progressions, and stylistic rhythmic patterns.

Despite these advantages, the design of effective 1D CNN architectures for music genre classification remains an open research question. Key considerations include the choice of input representation (raw waveform vs. feature sequences), kernel sizes and strides, network depth, pooling strategies, and the integration of regularization techniques. Furthermore, while 1D CNNs offer computational benefits, they may face challenges in modeling long-range dependencies compared to recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformer-based architectures, necessitating careful architectural design or hybrid approaches. Comparative studies between 1D CNNs and alternative architectures are still relatively sparse in the literature, particularly in the context of standardized benchmarks and controlled experimental settings.

The present work seeks to systematically explore and evaluate 1D CNN architectures for music genre classification. By analyzing various configurations of convolutional layers, pooling strategies, and activation functions, we aim to identify design patterns that yield robust and accurate classification performance across different datasets. Our investigation also considers the trade-offs between model complexity, training efficiency, and generalization capability. In doing so, we contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the suitability of 1D CNNs for audio classification tasks and their potential role as a lightweight, effective alternative to more computationally demanding architectures. Ultimately, this research aspires to inform the development of next-generation MIR systems that can efficiently and accurately categorize music in real-world applications.
conclusion: This study has explored the application of one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN) architectures for music genre classification, demonstrating their effectiveness in capturing temporal and spectral patterns from audio signals. By operating directly on extracted feature sequences, 1D CNNs reduce computational complexity compared to two-dimensional approaches while maintaining competitive accuracy. The experimental results indicate that carefully designed convolutional layers, kernel sizes, and pooling strategies can significantly enhance classification performance. Furthermore, the models exhibit robustness to variations in audio quality and genre overlap, underscoring their suitability for real-world applications. While promising, the findings also highlight the importance of balanced datasets and appropriate preprocessing to mitigate bias and overfitting. Future work could investigate hybrid architectures combining 1D CNNs with recurrent or attention-based mechanisms to further improve temporal context modeling. Overall, the results confirm that 1D CNNs present a viable and efficient solution for automated music genre classification, offering a strong foundation for subsequent research and practical deployment.

title: 3D simulations of photochemical hazes in the atmosphere of hot Jupiter HD 189733b
abstract: We present three-dimensional general circulation model (GCM) simulations of photochemical haze formation and transport in the atmosphere of the hot Jupiter HD 189733b. Using a coupled framework that integrates atmospheric dynamics, radiative transfer, and a simplified photochemical haze microphysics scheme, we investigate how stellar irradiation, atmospheric circulation, and vertical mixing shape the spatial distribution of haze particles. The model accounts for the production of haze precursors via photolysis of methane and other hydrocarbons in the upper atmosphere, followed by particle growth, coagulation, and sedimentation. Our simulations reveal strong longitudinal and latitudinal variations in haze abundance, with the highest concentrations forming on the dayside at high altitudes, where ultraviolet flux is greatest. Zonal jets transport haze-rich air toward the nightside, where lower temperatures promote particle growth and settling. The resulting three-dimensional haze structure significantly influences the planet’s thermal structure and observable spectra, with enhanced optical scattering in the blue and reduced infrared emission on the nightside. Comparisons with available HST and Spitzer observations suggest that photochemical hazes can account for the observed featureless optical transmission spectrum and muted water absorption features. We find that haze particle sizes and vertical distributions are highly sensitive to the assumed eddy diffusion coefficient and precursor production rates, indicating that observational constraints on these parameters are critical for accurate modeling. Our results underscore the importance of incorporating fully three-dimensional haze transport and radiative feedback in models of hot Jupiter atmospheres to correctly interpret spectroscopic observations and constrain underlying chemical and dynamical processes.
introduction:
Hot Jupiters, gas giant exoplanets orbiting extremely close to their host stars, provide unique laboratories for studying atmospheric dynamics and chemistry under intense stellar irradiation. Among these, HD 189733b has emerged as one of the most extensively observed, owing to its proximity, large transit depth, and favorable host star properties. Observations across a broad wavelength range have revealed spectral features suggestive of high-altitude aerosols, which can significantly influence the planet’s observed transmission and emission spectra. In particular, photochemical hazes—complex organic particles formed via the photolysis of atmospheric precursors—have been proposed as a key contributor to the muted spectral features and enhanced optical scattering detected for HD 189733b.

Photochemical haze formation is driven by the interaction of stellar ultraviolet (UV) photons with atmospheric molecules such as methane, ammonia, and other hydrocarbons, leading to complex chemical pathways that produce condensable macromolecules. While one-dimensional (1D) models have provided valuable insights into the chemical kinetics and vertical distribution of hazes, they cannot capture the inherently three-dimensional (3D) nature of atmospheric circulation. In tidally locked hot Jupiters, strong day–night temperature contrasts drive vigorous winds and global-scale advection, redistributing both gas-phase species and aerosol particles. This coupling between chemistry, microphysics, and dynamics can substantially modify the spatial distribution, particle size spectra, and optical properties of hazes.

Recent advances in 3D general circulation models (GCMs) now allow for the inclusion of simplified aerosol microphysics and photochemistry, enabling more realistic predictions of haze spatial variability. For HD 189733b, such models can help explain observational trends such as wavelength-dependent transit depths, phase curve asymmetries, and thermal emission suppression in certain bands. Furthermore, understanding haze transport and evolution is critical for interpreting the planet’s albedo, energy balance, and potential departures from chemical equilibrium.

In this work, we present 3D numerical simulations of photochemical haze formation and transport in the atmosphere of HD 189733b. We couple a parameterized photochemical production scheme to a GCM that includes advection, sedimentation, and particle growth, allowing us to explore the interplay between haze microphysics and atmospheric circulation. By comparing the simulated haze distributions to observational constraints, we aim to assess the role of photochemical aerosols in shaping the observable properties of this benchmark hot Jupiter and to provide guidance for future observational and modeling efforts.
conclusion:
In this study, we have presented the first fully three-dimensional simulations of photochemical haze formation and transport in the atmosphere of the hot Jupiter HD 189733b, coupling a general circulation model with a simplified haze microphysics scheme. By incorporating both the dynamical and chemical timescales relevant to haze particle production, growth, and advection, we have been able to explore the spatial distribution, vertical extent, and potential observational signatures of photochemical hazes under realistic irradiated planetary conditions.

Our results demonstrate that haze formation is strongly modulated by the planet’s atmospheric circulation. The global-scale day–night temperature contrast drives vigorous equatorial superrotation, which redistributes haze precursors and particles longitudinally. Photochemical production is maximized on the dayside upper atmosphere, where strong stellar UV flux initiates the formation of complex hydrocarbons. However, the rapid advection by zonal winds leads to a substantial transport of these precursors into the nightside, where lower temperatures allow for more efficient particle growth and reduced photolysis rates. As a result, we find a pronounced asymmetry between day and night hemispheres in particle size distributions and number densities.

Vertically, haze particles are lofted to pressures as low as a few microbars on the dayside, consistent with the high-altitude opacity inferred from transmission spectra. Downward mixing and sedimentation produce a gradual decline in haze abundance with depth, but the interplay of vertical mixing and particle growth leads to a non-uniform vertical profile. In particular, our simulations suggest that large particles can form at intermediate pressures (0.1–10 mbar) on the nightside, potentially enhancing scattering opacity in the near-infrared.

The three-dimensional nature of our model reveals that latitudinal variations are also significant. Cooler polar regions exhibit reduced photochemical production but can serve as reservoirs for haze particles transported from equatorial regions. These patterns are not captured in one-dimensional or even two-dimensional models, underscoring the importance of full 3D treatments when interpreting observational data.

From an observational standpoint, the simulated haze distributions imply notable consequences for both transmission and emission spectra. The extended, optically thick haze layers at the limb regions can mute molecular absorption features, consistent with the relatively featureless optical transmission spectrum observed for HD 189733b. In emission, longitudinal differences in haze opacity could contribute to phase curve asymmetries, particularly at wavelengths where scattering dominates over absorption. Our results also suggest that high-altitude hazes may remain photochemically active over a wide range of longitudes, complicating the retrieval of temperature and composition profiles from secondary eclipse data.

While the microphysics scheme adopted here is simplified, it captures the essential coupling between photochemical production, particle growth, and atmospheric dynamics. Future work incorporating more detailed chemical pathways, heterogeneous chemistry on particle surfaces, and a broader range of particle compositions will help refine these predictions. Additionally, coupling the haze model to radiative transfer in a self-consistent manner will allow us to quantify the feedback of haze opacity on atmospheric circulation, which may alter wind patterns and temperature structures.

In summary, our three-dimensional simulations highlight the complex and inherently non-uniform nature of photochemical haze formation on HD 189733b. The interplay of stellar irradiation, atmospheric dynamics, and particle microphysics leads to rich spatial structures that can significantly affect observational signatures. These findings reinforce the necessity of multidimensional modeling in the interpretation of current and future spectroscopic and photometric observations of exoplanetary atmospheres, particularly as forthcoming facilities such as the James Webb Space Telescope and Ariel will provide unprecedented constraints on both the chemical and aerosol properties of distant worlds.

title: Layer-layer competition in multiplex complex networks
abstract: We investigate the emergence of competition between layers in multiplex complex networks, where the same set of nodes interacts through distinct types of connections. In such systems, the activity of each node may be distributed heterogeneously across layers, and inter-layer coupling can induce nontrivial redistribution of dynamical processes. We develop a theoretical framework to quantify layer-layer competition by introducing a tunable parameter that controls inter-layer switching costs. Using both analytical arguments and numerical simulations on synthetic and real-world multiplex topologies, we identify regimes in which one layer dominates the dynamics, as well as coexistence phases where activity is shared. Our results reveal that structural heterogeneities, such as degree correlations and layer overlap, strongly influence the competition outcome. In particular, we find that increasing inter-layer coupling can trigger abrupt transitions between layer-dominant states, reminiscent of first-order phase transitions. These findings provide insight into scenarios such as competing communication platforms, multimodal transportation systems, or overlapping social contexts, where individuals or entities divide their participation among alternatives. The proposed approach offers a general methodology for studying competitive interactions in multiplex networks and highlights the critical role of structural and dynamical interplay in shaping collective behavior.
introduction:
In recent years, the study of complex networks has emerged as a powerful framework for understanding the structure and dynamics of a broad range of systems, from social and technological infrastructures to biological and ecological interactions. Traditional network theory has primarily focused on single-layer representations, where all interactions between units are aggregated into a single set of connections. However, many real-world systems are inherently multilayered, with the same set of nodes participating in different types of relationships or operating in different contexts. This has given rise to the formalism of multiplex networks, where nodes are connected through multiple layers, each representing a distinct mode of interaction or functional relation.

Multiplex networks capture a richer and more realistic description of system architecture than their monoplex counterparts. In such settings, each layer may correspond to a different communication medium in social systems, a different transportation mode in infrastructural systems, or a distinct biochemical pathway in cellular systems. The interplay between layers can give rise to emergent phenomena that cannot be inferred from the analysis of each layer in isolation. Interdependencies and correlations between layers can enhance or inhibit dynamical processes such as diffusion, synchronization, and epidemic spreading.

An important and less explored aspect of multiplex network dynamics is the competition between layers for node activity or resource allocation. In many systems, nodes have finite capacity to participate or invest in different layers simultaneously. For example, in social multiplex networks, individuals may divide their attention and communication effort between face-to-face interactions and online platforms. In transportation networks, passengers may choose between alternative modes such as rail or bus, depending on efficiency and cost. In biological networks, proteins may be involved in different pathways that compete for their functional engagement. This competition can lead to complex allocation patterns, where the activity or influence of one layer suppresses or constrains the activity of another.

Layer–layer competition introduces a coupling mechanism that is fundamentally different from cooperative interdependencies traditionally studied in multilayer systems. While cooperative coupling often facilitates cascading effects and mutual reinforcement, competition can lead to segregation of activity, dominance of one layer, or coexistence regimes depending on system parameters. Theoretical models have begun to formalize such competitive interactions by introducing constraints on node states across layers, defining cost–benefit trade-offs, or implementing dynamical rules that redistribute resources. These frameworks allow the investigation of phase transitions between different regimes of layer dominance, the stability of coexistence states, and the impact of network topology on competitive outcomes.

Understanding layer–layer competition is not only of theoretical interest but also of practical relevance. In communication infrastructures, competitive dynamics may determine the resilience of parallel channels to congestion or failure. In socio-economic systems, competition between platforms or services can shape market structure and innovation trajectories. In ecological contexts, species interactions across different trophic or spatial layers may involve competition for shared resources, influencing community stability and biodiversity. The ability to model and predict the outcomes of such competition can inform the design and management of multilayer systems, guiding interventions that promote desired behaviors or mitigate systemic risks.

This work aims to contribute to the growing body of research on multiplex networks by focusing specifically on the mechanisms and consequences of layer–layer competition. We develop a modeling framework that captures the redistribution of node activity across layers and explore how network structure, coupling strength, and dynamical rules affect the resulting macroscopic states. By combining analytical approaches with numerical simulations, we elucidate the conditions under which layers can coexist, one layer dominates, or complex switching dynamics emerge. Our findings provide new insights into the competitive interactions that shape the functioning of multiplex systems and open avenues for future research on strategic control and optimization in multilayer contexts.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the phenomenon of layer–layer competition in multiplex complex networks, focusing on how the structural and dynamical properties of interconnected layers influence the distribution of activity and the emergence of dominance or coexistence between layers. By modelling the multiplex as a set of coupled network layers with shared nodes but distinct intralayer connectivity patterns, we have been able to explore the interplay between topological heterogeneity, interlayer coupling strength, and node-level preferences. Our results highlight the delicate balance between cooperative and competitive interactions across layers, and how this balance shapes the global organization of activity in multiplex systems.

A central finding of our study is that the competition between layers is not solely determined by the intrinsic attractiveness or efficiency of each layer in isolation, but emerges from the mutual constraints that the layers impose on each other through their shared nodes. When interlayer coupling is weak, nodes can act relatively independently in each layer, allowing structurally advantageous layers to dominate activity. However, as coupling strength increases, the capacity for one layer to monopolize activity is reduced, and the system tends toward more balanced participation across layers. This transition is neither abrupt nor universal; rather, it depends sensitively on the alignment or mismatch of the degree distributions, clustering patterns, and centrality structures of the layers involved.

Our analysis also reveals that heterogeneity in node-level preferences plays a critical role in mediating competition. In scenarios where nodes’ intrinsic biases toward particular layers are homogeneous, the outcome of competition is largely dictated by structural asymmetries between the layers. Conversely, when preferences are heterogeneous, even structurally disadvantaged layers can retain significant levels of activity if they are strongly favored by certain subsets of nodes. This finding suggests that interventions aimed at redistributing activity across layers—such as incentives in communication platforms or routing strategies in transport systems—need to consider both the structural context and the heterogeneity of user or agent preferences.

From a methodological perspective, the framework we have developed provides a flexible means of quantifying layer–layer competition, capturing both microscopic (node-level) and macroscopic (system-level) aspects of the phenomenon. By incorporating adjustable interlayer coupling, the model allows us to interpolate between regimes of near-independence and strong interdependence, offering insights into how multiplex systems might respond to changes in coupling brought about by technological integration, policy shifts, or evolving user behaviors. The use of both analytical approximations and numerical simulations has enabled us to map the parameter space of competition outcomes and to identify regions where coexistence, domination, or oscillatory dynamics are likely to occur.

These results have broad implications for the design and management of multiplex systems in various domains. In social and communication networks, understanding the competitive dynamics between platforms or channels can inform strategies to foster diversity of engagement rather than monopolization by a single medium. In infrastructure systems such as transportation or power grids, recognizing how competition between parallel subsystems unfolds can guide investment in redundancy and resilience. Moreover, in biological contexts—such as neural or ecological multiplexes—layer–layer competition may underpin functional specialization or adaptive shifts, with potential consequences for stability and adaptability.

It is important to acknowledge the limitations of our approach. The model presented here assumes static topologies within each layer and static interlayer connections, whereas in many real systems both may evolve over time in response to the dynamics of competition itself. Additionally, our treatment of preferences and coupling is stylized, and richer forms of interdependence—such as multilayer feedback loops or context-dependent coupling—could yield qualitatively different behaviors. Future research should extend the present framework to incorporate temporal evolution, adaptive coupling, and stochasticity, as well as to validate theoretical predictions against empirical multiplex datasets.

In conclusion, our study advances the understanding of how competition between layers in multiplex networks arises from the complex interplay of structural, dynamical, and preferential factors. By elucidating the conditions under which one layer dominates, layers coexist, or activity fluctuates between them, we contribute to a more nuanced picture of multiplex organization and function. Such insights are increasingly relevant in a world where systems of communication, transportation, energy, and social interaction are inherently multilayered and interdependent. Continued exploration of layer–layer competition, grounded in both theory and empirical observation, will be essential for designing, regulating, and sustaining the multiplex systems that underpin modern life.

title: How to design a 2D active grid for dynamic inflow modulation
abstract: Active grids are increasingly employed in wind tunnel and flow simulation studies to generate controlled, time-varying turbulence profiles. This paper presents the design methodology for a two-dimensional (2D) active grid capable of dynamic inflow modulation for aerodynamic and aeroelastic testing. The system consists of an orthogonal array of independently actuated vanes, arranged to form a reconfigurable lattice that manipulates the incident flow field in both spatial and temporal domains. Design requirements were established based on target turbulence intensity, spectral content, and correlation length scales, with emphasis on achieving rapid modulation across a wide frequency range. Mechanical design considerations included vane geometry, structural stiffness, and actuation torque to minimize flow blockage while ensuring precise control. A modular actuation system using stepper motors and closed-loop control was implemented to enable programmable motion patterns and real-time adaptation. Computational fluid dynamics simulations informed the aerodynamic optimization of vane profiles and spacing, while preliminary wind tunnel tests validated the grid’s capability to produce reproducible inflow variations. Measured results demonstrated a high degree of control over turbulence characteristics, including the generation of intermittent gusts and prescribed spectral energy distributions. The proposed 2D active grid design offers a versatile platform for experimental studies requiring dynamic inflow conditions, with applications in wind energy, vehicle aerodynamics, and unsteady load characterization.
introduction:
The generation of controlled, spatially and temporally varying flow fields is of increasing importance in experimental fluid dynamics, particularly for the study of unsteady aerodynamic and hydrodynamic phenomena. Active grids, which employ individually actuated elements to manipulate incoming flow, have emerged as a versatile tool for producing tailored turbulence characteristics in wind tunnels and water channels. While most active grid designs to date have been one-dimensional arrays of rotating paddles or flaps, the need for more complex and realistic inflow conditions has motivated the development of two-dimensional (2D) configurations. A 2D active grid, composed of a matrix of independently controllable vanes or wings, offers the capability to modulate the flow field both in space and time across the cross-section of the test section.

Dynamic inflow modulation using a 2D active grid enables the reproduction of transient gusts, coherent structures, and heterogeneous turbulence patterns that more closely resemble real-world environments, such as atmospheric boundary layers or wake interactions in wind farms. This added flexibility is particularly relevant for applications in renewable energy research, aircraft and rotorcraft aerodynamics, and the validation of computational models under unsteady inflow conditions. However, the design of a 2D active grid poses significant challenges, including the mechanical integration of multiple actuators, the synchronization and control of their motions, the minimization of flow blockage, and the accurate characterization of the resulting flow fields.

This work presents a systematic approach to designing a 2D active grid for dynamic inflow modulation. Key considerations include actuator selection, vane geometry, control strategies, and structural layout. The proposed design methodology aims to balance mechanical feasibility, flow quality, and control bandwidth, providing a foundation for constructing a device capable of generating reproducible, complex inflow conditions for a wide range of experimental studies.
conclusion: The proposed design methodology enables effective creation of a 2D active grid capable of precise dynamic inflow modulation. By integrating optimized actuator placement and control algorithms, the system achieves enhanced turbulence generation and flow variability, supporting advanced experimental studies in aerodynamics and renewable energy applications with improved accuracy and flexibility.

title: Voting Rights, Markov Chains, and Optimization by Short Bursts
abstract: This paper investigates the intersection of voting rights, stochastic modeling, and computational optimization, introducing a novel framework that leverages Markov chains to analyze and improve equitable access to voting. We model voter participation and accessibility dynamics as state transitions in a discrete-time Markov process, capturing the probabilistic effects of policy changes, demographic shifts, and logistical constraints. The framework enables the identification of long-term equilibrium distributions of participation rates across different population segments, thereby quantifying disparities in voting rights realization. Building upon this modeling, we develop an optimization approach based on short computational bursts, wherein iterative refinements are performed within constrained time or resource budgets. This approach is particularly suited to policy environments requiring rapid scenario evaluation and adaptive decision-making. We demonstrate the method’s effectiveness through simulations informed by empirical data on voter registration, polling place distribution, and turnout patterns. Results indicate that the combination of Markov chain modeling and burst-based optimization can guide targeted interventions that measurably reduce inequities. The proposed methodology offers both a theoretical contribution to the modeling of democratic processes and a practical tool for policymakers seeking to promote fair and robust electoral participation.
introduction:
The protection and exercise of voting rights are central to the functioning of democratic societies. Across jurisdictions, the design of electoral systems, the accessibility of voting mechanisms, and the fairness of representation have long been subjects of legal, political, and mathematical scrutiny. In recent decades, the quantitative analysis of voting has expanded beyond traditional political science models to incorporate tools from probability theory, optimization, and computational methods. These approaches enable the study of voting as a dynamic process, subject to changing participation rates, evolving district boundaries, and varying institutional constraints. This paper situates itself at the intersection of voting rights analysis, Markov chain modeling, and optimization techniques, with the aim of developing a framework for understanding and improving electoral systems through iterative, computationally tractable methods.

Markov chains provide a natural mathematical framework for modeling the evolution of probabilistic systems over time. In the context of voting, they can be used to represent transitions between different states of voter participation, shifts in partisan composition, or the progression of legislative outcomes as shaped by electoral events. The Markov property—the assumption that future states depend only on the present state and not on the history—offers analytical tractability while still enabling the capture of complex dynamics when the state space is appropriately defined. For example, a state might encode turnout levels in different demographic groups, the partisan configuration of a legislative body, or the degree of compliance with voting rights legislation. By analyzing the steady-state distributions or transient behaviors of such Markov models, researchers can assess the long-term consequences of policy interventions or structural reforms.

However, the mere modeling of electoral processes is insufficient for guiding practical improvements. The optimization of voting systems—whether to maximize fairness, minimize disenfranchisement, or enhance representational accuracy—requires algorithms capable of navigating large and often combinatorial state spaces. Classical optimization approaches may be computationally prohibitive or may require assumptions that oversimplify the underlying problem. This motivates the exploration of “short burst” optimization techniques: iterative procedures that apply localized, computationally inexpensive adjustments to a system, evaluate the resulting changes, and repeat the process. Such methods can be seen as a compromise between exhaustive optimization, which is often infeasible, and static analysis, which may overlook actionable improvements.

The integration of Markov chain models with short-burst optimization offers several advantages for the study of voting rights. First, the Markov framework provides a probabilistic foundation for simulating the effects of changes—such as modifying district boundaries, altering voting technology, or implementing targeted voter outreach—on long-run electoral outcomes. Second, short-burst optimization allows for the incremental refinement of these interventions, guided by performance metrics tied to legal and normative criteria, such as proportionality, competitiveness, and inclusivity. Third, this combined approach is adaptable to varying levels of data availability, from richly detailed voter files to aggregated demographic statistics, making it applicable in diverse political and legal contexts.

This paper seeks to contribute to the literature in three ways. It develops a formalism for representing voting rights–relevant processes as Markov chains with state spaces aligned to legal and policy concerns. It proposes an optimization scheme based on short bursts, suitable for computational exploration of reforms under realistic constraints. And it demonstrates the approach through case studies, illustrating how probabilistic modeling and iterative optimization can identify both vulnerabilities and opportunities in electoral systems. By bridging mathematical modeling with normative commitments to fair and equal participation, the framework advanced here aims to support evidence-based policy design and to enrich the interdisciplinary dialogue on safeguarding democratic rights.
conclusion:
This study has examined the interplay between voting rights, stochastic modeling through Markov chains, and the optimization of decision-making processes via short bursts of computational or procedural effort. By integrating these three domains, we have sought to provide both a conceptual framework and a methodological toolkit for analyzing collective decision mechanisms in contexts where participation, influence, and procedural efficiency are all at stake.

Our investigation began with the recognition that voting rights are not merely formal entitlements but dynamic quantities whose effective value can fluctuate over time due to changes in coalition structures, agenda sequencing, and participation patterns. Modeling these fluctuations requires a probabilistic approach capable of capturing transitions between states of influence. Markov chains emerged as an appropriate formalism, allowing us to represent the evolution of voting power distributions as a sequence of state transitions governed by fixed or adaptive probabilities. This representation made it possible to study long-run equilibria, transient dynamics, and the sensitivity of outcomes to structural parameters such as quorum thresholds or agenda control rules.

Through the Markov chain framework, we demonstrated how different institutional arrangements can lead to markedly different stationary distributions of voting power, even when the nominal rights of participants are held constant. This finding reinforces the idea that legal or constitutional guarantees alone do not determine actual influence; process design and the probabilistic structure of interactions play equally decisive roles. Moreover, the stochastic approach allowed us to capture the effects of uncertainty—both in the form of random participation and in the strategic unpredictability of alliances—on the ultimate realization of collective choices.

The second major strand of our work concerned the optimization of decision-making processes under constraints of time, information, or computational resources. We introduced the notion of “short bursts” optimization: rather than attempting to solve complex allocation or scheduling problems in a single, exhaustive effort, decision-makers can achieve near-optimal outcomes by iterating brief, targeted computational or deliberative episodes. In the context of voting, this could correspond to limited rounds of preference aggregation, partial explorations of coalition possibilities, or focused simulations of policy impacts.
