Furthermore, the use of natural language prompts offers an interpretable and flexible mechanism for incorporating expert knowledge into generation pipelines. These findings suggest that prompt-driven few-shot learning holds promise for scalable, data-efficient clinical text generation. Future work will investigate more robust prompt optimization strategies, integration with multimodal visual features, and evaluation in real-world reporting workflows to ensure clinical reliability and utility in diverse healthcare settings.

title: Thermalization of rate-independent processes by entropic regularization
abstract: We investigate the thermalization of rate-independent processes through an entropic regularization framework. By augmenting the classical energetic formulation with an entropy term, we introduce a small thermal parameter that smooths the inherently non-smooth dissipation, yielding a thermodynamically consistent evolution. The resulting regularized problem admits well-posed solutions and captures thermal fluctuations at finite temperature. We analyze the asymptotic behavior as the thermal parameter vanishes, recovering the rate-independent limit, and illustrate the approach with examples demonstrating improved stability and computational tractability.
introduction:
Rate-independent processes arise in a variety of physical and engineering contexts, including plasticity, damage mechanics, and frictional contact, where the evolution depends solely on the path of loading and not on its rate. Mathematically, such systems are typically described by energetic formulations involving a dissipation potential that is positively homogeneous of degree one. While this framework captures the quasi-static, irreversible nature of the phenomena, it neglects thermal fluctuations and stochastic effects that can be relevant at small scales or in soft materials. Incorporating thermalization into rate-independent models poses conceptual and analytical challenges, as the underlying dynamics lack a natural timescale for relaxation.

A promising approach to this problem is entropic regularization, in which the deterministic rate-independent evolution is perturbed by a term proportional to the entropy of the system. This modification can be interpreted as introducing a probabilistic description of state transitions, consistent with statistical mechanics, that smooths the abrupt switching inherent in the original formulation. The regularization parameter controls the balance between purely rate-independent behavior and thermally activated dynamics, and in the vanishing limit one recovers the original rate-independent process.

From a mathematical perspective, entropic regularization leads to evolution equations of gradient-flow type in a suitable metric space, with entropy acting as a driving functional. This connection enables the use of tools from optimal transport, large-deviation theory, and variational convergence to analyze the limit behavior. In particular, one may study the passage from stochastic, thermally influenced trajectories to deterministic energetic solutions via asymptotic analysis.

In this work, we develop a systematic framework for the thermalization of rate-independent processes through entropic regularization. We establish well-posedness of the regularized problem, investigate its qualitative properties, and rigorously characterize the zero-temperature limit. Applications to prototypical models illustrate how thermal fluctuations manifest in macroscopic response and how entropic regularization provides a physically motivated and mathematically tractable pathway from stochastic to rate-independent behavior.
conclusion: We have investigated the thermalization of rate‑independent processes through entropic regularization, demonstrating how introducing an entropy term yields a smoothened evolution that captures thermal effects while preserving essential structural properties. The proposed framework bridges purely rate‑independent models and thermally activated dynamics, offering a consistent variational formulation. Analytical results establish convergence to the original rate‑independent limit as the regularization vanishes, while numerical illustrations confirm the predicted behavior. This approach opens new perspectives for modeling complex materials and systems where both mechanical dissipation and thermal fluctuations play significant, interacting roles.

title: Characterization and computation of control invariant sets within target regions for linear impulsive control systems
abstract: This paper addresses the characterization and computation of control invariant sets contained within prescribed target regions for discrete-time linear impulsive control systems. Such systems, featuring continuous evolution interspersed with instantaneous state jumps induced by control impulses, arise in numerous engineering applications including networked control, sampled-data systems, and hybrid process regulation. We focus on the problem of determining the largest subset of a given target region from which all trajectories can be maintained within the region for all future time through admissible impulsive control actions. Building on the concept of control invariance for linear systems, we extend the definition to the impulsive setting, accounting for both the continuous-time flow between impulses and the discrete-time state resets. The proposed characterization exploits the system’s hybrid structure by formulating invariance conditions as linear matrix inequalities coupled with set containment constraints. We develop an iterative computational procedure, based on backward reachability under impulse and flow dynamics, that converges to the maximal control invariant set inside the target region. The method accommodates polyhedral and ellipsoidal target sets and can incorporate input constraints on the impulsive actions. Numerical examples illustrate the approach, demonstrating computational efficiency and the ability to capture subtle interactions between continuous and impulsive dynamics. The results provide a constructive framework for safety verification and reference governor design in impulsive control systems, enabling systematic synthesis of control laws that guarantee constraint satisfaction. This work thus extends classical invariant set theory to a broad class of hybrid systems with impulsive controls, offering both theoretical characterization and practical algorithms for embedded and networked control applications.
introduction:
Control invariant sets play a central role in the analysis and synthesis of control strategies for dynamical systems, as they capture the notion of states from which the system can be maintained within prescribed constraints for all future times under admissible control actions. In recent years, their computation has been extensively studied in the context of continuous-time and discrete-time systems, motivated by applications in safety-critical control, constrained regulation, and model predictive control. For linear systems, convexity and polyhedrality properties have enabled the development of efficient computational procedures for maximal control invariant sets and related viability kernels. However, in many engineering applications, system dynamics are not purely continuous or purely discrete, but exhibit impulsive phenomena—abrupt changes in the state induced by instantaneous control actions—superimposed on continuous evolution. Examples include sampled-data systems with impulsive updates, switched electrical circuits, mechanical systems with impacts, and hybrid networked control systems with reset events.

Linear impulsive control systems constitute a fundamental class of hybrid systems in which the state evolves according to a linear differential equation between impulses, and undergoes instantaneous jumps at discrete instants determined by a given sequence or triggering rule. The presence of impulsive actions enriches the control possibilities, enabling rapid state corrections, but also complicates the analysis of invariant behavior due to the intertwined continuous–discrete evolution. While the theory of invariance for purely continuous or purely discrete systems is well established, the characterization of control invariant sets for impulsive systems remains less developed. In particular, most existing approaches focus on global invariance properties without considering additional spatial restrictions on the admissible state space.

In practical scenarios, the invariance property is often required not with respect to the entire state space, but within a specific *target region* representing operational or safety limits. Such a target region may be dictated by physical constraints, performance specifications, or safety envelopes, and the control objective becomes to ensure that the state remains inside this region indefinitely, starting from a set of admissible initial conditions. This motivates the study of *control invariant sets within target regions*—the largest subsets of the target region from which there exists an admissible impulsive control strategy that prevents exit from the region for all future times. The computation of such sets is crucial for guaranteeing constraint satisfaction and for determining feasibility domains in constrained control design.

This paper addresses the problem of characterizing and computing control invariant sets within given target regions for linear impulsive control systems. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for invariance under both continuous and impulsive control actions, and propose computational algorithms that exploit the structure of the target region and the system dynamics. The results extend classical invariance theory to a hybrid impulsive setting, bridging the gap between continuous/discrete invariance analysis and the needs of impulsive control applications. Illustrative examples demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of the proposed methods in determining admissible sets for constrained impulsive control.
conclusion:
This work has addressed the problem of characterizing and computing control invariant sets that are entirely contained within prescribed target regions for linear impulsive control systems. By integrating techniques from set invariance theory with the hybrid dynamics induced by impulsive actions, we have established conditions under which such sets exist and remain robust to system constraints and impulsive interventions. The proposed computational framework leverages the structure of linear dynamics between impulses and the discrete updates at impulse instants to iteratively approximate the maximal control invariant set within the target region. This approach accommodates both state and input constraints, ensuring practical applicability to safety-critical scenarios.  

Theoretical developments were supported by illustrative examples, demonstrating both the feasibility of the proposed method and its capacity to capture the interplay between continuous evolution and impulsive control in shaping admissible state trajectories. The results extend classical invariant set computation methods to a broader class of hybrid systems, highlighting the influence of impulse timing and magnitude on invariance properties. Future work may focus on extending the methodology to uncertain or nonlinear impulsive systems, and on developing more efficient algorithms for high-dimensional problems. Overall, the presented framework contributes a rigorous and computationally tractable tool for safety verification and target set maintenance in impulsive control applications.

title: Interaction of escaping cosmic rays with molecular clouds
abstract: We investigate the interaction between cosmic rays escaping from supernova remnants and nearby molecular clouds, focusing on particle transport, energy-dependent diffusion, and resultant non-thermal emissions. Using numerical models and multi-wavelength observational constraints, we examine gamma-ray signatures arising from hadronic interactions. Our results demonstrate that escaping cosmic rays significantly enhance cloud ionization and gamma-ray luminosity, providing a diagnostic of cosmic-ray propagation and feedback in the interstellar medium.
introduction:
Cosmic rays (CRs) are high-energy particles, predominantly protons and atomic nuclei, that permeate the interstellar medium (ISM) and play a central role in shaping its physical and chemical properties. Supernova remnants (SNRs) are widely regarded as the primary accelerators of Galactic CRs through diffusive shock acceleration. While the internal acceleration processes in SNRs have been extensively studied, the transport and interaction of CRs after escaping their acceleration sites remain less well constrained. Understanding these processes is essential for linking CR sources to the observed diffuse CR spectrum and associated non-thermal emission.

Molecular clouds (MCs), dense and magnetised structures within the ISM, are natural laboratories for studying CR propagation. Due to their high column densities, MCs act as effective targets for CR interactions, leading to the production of secondary particles and high-energy photons via inelastic proton–proton collisions. Gamma-ray observations of MCs in the vicinity of SNRs have revealed spatial and spectral signatures indicative of enhanced CR densities above the Galactic background. These enhancements are interpreted as evidence of freshly accelerated CRs escaping from nearby SNR shocks and diffusing into surrounding dense gas.

The interaction of escaping CRs with MCs provides a valuable probe of CR transport properties, such as diffusion coefficients and anisotropies, in regions with non-uniform magnetic field structures. Moreover, such interactions can influence the chemical evolution of molecular gas through ionisation processes, thereby impacting star formation activity. However, the complexity of CR propagation in turbulent and inhomogeneous environments introduces significant uncertainties, requiring a combination of observational constraints and theoretical modelling.

In this work, we investigate the mechanisms governing the interaction between escaping CRs and MCs, focusing on the resulting non-thermal emission signatures. By comparing model predictions with multi-wavelength observational data, we aim to constrain CR diffusion in the vicinity of SNRs and improve our understanding of the link between CR sources and the Galactic CR population.
conclusion:
The present study has examined the interaction between cosmic rays escaping from supernova remnants and nearby molecular clouds, focusing on the resulting signatures in non-thermal emission and the implications for particle transport. Our analysis indicates that the spatial and spectral characteristics of gamma-ray emission from such systems can be consistently explained by the diffusion of high-energy particles into dense cloud material, with energy-dependent propagation shaping the observed spectra. The comparison between model predictions and observational data suggests that diffusion coefficients in the vicinity of accelerators are significantly suppressed relative to Galactic averages, supporting the concept of locally enhanced magnetic turbulence induced by the escaping cosmic rays themselves.

Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of cloud morphology and density distribution in modulating the penetration depth of particles and the corresponding emission profiles. The coupling between cosmic-ray transport and the microphysics of the cloud environment emerges as a key factor in interpreting current and future observations from high-energy facilities. This work underscores that molecular clouds act as natural laboratories for probing the physics of cosmic-ray escape and propagation, offering constraints on both acceleration efficiency and the surrounding interstellar medium conditions.

Future progress will benefit from combined multi-wavelength campaigns and improved theoretical models that incorporate anisotropic diffusion, magnetic field structure, and time-dependent injection. Such efforts will refine our understanding of the feedback processes between energetic particles and their environments, contributing to a more comprehensive picture of the life cycle of cosmic rays in our Galaxy.

title: Soft Motion Trajectory Planner for Service Manipulator Robot
abstract: This paper presents a soft motion trajectory planner designed for a service manipulator robot, enabling smooth and safe movements in human-centered environments. The proposed approach generates continuous position, velocity, and acceleration profiles while respecting the robot’s dynamic constraints and task requirements. By employing polynomial interpolation and online trajectory adjustment, the planner ensures minimal jerks and reduced mechanical stress, improving both safety and operational lifespan. Experimental validation on a 6-DOF manipulator demonstrates effective adaptation to varying payloads and environmental conditions, achieving precise end-effector tracking and collision avoidance. The results indicate that the planner enhances interaction comfort, reduces energy consumption, and maintains high task efficiency, making it suitable for domestic, healthcare, and collaborative service robotics applications.
introduction:
Service robots are increasingly deployed in domestic, healthcare, and industrial environments to assist humans with a wide range of manipulation tasks. These robots are expected to operate safely and efficiently in unstructured and dynamic surroundings, often in close proximity to people. A critical requirement in such contexts is the ability to generate smooth and feasible motion trajectories that respect both the physical limitations of the manipulator and the safety of nearby humans. Traditional trajectory planning methods, while effective in structured industrial settings, often fail to adequately address the need for human–robot interaction comfort, adaptability to environmental changes, and compliance with variable task constraints.

Trajectory planning for service manipulators involves computing a sequence of joint or Cartesian positions, velocities, and accelerations that enable the robot to move from an initial to a goal configuration while satisfying kinematic, dynamic, and environmental constraints. In practice, these trajectories must avoid abrupt changes in velocity or acceleration, as such discontinuities can lead to excessive wear on mechanical components, increased control effort, and potentially unsafe motions. The concept of “soft motion” refers to the generation of trajectories with continuous profiles in position, velocity, and acceleration, thereby ensuring smooth transitions and reduced mechanical stress. Soft motion planning is particularly relevant for service robots, where motion quality influences not only efficiency but also user trust and acceptance.

Existing approaches to soft motion trajectory generation include polynomial interpolation, spline-based methods, and optimization-based planning. While these techniques can produce smooth paths, they may encounter difficulties when real-time adaptation is required due to unforeseen obstacles or changes in task requirements. Furthermore, many existing frameworks prioritize geometric path planning over dynamic feasibility, potentially leading to motions that a real manipulator cannot execute within its torque and velocity limits. Hence, there is a need for a planning framework that unifies smoothness, dynamic feasibility, and responsiveness to environmental variations.

This work presents a soft motion trajectory planner tailored for service manipulator robots, designed to generate dynamically feasible, smooth trajectories in real time. The proposed planner integrates motion profile generation with constraint-aware path adaptation, enabling the robot to respond gracefully to changes in task or environment without sacrificing motion quality. By incorporating jerk-limited profiles and efficient online computation, the planner ensures human-safe and mechanically gentle motions. The effectiveness of the approach is validated through simulations and experimental trials on a service manipulator platform, demonstrating improvements in trajectory smoothness, execution reliability, and interaction safety compared to conventional methods.
conclusion: The proposed soft motion trajectory planner demonstrated effective generation of smooth, continuous paths for a service manipulator robot, ensuring reduced mechanical stress and improved operational safety. By integrating velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints, the method achieved high motion quality while maintaining task efficiency. Simulation and experimental results confirmed its capability to adapt to varying task requirements and workspace conditions, highlighting its potential for real-world service robotics applications. The planner’s computational efficiency supports real-time implementation, enabling responsive and adaptive manipulation. Future work will focus on extending the approach to dynamic environments with moving obstacles, as well as incorporating learning-based optimization to further enhance adaptability and performance in complex service scenarios.

title: (Nearly) Efficient Algorithms for the Graph Matching Problem on Correlated Random Graphs
abstract: We study the graph matching problem in the correlated Erdős–Rényi random graph model, where two graphs are generated from a common underlying structure by independently subsampling edges with correlation parameter \(\rho\). This model captures a fundamental setting for network alignment, with applications in data integration, computer vision, and social network analysis. While information-theoretic limits for exact recovery are well understood, achieving these limits efficiently remains challenging. We present new algorithms that nearly match the optimal correlation threshold for recovery, running in polynomial time for a wide range of sparsity regimes. Our approach combines spectral methods with a refined neighborhood aggregation scheme that amplifies weak correlation signals into strong alignment cues. We prove that, for constant edge density, our algorithm succeeds down to correlation \(\rho = (1+o(1)) \sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\), matching the information-theoretic limit up to lower-order terms. For sparser graphs, we obtain analogous guarantees within logarithmic factors of the threshold. Our results narrow the gap between statistical and computational feasibility for graph matching in correlated random graphs, and introduce techniques that may be of independent interest for related high-dimensional inference problems.
introduction: The graph matching problem, which seeks a correspondence between the vertex sets of two graphs that best preserves edge structure, is fundamental in computer science, combinatorics, and network analysis. Despite its NP-hardness in general, recent work has focused on average-case models, particularly correlated random graphs, where structural similarity arises from a shared noisy origin. Such models capture applications in social networks, biology, and computer vision. In this work, we study (nearly) efficient algorithms for graph matching on correlated Erdős–Rényi graphs, providing rigorous performance guarantees and advancing the understanding of the computational–statistical tradeoffs in this important probabilistic setting.
conclusion:
We have studied the graph matching problem in the setting of correlated random graphs, focusing on the trade-off between statistical and computational efficiency. Our results provide algorithms that, while not fully optimal, achieve nearly information-theoretic performance with significantly improved computational guarantees compared to prior work. By leveraging structural properties of correlated Erdős–Rényi models and refined probabilistic analysis, we demonstrated that a careful combination of spectral methods, neighborhood statistics, and iterative refinement yields recovery guarantees that approach the fundamental threshold up to lower-order terms.  

These findings contribute to the growing understanding of the algorithmic landscape for graph matching, suggesting that in many regimes the gap between statistical possibility and polynomial-time computability can be made arbitrarily small. While our methods are tailored to specific random graph models, the underlying techniques are adaptable to broader settings, including sparse graphs and more general correlation structures.  

Several open directions remain. Closing the remaining gap to the information-theoretic limit, extending the approach to handle substantial model misspecification, and integrating robustness to adversarial noise are promising avenues for future work. More generally, our results support the view that, for structured random instances, efficient algorithms can often match the performance of intractable methods up to vanishing discrepancies, offering both practical applicability and theoretical insight into the limits of efficient graph inference.

title: L-RCM: a method to detect connected components in undirected graphs by using the Laplacian matrix and the RCM algorithm
abstract: We propose **L-RCM**, a novel method for detecting connected components in undirected graphs by leveraging the graph Laplacian matrix in combination with the Reverse Cuthill–McKee (RCM) algorithm. The approach begins by constructing the Laplacian matrix from the adjacency representation of the input graph. The RCM algorithm is then applied to reorder the matrix, producing a permutation that tends to cluster nonzero entries close to the diagonal. This reordering reveals a block diagonal structure in the Laplacian, where each block corresponds to a connected component of the original graph. The method exploits the property that the Laplacian of a disconnected graph is reducible, enabling efficient identification of components without repeated graph traversals. L-RCM is simple to implement, computationally efficient, and scales well for large, sparse graphs. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that L-RCM accurately recovers connected components while offering performance comparable to traditional search-based methods. This work provides a matrix-based alternative for a fundamental graph analysis task, bridging numerical linear algebra and graph theory.
introduction:
Graphs are fundamental structures in mathematics and computer science, widely used to model relationships and interactions in numerous domains, including social networks, communication systems, biological networks, and transportation infrastructures. In many applications, it is essential to identify the connected components of an undirected graph—subsets of vertices where each pair of vertices is linked by at least one path, and no additional vertices are connected to any vertex in the subset. Detecting connected components is a basic yet crucial task, forming the foundation for more complex graph analyses such as community detection, network resilience assessment, and graph partitioning.

Traditional methods for finding connected components typically rely on traversal algorithms such as Depth-First Search (DFS) or Breadth-First Search (BFS). These algorithms are straightforward, efficient, and well-studied, with linear time complexity in the size of the graph. However, in contexts where the graph is already represented in matrix form—particularly in fields such as numerical linear algebra, scientific computing, and spectral graph theory—it can be advantageous to exploit matrix-based methods. In such cases, operations on the graph's adjacency matrix or Laplacian matrix can reveal structural properties without reverting to purely combinatorial algorithms.

The Laplacian matrix of a graph encodes essential information about its connectivity. Defined as \( L = D - A \), where \( D \) is the degree matrix and \( A \) is the adjacency matrix, the Laplacian has several well-known properties that relate directly to connected components. In particular, the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of \( L \) equals the number of connected components in the graph, and the corresponding eigenvectors can be used to identify the vertices belonging to each component. While eigenvalue-based methods provide a powerful theoretical framework, they can be computationally expensive for large-scale graphs, especially when only the connected component structure is desired.

The Reverse Cuthill–McKee (RCM) algorithm is a reordering strategy originally designed to reduce the bandwidth of sparse symmetric matrices. By permuting the rows and columns of a matrix, RCM tends to cluster nonzero entries closer to the diagonal, thereby improving computational efficiency in various numerical methods. In the context of graph theory, applying RCM to the adjacency or Laplacian matrix effectively reorders vertices such that vertices in the same connected component are placed in contiguous index ranges. This property suggests that RCM can be used, perhaps indirectly, to detect connected components without explicit graph traversal.

Despite the potential of combining Laplacian-based representations with RCM reordering, this approach has received limited attention as a direct method for connected component detection. Most existing works treat RCM purely as a preprocessing step for numerical solvers, while connected component detection remains in the domain of DFS/BFS or spectral clustering. However, a method that leverages the Laplacian matrix's structural encoding of connectivity, coupled with RCM's ability to group related vertices, could offer a simple, matrix-oriented alternative well-suited for applications where the graph is already represented in sparse matrix form.

The method proposed in this work, termed **L-RCM**, addresses this opportunity. L-RCM constructs the Laplacian matrix of the given undirected graph, applies the RCM algorithm to reorder it, and then exploits the resulting permutation to identify connected components. The rationale is that the Laplacian's sparsity pattern inherently reflects adjacency relationships, and RCM's breadth-first-like traversal from a pseudo-peripheral vertex naturally groups connected vertices together. By inspecting the reordered Laplacian, the boundaries between connected components become evident as block-diagonal structures, enabling efficient detection without explicit search over the original graph structure.

The advantages of L-RCM are twofold. First, it is particularly convenient in workflows where the Laplacian matrix is already computed for other purposes, such as spectral analysis, finite element simulations, or network synchronizability studies. In such cases, no additional graph traversal is required, and connected components can be extracted directly from the reordered matrix. Second, the approach is compatible with sparse matrix libraries and parallel linear algebra frameworks, potentially benefiting large-scale computations.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background on graph Laplacians, connected components, and the RCM algorithm. Section 3 details the proposed L-RCM method, including its theoretical underpinnings and practical implementation steps. Section 4 presents experimental results on a range of synthetic and real-world graphs, comparing L-RCM with traditional algorithms in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and scalability. Section 5 discusses the implications of the method, its limitations, and potential extensions. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the contributions and outlines directions for future research.

By uniting the Laplacian matrix's connectivity-encoding properties with RCM's reordering capabilities, L-RCM offers a novel, matrix-based approach to connected component detection. This work aims to demonstrate that such a combination can yield a practical and efficient alternative to classical traversal algorithms, particularly in matrix-centric computational environments.
conclusion: The proposed L-RCM method offers an effective approach for detecting connected components in undirected graphs by combining the spectral properties of the Laplacian matrix with the ordering capabilities of the Reverse Cuthill–McKee algorithm. By leveraging the Laplacian’s ability to capture structural information and RCM’s reordering to cluster related vertices, the method facilitates a straightforward identification of component boundaries without extensive graph traversal. Experimental results indicate that L-RCM achieves accurate component detection with competitive computational performance, particularly for sparse graphs. Furthermore, the method’s reliance on established linear algebra operations ensures compatibility with existing numerical libraries, enhancing its practical applicability. The approach is conceptually simple, easy to implement, and scalable, making it a valuable alternative to traditional search-based algorithms. Future work may investigate extensions to weighted or dynamic graphs, as well as integration with parallel computing techniques to handle very large-scale network datasets efficiently.

title: Toy models of black hole, white hole and wormhole: thermal effects and information loss problem
abstract: We investigate simplified toy models of black holes, white holes, and wormholes to explore thermal effects and their implications for the information loss problem. Using idealized spacetimes and effective field theory approaches, we examine particle creation, horizon thermodynamics, and correlations between in- and out-going modes. The models incorporate both static and dynamical geometries, allowing us to analyze evaporation, time-reversal phenomena, and traversable connections. We discuss how thermal radiation emerges in each case, highlighting similarities and contrasts between black hole Hawking radiation, white hole emission, and wormhole thermal signatures. Our analysis addresses the fate of quantum information, identifying conditions under which unitarity may be preserved or violated. These insights aim to clarify conceptual aspects of gravitational thermodynamics and spacetime topology in a tractable framework.
introduction:
The study of black holes, white holes, and wormholes occupies a central place in modern theoretical physics, providing profound insights into the interplay between gravity, quantum theory, and thermodynamics. Black holes, predicted by general relativity and confirmed through astrophysical observations, are regions of spacetime from which nothing, not even light, can escape. Their defining property—the existence of an event horizon—leads to remarkable thermodynamic behavior, most famously encapsulated in Hawking’s discovery that black holes emit thermal radiation. This Hawking radiation implies that black holes possess a finite temperature and entropy, linking gravitational physics to statistical mechanics and quantum field theory in curved spacetime. However, the thermal nature of the radiation also gives rise to the long-standing information loss problem: if the radiation is purely thermal, it appears to carry no information about the matter that formed the black hole, suggesting a possible violation of unitarity in quantum mechanics.

White holes, in contrast, are hypothetical time-reversed counterparts of black holes. In classical general relativity, they represent regions from which matter and energy can emerge but into which nothing can enter. Although no observational evidence for white holes exists, their theoretical exploration deepens our understanding of spacetime symmetries, causal structure, and the possible extensions of solutions to Einstein’s equations. Similarly, wormholes—tunnels connecting disparate regions of spacetime—arise as solutions to the Einstein field equations under certain exotic conditions. Traversable wormholes, if they exist, would permit rapid travel between distant points or even allow for shortcuts through time, but their stability typically requires matter that violates known energy conditions.

The thermal properties and quantum aspects of these exotic spacetime structures have been extensively studied within semiclassical gravity. However, the complex and highly nonlinear nature of the full Einstein equations, coupled with quantum field theory, makes exact treatment intractable in most realistic scenarios. As a result, simplified “toy models” have become indispensable tools for probing conceptual issues. Such models typically strip away inessential complexities while retaining the key features relevant to the phenomena under investigation. For instance, two-dimensional dilaton gravity models, effective field theory approaches, and analogue gravity systems provide controlled environments to study horizon thermodynamics, Hawking-like radiation, and backreaction effects. By working in reduced settings, researchers can compute radiation spectra, entropy evolution, and correlation functions with greater clarity, thereby testing ideas about unitarity, information recovery, and the microscopic origin of black hole entropy.

In the context of the information loss problem, toy models have been particularly valuable in illustrating possible resolutions. They have been used to explore scenarios ranging from complete information destruction to subtle information encoding in correlations within Hawking radiation, and even to proposals involving remnants or quantum-gravitational modifications of spacetime structure. Extending these insights to white holes and wormholes can illuminate whether similar thermal and informational issues arise in other horizon-bearing or causally nontrivial spacetimes. For example, time-symmetric models linking black hole and white hole phases, or wormhole geometries incorporating quantum effects, can serve as laboratories for testing whether information can be preserved or transmitted in unconventional ways.

The present work develops and analyzes toy models of black holes, white holes, and wormholes with a focus on their thermal properties and implications for the information loss problem. By formulating tractable models that capture the essential causal and thermodynamic features, we aim to clarify how horizon thermality emerges, how it might be modified by quantum effects, and whether such modifications can address the apparent loss of information. This approach not only deepens our theoretical understanding of these exotic spacetimes but also contributes to the broader effort to reconcile the principles of general relativity with those of quantum mechanics.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined simplified, yet physically motivated, toy models of black holes, white holes, and wormholes, with a particular focus on their thermal properties and implications for the information loss problem. By abstracting the essential causal and thermodynamic features of these spacetimes, we have been able to explore the interplay between horizon dynamics, particle creation, and information flow in a tractable framework. The comparative analysis demonstrates that, while black holes exhibit the well-known Hawking radiation and associated entropy increase, white holes, in their idealized form, correspond to time-reversed processes that challenge conventional thermodynamic intuition, and wormholes open the possibility for nontrivial causal structures that may circumvent standard horizon-based arguments.

Our investigation of thermal effects within these models reinforces the robustness of semiclassical particle production in the presence of horizons, but also highlights the sensitivity of information retrieval prospects to the global spacetime structure. In particular, wormhole geometries—when treated as traversable or supported by exotic matter—can, in principle, provide channels for preserving correlations that would otherwise be lost in black hole evaporation. Conversely, the instability and unphysical properties of idealized white holes limit their role to theoretical probes of time symmetry and reversibility.

From the perspective of the information loss problem, the toy models underline the importance of horizon complementarity and the possible breakdown of semiclassical reasoning near the Planck scale. While the models cannot resolve the full quantum gravity dynamics, they clarify how different causal structures influence the fate of information, suggesting that modifications to the near-horizon region or to global topology could play a crucial role.

Overall, these simplified constructions serve as valuable laboratories for testing ideas about quantum thermodynamics in curved spacetime. They reveal both the universality of certain thermal effects and the diversity of possible information flow scenarios. Future work should integrate more realistic matter content, dynamical backreaction, and quantum gravitational corrections to assess whether insights from these toy models persist in a fully consistent theory, potentially guiding the resolution of the information loss paradox.

title: Intrinsic Gravitomagnetism and Non-commutative effects
abstract: We investigate the interplay between intrinsic gravitomagnetism and non-commutative geometric effects within the framework of modified general relativity. By incorporating non-commutative spacetime corrections into the weak-field approximation, we derive modified gravitomagnetic potentials and precession rates. Our results reveal that non-commutativity induces measurable deviations in frame-dragging phenomena, potentially detectable by high-precision satellite experiments. The analysis suggests that intrinsic gravitomagnetic fields serve as sensitive probes of Planck-scale structure, offering a novel avenue for testing quantum gravity-inspired modifications to classical gravitational dynamics.
introduction:
The interplay between gravitation and quantum mechanics remains one of the most profound open questions in modern theoretical physics. While general relativity provides a remarkably successful classical description of gravitational phenomena over a wide range of scales, it is inherently incompatible with the principles of quantum theory at the most fundamental level. One promising route toward bridging this gap lies in the investigation of gravitational analogues to well-established electromagnetic concepts, as well as in the exploration of possible modifications to spacetime structure at the Planck scale. In this context, intrinsic gravitomagnetism and non-commutative geometry emerge as complementary conceptual frameworks that can shed light on the quantum aspects of gravity and spacetime.

Gravitomagnetism arises naturally within general relativity when the Einstein field equations are linearised in the weak-field, slow-motion approximation. In this regime, the formal analogy with Maxwell’s equations for electromagnetism becomes manifest, leading to the introduction of gravitoelectric and gravitomagnetic fields. The former corresponds to the familiar Newtonian gravitational field, while the latter is sourced by mass-energy currents and is responsible for phenomena such as the Lense–Thirring effect, or frame-dragging. These effects have been experimentally confirmed, most notably by the Gravity Probe B mission and by precise satellite laser ranging measurements of the LAGEOS satellites. Such observations have firmly established the physical reality of gravitomagnetic phenomena, at least in their extrinsic form, i.e. those associated with the motion of masses relative to an inertial frame.

Intrinsic gravitomagnetism, however, refers to a deeper aspect of the gravitational field: the gravitomagnetic field generated by the intrinsic rotation, or spin, of a massive body, even in the absence of translational motion. In analogy to the intrinsic magnetic moment of an electron due to its spin, intrinsic gravitomagnetism is linked to the angular momentum content of spacetime itself. In general relativity, this is exemplified by the Kerr solution, where the spacetime geometry around a rotating mass contains off-diagonal metric elements encoding the gravitomagnetic potential. The study of intrinsic gravitomagnetism is of interest not only for its astrophysical implications, such as in the environment of rotating neutron stars and black holes, but also for its potential role in probing the microscopic structure of spacetime when coupled with quantum theory.

Parallel to the development of gravitomagnetic concepts, non-commutative geometry has emerged as a compelling candidate for describing spacetime at the smallest scales. Motivated by considerations from string theory, loop quantum gravity, and other approaches to quantum gravity, non-commutative geometry postulates that spacetime coordinates do not commute, but instead obey commutation relations of the form \([x^\mu, x^\nu] = i \theta^{\mu\nu}\), where \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\) is an antisymmetric constant tensor or, in more general constructions, a dynamical quantity. This modification introduces a fundamental length scale into the theory, below which the classical notion of a smooth spacetime manifold ceases to be valid. The non-commutativity of coordinates leads to modifications in the dispersion relations, symmetry structures, and interaction dynamics of physical fields, with potentially observable consequences in high-energy astrophysics, precision measurements, and cosmology.

The study of non-commutative effects in gravitational systems has attracted considerable attention over the past two decades. Non-commutative versions of general relativity, or effective models incorporating non-commutative corrections to the metric or to geodesic motion, have been proposed and analysed. These models predict small deviations from classical gravitational behaviour, which could, in principle, be detectable in certain regimes. In particular, the coupling between non-commutative geometry and gravitomagnetic fields offers a rich arena for theoretical exploration. Since gravitomagnetism is inherently linked to the off-diagonal components of the metric tensor, and non-commutativity often modifies such components in a nontrivial way, one may anticipate novel effects arising in the presence of intrinsic gravitomagnetic fields.

From a quantum mechanical perspective, the motion of test particles, especially those with intrinsic spin, in a gravitomagnetic background is sensitive to the detailed structure of spacetime. Phenomena such as gravitational Aharonov–Bohm effects, spin precession, and phase shifts in interferometric experiments can, in principle, encode information about both intrinsic gravitomagnetic fields and any underlying non-commutative deformation. For example, the gravitational analogue of the Berry phase may acquire corrections due to the non-commutative structure, leading to potentially measurable deviations from predictions based solely on classical general relativity. This suggests that high-precision experiments involving matter-wave interferometry, gyroscopes, or clock comparisons could serve as probes of such combined effects.

In astrophysical contexts, rotating compact objects provide natural laboratories for studying intrinsic gravitomagnetism. The strong-field regime near Kerr black holes or rapidly spinning neutron stars is expected to exhibit pronounced gravitomagnetic effects, which could, in principle, be modified by Planck-scale physics. While direct detection of non-commutative corrections in such environments is currently beyond reach, theoretical models can guide the search for subtle signatures in gravitational waveforms, pulsar timing measurements, or accretion disk dynamics. Moreover, the development of a consistent framework incorporating both intrinsic gravitomagnetism and non-commutative geometry could offer insights into the nature of spacetime singularities, the behaviour of horizons, and the thermodynamics of rotating black holes.

The purpose of the present work is to investigate the interplay between intrinsic gravitomagnetism and non-commutative geometry, with a view to identifying potential observational signatures and deepening our understanding of gravitational phenomena in the quantum regime. By formulating the dynamics of test particles and fields in a non-commutative extension of the Kerr spacetime, we aim to elucidate how intrinsic rotation and spacetime non-commutativity jointly influence measurable quantities. This approach not only extends the analogy between electromagnetism and gravitation into the quantum domain but also provides a concrete setting in which to explore the phenomenological implications of non-commutative geometry. Ultimately, the synthesis of these two lines of inquiry may contribute to the broader effort to reconcile general relativity with quantum mechanics, and to uncover the structure of spacetime at its most fundamental level.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the interplay between intrinsic gravitomagnetism and non-commutative geometrical effects, highlighting how modifications to the phase space structure can influence gravitational phenomena. By extending the conventional gravitomagnetic framework to incorporate non-commutative parameters, we have shown that subtle deformations in the underlying algebra lead to measurable corrections in the gravitomagnetic field and associated observables. These corrections, though typically small, could become significant in regimes involving strong gravitational fields or high-precision measurements. Our results suggest that non-commutative geometry provides a natural platform to explore deviations from classical general relativity, potentially offering insights into quantum gravity. Furthermore, the formalism developed here can be applied to astrophysical scenarios, such as rotating compact objects, where intrinsic gravitomagnetic effects are prominent. Future investigations should address the experimental feasibility of detecting such corrections, and explore the implications for fundamental symmetries. Ultimately, the synergy between gravitomagnetism and non-commutative geometry deepens our understanding of spacetime structure at both classical and quantum levels.

title: Coevolution of Quantum Wave Functions and the Friedmann Universe
abstract: We investigate the coupled evolution of quantum wave functions and the dynamical geometry of a Friedmann universe. Employing a semiclassical framework, matter fields are treated quantum mechanically while spacetime evolves according to Einstein’s equations sourced by expectation values. The analysis reveals feedback between quantum state evolution and cosmic expansion, influencing both large-scale dynamics and microscopic coherence. Results suggest that quantum–cosmological backreaction may leave observable imprints on early-universe structure formation and offers insight into unifying quantum theory with relativistic cosmology.
introduction:
The interplay between quantum mechanics and cosmology remains one of the most profound frontiers in theoretical physics. While the standard model of cosmology, grounded in the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric, successfully describes the large-scale evolution of a homogeneous and isotropic universe, it does not intrinsically account for the quantum nature of matter and fields that pervade spacetime. Conversely, quantum mechanics, with its probabilistic wave functions governed by the Schrödinger or Dirac equations, is conventionally formulated in a fixed background, rendering it insufficient for scenarios in which spacetime itself is dynamic. A complete understanding of the early universe, particularly near the Planck epoch, demands a framework in which quantum states and the geometry of the universe coevolve.

The concept of wave function evolution in an expanding or contracting spacetime has been explored in various contexts, from quantum field theory in curved spacetime to minisuperspace models of quantum cosmology. However, these approaches often treat the background metric as a pre-specified function, neglecting the feedback of quantum matter on the geometry except in semiclassical approximations. The Friedmann equations, derived from general relativity, couple the energy density and pressure to the expansion rate, suggesting that quantum expectation values of these quantities could, in principle, influence cosmic dynamics. This mutual dependence points toward a coevolutionary picture: the quantum state evolves in a time-dependent background determined by the Friedmann equations, while the background’s evolution is shaped by the quantum state’s energy–momentum content.

Investigating this coevolution is not only of conceptual significance for unifying quantum theory and general relativity but may also have observable consequences. Quantum fluctuations in the primordial universe are believed to seed large-scale structure, and their precise characteristics depend on the dynamical interplay between quantum fields and spacetime expansion. A consistent treatment of this interaction could refine predictions for cosmic microwave background anisotropies and the distribution of matter on cosmological scales. This work aims to develop and analyze a model in which quantum wave functions and the Friedmann universe evolve together self-consistently, illuminating the mutual constraints and possible emergent phenomena that arise from their coupled dynamics.
conclusion: This study highlights the mutual influence between quantum wave function dynamics and the evolving Friedmann universe, revealing feedback mechanisms that shape both cosmological expansion and quantum states, suggesting deeper interconnections between quantum theory and general relativity in describing cosmic evolution.

title: Distributed Computing with Channel Noise
abstract: We investigate the problem of distributed computation over networks subject to channel noise, focusing on the interplay between communication constraints, error resilience, and computational efficiency. In many distributed systems, nodes must exchange intermediate results over unreliable links, where noise can distort messages and impair correctness. We present a general framework for analyzing distributed algorithms under stochastic and adversarial noise models, incorporating both synchronous and asynchronous communication patterns. Our approach characterizes the trade-offs between redundancy, error correction, and computational latency, providing bounds on the achievable accuracy for a range of fundamental tasks, including consensus, aggregation, and distributed function evaluation. By combining probabilistic coding techniques with algorithmic fault tolerance, we design protocols that maintain correctness with high probability while minimizing communication overhead. We further explore how network topology and noise distribution influence the required redundancy levels, identifying conditions under which near-optimal performance is attainable. Experimental simulations on representative network models validate our theoretical bounds, demonstrating robust computation even under high noise rates. This work contributes both analytical tools and practical design principles for building noise-resilient distributed computing systems, with applications spanning sensor networks, decentralized control, and large-scale data processing in unreliable environments.
introduction:
Distributed computing has emerged as a foundational paradigm in modern information processing, enabling multiple computational entities to collaboratively solve problems that exceed the capacity or reliability of a single machine. From large-scale data analytics to decentralized control in sensor networks, distributed systems are deployed in diverse settings where resources, tasks, and information must be shared among spatially separated nodes. A key enabler of such collaboration is communication: nodes exchange messages to coordinate actions, share intermediate results, and achieve global objectives. However, in practical deployments, communication channels are rarely perfect. Physical limitations, environmental factors, and interference introduce noise into transmitted signals, leading to errors in the received data. The presence of channel noise fundamentally affects the design and performance of distributed computing systems, influencing both their efficiency and reliability.

The study of distributed computing in noisy environments lies at the intersection of distributed algorithms, information theory, and communication complexity. Classical models of distributed computation often assume that messages are transmitted reliably, abstracting away the physical layer and focusing on algorithmic coordination under adversarial or stochastic delays. Conversely, information-theoretic models of communication over noisy channels examine the limits of reliable data transmission, typically for point-to-point or broadcast channels, without addressing the structure of the computation being performed. Bridging these perspectives is essential for understanding the true capabilities and limitations of distributed systems operating over imperfect communication links.

Noise in communication channels can be modeled in various ways, from simple binary symmetric channels to more complex fading and interference models. The impact of such noise is twofold. First, it can corrupt the content of messages, leading to incorrect data being used in subsequent computations. Second, it can necessitate additional communication in the form of retransmissions, error correction, or redundancy, thereby increasing latency and resource consumption. When nodes operate under constraints on bandwidth, energy, or computation time, the interplay between noise mitigation and task execution becomes a critical design consideration. In many real-world settings such as wireless sensor networks, robotic swarms, or distributed machine learning systems, these trade-offs directly determine the feasibility of timely and accurate computation.

Recent research has begun to explore fundamental limits and optimal strategies for distributed computation under noisy communication. For example, in scenarios where the goal is to compute a global function of distributed inputs, the presence of noise may require more communication rounds or more sophisticated coding strategies to achieve a given level of accuracy. The complexity of distributed algorithms must therefore be analyzed jointly with the error characteristics of the underlying channels. This integrated viewpoint has led to new theoretical insights, such as bounds on the minimum communication cost for specific functions under noisy conditions, and the design of algorithms that are inherently robust to stochastic errors.

Moreover, channel noise interacts with other sources of uncertainty in distributed systems, such as asynchrony, node failures, and dynamic network topologies. In certain cases, noise can be treated similarly to adversarial faults, allowing fault-tolerant algorithmic techniques to be repurposed. In other cases, the stochastic nature of channel errors calls for probabilistic analysis and randomized algorithms. Understanding these interactions is crucial for developing general frameworks that can guide the design of practical systems.

The motivation for studying distributed computing with channel noise extends beyond theoretical elegance. Emerging applications such as edge computing for the Internet of Things, federated learning across mobile devices, and cooperative autonomous systems all rely on communication over inherently noisy wireless links. In such environments, conventional assumptions of reliable, instantaneous message delivery do not hold, and ignoring noise can lead to performance degradation or even system failure. By explicitly incorporating channel noise into distributed computing models, researchers can develop algorithms and protocols that are both efficient and resilient, ultimately enabling robust performance in challenging real-world conditions.

This paper contributes to this growing body of work by analyzing distributed computation in the presence of channel noise, identifying key trade-offs between communication efficiency, computational accuracy, and system resources. We present both theoretical bounds and algorithmic constructions that illuminate the fundamental challenges and opportunities in this setting, aiming to advance our understanding of how noise shapes the capabilities of distributed systems.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated the problem of distributed computing in the presence of channel noise, focusing on both theoretical performance limits and practical algorithmic strategies. By modeling communication links as noisy channels with varying error characteristics, we analyzed the trade-offs between redundancy, coding complexity, and computational efficiency. Our results demonstrate that, while noise inevitably degrades performance, carefully designed error-control mechanisms and adaptive protocols can substantially mitigate its impact, enabling reliable computation even under adverse conditions. We further showed that the choice of coding schemes must balance latency and fault tolerance, as excessive redundancy can hinder overall throughput. The proposed analytical framework provides a unified basis for comparing different noise-resilient distributed algorithms and offers insights into optimal resource allocation. Experimental evaluations confirm the validity of our theoretical predictions across a range of network topologies and noise models. Overall, this study underscores the importance of integrating communication error models into distributed algorithm design, paving the way for more robust and efficient large-scale computing systems operating in imperfect and unpredictable environments. Future work will explore dynamic adaptation to time-varying noise and the integration of machine learning techniques for predictive error correction.

title: Multimodal Generative Learning Utilizing Jensen-Shannon-Divergence
abstract: We propose a multimodal generative learning framework that leverages the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) to achieve robust cross-modal alignment and synthesis. Our method models heterogeneous data distributions by minimizing the JSD between modality-specific latent representations, enabling balanced training that mitigates mode collapse and overfitting. The approach integrates variational inference with adversarial optimization, ensuring stable convergence across image, text, and audio modalities. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate superior generative quality and semantic coherence compared to existing multimodal GAN and VAE variants. Furthermore, the use of JSD facilitates interpretable latent space geometry, improving transferability to unseen modalities. This work highlights the efficacy of divergence-based objectives for scalable, high-fidelity multimodal generation and representation learning.
introduction:
The rapid proliferation of multimodal data across domains such as healthcare, autonomous driving, and human-computer interaction has catalyzed significant interest in learning frameworks capable of integrating heterogeneous sources of information. Multimodal generative learning aims to model the joint distribution of multiple modalities—such as text, images, audio, and sensor signals—so as to enable coherent synthesis, translation, and inference across domains. By capturing complex cross-modal dependencies, such models facilitate a deeper semantic understanding and allow for richer, context-aware generation. However, the design of generative frameworks that can efficiently and accurately learn from multimodal data remains a formidable challenge, particularly when modalities vary widely in structure, dimensionality, and noise characteristics.

Recent advances in generative modeling, notably variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and diffusion-based models, have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in single-modality contexts. Extending these architectures to the multimodal setting requires careful consideration of joint representation learning, modality-specific encodings, and robust training objectives. A critical aspect of this challenge lies in devising effective divergence measures to align latent distributions across modalities, ensuring that the shared latent space captures both modality-specific nuances and cross-modal correlations. Conventional approaches often rely on Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence or related measures to enforce such alignment. While KL divergence is analytically convenient, it can be sensitive to support mismatches between distributions, leading to unstable training or mode collapse in generative scenarios.

The Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) offers an appealing alternative for multimodal generative learning. As a symmetric and bounded divergence measure derived from KL divergence, JSD mitigates some of the limitations of KL-based objectives, particularly when distributions exhibit partial or disjoint support. Its bounded nature provides numerical stability, while its symmetry ensures that misalignment is penalized consistently in both directions. In the context of adversarial training, JSD emerges naturally as the divergence minimized by the optimal discriminator in the original GAN formulation, suggesting its suitability for generative tasks. Furthermore, JSD’s capacity to provide meaningful gradients even when distributions are far apart renders it advantageous for aligning multimodal latent representations.

Despite these theoretical advantages, the explicit utilization of JSD in multimodal generative frameworks has received relatively limited attention. Prior works have predominantly leveraged JSD implicitly through adversarial objectives or have applied it in unimodal contexts. A systematic exploration of JSD as the principal divergence metric for multimodal generative learning—spanning architecture design, optimization strategies, and evaluation—remains scarce. Such an investigation holds the potential to improve cross-modal coherence, enhance sample diversity, and stabilize training dynamics.

In this work, we propose a multimodal generative learning framework that explicitly employs Jensen–Shannon divergence to align latent distributions across modalities. We integrate JSD-based objectives into both reconstruction and adversarial components of the model, enabling joint optimization that balances modality-specific fidelity with cross-modal consistency. Through empirical evaluation on benchmark multimodal datasets, we demonstrate that our approach yields more coherent and semantically aligned generations compared to KL-based baselines, underscoring the value of JSD in advancing multimodal generative learning.
conclusion: This work has explored a multimodal generative learning framework grounded in the Jensen–Shannon divergence, enabling effective alignment and synthesis across heterogeneous data modalities. By leveraging the symmetric and bounded properties of the Jensen–Shannon divergence, the proposed approach enhances training stability and improves the quality of cross-modal representations. Experimental results demonstrate competitive performance in both generative fidelity and modality translation, underscoring the method’s capacity to capture shared semantic structures while preserving modality-specific nuances. The formulation offers a principled means of balancing modality contributions, mitigating mode collapse, and fostering richer latent space organization. These findings suggest that Jensen–Shannon–based objectives can serve as a robust foundation for multimodal generative models, particularly in scenarios requiring coherent integration of diverse data sources. Future research may extend this framework to larger-scale datasets, incorporate additional modalities, and investigate adaptive divergence measures for further performance gains and generalization capabilities.

title: K 1-6: an asymmetric planetary nebula with a binary central star
abstract: We present imaging and spectroscopic observations of the planetary nebula K 1-6, revealing a strongly asymmetric morphology and evidence for a binary central star. Deep narrowband Hα and [O III] images obtained with medium-resolution CCD photometry show a bright, arc-like structure to the north and a diffuse, elongated envelope extending southward, suggestive of interaction with the interstellar medium and possible shaping by binary-driven outflows. Low-dispersion spectroscopy confirms the nebular nature through prominent recombination and forbidden emission lines, and indicates a moderately high excitation class. Time-series photometry of the central source reveals periodic variability consistent with a close binary system, while the spectral energy distribution suggests a hot subdwarf primary and a cooler late-type companion. The spatial offset between the central star and the geometric center of the nebula further supports a scenario of asymmetric mass loss influenced by binary orbital motion and external interaction. We discuss the shaping mechanisms in the context of current models for binary central stars in planetary nebulae, and highlight K 1-6 as an important addition to the small sample of asymmetric nebulae with confirmed binaries. These findings provide new constraints on the role of binarity in the morphological evolution of planetary nebulae.
introduction:
Planetary nebulae (PNe) represent a brief but crucial phase in the late evolution of low- to intermediate-mass stars (1–8 M⊙), during which the star expels its outer envelope and exposes its hot core, now evolving toward the white dwarf stage. The rich variety of PN morphologies—from spherical to axisymmetric and highly irregular—reflects the complex interplay of stellar winds, ionization fronts, and shaping mechanisms. While early models assumed spherical symmetry, high-resolution imaging surveys have revealed that strongly asymmetric and bipolar structures are common, suggesting that single-star evolution alone is insufficient to account for the observed diversity. Increasing evidence points toward binary interactions as a significant factor in the formation and shaping of many PNe.

Close binary central stars, often the products of common-envelope (CE) evolution, are particularly relevant in this context. During the CE phase, the companion spirals inward, depositing orbital energy and angular momentum into the envelope, which can lead to its ejection and imprint non-spherical geometries on the emerging nebula. Observational studies have established correlations between close binarity and certain morphological traits, such as bipolar lobes, equatorial rings, and jets. However, the detailed physical processes governing the shaping remain incompletely understood, and each new system with well-constrained stellar and nebular parameters adds valuable constraints to theoretical models.

K 1-6 is a relatively under-studied planetary nebula notable for its asymmetric appearance and central star characteristics. Its morphology departs from classical bipolar or elliptical forms, instead exhibiting irregular structures suggestive of complex ejection histories and possible interaction with the interstellar medium. Preliminary photometric and spectroscopic evidence has hinted at binarity in the central star system, but confirmation and characterization of the companion have been lacking. Given its unusual morphology and potential binary nature, K 1-6 offers an important opportunity to investigate the links between central star binarity and nebular asymmetry.

In this work, we present new imaging, spectroscopic, and time-series photometric observations of K 1-6, aimed at confirming the binary status of its central star and analyzing the nebular structure in detail. We discuss the observational evidence for binarity, characterize the stellar components, and consider the implications for the shaping and evolution of this asymmetric planetary nebula.
conclusion:
The study of K 1-6 presented here has revealed that it is an asymmetric planetary nebula whose morphology and kinematics are strongly influenced by the presence of a binary central star system. Our multi-wavelength analysis, combining optical narrow-band imaging, spectroscopic data, and ultraviolet photometry, has allowed us to disentangle the structural components of the nebula and to identify signatures of interaction between stellar winds, ionization fronts, and possible binary-induced shaping mechanisms. The results demonstrate that K 1-6 departs significantly from the classical picture of a spherically symmetric planetary nebula, instead exhibiting a complex and irregular envelope, brightened in certain regions and marked by asymmetries in both emission-line distribution and velocity structure.

The central star system of K 1-6 is confirmed to be a close binary, with photometric variability and spectral characteristics consistent with a hot subdwarf primary and a cooler, likely main-sequence or slightly evolved, companion. This configuration is consistent with theoretical models in which binary interaction, particularly during the late asymptotic giant branch (AGB) and post-AGB phases, can lead to non-spherical mass loss and the shaping of planetary nebulae into bipolar, elliptical, or otherwise asymmetric forms. The observed displacement of the central star from the nebular geometric centre, coupled with brightness enhancements along one side of the nebula, suggests that additional factors, such as systemic motion through the interstellar medium (ISM) and anisotropic mass ejection, are at play.

Our spectroscopic analysis has revealed variations in excitation conditions across the nebula, with higher ionization levels preferentially located near regions facing the central source, and lower ionization zones coinciding with fainter, more diffuse structures. The velocity field, while limited in spatial coverage, indicates a departure from simple radial expansion, showing localized deviations that may be indicative of collimated outflows, shocks, or interaction with ambient ISM material. The asymmetry in expansion velocities further supports the conclusion that binary-induced shaping and environmental effects have significantly influenced the present morphology.

The ultraviolet excess detected in the central star system points to the presence of a hot component capable of sustaining the ionization of the nebula, while the optical light curve and colour variations signal the influence of the cooler companion and possible reflection or heating effects. These findings align with other well-studied binary central star systems in planetary nebulae, in which irradiation and tidal interactions can produce photometric modulations as well as influence the circumstellar environment. The case of K 1-6 thus adds to the growing body of evidence that binarity is a key driver of morphological diversity in planetary nebulae.

When placed in a broader context, K 1-6 exemplifies the challenges of interpreting planetary nebula structures without detailed knowledge of their central stars. The complexity of its morphology, including filamentary features, brightness asymmetries, and an incomplete shell, could easily be misattributed to single-star evolutionary processes if the binary nature of the central system were not established. This underscores the importance of coordinated observational campaigns that integrate imaging, spectroscopy, and time-domain photometry to fully characterise both the nebular and stellar components.

The interaction of K 1-6 with the ISM is also a plausible contributor to its current appearance. The apparent bow-shock-like enhancement and the offset central star position relative to the nebular centroid are consistent with motion through the surrounding medium. Such interaction can compress and brighten the leading edge of the nebula while allowing the trailing regions to dissipate more freely, resulting in the observed asymmetry. This environmental influence, superimposed on the binary shaping processes, highlights the multifaceted nature of planetary nebula evolution, where internal and external factors combine to produce the observed diversity.

Future investigations of K 1-6 would benefit from high-resolution integral field spectroscopy to map the velocity field in detail, enabling a clearer distinction between expansion asymmetries, collimated flows, and ISM interaction signatures. Deep, multi-band imaging, including infrared observations, could reveal any remnant dust structures or jets that might further constrain the mass-loss history. Radial velocity monitoring of the central binary could refine orbital parameters and offer insights into past mass transfer episodes, while ultraviolet spectroscopy of the hot component could yield precise temperature and luminosity estimates, improving photoionization models of the nebula.

In summary, K 1-6 emerges as a compelling example of an asymmetric planetary nebula shaped by the combined influences of a close binary central star and interaction with the surrounding interstellar environment. Its morphological and kinematic characteristics cannot be explained by isotropic mass loss from a single progenitor, but instead point toward a complex evolutionary pathway involving binary interaction, possibly including common-envelope evolution, anisotropic outflows, and environmental shaping. The case of K 1-6 strengthens the paradigm that binarity plays a central role in the formation of non-spherical planetary nebulae and illustrates the necessity of multi-faceted observational approaches to disentangle the interplay of internal and external shaping mechanisms. As surveys continue to uncover more binary central stars, systems like K 1-6 will provide crucial laboratories for testing and refining our theoretical understanding of late stellar evolution and the diverse morphologies of planetary nebulae.

title: The NSVZ scheme for ${\cal N}=1$ SQED with $N_f$ flavors, regularized by the dimensional reduction, in the three-loop approximation
abstract: We investigate the three-loop structure of the renormalization group functions in \({\cal N}=1\) supersymmetric QED with \(N_f\) flavors, employing dimensional reduction as the regularization scheme. The focus is on the realization of the exact Novikov–Shifman–Vainshtein–Zakharov (NSVZ) relation between the \(\beta\)-function and the anomalous dimension of the matter superfields within this framework. Using the \(\overline{\mathrm{DR}}\) prescription, we compute the relevant three-loop contributions to the \(\beta\)-function and the two-loop anomalous dimension, and analyze their dependence on the subtraction scheme. We demonstrate explicitly that the NSVZ relation does not hold automatically in \(\overline{\mathrm{DR}}\) with dimensional reduction, but can be restored by a finite renormalization of the gauge coupling and matter superfields. This procedure defines a subtraction scheme—referred to as the NSVZ scheme—compatible with dimensional reduction, in which the exact relation is satisfied at the three-loop level. Our results clarify the interplay between regularization, renormalization, and exact supersymmetric constraints, and provide a consistent framework for higher-loop calculations in \({\cal N}=1\) SQED with multiple flavors.
introduction:
