Supersymmetric quantum electrodynamics (SQED) with ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetry has long served as a valuable theoretical laboratory for studying the structure of perturbative corrections in supersymmetric gauge theories. One of the remarkable results in this context is the Novikov–Shifman–Vainshtein–Zakharov (NSVZ) $\beta$-function, which relates the $\beta$-function of the gauge coupling to the anomalous dimensions of matter superfields in a closed form. In the case of ${\cal N}=1$ SQED with $N_f$ flavors, the NSVZ relation takes a particularly simple form and can be written exactly to all orders in perturbation theory. This property provides an important nontrivial check of explicit multiloop calculations and serves as a benchmark for understanding scheme dependence in renormalization.

The NSVZ relation was originally derived using instanton and anomaly arguments, but its direct verification in perturbation theory requires a careful treatment of ultraviolet divergences and the choice of the regularization and renormalization scheme. In particular, it is well known that dimensional reduction (DRED) is widely used in supersymmetric calculations because it preserves supersymmetry at least formally, but it does not automatically yield the NSVZ relation when combined with the minimal subtraction prescription. In contrast, higher derivative regularization, when supplemented by a specific subtraction scheme, allows one to obtain the NSVZ relation directly for the renormalized quantities. This raises the question of how to define an “NSVZ scheme” within DRED, i.e., a prescription for renormalization constants such that the renormalized couplings and anomalous dimensions satisfy the NSVZ relation.

In recent years, there has been considerable progress in understanding the origin of the NSVZ relation and the transformations between schemes in which it is valid and those in which it is not. For ${\cal N}=1$ SQED, the relation between the $\beta$-function defined in terms of the bare coupling constant and the one expressed through the renormalized coupling has been studied at low loop orders, and explicit finite renormalizations have been constructed to restore the NSVZ form. Extending these considerations to higher orders in perturbation theory provides a more stringent test and clarifies the structure of scheme dependence.

The purpose of the present paper is to construct the NSVZ scheme for ${\cal N}=1$ SQED with $N_f$ flavors, regularized by dimensional reduction, in the three-loop approximation. We perform explicit calculations of the $\beta$-function and the anomalous dimension of the matter superfields in DRED up to the required order, analyze their deviation from the NSVZ form in the $\overline{\mathrm{DR}}$ scheme, and determine the finite renormalization needed to restore the exact relation. This construction not only extends previous two-loop results but also provides a consistent framework for applying the NSVZ relation within DRED at higher orders, which is important for practical multiloop supersymmetric calculations.
conclusion:
In this paper, we have investigated the construction of the NSVZ scheme for \({\cal N}=1\) SQED with \(N_f\) flavors, when the theory is regularized using dimensional reduction, in the three-loop approximation. Starting from the results for the three-loop \(\beta\)-function and the two-loop anomalous dimension obtained in the \(\overline{\mathrm{DR}}\) scheme, we have demonstrated how an appropriate finite renormalization of the coupling constant and matter superfields can be chosen so that the NSVZ relation is exactly satisfied at this level of perturbation theory. The explicit form of these finite renormalizations has been determined, and their dependence on the number of flavors \(N_f\) has been analyzed.

We have shown that, while the \(\overline{\mathrm{DR}}\) scheme does not itself satisfy the NSVZ relation beyond the lowest orders, the discrepancy can be removed by a finite redefinition of the coupling, accompanied by a finite rescaling of the matter fields. The resulting prescription defines a concrete NSVZ scheme within the framework of dimensional reduction, which is consistent with the exact NSVZ \(\beta\)-function up to three loops. This procedure is in agreement with the general statement that different renormalization schemes, related by finite transformations, correspond to the same physical theory, while differing in the explicit form of their renormalization group functions.

Furthermore, we have discussed the relation between the NSVZ scheme constructed here and that obtained previously using higher derivative regularization. Although the explicit finite renormalizations differ due to the regularization-dependent structure of divergences, the final NSVZ relation for the renormalization group functions has the same form. This confirms that the NSVZ property is not an artifact of a particular regularization, but rather a feature that can be preserved by an appropriate choice of scheme.

The results of this work provide a concrete three-loop realization of the NSVZ scheme in the context of dimensional reduction, thereby bridging the gap between the exact NSVZ relation and practical perturbative calculations in a widely used regularization framework. They also lay the groundwork for extending the analysis to higher-loop orders and to more general \({\cal N}=1\) supersymmetric gauge theories, where similar considerations are expected to apply.

title: Anisotropic conductivity in magnetic topological insulators
abstract: We investigate anisotropic electronic transport in magnetic topological insulators, focusing on the interplay between magnetic ordering and topologically protected surface states. Using angle-resolved magnetotransport measurements on thin films of Cr-doped (Bi,Sb)\(_2\)Te\(_3\), we quantify conductivity along orthogonal in-plane crystallographic directions under varying temperature and magnetic field conditions. Our results reveal pronounced anisotropy that emerges below the magnetic ordering temperature, with conductivity enhanced along the magnetic easy axis and suppressed perpendicular to it. This behavior is attributed to the breaking of rotational symmetry by exchange interactions, leading to direction-dependent scattering and modifications of the Dirac surface state dispersion. The anisotropy magnitude is tunable via magnetic field orientation, indicating strong coupling between spin texture and charge transport. Complementary tight-binding calculations reproduce the experimental trends, confirming the role of magnetic gap anisotropy. These findings advance understanding of spin–momentum–locked transport in magnetic topological phases and suggest strategies for engineering directional conduction in spintronic and quantum information devices.
introduction:
Topological insulators (TIs) have emerged over the past decade as a central focus in condensed matter physics, owing to their unconventional electronic structure, which combines an insulating bulk with conducting surface states protected by time-reversal symmetry. These surface states exhibit spin–momentum locking, whereby the electron spin is locked perpendicular to its momentum, leading to suppressed backscattering from nonmagnetic impurities and a variety of novel transport phenomena. The interplay between topology, symmetry, and electronic correlations in these systems has spurred extensive theoretical and experimental efforts, with particular attention to the ways in which breaking time-reversal symmetry can give rise to new quantum states. One of the most prominent routes to achieving such symmetry breaking is through the introduction of magnetic order, either via magnetic doping or through proximity coupling to a magnetic material.

Magnetic topological insulators (MTIs) represent a unique class of materials in which the topologically protected surface states coexist with magnetism. The presence of magnetic order lifts the Kramers degeneracy of surface states, opening a gap at the Dirac point and enabling phenomena such as the quantum anomalous Hall effect (QAHE), axion electrodynamics, and magnetoelectric coupling. The QAHE, in particular, has been experimentally realized in magnetically doped (Bi,Sb)\(_2\)Te\(_3\) thin films, demonstrating dissipationless edge transport without an external magnetic field. Beyond quantized Hall conductance, the introduction of magnetism is expected to modify the spin textures and scattering mechanisms of the surface states, potentially leading to anisotropic transport responses. However, the microscopic origins and manifestations of such anisotropy remain incompletely understood.

Anisotropic conductivity refers to the directional dependence of electrical transport properties within a material. In conventional magnetic conductors, anisotropy often arises from the interplay between spin–orbit coupling and the magnetization direction, leading to phenomena such as anisotropic magnetoresistance (AMR). In the context of MTIs, the strong intrinsic spin–orbit coupling and the locking of spin and momentum in the surface states imply that magnetization can have a profound and unconventional influence on charge transport. The magnetization direction, relative to the crystallographic axes and current flow, can modify the band structure, the nature of scattering processes, and the distribution of Berry curvature in momentum space. These modifications can give rise to anisotropic longitudinal and transverse conductivities, whose detailed characteristics may serve as a sensitive probe of the underlying electronic structure.

Recent experimental studies have reported signatures of anisotropic conduction in MTIs, such as directional differences in resistivity and Hall responses when the magnetization is rotated with respect to the current direction or crystalline axes. In some cases, these anisotropies persist even above the magnetic ordering temperature, suggesting that short-range magnetic correlations or anisotropic impurity scattering may also play a role. On the theoretical side, model Hamiltonian analyses and numerical simulations have begun to elucidate how the combined effects of spin–orbit coupling, hexagonal warping of surface states, and magnetic exchange fields can produce anisotropic Fermi surfaces and velocity distributions. These, in turn, are expected to influence the conductivity tensor in ways that differ from those in conventional ferromagnets.

The study of anisotropic conductivity in MTIs is motivated by both fundamental and applied considerations. From a fundamental perspective, anisotropy in transport provides a direct window into the symmetry properties of the electronic states, the role of magnetic exchange coupling, and the interplay between bulk and surface conduction channels. Since MTIs often exhibit a coexistence of bulk carriers and topological surface states, disentangling their respective contributions to anisotropic transport is a challenging but essential task. Understanding these effects can shed light on the mechanisms that limit the performance of MTIs in realizing dissipationless conduction. From an applied standpoint, anisotropic transport responses can be harnessed for spintronic devices that exploit direction-dependent conductance, such as magnetic sensors, nonvolatile memory elements, and low-power logic components. The high tunability of MTIs through chemical composition, magnetic doping concentration, film thickness, and external fields provides a versatile platform for engineering anisotropic transport properties.

Despite these motivations, systematic investigations into the anisotropic conductivity of MTIs remain relatively scarce. Many experimental reports focus on magnetotransport measurements in a limited set of geometries, often without a detailed angular dependence study or without isolating the contributions from surface and bulk. Moreover, theoretical models frequently adopt simplified assumptions about the magnetization configuration or neglect the role of disorder and inhomogeneity, which are known to be significant in real samples. Bridging this gap requires a combination of precise material synthesis, high-resolution angular-dependent transport measurements, and theoretical modeling that incorporates realistic band structures and disorder effects.

In this work, we address the problem of anisotropic conductivity in magnetic topological insulators by combining experimental measurements and theoretical analysis. We focus on epitaxial thin films of magnetically doped TIs, in which the magnetic order is well characterized and the surface states can be probed with minimal bulk conduction. By systematically varying the orientation of the magnetization relative to the current and crystal axes, and by measuring both longitudinal and transverse conductivities over a range of temperatures and magnetic fields, we extract the angular dependence of the conductivity tensor. We interpret these results within a framework that accounts for spin–orbit coupling, magnetization-induced band structure modifications, and anisotropic scattering. Our findings reveal clear signatures of anisotropic transport linked to the interplay between magnetic order and topological electronic structure, and provide guidelines for tailoring anisotropic responses in MTI-based devices.

Through this approach, we aim to advance the understanding of how magnetic order modifies charge transport in topological materials, and to establish anisotropic conductivity as a sensitive probe of the rich physics at the intersection of topology and magnetism.
conclusion: In summary, we have investigated the anisotropic conductivity of magnetic topological insulators, elucidating the interplay between magnetic ordering, spin–orbit coupling, and topologically protected surface states. Our analysis demonstrates that the breaking of time-reversal symmetry by magnetic order induces a pronounced directional dependence in charge transport, closely linked to the orientation of the magnetization and crystalline axes. The observed anisotropy arises from the combined effects of spin-momentum locking and band structure modifications, which selectively enhance or suppress carrier mobility along specific directions. These findings highlight the importance of symmetry considerations in tailoring transport properties for device applications. Furthermore, our results suggest that controlled manipulation of magnetic orientation could provide a robust mechanism for tuning anisotropic response, enabling novel functionalities in spintronic and quantum information technologies. Future studies integrating microscopic modeling with high-resolution transport measurements will be essential to fully map the parameter space governing anisotropic conduction in this class of topological materials.

title: A novel teleoperator testbed to understand the effects of master-slave dynamics on embodiment and kinesthetic perception *
abstract: We present a novel teleoperator testbed designed to investigate how master–slave dynamics influence embodiment and kinesthetic perception. The system enables precise control over communication delays, motion scaling, and force feedback between a human-operated master device and a robotic slave manipulator. By systematically varying these parameters, we assess their impact on users’ sense of agency, body ownership, and perceived effort during manipulation tasks. The testbed incorporates high-fidelity motion tracking and force sensing to capture both objective performance metrics and subjective experiential reports. Preliminary experiments reveal that altered dynamic mappings can significantly modulate kinesthetic cues and the degree to which operators feel embodied in the remote system. This platform offers a controlled environment for probing fundamental questions in teleoperation, with applications in surgical robotics, remote exploration, and rehabilitation technologies.
introduction:
Teleoperation systems enable human operators to interact with remote or virtual environments through a master interface that controls a slave device. These systems are critical in domains such as minimally invasive surgery, hazardous material handling, and space exploration, where direct human presence is impractical or unsafe. A central challenge in teleoperation research is understanding how the dynamics between the master and slave subsystems affect the operator’s sense of embodiment—the subjective experience of owning and controlling the remote device—and kinesthetic perception, the awareness of movement and position through proprioceptive cues.

Previous studies have examined factors such as time delays, force feedback fidelity, and kinematic mapping in relation to task performance and operator workload. However, the complex interplay between mechanical dynamics, control strategies, and human sensory integration remains insufficiently characterized. In particular, the dynamic behavior of the master-slave pair, including mismatches in inertia, damping, and stiffness, may alter the naturalness of interaction and disrupt sensorimotor contingencies. These disruptions can degrade the operator’s ability to accurately perceive forces and positions, ultimately affecting both performance and the subjective sense of “being there” in the remote environment.

Despite the recognized importance of embodiment in teleoperation, experimental platforms that allow systematic manipulation of master-slave dynamics under controlled conditions are scarce. Existing testbeds often prioritize task execution over perceptual assessment, limiting their utility for studying fundamental human–machine interaction mechanisms. There is a need for an experimental framework that can flexibly adjust mechanical and control parameters, capture both objective performance data and subjective perceptual reports, and thus reveal how specific dynamic properties influence kinesthetic and embodiment-related outcomes.

This work presents a novel teleoperator testbed designed to address these needs. The system enables precise tuning of master and slave dynamics, supports high-fidelity bidirectional force feedback, and incorporates measurement protocols for both behavioral and psychophysical assessment. By providing a controlled environment for investigating the links between dynamic properties, sensory integration, and embodiment, this platform offers new opportunities to inform the design of teleoperation systems that are not only effective but also perceptually transparent to the operator.
conclusion: This work presented a novel teleoperator testbed designed to investigate how master–slave dynamics influence embodiment and kinesthetic perception. By enabling precise control and measurement of interaction parameters, the system provides a versatile platform for isolating and analyzing key factors underpinning sensorimotor integration in teleoperation. Preliminary results suggest that dynamic coupling characteristics significantly modulate users’ sense of agency and bodily ownership. These findings can inform future teleoperator interface designs, enhancing performance, comfort, and intuitiveness in a wide range of remote manipulation applications.

title: The Cayley-Dickson Construction in Homotopy Type Theory
abstract: We investigate the Cayley-Dickson construction within Homotopy Type Theory, developing higher-dimensional algebraic structures, formalizing their properties, and exploring implications for constructive mathematics, synthetic homotopy theory, and the internal study of normed division algebras.
introduction:
The Cayley–Dickson construction is a classical algebraic process that generates a sequence of normed algebras over the real numbers, beginning with the reals, complexes, quaternions, and octonions, and continuing to higher-dimensional, non-associative structures. This iterative doubling procedure plays a central role in the study of composition algebras, division algebras, and their applications in geometry, topology, and theoretical physics. Its well-known connection to the Hurwitz theorem and to phenomena such as triality highlights its deep structural significance.

Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) offers a modern, foundational framework for mathematics, combining constructive type theory with insights from homotopy theory. Within HoTT, algebraic and higher-categorical structures can be expressed in a manner that is both syntactic—amenable to formal verification—and homotopically meaningful. The formalization of algebraic constructions in HoTT not only ensures rigor but also facilitates computer-checked proofs in proof assistants such as Agda, Coq, or Lean.

In this work, we investigate the Cayley–Dickson construction from the perspective of Homotopy Type Theory. Our aim is twofold: first, to give a type-theoretic formulation of the construction that is faithful to its algebraic properties, and second, to study the extent to which its classical features—such as norm multiplicativity, alternativity, and the emergence of non-associativity—can be recovered or reformulated in a constructive and homotopical setting. This entails careful treatment of foundational issues, including the definition of real and complex numbers in HoTT, the handling of higher inductive types, and the encoding of bilinear and conjugation operations.

By situating the Cayley–Dickson process within HoTT, we bridge a gap between a historically rich algebraic tradition and a contemporary foundational framework. This synthesis promises not only new insights into the algebraic hierarchy generated by the construction, but also contributes to the growing body of formally verified mathematics in homotopy type theory, potentially informing further explorations in algebra, topology, and mathematical physics.
conclusion:
In this work we have explored the Cayley–Dickson construction from the perspective of homotopy type theory, emphasizing its structural and computational aspects when formulated in a constructive, type-theoretic setting. By reinterpreting the iterative doubling process of algebras over the reals within the framework of higher inductive types and univalent foundations, we have shown how the familiar sequence of normed division algebras—real numbers, complex numbers, quaternions, and octonions—can be reconstructed in a way that is compatible with the intensional nature of type theory. The formalization highlights not only the algebraic coherence of the construction, but also the subtleties that arise when classical proofs relying on choice principles or point-set topology are replaced by arguments respecting constructive constraints.

A key outcome has been the identification of the precise type-theoretic ingredients needed for each stage of the doubling process, including the handling of involutive anti-automorphisms, bilinear products, and norms, as well as the management of associativity and alternativity properties in higher stages. The homotopical viewpoint clarifies the role of identity types in expressing algebraic equalities up to coherent higher paths, making explicit the homotopy-theoretic content of algebraic laws often taken for granted in set-theoretic contexts.

Furthermore, our analysis underscores the way in which the Cayley–Dickson process interacts with the hierarchy of truncations and the distinction between mere propositions and higher types. Certain classical results, such as the non-existence of further normed division algebras beyond the octonions, acquire a refined interpretation in the univalent setting, where the failure of division or norm preservation can be expressed as the inhabitation of specific higher types encoding obstructions.

The constructive formalization of these ideas opens the door to machine-verified proofs of deep algebraic facts, leveraging proof assistants based on homotopy type theory. This not only strengthens the reliability of results but also facilitates experimentation with variations of the construction, such as modifications over other base types or in different homotopical universes. Future work could investigate connections to higher-categorical analogues of composition algebras, explore the role of the Cayley–Dickson process in the study of structured ring spectra, or extend the formalization to encompass non-normed generalizations. In sum, the homotopy type theoretic treatment of the Cayley–Dickson construction enriches both the algebraic theory and the constructive foundations, offering a bridge between classical algebraic structures and modern, computationally grounded mathematics.

title: An AI-Assisted Design Method for Topology Optimization Without Pre-Optimized Training Data
abstract: This paper presents a novel AI-assisted design method for structural topology optimization that eliminates the dependence on pre-optimized training datasets. Conventional AI-based approaches to topology optimization often require large volumes of high-quality, pre-computed solutions to learn design-performance relationships, incurring significant computational and storage costs. In contrast, the proposed method integrates a generative neural network with an iterative finite element analysis (FEA) loop, enabling the model to learn and adapt directly from in-process optimization data. The framework employs a reinforcement learning–inspired update mechanism, where performance feedback from FEA guides the refinement of design candidates in real time. This self-improving process accelerates convergence toward optimal topologies while preserving design diversity and adaptability to varying boundary conditions and load cases. Benchmark tests on standard 2D and 3D topology optimization problems demonstrate that the method achieves comparable or superior performance to traditional optimization algorithms and deep learning models trained on large datasets, while substantially reducing the upfront preparation effort. The results highlight the potential of this data-independent, AI-assisted approach to streamline the topology optimization workflow, making it more accessible for rapid design exploration in engineering applications without sacrificing solution quality.
introduction: Topology optimization is a powerful computational tool for designing high-performance structures by optimally distributing material within a given domain. Traditional approaches, such as density-based or level-set methods, often require iterative solvers with high computational cost. Recently, machine learning techniques have been introduced to accelerate topology optimization, but most rely on large datasets of pre-optimized designs for supervised training, limiting their applicability to predefined problem settings. This dependency constrains adaptability to new boundary conditions, loads, or design domains. To address these limitations, we propose an AI-assisted design method that eliminates the need for pre-optimized training data. By leveraging generative models and physics-based constraints, our approach enables efficient, flexible topology optimization while maintaining structural performance, offering a scalable framework for diverse engineering applications without the overhead of dataset generation.
conclusion:
This work has introduced an AI-assisted design method for topology optimization that eliminates the dependence on pre-optimized training data, thereby addressing a key limitation in current data-driven optimization approaches. By integrating physics-based simulation directly into the learning loop, the proposed framework enables the generation of optimized structures through iterative prediction–evaluation cycles, without requiring a large corpus of reference solutions. This not only reduces the data preparation burden but also broadens the applicability of AI methods to new problem domains where such datasets are unavailable or expensive to produce.

The method leverages neural network models to propose candidate topologies, which are then refined through feedback from finite element analysis. This closed-loop process allows the model to learn structural patterns and performance–design relationships in situ, adapting to problem-specific constraints and objectives. Compared with conventional topology optimization, the approach offers significant computational acceleration once the learning process stabilizes, while retaining the capacity to explore diverse design spaces. Compared with supervised AI-based methods, it demonstrates greater flexibility and generalizability, since it does not inherit biases from a fixed training dataset.

Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method can achieve competitive or superior structural performance relative to classical optimization techniques, while producing topologies that are both efficient and manufacturable. The results also highlight the method’s robustness to variations in boundary conditions, material properties, and load cases, indicating its potential for wider adoption in practical engineering design scenarios. Furthermore, by embedding the optimization within a machine learning framework that is continuously informed by physics, the approach maintains interpretability and physical consistency—qualities often sacrificed in purely data-driven models.

Despite these advantages, several aspects warrant further investigation. The current implementation focuses on two-dimensional, static load problems; extending the framework to three-dimensional, dynamic, or multi-physics cases will be essential for broader applicability. Additionally, while the elimination of pre-optimized data reduces initial preparation costs, the iterative simulation–learning cycles can still be computationally intensive, suggesting opportunities for parallelization, surrogate modeling, or adaptive sampling strategies to enhance efficiency. The integration of manufacturing constraints and multi-objective criteria within the learning process also represents a promising direction for future work.

In summary, the proposed AI-assisted topology optimization method represents a step toward more autonomous, adaptable, and data-efficient design tools. By removing the dependency on pre-optimized datasets and embedding physical reasoning directly into the optimization loop, it opens new possibilities for rapid, informed design exploration across a wide range of engineering applications.

title: Entanglement Entropy in Integrable Field Theories with Line Defects II. Non-topological Defect
abstract: We investigate the bipartite entanglement entropy in integrable quantum field theories in the presence of purely transmissive, non-topological line defects. Extending previous analyses for topological defects, we employ the replica trick and form factor bootstrap to compute leading corrections to the entanglement entropy in massive theories. The non-topological nature of the defect modifies the transmission amplitudes and introduces defect-dependent exponential corrections in the large-interval regime. We analyse explicit examples, focusing on the sinh-Gordon model, and compare analytic predictions with numerical results from truncated conformal space approach. Our findings reveal how non-topological defects interpolate between transparent and reflective limits, offering insight into defect-induced modifications of quantum correlations in integrable systems.
introduction:
Quantum entanglement has emerged as a central concept in modern theoretical physics, providing deep insights into the structure of quantum many-body systems, quantum field theories (QFTs), and quantum gravity. Among various measures of entanglement, the entanglement entropy (EE) has proven particularly fruitful, serving both as a diagnostic of quantum correlations and as a tool for probing universal aspects of critical phenomena. In (1+1)-dimensional integrable quantum field theories, the computation of EE has benefitted from the availability of exact methods, notably the form factor bootstrap and the replica trick. These approaches allow one to capture non-perturbative information, even in interacting settings, and to explore the effects of integrability-preserving perturbations. 

An important generalization of the study of EE in integrable models involves the introduction of defects or impurities. Defects in QFT can model a wide range of physical situations, from domain walls in condensed matter systems to impurity lines in spin chains and junctions in quantum wires. In integrable field theories, defects can be classified according to their scattering properties. A particularly tractable class is that of *topological defects*, which are purely transmitting and preserve the energy–momentum tensor across their worldline. For such defects, the computation of EE is often simplified, as the defect can be moved without affecting the correlators of local operators, except for possible transmission factors. In a previous work, we analyzed the EE in integrable models with topological line defects, obtaining exact expressions for the leading and subleading contributions in various regimes.

However, in many physically relevant contexts, defects are *non-topological*, meaning that they generally lead to both transmission and reflection of excitations. These defects break part of the symmetry enjoyed by the bulk theory, while still preserving integrability under appropriate conditions. They are characterized by nontrivial defect scattering matrices, which encode both the forward scattering and the reflection amplitudes. Non-topological defects can interpolate between different boundary conditions in limiting cases, and they allow for richer dynamical behaviour than their topological counterparts. From the standpoint of entanglement, the presence of reflection introduces qualitatively new features, such as the possibility of localized modes near the defect and modified scaling behaviour of EE.

The study of EE in the presence of non-topological defects raises both conceptual and technical challenges. On the conceptual side, it is not immediately clear how the defect modifies the universal scaling forms known from conformal field theory (CFT) in the ultraviolet (UV) limit, or how it affects the saturation values in massive theories in the infrared (IR) regime. The interplay between bulk integrability and defect-induced reflections may lead to crossover behaviour that is absent in purely transmitting cases. On the technical side, the reflection and transmission amplitudes enter the computation of correlation functions via the defect form factors, which now depend on both rapidity and the defect’s internal degrees of freedom. This complicates the application of the replica method to compute Rényi and von Neumann entropies, as the analytic continuation in the replica index must be performed in the presence of these additional scattering structures.

In this work, we extend the analysis of entanglement entropy in integrable field theories to include non-topological line defects. We focus on massive relativistic integrable models in (1+1) dimensions, and employ the form factor bootstrap adapted to defect theories to evaluate the branch-point twist field correlators required in the replica approach. In contrast to the topological case, the presence of reflection modifies both the UV and IR behaviour of the EE, leading to defect-dependent corrections that can be computed systematically. We analyse the leading large-distance behaviour in the IR, where the entropy saturates to a constant determined by the defect’s scattering data, and we investigate the subleading exponential corrections governed by the particle spectrum. In the UV limit, we explore how the defect strength interpolates between the CFT result without a defect and the limiting behaviour corresponding to a purely reflecting boundary.

Our results provide an exact characterization of how non-topological integrable defects modify quantum entanglement, complementing and generalizing the topological case previously studied. Beyond their intrinsic theoretical interest, these findings have potential implications for low-dimensional condensed matter systems with localized impurities, and for the design of quantum devices where control over transmission and reflection at the quantum level is required. They also serve as a further step towards a systematic classification of defect effects on entanglement in integrable quantum field theories.
conclusion:
In this work we have extended the analysis of entanglement entropy in integrable quantum field theories to the case of non-topological line defects. Building on the framework developed in the first part of this study for topological defects, we have considered defect lines that generically modify the scattering processes without preserving the full transmission properties characteristic of the topological case. Our approach has relied on the form factor bootstrap for defect operators, enabling an explicit evaluation of correlation functions of branch-point twist fields in the presence of such defects.

We have shown that non-topological defects introduce qualitatively new features into the entanglement structure. In particular, the defect transmission and reflection amplitudes enter directly into the form factor expansions, leading to corrections in the ultraviolet and infrared scaling of the Rényi entropies. At short distances, while the universal logarithmic growth dictated by conformal symmetry is preserved, the non-topological defect modifies the overall constant term, which now depends on the defect parameters. This reflects the partial breaking of conformal invariance induced by the defect, and signals that even in integrable settings, non-topological impurity lines can leave a persistent imprint on short-distance quantum correlations.

In the infrared regime, where the correlation length becomes large compared to the subsystem size, the entropy saturates to a constant value determined by the defect’s reflection and transmission coefficients. Unlike the topological case, where the saturation value is independent of the defect due to perfect transmission, here the reduced transmission probability effectively partitions the system into weakly coupled regions, lowering the asymptotic entropy. This behavior is consistent with physical intuition from lattice models with impurities, and our results provide a precise quantitative formulation in the continuum integrable framework.

We have also explored intermediate distance scales, where the defect induces nontrivial crossover behavior in the entropy. The interplay between bulk mass scales and defect scattering data yields a rich structure, which can be systematically captured within the form factor expansion. Our explicit computations in representative models, such as the sinh-Gordon theory with a purely transmitting or partially reflecting defect, illustrate how the general formalism can be applied to extract numerical predictions for the entropy at all length scales.

The methods developed here open several directions for further research. One natural extension is to consider defects with internal degrees of freedom, which could lead to additional contributions to the entanglement entropy from defect-bound states. Another avenue is the analysis of time-dependent scenarios, such as quantum quenches in the presence of non-topological defects, where the interplay between defect scattering and entanglement growth could reveal new dynamical universality classes. Finally, it would be interesting to explore the connection between the defect-induced constant terms in the entropy and boundary or defect g-functions, potentially providing a unifying thermodynamic interpretation.

In summary, our analysis demonstrates that non-topological defects in integrable quantum field theories produce distinctive and calculable modifications to the entanglement entropy at all scales. These results deepen the understanding of impurity effects in low-dimensional quantum systems and enrich the broader picture of how locality, integrability, and defect structure intertwine in shaping quantum correlations.

title: GRB 130925A: an ultra-long Gamma Ray Burst with a dust-echo afterglow, and implications for the origin of the ultra-long GRBs
abstract: We present a detailed analysis of GRB 130925A, an ultra-long gamma-ray burst (GRB) distinguished by prompt high-energy emission lasting approximately 20 ks, making it one of the longest GRBs recorded to date. Multi-wavelength follow-up observations reveal an X-ray afterglow with an unusual temporal and spectral evolution, inconsistent with the standard synchrotron afterglow model. We interpret the late-time X-ray emission as being dominated by a dust-scattered echo of the prompt emission, produced by intervening dust in the host galaxy. Spectral softening and a shallow temporal decay are well reproduced by a dust-scattering model, allowing us to constrain the distribution and properties of circumburst dust. The negligible contribution from a conventional external-shock afterglow suggests a low-density circumburst environment, consistent with a progenitor embedded in a relatively isolated region. We discuss the implications of these findings for the origin of ultra-long GRBs, considering both the collapse of blue supergiant stars and tidal disruption events (TDEs) of stars by massive black holes. The observed energetics, spectral characteristics, and host galaxy properties favor a massive star origin, with the extreme duration arising from the extended envelope of a blue supergiant. GRB 130925A thus provides compelling evidence that at least some ultra-long GRBs are produced by the core collapse of massive stars with large radii, and that dust-scattered echoes can dominate their late-time X-ray emission.
introduction:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic explosions in the Universe, typically releasing energies of order 10^51–10^54 erg in the form of high-energy photons over timescales ranging from milliseconds to several minutes. They are conventionally divided into two broad classes based on their prompt emission duration: short GRBs, with T90 < 2 s, and long GRBs, with T90 > 2 s, the latter generally associated with the collapse of massive stars (“collapsars”). However, in recent years a small but intriguing population of events has emerged with durations vastly exceeding those of canonical long bursts, in some cases lasting several thousand seconds. These so-called “ultra-long” GRBs challenge the standard progenitor models, raising questions about their origin, central engine activity, and the environments in which they occur.

GRB 130925A is one of the most striking examples of this ultra-long class. Detected by the Swift Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) on 2013 September 25, the burst exhibited prompt gamma-ray emission persisting for approximately 20,000 seconds, making it one of the longest GRBs ever recorded. Its light curve displayed multiple, widely spaced episodes of high-energy emission, interspersed with extended periods of relative quiescence, suggesting prolonged or recurrent activity of the central engine. Observations across the electromagnetic spectrum revealed unusual afterglow properties, most notably a late-time X-ray decay inconsistent with the standard external shock model. Instead, the X-ray light curve was dominated by a component consistent with a dust-scattered echo of the prompt emission.

Dust scattering halos and echoes have been observed in the X-ray afterglows of some GRBs, but in GRB 130925A the dust echo was unusually prominent, effectively replacing the canonical afterglow emission. This implies a dense, dusty environment along the line of sight, likely within the host galaxy. In such a scenario, prompt X-ray photons are scattered by interstellar dust grains into the line of sight with a time delay, producing a temporally extended and spectrally softened component. The presence of such a strong dust echo provides a valuable diagnostic of the circumburst medium and the location of the burst within its host galaxy, as well as a means to probe the properties of interstellar dust at cosmological distances.

The extreme duration and distinctive afterglow behaviour of GRB 130925A have important implications for the nature of ultra-long GRBs. Proposed progenitor scenarios include the collapse of blue supergiants with extended envelopes, tidal disruption events (TDEs) involving the disruption of a star by an intermediate-mass black hole, and magnetar-powered events with unusually prolonged energy injection. The dense, dusty environment inferred for GRB 130925A may favour progenitors in regions of active star formation, consistent with massive stellar origins, but the unusually slow evolution of the prompt emission also invites consideration of alternative models.

In this paper we present a detailed analysis of GRB 130925A, focusing on the properties of its prompt emission, the derivation and modelling of its dust-echo afterglow, and the constraints these observations place on progenitor scenarios. By comparing GRB 130925A to other ultra-long GRBs and to the broader GRB population, we aim to clarify whether ultra-long events represent an extension of the long GRB distribution or a distinct class with separate physical origins.
conclusion:
GRB 130925A stands out as one of the most extreme examples of the ultra-long gamma-ray burst (ULGRB) class, with prompt high-energy emission lasting over 20,000 seconds, and with an afterglow dominated at late times by X-ray emission consistent with a dust-scattered echo of the prompt and early afterglow photons. The combination of prolonged prompt emission and a distinctive afterglow signature has enabled a rare and detailed exploration of both the circumburst environment and the physical parameters of the progenitor system.

Our analysis shows that the temporal and spectral evolution of the late X-ray light curve is inconsistent with the canonical synchrotron afterglow model, but can be well reproduced by dust scattering models, requiring a distribution of dust at distances of tens to hundreds of parsecs from the burst site. This is indicative of a dense, dusty host environment, plausibly associated with regions of active star formation. The dust echo interpretation also implies that the underlying forward shock emission was unusually faint, suggesting either a low circumburst density or an intrinsically low kinetic energy in the outflow. This is in contrast to the typical bright afterglows of long-duration GRBs and points towards diverse energy-partition scenarios within the ULGRB population.

The extraordinary duration of the prompt emission challenges the standard collapsar framework. While fallback accretion in a massive star collapse could, in principle, sustain extended central engine activity, the timescales observed in GRB 130925A are more naturally explained if the progenitor was an extended, low-density star such as a blue supergiant, whose large stellar radius and envelope structure permit a prolonged jet breakout and accretion phase. Alternatively, tidal disruption of a star by an intermediate-mass black hole could also produce ultra-long high-energy emission, though in this case the association of GRB 130925A with a star-forming region within its host galaxy, and the presence of substantial dust, favour a massive stellar origin over a nuclear transient.

The characteristics of GRB 130925A suggest that ULGRBs are not merely the tail of the duration distribution of long GRBs, but may represent a distinct physical subclass with different progenitor properties and environments. The prevalence of dust echoes in such events could bias afterglow-based energetics and redshift estimates if not properly accounted for, and may explain the faintness of some ULGRB afterglows in the optical and near-infrared. Future systematic searches for dust echo signatures will be important to constrain the true frequency of such environments and to refine the inferred energetics of the ULGRB population.

In summary, GRB 130925A provides compelling evidence that ultra-long gamma-ray bursts can arise from progenitors embedded in dense, dusty star-forming regions, with prompt emission durations far exceeding those of typical collapsars and afterglows shaped by dust scattering rather than purely by synchrotron emission. Its properties support models invoking large-radius progenitors and extended engine activity, and highlight the need for multi-wavelength, long-term monitoring to disentangle intrinsic afterglow physics from environmental effects. As more ULGRBs are discovered and studied in detail, the diversity of their environments and progenitors will offer valuable insights into the extreme endpoints of stellar evolution and the variety of pathways to relativistic jet production.

title: The Effect of the Uncertainty of Load and Renewable Generation on the Dynamic Voltage Stability Margin
abstract: This paper investigates the impact of load and renewable generation uncertainties on the dynamic voltage stability margin (DVSM) of power systems. Variability in load demand and the intermittent nature of renewable resources introduce stochastic fluctuations that can significantly influence system voltage dynamics. A probabilistic assessment framework is developed, integrating time-domain simulations with Monte Carlo sampling to capture a wide range of operating scenarios. The approach quantifies the statistical distribution of DVSM under uncertain conditions, revealing critical interactions between load variability, renewable penetration levels, and system stability limits. Case studies on a modified IEEE test system demonstrate that higher uncertainty levels reduce the mean DVSM and increase the probability of voltage instability. The results highlight the necessity of incorporating uncertainty into stability assessments to ensure reliable operation in modern, renewable-rich power systems.
introduction:
The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources, particularly wind and solar power, has introduced significant challenges to the secure and reliable operation of modern power systems. Unlike conventional synchronous generators, renewable generation is inherently variable and uncertain due to its strong dependence on weather conditions and limited dispatchability. At the same time, the demand side is evolving with the proliferation of electric vehicles, flexible loads, and distributed energy resources, adding further uncertainty to net system load. These changes have profound implications for system stability, especially for voltage stability, which is a critical aspect of power system security. Voltage instability events, if not anticipated and mitigated, can lead to wide-area blackouts, resulting in economic losses and threats to safety.

Dynamic voltage stability refers to the ability of the power system to maintain acceptable voltages at all buses following a disturbance, such as a fault, line trip, or sudden change in generation or load, while considering the time-dependent response of system components. The dynamic voltage stability margin (DVSM) quantifies the distance between the current operating point and the point of voltage instability, thus providing a measure of the system’s resilience to disturbances. Accurate assessment of the DVSM is essential for secure system operation, as it enables operators to determine operating limits, plan corrective actions, and design appropriate control strategies.

In traditional power systems dominated by thermal and hydro generation, the uncertainties influencing DVSM were relatively limited and could be addressed using well-established deterministic methods. However, with the growing share of renewable generation and stochastic load behavior, these uncertainties have become more pronounced and cannot be neglected. Renewable generation output fluctuates due to variations in wind speed, solar irradiance, and ambient temperature, often on time scales comparable to system dynamics. Similarly, load demand exhibits random fluctuations driven by consumer behavior, weather conditions, and the increasing presence of responsive loads. The combined effect of these uncertainties can cause the DVSM to vary significantly over time, potentially reducing the system’s ability to withstand disturbances.

Conventional stability assessment methods often rely on worst-case deterministic scenarios or steady-state approximations, which may result in overly conservative or optimistic operating limits when uncertainty is high. Recent research has highlighted the need for probabilistic and dynamic approaches that incorporate the stochastic nature of both generation and demand. Such approaches offer a more realistic representation of system behavior, enabling more informed operational decisions. However, the integration of uncertainty into dynamic voltage stability analysis presents considerable challenges, including the need for advanced modeling techniques, efficient computational algorithms, and accurate statistical characterization of input uncertainties.

A rigorous understanding of how uncertainty in load and renewable generation affects the DVSM is crucial for multiple reasons. First, it supports the development of adaptive stability margins that can be updated in real time as operating conditions change. Second, it informs the design of control and protection schemes that can respond effectively to rapid fluctuations. Third, it contributes to more robust planning practices by identifying critical operating conditions that are likely to occur under uncertain scenarios.

This paper investigates the impact of combined load and renewable generation uncertainty on the dynamic voltage stability margin of power systems. By employing probabilistic modeling and dynamic simulation techniques, the study aims to quantify the influence of uncertainty on DVSM and identify key factors that determine system vulnerability. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of more resilient operational strategies and control mechanisms in power systems with high renewable penetration.
conclusion: This study investigated the influence of uncertainties in load demand and renewable generation on the dynamic voltage stability margin of power systems. The results demonstrate that variability in both factors can significantly reduce the available stability margin, with high renewable penetration amplifying the impact of load fluctuations. Stochastic modeling and time-domain simulations revealed that the combined effects of uncertain inputs lead to earlier onset of voltage instability compared to deterministic scenarios. Furthermore, the sensitivity analysis indicates that the correlation between load and renewable variations plays a critical role in shaping system resilience. These findings highlight the necessity for incorporating uncertainty-aware assessment methods into stability studies, enabling more robust operational planning and preventive control strategies. Future work should explore adaptive control schemes and enhanced forecasting techniques to mitigate the adverse effects of uncertainty, ensuring secure and reliable integration of renewable energy sources in evolving power networks.

title: Constraining nonstandard neutrino interactions at electron colliders
abstract: We investigate the potential of high–energy electron colliders to probe nonstandard neutrino interactions (NSIs) beyond the Standard Model. Such interactions, parameterized by effective four–fermion operators, can modify neutrino–electron scattering rates and angular distributions, offering a sensitive window to new physics. We focus on processes involving final–state neutrinos at future facilities such as the ILC and CLIC, where precise measurements of missing energy signatures can be used to constrain vector and axial–vector NSI couplings. Using simulated event samples and realistic detector assumptions, we perform a statistical analysis of differential cross sections, accounting for Standard Model backgrounds and systematic uncertainties. Projected bounds are derived for representative center–of–mass energies and integrated luminosities, demonstrating that electron colliders can improve current limits from oscillation and scattering experiments by up to an order of magnitude. Our results highlight the complementary role of lepton colliders in the global NSI program, particularly for flavor–dependent couplings involving electron neutrinos.
introduction: Neutrinos, as neutral and feebly interacting particles, provide a unique window into physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). While the SM successfully describes neutrino interactions via weak charged and neutral currents, a variety of theoretical frameworks predict additional nonstandard neutrino interactions (NSIs) that could arise from new mediators or higher-dimensional operators. These NSIs can modify neutrino production, propagation, and detection, leaving subtle imprints in precision measurements. Electron–positron colliders, with their clean experimental environment and well-understood kinematics, offer an excellent platform to probe such effects. Processes involving neutrinos in the final state, such as \( e^+ e^- \to \nu \bar{\nu} \gamma \), are particularly sensitive to deviations from SM expectations. Recent advances in luminosity and detector capabilities at current and future facilities, including Belle II and proposed high-energy colliders, open new opportunities for stringent NSI constraints. In this work, we systematically investigate the sensitivity of electron colliders to NSIs, quantify potential bounds, and compare their reach with existing terrestrial and astrophysical limits.
conclusion:
In this work, we have explored the potential of high-energy electron–positron colliders to probe nonstandard neutrino interactions (NSIs) through precision measurements and dedicated searches. By considering a general effective field theory framework, we parametrized possible deviations from the Standard Model in terms of dimension-six four-fermion operators involving neutrinos and electrons. This approach allowed us to capture a wide range of new physics scenarios without committing to a specific ultraviolet completion, thereby enabling a model-independent interpretation of collider sensitivities.

Our analysis has demonstrated that future high-luminosity electron colliders, such as those envisaged in the International Linear Collider (ILC) or Compact Linear Collider (CLIC) programs, will be able to significantly improve upon current bounds on various NSI parameters. In particular, we showed that processes such as \( e^+ e^- \to \nu \bar{\nu} \gamma \) and \( e^+ e^- \to e^+ e^- \nu \bar{\nu} \) are especially sensitive to contact interactions involving neutrinos, owing to their clean experimental signatures and the suppression of Standard Model backgrounds at high center-of-mass energies. The capability to polarize electron and positron beams further enhances sensitivity by selectively amplifying or suppressing certain helicity amplitudes, thereby improving the discrimination between NSI effects and Standard Model contributions.

By performing a detailed simulation of relevant signal and background processes, including realistic detector effects, we have derived projected exclusion limits for representative NSI coefficients. For benchmark collider energies and integrated luminosities, our results indicate that electron colliders can probe effective scales well into the multi-TeV regime, complementing and in some cases surpassing the reach of neutrino scattering experiments and astrophysical constraints. This complementarity arises because collider observables are sensitive to different combinations of couplings and kinematic regimes, thus providing independent and robust tests of new physics in the neutrino sector.

We have also highlighted the importance of combining collider data with results from oscillation experiments, coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering, and astrophysical measurements. Such a global approach would enable the disentanglement of potential NSI effects from other new physics scenarios, such as additional gauge bosons or leptoquarks, and would strengthen the overall interpretability of any observed deviation from Standard Model predictions.

In conclusion, the study affirms that electron–positron colliders offer a powerful and complementary avenue for constraining nonstandard neutrino interactions. Their clean experimental environment, tunable beam polarization, and high precision make them ideally suited to explore subtle effects in the neutrino sector. As experimental programs advance and statistical samples grow, the sensitivity to NSIs will continue to improve, potentially revealing indirect signs of physics beyond the Standard Model. Continued theoretical and phenomenological efforts will be essential to refine these predictions, incorporate higher-order corrections, and extend the analysis to a broader class of operators. Ultimately, the synergy between collider experiments and other neutrino probes holds great promise for deepening our understanding of neutrino properties and their role in the fundamental laws of nature.

title: Tropicalization and tropical equilibration of chemical reactions
abstract: We investigate the tropicalization and tropical equilibration of chemical reaction networks, focusing on their application to model reduction and qualitative analysis. Tropicalization replaces nonlinear kinetic terms by piecewise-linear counterparts through valuation analysis, enabling the identification of dominant reaction pathways. Tropical equilibration identifies parameter regimes where competing monomials balance, revealing slow–fast dynamics and metastable states. We develop a systematic framework combining asymptotic analysis with tropical geometry to characterize such equilibrations in mass-action systems. Applications to representative biochemical networks demonstrate accurate approximation of dynamics, reduced computational complexity, and insight into structural stability, offering a powerful tool for multiscale chemical kinetics.
introduction: Chemical reaction networks often involve nonlinear dynamics spanning multiple timescales, making their analysis and simulation challenging. Tropical geometry offers a powerful framework for approximating such systems by replacing smooth nonlinear terms with piecewise-linear counterparts, a process known as tropicalization. This approach preserves essential qualitative behaviors while enabling computational simplifications. A related concept, tropical equilibration, identifies regimes where dominant reaction terms balance, revealing key asymptotic structures of the dynamics. Together, these techniques provide insight into the hierarchy of timescales, the identification of slow invariant manifolds, and the reduction of complex kinetic models. Recent developments have demonstrated their applicability in biochemical networks, metabolic pathways, and systems biology. This work explores the interplay between tropicalization and tropical equilibration, emphasizing their theoretical foundations, methodological integration, and potential for advancing the analysis of multiscale chemical reaction systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the processes of tropicalization and tropical equilibration as applied to the analysis of chemical reaction networks. By reformulating the governing kinetic equations in a tropical framework, we have been able to identify dominant balances and asymptotic regimes that are not immediately apparent in the original polynomial or rational formulations. The tropicalization procedure, which replaces sums of terms by the maximum of their orders of magnitude, provides a systematic reduction from nonlinear differential equations to piecewise-linear dynamics. This reduction preserves key structural features of the original system while greatly simplifying the identification of slow and fast variables, as well as the decomposition into quasi-steady-state and quasi-equilibrium subsystems.

The concept of tropical equilibration further refines this analysis by identifying parameter and variable scalings for which several competing terms attain the same asymptotic order. Such conditions correspond to regions in parameter space where the interplay between reaction pathways leads to critical transitions in system behavior, such as the onset of bistability, oscillations, or multiscale transients. In this regard, tropical equilibration serves both as a diagnostic tool for detecting sensitive dependencies and as a predictive tool for locating bifurcation points or critical manifolds.

Our results demonstrate that tropical methods can be applied systematically to a broad class of chemical systems, including those with multiple timescales, conservation laws, and complex stoichiometries. By providing an explicit link between algebraic structures in reaction rate laws and the qualitative features of the dynamics, the tropical perspective complements and enriches existing singular perturbation and asymptotic analysis techniques. Moreover, the piecewise-linear approximations obtained by tropicalization lend themselves to efficient computational exploration, facilitating parameter screening and model reduction in high-dimensional systems.

The study also highlights certain limitations and open questions. The accuracy of tropical approximations depends on the extent of separation between dominant and subdominant terms, and the identification of relevant scalings may require careful analysis when such separation is weak. Furthermore, while tropical methods capture leading-order behavior, incorporating corrections to account for small but non-negligible terms remains a challenge for future work.

Overall, tropicalization and tropical equilibration offer a powerful, conceptually transparent, and computationally tractable framework for the study of chemical reaction networks. They bridge discrete combinatorial structures and continuous dynamical behavior, opening avenues for deeper theoretical understanding and for the development of practical tools in chemical kinetics, systems biology, and related fields.

title: The Globular Cluster Systems of Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies in the Coma Cluster
abstract: We present a comprehensive study of the globular cluster (GC) systems associated with a sample of ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) in the Coma Cluster, based on deep *Hubble Space Telescope* imaging in the F606W and F814W bands. Our analysis targets 48 UDGs spanning a range of luminosities and effective radii, enabling a statistical characterization of their GC populations. Candidate GCs were identified via point-source selection criteria and color–magnitude cuts optimized for the Coma distance. We find that the GC specific frequencies (S\(_N\)) of these UDGs exhibit a wide dispersion, from values comparable to those of dwarf ellipticals to extreme cases exceeding those of giant ellipticals. A subset of UDGs hosts remarkably rich GC systems, with inferred GC counts up to \(\sim\)70, while others are consistent with having few or no GCs. We investigate correlations between GC abundance and galaxy structural parameters, and find that GC-rich UDGs tend to be larger and more spheroid-dominated, whereas GC-poor systems show no such trends. The total GC system mass is used to estimate host halo masses via empirical scaling relations, suggesting that GC-rich UDGs reside in dark matter halos comparable to those of \(L^*\) galaxies, while GC-poor UDGs are more consistent with dwarf-scale halos. These results support the scenario that UDGs are not a homogeneous population: some may be “failed” massive galaxies quenched early, while others are extended dwarfs shaped by environmental processes in the Coma Cluster. Our findings reinforce the utility of GC system properties as tracers of UDG formation histories and underlying dark matter content.
introduction: Ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) are a recently recognized population of galaxies characterized by low surface brightness, large effective radii, and stellar masses typical of dwarf galaxies. Despite their diffuse appearance, some UDGs host surprisingly rich globular cluster (GC) systems, raising questions about their formation histories and dark matter content. The Coma Cluster, with its high-density environment and abundant UDG population, provides an ideal laboratory for studying these galaxies and their GC systems. Previous studies have revealed a wide diversity in GC abundance among UDGs, suggesting multiple formation pathways, ranging from tidally heated dwarfs to failed massive galaxies. The number and spatial distribution of GCs offer valuable insights into the total halo mass and assembly history of these systems. However, systematic studies of UDG GC systems in Coma remain limited, particularly at faint luminosities and low GC numbers. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of GC populations associated with a sample of UDGs in the Coma Cluster, aiming to constrain their halo masses, explore environmental dependencies, and assess their place in the broader galaxy formation framework. Our results provide new constraints on UDG origins and evolutionary scenarios.
conclusion:
In this study, we have investigated the globular cluster (GC) systems associated with a sample of ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) in the Coma cluster, combining deep imaging, careful background subtraction, and statistical analysis to quantify their GC populations and spatial distributions. Our results indicate that while UDGs span a wide range in GC abundance, a significant fraction host rich GC systems with specific frequencies comparable to, or exceeding, those of much more luminous galaxies. This reinforces earlier suggestions that some UDGs may reside in relatively massive dark matter halos, inconsistent with the expectations for diffuse, low-mass dwarfs formed through extreme feedback-driven puffing up.

The radial distributions of GCs around our UDG sample are generally extended, with half-number radii comparable to or larger than the stellar effective radii, and in some cases approaching those of GCs around normal giant ellipticals. This spatial correspondence supports the interpretation that the GCs are physically associated with the UDGs, not merely projected background contaminants. Furthermore, the richness of the GC systems correlates only weakly, if at all, with the galaxies’ present-day stellar luminosity, suggesting that GC abundance is a more reliable tracer of the underlying halo mass than optical light in these extreme systems.

By comparing our measurements with predictions from empirical GC–halo mass relations, we estimate that the most GC-rich UDGs in our sample inhabit halos with virial masses in excess of 10¹¹ M☉, placing them firmly in the regime of Milky Way–mass systems despite their extremely low stellar masses and surface brightnesses. Conversely, GC-poor UDGs appear consistent with dwarf-galaxy–mass halos, implying that the UDG class is heterogeneous in origin. This diversity is consistent with multiple formation channels: some UDGs may be “failed” massive galaxies whose star formation was truncated early, while others may be diffuse dwarfs shaped by environmental processes such as tidal heating or ram-pressure stripping within the Coma cluster.

Our findings have implications for both galaxy formation theory and the use of GC systems as probes of halo mass in low-surface-brightness regimes. The presence of populous GC systems in some UDGs strengthens the case for a high-mass subset, challenging models in which all UDGs are simply high-spin dwarfs. At the same time, the coexistence of GC-poor UDGs underscores the necessity of targeted studies to disentangle the various evolutionary pathways leading to such diffuse stellar systems.

Future work should extend this analysis to larger samples across different environments, employ spectroscopic confirmation of GC membership to reduce statistical uncertainties, and explore the internal kinematics of both stars and GCs to directly constrain dynamical masses. Such efforts will help clarify the role of environment, feedback, and halo assembly history in shaping the globular cluster systems and structural properties of ultra-diffuse galaxies. In this way, UDGs and their GCs can serve as key laboratories for testing the interplay between baryons and dark matter in the low-luminosity frontier of galaxy formation.

title: A Fast Parallel Tensor Decomposition with Optimal Stochastic Gradient Descent: an Application in Structural Damage Identification
abstract: Tensor decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for extracting latent structures from multi-dimensional data, with applications spanning signal processing, machine learning, and structural health monitoring. However, large-scale tensor data pose significant computational challenges, particularly when real-time or near-real-time analysis is required. This paper presents a fast parallel tensor decomposition framework based on an optimally tuned stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm, designed to accelerate convergence while maintaining high accuracy. The proposed method leverages a novel adaptive learning rate schedule derived from convergence analysis, combined with parallelization strategies that exploit both shared-memory and distributed-memory architectures. The algorithm is applied to structural damage identification, where vibration response data from sensor networks are modeled as high-order tensors capturing spatial, temporal, and modal information. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves substantial speedup compared to conventional alternating least squares and standard SGD-based methods, without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity. The adaptive SGD ensures stable convergence under noisy conditions, critical for field monitoring scenarios, and the parallel implementation scales efficiently with the number of processing units. In damage localization tasks, the method reliably identifies damage patterns with higher sensitivity and lower false positive rates. This work highlights the potential of combining advanced stochastic optimization with high-performance computing to enable efficient, accurate, and scalable tensor analysis for engineering diagnostics, offering a pathway toward real-time structural health monitoring in complex infrastructures.
introduction:
Tensor decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing multidimensional data across various scientific and engineering domains. Its ability to extract latent factors from high-order data makes it particularly valuable in applications such as signal processing, computer vision, and structural health monitoring. However, conventional decomposition algorithms often suffer from high computational costs, especially when applied to large-scale tensors, limiting their usability in real-time or resource-constrained scenarios. The advent of parallel computing and stochastic optimization has opened new avenues for accelerating these methods without compromising accuracy.  

In structural damage identification, timely and accurate detection is critical to ensuring safety and reducing maintenance costs. Structural response data, often collected from distributed sensor networks, naturally form high-order tensors capturing spatial, temporal, and modal information. Efficient tensor decomposition can reveal subtle patterns associated with damage initiation and progression. Yet, existing approaches frequently face challenges in scalability, convergence speed, and robustness to noise.  

This study proposes a fast parallel tensor decomposition framework based on an optimal stochastic gradient descent strategy. The method leverages parallelism to handle large-scale data and employs an optimized learning rate schedule to enhance convergence stability. We demonstrate its effectiveness in structural damage identification, highlighting significant improvements in computational efficiency and detection accuracy over conventional algorithms.
conclusion: This study presented a fast parallel tensor decomposition framework integrated with an optimal stochastic gradient descent strategy, aimed at improving both computational efficiency and convergence stability. By leveraging parallel processing, the proposed method significantly reduced execution time for large-scale tensor data while maintaining high decomposition accuracy. The incorporation of an adaptive learning rate scheme within the stochastic gradient descent ensured robust convergence, even under noisy or incomplete data conditions. Application to structural damage identification demonstrated the method’s capability to extract meaningful latent features from complex vibration response tensors, enabling accurate localization and quantification of damage. Comparative experiments against baseline tensor decomposition approaches confirmed superior performance in terms of speed, scalability, and detection precision. The approach’s efficiency makes it particularly suited for real-time or near-real-time structural health monitoring scenarios, where timely decision-making is critical. Future work will focus on extending the method to handle streaming tensor data and integrating domain-specific constraints to further enhance interpretability. Overall, the proposed parallel and adaptive optimization framework offers a powerful and practical tool for large-scale tensor analysis in engineering diagnostics and beyond.

title: NuSTAR spectral analysis of two bright Seyfert 1 galaxies: MCG +8-11-11 and NGC 6814
abstract: We present a detailed broadband X-ray spectral analysis of two bright Seyfert 1 galaxies, MCG +8‑11‑11 and NGC 6814, based on observations with the *Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array* (*NuSTAR*). The high sensitivity of *NuSTAR* in the 3–79 keV band allows us to model the primary continuum, reflection features, and high-energy cutoffs with unprecedented precision. For both sources, we fit the spectra with physically motivated models incorporating a cutoff power-law continuum, relativistic disk reflection, and distant neutral reflection. In MCG +8‑11‑11, we find a photon index of Γ ≈ 1.75 and a high-energy cutoff at E_cut ≈ 200 keV, along with a moderately broadened Fe Kα emission line and a reflection fraction R ≈ 0.3, consistent with a compact corona and modest relativistic effects. NGC 6814 exhibits a softer continuum (Γ ≈ 1.84) and a lower cutoff energy, E_cut ≈ 110 keV, with a stronger reflection component (R ≈ 0.6) and a narrow Fe Kα line indicative of distant reprocessing. No significant evidence for ultra-fast outflows is detected in either source. Our results provide constraints on the coronal temperatures and geometries in these Seyfert 1 nuclei, supporting scenarios in which coronal properties vary between sources while accretion disk reflection remains an important contributor to their hard X-ray spectra.
introduction:
Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are among the most luminous persistent sources in the Universe, powered by accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) at the centres of galaxies. Seyfert 1 galaxies, a subclass of AGN, display broad optical emission lines and strong X-ray emission, making them ideal laboratories for studying the innermost regions of the accretion flow.
