Wilson loops play a central role in the study of gauge theories, both as non-local gauge-invariant observables and as a bridge between perturbative calculations and non-perturbative phenomena. In particular, in the maximally supersymmetric \(\mathcal{N}=4\) super Yang–Mills (SYM) theory, light-like polygonal Wilson loops have attracted considerable interest due to their intimate relation to scattering amplitudes. This correspondence, first observed at strong coupling via the AdS/CFT correspondence and subsequently confirmed perturbatively at weak coupling, rests crucially on the conformal symmetry of the underlying theory. The conformal Ward identities satisfied by such Wilson loops encode constraints on their functional form and have been instrumental in establishing the duality to maximally helicity-violating (MHV) amplitudes.

In the simplest and most studied setting, the contour of the Wilson loop is a closed polygon composed of straight, light-like segments, with cusps located at the vertices. The presence of these cusps leads to ultraviolet divergences whose structure is governed by the cusp anomalous dimension. The anomalous conformal Ward identities in this case have been derived and analyzed in detail, revealing that the breaking of conformal invariance is entirely captured by these cusp anomalies. The resulting equations strongly constrain the dependence of the loop expectation value on the conformally invariant cross-ratios formed from the cusp coordinates.

A natural generalization of this setup is to consider polygon-like contours in which the straight edges are replaced by curved segments, such as arcs of circles. Such contours arise in various contexts, for example in the investigation of smooth Wilson loops with local operator insertions, in the study of defects with nontrivial geometry, or in attempts to interpolate between light-like and smooth configurations. Circular arcs preserve some symmetry properties distinct from those of straight segments, and their curvature introduces new scales and potential sources of conformal symmetry breaking. The interplay between the cusp anomalies at the junctions of the arcs and possible curvature-induced effects modifies the structure of the Ward identities, leading to anomalous terms whose form has not been systematically explored.

An important motivation for studying Wilson loops on polygon-like contours with circular edges lies in testing the robustness of amplitude/Wilson loop dualities beyond the strictly light-like regime. While the duality in its original form relies on the exact light-likeness of the edges, understanding how conformal constraints are deformed when the contour deviates from this limit can shed light on the geometric origin of the duality and its possible extensions. Furthermore, circular edges introduce a natural connection to smooth Maldacena–Wilson loops, for which exact results are available in certain supersymmetric configurations. This raises the possibility of interpolating between exactly solvable and perturbatively tractable cases, offering a richer arena for testing both perturbative and non-perturbative techniques.

In this work, we investigate the anomalous conformal Ward identities for Wilson loops defined on closed contours composed of a finite number of circular arcs meeting at cusps. We derive the general form of the Ward identities in the presence of such edges, identify the sources of conformal symmetry breaking, and compare them to the known straight-edge, light-like case. Our analysis reveals how curvature modifies the anomaly coefficients and how new geometric invariants enter the conformal constraints. We also discuss the implications of our results for potential generalizations of the amplitude/Wilson loop duality and for the classification of conformal anomalies in gauge theory observables. By systematically extending the study of anomalous conformal Ward identities to this broader class of contours, we aim to deepen the understanding of the geometric and symmetry principles governing Wilson loops in conformal field theories.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the structure of anomalous conformal Ward identities for Wilson loops defined on polygon-like contours whose edges are replaced, in part or in whole, by circular arcs. Our motivation was twofold: to extend the understanding of conformal symmetry breaking effects beyond the well-studied case of piecewise-linear lightlike polygons, and to explore how smooth, curved segments modify both the ultraviolet singularity structure and the functional form of the anomaly. By formulating the problem in terms of a regulated contour and carefully tracking the dependence of the Wilson loop expectation value on the conformal parameters, we have been able to derive explicit Ward identities that capture the interplay between cusps, finite curvature, and global conformal transformations.

Our analysis shows that while the general form of the anomalous Ward identities retains a close kinship with the polygonal case, the introduction of circular edges leads to qualitatively new contributions. In particular, we have found that the conformal anomaly acquires additional terms depending on the radii of curvature of the arcs, which persist even in the limit where these arcs become infinitesimally short. This indicates that the anomaly is sensitive not only to the local cusp angles but also to the curvature distribution along the contour. From the point of view of conformal field theory, this can be interpreted as a manifestation of the fact that local conformal transformations act nontrivially on curved segments, thereby producing integrated contributions that have no analogue for straight edges.

We have also clarified the role of regularization and renormalization in the presence of curved edges. The dimensional regularization scheme, while preserving much of the conformal structure in the absence of anomalies, requires a careful separation between cusp divergences and curvature-induced divergences. In the resulting renormalized Ward identities, the anomalous terms can be organized into a sum over cusps, as in the standard case, plus an integral along each curved segment weighted by a local curvature-dependent coefficient. This decomposition suggests a natural generalization of the cusp anomalous dimension to a “curvature anomalous density,” which may be of independent interest for the study of smooth Wilson loops.

Beyond the formal derivation, we have checked our Ward identities against explicit perturbative calculations at weak coupling in a representative gauge theory. The agreement between the calculated variation under special conformal transformations and the predicted anomaly structure provides strong evidence for the validity of our general expressions. Furthermore, we have argued that similar considerations should apply at strong coupling via the AdS/CFT correspondence, where the minimal surface in AdS space bounded by a contour with circular arcs should encode the same curvature-sensitive anomaly.

The results presented here open several avenues for further investigation. It would be natural to pursue a systematic classification of contour shapes according to their conformal anomaly structure, interpolating between purely polygonal loops and fully smooth curves. Another promising direction is to explore whether the curvature anomalous density admits a universal form across different gauge theories, or whether it carries detailed dynamical information. Finally, the interplay between curvature effects and other sources of conformal symmetry breaking, such as mass scales or background fields, remains largely unexplored. We hope that the framework developed in this work will provide a useful starting point for such studies, and that it will contribute to a more complete understanding of the rich structure of conformal anomalies in gauge-invariant observables.

title: The non-symmetric Wilson polynomials are the Bannai-Ito polynomials
abstract: We establish that the non-symmetric Wilson polynomials, arising in the framework of double affine Hecke algebras of rank one, coincide with the Bannai–Ito polynomials after an explicit parameter transformation. This identification is achieved through a detailed analysis of their recurrence relations, orthogonality properties, and eigenvalue equations. Our results provide a unifying perspective linking these two families, clarifying their place within the Askey scheme and offering new insights into the structure of associated algebraic and spectral problems.
introduction:
The Bannai–Ito polynomials occupy an important position at the top level of the discrete part of the Askey scheme, arising as the \(q \to -1\) limit of the \(q\)-Racah polynomials. They were originally introduced in connection with association schemes and have since appeared in diverse contexts, including representation theory of the orthosymplectic Lie superalgebra \(\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)\) and the study of Leonard pairs. More recently, attention has turned to their “non-symmetric” analogues, which arise naturally in Dunkl-type settings and bear close connections to double affine Hecke algebras (DAHA) of rank one at special parameter values.

On the other hand, the non-symmetric Wilson polynomials form a family of orthogonal polynomials associated with the DAHA of type \((C_1^\vee, C_1)\) in the rational degeneration. These polynomials, depending on four parameters, extend the symmetric Wilson polynomials by relaxing invariance under the reflection operator, and they possess rich algebraic and analytic structures. In particular, they can be described as eigenfunctions of certain Dunkl-type operators and enjoy explicit orthogonality relations with respect to discrete or continuous measures, depending on parameter regimes.

The purpose of this work is to demonstrate that the non-symmetric Wilson polynomials, under a suitable limit transition and parameter identification, coincide with the Bannai–Ito polynomials. This identification provides a unified perspective linking two seemingly different families within the Askey scheme and clarifies the role of Bannai–Ito polynomials within the framework of non-symmetric orthogonal polynomials associated with DAHAs. Our approach reveals structural correspondences in their recurrence relations, eigenvalue equations, and operator realizations, thereby deepening the understanding of both families and suggesting new avenues for generalization.
conclusion:
In this work, we have established a precise correspondence between the non-symmetric Wilson polynomials and the Bannai–Ito polynomials. By analyzing the underlying algebraic structures and recurrence relations, we demonstrated that the non-symmetric Wilson family, originally defined in the framework of double affine Hecke algebras of rank one, admits an explicit transformation into the Bannai–Ito form. This identification relies on a limiting process combined with a reinterpretation of the spectral parameters, revealing that the Bannai–Ito polynomials arise naturally as a degenerate yet structurally rich case of the more general non-symmetric Wilson system.

The equivalence we have shown is not merely formal, but extends to orthogonality properties, difference-reflection operator actions, and explicit bispectrality. This unification clarifies the position of the Bannai–Ito polynomials within the Askey–Wilson scheme and its non-symmetric generalizations, providing a bridge between continuous and discrete orthogonal polynomial theories. Moreover, it deepens the understanding of how certain “−1” limits of \( q \)-polynomials inherit the representation-theoretic and algebraic features of their symmetric and non-symmetric progenitors.

Our results open the way for several further investigations. In particular, the explicit mapping between the two families suggests new interpretations of Bannai–Ito polynomials in harmonic analysis on reflection groups and potential applications in integrable models with discrete symmetries. It would also be of interest to explore multivariate extensions and to examine whether similar correspondences hold for other non-symmetric polynomial families under appropriate degenerations. Overall, the identification presented here contributes to the ongoing effort to unify disparate branches of orthogonal polynomial theory under a common algebraic and analytic framework.

title: Eye-CU: Sleep Pose Classification for Healthcare using Multimodal Multiview Data
abstract: Continuous patient monitoring in intensive care units (ICUs) is critical for timely medical intervention, yet manual observation of patient sleep poses is labor-intensive and prone to human error. This paper presents **Eye-CU**, a novel multimodal, multiview system for automated sleep pose classification in healthcare settings. Eye-CU integrates synchronized RGB, depth, and thermal imaging from multiple camera viewpoints to robustly capture patient postures under challenging conditions such as occlusions, variable lighting, and bedding coverage. We propose a feature fusion framework that combines complementary modalities and viewpoints to enhance classification accuracy. The system is evaluated on a newly collected multimodal dataset of ICU-relevant sleep poses, annotated by clinical experts. Experimental results demonstrate that Eye-CU achieves significant improvements over single-modality and single-view baselines, particularly in scenarios with partial visibility. Our findings indicate that multimodal, multiview integration substantially increases robustness and reliability, enabling real-time, non-intrusive monitoring of patient sleep poses. Eye-CU has the potential to support clinical decision-making, improve patient safety, and reduce the burden on healthcare staff in critical care environments.
introduction:
Sleep is a critical physiological process that plays a central role in physical restoration, cognitive functioning, and emotional well-being. In healthcare settings, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs) and long-term care facilities, monitoring patient sleep is essential for assessing recovery, detecting complications, and improving overall quality of care. Sleep posture, in particular, is a valuable indicator of patient comfort, mobility, and health status. Abnormal or prolonged postures can be early signs of pressure ulcers, respiratory distress, or neurological impairments. Continuous and accurate classification of sleep poses can thus offer caregivers timely insights to intervene and adjust care plans. However, traditional sleep monitoring techniques, such as polysomnography, are intrusive, resource-intensive, and not always feasible for continuous bedside deployment outside specialized sleep laboratories.

Recent advances in computer vision and sensing technologies have opened new possibilities for unobtrusive, automated sleep posture recognition. Vision-based monitoring systems, when integrated into the healthcare environment, can provide non-contact, continuous observation without interfering with patient rest. Yet, the real-world deployment of such systems in clinical environments is challenging due to factors such as varying illumination, occlusion from bedding or medical equipment, and differences in patient body shapes, sizes, and clothing. Moreover, ICUs are highly dynamic environments with frequent caregiver interactions, fluctuating lighting conditions, and the presence of multiple monitoring devices, all of which complicate robust pose classification.

To address these challenges, researchers have explored multimodal and multiview approaches. Multimodal data fusion leverages complementary sensing modalities—such as RGB imagery, depth sensing, infrared imaging, and pressure mapping—to overcome the limitations inherent to any single modality. For example, depth sensors are less sensitive to changes in illumination and can capture structural information about body posture, while infrared cameras are effective for nighttime monitoring without disturbing patients. Multiview systems, which capture data from multiple camera angles, can mitigate occlusions and provide more complete spatial coverage, enabling more reliable pose classification in cluttered or partially obstructed environments. The integration of multimodal and multiview data thus holds promise for achieving high classification accuracy under the challenging conditions present in healthcare settings.

Despite these advantages, the effective use of multimodal, multiview data presents significant research challenges. Data from different sensors and viewpoints often vary in resolution, field of view, and temporal synchronization, requiring sophisticated calibration and fusion strategies. Moreover, the variability in patient positioning, bedding arrangements, and the presence of medical apparatus demands robust feature extraction methods that can generalize across a wide range of conditions. Machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning, have shown strong potential in automatically learning discriminative features from complex, heterogeneous data. However, such models require carefully curated datasets that reflect the diversity and unpredictability of real-world clinical environments—a resource that is still scarce in the domain of sleep pose classification.

In addition to technical challenges, privacy and ethical considerations must be addressed when deploying vision-based monitoring systems in healthcare. The use of RGB imagery raises concerns about identifiable patient information, necessitating privacy-preserving approaches such as using depth or infrared data, anonymization techniques, or on-device processing to minimize the storage and transmission of sensitive visual information. Designing systems that respect patient dignity while delivering actionable insights to caregivers is essential for the widespread adoption of such technologies.

This work presents *Eye-CU*, a novel framework for sleep pose classification tailored for healthcare environments, leveraging multimodal, multiview data to achieve robust performance under real-world ICU conditions. Our approach integrates RGB, depth, and infrared modalities captured from multiple viewpoints to address occlusion, lighting variation, and patient diversity. By employing a deep learning architecture designed for multimodal fusion and spatial-temporal reasoning, *Eye-CU* is capable of accurately classifying a range of clinically relevant sleep poses. We evaluate our method on a dataset collected in a simulated ICU setting that incorporates realistic challenges such as variable lighting, partial occlusions, and diverse subject profiles. Experimental results demonstrate that our multimodal, multiview fusion strategy significantly outperforms single-modality or single-view baselines, underscoring the value of integrated sensing for patient monitoring.

The contributions of this work are threefold: (1) we propose a multimodal, multiview framework for sleep pose classification in healthcare settings; (2) we design and implement a deep learning-based fusion architecture that effectively combines heterogeneous sensor data; and (3) we provide a comprehensive evaluation on a challenging dataset, offering insights into the relative importance of different modalities and views. By addressing both the technical and practical challenges of sleep pose monitoring in ICUs, *Eye-CU* moves toward enabling continuous, unobtrusive patient observation that can enhance clinical decision-making and improve patient outcomes.
conclusion:
This work presented *Eye-CU*, a multimodal, multiview framework for sleep pose classification in healthcare settings, addressing the critical need for accurate, non-intrusive patient monitoring. By integrating RGB, depth, and pressure sensor data across multiple camera viewpoints, the proposed system overcomes common limitations of single-modality or single-view approaches, such as occlusion, lighting variation, and viewpoint dependency. The fusion of complementary sensing modalities, combined with robust feature extraction and classification techniques, enables reliable recognition of a range of patient poses under realistic hospital conditions.

Experimental results demonstrated that the multimodal multiview fusion strategy consistently outperforms unimodal or single-view baselines, achieving high classification accuracy across diverse scenarios, including partial occlusions from medical equipment or bedrails. The system showed strong generalization to different subjects and environmental conditions, highlighting its potential for deployment in real-world clinical environments where variability is inevitable. The results also confirmed that incorporating heterogeneous sensor data not only enhances predictive performance but also increases resilience to sensor failures or data degradation, an important consideration in continuous patient monitoring.

From a clinical perspective, *Eye-CU* supports healthcare providers by enabling automated, round-the-clock pose monitoring, which is essential for preventing complications such as pressure ulcers, detecting abnormal movements, and assessing recovery progress. The system’s non-invasive nature preserves patient comfort, while its scalability allows integration into existing hospital infrastructures without significant workflow disruption. Furthermore, the methodology is adaptable, allowing for extension to other monitoring tasks, such as detecting vital sign changes or other activity patterns relevant to patient care.

While the current study validates the feasibility and effectiveness of multimodal multiview fusion for sleep pose classification, further work is warranted to address remaining challenges. These include optimizing sensor placement for different room layouts, improving real-time processing capabilities, and refining algorithms to handle rare or transitional poses. Additionally, expanding the dataset to include a broader range of patient conditions, demographics, and clinical settings will enhance the robustness and fairness of the system.

In summary, *Eye-CU* contributes a practical and accurate solution to patient pose monitoring by leveraging the strengths of multimodal and multiview data fusion. Its demonstrated performance and adaptability position it as a promising tool for enhancing patient safety, supporting clinical decision-making, and paving the way for more intelligent and responsive healthcare monitoring systems.

title: Reconstruction of attosecond pulses in the presence of interfering dressing fields using the 100 kHz ELI-ALPS HR-1 laser system
abstract: We report on the reconstruction of attosecond pulse trains generated and characterised in the presence of multiple, interfering dressing fields, using the 100 kHz HR-1 laser system at ELI-ALPS. The high repetition rate of the source enables acquisition of high signal-to-noise datasets while preserving sub-cycle temporal resolution. We investigate the influence of controlled dressing fields, temporally and spectrally overlapped with the extreme ultraviolet (XUV) pulses, on standard attosecond pulse characterisation techniques. Interference between the dressing fields modifies both the spectral phase and amplitude of the measured photoelectron spectra, requiring adapted retrieval algorithms. We present a reconstruction methodology that accounts for the coherent superposition of fields and disentangles the contribution of each dressing component. Experimental results are supported by numerical simulations, demonstrating accurate recovery of the attosecond pulse temporal profile despite strong perturbations. This approach enables robust pulse characterisation in complex experimental configurations, extending the applicability of attosecond metrology to scenarios involving multi-colour control fields. Our findings are relevant for ultrafast studies where precise knowledge of the driving and dressing field interplay is essential for interpreting electron dynamics on the attosecond timescale.
introduction:
The generation and characterization of attosecond light pulses has opened unprecedented opportunities for probing and controlling ultrafast electronic dynamics in atoms, molecules, and condensed matter systems. Such pulses, with durations on the order of a few hundred attoseconds or less, enable time-resolved studies of electron motion on its natural timescale, allowing fundamental processes such as photoionization, charge migration, and electron correlation to be examined in real time. The reliable reconstruction of the temporal structure and phase of attosecond pulses is therefore a key prerequisite for advancing attosecond science.

A variety of techniques have been developed for attosecond pulse characterization, including reconstruction methods based on photoelectron spectroscopy, streaking, and interferometric measurements. Among these, attosecond streaking and the reconstruction of attosecond beating by interference of two-photon transitions (RABBITT) have emerged as widely used approaches. Both rely on the interaction of the attosecond pulse train or isolated pulse with a synchronized infrared (IR) or near-infrared (NIR) dressing field, which induces energy shifts in the photoelectron spectrum that carry information about the pulse temporal profile and phase. In idealized scenarios, the dressing field is well-defined and free of significant spatio-temporal distortions, enabling straightforward retrieval of the attosecond pulse characteristics through established inversion algorithms.

In practice, however, experimental conditions often depart from this idealization. The presence of multiple dressing fields, whether arising from intentional experimental design or from spurious reflections, beam-splitter leakage, or nonlinear propagation effects, can lead to complex interference patterns in the measured photoelectron spectra. These interfering dressing fields may differ in polarization, spectrum, phase, or spatial mode, thereby introducing additional modulations in the streaking or sideband signals that complicate the retrieval process. Understanding and mitigating these effects is essential for accurate attosecond pulse reconstruction, especially in state-of-the-art laser facilities where high repetition rates and complex optical arrangements are employed.

The Extreme Light Infrastructure Attosecond Light Pulse Source (ELI-ALPS) provides a unique environment for investigating such challenges. Its High Repetition rate (HR-1) laser system delivers carrier-envelope phase (CEP) stable few-cycle pulses at a repetition rate of 100 kHz, enabling experiments with high statistical precision while maintaining the temporal resolution required for attosecond metrology. The high repetition rate is particularly advantageous for averaging over noise and for systematic studies of subtle interference phenomena, but it also increases the likelihood that weak parasitic fields or residual reflections contribute to the effective dressing field experienced by the target. This makes ELI-ALPS HR-1 an excellent platform for exploring attosecond pulse reconstruction in the presence of interfering dressing fields.

In this work, we address the problem of reconstructing attosecond pulses under such non-ideal conditions. We focus on the effects of multiple, potentially phase-locked or partially coherent dressing fields on the temporal retrieval of attosecond pulse trains generated by high-order harmonic generation (HHG). By combining experimental measurements at the HR-1 beamline with theoretical modeling, we identify characteristic signatures of dressing field interference in the photoelectron spectra and assess their impact on established reconstruction algorithms. We demonstrate that conventional approaches, which assume a single, well-characterized dressing field, may yield significant systematic errors in the retrieved pulse duration and phase in the presence of multiple fields. Furthermore, we propose and validate modified retrieval strategies that incorporate the additional dressing field components into the inversion procedure, thereby restoring accurate pulse characterization.

Our study not only provides practical solutions for experiments at ELI-ALPS and similar facilities but also deepens the understanding of how complex field environments affect attosecond metrology. The insights gained here are relevant to a broad range of ultrafast spectroscopic techniques where interfering fields may be present, including pump–probe experiments with multiple synchronized sources and studies in which higher-order nonlinearities generate unintended radiation. By explicitly accounting for such effects, we enable more reliable extraction of attosecond pulse properties, thereby enhancing the fidelity of ultrafast measurements and the scope of attosecond science.
conclusion: In this work, we have demonstrated the successful reconstruction of attosecond pulses in the presence of interfering dressing fields using the 100 kHz ELI-ALPS HR‑1 laser system. By implementing tailored analysis strategies, we accounted for the complex temporal and spectral modulations introduced by multiple dressing fields, enabling accurate retrieval of the pulse characteristics. The high repetition rate of the HR‑1 source facilitated improved signal-to-noise ratios and robust statistical analysis, supporting reliable reconstruction even under challenging interference conditions. Our results highlight the feasibility of precise attosecond pulse characterization in multi-field environments, paving the way for advanced pump–probe experiments and ultrafast dynamics studies where controlled field interference can be exploited for enhanced temporal resolution and novel spectroscopic capabilities.

title: A la Carte of Correlation Models: Which One to Choose?
abstract: Selecting an appropriate correlation model is critical for accurately capturing dependencies among variables in diverse fields such as finance, engineering, and environmental science. This paper presents a comparative framework for evaluating a broad spectrum of correlation models, ranging from classical Pearson and Spearman measures to advanced copula-based and dynamic correlation approaches. Criteria for selection include data characteristics, underlying assumptions, computational complexity, and interpretability. Through theoretical discussion and empirical illustrations, we highlight trade-offs and practical considerations. The proposed “a la carte” perspective enables researchers and practitioners to tailor correlation model choice to specific analytical contexts, enhancing robustness and insight.
introduction:
In the analysis of multivariate data, the accurate modeling of dependence structures is of central importance across a wide array of disciplines, including finance, insurance, environmental sciences, genomics, and engineering. Correlation models, which aim to capture the strength and nature of relationships between random variables, serve as fundamental tools for understanding complex systems and for making informed predictions. Yet, the seemingly straightforward task of “choosing a correlation model” can be deceptively intricate. The proliferation of available models—ranging from the classical Pearson linear correlation to a variety of rank-based measures, copula-based dependencies, dynamic correlation structures, and high-dimensional shrinkage estimators—has created a landscape in which practitioners must navigate a series of methodological and practical trade-offs. Selecting an appropriate model requires balancing theoretical assumptions, computational feasibility, interpretability, and robustness to data imperfections.

The notion of correlation itself is multifaceted. In its simplest form, correlation is often understood as a scalar summary statistic describing the linear association between two variables. However, real-world data frequently exhibit nonlinear, non-Gaussian, or time-varying dependencies that cannot be adequately captured by the Pearson coefficient alone. This has motivated the development of alternative measures, such as Spearman’s rank correlation, Kendall’s tau, and distance correlation, each of which relaxes certain assumptions or targets particular types of association. Beyond pairwise measures, correlation modeling extends to the estimation of full correlation or covariance matrices, which form the backbone of multivariate statistical analysis, portfolio optimization, and risk management. In these contexts, the choice of model directly influences downstream inference, prediction accuracy, and decision-making quality.

The “à la carte” metaphor is apt for the contemporary state of correlation modeling. Researchers and practitioners are now presented with a menu of models, each with distinct flavors, ingredients, and preparation methods. Some models, such as constant correlation estimators, are simple and computationally convenient, but may fail to capture important structural features of the data. Others, like dynamic conditional correlation (DCC) models or copula-based approaches, offer greater flexibility and the ability to model heterogeneous dependency patterns, but at the cost of increased complexity, data requirements, and parameter uncertainty. High-dimensional applications further complicate matters, as sample covariance matrices become unstable and shrinkage or regularization techniques must be applied to ensure reliable estimation. The “best” choice is rarely universal; instead, it depends on the specific characteristics of the dataset, the research objectives, and the tolerance for model risk.

The consequences of mis-specifying the correlation structure can be substantial. In finance, an underestimation of asset correlations may lead to under-hedged portfolios and unexpected losses during market stress. In environmental modeling, ignoring nonlinear dependencies between climate variables could result in flawed projections and misguided policy recommendations. In bioinformatics, inappropriate correlation measures may obscure biologically meaningful relationships or inflate false discovery rates. These risks underscore the necessity of careful model selection, grounded in both statistical theory and domain knowledge.

Despite the importance of this choice, guidance on selecting among competing correlation models is often fragmented across specialized literatures. Many studies focus narrowly on developing or testing a single model, without situating it in a broader comparative framework. Consequently, practitioners may rely on convention, convenience, or familiarity, rather than on a systematic evaluation of the available options. This paper aims to address this gap by offering a structured overview of correlation models, their assumptions, strengths, and limitations, along with considerations for their application in different empirical contexts. By framing the selection process as an informed choice from an à la carte menu, we emphasize the active role of the analyst in tailoring the model to the problem at hand.

In doing so, we will first review the conceptual foundations of correlation and dependence, clarifying the distinctions between linear and nonlinear association, symmetric and asymmetric dependence, and static versus dynamic correlation structures. We will then survey a range of correlation models, categorizing them according to their statistical underpinnings and their suitability for various data characteristics, such as dimensionality, distributional form, and temporal dynamics. Special attention will be given to the trade-offs between model flexibility and estimation stability, as well as to diagnostic tools for assessing model adequacy. Finally, we will illustrate the practical implications of model choice through empirical examples drawn from diverse application areas.

By synthesizing methodological insights and practical considerations, this work seeks to equip researchers and practitioners with a coherent framework for navigating the rich but sometimes bewildering landscape of correlation models. In an era of abundant data and increasingly complex analytical challenges, the ability to select an appropriate correlation model is not merely a technical detail, but a critical determinant of the validity and impact of statistical analysis.
conclusion:
The comparative analysis of correlation models presented in this study underscores that there is no universally optimal choice; rather, model selection should be guided by the specific characteristics of the data, the research objectives, and the trade-off between interpretability and predictive performance. Classical linear correlation measures, such as Pearson’s coefficient, remain appropriate for settings where relationships are symmetric, continuous, and approximately normally distributed. In contrast, rank-based methods like Spearman’s rho and Kendall’s tau demonstrate greater robustness to nonlinearity and outliers, making them suitable for ordinal data or monotonic but nonlinear associations.  

For more complex dependencies, particularly those involving tail behavior, copula-based approaches offer a flexible framework to disentangle marginal distributions from dependence structures, although they require careful model specification and greater computational resources. Similarly, distance correlation and mutual information measures can capture non-monotonic and higher-order associations, expanding the analytical toolkit for high-dimensional or nonparametric contexts. Nevertheless, these methods may present interpretability challenges for practitioners unfamiliar with their theoretical underpinnings.  

The findings highlight that empirical validation, through simulation or cross-validation, is essential before committing to a correlation model, especially in applied domains where model assumptions are frequently violated. Furthermore, hybrid strategies—combining multiple correlation measures or embedding them within machine learning pipelines—can leverage complementary strengths, though at the cost of increased complexity.  

Ultimately, the choice of correlation model should be viewed as part of a broader inferential or predictive strategy, rather than a purely technical decision. By aligning model capabilities with data properties and analytical goals, researchers can ensure that their correlation assessments are both statistically sound and substantively meaningful. This tailored, a la carte approach empowers analysts to navigate the diverse landscape of correlation models with rigor and adaptability.

title: On the Geometry of Bayesian Graphical Models with Hidden Variables
abstract: We investigate the geometric structure of Bayesian graphical models in the presence of hidden variables, focusing on the algebraic and differential properties of their parameter spaces. By characterizing the singularities induced by marginalization, we reveal how hidden variables affect identifiability and model selection. Our analysis combines tools from algebraic geometry and information geometry to describe parameter equivalence classes and likelihood surfaces. These results provide insight into the complexity of inference and suggest new criteria for model comparison in latent-variable settings.
introduction:
Probabilistic graphical models provide a powerful framework for representing and reasoning about complex stochastic systems. By encoding conditional independence relations among random variables through graph structures, these models enable compact representation of high-dimensional probability distributions and support efficient inference and learning algorithms. Within this framework, Bayesian networks—directed acyclic graphs in which nodes correspond to random variables and edges encode direct probabilistic dependencies—have become a central tool in statistics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. Their appeal lies in the combination of a clear semantic interpretation, grounded in probability theory, with algorithmic techniques for estimation, prediction, and decision-making.

A Bayesian graphical model specifies a parametric family of joint probability distributions subject to independence constraints encoded by the graph. When all variables in the model are observed, the parameter space often admits a simple characterization: it is typically a smooth manifold, possibly with a product or exponential family structure, and can be studied using established tools from statistical theory and differential geometry. In such cases, the asymptotic behavior of estimators, identifiability of parameters, and the geometry of the likelihood function are well understood. However, in many realistic scenarios some variables are not directly observed; they are latent or hidden. These hidden variables may represent unmeasured factors, missing data, or abstract constructs introduced to capture dependencies among observed variables. While latent structure models expand expressiveness and flexibility, they also complicate the statistical and geometric analysis.

The presence of hidden variables fundamentally alters the geometry of the model space. The set of observable distributions obtained by marginalizing over latent variables is often no longer a smooth manifold; instead, it may exhibit singularities, boundaries, and non-identifiable parameterizations. These geometric irregularities have profound implications. They can lead to non-standard asymptotics, where likelihood ratios do not follow chi-squared distributions and maximum likelihood estimators may converge at slower rates. Moreover, they challenge the application of classical tools from information geometry, which rely on regularity assumptions. Understanding the geometry of Bayesian graphical models with hidden variables is therefore essential for both theoretical insight and practical methodology.

This geometric perspective has been explored in a variety of contexts. In algebraic statistics, the set of distributions represented by a graphical model is studied as an algebraic variety or semi-algebraic set, allowing the use of tools from commutative algebra and algebraic geometry to describe its structure. In information geometry, the focus is on the Riemannian metric induced by the Fisher information and the associated affine connections, which capture the curvature and geodesic structure of the model manifold. For models with hidden variables, both approaches reveal that the observable model can have components of different dimensions, intersecting in singular loci, and that the parametrization map from the full model to the observable space can be many-to-one. These features underscore the need for a careful analysis that bridges statistical, geometric, and algebraic viewpoints.

The study of such geometry is not purely of theoretical interest. In practice, hidden-variable models are ubiquitous: mixture models, hidden Markov models, factor analysis, and topic models are only a few prominent examples. The singularities and identifiability issues inherent in these models affect likelihood-based inference, Bayesian posterior behavior, and model selection criteria such as the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). Recent advances have shown that modifications of BIC that take into account the model’s singularities—through quantities like the real log canonical threshold—can yield more accurate asymptotic approximations to the marginal likelihood. These developments illustrate how a deep understanding of the model’s geometric structure can inform improved statistical procedures.

In this work, we investigate the geometry of Bayesian graphical models with hidden variables, with an emphasis on the interplay between the combinatorial structure of the underlying graph and the analytic and algebraic properties of the induced family of observable distributions. We aim to characterize the nature and location of singularities, quantify the dimensions of model components, and explore the consequences for statistical inference. Our approach draws on techniques from algebraic geometry, information geometry, and the theory of semi-algebraic sets, and applies them to classes of models of practical relevance. By elucidating the geometric landscape of these models, we seek to contribute both to the foundational understanding of probabilistic graphical models and to the development of robust inference methods in the presence of latent structure.
conclusion: We have examined the geometric structure of Bayesian graphical models with hidden variables, highlighting how latent components induce nontrivial algebraic and topological features. Our analysis clarifies identifiability boundaries and reveals singularities shaping model complexity. These insights bridge statistical theory and algebraic geometry, offering a foundation for improved inference algorithms and guiding future work on model selection and learning in complex probabilistic systems.

title: Galaxy Zoo: Morphological classification of galaxy images from the Illustris simulation
abstract: We present the results of a morphological classification study of galaxy images generated from the Illustris cosmological simulation, using the citizen science platform Galaxy Zoo. Our aim is to investigate the reliability and statistical properties of visual classifications performed on synthetic data, and to compare them with established trends from observational surveys. A sample of 20,000 galaxies at redshift \( z = 0 \) was selected from the Illustris-1 simulation, rendered in mock optical images with realistic observational effects, including point spread function convolution, noise, and sky background consistent with Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) conditions. These images were classified by Galaxy Zoo volunteers via a decision tree covering basic morphological features such as smoothness, presence of a disk, and signs of disturbance. We analyse the aggregated vote fractions for each morphological category, quantify inter-classifier agreement, and explore correlations with intrinsic galaxy properties such as stellar mass, star formation rate, and kinematics. Our results demonstrate that non-expert classifiers can successfully recover broad morphological distinctions in simulated data, with classification trends broadly consistent with observational Galaxy Zoo results: massive quiescent galaxies are predominantly smooth, while low-mass star-forming systems are more often classified as having disks or irregular features. However, we identify systematic differences, including an overabundance of smooth classifications for intermediate-mass galaxies, potentially linked to differences in the simulated galaxy population or rendering process. This work highlights the potential and limitations of applying citizen science morphological classification to simulated galaxy data, and provides a framework for direct, quantitative comparisons between simulations and observations in the era of large cosmological surveys.
introduction:
Understanding the morphological diversity of galaxies is central to the study of their formation and evolution. Morphology encodes information about a galaxy’s dynamical state, its star formation history, and the influence of environmental processes. Since the pioneering work of Hubble, visual classification has remained a fundamental approach, enabling astronomers to organize galaxies into broad categories such as ellipticals, spirals, and irregulars, and further into subtler morphological subtypes. Such classifications have traditionally relied on human inspection of imaging data, which, while effective, is labor-intensive and subject to biases. The advent of large-scale imaging surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), has dramatically increased the volume of available galaxy images, making traditional expert classification impractical at scale.

Citizen science initiatives, notably Galaxy Zoo, have addressed this challenge by engaging hundreds of thousands of volunteers to visually classify galaxies. This approach has produced large, high-quality morphological catalogues that have enabled a wide range of astrophysical studies, from the role of bars in disk galaxies to the impact of mergers on star formation. The success of Galaxy Zoo and similar projects demonstrates the value of human pattern recognition in astronomy, especially when combined with careful aggregation and debiasing techniques.

Parallel to observational efforts, cosmological hydrodynamical simulations have advanced to the point where they can produce realistic galaxy populations. The Illustris simulation, and its successor IllustrisTNG, model the co-evolution of dark matter, gas, stars, and black holes across cosmic time, yielding synthetic galaxy images that can be directly compared with observations. These simulations provide a controlled laboratory for studying the emergence of morphological features, testing classification methodologies, and linking morphology to underlying physical properties such as stellar mass, kinematics, and merger history.

Despite the potential of simulated datasets, systematic visual classification of simulated galaxies has been less extensively explored than for observational data. Applying the Galaxy Zoo methodology to synthetic images from simulations like Illustris offers several advantages: it enables direct comparison between simulated and observed morphological distributions, facilitates the calibration of automated classification algorithms, and allows investigation into the origins of morphological diversity in a physically consistent context. Moreover, classification of simulated galaxies can help identify discrepancies between simulations and observations, providing valuable feedback for improving subgrid physics models.

In this work, we present morphological classifications of galaxy images generated from the Illustris simulation, obtained through the Galaxy Zoo platform. Volunteers were tasked with examining synthetic images designed to mimic SDSS-like observations, following a decision tree similar to that used in previous Galaxy Zoo projects. We describe the preparation of the simulated dataset, the classification process, and the methods used to aggregate and interpret the volunteer responses. By comparing the morphological trends in the Illustris sample to those measured in real galaxies, we aim to assess the realism of the simulated galaxy population, explore the physical drivers of morphology in the simulation, and lay the groundwork for future studies that integrate citizen science and cosmological simulations.
conclusion: In this work, we have presented morphological classifications of galaxy images from the Illustris simulation using the Galaxy Zoo citizen science framework. By engaging a large number of volunteers, we obtained robust visual assessments that complement automated classification methods and enable detailed comparisons between simulated and observed galaxy populations. Our results demonstrate that simulated galaxies exhibit a wide range of morphologies broadly consistent with those seen in the real Universe, while also revealing subtle discrepancies that can inform future improvements in galaxy formation models. The combination of human visual expertise and high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations offers a powerful approach to understanding the physical drivers of galaxy structure. This study highlights the value of citizen science in bridging simulation and observation, and sets the stage for expanded morphological analyses in forthcoming simulation datasets.

title: Subhalo sinking and off-center massive black holes in dwarf galaxies
abstract: We investigate the orbital decay of dark matter subhalos hosting massive black holes (MBHs) within dwarf galaxies, focusing on the emergence of off-center MBHs. Using high-resolution N-body simulations, we track subhalo sinking driven by dynamical friction and tidal stripping in realistic dwarf galaxy potentials. Our results show that low-mass subhalos often stall at kiloparsec scales, leaving MBHs displaced from the galactic center for gigayear timescales. Such off-center MBHs may evade detection in dynamical surveys and contribute to low-luminosity accretion signatures. We discuss implications for MBH occupation fractions, gravitational wave event rates, and the interpretation of central kinematics in low-mass galaxies.
introduction:
Massive black holes (MBHs) are now believed to reside not only in the centers of massive galaxies but also in a fraction of dwarf galaxies. The occupation fraction, mass distribution, and dynamical state of MBHs in the low-mass regime provide crucial constraints on the formation channels of the first black hole seeds and their subsequent growth. Dwarf galaxies, with their shallow gravitational potentials, low stellar densities, and often irregular morphologies, offer a unique laboratory for investigating these processes. In particular, the dynamical settling of MBHs toward the centers of their host galaxies is not guaranteed. Observations have begun to reveal candidates for off-nuclear MBHs in nearby dwarfs, challenging the common assumption that MBHs always reside at the potential minimum.

In the hierarchical structure formation paradigm of ΛCDM cosmology, dwarf galaxies are assembled through the accretion and merging of smaller systems, including dark matter subhalos. If a subhalo hosts a MBH, the merger process can deliver the MBH into the larger dwarf galaxy. The fate of such an infalling MBH depends on the complex interplay between dynamical friction, tidal stripping, and the structure of the host galaxy. In massive galaxies, the deep potential wells and dense stellar cusps promote rapid orbital decay of inspiraling MBHs toward the center. In dwarfs, however, the low central densities and core-like dark matter profiles inferred in many systems can significantly prolong sinking timescales. This raises the possibility that a substantial fraction of MBHs in dwarfs remain wandering at kiloparsec scales from their host centers for cosmologically significant times.

Theoretical studies have examined the efficiency of dynamical friction in various host environments, noting that cored density profiles in particular can lead to a stalling of inspiral, sometimes referred to as “core stalling.” This effect, coupled with the stripping of the infalling subhalo’s mass, can leave the MBH stranded far from the galactic nucleus. Such off-center MBHs may still retain a bound stellar cluster or compact remnant of their parent subhalo, potentially aiding their detection. The long-lived presence of these objects has implications for gravitational wave event rates, the interpretation of MBH–host scaling relations, and the accretion signatures observed in dwarf galaxies.

Numerical simulations have begun to explore the sinking of MBHs in low-mass systems, but the parameter space relevant to dwarf galaxies remains only partially mapped. Questions remain regarding the role of baryonic feedback in shaping the density profile of the host, the influence of orbital eccentricity and inclination on decay timescales, and the survival of subhalo cores against tidal forces. Moreover, the relative importance of multiple MBHs delivered by successive mergers, and their potential interactions, is not well understood in the dwarf regime.

Observationally, the identification of off-center MBHs is challenging. High-resolution imaging and spectroscopy are required to distinguish them from massive star clusters or supernova remnants. Nevertheless, recent reports of offset active galactic nuclei and compact radio or X-ray sources in dwarfs suggest that wandering MBHs may be more common than previously appreciated. If confirmed, these detections would offer direct evidence for incomplete dynamical settling and the long-term survival of subhalo-delivered MBHs.

In this work, we investigate the sinking of MBHs brought into dwarf galaxies via the accretion of subhalos, focusing on the dynamical conditions that determine whether the MBH reaches the galactic center or remains off-nuclear. Using controlled numerical experiments, we explore a range of host density profiles, subhalo masses, and orbital parameters. Our aim is to quantify the sinking timescales, identify the regimes in which inspiral is stalled, and assess the prevalence and properties of off-center MBHs in dwarf galaxies. By connecting the theory of MBH orbital decay to emerging observational evidence, we seek to clarify the role of subhalo sinking in shaping the demographics and spatial distribution of MBHs in the low-mass galaxy population.
conclusion:
Our investigation of subhalo sinking and the resulting off-center massive black holes (MBHs) in dwarf galaxies demonstrates that dynamical friction, tidal stripping, and the host galaxy’s evolving potential combine to produce long-lived spatial offsets between MBHs and the stellar or gaseous centers of their hosts. Using high-resolution simulations, we find that subhalos containing MBHs frequently stall at kiloparsec-scale radii, particularly in low-mass dwarfs with shallow central density profiles. This stalling is enhanced when the host experiences significant mass loss, either through tidal interactions or stellar feedback, which lowers the central density and reduces the efficiency of dynamical friction.  

Our results imply that a substantial fraction of MBHs in present-day dwarf galaxies may remain displaced from the photometric center over cosmological timescales. Such offsets have important observational consequences: traditional dynamical or accretion-based searches that assume a nuclear location may systematically miss these MBHs. Moreover, the orbital decay timescales we derive are consistent with the persistence of off-center MBHs even in isolated dwarfs, suggesting that their detection is not limited to systems undergoing strong environmental interactions.  

The connection between subhalo sinking and MBH offsets also offers insight into the assembly history of dwarf galaxies. Off-center MBHs may trace past minor mergers, with the remnant subhalo core surviving as a distinct stellar or dark matter overdensity. This scenario provides a potential link between the frequency of off-center MBHs and the merger rate in the low-mass galaxy regime.  

Future observational programs with high spatial resolution and sensitivity, such as those enabled by the James Webb Space Telescope and upcoming extremely large telescopes, will be critical for identifying and characterizing displaced MBHs in dwarfs. Such measurements will test the predictions presented here, constrain the efficiency of dynamical friction in low-density environments, and refine our understanding of black hole–galaxy co-evolution in the least massive galactic systems.

title: The CAST experiment: status and perspectives
abstract: The CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) is a pioneering experiment dedicated to the search for solar axions, hypothetical particles that could solve the strong CP problem in quantum chromodynamics and constitute a component of dark matter. Utilizing a decommissioned LHC test magnet with a strong transverse magnetic field, CAST aims to convert axions into detectable X-ray photons via the Primakoff effect. Since its inception, the experiment has undergone several phases, improving sensitivity through enhanced detectors, extended tracking capabilities, and operation with different buffer gases to probe higher axion masses. Current results have set some of the most stringent limits on the axion–photon coupling over a wide mass range. Ongoing upgrades, including advanced X-ray optics and low-background detectors, promise significant sensitivity gains. Future perspectives involve exploring broader parameter space and contributing to the global effort to detect axion-like particles, thereby advancing our understanding of fundamental physics and cosmology.
introduction:
The CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) is a pioneering experiment dedicated to the search for axions and axion-like particles (ALPs), hypothetical pseudoscalar bosons originally postulated in the context of the Peccei–Quinn solution to the strong CP problem in quantum chromodynamics. Beyond their role in addressing this theoretical challenge, axions are compelling candidates for the dark matter that constitutes a substantial fraction of the Universe’s mass-energy content. In particular, solar axions could be produced in the Sun’s core via the Primakoff effect, whereby thermal photons are converted into axions in the presence of electromagnetic fields generated by plasma constituents.  

CAST exploits the inverse Primakoff effect to reconvert solar axions into detectable X-ray photons as they traverse a strong laboratory magnetic field. The experiment employs a refurbished superconducting LHC prototype dipole magnet, providing a field of up to 9 T over a length of 9.26 m, mounted on a platform capable of tracking the Sun during sunrise and sunset periods. X-ray detectors placed at both ends of the magnet bore record potential photon signals coincident with solar alignment. By scanning over various buffer gas pressures introduced into the magnet bores, CAST is able to extend its sensitivity to higher axion masses through coherent conversion.

Since beginning operation in 2003, CAST has set the most stringent experimental limits on the axion–photon coupling constant for a broad range of masses, surpassing previous helioscope searches. The experiment continues to evolve, with upgrades to detector technology and data acquisition systems, as well as new analysis techniques. These developments enhance sensitivity and broaden the physics reach, providing valuable input to the global effort to explore the axion parameter space and, more generally, to probe physics beyond the Standard Model.
conclusion: The CAST experiment has played a pivotal role in advancing the search for solar axions and axion-like particles, pushing the sensitivity frontier of helioscope techniques. Over its operational phases, CAST has implemented significant technological improvements, from enhanced X-ray detectors and low-background environments to upgraded tracking and magnet systems, enabling more stringent limits on the axion-photon coupling constant over a wide mass range. The most recent results have set some of the strongest laboratory-based constraints to date, complementing astrophysical bounds and informing theoretical axion models. In addition to its primary objectives, CAST has provided a valuable testbed for innovative detector concepts and analysis methods applicable to future axion searches. As the experiment approaches its ultimate sensitivity within current design limits, the lessons learned offer critical guidance for the next generation of helioscope projects, such as the International Axion Observatory (IAXO). With continued international collaboration and technological refinement, the search for axions remains a promising avenue to address fundamental questions in particle physics and cosmology, potentially shedding light on the dark matter puzzle and the strong CP problem.

title: Human cell recovery after microwave irradiation
abstract: Microwave irradiation is increasingly explored for biomedical applications, yet its effects on human cell viability and recovery remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigates the immediate and delayed responses of cultured human epithelial cells following controlled microwave exposure at sub-lethal power levels. Cells were subjected to irradiation for varying durations, and viability, metabolic activity, and membrane integrity were assessed over a 72-hour recovery period. Results demonstrated a transient decline in metabolic activity within the first 6 hours post-irradiation, accompanied by mild membrane perturbations. However, most cultures exhibited substantial recovery by 48 hours, with metabolic rates approaching baseline. Prolonged exposure induced more persistent impairments, suggesting a threshold beyond which recovery is incomplete. These findings provide insight into the temporal dynamics of cellular repair mechanisms following microwave stress and highlight critical parameters for safe biomedical application of microwave technologies.
introduction:
Microwave irradiation has become an increasingly relevant subject of study in the context of biological systems, owing to the ubiquity of microwave-emitting devices in modern life and the expanding application of microwave-based technologies in biomedical research and therapy. Microwaves, defined as electromagnetic waves with frequencies between 300 MHz and 300 GHz, occupy a significant portion of the electromagnetic spectrum and are widely used in communications, industrial processing, and diagnostic and therapeutic medical devices. Although the thermal effects of microwave exposure are well established and have been exploited in procedures such as microwave ablation of tumors, the potential for non-thermal biological effects and the capacity of human cells to recover from microwave-induced damage remain areas of active investigation and debate.

The interaction of microwaves with biological tissue is influenced by several factors, including frequency, power density, exposure duration, and the dielectric properties of the target material. At sufficient intensities, microwaves can induce dielectric heating, leading to thermal stress, protein denaturation, and membrane disruption. However, even at lower power levels where bulk heating is minimal, microwaves may still influence cellular processes through mechanisms that are not yet fully understood. These may include perturbations of membrane potential, modulation of ion channel activity, and alterations in intracellular signaling cascades. Understanding the full spectrum of microwave–cell interactions is critical for assessing potential health risks and for developing safe and effective biomedical applications.

Cellular recovery after microwave exposure involves a coordinated series of events that aim to restore homeostasis and repair damaged structures. Depending on the severity and nature of the insult, cells may activate stress response pathways, upregulate heat shock proteins, initiate DNA repair mechanisms, or engage in autophagic processes to remove irreversibly damaged components. In cases where damage is too extensive, programmed cell death pathways such as apoptosis may be triggered to prevent the propagation of compromised cells. The balance between successful recovery and progression to cell death is influenced by cell type, physiological state, and the surrounding microenvironment.

Despite the practical importance of these processes, systematic studies on recovery dynamics in human cells following microwave irradiation remain relatively limited. Much of the existing literature has focused either on acute cytotoxicity or on long-term epidemiological associations, without detailed examination of the temporal sequence of cellular repair responses. Furthermore, studies often differ widely in their experimental parameters—such as microwave frequency, modulation pattern, power output, and exposure duration—making direct comparisons and generalizations challenging. This lack of standardization underscores the need for carefully controlled experimental models that can isolate specific factors and evaluate their impact on recovery outcomes.

In recent years, advances in live-cell imaging, molecular profiling, and high-throughput screening have opened new possibilities for dissecting the mechanisms of cellular recovery at high temporal and spatial resolution. For example, fluorescence-based reporters can track the activation of stress-responsive transcription factors in real time, while omics approaches can reveal global changes in gene expression, protein abundance, or metabolite levels after exposure. These tools enable a more nuanced understanding of how human cells detect and respond to microwave-induced perturbations, and how the efficiency of recovery may vary among different cell types or under different environmental conditions.

The relevance of such research extends beyond basic science, as microwave irradiation is increasingly incorporated into therapeutic strategies. Microwave hyperthermia, for example, is used to sensitize cancer cells to chemotherapy or radiotherapy, exploiting their reduced capacity for recovery compared to normal cells. Conversely, in regenerative medicine and tissue engineering, it is important to ensure that any microwave-based processing steps do not irreversibly impair cell viability or function. Moreover, with the proliferation of wireless communication technologies and the growing public concern about potential health effects of chronic low-level exposure, there is a pressing societal interest in understanding whether and how human cells can recover from such exposures.

The present study aims to address these gaps by examining the recovery kinetics of cultured human cells following controlled microwave irradiation. By systematically varying exposure parameters and assessing multiple markers of cellular stress and viability over defined time intervals, we seek to elucidate the relationship between the extent of initial damage and the efficiency of subsequent repair. Through this approach, we hope to contribute to a clearer understanding of the biological implications of microwave exposure and to provide an empirical basis for both safety guidelines and the rational design of microwave-based biomedical interventions.
conclusion: Our findings indicate that human cells exhibit partial recovery following microwave irradiation, with viability depending on exposure parameters. While short, low-intensity treatments caused reversible effects, prolonged or high-intensity exposure led to significant damage. These results highlight the importance of optimizing irradiation conditions to minimize cellular harm and support potential biomedical applications.

title: Fusion of stereo and still monocular depth estimates in a self-supervised learning context
abstract: We present a self-supervised framework that fuses depth estimates from stereo image pairs and single-view monocular cues to improve accuracy and robustness in diverse scenes. While stereo-based methods excel in textured regions with sufficient baseline, they degrade in low-texture or occluded areas; conversely, monocular methods leverage learned priors to infer plausible depth where stereo fails but lack geometric grounding. Our approach integrates both modalities within a unified network, trained end-to-end using photometric reconstruction losses without ground-truth depth. A confidence-guided fusion module adaptively weights stereo and monocular predictions at the pixel level. Experiments on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses individual stereo-only and monocular-only baselines, particularly in challenging regions. This work highlights the complementary nature of stereo geometry and monocular priors in self-supervised depth estimation and offers a pathway toward more reliable depth perception in unconstrained environments.
introduction:
Depth estimation is a fundamental problem in computer vision, underpinning a wide range of downstream tasks such as autonomous navigation, scene understanding, augmented reality, and robotic manipulation. Accurate recovery of scene geometry from visual inputs enables machines to interact with their environment in a safe, efficient, and intelligent manner. Traditionally, depth can be inferred from multiple modalities, including stereo vision, where depth arises from geometric triangulation between synchronized camera views, and monocular vision, where depth is predicted from a single image by exploiting learned priors. Each approach presents distinct advantages and limitations: stereo methods are grounded in well-established geometric principles and can deliver metric depth without explicit learning, but their performance deteriorates in textureless regions, under occlusions, or in low-light conditions. Monocular methods, particularly those based on deep learning, are capable of inferring plausible depth even in challenging conditions by leveraging semantic and contextual cues, but they are prone to scale ambiguity and may generalize poorly outside their training distribution.

Recent advances in self-supervised learning have significantly expanded the scope of monocular and stereo depth estimation. Self-supervised frameworks eliminate the need for costly ground truth depth annotations by formulating view synthesis as a supervisory signal, typically using photometric reconstruction losses between observed and synthesized images. For monocular settings, sequences from a moving camera provide the temporal parallax necessary to learn depth and ego-motion jointly; for stereo settings, rectified stereo pairs offer a known baseline that constrains depth prediction. These paradigms have yielded competitive results compared to supervised methods, while greatly easing data collection requirements. Nevertheless, most self-supervised approaches treat stereo and monocular learning separately, failing to exploit the complementary strengths that could emerge from their fusion.

The fusion of stereo and monocular depth estimation holds particular promise. Stereo depth prediction benefits from metric scale and robustness in well-textured regions, while monocular estimation can fill in gaps where stereo fails, such as in low-texture or occluded regions. Furthermore, monocular methods can operate when stereo baselines are unavailable, providing continuity of depth perception. Combining the two modalities in a unified framework could produce depth maps that are more accurate, complete, and robust than either modality alone. However, integrating stereo and monocular cues is non-trivial, particularly in a self-supervised setting. The different nature of the cues—geometric triangulation versus learned semantic inference—means that their respective error modes, confidence levels, and spatial resolutions differ. Effective fusion therefore requires strategies for reconciling these differences, weighting contributions appropriately, and preserving the benefits of both modalities without amplifying their weaknesses.

Several recent works have begun to explore multi-cue fusion for depth estimation, often in supervised contexts or with additional sensors such as LiDAR to provide ground truth supervision. In contrast, the self-supervised fusion of stereo and still monocular depth estimates remains relatively underexplored. In this setting, the challenge is to design loss functions, architectures, and fusion mechanisms that can jointly train on heterogeneous inputs without explicit depth labels. Temporal information, available in video sequences, can be exploited for monocular self-supervision, while stereo pairs can provide a metric constraint. A unified model must learn to integrate these constraints coherently, balancing spatial consistency, temporal stability, and photometric accuracy.

Moreover, the fusion problem can be approached not only at the level of training but also at inference time. One can envisage a system where separate stereo and monocular networks are trained self-supervisedly and their outputs combined post hoc, for example via learned confidence maps, probabilistic fusion, or optimization-based refinement. Alternatively, a single architecture could be designed to ingest both stereo and monocular inputs and produce a fused depth map in one forward pass. Each approach presents trade-offs in terms of accuracy, computational cost, and adaptability to varying input availability.

In this work, we investigate the fusion of stereo and still monocular depth estimates within a purely self-supervised learning framework. We aim to leverage the complementary strengths of each modality to produce dense, accurate depth maps without reliance on ground truth depth annotations. Our contributions are threefold: first, we propose a fusion strategy that combines independently trained self-supervised stereo and monocular depth predictions through a learned confidence-based weighting scheme; second, we demonstrate that our approach significantly improves depth estimation performance over either modality alone, particularly in challenging regions; third, we provide an extensive evaluation on standard benchmarks, analyzing the impact of fusion under varying scene conditions and input configurations. By bridging the gap between stereo and monocular self-supervised depth estimation, our approach opens the door to more versatile and robust depth perception systems suitable for real-world applications where sensor configurations and environmental conditions may vary dynamically.
conclusion:
This work has investigated the fusion of stereo-based and still monocular depth estimates within a self-supervised learning framework, with the goal of exploiting the complementary strengths of these two paradigms. While stereo depth estimation benefits from explicit geometric constraints and can provide metrically accurate measurements in regions with adequate texture and disparity, it often struggles in textureless areas, occluded regions, or over large baselines. Conversely, still monocular depth estimation, trained in a self-supervised manner from monocular sequences, can infer plausible depth in challenging regions by leveraging learned scene priors, yet suffers from scale ambiguity and may lack metric accuracy. Our approach has demonstrated that these modalities, when combined appropriately, can yield depth maps that are both more accurate and more complete than those produced by either method in isolation.

We have shown that a fusion strategy, informed by confidence measures derived from each modality, enables the system to select or blend depth values in a way that preserves the high-fidelity geometry of stereo where it is reliable, while filling in its failure cases with the contextually plausible predictions of monocular inference. The proposed self-supervised training regime allows the network to learn to reconcile these sources without requiring dense ground truth depth, thus maintaining scalability and applicability to diverse environments. The design of the fusion module, together with the joint optimization scheme, has proven effective in aligning the scale and distribution of the monocular estimates with stereo outputs, mitigating inconsistencies that could otherwise hinder performance.

Extensive experimental results on benchmark datasets have confirmed that this fusion approach consistently outperforms standalone stereo or monocular baselines in terms of both quantitative error metrics and qualitative perceptual quality. Notably, the improvements are most pronounced in regions that are inherently challenging for stereo matching, such as reflective surfaces, repetitive patterns, or low-texture expanses, where monocular predictions contribute valuable structural cues. At the same time, the incorporation of stereo constraints helps anchor the monocular estimates to physically plausible scales, reducing the drift and distortion that can arise in purely monocular self-supervised frameworks.

Beyond the immediate performance gains, this work underscores the broader principle that heterogeneous depth cues can be synergistically integrated in a learning-based setting, even when each cue is itself learned without supervision from ground truth.
