The results suggest that self-supervised fusion can serve as a powerful paradigm for leveraging the diversity of available sensory modalities in robotics, autonomous driving, and augmented reality, where robustness to environmental variability is critical.

Future research directions include extending the fusion framework to incorporate additional cues such as sparse LiDAR, event cameras, or semantic priors, which could further enhance performance in adverse conditions. Moreover, exploring adaptive, context-aware fusion policies that dynamically adjust the weighting of each modality in response to scene content and estimated uncertainty may yield further gains. Finally, investigating lightweight architectures and efficient training schemes will be important for deploying such systems on resource-constrained platforms. In summary, the fusion of stereo and still monocular depth estimates in a self-supervised context offers a promising avenue toward more accurate, robust, and versatile depth perception systems.

title: Beyond Road Extraction: A Dataset for Map Update using Aerial Images
abstract: Timely and accurate map updates are essential for navigation, urban planning, and disaster response. While recent advances in computer vision have improved road extraction from aerial imagery, existing datasets focus primarily on detecting road networks, overlooking broader map update needs such as identifying newly constructed, modified, or removed structures. We introduce a novel dataset specifically designed to support comprehensive map update tasks using high-resolution aerial images. The dataset includes temporally paired imagery and corresponding vector map annotations, enabling detection of diverse change types beyond roads, including buildings, open spaces, and other man-made features. It covers varied geographic regions, seasons, and imaging conditions to promote robust model generalization. To establish benchmarks, we evaluate multiple state-of-the-art change detection and segmentation models on our dataset, highlighting challenges in multi-class change detection from aerial views. By bridging the gap between road-centric datasets and the broader requirements of map maintenance, our work provides a valuable resource for advancing automated, scalable, and accurate map updating methods.
introduction:
In recent years, the rapid growth of urban areas, the continuous development of transportation networks, and the increasing frequency of natural and anthropogenic changes to landscapes have highlighted the need for timely and accurate map updates. Traditional mapping approaches, which often rely on labor-intensive field surveys or manual interpretation of high-resolution imagery, are costly, time-consuming, and inherently limited in scalability. The proliferation of aerial imagery, captured by manned aircraft, drones, and satellites, offers an unprecedented opportunity to automate the map update process by leveraging advances in computer vision and machine learning. However, most existing research in this domain has focused narrowly on road extraction as a proxy for map updating, overlooking the broader range of map elements and the contextual information necessary for comprehensive and reliable updates.

Road extraction has indeed been a central task in remote sensing and photogrammetry, due to the critical role of road networks in navigation, urban planning, and disaster response. Numerous datasets have been introduced to train and evaluate algorithms for detecting and delineating roads from aerial and satellite images. While these benchmarks have driven significant progress, they often fail to capture the complexity of real-world map maintenance scenarios. In practice, updating a map involves not only adding or removing roads, but also detecting new buildings, changes in land use, alterations in road geometry, and the emergence or disappearance of other cartographic features. A dataset tailored exclusively to road extraction is therefore insufficient for developing and evaluating systems intended for end-to-end, automated map updating.

Another key limitation of existing datasets is their lack of temporal dimension. Map updates inherently require comparing the current state of the world to an existing representation, often in the form of a previously collected map or an earlier image. Temporal aerial datasets that explicitly link imagery to corresponding map data are rare, and those that do exist tend to be small in scale, geographically limited, or not publicly available due to licensing restrictions. Without temporally aligned image–map pairs, it is challenging to design algorithms that can detect meaningful changes and distinguish them from noise, seasonal variations, or imaging artifacts.

In addition, the diversity of environments represented in publicly available datasets remains limited. Many benchmarks are biased toward urban areas with well-defined infrastructure, whereas rural regions, informal settlements, and transitional landscapes are underrepresented. This lack of diversity hampers the generalization of trained models and limits their applicability to global-scale mapping tasks. Furthermore, the absence of standardized evaluation protocols for map update tasks makes it difficult to compare methods and measure progress in a consistent manner.

To address these gaps, we introduce a new dataset specifically designed for the broader task of map updating using aerial images. Our dataset goes beyond road extraction by including multiple map feature types, temporal image–map pairs, and diverse geographic contexts. By providing both historical and recent aerial imagery aligned with vector map data, it enables the development and rigorous evaluation of algorithms capable of detecting, classifying, and integrating changes into existing maps. We anticipate that this resource will foster research toward more holistic and automated mapping solutions, ultimately contributing to faster, more accurate, and more globally inclusive map updates.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced a novel dataset designed to advance research on map updating from aerial imagery, moving beyond traditional road extraction tasks. Our dataset captures diverse scenarios, including road network changes, new constructions, and altered landscapes, enabling the development of models that address real-world mapping challenges. By incorporating both temporal and spatial variations, it supports robust evaluation of change detection and map alignment methods. We believe this resource will foster progress in automated cartography, supporting applications in navigation, urban planning, and disaster response. Future work will explore broader geographic coverage, multi-modal data integration, and benchmarks for end-to-end map update pipelines.

title: The clustering amplitude of X-ray selected AGN at z=0.8: Evidence for a negative dependence on accretion luminosity
abstract: We investigate the large-scale clustering properties of X-ray selected active galactic nuclei (AGN) at intermediate redshift, focusing on the dependence of clustering amplitude on accretion luminosity. Our sample comprises 482 AGN drawn from a combination of deep and wide X-ray surveys, with robust spectroscopic or high-quality photometric redshifts in the range \(0.6 < z < 1.0\). X-ray luminosities span \(10^{42} < L_{\mathrm{X}}(2-10 \ \mathrm{keV}) < 10^{45} \ \mathrm{erg \ s^{-1}}\), enabling a direct comparison between moderate- and high-luminosity accretors. We compute the projected two-point correlation function \(w_p(r_p)\) for subsamples divided by \(L_{\mathrm{X}}\), modelling the results with a halo occupation distribution framework to derive the bias parameter and typical dark matter halo masses. The full sample exhibits a bias \(b = 1.65 \pm 0.15\), corresponding to a characteristic halo mass of \(\log (M_{\mathrm{h}}/h^{-1} M_\odot) \approx 12.8\). However, we detect a statistically significant trend in which lower-luminosity AGN cluster more strongly than their higher-luminosity counterparts. AGN with \(L_{\mathrm{X}} < 10^{43.5} \ \mathrm{erg \ s^{-1}}\) reside in halos of mass \(\log M_{\mathrm{h}} \approx 13.2\), whereas those with \(L_{\mathrm{X}} > 10^{44} \ \mathrm{erg \ s^{-1}}\) are found in halos of \(\log M_{\mathrm{h}} \approx 12.4\). This negative luminosity dependence of the clustering amplitude is robust against sample selection effects and redshift evolution within our range. Our findings suggest that the most luminous AGN at \(z \sim 0.8\) are preferentially hosted by lower-mass halos, possibly reflecting differences in triggering mechanisms, gas supply, or evolutionary stage relative to moderate-luminosity systems. These results provide new constraints on the connection between black hole growth and large-scale environment at cosmic noon.
introduction:
Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are among the most luminous persistent sources in the Universe, powered by accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs). They play a central role in galaxy evolution through feedback processes that regulate star formation and influence the growth of their host galaxies. Understanding the large-scale environments of AGN provides key insights into the connection between black hole accretion and the underlying dark matter distribution. Clustering measurements, in particular, yield estimates of the typical dark matter halo (DMH) masses that host AGN, thereby constraining models of SMBH fueling and co-evolution with galaxies.  

Previous studies of AGN clustering have employed samples selected at optical, infrared, radio, and X-ray wavelengths, often revealing that moderate-luminosity AGN reside in halos of mass ∼10¹²–10¹³ h⁻¹ M☉. However, the dependence of clustering strength on accretion luminosity remains debated. Optical quasar surveys have reported a weak or absent luminosity dependence at z ≲ 2, whereas results from X-ray selected samples have been more mixed, in part due to limited sample sizes and heterogeneous selection. X-ray surveys are particularly valuable for this investigation, as they provide a relatively unbiased census of AGN activity across a wide range of obscuration and accretion rates.  

In this work, we present a clustering analysis of X-ray selected AGN at redshift z ≈ 0.8, drawn from a large-area, homogeneous survey. We investigate the relationship between clustering amplitude and X-ray luminosity, focusing on whether more luminous AGN inhabit more massive dark matter halos, as predicted by simple halo occupation models, or whether an inverse trend is present. Our results point to evidence for a negative dependence of clustering strength on accretion luminosity, challenging prevailing assumptions about the link between AGN power and environment, and offering new constraints on the triggering mechanisms of black hole growth.
conclusion:
We have presented a measurement of the clustering properties of X-ray selected active galactic nuclei (AGN) at a median redshift of \( z \approx 0.8 \), based on a large, homogeneous sample with well-constrained spectroscopic redshifts and robust X-ray luminosities. By splitting the sample into bins of accretion luminosity, we investigated the dependence of the AGN clustering amplitude on intrinsic X-ray power. Our analysis reveals a statistically significant trend in which lower-luminosity AGN exhibit stronger large-scale clustering, corresponding to host dark matter haloes of higher typical mass, compared to their higher-luminosity counterparts.  

This negative correlation between clustering strength and accretion luminosity contrasts with the predictions of simple models in which higher-luminosity AGN are associated with more massive haloes and denser environments. Instead, our findings support a scenario in which distinct fuelling mechanisms dominate in different halo mass regimes. In massive haloes, AGN activity may be sustained primarily through the accretion of hot gas or through stochastic processes within group or cluster environments, leading to lower instantaneous accretion rates. Conversely, high-luminosity AGN in less massive haloes could be triggered more efficiently by processes such as major mergers or cold gas inflows, which are more prevalent in lower-density environments at this redshift.  

The observed luminosity dependence also aligns with the notion of two broad AGN modes: a “maintenance” or low-Eddington mode in rich environments and a “quasar” or high-Eddington mode in less massive haloes. These results are consistent with previous optical and X-ray clustering studies that have hinted at a complex, non-monotonic relationship between AGN luminosity and host halo mass, but our work provides stronger statistical evidence in the intermediate-redshift regime.  

Future progress will benefit from larger, deeper X-ray surveys with extensive spectroscopic follow-up, enabling finer binning in both luminosity and redshift, as well as improved constraints on halo occupation distributions. Incorporating multi-wavelength data to probe host galaxy properties will also help disentangle the roles of environment, stellar mass, and fuelling mechanism. Our results highlight the importance of considering luminosity-dependent clustering in models of black hole growth and its connection to large-scale structure, and they suggest that the link between AGN power and environment is more nuanced than previously assumed.

title: First time-series optical photometry from Antarctica
abstract: We present the first time-series optical photometry obtained from Antarctica, demonstrating the unique capabilities of the polar environment for continuous high-precision observations. Using a dedicated instrument at Dome A, we monitored selected stellar fields over several weeks during the austral winter. The exceptionally stable atmospheric conditions and extended darkness enabled uninterrupted light curves with millimagnitude precision. Our data reveal new variable stars and provide improved parameters for known systems. These results confirm Antarctica’s potential for long-duration photometric monitoring, supporting future large-scale surveys from the continent to address key questions in stellar variability, exoplanet detection, and time-domain astrophysics.
introduction: Antarctica offers unique advantages for ground-based astronomical observations, including prolonged periods of darkness during the austral winter, exceptionally low atmospheric water vapor, and a stable atmosphere that can provide superior seeing conditions. These factors make the Antarctic plateau an ideal site for high-precision optical and infrared photometry. While previous astronomical studies from Antarctica have focused primarily on site testing, infrared observations, and cosmic microwave background measurements, time-series optical photometry has remained largely unexplored due to logistical and technical challenges. Continuous monitoring of stellar brightness variations is a powerful tool for studying variable stars, detecting exoplanets via transits, and probing stellar oscillations. Such observations benefit greatly from uninterrupted coverage, which is difficult to achieve at temperate latitudes due to the day-night cycle and weather interruptions. The extended polar night at Antarctic stations presents an unparalleled opportunity for high-duty-cycle time-series measurements. Here, we present the first dedicated time-series optical photometry obtained from Antarctica, demonstrating both the feasibility and scientific potential of such observations. We describe the observing site, instrumentation, and data reduction procedures, and we assess the quality of the photometric time-series. These results establish a foundation for future Antarctic optical astronomy programs aimed at continuous, high-precision monitoring of astrophysical phenomena.
conclusion:
The time-series optical photometry presented here constitutes the first such dataset obtained from an Antarctic site, demonstrating both the feasibility and the scientific potential of conducting high-precision time-domain astronomy from the continent. Over the course of the observing campaign, we obtained continuous, high-cadence measurements under uniquely stable atmospheric conditions, resulting in photometric precision comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, that achieved at premier mid-latitude observatories. These results validate the suitability of the Antarctic plateau for extended monitoring of variable and transient sources, particularly in optical bands where low sky brightness and exceptional seeing can be exploited.  

The stability of the light curves and the low photometric scatter underscore the advantages of the site’s prolonged periods of darkness, reduced scintillation noise, and minimal weather interruptions. Our analysis further illustrates that the logistical challenges of operating in such an environment can be overcome with robust instrumentation and autonomous data acquisition strategies. The successful deployment and operation of the photometric system provide a framework for future Antarctic facilities dedicated to time-domain studies.

From a scientific perspective, the data quality enabled the detection of subtle flux variations and periodicities that would be difficult to capture from more temperate sites. This capability opens the door to a wide range of astrophysical investigations, including exoplanet transit searches, asteroseismology, and the monitoring of variable stars and transient events, with improved temporal coverage and sensitivity to low-amplitude signals.

Looking ahead, expanding the temporal baseline and spectral coverage of Antarctic photometry will further enhance its impact. Multi-season campaigns, complemented by simultaneous observations at other wavelengths, will allow for comprehensive characterization of astrophysical phenomena. Moreover, integration with global networks of telescopes could mitigate the gaps inherent to any single-site operation, while leveraging Antarctica’s unique observational advantages.

In summary, this work demonstrates that Antarctica offers a world-class platform for high-precision, time-resolved optical astronomy. The success of this pioneering experiment not only establishes a proof of concept for sustained photometric monitoring from the continent, but also points toward a future where Antarctic observatories play a central role in the global time-domain astronomy effort.

title: Physical conditions in potential sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays: Updated Hillas plot and radiation-loss constraints
abstract: We present an updated assessment of physical conditions in potential astrophysical accelerators of ultra‑high‑energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), combining the classical Hillas criterion with constraints from radiation losses. Using recent observational data, we refine size–magnetic field parameter space estimates for candidate sources, including active galactic nuclei, gamma‑ray bursts, and galaxy clusters. We incorporate synchrotron and inverse Compton loss limits to identify the maximum achievable particle energies under realistic conditions. The resulting updated Hillas plot highlights viable regions for proton and heavy‑nuclei acceleration. Our analysis narrows the range of plausible UHECR sources and provides improved guidance for future multi‑messenger observations.
introduction:
Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs), with energies exceeding \(10^{18}\) eV, remain among the most enigmatic phenomena in high-energy astrophysics. Despite decades of observational and theoretical effort, their origin, acceleration mechanisms, and propagation effects are not fully understood. The extreme energies involved imply that their sources must host environments with exceptional physical conditions, capable of confining and accelerating charged particles to energies approaching or exceeding \(10^{20}\) eV. Identifying such environments requires combining constraints from particle acceleration theory with observationally inferred source properties.

A widely used tool for assessing the feasibility of candidate UHECR sources is the Hillas plot, which represents the magnetic field strength \(B\) and size scale \(R\) of astrophysical objects, and delineates the parameter space in which confinement of particles of a given rigidity is possible. In its simplest form, the Hillas criterion follows from the requirement that the particle gyroradius not exceed the size of the acceleration region. This geometric constraint, however, is necessary but not sufficient: in realistic astrophysical environments, energy losses due to synchrotron radiation, inverse Compton scattering, photo-hadronic interactions, and adiabatic expansion can significantly limit the maximum attainable energy.

Recent observational advances — including high-resolution radio, optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray measurements of active galactic nuclei (AGN), gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), and large-scale structure shocks — have refined estimates of \(B\) and \(R\) for many candidate sources. At the same time, progress in multimessenger astronomy, particularly the detection of high-energy neutrinos and improved UHECR composition measurements, provides additional constraints on the physical conditions within acceleration sites. These developments motivate an updated examination of the Hillas parameter space, incorporating not only the geometric confinement condition but also the competing effects of acceleration and radiation-loss timescales.

In this work, we revisit the Hillas plot in light of current observational data, and systematically apply radiation-loss constraints to identify physically plausible regions for UHECR acceleration. We consider several representative acceleration mechanisms — including diffusive shock acceleration, shear acceleration, and unipolar induction — and evaluate the maximum energies attainable for different particle species under realistic source conditions. Our analysis highlights the interplay between magnetic field strength, source size, and loss processes, and its implications for the viability of various astrophysical objects as UHECR sources. By combining updated source parameters with refined theoretical limits, we aim to provide a more stringent framework for interpreting present and future UHECR observations, and to guide the search for their most promising astrophysical accelerators.
conclusion: Our updated Hillas plot, incorporating radiation-loss constraints, refines the parameter space for potential ultra-high-energy cosmic ray sources. The results highlight stringent physical conditions required for acceleration, reducing viable candidates and guiding future observational and theoretical efforts to identify the most plausible astrophysical accelerators.

title: Automated Machine Learning for Deep Recommender Systems: A Survey
abstract: Deep recommender systems have achieved remarkable success in delivering personalized content across diverse domains. However, their design involves numerous architectural, hyperparameter, and feature engineering choices, often requiring extensive expert intervention. Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) offers promising solutions by automating these stages, enabling more efficient and accessible model development. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of AutoML techniques applied to deep recommender systems, covering search spaces, optimization strategies, and evaluation protocols. We categorize existing methods into architecture search, hyperparameter optimization, and automated feature engineering, highlighting their contributions and limitations. Furthermore, we discuss challenges unique to recommender settings, including scalability, dynamic data, and cold-start problems. Finally, we outline future research directions toward more adaptive, resource-efficient, and interpretable automated recommendation pipelines, aiming to bridge the gap between AutoML research and practical large-scale recommender system deployment.
introduction:
Recommender systems have become an indispensable component of modern online services, shaping user experiences in domains such as e-commerce, media streaming, social media, and personalized information retrieval. By filtering and ranking large volumes of items according to inferred user preferences, these systems address the problem of information overload and improve user engagement. Over the past decade, deep learning has emerged as a dominant paradigm for building recommender systems, owing to its ability to automatically learn high-level feature representations from complex, heterogeneous data sources. Deep recommender systems leverage architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), attention mechanisms, and graph neural networks (GNNs) to capture intricate user–item interactions, temporal dynamics, and contextual factors. However, the design of effective deep recommender models remains a challenging and resource-intensive process, requiring expertise in model architecture, feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, and training strategies.

Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) aims to alleviate these challenges by automating various stages of the machine learning pipeline, including data preprocessing, feature selection, model selection, architecture search, and hyperparameter optimization. In the context of deep recommender systems, AutoML offers the potential to democratize the development process, enabling practitioners without extensive machine learning expertise to build high-performance models, while also allowing experts to explore larger search spaces more efficiently. The integration of AutoML into recommender system development can address several persistent issues: the high cost of manual trial-and-error design, the difficulty of adapting models to different domains or data distributions, and the need for scalable, reproducible workflows.

The application of AutoML to deep recommender systems introduces unique opportunities and challenges. Unlike standard supervised learning tasks, recommendation often involves implicit feedback, highly sparse user–item interaction matrices, and the need to optimize ranking-based objectives rather than simple classification accuracy. Moreover, recommendation scenarios frequently operate under strict latency constraints and require continuous model updates to reflect evolving user preferences. Consequently, AutoML techniques must be adapted to handle these domain-specific characteristics, balancing predictive performance with computational efficiency and model interpretability. Emerging approaches have explored neural architecture search (NAS) to discover novel deep recommendation architectures, meta-learning to enable rapid adaptation to new recommendation tasks, and automated feature engineering to construct informative user and item representations from multimodal data.

Despite growing interest, research on AutoML for deep recommender systems remains fragmented, with studies often focusing on isolated components such as hyperparameter tuning or architecture search, without a comprehensive view of the full automation pipeline. Furthermore, the interaction between AutoML methods and core recommendation challenges—such as cold start, data sparsity, scalability, and fairness—has yet to be systematically examined. A consolidated survey of the state of the art is therefore essential to map the existing landscape, identify promising directions, and highlight gaps in current approaches.

This survey aims to provide a structured and comprehensive overview of Automated Machine Learning techniques applied to deep recommender systems. We begin by outlining the fundamentals of deep recommendation models and the AutoML paradigm, establishing a common vocabulary and conceptual framework. We then categorize existing work according to the stages of the AutoML process, including data preprocessing automation, automated feature engineering, hyperparameter optimization, and neural architecture search, with an emphasis on how these techniques are tailored to recommendation-specific requirements. We also examine evaluation methodologies, benchmark datasets, and performance metrics, discussing their suitability for automated approaches. Finally, we identify open challenges—such as handling dynamic environments, optimizing for multiple objectives, ensuring fairness and transparency, and reducing computational cost—and suggest future research directions.

By synthesizing and analyzing the literature, this work seeks to guide both researchers and practitioners in understanding the current capabilities and limitations of AutoML in the realm of deep recommender systems, fostering further innovation at the intersection of automation and personalized recommendation.
conclusion: This survey has reviewed recent advances in automated machine learning techniques for deep recommender systems, highlighting developments in architecture search, hyperparameter optimization, and feature engineering. We have examined how AutoML can reduce manual effort, improve model performance, and adapt to dynamic user-item environments. Despite promising progress, challenges remain in scalability, interpretability, and integration with real-world recommendation pipelines. Future research should focus on efficient search strategies, better handling of sparse and streaming data, and combining domain knowledge with automation to balance performance and transparency, ultimately enabling more accurate, adaptive, and trustworthy recommender systems.

title: Clock Auto-synchronizing Method for BES III ETOF Upgrade
abstract: The Endcap Time-of-Flight (ETOF) detector upgrade for the BES III experiment requires precise clock synchronization to ensure optimal timing resolution for particle identification. Variations in cable length, temperature, and electronic components can introduce phase drift between distributed clock signals, degrading system performance. To address this challenge, we propose a clock auto-synchronizing method based on real-time phase monitoring and adjustment within the ETOF electronics. The method employs a feedback control mechanism to detect phase differences between the master and local clocks and automatically aligns them with sub-nanosecond accuracy. Implementation in field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) allows continuous online calibration without interrupting data acquisition. Laboratory and beam tests demonstrate that the technique maintains synchronization stability over extended operation periods. This approach enhances the reliability of the upgraded ETOF system and can be applied to other high-energy physics experiments requiring high-precision timing.
introduction:
The Beijing Spectrometer III (BESIII) experiment, operating at the Beijing Electron Positron Collider II (BEPCII), plays a crucial role in the study of hadron spectroscopy, charmonium physics, and the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model. To enhance its particle identification capability, an upgrade of the Endcap Time-of-Flight (ETOF) system has been undertaken, replacing the original scintillator-based detectors with Multi-gap Resistive Plate Chambers (MRPCs). This upgrade significantly improves the time resolution, thereby enabling more precise measurement of particle flight times and enhancing the separation power between charged particles.

A key requirement for the upgraded ETOF system is precise and stable synchronization of the distributed clock signals across all detector electronics. The accuracy of time-of-flight measurements depends critically on minimizing timing jitter and phase drift in the clock distribution network. In the BESIII environment, the clock signals must be transmitted over long distances from the central clock source to the front-end electronics, where variations in transmission paths and temperature fluctuations can induce phase differences. Traditional manual calibration methods for phase alignment are time-consuming, prone to human error, and unsuitable for maintaining long-term stability during continuous operation.

To address these challenges, a clock auto-synchronizing method has been developed for the BESIII ETOF upgrade. This method enables automatic phase detection and adjustment in real time, ensuring that the distributed clock signals remain aligned without operator intervention. By integrating this mechanism into the ETOF electronics, the system can dynamically compensate for environmental drifts and maintain optimal timing performance. The proposed approach not only improves operational efficiency but also enhances the reliability and precision of the upgraded detector system.
conclusion: The proposed clock auto-synchronizing method for the BESIII ETOF upgrade has been successfully designed, implemented, and validated. Experimental results demonstrate that the system achieves reliable, precise, and stable clock alignment without manual intervention, thereby improving timing resolution and operational efficiency. The method adapts automatically to phase variations and environmental changes, ensuring consistent performance during long-term operation. Its robustness and scalability make it suitable for future detector upgrades. This work provides a practical and effective solution, contributing to the enhanced performance and maintainability of the BESIII experiment’s time-of-flight system.

title: Using the Mean Absolute Percentage Error for Regression Models
abstract: This paper examines the use of the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) as a performance metric for regression models. We analyze its mathematical properties, interpretability, and limitations, particularly under zero or near-zero targets. Comparative experiments with alternative error measures are conducted, highlighting scenarios where MAPE offers intuitive insights and where caution or alternative metrics are warranted.
introduction:
Accurate prediction is a central objective in the development and evaluation of regression models across diverse disciplines, including economics, engineering, environmental science, and healthcare. The selection of an appropriate performance metric is critical, as it directly influences both the interpretation of model outputs and the comparative assessment of alternative approaches. Among the variety of error measures available, the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) has emerged as a widely used indicator due to its intuitive interpretation in percentage terms, which facilitates communication of results to audiences with varying levels of statistical expertise. By expressing predictive errors as a proportion of the actual values, MAPE provides a scale-independent measure that is easily comparable across datasets and contexts.

Despite its popularity, the use of MAPE is not without limitations. Its reliance on percentage errors makes it sensitive to observations with small actual values, potentially inflating the overall error metric and leading to misleading conclusions. Additionally, MAPE is asymmetric in the sense that it penalizes overestimation and underestimation differently, which may bias model evaluation in certain applications. These characteristics have prompted ongoing discussions in the literature regarding the conditions under which MAPE is most appropriate, as well as the development of alternative or adjusted formulations designed to mitigate its shortcomings.

Nevertheless, MAPE remains a practical and interpretable choice in many real-world prediction tasks, particularly when stakeholders require a clear understanding of relative prediction accuracy. In applied settings such as retail demand forecasting, energy consumption prediction, and financial time series modeling, its percentage-based representation aligns naturally with decision-making processes that depend on proportional errors rather than absolute deviations. This paper examines the theoretical properties, advantages, and limitations of MAPE as a performance measure for regression models, and explores strategies for its effective application. By situating MAPE within a broader framework of error metrics, we aim to provide guidance for researchers and practitioners in selecting and implementing appropriate accuracy measures that balance interpretability with statistical robustness.
conclusion: This study examined the applicability and interpretability of the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) as an evaluation metric for regression models. Our analysis highlighted MAPE’s intuitive appeal, as it expresses prediction errors in percentage terms, facilitating communication with non-technical audiences. However, we also discussed its limitations, particularly its sensitivity to values near zero and its asymmetric penalization of over- and under-estimations. Comparative experiments demonstrated that while MAPE can offer valuable insights, it should be applied with caution and, when appropriate, complemented by alternative error measures. Future research could explore robust adaptations of MAPE that mitigate its drawbacks while retaining interpretability. Overall, MAPE remains a useful tool for model assessment when its assumptions and constraints are explicitly acknowledged in the evaluation process.

title: Energy-Efficient Power Allocation in Cognitive Radio Systems with Imperfect Spectrum Sensing
abstract: This paper investigates energy-efficient power allocation strategies for cognitive radio (CR) systems operating under imperfect spectrum sensing conditions. In CR networks, secondary users (SUs) opportunistically access underutilized licensed spectrum while minimizing interference to primary users (PUs). However, spectrum sensing errors, such as missed detections and false alarms, degrade system performance and complicate power allocation design. We formulate an optimization problem that maximizes the energy efficiency, defined as the ratio of achievable throughput to total power consumption, subject to average interference and transmit power constraints. The impact of sensing inaccuracy is explicitly incorporated through probabilistic models of detection and false alarm rates. To solve the non-convex problem, we employ fractional programming combined with Lagrangian dual decomposition, yielding closed-form expressions for optimal power allocation under different sensing outcomes. Analytical results reveal the trade-off between sensing reliability and energy efficiency, highlighting regimes where improved sensing accuracy significantly enhances performance. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms conventional throughput-oriented allocation methods, achieving notable energy savings even with moderate sensing errors. The findings provide valuable design insights for green cognitive radio systems operating in practical, imperfect sensing environments.
introduction: This work investigates energy-efficient power allocation strategies for cognitive radio systems under imperfect spectrum sensing, aiming to balance spectral efficiency, energy consumption, and interference constraints for reliable wireless communication.
conclusion: The proposed scheme enhances energy efficiency in cognitive radio systems, effectively mitigating imperfect sensing impacts while maintaining reliable communication and spectrum utilization performance.

title: Constraining stellar parameters and atmospheric dynamics of the carbon AGB star V Oph
abstract: We present a detailed study of the stellar parameters and atmospheric dynamics of the carbon-rich asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star V Oph, combining multi-epoch interferometric observations with spectroscopic and photometric data. Using near- and mid-infrared long-baseline interferometry obtained with VLTI instruments, we constrain the angular diameter variations across the pulsation cycle and probe the spatial distribution of molecular and dust layers. Complementary high-resolution spectra in the optical and infrared allow us to derive effective temperatures, C/O ratio, and radial velocity curves, providing insight into the coupling between pulsation and atmospheric motion. We model the data with dynamic model atmospheres for carbon stars that self-consistently include pulsation-induced shocks and dust formation. The best-fitting models indicate a photospheric radius variation of ≈ 8–10% and effective temperatures ranging from 2550 K to 2800 K over the cycle. The derived luminosity of (8.5 ± 1.0) × 10³ L⊙ and a distance estimate of 630 ± 50 pc place V Oph near the tip of the thermally pulsing AGB. The interferometric visibilities reveal extended molecular layers dominated by C₂H₂ and HCN at 1.5–2.0 stellar radii, with temporal changes consistent with pulsation-driven levitation. We detect phase-dependent asymmetries in the visibility data, suggestive of large-scale inhomogeneities or clumpy dust formation. Our results provide robust constraints on the fundamental parameters of V Oph and demonstrate the interplay between pulsation, molecular layer dynamics, and dust formation in carbon-rich AGB stars. These findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of mass-loss processes and late-stage stellar evolution for low- to intermediate-mass stars.
introduction:
Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars represent a late evolutionary stage of low- to intermediate-mass stars, characterized by extensive mass loss, large-amplitude pulsations, and complex atmospheric dynamics. Carbon-rich AGB stars, in which the surface carbon-to-oxygen ratio exceeds unity due to dredge-up events, play a crucial role in enriching the interstellar medium with carbonaceous material and dust. Understanding their fundamental parameters and atmospheric processes is essential for constraining stellar evolution models and the feedback of evolved stars on galactic chemical evolution.  

V Oph is a well-studied carbon-rich Mira variable exhibiting pronounced variability in brightness and spectral features over its pulsation cycle. Its extended atmosphere hosts molecular layers, shock fronts, and dust formation zones, making it an ideal target for probing the interplay between pulsation, atmospheric dynamics, and mass loss. However, the determination of precise stellar parameters—such as effective temperature, radius, and luminosity—remains challenging due to the temporal and spatial inhomogeneities in the atmosphere.  

Advances in high-angular-resolution interferometry and spectro-interferometry now permit direct constraints on the spatial structure and temporal evolution of AGB atmospheres. By combining such observations with dynamic model atmospheres tailored for carbon-rich stars, we can investigate the physical conditions in V Oph’s atmosphere, test pulsation-driven wind models, and refine estimates of its fundamental parameters, thereby improving our understanding of evolved stellar envelopes.
conclusion:
In this work, we have combined high‑angular‑resolution interferometric observations with detailed radiative transfer modelling to constrain the fundamental stellar parameters and investigate the atmospheric dynamics of the carbon‑rich asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star V Oph. By integrating spectrally dispersed visibility data with contemporaneous photometric and spectroscopic measurements, we have derived a consistent set of parameters that describe both the stellar photosphere and the surrounding molecular and dusty layers. The approach has enabled us to disentangle the relative contributions of the photospheric continuum, molecular opacities, and dust emission to the observed flux distribution, thereby providing new insights into the physical conditions in the extended atmosphere of this pulsating carbon star.

Our analysis yields a limb‑darkened angular diameter that, when combined with an updated parallax, leads to a robust estimate of the stellar radius. Together with the bolometric flux, this allows us to place V Oph on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, confirming its location on the thermally pulsing AGB sequence. The effective temperature derived from our modelling is consistent with previous estimates for carbon stars of similar variability type, while the luminosity is in agreement with predictions from stellar evolution calculations for a star of intermediate initial mass in the late stages of the AGB. The variability phase coverage of our interferometric data also enables us to quantify changes in angular diameter and effective temperature across the pulsation cycle, revealing a modest but significant variability in both parameters.

The interferometric visibilities exhibit clear signatures of extended molecular layers beyond the photosphere, most notably from C₂H₂ and HCN in the near‑infrared. Our radiative transfer models indicate that these layers are warm (∼1500–2000 K) and reside at radii of 1.5–2.0 R⋆, consistent with the predictions of dynamic model atmospheres for carbon‑rich Mira‑like variables. The data also show an excess at longer wavelengths attributable to amorphous carbon dust, with the onset of dust formation occurring at ∼2–3 R⋆. The coexistence of warm molecular layers and dust at these radii suggests that pulsation‑driven shocks levitate atmospheric material to distances where dust condensation becomes efficient, thereby facilitating mass loss through a radiation‑driven wind.

By comparing our observations with time‑dependent hydrodynamic models, we find qualitative agreement in the overall structure and variability of the atmosphere, but also some discrepancies in the detailed wavelength dependence of the visibilities. These differences point to the need for improved molecular opacity data and more comprehensive treatment of non‑equilibrium chemistry in the dynamic models. Our results highlight the importance of simultaneous constraints on the stellar continuum, molecular absorption, and dust emission in order to refine the physical description of AGB star atmospheres.

The derived mass‑loss rate and dust properties are consistent with V Oph being in an intermediate mass‑loss regime, likely preceding the onset of the superwind phase. The presence of both molecular and dust signatures at relatively small radii supports a scenario in which the mass‑loss process is already well established, even though the circumstellar envelope has not yet reached the high optical depths observed in more evolved carbon Miras. This transitional status makes V Oph an important laboratory for studying the coupling between pulsation, atmospheric dynamics, and dust‑driven winds.

In summary, our study provides a coherent set of stellar parameters for V Oph and reveals the spatial and temporal complexity of its extended atmosphere. The combination of high‑resolution interferometry and detailed modelling has allowed us to probe regions of the atmosphere that are inaccessible to purely spectroscopic techniques, offering direct constraints on the physical processes governing mass loss in carbon‑rich AGB stars. Future work should aim to extend the temporal coverage to multiple pulsation cycles, to obtain simultaneous multi‑wavelength interferometric data spanning the near‑ to mid‑infrared, and to incorporate advances in dynamic atmosphere and wind models. Such efforts will further elucidate the interplay between pulsation, shock dynamics, molecular layer formation, and dust condensation, and will ultimately improve our understanding of the late‑stage evolution and mass‑loss mechanisms of carbon‑rich evolved stars.

title: Effects of staggered Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions in a quasi-two-dimensional Shastry-Sutherland model
abstract: We investigate the influence of staggered Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) interactions on the magnetic properties of a quasi-two-dimensional Shastry–Sutherland model, motivated by experimental observations in frustrated quantum magnets. Using a combination of perturbative continuous unitary transformations and exact diagonalization, we analyze the evolution of the excitation spectrum, magnetization process, and spin correlations as a function of DM strength and orientation. The staggered DM terms lift degeneracies in the triplet manifold, induce anisotropic dispersion, and modify the field-induced plateau structure. Our results reveal a pronounced sensitivity of low-energy excitations to the DM pattern, suggesting an essential role in stabilizing or destabilizing magnetization plateaus. The findings provide insight into anisotropic exchange effects in layered frustrated spin systems.
introduction:
Frustrated quantum magnets have long served as a fertile ground for exploring exotic quantum states of matter, owing to the interplay between competing interactions, low dimensionality, and quantum fluctuations. Among the various lattice geometries that realize such physics, the Shastry–Sutherland model (SSM) occupies a special place. Originally introduced as an exactly solvable two-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model with orthogonal dimers, it exhibits a rich phase diagram encompassing a product singlet ground state, magnetically ordered phases, and magnetization plateaus. The model has received renewed attention due to its realization in the quasi-two-dimensional compound SrCu\(_2\)(BO\(_3\))\(_2\), where Cu\(^{2+}\) spins form a network of orthogonal dimers in the crystallographic \(ab\)-plane, weakly coupled in the third dimension.

In real materials, however, deviations from the idealized SSM are inevitable. In particular, the lack of inversion symmetry at certain Cu–O–Cu bonds allows for antisymmetric exchange interactions of the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) type. The DM interaction, \(\mathbf{D}_{ij} \cdot (\mathbf{S}_i \times \mathbf{S}_j)\), arises from spin–orbit coupling and can profoundly influence both the static and dynamic properties of quantum magnets. While uniform DM interactions have been widely studied, staggered DM patterns—where the DM vectors alternate in orientation or magnitude across the lattice—introduce additional complexity. In SrCu\(_2\)(BO\(_3\))\(_2\), neutron scattering, ESR, and NMR experiments have revealed the presence of both intra-dimer and inter-dimer DM terms, some of which exhibit a staggered arrangement dictated by crystal symmetries.

The role of staggered DM interactions in the SSM and related models is twofold. First, they can break spin rotational symmetries partially or completely, altering the excitation spectrum and lifting degeneracies. For instance, in a pure Heisenberg dimer system, triplet excitations are degenerate in the absence of anisotropy; staggered DM terms can split these modes and modify their dispersion. Second, staggered DM couplings can induce weak canting of spins and generate novel collective modes, influencing finite-field properties such as magnetization plateaus and spin textures. In the quasi-two-dimensional setting, interlayer couplings combined with staggered DM interactions may stabilize anisotropic three-dimensional orders or modify critical fields.

Theoretical studies have addressed the influence of uniform DM terms in various low-dimensional frustrated magnets, but the staggered case—especially in the context of the SSM—remains comparatively less explored. Perturbative analyses, exact diagonalization, and density matrix renormalization group calculations have provided valuable insights into the pure SSM and its uniform DM extensions, yet the combined effects of frustration, dimensionality, and staggered antisymmetric exchange require further systematic investigation. Moreover, the experimental relevance of staggered DM interactions in SrCu\(_2\)(BO\(_3\))\(_2\) and related materials motivates the development of quantitative theoretical frameworks that go beyond the idealized isotropic limit.

In this work, we study the effects of staggered Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions in a quasi-two-dimensional Shastry–Sutherland model. By incorporating both intra- and inter-dimer staggered DM terms into a realistic Hamiltonian, we analyze their impact on the ground state, excitation spectrum, and field-induced phases. Our results elucidate how staggered anisotropies modify the stability of the singlet phase, alter the dispersion of triplet excitations, and influence the nature of magnetization plateaus in weakly coupled SSM layers. This study provides a step toward bridging the gap between idealized theoretical models and the complex behavior observed in real frustrated quantum magnets.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the influence of staggered Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya (DM) interactions on the magnetic properties of a quasi-two-dimensional Shastry–Sutherland model, motivated by their relevance to real materials such as SrCu₂(BO₃)₂. Using a combination of analytical perturbative approaches and numerical exact diagonalization on finite clusters, we have characterized how the interplay between frustrated exchange couplings and anisotropic spin–orbit-induced terms modifies the low-energy spectrum and the nature of magnetic excitations.

Our results demonstrate that staggered DM interactions lift certain degeneracies inherent to the pure Shastry–Sutherland lattice, leading to a mixing of singlet and triplet sectors and a finite dispersion of otherwise localized triplet excitations. This effect manifests in a measurable shift of the spin gap and in the emergence of anisotropic features in the dynamical structure factor, which could be probed directly by inelastic neutron scattering or electron spin resonance experiments. Moreover, we find that the induced dispersion depends sensitively on the directionality and magnitude of the staggered DM vectors, revealing that different symmetry-allowed patterns can produce qualitatively distinct modifications to the excitation spectrum.

In the magnetized regime, the staggered DM terms affect the stability and sequence of magnetization plateaus. They tend to destabilize certain commensurate states by introducing competing kinetic processes for triplon quasiparticles, thereby facilitating the onset of incommensurate phases. This observation provides a possible route to reconcile discrepancies between experimentally observed plateau widths and those predicted by isotropic Heisenberg models.

Overall, our study underscores the importance of incorporating realistic anisotropic interactions when modeling frustrated quantum magnets with low crystallographic symmetry. Staggered DM interactions, though often treated as a perturbation, can have profound consequences for both static and dynamic properties. Future work could extend our analysis to larger system sizes via tensor network or quantum Monte Carlo methods adapted to handle sign problems introduced by DM terms, as well as to finite-temperature regimes where additional thermal effects may interplay with the anisotropic exchange. Our findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the microscopic mechanisms governing the rich phenomenology of Shastry–Sutherland magnets and offer concrete predictions for forthcoming high-resolution spectroscopic measurements.

title: Multimodal Hate Speech Detection from Bengali Memes and Texts
abstract: The rapid growth of social media platforms has led to an unprecedented spread of multimodal content, including images, memes, and texts, which often serve as vehicles for hate speech. While automated hate speech detection has gained considerable attention in recent years, most research focuses on English or other high-resource languages, leaving low-resource languages like Bengali underexplored. This paper presents a comprehensive study on multimodal hate speech detection in Bengali, with a particular focus on memes and text-based posts. We construct and release a novel annotated dataset comprising Bengali memes that combine textual and visual elements, alongside standalone Bengali texts, labeled for varying degrees and targets of hate speech. Leveraging this resource, we evaluate a range of unimodal and multimodal deep learning architectures, including transformer-based language models for text and convolutional neural networks for images, as well as fusion strategies that integrate visual and textual features. Our experiments demonstrate that multimodal fusion consistently outperforms unimodal baselines, particularly in cases where textual cues alone are ambiguous or visual components carry implicit hateful connotations. We also analyze error patterns, highlighting challenges such as figurative language, culturally specific references, and low-quality meme text extraction. The results underscore the importance of incorporating both visual and textual modalities for effective hate speech detection in Bengali and other low-resource languages. By making our dataset and experimental framework publicly available, we aim to facilitate future research on multilingual and multimodal content moderation, contributing toward safer and more inclusive online environments. Our findings suggest that multimodal approaches hold significant promise for addressing the nuanced and culturally specific nature of hate speech in diverse linguistic contexts.
introduction: Hate speech detection in Bengali remains challenging, particularly in multimodal contexts combining text and images. Memes often embed offensive content subtly through cultural references and visuals. This study addresses detecting such hate speech using multimodal approaches, advancing computational understanding of Bengali social media discourse.
conclusion:
This study addressed the challenge of multimodal hate speech detection in the context of Bengali memes and textual content, a domain that remains underexplored despite the rapid growth of social media in the Bengali-speaking community. By integrating both textual and visual modalities, we demonstrated that multimodal fusion techniques can significantly enhance the detection of hateful and offensive content compared to unimodal approaches. Our experiments showed that combining features extracted from meme images with deep language representations of Bengali text enables more robust modeling of nuanced and context-dependent hate expressions. The results highlight the importance of considering cultural and linguistic particularities in model design, as direct adaptations from English-centric datasets and architectures often fail to capture the subtleties inherent in Bengali communication.

Beyond empirical performance, this work underscores the necessity of building diverse, representative, and ethically sourced multimodal datasets for low-resource languages. While promising, our approach is not without limitations, including potential biases in annotation and challenges in interpreting sarcasm or coded language. Future research should explore larger-scale datasets, advanced fusion architectures, and cross-lingual transfer learning to further improve performance and generalizability. Ultimately, our findings contribute to the growing effort to create safer online spaces by enabling more accurate, culturally aware, and multimodal hate speech detection systems for Bengali and other low-resource languages.

title: A stochastic model of catalytic reaction networks in protocells
abstract: We present a stochastic model for catalytic reaction networks confined within protocellular compartments, aiming to investigate the interplay between molecular noise, network topology, and compartmentalization in early chemical evolution. The model represents molecular species as nodes in a randomly generated catalytic network, with reaction events simulated using Gillespie’s algorithm to capture intrinsic stochasticity. Protocells are modeled as semi-permeable compartments allowing selective exchange of small molecules with the environment, while larger catalysts remain enclosed. The framework incorporates protocell growth through the accumulation of internal components and division once a threshold volume is reached, distributing molecular contents between daughter compartments. We explore the conditions under which autocatalytic cycles emerge and persist, and how fluctuation-driven extinctions influence the stability of chemical diversity. Numerical simulations reveal that compartmentalization can enhance the survival of weakly populated catalytic species by reducing dilution effects, but also introduces variability in network composition after division events. Our results suggest that stochastic effects, coupled with the discrete nature of protocells, can promote the maintenance of complex reaction networks even under unfavorable average conditions. This work provides quantitative insights into how early protocellular systems might have sustained catalytic organization before the advent of genetic replication, highlighting the role of noise as a constructive factor in prebiotic evolution.
introduction:
The emergence of life from non-living matter is thought to have involved the self-organization of simple molecular components into complex, self-sustaining networks of chemical reactions. Among the many hypotheses proposed to explain this transition, catalytic reaction networks (CRNs) have received considerable attention as plausible precursors to modern metabolic systems. In such networks, molecules catalyze the formation of other molecules, collectively enabling the propagation and maintenance of the network’s composition. When embedded in compartments such as lipid vesicles, these networks may constitute protocells—primitive cell-like entities capable of growth, division, and evolution. Understanding the dynamics of CRNs within protocells is therefore central to elucidating potential pathways for the origin of life.

Catalytic reaction networks are inherently stochastic at the molecular scale. In protocells, where the number of molecules of each species can be small, fluctuations in reaction events can have significant consequences for the stability and functionality of the network. This stochasticity can result in phenomena such as the extinction of essential molecular species, spontaneous switching between metastable states, and the emergence of novel dynamical behaviors not predicted by deterministic models. Consequently, a rigorous theoretical framework that incorporates the discrete and probabilistic nature of chemical reactions is required to describe and predict the behavior of protocellular CRNs.

Previous studies have employed both deterministic rate equations and stochastic simulation algorithms to investigate CRNs in well-mixed environments and in spatially structured systems. Deterministic models, while providing insights into average behaviors and steady-state properties, fail to capture fluctuations that are intrinsic to small systems. Stochastic models, particularly those based on the chemical master equation and Gillespie-type algorithms, offer a more accurate representation of the temporal evolution of molecular populations in protocells. These approaches have revealed that noise can play constructive roles in protocell dynamics, for example by enabling adaptive responses to environmental changes or by facilitating evolutionary transitions through rare events.

Despite these advances, the interplay between network topology, catalytic efficiency, and compartmentalization remains incompletely understood. In realistic prebiotic scenarios, protocells are likely to exchange material with their surroundings, grow by incorporating additional membrane components, and divide when reaching a critical size. These processes couple the internal chemical dynamics with the physical properties of the compartment, leading to rich and complex behaviors. Moreover, the stochastic nature of reaction events in such coupled systems may crucially influence the persistence and evolvability of protocells.

In this work, we develop a stochastic model of catalytic reaction networks within growing and dividing protocells. Our approach explicitly accounts for the discrete nature of molecular populations, the probabilistic occurrence of reaction events, and the coupling between chemical dynamics and protocell volume changes. By systematically exploring different network topologies and kinetic parameters, we aim to characterize the conditions under which protocells can sustain functional CRNs over multiple generations. This study contributes to a quantitative understanding of how stochastic effects shape the viability of protocells and provides insights into the principles governing early biochemical organization.
conclusion: In this work, we have developed and analyzed a stochastic model of catalytic reaction networks operating within protocellular compartments. By explicitly accounting for molecular fluctuations and finite system size, the model captures emergent behaviors inaccessible to deterministic approaches, including variability in reaction pathways, transient dominance of specific catalysts, and stochastic switching between network states. Our results demonstrate that confinement within a protocell not only modulates reaction kinetics through spatial and population constraints, but also enhances the robustness of certain network motifs against perturbations. This suggests that stochastic effects, often regarded as noise, can play a constructive role in sustaining functional chemical organization during early stages of life. Furthermore, simulations reveal that protocell division and molecular partitioning introduce additional layers of variability, potentially influencing evolutionary trajectories of prebiotic chemical systems. The framework presented here provides a quantitative foundation for exploring how catalytic networks could maintain functionality under primitive conditions. Future work will extend the model to include molecular inflow and outflow, heterogeneous membrane properties, and coupling between multiple protocells. Such extensions may offer deeper insight into the interplay between stochastic dynamics, spatial structure, and evolutionary selection in the origin of life.

title: Spectral performance of Square Kilometre Array Antennas II: Calibration performance
abstract: We investigate the calibration performance of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) antennas with particular emphasis on the spectral behaviour of the instrumental response and its impact on high-dynamic-range science goals. This study forms the second part of a two-paper series, building on prior characterisation of the spectral performance of SKA antenna designs. Using detailed electromagnetic simulations of representative SKA1-Mid and SKA1-Low antenna models, we generate realistic visibility datasets incorporating frequency-dependent primary beam patterns, mutual coupling effects, and receiver noise. We apply a suite of calibration strategies, including direction-independent and direction-dependent methods, to assess the achievable suppression of instrumental spectral structure across the full operational frequency range. Calibration residuals are quantified in terms of fractional amplitude and phase errors, and their spectral correlation properties are analysed. We further evaluate the performance in the context of key science cases sensitive to spectral systematics, such as detection of the Epoch of Reionisation signal and precision continuum imaging. Our results show that while standard direction-independent calibration can reduce large-scale spectral structure effectively, fine-scale residuals persist at levels that may bias power spectrum measurements if unmodelled. Direction-dependent calibration, incorporating beam and ionospheric models, significantly improves performance, particularly for wide-field low-frequency observations, but at the cost of increased computational complexity. We identify critical trade-offs between calibration accuracy, solution stability, and processing efficiency, and discuss requirements for sky models and beam characterisation to meet SKA science objectives. Our findings provide quantitative benchmarks for acceptable spectral calibration residuals and inform the design of calibration pipelines for early SKA operations, ensuring that instrumental spectral features remain below the thresholds necessary for the most challenging cosmological and astrophysical measurements.
introduction: The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will be the world’s largest radio telescope, designed to deliver unprecedented sensitivity and survey speed across a broad frequency range. Achieving the SKA’s ambitious science goals requires exquisite control over instrumental and environmental effects that can distort received signals. Of particular importance is the calibration of antenna spectral response, since frequency-dependent gain and phase errors can limit dynamic range and hinder the detection of faint astrophysical signals. In this second paper of the series on SKA antenna spectral performance, we focus on calibration performance, building on the characterisation of intrinsic spectral behaviour presented in Paper I. We assess the ability of standard and advanced calibration schemes to recover true sky spectra in the presence of realistic instrumental imperfections. This work quantifies calibration accuracy as a function of spectral complexity, signal-to-noise ratio, and calibration strategy, providing essential input for SKA system design and data processing pipelines.
conclusion: This study has evaluated the calibration performance of Square Kilometre Array (SKA) antennas with a focus on their spectral behaviour. Through detailed simulations and analysis, we have quantified the impact of instrumental and environmental effects on calibration accuracy across the operational frequency range. The results demonstrate that achieving the required spectral smoothness is feasible with appropriate calibration strategies, though performance is sensitive to array configuration, receiver stability, and model completeness. Residual spectral structure can be mitigated through advanced algorithms and careful system design. These findings provide critical guidance for SKA calibration planning, informing both hardware specifications and data processing pipelines to meet the stringent requirements for high-dynamic-range, wideband radio astronomy observations.

title: Theory of Multi-Orbital Topological Superconductivity in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
abstract: We develop a theoretical framework for multi-orbital topological superconductivity in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), focusing on the interplay between strong spin–orbit coupling, orbital hybridization, and unconventional pairing. Using a multi-band tight-binding model derived from first-principles calculations, we analyze symmetry-allowed pairing channels and identify conditions for realizing time-reversal-invariant and chiral topological superconducting states. The multi-orbital nature introduces momentum-dependent interorbital pairing that stabilizes nontrivial topological phases beyond single-orbital models. We compute topological invariants and edge-state spectra, revealing robust Majorana modes protected by crystal symmetries. Our results suggest that gating, strain, or proximity effects can tune TMDs into distinct topological regimes, offering a pathway to engineer and control multi-orbital topological superconductivity in two-dimensional materials for quantum information applications.
introduction:
Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as a versatile platform for exploring a wealth of quantum phenomena, including charge density waves, Mott physics, valley polarization, and unconventional superconductivity. Their layered crystal structures, strong spin–orbit coupling (SOC), and tunable electronic properties via electrostatic gating, chemical doping, or pressure make them ideal candidates for engineering and studying exotic quantum states. In recent years, the discovery of superconductivity in both bulk and monolayer TMDs, such as MoS₂, NbSe₂, and TaS₂, has stimulated intense research into the interplay between multi-orbital band structures, SOC, and pairing mechanisms. Notably, the reduced symmetry in monolayer TMDs, combined with Ising-type SOC, can stabilize superconductivity against in-plane magnetic fields far beyond the conventional Pauli limit, suggesting the presence of unconventional and potentially topological pairing states.

While conventional BCS theory accounts for many features of superconductivity in simple metals, the multi-orbital nature of the low-energy bands in TMDs introduces qualitatively new physics. The conduction and valence bands near the K and K′ valleys are primarily composed of transition metal d-orbitals with distinct angular momentum character, leading to complex orbital textures in momentum space. Additionally, the lack of inversion symmetry in monolayers gives rise to spin–valley locking, which, when combined with inter-orbital hybridization and SOC, can profoundly influence the structure of the superconducting gap. In such systems, the pairing symmetry may acquire admixtures of spin-singlet and spin-triplet components, and the multi-orbital degrees of freedom can enable nontrivial topological superconducting phases.

Topological superconductivity has attracted considerable attention for its potential to host Majorana bound states, which obey non-Abelian statistics and are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computation. The realization of such phases in intrinsic materials, rather than engineered heterostructures, remains a central goal in condensed matter physics. Multi-orbital TMDs offer a promising route toward this objective because their intrinsic electronic structure naturally supports a variety of topologically nontrivial pairing channels. Theoretical studies have shown that in systems with strong SOC and broken inversion symmetry, unconventional Cooper pairing can arise from either electron–phonon or electron–electron interactions, with symmetry-protected band crossings and spin–momentum locking enabling topological gap structures. However, a comprehensive theory that accounts for the full multi-orbital character of TMDs and its role in stabilizing topological superconductivity is still lacking.

Previous approaches have often relied on simplified single-orbital models or effective low-energy theories that capture only the vicinity of the Fermi surface near a single valley. While such models can provide qualitative insight, they cannot fully describe the intricate interplay between orbital hybridization, SOC, and interlayer coupling in few-layer systems. Moreover, the orbital content of the Fermi surface can vary significantly with carrier density, gating, or strain, leading to changes in the pairing symmetry and topology of the superconducting state. A systematic treatment of these effects requires a realistic multi-orbital framework that incorporates the microscopic symmetries of the TMD lattice and the spin–orbit entanglement inherent in their band structures.

In this work, we develop a theory of multi-orbital topological superconductivity tailored to transition metal dichalcogenides, with an emphasis on the role of orbital degrees of freedom, SOC, and crystal symmetries in determining the nature of the pairing state. By constructing a multi-orbital tight-binding model anchored in first-principles calculations and analyzing its superconducting instabilities within a symmetry-based classification scheme, we identify the conditions under which topologically nontrivial superconducting phases emerge. Our results provide a unified framework for understanding existing experimental observations and suggest concrete pathways for realizing and controlling topological superconductivity in TMD materials.
conclusion:
In this work, we have developed a theoretical framework for understanding multi-orbital topological superconductivity in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), focusing on the interplay between orbital degrees of freedom, spin–orbit coupling, and unconventional pairing symmetry. By constructing a multi-orbital tight-binding model that incorporates realistic band structures and symmetry-allowed pairing channels, we have elucidated how the intrinsic multi-orbital character of TMDs enriches the topological superconducting phase diagram beyond that of single-orbital systems. Our analysis demonstrates that the coexistence of strong Ising spin–orbit coupling and inter-orbital hybridization can stabilize a variety of topologically nontrivial superconducting states, including both time-reversal-invariant and time-reversal-breaking phases.  

The results highlight that orbital-selective pairing, driven by the distinct symmetry properties of the constituent d-orbitals, plays a decisive role in determining the topological invariants of the superconducting state. In particular, we find that inter-orbital pair amplitudes can induce nontrivial band inversions in the Bogoliubov–de Gennes quasiparticle spectrum, leading to protected Majorana edge modes under appropriate boundary conditions. Furthermore, the competition between on-site and extended orbital pairing channels can generate nodal-to-fully-gapped transitions, which are accompanied by changes in the topological classification. These findings underscore the necessity of treating orbital degrees of freedom on equal footing with spin and momentum in the search for topological superconductivity.  

From a materials perspective, the theory provides a concrete route to identifying experimentally accessible regimes in monolayer and few-layer TMDs where topological superconductivity is favored. By tuning carrier density, applying in-plane or out-of-plane magnetic fields, or engineering strain, one can selectively enhance orbital mixing and manipulate the effective pairing symmetry. Our results suggest that several group-V and group-VI TMDs with partially filled d-manifolds are promising candidates for realizing robust Majorana quasiparticles without the need for external proximity effects.  

Looking forward, the framework presented here can be extended to incorporate interaction-driven effects beyond mean-field theory, disorder, and coupling to substrate degrees of freedom. Such generalizations will be essential for quantitatively connecting theory to spectroscopic and transport experiments. Moreover, the multi-orbital perspective introduced in this study is applicable to a broader class of layered materials with strong spin–orbit coupling, potentially opening new avenues for topological quantum computation platforms. In summary, our work establishes a foundational theoretical basis for multi-orbital topological superconductivity in TMDs, revealing the critical role of orbital physics in stabilizing and controlling exotic superconducting phases and their associated boundary excitations.

title: DC-Prophet: Predicting Catastrophic Machine Failures in DataCenters
abstract: We present **DC-Prophet**, a predictive framework for anticipating catastrophic machine failures in large-scale datacenters. Such failures, though infrequent, can cause substantial service disruptions and economic loss. DC-Prophet leverages fine-grained telemetry and operational logs to model the temporal dynamics of machine health, combining feature engineering with a hybrid learning architecture that integrates gradient boosting for feature selection and recurrent neural networks for sequential prediction. By focusing on early detection, the system enables proactive mitigation strategies, such as workload migration and preventive maintenance, reducing downtime and recovery costs.
