On the theoretical side, developing closure models that accurately encapsulate the net effect of local turbulence on global evolution is essential. On the numerical side, progress in high-performance computing, adaptive algorithms, and data assimilation techniques will be critical to integrate disparate scales in a tractable manner. On the observational side, targeted campaigns aimed at isolating signatures of specific transport mechanisms can help calibrate and discriminate between competing models. Furthermore, cross-disciplinary engagement with plasma physics, fluid dynamics, and applied mathematics can stimulate new approaches to multiscale modeling, stability analysis, and turbulence characterization.

In summary, the next generation of accretion theory must transcend the traditional dichotomy between local and global perspectives. The physics of angular momentum and energy transport is inherently multiscale, with feedbacks that challenge simple separation of processes. By explicitly embracing this complexity—through hybrid modeling frameworks, synergistic numerical and theoretical development, and close integration with multiwavelength observations—we can move toward a predictive, physically grounded theory that is applicable across the rich diversity of accreting systems. The path forward is demanding, but the potential rewards include not only a deeper understanding of accretion itself, but also new insights into the broader astrophysical phenomena that accretion powers and regulates.

title: Tensor Programs I: Wide Feedforward or Recurrent Neural Networks of Any Architecture are Gaussian Processes
abstract: We study the behavior of wide neural networks—feedforward, recurrent, and of arbitrary architecture—through the framework of *tensor programs*, a unifying mathematical language for describing neural network computations. By analyzing the infinite-width limit, we prove that, under broad conditions on initialization and nonlinearity, the pre-activations of such networks converge in distribution to Gaussian processes. Our approach generalizes and systematizes prior results that were restricted to specific architectures, offering a single proof technique that applies to multi-layer, weight-tied, and recurrent settings alike. The tensor program formalism enables rigorous tracking of correlations across neurons and layers, even in the presence of parameter sharing. This yields explicit formulas for the covariance kernels corresponding to arbitrary computation graphs. Our results provide both theoretical insight into the behavior of wide networks and practical tools for designing architectures with predictable limiting behavior, bridging deep learning theory with classical probabilistic modeling.
introduction:
The study of wide neural networks has revealed deep and surprising connections between modern machine learning models and classical probabilistic objects. In particular, as the width of a neural network layer tends to infinity, the distribution over functions represented by the network converges to a Gaussian process (GP) under fairly general conditions. This correspondence was first established for simple fully connected feedforward architectures with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) parameters, but subsequent work has demonstrated that the phenomenon is far more general. The Gaussian process perspective provides both theoretical insight and practical tools: it allows for principled uncertainty quantification, connects neural networks to Bayesian nonparametrics, and yields analytical predictions for training dynamics in certain regimes.

Despite its importance, most existing results on the GP limit of neural networks focus on specific architectures and weight initialization schemes. Early derivations, such as those by Neal (1996), considered fully connected feedforward networks with a single hidden layer and Gaussian-distributed weights. More recent treatments extended the analysis to deep fully connected networks, certain convolutional networks, and residual networks, often relying on independence assumptions and specific activation functions. However, modern architectures in practice exhibit far greater structural diversity, including arbitrary connectivity patterns, weight sharing, and recurrent connections. Moreover, the ability to reason systematically about the GP limit for such general architectures has been limited by the lack of a unifying analytical framework.

The tensor program framework addresses this gap by providing a rigorous and flexible formalism for tracking the distributional evolution of signals through arbitrary compositions of linear and nonlinear operations in the infinite-width limit. In this framework, a neural network computation—whether feedforward, recurrent, or of more exotic design—is represented as a “program” built from basic tensor operations. By analyzing the program’s execution under random initialization, one can characterize the joint distribution of all intermediate signals as widths tend to infinity. A central result is that, under mild conditions on the initialization and nonlinearity, these joint distributions converge to Gaussian distributions whose covariance structure can be computed recursively from the program structure. In the special case of network outputs, this yields the GP correspondence.

This unifying perspective has several important consequences. First, it shows that the GP limit is not an idiosyncratic feature of a few simple architectures, but a universal property of a broad class of randomly initialized wide networks. The result holds regardless of the specific arrangement of layers, the presence of skip connections, or the use of recurrent loops, as long as certain technical conditions are satisfied. Second, it provides a constructive method for determining the kernel of the limiting GP directly from the architecture and initialization, enabling the analysis of architectures that were previously intractable. Third, it clarifies the relationship between different special cases studied in the literature: many prior results can be recovered as specific instances of the general tensor program theorem.

From a practical standpoint, the GP correspondence in the infinite-width limit serves as a foundation for further theoretical developments, such as the derivation of neural tangent kernels (NTKs) that govern gradient descent dynamics in wide networks. It also offers a baseline for understanding the impact of finite-width effects, parameter sharing, and structured priors on network behavior. By situating diverse architectures within a single analytical framework, the tensor program approach opens the door to systematic studies of how architectural choices influence expressivity, generalization, and trainability.

In this work, we present the theory of tensor programs and prove that any feedforward or recurrent neural network architecture composed of standard linear and nonlinear operations, when initialized with i.i.d. parameters of suitable variance, converges in distribution to a Gaussian process as its widths go to infinity. We formalize the execution of such networks as tensor programs, establish conditions for convergence, and derive recursive formulas for the limiting covariances. Through this general theorem, we recover and extend all known GP correspondence results for neural networks, demonstrating that the Gaussian process limit is a universal property of wide architectures. This provides a powerful theoretical lens through which to view the behavior of modern deep learning systems in the large-width regime.
conclusion:
In this work, we have established a general theoretical framework for analyzing the infinite-width limit of a broad class of neural network architectures, encompassing both feedforward and recurrent structures. By formulating the computation of such networks as tensor programs, we demonstrated that, under mild conditions on the initialization and nonlinearity, the pre-activations in each layer converge in distribution to jointly Gaussian random variables as the width tends to infinity. This convergence holds irrespective of architectural details such as depth, skip connections, or weight sharing patterns, thereby unifying and extending prior results that were limited to specific network configurations.  

Our approach not only recovers the well-known correspondence between wide neural networks and Gaussian processes, but also clarifies the precise conditions under which this equivalence arises. The tensor program formalism provides a systematic means of tracking the propagation of means and covariances through arbitrary computation graphs, enabling principled derivations of kernel functions for the induced Gaussian processes. This generality opens a path for rigorous analysis of architectures previously treated only heuristically, including those with tied weights or recurrent dynamics.  

The implications of this result are twofold. First, it furnishes a solid theoretical foundation for using Gaussian process theory to study the behavior, expressivity, and generalization of wide networks. Second, it offers practical tools for designing and initializing architectures to achieve desired statistical properties at infinite width, which may inform finite-width approximations. Future work may extend this framework to incorporate training dynamics, non-Gaussian initializations, and structured forms of randomness, thereby bridging the gap between the static infinite-width regime and the finite, trained networks employed in practice. Through this lens, tensor programs serve as a versatile and unifying language for the asymptotic theory of neural networks.

title: Contagions in Social Networks: Effects of Monophilic Contagion, Friendship Paradox and Reactive Networks
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of contagion processes in social networks under three intertwined phenomena: monophilic contagion, the friendship paradox, and network adaptivity through reactive rewiring. Monophilic contagion captures the tendency of individuals to adopt behaviors or states based on the states of their friends’ friends, extending the scope of influence beyond immediate neighbors. The friendship paradox—the observation that most individuals have fewer connections than their friends on average—amplifies the impact of highly connected nodes and alters effective transmission probabilities. We develop a mathematical framework that integrates these mechanisms into a discrete-time susceptible–infected–susceptible (SIS) model on time-varying networks. Reactive networks are modeled by allowing the topology to adapt in response to the state of the contagion, capturing avoidance, reinforcement, or other behaviorally driven rewiring patterns. Analytical results reveal that monophilic contagion lowers epidemic thresholds relative to purely dyadic contagion, and that the friendship paradox further accelerates spread by biasing exposure toward high-degree nodes. In reactive networks, rewiring can either suppress or sustain contagion depending on the interplay between adaptation rates and network heterogeneity. Numerical simulations on synthetic and empirical networks corroborate the theoretical predictions, highlighting the combined and sometimes counterintuitive effects of higher-order influence, structural bias, and adaptive topology on contagion dynamics.
introduction:
The spread of behaviors, ideas, and diseases in social networks has attracted significant attention across disciplines ranging from sociology and epidemiology to computer science and economics. Classical contagion models, such as the Susceptible–Infected–Susceptible (SIS) framework, typically assume that individuals’ adoption or infection states evolve over a fixed network structure and are influenced directly by their immediate neighbors. However, recent empirical and theoretical work suggests that more nuanced mechanisms can substantially alter contagion dynamics. In particular, monophilic contagion—where individuals are influenced not only by their direct contacts but also by contacts of contacts—has emerged as a relevant extension, reflecting real-world scenarios in which second-degree connections impact decision-making and exposure.

A related structural phenomenon, the friendship paradox, states that on average, most individuals have fewer connections than their friends do. This paradox implies that sampling neighbors or friends-of-friends skews observations toward higher-degree nodes, which can accelerate or otherwise alter contagion spread. When combined with monophilic contagion processes, the friendship paradox suggests the potential for faster diffusion, as individuals are indirectly exposed to more highly connected—and thus more influential—nodes.

Furthermore, in many real systems, the network itself is not static but evolves in response to the contagion state. Such reactive networks can arise when individuals rewire connections to avoid infection, seek out information, or form protective clusters, thereby coupling the dynamics of network topology with the contagion process. This co-evolution introduces complex feedback loops, as changes in network structure influence contagion spread, which in turn drives further structural adaptation.

This paper investigates the interplay between monophilic contagion, the friendship paradox, and reactive network dynamics in shaping contagion outcomes. By integrating these mechanisms into mathematical and simulation-based models, we aim to characterize their individual and joint effects on thresholds, prevalence, and stability of contagions. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of how higher-order social influence, structural biases in perception, and adaptive connectivity together govern diffusion processes in complex networks.
conclusion:
This study has examined the dynamics of contagion processes in social networks under the joint influence of monophilic contagion mechanisms, the friendship paradox, and reactive network structures. By integrating these phenomena into a unified analytical framework, we have shown that network topology, perception biases, and adaptive structural responses can significantly alter both the threshold conditions for contagion spread and the eventual extent of diffusion. Monophilic contagion, in which adoption decisions are influenced by neighbors of neighbors, amplifies the effective reach of influence and can lower critical thresholds. The friendship paradox, whereby individuals are more likely to encounter better-connected peers, further enhances exposure in early stages, accelerating growth rates. At the same time, reactive networks—where connectivity patterns evolve in response to contagion prevalence—can either suppress or facilitate spread depending on the nature of the rewiring rules and the interplay with the other mechanisms.

The results highlight the importance of considering higher-order social perception effects and endogenous network evolution in models of diffusion, particularly in contexts such as information dissemination, behavioral adoption, or epidemic control. Ignoring these factors may lead to underestimation or overestimation of contagion potential. Future work could extend the framework to heterogeneous contagion rules, multiplex networks, or empirical calibration with real-time network data. Overall, the findings underscore that contagion in social networks is not solely a function of static structural properties, but is shaped by the interaction of cognitive biases and adaptive network responses.

title: Excluding the Light Dark Matter Window of a 331 Model Using LHC and Direct Dark Matter Detection Data
abstract: We investigate the viability of a light dark matter (DM) candidate within the framework of a 331 gauge extension of the Standard Model, where the DM particle arises as a neutral component of an extended scalar sector stabilized by a discrete symmetry. Focusing on the mass range below 100 GeV, we combine constraints from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and current direct detection experiments to delineate the allowed parameter space. Collider bounds on new gauge bosons and exotic fermions, together with Higgs boson invisible decay measurements, significantly restrict the couplings between the DM candidate and Standard Model particles. Direct detection limits from XENON1T, LUX, and PandaX further exclude regions with sizeable spin-independent scattering cross sections. Our analysis demonstrates that, once all constraints are applied, the parameter space accommodating a light scalar or fermionic DM candidate is effectively ruled out for masses below approximately 60 GeV. These results close the light DM window in this class of 331 models, guiding future searches toward heavier mass regimes and complementary experimental probes.
introduction:
The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics has been remarkably successful in describing a wide range of fundamental phenomena, culminating in the discovery of the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Nevertheless, a variety of experimental and observational results point to the existence of new physics beyond the SM. Among the most compelling of these is the evidence for non-baryonic dark matter (DM), inferred from galactic rotation curves, gravitational lensing, cosmic microwave background measurements, and large-scale structure formation. Despite its overwhelming astrophysical evidence, the particle nature of dark matter remains unknown. This gap in our understanding has motivated a vast array of theoretical extensions of the SM that can accommodate viable dark matter candidates, alongside potentially addressing other theoretical shortcomings.

One appealing class of models extends the SM gauge group to \( SU(3)_C \times SU(3)_L \times U(1)_X \), commonly known as 331 models. In these frameworks, the electroweak sector is enlarged from \( SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y \) to \( SU(3)_L \times U(1)_X \), leading to a richer particle spectrum and new interactions. Besides offering intriguing explanations for the number of fermion families and the quantization of electric charge, 331 models naturally predict new gauge bosons, exotic fermions, and scalar multiplets. In certain realizations, these additional fields can provide stable, neutral particles that serve as dark matter candidates, stabilized by residual symmetries emerging after spontaneous symmetry breaking.

A particularly interesting possibility in some variants of the 331 model is the existence of a *light* dark matter candidate, with a mass in the sub- to few-GeV range. Such light dark matter (LDM) scenarios have attracted increased attention in recent years because they can evade conventional constraints that typically exclude heavier WIMP-like candidates, while remaining consistent with the relic density inferred from cosmological observations. However, the viability of LDM is subject to stringent and complementary bounds from both direct detection experiments and high-energy collider searches. 

Direct detection experiments, which aim to measure the nuclear recoil from DM-nucleus scattering, have improved their sensitivity to low-mass dark matter significantly, with cutting-edge detectors such as CRESST, DarkSide-50, and SuperCDMS exploring the sub-GeV to few-GeV mass range. For light dark matter, the scattering cross section can be suppressed due to kinematic effects, but the increasing precision of low-threshold detectors is beginning to probe previously unconstrained parameter space. In parallel, collider searches at the LHC can place powerful constraints on LDM candidates by looking for missing transverse momentum signatures in association with Standard Model particles, as well as setting mass limits on mediators predicted by the model. In the 331 scenario, new gauge bosons and scalars can mediate interactions between the dark matter and SM fields, and non-observation of their signatures sets strong bounds on their masses and couplings.

The interplay between LHC and direct detection constraints is particularly relevant in testing the 331 model’s parameter space. While collider searches are sensitive to mediator production regardless of the DM mass, direct detection bounds are highly dependent on the DM mass and the mediator coupling to nucleons. By combining these complementary approaches, one can robustly test the light dark matter window and, in some cases, exclude it entirely. This is especially significant for models where the relic density constraint can be satisfied for light masses through resonant annihilation or co-annihilation processes involving new states.

Previous studies have analyzed the heavy dark matter regime of 331 models, often focusing on TeV-scale candidates and the corresponding high-energy phenomenology. In contrast, the light mass region has received less attention, partly due to the challenges in probing it experimentally and the subtleties in the model’s parameter correlations. However, with recent advances in both collider analyses and direct detection techniques, the LDM sector of the 331 model can now be scrutinized with unprecedented precision.

In this work, we revisit the light dark matter scenario in a representative 331 model, taking into account the latest data from LHC Run 2 searches and state-of-the-art direct detection results. We perform a comprehensive scan over the relevant parameter space, incorporating theoretical requirements such as perturbativity, vacuum stability, and the correct pattern of symmetry breaking, as well as cosmological constraints from the observed relic abundance. Our analysis focuses on the viability of a light, stable particle arising from the extended gauge and scalar sectors, and we assess whether any region of the LDM mass range remains consistent with all current experimental bounds.

The structure of this paper is as follows. In Section 2, we briefly review the theoretical framework of the 331 model under consideration, highlighting the features relevant for the dark matter phenomenology. Section 3 outlines the methodology of our parameter space exploration, including the implementation of collider and direct detection constraints. Section 4 presents the results of our combined analysis, emphasizing the impact of LHC limits on mediator masses and couplings, and the exclusion power of low-threshold direct detection experiments. Finally, in Section 5, we summarize our findings and discuss the implications for future searches, concluding that the combination of collider and direct detection data can decisively test—and in some cases exclude—the light dark matter window of the 331 model.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the viability of the light dark matter window in a specific realization of the 331 model by confronting its parameter space with the most recent constraints from LHC searches and direct dark matter detection experiments. Collider limits on new gauge bosons and exotic fermions, combined with bounds on invisible Higgs decays, significantly restrict the region where a light dark matter candidate could survive. Furthermore, the latest results from experiments such as XENONnT and LZ impose stringent upper limits on the spin-independent scattering cross section, excluding most of the low-mass parameter space consistent with relic density requirements. The complementarity of collider and direct detection data leaves only a marginal region viable, which is expected to be probed in upcoming experimental runs. Our results therefore indicate that the light dark matter scenario within this 331 framework is highly disfavored, highlighting the power of combined experimental constraints in testing beyond Standard Model constructions.

title: Software Engineering in Civic Tech: A Case Study about Code for Ireland
abstract: This paper examines the role of software engineering practices in the civic technology sector through a case study of Code for Ireland, a volunteer-driven organisation developing digital solutions for social good. Civic tech initiatives face unique challenges, including limited resources, heterogeneous stakeholder needs, and sustaining volunteer engagement, which influence both the development process and project outcomes. Drawing on qualitative data from interviews, project documentation, and participant observation, this study investigates how Code for Ireland organises its workflows, applies software engineering methodologies, and balances technical goals with civic impact. The findings highlight the adaptation of agile principles to accommodate fluctuating team composition, the importance of lightweight documentation for continuity, and the integration of user feedback from community partners. Additionally, the research identifies strategies for fostering collaboration and maintaining project momentum despite non-commercial constraints. By situating these practices within broader software engineering discourse, the paper contributes insights into how engineering principles can be effectively tailored to civic contexts, offering guidance for practitioners and researchers seeking to enhance the sustainability and societal value of civic tech projects.
introduction:
In recent years, the intersection of software engineering and civic engagement has emerged as a dynamic and transformative domain, often referred to as “civic technology” or “civic tech.” Civic tech encompasses the design, development, and deployment of digital tools and platforms that enable greater participation in public life, improve the delivery of government services, and foster transparency and accountability. This field sits at the confluence of computer science, public administration, and social innovation, and has gained prominence as governments, non-profit organisations, and volunteer communities increasingly recognise the potential of technology to address societal challenges. While much of the scholarly discourse on software engineering has traditionally focused on commercial, industrial, or open-source contexts, there is a growing need to examine how engineering principles, processes, and practices translate into the civic technology arena, particularly in grassroots, volunteer-driven initiatives.

Code for Ireland is one such initiative, operating as part of the wider Code for All network, which has chapters in multiple countries. Founded in 2013, Code for Ireland brings together volunteer software developers, designers, data analysts, and civic-minded citizens to co-create technological solutions that address real-life issues facing communities in Ireland. Working closely with civil society organisations, local authorities, and other stakeholders, the group develops applications, data visualisations, and digital services aimed at improving aspects of civic life—from environmental monitoring to community information systems. Unlike corporate or government-led software projects, Code for Ireland operates without a formal hierarchical structure, relying instead on collaborative, project-based teams and voluntary contributions of time and expertise. This makes it an illuminating case for exploring how software engineering practices are adapted, modified, or reinterpreted in a civic tech context.

The study of software engineering in civic tech settings is particularly important for several reasons. First, such projects often operate under constraints that differ from those in commercial environments, including limited funding, reliance on volunteer labour, and fluctuating participation levels. These constraints influence project planning, requirements gathering, design choices, and maintenance strategies. Second, civic tech projects frequently involve diverse teams with varying levels of technical expertise, necessitating inclusive and flexible development approaches. Third, the end-users and stakeholders are often members of the public or representatives of non-profit organisations, whose needs may not be easily captured through traditional software requirements elicitation methods. Understanding how software engineering principles are applied in such contexts can contribute to both theory and practice, offering lessons for practitioners and insights for researchers interested in human-centred, socially impactful technology.

While the academic literature on civic technology has expanded in scope, much of it has focused on the social and political impacts of civic tech initiatives, open data movements, and participatory governance platforms. Less attention has been paid to the software engineering processes underpinning these systems, particularly in volunteer-driven groups like Code for Ireland. Existing research on community-based software projects, such as open-source software development, offers useful parallels, but civic tech often entails unique challenges: balancing technical feasibility with social value, engaging non-technical stakeholders in iterative design, and sustaining projects beyond initial deployment in the absence of commercial incentives. Investigating these challenges through an in-depth case study can shed light on how engineering practices evolve in such environments.

This paper presents a case study of Code for Ireland, with the aim of examining how software engineering is practiced within a civic tech organisation that relies on volunteer contributions. The study explores the group’s organisational structure, project workflows, and development methodologies, as well as the ways in which they manage requirements, coordinate work, and ensure the quality and sustainability of their products. By situating the analysis within the broader discourse on software engineering and civic technology, the paper seeks to contribute to a better understanding of how established engineering practices are adapted to meet the needs of socially-driven, resource-constrained projects. Furthermore, the case study highlights the opportunities and limitations inherent in volunteer-led software development for civic purposes, offering reflections that may inform both practitioners engaged in similar initiatives and researchers seeking to theorise about software engineering in non-traditional contexts.

In doing so, this research addresses a gap in the literature by linking the technical aspects of software engineering with the civic and participatory goals of technology projects. It underscores the importance of understanding not only the social impact of civic tech but also the engineering practices that enable such impact to be realised. Through the lens of Code for Ireland, the paper illuminates the interplay between technical rigour and civic mission, demonstrating how software engineering can serve as both a means and a catalyst for community empowerment.
conclusion:
This case study of Code for Ireland has explored how software engineering practices can be applied effectively within the civic technology domain to address societal challenges. By examining the organisation’s structure, project life cycles, and community-driven ethos, the study has demonstrated that the principles of professional software development—such as iterative design, collaborative problem-solving, and rigorous testing—are not only relevant to civic tech but also crucial for sustaining volunteer engagement and delivering impactful solutions. The findings underscore that successful civic technology initiatives require a careful balance between technical excellence, user-centred design, and community participation.

A key insight emerging from this research is the adaptability of software engineering methodologies in contexts where resources are limited, and contributors may have varying levels of expertise. Code for Ireland’s emphasis on agile practices, open-source collaboration, and incremental delivery has enabled it to produce functional and relevant digital tools while fostering an inclusive environment for volunteers. This adaptability, however, is contingent on strong facilitation, clear communication, and the ability to align diverse stakeholder expectations with achievable technical outcomes.

Moreover, the case highlights the importance of sustained engagement beyond initial project launches. Many civic tech initiatives face challenges in long-term maintenance, reflecting broader issues in volunteer-led software development. Code for Ireland’s approach—building modular solutions, encouraging documentation, and nurturing a sense of ownership among contributors—offers valuable lessons for maintaining project viability over time. This reinforces the view that civic technology projects benefit from embedding maintainability and sustainability considerations from the outset, rather than treating them as afterthoughts.

The study also reveals that civic tech organisations occupy an intersection between grassroots activism and professional software engineering. This positioning creates opportunities for innovation that draw on both the creativity of civic-minded volunteers and the discipline of established engineering processes. It also suggests that the success of such initiatives depends on the ability to mediate between social goals and technical feasibility, ensuring that solutions are both meaningful to communities and grounded in robust engineering principles.

In conclusion, the experience of Code for Ireland illustrates that software engineering can serve as a powerful enabler of civic innovation when applied with sensitivity to community contexts and constraints. Through a combination of agile methodologies, open collaboration, and a commitment to social impact, civic tech organisations can deliver solutions that are both technically sound and socially relevant. Future research could extend these insights by comparing multiple civic tech groups across different cultural and institutional environments, deepening our understanding of how software engineering practices can be tailored to maximise societal benefit.

title: The Riemann Problem for Hyperbolic Equations under a Nonconvex Flux with Two Inflection Points
abstract: We investigate the Riemann problem for a class of scalar hyperbolic conservation laws whose flux functions are smooth but nonconvex, exhibiting two distinct inflection points. Such flux profiles arise in various physical contexts, including multiphase flows, traffic models with phase transitions, and nonlinear elasticity. The presence of two inflection points leads to richer wave structures than in the single-inflection or purely convex cases, allowing for the coexistence of multiple shock and rarefaction families, as well as nonclassical waves governed by additional admissibility criteria. We perform a detailed analysis of the solution structure by combining phase plane methods, convex–concave envelope constructions, and the theory of entropy conditions, with particular attention to the Liu and Lax criteria. The multiplicity of inflection points necessitates a careful classification of wave interactions and intermediate states, as several qualitatively distinct self-similar patterns can emerge from the same set of initial states. We present a complete characterization of the admissible wave sequences, identify regions in the state space corresponding to compound and transitional waves, and discuss the role of undercompressive shocks in the global solution. The results extend existing theory for nonconvex fluxes with a single inflection point, highlighting new bifurcation phenomena in the wave pattern diagram. Numerical simulations based on high-resolution finite volume schemes are included to illustrate the analytical predictions and confirm the intricate structure of the solutions. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between flux geometry and nonlinear wave dynamics in hyperbolic conservation laws.
introduction:
The Riemann problem, which consists of solving a system of hyperbolic conservation laws with initial data given by two constant states separated by a single discontinuity, is a cornerstone in the theory of nonlinear waves. Its solution structure provides fundamental insight into the qualitative behavior of more general initial value problems and underlies the construction of many numerical methods for hyperbolic partial differential equations. Classical theory has been extensively developed for convex flux functions, where characteristic fields exhibit genuine nonlinearity or linear degeneracy, and solution patterns are composed of simple waves such as rarefactions, shocks, and contact discontinuities. In this setting, the Lax entropy conditions and self-similar solutions offer a complete description of admissible wave structures.

When the flux function is nonconvex, the situation becomes significantly more complicated. Nonconvexity may arise in numerous physical models, including multiphase flow in porous media, magnetohydrodynamics, traffic flow, and nonlinear elasticity, where the constitutive relations or state equations lead to changes in the sign of the characteristic speed derivatives. In such cases, the occurrence of inflection points in the flux function allows for richer wave phenomena: composite waves formed by the concatenation of shocks and rarefactions, undercompressive shocks, and other nonclassical structures. The presence of even a single inflection point already requires a refined analysis, involving the construction of convex and concave envelopes to determine admissible solution branches.

The focus of this work is on the Riemann problem for a scalar conservation law with a flux function exhibiting two distinct inflection points. This configuration enlarges the complexity of the wave interactions and admissibility criteria. Multiple inflection points partition the state space into regions of alternating convexity and concavity, enabling the coexistence of various wave families and the possibility of transitions between them within a single Riemann solution. In particular, the solution may contain multiple composite waves, sequences of rarefaction–shock or shock–rarefaction structures, and intermediate states determined by intricate matching conditions. The analysis must account for the interplay between genuinely nonlinear segments and those where the characteristic field changes convexity, as well as the role of entropy conditions beyond the classical Lax framework.

The study of such problems is motivated both by applications and by the need to extend the theoretical framework of hyperbolic conservation laws. Understanding the precise structure of solutions for fluxes with two inflection points is essential for the design of accurate numerical solvers, especially those preserving physically admissible structures without introducing spurious oscillations. In this paper, we develop a systematic approach to classify all possible Riemann solutions in this setting, construct the associated wave curves, and characterize the admissibility of composite structures. The results contribute to the broader understanding of nonconvex hyperbolic problems and provide a foundation for further analytical and computational investigations.
conclusion: We have examined the Riemann problem for a hyperbolic conservation law with a nonconvex flux exhibiting two inflection points. The analysis identified the rich wave structures arising from the interplay of rarefaction, shock, and composite waves. Through careful classification of admissible solutions, we clarified transition criteria between regimes. These results extend existing theory, offering a more complete framework for understanding complex flux geometries in nonlinear wave propagation problems.

title: Topological invariant and cotranslational symmetry in strongly interacting multi-magnon systems
abstract: We investigate the emergence of topological invariants in strongly interacting multi-magnon systems by exploiting cotranslational symmetry—a generalized translational invariance defined in the center-of-mass frame of multiple particles. Considering a class of spin models with strong exchange interactions, we formulate an effective description of bound magnon states and demonstrate that the cotranslational symmetry enables the definition of a topological invariant directly in the multi-particle Hilbert space. Using this framework, we construct a multi-magnon Chern number, capturing the global topological properties of the bound-state bands even in the presence of strong interactions that break single-particle translational symmetry. Numerical calculations for representative lattice geometries reveal nontrivial topological phases characterized by robust edge modes in the interacting spectrum. Our results show that cotranslational symmetry provides a natural route to generalize bulk-boundary correspondence to interacting quasiparticles, offering a unified description of topology in multi-particle sectors. This approach opens new avenues for exploring topological phenomena in strongly correlated spin systems and related platforms where interaction effects are essential.
introduction:
Topological phases of matter have attracted tremendous interest over the past decades, owing to their remarkable robustness against local perturbations and their potential applications in quantum information processing and spintronics. While most pioneering studies have focused on noninteracting or weakly interacting systems, recent advances have opened new avenues for exploring topological phenomena in strongly correlated regimes, where interactions can qualitatively modify the nature of excitations and their topological properties. In particular, the interplay between strong interactions and topology can give rise to emergent quasiparticles whose collective behavior transcends the single-particle picture.

Magnons, the quantized excitations of spin systems, provide a versatile platform for investigating such interaction-induced topological effects. In the linear spin-wave approximation, magnons behave as noninteracting bosonic quasiparticles, and their band topology can be characterized by conventional invariants such as the Chern number. However, in the presence of strong spin–spin interactions, multi-magnon bound states can form, leading to rich many-body dynamics beyond the reach of single-magnon theories. Understanding the topological nature of these bound states is essential for a comprehensive description of strongly interacting spin systems.

A key challenge in this context is the identification of appropriate symmetries and invariants that can characterize topological phases of bound multi-magnon states. Traditional translational symmetry is insufficient, as the center-of-mass and relative motions of bound magnons are intertwined by interactions. Recently, the concept of *cotranslational symmetry*—a generalized translational invariance of the entire multi-particle wavefunction—has emerged as a powerful tool to address this problem. By exploiting cotranslational symmetry, it becomes possible to define an effective Brillouin zone for the center-of-mass motion, enabling the extension of Berry-phase-based topological invariants to interacting multi-particle systems.

Previous works have demonstrated that such an approach can reveal nontrivial topology in few-body bound states in one- and two-dimensional lattice models. Nevertheless, the characterization of topological invariants in strongly interacting multi-magnon systems remains largely unexplored, particularly in regimes where the bound states are deeply localized in relative coordinates but still possess dispersive center-of-mass motion. Moreover, the connection between interaction strength, cotranslational symmetry, and the stability of topological phases has yet to be systematically established.

In this work, we investigate the topological properties of strongly interacting multi-magnon bound states in translationally invariant spin systems. By formulating a cotranslational symmetry framework, we construct many-body topological invariants that remain well-defined in the presence of strong interactions. Our analysis uncovers interaction-driven topological phase transitions and provides insight into how multi-magnon excitations inherit and modify topological features from their underlying spin models. This study paves the way for probing interaction-induced topology in quantum magnetic materials and engineered spin systems.
conclusion: In this work, we have explored the role of cotranslational symmetry in defining topological invariants for strongly interacting multi-magnon systems. By extending the concept of translational symmetry to collective motion of bound magnons, we identified a natural framework in which the many-body Bloch states can be constructed and their Berry curvature defined. This allowed us to generalize the notion of Chern numbers to a highly correlated regime, beyond the single-particle picture. Our analysis reveals that the emergence of nontrivial topological invariants is intrinsically tied to the bound-state nature of multi-magnon excitations, and that these invariants remain robust under strong interactions. The approach provides a unified description of topological phases in interacting spin systems, bridging the gap between single-particle band theory and genuine many-body effects. The results suggest that cotranslational symmetry offers a powerful tool for classifying and predicting topological properties in a broad class of quantum magnets. Future work may extend these ideas to higher dimensions, finite temperatures, and systems with disorder, potentially guiding experimental efforts to detect interaction-induced topological phenomena in spin chains and related quantum platforms.

title: Modelling the mass-metallicity relation of star-forming galaxies from z ~ 3.5 to z ~ 0
abstract: We present a comprehensive study of the evolution of the mass–metallicity relation (MZR) for star-forming galaxies from redshift \( z \sim 3.5 \) to the local Universe (\( z \sim 0 \)), using a combination of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations and observational constraints. Our modelling framework incorporates gas inflow, star formation, chemical enrichment, and feedback processes, calibrated against recent spectroscopic surveys spanning a broad range in stellar mass (\( 10^{8} \lesssim M_{\star}/M_{\odot} \lesssim 10^{11} \)) and redshift. We employ a physically motivated parameterisation of the MZR that captures both its slope and normalisation evolution, and test the influence of varying gas accretion histories and outflow mass-loading factors. The model successfully reproduces the observed flattening of the relation at high stellar masses and the systematic increase in metallicity from high to low redshift. We find that the primary driver of MZR evolution is the interplay between declining gas fractions and reduced metal loss via galactic winds over cosmic time. At \( z \gtrsim 2.5 \), rapid gas accretion dilutes the interstellar medium, maintaining lower metallicities, while at \( z \lesssim 1 \), the suppression of inflows and cumulative enrichment lead to near-solar abundances in massive systems. Our results suggest that the MZR’s redshift dependence can be largely explained without invoking strong evolution in feedback efficiency, but requires a gradual change in the balance between inflow, star formation, and outflow. This framework provides a predictive tool for interpreting upcoming deep spectroscopic surveys of high-redshift galaxies.
introduction:
The mass–metallicity relation (MZR), describing the correlation between the stellar mass of a galaxy and the metallicity of its interstellar medium, provides a fundamental constraint on galaxy formation and evolution models. First established in the local Universe with large spectroscopic surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the MZR has since been traced to progressively higher redshifts, revealing systematic evolution over cosmic time. At a given stellar mass, high-redshift star-forming galaxies exhibit lower gas-phase metallicities than their low-redshift counterparts, reflecting the combined effects of gas inflows, outflows, and star formation history on chemical enrichment. Understanding the physical drivers of the MZR and its redshift evolution is key to disentangling the interplay between baryonic processes that govern galaxy growth.  

From a theoretical perspective, the MZR emerges naturally in hierarchical galaxy formation models, where stellar feedback regulates star formation and drives metal-enriched outflows, while gas accretion from the intergalactic medium dilutes the metallicity of the interstellar medium. Semi-analytic models and hydrodynamical simulations have reproduced the general form of the relation, but discrepancies remain in matching both the slope and normalisation across the full redshift range. Moreover, observational studies indicate that the MZR may be part of a more fundamental relation linking stellar mass, metallicity, and star formation rate – the so-called “fundamental metallicity relation” (FMR) – whose universality across cosmic time remains debated.  

At redshifts z ≳ 3, the observational constraints on the MZR are sparse due to the challenges of measuring robust metallicities for faint, distant galaxies. Spectroscopic surveys using rest-frame optical emission lines, enabled by near-infrared instruments, have begun to fill this gap, but systematic uncertainties in metallicity calibrations complicate comparisons across epochs. Nonetheless, recent datasets now allow the MZR to be probed from z ~ 3.5 to the present day, providing an unprecedented window into the chemical evolution of star-forming galaxies over more than 12 billion years.  

In this work, we present a modelling framework aimed at reproducing the observed MZR evolution from z ~ 3.5 to z ~ 0, incorporating physically motivated prescriptions for gas inflow, star formation, and feedback. By confronting the model predictions with a compilation of observational measurements across redshift, we seek to identify the dominant mechanisms shaping the MZR and to assess their relative importance over cosmic time. This approach allows us to interpret the observed trends within a coherent evolutionary context, offering new insights into the baryon cycle and the regulation of galaxy metallicities.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a detailed investigation of the mass–metallicity relation (MZR) for star-forming galaxies over a wide range of cosmic time, from redshift \( z \sim 3.5 \) to the present day. By combining observational constraints from spectroscopic surveys with physically motivated models of galaxy evolution, we have explored how the interplay between stellar mass growth, metal production, and gas flows shapes the observed scaling between stellar mass and gas-phase metallicity. Our approach has allowed us to track both the normalization and slope of the MZR across more than 11 billion years of cosmic history, providing a coherent framework for interpreting its evolution in the context of galaxy formation theory.

Our results confirm that the MZR is already in place at \( z \approx 3.5 \), albeit with a significantly lower normalization compared to the local Universe. The evolution is most pronounced at low and intermediate stellar masses, where metallicities increase by up to \(\sim 0.5\) dex from the highest redshifts to \( z \approx 0 \). At the massive end, the relation shows a degree of saturation even at early times, consistent with the idea that the most massive systems enriched rapidly in the early Universe and subsequently evolved more quiescently. The slope of the relation steepens modestly with redshift, reflecting the stronger impact of inflows and outflows on less massive systems in the early epochs. These findings are consistent with a scenario in which the balance between metal enrichment from star formation and dilution by pristine or low-metallicity inflows shifts gradually as galaxies grow in mass and as the cosmic gas supply declines.

By implementing a range of chemical evolution models, including both equilibrium and non-equilibrium formulations, we find that no single, static parameter set can reproduce the MZR at all epochs. Instead, the data favour models in which key feedback and accretion parameters evolve with redshift. In particular, high-redshift galaxies require stronger mass-loading factors and higher specific accretion rates to match the observed low metallicities, while at later times, reduced inflow rates and more effective recycling of enriched material can account for the higher metallicities at fixed mass. This evolution is naturally explained within the framework of hierarchical galaxy formation, where early growth is dominated by rapid gas accretion from the cosmic web, and later stages are regulated more by internal processes and declining external supply.

An important outcome of this study is the role of gas fraction in driving the MZR evolution. Galaxies at high redshift have substantially higher gas fractions, which both dilute their metallicities and sustain elevated star formation rates. As gas fractions decline over time, the efficiency of metal retention increases, leading to the observed rise in metallicity. Incorporating gas fraction evolution into our models not only improves the fit to the MZR at all redshifts but also naturally links the MZR to the so-called fundamental metallicity relation, which connects stellar mass, metallicity, and star formation rate. Our results support the view that the MZR is not an isolated scaling law but part of a broader set of interrelated relations governed by baryon cycling processes.

While our modelling provides a consistent picture of the MZR evolution, several uncertainties remain. The choice of metallicity calibration introduces systematic offsets in normalization, and the treatment of inflows and outflows remains simplified in our framework. Furthermore, environmental processes, mergers, and radial metallicity gradients are not explicitly included, yet they may play a non-negligible role, especially in the most massive systems and at intermediate redshifts. Future work combining spatially resolved spectroscopy from upcoming facilities with cosmological hydrodynamical simulations will be essential to disentangle these effects and refine our understanding of the underlying physical drivers.

In summary, the evolution of the mass–metallicity relation from \( z \sim 3.5 \) to the present reflects the changing balance between gas accretion, star formation, feedback, and recycling in galaxies of different masses. Our results highlight the need for redshift-dependent modelling of baryon cycling to reproduce the observed trends, and they reinforce the interpretation of the MZR as a manifestation of the coupled growth of stellar mass and chemical enrichment in a cosmological context. As new large, deep spectroscopic surveys extend precise metallicity measurements to earlier epochs and lower masses, the framework developed here will provide a valuable tool for probing the physical processes that govern galaxy evolution across cosmic time.

title: C3SASR: Cheap Causal Convolutions for Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation
abstract: We propose C3SASR, a novel framework that enhances self-attentive sequential recommendation by integrating cheap causal convolutions into transformer-based architectures. While self-attention excels at modeling complex item dependencies, its quadratic complexity in sequence length limits scalability for long user histories. C3SASR addresses this challenge by replacing part of the attention computation with lightweight causal convolutional layers that efficiently capture local context while preserving temporal order. These causal convolutions act as complementary feature extractors, enabling the model to focus attention on more informative, long-range dependencies. To further improve efficiency, we design a hybrid interaction module that adaptively fuses convolutional and attention-based representations. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that C3SASR achieves superior recommendation accuracy compared to strong baselines, while significantly reducing computational cost and memory usage. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the convolution-attention hybridization and the adaptive fusion mechanism. Our approach provides a practical solution for large-scale, real-time sequential recommendation systems without sacrificing predictive performance.
introduction:
Sequential recommendation has emerged as a crucial problem in personalized information access, where the goal is to predict the next item a user is likely to interact with based on their historical behavior. This paradigm underlies many modern recommender systems in domains such as e-commerce, streaming media, and online advertising, where user–item interactions naturally form temporal sequences. By modeling the order and context of these interactions, sequential recommenders can capture dynamic user preferences and short-term interests beyond what static user profiles provide.

Recent advances in deep learning have substantially improved sequential recommendation by leveraging architectures originally developed for natural language processing and computer vision. Among these, self-attention networks, inspired by the Transformer model, have shown remarkable effectiveness. Self-attention enables each position in the sequence to attend to all others, thereby modeling both short- and long-range dependencies without the recurrence constraints of RNNs or the locality bias of CNNs. Models such as SASRec and BERT4Rec have demonstrated that self-attention can outperform prior recurrent and convolutional approaches in accuracy and scalability.

Despite their success, self-attentive sequential recommenders have notable limitations. First, the quadratic time and memory complexity of self-attention with respect to sequence length can be prohibitive for long user histories, leading to high computational cost and latency in both training and inference. Second, while self-attention captures global dependencies, it does not explicitly encode local continuity patterns that are often present in user–item interaction sequences — for example, binge-watching episodes of a TV series, purchasing items from a specific category in succession, or listening to songs from the same album. Local context modeling, when combined with global attention, can provide richer sequence representations and improve recommendation accuracy.

To address these limitations, researchers have explored hybrid architectures that combine self-attention with convolutional or recurrent components, aiming to balance efficiency, locality bias, and global context modeling. Convolutional layers, in particular, are attractive due to their ability to capture local patterns through sliding windows, their parallelizable computation, and their generally lower computational complexity compared to self-attention over long sequences. However, naïve integration of standard convolutions into self-attentive models may not yield optimal efficiency gains, especially when causal (autoregressive) sequence modeling is required to preserve the order and avoid information leakage from future items.

Causal convolutions, which enforce that the representation at each time step depends only on current and past inputs, have been widely used in sequence modeling tasks such as language modeling and time series forecasting. They can efficiently capture fixed-size local dependencies, and when stacked, can extend their receptive field to model longer contexts. Nevertheless, standard causal convolutions with large receptive fields can still incur non-trivial computational costs, particularly if the kernel size or the number of layers is large.

In this work, we propose **C3SASR** — *Cheap Causal Convolutions for Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation* — a novel architecture that augments self-attention with a lightweight causal convolutional module designed to efficiently enhance local context modeling. The key idea is to replace expensive wide-kernel convolutions with a parameter- and computation-efficient alternative that leverages depthwise separable convolutions and dilations to expand the receptive field without proportionally increasing cost. By integrating this cheap causal convolutional block before the self-attention layers, C3SASR enriches the input representations with localized sequential patterns, allowing the subsequent attention mechanism to focus on modeling higher-order, global dependencies.

Our proposed architecture offers several benefits. First, it significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with modeling local dependencies compared to using additional self-attention layers. Second, the causal design ensures strict autoregressive behavior, enabling the model to be applied in both next-item prediction and streaming recommendation settings without retraining. Third, by explicitly introducing an inductive bias toward locality, C3SASR can improve recommendation accuracy in scenarios where short-term patterns are strong predictors of user behavior.

We conduct extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets for sequential recommendation, comparing C3SASR against state-of-the-art self-attentive and hybrid models. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or superior accuracy while reducing computational cost, validating the effectiveness of cheap causal convolutions as a complement to self-attention. Further ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component and highlight the trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: (1) We identify the inefficiency of pure self-attention models in capturing local dependencies for sequential recommendation and motivate the need for a lightweight locality-enhancing module. (2) We design a novel cheap causal convolutional block that efficiently encodes local sequential patterns without future leakage. (3) We integrate this block with self-attention in the C3SASR architecture, achieving an effective balance between accuracy and efficiency. (4) We provide comprehensive empirical evidence of the advantages of our approach on multiple datasets.

By bridging the gap between local and global sequence modeling in a computationally efficient manner, C3SASR offers a practical and high-performance solution for real-world sequential recommendation systems.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced C3SASR, a lightweight yet effective framework that integrates cheap causal convolutions with self-attentive architectures for sequential recommendation. By replacing expensive attention layers in the early stages with causal convolutions, C3SASR reduces computational cost while preserving the ability to capture both short- and long-range dependencies. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrated that our approach achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, while significantly improving efficiency in terms of memory usage and inference time. These results highlight the potential of combining convolutional and attention-based mechanisms in a cost-aware manner for large-scale recommendation scenarios. Future work will explore adaptive hybrid architectures and more sophisticated convolutional designs to further enhance scalability and generalization in diverse sequential recommendation tasks.

title: Tidal decay and orbital circularization in close-in two-planet systems
abstract: We investigate the long-term tidal evolution of close-in two-planet systems, focusing on the coupled processes of orbital decay and eccentricity damping. Using a combination of secular perturbation theory and direct numerical integrations, we explore the interplay between mutual gravitational interactions and tidal dissipation in the innermost planet. Our model includes equilibrium tide prescriptions with constant time lag, and accounts for stellar tides as well as planetary tides, allowing for energy dissipation in both bodies. We examine a range of system architectures with varying planet masses, orbital separations, and initial eccentricities, representative of observed compact multi-planet systems. The results show that tidal dissipation in the inner planet can lead to significant inward migration on Gyr timescales, accompanied by rapid eccentricity damping. However, secular forcing from the outer companion can maintain a finite eccentricity in the inner orbit, enhancing tidal heating and accelerating decay. We find that, depending on the mass ratio and spacing, the coupled evolution may lead to resonant passage, apsidal alignment, or complete dynamical decoupling. In some cases, orbital decay of the inner planet triggers instability in the outer planet’s orbit, potentially leading to scattering or ejection. The timescales for circularization and decay are sensitive to the tidal quality factors of both planets and the host star. Our findings highlight the importance of multi-planet interactions in shaping the orbital architecture of close-in systems, and suggest that observed eccentricities and period ratios may encode information about past tidal and dynamical evolution.
introduction:
The discovery of close-in exoplanets with orbital periods of only a few days has prompted intense investigation into the dynamical processes that shape their present-day configurations. In particular, systems hosting multiple planets in compact arrangements provide valuable laboratories for studying the interplay between planetary migration, tidal dissipation, and long-term orbital evolution. Tidal interactions between a planet and its host star can lead to orbital decay—where the semimajor axis decreases over time—and to orbital circularization, whereby eccentricity is damped. While tidal effects have been extensively studied for single-planet systems, their role in multi-planet systems, where mutual gravitational perturbations are significant, is less well constrained.

In close-in two-planet systems, the secular exchange of angular momentum between planets can maintain finite eccentricities despite tidal damping. This sustained eccentricity can enhance tidal dissipation in the inner planet, potentially accelerating its orbital decay. Conversely, strong tidal damping can quench secular excitation, leading to rapid circularization and decoupling of the planets’ orbital evolution. The balance between these processes depends on planetary masses, orbital spacings, eccentricities, and the efficiency of tidal dissipation in both the planets and the star. Moreover, near-resonant configurations may amplify or suppress tidal effects, further complicating the evolutionary pathways.

Recent observations have revealed two-planet systems in which the inner planet’s proximity to the host star suggests significant past tidal evolution, yet the architecture of the outer companion hints at ongoing dynamical interactions. Understanding how tidal decay and circularization operate in such systems is crucial for interpreting their current orbital parameters and constraining their formation histories. Theoretical models that couple tidal dissipation with N-body dynamics offer a means to explore the range of possible evolutionary outcomes, but require careful treatment of both short-term perturbations and long-term secular trends.

In this work, we investigate the coupled tidal and dynamical evolution of close-in two-planet systems, focusing on the conditions that lead to significant orbital decay and circularization of the inner planet. By combining analytic secular theory with numerical integrations that include tidal forces, we aim to identify the regimes in which tidal dissipation reshapes system architecture and to compare these predictions with the observed exoplanet population.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the coupled processes of tidal decay and orbital circularization in close-in two-planet systems, with a focus on how mutual gravitational interactions and tidal dissipation within the planets and the host star shape the long-term dynamical evolution. By combining secular perturbation theory with tidal evolution models, we have quantified the interplay between eccentricity damping, semi-major axis decay, and the exchange of angular momentum between planets in configurations where the inner planet resides in a short-period orbit and the outer companion lies at modest orbital separation. Our analysis highlights that the presence of an additional planet can significantly alter the tidal evolution timescales compared to single-planet cases, both accelerating and decelerating orbital decay depending on the initial orbital architecture.

We have shown that the gravitational perturbations from an outer companion can maintain a finite eccentricity in the inner planet, even in the presence of strong tidal damping. This sustained eccentricity, in turn, enhances tidal dissipation and can lead to more rapid inward migration of the inner planet toward the host star. Conversely, in some configurations, the secular coupling may act to reduce the eccentricity forcing on the inner planet, thereby prolonging its survival in a close-in orbit. The efficiency of these mechanisms is found to depend sensitively on the planetary mass ratio, orbital spacing, and mutual inclination, as well as on the tidal quality factors adopted for the planets and the star.

Our results indicate that tidal circularization is not simply a monotonic process determined by the inner planet’s proximity to the star, but rather emerges from a complex interaction between tides and multi-planet dynamics. In particular, the pathway toward a circularized orbit can be significantly extended if angular momentum exchange with the outer planet counteracts the tidal damping of eccentricity. This finding has important implications for the interpretation of observed eccentricities in close-in exoplanets, suggesting that non-zero eccentricities in apparently old systems may be sustained by undetected companions.

We have further demonstrated that the combined action of tidal decay and secular forcing can produce distinctive evolutionary tracks in the semi-major axis–eccentricity plane, which may be used to constrain the tidal properties of planets and stars when combined with precise orbital measurements. Our models also suggest that in some cases the inner planet may undergo runaway tidal decay once its eccentricity is sufficiently excited, potentially leading to ingestion by the star on timescales much shorter than would be predicted assuming isolated tidal evolution.

Future observational surveys, particularly those capable of detecting low-mass, long-period companions to close-in planets, will be essential for testing these theoretical predictions. The integration of transit timing variation analyses, radial velocity follow-up, and astrometric constraints will provide the necessary dynamical context to disentangle the role of multi-planet interactions in shaping tidal evolution. Continued refinement of tidal dissipation models, informed by both laboratory experiments and detailed interior structure calculations, will be crucial for improving the quantitative accuracy of such studies. Ultimately, understanding the coupled tidal and dynamical evolution of close-in multi-planet systems will shed light on the final stages of planetary system architecture and the fate of short-period planets.

title: Hydrodynamic simulations of moonlet induced propellers in Saturn's rings: Application to Bleriot
abstract: We present three–dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of propeller–shaped disturbances in Saturn’s A ring generated by embedded moonlets, with specific application to the prominent propeller feature Blériot. Using a locally isothermal, viscous disk model, we solve the Navier–Stokes equations in a corotating frame to investigate the nonlinear interaction between a moonlet and the surrounding ring material. The simulations employ high spatial resolution to resolve both the immediate Hill sphere region and the extended S–shaped density perturbations. By varying moonlet mass, kinematic viscosity, and background surface density, we quantify their influence on propeller morphology, gap opening efficiency, and azimuthal extent. Our models reproduce key observational characteristics of Blériot measured by the Cassini spacecraft, including the radial separation of partial gaps and the longitudinal asymmetry between leading and trailing lobes. We find that the azimuthal decay length of the propeller wakes is strongly dependent on the effective ring viscosity, while the radial width is primarily determined by the moonlet’s Hill radius. Synthetic optical depth profiles extracted from the simulations compare favorably with Cassini UVIS and ISS data, supporting the validity of the hydrodynamic approach for dense ring systems. The results suggest that Blériot’s observed morphology can be explained by a moonlet of radius ∼0.75 km embedded in a ring region with kinematic viscosity of order 50 cm² s⁻¹. Our study demonstrates that high–resolution hydrodynamic modeling provides a robust framework for interpreting propeller features, constraining the physical properties of Saturn’s rings, and probing the dynamics of embedded moonlets in particulate disks.
introduction:
Saturn’s rings exhibit a wealth of fine-scale structures that reflect the complex interplay between gravitational perturbations, self-gravity, and collisional dynamics within the dense disk of icy particles. Among the most intriguing of these structures are the so-called “propellers,” localized disturbances generated by embedded moonlets too small to clear complete gaps in the surrounding ring material. These features, first identified in Cassini spacecraft images, manifest as characteristic, elongated bright and dark lobes extending both azimuthally and radially from the moonlet’s location. Their morphology encodes information about the mass, size, and orbital parameters of the embedded bodies, as well as the local dynamical and collisional environment of the rings.

The propeller named Bleriot is one of the largest and most persistent such features observed in Saturn’s outer A ring. Its relatively well-defined shape and long-lived visibility make it an ideal candidate for detailed study. Previous observational analyses have provided constraints on the moonlet’s orbit and estimates of its size, while analytic theories and simplified numerical models have elucidated the basic mechanisms by which a moonlet perturbs the surrounding ring material. However, fully capturing the dynamical evolution of the propeller structure, including the response of ring particles to the moonlet’s gravitational field, requires high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations that account for viscosity, pressure, and self-gravity in an appropriate approximation.

Hydrodynamic models treat the ring as a continuum fluid, enabling the study of large-scale features without resolving individual particles. This approach is particularly advantageous when computational resources limit the applicability of direct N-body simulations over the spatial and temporal scales relevant to observed propellers. By calibrating the effective viscosity and other transport coefficients against local N-body simulations or observations, hydrodynamic simulations can reproduce the large-scale morphology and evolution of moonlet-induced perturbations with reasonable fidelity.

In this work, we apply a two-dimensional, isothermal hydrodynamic model to simulate the propeller structure generated by a moonlet with parameters consistent with those inferred for Bleriot. We investigate how the resulting density perturbations evolve under the combined influence of the moonlet’s gravity and the viscous spreading of the ring. By comparing our simulations to Cassini imaging data, we assess the ability of the hydrodynamic approach to reproduce the observed shape, size, and contrast of the propeller lobes. This study not only refines our understanding of Bleriot’s properties but also provides a framework for interpreting other propeller features in Saturn’s rings, thereby contributing to a more comprehensive picture of the dynamics of embedded moonlets in dense planetary rings.
conclusion: Our hydrodynamic simulations reproduce key morphological features of the propeller structure generated by the moonlet Blériot in Saturn’s A ring. By incorporating realistic ring viscosity and self-gravity wakes, the models capture both the radial gap profile and the azimuthal density variations observed by Cassini. The results indicate that the propeller’s asymmetry and wake damping scale are sensitive to the moonlet’s mass and the local ring viscosity, providing constraints on these quantities. Comparison with high-resolution imaging suggests that Blériot’s gravitational perturbations are well described by a nonlinear hydrodynamic framework. These findings support the use of such models to interpret other propeller structures, offering insight into moonlet–ring interactions and the dynamical evolution of Saturn’s rings.

title: 3D Unoriented loop models and the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model
abstract: We investigate three-dimensional statistical loop models in which loops are unoriented and mutually nonintersecting, and establish their connection to the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ nonlinear sigma model. Using analytical arguments and numerical simulations, we explore the critical properties of these models, focusing on universality classes and phase transitions. The mapping to the sigma model elucidates the role of topological defects and the influence of loop fugacity $n$ on scaling behaviour. Our results provide new insights into the continuum limit of unoriented loop ensembles in three dimensions.
introduction:
Loop models are a central paradigm in the study of statistical mechanics, providing a unifying language for a variety of physical systems ranging from polymers and percolation to spin systems and field theories. In their most basic form, loop models describe ensembles of non‑intersecting closed paths on a lattice or in the continuum, with statistical weights assigned according to their length, topology, or other geometric features. They can serve as graphical representations of high‑temperature expansions of spin models, as worldline formulations of quantum systems, or as path integrals in certain gauge theories. In two dimensions, such models have been extensively studied and are often exactly solvable, giving rise to deep connections with conformal field theory, Coulomb gas methods, and integrable systems.

A particularly rich class of loop models is that of *unoriented* loops, in which the loops have no intrinsic direction. In the lattice representation, these correspond to configurations in which the local degrees of freedom do not distinguish between a path traversed clockwise or counterclockwise. This unoriented nature arises naturally in the graphical expansions of discrete spin models with real rather than complex or vector spins, such as the Ising model or more generally the $O(n)$ models with real $n$. When the local degrees of freedom transform under the orthogonal group, the loops carry an index structure that is contracted at vertices, and in the unoriented case the index contractions respect a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ identification, effectively quotienting by reflection.
