Such a quotient leads directly to a connection with projective spaces, most notably the real projective space $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$.

The $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model is a nonlinear field theory whose fields take values in the manifold $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$, the space of lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Equivalently, it may be thought of as an $O(n)$ vector field with a local $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge redundancy, identifying $\mathbf{S}$ with $-\mathbf{S}$. This $\mathbb{Z}_2$ identification precisely captures the absence of orientation in the underlying loop representation. The $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model has been studied in various contexts, including nematic liquid crystals, frustrated magnetism, and gauge theories with discrete symmetries. Its renormalization group behaviour and possible phases are sensitive to both the spatial dimension and the value of $n$.

In two dimensions, the mapping between unoriented loop models and the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model is well‑established. Starting from a high‑temperature expansion of the lattice $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ model, one finds a sum over configurations of non‑intersecting unoriented loops, each loop contributing a factor of $n$ to the partition function. Conversely, certain two‑dimensional loop models can be reformulated as $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma models in the continuum limit, with the loop fugacity playing the role of the number of components $n$. This correspondence has been exploited to study critical points, universality classes, and topological defects, such as $\mathbb{Z}_2$ vortices, that are characteristic of $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ target spaces.

In three dimensions, however, the situation is less well explored. Loop models in 3D no longer map trivially to local height or Coulomb gas models, and the powerful machinery of two‑dimensional conformal field theory is no longer available. Nevertheless, loop representations remain a valuable tool, both for computational approaches such as Monte Carlo simulations and for analytical insights into the structure of field theories. Unoriented loop models in 3D are particularly interesting, as they may capture the physics of nematic ordering, line defects in ordered media, and certain gauge theories with discrete symmetries. Moreover, the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model itself has a nontrivial phase structure in three dimensions, including possible ordered, disordered, and topologically ordered phases, and the loop representation offers a complementary perspective on these phases.

The aim of this work is to investigate the connection between 3D unoriented loop models and the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model, elucidating how the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge structure inherent in the field theory manifests in the loop ensemble, and how the statistical properties of the loops encode the continuum behaviour of the sigma model. We will construct explicit lattice realizations of unoriented loop models whose continuum limits are expected to be described by $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ field theories, and we will explore their phase diagrams using a combination of analytical arguments and numerical simulations. Our focus will be on universal properties, such as critical exponents and scaling functions, as well as on the role of topological excitations like $\mathbb{Z}_2$ vortices and their interplay with the loop geometry.

By establishing a clear correspondence between three‑dimensional unoriented loop ensembles and the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model, we aim to provide a framework for understanding a broad class of physical systems within a unified description. This approach not only sheds light on the critical behaviour of these systems but also offers a route to study topological aspects and defect dynamics in a tractable, geometrical language. In doing so, it bridges the gap between the well‑developed two‑dimensional theory of loops and the more complex, but physically rich, three‑dimensional setting.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the relationship between three-dimensional unoriented loop models and the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ nonlinear sigma model, with particular attention to the mapping between the loop configurations and field-theoretic degrees of freedom. By formulating the statistical mechanics of unoriented loops in terms of local Boltzmann weights and topological constraints, we have shown how the configuration space naturally encodes an $\mathrm{O}(n)$ symmetry with a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ identification, leading to an effective continuum description in terms of the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ target manifold. This identification clarifies the role of orientation reversal in the loop model and demonstrates how the absence of a global loop orientation modifies the universality class relative to oriented loop ensembles.

Through a combination of analytic arguments and numerical evidence, we have established that at long wavelengths the unoriented loop model flows to the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model with a coupling constant determined by the loop fugacity and local interaction strengths. In particular, the mapping is robust to a range of microscopic details, underscoring its universality. The nontrivial topology of $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$, with fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}_2$, has important consequences for the nature of excitations and defect configurations in the continuum theory. We have highlighted how this manifests in the loop picture as the presence of domain wall-like structures and the absence of vortex charges associated with full $\mathrm{O}(n)$ symmetry.

Our study also sheds light on the critical behaviour of three-dimensional unoriented loop models. The correspondence with the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model provides a natural framework for understanding the phase structure, including the possibility of continuous phase transitions governed by nontrivial fixed points, as well as first-order transitions in certain parameter regimes. The presence of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge-like identification suggests that some transitions may be accompanied by emergent gauge fields in the infrared, an avenue that merits further exploration both analytically and numerically.

Furthermore, by comparing to known results in two dimensions, where the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ model is asymptotically free for $n>2$ and exhibits rich topological phenomena, we have been able to discern both similarities and qualitative differences arising in three dimensions. Notably, the role of topological defects changes, and the interplay between loop fugacity, interaction range, and lattice geometry becomes more prominent in dictating the universality class. This highlights the importance of dimensionality in determining the mapping between discrete statistical models and their continuum counterparts.

In addition to these theoretical insights, our results offer practical guidance for Monte Carlo simulations and other numerical studies. The identification of the low-energy effective theory allows one to predict scaling forms and critical exponents, and to design observables sensitive to the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ structure inherent in the unoriented model. This connection also facilitates the transfer of analytical techniques developed for sigma models, such as large-$n$ expansions and renormalization group analyses, to the study of loop ensembles.

In conclusion, the mapping between three-dimensional unoriented loop models and the $\mathrm{RP}^{n-1}$ sigma model provides a coherent and physically transparent understanding of the emergent continuum behaviour of these systems. It unifies seemingly disparate perspectives from lattice statistical mechanics and field theory, and clarifies the role of symmetry and topology in shaping the phase diagram. Future work could extend these ideas to include anisotropic interactions, coupling to additional degrees of freedom, or the effects of quenched disorder, potentially revealing new universality classes and deepening our understanding of topological and geometrical aspects of critical phenomena in three dimensions.

title: On the Formation Height of the SDO/HMI Fe 6173 Doppler Signal
abstract: We investigate the effective formation height of the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) Fe I 6173 Å Doppler velocity signal using high–resolution three–dimensional, radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations of the solar photosphere. Synthetic line profiles are computed from the simulations with a realistic treatment of radiative transfer, and the HMI instrumental transmission profiles are applied to generate observables directly comparable to spacecraft data. The contribution of different atmospheric layers to the measured Doppler shifts is quantified through response function analysis and cross–correlation techniques between simulated velocities and synthesized observables. Our results indicate that, for quiet–Sun conditions at disk center, the HMI Doppler signal is most sensitive to velocities at a mean geometric height of approximately 100 km above the continuum optical depth unity level at 5000 Å, with substantial contributions extending over a range of ±75 km. This height is found to vary with viewing angle, increasing toward the limb due to line–of–sight projection effects, and with local magnetic activity, which modifies the thermodynamic and velocity structure of the atmosphere. We discuss the implications of these results for helioseismic inversions and for the interpretation of observed Doppler shifts in active regions. Our analysis provides a refined characterization of the HMI velocity measurement formation height, enabling more accurate comparisons between observations and numerical models of solar dynamics.
introduction:
The Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) has provided an unprecedented continuous view of the Sun’s photospheric dynamics since its launch in 2010. Operating in the Fe I 6173.3 Å spectral line, HMI delivers high-cadence, full-disk Dopplergrams, magnetograms, and continuum intensity maps that have become fundamental for studies in global and local helioseismology, surface flow tracking, and magnetic field evolution. The interpretation of these observations, particularly the Doppler velocity signal, requires a solid understanding of the spectral line’s formation properties in the solar atmosphere. In particular, the effective “formation height” of the measured Doppler signal is a key quantity for connecting the observed velocities to the underlying physical processes.

The concept of formation height refers to the range of atmospheric layers that contribute most significantly to the emergent intensity or to derived quantities such as Doppler shifts. For a given spectral line, this depends on the atomic parameters of the transition, the thermodynamic and dynamic state of the atmosphere, and the instrumental transmission profile. In practice, the formation height is not a sharply defined level but rather a contribution function that is typically broad in height. For solar Doppler measurements, the effective height is further influenced by the method of line sampling and the inversion or fitting algorithms used to derive velocities. Understanding this height is particularly important in helioseismology, where travel-time measurements are interpreted in terms of subsurface flows and wave propagation, and in studies of oscillations and waves in active regions, where phase differences between observables formed at different heights provide diagnostic information about atmospheric structure and dynamics.

For the Fe I 6173 Å line, previous studies have provided estimates of formation heights based on both classical one-dimensional (1D) semi-empirical atmospheric models and modern three-dimensional (3D) radiation magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. These works indicate that the line core is formed in the mid-photosphere, while the wings sample deeper layers. However, the HMI Doppler signal is not derived from a simple line-core measurement; instead, the instrument samples the line at six wavelength positions, symmetrically placed around the nominal line center, and applies a Fourier phase method to estimate the Doppler shift. As a result, the effective formation height of the final Dopplergrams is determined by a weighted combination of the contributions from all sampled wavelengths, integrated over the instrumental spectral transmission profiles and the pixel’s spatial resolution. This makes the determination of the formation height a non-trivial problem that requires realistic forward modeling.

The accuracy of such an estimate has direct implications for the interpretation of multi-height velocity measurements, especially when comparing HMI data with observations from other instruments such as the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on SDO or ground-based spectroscopic facilities. In addition, the temporal and spatial resolution of HMI Dopplergrams, combined with their formation height, define the sensitivity of the data to waves and flows at different atmospheric depths. For example, phase shifts between Doppler velocities and intensity fluctuations, or between Doppler signals at different heights, are commonly used to infer upward or downward wave propagation. Misestimation of the formation height may lead to incorrect inferences about wave speeds, energy fluxes, or the depth of flow structures.

Given the central role of HMI data in solar physics research, it is therefore essential to quantify the formation height of the Fe I 6173 Å Doppler signal with the highest possible accuracy. This requires realistic modeling of the solar atmosphere, including the effects of convection, oscillations, and magnetic fields, as well as a faithful representation of the instrument’s spectral sampling and data processing pipeline. In this work, we employ state-of-the-art 3D radiative MHD simulations of the solar photosphere to compute synthetic Fe I 6173 Å spectra, apply the HMI measurement and velocity-retrieval procedures, and determine the corresponding height response of the Doppler signal. By analyzing both quiet-Sun and magnetically active regions, we assess the dependence of the effective formation height on local atmospheric conditions. Our results provide a refined reference for the interpretation of HMI Dopplergrams in a wide range of solar applications, from helioseismology to wave diagnostics and magnetic field studies.
conclusion:
In this study, we have investigated the formation height of the Doppler velocity signal derived from the Fe I 6173 Å line as measured by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). Using a combination of realistic radiative transfer calculations in a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulation and a detailed modeling of the HMI filter transmission profiles, we evaluated the contribution of different atmospheric layers to the observed signal. By comparing the synthetic HMI Dopplergrams with the actual line-of-sight velocities in the simulation, we determined the effective height at which the measured velocities most closely represent the true solar motions.

Our results indicate that the HMI Doppler signal is formed over a relatively broad range in the photosphere, with the peak sensitivity located at approximately 100–150 km above the continuum optical depth unity at 5000 Å. The precise height depends on the local thermodynamic and magnetic conditions, as well as on the viewing angle. We find that the contribution functions are asymmetric, with extended tails toward higher layers, implying that high photospheric dynamics can influence the measured velocities. This vertical smearing must be considered in the interpretation of HMI Doppler data, particularly in studies of wave propagation, convective motions, and helioseismic inversions.

We also examined the robustness of our height estimates to variations in spectral sampling, filter characteristics, and line broadening. The derived formation heights remain consistent within about ±20 km, suggesting that our conclusions are not strongly sensitive to moderate uncertainties in the instrumental parameters. However, the presence of strong magnetic fields can shift the effective height upward due to Zeeman splitting and line weakening.

In summary, we provide a physically motivated estimate of the HMI Doppler signal formation height that can aid in the quantitative interpretation of SDO observations. These results underscore the importance of accounting for the extended response function when relating observed velocities to specific atmospheric layers, and they offer a foundation for improved forward modeling in helioseismic and photospheric dynamics studies.

title: Accuracy of cosmological parameters using the baryon acoustic scale
abstract: We present an analysis of the accuracy of cosmological parameter estimation derived from measurements of the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) scale. Using simulated galaxy survey data and incorporating realistic observational uncertainties, we quantify the precision with which key parameters such as the Hubble constant, matter density, and dark energy equation-of-state can be constrained. The BAO feature, acting as a standard ruler, provides robust distance measurements across a range of redshifts, enabling tight constraints on the expansion history of the Universe. We investigate the impact of survey volume, redshift coverage, and systematic effects on parameter recovery, and compare results with complementary probes such as supernovae and cosmic microwave background data. Our findings demonstrate that BAO measurements alone can achieve percent-level accuracy for several parameters, while combined analyses offer significant improvements. These results highlight the critical role of BAO observations in future cosmological surveys, particularly in testing models of dark energy and possible deviations from the standard ΛCDM framework.
introduction:
The determination of cosmological parameters with high precision is a central goal of modern observational cosmology, as these parameters underpin our understanding of the composition, geometry, and evolution of the Universe. Over the past two decades, a variety of probes have been developed and refined to constrain key quantities such as the Hubble constant, the matter density parameter, and the equation of state of dark energy. Among these probes, the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) feature in the large-scale distribution of galaxies and other tracers has emerged as a robust standard ruler, offering a relatively clean and well-understood physical scale anchored in early-Universe physics. The BAO signal originates from sound waves propagating in the photon–baryon plasma prior to recombination, leaving an imprint in the matter distribution that can be observed today as a preferred clustering scale of order 150 Mpc. 

The baryon acoustic scale is determined primarily by the physics of the early Universe, and its size can be calculated from first principles using measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). When this physical scale is measured in the late-time galaxy distribution, it provides a geometric test of the cosmological model, enabling constraints on the expansion history and the growth of structure. BAO measurements are particularly valuable because the underlying physics is linear to a high degree, making them less sensitive to complex astrophysical processes that affect small-scale clustering. This allows for robust comparisons between theoretical predictions and observations, with minimal dependence on poorly constrained parameters.

In recent years, large spectroscopic surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS), and the extended BOSS (eBOSS) have delivered increasingly precise BAO distance measurements across a broad range of redshifts. These results have been complemented by alternative tracers, such as the Lyman-α forest and emission line galaxies, which extend the reach of BAO observations to higher redshifts. Together with CMB data from missions such as Planck, BAO measurements have become a cornerstone of the “standard cosmological model,” the ΛCDM framework, enabling precise determination of parameters such as Ω_m, Ω_Λ, and H_0.

However, as observational precision improves, it becomes increasingly important to assess the accuracy and consistency of cosmological parameters inferred from BAO relative to other probes. Tensions between different datasets — most notably the current discrepancy in the value of H_0 measured from the CMB and from local distance ladders — motivate careful examination of potential systematics and the cross-validation of different methods. Understanding how the choice of datasets, analysis techniques, and fiducial cosmologies affects the inferred baryon acoustic scale is essential for ensuring the reliability of cosmological conclusions.

This work investigates the accuracy of cosmological parameters determined using the baryon acoustic scale, with an emphasis on quantifying uncertainties and identifying possible sources of bias. By systematically comparing BAO-based parameter constraints with those from complementary approaches, we aim to clarify the role of the baryon acoustic scale as a precision tool for cosmology and to assess its capacity to illuminate current tensions in the cosmological model.
conclusion: Our analysis demonstrates that the baryon acoustic scale provides a robust and precise probe for determining cosmological parameters. The results confirm consistency with current ΛCDM constraints, highlighting the method’s reliability and potential for improving future measurements in large-scale structure surveys.

title: Propagating, evanescent, and localized states in carbon nanotube-graphene junctions
abstract: We investigate the electronic states arising at seamless junctions between single-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and graphene sheets, focusing on the interplay between propagating, evanescent, and spatially localized modes. Using a combination of continuum Dirac theory and tight-binding numerical simulations, we analyze junctions formed by connecting armchair or zigzag CNTs to graphene via defect-mediated topological reconstructions, typically involving heptagon–pentagon pairs. The underlying curvature and lattice mismatch at the junction induce local modifications of the electronic structure, leading to nontrivial scattering and confinement phenomena. We show that for energies near the Dirac point, propagating modes in the graphene sheet can couple to CNT subbands with matching symmetry, resulting in partial transmission and characteristic interference patterns in the local density of states (LDOS). Evanescent modes, originating from subbands lying above or below the incident energy, are found to dominate the near-junction LDOS decay and play a crucial role in mediating the crossover between extended graphene states and quantized CNT modes. Furthermore, for certain defect configurations and tube chiralities, quasi-bound states emerge within the junction region, exhibiting strong spatial localization and sharp resonances in the scattering spectrum. These localized states are traced to the interplay between curvature-induced gauge fields and the discrete rotational symmetries of the CNT, which selectively suppress coupling to continuum graphene modes. Our results reveal a sensitive dependence of the transport characteristics on the nanotube chirality, junction geometry, and defect arrangement, with implications for designing hybrid carbon-based nanostructures with tailored electronic functionality. The theoretical framework developed here provides a unified description of propagating, evanescent, and localized states in CNT–graphene junctions, bridging the gap between continuum models and atomistic simulations. Potential applications include nanoscale electron waveguides, resonant tunneling devices, and quantum dots integrated into two-dimensional carbon platforms.
introduction:
Carbon-based nanostructures have attracted sustained attention over the past three decades due to their remarkable electronic, mechanical, and thermal properties, as well as their potential for integration into nanoscale devices. Among these materials, graphene and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) occupy a central position. Graphene, a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice of carbon atoms, exhibits a linear low-energy dispersion relation near the Dirac points in the Brillouin zone, leading to massless Dirac fermion behavior and high carrier mobilities. CNTs, in turn, can be viewed as rolled-up graphene sheets, with their electronic properties determined by the chirality and diameter of the tube. Depending on their geometrical parameters, CNTs can be metallic or semiconducting, and their one-dimensional nature yields a discrete set of subbands derived from the quantization of the transverse momentum.

The seamless integration of these two allotropes into hybrid architectures—such as carbon nanotube-graphene junctions—offers opportunities to engineer novel electronic functionalities by combining the distinct band structures and dimensionalities of graphene and CNTs. Such junctions can be realized experimentally through chemical vapor deposition growth, electron beam sculpting, or chemical functionalization, producing structures in which a CNT protrudes from or is embedded into a graphene sheet. These hybrid systems hold promise for nanoelectronic interconnects, field emitters, sensors, and energy devices, as they may exploit the high current-carrying capacity of CNTs together with the planar connectivity and tunability of graphene.

From a theoretical standpoint, the electronic states in carbon nanotube-graphene junctions are determined by the interplay between the extended Bloch states of the graphene sheet and the quantized modes of the CNT, mediated by the atomic structure of the junction region. Depending on the energy and symmetry of the states, electrons incident from the graphene side can either propagate into the CNT, decay evanescently, or become localized near the junction. Propagating states correspond to modes that can carry current through the junction, evanescent states decay exponentially into one or both sides and contribute to tunneling phenomena, while localized states remain confined to the vicinity of the structural interface, potentially giving rise to resonances in transport and signatures in scanning tunneling spectroscopy.

The classification and characterization of propagating, evanescent, and localized states in these systems is not only of fundamental interest but also critical for device applications. For example, in a CNT-graphene interconnect, the efficiency of carrier injection depends on the matching between available propagating modes in the two subsystems. Conversely, localized states induced by topological defects at the junction—such as pentagon-heptagon pairs required to accommodate curvature—can act as scattering centers, reducing conductance, or serve as quantum dots for single-electron devices. Evanescent modes are essential in understanding subthreshold conduction and near-field coupling phenomena in closely spaced junctions.

Several theoretical studies have addressed electronic transport across CNT-graphene junctions, often using tight-binding models or density functional theory (DFT) to describe the atomic-scale structure and the corresponding electronic spectrum. Early works focused on idealized geometries, such as perfect armchair or zigzag CNTs connected to graphene through minimal defect lines, to elucidate the role of chirality and momentum conservation. More recent approaches incorporate realistic structural relaxation and disorder, uncovering the complex interplay between lattice mismatch, defect-induced states, and mode matching. However, a systematic analysis that distinguishes clearly between propagating, evanescent, and localized states for a broad range of energies and junction types remains limited.

The physics of these states is closely related to the boundary conditions imposed by the junction geometry on the Dirac-like quasiparticles of graphene and CNTs. In graphene, the low-energy excitations are described by a two-component spinor formalism, where the pseudospin encodes the sublattice degree of freedom. The wrapping of graphene into a CNT imposes quantization along the circumferential direction, leading to discrete transverse momenta. At the junction, the continuity of the wave function and current must be satisfied across a curved and defect-decorated interface, which can mix valleys and modify selection rules. This mixing can open gaps, create bound states, or alter the decay lengths of evanescent modes. Understanding these effects requires an interplay between continuum models, which capture the long-wavelength physics, and atomistic simulations, which include the detailed topology of the junction.

Experimentally, scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS) provide direct access to the local density of states near CNT-graphene junctions, enabling the identification of localized resonances and the mapping of spatial decay of electronic states. Transport measurements in devices incorporating such junctions yield information on conductance quantization, contact resistance, and the role of interface states. The interpretation of these experiments hinges on a clear theoretical framework that can predict the conditions under which certain types of states dominate.

In this work, we present a comprehensive study of propagating, evanescent, and localized electronic states in carbon nanotube-graphene junctions, combining analytical considerations with numerical tight-binding calculations. By systematically varying the chirality of the CNT, the orientation of the graphene lattice, and the detailed atomic structure of the junction, we classify the resulting electronic states according to their spatial behavior and spectral characteristics. We identify the energy ranges where propagating modes are allowed, determine the decay lengths of evanescent states, and characterize the symmetry and localization of bound states induced by topological defects. Our approach elucidates how the matching of transverse momenta between the graphene and CNT subsystems governs the transmission properties, and how deviations from ideal matching lead to the emergence of non-propagating states.

The results presented here provide insight into the microscopic mechanisms governing charge transport in CNT-graphene hybrid structures and establish guidelines for engineering junctions with desired electronic properties. By distinguishing explicitly between propagating, evanescent, and localized states, our framework offers a unified perspective applicable to a wide range of carbon-based nanostructures and heterojunctions. This understanding is a necessary step toward the rational design of nanoscale devices that exploit the unique interplay between the dimensionalities and band structures of graphene and carbon nanotubes.
conclusion:
In this work, we have undertaken a systematic theoretical investigation of the electronic states arising in carbon nanotube–graphene junctions, with particular emphasis on the interplay between propagating, evanescent, and localized modes. By employing a combination of continuum Dirac theory and atomistic tight-binding calculations, we have analyzed the spatial structure, energy dispersion, and coupling characteristics of these distinct states, elucidating the conditions under which each type emerges and dominates transport or spectral response.

Our results demonstrate that the seamless connection between the quasi-one-dimensional nanotube and the two-dimensional graphene sheet leads to a rich mode structure, arising from the mismatch in dimensionality and symmetry. Propagating states, which carry current across the junction, were found to be strongly influenced by the chirality and diameter of the nanotube as well as the relative orientation of the graphene lattice. In particular, certain chiralities promote efficient mode matching, resulting in minimal reflection and high transmission, while others lead to pronounced backscattering due to momentum mismatch and sublattice asymmetry.

Evanescent modes, characterized by exponential decay away from the junction interface, play a crucial role in mediating coupling between otherwise mismatched propagating states. We have shown that these modes can significantly affect the tunneling conductance, especially near the Dirac point where the density of states in the leads is low. The spatial decay length of the evanescent components depends sensitively on both the junction geometry and the energy of the incident electrons, revealing a tunable regime in which evanescent contributions dominate short-range transport.

Localized states, arising from either topological defects at the junction seam or from the abrupt change in dimensionality, constitute another important class of solutions. These states, often pinned near specific energies, can act as resonant scatterers and give rise to sharp features in the local density of states. Our atomistic calculations have identified specific defect configurations—such as pentagon–heptagon pairs—that stabilize midgap localized modes, whose spatial confinement is on the order of a few lattice constants. The presence of such localized states has implications for both coherent transport and scanning probe spectroscopy, potentially enabling their detection and manipulation.

An important outcome of this study is the clear identification of the regimes in which each type of state dominates the low-energy physics of the junction. At energies well above the Dirac point, propagating modes in both the nanotube and graphene dominate, and the junction behaves as a relatively transparent contact, with evanescent and localized contributions playing a minor role. In contrast, near charge neutrality, the scarcity of available propagating channels in the nanotube enhances the relevance of evanescent and localized states, leading to reduced conductance and the appearance of resonant features. This energy-dependent crossover underscores the necessity of a unified treatment of all three types of states when modeling realistic devices.

From a broader perspective, our findings have direct implications for the design of hybrid nanotube–graphene electronic components. Understanding the detailed mode structure enables targeted engineering of junction properties through control of chirality, orientation, and interface morphology. For instance, minimizing defect-induced localized states can improve conductance in interconnect applications, while deliberately introducing such states could be exploited in sensing or quantum information contexts. Moreover, the tunability of evanescent mode penetration through electrostatic gating suggests possible applications in switchable tunneling devices.

In summary, the carbon nanotube–graphene junction is a versatile platform where the coexistence and competition of propagating, evanescent, and localized electronic states give rise to complex yet controllable transport behavior. By characterizing these states and their dependencies on structural and energetic parameters, this work lays the groundwork for both fundamental studies of mixed-dimensional systems and the rational design of next-generation carbon-based nanoelectronic devices.

title: Binary Classifier Calibration: Bayesian Non-Parametric Approach
abstract: We propose a Bayesian non-parametric framework for calibrating probabilistic outputs of binary classifiers. While modern classifiers often achieve high accuracy, their predicted probabilities can be poorly calibrated, leading to suboptimal decision-making in risk-sensitive applications. Our approach models the unknown calibration function using Gaussian process priors, enabling flexible, data-driven adaptation without restrictive parametric assumptions. The Bayesian formulation naturally quantifies uncertainty in the calibrated probabilities, allowing for principled downstream integration in decision-theoretic pipelines. We derive an efficient inference scheme based on variational approximations, ensuring scalability to large datasets. The method accommodates diverse base classifiers and is robust to overfitting, particularly in low-data regimes. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate superior calibration performance compared to established techniques such as Platt scaling, isotonic regression, and spline-based methods, as measured by expected calibration error and log-loss. Our results highlight the advantages of combining non-parametric flexibility with Bayesian uncertainty quantification for reliable probability calibration in binary classification tasks.
introduction:
The performance of binary classifiers is often measured not only by their ability to separate classes, but also by the reliability of the probabilities they output. In many applications, particularly in domains such as medical diagnosis, risk assessment, weather forecasting, and financial decision-making, the predicted probabilities themselves are of primary interest. A classifier is said to be well-calibrated if, among all instances to which it assigns a probability \(p\) of belonging to the positive class, approximately a fraction \(p\) of them truly belong to that class. While modern machine learning algorithms, such as gradient boosted trees, deep neural networks, and support vector machines, can achieve high discriminative power, their raw probability scores are often poorly calibrated. This mismatch between predicted and true probabilities can lead to suboptimal decision-making, especially in cost-sensitive or safety-critical settings.

Calibration methods aim to transform the output scores of a classifier into well-calibrated probabilities. Classical approaches include Platt scaling, which fits a logistic regression model to the classifier scores, and isotonic regression, which performs a non-parametric monotonic transformation. More recent advances have explored temperature scaling and other post-processing methods, particularly in deep learning contexts. However, many of these methods impose restrictive parametric forms or rely on strong smoothness assumptions, potentially limiting their flexibility in modeling complex score–probability relationships. Additionally, some approaches are prone to overfitting when data is scarce, while others may fail to capture local variations in calibration due to their global nature.

Bayesian methods offer a principled framework to address uncertainty in calibration. By treating the calibration function as a random object and placing a prior distribution over it, Bayesian calibration models can naturally quantify uncertainty in the calibrated probabilities, which is particularly valuable when making decisions under uncertainty. Moreover, Bayesian inference allows for the incorporation of prior knowledge about the calibration function, such as monotonicity or smoothness, in a coherent probabilistic manner. While Bayesian parametric models, such as those based on logistic regression, have been employed for calibration, they inherit the limitations of their parametric forms and may struggle to adapt to complex or irregular calibration curves.

A Bayesian non-parametric approach provides a flexible alternative by allowing the data to dictate the shape of the calibration function without imposing a rigid functional form. Gaussian process (GP) priors, Dirichlet process mixtures, and Bayesian spline models are examples of non-parametric tools that can adaptively capture nonlinearities and local variations in the mapping from classifier scores to true probabilities. Such approaches are particularly appealing in settings where the relationship between scores and true probabilities is complex, heterogeneous across the score range, or only partially observed. They also provide a natural mechanism to balance flexibility with regularization, through the interplay between prior assumptions and observed data.

This work investigates a Bayesian non-parametric approach to binary classifier calibration, motivated by the need for flexible, uncertainty-aware, and data-efficient calibration methods. We consider the calibration problem as one of learning an unknown monotonic mapping from classifier scores to well-calibrated probabilities, and we place a suitable non-parametric prior over this mapping. Our framework accommodates various prior choices, enabling adaptation to different problem settings and allowing for quantification of both epistemic uncertainty (due to limited data) and aleatoric uncertainty (due to inherent randomness in outcomes). The Bayesian formulation also facilitates coherent integration with downstream decision-making processes that require probabilistic inputs.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we develop a Bayesian non-parametric calibration model grounded in flexible prior structures that can capture complex calibration curves while respecting monotonicity constraints. Second, we derive efficient inference procedures for learning the calibration function from data, leveraging modern Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and variational inference techniques to ensure scalability to large datasets. Third, we evaluate our approach on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing it against established calibration methods in terms of calibration error, predictive log-likelihood, and decision-theoretic utility. Our empirical results demonstrate that the proposed Bayesian non-parametric model achieves competitive or superior calibration performance, particularly in low-data regimes and in cases where the true calibration function exhibits substantial local variability.

By uniting the flexibility of non-parametric modeling with the principled uncertainty quantification of Bayesian inference, our approach offers an interpretable and robust solution to the calibration problem for binary classifiers. We argue that such methods are increasingly important as machine learning systems are deployed in sensitive applications where not only the accuracy, but also the trustworthiness of their probabilistic predictions, is of paramount importance.
conclusion: This work has explored a Bayesian non-parametric framework for calibrating binary classifiers, addressing limitations of traditional parametric methods in capturing complex, data-driven reliability structures. By leveraging flexible priors, the proposed approach adapts to heterogeneous score distributions without imposing restrictive functional forms, enabling robust calibration even in low-data regimes. Empirical evaluations demonstrated consistent improvements in calibration metrics while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy across diverse datasets. The fully probabilistic formulation further provides principled uncertainty quantification, offering more informative decision support for downstream applications. Compared to existing techniques, the method balances adaptability with interpretability, highlighting the value of Bayesian non-parametrics in bridging theory and practice. Future work may extend this framework to multi-class settings, incorporate hierarchical modeling for domain adaptation, and explore computational optimizations for large-scale deployment. Overall, the results underscore the promise of Bayesian non-parametric calibration as a versatile and reliable tool for enhancing the trustworthiness of probabilistic predictions in real-world binary classification tasks.

title: On the hidden treasure of dialog in video question answering
abstract: This paper investigates the underexplored role of dialog as a rich source of semantic grounding in video question answering (VideoQA). While most existing approaches focus primarily on visual and temporal cues, we argue that dialog—whether derived from subtitles, transcripts, or conversational interactions—can provide complementary context that enhances reasoning over complex events. We present a systematic analysis of how dialog content interacts with visual evidence, revealing patterns where language captures subtle narrative relations, implicit causal links, and off-screen events that vision alone may miss. Building on these insights, we design a multimodal framework that integrates dialog-aware representations with visual-temporal features, enabling finer-grained understanding and more accurate question answering. Experiments on benchmark VideoQA datasets augmented with dialog annotations demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse question types, particularly those requiring high-level inference. Our findings highlight dialog as a hidden but valuable treasure in VideoQA, opening new directions for multimodal reasoning research and dataset design.
introduction:
In recent years, video question answering (VideoQA) has emerged as a prominent research area at the intersection of computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal reasoning. The task generally requires a system to comprehend the dynamic visual content of a video and answer natural language questions about it. This entails recognizing objects, actions, and events, tracking entities across time, and integrating contextual cues to infer implicit information. Early work in VideoQA primarily relied on visual frames and, in some cases, accompanying subtitles to derive answers, focusing on static frame-level features or temporally aggregated video representations. While these approaches have demonstrated promising results, they often overlook a rich and readily available source of semantic information in many videos: dialog.

Dialog, in the context of VideoQA, refers to the spoken interactions between characters, narrators, or other entities present in the audiovisual material. This modality is distinct from simple subtitles or closed captions, which typically offer verbatim transcripts of speech without capturing the pragmatic, interactive, and narrative structures embodied in conversation. Dialog carries nuanced information about relationships, intentions, emotions, and causal links between events, often filling in details that may be ambiguous or absent in the visual stream. For example, in a movie clip, a character’s off-screen comment can reveal unseen events, clarify motivations, or foreshadow future actions, all of which may be crucial for correctly answering a question.

Despite its potential, dialog has remained an underutilized resource in VideoQA research. Several factors contribute to this oversight. First, many benchmark datasets have been constructed from sources with limited or no conversational content, such as instructional videos or sports footage, leading to a research focus on visual cues. Second, incorporating dialog requires sophisticated processing pipelines, including automatic speech recognition (ASR) for transcription, speaker diarization, and natural language understanding capable of handling colloquial and context-dependent expressions. Third, aligning dialog with visual events introduces additional challenges, as utterances may refer to off-screen actions or temporally displaced events.

Nevertheless, there is growing evidence that dialog can substantially improve multimodal reasoning in VideoQA systems. Dialog complements visual information by providing explicit references, temporal anchors, and causal explanations that are difficult to infer from visual data alone. It also offers redundancy that can be valuable when visual cues are noisy, occluded, or ambiguous. Moreover, dialog can bridge gaps between different scenes, maintaining narrative coherence and enabling reasoning across temporally distant segments of video.

This paper explores the “hidden treasure” of dialog in VideoQA, advocating for its systematic integration into multimodal architectures. We argue that exploiting dialog requires rethinking not only feature extraction but also the design of reasoning mechanisms capable of jointly processing visual observations and conversational context. To this end, we examine the characteristics of dialog in representative VideoQA datasets, analyze its contributions to different types of questions, and propose modeling strategies that effectively fuse dialog with visual and textual modalities. Through empirical studies, we demonstrate that dialog-aware VideoQA models can achieve significant performance gains, particularly on questions requiring high-level reasoning, inference of unobserved events, or understanding of character relationships. In doing so, we aim to broaden the scope of VideoQA research and highlight dialog as a valuable, yet often overlooked, modality for advancing the state of the art.
conclusion: This work has explored the underexamined role of dialog as a rich and multifaceted resource in video question answering. By investigating how conversational exchanges capture temporal dependencies, contextual cues, and implicit commonsense knowledge, we have shown that dialog offers more than a supplementary annotation—it can fundamentally shape model understanding and reasoning. Our findings suggest that leveraging dialog structures enables systems to bridge visual and linguistic modalities more effectively, facilitating nuanced comprehension of events and intentions. Moreover, the integration of dialog-driven features demonstrated measurable improvements across multiple evaluation settings, highlighting its potential as a core component of future architectures. We believe that continued research into dialog-informed representations, particularly in multimodal and interactive contexts, will yield deeper insights into human–AI communication. Ultimately, treating dialog not as peripheral but as a hidden treasure may unlock new frontiers in robust, context-aware video question answering systems.

title: Nested LSTMs
abstract: We introduce Nested Long Short-Term Memory (Nested LSTM) networks, a novel recurrent architecture designed to enhance the ability of sequence models to capture complex temporal dependencies. Unlike conventional LSTMs, which employ a single memory cell per unit, Nested LSTMs incorporate an additional internal LSTM cell within each memory cell, enabling hierarchical memory representation. This nested structure allows the model to retain and process information at multiple temporal scales, improving long-term dependency modeling while maintaining manageable parameter growth. We evaluate Nested LSTMs on a range of sequential tasks, including character-level language modeling and sequential prediction benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over standard LSTMs and gated recurrent units. Analysis shows that the nested design yields richer internal dynamics and more interpretable memory usage. These results suggest that nesting memory structures is a promising direction for advancing recurrent neural network architectures.
introduction:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have emerged as a powerful class of models for sequential data, enabling significant advances in applications such as language modeling, speech recognition, and time series forecasting. Among the various RNN architectures, the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network has become particularly prominent due to its ability to mitigate the vanishing and exploding gradient problems, thereby facilitating the learning of long-range temporal dependencies. By incorporating gating mechanisms that regulate the flow of information, LSTMs can capture complex temporal structures that exceed the capabilities of simple RNNs. Over the past decade, LSTMs have formed the backbone of numerous state-of-the-art systems in natural language processing, machine translation, video analysis, and other sequence modeling domains.

Despite their success, standard LSTMs face limitations when modeling sequences with multiple interacting timescales or with hierarchical temporal dependencies. In many real-world scenarios, such as narrative text, musical compositions, and multi-resolution sensor data, relevant information may be organized at different temporal granularities. For example, in language, syntactic and semantic relationships often span varying distances, from local word-to-word dependencies to discourse-level coherence over paragraphs. While stacking multiple LSTM layers can, in principle, provide a form of hierarchical representation, such architectures may suffer from inefficient credit assignment across layers and time steps, and may not effectively disentangle different temporal abstractions. Furthermore, simply increasing the depth of LSTM networks can lead to higher computational costs and training instability without necessarily improving the modeling of nested temporal relationships.

To address these challenges, recent research has explored architectural modifications that embed richer internal dynamics within recurrent units. One promising direction is the concept of Nested LSTMs, in which each memory cell contains an inner LSTM, effectively introducing a hierarchy of temporal processing within a single recurrent step. In this formulation, the outer LSTM governs the high-level sequence progression, while the inner LSTM operates over the cell state itself, enabling a more nuanced internal memory update. This nesting mechanism allows the network to represent and manipulate information at multiple timescales in a more integrated fashion than conventional stacked architectures. By explicitly modeling temporal hierarchies within the recurrent unit, Nested LSTMs aim to improve the capture of long-term dependencies without sacrificing the responsiveness to short-term patterns.

The intuition behind Nested LSTMs is grounded in the observation that temporal abstraction can be beneficially structured. In stacked LSTMs, each layer processes the entire sequence at the same rate, passing outputs to the subsequent layer at each time step. In contrast, nesting allows the inner LSTM to maintain and update its state based on the evolving outer cell state, potentially at a different effective temporal resolution. This design can facilitate selective retention or transformation of information, thereby enhancing the model’s capacity to manage context over extended sequences. Such an approach may be particularly advantageous in domains where important events occur over variable and overlapping timescales, as it provides an architectural bias towards capturing these patterns.

Empirical studies have begun to demonstrate that Nested LSTMs can outperform baseline LSTM architectures on tasks requiring multi-scale temporal reasoning, including character-level language modeling and synthetic sequence prediction benchmarks. These results suggest that nesting can lead to more compact and efficient representations of temporal dependencies, possibly due to the richer dynamics afforded by the inner recurrent structure. Nevertheless, the theoretical understanding of why and when nesting yields performance gains remains limited, and systematic evaluations across diverse tasks are still scarce. Moreover, the computational trade-offs of nesting, including the increased parameter count and potential for overfitting, warrant careful analysis.

In this work, we investigate the Nested LSTM architecture in depth, aiming to provide both empirical evidence and conceptual clarity regarding its advantages and limitations. We situate Nested LSTMs within the broader landscape of hierarchical and multi-timescale recurrent models, contrasting them with alternative approaches such as clockwork RNNs, hierarchical multiscale RNNs, and gated feedback architectures. Through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, we examine the extent to which nesting improves the modeling of sequences with complex temporal structure, and we analyze the learned dynamics to elucidate the mechanisms by which nesting influences memory retention and information flow. By doing so, we seek to contribute a more comprehensive understanding of Nested LSTMs and their potential role in advancing sequence modeling methodologies.
conclusion: This work has explored the concept and effectiveness of Nested Long Short-Term Memory (NLSTM) networks, highlighting their capacity to capture hierarchical temporal dependencies more effectively than conventional LSTMs. By nesting memory cells within memory cells, NLSTMs provide a deeper, more structured representation of sequential data, enabling improved performance on tasks involving long-range context. Experimental results demonstrate that this architecture can yield superior accuracy and stability across diverse sequence modeling benchmarks. Furthermore, the nested design offers a promising direction for integrating multi-scale temporal reasoning into recurrent neural networks. Future research may investigate optimizing training efficiency, exploring hybrid architectures, and extending the approach to multimodal and real-time applications, further advancing the potential of NLSTMs in complex sequential learning problems.

title: Creating and understanding email communication networks to aid digital forensic investigations
abstract: This paper presents a framework for constructing and analyzing email communication networks to support digital forensic investigations. By extracting metadata from email headers, we model interactions as graph structures, enabling the identification of key actors, communication patterns, and potential anomalies. The approach integrates network analysis techniques, including centrality measures and community detection, to reveal hidden relationships and organizational structures. We demonstrate the method using real-world datasets, highlighting its effectiveness in uncovering relevant connections and supporting investigative hypotheses. Our results show that visual and quantitative analyses of email networks can significantly enhance the efficiency and accuracy of forensic examinations, providing investigators with actionable insights into complex communication ecosystems.
introduction:
The proliferation of digital communication technologies has transformed the way individuals, organizations, and societies exchange information. Among these technologies, email remains one of the most widely used and enduring forms of digital communication, playing a critical role in both personal and professional contexts. The ubiquity of email has made it a valuable source of evidence in digital forensic investigations, where uncovering hidden relationships, tracing information flows, and reconstructing communication patterns can be crucial to understanding events and attributing actions. However, the immense volume of email data, coupled with its complex and often unstructured nature, presents significant challenges for investigators seeking to extract meaningful insights.

Digital forensics traditionally focuses on the acquisition, preservation, analysis, and presentation of digital evidence in a manner that is legally admissible. In the context of email analysis, this involves identifying relevant messages, parsing metadata, recovering deleted communications, and verifying authenticity. Beyond these foundational tasks, investigators increasingly recognize the value of representing email data as social or communication networks, where nodes correspond to individuals or accounts, and edges represent interactions between them. Such network-based representations enable the application of graph theory, social network analysis, and computational methods to detect patterns, central actors, communities, and anomalies that may otherwise remain obscured in raw datasets.

The construction of accurate and interpretable email communication networks requires careful consideration of technical and methodological factors. Email metadata, such as sender and recipient addresses, timestamps, and subject lines, must be extracted, cleaned, and normalized to account for aliases, mailing lists, and automated systems. Decisions must be made regarding whether to treat carbon copies (CC) and blind carbon copies (BCC) as equivalent to direct communications, and how to handle group messages or mailing list distributions. Furthermore, temporal aspects of communication—such as the frequency and directionality of exchanges—can significantly influence the interpretation of network structures, particularly in dynamic or evolving investigative contexts.

Research in this domain has demonstrated the potential of email communication network analysis in diverse applications, including corporate fraud detection, insider threat assessment, criminal network mapping, and historical event reconstruction. For example, the analysis of the Enron email corpus has provided valuable methodological insights and served as a benchmark for developing algorithms to identify influential actors and uncover organizational substructures. In law enforcement and cybersecurity investigations, communication network models can help prioritize investigative leads, correlate disparate data sources, and reveal covert interactions that are not immediately apparent through keyword searches or conventional content analysis.

Despite these advances, several challenges remain. Privacy considerations impose constraints on the scope and granularity of network analyses, necessitating techniques that balance investigative utility with ethical and legal obligations. The dynamic nature of communication, including shifts in interaction patterns over time, can complicate both the construction and interpretation of networks. Moreover, the presence of noise, such as spam and automated notifications, can distort network structures if not properly filtered. Addressing these challenges requires a multidisciplinary approach that integrates expertise from digital forensics, data science, network theory, and legal studies.

This paper aims to contribute to the field by presenting a structured framework for creating and understanding email communication networks in support of digital forensic investigations. We outline methodologies for data extraction, preprocessing, and network construction, and we explore analytical techniques to identify key actors, communities, and temporal patterns. By bridging the gap between raw email data and actionable investigative insights, our approach seeks to enhance the efficiency, accuracy, and interpretability of forensic analyses, ultimately supporting more informed decision-making in investigative and judicial processes.
conclusion: This study has demonstrated that constructing and analysing email communication networks can significantly enhance the effectiveness of digital forensic investigations. By transforming raw email data into structured network representations, investigators can uncover hidden relationships, identify key actors, and detect anomalous patterns that may be indicative of malicious activity. The network-based approach facilitates both macro-level insights into the overall communication structure and micro-level examinations of specific interactions, thereby bridging the gap between large-scale data analysis and detailed forensic scrutiny. Furthermore, integrating temporal dynamics into these networks allows for a richer understanding of evolving behaviours over time, which is crucial for reconstructing events and establishing timelines. While methodological challenges remain, such as ensuring data completeness and managing privacy considerations, the findings underscore the value of combining social network analysis techniques with traditional forensic methods. Future work should explore automated tools that can seamlessly ingest diverse email formats, enhance visualisation capabilities, and incorporate advanced anomaly detection algorithms. Overall, email communication network analysis represents a powerful complement to existing investigative practices, offering a systematic, scalable, and insightful means of interpreting complex digital evidence.

title: AiR-ViBeR: Exfiltrating Data from Air-Gapped Computers via Covert Surface ViBrAtIoNs
abstract:
Air-gapped computers are commonly deployed in high-security environments to isolate sensitive information from external networks. However, such isolation does not eliminate the risk of data exfiltration via unconventional side channels. This paper presents **AiR-ViBeR**, a novel covert communication technique that exploits surface-borne vibrations to bridge air gaps. We demonstrate that a computer’s internal components, particularly cooling fans and mechanical drives, can be manipulated to generate carefully modulated vibration patterns that propagate through a shared physical surface, such as a desk or shelf. These vibrations are then detected by a nearby device equipped with an accelerometer, such as a smartphone or embedded sensor, and decoded into the original data.  

We design and implement a proof-of-concept system that encodes binary information into subtle oscillation frequencies without noticeably affecting system performance or triggering conventional intrusion detection. Experimental evaluation in realistic office settings shows that AiR-ViBeR can achieve bit rates of up to 20 bits per second over distances of up to 2 meters through common surfaces, with a bit error rate below 5% under controlled conditions. We also assess the channel’s resilience to environmental noise and its limitations in different material contexts. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures, including vibration damping, sensor access restrictions, and anomaly detection in system fan control. Our findings highlight the feasibility of vibration-based exfiltration in air-gapped scenarios and underscore the need for expanded threat models that account for physical emanations beyond electromagnetic and acoustic channels.
introduction:
Air-gapped computers, physically isolated from external networks, are widely deployed in environments that demand strong security assurances, such as military facilities, critical infrastructure control systems, and financial institutions. This physical separation is intended to mitigate the risk of remote cyberattacks and to prevent unauthorized data exfiltration. However, recent research has demonstrated that air gaps are not an absolute barrier; adversaries can exploit unconventional side channels to bridge the isolation, including electromagnetic emissions, acoustic signals, thermal fluctuations, and optical channels. These methods typically rely on subtle, often overlooked physical emanations produced by a system during normal operation.

In this work, we introduce AiR-ViBeR, a novel covert channel that leverages surface-borne vibrations generated by an air-gapped computer’s internal components to exfiltrate data. Specifically, we show that controlled operation of the computer’s cooling fans or other movable parts can induce measurable vibrations in the surface on which the system rests. These vibrations can propagate through desks, floors, or adjacent structures and be detected by a nearby device equipped with an accelerometer, such as a smartphone or IoT sensor. By modulating these vibrations, it becomes possible to transmit encoded information without any direct network or wireless connection.

The AiR-ViBeR approach expands the attack surface for air-gapped systems, highlighting the need to account for mechanical as well as electromagnetic or acoustic leakage. We evaluate the channel’s feasibility, achievable bit rates, and operational constraints under realistic environmental conditions. Our findings underscore that physical isolation alone cannot guarantee security, and that defending against covert vibration-based channels requires a combination of environmental controls, system hardening, and vigilant monitoring of seemingly innocuous sensor-equipped devices in proximity to sensitive systems.
conclusion: This work has presented AiR-ViBeR, a novel method for exfiltrating data from air-gapped computers by exploiting covert surface vibrations. We demonstrated that malware can deliberately generate controlled vibrations using a computer’s internal components, which can then be detected by nearby accelerometer-equipped devices. Through experimental evaluation, we showed that this channel is viable over short distances, resilient to certain environmental noise conditions, and capable of transmitting meaningful data at a low but practical bitrate. Our findings highlight that even systems physically isolated from networks remain vulnerable to unconventional side-channel attacks. This underscores the necessity for a broader security perspective that includes non-traditional emanations and physical signal leakage. Potential countermeasures, such as restricting sensor access on mobile devices, vibration dampening, and stricter physical isolation policies, should be considered as part of a comprehensive defense strategy. Ultimately, AiR-ViBeR expands the understanding of air-gap threat models and reinforces the importance of continually reassessing the assumptions underlying high-security environments.

title: A flexible method to evolve collisional systems and their tidal debris in external potentials
abstract: We present a novel method for evolving collisional stellar systems and their unbound tidal debris within arbitrary, time-dependent external potentials. Our approach couples direct \(N\)-body integration for the dense core with an adaptive, particle-spray scheme for escaped material, ensuring accurate dynamical evolution over large spatial scales at reduced computational cost. The method flexibly incorporates external gravitational fields from analytic models or numerical simulations, enabling studies of star clusters, dwarf galaxies, and their tidal streams in realistic galactic environments. We validate the technique against full \(N\)-body simulations and demonstrate its efficiency and precision in capturing both internal dynamics and large-scale debris morphology.
introduction:
The study of collisional stellar systems—such as star clusters, dwarf galaxies, and dense stellar associations—has long been central to our understanding of galactic structure and evolution. These systems evolve under the combined influence of internal gravitational encounters between stars and external tidal fields generated by their host galaxy or nearby structures. Over time, the interplay between internal relaxation processes and external perturbations drives mass loss, shapes tidal debris, and determines the long-term survival of the system. Understanding this coupled evolution is essential for interpreting a wide range of astrophysical phenomena, from the morphology of tidal streams to the dissolution timescales of star clusters in different galactic environments.

Traditional approaches to modelling collisional systems rely on direct N-body simulations, which integrate the equations of motion for all constituent stars while self-consistently accounting for their mutual gravitational interactions. These methods, while accurate, are computationally expensive; the cost scales steeply with the number of particles, making it challenging to follow systems with realistic particle numbers over many relaxation times. Furthermore, including the effects of a realistic, time-dependent external potential—such as that arising from a galaxy with a complex mass distribution or evolving substructure—adds additional computational and modelling complexity. As a result, many studies simplify the external potential or treat the evolution of tidal debris separately from the internal dynamics of the bound system.

Alternative methods, such as orbit-averaged Fokker–Planck models, Monte Carlo techniques, and hybrid schemes, have been developed to alleviate the computational burden. These methods can capture the essential physics of relaxation and mass loss without resolving every stellar encounter in detail. However, they generally rely on simplifying assumptions about the geometry, symmetry, or steadiness of the external field, and may not be easily adaptable to situations where the tidal environment varies on timescales comparable to the internal dynamical time of the system. Moreover, the treatment of unbound stars—those that have escaped the cluster but remain dynamically correlated in tidal tails—often requires separate modelling, limiting the ability to capture the continuous transition from bound system to tidal debris.

Recent observational advances have highlighted the need for more flexible and integrated modelling approaches. Wide-field photometric and astrometric surveys, such as those conducted by *Gaia*, have revealed extended stellar streams and substructures associated with dissolving clusters and dwarf galaxies. These features often bear the imprints of the host galaxy’s gravitational potential, as well as the internal dynamics of their progenitors. Interpreting these observations demands models that can simultaneously track the internal evolution of collisional systems and the spatial and kinematic distribution of their escaping stars in a realistic and possibly time-dependent external potential.

In this work, we present a general and adaptable method for evolving collisional stellar systems and their tidal debris in arbitrary external gravitational fields. The approach aims to retain the essential dynamical fidelity of direct N-body simulations while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling the study of a wide range of astrophysical scenarios. By coupling the internal collisional evolution to the motion of both bound and unbound stars in a unified framework, our method provides a powerful tool for exploring the life cycle of collisional systems, from formation to dissolution, in complex galactic environments.
conclusion:
We have presented a new, flexible method for evolving collisional stellar systems and their associated tidal debris in arbitrary, time-dependent external potentials. By coupling a direct or Monte Carlo integrator for the internal dynamics of the collisional system with an orbit integration scheme for escaping particles, our approach bridges the gap between high-fidelity cluster simulations and efficient modelling of large-scale tidal structures. This method allows for a consistent treatment of the internal two-body relaxation driving mass loss, while simultaneously following the long-term evolution of debris in a galactic context without resorting to full N-body calculations for all particles.  

The key advantages of the framework lie in its modularity and computational efficiency. The internal subsystem can be modelled with any appropriate collisional code, enabling the use of sophisticated treatments of stellar evolution, binaries, and tidal heating. Escaped stars, once beyond the tidal boundary, are transferred to a separate integrator that evolves their orbits in the external potential with negligible additional computational cost. This separation of scales permits high particle resolution in the debris without compromising the accuracy of the collisional evolution. Importantly, the method is adaptable to arbitrary smooth host potentials, including time-dependent and non-axisymmetric forms, making it suitable for studies of clusters in realistic galactic environments or merging galaxies.

Validation against direct N-body simulations demonstrates that the method reproduces both the internal structural evolution of the bound cluster and the spatial and kinematic properties of the tidal debris with high fidelity. The agreement holds over many dynamical times, confirming that the transition between the collisional and collisionless regimes is handled consistently. The approach thus opens the possibility to explore parameter spaces and timescales that would be prohibitively expensive for pure N-body methods, including the evolution of massive clusters over gigayear times in complex galactic potentials.

Beyond modelling the disruption of star clusters, the method is applicable to a broad set of astrophysical systems in which a dense collisional core is embedded in and exchanges mass with a collisionless halo or background. Examples include dwarf galaxies interacting with the Milky Way, nuclear star clusters in galactic nuclei, and globular clusters in tidal streams. Future work will extend the framework to incorporate self-gravity of the debris, more sophisticated escape criteria, and coupling to cosmological simulations, further enhancing its predictive power for interpreting the growing wealth of observational data on stellar streams and disrupted systems.

title: A Quantitative Theory of Bottleneck Structures for Data Networks
abstract: We develop a quantitative framework for analyzing bottleneck structures in data networks, with the goal of characterizing their formation, persistence, and impact on overall system performance. Bottlenecks—nodes or links whose limited capacity constrains end-to-end throughput—are a critical determinant of latency, congestion, and reliability in large-scale communication systems. Our approach integrates graph-theoretic representations of network topology with stochastic models of traffic flow, enabling the identification of structural features that give rise to persistent bottlenecks under varying load conditions. We introduce a set of metrics that quantify bottleneck severity, based on flow allocation, queueing dynamics, and capacity utilization, and derive analytical bounds for performance degradation associated with these structures. Using both synthetic and empirical network data, we validate our theory through simulations and compare predicted bottleneck locations with those detected via standard measurement techniques. Results demonstrate that the proposed model accurately predicts both the onset of congestion and the spatial distribution of load imbalances, outperforming heuristic-based detection methods in precision and computational efficiency. We further explore the implications of our findings for network design and optimization, showing that targeted structural modifications informed by our metrics can significantly alleviate bottleneck effects without requiring large-scale capacity upgrades. This work provides a principled basis for diagnosing and mitigating performance-limiting structures in diverse data networking environments, from backbone infrastructures to distributed cloud architectures.
introduction:
In modern communication systems, data networks form the backbone of information exchange across a wide range of applications, from cloud computing and distributed storage to real-time streaming, autonomous systems, and large-scale scientific collaborations. As these networks grow in size and complexity, their performance increasingly depends on the structural and dynamical properties of the underlying topology. One recurring and critical phenomenon in such systems is the emergence of bottlenecks—restricted regions in the network through which a disproportionate fraction of traffic must pass. Bottlenecks can arise from physical limitations, such as limited-capacity links, or from logical constraints, such as policies governing routing and resource allocation. Understanding the formation, persistence, and impact of bottlenecks is essential for predicting network behavior and designing strategies for optimization and control.

Bottleneck structures in data networks are not merely incidental anomalies; rather, they often emerge as an intrinsic consequence of the interplay between network topology, traffic patterns, and capacity constraints.
