The phenomenon of counteralignment is of particular interest because a retrograde circumbinary disc interacts with the binary in a qualitatively different way from a prograde one. In the retrograde case, resonant torques that operate in the prograde configuration are largely absent, potentially allowing more efficient accretion of material onto the binary and a different pathway for binary orbital evolution. In the context of supermassive black hole binaries, retrograde circumbinary discs have been proposed as a mechanism for driving rapid binary coalescence, with implications for gravitational wave event rates. In young stellar binaries, counteraligned discs could influence planet formation by altering the dynamics and stability of planetesimals.

Despite the importance of this process, the stability of a counteraligned circumbinary disc has not been fully characterized. In particular, it is not yet clear under what conditions counteralignment, once achieved, remains dynamically stable over viscous timescales, or whether subsequent perturbations might drive the disc back towards alignment or produce further structural changes. Additionally, the role of disc thickness, viscosity, and binary eccentricity in determining the stability of the counteraligned state remains incompletely understood. Addressing these questions requires a combination of analytic theory and high-resolution numerical simulations capable of following the coupled evolution of the disc and binary over many orbital periods.

In this work, we investigate the conditions under which a circumbinary disc can achieve and maintain a stable counteraligned configuration. We present a series of three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations exploring a range of binary mass ratios, eccentricities, and disc parameters, and compare the outcomes to analytic stability criteria. Our results clarify the parameter space for stable counteralignment and provide new insight into the dynamical pathways that lead to long-lived retrograde discs.
conclusion:
We have investigated the dynamical evolution and long-term stability of a circumbinary disc that is initially misaligned with respect to the binary orbital plane. Using a combination of analytic arguments and numerical simulations, we have demonstrated that, under a broad range of parameters, dissipative torques can drive the disc into a state of stable counteralignment, in which the disc angular momentum is antiparallel to that of the binary. This outcome contrasts with the more commonly discussed coplanar alignment, and arises when the initial tilt exceeds a critical value determined by the ratio of the disc and binary angular momenta.

Our results show that the counteraligned configuration is not merely a transient state, but can persist over many viscous timescales provided that external torques and mass inflow rates are modest. The binary potential induces coherent precession of disc annuli, and viscous dissipation damps the relative tilt until the disc achieves a uniform, counterrotating orientation. Once established, the counteraligned disc remains dynamically stable, with warp amplitudes and internal stresses settling to low levels. The stability is enhanced for binaries with high mass ratios and modest eccentricities, where the differential precession rate is more uniform across the disc.

These findings have important implications for the evolution of circumbinary systems in astrophysical contexts, including young stellar binaries, supermassive black hole pairs, and post-common-envelope binaries. Counteraligned discs can efficiently extract angular momentum from the binary, potentially accelerating orbital decay and influencing merger timescales. They may also alter accretion signatures, producing observational diagnostics distinct from those of aligned systems.

Future work should extend these studies to include the effects of substantial eccentricities, self-gravity in massive discs, and sustained mass feeding from larger-scale reservoirs. Such investigations will further clarify the conditions under which counteralignment emerges, and its role in shaping the co-evolution of binaries and their surrounding discs.

title: Analytic constraints on the energy-momentum tensor in conformal field theories
abstract: We investigate general analytic constraints on the energy-momentum tensor in conformal field theories across arbitrary spacetime dimensions. Using the operator product expansion and conformal Ward identities, we derive bounds on the tensor’s correlation functions that follow from unitarity, crossing symmetry, and causality. Particular emphasis is placed on the structure of three-point functions involving the energy-momentum tensor and conserved currents, where conformal symmetry fixes the functional form up to a finite set of coefficients. We show that positivity conditions from the conformal collider setup impose stringent inequalities on these parameters, recovering and generalizing known results in four dimensions. Our analysis highlights the interplay between symmetry, analyticity, and unitarity, and clarifies the role of the energy-momentum tensor as a central object in constraining conformal field theory dynamics.
introduction:
Conformal field theories (CFTs) occupy a central role in modern theoretical physics, providing a framework for describing systems at criticality, furnishing exactly solvable models in two dimensions, and serving as the holographic duals of certain gravitational theories in higher dimensions. A key structural element of any CFT is the energy-momentum tensor \(T_{\mu\nu}\), whose conservation and tracelessness encode the invariance of the theory under spacetime translations, rotations, and local scale transformations. Beyond these kinematic constraints, the energy-momentum tensor carries dynamical information: its correlation functions encapsulate the response of the theory to background geometry and provide order parameters for various physical observables.

In recent years, there has been significant progress in deriving nontrivial bounds on the behavior of \(T_{\mu\nu}\) using general principles such as unitarity, causality, and crossing symmetry. In conformal collider physics, for instance, the analysis of energy flux measurements in hypothetical detectors leads to inequalities on the three-point functions involving \(T_{\mu\nu}\), constraining the allowed space of CFT data. Similarly, the conformal bootstrap program has exploited the operator product expansion (OPE) and crossing symmetry to map out the space of consistent scaling dimensions and OPE coefficients, with the energy-momentum tensor appearing as a universal operator in every unitary CFT. These developments highlight the power of combining symmetry considerations with analytic constraints to obtain rigorous, model-independent results.

The analytic structure of correlation functions plays a crucial role in this endeavor. In Lorentzian signature, causality imposes stringent restrictions on the singularity structure and discontinuities of correlators, while unitarity enforces positivity of certain spectral densities. For the energy-momentum tensor, these requirements can be translated into sum rules and inequalities involving its OPE coefficients with other operators. In some cases, these constraints are directly related to the averaged null energy condition (ANEC), which asserts the positivity of the integral of the null-null component of \(T_{\mu\nu}\) along complete null geodesics. The ANEC has been proven in general quantum field theories under mild assumptions, and in conformal settings it leads to a hierarchy of “higher-spin” ANEC constraints involving conserved currents of spin greater than two.

This work is devoted to a systematic analysis of analytic constraints on the energy-momentum tensor in CFTs across dimensions. We focus on the interplay between conformal symmetry, OPE structure, and the analytic properties of correlation functions in Lorentzian signature, with an emphasis on the implications for the allowed tensor structures and coefficients in \( \langle TTT \rangle \) and mixed correlators. Our approach synthesizes techniques from conformal collider bounds, dispersion relations, and the lightcone bootstrap, leading to new inequalities and exclusion regions in the space of CFT data. By clarifying the precise manner in which analyticity and causality shape the dynamics of \(T_{\mu\nu}\), we aim to deepen the understanding of universal constraints in conformal theories and to provide a framework for future explorations of their phenomenological and holographic applications.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated a set of analytic constraints on the energy–momentum tensor in conformal field theories, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between unitarity, conformal symmetry, and causality. By analyzing the structure of correlation functions, both in position and momentum space, we have shown that the conformal Ward identities, together with positivity conditions derived from reflection positivity and lightcone bootstrap arguments, significantly restrict the allowed space of tensor structures and operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients involving the stress tensor. Our results demonstrate that these constraints are not merely formal, but have direct implications for the spectrum and dynamics of CFTs in various spacetime dimensions.

In particular, we have provided a systematic derivation of bounds on the three–point function coefficients of the stress tensor with itself and with other low-spin operators, recovering and extending known results from collider-type energy conditions and conformal collider bounds. The approach taken here, based on the analytic continuation of Euclidean correlators to appropriate Lorentzian configurations, has allowed us to unify several seemingly disparate arguments into a coherent framework. In doing so, we have clarified the relationship between the Hofman–Maldacena bounds, higher-spin positivity conditions, and more recent bootstrap constraints, showing that they emerge from a common set of analyticity and positivity requirements on conformal correlators.

Moreover, our analysis sheds light on how these constraints manifest differently in various spacetime dimensions. While in four dimensions the structure of the stress tensor three–point function is controlled by three independent parameters, in three dimensions it reduces to two, and our methods naturally yield the corresponding allowed regions in parameter space. In two dimensions, where the Virasoro algebra controls the dynamics, our formalism reproduces the central charge positivity condition as the sole nontrivial restriction. This dimensional dependence highlights the universality of the analytic approach while also revealing its sensitivity to the underlying representation theory of the conformal group.

We have also discussed the implications of our results for holographic CFTs with a weakly coupled gravity dual. In that context, the analytic bounds derived here translate into constraints on the higher-derivative couplings in the bulk effective action, thereby providing a CFT-based derivation of certain causality bounds in AdS gravity. This connection further reinforces the idea that fundamental consistency conditions in quantum gravity can be encoded in universal properties of the stress tensor sector of the dual CFT.

Looking ahead, the methods developed here can be extended in several directions. One promising avenue is the inclusion of spinning operators beyond the stress tensor, where similar analyticity arguments may yield new constraints on mixed correlators. Another is the exploration of nontrivial RG flows, where approximate conformal symmetry at intermediate scales might still enforce remnants of the constraints we have described. Finally, a systematic numerical implementation of these analytic bounds, embedded in the broader conformal bootstrap program, could sharpen our understanding of the landscape of consistent conformal field theories.

In summary, the analytic constraints on the energy–momentum tensor derived in this work represent a unifying framework that captures and extends a wide range of known results. They reinforce the central role of the stress tensor as a probe of fundamental consistency conditions in conformal field theory, and open the door to further applications across both field theory and holography.

title: Mapping far-IR emission from the central kiloparsec of NGC 1097
abstract: We present far-infrared (far-IR) imaging of the central kiloparsec of the nearby barred spiral galaxy NGC 1097, obtained with the *Herschel* Space Observatory’s PACS instrument at 70, 100, and 160 µm. These data provide unprecedented spatial resolution in the far-IR for this galaxy, enabling us to resolve the circumnuclear starburst ring and investigate the distribution of dust emission associated with recent star formation. The 70 and 100 µm maps clearly trace the bright, ∼900 pc diameter ring, with additional emission from the dust lanes along the large-scale bar. Radial profiles indicate that the ring dominates the far-IR output within the central kiloparsec, contributing more than two-thirds of the total flux in this region. We compare the far-IR morphology with archival mid-IR imaging from *Spitzer*/IRAC and MIPS, Hα maps, and CO(J=2–1) molecular gas distributions, finding a close correspondence between far-IR peaks, sites of intense star formation, and concentrations of molecular gas. The azimuthal variation in far-IR surface brightness along the ring is modest (<30%), suggesting either a relatively uniform star formation rate around the ring or rapid dispersal of dust-heating sources compared to the orbital timescale. Spectral energy distributions (SEDs) extracted from the ring and nucleus indicate characteristic dust temperatures of 25–35 K, consistent with heating by young stellar populations. The nucleus itself is faint in the far-IR, contributing less than 10% of the central kiloparsec flux, in agreement with its classification as a low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN). Our results demonstrate the power of high-resolution far-IR observations in disentangling the spatially resolved dust heating mechanisms in nearby galaxies, and provide important constraints for models of starburst rings fueled by bar-driven gas inflows. These observations of NGC 1097 add to the growing evidence that circumnuclear star-forming rings can dominate the far-IR luminosity in barred spirals, with relatively uniform conditions conducive to sustained star formation.
introduction:
NGC 1097 is a nearby barred spiral galaxy (type SBb) located at a distance of approximately 14.5 Mpc, notable for its pronounced circumnuclear star-forming ring and its classification as a low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (LLAGN). The galaxy’s central kiloparsec harbors a complex interplay between nuclear activity, intense star formation, and large-scale gas inflow driven by its prominent bar. This combination makes NGC 1097 an ideal laboratory for studying the physical conditions and energetics of the interstellar medium (ISM) in environments where both secular processes and nuclear activity shape the evolution of the central regions.

The circumnuclear ring, with a diameter of roughly 1 kpc, is one of the most remarkable features of NGC 1097. It is delineated by sites of massive, young star clusters, formed as gas accumulates at resonances set by the bar’s gravitational potential. Molecular gas observations have revealed large reservoirs of fuel in the ring, and optical and near-infrared imaging have traced the distribution of young stellar populations and dust lanes feeding the ring. However, while extensive work has been carried out at optical, near-IR, and radio wavelengths, the far-infrared (far-IR) domain remains less explored at comparable spatial resolution. Since the far-IR emission is dominated by thermal dust emission heated by young stars and, to some extent, by the AGN, mapping this regime is essential for obtaining a complete picture of the star formation and dust properties in the nuclear region.

Far-IR observations are particularly sensitive to cool dust (T ≈ 20–50 K), which constitutes the bulk of the dust mass and dominates the bolometric output of dusty star-forming regions. In the central kiloparsec of galaxies such as NGC 1097, the far-IR continuum can reveal variations in dust temperature, optical depth, and heating sources that are not evident at shorter wavelengths, where emission from warmer dust and starlight can dominate. Furthermore, the far-IR provides a relatively unobscured view of embedded star formation, allowing for a more accurate assessment of the star formation rate (SFR) and distribution in heavily dust-enshrouded environments. Spectral lines in the far-IR, such as [C II] 158 μm and [O I] 63 μm, can also serve as diagnostics of the ISM’s physical state, although here we focus on the continuum emission.

Recent advances in far-IR instrumentation, particularly with the Herschel Space Observatory’s PACS and SPIRE instruments, have enabled mapping of nearby galaxies at resolutions sufficient to resolve circumnuclear structures on scales of a few hundred parsecs. For NGC 1097, this makes it possible to separate the contributions of the nuclear point source, the circumnuclear ring, and the surrounding disk, and to study spatial variations in dust temperature and surface brightness within the central kiloparsec. Such information is crucial for constraining models of star formation efficiency, feedback, and the transport of gas and dust in barred galaxy nuclei.

In this work, we present new far-IR maps of NGC 1097’s central kiloparsec, obtained with Herschel/PACS at 70, 100, and 160 μm. Our aims are to characterize the morphology of the far-IR emission, quantify the relative contributions from the nucleus and the circumnuclear ring, and derive spatially resolved dust temperatures and luminosities. By comparing the far-IR results with data at other wavelengths, we assess the connection between dust heating, star formation, and nuclear activity. This study contributes to a more complete understanding of the energetics and structure of the ISM in NGC 1097’s central region, offering insights into the processes that regulate starburst and AGN coexistence in barred spiral galaxies.
conclusion:
Our far-infrared mapping of the central kiloparsec of NGC 1097 has revealed a detailed view of the dust emission morphology and its relationship to the circumnuclear star-forming ring and central active nucleus. The high spatial resolution achieved in the far-IR allows us to disentangle the contributions from the ring, the bar dust lanes, and the nuclear region, providing new constraints on the distribution and heating of dust in this composite starburst–AGN system. The far-IR emission is strongly concentrated along the ∼900 pc diameter ring, with prominent knots coinciding with previously identified star-forming complexes. The spatial correspondence between far-IR peaks, tracers of massive star formation, and molecular gas reservoirs supports the interpretation that the dust is predominantly heated by young stars in these regions.

We find only a modest far-IR contribution from the nucleus itself, consistent with earlier indications that the AGN in NGC 1097 is of low luminosity and that its infrared output is overwhelmed by circumnuclear star formation. The colour temperature map derived from the far-IR bands shows warmer dust along the ring and cooler dust in the inter-ring regions, indicating localized heating and possible age gradients in the stellar populations. The inner bar dust lanes are detected in the far-IR continuum, suggesting that cold dust is being funneled toward the central regions, potentially sustaining the ongoing starburst.

Our analysis indicates that the far-IR emission traces both the current star formation and the dust mass distribution, with the ring dominating the energetics of the central kiloparsec. The lack of a significant far-IR excess at the nucleus further constrains the contribution of the AGN to the total infrared luminosity. These results reinforce the view that NGC 1097’s central IR output is driven largely by star formation within its circumnuclear ring, with the AGN playing only a secondary role in the far-IR regime.

Future work combining these far-IR maps with high-resolution spectroscopy and submillimetre interferometry will allow a more complete characterization of the dust heating mechanisms, gas dynamics, and star formation history in the central kiloparsec. Such studies will be essential for understanding the interplay between nuclear activity, circumnuclear starbursts, and the transport of gas and dust in barred spiral galaxies like NGC 1097.

title: Estimating hyperbolicity of chaotic bidimensional maps
abstract: We investigate numerical methods for estimating the degree of hyperbolicity in chaotic two–dimensional discrete–time dynamical systems. Hyperbolicity, characterized by the uniform separation of stable and unstable manifolds, plays a central role in the structural stability and predictability of chaotic maps. Using prototypical examples such as the Hénon map and the standard map in chaotic regimes, we evaluate local angles between covariant Lyapunov vectors to quantify deviations from uniform hyperbolicity. Our approach combines long–term trajectory sampling with finite–time Lyapunov exponent computations to construct probability distributions of manifold intersection angles, enabling a statistical characterization of hyperbolicity violations. We analyze the influence of numerical precision, trajectory length, and sampling density on the robustness of the estimates. The results show that even in strongly chaotic regimes, small but non–negligible occurrences of near–tangencies persist, implying partial hyperbolicity breakdown. We discuss the implications for shadowing properties, predictability horizons, and control of chaos, and outline possible extensions to higher–dimensional mappings and experimental data from physical systems.
introduction:
Chaotic dynamical systems exhibit sensitive dependence on initial conditions, making their long-term evolution intrinsically unpredictable. In two-dimensional maps, such as those arising in discrete-time models of physical, biological, or engineering processes, chaos is often accompanied by complex geometrical structures in phase space. A central concept in the study of such systems is *hyperbolicity*, which characterizes the uniform separation of trajectories along stable and unstable manifolds. Hyperbolic systems are structurally stable, meaning their qualitative behavior is robust under small perturbations. However, many physically relevant chaotic maps are only partially hyperbolic or display regions where hyperbolicity breaks down, leading to intricate dynamical phenomena.

Quantifying the degree of hyperbolicity in a given system is of both theoretical and practical relevance. From a theoretical perspective, it provides insight into the interplay between stability and instability in chaotic dynamics. From an applied standpoint, it can inform the reliability of numerical simulations, the predictability of model outputs, or the design of control strategies. While rigorous criteria for hyperbolicity exist, they are often difficult to verify in complex or experimentally obtained systems. Consequently, numerical estimation methods play a crucial role in assessing hyperbolic properties from finite data sets or simulated trajectories.

In this work, we focus on the estimation of hyperbolicity in chaotic bidimensional maps using computational approaches that analyze local expansion and contraction rates along trajectories. We discuss how finite-time Lyapunov exponents, covariant Lyapunov vectors, and angular separation between invariant directions can be used to diagnose violations of hyperbolicity. Our study emphasizes the challenges posed by finite-precision computations, short data series, and the presence of tangencies between stable and unstable manifolds. By applying these methods to prototypical chaotic maps, we aim to evaluate their effectiveness and limitations, offering guidelines for interpreting numerical estimates of hyperbolicity in realistic settings. This approach contributes to a deeper understanding of the geometric structure underlying two-dimensional chaotic dynamics.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the estimation of hyperbolicity in chaotic bidimensional maps through a systematic analysis of their dynamical properties. By employing numerical techniques to evaluate local Lyapunov exponents and angular distributions between stable and unstable manifolds, we have quantified deviations from uniform hyperbolicity and identified regions of phase space where tangencies are more likely to occur. Our findings demonstrate that even in maps exhibiting strong chaotic behavior, hyperbolicity can be significantly non-uniform, with localized breakdowns that may influence long-term predictability and transport phenomena.  

The proposed methodology offers a practical framework for assessing hyperbolic characteristics without requiring explicit analytical expressions for invariant manifolds, making it applicable to a broad class of discrete-time dynamical systems. Comparisons between different parameter regimes revealed a clear correlation between the degree of hyperbolicity and the global stability structure of the attractor, suggesting that hyperbolicity estimates can serve as sensitive indicators of bifurcation onset.  

These results contribute to a more refined understanding of the geometric structure underlying chaotic dynamics, bridging the gap between theoretical criteria for hyperbolicity and computational diagnostics. Future work should extend this approach to higher-dimensional systems and explore the role of hyperbolicity fluctuations in controlling mixing rates and transport barriers. Such developments could enhance the predictive modeling of complex physical processes governed by nonlinear maps and support the design of control strategies in chaotic regimes.

title: Rayleigh scattering in the transmission spectrum of HAT-P-18b
abstract: We present optical transmission spectroscopy of the Saturn-mass exoplanet HAT-P-18b, obtained with the FORS2 instrument at the Very Large Telescope. The measured transmission spectrum spans 0.44–0.93 μm and reveals a pronounced slope toward shorter wavelengths consistent with Rayleigh scattering in the planet’s atmosphere. No significant detection of pressure-broadened alkali absorption features is found, suggesting the presence of high-altitude haze that masks molecular signatures. The observed spectral slope corresponds to an atmospheric temperature broadly consistent with the planet’s equilibrium temperature, assuming scattering by small particles. Our results add HAT-P-18b to the growing sample of exoplanets exhibiting scattering-dominated optical spectra, highlighting the prevalence of aerosols in low-gravity, gas giant atmospheres. This study demonstrates the capability of ground-based facilities to characterize atmospheric scattering properties in transiting exoplanets with moderate equilibrium temperatures.
introduction:
The study of exoplanetary atmospheres through transmission spectroscopy has become a powerful tool for probing the physical and chemical properties of planets beyond our Solar System. By measuring the wavelength-dependent transit depth as a planet passes in front of its host star, it is possible to infer the presence of molecular species, clouds, and hazes in the planetary atmosphere. In particular, short-wavelength observations are sensitive to scattering processes, including Rayleigh scattering by small particles or molecules, which imprint a characteristic slope on the transmission spectrum. The detection and characterization of such scattering signatures provide key insights into atmospheric composition, temperature structure, and the nature of aerosol particles.

HAT-P-18b is a Saturn-mass, low-density gas giant orbiting a K2 dwarf star with an orbital period of approximately 5.5 days. Its relatively low surface gravity and equilibrium temperature of around 850 K make it an interesting target for atmospheric characterization, as the extended scale height enhances spectral features in transmission. Previous studies of similar warm Saturns have revealed a variety of atmospheric behaviors, ranging from clear atmospheres with prominent molecular absorption to strongly muted features indicative of high-altitude clouds or hazes. In some cases, blue-optical slopes consistent with Rayleigh scattering have been observed, suggesting the presence of small-particle aerosols in the upper atmosphere.

While the atmospheric properties of a number of hot Jupiters and warm Neptunes have been explored in detail, fewer observational constraints exist for planets in the mass and temperature regime of HAT-P-18b. Early photometric and spectroscopic transit measurements of this planet have hinted at the possibility of a scattering slope in the optical, but the precision and wavelength coverage of available data have so far limited robust interpretation. Detecting and quantifying Rayleigh scattering in HAT-P-18b’s atmosphere would contribute to a broader understanding of aerosol formation and survival in low-gravity, moderately irradiated gas giants, and help place this planet in the context of atmospheric diversity among exoplanets.

In this work, we present new optical transmission spectroscopy of HAT-P-18b, obtained with high-precision ground-based observations spanning the blue to red optical regime. We aim to investigate the presence and characteristics of a Rayleigh scattering signature, constrain the atmospheric scale height and potential aerosol properties, and compare our findings with theoretical models and trends identified in other exoplanets. Our results provide new empirical constraints on the atmospheric composition and scattering processes in HAT-P-18b, contributing to the growing body of comparative exoplanetology.
conclusion: Our analysis of the transmission spectrum of HAT-P-18b reveals a pronounced slope toward shorter wavelengths, consistent with Rayleigh scattering by small particles in the planet’s atmosphere. This finding supports the presence of a haze layer that obscures molecular absorption features, in agreement with previous studies of similar exoplanets. The detection of scattering signatures contributes to the growing evidence for diverse atmospheric compositions among hot Saturns. Future higher-precision measurements, particularly at blue optical wavelengths, will help constrain particle properties and refine models of atmospheric structure and cloud formation in HAT-P-18b.

title: Transverse momentum distribution of charged particles and identified hadrons in p-Pb collisions at the LHC with ALICE
abstract: The transverse momentum (\(p_{\mathrm{T}}\)) spectra of charged particles and identified hadrons produced in proton–lead (p–Pb) collisions at a nucleon–nucleon centre-of-mass energy of \(\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 5.02\) TeV have been measured with the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The analysis covers a broad \(p_{\mathrm{T}}\) range, from 0.15 GeV/\emph{c} up to 50 GeV/\emph{c} for charged particles, and up to 14 GeV/\emph{c} for pions, kaons, and protons, identified via specific energy loss and time-of-flight measurements. The results are presented for minimum-bias events and compared to proton–proton (\(pp\)) reference spectra at the same energy, scaled by the number of binary nucleon–nucleon collisions. The nuclear modification factor \(R_{\mathrm{pPb}}\) is found to be consistent with unity for \(p_{\mathrm{T}} \gtrsim 2\) GeV/\emph{c}, indicating the absence of strong final-state effects at high \(p_{\mathrm{T}}\). At lower \(p_{\mathrm{T}}\), a moderate enhancement is observed, consistent with initial-state multiple scattering (Cronin effect). Particle species dependence of the spectra and \(R_{\mathrm{pPb}}\) is discussed in the context of collective phenomena and cold nuclear matter effects. These measurements provide essential constraints on models of particle production in small collision systems and serve as a crucial baseline for interpreting heavy-ion results at the LHC.
introduction:
High-energy proton–nucleus (p–A) collisions provide a unique environment to investigate the interplay between hard and soft processes in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), and to disentangle initial-state nuclear effects from the final-state phenomena observed in heavy-ion collisions. At the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC), proton–lead (p–Pb) collisions at multi-TeV energies allow the study of particle production over a broad transverse momentum (\(p_{\mathrm{T}}\)) range, offering insights into parton distribution modifications, multiple scattering, and possible collective dynamics in small systems.  

The transverse momentum distribution of charged particles is a fundamental observable that reflects the underlying particle production mechanisms. At low \(p_{\mathrm{T}}\), particle yields are dominated by soft processes, typically described by hydrodynamic or phenomenological models, whereas at high \(p_{\mathrm{T}}\) they are sensitive to hard parton scattering calculable in perturbative QCD. Measurements of identified hadrons, such as pions, kaons, and protons, further constrain hadronization models and baryon-to-meson production mechanisms, and can reveal possible mass-dependent effects or radial flow patterns.  

The ALICE detector, with its excellent particle identification capabilities over a wide momentum range, is well suited for such studies. By comparing p–Pb results to those from proton–proton (pp) and lead–lead (Pb–Pb) collisions, one can quantify nuclear modification factors and assess the role of initial-state effects, such as nuclear shadowing or saturation, and final-state effects, including possible collective flow. This paper presents measurements of the \(p_{\mathrm{T}}\) spectra of charged particles and identified hadrons in p–Pb collisions at \(\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 5.02\) TeV, recorded with ALICE, and discusses their implications for particle production mechanisms in small collision systems.
conclusion: The transverse momentum distributions of charged particles and identified hadrons in p–Pb collisions at the LHC have been measured with the ALICE detector. The results reveal characteristic features of particle production across different momentum ranges, providing insights into initial- and final-state effects. Comparisons with theoretical models suggest that collective phenomena may play a role even in small systems, contributing to a deeper understanding of the dynamics in proton–nucleus interactions.

title: Competition among alliances of different sizes
abstract: We analyze competition between strategic alliances that differ in size, focusing on how asymmetries in membership affect performance and stability. Using a game-theoretic framework, we model alliances as cooperative groups competing for a common market while internally sharing costs and benefits. The model incorporates both inter-alliance competition and intra-alliance coordination, allowing us to examine how the size of an alliance influences its strategic behavior, resource allocation, and payoff distribution. Our results show that larger alliances can exploit economies of scale and exert greater market influence, but face higher coordination costs and potential internal conflicts. Smaller alliances, while less influential, may adapt more quickly and maintain higher internal cohesion. We identify conditions under which alliances of different sizes can coexist in equilibrium and when one type dominates. These findings contribute to understanding the trade-offs inherent in alliance formation and provide insights into competitive dynamics in industries characterized by collaborative rivalry.
introduction:
In many economic, technological, and political arenas, collaboration among distinct actors has emerged as a strategic response to increasingly complex and competitive environments. Firms, institutions, and even nations often join forces in alliances to pool resources, share risks, and jointly pursue opportunities that would be difficult to seize individually. Such alliances can vary greatly in scale, ranging from small, tightly knit partnerships to large, loosely connected consortia. The size of an alliance shapes its internal dynamics, coordination mechanisms, and capacity for collective action. At the same time, alliances do not operate in isolation: they compete with other alliances—often of different sizes—for market share, technological leadership, policy influence, or other strategic advantages. Understanding the nature of competition among alliances of different sizes is therefore a critical task for scholars and practitioners alike.

Research on interorganizational alliances has tended to focus on dyadic partnerships or homogeneous networks, often assuming that competitors are similar in structure and scale. Yet in many real-world settings, alliances are heterogeneous in size, composition, and scope. For example, in global industries such as commercial aviation, strategic alliances encompass both large, multi-firm constellations spanning continents and smaller regional groupings with focused market niches. Similar patterns are evident in technology sectors, where large open-source communities compete against compact, proprietary development teams, and in international relations, where broad coalitions of states interact with smaller, more specialized blocs. In such circumstances, differences in size can influence not only the resources available to each alliance but also their agility, decision-making processes, and ability to adapt to environmental change.

The strategic literature suggests that size confers both advantages and disadvantages. Larger alliances may benefit from economies of scale, greater resource diversity, and broader geographic reach, enhancing their competitive capacity. They may be better able to absorb shocks, undertake large-scale projects, and influence industry standards or regulations. At the same time, greater size can introduce coordination challenges, increase the risk of internal conflict, and slow down strategic responses. Conversely, smaller alliances may suffer from resource constraints and limited bargaining power, yet they can often capitalize on flexibility, cohesion, and rapid decision-making. These contrasting attributes raise important questions about how alliances of different sizes perform when they compete directly in the same domain and what factors mediate or moderate the outcomes of such competition.

Existing theoretical frameworks provide partial insights into these dynamics but do not fully integrate the implications of size heterogeneity into models of alliance competition. Resource-based perspectives highlight the role of complementary assets and capabilities, but often without explicit consideration of how alliance size shapes the configuration and deployment of these resources. Network theories shed light on structural advantages and the flow of information, yet they typically examine networks of a given scale or density. Strategic management studies have examined competitive interactions among firms of different sizes, but the extension of these insights to collective entities such as alliances requires attention to additional layers of complexity, including inter-partner coordination, governance arrangements, and the distribution of benefits among members.

Moreover, empirical evidence on the competition between alliances of different sizes remains fragmented. Case studies reveal instances where large alliances dominate markets through coordinated strategies, as well as examples in which smaller alliances outmaneuver larger rivals by exploiting niche opportunities or innovating more swiftly. Quantitative studies, however, have seldom been designed to compare systematically the competitive performance of differently sized alliances, often due to data limitations or definitional ambiguities regarding alliance boundaries and membership. As a result, our understanding of the conditions under which size differences matter most—and of the mechanisms through which size influences competitive outcomes—remains incomplete.

Addressing this gap is important for both theory and practice. From a theoretical standpoint, integrating alliance size into models of inter-alliance competition can enhance our understanding of collective strategic behavior and contribute to a more nuanced account of competitive advantage at the group level. In practical terms, alliance managers and policymakers face choices about whether to expand or contract alliance membership, merge with other alliances, or maintain a particular scale. These decisions rest on assumptions about how size affects competitive performance, assumptions that require empirical validation. Furthermore, as global challenges increasingly demand coordinated responses across multiple actors—whether in business, science, or governance—the design of effective alliances capable of prevailing in competitive environments becomes a matter of pressing concern.

This study seeks to advance knowledge in this area by examining the competitive interactions between alliances of different sizes, exploring how variations in scale influence strategic behavior, performance outcomes, and adaptive capacity. By drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives and leveraging both qualitative and quantitative evidence, the analysis aims to identify the advantages and disadvantages associated with different alliance sizes and to clarify the contingencies that shape competitive success. In doing so, it contributes to a richer understanding of alliance competition and offers actionable insights for those engaged in forming, managing, or competing against alliances of varying scales.
conclusion:
The analysis presented in this study has examined the dynamics of competition among alliances of varying sizes, highlighting the interplay between structural advantages, coordination mechanisms, and strategic positioning. By comparing alliances composed of a small number of tightly connected members with those encompassing larger, more diverse networks, this research has demonstrated that size alone does not determine competitive outcomes. Instead, performance and resilience emerge from the interaction between alliance size, internal governance, and the ability to adapt to environmental uncertainties.

Smaller alliances often benefit from agility, cohesion, and lower coordination costs, enabling rapid decision-making and responsiveness to changing market conditions. These advantages, however, can be offset by limited resource pools and reduced capacity to absorb shocks, particularly in industries characterized by high capital requirements or volatile demand. Larger alliances, by contrast, can draw upon broader resources, diversified capabilities, and greater market reach, but they frequently face challenges in maintaining trust, managing complexity, and avoiding strategic drift. The empirical findings suggest that these trade-offs are not static; they evolve over time as alliances learn, reconfigure, and respond to external pressures.

A key contribution of this study lies in identifying the conditions under which alliances of different sizes can coexist and compete effectively. The results indicate that heterogeneity in member capabilities, alignment of strategic goals, and the development of robust coordination frameworks are more critical than scale per se. Furthermore, the analysis underscores the role of institutional and environmental contexts in shaping competitive trajectories: regulatory regimes, technological turbulence, and cultural factors can amplify or diminish the inherent advantages of a particular alliance size.

From a managerial perspective, the findings imply that alliance leaders should focus less on pursuing growth in membership for its own sake and more on optimizing the fit between alliance structure, strategic objectives, and the competitive environment. For policymakers, the coexistence of varying alliance sizes suggests that fostering a diverse alliance ecosystem can enhance overall market dynamism and innovation potential.

While this study has advanced understanding of alliance size competition, it also opens pathways for further research. Longitudinal studies could better capture the temporal dynamics of alliance performance, and cross-sectoral analyses may reveal whether the observed patterns hold across different competitive landscapes. Ultimately, the evidence affirms that in the competition among alliances, size matters—but only in conjunction with the strategic and organizational factors that convert potential scale into sustained advantage.

title: Compressive Sensing Imaging of 3-D Object by a Holographic Algorithm
abstract: We present a novel holographic algorithm for compressive sensing imaging of three-dimensional objects, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction from significantly reduced measurement data. The proposed method integrates principles of compressive sensing with computational holography to exploit sparsity in both spatial and depth domains. By employing a tailored measurement matrix and iterative reconstruction, the approach effectively recovers amplitude and phase information, preserving fine structural details while reducing acquisition time and data volume. Numerical simulations and experimental results demonstrate that the algorithm achieves accurate 3-D reconstructions with fewer holographic projections compared to conventional methods. The technique is robust to measurement noise and adaptable to various optical configurations, making it suitable for applications in microscopy, remote sensing, and non-destructive testing. This work advances the efficiency and practicality of holographic 3-D imaging through synergistic use of compressive sensing theory.
introduction: Compressive sensing (CS) has emerged as a powerful framework for acquiring and reconstructing signals with significantly fewer measurements than required by the Nyquist criterion. In optical imaging, CS enables efficient data acquisition, reducing acquisition time and storage demands. Three-dimensional (3-D) object reconstruction benefits greatly from CS by exploiting spatial sparsity and structural priors. Holographic imaging, which records both amplitude and phase information, offers a robust platform for 3-D visualization. Integrating CS with holographic algorithms allows high-resolution reconstruction from undersampled measurements, mitigating noise and hardware limitations. This work presents a novel CS-based holographic approach for accurate, efficient imaging of 3-D objects.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a holographic algorithm for compressive sensing imaging of three-dimensional objects, demonstrating its effectiveness in reconstructing high-fidelity spatial information from undersampled measurements. By integrating compressive sensing theory with holographic reconstruction, the proposed method significantly reduces data acquisition requirements while preserving depth and structural accuracy. Simulation and experimental results verify that this approach achieves robust performance under noise and limited sampling conditions. The method offers potential advantages for applications in optical imaging, remote sensing, and microscopy. Future work will focus on optimizing reconstruction speed, extending to dynamic scenes, and exploring hardware implementations for real-time 3D imaging.

title: Spatial Point Pattern Analysis of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in France
abstract: This study presents a spatial point pattern analysis of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) reports in France, using a georeferenced dataset spanning multiple decades. Employing techniques from spatial statistics, including kernel density estimation, nearest-neighbor analysis, and Ripley’s K-function, we investigate whether the spatial distribution of UAP observations deviates from complete spatial randomness. Results reveal significant clustering in specific regions, particularly in proximity to military installations, high-population areas, and certain geographic features, suggesting potential reporting or observational biases. Temporal stratification indicates that clustering patterns persist over time, though their intensity varies across decades. The findings support the hypothesis that sociocultural, environmental, and infrastructural factors may influence both the occurrence and reporting of UAPs. By integrating spatial analysis with contextual geographic data, this research contributes a systematic, quantitative perspective to the study of UAP phenomena in France, offering a replicable framework for comparative studies in other national contexts.
introduction: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) have long attracted public interest and scientific inquiry, yet systematic spatial analyses of their reported occurrences remain limited. In France, the centralized documentation of UAP by the Groupe d’Études et d’Informations sur les Phénomènes Aérospatiaux Non-identifiés (GEIPAN) offers a unique opportunity to study their geographical distribution. Spatial point pattern analysis, a set of statistical techniques for examining the arrangement of events in space, provides a rigorous framework for investigating whether reported UAP sightings are randomly distributed, clustered, or regularly spaced. Understanding these patterns can yield insights into potential underlying causes, whether related to physical phenomena, environmental conditions, or sociocultural factors affecting observation and reporting. Previous research on anomalous aerial sightings has often been descriptive, focusing on case studies or temporal trends, with less emphasis on spatial statistical methods. This study applies spatial point pattern analysis to the French UAP dataset to identify significant spatial structures and possible correlations with geographic or demographic variables. By integrating geospatial statistics with official UAP records, the analysis aims to contribute to a more systematic understanding of the phenomenon’s spatial characteristics and to inform future multidisciplinary research.
conclusion:
The spatial point pattern analysis of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) reports in France has provided important insights into the geographic distribution and potential correlates of these events. By applying quantitative spatial statistics to a comprehensive dataset, this study has moved beyond anecdotal accounts to identify significant clustering patterns and spatial heterogeneity across the French territory. The results indicate that UAP reports are not randomly distributed but tend to concentrate in specific regions, suggesting the influence of both environmental and socio-demographic factors. Proximity to population centers, transportation networks, and certain military or industrial sites appears to be associated with higher reporting densities, although these relationships are complex and warrant further investigation.

The detection of statistically significant clusters highlights the value of spatial analytical approaches in fields where data quality and completeness can vary. While the observed patterns may reflect genuine differences in the occurrence of phenomena, they could also be shaped by variations in observation opportunities, reporting practices, and cultural factors. The incorporation of control variables and comparison with null models has strengthened the robustness of the findings, yet limitations remain. In particular, the self-reported nature of the data and potential biases in temporal coverage underscore the need for cautious interpretation.

This research contributes to the broader understanding of unexplained aerial reports by demonstrating how spatial point pattern methods can uncover latent structures in the data. It also provides a methodological framework that can be applied to other national or regional datasets, enabling cross-cultural comparisons and temporal trend analyses. Future work should aim to integrate additional covariates, such as meteorological conditions and air traffic data, and to explore multi-scale spatial processes that may influence UAP distribution.

In conclusion, the French UAP dataset exhibits non-random spatial organization, with identifiable clusters that invite further scientific scrutiny. While the causes underlying these patterns remain uncertain, the present analysis underscores the importance of systematic, spatially explicit approaches in advancing the empirical study of UAP. Such work deepens our understanding of the phenomenon’s geography and lays the groundwork for more targeted and interdisciplinary investigations.

title: A minimal model for structure, dynamics, and tension of monolayered cell colonies
abstract: We present a minimal theoretical and computational framework to describe the structure, collective dynamics, and mechanical tension of confluent monolayered cell colonies. The model treats cells as deformable units with an effective area elasticity, cortical contractility, and active self-propulsion, while cell–cell interfaces transmit both adhesive and tensile forces. Intercellular interactions are encoded through a reduced set of parameters governing junctional mechanics and motility, enabling direct connection to measurable biophysical quantities. By systematically varying these parameters, we identify distinct regimes of colony organization, ranging from fluid-like rearranging tissues to solid-like jammed states. The model predicts how active forces and cell–cell adhesion jointly determine spatial order, velocity correlations, and stress transmission across the colony. Analytical estimates and numerical simulations reveal a simple scaling relation between colony-wide tension and the balance of actomyosin contractility with adhesive coupling. Furthermore, we show that mechanical heterogeneity naturally emerges from local fluctuations in cell shape and motility, leading to nonuniform stress patterns and collective modes such as swirling and coherent migration. Comparison with published experimental data on epithelial monolayers demonstrates that the minimal model reproduces key trends in tissue mechanics and kinematics without requiring detailed subcellular descriptions. This parsimonious approach provides a tractable platform for exploring the interplay between activity, mechanics, and topology in living tissues, and offers predictive insights into how monolayered colonies respond to perturbations in adhesion, contractility, or substrate interactions.
introduction:
The collective behavior of cells within epithelial tissues underlies numerous biological processes, ranging from embryonic morphogenesis and wound healing to cancer invasion. In these contexts, cells often assemble into confluent, monolayered colonies whose mechanical and dynamical properties emerge from the interplay between cell–cell adhesion, active force generation, and constraints imposed by geometry and the substrate. Understanding how these factors combine to determine colony structure, internal stresses, and spatiotemporal patterns of motion remains a central challenge in biophysics. While experimental studies have revealed rich phenomenology—such as coordinated flows, pulsations, and stress transmission across many cell diameters—there is a need for theoretical frameworks that can capture these behaviors in a minimal yet predictive manner.

Existing modeling approaches span a wide range of complexity, from continuum hydrodynamic descriptions of active matter to detailed vertex or cellular Potts models that track individual cell shapes and fluctuations. Continuum theories can efficiently capture large-scale flows and stress patterns, but often rely on coarse-grained parameters whose microscopic origins are difficult to identify. In contrast, highly detailed cell-based models incorporate explicit representations of junctional mechanics and cytoskeletal activity, but the large number of parameters and computational cost can obscure the essential physical mechanisms. Between these extremes lies the opportunity for minimal models that retain only the key ingredients needed to reproduce the salient structural and dynamical features of monolayered colonies, while allowing for analytical insight and efficient numerical exploration.

A central aspect of epithelial mechanics is the generation and transmission of tension. Tension arises from actomyosin contractility within cells, adhesion-mediated coupling between neighbors, and interactions with the extracellular matrix. These forces not only determine the equilibrium or steady-state geometry of the tissue but also influence its ability to remodel and migrate collectively. Experimental measurements using techniques such as traction force microscopy and laser ablation have demonstrated that tension is spatially heterogeneous and dynamically regulated, often correlating with patterns of cell rearrangements and collective flows. Capturing the origin and distribution of such tension within a theoretical framework is essential for linking cellular activity to emergent tissue-scale behavior.

Here, we develop a minimal, cell-resolved model for confluent monolayered colonies that unifies structure, dynamics, and tension within a single framework. Our approach is motivated by the need to identify the minimal set of mechanical interactions and active processes that can reproduce experimentally observed features, such as the distribution of cell shapes, the correlation of neighbor exchanges with stress patterns, and the emergence of coherent flows. We consider each cell as a deformable unit characterized by a target area, perimeter elasticity, and active contractile stress, coupled to its neighbors via adhesive junctions. The colony is confined to a two-dimensional substrate, with frictional coupling to the underlying surface providing resistance to motion. This formulation allows us to track the evolution of cell shapes and positions over time, directly compute intercellular tensions, and explore how changes in activity or adhesion affect collective dynamics.

By systematically varying the model parameters, we identify regimes corresponding to solid-like, fluid-like, and actively flowing colonies, and relate these to experimentally relevant control variables such as actomyosin contractility and cadherin-mediated adhesion. We further demonstrate that the model captures the scaling of internal stress with colony size and predicts distinctive spatial patterns of tension that can be tested against experimental data. Ultimately, our minimal model provides a tractable platform for investigating the mechanical principles of epithelial organization, offering insight into how cellular-level forces and interactions give rise to the emergent structure, dynamics, and tension of monolayered cell colonies.
conclusion:
In this work, we have introduced and analyzed a minimal theoretical framework that captures the essential structural organization, dynamical behavior, and tension regulation of monolayered cell colonies. By reducing the complexity of cellular interactions to a tractable set of parameters and rules, our model bridges the gap between detailed mechanistic simulations and coarse-grained continuum descriptions. It elucidates how local cell–cell adhesion, active motility, and mechanical feedback collectively give rise to emergent colony-scale patterns and stress distributions.

Our results demonstrate that even with minimal ingredients, the model reproduces key experimentally observed features of epithelial monolayers, including the maintenance of a cohesive structure, the emergence of collective motion, and the spatial heterogeneity of mechanical tension. The interplay between active forces generated by individual cells and the elastic-like response of the colony generates a robust balance that sustains both structural integrity and dynamic adaptability. In particular, we have shown that tension profiles arise naturally from the competition between adhesion-mediated cohesion and motility-driven rearrangements, leading to characteristic gradients from the colony edge to its interior. These findings are consistent with experimental reports of peripheral tension enrichment and central stress relaxation.

The simplicity of the model allows for analytical insights into the parameter regimes governing morphological stability and dynamical transitions. For example, varying adhesion strength or motility amplitude can drive the colony from a quiescent, solid-like state to a fluid-like regime with enhanced neighbor exchanges, reflecting the plasticity observed in living tissues during morphogenesis or wound healing. Moreover, the framework accommodates extensions to incorporate additional biological processes, such as proliferation, apoptosis, or substrate interactions, without losing interpretability.

Beyond reproducing known behaviors, the minimal model offers predictive power. It suggests specific perturbations—such as modulating adhesion molecules or cytoskeletal activity—that could be experimentally tested to tune colony tension and dynamics. This predictive capability makes it a useful tool for designing experiments and interpreting data in the context of tissue engineering, developmental biology, and disease progression.

In summary, the model presented here captures the fundamental physics underlying the structure, dynamics, and tension regulation of monolayered cell colonies with a minimal set of assumptions. It highlights the sufficiency of simple mechanical and motility rules to generate complex collective phenomena, and it provides a foundation for systematic exploration of more intricate biological scenarios. Future work will focus on coupling this framework to biochemical signaling networks and heterogeneous cell populations, thereby enabling a deeper understanding of the reciprocal interplay between mechanics and biology in tissue organization.

title: Graded Orbital Occupation near Interfaces in a La2NiO4 - La2CuO4 Superlattice
abstract: We investigate the spatial variation of orbital occupation in a La₂NiO₄–La₂CuO₄ superlattice using resonant soft x-ray scattering and x-ray absorption spectroscopy. By tuning the photon energy to the Ni and Cu L-edges, we selectively probe the electronic states in each constituent layer. Analysis of polarization-dependent spectra reveals a graded occupation of the Ni \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{3z^2-r^2}\) orbitals near the interface, in contrast to the more uniform orbital configuration in the bulk-like interior. The Cu orbital population remains comparatively invariant across the interface. Model calculations based on crystal field and covalency effects reproduce the observed depth-dependent orbital polarization, indicating a redistribution of hole density from Ni to Cu layers mediated by interfacial hybridization. These results demonstrate that controlled interface engineering in transition-metal oxide heterostructures can tailor orbital configurations, with implications for emergent electronic and magnetic phenomena.
introduction:
Transition metal oxides with layered perovskite structures exhibit a rich variety of correlated electronic phases, including unconventional superconductivity, charge and spin order, and metal–insulator transitions. Among these, the Ruddlesden–Popper series La\(_2\)NiO\(_4\) and La\(_2\)CuO\(_4\) have attracted sustained interest owing to their structural similarity yet strikingly different ground states. La\(_2\)CuO\(_4\), the undoped parent compound of high-\(T_c\) cuprate superconductors, is a charge-transfer insulator with antiferromagnetic order, while La\(_2\)NiO\(_4\) is a correlated insulator displaying strong electron–lattice coupling and charge stripe tendencies. Their closely matched lattice parameters and layered structures make them suitable candidates for constructing atomically precise superlattices, enabling systematic exploration of interfacial effects on orbital, charge, and spin degrees of freedom.

Heterostructuring dissimilar correlated oxides can give rise to novel emergent states not present in the bulk constituents. Band alignment, polar discontinuities, and strain fields can drive charge transfer across the interface, altering the local electronic configuration. In transition metal oxides, such modifications are often accompanied by changes in the occupation of the \(d\) orbitals, which govern magnetic exchange, transport, and coupling to the lattice. In particular, for layered nickelates and cuprates, the competition between \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{3z^2-r^2}\) orbital occupation plays a central role in determining their low-energy physics. Understanding how orbital polarization evolves near interfaces is thus essential for rational design of functional oxide heterostructures.

Previous work on oxide superlattices has revealed that orbital polarization can be strongly influenced by epitaxial strain, quantum confinement, and covalency effects. In nickelate-based heterostructures, x-ray linear dichroism studies have demonstrated substantial redistribution between the \(e_g\) orbitals, while in cuprate heterostructures, subtle distortions of the CuO\(_6\) octahedra can modulate the crystal field splitting. However, the spatial profile of orbital occupation across an interface, particularly in systems combining nickelates and cuprates, remains incompletely characterized. It is not yet clear whether the orbital configuration changes abruptly at the interface or varies gradually over several unit cells, and how such variation correlates with structural relaxation and charge redistribution.

In this work, we investigate a superlattice composed of alternating layers of La\(_2\)NiO\(_4\) and La\(_2\)CuO\(_4\), grown by molecular beam epitaxy with atomic-layer precision. By combining resonant soft x-ray scattering and x-ray absorption spectroscopy with polarization control, we probe the depth-dependent orbital occupation near the interfaces. The analysis reveals a graded variation of \(e_g\) orbital polarization extending several unit cells into both constituents, rather than a sharp interface. This graded orbital occupation is accompanied by subtle modifications of the local lattice environment, suggesting a cooperative interplay between structural relaxation and electronic reconstruction.

Our findings demonstrate that in the La\(_2\)NiO\(_4\)–La\(_2\)CuO\(_4\) system, the interfacial region hosts a distinct orbital configuration that cannot be simply described by a bulk-like termination of either material. Instead, the interface acts as a transitional zone in which the orbital degrees of freedom adjust continuously to reconcile the differing electronic preferences of Ni and Cu sites. Such graded orbital profiles may be a general feature of correlated oxide heterostructures, with implications for engineering interface-driven functionalities in complex oxide devices.
conclusion:
In summary, resonant soft x-ray scattering measurements of the La₂NiO₄–La₂CuO₄ superlattice reveal a pronounced modulation of the Ni \(d\)-orbital occupation localized near the heterointerfaces. By tuning to the Ni \(L_{2,3}\) edges and analyzing the momentum-dependent scattering intensities, we directly probed variations in the \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{3z^2-r^2}\) occupancies across the superlattice period. The data demonstrate a graded orbital polarization extending over several unit cells, rather than an abrupt change confined to a single atomic plane. This spatially extended profile is consistent with electronic reconstruction driven by both polar discontinuities and local strain fields at the interfaces.  

Comparison with model calculations indicates that the occupation gradient arises from a combination of charge transfer between layers and crystal field modifications induced by lattice distortions. The results highlight that in layered nickelate–cuprate heterostructures, orbital degrees of freedom can be engineered continuously across interfaces, offering a finer level of control than purely chemical substitution. Such control over orbital polarization has direct implications for tailoring the anisotropic transport and magnetic properties in correlated oxide heterostructures.  

Our findings underscore the importance of spatially resolved probes in capturing subtle interfacial phenomena that are averaged out in bulk measurements. The graded orbital occupation observed here provides a new platform for exploring interface-driven emergent states, and suggests that deliberate interface design could be an effective route to realize novel functionalities in transition-metal oxide superlattices.

title: Space-like and time-like pion-rho transition form factors in the light-cone formalism
abstract: We investigate the space-like and time-like pion–rho transition form factors within the light-cone formalism, employing light-front wave functions derived from phenomenological models constrained by experimental data. The framework allows a unified treatment of both kinematic regions, enabling consistent analytic continuation from space-like to time-like momentum transfers. We compute the transition form factors over a wide range of \(Q^2\) and compare the results with available measurements and other theoretical approaches. Our analysis reveals that the light-cone approach captures essential relativistic effects and yields predictions in good agreement with experimental trends. The study provides insights into the nonperturbative structure of light mesons and offers a consistent method to describe hadronic transition processes in both space-like and time-like domains.
introduction:
The study of meson transition form factors provides a crucial window into the nonperturbative dynamics of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). In particular, the transition between the pion (\(\pi\)) and rho (\(\rho\)) mesons probes the interplay between quark spin, orbital angular momentum, and the strong interaction binding effects in light meson systems. The pion, as the lightest pseudoscalar meson and the pseudo–Goldstone boson of spontaneously broken chiral symmetry, and the rho, as the lightest vector meson, represent fundamental building blocks in the description of hadronic structure. The pion–rho (\(\pi\)–\(\rho\)) transition form factors encode information about the internal quark–gluon wave functions beyond what is accessible from elastic form factors alone, making them an indispensable tool for exploring hadron structure in both the space-like and time-like momentum transfer regions.

Experimentally, the \(\pi\)–\(\rho\) transition can be studied through processes such as electroproduction, radiative decays, and electron–positron annihilation. The space-like form factors can be extracted from exclusive electroproduction processes where a virtual photon induces a transition between a pion and a rho meson, while time-like form factors are accessible via annihilation channels such as \(e^+ e^- \to \pi \rho\) or from the Dalitz decays of heavier mesons. Measurements in both regions are complementary: the space-like domain is directly related to the Fourier transform of the light-front wave functions, while the time-like domain provides insight into resonance structures and analytic continuation properties of the form factors. A unified theoretical description that consistently treats both kinematic regions is therefore highly desirable.

From the theoretical standpoint, the calculation of \(\pi\)–\(\rho\) transition form factors requires a framework capable of incorporating both the relativistic nature of light mesons and the nonperturbative binding effects of QCD. The light-cone (or light-front) formalism has emerged as a powerful approach in this regard. By quantizing QCD at fixed light-cone time, one obtains a description in terms of relativistic wave functions that have a direct partonic interpretation. These light-cone wave functions are boost invariant along the longitudinal direction and allow for a clear separation between longitudinal momentum fractions and transverse momentum degrees of freedom. Moreover, exclusive processes can be described in a manner that naturally incorporates relativistic spin effects through the Melosh–Wigner rotation, which is particularly important for light meson systems.

Within the light-cone framework, form factors appear as overlaps of light-front wave functions corresponding to different Fock states of the hadrons involved. For the \(\pi\)–\(\rho\) transition, the dominant contribution typically arises from the minimal valence quark–antiquark Fock component, although higher Fock states may become relevant at small momentum transfers or in the time-like region near resonances. The formalism provides a unified treatment of space-like and time-like momentum transfers through analytic continuation, offering a consistent description of the transition form factors in both regions. Furthermore, the light-cone approach can incorporate constraints from perturbative QCD at large momentum transfers and from chiral symmetry in the low-energy regime.

Previous investigations of \(\pi\)–\(\rho\) transition form factors have employed a variety of methods, including QCD sum rules, lattice QCD, effective field theories, and constituent quark models. While these approaches have provided important insights, each has limitations in simultaneously addressing the relativistic and nonperturbative aspects across the full kinematic range. The light-cone formalism offers a complementary perspective that can bridge the gap between low- and high-energy descriptions, and it facilitates direct comparison with experimental observables expressed in terms of partonic variables.

In this work, we present a detailed study of the space-like and time-like \(\pi\)–\(\rho\) transition form factors within the light-cone formalism, focusing on the role of relativistic effects and the analytic continuation between the two kinematic regions. We construct the light-front wave functions for the pion and rho mesons using a phenomenologically motivated model that incorporates both the radial momentum distribution and the spin–orbital structure through the Melosh rotation. The resulting expressions for the transition form factors are evaluated over a wide range of momentum transfers, and the predictions are compared with available experimental data and other theoretical models. Our analysis highlights the advantages of the light-cone approach in providing a coherent and physically transparent description of the \(\pi\)–\(\rho\) transition, and it sheds light on the underlying quark–gluon dynamics that govern this fundamental process.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the space-like and time-like pion–rho transition form factors within the light-cone formalism, employing a phenomenologically motivated light-cone wave function for both the pion and the rho meson. By constructing the relevant helicity amplitudes and carefully treating the non-valence (or higher Fock state) contributions in the time-like region, we have obtained a unified description of the transition form factor across the full kinematic domain. Our results in the space-like region are consistent with available experimental data and exhibit the expected asymptotic behavior dictated by perturbative QCD, while in the time-like region the calculated form factors reproduce the general trends and magnitudes observed in processes such as \( e^+ e^- \to \pi \rho \).

The analysis demonstrates that the light-cone framework provides a natural and efficient way to incorporate relativistic effects, particularly the spin-orbit coupling encoded in the Melosh rotation, which plays a significant role in shaping the \( Q^2 \)-dependence of the form factors. The separation between valence and non-valence contributions, and their respective dominance in different kinematic regimes, has been made explicit. We find that while the space-like form factor is primarily governed by the valence sector, the time-like form factor receives substantial contributions from higher Fock states, emphasizing the importance of a consistent treatment of non-perturbative dynamics.

Our study thus extends the applicability of the light-cone formalism to transition processes involving vector and pseudoscalar mesons, offering a coherent picture that bridges space-like and time-like momentum transfers. Future work may focus on refining the input wave functions through lattice-QCD constraints or global fits to a wider set of exclusive processes, and on extending the approach to other meson transitions. These developments would further test the universality of the light-cone wave functions and deepen our understanding of hadronic structure in QCD.

title: Field induced multiple order-by-disorder state selection in antiferromagnetic honeycomb bilayer lattice
abstract: We investigate the magnetic field–induced selection of ordered states in an antiferromagnetic honeycomb bilayer lattice with competing interactions. Using a combination of classical Monte Carlo simulations and linear spin-wave theory, we demonstrate that thermal and quantum order-by-disorder mechanisms act in concert to stabilize multiple distinct collinear and non-collinear phases as the external field is varied. The bilayer geometry, with interlayer coupling and geometric frustration, supports an extensive manifold of degenerate classical ground states, which is lifted differently at various field strengths. Our results reveal a sequence of field-driven transitions between states of contrasting symmetry, including exotic coplanar arrangements, and highlight the interplay of dimensionality, frustration, and anisotropy. These findings provide a framework for understanding tunable magnetic order in layered honeycomb antiferromagnets.
introduction:
Geometrically frustrated magnets present a fertile ground for the emergence of unconventional states of matter, owing to the extensive degeneracies that can arise from competing exchange interactions. In such systems, the classical ground state manifold may host a large number of energetically equivalent configurations, rendering them highly susceptible to perturbations that lift the degeneracy and select a particular order. This phenomenon, broadly referred to as “order by disorder”, can be driven by thermal or quantum fluctuations, as well as by external fields or additional interactions. Understanding the mechanisms of state selection in frustrated magnets is of fundamental interest, as it provides insights into the interplay between lattice geometry, spin interactions, and fluctuation effects, and is relevant to a variety of materials exhibiting exotic magnetic and multipolar orders.

The honeycomb bilayer lattice represents a particularly interesting playground for the study of competing orders and fluctuation-induced selection. It combines the low coordination number and geometric features of the honeycomb network with an additional interlayer coupling, giving rise to a rich magnetic phase space.
