The cross distillation mechanism allows each client to benefit from complementary representations learned by others, mitigating the adverse effects of non-IID data distributions. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrated that FedX consistently outperforms existing unsupervised and semi-supervised federated learning baselines in terms of accuracy, convergence stability, and robustness to client data imbalance. Furthermore, the method exhibits strong adaptability to varying client participation rates and communication constraints. These findings highlight the potential of knowledge-centric collaboration in federated settings, particularly when annotation resources are scarce or unavailable. Future work will explore extending FedX to multimodal data, incorporating adaptive knowledge selection strategies, and investigating its performance under adversarial conditions. Overall, FedX offers a promising direction for advancing unsupervised federated learning and broadening its applicability to real-world, privacy-sensitive, and label-deficient scenarios.

title: NIR and optical observations of the failed outbursts of black hole binary XTE J1550-564
abstract: We present near-infrared (NIR) and optical photometric monitoring of the black hole X-ray binary XTE J1550-564 during its 2001 and 2003 low-luminosity outbursts, commonly referred to as “failed” outbursts due to the absence of a full transition to the soft X-ray spectral state. Observations were obtained with the [instrument/telescope names], spanning the \(J\), \(H\), \(K_s\), and optical \(V\), \(R\), \(I\) bands, contemporaneous with X-ray coverage from the *Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer* (RXTE). The light curves reveal modest flux enhancements, peaking at \(\sim 0.5{-}1\) mag above quiescence in the NIR and optical, with durations of less than two months. Colour–magnitude diagrams and spectral energy distributions (SEDs) constructed at multiple epochs show a relatively flat NIR–optical spectral slope, consistent with optically thick synchrotron emission from a compact jet, combined with a cooler thermal component from the outer accretion disc. No significant colour evolution is detected, suggesting that the jet contribution remains dominant throughout the outburst cycles. Comparison with major outbursts of XTE J1550-564 indicates that the failed events occur at lower overall luminosities and without the strong thermal disc signature characteristic of the soft state. The contemporaneous X-ray hardness–intensity diagrams confirm that the source remained in a hard spectral state at all times. Our results support the view that failed outbursts are powered predominantly by a persistent compact jet coupled with a truncated accretion disc, and that NIR/optical monitoring provides a sensitive probe of jet behaviour in low-luminosity accretion regimes. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of the diversity of outburst phenomenology in black hole X-ray binaries.
introduction:
Black hole X-ray binaries (BHXBs) are systems in which a stellar-mass black hole accretes matter from a companion star, typically via Roche-lobe overflow. The accreted material forms a geometrically thin, optically thick accretion disc, whose thermal emission dominates the optical and soft X-ray bands, while a hot, optically thin corona and relativistic jets contribute to harder X-ray and radio emission. These systems exhibit transient outbursts during which their luminosity can increase by several orders of magnitude, accompanied by dramatic changes in spectral and timing properties. Outbursts are interpreted within the framework of the disc instability model (DIM), in which thermal–viscous instabilities in the disc trigger enhanced accretion onto the compact object. During a typical outburst, the source evolves through distinct accretion states, from the low-hard state dominated by non-thermal emission, through intermediate states, to the high-soft state where thermal disc emission prevails, before returning to quiescence.

Not all outbursts proceed through the canonical sequence of states. In so-called “failed outbursts,” the source brightens but remains in the hard state, never making the transition to the soft state. Such behaviour has been observed in a number of BHXBs and is thought to reflect either insufficient mass accretion rate to trigger the full state transition, or changes in the inner disc–jet–corona coupling. Failed outbursts provide a valuable opportunity to study the conditions under which state transitions occur, the role of mass accretion rate, and the relative contributions of the jet, corona, and disc to the observed emission.

Multiwavelength observations, spanning radio to X-rays, are crucial for disentangling these components. In particular, near-infrared (NIR) and optical data trace both the outer accretion disc and the compact jet. In the hard state, the NIR–optical spectrum can contain a significant synchrotron contribution from the jet, in addition to reprocessed X-ray emission from the disc and possible contributions from the companion star. Monitoring these bands during failed outbursts allows constraints on jet properties, disc irradiation, and the interplay between inflow and outflow.

The black hole binary XTE J1550–564, discovered during a bright outburst in 1998, has exhibited multiple outbursts over the past two decades. It is a well-studied system with a dynamically confirmed black hole of mass ≈ 9–10 M⊙ and an orbital period of 1.54 days. While some of its outbursts have followed the canonical pattern, others have been of low amplitude and have remained in the hard state, qualifying as failed outbursts. These events offer a rare laboratory to investigate the accretion physics under subcritical conditions in a source whose parameters are relatively well constrained.

In this work, we present NIR and optical observations of XTE J1550–564 during its failed outbursts, obtained contemporaneously with X-ray monitoring. Our goals are to characterise the spectral energy distribution in the NIR–optical regime, assess the relative contributions of the jet and irradiated disc, and compare these properties with those observed during full outbursts. By combining multi-band photometry with X-ray data, we aim to shed light on the mechanisms governing failed outbursts and to place them in the broader context of black hole accretion and jet production.
conclusion:
We have presented a detailed analysis of near-infrared (NIR) and optical observations of the black hole X-ray binary XTE J1550–564 during its failed outbursts. Our multiwavelength dataset, obtained contemporaneously with X-ray monitoring, enables us to probe the accretion flow and jet contributions in a regime where the source did not undergo a full transition to the soft state. The NIR and optical light curves exhibit modest variability correlated with the X-ray flux, consistent with the source remaining in the hard spectral state throughout the events. The spectral energy distributions suggest a combination of thermal emission from the outer accretion disc and non-thermal synchrotron emission from a compact jet. 

We find no evidence for the strong disc brightening typically associated with state transitions, supporting the classification of these episodes as failed outbursts. The NIR colours remain relatively constant, indicating a stable contribution from the jet or outer disc, while the modest optical variability is consistent with X-ray reprocessing in the disc. The lack of significant changes in the spectral slopes between epochs further points to a persistent hard-state geometry, with the inner disc likely truncated and a radiatively inefficient hot flow dominating the innermost regions.

Comparisons with previous full outbursts of XTE J1550–564 reveal that the NIR/optical emission during failed outbursts is fainter and less variable, reinforcing the view that the mass accretion rate did not reach the threshold required for the transition to the soft state. These results highlight the diagnostic power of coordinated NIR, optical, and X-ray observations for understanding the interplay between inflow and outflow in black hole binaries. 

Future monitoring of similar events in other systems will help to establish whether the spectral and variability patterns observed here are generic features of failed outbursts, and will provide further constraints on the physical conditions that govern state transitions in accreting black holes.

title: Selection biases in empirical p(z) methods for weak lensing
abstract: Weak gravitational lensing cosmology relies on accurate estimates of the redshift distributions, \(p(z)\), of source galaxy samples. Empirical methods, which derive \(p(z)\) from spectroscopic subsamples via direct calibration or machine-learning approaches, are susceptible to selection biases arising from mismatches between the spectroscopic training set and the full photometric sample. In this work, we investigate the impact of such selection effects on empirical \(p(z)\) estimation in the context of forthcoming Stage-IV weak lensing surveys. Using simulated galaxy catalogs with realistic photometric errors and spectroscopic targeting incompleteness, we quantify biases introduced when the spectroscopic sample is not fully representative in color–magnitude–morphology space. We demonstrate that even small deviations in selection can lead to coherent shifts in the recovered \(p(z)\), which propagate into biased shear–redshift calibration and ultimately biased cosmological parameter inference. We explore mitigation strategies, including reweighting techniques, targeted spectroscopic supplementation, and hybrid empirical–template approaches, and assess their performance across a range of selection scenarios. Our results highlight that controlling spectroscopic selection functions to high precision, or applying robust corrections for their effects, is essential to meet the stringent systematic-error requirements of upcoming lensing analyses. This study provides quantitative guidance for spectroscopic survey design and calibration strategy, ensuring unbiased \(p(z)\) estimation for precision weak lensing cosmology.
introduction:
Weak gravitational lensing has emerged as one of the most powerful tools for probing the growth of structure and constraining cosmological parameters. By measuring the coherent distortions in the shapes of distant galaxies induced by large-scale structure, current and upcoming surveys such as the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope aim to map the matter distribution with unprecedented precision. A critical ingredient in this endeavour is the accurate estimation of the redshift distribution, \(p(z)\), of the lensed galaxy sample. Since direct spectroscopic measurements are infeasible for the vast number of galaxies involved, photometric redshift (photo-\(z\)) techniques are employed, often calibrated using smaller spectroscopic subsamples.

Empirical \(p(z)\) methods—where a spectroscopic training set is used to infer the redshift distributions of photometric samples—offer a flexible and data-driven approach. However, their accuracy depends critically on the representativeness of the spectroscopic sample. In practice, spectroscopic samples are subject to selection effects arising from magnitude limits, color cuts, target prioritization, and observational constraints, which may lead to systematic differences from the photometric sample. If unaccounted for, these selection biases can distort the inferred \(p(z)\), potentially leading to biased cosmological inferences from weak lensing analyses.

The impact of such biases is particularly insidious because they can arise from subtle correlations between galaxy properties—such as color, surface brightness, or environment—and redshift. Furthermore, selection functions may be difficult to characterize fully, especially when spectroscopic data are compiled from heterogeneous surveys. While techniques have been developed to mitigate these effects, including reweighting and clustering-based redshift estimation, the robustness of empirical \(p(z)\) methods in the presence of complex selection biases remains an open question.

In this work, we investigate the influence of spectroscopic selection effects on empirical \(p(z)\) estimation for weak lensing applications. We quantify the resulting biases in redshift distributions and assess their impact on cosmological parameters. Our aim is to provide practical guidelines for survey design and calibration strategies that minimize the propagation of selection biases into weak lensing cosmology.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined how selection effects influence empirical determinations of the redshift distribution, \(p(z)\), for weak gravitational lensing source samples. Using a combination of simulated surveys and realistic mock catalogues, we quantified the biases that arise when the spectroscopic calibration set is not fully representative of the photometric sample due to implicit or explicit selection criteria. Our analysis demonstrates that even moderate mismatches in colour–magnitude space, or in the distribution of morphological parameters, can lead to systematic shifts in \(p(z)\) estimates that are comparable to, or exceed, the statistical uncertainties in forthcoming Stage IV weak lensing surveys.

We have shown that the empirical \(p(z)\) methods, while powerful, inherit the selection functions of their training data in a non-trivial way. In particular, common quality cuts—such as those based on photometric signal-to-noise, size relative to the PSF, or star–galaxy separation—can imprint redshift-dependent biases if they are applied differently to the spectroscopic and photometric samples. These effects persist even when the spectroscopic sample is reweighted to match the photometric sample in observed colour–magnitude space, indicating that hidden variables correlated with redshift, but not captured in the matching, can cause significant bias.

Our results underscore the necessity for calibration strategies that explicitly account for these hidden selection effects. This can be achieved through improved spectroscopic targeting that aims for complete coverage in the multi-dimensional space of observables, the use of hybrid methods that combine empirical and model-based \(p(z)\) estimates, or forward-modelling approaches that simulate both the photometric and spectroscopic selection processes. In all cases, robust uncertainty quantification must include contributions from potential residual selection biases.

Given the stringent requirements on redshift accuracy for cosmological weak lensing analyses—often at the level of \(\Delta z \lesssim 0.002(1+z)\)—these biases are not negligible. Our findings suggest that without careful mitigation, selection-induced errors in \(p(z)\) could constitute a dominant source of systematic uncertainty, potentially biasing cosmological parameter inference. Future survey designs, calibration programmes, and analysis pipelines must therefore incorporate comprehensive diagnostics for selection bias, ensuring that the promise of high-precision weak lensing cosmology can be fully realised.

title: Isgur-Wise function within a QCD quark model with Airy's function as the wave function of heavy-light mesons
abstract: We investigate the Isgur–Wise function within a QCD-inspired quark model employing Airy’s function as the spatial wave function for heavy–light mesons. The model parameters are fixed from spectroscopy, and the resulting Isgur–Wise function is analyzed for slope and curvature. Our results are consistent with heavy quark symmetry constraints, offering a simple yet effective framework for describing semileptonic heavy–light meson decays.
introduction:
The study of hadrons containing a single heavy quark provides a unique window into the interplay between perturbative and nonperturbative aspects of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). Heavy-light mesons, composed of one heavy quark (such as charm or bottom) and one light antiquark, are particularly important in this regard. The large mass of the heavy quark introduces a natural separation of scales, allowing the application of Heavy Quark Effective Theory (HQET) to simplify the dynamics. Within HQET, many of the nonperturbative aspects of the strong interaction are encapsulated in a universal form factor known as the Isgur–Wise (IW) function. This function governs the leading-order behavior of semileptonic decays of heavy mesons in the heavy-quark limit and plays a central role in extracting elements of the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa (CKM) matrix from experimental data.

The IW function, denoted as \(\xi(\omega)\), where \(\omega = v \cdot v'\) is the product of the initial and final meson four-velocities, is normalized to unity at zero recoil (\(\omega = 1\)) as a consequence of heavy quark symmetry. Its slope and curvature at zero recoil encode important information about the spatial structure and dynamics of heavy-light mesons. Accurate theoretical determination of the IW function is therefore crucial for precision tests of the Standard Model. While HQET provides the symmetry relations and normalization, the shape of the IW function must be computed using nonperturbative methods.

Various approaches have been employed to estimate the IW function, including lattice QCD simulations, QCD sum rules, and quark models. Among these, potential models have proven to be a valuable phenomenological tool, offering intuitive insight into the spatial wave functions of mesons. In such models, the heavy-light meson is described as a bound state in an effective potential inspired by QCD, typically incorporating a short-range Coulombic term from one-gluon exchange and a long-range confining term, often taken to be linear in the interquark separation. The Schrödinger equation for a linear potential admits solutions in terms of Airy functions, which naturally encode the physics of confinement in a simple and analytically tractable form.

The use of Airy functions as meson wave functions is motivated by the form of the potential energy in the nonrelativistic limit of QCD-inspired quark models. A purely linear potential, \( V(r) = \sigma r \), where \(\sigma\) is the string tension, leads to radial wave functions governed by the Airy differential equation. These functions have the desirable property of vanishing at large distances in a manner consistent with confinement, while also exhibiting an oscillatory structure at short distances that reflects the bound-state nature of the system. When augmented with relativistic corrections and short-range interactions, Airy function–based wave functions can provide a realistic description of heavy-light mesons.

Incorporating Airy functions into the computation of the IW function offers a pathway to connect the confining dynamics directly with observable form factors. The overlap integrals that define \(\xi(\omega)\) in quark models depend explicitly on the spatial wave functions of the initial and final mesons. By adopting Airy functions derived from a linear potential as the leading-order wave functions, one can calculate the slope (or charge radius) and curvature of the IW function in a manner that is analytically transparent and physically motivated. Moreover, such an approach allows systematic inclusion of perturbative corrections from the Coulombic term and relativistic effects, which can be treated as perturbations to the Airy-based solution.

Previous works using potential models have often relied on harmonic oscillator wave functions for their mathematical convenience. While this choice facilitates analytic computations, it does not reflect the linear nature of QCD confinement at large distances. The Airy function approach, by contrast, is more directly tied to the linear potential and hence to the string-like behavior of the QCD flux tube. This is particularly relevant for heavy-light systems, where the light quark probes the confining potential deeply, and the wave function’s tail plays a significant role in determining the IW function’s shape.

In this work, we develop a QCD-inspired quark model for heavy-light mesons in which the spatial wave function is taken to be the Airy function solution of the Schrödinger equation with a linear potential. We compute the Isgur–Wise function by evaluating the overlap integrals between boosted wave functions, following the standard formalism in the heavy-quark limit. The slope and curvature of the IW function are extracted and compared with experimental constraints and results from other theoretical approaches. By doing so, we aim to assess the viability of the Airy function–based model as a tool for describing heavy-light meson structure and for providing reliable inputs to phenomenological analyses of semileptonic decays.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we outline the theoretical framework, introducing the quark model Hamiltonian, the Airy function solutions, and the method for computing the IW function. Section 3 presents the results for the slope and curvature parameters, along with a comparison to alternative models and available data. Section 4 discusses the physical implications of the findings, including the sensitivity of the IW function to the choice of potential parameters and the role of relativistic corrections. Finally, Section 5 summarizes our conclusions and outlines directions for future work, including possible extensions to finite heavy-quark masses and higher-order HQET corrections.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the Isgur–Wise (IW) function within the framework of a QCD-inspired quark model, employing Airy’s function as the spatial wave function for heavy–light mesons. By adopting the Airy function form, motivated by the linear confinement potential in the heavy–light system, we have been able to capture essential nonperturbative features of QCD in a tractable analytic form. The analysis has focused on the calculation of the IW function and its derivatives at zero recoil, namely the slope (charge radius) and curvature parameters, which play a central role in the heavy quark effective theory (HQET) description of semileptonic decays.

Our results demonstrate that the Airy-function-based wave function provides a realistic and consistent description of the heavy–light meson ground state, yielding an IW function that satisfies the required normalization at zero recoil, \(\xi(1) = 1\), as dictated by heavy quark symmetry. The computed slope parameter \(\rho^2\) lies within the range suggested by phenomenological fits and lattice QCD estimates, indicating that the model effectively captures the spatial distribution and dynamics of the light degrees of freedom in the meson. Similarly, the curvature parameter \(C\) is found to be compatible with theoretical bounds, further supporting the reliability of the chosen wave function form.

One of the notable features of the Airy function approach is its natural emergence from the solution of the Schrödinger equation with a linear confining potential, which is a widely accepted feature of QCD in the nonperturbative regime. Unlike purely harmonic oscillator or power-law trial functions, the Airy function inherently encodes the asymmetry between the heavy and light constituents, reflecting the realistic potential shape at large distances. This leads to an IW function with a smooth fall-off in the recoil variable \(w\), consistent with expectations from HQET and dispersion relation constraints.

The comparison with other quark model predictions shows that our approach yields results of comparable accuracy, but with the added advantage of a more direct connection to the confining potential. Moreover, the absence of arbitrary fitting parameters beyond those fixed by spectroscopy enhances the predictive power and theoretical transparency of the model. The consistency of our slope and curvature values with both experimental data from semileptonic \(B \to D^{(*)}\) transitions and lattice QCD determinations supports the applicability of the Airy function wave function in heavy–light meson phenomenology.

In summary, the present study reinforces the utility of analytically motivated wave functions derived from physically realistic potentials in the modeling of nonperturbative QCD effects. The Airy function form not only provides a coherent and theoretically grounded description of the heavy–light meson structure, but also yields quantitatively reliable predictions for the IW function and its derivatives. Future extensions of this work could involve incorporating relativistic corrections, higher excited states, and finite heavy–quark mass effects, as well as applying the formalism to a wider range of processes in heavy flavor physics. Such developments would further test the robustness of the Airy function approach and deepen our understanding of hadronic structure in the heavy quark sector.

title: A holistic view on ram pressure stripping in the Virgo cluster - The first complete model-based time sequence
abstract: We present the first comprehensive, model-based temporal sequence of ram pressure stripping (RPS) in the Virgo cluster, integrating observational constraints with dynamical simulations to provide a holistic view of the process from initial gas displacement to the eventual quenching of star formation. Using a representative sample of spiral galaxies spanning a range of projected cluster-centric distances and orbital parameters, we combine spatially resolved H I and H α observations with tailored hydrodynamical models to reconstruct individual stripping histories. Our approach allows us to align galaxies along a physically motivated timeline, identifying distinct evolutionary phases: (1) pre-stripping compression and mild asymmetries; (2) peak ram pressure with rapid gas removal; (3) post-peak tail fading and disk truncation; and (4) long-term quenching. The models incorporate a realistic intracluster medium density distribution based on X-ray observations and account for galaxy inclination, velocity vector, and mass distribution. Comparison between simulated gas morphologies, velocity fields, and observed data yields consistent estimates for stripping onset timescales, peak durations (typically <200 Myr), and total gas depletion times (~1 Gyr). We find that the sequence is robust across a range of orbits, with variations primarily driven by impact parameter and inclination relative to the ICM wind. This unified framework enables a direct mapping between observed gas/stellar features and specific dynamical stages, offering new predictive power for interpreting cluster galaxy populations. Our results provide a benchmark for future studies of environmental quenching, demonstrating that RPS in Virgo is a rapid, yet multi-phase process whose imprints on morphology and star formation can be chronologically ordered with high fidelity.
introduction:
Galaxies residing in clusters evolve under the combined influence of gravitational interactions, the dense intracluster medium (ICM), and the cluster’s large-scale potential. One of the most striking environmental processes in such dense regions is ram pressure stripping (RPS), whereby the interstellar medium (ISM) of a galaxy is removed through hydrodynamical interaction with the surrounding ICM as the galaxy moves through it. First proposed by Gunn & Gott (1972), RPS has since been recognized as a key mechanism in shaping the morphology, star formation activity, and gas content of cluster galaxies. Observational evidence for RPS is abundant in the nearby Virgo cluster, the closest rich galaxy cluster to the Milky Way, where numerous galaxies exhibit truncated gas disks, asymmetric gas distributions, and extended tails of stripped material.

The Virgo cluster provides a unique laboratory for studying RPS in detail due to its proximity (∼16.5 Mpc), modest size, and well-characterized galaxy population. Over the past decades, multi-wavelength observations—from radio H I mapping to optical imaging and X-ray studies—have revealed a diversity of RPS morphologies and intensities, indicating that the process is highly time-dependent and sensitive to orbital parameters, ICM density variations, and the internal structure of the galaxies. Despite significant progress, most existing studies have either focused on single snapshots in time or on simplified analytic models, limiting our understanding of the full temporal evolution of RPS in real cluster environments.

Recent advances in high-resolution simulations and dynamical modeling now allow for a more comprehensive, model-based reconstruction of the stripping history of individual galaxies. By combining observational constraints with physically motivated models of galaxy orbits, ICM density profiles, and gas removal efficiencies, it is possible to place galaxies along a continuous timeline of RPS evolution. Such an approach not only provides insight into the mechanisms and timescales involved but also enables a holistic interpretation of the observed variety of RPS signatures in a coherent framework.

In this work, we present the first complete, model-based time sequence of ram pressure stripping in the Virgo cluster, integrating observational data with dynamical modeling to trace the process from initial onset to its aftermath. This holistic view offers new perspectives on the role of RPS in galaxy transformation and provides a benchmark for interpreting RPS phenomena in more distant clusters.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented the first complete, model-based time sequence of ram pressure stripping for a spiral galaxy in the Virgo cluster, constructed from a synthesis of dynamical modeling, multi-wavelength observations, and physically motivated assumptions about the intracluster medium (ICM) structure and galaxy orbits. By integrating the temporal evolution of gas removal with the morphological and kinematic signatures observed at different stripping stages, we have developed a coherent framework that connects initial infall conditions to the present-day appearance of stripped systems. This holistic approach allows for a consistent interpretation of the diverse observational manifestations of ram pressure stripping in a unified temporal context.

Our sequence captures the onset of ram pressure effects well before the peak pressure event, highlighting the importance of gradual, low-level gas loss and disk asymmetry in the early infall phase. These subtle features, often overlooked in purely observational studies, are shown to be consistent with model predictions of pre-peak stripping at large cluster-centric radii. As the galaxy approaches pericenter, our models reproduce the rapid gas truncation, extraplanar gas tails, and enhanced star formation along the leading edge—signatures widely reported in Virgo spirals. The peak ram pressure phase, while short-lived, is revealed here as the critical juncture that determines the final extent of the stripped disk and the fate of the dense molecular component. Post-peak, the models track the dispersal of stripped gas into the ICM, the fading of extraplanar star formation, and the gradual settling of the stellar disk, offering a quantitative link between recently stripped and fully quenched systems.

A key outcome of this study is the demonstration that a single, physically consistent time sequence can account for the range of observed gas morphologies and star formation patterns in the Virgo cluster. This suggests that much of the apparent diversity in stripping signatures can be attributed to differences in viewing angle, orbital phase, and initial gas content, rather than to fundamentally different physical mechanisms. The close agreement between modeled and observed HI, Hα, and UV morphologies at multiple stages strengthens the case for ram pressure stripping as the dominant environmental process shaping spiral galaxies in the dense regions of Virgo.

Furthermore, by anchoring our time sequence to realistic cluster orbits and ICM density profiles, we have been able to place quantitative constraints on the duration and efficiency of gas removal. Our results indicate that the bulk of atomic gas loss occurs within ~300 Myr around peak pressure, with significant pre-processing occurring up to 500 Myr earlier. This temporal framework provides a natural explanation for the observed correlation between gas truncation radius and projected cluster-centric distance, as well as for the presence of galaxies with truncated gas disks but ongoing central star formation.

The holistic model also offers predictive power for future observational campaigns. It identifies specific combinations of gas morphology, kinematics, and star formation distribution that correspond to well-defined orbital phases. By applying these diagnostics to large samples, it will be possible to reconstruct the recent orbital histories of cluster spirals and to map out the spatial and temporal distribution of stripping events across the cluster. This, in turn, will yield new insights into the dynamical state of the cluster and the role of the ICM in regulating galaxy evolution.

While our sequence is tailored to the Virgo cluster, the methodology is readily adaptable to other environments. Variations in ICM density, cluster potential, and galaxy mass can be incorporated to generate analogous timelines for different systems, enabling comparative studies across a range of cluster masses and redshifts. Such extensions will help to clarify the universality of the stripping process and to distinguish it from other environmental mechanisms such as tidal interactions or harassment.

In summary, the complete model-based time sequence presented here provides a robust, physically grounded framework for interpreting the complex, transient phenomena associated with ram pressure stripping. By bridging the gap between instantaneous observations and the full evolutionary context, it advances our understanding of how the cluster environment transforms galaxies, and lays the groundwork for a new generation of systematic, time-resolved studies of environmental galaxy evolution.

title: Relative velocities among accreting planetesimals in binary systems: the circumbinary case
abstract: We investigate the relative velocities among accreting planetesimals embedded in circumbinary disks, focusing on the dynamical effects induced by the binary’s gravitational perturbations. Using numerical N-body simulations coupled with a prescription for gas drag, we explore a range of binary mass ratios, orbital separations, and eccentricities. Our results show that secular perturbations from the binary significantly excite planetesimal eccentricities, leading to impact velocities that may exceed the threshold for collisional growth, particularly for small bodies strongly coupled to the gas. However, for certain combinations of binary parameters and disk properties, gas drag can damp relative velocities sufficiently to allow accretion to proceed. We identify regions in parameter space where growth is favored, and others where fragmentation is likely. These findings provide constraints on the initial conditions for planet formation in circumbinary systems, and help explain the observed distribution of planets around close binaries detected by Kepler and other surveys.
introduction:
Planet formation is a multi–stage process that begins with the coagulation of dust grains into kilometer–sized planetesimals and proceeds through mutual accretion to form planetary embryos. In this scenario, the relative velocity between colliding bodies is a key parameter: low–velocity encounters favour accretion through gravitational focusing, whereas high–velocity impacts tend to result in erosion or catastrophic disruption. While the evolution of relative velocities has been extensively studied for planetesimals orbiting single stars, the situation in binary systems is more complex. Gravitational perturbations from the companion star can significantly alter planetesimal orbits, potentially increasing relative velocities to levels incompatible with growth.

A large fraction of solar–type stars are found in binary or multiple systems, and observational surveys have revealed planets in both circumprimary (S–type) and circumbinary (P–type) configurations. The discovery of circumbinary planets by missions such as *Kepler* demonstrates that planet formation can proceed in dynamically rich environments. In the circumbinary configuration, planetesimals orbit the common centre of mass of the two stars. The binary’s gravitational potential is inherently non–axisymmetric and time–dependent, leading to secular and resonant perturbations on the orbits of small bodies. These perturbations can excite eccentricities and inclinations, thereby modifying encounter velocities.

Previous work on planetesimal dynamics in binary systems has largely focused on circumstellar discs, where the companion star acts as an external perturber. The circumbinary case has received comparatively less attention, despite its relevance to the growing sample of known circumbinary planets. In particular, the interplay between the binary–driven orbital excitation and the damping effects of the gaseous disc in which planetesimals are embedded remains an open question. Gas drag can align pericentres and reduce eccentricities, lowering impact speeds, but the efficiency of this mechanism depends sensitively on planetesimal size, gas density, and the binary orbital parameters.

Understanding the regime of relative velocities among accreting planetesimals in circumbinary systems is essential for assessing the viability of planet formation in such environments. If relative velocities remain low enough for accretion to dominate over fragmentation, the standard core–accretion scenario may proceed largely unimpeded. Conversely, if binary perturbations drive velocities into the erosive regime, alternative formation pathways or migration from more benign regions may be required. In this work, we investigate the distribution of encounter velocities as a function of binary and planetesimal parameters in the circumbinary case, aiming to delineate the conditions conducive to the early stages of planet formation around close stellar binaries.
conclusion: We have investigated the relative velocities among accreting planetesimals embedded in circumbinary disks, focusing on the dynamical consequences of the binary’s gravitational perturbations. Our results show that, while secular forcing from the central binary excites eccentricities, the combined action of gas drag and mutual gravitational interactions among planetesimals can lead to partial orbital alignment, moderating impact speeds. The efficiency of this alignment depends sensitively on the binary’s mass ratio, eccentricity, and the radial location within the disk. In regions sufficiently far from the binary, relative velocities remain low enough to permit accretional growth, whereas closer to the binary, increased excitation can drive collisional erosion. These findings suggest that planet formation in circumbinary environments is favored beyond a critical distance, the exact value of which varies with system parameters. Our study highlights the importance of accurately modelling both gravitational perturbations and dissipative forces when assessing growth conditions. Future work incorporating more realistic gas disk structures and size distributions will further clarify the viability of planetesimal accretion in binary systems.

title: MAEEG: Masked Auto-encoder for EEG Representation Learning
abstract: We present MAEEG, a Masked Auto-encoder framework for self-supervised EEG representation learning. MAEEG leverages the inherent spatio-temporal structure of EEG signals by randomly masking segments in both time and channel dimensions, and reconstructing the missing data from the visible context. This approach encourages the encoder to capture rich, high-level neural patterns without reliance on labeled data. We design a lightweight transformer-based architecture tailored to EEG characteristics, enabling efficient learning from large-scale recordings. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that MAEEG achieves superior performance in downstream tasks such as emotion recognition, motor imagery classification, and sleep stage scoring, compared to existing self-supervised and supervised baselines. Our results highlight the effectiveness of masked reconstruction for EEG and suggest MAEEG as a general-purpose pretraining method for diverse brain–computer interface applications.
introduction:
Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive technique that records brain activity with high temporal resolution and has been widely applied in neuroscience research, brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), and clinical diagnosis. Despite its potential, EEG signals are inherently noisy, subject-specific, and non-stationary, making robust feature extraction a critical challenge. Traditional EEG analysis pipelines often rely on handcrafted features or supervised learning models trained on limited labeled datasets. However, obtaining large-scale, high-quality annotations for EEG is costly and time-consuming, which limits the scalability and generalization of such approaches.  

Recent advances in self-supervised learning (SSL) have demonstrated remarkable success in extracting transferable representations from unlabeled data, particularly in computer vision and natural language processing. Among these, masked auto-encoders (MAEs) have emerged as an effective paradigm, learning to reconstruct missing portions of the input from partial observations. This strategy encourages the model to capture high-level semantic structures and robust patterns without explicit supervision. While MAEs have been extensively explored in image and speech domains, their application to EEG remains underexplored, partly due to the unique temporal–spectral characteristics and high inter-subject variability of EEG signals.  

In this work, we propose **MAEEG**, a novel masked auto-encoder framework tailored for EEG representation learning. By randomly masking segments of multichannel EEG signals and training the model to reconstruct the missing data, MAEEG learns to encode meaningful temporal and frequency-domain patterns that are informative for downstream tasks. We design the architecture to accommodate the multi-scale nature of EEG and evaluate its effectiveness across diverse datasets and tasks, including emotion recognition and motor imagery classification. Our experiments show that MAEEG outperforms existing self-supervised baselines and yields representations that transfer well across subjects and datasets, highlighting its potential as a general-purpose EEG feature learning approach.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed MAEEG, a masked auto-encoder framework tailored for EEG representation learning. By leveraging a masking strategy and self-supervised pretraining, MAEEG effectively captures both local and global temporal patterns, enabling robust feature extraction without extensive labeled data. Experimental results across multiple EEG benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines in classification and transfer learning tasks. Furthermore, MAEEG shows strong generalization to diverse recording conditions and subject variations. These findings highlight the potential of masked auto-encoding for advancing EEG analysis, paving the way for more scalable, label-efficient, and generalizable neural signal processing methods in neuroscience and brain–computer interfaces.

title: On an index reduction method by deflation for differential-algebraic equations
abstract: We present a deflation-based method for index reduction of linear differential-algebraic equations (DAEs). The approach constructs a sequence of reduced systems, each with lower index, by eliminating constraints through structured transformations. At each step, algebraic variables are identified and removed while preserving solution equivalence. The process terminates with an ordinary differential equation or a regular DAE of minimal index. We analyze correctness, termination, and numerical stability, and illustrate the method’s efficiency with examples, highlighting its advantages over traditional index reduction techniques.
introduction:
Differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) arise naturally in the mathematical modeling of constrained dynamical systems, including multibody mechanics, electrical circuits, chemical processes, and control systems. Unlike ordinary differential equations (ODEs), DAEs involve both differential and algebraic components, leading to structural and numerical challenges. A key difficulty is the *index* of a DAE, a measure of the inherent complexity related to the number of differentiations required to obtain an explicit ODE form. High-index systems are particularly sensitive to perturbations and pose significant obstacles for numerical integration, often resulting in instability or loss of accuracy.

Index reduction techniques aim to transform a high-index DAE into an equivalent system of lower index, ideally index one, while preserving the solution set. Classical approaches include differentiation of constraints, substitution, and projection methods. However, these methods can lead to increased system size, hidden constraints, or ill-conditioning. In recent years, *deflation* has emerged as a promising strategy for index reduction. Originally developed for polynomial systems, deflation iteratively removes singularities by augmenting the system with derivative information, thereby reducing complexity without excessive equation growth.

This paper investigates a deflation-based method tailored for DAEs, providing a systematic procedure for lowering the index while maintaining numerical stability. The approach leverages structural properties of the system matrices and constraint equations, enabling efficient computation and clearer insight into the underlying dynamics. We present theoretical foundations, algorithmic details, and illustrative examples demonstrating the effectiveness of the method. The proposed technique offers a robust alternative to traditional index reduction strategies, with potential applicability across diverse areas of engineering and applied science.
conclusion: We have presented a deflation-based approach for the index reduction of linear differential-algebraic equations, providing a systematic procedure that successively lowers the index through the solution of associated linear systems. The method preserves the original problem structure while avoiding the introduction of additional variables, and it yields at each step a reduced system that can be solved more efficiently. The theoretical foundation ensures that consistency of initial conditions is maintained, and the approach can be readily integrated with existing numerical solvers. Numerical experiments confirm its effectiveness and robustness, particularly for high-index problems. Future work will address extensions to nonlinear systems, adaptive stopping criteria, and the incorporation of error control strategies to enhance stability and accuracy in practical applications.

title: Efficient Context Management and Personalized User Recommendations in a Smart Social TV environment
abstract: This paper presents an approach for efficient context management and personalized user recommendations within a Smart Social TV environment. The proposed framework integrates real-time context acquisition, semantic modeling, and adaptive recommendation strategies to enhance user engagement and content relevance. Context data, including viewing history, social interactions, device capabilities, and environmental factors, is dynamically processed using a scalable context management architecture. Personalized recommendations are generated through a hybrid filtering mechanism combining collaborative, content-based, and context-aware techniques. The system also incorporates social features to encourage shared viewing experiences and dynamic adaptation to evolving preferences. Experimental evaluation demonstrates improvements in recommendation accuracy, response time, and user satisfaction compared to baseline methods. The results highlight the potential of context-aware personalization to transform interactive media consumption in next-generation Smart TV platforms.
introduction:
The rapid evolution of digital television and internet-based media services has given rise to Smart Social TV environments, where users can seamlessly interact with both content and other viewers in real time. These platforms integrate traditional broadcasting with social networking features, enabling personalized, interactive, and socially enriched viewing experiences. As user engagement grows, the ability to manage contextual information efficiently becomes critical for delivering relevant and timely recommendations. Context in this setting encompasses diverse factors, including viewing history, user preferences, social interactions, device capabilities, and temporal or situational variables. Managing such multifaceted context in real time poses significant challenges in terms of scalability, relevance, and privacy.  

Personalized user recommendations play a central role in enhancing user satisfaction and retention in Smart Social TV. By leveraging contextual data, recommendation systems can adapt content delivery to individual tastes, viewing habits, and social influences. However, achieving high-quality personalization requires advanced techniques for context acquisition, modeling, and processing, as well as efficient integration with recommendation algorithms. Furthermore, the dynamic and interactive nature of Smart Social TV demands that these systems continually update and refine recommendations as contexts evolve. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a framework for efficient context management coupled with adaptive, personalized recommendation strategies tailored to the Smart Social TV environment.
conclusion: This work has presented an approach for efficient context management and personalized user recommendations within a Smart Social TV environment. By integrating dynamic context acquisition, semantic modeling, and adaptive recommendation algorithms, the proposed framework effectively addresses the challenges of delivering relevant and engaging content in real time. The system leverages both explicit user preferences and implicit behavioral cues, enabling a more accurate understanding of viewer interests and situational context. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that this approach enhances recommendation precision while maintaining computational efficiency, a critical factor for interactive, resource-constrained environments such as Smart TVs. Moreover, the incorporation of social interaction data enriches the personalization process, fostering a more immersive and community-driven viewing experience. These results suggest that context-aware personalization can significantly improve user satisfaction and engagement in next-generation television platforms. Future work will focus on expanding the contextual dimensions considered, refining real-time processing capabilities, and exploring privacy-preserving mechanisms to ensure user trust. Overall, the proposed solution provides a robust foundation for intelligent, user-centered media services, bridging the gap between technological capability and the evolving expectations of socially connected audiences.

title: On A New Convergence Class in Sup-sober Spaces
abstract: We introduce and investigate a new convergence class in sup-sober spaces, motivated by recent developments in domain theory and general topology. This class is defined via a refinement of net convergence that preserves key order-theoretic and topological properties inherent to sup-sobriety. Fundamental structural characteristics are established, including stability under subspace formation, product spaces, and continuous mappings. We further examine the relationship between the proposed convergence and existing notions such as Scott and \(I\)-convergence, highlighting both generalizations and distinctions. Several characterizations are provided, offering insight into its role in the broader framework of convergence theory. Our results demonstrate that the new class captures subtle continuity behaviors, enriching the analysis of sup-sober spaces and opening avenues for applications in order-theoretic topology.
introduction:
The study of convergence classes has played a central role in the investigation of topological and order-theoretic structures, providing a unifying framework for describing various modes of convergence beyond the realm of sequences and nets. In particular, the interplay between domain theory and topology has led to the development of specialized convergence notions that capture subtle continuity properties in non-Hausdorff settings. Sup-sober spaces, introduced as a natural generalization of sober spaces, have emerged as an important class in this context. They retain the essential feature that every irreducible closed set is the closure of its supremum, yet allow for richer structures that arise naturally in theoretical computer science and lattice-theoretic topology.

Existing work has largely focused on characterizing sup-sober spaces via their specialization order, Scott topology, and known convergence classes such as the Scott convergence. However, many questions remain open regarding the refinement and extension of these convergence notions to capture additional order-theoretic behaviors. Motivated by these considerations, the present paper introduces a new convergence class specifically tailored to sup-sober spaces. This class is designed to preserve desirable topological properties while extending the applicability of convergence methods to settings where existing approaches are inadequate. We investigate its fundamental properties, establish relationships with known convergence structures, and provide characterizations that illuminate its role within the broader theory of sup-sober spaces. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of convergence phenomena in non-Hausdorff environments and open new avenues for further research in the area.
conclusion:
In this work, we have introduced and investigated a new convergence class in the setting of sup-sober spaces. By formulating the class through the interplay between directed suprema and the intrinsic topological structure, we have been able to capture convergence behaviors that extend beyond those described by existing frameworks. Our results establish that the proposed convergence class is well-behaved under natural operations, aligns with known notions in special cases, and yields a unifying perspective for several earlier convergence concepts. In particular, we demonstrated that the class is topological and compatible with the specialization order, thereby ensuring its applicability within both order-theoretic and topological contexts.

Moreover, we provided characterizations of this convergence in terms of net and filter convergence, revealing its stability properties and its relationship to other convergences in the literature. Examples illustrated that the new class strictly extends previously studied ones, while retaining desirable limit uniqueness properties inherent to the sup-sober framework. This suggests that the class can serve as a robust tool in studying continuity, compactness, and completeness in non-Hausdorff settings.

The convergence class introduced here opens up several promising directions for further research, including its interaction with domain-theoretic constructions and its potential to refine separation axioms in generalized spaces. We anticipate that subsequent work will deepen its integration into the broader theory of convergence spaces, enhancing our understanding of the fine structure of sup-sober spaces.

title: SuperSpec: design concept and circuit simulations
abstract: SuperSpec is a proposed on-chip spectrometer architecture designed for broadband, moderate-resolution (R ≈ 100–500) spectroscopy at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths. The concept employs a series of lithographically fabricated superconducting resonators, each tuned to a specific frequency channel and coupled to a common feedline, with power detected by kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs). This architecture enables compact, scalable, and highly multiplexed spectroscopic instruments suitable for large-format arrays. We present the design concept, emphasizing the trade-offs among spectral resolution, coupling efficiency, and fabrication tolerances. Circuit simulations based on transmission line models are used to predict device performance, including channel profiles, cross-talk, and overall optical efficiency. Simulation results demonstrate that careful control of resonator quality factors and coupling geometries can achieve the desired resolution while maintaining high throughput. The SuperSpec approach offers a promising platform for future cryogenic spectroscopic surveys, enabling efficient mapping of faint astronomical sources across wide spectral bands with significantly reduced instrument volume and complexity.
introduction:
The development of highly sensitive, efficient, and compact spectrometers is of central importance to advancing observational astrophysics, particularly in the millimeter- and submillimeter-wave regimes. Observations in these frequency ranges enable the study of a broad range of astrophysical processes, from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) to the thermal emission of interstellar dust and the molecular line emission from the cool interstellar medium in galaxies. Spectroscopic measurements at these wavelengths provide critical diagnostics of the physical conditions, chemical abundances, and kinematics of astrophysical sources, thereby offering unique insight into galaxy formation and evolution across cosmic history. However, traditional spectrometer architectures for these frequencies tend to be bulky, mechanically complex, and difficult to scale to large-format arrays, limiting their utility for wide-field surveys or multi-object observations.

SuperSpec is a new on-chip spectrometer concept designed to address these limitations. The instrument uses superconducting transmission line technology to implement a filter-bank spectrometer directly on a lithographed chip. Each channel consists of a narrow-band filter that selects a specific frequency from a broadband input signal, coupled to a superconducting detector that measures the power in that channel. By arranging many such filters in parallel, SuperSpec achieves simultaneous spectral coverage over a wide bandwidth with moderate resolving power, while maintaining a form factor compatible with large detector arrays. This integrated approach eliminates the need for large free-space optics or mechanically tuned components, enabling a scalable, robust, and cryogenically compatible spectrometer platform.

The motivation for the SuperSpec concept arises from the scientific goals of future submillimeter and millimeter-wave surveys, which demand both high sensitivity and multiplexing capability. For example, intensity mapping experiments, aimed at measuring the aggregate emission from spectral lines such as [C II] at high redshift, require instruments with hundreds to thousands of spectral channels operating simultaneously over wide instantaneous bandwidths. Similarly, follow-up spectroscopy of faint sources detected in photometric surveys demands compact spectrometers that can be deployed in large numbers on multi-object platforms. The combination of superconducting microstrip technology and lithographic fabrication offers a pathway to meeting these requirements, leveraging the advances in superconducting detector arrays developed for CMB and submillimeter imaging.

At the heart of the SuperSpec architecture is a set of half-wave resonators fabricated from superconducting microstrip lines. These resonators are weakly coupled to a common feedline on one side and to a kinetic inductance detector (KID) on the other. Each resonator is tuned to a specific frequency by adjusting its physical length and coupling strengths, thereby setting the spectral resolution and channel spacing. The filter bank is designed to cover the target frequency range with minimal gaps and overlap between adjacent channels, optimizing both throughput and spectral fidelity. The KIDs serve as the power detectors for each spectral channel, converting the absorbed millimeter-wave energy into a measurable shift in resonator frequency due to changes in the kinetic inductance of the superconducting film.

Realizing the full potential of SuperSpec requires careful design of the filter bank and precise control over the electromagnetic properties of the superconducting transmission lines. Circuit simulations play a crucial role in this process, enabling the prediction of channel responses, coupling efficiencies, and system-level performance prior to fabrication. By modeling the distributed nature of the transmission lines and the interactions between resonators, designers can explore trade-offs between resolution, bandwidth, and fabrication tolerance. These simulations inform design choices such as the number of channels, their frequency placement, the degree of coupling to the feedline and detectors, and the material properties of the superconducting films and dielectric layers.

In this work, we present the design concept and circuit simulation results for a SuperSpec prototype. We describe the underlying principles of the filter-bank spectrometer, the specific implementation choices made for the prototype, and the simulation methods used to evaluate performance. The results illuminate both the opportunities and challenges inherent in implementing a high-performance spectrometer on a chip, including issues of channel isolation, fabrication tolerances, and detector coupling. By combining a scalable lithographic architecture with advanced superconducting detection, SuperSpec offers a promising route toward the next generation of millimeter- and submillimeter-wave spectroscopic instrumentation.
conclusion:
The design concept and circuit simulations of SuperSpec presented in this work demonstrate the feasibility and promise of an ultra-compact, lithographically fabricated spectrometer operating at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths. By integrating a filter bank architecture directly onto a planar substrate, SuperSpec offers a transformative approach to spectroscopy for astronomical instrumentation, enabling high spectral resolution within a significantly reduced footprint compared to conventional dispersive spectrometers. The modular nature of the design permits scalable fabrication, while its on-chip implementation facilitates integration with large-format detector arrays, thereby opening the path toward wide-field, multiplexed spectroscopic surveys.

Through detailed circuit simulations, we have validated the core principles underpinning the SuperSpec architecture. The modeling results confirm that the filter bank can be engineered to provide the desired spectral resolution and channel uniformity over the targeted frequency band. The simulations further highlight the critical role of resonator quality factors, coupling strengths, and fabrication tolerances in achieving optimal performance. In particular, we have shown that careful control of coupling capacitances and resonator dimensions is essential to ensuring both high efficiency and minimal spectral leakage between channels. The agreement between theoretical predictions and simulation outcomes provides confidence in the robustness of the design and its readiness for subsequent prototyping and experimental verification.

Beyond confirming the viability of the concept, the simulation campaign has yielded valuable insights into design trade-offs inherent in the system. For instance, increasing channel density improves spectral coverage but imposes stricter requirements on resonator spacing and fabrication precision. Similarly, while higher-Q resonators enhance spectral resolution, they also increase susceptibility to loss mechanisms and production variability. These considerations will guide the optimization of future iterations of the device, balancing performance goals with manufacturability and operational stability.

The compactness, scalability, and potential for high multiplexing position SuperSpec as a compelling technology for next-generation submillimeter and millimeter-wave astronomy. Its ability to perform simultaneous, multi-object spectroscopy over wide fields of view could enable large-scale surveys of the high-redshift universe, detailed mapping of molecular clouds, and sensitive measurements of faint spectral lines from distant galaxies. Moreover, the planar fabrication process is compatible with existing superconducting detector technologies, suggesting a straightforward integration pathway into current and planned observatories.

In summary, the work presented here establishes a solid foundation for the realization of SuperSpec. The demonstrated alignment between design objectives and simulation results provides a clear roadmap toward fabrication and laboratory testing. Future efforts will focus on translating the simulated performance into measured results, refining the design based on empirical data, and exploring system-level integration in astronomical instruments. The SuperSpec concept thus represents a significant step toward compact, high-performance, on-chip spectrometers that can expand the frontiers of observational astrophysics.

title: Minimal warm inflation with complete medium response
abstract: We investigate a minimal warm inflationary scenario incorporating the complete medium response of the thermal bath to dissipative dynamics. By consistently including both the inflaton dissipation and the backreaction of produced radiation, we derive the background evolution and perturbation spectra without relying on quasi-static or truncated approximations. The analysis employs a minimal field content and interaction structure sufficient to sustain slow-roll inflation in the warm regime. We show that the medium’s full dynamical response modifies the inflationary observables, leading to distinctive signatures in the scalar spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio. Our results provide a self-consistent framework for assessing minimal warm inflation against current and future cosmological data.
introduction:
The inflationary paradigm has become a central component of modern cosmology, providing a compelling mechanism for generating the observed homogeneity, isotropy, and nearly scale-invariant spectrum of primordial perturbations. In its conventional “cold” formulation, inflation is driven by the potential energy of a scalar field, the inflaton, which evolves in near isolation from other degrees of freedom. In this picture, the Universe undergoes a period of accelerated expansion followed by a reheating phase, during which the inflaton’s energy is transferred to a thermal bath of particles, initiating the standard hot Big Bang evolution. While successful in explaining a wide range of observations, cold inflation implicitly assumes that dissipative effects and associated thermal fluctuations during inflation are negligible.

Warm inflation offers an alternative framework in which the inflaton remains coupled to other fields throughout inflation, leading to a continuous transfer of energy into a radiation bath. In this scenario, the Universe maintains a finite temperature during inflation, eliminating the need for a separate reheating phase and altering both the background dynamics and the generation of primordial fluctuations. Dissipative effects modify the inflaton’s equation of motion, and thermal fluctuations in the medium can dominate over quantum fluctuations in sourcing the curvature perturbations. This opens the possibility for distinct observational signatures, such as a modified scalar spectral index and a suppressed tensor-to-scalar ratio. Furthermore, warm inflation may alleviate some of the fine-tuning issues associated with cold inflation by allowing inflation to proceed on steeper potentials.

A crucial ingredient in the theoretical description of warm inflation is the treatment of the medium’s response to the dissipative dynamics. In early studies, the radiation bath was often modeled in a minimal way, with a constant or phenomenological dissipation coefficient and without fully incorporating the feedback of the produced radiation on the inflaton’s evolution. More refined approaches have introduced temperature- and field-dependent dissipation coefficients derived from quantum field theory, as well as hydrodynamic treatments of the radiation. However, many analyses still approximate the medium’s response in a simplified or incomplete manner, which can obscure the range of viable models and their predictions.

In this work, we present a minimal warm inflation framework that incorporates the complete medium response in a self-consistent manner. By “complete” we mean that the coupled dynamics of the inflaton, radiation energy density, and perturbations are treated without neglecting terms arising from the backreaction of the thermal bath, including the full dependence of dissipation on both temperature and inflaton field value. This approach allows us to clarify the parameter space in which warm inflation is consistent with current cosmological observations, and to identify the minimal set of assumptions required to maintain internal consistency. We demonstrate that even in a minimal realization—avoiding elaborate particle physics model-building—accounting for the full medium response can significantly influence the inflationary dynamics, the duration of inflation, and the primordial perturbation spectra. Our results highlight the importance of a consistent treatment of dissipation and thermal effects in assessing the viability of warm inflation and in confronting it with precision cosmological data.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined a minimal realization of warm inflation in which the dissipative dynamics are treated with a complete medium response, incorporating both the real and imaginary parts of the inflaton self-energy within a consistent nonequilibrium framework. By doing so, we have moved beyond the commonly used adiabatic-Markovian approximation and explicitly accounted for the finite-time correlations and spectral properties of the thermal bath. This refinement provides a more accurate description of the inflaton’s dissipative coefficient and its temperature dependence, particularly in regimes where the microscopic interactions have nontrivial frequency structures or when the relaxation times of the bath fields are comparable to the Hubble time.

Our analysis demonstrates that, even in the minimal setup with a single scalar inflaton coupled to light degrees of freedom, the inclusion of the complete medium response can lead to quantitative and qualitative modifications of the inflationary dynamics. In particular, the slow-roll conditions and the evolution of the inflaton field are sensitive to the detailed form of the dissipation kernel, which in turn affects the duration of the inflationary phase and the magnitude of the generated density perturbations. The spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio are shifted relative to predictions based on simplified treatments, and these shifts can be comparable to current observational uncertainties, especially in the moderately strong dissipative regime.

We have also shown that the complete medium response naturally regulates potential divergences and inconsistencies that arise in instantaneous response approximations, ensuring the physicality of the energy-momentum exchange between the inflaton and the thermal bath throughout the inflationary period. This feature reinforces the internal consistency of warm inflation as a viable alternative to conventional cold inflation scenarios, while opening up a more robust parameter space for model building compatible with current CMB constraints.

An important implication of our results is that precise confrontation of warm inflation models with observational data requires a careful treatment of the microphysical dissipation process. The methodology employed here can be extended to more complex particle physics realizations, including supersymmetric and gauge-mediated models, where the medium response functions may have richer structures. Moreover, our framework can be adapted to study the transition from the inflationary epoch to the subsequent radiation-dominated era, providing a unified description of reheating and thermalization in warm inflation settings.

In summary, the minimal warm inflation scenario with complete medium response offers a theoretically consistent and phenomenologically rich framework that captures essential nonequilibrium effects often neglected in earlier analyses. By bridging the gap between microphysical dynamics and cosmological observables, this approach enhances the predictive power of warm inflation and motivates further investigation into its embedding within fundamental theories and its potential signatures in forthcoming cosmological surveys.

title: Predicting The Stock Trend Using News Sentiment Analysis and Technical Indicators in Spark
abstract: This study presents a scalable framework for predicting stock market trends by integrating news sentiment analysis with technical indicators using Apache Spark. The proposed approach leverages large-scale financial news data to extract sentiment scores through natural language processing techniques, while concurrently computing technical indicators from historical price data. These heterogeneous features are combined to train machine learning models in Spark’s distributed environment, enabling efficient processing of high-volume data streams. Experiments were conducted on historical stock data and corresponding news articles, assessing multiple classification algorithms for trend prediction. Results demonstrate that incorporating sentiment features alongside technical indicators improves predictive accuracy compared to models relying solely on price-based metrics. The framework’s distributed architecture ensures rapid computation and adaptability to real-time applications. This work highlights the potential of combining textual sentiment and quantitative market signals for enhanced decision-making in algorithmic trading and financial forecasting.
introduction:
In recent years, the prediction of stock market trends has gained significant attention from both academic researchers and industry practitioners due to its potential for guiding investment decisions and managing financial risk. The stock market is inherently volatile and influenced by a wide range of factors, including macroeconomic indicators, corporate performance, geopolitical developments, and investor sentiment. Traditional forecasting approaches have primarily relied on historical price and volume data, employing statistical models and technical indicators to identify patterns. While these methods capture certain aspects of market dynamics, they often fall short in accounting for the qualitative information embedded in financial news and other unstructured textual sources.

With the rise of big data analytics and advancements in natural language processing (NLP), sentiment analysis of financial news has emerged as a promising complementary tool for market prediction. News sentiment reflects the collective emotional state of investors, which can influence trading behavior and, consequently, price movements. Integrating sentiment analysis with established technical indicators offers the potential to develop more robust predictive models that incorporate both quantitative and qualitative signals.

Apache Spark, a distributed computing framework, provides the scalability and efficiency necessary to process and analyze large volumes of heterogeneous financial data in near real-time. The combination of Spark’s parallel processing capabilities with machine learning libraries enables the integration of structured market data and unstructured textual content into predictive workflows. This approach facilitates the extraction of sentiment scores from news articles, their alignment with corresponding market data, and the training of predictive models that can generalize to unseen market conditions.

This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of combining news sentiment analysis with traditional technical indicators for predicting stock market trends within a Spark-based environment. By leveraging both historical price patterns and contemporaneous sentiment signals, the proposed framework seeks to improve trend prediction accuracy and provide actionable insights for traders, analysts, and automated trading systems.
conclusion: This study demonstrated an integrated approach to predicting stock market trends by combining news sentiment analysis with technical indicators using Apache Spark. Leveraging Spark’s distributed processing capabilities enabled efficient handling of large-scale financial and textual data. Experimental results indicated that incorporating sentiment scores from financial news alongside historical market indicators improves predictive accuracy compared to using technical features alone. The findings highlight the importance of fusing qualitative and quantitative information for market forecasting. Furthermore, the scalability of the Spark framework makes the approach suitable for real-time applications in dynamic trading environments. Future work may explore deep learning models, richer linguistic features, and alternative data sources to further enhance prediction performance and adaptability in rapidly evolving financial markets.

title: Long-term multi-frequency monitoring of microquasars
abstract: We present the results of a long-term, multi-frequency monitoring campaign of a representative sample of Galactic microquasars, aimed at investigating their variability, spectral evolution, and jet–accretion coupling over timescales from days to years. Observations were conducted using a coordinated network of radio, millimetre, infrared, and X-ray facilities, providing continuous coverage between 1 GHz and 100 keV. The dataset spans over 12 years, enabling the characterization of both transient outbursts and persistent emission states. We report correlated variability patterns across frequencies, with radio flares often lagging X-ray peaks by hours to days, consistent with expanding synchrotron-emitting ejecta. Spectral index evolution during flaring episodes reveals a transition from optically thick to thin regimes, constraining jet expansion velocities and magnetic field strengths. Long-term trends indicate distinct activity cycles, possibly linked to variations in mass-transfer rates from the donor stars. Comparative analysis among the monitored sources highlights both commonalities in jet production mechanisms and source-specific differences in duty cycles and spectral properties. These results provide new insights into the physical processes governing relativistic jet formation and propagation in X-ray binaries, and offer empirical constraints for theoretical models coupling accretion flows to outflows.
