The comprehensive, multi-frequency dataset will serve as a valuable reference for future time-domain studies of compact objects.
introduction: Microquasars are X-ray binary systems exhibiting relativistic jets, serving as nearby laboratories for studying accretion and jet physics. Their emission spans from radio to gamma rays, with variability on timescales from seconds to years. Long-term, multi-frequency monitoring is crucial for understanding the coupling between accretion flows and jet ejections, as well as probing particle acceleration and energy transport. By correlating spectral and temporal behaviors across bands, we can constrain theoretical models and identify triggering mechanisms of outbursts. This study presents extended, coordinated observations of selected microquasars over multiple years.
conclusion: Our long-term, multi-frequency monitoring of microquasars has revealed persistent variability patterns and correlated changes across radio and X-ray bands, underscoring the complex interplay between accretion processes and relativistic jet production. The temporal coverage and spectral resolution achieved allow us to identify both transient flares and gradual evolutionary trends, offering new constraints on emission mechanisms. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, broadband observations for disentangling the physical drivers of microquasar activity, and they lay a foundation for future studies aimed at linking variability properties to fundamental system parameters.

title: Limiting effects in tori clusters
abstract: We investigate the emergence of limiting effects in clusters of coupled tori, focusing on the interplay between geometric confinement, inter-torus interactions, and collective dynamical modes. Using a combination of analytical modeling and numerical simulations, we examine how the topology and spatial arrangement of multiple tori influence energy distribution, resonance patterns, and stability thresholds. Our results reveal that beyond a critical coupling strength, the system exhibits saturation phenomena in oscillatory amplitudes and frequency shifts, attributable to nonlinear mode mixing and mutual inductive or elastic constraints. Furthermore, the limiting behavior is shown to depend sensitively on cluster size, symmetry, and boundary conditions, with distinct scaling laws for densely packed versus sparse configurations. These findings provide new insights into the fundamental physics of toroidal assemblies, with potential applications ranging from metamaterial design to plasma confinement systems, where controlled limiting effects can be exploited to enhance performance and stability.
introduction:
The study of collective dynamics in clustered toroidal structures has attracted increasing attention in recent years, driven both by advances in fabrication techniques and by the broad range of natural and engineered systems in which such geometries occur. Tori clusters arise in contexts as diverse as magnetic confinement devices, photonic crystal arrangements, fluid vortices, and topologically constrained nanostructures. Their distinctive topology, characterized by a closed-loop geometry with a central void, leads to unique interaction profiles when multiple tori are brought into proximity. These interactions can give rise to emergent behaviours not present in isolated systems, including coupled oscillations, synchronization phenomena, and constrained transport processes.

A central question concerns the limiting effects that emerge as the number of constituent tori increases or as their spatial separation decreases. In many physical systems, inter-unit coupling is mediated by fields or flows whose properties are altered by the topology of each element. In clusters of tori, the geometry imposes constraints on how such couplings scale, potentially leading to saturation effects, symmetry-breaking transitions, or suppression of certain modes. Understanding these limits is essential for predicting the performance and stability of toroidal assemblies under operational conditions.

Previous studies have examined pairwise interactions between tori, often focusing on idealized configurations or simplified coupling mechanisms. While such approaches have clarified basic features of mutual influence, they do not fully capture the collective constraints that arise in larger ensembles. In particular, the interplay between local curvature, global topology, and inter-torus distance can produce nonlinear responses that are not apparent from two-body analyses. Furthermore, material properties, boundary conditions, and external driving fields can all modulate the onset and character of limiting effects.

The present work aims to provide a systematic investigation of limiting behaviours in tori clusters, combining analytical modelling with numerical simulations to capture both geometric and dynamical aspects. We seek to identify universal scaling relations that describe how key observables, such as energy transfer rates or mode amplitudes, evolve with cluster size and configuration. By delineating the regimes in which coupling saturates or destabilizes the system, our results contribute to a deeper understanding of toroidal assemblies in both fundamental and applied settings. These insights have potential implications for the design of resilient devices, the control of collective modes, and the exploitation of topological effects in complex physical systems.
conclusion: The present study has examined the limiting effects that emerge in clusters of tori, with particular attention to the interplay between geometric constraints, inter-torus coupling, and boundary conditions. Our analysis demonstrates that as the number of constituent tori increases, collective behaviors arise that are not trivially predictable from the properties of individual elements. Specifically, we have shown that the spatial arrangement within the cluster imposes characteristic limits on both the achievable modes of oscillation and the distribution of stresses, leading to saturation effects at higher cluster densities. Theoretical modelling, supported by numerical simulations, confirms that these limitations are strongly dependent on the ratio of toroidal radii and the relative orientation of the tori, suggesting a tunable pathway for controlling cluster performance. Furthermore, the observed threshold phenomena indicate the presence of distinct regimes, wherein small perturbations can trigger disproportionate structural or dynamical responses. These findings advance our understanding of toroidal assemblies in both mechanical and electromagnetic contexts, and they provide a framework for optimizing cluster configurations for practical applications. Future work should extend the current model to incorporate non-ideal material properties and environmental interactions, thereby enabling more accurate predictions for real-world systems and guiding the design of robust, efficient toroidal clusters.

title: Hints for families of GRBs improving the Hubble diagram
abstract: We investigate the potential of employing distinct families of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) to refine the Hubble diagram at high redshifts. GRBs, as the most luminous explosions in the universe, can be observed well beyond the reach of Type Ia supernovae, yet their large intrinsic diversity limits their utility as standardizable candles. By identifying subsets of GRBs that share common physical properties and spectral–temporal correlations, we aim to reduce dispersion in luminosity distance estimates. Using a curated sample of well-measured GRBs with known redshifts, we apply multi-parameter correlation analyses to distinguish families based on prompt emission characteristics, afterglow behavior, and energetics. For each family, we recalibrate empirical luminosity relations, such as the Amati and Yonetoku correlations, and assess their scatter. Our results indicate that certain families, defined through tighter spectral-energy criteria, yield significantly improved distance moduli, leading to a more precise high-redshift Hubble diagram. This approach mitigates systematic uncertainties arising from population heterogeneity and may extend cosmological parameter constraints to earlier epochs. We discuss the implications for probing dark energy evolution and testing cosmological models beyond z ≈ 6. The identification of physically motivated GRB families thus represents a promising route to enhancing the cosmological utility of GRBs.
introduction:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic phenomena in the Universe, releasing vast amounts of energy over timescales ranging from milliseconds to several minutes. Detected at cosmological distances, they have been proposed as potential standardizable candles, complementing Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) in tracing the expansion history of the Universe. Unlike SNe Ia, which are limited to redshifts \( z \lesssim 2 \), GRBs have been observed up to \( z \gtrsim 9 \), thus offering a unique opportunity to extend the Hubble diagram deep into the early Universe. However, the intrinsic diversity of GRB prompt and afterglow emissions, as well as the complex physics of their progenitors and environments, make their standardization challenging. Empirical correlations between observable quantities—such as the Amati relation between the rest-frame spectral peak energy \( E_{\rm p} \) and the isotropic-equivalent radiated energy \( E_{\rm iso} \), or the Ghirlanda relation involving collimation-corrected energies—have been proposed to reduce the scatter in luminosity indicators. Yet, these correlations often exhibit significant dispersion when applied to heterogeneous GRB samples, limiting their cosmological utility.

One promising avenue to improve the standardization of GRBs is to identify distinct sub-classes, or “families,” that share common physical properties and follow tighter luminosity correlations. Such families may correspond to different progenitor channels, circumburst environments, or jet structures, each imprinting characteristic signatures on the observed emission. Advances in time-resolved spectroscopy, broadband afterglow monitoring, and statistical classification techniques have made it increasingly feasible to disentangle these sub-populations within large GRB datasets. By isolating more homogeneous families, the intrinsic scatter in luminosity relations can be reduced, thereby enhancing the precision of GRB-based distance measurements.

Improved calibration of GRB luminosity indicators through family identification has direct implications for cosmology. A refined GRB Hubble diagram can bridge the redshift gap between SNe Ia and the cosmic microwave background (CMB), providing independent constraints on the dark energy equation of state at epochs inaccessible to other probes. Moreover, robust high-\( z \) distance indicators are crucial for testing departures from the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM model, probing early Universe physics, and constraining models of cosmic reionization.

In this work, we investigate the potential of GRB family identification to enhance the quality of the GRB Hubble diagram. We discuss criteria for defining homogeneous families, explore their impact on the scatter of key correlations, and assess the resulting improvements in cosmological parameter estimation. Our results aim to clarify the role of GRBs as precision tools for observational cosmology and to outline strategies for exploiting forthcoming GRB samples from next-generation missions.
conclusion: In this work, we have explored the potential of identifying and utilizing families of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) with shared intrinsic properties to improve the construction of the Hubble diagram at high redshift. By systematically grouping GRBs according to correlations among their prompt emission and afterglow parameters, we have shown that it is possible to reduce the intrinsic scatter in luminosity indicators, thereby enhancing their utility as standardizable candles. The refined Hubble diagram derived from these families exhibits improved consistency with the concordance cosmological model, while also extending the redshift reach beyond that accessible to Type Ia supernovae. This approach not only strengthens the statistical weight of GRB-based cosmology but also offers an independent probe for testing the evolution of dark energy and the geometry of the Universe at early epochs. Although the sample size remains limited and selection effects must be further constrained, our results indicate that the family-based methodology can significantly mitigate calibration uncertainties. Future work, incorporating larger, uniformly observed GRB datasets and more sophisticated clustering algorithms, will be critical to fully realizing the promise of GRB families as cosmological tools. Such advances may ultimately allow GRBs to play a central role in precision cosmology alongside other established distance indicators.

title: Non-Convex Utility Maximization in Gaussian MISO Broadcast and Interference Channels
abstract: We study non-convex utility maximization problems in Gaussian multiple-input single-output (MISO) broadcast and interference channels, where the objective captures general system-level performance measures beyond weighted sum-rate. Such formulations arise in scenarios involving fairness, quality-of-service constraints, and heterogeneous service requirements, but are challenging due to the inherent non-convexity of the rate region. We develop a unified optimization framework based on successive convex approximation, leveraging rate–MMSE relationships and convex–concave decompositions to derive efficient iterative algorithms with provable convergence to stationary points. The proposed methods accommodate both centralized and distributed implementations, enabling scalability in networks with many users and antennas. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our algorithms achieve significant performance gains over existing baselines for various utility functions, including proportional fairness and max–min fairness. These results highlight the effectiveness and flexibility of the approach for practical multiuser MISO systems operating under general utility-driven design criteria.
introduction:
The design of efficient transmission strategies in multiuser wireless communication systems has long been a central topic in information theory and signal processing. In particular, the Gaussian multiple-input single-output (MISO) broadcast channel (BC) and the Gaussian MISO interference channel (IC) serve as fundamental models for downlink multiuser communication and for networks with multiple interfering transmitter-receiver pairs, respectively. In these settings, the transmitter(s) are equipped with multiple antennas, enabling spatial multiplexing and beamforming, while each receiver is equipped with a single antenna. These configurations are highly relevant to modern and emerging wireless systems, including cellular base stations, coordinated multi-point transmission, and device-to-device communication.

A common objective in the design of transmission strategies is the maximization of a network utility function that captures performance trade-offs among users. Such utility functions can represent various system-level goals, including weighted sum-rate maximization, proportional fairness, and max–min fairness. In practical scenarios, utility functions are often non-convex in the beamforming vectors or transmit covariance matrices, due to the inherent coupling of users’ signals through interference. This non-convexity poses significant challenges for both analysis and algorithm design, as standard convex optimization techniques are not directly applicable.

In the Gaussian MISO BC, the optimal precoding structure under certain utility functions can be characterized using techniques such as dirty paper coding (DPC) and its variants. However, DPC is difficult to implement in practice, and thus linear precoding schemes such as zero-forcing beamforming or regularized zero-forcing are widely employed. In these linear schemes, the achievable rate region is generally non-convex with respect to the beamforming vectors, making exact utility maximization intractable in most cases. Similarly, in the Gaussian MISO IC, each transmitter’s signal causes interference to unintended receivers, and the achievable rates are coupled in a highly non-linear manner. The resulting optimization problems are typically NP-hard, even for simple utility functions like the weighted sum rate.

The study of non-convex utility maximization problems in these channels has led to the development of various approximation and iterative algorithms, including successive convex approximation, weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) methods, alternating optimization, and game-theoretic approaches. These methods often provide locally optimal solutions that satisfy certain stationarity conditions, such as the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, but offer no guarantee of global optimality. Nonetheless, they have proven effective in practice, delivering substantial performance gains over naive designs.

From a theoretical standpoint, understanding the structure of optimal solutions and the properties of the achievable rate region remains an important challenge. For instance, in the MISO BC, the capacity region with DPC is convex, but the region achieved with practical linear precoding is not. In the MISO IC, even characterizing the Pareto boundary of the achievable rate region is nontrivial. These difficulties are compounded when fairness or quality-of-service constraints are imposed, as they often lead to highly non-convex feasible sets.

This work focuses on the formulation and analysis of non-convex utility maximization problems in Gaussian MISO BC and IC settings. We aim to elucidate the impact of channel conditions, interference structure, and utility definitions on problem tractability, as well as to develop efficient algorithms that can approach optimal performance in practice. By bridging the gap between theoretical formulation and algorithmic implementation, our study contributes to the design of high-performance transmission strategies for multiuser wireless networks operating in interference-limited regimes.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated non-convex utility maximization problems in Gaussian MISO broadcast and interference channels. By leveraging problem structure and advanced optimization techniques, we derived algorithms capable of efficiently handling the inherent non-convexity while ensuring convergence to high-quality stationary solutions. Our analysis demonstrated significant performance gains over conventional convex approximations, particularly in scenarios with stringent interference constraints. The results highlight the importance of tailored non-convex optimization methods for practical multi-antenna systems and motivate further exploration of scalable algorithms for large network deployments.

title: Pricing options and computing implied volatilities using neural networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of neural networks to option pricing and the computation of implied volatilities. Traditional numerical methods for these tasks, such as finite-difference schemes and iterative root-finding, can be computationally expensive and sensitive to model assumptions. We develop feedforward architectures trained on synthetic datasets generated from standard option pricing models, enabling efficient mapping between market inputs, option prices, and implied volatilities. The proposed approach achieves high accuracy while significantly reducing computation time, making it suitable for real-time applications. We evaluate performance across varying moneyness, maturities, and volatility regimes, demonstrating robust generalization beyond the training range. Our results highlight neural networks as a flexible, fast, and accurate alternative to conventional pricing and inversion techniques in quantitative finance.
introduction:
In modern financial markets, the accurate pricing of derivative securities and the estimation of their implied volatilities are of central importance to both practitioners and researchers. Options, in particular, serve as essential instruments for hedging, speculation, and risk management. Classical models, such as the Black–Scholes–Merton framework, provide closed-form solutions under simplifying assumptions, including constant volatility and frictionless markets. While these models offer valuable theoretical insights, empirical evidence consistently demonstrates deviations from their assumptions, leading to systematic mispricings, volatility smiles, and skews. Consequently, more sophisticated approaches have been developed, including stochastic volatility models, jump-diffusion processes, and numerical methods such as finite differences and Monte Carlo simulations. These methods, although more flexible, often incur significant computational costs, especially in high-dimensional settings or when rapid recalibration is required.

In recent years, advances in machine learning, and particularly in neural networks, have offered promising alternatives for option pricing and implied volatility estimation. Neural networks are capable of approximating complex, nonlinear functions and can learn directly from large datasets without requiring explicit model specification. This data-driven paradigm enables the capture of intricate patterns in option prices that may be difficult to model analytically. Moreover, once trained, neural networks can provide near-instantaneous predictions, making them highly attractive for real-time applications such as high-frequency trading or dynamic hedging.

The use of neural networks in the context of derivative pricing addresses two related but distinct tasks: the direct prediction of option prices given underlying parameters, and the inversion problem of computing implied volatilities from observed market prices. The latter is traditionally solved through iterative root-finding methods, which may be computationally intensive and sensitive to initial conditions. Neural networks offer a non-iterative alternative, mapping observed market data directly to implied volatilities.

This paper investigates the application of neural network architectures for both option pricing and implied volatility computation. We aim to evaluate their accuracy, efficiency, and robustness compared to conventional numerical techniques, and to explore the trade-offs between model complexity, training requirements, and prediction performance. By leveraging synthetic and market datasets, we demonstrate that neural networks can achieve high precision while substantially reducing computation times, thus offering a viable and scalable tool for modern financial engineering.
conclusion:
This study set out to investigate the potential of neural network architectures for accurately and efficiently pricing options and computing implied volatilities, tasks that are central to modern financial engineering. By leveraging the universal function approximation capabilities of neural networks, we have demonstrated that such models can learn the complex, nonlinear relationships inherent in option pricing models, both under theoretical frameworks such as Black–Scholes and in more realistic market settings that incorporate stochastic volatility and jumps. Our empirical results indicate that well‑designed networks can achieve high accuracy across a wide range of strike prices, maturities, and market conditions, while substantially reducing the computational burden relative to traditional numerical methods.

A key contribution of this work is the demonstration that neural networks can serve as effective surrogates for iterative root‑finding procedures in the computation of implied volatilities. Conventional methods, such as Newton–Raphson or bisection, are computationally intensive when applied to large option datasets or in real‑time trading environments. Our findings show that, once trained, neural networks can produce implied volatility estimates orders of magnitude faster, without significant loss of precision. This performance gain has immediate implications for risk management, derivatives trading, and regulatory reporting, where speed and scalability are critical.

In addition to speed and accuracy, the flexibility of neural networks allows them to adapt to different option types and underlying asset dynamics without the need for explicit model specification. This adaptability is particularly valuable in markets where underlying assumptions of parametric models may be violated. However, the black‑box nature of neural networks poses interpretability challenges, and their performance can be sensitive to the quality and representativeness of the training data. Careful architecture selection, regularization, and validation are therefore essential to ensure robustness and generalization.

Our results suggest promising avenues for further research. One direction is the integration of domain knowledge, such as no‑arbitrage constraints or known asymptotic behaviors, directly into the network architecture or loss function, potentially improving both accuracy and interpretability. Another is the exploration of transfer learning and continual learning approaches, enabling models to adapt quickly to evolving market conditions without retraining from scratch. Moreover, extending the methodology to exotic derivatives and multi‑asset options could broaden its applicability.

In conclusion, neural networks offer a viable and powerful alternative to conventional option pricing and implied volatility computation methods. While challenges remain, particularly in interpretability and data dependence, the demonstrated efficiency and accuracy gains position these models as valuable tools for both academic research and industry practice, with the potential to reshape computational finance workflows.

title: Differential invariants of Kundt spacetimes
abstract: We investigate the differential invariants characterizing Kundt spacetimes, employing the Cartan–Karlhede algorithm. Explicit invariant classifications are derived, revealing geometric structures and equivalence criteria, with implications for exact solutions, curvature homogeneity, and algebraic specialization within general relativity.
introduction:
Kundt spacetimes form an important and intriguing class of exact solutions in general relativity, characterized by the existence of a null congruence that is geodesic, expansion-free, shear-free, and twist-free. These geometries encompass a wide variety of physically and mathematically significant metrics, including pp-waves, VSI (vanishing scalar invariants) and CSI (constant scalar invariants) spacetimes, as well as certain exact solutions of supergravity and string theory. Their rich structure and broad applicability have made them a subject of sustained interest in both mathematical relativity and theoretical physics.

A central question in the study of any spacetime is the determination of its local equivalence class under diffeomorphisms. Differential invariants—quantities constructed from the curvature tensor and its covariant derivatives that remain unchanged under coordinate transformations—provide a systematic means for solving the equivalence problem. In particular, the Cartan–Karlhede algorithm offers a constructive procedure for identifying the minimal set of functionally independent invariants required to uniquely characterize a given geometry. For Kundt spacetimes, the analysis of differential invariants is especially subtle: many members of this class exhibit degeneracies in their scalar polynomial curvature invariants, necessitating the use of higher-order covariant derivatives or frame components to achieve a complete classification.

Recent work has highlighted the role of curvature operators and alignment theory in understanding the algebraic and differential properties of Kundt metrics. Invariant classification not only facilitates the identification of isometries and the separation of physically distinct solutions, but also deepens our understanding of the geometric mechanisms underlying special properties such as the absence of gravitational wave tails or the preservation of certain supersymmetries. Moreover, the study of differential invariants in the Kundt class has implications for quantum gravity, where spacetimes with degenerate invariants may evade conventional curvature-based singularity diagnostics.

In this paper, we undertake a systematic investigation of the differential invariants associated with various subclasses of Kundt spacetimes. By applying and refining the Cartan–Karlhede algorithm, we determine the invariant structures that distinguish these geometries, elucidate their hierarchical relationships, and clarify the extent to which scalar polynomial invariants suffice for their classification.
conclusion: In this work we have investigated the structure of differential invariants associated with Kundt spacetimes, with particular emphasis on their role in the local equivalence problem. By systematically analysing the Cartan–Karlhede algorithm for various subclasses, we have shown that the degeneracy of polynomial curvature invariants in these geometries necessitates the use of higher-order differential invariants to achieve a complete invariant characterization. Our results clarify the hierarchy of such invariants and demonstrate how they distinguish between metrics that share identical sets of scalar polynomial invariants. Moreover, we have illustrated that the differential invariants are intimately related to the underlying null congruence structure, capturing geometric features that remain hidden to purely algebraic classifications. The explicit invariant bases we have constructed provide a practical tool for identifying Kundt metrics and for exploring their physical applications, including exact solutions of Einstein’s equations with aligned matter fields. This study thus reinforces the significance of differential invariants in understanding the rich geometry of Kundt spacetimes and lays the groundwork for further investigations into their role in broader classes of Lorentzian manifolds.

title: Timing analysis for 20 millisecond pulsars in the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array
abstract: We present updated timing solutions for 20 millisecond pulsars observed as part of the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array (PPTA) project. These pulsars have been regularly monitored with the Parkes 64-m radio telescope over time spans of up to 18 years, using multiple receiver systems and backends to achieve high-precision pulse time-of-arrival measurements. We describe the procedures used to correct for instrumental delays, account for variations in dispersion measure, and model timing noise. Our analysis incorporates improved astrometric parameters, proper motions, and, where measurable, annual parallax. Several pulsars exhibit significant red noise, which we model using a power-law spectrum, and we report updated binary parameters for pulsars in compact systems. The resulting timing residuals reach sub-microsecond precision for the best sources, demonstrating the long-term stability of these pulsars and the effectiveness of our calibration methods. These results provide a refined dataset for ongoing efforts to detect nanohertz-frequency gravitational waves and to study the interstellar medium using pulsar timing techniques.
introduction: The Parkes Pulsar Timing Array (PPTA) monitors a set of millisecond pulsars with exceptional rotational stability to investigate phenomena such as gravitational waves, time standards, and the interstellar medium. This study presents updated timing analyses for 20 millisecond pulsars observed over extended time spans with the Parkes radio telescope. By refining pulse arrival times and characterizing timing residuals, we improve constraints on pulsar parameters and noise processes. These results contribute to ongoing efforts to enhance the sensitivity of pulsar timing arrays to nanohertz-frequency gravitational wave signals.
conclusion: We have presented a comprehensive timing analysis of 20 millisecond pulsars observed as part of the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array project. Our results demonstrate sub-microsecond timing precision for the majority of the sample, enabling stringent tests of pulsar stability and sensitivity to low-frequency gravitational waves. The updated timing models incorporate improved dispersion measure corrections and refined astrometric parameters, enhancing long-term stability. These findings provide a robust foundation for future PTA analyses, contributing to the broader effort to detect nanohertz gravitational waves and to probe the astrophysics of pulsars and the interstellar medium.

title: Lifted Relational Neural Networks
abstract: We introduce Lifted Relational Neural Networks (LRNNs), a framework that integrates relational logic representations with neural computation through a lifted template-based architecture. LRNNs exploit parameter sharing across isomorphic substructures, enabling efficient learning in domains with rich relational structure. By grounding only relevant portions of the lifted model, our approach scales to large, complex datasets while maintaining the expressiveness of first-order logic. We propose a differentiable formulation that supports gradient-based optimization, allowing the joint learning of symbolic and subsymbolic components. Experiments on relational classification and link prediction tasks demonstrate that LRNNs achieve competitive or superior accuracy compared to propositional baselines, while requiring significantly fewer parameters and retaining interpretability through the underlying logical rules.
introduction:
Relational reasoning lies at the heart of human intelligence, enabling the integration of structured knowledge with perceptual information to make inferences that generalize beyond observed instances. Over the past decades, statistical relational learning (SRL) has provided a principled framework for combining the expressivity of first-order logic with the robustness of probabilistic models. By representing knowledge in terms of entities, relations, and logical rules, SRL methods can capture complex dependencies and exploit symmetries in the data. However, traditional SRL approaches often rely on handcrafted features or inference procedures that scale poorly to large datasets and high-dimensional perceptual inputs.

In parallel, neural networks have demonstrated remarkable success in learning from raw, unstructured data such as images, text, and speech, largely due to their ability to automatically extract task-relevant features through end-to-end training. While deep learning excels in perceptual domains, it struggles to incorporate explicit relational structure and to generalize systematically across varying object configurations. Recent work at the intersection of deep learning and relational modeling seeks to bridge this gap, giving rise to neural-symbolic systems that combine the representational power of logic with the function-approximation capabilities of neural architectures.

A key challenge in unifying these paradigms is how to represent and process relational knowledge in a way that is both computationally efficient and amenable to gradient-based learning. Naïvely grounding all possible instantiations of relational rules leads to combinatorial blow-up, making inference and learning intractable for domains with many objects. In SRL, *lifted inference* techniques address this problem by reasoning directly about groups of indistinguishable objects, thereby exploiting symmetries to reduce computational complexity. Bringing the idea of lifted representations into the neural setting offers the potential to achieve similar efficiency gains while retaining the flexibility of deep learning.

This work introduces *Lifted Relational Neural Networks* (LRNNs), a novel framework that integrates lifted relational representations with neural computation. LRNNs encode knowledge in the form of weighted first-order rules, which are compiled into a neural network whose structure reflects the relational dependencies in the domain. Crucially, the compilation operates at the lifted level, avoiding full grounding and thus enabling scalability to larger domains. This allows the network to share parameters across symmetric structures, improving data efficiency and facilitating generalization to novel object configurations. By training the network end-to-end, LRNNs can learn both the parameters associated with relational rules and the embeddings of constants and predicates, blending declarative knowledge with distributed representations.

The proposed approach builds on and extends prior work in neural-symbolic integration, graph neural networks, and lifted inference. Unlike standard graph neural networks, which operate on individual grounded graphs, LRNNs maintain an explicit lifted structure that reflects the underlying logical theory. This distinction enables systematic parameter sharing and avoids redundant computation over isomorphic substructures. Compared to earlier neural-symbolic models, LRNNs support differentiable reasoning over arbitrary relational arities and can incorporate domain knowledge in a transparent, interpretable form.

We evaluate LRNNs on benchmark relational learning tasks, including molecular property prediction, family-relationship reasoning, and knowledge base completion. Experimental results demonstrate that LRNNs achieve competitive or superior accuracy compared to both purely neural and purely symbolic baselines, particularly in settings with limited training data or requiring strong generalization to unseen entities. Moreover, the lifted formulation leads to significant computational savings in both training and inference.

By uniting the efficiency of lifted reasoning with the adaptability of neural networks, LRNNs provide a promising direction for scalable, interpretable, and generalizable relational learning. This framework opens avenues for further research on integrating structured knowledge into deep learning systems, with potential applications in scientific discovery, natural language understanding, and robotics.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced Lifted Relational Neural Networks, a framework that integrates the strengths of statistical relational learning with the representational power of deep neural architectures. By leveraging lifted inference principles, our approach exploits symmetries in relational structures to enable efficient learning and reasoning without sacrificing expressiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves competitive or superior performance across a range of relational tasks while reducing computational overhead compared to grounded counterparts. Moreover, the framework’s modularity facilitates incorporation of domain knowledge and supports flexible adaptation to heterogeneous data sources. These results suggest that lifted neural approaches offer a promising direction for scalable, interpretable, and data-efficient relational learning. Future work will explore extensions to dynamic and temporal domains, as well as deeper integration with probabilistic logic programming to further enhance reasoning capabilities.

title: PI-Net: A Deep Learning Approach to Extract Topological Persistence Images
abstract: We propose **PI-Net**, a novel deep learning framework designed to directly extract persistence images from raw data, bridging the gap between topological data analysis (TDA) and modern neural architectures. Persistence images are a stable, vectorized representation of persistence diagrams, which encode the birth and death of topological features across multiple scales. Traditional computation of persistence images relies on a two-step pipeline: first constructing a filtration and computing persistence diagrams via combinatorial algorithms, then applying a fixed transformation to obtain the image representation. PI-Net streamlines this process by embedding differentiable topological feature extraction within a neural network, enabling end-to-end learning of persistence-informed representations. Our architecture incorporates a differentiable approximation of the persistence diagram computation, followed by a learned mapping into the image domain, allowing joint optimization with downstream objectives. This integration not only reduces computational overhead but also allows the network to tailor topological features to the task at hand. We evaluate PI-Net on synthetic and real-world datasets, including shape classification and molecule property prediction, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness compared to baseline TDA pipelines. The results highlight the potential of deep, differentiable topology-aware models for advancing representation learning in domains where shape, connectivity, and multi-scale structure are critical.
introduction:
Topological data analysis (TDA) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for uncovering intrinsic structural patterns in complex, high-dimensional datasets. By focusing on the shape of data rather than solely on its statistical properties, TDA offers complementary insights to conventional machine learning methods. Among the most widely used tools in TDA is persistent homology, which encodes the birth and death of topological features—such as connected components, loops, and voids—across multiple scales. The outcome of persistent homology is typically represented as a persistence diagram, a multiset of points in a plane where each point corresponds to a topological feature’s lifespan in the filtration. While persistence diagrams are stable and theoretically rich, they are not directly amenable to standard machine learning pipelines, which often require fixed-size vector representations.

To bridge this gap, several vectorization techniques have been proposed, with the persistence image (PI) being one of the most prominent. Persistence images map points from a persistence diagram into a discretized grid through kernel density estimation, producing a fixed-dimensional representation that preserves topological structure while enabling the use of conventional learning algorithms. This transformation has proven effective in a variety of domains, from material science and neuroscience to sensor networks and time-series analysis. Despite its success, the conventional computation of persistence images involves a sequence of discrete steps: computing the persistence diagram from raw data, selecting kernel parameters and grid resolution, and finally rendering the diagram into an image. Each of these steps is typically hand-crafted, independent of downstream tasks, and potentially suboptimal for specific learning objectives.

Recent advances in deep learning suggest the possibility of integrating representation learning directly with task-driven optimization. Neural networks can be trained end-to-end to discover features that are most relevant for classification, regression, or other supervised or unsupervised tasks. However, the integration of topological feature extraction into deep neural architectures remains challenging. Persistent homology is inherently combinatorial and non-differentiable with respect to raw data inputs, which complicates gradient-based optimization. Therefore, most existing approaches either treat the persistence computation as a fixed preprocessing step or rely on differentiable approximations that may lose some of the theoretical guarantees of persistent homology.

The motivation for this work stems from the observation that, while persistence images provide a bridge between topology and machine learning, their current generation process remains detached from the learning pipeline. As a result, the parameters governing the transformation—from the placement of kernel centers to the weighting of topological features—are not optimized for the specific prediction or inference task at hand. A learnable persistence image representation could, in principle, adapt these parameters in a data-driven manner, enhancing both discriminative power and robustness.

In this paper, we introduce PI-Net, a deep learning framework that directly extracts and optimizes persistence images in an end-to-end fashion. PI-Net is designed to be fully differentiable with respect to its inputs, allowing gradient-based training alongside other neural network components. The architecture incorporates a novel differentiable module that approximates the mapping from raw data to persistence diagrams and subsequently to persistence images, parameterizing kernel functions and weighting schemes in a trainable form. This enables the network to learn topological representations that are tuned to the ultimate learning objective, rather than relying on fixed, handcrafted settings.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we propose a differentiable persistence image layer that can be seamlessly integrated into deep architectures, making it possible to jointly learn topological descriptors and downstream task parameters. Second, we demonstrate that PI-Net can capture relevant topological patterns more effectively than static persistence image computation, as evidenced by improved performance across multiple benchmark datasets. Third, we provide an extensive analysis of the learned parameters, offering insights into how neural networks adapt topological feature extraction to specific data domains.

We validate PI-Net on a range of supervised learning tasks, including shape classification, time-series analysis, and graph-based data scenarios, where topological features play a critical role. Comparisons with standard persistence image pipelines and recent differentiable TDA methods reveal consistent gains in accuracy and robustness. Moreover, our experiments highlight cases where PI-Net learns non-intuitive kernel placements or weightings that align with domain-specific invariances, underscoring the benefits of task-aware topological representation learning.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing related work in topological data analysis, persistence image computation, and differentiable topology layers. We then describe the architecture and training methodology of PI-Net in detail, including the design of the differentiable persistence image module. Following this, we present empirical evaluations on diverse datasets, analyze the learned representations, and discuss their interpretability. Finally, we conclude with a summary of our findings and potential directions for future research, including extensions to other topological summaries and integration with geometric deep learning frameworks.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced PI-Net, a novel deep learning framework for extracting and leveraging topological persistence images directly from data. By integrating concepts from topological data analysis with end-to-end trainable architectures, PI-Net bridges the gap between handcrafted topological descriptors and modern representation learning. Our experiments demonstrate that PI-Net not only captures rich topological features but also adapts them to specific tasks, yielding competitive or superior performance compared to traditional persistence image pipelines. The ability to jointly optimize feature extraction and task objectives enables more expressive and task-relevant topological embeddings. Furthermore, the proposed approach is flexible and can be extended to various data modalities and problem domains. Future work will explore scaling PI-Net to larger datasets, incorporating multi-scale topological summaries, and investigating its interpretability. Overall, PI-Net represents a step forward in unifying topological analysis and deep learning for robust and informative data representations.

title: Fibonacci Sequence, Recurrence Relations, Discrete Probability Distributions and Linear Convolution
abstract: This paper explores the interconnections between the Fibonacci sequence, recurrence relations, discrete probability distributions, and linear convolution, highlighting their theoretical foundations and practical applications. The Fibonacci sequence, a classic example of a second-order linear recurrence, serves as a unifying framework to investigate patterns and structural properties in discrete mathematics. We examine how recurrence relations provide a systematic approach for deriving closed-form expressions and generating functions, enabling deeper insights into sequence behavior. Discrete probability distributions are incorporated to model stochastic processes related to sequence generation, with emphasis on probability mass functions and expected values in discrete settings. Furthermore, linear convolution is analyzed as a computational tool for combining sequences, demonstrating its role in signal processing, combinatorial enumeration, and probabilistic modeling. By integrating these concepts, the study reveals how deterministic and probabilistic structures interact in discrete systems. The findings underscore the versatility of these mathematical constructs and their potential for cross-disciplinary applications in computer science, engineering, and applied mathematics.
introduction: The Fibonacci sequence, a classical object in mathematics, arises naturally from a simple recurrence relation and exhibits intriguing structural and combinatorial properties. Recurrence relations, in general, form a foundational tool in discrete mathematics, enabling the description and analysis of sequences and processes evolving over discrete steps. Discrete probability distributions further enrich this framework by quantifying uncertainty in systems with countable outcomes, providing essential models in statistics, computer science, and engineering. Linear convolution, a fundamental operation in signal processing and discrete systems analysis, relates closely to these concepts through its role in combining sequences and modeling system responses. This paper explores the interplay between these areas, highlighting their mathematical connections and applications. By examining the Fibonacci sequence through recurrence relations, interpreting its probabilistic aspects, and relating sequence operations to convolution, we aim to demonstrate the unified nature of these discrete structures and their significance in theoretical and applied contexts.
conclusion: The exploration of the Fibonacci sequence and recurrence relations illustrates the power of mathematical structures in modeling complex patterns. Discrete probability distributions provide a framework for quantifying uncertainty, while linear convolution demonstrates the systematic combination of sequences in both theoretical and applied contexts. Together, these concepts reveal deep interconnections between number theory, probability, and signal processing. Their integration enhances analytical capabilities, supports problem-solving across diverse domains, and fosters a deeper appreciation of mathematical coherence. Future work may extend these relationships to more generalized forms, enriching both theoretical understanding and practical applications in science and engineering.

title: Extending set functors to generalised metric spaces
abstract: We investigate the extension of set functors to the enriched context of generalised metric spaces, formulated within the framework of Lawvere’s approach to enriched category theory. Many constructions in theoretical computer science, such as behavioural pseudometrics and quantitative semantics, require lifting endofunctors on **Set** to categories enriched over \([0,\infty]\)-valued metrics. We develop a systematic method for producing such extensions, preserving limits, colimits, and relevant enrichment structure. Our approach generalises the Kantorovich and Wasserstein liftings, providing a unifying categorical perspective. We identify necessary and sufficient conditions on a set functor to admit a nonexpansive or Lipschitz lifting, and we analyse the preservation of completeness, cocompleteness, and fixed points in the enriched setting. Applications include coalgebraic modelling of quantitative systems and compositional reasoning about metric invariants. This work bridges the gap between classical functorial constructions and metric enrichment, offering new tools for quantitative algebra and coalgebra.
introduction:
The theory of functors on the category of sets and functions underlies a substantial portion of modern mathematics and theoretical computer science. Functorial constructions allow the systematic transport of structure along maps, and many important examples—ranging from polynomial functors to powerset and distribution functors—arise naturally in diverse contexts. When moving beyond purely set-theoretic domains, however, it becomes necessary to ask how such functors can be meaningfully extended to richer categories that carry additional structure. One particularly fruitful setting is that of generalised metric spaces, where objects are equipped with a notion of distance that may take values in a quantale or other enriched structure, and morphisms respect the metric in a suitably non-expansive sense.

Generalised metric spaces, in the sense of Lawvere, provide a unifying framework in which classical metric spaces, (pre)orders, and various quantitative structures can be treated on the same footing. They are instances of categories enriched over the monoidal poset \(([0,\infty], \geq, 0, +)\) or over more general commutative quantales. This setting supports a well-developed theory of limits, colimits, and categorical constructions that mirror and extend familiar metric notions. From the perspective of applications, generalised metric structures arise in semantics of programming languages, quantitative domain theory, probabilistic systems, and areas of analysis where asymmetry or extended distances are natural.

A central question, both conceptually and technically, is: given a functor \(F : \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Set}\), when and how can it be extended to a functor \(\bar{F}\) on a category of generalised metric spaces, \(\mathbf{Met}_\mathcal{V}\), in such a way that the enrichment is respected? The requirement is not trivial: while any set functor acts on the underlying sets of generalised metric spaces, the challenge lies in defining a compatible metric on \(\bar{F}X\) for each space \(X\), and in ensuring that \(\bar{F}\) preserves the non-expansive nature of morphisms. Different choices of metric extension may lead to different enriched functors, and some set functors may admit no nontrivial extension satisfying natural coherence conditions.

This problem is closely related to, but distinct from, the well-studied theory of lifting functors to categories of algebras, coalgebras, or other structured objects. In the enriched setting, the additional quantitative data impose constraints that have no analogue in the purely set-theoretic case. For example, the powerset functor on sets has several possible metric liftings, depending on whether one uses Hausdorff, Kantorovich, or other distance constructions; each choice reflects a different conceptual stance on how the functor interacts with the metric structure.

Recent work has investigated the lifting of set functors to categories of metric spaces, often with an eye toward applications in coalgebraic semantics, quantitative reasoning, and probabilistic transition systems. Techniques from enriched category theory, such as the use of relation liftings, Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality, and the theory of modules (profunctors), have proved to be powerful tools in this context. However, most existing results either focus on specific, well-behaved functors or restrict attention to symmetric, finite-valued metrics. There remains a need for a systematic account that accommodates generalised metrics, possibly asymmetric or extended, and that clarifies the categorical conditions under which extensions exist and are unique.

In this work, we develop a general framework for extending set functors to categories of generalised metric spaces. Our approach draws on the theory of enriched categories, in particular the characterisation of \(\mathcal{V}\)-categories and \(\mathcal{V}\)-functors in terms of \(\mathcal{V}\)-relations and their liftings. We identify necessary and sufficient conditions for a set functor to admit a canonical extension, describe constructions that produce the corresponding enriched functor, and illustrate the theory with a range of examples, including probabilistic and nondeterministic powerdomains. In doing so, we unify and generalise several disparate strands of previous work, and lay the groundwork for further applications in quantitative semantics and analysis.
conclusion:
We have investigated the problem of extending set functors to categories of generalised metric spaces, focusing on constructions that preserve the essential structure while accommodating enriched categorical settings. By systematically analysing the interaction between set-based behaviour and metric enrichment, we identified conditions under which such extensions exist and remain faithful to the underlying functorial properties. Our approach clarified how limits, colimits, and other categorical constructs behave under these enriched extensions, and demonstrated that several familiar functors from Set admit natural liftings to categories such as Lawvere metric spaces. 

These results broaden the scope of categorical methods in the study of metric-like structures, allowing techniques from coalgebra, algebra, and topology to be applied in a richer quantitative context. In particular, our findings suggest that the extended functors retain sufficient structural fidelity to support the transfer of fixed-point and coinductive reasoning principles from the discrete to the metric-enriched setting. 

Future work may explore the interplay between such extensions and notions of completeness, compactness, or continuity in enriched categories, as well as applications to semantics of quantitative systems. We believe these insights contribute both to the theory of enriched category extensions and to their potential use in modelling and analysis across mathematics and computer science.

title: Search for lepton number and flavour violation in $K^{+}$ and $\pi^{0}$ decays
abstract: We present a search for lepton number and lepton flavour violating decays of the charged kaon and neutral pion using high-statistics data collected with a dedicated detector system. Candidate events for processes such as $K^{+}\to\pi^{-}\ell^{+}\ell^{+}$ and $\pi^{0}\to\mu^{\pm}e^{\mp}$ were examined. No significant excess above expected backgrounds was observed. Upper limits on the branching fractions are set at the $10^{-10}$–$10^{-9}$ level, improving existing constraints. These results provide stringent tests of physics beyond the Standard Model, including scenarios with heavy neutrinos or leptoquarks.
introduction:
The conservation of lepton number and lepton flavour has long been regarded as a fundamental feature of the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics. In the SM, charged lepton flavour is conserved exactly in all interactions, and total lepton number is preserved in both perturbative and non-perturbative processes. However, the discovery of neutrino oscillations has provided unambiguous evidence for lepton flavour violation (LFV) in the neutral lepton sector, demonstrating that lepton flavour conservation is not an exact symmetry of nature. This motivates dedicated searches for LFV and lepton number violation (LNV) in processes involving charged leptons, which are forbidden or highly suppressed within the SM framework.  

In the SM extended to include non-zero neutrino masses, LFV in charged lepton processes is expected at unobservably small rates, typically many orders of magnitude below current experimental sensitivities. In contrast, a variety of theories beyond the SM—such as models with heavy Majorana neutrinos, supersymmetric extensions, leptoquarks, or additional gauge bosons—predict sizeable enhancements to LFV and LNV decay rates, potentially within reach of present or near-future experiments. Observation of such processes would constitute clear evidence of new physics and provide insight into the mechanism of neutrino mass generation, the nature of lepton number conservation, and the structure of flavour symmetries.  

Rare kaon and pion decays provide a particularly clean and sensitive laboratory for such searches. The decays of charged kaons, $K^{+} \to \pi^{-} \ell^{+} \ell^{+}$, violate total lepton number by two units, while processes such as $K^{+} \to \pi^{+} \mu^{\pm} e^{\mp}$ or $\pi^{0} \to \mu^{\pm} e^{\mp}$ violate charged lepton flavour. In the SM, these decays are either strictly forbidden or suppressed to branching ratios below $10^{-50}$, rendering any measurable signal a clear signature of physics beyond the SM. The excellent particle identification, kinematic reconstruction, and large data samples achievable in modern kaon and pion decay experiments enable stringent limits to be placed on such rare processes.  

In this work we present a search for LNV and LFV in specific $K^{+}$ and $\pi^{0}$ decay modes using high-statistics datasets collected with state-of-the-art detectors. The analysis strategy, background suppression techniques, and statistical treatment are designed to maximise sensitivity to branching ratios at the level of $10^{-10}$–$10^{-11}$, probing unexplored regions of parameter space for a range of new physics scenarios.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a search for lepton number violation (LNV) and lepton flavour violation (LFV) in rare decays of charged kaons and neutral pions, using high-statistics datasets collected with a modern fixed-target experiment. The analysis focused on decay channels such as \(K^{+} \to \pi^{-} \ell^{+} \ell^{+}\), \(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} \mu^{\pm} e^{\mp}\), and \(\pi^{0} \to \mu^{\pm} e^{\mp}\), which are forbidden or highly suppressed within the Standard Model (SM) but arise naturally in various extensions incorporating Majorana neutrinos, leptoquarks, or other new mediators. No significant excess above the expected background was observed in any of the investigated channels.

We have established new upper limits on the branching fractions for these processes at the 90% confidence level. In several cases, the obtained limits improve upon previous experimental constraints by factors of two to ten, depending on the decay mode. These results thus provide the most stringent bounds to date for some of the searched channels, further constraining the parameter space of theoretical models predicting LNV or LFV processes in the light meson sector.

The absence of a signal is consistent with the SM expectation of negligible rates for such decays. However, the improved sensitivities extend the reach of experimental tests into regions relevant for models involving heavy sterile neutrinos with masses in the MeV–GeV range, supersymmetric scenarios with R-parity violation, or frameworks with extended Higgs sectors. In particular, the limits obtained here translate into new constraints on effective couplings governing four-fermion operators that mediate these rare processes.

Future experimental efforts, benefiting from increased beam intensities, enhanced detector capabilities, and refined analysis techniques, will allow further improvements in sensitivity by at least one order of magnitude. Such progress will be crucial for probing the full range of viable model predictions and for testing the Majorana nature of neutrinos and possible sources of charged lepton flavour violation. The present study demonstrates the continuing importance of rare kaon and pion decays as precision probes for physics beyond the SM, complementing searches at high-energy colliders and in other low-energy precision experiments.

title: A time - luminosity correlation for Gamma Ray Bursts in the X - rays
abstract: We present an analysis of a statistically significant sample of 192 Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) with well-sampled X-ray afterglow light curves, aimed at investigating a correlation between a characteristic time scale and the corresponding luminosity. Using data from the *Swift* X-Ray Telescope, we identify the end time of the plateau phase, \(T_a\), and compute the rest-frame X-ray luminosity, \(L_a\), at that epoch. Our results confirm the existence of a tight anti-correlation between \(L_a\) and \(T_a\) across more than three orders of magnitude in luminosity and two in time. The best-fit relation, derived via a Bayesian regression method accounting for uncertainties in both variables and intrinsic scatter, shows a slope consistent with previous smaller-sample studies, but with reduced statistical uncertainties. We investigate possible redshift evolution effects and selection biases, finding the correlation to be intrinsic to the GRB population. This time–luminosity relation provides a potential standardization tool for GRB afterglows, with implications for their use as cosmological probes. We discuss physical interpretations in the context of energy injection models and magnetar spin-down scenarios, and consider the prospects for improving constraints with future X-ray missions.
introduction:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most energetic transient phenomena in the universe, releasing vast amounts of energy within timescales ranging from milliseconds to several minutes. Following the prompt gamma-ray emission, GRBs exhibit a multi-wavelength afterglow, with X-ray observations playing a central role in probing their emission mechanisms and the properties of their progenitors. The advent of rapid follow-up capabilities, particularly with the *Swift* satellite, has enabled the systematic study of GRB afterglows from the earliest phases, revealing a complex temporal evolution in the X-ray light curves. These typically display an initial steep decay, a plateau phase, and a subsequent normal decay, though significant variability exists among individual events.

A key pursuit in GRB research is the identification of empirical correlations between observable quantities, as such relations can provide insights into the underlying physics and potentially enable the standardization of GRBs as cosmological probes. Several correlations have been reported, linking the energetics of the prompt emission to afterglow properties or connecting temporal and spectral parameters. In the X-ray regime, one of the most intriguing findings is the apparent anti-correlation between the luminosity at the end of the plateau phase and the corresponding break time in the rest frame. This so-called time–luminosity correlation suggests that brighter plateaus tend to end earlier, while dimmer plateaus persist for longer durations.

The existence of such a correlation has been interpreted in various theoretical frameworks, including models invoking energy injection from a long-lived central engine, such as a magnetar, or the interaction of the relativistic ejecta with the circumburst medium under specific density profiles. The correlation’s slope and normalization may encode information about the total energy budget, jet collimation, and the nature of the energy injection mechanism. Moreover, if sufficiently tight and free from strong selection biases, the time–luminosity relation could serve as a distance indicator, enabling the use of GRBs as complementary probes to supernovae in mapping the expansion history of the universe to higher redshifts.

Despite its potential significance, the robustness and universality of the time–luminosity correlation remain under active investigation. Different studies have reported varying degrees of scatter, sample dependence, and sensitivity to analysis methods, suggesting that observational biases, incomplete sampling of the early afterglow, and intrinsic diversity among GRBs may all influence the observed relation. Furthermore, the physical interpretation of the plateau phase itself—whether it arises from ongoing central engine activity, structured jets, or other mechanisms—remains unsettled. In this work, we investigate the time–luminosity correlation in the X-ray afterglows of GRBs using an updated and well-characterized sample, aiming to assess its statistical significance, explore possible physical origins, and examine its implications for GRB phenomenology and cosmology.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the existence and robustness of a correlation between characteristic timescales and luminosities in the X-ray afterglow phase of Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs). By analysing a well-defined sample of events with high-quality X-ray follow-up observations, we identified a statistically significant relationship linking the rest-frame break time in the afterglow light curve to the corresponding luminosity at that epoch. This time–luminosity correlation, manifest across a wide range of redshifts and energies, appears to be intrinsic to the GRB phenomenon rather than an artefact of selection effects or instrumental thresholds. Our analysis has incorporated careful treatment of k-corrections, cosmological time dilation, and biases introduced by incomplete sampling, thereby reinforcing the reliability of the reported trend.

The results presented here extend and refine earlier studies that hinted at similar correlations, but often with smaller or less homogeneous datasets. By exploiting the wealth of data from recent missions, particularly those with rapid and sustained X-ray coverage, we have been able to constrain the slope and scatter of the correlation with improved precision. The observed relation suggests that the physical processes governing the energy release and afterglow evolution are closely coupled, likely reflecting fundamental aspects of the jet dynamics, circumburst environment, or central engine activity. The consistency of the correlation across diverse bursts, including both long and short-duration classes, points toward a universal mechanism at work, albeit with possible subclass-dependent normalisations.

From a theoretical standpoint, the time–luminosity correlation may be interpreted in the context of afterglow models where the break time corresponds to a dynamical transition, such as a jet break or cessation of energy injection. In these scenarios, a tighter connection between the afterglow brightness and the characteristic timescale would naturally arise if the energetics and geometry of the outflow are regulated by a common set of parameters. For instance, within the standard synchrotron-shock framework, the correlation could reflect a scaling between the kinetic energy of the blastwave and the collimation angle, or between the energy reservoir and the density of the surrounding medium. Alternatively, models invoking prolonged central engine activity would predict that the luminosity at the plateau termination is tied to the total injected energy and the duration of the injection phase, which in turn sets the observed break time.

The practical implications of this correlation are twofold. First, it offers a potential diagnostic tool for probing the physics of GRBs, enabling constraints on key parameters that are otherwise difficult to measure directly. Second, if the correlation can be calibrated with sufficient accuracy and shown to be free from significant evolutionary effects, it might serve as a standardisable candle for cosmological applications, complementing other GRB luminosity relations and extending the reach of distance measurements beyond the redshift range accessible to type Ia supernovae. While the current scatter in the relation limits its immediate utility for precision cosmology, future improvements in data quality and uniformity, as well as better understanding of the underlying physics, could enhance its predictive power.

Nonetheless, several caveats must be acknowledged. Although we have taken steps to mitigate observational biases, residual selection effects cannot be entirely ruled out, particularly at the faint end of the luminosity distribution and for bursts with incomplete temporal coverage. The intrinsic diversity of GRB environments and progenitors may also contribute to the observed scatter, potentially masking secondary correlations or introducing systematic shifts. Moreover, uncertainties in the determination of break times, especially in cases with complex light curve morphologies, remain a source of error that should be addressed through more sophisticated fitting techniques and higher-cadence observations.

Looking ahead, the forthcoming generation of high-sensitivity, wide-field X-ray instruments will significantly expand the sample of GRBs with well-characterised afterglows, enabling more stringent tests of the time–luminosity correlation. In parallel, advances in theoretical modelling and numerical simulations should help to elucidate the physical origin of the relation and its dependence on progenitor properties, jet structure, and environmental conditions. Coordinated multi-wavelength campaigns, combining X-ray, optical, and radio data, will be particularly valuable for breaking degeneracies among competing models and for probing the connection between the prompt emission and the afterglow phase.

In summary, our study provides compelling evidence for a correlation between rest-frame X-ray luminosity and characteristic timescale in GRB afterglows. This finding strengthens the case for a common physical mechanism regulating the temporal and energetic properties of these events and opens new avenues for both astrophysical insight and cosmological application. Continued observational and theoretical efforts will be essential to fully exploit the potential of this relation and to integrate it into a coherent framework for understanding the GRB phenomenon.

title: MCDF-RCI predictions for structure and width of $K\alpha_{1,2}$ x-ray line of Al and Si
abstract: Multiconfiguration Dirac–Fock calculations including relativistic configuration interaction (MCDF-RCI) are performed to predict energies and natural widths of the $K\alpha_{1,2}$ x-ray lines in aluminum and silicon. Predicted transition energies and widths are compared with available experimental data, showing good agreement and confirming the reliability of the MCDF-RCI approach for accurate x-ray spectral structure analysis.
introduction:
Accurate theoretical predictions of x-ray transition energies and natural line widths are essential for the interpretation of high-resolution spectroscopic measurements and for applications in materials science, plasma diagnostics, and fundamental atomic physics. Among these transitions, the $K\alpha_{1,2}$ lines, arising from the $2p_{3/2,1/2} \rightarrow 1s_{1/2}$ radiative decays following a $K$-shell vacancy, are of particular importance. Their energies and profiles are sensitive to relativistic effects, electron correlation, and quantum electrodynamic (QED) contributions, making them valuable benchmarks for advanced atomic theory.

In light and medium-$Z$ elements such as aluminium ($Z=13$) and silicon ($Z=14$), the relatively small nuclear charge allows for high-precision calculations that can be directly compared with experimental data. However, accurate modeling still requires a careful treatment of relativistic interactions and electron correlation, as well as a consistent description of the initial and final states involved in the transition. The multiconfiguration Dirac–Fock (MCDF) method, supplemented by relativistic configuration interaction (RCI) calculations, provides a robust framework for such investigations. By generating wave functions from a self-consistent relativistic field and systematically including configuration mixing, one can account for both Coulomb correlation and the Breit interaction, while QED corrections can be incorporated perturbatively.

In this work, we present MCDF–RCI calculations for the energies and natural widths of the $K\alpha_{1,2}$ x-ray lines of Al and Si. We analyze the influence of electron correlation, relativistic effects, and radiative and non-radiative decay channels on the line structure, and compare our results with available experimental data. The aim is to provide reliable theoretical reference values and to assess the predictive capability of the MCDF–RCI approach for low-$Z$ $K$-shell x-ray spectra.
conclusion:
The present work has employed the multiconfiguration Dirac–Fock method, supplemented by relativistic configuration interaction, to compute the structure and natural width of the $K\alpha_{1,2}$ x-ray lines in neutral Al and Si. The inclusion of extensive configuration expansions, together with the full treatment of relativistic effects and electron correlation, has yielded transition energies in very good agreement with available high-resolution experimental data. The calculated line widths, obtained from the total radiative and Auger decay rates of the initial $1s^{-1}$ states, also reproduce the measured values within the quoted uncertainties, thereby validating the accuracy of the present approach.  

Detailed analysis of the individual contributions demonstrates that both relativistic and correlation effects are essential for an accurate description of these low-$Z$ systems, with correlation effects exerting a slightly stronger influence on the line widths. The fine-structure splitting of the $K\alpha_{1}$ and $K\alpha_{2}$ components is well reproduced, confirming the reliability of the MCDF–RCI treatment in this energy region.  

These results provide benchmark theoretical values for the $K\alpha_{1,2}$ lines of Al and Si and underline the importance of a balanced relativistic and correlation treatment in x-ray spectroscopy. The methodology can be readily extended to other elements and charge states, offering predictive capability for future experimental and applied spectroscopic studies.

title: WeNet: Production oriented Streaming and Non-streaming End-to-End Speech Recognition Toolkit
abstract: We present **WeNet**, an open-source, production-oriented end-to-end speech recognition toolkit designed to support both streaming and non-streaming scenarios within a unified framework. WeNet adopts a unified two-pass approach that integrates streaming and non-streaming modes by sharing the same model architecture and parameters, thereby simplifying deployment and maintenance in real-world applications. The toolkit is built upon a state-of-the-art Conformer-based encoder and attention-based decoder, augmented with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) for efficient alignment and decoding. For streaming recognition, WeNet employs a chunk-by-chunk processing strategy with minimal latency, while non-streaming recognition benefits from full-context modeling for improved accuracy. The system includes optimized training recipes, portable runtime support, and bindings for multiple platforms, enabling seamless integration into production pipelines on both server and edge devices. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, including AISHELL-1 and Librispeech, demonstrate competitive or superior performance compared to existing open-source toolkits, in both streaming and non-streaming modes.
