By unifying research-friendly design with production readiness, WeNet aims to bridge the gap between academic development and industrial deployment, fostering broader adoption of end-to-end speech recognition technologies.
introduction:
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has witnessed remarkable progress over the past decade, driven largely by advances in deep learning and the availability of large-scale datasets. Traditional ASR systems typically adopt a hybrid approach that decomposes the task into multiple components, including acoustic modeling, pronunciation modeling, and language modeling. While effective, these systems require significant engineering effort, domain expertise, and careful integration of heterogeneous modules, which can hinder rapid development and deployment, especially for new languages and application scenarios. In recent years, end-to-end (E2E) ASR methods have emerged as a compelling alternative, offering a unified modeling framework that directly maps acoustic features to word or subword sequences. By jointly optimizing all components within a single neural network, E2E systems simplify model development and have shown competitive or superior performance compared to traditional pipelines.

Among E2E approaches, architectures such as connectionist temporal classification (CTC), recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T), and attention-based encoder–decoder models have been extensively studied. These models differ in alignment mechanisms and decoding strategies, but all share the advantage of eliminating the need for handcrafted pronunciation lexicons and intermediate representations. Further improvements have been achieved by combining the strengths of different architectures, for instance through multi-task learning or joint CTC/attention objectives, which enhance convergence speed, improve alignment, and yield better generalization. As a result, E2E ASR has been adopted in a wide range of applications, from voice assistants to dictation systems and real-time transcription services.

Despite the algorithmic advances, a persistent challenge remains: bridging the gap between research-oriented ASR toolkits and production-level deployment. Many open-source toolkits, such as ESPnet, Kaldi, and Fairseq, have played a crucial role in fostering research innovations, but they often focus primarily on offline, non-streaming recognition. In contrast, real-world applications frequently require streaming ASR, where transcriptions are generated in real time as speech is received. Streaming ASR imposes additional constraints on model architecture, latency, and decoding algorithms, and often necessitates specialized optimization for low-latency inference on diverse hardware platforms. Moreover, production systems must address robustness, scalability, and ease of integration with upstream and downstream components in industrial pipelines.

While some proprietary systems offer both streaming and non-streaming capabilities, there is a lack of open-source solutions that are simultaneously research-friendly and production-oriented, capable of supporting both modes within a unified framework. This gap limits the ability of researchers to prototype models that can be directly deployed in production without significant re-engineering, and it constrains industrial practitioners from leveraging state-of-the-art research in a cost-effective and maintainable manner. In addition, the development of streaming and non-streaming models often proceeds in isolation, leading to duplicated efforts and inconsistencies between the two modes.

To address these challenges, we introduce **WeNet**, an open-source, production-oriented end-to-end speech recognition toolkit that unifies streaming and non-streaming ASR within a single framework. WeNet is designed with the dual goals of facilitating cutting-edge research and enabling seamless transition to industrial deployment. It incorporates efficient and modular implementations of popular E2E architectures, supports multiple training criteria such as CTC and attention-based losses, and provides a consistent interface for both offline and online decoding. By adopting a unified streaming and non-streaming modeling approach, WeNet reduces the engineering overhead of maintaining separate codebases and enables model reuse across different application scenarios.

A key feature of WeNet is its *Unified Two-pass* (U2) model, which is capable of operating in both streaming and non-streaming modes with minimal architectural changes. In streaming mode, U2 produces low-latency partial transcriptions while maintaining competitive accuracy; in non-streaming mode, it leverages full-context information for optimal recognition performance. This flexibility allows developers to deploy the same model architecture across heterogeneous applications, from real-time transcription to batch processing, without retraining from scratch. Furthermore, WeNet emphasizes production readiness by providing optimized inference engines, efficient runtime deployment on CPUs and GPUs, and integration with popular serving frameworks.

WeNet also prioritizes openness and community collaboration. It is released under a permissive license, accompanied by comprehensive documentation, recipes, and pre-trained models for multiple languages. The toolkit is designed to be extensible, enabling researchers to experiment with novel architectures, training strategies, and decoding algorithms while retaining compatibility with production deployment pipelines. Through this combination of research flexibility and industrial applicability, WeNet aims to accelerate innovation in speech recognition and lower the barrier to deploying high-quality ASR systems across diverse domains.

In summary, the motivation for WeNet stems from the need for an open-source, end-to-end ASR toolkit that bridges research and production, unifies streaming and non-streaming recognition, and delivers both high accuracy and low latency. By providing a practical, extensible, and efficient platform, WeNet seeks to foster collaboration between academia and industry, streamline the path from model development to real-world application, and ultimately advance the state of speech recognition technology.
conclusion: We presented WeNet, an open-source end-to-end speech recognition toolkit designed for both streaming and non-streaming scenarios with a focus on production deployment. By integrating a unified two-pass framework, advanced modeling techniques, and efficient decoding strategies, WeNet achieves competitive accuracy while maintaining low latency and scalability. Its modular design and rich recipe collection enable rapid adaptation to diverse languages and application domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world conditions. WeNet bridges the gap between research and production, providing a practical, extensible, and high-performance ASR solution that empowers both academic exploration and large-scale industrial applications.

title: Pseudodoping of Metallic Two-Dimensional Materials
abstract: We investigate pseudodoping phenomena in metallic two-dimensional (2D) materials, where hybridization with supporting substrates induces apparent charge transfer without significant electron redistribution. Using first-principles calculations and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we demonstrate that band structure modifications mimic heavy doping, despite negligible changes in carrier density. Our results reveal that pseudodoping arises from momentum-dependent orbital mixing, leading to shifts in Fermi surface topology and transport properties. We further develop a minimal theoretical model capturing the essential physics. These insights provide a framework for engineering electronic properties in 2D metals via substrate interactions, enabling novel device functionalities without chemical modification.
introduction:
Two-dimensional (2D) materials with metallic character have emerged as a fertile platform for exploring novel electronic phenomena and for enabling next-generation device architectures. Since the isolation of graphene, a variety of atomically thin systems such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), group-VA elements, and metallic MXenes have been synthesized, revealing a wide spectrum of electronic properties governed by their reduced dimensionality and unique band structures. In metallic 2D systems, high carrier densities and tunable Fermi surfaces make them ideal candidates for applications in nanoelectronics, catalysis, and plasmonics. A central challenge in harnessing these properties lies in controlling the electronic structure, particularly the carrier concentration, without introducing disorder or compromising structural integrity.

Traditionally, carrier density in 2D materials is modulated through chemical doping, electrostatic gating, or adsorption of foreign species. While effective, these methods can lead to undesirable side effects, including defect formation, inhomogeneous charge distribution, and stability issues. Recent research has brought attention to an alternative mechanism, termed *pseudodoping*, in which apparent changes in carrier concentration arise not from actual charge transfer, but from modifications in band alignment and hybridization induced by the substrate or nearby layers. Pseudodoping can result from interfacial hybridization between the 2D material and a metallic or semiconducting support, leading to shifts in the Fermi level and changes in the occupancy of electronic states that mimic the effects of doping, even in the absence of significant net charge transfer.

This phenomenon is particularly relevant for metallic 2D materials, where subtle changes in the density of states near the Fermi level can strongly influence transport, magnetism, and superconductivity. Understanding pseudodoping is essential for correctly interpreting spectroscopic measurements such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS), which are sensitive to the apparent carrier concentration. Moreover, pseudodoping offers an opportunity to engineer electronic properties in a reversible and non-invasive manner, avoiding many pitfalls of conventional doping strategies.

In this work, we investigate the microscopic origins and consequences of pseudodoping in metallic 2D materials, focusing on prototypical systems interfaced with various substrates. By combining first-principles calculations with experimental data, we elucidate the interplay between hybridization, band renormalization, and Fermi surface topology. Our results provide guidelines for exploiting pseudodoping as a design principle for tailored functionalities in 2D metals and underscore the importance of distinguishing it from genuine charge doping in both fundamental studies and practical applications.
conclusion: In summary, we have demonstrated that pseudodoping offers a compelling mechanism to tailor the electronic properties of metallic two-dimensional materials without introducing significant chemical disorder. By exploiting substrate interactions, charge transfer, and hybridization effects, it is possible to achieve tunable shifts in band structure and carrier concentration that mimic conventional doping while preserving intrinsic structural integrity. Our analysis highlights the interplay between interfacial coupling strength and the resulting electronic modifications, providing a framework for predictive control in device applications. These findings not only deepen the understanding of substrate-mediated phenomena in low-dimensional systems but also open viable pathways for engineering functional heterostructures with optimized performance for nanoelectronic, optoelectronic, and quantum technologies.

title: MOND, dark matter, and conservation of energy
abstract: We examine the implications of Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) and dark matter hypotheses for galactic dynamics, focusing on the consistency of each framework with energy conservation. Analytical and numerical analyses highlight conditions under which MOND respects conservation laws, contrasting them with dark matter models, and discussing observational constraints.
introduction:
The apparent discrepancy between the observed dynamics of galaxies and the predictions derived from Newtonian gravity has been a central challenge in astrophysics for decades. Rotation curves of spiral galaxies remain flat at large radii, contrary to the decline expected from visible mass distributions. The prevailing explanation invokes dark matter, a non-luminous component that interacts primarily through gravity, whose presence reconciles observations with standard gravitational theory. Despite its success in explaining a wide range of cosmological phenomena, the dark matter paradigm remains empirically elusive, with no direct detection to date.  

An alternative approach, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND), proposes a modification to Newton’s second law or the law of gravitation at accelerations below a characteristic scale. MOND has achieved notable success in fitting galactic rotation curves with fewer free parameters, suggesting a possible underlying regularity. However, MOND’s status as a fundamental theory remains debated, particularly regarding its compatibility with conservation laws. While certain relativistic extensions preserve energy–momentum conservation, the original non-relativistic formulation raises questions about the general applicability of these principles.  

The conservation of energy is a foundational principle in physics, closely linked to symmetries via Noether’s theorem. Any modification to gravitational dynamics must be assessed for consistency with this principle. This paper examines the interplay between MOND, dark matter, and energy conservation, aiming to clarify whether the modifications implied by MOND can be reconciled with standard conservation laws, and to evaluate the implications for our understanding of galactic dynamics and the nature of gravitation.
conclusion: In summary, the comparison between MOND and dark matter frameworks highlights fundamental differences in their treatment of galactic dynamics and the conservation of energy. While MOND offers an alternative to unseen mass by modifying Newtonian dynamics, challenges remain in reconciling it with energy conservation in complex systems. Dark matter models, though not yet directly confirmed, preserve established conservation laws more naturally. Future theoretical and observational advances will be essential to determine which framework, or synthesis, most accurately describes cosmic structure and motion.

title: Bose-Einstein correlations and the stochastic scale of light hadrons emitter source
abstract: Bose–Einstein correlations (BEC) of identical bosons provide a powerful tool for probing the space–time structure of particle emission sources in high-energy collisions. In this study, we investigate the stochastic scale characterizing the emitter source of light hadrons by analyzing two-particle correlation functions within a quantum statistical framework. The stochastic scale parameter is introduced to quantify the influence of chaotic and coherent components in the emission process, as well as medium-induced distortions. Using experimental data from proton–proton and heavy-ion collisions at various center-of-mass energies, we extract the dependence of the stochastic scale on kinematic variables and collision characteristics. The results indicate a nontrivial energy and multiplicity dependence, suggesting sensitivity to the source’s geometry and dynamical evolution. This approach provides refined insight into the microscopic space–time picture of hadronization and the role of quantum interference in strongly interacting systems.
introduction:
The study of multiparticle production processes in high-energy collisions provides a unique window into the space-time structure of the hadronization region and the underlying dynamics of strong interactions. Among the most effective tools for probing the geometry and dynamics of the particle-emitting source are Bose–Einstein correlations (BEC) between identical bosons, most commonly observed in the form of an enhancement of the production probability for pairs of identical pions with small relative momenta. Rooted in the symmetrization requirement of the quantum-mechanical wave function for identical bosons, these correlations carry rich information about the spatial extent, lifetime, and internal dynamics of the emitter. Since the pioneering Hanbury Brown–Twiss (HBT) interferometry measurements in astronomy, analogous techniques have been adapted to particle physics, enabling femtoscopic resolution of the source created in high-energy interactions.

In high-energy proton–proton, proton–nucleus, and nucleus–nucleus collisions, the BEC effect manifests itself in the two-particle correlation function, typically parameterized in terms of a correlation radius (or correlation length) and a chaoticity parameter that encodes the degree of coherence of particle emission. In the simplest interpretations, the correlation radius reflects the characteristic size of the emission region at freeze-out, while the chaoticity parameter accounts for partial coherence, resonance decays, and other dynamical effects. However, recent advances in both experimental precision and theoretical modeling have indicated that this picture is incomplete. The emitter is not a static, uniform sphere, but rather a complex, fluctuating system subject to stochastic forces arising from the underlying quantum chromodynamic (QCD) field environment, hadronic rescattering, and collective expansion.

These stochastic influences suggest the need for a more refined characterization of the source, introducing the concept of a *stochastic scale*. This scale represents the effective range over which such random, chaotic forces act on the emitted bosons, thereby modifying the observed correlation pattern. In particular, the interplay between the thermal motion of particles, medium-induced fluctuations, and residual final-state interactions can lead to a correlation function whose shape and extracted parameters differ from those predicted by purely geometric models. In this framework, the stochastic scale is not merely a geometric size, but a dynamical quantity reflecting the degree of disorder and the strength of environmental perturbations in the hadronization zone.

Light hadrons, such as charged pions and kaons, are especially well suited for such studies. Their copious production rates in high-energy collisions and their bosonic nature make them ideal probes of BEC effects, while their relatively small masses ensure sensitivity to the fine details of the source evolution. Moreover, the comparison of BEC parameters across different collision systems, energies, and multiplicity classes provides insight into the scaling properties of the stochastic scale and its dependence on global event characteristics. Precise measurements of these correlations at modern facilities, such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), have opened the possibility of systematically disentangling geometric and stochastic contributions to the emitter properties.

The present work focuses on the theoretical interpretation of BEC measurements in terms of the stochastic scale of the light hadron emitter source. We aim to elucidate how this scale emerges from the interplay between the intrinsic geometry of the emission region and the dynamic fluctuations induced by the surrounding medium. By employing a quantum-statistical approach augmented with considerations from stochastic dynamics, we derive relations connecting experimentally accessible correlation parameters to the underlying stochastic scale. This allows for a more nuanced understanding of BEC data and provides a framework for interpreting current and future measurements in a consistent manner. The analysis presented here thus contributes to the broader effort of using femtoscopic observables as precision tools to probe the microscopic dynamics of high-energy hadronic collisions.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the role of Bose–Einstein correlations (BEC) in extracting information about the space–time structure and stochastic properties of the emitter source of light hadrons in high-energy collisions. By employing a framework that incorporates both quantum statistical effects and additional stochastic influences, we have extended the interpretation of correlation measurements beyond the conventional static or purely geometric source models. Our analysis emphasizes that the measured two-particle correlation function embodies not only the underlying quantum interference due to the symmetrization of identical boson wave functions, but also the dynamical and environmental factors that affect the coherence and localization of the produced particles.

The introduction of a stochastic scale parameter has proven to be a valuable refinement in the characterization of the emitter source. This parameter encapsulates the degree to which external random forces, medium fluctuations, and hadronization dynamics influence the spatial and temporal spread of the emission region. Its extraction from experimental data offers a complementary measure to the traditional “source radius” obtained from BEC fits. We have shown that the stochastic scale provides a more nuanced understanding of the interplay between coherent and incoherent emission processes and can signal variations in the hadronization environment across different collision systems and energies.

Our discussion has demonstrated that, within the adopted theoretical model, the stochastic scale is sensitive to both the temperature of the hadronic medium and the mass of the emitted bosons. This mass dependence, often overlooked in simplified treatments, becomes particularly relevant when comparing BEC results for pions, kaons, and other light mesons. The observed trend suggests that heavier bosons, being less affected by thermal motion, may exhibit smaller apparent stochastic scales, thereby reflecting a reduced influence of environmental randomness on their emission profiles. Conversely, for lighter particles, the stochastic effects can be more pronounced, leading to broader effective source distributions.

Furthermore, our findings indicate that the stochastic scale is not an entirely independent quantity from the conventional BEC parameters, but rather a complementary descriptor that can help disentangle different physical contributions to the correlation function. In particular, variations in the stochastic scale with collision energy or multiplicity may reveal changes in the microscopic structure of the emitting system, such as the onset of collective phenomena, modifications in the hadronization mechanism, or the degree of final-state interactions.

From a phenomenological standpoint, the simultaneous analysis of the geometric radius and the stochastic scale offers a richer picture of the emitter source. This dual characterization allows for a more consistent comparison between different experimental setups and theoretical models, and can help bridge the gap between femtoscopic measurements and the underlying dynamics of particle production. In this context, the stochastic scale emerges as a promising observable for probing the fine-grained structure of the hadron emission process, potentially serving as a diagnostic tool for the properties of the medium created in high-energy collisions.

In summary, the incorporation of stochastic effects into the study of Bose–Einstein correlations provides a deeper insight into the nature of the light hadron emitter source. By moving beyond purely geometric interpretations, we gain access to information about the dynamical and environmental influences shaping particle emission. Future experimental analyses that systematically extract both the emitter radius and the stochastic scale across a broad range of energies, particle species, and collision systems will be essential to fully exploit the potential of this approach and to refine our understanding of the femtoscopic structure of hadronic matter.

title: Two-jet astrosphere model: effect of azimuthal magnetic field
abstract: A two-jet model of the astrosphere is developed to investigate the dynamical influence of an azimuthal interstellar magnetic field on the global structure of a stellar wind interaction region. The study extends previous axisymmetric magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations by incorporating a purely azimuthal magnetic component in the stellar wind and examining its role in shaping outflow morphology. Numerical solutions of the steady-state, ideal MHD equations are obtained for a range of magnetic field strengths, characterized by the wind magnetization parameter. The results reveal that the azimuthal magnetic field produces a strong collimation effect along the stellar rotation axis, leading to the formation of two oppositely directed, high-velocity jets extending beyond the termination shock. Magnetic hoop stresses compress the plasma toward the axis, enhancing jet density and velocity, while the equatorial regions become depleted and broadened. Increasing field strength reduces the astrospheric size in the equatorial plane and increases the jet opening angle, with a transition from nearly spherical to strongly bipolar morphologies. Comparison with non-magnetized and poloidal field cases shows that the azimuthal configuration leads to more efficient focusing of the outflow and higher asymmetry between polar and equatorial directions. The model predictions are discussed in the context of observed bipolar structures around evolved stars and astrospheres of fast-rotating massive stars, suggesting that azimuthal magnetic fields of moderate strength can account for the observed jet-like morphologies without invoking additional collimation mechanisms. These findings highlight the importance of magnetic topology in determining the large-scale structure of astrospheres and provide a framework for interpreting current and future high-resolution observations.
introduction:
The interaction between a stellar wind and the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) gives rise to a complex astrospheric structure, governed by the interplay of plasma dynamics, magnetic fields, and radiative processes. In the simplest hydrodynamic picture, a star moving relative to the ISM produces a bow shock, a contact discontinuity, and a wind termination shock. However, the inclusion of magnetic fields—both stellar and interstellar—introduces additional anisotropies and structural features that cannot be captured by purely hydrodynamic models. Among these, the azimuthal component of the stellar magnetic field, arising naturally from stellar rotation, plays a particularly significant role in shaping the large-scale morphology of the astrosphere.

Previous studies have demonstrated that magnetized stellar winds can produce collimated outflows or jet-like structures along the star’s rotation axis, especially in the limit of a dominant azimuthal field. Such configurations may lead to a two-jet topology, in which the stellar wind is funneled into polar directions, while equatorial regions are compressed. This configuration alters the locations and shapes of the termination shock, astropause, and bow shock, and modifies the distribution of plasma parameters throughout the astrosphere. Understanding these effects is essential for interpreting observational signatures, including nonthermal radio emission, energetic neutral atom (ENA) fluxes, and far-UV structures observed around nearby astrospheres.

Despite these advances, the quantitative influence of the azimuthal magnetic field on global astrospheric geometry remains incompletely understood. In particular, the transition from quasi-spherical to two-jet configurations as a function of magnetic field strength and stellar wind parameters has not been fully explored. In this work, we employ a magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model of a stellar wind–ISM interaction to investigate how an azimuthal magnetic field modifies the morphology and internal structure of the astrosphere. We focus on identifying the conditions that give rise to two-jet structures and on quantifying the resulting changes in shock positions, flow patterns, and pressure distributions.
conclusion:
In this study, we have investigated the structure and dynamics of a two-jet astrosphere model in the presence of an azimuthal magnetic field, with the aim of assessing the role of magnetic effects on the global flow configuration. By incorporating the azimuthal magnetic component into the magnetohydrodynamic formulation and considering steady-state, axisymmetric solutions, we have been able to explore how the magnetic tension and pressure modify the morphology of the astrosphere and the properties of the jets.

Our results demonstrate that the azimuthal magnetic field exerts a significant collimating influence on the outflow, enhancing the stability and coherence of the jets over large distances from the central star. The magnetic pressure associated with the azimuthal component contributes to confining the plasma in the jet channels, reducing lateral expansion and mitigating instabilities that might otherwise disrupt the flow. This effect is particularly pronounced in regions where the magnetic energy density becomes comparable to or exceeds the kinetic energy density, leading to a more elongated and narrow jet structure.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the azimuthal field alters the pressure balance and shock structure within the astrosphere. The termination shock position and the shape of the astropause are modified, reflecting the redistribution of momentum and energy between the plasma and the magnetic field. The jets emerging along the symmetry axis are found to be faster and more collimated than in purely hydrodynamic models, while the surrounding astrosheath exhibits changes in density and temperature profiles consistent with enhanced magnetic confinement.

These findings suggest that for stars with sufficiently strong magnetic fields, the azimuthal component plays a decisive role in shaping the large-scale astrospheric environment. The two-jet configuration, stabilized and focused by magnetic effects, may have important implications for the transport of stellar wind material into the interstellar medium, as well as for the observational signatures of such systems in various wavelength regimes. Future work should extend this analysis to fully three-dimensional simulations, include realistic stellar rotation and wind anisotropies, and explore the consequences of time-dependent magnetic field variations. By doing so, a more comprehensive understanding of magnetically influenced astrospheres and their jets can be achieved, bridging the gap between theoretical models and observational constraints.

title: Radiatively induced Fermi scale and unification
abstract: We investigate a framework in which the electroweak (Fermi) scale emerges radiatively from a higher unification scale, rather than being set by fundamental parameters. Within a classically scale-invariant extension of the Standard Model embedded in a grand unified theory, quantum corrections dynamically generate the Fermi scale via the Coleman–Weinberg mechanism. The scalar sector features an enlarged symmetry, spontaneously broken at the unification scale, with the electroweak scale induced through vacuum misalignment. We analyse the renormalisation group evolution of couplings, ensuring perturbativity and gauge coupling unification, and explore constraints from current collider and precision data. Our results demonstrate that a naturally light Higgs and a stable hierarchy can be obtained without fine-tuning, offering a predictive connection between electroweak symmetry breaking and high-scale unification.
introduction:
The origin of the electroweak (EW) scale remains one of the central open questions in particle physics. Within the Standard Model (SM), the Higgs potential is parameterised by a dimensionful mass term whose magnitude must be finely tuned to reproduce the observed value of the Fermi scale, \( v \simeq 246 \) GeV. This hierarchy problem motivates the exploration of frameworks in which the EW scale emerges dynamically, potentially alleviating the need for unnatural parameter choices. Among the proposed mechanisms, radiative symmetry breaking à la Coleman–Weinberg offers an appealing avenue, whereby quantum corrections induce the vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field from a scale-invariant tree-level Lagrangian. In such scenarios, the Fermi scale can be generated radiatively from a more fundamental scale, opening the possibility of a natural connection to high-energy physics.

An equally compelling aspect of physics beyond the SM is the unification of gauge interactions. Grand Unified Theories (GUTs) provide an elegant framework in which the SM gauge couplings meet at a high scale, potentially linked to the scale of quantum gravity. However, conventional unification scenarios typically treat the EW scale as an independent input rather than a derived quantity. Embedding radiatively induced symmetry breaking into a unified theory raises the prospect of explaining the Fermi scale in terms of unified parameters, thereby addressing two structural features of the SM within a single framework.

In this work, we investigate models in which the Fermi scale arises radiatively in the context of gauge coupling unification. We analyse the dynamics of radiative breaking, its compatibility with unification constraints, and the resulting predictions for the Higgs sector and new physics thresholds. Our aim is to assess the viability of this unified radiative mechanism, identify its phenomenological signatures, and outline the conditions under which it can naturally reconcile the observed hierarchy between the EW and unification scales.
conclusion: In this work we have examined the possibility that the electroweak scale is not a fundamental input, but rather emerges radiatively from dynamics at a much higher unification scale. By embedding the Standard Model within a framework in which the Higgs sector is linked to new scalar degrees of freedom and additional gauge interactions, we have shown that the Fermi scale can be generated through quantum corrections, thereby alleviating the hierarchy problem. The analysis demonstrates that the required separation of scales can be achieved without severe fine-tuning, provided that the couplings satisfy perturbativity and stability constraints up to the unification point. Furthermore, we explored the implications for gauge coupling unification, finding that the radiatively induced Fermi scale is compatible with precise meeting of the couplings at high energy, potentially within a grand unified or extended symmetry context. This scenario offers a predictive framework in which low-energy observables, such as Higgs and vector boson masses, are correlated with high-scale parameters. Our results motivate further investigation into specific ultraviolet completions, their phenomenological signatures, and the role of radiative mechanisms in naturally connecting the electroweak and unification scales.

title: Study of Asymptotic Velocity in the Bondi-Hoyle Accretion Flows in the Domain of Kerr and 4-D Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet Gravities
abstract: We investigate the asymptotic velocity structure of relativistic Bondi–Hoyle accretion flows onto rotating black holes within the frameworks of Kerr geometry and four-dimensional Einstein–Gauss–Bonnet (EGB) gravity. Our analysis focuses on the steady-state, axisymmetric regime, where a uniform supersonic flow encounters the gravitational field of a compact object, leading to the formation of an accretion cone. We employ the relativistic hydrodynamic equations in each spacetime and derive the governing relations for the far-field velocity components, paying particular attention to the influence of black hole spin and the Gauss–Bonnet coupling parameter. The asymptotic velocity is examined in the limit where the radial coordinate greatly exceeds the gravitational radius, allowing a perturbative expansion around the uniform inflow state. In the Kerr case, frame-dragging effects introduce characteristic anisotropies in the velocity field, which are quantified for various spin parameters. In the 4-D EGB case, modifications to the spacetime curvature alter the gravitational focusing of streamlines, leading to distinctive signatures in the asymptotic velocity profile. We present analytical expressions in the weak-field approximation and complement them with numerical integrations extending into the nonlinear regime. Our results indicate that while both rotation and Gauss–Bonnet corrections modify the far-field flow, their imprints are separable in the asymptotic domain, providing a potential diagnostic for alternative gravity effects in high-energy astrophysical environments. The study contributes to a more complete understanding of accretion dynamics in modified gravity theories and offers a framework for interpreting future observational data on relativistic flows near rotating compact objects.
introduction:
Accretion processes play a central role in high-energy astrophysics, governing the growth of compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars, and influencing the energetic feedback into their surrounding environments. Among the various accretion scenarios, the Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton (BHL) model describes the steady-state accretion of matter onto a moving compact object from a uniform medium. This framework has been applied extensively to study astrophysical situations ranging from stellar-mass black holes in X-ray binaries to supermassive black holes traversing the interstellar medium. A key quantity in such flows is the asymptotic velocity of the accreting gas far from the gravitational influence of the compact object, which determines the accretion rate and the morphology of the flow.

While the original BHL theory was formulated in Newtonian gravity, modern applications require a general relativistic treatment, especially in the vicinity of black holes where strong-field effects become significant. In particular, rotating black holes described by the Kerr metric introduce frame-dragging and anisotropic gravitational effects that can substantially modify the accretion dynamics. The general relativistic extension of BHL accretion in Kerr spacetime has been the subject of several analytical and numerical studies, revealing deviations from the Schwarzschild case in terms of shock formation, accretion rate, and flow structure.

Beyond general relativity, alternative theories of gravity have been proposed to address fundamental issues such as the nature of singularities, the unification with quantum theory, and cosmological observations. Among these, the Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (EGB) theory represents a natural higher-curvature generalization of general relativity, originally motivated by low-energy limits of string theory. Although the Gauss-Bonnet term in four dimensions is topological and does not affect the field equations, recent proposals for a rescaled coupling in the limit \( D \to 4 \) have led to non-trivial modifications of black hole solutions. The resulting 4-D Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (4DEGB) black holes exhibit corrections to their spacetime geometry that can, in principle, be probed through astrophysical processes such as accretion.

The asymptotic velocity in relativistic BHL flows serves as an important diagnostic for understanding the interplay between gravity and hydrodynamics in different gravitational theories. A comparative study of Kerr and 4DEGB spacetimes can shed light on how rotation and higher-curvature corrections influence the large-scale flow properties, potentially leading to observational signatures distinguishable in high-energy astrophysical systems. In this work, we investigate the asymptotic velocity profiles for relativistic Bondi-Hoyle accretion in both Kerr and 4DEGB backgrounds, aiming to quantify the deviations introduced by the modified gravity effects and to explore their astrophysical relevance.
conclusion:
In this work, we have undertaken a comparative investigation of the asymptotic velocity profiles in Bondi–Hoyle accretion flows within the frameworks of Kerr spacetime and its extension to four-dimensional Einstein–Gauss–Bonnet (EGB) gravity. By formulating the hydrodynamical equations governing steady-state, axisymmetric accretion in these geometries, and implementing appropriate boundary conditions for supersonic flows far from the black hole, we have been able to extract the influence of spacetime rotation and higher-curvature corrections on the asymptotic behaviour of the inflowing matter.

Our analysis reveals that in the Kerr background, the asymptotic velocity is sensitive to both the black hole spin parameter and the inclination of the accretion flow with respect to the rotation axis. As expected, frame-dragging effects introduce anisotropies in the velocity field at large radii, with the magnitude of these deviations increasing for rapidly rotating black holes. The velocity field asymptotically approaches the uniform upstream value, but the approach is modulated by the angular momentum of the spacetime, producing measurable differences between prograde and retrograde flow configurations.

In the 4-D EGB scenario, where the Gauss–Bonnet coupling \(\alpha_{GB}\) encodes leading-order higher-curvature effects, we find additional modifications to the asymptotic velocity, even in the non-rotating limit. These corrections arise from the altered effective gravitational potential, which modifies the compression and acceleration of the inflowing gas. For rotating EGB black holes, the interplay between frame dragging and Gauss–Bonnet terms produces a richer parameter dependence: the asymptotic velocity can either increase or decrease relative to the Kerr case, depending on the sign and magnitude of \(\alpha_{GB}\), as well as on the spin parameter. This is particularly evident in the transonic transition region, whose structure influences the far-field velocity profile.

A key outcome of this study is the identification of scaling relations between the asymptotic velocity deficit (relative to the upstream velocity) and the black hole parameters in both gravitational theories. In Kerr spacetime, the deficit grows approximately linearly with spin for moderate values, whereas in EGB gravity, the dependence on \(\alpha_{GB}\) is non-linear and can partially offset or enhance the spin-induced effects. This suggests that precise measurements of asymptotic velocity profiles in astrophysical accretion flows could, in principle, serve as probes of both rotation and higher-curvature corrections, provided other environmental factors are controlled.

Our results also highlight the robustness of the Bondi–Hoyle formalism in accommodating modifications to the underlying gravitational theory. The structure of the governing equations remains formally similar, but the metric functions, and hence the effective gravitational potential, encode the specific features of Kerr and EGB geometries. This allows for a unified treatment, facilitating direct comparison between different theories. Moreover, the asymptotic velocity emerges as a relatively clean observable, less contaminated by near-horizon microphysics, and thus potentially more accessible to modelling in large-scale numerical simulations and observations.

Looking ahead, it will be important to extend this work beyond the idealised, steady-state, axisymmetric assumptions adopted here. Incorporating magnetic fields, turbulence, radiative processes, and realistic equations of state may reveal additional interplay between gravitational effects and fluid microphysics. Furthermore, exploring the parameter space of EGB gravity in the context of strong-field tests, such as those enabled by very-long-baseline interferometry of black hole shadows or high-resolution spectroscopy of accretion flows, could provide complementary constraints. In summary, the comparative study presented here underscores the diagnostic potential of asymptotic velocity measurements in accretion flows as a means to discriminate between general relativity and its higher-curvature extensions, while offering new insights into the coupled dynamics of matter and spacetime.

title: Throughput Optimal Routing in Overlay Networks
abstract: We investigate the problem of throughput optimal routing in overlay networks, where only a subset of nodes can perform dynamic routing while the remaining nodes forward traffic along predetermined physical paths. Such constraints arise naturally in practical deployments where legacy infrastructure coexists with controllable overlay nodes. We model the system as a constrained queuing network and develop a policy that jointly exploits overlay routing flexibility and underlying path structures. The proposed algorithm, based on backpressure principles adapted to the overlay setting, is proven to achieve the maximum possible throughput region under the given constraints. Our analysis characterizes the impact of overlay node placement and topology on performance, and demonstrates robustness to stochastic traffic variations. Simulation results on diverse network topologies validate the theoretical findings, showing significant throughput gains over conventional shortest-path routing. This work provides a foundation for designing efficient routing strategies in partially controllable network environments.
introduction:
The rapid proliferation of data-intensive applications and services has placed unprecedented demands on communication networks. From cloud computing and video streaming to large-scale data analytics and the Internet of Things (IoT), modern networked systems must deliver ever-increasing throughput while maintaining low latency and high reliability. In parallel, the complexity of network infrastructures has grown, incorporating heterogeneous technologies, dynamic topologies, and diverse traffic patterns. In such environments, efficient routing strategies—mechanisms for determining the paths that data packets take through a network—are crucial to ensuring that available resources are utilized effectively and that performance objectives are met.

Traditional routing protocols, such as those employed in the Internet Protocol (IP) layer, are generally designed for static or slowly varying topologies and rely on shortest-path heuristics or precomputed routing tables. While these approaches have been successful in large-scale deployment, they often fail to fully exploit available network capacity under dynamic and bursty traffic conditions. In particular, when traffic demands exceed what can be supported along predetermined paths, congestion arises, leading to increased delays and packet losses. This limitation motivates the study of *throughput optimal routing*, i.e., routing policies that can sustain the maximum possible traffic load that the network can theoretically support, as characterized by its capacity region.

The concept of throughput optimality is well established in the literature on queueing networks and stochastic control. A throughput optimal policy ensures network stability under any arrival rate vector that lies within the network’s capacity region, without requiring prior knowledge of traffic statistics. One of the most celebrated results in this area is the backpressure routing algorithm, introduced by Tassiulas and Ephremides, which uses queue differentials to dynamically select routes that maximize throughput. Backpressure routing has been shown to be throughput optimal in a variety of settings, including wireless ad hoc networks, but it has also been criticized for potentially incurring high delays and requiring significant coordination overhead.

Overlay networks have emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing the functionality and performance of underlying physical networks without requiring changes to their infrastructure. In an overlay network, a set of participating nodes—often referred to as overlay nodes or peers—are connected by virtual links that correspond to paths in the underlying network. Overlay routing protocols can be deployed at the application layer or in dedicated software modules, enabling rapid innovation and specialized functionality, such as enhanced fault tolerance, content distribution, or security. The flexibility of overlays makes them an attractive platform for implementing advanced routing algorithms, including those that aim for throughput optimality.

However, achieving throughput optimal routing in overlay networks presents unique challenges. Unlike traditional networks, overlay nodes may have only partial visibility into the underlying topology and may not control the routing decisions made at intermediate physical nodes. The paths corresponding to overlay links may share underlying resources, leading to complex interactions between flows and potential bottlenecks. Furthermore, overlay networks are often deployed over wide-area infrastructures with heterogeneous link capacities and latencies, adding further variability to performance. These constraints necessitate the development of routing algorithms that can operate effectively with limited information, adapt to dynamic conditions, and still guarantee throughput optimality.

Recent research has begun to explore the design of throughput optimal routing policies tailored to overlay environments. One line of work adapts backpressure principles to the overlay setting, using queue backlogs at overlay nodes to guide decisions about which overlay links to use for forwarding traffic. Another approach leverages multi-path routing, splitting traffic across multiple overlay paths to balance load and avoid congestion. These methods must contend with the fact that the relationship between overlay link usage and physical resource consumption may be opaque, requiring estimation or indirect measurement. Moreover, the control timescales in overlays may be constrained by application-level protocols and transport-layer dynamics, influencing the responsiveness and stability of routing algorithms.

The importance of throughput optimal routing in overlays is underscored by the increasing reliance on overlay architectures in practice. Content delivery networks (CDNs), virtual private networks (VPNs), peer-to-peer systems, and emerging software-defined overlay fabrics in data centers all exemplify scenarios where overlay routing decisions directly impact performance. In these contexts, the ability to sustain high throughput under varying traffic loads can translate into better quality of service, more efficient resource utilization, and improved user experience. At the same time, overlays offer a testbed for deploying sophisticated routing algorithms incrementally, without requiring wholesale changes to entrenched networking infrastructure.

This paper contributes to the growing body of work on throughput optimal routing by focusing specifically on the overlay network setting. We investigate the fundamental limits of achievable throughput given the constraints of overlay operation, and we propose routing strategies that approach these limits in a scalable and implementable manner. Our work builds on the theoretical foundations of dynamic routing in queueing networks, adapting and extending them to account for the layered structure and partial observability inherent in overlays. We also address practical considerations, such as the measurement of congestion signals, the coordination of routing decisions among distributed overlay nodes, and the trade-offs between throughput, delay, and implementation complexity.

By uniting rigorous performance guarantees with the operational realities of overlay deployment, our study aims to bridge the gap between theory and practice in high-performance routing. The results presented here have implications not only for overlay networks in the conventional sense but also for any layered or virtualized networking environment where logical connectivity is decoupled from the physical substrate. In the sections that follow, we formalize the overlay network model, characterize its capacity region, develop throughput optimal routing policies, and evaluate their performance through analysis and simulation. Through this exploration, we aim to advance the understanding of how to design and implement routing mechanisms that can fully realize the throughput potential of modern networked systems.
conclusion: This work investigated throughput optimal routing strategies in overlay networks, addressing the challenges posed by partial control over network nodes and links. By formulating the problem within a rigorous analytical framework, we demonstrated that carefully designed dynamic routing policies can achieve throughput optimality despite underlying constraints. Simulation results validated the theoretical guarantees, showing significant performance gains over baseline approaches. Our findings highlight the importance of exploiting both topological knowledge and real-time traffic information. Future research may extend these methods to accommodate stochastic link failures, heterogeneous quality-of-service requirements, and scalable distributed implementations.

title: Deep Domain Adaptation for Detecting Bomb Craters in Aerial Images
abstract: Detecting bomb craters in aerial imagery is critical for post-conflict assessment, environmental monitoring, and historical analysis. However, variations in sensor type, resolution, and environmental conditions hinder the generalization of detection models across domains. This work proposes a deep domain adaptation framework that leverages labeled source-domain data and unlabeled target-domain imagery to improve crater detection performance in unseen environments. Our approach integrates convolutional feature extraction with adversarial domain alignment to minimize distributional discrepancies, while a crater-specific attention module enhances the representation of subtle circular depressions. We evaluate the method on multiple aerial datasets covering diverse geographic and temporal contexts, demonstrating superior detection accuracy compared to baseline CNN and domain-adaptation techniques. Results show that our model maintains robust performance despite significant domain shifts, reducing false detections in cluttered terrains. This study highlights the potential of deep domain adaptation for reliable, scalable damage assessment using heterogeneous aerial imagery sources.
introduction:
The detection of bomb craters in aerial imagery is a critical task in post-conflict assessment, humanitarian demining, and forensic analysis of conflict zones. Accurate identification and mapping of such craters can provide valuable information for estimating the intensity and spatial distribution of bombardments, assessing damage to infrastructure and ecosystems, and supporting legal investigations into violations of international humanitarian law. Traditionally, crater detection has relied on manual annotation or classical image processing techniques, which are often labor-intensive, time-consuming, and highly sensitive to variations in lighting, scale, and terrain conditions.

Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved object detection and semantic segmentation in remote sensing imagery. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and their variants have demonstrated remarkable performance across a variety of aerial image analysis tasks, including building footprint extraction, vehicle detection, and land-cover classification. However, the application of deep learning to bomb crater detection faces unique challenges. One of the most pressing is the scarcity of labeled training data from target regions. Bombardments occur in geographically distinct and often inaccessible areas, making it difficult to collect large-scale annotated datasets that capture the full diversity of crater appearances. Furthermore, differences in sensor characteristics, resolution, atmospheric conditions, and landscape features between available source datasets and the target domain can significantly degrade the performance of models trained in a conventional supervised setting.

Domain adaptation offers a promising solution to this problem by enabling the transfer of knowledge from a source domain, where labeled data is abundant, to a target domain with little or no labeled data. Deep domain adaptation techniques, in particular, leverage feature alignment, adversarial learning, and domain-invariant representation learning to mitigate the adverse effects of domain shift. In the context of bomb crater detection, these methods can help bridge the gap between synthetic or geographically disparate datasets and real-world target imagery.

This work investigates deep domain adaptation approaches for the detection of bomb craters in aerial images, with the aim of improving generalization across differing geographic and environmental conditions. By integrating domain adaptation into the deep learning pipeline, we seek to develop robust detection models that maintain high accuracy despite substantial variations in input data distributions, ultimately supporting more effective post-conflict analysis and humanitarian response.
conclusion:
This work has presented a deep domain adaptation framework for the detection of bomb craters in aerial imagery, addressing the critical challenge of transferring knowledge from labeled source domains to unlabeled or sparsely labeled target domains with distinct visual characteristics. By leveraging adversarial feature alignment and domain-invariant representation learning, the proposed approach successfully mitigates the performance degradation typically caused by variations in imaging conditions, geographic contexts, and sensor modalities. Experimental evaluations on multiple aerial datasets demonstrated that our method consistently outperforms conventional supervised baselines and non-adaptive deep learning models, achieving higher detection accuracy and robustness across diverse target domains.

The ability to adapt to new operational environments without extensive manual annotation is particularly important in conflict monitoring and post-strike assessment scenarios, where timely and reliable information can support humanitarian relief, reconstruction planning, and accountability efforts. Our results show that incorporating domain adaptation not only improves detection rates but also reduces false positives, thereby enhancing the practical utility of automated crater recognition systems. Furthermore, visual inspections and quantitative analyses confirmed that the learned feature space effectively bridges domain gaps, allowing the network to generalize to unseen regions and imaging conditions.

While the proposed framework demonstrates strong potential, several avenues for future research remain. Enhancing the interpretability of the learned representations could aid expert validation and foster trust in automated assessments. Integrating multi-modal data, such as synthetic aperture radar or hyperspectral imagery, may further improve detection in challenging conditions, including cloud cover or low-light environments. Additionally, exploring semi-supervised and continual adaptation strategies could enable systems to incrementally refine their performance as new data becomes available in dynamic operational contexts.

In summary, this study underscores the value of deep domain adaptation for reliable bomb crater detection in aerial images, offering a scalable solution to the scarcity of labeled target-domain data and the variability of real-world conditions. By advancing the adaptability and accuracy of automated detection systems, our approach contributes to the broader goal of developing robust, data-efficient tools for remote sensing applications in security, humanitarian, and environmental monitoring domains.

title: Planning with Submodular Objective Functions
abstract: We investigate planning problems where the objective function is submodular, a common structure in information gathering, sensor placement, and active learning. Submodularity captures the diminishing returns property, enabling efficient approximation algorithms with provable guarantees. We present a unified framework for planning under submodular criteria, encompassing deterministic and stochastic settings. Our approach leverages greedy and adaptive strategies, extending classical results to accommodate complex constraints such as budgets, paths, and uncertainty. We provide theoretical bounds on performance and demonstrate empirical benefits on diverse domains. Results indicate that exploiting submodularity yields scalable, near-optimal planning solutions in high-dimensional, resource-constrained environments.
introduction:
Planning problems arise in a wide range of domains, from robotics and sensor networks to environmental monitoring, logistics, and information gathering. In many of these settings, an agent or a team of agents must select a sequence of actions, locations, or tasks in order to achieve a goal while respecting resource constraints such as time, energy, or budget. A central challenge in these problems is to design planning strategies that make the best possible use of limited resources while accounting for uncertainty, dynamic environments, and potentially large decision spaces. In recent years, a unifying perspective has emerged in which the quality of a plan can be quantified by a set function that measures the utility or coverage of the chosen actions, and where the key structural property of this function is *submodularity*.

A set function \( f: 2^V \to \mathbb{R} \) defined on a finite ground set \(V\) is called submodular if it exhibits the property of diminishing returns: for every \( A \subseteq B \subseteq V \) and every \( s \in V \setminus B \), the marginal gain from adding \(s\) to \(A\) is at least as large as the marginal gain from adding \(s\) to \(B\). This property captures the intuitive idea that the benefit of acquiring additional resources, information, or coverage decreases as one’s existing set grows. Many objective functions encountered in planning naturally exhibit submodularity. For example, in sensor placement for environmental monitoring, the informativeness of a new sensor location often decreases as more sensors are deployed; in active learning, the value of labeling a new data point diminishes as the labeled dataset grows; and in path planning for data collection, the incremental information gain from visiting an additional location depends on which locations have already been visited.

The significance of submodularity in planning stems from two key facts. First, the property enables the design of efficient approximation algorithms with strong theoretical guarantees. In the classical setting of selecting a subset of items subject to a cardinality constraint, a simple greedy algorithm that iteratively adds the item with the largest marginal gain achieves a \((1 - 1/e)\)-approximation to the optimal objective value, and this bound is tight. Second, many more complex combinatorial constraints—such as matroid constraints, knapsack constraints, or path constraints—can be incorporated into the submodular optimization framework, often with analogous approximation results. This combination of modeling power and algorithmic tractability makes submodular optimization a compelling tool for planning in high-dimensional, uncertain, and resource-limited environments.

Despite these advantages, planning with submodular objective functions presents several important challenges. In many practical applications, the set of feasible plans is not simply the collection of all subsets of a ground set; instead, feasibility may be determined by temporal ordering, spatial connectivity, or other combinatorial structures. In robotic exploration, for example, a feasible plan corresponds to a path through a physical environment that satisfies motion constraints. In such settings, the problem becomes one of optimizing a submodular function over a structured domain, such as the set of walks in a graph, which is in general computationally more demanding than unconstrained subset selection. Moreover, in real-world deployments, the objective function may not be known in advance but must be estimated from noisy measurements or learned online, introducing an additional layer of uncertainty.

Another practical consideration is that many planning problems require adaptive decision-making, in which actions are selected sequentially based on observations obtained during execution. The notion of *adaptive submodularity*, an extension of submodularity to stochastic settings, provides a framework for analyzing greedy strategies in such adaptive contexts, yielding performance guarantees analogous to the non-adaptive case. For instance, in active information gathering with uncertain outcomes, an adaptive greedy policy that selects the next action to maximize the expected marginal gain can be provably near-optimal when the objective is adaptively submodular. This theory has found applications in domains such as search-and-rescue, medical diagnosis, and adaptive sensing.

The growing interest in submodular planning has led to a rich body of work on specialized algorithms, approximation bounds, and practical heuristics. Researchers have investigated techniques for accelerating greedy selection through lazy evaluations, exploiting structure in the objective function for scalable computation, and integrating submodular optimization with probabilistic inference to handle uncertainty. Other work has examined the interplay between submodularity and other problem properties, such as monotonicity, curvature, or decomposability, to refine approximation guarantees or enable distributed implementation.

At the same time, there remain open questions at the intersection of theory and practice. In particular, bridging the gap between the elegant guarantees of submodular optimization and the complex realities of planning in dynamic, partially observable environments is an ongoing challenge. Issues such as non-monotonicity, where adding elements can sometimes decrease utility, require more sophisticated algorithms and analysis. Similarly, multi-agent settings introduce coordination constraints that complicate the optimization landscape, and online or streaming scenarios demand algorithms that operate under tight computational and memory budgets.

In this paper, we investigate planning problems in which the objective function is submodular and the feasible set of plans is shaped by combinatorial constraints arising from the application domain. Our goals are twofold: to develop algorithmic strategies that leverage submodularity for efficient and effective planning, and to provide theoretical and empirical evaluations of these strategies in representative scenarios. We build on the foundational theory of submodular optimization, extending it to accommodate structured plan spaces and, where applicable, adaptive decision-making. By doing so, we aim to contribute both to the theoretical understanding of submodular planning and to its practical deployment in real-world systems.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing relevant background on submodular functions, their properties, and existing optimization results. We then formalize the planning problems of interest and describe the combinatorial constraints that define feasible plans. Next, we present our proposed algorithms, along with analyses of their approximation performance and computational complexity. We evaluate these methods on synthetic and real-world datasets from domains such as environmental monitoring and robotic exploration. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future research on planning with submodular objectives, highlighting directions for extending the framework to richer and more challenging settings.
conclusion: In this work, we examined planning problems where the objective function exhibits submodularity, a property that naturally captures diminishing returns and arises in numerous real-world applications. We analyzed algorithmic approaches that exploit this structure, highlighting both theoretical guarantees and practical performance. Our results demonstrate that leveraging submodularity enables efficient approximation algorithms with provable bounds, even in complex planning domains. Empirical evaluations confirm the effectiveness of these methods, showing substantial improvements over baselines that do not exploit submodular properties. Furthermore, we discussed extensions to settings with additional constraints and uncertainty, illustrating the broad applicability of our framework. Overall, our findings underscore the value of integrating submodular optimization principles into planning, offering a principled pathway to scalable, high-quality solutions in diverse domains such as robotics, sensor placement, and information gathering, and motivating further exploration of submodular planning paradigms.

title: Simulation-guided Beam Search for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) leverages deep learning to tackle discrete optimization problems, yet its performance often depends on the efficiency of search strategies during inference. Beam search is a widely used decoding method for sequence-based NCO models, but conventional implementations may waste computational resources on suboptimal candidate solutions. We propose a simulation-guided beam search (SGBS) framework that integrates fast rollout simulations into the beam expansion process to more accurately estimate future rewards. At each step, candidate partial solutions are evaluated through lightweight simulations, enabling the pruning of low-potential beams and the prioritization of promising trajectories. This approach balances exploration and exploitation while keeping computational overhead manageable. We apply SGBS to several canonical NCO tasks, including the traveling salesman problem and vehicle routing problem, demonstrating consistent improvements over baseline beam search and sampling-based methods. Experiments reveal that SGBS achieves superior solution quality under fixed inference budgets, highlighting the potential of simulation-guided strategies for enhancing neural combinatorial optimization performance.
introduction:
Combinatorial optimization problems are ubiquitous in operations research, computer science, and engineering, arising in domains such as logistics, telecommunications, scheduling, and circuit design. Many of these problems, including the traveling salesman problem (TSP), vehicle routing problem (VRP), and job shop scheduling, are NP-hard, rendering exact solutions computationally impractical for large instances. Classical approaches, such as branch-and-bound, dynamic programming, and integer linear programming, often rely on sophisticated heuristics, relaxations, or problem-specific insights to prune the search space and improve scalability. While these methods can yield high-quality solutions for structured instances, their performance may degrade on large-scale or highly irregular problem instances, and adapting them to new problem classes often requires substantial manual effort.

Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep neural networks, have inspired a new line of research termed neural combinatorial optimization (NCO). In NCO, models are trained to directly construct or guide the search for high-quality solutions, often learning heuristics from large datasets and generalizing to unseen instances. Sequence-to-sequence architectures, attention mechanisms, and reinforcement learning have been leveraged to produce competitive results on canonical combinatorial optimization problems. For example, pointer networks and transformer-based policies have been used to sequentially generate solutions, while policy gradient and actor–critic methods facilitate learning from delayed rewards. These approaches have demonstrated the potential for data-driven methods to complement or even surpass handcrafted heuristics in certain settings.

Despite promising progress, neural methods for combinatorial optimization face several challenges. First, purely learned construction policies may produce suboptimal solutions for difficult instances, particularly when generalization to distributions different from the training data is required. Second, while neural policies can be combined with classical search algorithms to improve solution quality, naively integrating them into search procedures such as beam search or Monte Carlo tree search can be computationally expensive or fail to fully exploit the model’s predictive capabilities. Third, existing NCO approaches often lack mechanisms to refine or validate intermediate solutions during the search, leading to inefficiencies and missed opportunities for improvement.

Beam search is a widely used heuristic search algorithm that maintains a fixed-size set of the most promising partial solutions at each step, expanding them in parallel. In the context of NCO, beam search can be guided by a learned policy to prioritize expansions that are likely to lead to high-quality complete solutions. However, the standard beam search procedure relies solely on policy scores for ranking partial solutions, without explicitly considering how these partial solutions might evolve into complete solutions through simulation or lookahead. This limitation can cause the search to focus on locally promising but globally suboptimal branches, especially in problems with deceptive reward landscapes or long-horizon dependencies.

To address these challenges, we propose a simulation-guided beam search framework for neural combinatorial optimization. Our key idea is to augment the beam search process with Monte Carlo–style simulations from partial solutions to complete solutions, using either learned models or fast heuristics to estimate the potential quality of each branch. By integrating simulation-based value estimates into the beam selection criterion, our approach balances the exploitation of high-probability expansions suggested by the policy with the exploration of branches that may yield better final solutions than their immediate scores indicate. This hybridization leverages the strengths of both learned policies and simulation-based evaluation, enabling more informed pruning and selection during the search.

The proposed framework is flexible and can be applied to various neural architectures and combinatorial optimization problems. During training, the neural policy learns to generate promising partial solutions, while the simulation component is tuned to efficiently approximate their completion quality. At inference time, the simulation-guided beam search dynamically allocates computational resources to explore the most promising regions of the search space, improving solution quality without incurring prohibitive search costs. Moreover, the simulation component can exploit problem-specific heuristics, domain knowledge, or lightweight learned value functions, allowing the method to adapt to problem characteristics and computational constraints.

We evaluate our approach on benchmark instances of the TSP and VRP, comparing against both classical heuristics and state-of-the-art neural baselines. Experimental results demonstrate that simulation-guided beam search consistently improves upon standard beam search guided solely by policy scores, yielding higher-quality solutions with modest additional computational overhead. The approach shows particular advantages on larger problem instances and in settings where the distribution of test instances differs from that of the training data, highlighting its robustness and generalization capabilities.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions: (1) we introduce a novel simulation-guided beam search framework that integrates Monte Carlo–style lookahead into neural combinatorial optimization; (2) we develop an effective combination of learned policies and simulation-based value estimation to guide search more intelligently; and (3) we empirically validate the benefits of our approach across multiple problem domains and scales. By bridging the gap between learned heuristics and simulation-based planning, our method advances the state of the art in neural approaches to combinatorial optimization and opens new directions for combining machine learning with classical search techniques.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced a simulation-guided beam search framework for neural combinatorial optimization, integrating predictive modeling with search-based refinement to improve solution quality. By leveraging simulations to estimate the downstream impact of partial solutions, our method effectively prioritizes promising candidates within the beam, reducing the risk of premature convergence to suboptimal solutions. Experimental results across benchmark combinatorial problems demonstrate consistent gains over conventional neural decoding strategies, including standard beam search and greedy approaches, particularly in complex instances where solution quality is sensitive to early decision errors. The proposed approach maintains computational efficiency while enabling more informed exploration of the search space, highlighting the value of combining learned heuristics with search-time evaluation. Beyond the demonstrated tasks, the framework is adaptable to a broad class of discrete optimization problems where neural models serve as policy generators. Future work will explore tighter integration of simulation models with neural architectures and extensions to stochastic or dynamic problem settings.

title: Inferring Unusual Crowd Events From Mobile Phone Call Detail Records
abstract: Understanding unusual crowd dynamics is critical for applications ranging from urban planning to public safety. This paper presents a novel approach for detecting and characterizing atypical crowd events by leveraging large-scale mobile phone Call Detail Records (CDRs). Unlike conventional crowd monitoring methods that require dedicated sensing infrastructure, our method exploits the pervasive coverage of cellular networks to infer collective human mobility patterns in real time. We first preprocess anonymized CDRs to extract spatiotemporal distributions of user activity, constructing dynamic mobility networks that capture the movement and congregation of individuals across urban spaces. We then introduce an event detection framework that identifies deviations from learned baseline patterns using statistical anomaly detection and clustering techniques. Our approach accounts for varying temporal resolutions, daily and weekly periodicities, and location-specific activity levels to reduce false positives caused by routine fluctuations. We evaluate our method using several months of CDR data from a large metropolitan area, demonstrating its ability to detect both planned events, such as concerts and sports matches, and unplanned incidents, including transportation disruptions and emergency situations. Comparative analysis against ground truth event logs and social media reports shows high precision and recall in identifying unusual gatherings.
