The analysis assumes a fixed number of latent states and first-order Markov transitions, which may not capture more complex dynamics. In addition, the model relies on available crash data, which may be subject to reporting biases or measurement errors. Future research could extend the approach by exploring higher-order state dependence, incorporating spatial correlations, or integrating real-time traffic and weather data to improve state identification.

Overall, the study demonstrates that the Markov switching multinomial logit model is a valuable tool for understanding the complex and evolving nature of accident injury severities. By capturing latent temporal heterogeneity, it offers both methodological advancement and practical insights for enhancing roadway safety and reducing the societal burden of traffic crashes.

title: Vocal effort modeling in neural TTS for improving the intelligibility of synthetic speech in noise
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of vocal effort modeling into neural text-to-speech (TTS) systems to enhance the intelligibility of synthetic speech in noisy listening environments. Conventional neural TTS models are typically optimized for naturalness in quiet conditions, resulting in degraded comprehension under background noise. We propose a method for conditioning a neural TTS model on a vocal effort parameter derived from recordings of human speech produced at varying effort levels. The model learns to adjust prosodic and spectral characteristics, such as pitch, intensity, and formant dispersion, to emulate Lombard-like speech adaptations. Objective evaluations using intelligibility metrics and subjective listening tests in simulated noise demonstrate that speech synthesized with moderate to high vocal effort significantly outperforms baseline TTS in word recognition accuracy without substantial loss of perceived naturalness. Our findings highlight the potential of explicit vocal effort control in neural TTS as a practical approach to improving speech robustness, with applications in assistive technologies, public announcement systems, and human–machine interaction.
introduction:
The growing adoption of text-to-speech (TTS) systems in diverse applications, ranging from virtual assistants and navigation systems to assistive technologies, has intensified the demand for synthetic speech that remains intelligible under challenging acoustic conditions. While modern neural TTS architectures, such as those based on sequence-to-sequence models with attention or non-autoregressive paradigms, have achieved remarkable naturalness and expressiveness in quiet environments, their intelligibility often deteriorates in the presence of background noise. This limitation poses a substantial barrier to deployment in real-world scenarios, where listeners may encounter speech in noisy streets, crowded public spaces, or while driving. Improving the robustness of synthetic speech to noise remains an open challenge that bridges speech synthesis, speech perception, and human communication research.

In natural spoken communication, talkers instinctively adapt their vocal effort to adverse listening conditions, a phenomenon commonly referred to as the Lombard effect. This adaptation manifests through systematic changes in acoustic and prosodic characteristics, such as increased vocal intensity, spectral tilt modification, formant shifts, and temporal adjustments. These modifications serve to enhance the audibility and intelligibility of speech for listeners in noisy environments. In contrast, most current neural TTS systems generate speech with a fixed vocal effort profile, optimized for naturalness in quiet but not for robustness in noise. Consequently, synthetic speech lacks the adaptive qualities that human speakers employ to maintain communication effectiveness in adverse conditions.

Previous work on improving synthetic speech intelligibility in noise has explored techniques such as spectral shaping, dynamic range compression, and explicit modeling of Lombard speech. Some approaches have incorporated signal processing post-filters, while others have attempted to retrain synthesis models on speech recorded under noisy conditions. However, these methods often face trade-offs between intelligibility gains and degradation of perceived naturalness, or require extensive Lombard speech corpora that are costly and time-consuming to collect. Moreover, many of these techniques treat vocal effort adaptation as a binary condition—either “normal” or “Lombard”—rather than as a continuous, controllable parameter reflecting the nuanced gradations of human vocal effort.

Recent advances in controllable neural TTS provide an opportunity to address this gap through explicit vocal effort modeling. By parameterizing vocal effort as a continuous dimension within the synthesis process, it becomes possible to generate speech with adaptive acoustic-prosodic characteristics that are optimized for intelligibility in varying noise conditions, while preserving naturalness. Such an approach aligns with the broader trend toward expressive and context-aware speech synthesis, where control over speaking style, emotion, and other paralinguistic features is increasingly integrated into neural architectures.

This work investigates the modeling of vocal effort in neural TTS as a means to improve the intelligibility of synthetic speech in noise. We propose a framework that learns a vocal effort representation from natural speech data and integrates it into a state-of-the-art TTS model, enabling fine-grained control over the effort level during synthesis. The contributions of this study are threefold: (1) the design of a neural TTS system with explicit vocal effort control; (2) an evaluation of its impact on intelligibility across different noise conditions; and (3) an analysis of the trade-off between intelligibility and perceived naturalness. Through this research, we aim to bring synthetic speech closer to the adaptive capabilities of human speakers, enhancing its utility in real-world noisy environments.
conclusion:
This work investigated the integration of vocal effort modeling into neural text-to-speech (TTS) systems with the aim of enhancing the intelligibility of synthetic speech under noisy listening conditions. By explicitly conditioning the synthesis process on vocal effort parameters derived from human speech production, we enabled the system to generate speech with adaptive prosodic and spectral characteristics that more closely resemble natural communicative strategies in adverse environments. Objective intelligibility measures and subjective listening tests consistently demonstrated that the proposed approach yields significant improvements over baseline neural TTS, particularly in moderate to high noise levels.  

The results indicate that modeling vocal effort not only enhances signal robustness but also preserves naturalness, suggesting that the neural TTS can dynamically balance clarity and expressiveness. The findings further highlight the importance of incorporating speech production principles into data-driven synthesis frameworks, bridging the gap between acoustic modeling and perceptual needs.  

Future work should explore finer-grained control of vocal effort parameters, potentially incorporating listener-specific adaptation to further optimize intelligibility. Extending the evaluation to diverse noise types and real-world communication scenarios would also validate the generalizability of the method. Overall, the study demonstrates that vocal effort modeling is a promising and effective strategy for improving the practical usability of neural TTS in noisy environments, with implications for assistive technologies, public announcement systems, and human–machine interaction in challenging acoustic conditions.

title: Tree Boosted Varying Coefficient Models
abstract: We propose a novel methodology that integrates varying coefficient models with gradient tree boosting to capture complex, nonlinear effect modification in high-dimensional data. Our approach, Tree Boosted Varying Coefficient Models (TBVCM), represents coefficient functions using ensembles of regression trees, enabling flexible modeling of interactions between covariates and effect modifiers. The boosting framework facilitates automatic variable selection, regularization, and scalability to large datasets. We establish theoretical properties, including consistency under mild conditions, and develop efficient algorithms for estimation. Simulation studies demonstrate superior predictive accuracy and interpretability compared to existing methods. Applications to real-world datasets illustrate the capacity of TBVCM to uncover nuanced, data-driven patterns in heterogeneous relationships.
introduction:
In many scientific and applied domains, the relationship between predictors and a response variable is rarely static. Rather than exerting a uniform influence across all observations, covariates often have effects that change with respect to other variables, such as time, spatial location, or environmental conditions. Varying coefficient models (VCMs) were introduced as a flexible framework to capture such dynamic relationships, allowing regression coefficients to vary smoothly as functions of effect modifiers. This approach has found widespread use in disciplines as diverse as biostatistics, econometrics, environmental science, and engineering, where understanding how effects evolve is critical for accurate modeling and interpretation.

Conventional VCMs are typically estimated using smoothing techniques, such as local polynomial fitting, spline bases, or kernel methods, which impose smoothness constraints and often assume relatively simple functional forms for the coefficient trajectories. While these methods are effective in low-dimensional settings and when the functional relationships are not overly complex, they can struggle when faced with high-dimensional predictors, complex nonlinearities, or intricate interactions between variables. Furthermore, such approaches frequently require careful manual specification of tuning parameters and basis functions, and their performance can degrade if the underlying coefficient functions exhibit abrupt changes or heterogeneous patterns across the covariate space.

In parallel, machine learning methods, and in particular tree-based ensemble models, have emerged as powerful nonparametric tools for predictive modeling. Gradient boosting machines (GBMs), random forests, and related algorithms excel at capturing complex nonlinearities, high-order interactions, and heterogeneous effects without requiring explicit parametric assumptions. Tree-based learners partition the predictor space into regions within which simple models—often constants—are fit, and ensemble methods aggregate many such trees to improve predictive accuracy and robustness. While these models have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in numerous predictive tasks, their interpretability in terms of varying coefficients and effect modification is less direct, as they do not naturally decompose the response into predictor-specific varying effects.

Recent methodological developments have sought to bridge the gap between statistical models that emphasize interpretability, such as VCMs, and machine learning approaches that prioritize predictive accuracy and flexibility. One line of research has focused on integrating structured model forms into machine learning algorithms, enabling them to retain a degree of interpretability while benefiting from the adaptability of nonparametric fitting. For example, partially linear tree-based models and generalized additive models with boosted components have been proposed to capture certain structured effects while modeling residual complexity with ensembles. However, these approaches often treat the varying coefficient structure in a limited or ad hoc manner, without fully integrating it into the core of the learning algorithm.

The idea of a tree boosted varying coefficient model is to combine the interpretability and structure of VCMs with the flexibility and predictive power of gradient boosting. In this framework, each coefficient function in the VCM is itself modeled using an ensemble of regression trees, trained via boosting to capture complex patterns in the effect modifiers. Rather than assuming that a coefficient varies smoothly according to a low-dimensional basis, the boosted trees can adaptively partition the modifier space, allowing for both smooth and abrupt changes, nonlinear dependencies, and interactions between modifiers. This approach retains the conceptual clarity of VCMs—regression coefficients that depend on other variables—while leveraging the strengths of modern machine learning for function estimation.

Such a modeling strategy offers several advantages. First, it allows for the simultaneous estimation of multiple varying coefficients in a data-driven manner, without requiring explicit specification of their functional form. Second, by using gradient boosting, it can handle high-dimensional modifier spaces and automatically select relevant variables and interactions that influence each coefficient. Third, the model can accommodate heterogeneous patterns, such as regime shifts or threshold effects, that are difficult to capture with traditional smoothers. Finally, by maintaining the coefficient-based representation, the model facilitates interpretation in terms of how the effect of each predictor changes with the modifiers, which is often of primary scientific interest.

Despite these appealing properties, the development of tree boosted varying coefficient models raises important methodological and computational questions. The boosting algorithm must be adapted to estimate multiple coefficient functions simultaneously, ensuring that updates are targeted appropriately and that overfitting is controlled. Regularization strategies, such as shrinkage, subsampling, and tree complexity constraints, play a critical role in balancing flexibility and generalization. Furthermore, interpretability requires careful consideration of how to summarize and visualize the estimated coefficient functions, especially when they depend on multiple modifiers. Theoretical analysis of consistency, convergence rates, and variable selection properties in this context is also an open area of research, given the nonparametric and high-dimensional nature of the problem.

In this work, we propose a unified framework for tree boosted varying coefficient models that addresses these challenges. We formalize the model structure, develop an efficient boosting algorithm for fitting, and discuss strategies for regularization and interpretation. Through simulation studies and applications to real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our approach can capture complex, high-dimensional coefficient variation while providing interpretable insights into effect modification. Our results suggest that integrating the structured interpretability of VCMs with the adaptive flexibility of tree boosting offers a promising direction for modern statistical modeling, particularly in domains where understanding dynamic relationships is as important as predictive performance.
conclusion: In this work, we have proposed tree boosted varying coefficient models as a flexible and interpretable framework for capturing complex, nonlinear relationships in regression settings where covariate effects vary with other variables. By integrating gradient boosting with varying coefficient structures, the method effectively balances predictive accuracy with interpretability, enabling practitioners to explore heterogeneous effects across diverse contexts. The tree-based boosting component allows for automatic detection of relevant effect modifiers and nonlinear interactions, while the varying coefficient formulation retains a clear, conditional interpretation of regression parameters. Empirical studies on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive or superior predictive performance compared to standard boosting and traditional varying coefficient models, particularly in scenarios with intricate effect heterogeneity. Moreover, the model’s structure facilitates visualization and domain-specific interpretation, supporting its utility in applied research. Future work could extend the framework to generalized response settings, incorporate regularization for enhanced stability, and explore scalable algorithms for high-dimensional data. Overall, tree boosted varying coefficient models provide a powerful, interpretable, and adaptable tool for modeling nuanced relationships in complex data environments.

title: Properties of Farey Sequence and their Applications to Digital Image Processing
abstract: The Farey sequence, a well-studied construct in number theory, comprises fractions in lowest terms arranged in ascending order with denominators bounded by a given integer. Its rich mathematical properties, including mediant generation, symmetry, and uniform distribution, have inspired applications beyond pure mathematics. This paper investigates the structural characteristics of Farey sequences and explores their potential in digital image processing. We examine how fraction ordering and spacing can be leveraged for tasks such as subpixel interpolation, edge detection, and pattern representation. By mapping pixel intensity ratios and geometric slopes to Farey fractions, we demonstrate efficient computation schemes that exploit their mediant property for adaptive resolution enhancement. Experimental results indicate that Farey-based methods can reduce computational complexity while maintaining accuracy in feature extraction. The study highlights the synergy between number-theoretic principles and image analysis, suggesting new pathways for low-cost, high-precision digital imaging algorithms.
introduction:
The Farey sequence, a sequence of completely reduced fractions between 0 and 1 arranged in increasing order with denominators less than or equal to a given positive integer, has long been a subject of interest in number theory. Named after the British geologist John Farey, who first described its properties in the early nineteenth century, the sequence exhibits a rich mathematical structure, including mediant properties, neighbor relationships, and connections to continued fractions. These characteristics have inspired extensive exploration in pure mathematics and have found growing relevance in applied fields. One significant area where the Farey sequence has demonstrated potential is in digital image processing, where rational approximations and hierarchical representations play an essential role in tasks such as image scaling, edge detection, and pattern recognition.

The inherent ordering and density properties of the Farey sequence make it particularly suitable for approximating real numbers with rational fractions of bounded denominators. This property is valuable in digital image processing, where pixel intensities, geometric transformations, and frequency components often require efficient and accurate quantization. By leveraging the mediant property, which states that for two neighboring fractions \( a/b \) and \( c/d \) in the sequence, their mediant \( (a+c)/(b+d) \) lies between them, algorithms can be designed to iteratively refine approximations without resorting to computationally expensive floating-point arithmetic. Consequently, Farey-based approaches can yield performance advantages in resource-constrained or real-time image processing applications.

Another notable feature of the Farey sequence is its connection to lattice point geometry and the modular group, which suggests underlying symmetry and scaling properties. In image processing, such properties can be exploited for tasks involving multi-resolution analysis, where different levels of detail are represented through rational approximations of transformation parameters. Furthermore, the sequence’s relationship to continued fractions offers a framework for understanding hierarchical structures in images, aiding in compression schemes and image analysis methods.

This paper investigates the mathematical properties of Farey sequences and their applicability to various domains of digital image processing. By bridging number theory and computational imaging, we aim to demonstrate how the intrinsic order and approximation capabilities of Farey sequences can be harnessed to develop efficient, accurate, and theoretically grounded image processing techniques. Through theoretical analysis and experimental validation, we highlight both the potential benefits and practical considerations of integrating Farey sequence concepts into contemporary imaging workflows.
conclusion: The study of the properties of the Farey sequence reveals a rich mathematical structure that offers practical advantages in digital image processing. By exploiting its ordered arrangement of rational numbers and mediant property, efficient algorithms for tasks such as edge detection, image segmentation, and frequency domain analysis can be developed. The intrinsic relationship between Farey sequences and continued fractions enables precise approximation of gradients and directional features, enhancing computational accuracy while reducing complexity. Furthermore, the sequence’s symmetry and density characteristics support adaptive resolution approaches, beneficial in multi-scale image analysis. These findings demonstrate that the intersection of number theory and image processing is not only theoretically significant but also technologically impactful. Future research may further integrate Farey-based methods with modern machine learning frameworks, unlocking new possibilities for robust and efficient image analysis techniques.

title: Chemical abundance ratios of galactic globular clusters from modelling integrated light spectroscopy
abstract: We present a detailed analysis of the chemical abundance ratios of a representative sample of Galactic globular clusters derived from modelling integrated-light spectroscopy. High signal-to-noise, medium- to high-resolution spectra were obtained for 25 clusters spanning a wide range in metallicity and horizontal branch morphology. The spectra were analysed using state-of-the-art population synthesis techniques coupled with theoretical isochrones and an extensive library of synthetic stellar spectra, enabling the simultaneous determination of [Fe/H] and a suite of key element ratios, including [Mg/Fe], [Ca/Fe], [Ti/Fe], and [Na/Fe]. Our method accounts for the effects of multiple stellar populations, variable horizontal branch contributions, and stochastic sampling of bright giants, allowing for a robust comparison with literature values derived from high-resolution spectroscopy of individual member stars. The resulting integrated-light abundances reproduce the well-known trends of α-enhancement at low metallicity, the decline of [α/Fe] toward solar values at higher [Fe/H], and the presence of the Na–O anticorrelation signature in the form of systematically elevated [Na/Fe] ratios. We find that the integrated-light approach yields metallicities accurate to within 0.05 dex and abundance ratios to within 0.1 dex for most elements, demonstrating its viability for extragalactic applications where individual stars cannot be resolved. The abundance patterns across our sample reflect the complex chemical enrichment histories of the clusters, consistent with early, rapid star formation and contributions from both core-collapse and Type Ia supernovae, as well as pollution from intermediate-mass asymptotic giant branch stars. Our results provide a benchmark for interpreting integrated-light spectra of unresolved stellar systems, enabling chemical tagging of globular clusters in nearby galaxies, and contribute to the broader effort of reconstructing the formation and evolutionary history of the Galactic halo through its oldest stellar populations.
introduction: Galactic globular clusters (GCs) are among the oldest stellar systems in the Milky Way and provide crucial insights into the early formation and chemical evolution of the Galaxy. Their stellar populations are typically old and metal-poor, preserving the chemical signatures of the interstellar medium at the time of their formation. While high-resolution spectroscopy of individual stars has yielded detailed abundance patterns for nearby clusters, such observations are challenging for distant or heavily reddened systems. Integrated light (IL) spectroscopy offers a complementary approach, enabling the study of unresolved clusters by modelling their combined stellar spectra. Advances in population synthesis and spectral fitting techniques now allow the determination of detailed chemical abundance ratios from IL data, extending the reach of chemical tagging to extragalactic systems. In this work, we apply state-of-the-art IL modelling to a representative sample of Galactic GCs, aiming to derive precise abundance ratios for key elements. These measurements provide constraints on nucleosynthetic processes, cluster formation environments, and the assembly history of the Milky Way.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a detailed analysis of chemical abundance ratios in Galactic globular clusters (GCs) derived from modelling integrated light (IL) spectroscopy. By employing state-of-the-art stellar population synthesis techniques in conjunction with high-resolution IL spectra, we have been able to extract robust abundance patterns for a representative sample of clusters spanning a wide range of metallicities, horizontal branch morphologies, and structural parameters. Our results demonstrate that IL spectroscopy, when coupled with physically motivated modelling, is capable of reproducing key abundance trends traditionally obtained from high-quality spectroscopy of individual cluster members, thereby offering a powerful approach for studying unresolved star clusters in both the Milky Way and external galaxies.

The derived abundance ratios for α-elements (e.g., Mg, Si, Ca, Ti) confirm the well-established enhancement relative to iron at low metallicities, consistent with early enrichment dominated by core-collapse supernovae. The relatively small scatter in these ratios across our sample suggests a high degree of chemical homogeneity within most clusters, reinforcing the notion that GCs formed rapidly from well-mixed gas. At the same time, we detect subtle but statistically significant variations in certain elements, such as Mg and Na, that point to the presence of multiple stellar populations and internal self-enrichment processes. These findings are in line with detailed stellar spectroscopy studies, indicating that IL analyses can recover signatures of intra-cluster chemical complexity, albeit with some limitations in resolving the full amplitude of abundance spreads.

Our measurements of iron-peak and neutron-capture elements further highlight the diagnostic power of IL methods. The behaviour of elements such as Ni and Cr tracks that of Fe closely, while variations in Ba and Eu abundances provide constraints on the relative contributions of the s- and r-process enrichment channels in the early history of each cluster. Notably, the [Ba/Eu] ratios in metal-poor clusters are low, consistent with a dominant r-process origin, while more metal-rich clusters exhibit modest s-process contributions, likely reflecting a longer formation timescale or pollution from asymptotic giant branch stars.

A key advantage of the modelling approach adopted here is its applicability to integrated spectra of unresolved systems. Our comparison between IL-based abundances and literature values from individual stars demonstrates that, with careful treatment of stellar population parameters, IL spectroscopy achieves an accuracy and precision sufficient for tracing chemical evolution in extragalactic GC systems. This capability is essential for extending Galactic chemical evolution studies beyond the Milky Way, enabling the investigation of star formation histories, mass assembly, and enrichment processes in diverse galactic environments.

In summary, this study confirms that modelling high-quality IL spectra provides a reliable means to recover detailed abundance patterns in globular clusters. The method reproduces known trends, detects multiple population signatures, and yields insights into nucleosynthetic enrichment pathways. Future work should focus on expanding the sample to include clusters in different galactic environments, improving the treatment of horizontal branch morphology and abundance spreads in the models, and extending the wavelength coverage to incorporate additional diagnostic features. Such efforts will further enhance the utility of IL spectroscopy as a tool for probing the chemical fingerprints of ancient stellar systems across the universe.

title: Robust Spoken Language Understanding via Paraphrasing
abstract: We propose a paraphrase-based framework to enhance the robustness of spoken language understanding (SLU) systems against variations in user input. Spoken utterances often exhibit lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity, leading to degraded performance in intent classification and slot filling. Our approach integrates a paraphrasing module that generates semantically equivalent reformulations of input utterances, enabling the SLU model to leverage multiple linguistic realizations during both training and inference. We evaluate the method on benchmark SLU datasets under noisy and out-of-distribution conditions, demonstrating significant improvements over strong baselines. Results show that paraphrasing mitigates performance drops caused by speech recognition errors and linguistic variability, offering a simple yet effective strategy for building more robust and adaptable SLU systems.
introduction:
Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) is a core component of modern conversational systems, enabling machines to extract structured semantic representations from human speech. It underpins a wide range of applications, from virtual assistants and customer service chatbots to voice-controlled devices and in-car dialogue systems. The effectiveness of SLU models directly impacts the quality of downstream tasks such as intent detection, slot filling, and dialogue state tracking. Despite continuous advances in deep learning and end-to-end architectures, SLU systems remain vulnerable to variations in user input, particularly those arising from paraphrasing. Users often express the same meaning in multiple linguistic forms, using different lexical choices, syntactic structures, or discourse markers. Robust handling of such paraphrastic variation is critical for ensuring consistent performance in real-world deployments.

A significant challenge arises from the fact that training data for SLU is often limited in diversity and may fail to capture the wide spectrum of paraphrases encountered in practice. This mismatch between training and test-time utterances can lead to degraded performance, especially in open-domain or noisy acoustic environments. Furthermore, spoken language exhibits disfluencies, colloquialisms, and idiosyncratic phrasing that differ from written text, making it difficult for models trained predominantly on canonical sentence forms to generalize. Paraphrasing can also interact with automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors, compounding the complexity of the SLU pipeline.

Recent research in natural language understanding has explored data augmentation techniques, domain adaptation, and robust representation learning to address variability in input expressions. Among these, paraphrasing-based approaches have emerged as a promising strategy to improve model robustness. By generating alternative formulations of training utterances, paraphrase augmentation can expose SLU models to a broader range of linguistic patterns, thereby reducing overfitting to narrow lexical or syntactic cues. Techniques for paraphrase generation span from rule-based transformations and statistical machine translation to neural sequence-to-sequence models, including large-scale pretrained language models capable of producing fluent and semantically faithful rewordings. Integrating these paraphrases into SLU training has the potential to enhance generalization, mitigate performance drops due to distributional shifts, and improve resilience against ASR-induced perturbations.

However, leveraging paraphrasing for SLU is not without challenges. Automatically generated paraphrases may introduce noise through semantic drift, grammatical errors, or unnatural constructions, which can in turn harm model performance. Controlling the quality and diversity of paraphrases is therefore essential. Moreover, the impact of paraphrasing on different SLU tasks—such as intent classification versus slot filling—may vary, necessitating careful evaluation. While prior work has demonstrated the benefits of data augmentation in text-based natural language understanding, the specific interplay between paraphrasing, ASR errors, and spoken language phenomena remains underexplored. There is a need for systematic investigation into how paraphrase generation methods, integration strategies, and training regimes influence robustness in SLU systems.

In this work, we address the problem of enhancing SLU robustness through paraphrasing by conducting a comprehensive study across multiple datasets, paraphrase generation techniques, and model architectures. We focus on realistic spoken language scenarios that incorporate ASR outputs, aiming to bridge the gap between controlled text-based experiments and noisy, real-world conditions. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we propose a framework for generating and integrating high-quality paraphrases into SLU training pipelines; (2) we analyze the effects of paraphrase diversity and fidelity on intent detection and slot filling performance under varying levels of ASR noise; and (3) we provide empirical evidence that targeted paraphrasing can significantly improve SLU robustness without requiring additional labeled speech data. Through this investigation, we seek to advance the development of conversational systems that can reliably understand user intent despite the inherent variability of human language.
conclusion: This work investigated the use of paraphrasing to enhance the robustness of spoken language understanding systems. By generating diverse paraphrastic variants of user utterances, our approach mitigates the impact of linguistic variability, recognition errors, and domain shifts. Experimental results demonstrated consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks, highlighting the effectiveness of integrating paraphrase-based augmentation into training pipelines. Furthermore, the method is model-agnostic and can be applied alongside existing architectures without significant overhead. Future work will explore adaptive paraphrase generation conditioned on context and user profiles, as well as extending the approach to multilingual and code-switched scenarios to further improve real-world deployment robustness.

title: Analysis of high-resolution spectra from a hybrid interferometric/dispersive spectrometer
abstract: We present an analysis of high-resolution optical spectra acquired using a hybrid interferometric/dispersive spectrometer that combines a Fabry–Pérot etalon with a grating-based device. This architecture enables simultaneous high spectral resolution and broad wavelength coverage by exploiting the etalon’s interference fringes for fine spectral discrimination, while the grating spectrometer separates overlapping orders. Experimental measurements were obtained from well-characterized atomic emission sources, and the resulting spectra were reconstructed using a calibration procedure that accounts for instrumental dispersion and etalon phase response. The hybrid approach achieved resolving powers exceeding 150,000 over a spectral range of several nanometers, with improved signal-to-noise compared to conventional configurations. We evaluate the system’s performance in terms of resolution, accuracy, and sensitivity, and demonstrate its applicability to precision spectroscopy in laboratory and field environments. The results highlight the potential of hybrid spectrometers for compact, high-performance spectral diagnostics across diverse scientific and industrial applications.
introduction:
High-resolution optical spectroscopy is a fundamental tool in the physical sciences, enabling precise characterization of atomic and molecular transitions, quantitative chemical analysis, and diagnostics of plasmas and other complex systems. The ability to resolve fine spectral features is critically important in applications ranging from environmental monitoring and biomedical sensing to astrophysics and quantum optics. Conventional high-resolution spectrometers typically employ either dispersive elements, such as diffraction gratings or prisms, or interferometric devices, such as Fabry–Pérot etalons or Fourier transform spectrometers (FTS). Each approach offers distinct advantages and limitations in terms of resolution, throughput, spectral coverage, and instrument footprint.

Dispersive spectrometers spatially separate wavelengths according to the angular dispersion of a grating or prism, with resolution determined by the groove density, illuminated aperture, and optical path length. They provide broad spectral coverage in a single acquisition and are relatively straightforward to align and operate. However, achieving very high resolving power requires large optical components and long optical paths, which can increase the system size and reduce portability. In addition, the spectral resolution is inherently linked to the physical dimensions of the dispersive element, imposing constraints on miniaturization.

Interferometric spectrometers, by contrast, encode spectral information in interference fringes formed by the superposition of multiple optical paths. Fabry–Pérot interferometers (FPIs) and FTS instruments can achieve extremely high resolution and precise wavelength calibration. FPIs, in particular, are well suited for resolving narrow spectral lines, as their finesse can be engineered to yield sub-picometer resolution. However, interferometric methods often require scanning or multiple exposures to cover a wide spectral range, and their performance can be sensitive to mechanical stability and environmental conditions. Furthermore, the narrow free spectral range of etalon-based systems can lead to order ambiguities without additional spectral discrimination.

Hybrid interferometric/dispersive spectrometers combine these two approaches to leverage their respective strengths while mitigating their limitations. In such systems, an interferometric element is used to generate high-resolution spectral modulation, while a dispersive stage separates overlapping interference orders and provides coarse spectral information. This combination allows for simultaneous acquisition of wide-range, high-resolution spectra in a compact form factor. The dispersive element effectively increases the interferometer’s free spectral range, while the interferometer enhances the resolution beyond that of the dispersive stage alone. Recent advances in optical design, detector technology, and computational reconstruction algorithms have enabled the development of hybrid instruments suitable for field deployment without sacrificing performance.

The analysis of high-resolution spectra from hybrid spectrometers presents unique challenges and opportunities. The recorded data often take the form of two-dimensionally encoded interferograms, in which the spectral information is distributed between spatial and interference fringe dimensions. Reconstruction of the underlying spectrum requires careful calibration of both the dispersive and interferometric responses, as well as algorithms capable of deconvolving the combined instrument function. Additionally, the hybrid modality can offer enhanced sensitivity to subtle spectral features, making it well suited for detecting weak absorption lines, resolving closely spaced transitions, or monitoring dynamic changes in spectral profiles.

In this work, we present a detailed analysis of high-resolution spectra obtained from a hybrid interferometric/dispersive spectrometer, focusing on the methods for data acquisition, calibration, and spectral reconstruction. We evaluate the instrument’s performance in terms of resolution, accuracy, and spectral fidelity, and we demonstrate its capabilities in resolving narrow spectral features across a broad wavelength range. Our results highlight the potential of hybrid spectrometers as versatile and powerful tools for applications requiring both high spectral resolution and compact, robust instrumentation.
conclusion:
The analysis of high‑resolution spectra obtained from the hybrid interferometric/dispersive spectrometer demonstrates the capability of this approach to combine the advantages of both Fourier transform and dispersive methodologies. By integrating interferometric modulation with a dispersive detection stage, the instrument achieves enhanced spectral resolution without sacrificing throughput, while maintaining compactness and mechanical stability. Experimental results confirm that the hybrid configuration effectively resolves fine spectral features that would be challenging to distinguish using either technique alone. The retrieval algorithms developed for the combined data domain proved robust in handling noise and instrumental artifacts, enabling accurate reconstruction of spectral line shapes and positions.

Comparisons with reference spectrometers indicate that the hybrid system attains resolution close to the theoretical limit predicted from its optical design, while delivering improved sensitivity in the target wavelength range. The ability to tailor the interferometric path difference and dispersive element parameters provides flexibility for diverse applications, from gas-phase spectroscopy to materials characterization. In addition, the approach offers inherent multiplexing benefits and reduced sensitivity to mechanical drift, which are advantageous for both laboratory and field measurements.

Overall, the results validate the hybrid interferometric/dispersive design as a practical and powerful tool for high‑resolution spectroscopy. The demonstrated performance suggests that further optimization of optical alignment, calibration routines, and retrieval algorithms could yield even higher accuracy and efficiency. Future work will focus on expanding the operational bandwidth, improving real‑time data processing capabilities, and exploring miniaturization for portable deployments. The present findings underscore the potential of hybrid spectrometers to address measurement challenges in scientific, industrial, and environmental monitoring contexts, bridging the gap between traditional high‑resolution instruments and the need for compact, versatile, and high‑performance spectral analysis systems.

title: Hydrodynamic electrons in Graphene: a viscous boundary-layer description
abstract: We develop a viscous boundary-layer framework for describing hydrodynamic electron flow in graphene, focusing on the interplay between momentum-conserving electron–electron scattering and momentum-relaxing boundary interactions. In the hydrodynamic regime, where carrier–carrier collisions dominate, spatial variations in velocity are confined to narrow regions near device edges, analogous to classical viscous boundary layers in fluids. By deriving and solving the governing Navier–Stokes–type equations with appropriate slip boundary conditions, we capture the emergence of shear-dominated edge currents and quantify their influence on overall transport. The theory predicts a characteristic scaling of the boundary-layer thickness with viscosity and momentum-relaxation rates, consistent with available experimental data. Our results provide a unified description bridging ballistic, hydrodynamic, and diffusive regimes, and offer analytical tools for interpreting nonlocal resistance and current-density profiles in mesoscopic graphene devices. This boundary-layer perspective establishes a simple, physically transparent framework for engineering hydrodynamic transport in two-dimensional electron systems.
introduction:
The study of electronic transport in graphene has revealed a remarkable regime in which charge carriers behave collectively, akin to a viscous fluid. In contrast to the conventional picture of electrons as independent quasiparticles undergoing momentum-relaxing collisions with impurities or phonons, hydrodynamic transport emerges when electron–electron scattering dominates. In this regime, local equilibrium is established rapidly, and the long-wavelength dynamics of the electronic system can be described by equations analogous to those governing classical fluids. Recent experimental advances have confirmed signatures of such hydrodynamic electron flow in high-mobility graphene devices, including negative nonlocal resistance, Poiseuille-like current profiles, and enhanced conductance in narrow channels.

A central feature of classical viscous flows is the formation of boundary layers, where velocity gradients are concentrated and dissipation is enhanced due to the no-slip or partial-slip conditions at solid boundaries. In the context of graphene, the microscopic nature of the sample edges, together with momentum relaxation from boundary scattering, determines the effective boundary conditions for the electron fluid. Understanding the interplay between viscous bulk flow and boundary-layer dynamics is crucial for predicting transport coefficients, current distributions, and potential profiles in experimentally relevant geometries. While hydrodynamic theories of electron transport have been developed for idealized bulk systems, a systematic description that incorporates viscous boundary layers in graphene remains incomplete.

In this work, we develop a theoretical framework for the hydrodynamic electron flow in graphene that explicitly accounts for viscous boundary layers. Starting from the linearized Navier–Stokes equations adapted to a two-dimensional electron fluid, we derive solutions for confined geometries in which the interplay between viscosity, boundary scattering, and external driving fields is captured. Our approach allows us to identify characteristic length scales associated with the viscous penetration depth and to quantify their impact on measurable quantities such as conductance and spatial current patterns. The analysis reveals how boundary layers mediate the transition between bulk-like hydrodynamic flow in the channel interior and the strongly sheared flow near the edges.

By providing a viscous boundary-layer description, we bridge the gap between idealized hydrodynamic models and realistic device conditions, enabling more accurate comparisons with experiments. The results reported here offer a pathway to extract microscopic parameters, such as the slip length and viscosity, from transport measurements, and to optimize device geometries for the observation and utilization of hydrodynamic effects in graphene. Our findings deepen the understanding of electron hydrodynamics and highlight the role of boundaries as active elements in shaping electronic flow.
conclusion:
In this work, we have developed a viscous boundary-layer framework for describing hydrodynamic electron flow in graphene, emphasizing the interplay between momentum-conserving electron–electron scattering and momentum-relaxing processes at device boundaries. By extending the conventional hydrodynamic equations with appropriate slip boundary conditions, we have shown that the spatial structure of the electron velocity field near edges is governed by a competition between viscous shear and boundary-induced momentum loss. The resulting boundary layer, characterized by a viscous penetration depth, plays a decisive role in determining measurable transport properties, including nonlocal resistance signals and current distribution patterns.  

Our analysis demonstrates that, in the hydrodynamic regime, the scale of the viscous boundary layer can be comparable to experimentally accessible device dimensions, leading to deviations from bulk Poiseuille-like flow and enhancing the sensitivity of transport measurements to boundary conditions. In particular, we find that partial slip at the edges can interpolate between ideal no-slip and free-slip limits, offering a quantitative means to account for diverse sample preparations and edge morphologies.  

The boundary-layer description not only captures the qualitative features observed in recent experiments but also provides a systematic route to extract viscosity and slip length from spatially resolved transport data. By framing hydrodynamic electron transport in graphene within a well-established fluid-mechanical paradigm, our approach bridges microscopic scattering processes with mesoscopic flow patterns, highlighting the universality of viscous boundary effects across different physical systems.  

Future work may extend this framework to include magnetic field effects, strain-induced gauge fields, and non-linear flow regimes, as well as to explore its applicability to other two-dimensional materials. Taken together, our results underscore the central role of viscous boundary layers in shaping electron hydrodynamics, offering both conceptual clarity and practical tools for interpreting and designing graphene-based transport experiments.

title: Optimizing quantization for Lasso recovery
abstract: We study the impact of quantization on sparse signal recovery using the Lasso estimator. By analyzing the trade-off between quantization resolution and recovery accuracy, we develop an optimization framework that jointly selects quantization parameters to minimize reconstruction error. Our approach leverages probabilistic error bounds and properties of high-dimensional geometry to guide parameter selection under measurement and bit-budget constraints. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly improves recovery performance over conventional uniform quantization, particularly in low-bit regimes, while maintaining computational efficiency.
introduction:
Sparse signal recovery has emerged as a central problem in high-dimensional statistics, signal processing, and machine learning. Among the various approaches, the Lasso estimator, which combines an ℓ₂ data fidelity term with an ℓ₁ regularization penalty, has proven to be a powerful and computationally efficient method for recovering sparse vectors from noisy linear measurements. A large body of theoretical work has established conditions under which Lasso achieves near-optimal recovery guarantees, assuming access to real-valued measurements with arbitrary precision. In practical scenarios, however, measurement and storage constraints necessitate the quantization of observed data, introducing a new layer of complexity into the recovery process.

Quantization—the process of mapping continuous-valued measurements to a finite set of discrete levels—arises in numerous applications, from digital communications to resource-limited sensing platforms. While coarse quantization schemes, such as one-bit quantization, have been extensively studied in the context of sparse recovery, the interplay between quantization design and the performance of standard recovery algorithms like Lasso remains less well understood. In particular, the choice of quantization parameters can significantly affect both the statistical accuracy of the recovered signal and the computational stability of the estimation procedure.

This work focuses on optimizing quantization schemes specifically for Lasso-based recovery. We aim to identify quantization strategies that preserve essential information about the underlying sparse signal while respecting bit-budget or resolution constraints. Our analysis builds on recent advances in high-dimensional statistics and quantized compressed sensing, extending them to address the nontrivial interaction between quantization noise, measurement design, and regularization. By characterizing the trade-offs between quantization resolution, measurement number, and reconstruction error, we provide principled guidelines for quantizer design tailored to Lasso. The resulting framework bridges the gap between theoretical recovery guarantees and practical signal acquisition systems, enabling more efficient and accurate sparse recovery under realistic constraints.
conclusion: This work investigated strategies for optimizing quantization in the context of Lasso recovery, focusing on balancing measurement precision and reconstruction accuracy. By analyzing the interplay between quantization step size, measurement noise, and sparsity structure, we derived conditions under which recovery performance is preserved despite reduced bit-depth. Numerical experiments confirmed that carefully tuned quantization parameters can achieve near-optimal recovery with significantly lower storage and transmission costs. Our results highlight the importance of jointly considering quantization design and sparse recovery algorithms. Future research may extend these methods to adaptive and non-uniform quantization schemes, further improving efficiency in large-scale and resource-constrained sensing systems.

title: Counterexample-Guided Prophecy for Model Checking Modulo the Theory of Arrays
abstract: We present a counterexample-guided prophecy approach for model checking systems with array-manipulating operations. Our method integrates prophecy variables into the verification process to anticipate future array accesses, enabling more precise reasoning about program states. Counterexamples from failed verification attempts guide the refinement of these prophecies, improving convergence and scalability. By working modulo the theory of arrays, our technique handles unbounded data structures while maintaining soundness. Experimental results on challenging benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements in verification performance compared to existing array reasoning methods.
introduction:
Model checking is a widely used formal verification technique for automatically establishing whether a given system model satisfies a desired specification, typically expressed in temporal logic. Its appeal lies in its ability to provide exhaustive guarantees over all possible system behaviors. However, the applicability of model checking to systems with complex data structures, such as arrays, is hindered by the state explosion problem and the intricacies of reasoning over theories that capture the semantics of such data structures. The theory of arrays, with operations of reading and writing at indexed positions, is particularly challenging due to the need to reason about unbounded index and value domains, as well as extensionality.

To address these challenges, Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers have been integrated into model checking frameworks, enabling reasoning “modulo” background theories. This integration has fueled advances in verifying systems with richer data models, but it also introduces new difficulties. In particular, the combination of state-space exploration and theory reasoning can result in spurious counterexamples: abstract traces that appear to violate the specification in the current abstraction but are not actually feasible in the concrete system. The presence of such spurious counterexamples calls for refinement techniques that can incrementally improve the abstraction, eliminating infeasible behaviors while preserving genuine ones.

Counterexample-Guided Abstraction Refinement (CEGAR) has emerged as a successful paradigm for dealing with spurious counterexamples in propositional model checking and its extensions to SMT-based settings. In the CEGAR loop, abstract model checking is performed first; when a counterexample is found, it is checked for feasibility with respect to the concrete system. If the counterexample is spurious, the abstraction is refined to rule it out. While CEGAR has been effective for many theories, its application to the theory of arrays remains nontrivial. The main difficulty lies in devising refinement strategies that capture the subtle dependencies between array accesses without overcomplicating the abstraction.

In recent years, the notion of prophecy variables has been explored as a means to anticipate future values in model checking, particularly for liveness verification. Prophecy variables allow the model to “guess” certain values that will be encountered later in a run, thus enabling the model checker to reason about future-dependent properties in a finite-state setting. When combined with abstraction and refinement, prophecy variables can also serve to encode constraints that disambiguate the feasibility of counterexamples involving complex data interactions.

This paper introduces Counterexample-Guided Prophecy (CEGP), a novel refinement framework for model checking modulo the theory of arrays. CEGP leverages prophecy variables to record and reason about array values that are crucial for assessing counterexample feasibility. Upon detecting a spurious counterexample, the method synthesizes prophecy variables and associated constraints that capture the necessary relationships between array reads and writes observed in the counterexample. The abstraction is then refined with these constraints, eliminating the infeasible trace while minimally impacting unrelated behaviors. We demonstrate that CEGP can significantly reduce the number of refinement iterations and improve verification performance on challenging array-intensive benchmarks, compared to traditional CEGAR approaches. By uniting prophecy-based reasoning with counterexample-guided refinement, our approach advances the state of the art in SMT-based model checking for systems with complex data structures.
conclusion:
In this work, we presented a counterexample-guided prophecy framework for model checking modulo the theory of arrays. Our approach integrates prophecy variables into the verification process to anticipate future array states, while iteratively refining them using counterexamples generated during model checking. This combination enables the verification of safety properties that depend on complex array manipulations, which are often challenging for existing methods. By leveraging the theory of arrays with extensionality, the method preserves logical soundness while improving convergence in the presence of quantified invariants.

Through experimental evaluation, we demonstrated that our technique can reduce spurious counterexamples and accelerate convergence compared to standard model checking approaches without prophecy guidance. The counterexample-guided refinement loop ensures that unnecessary prophecy variables are eliminated, while essential ones are instantiated with precision to capture the required future state information. This results in more efficient exploration of the state space and increased automation in invariant discovery.

Our results indicate that prophecy variables, when systematically managed through counterexample analysis, offer a promising mechanism for scaling model checking to richer data structures. Future work will explore extending this framework to other theories, such as algebraic data types, and integrating it into industrial verification pipelines for software and hardware systems.

title: Electric field control of magnetic properties and magneto-transport in composite multiferroics
abstract: We investigate the electric field control of magnetic properties and magneto-transport in composite multiferroic heterostructures comprising ferromagnetic and ferroelectric layers. Using a combination of experimental measurements and theoretical modeling, we demonstrate that interfacial strain coupling and charge-mediated effects enable reversible tuning of magnetization, coercivity, and anisotropy via applied electric fields at room temperature. Magneto-transport characterization reveals significant modulation of anisotropic magnetoresistance and spin-dependent conduction, correlated with the electric-field-induced magnetic changes. Our results show that the coupling strength is sensitive to layer thickness, interface quality, and ferroelectric polarization state, allowing optimization of device performance. The findings provide quantitative insight into the mechanisms governing magneto-electric coupling in composite systems and highlight pathways for low-power, voltage-controlled spintronic devices. This work advances the understanding of multifunctional oxide heterostructures and offers a framework for engineering electrically tunable magnetic and transport properties for next-generation memory and logic applications.
introduction:
Multiferroic materials, in which two or more primary ferroic orders such as ferroelectricity, ferromagnetism, and ferroelasticity coexist, have attracted considerable attention due to their potential for novel device applications and the intriguing fundamental physics they exhibit. Of particular interest are composite multiferroics, in which ferroelectric and magnetic phases are combined in a heterostructure or composite form, enabling magnetoelectric (ME) coupling via elastic, charge, or exchange-mediated interactions. Such coupling allows the control of magnetic properties by an electric field and, conversely, the control of electric polarization by a magnetic field. Harnessing these cross-coupling effects opens pathways toward low-power spintronics, non-volatile memories, sensors, and tunable microwave devices.

In single-phase multiferroics, the coexistence of ferroelectric and ferromagnetic orders at room temperature is rare due to conflicting electronic and structural requirements for each order parameter. Composite architectures, however, circumvent this limitation by combining distinct ferroelectric and magnetic constituents, each optimized for their respective ferroic property, and coupling them through interfacial interactions. The most widely explored mechanisms of magnetoelectric coupling in such composites are strain-mediated coupling via the piezoelectric and magnetostrictive effects, charge-mediated coupling at the interface, and exchange-bias coupling in multiferroic–ferromagnet bilayers. Among these, strain-mediated coupling has demonstrated particularly strong effects at room temperature, enabling efficient electric field control of magnetization, coercivity, and magnetic anisotropy.

Electric field manipulation of magnetic properties is highly attractive for energy-efficient spintronic devices, as it offers a route to circumvent the high energy consumption associated with conventional current-driven magnetic switching. In strain-mediated multiferroic heterostructures, an applied electric field induces strain in the ferroelectric layer, which is transferred to the adjacent magnetic layer, thereby modifying its magnetic anisotropy and magnetization state. This approach has been demonstrated in various systems, including epitaxial thin-film heterostructures, laminate composites, and nanopillar arrays. Charge-mediated effects, on the other hand, rely on the modulation of carrier density or screening at the ferroelectric/ferromagnet interface, influencing exchange interactions and magnetic ordering in ultrathin magnetic layers. The relative strength, reversibility, and speed of these mechanisms depend sensitively on the materials choice, interface quality, and device geometry.

An important manifestation of electric field control in multiferroic composites is the modulation of magneto-transport properties, such as anisotropic magnetoresistance (AMR), tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR), and anomalous Hall effect (AHE). By tuning the magnetic state electrically, one can achieve non-volatile and reversible control of resistance states in magnetic tunnel junctions or spin valves, offering significant potential for multifunctional logic and memory devices. Furthermore, electric field-induced changes in domain structure and magnetic anisotropy can influence spin-dependent scattering and transport phenomena, providing a versatile platform to study magneto-transport in correlated systems.

Recent advances in thin-film growth techniques, such as pulsed laser deposition, molecular beam epitaxy, and sputtering, have enabled atomically sharp interfaces and precise control of strain, stoichiometry, and layer thickness in multiferroic composites. These developments have facilitated systematic investigations into the fundamental mechanisms of magnetoelectric coupling and the optimization of functional responses. Concurrently, progress in nanoscale characterization methods, including scanning probe microscopy, X-ray magnetic circular dichroism, and transmission electron microscopy, has provided new insights into the interplay between ferroelectric and magnetic domains and the role of defects, interfacial chemistry, and lattice distortions.

Despite these advances, several challenges remain for the practical implementation of electric field control of magnetism in composite multiferroics. These include enhancing the magnitude and stability of the ME response at room temperature, achieving fast and fatigue-resistant switching, and understanding the interplay between different coupling mechanisms in complex geometries. Addressing these challenges will require a combination of materials design, interface engineering, and theoretical modeling.

In this work, we investigate the electric field control of magnetic properties and magneto-transport in composite multiferroic heterostructures, focusing on the mechanisms that govern the coupling between ferroelectric and magnetic layers. By systematically varying structural parameters and probing both static and dynamic responses, we aim to elucidate the pathways for optimizing ME coupling strength and functional performance. Our findings provide insights into the design principles of next-generation spintronic and multifunctional electronic devices based on multiferroic composites.
conclusion: In summary, we have investigated the electric field control of magnetic properties and magneto-transport in composite multiferroic systems, emphasizing the interplay between ferroelectric and ferromagnetic components mediated by interfacial coupling. Our results demonstrate that applied electric fields can effectively modulate magnetization, coercivity, and anisotropy, enabling reversible and energy-efficient tuning of magnetic states. The observed changes in magneto-transport, including electric-field-induced variations in magnetoresistance, highlight the potential of such composites for multifunctional device applications. The coupling mechanisms, attributed to strain transfer, charge modulation, and exchange bias effects, offer versatile pathways for tailoring the magnetic response without direct magnetic fields. This work underscores the promise of composite multiferroics as a platform for low-power spintronic devices, non-volatile memory elements, and reconfigurable logic. Future studies should address scaling effects, interface engineering, and dynamic response under combined electric and magnetic stimuli to optimize performance. Overall, our findings contribute to the understanding and practical exploitation of electric-field control in magneto-functional materials, paving the way toward novel, compact, and energy-efficient device architectures.

title: Hydrodynamic and Solid Mechanics Analysis of Capillary Force-Induced Mold Deformation in Sub-10 nm UV Nanoimprint Lithography
abstract: This study investigates capillary force-induced deformation of mold structures in sub-10 nm ultraviolet nanoimprint lithography (UV-NIL) through coupled hydrodynamic and solid mechanics analysis. A lubrication approximation is employed to model resist filling dynamics, while finite element simulations quantify the resulting bending and stress in high-aspect-ratio mold features. The interplay between surface tension, viscous forces, and mold elasticity is examined to identify critical feature geometries susceptible to collapse during resist infiltration. Parametric studies reveal how line width, spacing, and resist viscosity influence transient pressure distributions and maximum deflection. Results indicate that sub-10 nm features with aspect ratios above a threshold exhibit significant deformation prior to complete filling, potentially compromising pattern fidelity. The analysis provides design guidelines for mold stiffness and resist properties, enabling improved structural integrity and pattern transfer fidelity in next-generation UV-NIL processes.
introduction:
Advances in ultraviolet nanoimprint lithography (UV-NIL) have enabled the fabrication of nanoscale patterns with critical dimensions well below 10 nm, offering a promising pathway for next-generation semiconductor manufacturing, photonic devices, and high-density data storage. In the UV-NIL process, a liquid resist is deposited onto a substrate and subsequently shaped by a transparent mold under low pressure, followed by UV curing to solidify the patterned features. As device dimensions approach the sub-10 nm regime, surface forces, particularly capillary forces arising from liquid menisci between mold protrusions, become increasingly significant relative to the mechanical stiffness of the mold. These nanoscale capillary interactions can induce local deformation of the mold features, potentially compromising pattern fidelity and limiting achievable resolution.

While UV-NIL has been extensively studied from the perspectives of material formulation, process optimization, and defect control, the interplay between hydrodynamic resist filling and the solid mechanics of mold structures under capillary loading at ultra-small scales remains insufficiently understood. In particular, the deformation of high-aspect-ratio mold features due to capillary pressure is a multi-physics problem involving fluid dynamics, surface tension, and elastic or elastic–plastic structural response. At sub-10 nm scales, the Laplace pressure associated with the curved resist meniscus can reach magnitudes comparable to or exceeding the yield strength of mold materials, even for stiff candidates such as quartz or silicon. This creates a critical need for predictive models that couple nanoscale hydrodynamics with structural mechanics, enabling the design of mold geometries and process parameters that mitigate deformation.

Previous research has addressed either the resist filling dynamics using continuum or molecular fluid models, or the mechanical stability of mold features under generic loading conditions. However, comprehensive analyses that integrate the transient capillary forces generated during UV-NIL filling with the resulting elastic deflection or potential collapse of mold features remain scarce. Such coupled analysis is essential for elucidating the scaling laws that govern deformation as feature sizes shrink, gap widths narrow, and aspect ratios increase. Furthermore, understanding the influence of resist viscosity, surface tension, contact angle, and imprint speed on capillary force generation is critical for balancing filling efficiency against mechanical integrity.

In this work, we present a hydrodynamic and solid mechanics analysis of capillary force-induced mold deformation in sub-10 nm UV-NIL. The study combines lubrication theory for nanoscale resist flow with elastic beam and plate models for mold protrusions, capturing the time evolution of both meniscus shape and structural deflection. The results provide quantitative guidelines for mold design, material selection, and process optimization to ensure high-fidelity pattern replication in the extreme nanoscale regime.
conclusion: This study has presented a coupled hydrodynamic and solid mechanics analysis to elucidate the mechanisms of capillary force-induced mold deformation in sub-10 nm UV nanoimprint lithography. By integrating fluid flow modeling of resist infiltration with structural deformation analysis of nanoscale mold features, the work quantifies the interplay between surface tension-driven pressure gradients and the elastic response of slender mold beams. The results demonstrate that, at sub-10 nm scales, capillary pressures increase sharply, leading to non-negligible bending and potential collapse of features with high aspect ratios. Parametric investigations reveal the critical dependence of deformation on beam width, height, and material modulus, as well as on resist viscosity and contact angle. The combined analysis provides predictive capability for identifying safe operating regimes that minimize mechanical failure without compromising pattern fidelity. These insights offer practical guidelines for mold design, material selection, and process parameter optimization in next-generation UV nanoimprint lithography. The methodology can be extended to other capillary-driven micro- and nanoscale manufacturing processes, supporting the development of robust patterning technologies at the ultimate resolution limits.

title: Checkpointing as a Service in Heterogeneous Cloud Environments
abstract: Checkpointing is a critical technique for enhancing fault tolerance and reducing recovery time in large-scale distributed systems. In heterogeneous cloud environments, where computational resources vary in architecture, performance, and reliability, implementing efficient checkpointing presents unique challenges. This paper proposes *Checkpointing as a Service* (CaaS), a cloud-native framework that abstracts checkpoint management from applications and offers adaptive, platform-agnostic support for diverse workloads. The service integrates resource-aware scheduling, incremental state capture, and optimized data placement strategies to minimize checkpoint overhead and recovery latency. By leveraging runtime profiling and machine learning models, CaaS dynamically selects checkpoint intervals and storage backends based on workload characteristics and node heterogeneity. We evaluate the framework on a multi-cloud testbed comprising heterogeneous CPU, GPU, and memory configurations. Experimental results demonstrate up to 38% reduction in checkpoint time and 27% improvement in recovery efficiency compared to conventional approaches, with negligible application performance degradation. Our findings highlight the feasibility and benefits of delivering checkpointing as an on-demand, adaptive service in heterogeneous cloud ecosystems.
introduction:
The increasing adoption of cloud computing for high‑performance and data‑intensive applications has amplified the demand for fault tolerance mechanisms that ensure reliability and minimize downtime. In heterogeneous cloud environments—comprising diverse hardware architectures, virtualization technologies, and network configurations—achieving efficient fault tolerance is particularly challenging. Checkpointing, the process of saving the execution state of an application at specific intervals, is a well‑established technique to enable recovery from failures without restarting computations from scratch. However, implementing checkpointing in heterogeneous clouds requires addressing variability in performance, resource availability, and fault characteristics across disparate nodes.

Traditional checkpointing solutions are often tightly coupled to specific system configurations, limiting their portability and scalability. Furthermore, the operational overhead of managing checkpoint schedules, storage, and recovery processes can be prohibitive for users lacking deep systems expertise. This creates a strong motivation for delivering checkpointing capabilities as an on‑demand, platform‑agnostic service—abstracting complexity while ensuring efficiency and resilience.

Checkpointing as a Service (CaaS) offers a promising paradigm in which checkpoint creation, storage, and restoration are orchestrated automatically, with optimizations tailored to heterogeneous infrastructures. By integrating adaptive scheduling, storage tiering, and fault prediction, CaaS can reduce checkpoint overhead while maintaining high recovery guarantees. This paper explores the design, implementation, and evaluation of a CaaS framework for heterogeneous cloud environments, aiming to bridge the gap between fault tolerance research and practical, user‑friendly cloud services. The proposed approach seeks to enhance application reliability, reduce operational complexity, and provide a scalable, cost‑effective solution for diverse workloads.
conclusion: This work has explored the design and implementation of Checkpointing as a Service (CaaS) in heterogeneous cloud environments, addressing the challenges posed by diverse hardware architectures, varying workload characteristics, and dynamic resource availability. By abstracting checkpointing operations into a service layer, our approach simplifies fault tolerance for application developers while enabling efficient resource utilization for cloud providers. The proposed framework demonstrates that adaptive strategies, informed by workload profiling and system monitoring, can significantly reduce checkpoint overhead and recovery time across heterogeneous nodes. Experimental evaluation confirms that CaaS can maintain high application throughput and resilience under failure scenarios, while accommodating the performance disparities inherent in mixed CPU, GPU, and specialized accelerators. Furthermore, the service-oriented model facilitates integration with orchestration tools, offering scalability and transparency. These findings suggest that CaaS can play a pivotal role in enabling reliable, performance-aware computing in next-generation cloud infrastructures. Future work will focus on incorporating predictive failure models, optimizing checkpoint placement policies, and extending support to emerging hardware paradigms, further enhancing robustness and efficiency in increasingly complex cloud ecosystems.

title: Efficient Enumeration of Chordless Cycles
abstract: We present an efficient algorithm for enumerating all chordless cycles in undirected graphs, a fundamental problem with applications in graph theory, network analysis, and computational biology. Unlike general cycle enumeration, chordless cycles—cycles without edges connecting nonconsecutive vertices—capture essential structural properties while avoiding redundancy. Our method leverages recursive exploration with pruning rules based on vertex ordering and adjacency constraints, ensuring that each cycle is generated exactly once. We analyze the time complexity and demonstrate that the algorithm achieves near-optimal performance for sparse and dense graphs alike. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show significant improvements in runtime and memory usage over existing approaches. The proposed framework provides a practical and scalable tool for structural graph analysis in diverse scientific and engineering domains.
introduction: Chordless cycles, also known as induced cycles, are fundamental structures in graph theory with significant applications in areas such as network analysis, computational biology, and social network mining.
