Such modeling supports device optimization by linking electrical parameters to physical processes, offering a valuable tool for design, analysis, and performance prediction of emerging organic photovoltaic technologies.

title: Scaling Neural Face Synthesis to High FPS and Low Latency by Neural Caching
abstract: We present a neural face synthesis framework that achieves high frame rates and low latency through a novel neural caching mechanism. Existing neural rendering approaches for photorealistic face synthesis often incur significant computational cost, limiting their applicability in real-time interactive settings such as telepresence, gaming, and virtual reality. Our method leverages temporal redundancy in video streams by reusing intermediate neural representations across consecutive frames. Specifically, we design a lightweight cache that stores and selectively updates latent features based on motion cues and scene changes, minimizing redundant computation while preserving visual fidelity. The cache is dynamically refreshed using an adaptive update policy informed by feature divergence metrics, ensuring robustness to rapid head motion and expression changes. We integrate the cache into a state-of-the-art face synthesis network, achieving up to a 4× speedup and rendering at over 120 FPS on consumer GPUs, with latency reduced to under 10 ms per frame. Quantitative and perceptual evaluations demonstrate that our approach maintains high image quality while substantially improving responsiveness, enabling fluid, real-time neural face synthesis for interactive applications.
introduction: Recent advances in neural rendering have enabled photorealistic face synthesis for applications in virtual reality, telepresence, and video games. However, achieving high frame rates and low latency remains challenging due to the substantial computational demands of deep generative models. Conventional acceleration techniques often degrade visual fidelity or require specialized hardware. In this work, we propose *neural caching*, a novel approach that reuses intermediate neural features across frames to significantly reduce redundant computation. Our method scales neural face synthesis to high FPS with minimal quality loss, enabling responsive, real-time experiences on commodity devices.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a novel framework for scaling neural face synthesis to high frame rates and low latency through the introduction of *neural caching*, a strategy that leverages temporal coherence in video synthesis to significantly reduce redundant computation. By decomposing the synthesis process into temporally stable and temporally variant components, we were able to cache and reuse intermediate neural representations between consecutive frames. This approach allowed us to bypass the need to recompute expensive feature transformations for static or slowly changing regions, while still adapting dynamically to motion, expression changes, and lighting variations.

Our experimental results demonstrate that neural caching enables substantial performance gains without compromising perceptual quality. Across diverse datasets and multiple network architectures, our method consistently achieved frame rate improvements of 2–4× compared to baseline real-time neural rendering pipelines, while reducing end-to-end latency by up to 45%. Importantly, the proposed caching mechanism operates orthogonally to other acceleration techniques such as model pruning, quantization, and architectural optimization, and thus can be combined with them for further efficiency gains. The achieved speedups make it feasible to deploy high-fidelity neural face synthesis in latency-sensitive applications such as live telepresence, virtual reality, and interactive entertainment.

We also established that the quality degradation introduced by caching is minimal when appropriate cache update policies are used. By exploiting temporal difference metrics to trigger selective recomputation, we maintained high structural similarity (SSIM) and perceptual quality (LPIPS) scores across sequences with varying motion dynamics. Moreover, our ablation studies confirmed that naive frame-to-frame reuse is insufficient for challenging scenarios, and that our proposed adaptive caching policy is essential to balance performance with fidelity.

Beyond quantitative metrics, user studies indicated that viewers found the cached outputs to be visually indistinguishable from the baseline in most cases, even under head movements and moderate expression changes. This finding underscores the perceptual redundancy present in sequential face synthesis and validates the core premise of our approach: that significant portions of neural rendering computation can be reused without harming the viewing experience.

Although our method achieves notable advancements in real-time performance, several limitations remain. The caching mechanism relies on temporal stability assumptions that may be violated under extreme motion, rapid illumination shifts, or occlusions, leading to occasional artifacts. While our adaptive update strategy mitigates these effects, further work is needed to make caching robust to these edge cases. Additionally, memory overhead from storing intermediate features can become non-negligible for very large models, suggesting that future research could explore compression techniques for cached representations.

Looking ahead, the principles underlying neural caching have broader applicability beyond facial synthesis. Any neural generation task with high temporal redundancy—such as full-body avatar animation, view synthesis in dynamic scenes, or video-to-video translation—could potentially benefit from similar decomposition and reuse strategies. Integration with neural video codecs may further blur the line between synthesis and compression, enabling new classes of low-bandwidth, high-quality telepresence systems. Moreover, advances in hardware-aware caching policies, possibly informed by learned predictors of scene change, could unlock even greater performance gains.

In summary, we have introduced a method that meaningfully advances the state of the art in efficient neural face synthesis by harnessing temporal coherence through neural caching. Our approach achieves high FPS and low latency without sacrificing perceptual fidelity, is compatible with existing acceleration techniques, and opens new research directions in temporally-aware neural rendering. We believe that neural caching represents an important step toward making photorealistic, interactive face synthesis ubiquitous across devices and applications, and anticipate that its core ideas will inspire further innovations in efficient neural video generation.

title: Topological Hall signatures of magnetic hopfions
abstract: Magnetic hopfions are three-dimensional topological spin textures characterized by a nontrivial Hopf invariant, offering unique opportunities for robust information storage and manipulation. Here we investigate their emergent electrodynamics and demonstrate that hopfion crystals give rise to distinct topological Hall signatures, arising from the real-space Berry curvature of conduction electrons coupled to the spin texture. Using micromagnetic simulations combined with semiclassical transport theory, we identify characteristic features in the Hall resistivity that differentiate hopfions from skyrmions and other chiral spin structures. The signal exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on magnetic field and hopfion density, reflecting the complex topology of the underlying spin configuration. Our findings establish the topological Hall effect as a sensitive probe for detecting hopfions in candidate materials and pave the way for their experimental identification in bulk and thin-film systems.
introduction:
Topologically nontrivial spin textures in magnetic materials have emerged as a fertile ground for exploring new physics and potential spintronic functionalities. While two-dimensional skyrmions—characterized by an integer-valued topological charge—have been extensively investigated both theoretically and experimentally, their three-dimensional counterparts remain comparatively less explored. Among these, magnetic hopfions, which are particle-like configurations classified by the Hopf invariant, represent a distinct class of solitonic textures stabilized by the topology of their intertwined field lines. Unlike skyrmions, hopfions exhibit no singular cores and are defined by the linking of preimages in the magnetization field, endowing them with unique spatial and dynamical properties.

The search for hopfions has been motivated not only by their topological stability but also by the prospect of novel electromagnetic responses arising from their complex spin structure. In analogy with the topological Hall effect (THE) observed in skyrmion-hosting materials, hopfions are expected to generate emergent electromagnetic fields that influence the motion of conduction electrons. These emergent fields originate from the real-space Berry curvature associated with the noncoplanar spin configuration, leading to transverse charge transport distinct from the ordinary and anomalous Hall effects. However, the absence of direct theoretical predictions and unambiguous experimental identification of hopfion-induced Hall signatures has so far limited our understanding of their transport fingerprints.

Recent advances in real-space magnetic imaging, such as Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, magnetic force microscopy, and X-ray magnetic tomography, have opened pathways toward the visualization of three-dimensional spin textures. Parallel progress in micromagnetic simulations and continuum field theories has begun to elucidate the stabilization mechanisms for hopfions, including contributions from frustrated exchange, Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions, and dipolar fields in confined geometries. These developments create an opportunity to investigate the interplay between the topological structure of hopfions and their electronic transport manifestations.

In this work, we address the question of whether and how magnetic hopfions can be detected via their topological Hall signatures. We develop a theoretical framework to compute the emergent gauge fields associated with hopfion textures and evaluate the resulting Hall response within a semiclassical transport formalism. By comparing these results to the well-established case of skyrmions, we identify qualitative and quantitative differences in the magnitude, spatial distribution, and symmetry of the emergent magnetic field. Our analysis demonstrates that hopfions can produce measurable transverse resistivity signals, with characteristic dependencies on sample geometry, hopfion size, and carrier mean free path.

The findings presented here provide a foundation for experimental searches for hopfions based on electrical transport measurements, complementing direct imaging techniques. Beyond their fundamental interest, the ability to detect and manipulate hopfions through their topological Hall effect could open new routes for three-dimensional spintronic devices, where information is encoded in robust, topologically protected magnetic structures.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the emergence of topological Hall signatures associated with magnetic hopfions, a class of three-dimensional topological solitons characterized by a nontrivial Hopf invariant. Through a combination of analytical modelling and numerical simulations, we have elucidated how the unique real-space topology of hopfions manifests in momentum-space Berry curvature and, consequently, in measurable transport properties. Our analysis demonstrates that the noncoplanar spin textures inherent to hopfions give rise to an emergent magnetic field that possesses distinct spatial distributions compared to those generated by two-dimensional skyrmions or other chiral spin structures.

By systematically comparing the emergent field profiles of hopfions with those of skyrmion tubes and bobbers, we have identified characteristic features in the topological Hall resistivity that can serve as fingerprints for hopfion phases. Notably, the three-dimensional winding of spin configurations leads to a redistribution of the emergent field along the thickness of the sample, yielding a Hall response that is sensitive to both the hopfion density and their internal twist. This dependence offers a pathway for distinguishing hopfions from other magnetic textures using purely electrical transport measurements, without the need for direct imaging.

Our results further reveal that the magnitude and sign of the topological Hall signal are tunable via external parameters such as magnetic field, temperature, and conduction electron mean free path. In particular, we find that the interplay between the hopfion core size and the electronic scattering length determines whether the Hall response is dominated by the real-space Berry phase or influenced by momentum-space band topology. These findings underline the importance of considering both intrinsic and extrinsic transport regimes when interpreting experimental data in candidate hopfion-hosting materials.

The theoretical framework developed here provides a basis for predicting the transport signatures of hopfions in realistic material platforms, including centrosymmetric magnets with competing exchange interactions and frustrated lattices. Our simulations suggest that the distinctive Hall features we report should be robust against moderate disorder and thermal fluctuations, enhancing their potential utility for experimental detection. Moreover, because hopfions are inherently three-dimensional, their topological charge is not simply projected onto a plane, and thus their Hall signature encodes richer information about the full spin texture.

The identification of reliable electrical signatures for hopfions is a critical step toward their incorporation into spintronic applications, where their stability and topological protection could be harnessed for robust information storage or logic devices. The tunability of their Hall response could also be exploited for sensing applications or for the electrical readout of three-dimensional magnetic states. Beyond applications, the ability to detect hopfions via transport measurements opens new avenues for exploring fundamental aspects of three-dimensional magnetism and topology, including interactions between hopfions, dynamics under current drive, and phase transitions involving changes in the Hopf invariant.

In summary, we have shown that magnetic hopfions give rise to distinctive topological Hall signatures that reflect their unique three-dimensional topology. Our work establishes clear criteria for identifying these signatures in experiment and provides a theoretical foundation for future studies aimed at controlling and exploiting hopfions in functional devices. Continued experimental efforts to probe these predictions will not only validate the proposed mechanisms but also deepen our understanding of topologically nontrivial spin textures in condensed matter systems.

title: Deep Kinematic Pose Regression
abstract: We present a deep learning framework for kinematic pose regression that directly estimates articulated body configurations from visual input while enforcing structural validity through an embedded kinematic model. Unlike conventional pose estimation approaches that predict joint positions independently, our method integrates a differentiable forward kinematics layer into a convolutional neural network, enabling end-to-end learning of joint angle parameters consistent with human skeletal constraints. This representation inherently preserves limb lengths and joint connectivity, reducing physically implausible predictions. We evaluate our approach on benchmark human pose datasets for both 2D and 3D scenarios, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness compared to baseline coordinate regression models. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting anatomically consistent poses under occlusion and varying viewpoints. Our results highlight the benefits of embedding domain-specific kinematic priors into deep regression networks, offering a principled path toward physically grounded, data-driven pose estimation in real-world human motion analysis applications.
introduction: Estimating human pose from visual data is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications in animation, human–computer interaction, augmented reality, and robotics. Traditional approaches often rely on detecting keypoints followed by geometric post-processing, which can suffer from accumulated errors and limited ability to enforce anatomical constraints. Recent deep learning methods have shown significant improvement by learning rich feature representations directly from images. However, many of these approaches treat joint locations as independent regression targets, neglecting the underlying kinematic structure of the human body. This can lead to physically implausible poses and reduced generalization across viewpoints and activities. In this work, we propose a deep kinematic pose regression framework that explicitly incorporates a differentiable kinematic model into the learning process. By embedding joint dependencies and bone length constraints within the network, our method produces anatomically consistent predictions while retaining the flexibility and accuracy of end-to-end training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive accuracy and improved physical plausibility compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated deep kinematic pose regression as a principled approach to estimating articulated body configurations from visual input. By integrating kinematic constraints directly into the regression process, our method enforces physically plausible predictions while maintaining the flexibility of deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive accuracy and improved generalization compared to unconstrained regressors, particularly in challenging poses. Furthermore, the explicit modeling of joint dependencies facilitates interpretability and robustness. Future research could explore extending the framework to dynamic sequences, multi-person interactions, and domain adaptation scenarios, further leveraging kinematic structure for enhanced 3D human pose estimation.

title: A Note on the Pricing of Basket Options Using Taylor Approximations
abstract: This paper investigates the pricing of basket options using Taylor series approximations. By expanding the basket payoff function around the mean asset prices, we derive tractable analytical expressions for option values. Numerical experiments demonstrate the method’s accuracy and efficiency compared to Monte Carlo simulation, offering a practical approach for multi-asset derivative valuation under correlated dynamics.
introduction:
Basket options are financial derivatives whose payoff depends on the weighted sum of multiple underlying assets. They are widely used in equity, commodity, and foreign exchange markets to hedge or speculate on the performance of a portfolio rather than on individual instruments. Despite their practical relevance, accurately pricing basket options remains a challenging problem. The difficulty arises primarily from the lack of closed-form solutions under standard models, except in special cases, due to the complexity of the joint distribution of the underlying assets and the nonlinearity of the payoff function. As a result, practitioners and researchers have developed a variety of approximation and numerical methods, including Monte Carlo simulation, moment-matching techniques, and analytical expansions.

Among these methods, Taylor series approximations have attracted attention for their ability to provide fast and reasonably accurate estimates. By expanding the option payoff or its value function around a chosen point—often the mean of the basket value—one can obtain tractable pricing formulas that capture the effects of asset correlations, volatilities, and weights. Such expansions can yield valuable insights into the sensitivities of basket option values and can serve as efficient substitutes for more computationally intensive methods, particularly in calibration or risk management contexts.

This note revisits the pricing of basket options using Taylor approximations, with emphasis on deriving explicit formulas and assessing their accuracy. Building on the framework of the multivariate Black–Scholes model, we examine both first- and second-order approximations and discuss their practical implementation. Numerical experiments illustrate the trade-off between computational efficiency and approximation error, providing guidance on the applicability of the approach for different market configurations. The results contribute to the ongoing effort to balance analytical tractability and numerical precision in multi-asset option pricing.
conclusion: This study has examined the use of Taylor series expansions to approximate the pricing of basket options, offering a tractable alternative to more computationally intensive methods. By expanding the option payoff and moments of the underlying basket distribution, we derived closed-form approximations that capture key dependencies on the weights, volatilities, and correlations of the constituent assets. Numerical experiments indicate that low-order expansions can deliver accurate results for moderate volatility and correlation levels, while higher-order terms improve performance in more extreme scenarios. The approach thus provides both analytical insight and practical efficiency, making it a valuable tool for risk management and derivative pricing in multi-asset settings.

title: Recurring sets of recurring starspot occultations on exoplanet-host Qatar-2
abstract: We present a detailed analysis of recurring starspot occultation events observed in the transiting hot Jupiter system Qatar-2, based on high-cadence photometry from the *Kepler* K2 mission and complementary ground-based follow-up. The light curves reveal multiple in-transit anomalies consistent with the planet repeatedly crossing the same long-lived starspots over consecutive orbital periods. By modeling these anomalies with a starspot occultation framework, we determine spot positions, sizes, and contrasts, and identify distinct sets of recurring features persisting for several stellar rotations. The recurrence patterns allow precise measurement of the stellar rotation period at the transit chord and provide constraints on the stellar obliquity. Our results indicate that the stellar equator is closely aligned with the planetary orbital plane, and that the spots are stable over tens of days, suggesting strong magnetic activity anchored to preferred longitudes. The observed recurrence also enables refinement of the planetary ephemeris and detection of subtle transit timing variations. This study demonstrates the utility of repeated starspot occultations as probes of stellar surface structure and spin–orbit geometry, and highlights Qatar-2 as a valuable laboratory for investigating the interplay between magnetic activity and close-in giant planets.
introduction:
The study of stellar activity in transiting exoplanet systems offers a unique opportunity to probe both stellar magnetic phenomena and the orbital geometry of the planet. Starspots—regions of reduced surface temperature caused by concentrations of magnetic flux—can produce detectable anomalies in high-precision transit light curves when occulted by an orbiting planet. These spot-crossing events manifest as temporary brightening features against the otherwise smooth transit profile. By tracing the recurrence of such features over multiple transits, it is possible to infer the rotational period of the host star, the latitude distribution of active regions, and the degree of spin–orbit alignment between the stellar rotation axis and the planetary orbital plane.

Qatar-2 is a K-dwarf star hosting a close-in hot Jupiter, Qatar-2b, with an orbital period of approximately 1.34 days. Previous photometric monitoring has revealed that Qatar-2 exhibits significant magnetic activity, consistent with its relatively young age and rapid rotation. The short orbital period of Qatar-2b, combined with the large planet-to-star radius ratio, makes this system particularly well suited for the detection of starspot occultations. In such configurations, a planet will repeatedly sweep across nearly the same chord of the stellar disk, potentially encountering the same active regions over successive stellar rotations.

Recurring sets of recurring starspot occultations—where the same spot-crossing signatures appear in sequences separated by the stellar rotation period—offer a powerful diagnostic for characterizing stellar surface features. These repetitions can reveal the persistence of individual spots on timescales of weeks, constrain the stellar rotation period to high precision, and shed light on the stability and evolution of active longitudes. Moreover, the detection of such patterns provides a means to probe the relative orientation of the stellar rotation axis and planetary orbit, complementing spectroscopic Rossiter–McLaughlin measurements.

In this work, we present a detailed analysis of high-cadence photometric observations of Qatar-2 obtained by the *K2* mission and ground-based facilities. We identify and characterize multiple sets of recurring starspot occultations, tracking their appearance across many consecutive transits. By modeling the timing and morphology of the spot-crossing anomalies, we measure the stellar rotation period and investigate the longevity of the active regions responsible. Our results contribute to the growing body of evidence that certain magnetically active stars host long-lived starspots or spot groups at preferred latitudes, and they demonstrate the utility of transit photometry for mapping stellar surface activity in the era of space-based exoplanet surveys.
conclusion:
Our analysis of the extensive photometric time series for Qatar-2 has revealed clear evidence for recurring sets of recurring starspot occultations, providing new insight into the stellar activity and spin–orbit geometry of this exoplanetary system. By identifying and tracking individual spot-crossing events across multiple consecutive transits, we have demonstrated that some starspots persist over many stellar rotations, and that their reappearance aligns with a consistent pattern expected for long-lived active regions on a slowly rotating K-dwarf. The recurrence of these occultations within specific transit phases supports the interpretation that the stellar rotation axis is closely aligned with the planetary orbital axis, in agreement with previous Rossiter–McLaughlin measurements.

The detection of multiple sets of recurring occultations indicates that active latitudes on Qatar-2 are stable over timescales of at least several tens of days, and possibly much longer. The longevity and spatial coherence of these active regions suggest that the magnetic field topology is dominated by large-scale structures, which may be characteristic of mid-K dwarfs. Our modelling of the occultation sequences has constrained the stellar rotation period independently, yielding values in good agreement with those derived from out-of-transit modulation, thereby reinforcing the robustness of our methodology.

These findings have important implications for understanding star–planet interactions and their observational signatures. The persistence of starspot occultations offers a unique opportunity to probe stellar differential rotation, the evolution of active regions, and the possible influence of the close-in giant planet on the host star’s magnetic activity. Furthermore, recurring occultation events can serve as precise markers for refining orbital ephemerides and testing for transit timing variations.

Future high-cadence, high-precision photometry—particularly from space-based platforms—will enable more detailed mapping of starspot distributions and evolution in systems like Qatar-2. Combined with spectroscopic monitoring, such studies can help disentangle the interplay between stellar activity cycles and planetary orbital dynamics. In summary, the recurring sets of recurring occultations observed in Qatar-2 not only illuminate the nature of stellar magnetism in exoplanet hosts but also provide a valuable diagnostic for the physical and dynamical properties of close-in planetary systems.

title: Efficient cosmological parameter sampling using sparse grids
abstract: We present a novel approach for efficient sampling of cosmological parameter spaces based on sparse grid interpolation techniques. Traditional Monte Carlo and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, while robust, often require prohibitively large numbers of model evaluations to achieve convergence in high-dimensional settings, such as those arising in modern cosmology. Our method constructs a surrogate model of the likelihood function using adaptive sparse grids, enabling accurate interpolation across the parameter domain with far fewer evaluations of the underlying cosmological model. This approach exploits the smoothness of the likelihood surface and the hierarchical structure of sparse grids to concentrate sampling in regions of high variation, thereby reducing computational cost without sacrificing accuracy. We demonstrate the method on representative cosmological inference problems, including parameter estimation from simulated cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure data. Comparisons with conventional MCMC show that our sparse grid strategy achieves similar or improved precision in posterior estimation with an order-of-magnitude reduction in model evaluations. This framework offers a scalable and adaptable tool for accelerating cosmological parameter inference, with potential applications to upcoming large-volume surveys and complex theoretical models.
introduction:
The determination of cosmological parameters from observational data is a central task in modern cosmology. Advances in survey capabilities, such as those provided by the Planck satellite, the Dark Energy Survey, and upcoming facilities like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory and the Euclid mission, have produced and will continue to generate vast quantities of high-precision data. Extracting reliable constraints on parameters describing the Universe’s composition, geometry, and evolution necessitates efficient and accurate statistical inference techniques. In the standard Bayesian framework, this involves the computation of likelihood functions over a high-dimensional parameter space, often requiring repeated evaluations of computationally expensive theoretical models such as Boltzmann solvers. Consequently, the sampling strategy adopted has a decisive impact on the feasibility and efficiency of cosmological analyses.

Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods have become the canonical choice for exploring posterior distributions in cosmology due to their asymptotic convergence properties and flexibility in handling complex likelihoods. However, their performance can be severely hampered in scenarios where the likelihood function is costly to evaluate, the parameter space is high-dimensional, or the posterior exhibits strong degeneracies. Alternative approaches, such as nested sampling, importance sampling, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, offer improvements under certain conditions, but they do not fundamentally eliminate the challenge posed by the curse of dimensionality and the need for a large number of likelihood evaluations. As cosmological models become increasingly sophisticated, there is a pressing need for methods that can reduce the computational burden while preserving accuracy.

Sparse grid methods, originating in numerical analysis for high-dimensional integration and interpolation, present a promising avenue in this context. By exploiting the structure of smooth functions in multiple dimensions, sparse grids achieve a substantial reduction in the number of required sampling points compared to full tensor-product grids, while retaining high-order accuracy. This efficiency gain stems from the hierarchical construction of the approximation, which selectively refines the grid in directions of greatest variation. In cosmological parameter estimation, where likelihood functions often exhibit smooth behaviour modulated by distinct scales of variation across parameters, sparse grids offer the potential to construct accurate surrogate models of the likelihood or posterior with far fewer evaluations.

Recent applications of sparse grids in uncertainty quantification, engineering design, and computational physics suggest their suitability for problems where evaluations are expensive and the effective dimensionality is moderate. In cosmology, however, their use remains relatively unexplored. This work aims to investigate the performance of sparse grid sampling strategies for cosmological parameter inference, assessing their accuracy, efficiency, and scalability relative to established methods. We focus on constructing surrogate likelihood approximations from sparse grid nodes and utilising these surrogates in Bayesian inference, thereby reducing the number of calls to the underlying cosmological model. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate that sparse grids can significantly accelerate parameter estimation without compromising the precision of cosmological constraints, making them a valuable addition to the computational toolbox of modern cosmology.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a novel approach for efficient cosmological parameter sampling based on sparse grid techniques. By exploiting the inherent smoothness of cosmological likelihood surfaces and the high-dimensional structure of parameter spaces, our method achieves substantial reductions in the number of required model evaluations compared to conventional dense sampling or brute-force Monte Carlo strategies. The adaptive refinement capabilities of sparse grids allow computational resources to be concentrated in regions of high posterior probability, while maintaining global coverage of the parameter space. This leads to improved convergence rates and more accurate parameter inferences within a fixed computational budget.

We have demonstrated that the sparse grid framework integrates naturally with established cosmological inference pipelines, including those based on Boltzmann solvers and large-scale structure simulations. The interpolation properties of the sparse grid representation enable rapid evaluation of the likelihood function once the grid is constructed, facilitating downstream analyses such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling or nested sampling with minimal additional cost. Furthermore, our results indicate that the method retains accuracy even in the presence of moderate non-linearities or parameter degeneracies, provided that the refinement criteria appropriately target these features.

Comparisons with traditional sampling schemes show that sparse grids can reduce the number of model evaluations by factors of several, especially in moderate- to high-dimensional parameter spaces typical in modern cosmology. This efficiency gain is particularly valuable when each model evaluation is computationally expensive, as is often the case when incorporating non-linear effects, baryonic physics, or full forward modelling of observables. The flexibility of sparse grids also opens the door to hybrid strategies, where coarse global approximations are combined with targeted high-resolution refinement in regions of scientific interest.

While the current implementation assumes smooth likelihood functions and Gaussian-distributed observational uncertainties, future work should explore extensions to handle more complex likelihood structures, including multi-modal distributions and non-Gaussian error models. Incorporating observational systematics into the sparse grid refinement process is another promising direction, as is the integration of machine learning surrogates to further accelerate grid construction. Additionally, applying this approach to joint analyses of multiple cosmological probes will test its robustness and scalability in realistic, high-dimensional inference problems.

In summary, sparse grid sampling offers a powerful and flexible tool for cosmological parameter estimation, capable of delivering significant computational savings without compromising accuracy. As cosmological datasets continue to grow in size and complexity, such methods will be critical for fully exploiting their constraining power and enabling timely, precise insights into the fundamental properties of the Universe.

title: M$^2$I Communication: From Theoretical Modeling to Practical Design
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of M$^2$I (Magnetic-Magnetic Inductive) communication, bridging theoretical foundations and practical system design. M$^2$I communication leverages coupled magnetic resonances to enable reliable, low-power data exchange in challenging environments where conventional radio frequency technologies face significant attenuation or scattering. We first develop a comprehensive theoretical model that captures the near-field magnetic coupling dynamics, mutual inductance variations, and the impact of coil geometry, alignment, and medium properties on communication performance. Analytical results are validated against full-wave electromagnetic simulations, demonstrating strong agreement across a range of operating frequencies and coil configurations. Building on the model, we present design guidelines for transceiver architecture, modulation schemes, and adaptive tuning techniques to optimize performance under real-world constraints such as misalignment, medium heterogeneity, and power limitations. A prototype implementation is developed and experimentally evaluated, confirming the feasibility of high-throughput, robust M$^2$I links in both controlled laboratory and field conditions. The proposed framework provides a systematic pathway from theory to practice, enabling the deployment of M$^2$I communication in underwater, underground, and embedded sensing applications.
introduction:
In recent years, the rapid proliferation of interconnected devices, the exponential growth of data traffic, and the evolution of intelligent applications have collectively driven the demand for communication systems that are not only high-performing but also adaptive, efficient, and scalable. Emerging paradigms such as the Internet of Things (IoT), machine-type communications, and intelligent transportation systems require a fundamental rethinking of how information is modeled, transmitted, and processed. These domains are characterized by heterogeneous requirements—ranging from ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) to massive machine-type communication (mMTC)—that challenge the traditional design trade-offs of communication theory. Against this backdrop, the concept of M$^2$I (Multi-Modal and Intelligent) communication has emerged as a promising framework that unites theoretical rigor with design-oriented practicality.

M$^2$I communication refers to systems that simultaneously exploit multiple modalities—such as heterogeneous signaling formats, diverse physical channels, and multi-domain resource allocations—while embedding intelligence throughout the communication chain. By modalities, we mean not only physical-layer diversity (e.g., time, frequency, space, and code) but also functional diversity across protocol layers, sensing capabilities, and semantic representations of information. Intelligence, in this context, encompasses both data-driven and model-based decision-making mechanisms that optimize communication strategies in real time, adapting to environmental variability and application-specific constraints. This integrated approach aims to transcend the limitations of conventional single-modality, static designs, enabling systems to operate efficiently in complex, dynamic, and resource-constrained environments.

From a theoretical perspective, M$^2$I communication builds upon foundational concepts of information theory, signal processing, and network optimization, while extending them to account for multi-modal interactions and intelligent adaptation. Traditional models often assume stationary channels, fixed modulation schemes, and well-defined performance metrics such as bit error rate or spectral efficiency. However, in M$^2$I systems, the performance of each modality is not independent but coupled—either synergistically or competitively—with others. This coupling necessitates new mathematical models capable of capturing cross-modal dependencies, joint resource allocation, and the interplay between communication and computation. Furthermore, intelligence introduces stochastic decision processes, online learning dynamics, and predictive control into the modeling framework, demanding hybrid approaches that combine analytical tractability with empirical adaptability.

On the practical side, M$^2$I communication must address real-world constraints such as hardware limitations, energy efficiency, latency budgets, and interoperability across heterogeneous platforms. Designing such systems entails translating theoretical insights into architectures, protocols, and algorithms that can be deployed on existing and emerging infrastructures. This transition from theory to practice is non-trivial: abstract models often rely on idealized assumptions that may be violated in operational settings, while practical designs must contend with incomplete information, measurement noise, and implementation overhead. Bridging this gap requires iterative co-design processes, where theoretical modeling informs design choices, and empirical evaluations feed back into refined models. This cycle ensures that M$^2$I systems are not only theoretically sound but also robust, scalable, and aligned with application needs.

The relevance of M$^2$I communication extends to a wide range of applications. In autonomous vehicular networks, for example, vehicles must exchange multi-modal information—such as sensor data, control commands, and environmental context—under strict latency and reliability constraints, while adapting to varying traffic and channel conditions. In industrial IoT scenarios, heterogeneous devices coordinate to maintain process efficiency, leveraging both wired and wireless modalities and dynamically adjusting communication parameters based on machine learning predictions. In augmented and virtual reality, multi-modal data streams (video, audio, tactile feedback) must be synchronized and optimized for immersive user experiences, requiring intelligent bandwidth allocation and predictive prefetching. These examples illustrate the breadth of scenarios in which M$^2$I principles can deliver substantial performance gains.

Despite its promise, the systematic study of M$^2$I communication remains in its infancy. Existing literature has tended to address either multi-modal diversity or intelligent adaptation in isolation, without fully exploring their combined potential. Moreover, while numerous works have proposed ad hoc solutions for specific applications, there is a lack of unified frameworks that connect rigorous theoretical analysis with end-to-end system design. This gap motivates the present work, which seeks to advance M$^2$I communication from conceptual underpinnings to practical realizations.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive treatment of M$^2$I communication that integrates theoretical modeling with practical design methodologies. We begin by formalizing the notion of multi-modal and intelligent communication, developing analytical models that capture the interactions between modalities and the role of learning-based adaptation. We then translate these models into design principles and concrete architectures, supported by simulation and experimental results. Through this dual perspective, our aim is to provide both the conceptual clarity and the engineering guidance necessary for the next generation of communication systems to meet the complex demands of future applications.
conclusion:
This work has explored the concept of M$^2$I communication from both a theoretical and practical perspective, establishing a coherent framework that bridges analytical modeling with real-world design considerations. Beginning with the development of a rigorous mathematical model, we characterized the fundamental propagation mechanisms, channel behavior, and performance limits inherent to M$^2$I systems. The theoretical analysis not only provided a deeper understanding of the signal transmission process but also revealed key parameters influencing efficiency, reliability, and scalability. These insights served as the foundation for translating abstract formulations into implementable design strategies.

On the practical side, we synthesized the derived models into a design methodology that addresses critical engineering trade-offs, including size constraints, energy consumption, material properties, and environmental variability. By aligning model predictions with empirical constraints, we demonstrated how M$^2$I communication can be optimized for diverse application scenarios, from low-power embedded systems to robust industrial networks. The iterative interplay between theory and practice proved essential, as experimental feedback informed refinements to the model, while theoretical predictions guided hardware configuration and protocol selection.

Our results indicate that the M$^2$I paradigm holds significant promise for enabling novel communication capabilities in environments where conventional wireless solutions encounter limitations. In particular, the ability to achieve stable performance in challenging propagation conditions, coupled with the inherent security and energy efficiency of the approach, positions M$^2$I as a viable alternative or complement to established technologies. Furthermore, the modularity of the proposed framework facilitates adaptation to emerging requirements, suggesting a long-term relevance of the methodology.

Nonetheless, several open challenges remain. The current models, while accurate under controlled conditions, require further extension to account for complex, dynamic environments and heterogeneous device characteristics. Similarly, the practical implementations could benefit from advances in materials science, miniaturization techniques, and adaptive signal processing algorithms. Addressing these issues will likely require interdisciplinary collaboration, bringing together expertise in electromagnetics, circuit design, information theory, and systems engineering.

In summary, this study has provided a comprehensive treatment of M$^2$I communication, advancing it from conceptual modeling to actionable design principles. By unifying analytical rigor with practical feasibility, we have laid the groundwork for future research and development in this promising field. The continued refinement and integration of theoretical insights with technological innovations will be crucial for realizing the full potential of M$^2$I systems in next-generation communication infrastructures.

title: A Method for Calculating Collision Probability Between Space Objects
abstract: This paper presents a computational method for estimating the collision probability between space objects in Earth orbit. The approach models relative motion using two-body dynamics with perturbative corrections and incorporates position and velocity uncertainties through a Gaussian error framework. Collision probability is derived via numerical integration over the encounter geometry, accounting for object dimensions and covariance propagation. The method is applicable to both cataloged satellites and tracked debris, enabling assessment over short-term conjunction events. Validation against Monte Carlo simulations demonstrates accuracy and computational efficiency suitable for operational use. The proposed technique supports improved conjunction assessment, facilitating timely decision-making for collision avoidance maneuvers and contributing to the mitigation of risks in the increasingly congested orbital environment.
introduction:
The rapid increase in the number of artificial satellites and debris in Earth orbit has raised growing concerns about the risk of collisions between space objects. Advances in satellite deployment, particularly the proliferation of large constellations, have intensified the density of objects in low Earth orbit (LEO) and other orbital regimes. This trend exacerbates the potential for catastrophic collisions, which can generate large amounts of debris, further increasing the probability of subsequent impacts in a self-sustaining process known as the Kessler Syndrome. As a result, accurate estimation of collision probability has become a critical component of space situational awareness (SSA) and traffic management strategies.

Collision probability assessment involves quantifying the likelihood that two objects with uncertain trajectories will come within a specified miss distance during a given time interval. This calculation is complicated by various factors, including the accuracy of orbital data, the stochastic nature of perturbations, and the often incomplete knowledge of physical object characteristics. Traditional methods, such as the use of hard-body radius approximations or covariance-based analytical formulations, have provided valuable tools for operational conjunction assessments. However, these approaches may be limited in accuracy when covariance information is incomplete, when orbital uncertainties are non-Gaussian, or when the encounter geometries are complex.

Recent research has explored more sophisticated probabilistic techniques, including numerical integration of relative motion probability density functions and Monte Carlo simulations, to improve reliability under such conditions. Nonetheless, these methods can be computationally expensive, particularly when applied to large numbers of potential conjunctions in real time. Therefore, there remains a need for efficient, robust methods capable of handling diverse uncertainty models while maintaining computational tractability.

This paper presents a method for calculating collision probability between space objects that balances accuracy and efficiency. The proposed approach incorporates realistic uncertainty representations and is adaptable to various encounter scenarios. By addressing both methodological rigor and operational constraints, this work contributes to improving the safety and sustainability of space activities in an increasingly congested orbital environment.
conclusion: The method presented provides a systematic and computationally efficient approach for estimating the collision probability between space objects, incorporating both orbital uncertainties and the relative geometry of encounter. By integrating probabilistic models with high-fidelity orbital propagation, the approach captures the influence of covariance evolution and encounter dynamics more accurately than simplified analytical approximations. Validation against simulated conjunction scenarios demonstrates that the method produces results consistent with established benchmarks while offering improved adaptability to diverse orbital regimes. This capability is particularly valuable for conjunction assessment in increasingly congested orbital environments, where timely and reliable probability estimates are essential for informed decision-making. Moreover, the framework is flexible and can be extended to incorporate non-spherical object shapes, atmospheric drag variations, and maneuver uncertainties, thereby improving realism in operational contexts. Future work may focus on optimizing computational performance for large-scale catalog processing and integrating the method into automated collision avoidance systems. Overall, the proposed approach contributes a robust and adaptable tool for enhancing space situational awareness and mitigating collision risks.

title: Orientation-guided Graph Convolutional Network for Bone Surface Segmentation
abstract: We propose an orientation-guided graph convolutional network (OG-GCN) for accurate bone surface segmentation from volumetric medical images. Unlike conventional CNN-based methods, our approach models the bone surface as a graph, where vertices represent sampled surface points and edges encode spatial relationships. To better capture anisotropic geometric patterns, we introduce orientation-guided convolution kernels that adaptively aggregate features according to local surface normal directions. This design enhances the network’s ability to delineate complex bone boundaries, especially in regions with high curvature or thin structures. Experiments on multiple CT datasets demonstrate that OG-GCN achieves superior segmentation accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its potential for clinical applications in orthopedic planning and image-guided surgery.
introduction:
Accurate bone surface segmentation from medical imaging data is a critical step for numerous clinical and research applications, including orthopedic surgery planning, biomechanical modeling, and disease diagnosis. Conventional segmentation methods, such as thresholding or region-growing techniques, often struggle to capture fine structural details in complex anatomical regions, particularly when image quality is degraded by noise or artifacts. Deep learning-based approaches, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated substantial improvements in segmentation performance. However, standard CNNs are typically designed for grid-structured data and may fail to effectively model the irregular geometry and topology of bone surfaces.

Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) provide a powerful framework for processing non-Euclidean data by operating directly on graph representations of anatomical structures. Nevertheless, existing GCN-based methods often overlook the intrinsic orientation information present in surface geometry, which can be crucial for distinguishing between adjacent structures with similar local features. To address this limitation, we propose an Orientation-guided Graph Convolutional Network (OG-GCN) that integrates local orientation cues into graph-based feature learning. By explicitly encoding orientation information into the node and edge features, our method enhances the discriminative capability of the network, leading to more accurate and robust bone surface segmentation.
conclusion: In this work, we proposed an orientation-guided graph convolutional network (OG-GCN) to address the challenge of accurate bone surface segmentation. By integrating orientation information into the graph construction and convolution process, our model effectively captures geometric context and enhances boundary delineation. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that OG-GCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and robustness, particularly in regions with complex structures or low contrast. The proposed framework leverages local orientation cues to guide feature propagation, resulting in improved surface continuity and reduced segmentation errors. Future work will explore integrating multi-scale orientation features and extending the method to other anatomical structures, further advancing graph-based medical image analysis.

title: Stable marriage problems with quantitative preferences
abstract: We investigate variants of the stable marriage problem in which agents express quantitative preferences over potential partners, rather than merely providing ordinal rankings. In this framework, each agent assigns a numerical score to every possible match, enabling a richer representation of preferences and compatibility. We examine how classical notions of stability can be extended to accommodate quantitative data, and propose several alternative stability criteria that capture different trade-offs between individual satisfaction and global optimality. Our analysis explores the computational complexity of finding stable matchings under these criteria, identifying cases that remain polynomial-time solvable as well as those that become NP-hard. We also study the structural properties of stable matchings in the quantitative setting, including existence guarantees, uniqueness conditions, and the relationships between various stability definitions. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets illustrate how quantitative preferences influence matching outcomes, revealing differences in fairness, efficiency, and robustness compared to ordinal approaches. These results demonstrate that incorporating quantitative information can yield more nuanced and potentially more desirable matchings, but also raises new challenges in algorithm design and evaluation. Our work provides a foundation for further research on stability concepts in quantitatively enriched matching markets.
introduction:
The stable marriage problem (SMP) is a cornerstone of algorithmic game theory and combinatorial optimization, originally formulated by Gale and Shapley in 1962. In its classical form, the problem involves two disjoint sets of agents—traditionally referred to as men and women—each of whom ranks all members of the opposite set in order of preference. A matching is a pairing of agents from the two sets such that each agent is matched to exactly one partner, and a matching is said to be stable if there is no pair of agents who would both prefer each other to their assigned partners. The SMP has inspired a rich body of research due to its elegant mathematical formulation, well-defined notions of stability, and wide-ranging applications in markets, resource allocation, and institutional design.

The standard SMP formulation assumes ordinal preferences: each agent’s preference list specifies only the relative ordering of potential partners, without any indication of the strength or magnitude of preference between alternatives. This abstraction has the advantage of simplicity and generality, enabling the design of efficient algorithms such as the Gale–Shapley deferred acceptance algorithm, which guarantees the existence of at least one stable matching for any set of complete, strict preference lists. However, in many real-world scenarios, preferences are inherently quantitative rather than purely ordinal; agents may assign scores, utilities, or weights to potential partners, reflecting varying intensities of preference. For instance, in college admissions, a university may score applicants based on multiple criteria, leading to numerical rankings; in job matching, employers may evaluate candidates using detailed performance metrics; and in online dating or recommendation systems, preference data is often derived from ratings, compatibility scores, or predicted match quality.

The introduction of quantitative preferences to the stable marriage setting gives rise to what is often termed the stable marriage problem with quantitative preferences (SMP-QP). In this variant, each agent assigns a numerical value to each potential partner, representing the degree of desirability or utility. Quantitative preferences open up new modeling opportunities, allowing for richer representations of agent priorities and more nuanced decision-making processes. At the same time, they introduce additional computational and theoretical challenges, as stability may need to be redefined or refined to account for the magnitude of mutual preference rather than merely its existence.

A straightforward approach to incorporating quantitative preferences is to convert them into ordinal rankings by sorting partners according to their assigned scores. However, such a transformation discards valuable information about preference intensities. Two matchings that are equally stable in the ordinal sense may differ significantly in terms of aggregate or individual satisfaction when the underlying quantitative preferences are considered. This motivates the exploration of stability concepts that explicitly integrate utility values, such as *α-stability*, where a blocking pair is considered significant only if both agents’ gains from deviation exceed a certain threshold, or *maximum weight stability*, where the objective is to find a stable matching that maximizes the sum of assigned preference scores.

The study of SMP-QP is not purely theoretical; it aligns closely with practical matching problems in economics, computer science, and operations research. Applications in centralized matching markets, such as the National Resident Matching Program for medical graduates, often have access to rich, quantitative evaluation data. Similarly, in matching students to schools or universities, quantitative criteria such as test scores, grades, and interview performance are central to decision-making. In these settings, designing algorithms that respect stability while optimizing for quantitative objectives can lead to more efficient and satisfactory outcomes for all participants.

Beyond application-specific motivations, SMP-QP engages with fundamental questions about fairness, efficiency, and trade-offs in multi-agent systems. While ordinal stability ensures that no pair can mutually improve their situation in terms of rank, it does not guarantee optimality with respect to the magnitude of preferences. Conversely, optimizing solely for aggregate score without regard for blocking pairs can lead to highly unstable matchings. Balancing these competing objectives requires careful definition of stability criteria and the development of algorithms that can navigate the resulting solution space.

Existing research on SMP-QP has considered a variety of approaches, including adaptations of classical deferred acceptance methods to handle weighted preferences, formulations as integer programming problems, and heuristic or approximation algorithms for large-scale instances. Some studies have introduced multi-objective frameworks that simultaneously seek to maximize total preference satisfaction while maintaining a chosen notion of stability. Others have investigated the structure of stable matchings under quantitative preferences, identifying conditions under which classical properties, such as the lattice structure of the set of stable matchings, still hold.

Despite these advances, many open problems remain. The computational complexity of finding matchings that are both quantitatively optimal and stable under refined definitions is not fully understood for general cases. Moreover, the impact of incomplete preference information, ties, and strategic manipulation in the quantitative setting warrants further investigation. From a practical perspective, there is a need for scalable algorithms that can handle the large, complex datasets typical of modern matching platforms while accommodating nuanced preference data.

In this work, we contribute to the growing literature on SMP-QP by formalizing stability notions that incorporate quantitative preferences, analyzing their theoretical properties, and developing algorithms that achieve favorable trade-offs between stability and preference satisfaction. We present both exact and approximate methods, evaluate their performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, and explore the implications of different stability definitions for participant welfare and system efficiency. By bridging the gap between purely ordinal models and the rich quantitative data available in practice, our study aims to provide a more expressive and applicable framework for stable matching in diverse domains.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined stable marriage problems in the context of quantitative preferences, extending the classical framework to settings where agents express graded evaluations rather than mere ordinal rankings. By incorporating numerical scores into preference structures, we have explored both theoretical properties and algorithmic implications, highlighting how stability can be redefined and measured when preference intensities are taken into account. Our analysis has shown that quantitative preferences enrich the solution space, allowing for finer distinctions between matchings that would otherwise be indistinguishable in the ordinal model, and enabling the design of mechanisms that balance stability with aggregate satisfaction. We have also discussed computational strategies for finding stable matchings under these extended definitions, noting trade-offs between optimality criteria and feasibility. Experimental observations suggest that leveraging quantitative information can lead to outcomes that are both stable and more satisfactory from a utilitarian perspective, though sensitivity to preference distributions remains an important consideration. This work opens several avenues for future research, including the study of robustness under noisy or incomplete quantitative data, the exploration of fairness metrics in the quantitative domain, and the adaptation of these concepts to many-to-one or dynamic matching scenarios. Overall, our findings demonstrate that moving beyond ordinal preferences offers a richer and more flexible foundation for stable matching theory, with potential applications in diverse real-world allocation problems.

title: Context-based Barrier Notification Service Toward Outdoor Support for the Elderly
abstract: The rapid growth of the elderly population highlights the need for accessible outdoor environments that support safe and independent mobility. However, physical barriers such as uneven surfaces, construction zones, and temporary obstacles can pose significant challenges, increasing the risk of falls and discouraging outdoor activity. This study presents the design and evaluation of a context-based barrier notification service aimed at assisting elderly individuals during outdoor navigation. The proposed system integrates real-time environmental sensing, crowdsourced barrier reports, and personalized context analysis to deliver timely and relevant notifications via a mobile application. By considering individual mobility profiles, location, and environmental conditions, the service prioritizes barrier alerts to minimize cognitive load while maximizing safety. Field trials with elderly participants demonstrated that the system effectively identified and communicated relevant obstacles, enhancing route safety and user confidence. The findings suggest that context-aware barrier notification services can play a vital role in promoting outdoor mobility, reducing accident risks, and supporting active aging. Future work will explore integration with wearable devices and expansion to broader urban accessibility applications.
introduction:
The global population is aging at an unprecedented rate, with the proportion of people aged 65 and over steadily increasing in many countries. As this demographic shift progresses, ensuring the mobility, safety, and independence of older adults has become a critical social and technological challenge. Outdoor mobility plays a crucial role in maintaining physical health, social engagement, and overall quality of life for the elderly. However, age-related declines in sensory, cognitive, and motor abilities can make navigating outdoor environments increasingly difficult. Hazards such as uneven pavements, construction zones, steep inclines, or temporary obstacles may pose significant risks, potentially leading to falls, injuries, or reduced willingness to go out.  

Conventional navigation systems are predominantly designed for the general population and are optimized for route efficiency rather than user safety in the presence of physical or situational barriers. While some assistive technologies provide basic guidance, they often fail to consider the specific needs, limitations, and preferences of elderly users. Furthermore, environmental conditions and urban infrastructure are dynamic, meaning that static maps or pre-defined alerts cannot provide timely and relevant information about emerging hazards. This gap underscores the need for context-aware solutions that can adapt in real time to environmental changes and personal user contexts.

A context-based barrier notification service offers a promising approach to addressing these challenges. By integrating real-time environmental sensing, geographic information systems, and user-specific profiles, such a service could identify potential hazards ahead of time and deliver tailored alerts to elderly pedestrians. Context awareness enables the system to account for factors such as mobility limitations, current weather, or personal comfort levels, thereby enhancing both safety and confidence during outdoor activities.  

This study explores the design and development of a context-based barrier notification service aimed at supporting outdoor mobility for older adults. We focus on identifying relevant contextual factors, determining effective methods of barrier detection and classification, and designing notification strategies that are both timely and comprehensible. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the creation of inclusive, adaptive urban navigation systems that empower elderly individuals to maintain active, independent lifestyles while minimizing risks in outdoor environments.
conclusion: This study presented a context-based barrier notification service designed to support elderly individuals in outdoor environments. By integrating environmental sensing, user context awareness, and adaptive notification delivery, the system enhances mobility and safety while reducing cognitive load. Field evaluations demonstrated that timely, personalized alerts can help older adults avoid obstacles and navigate more confidently. The approach highlights the importance of combining real-time data with user-specific needs to maximize effectiveness. Future work will focus on expanding sensor coverage, refining context inference, and exploring multimodal feedback to accommodate diverse sensory and cognitive abilities. Ultimately, this service has the potential to promote independent living and improve quality of life for the aging population in urban and suburban settings.

title: Unsupervised Part Discovery by Unsupervised Disentanglement
abstract: We propose a novel framework for unsupervised part discovery through disentangled representation learning, without relying on manual annotations or predefined semantic categories. Our method leverages an unsupervised disentanglement objective to separate latent factors corresponding to distinct object parts, enabling interpretable and spatially localized feature representations. Specifically, we combine part-aware spatial attention with a factorized latent space, encouraging each dimension to capture a consistent, spatially coherent component across instances. This approach facilitates emergent part segmentation by aligning disentangled factors with recurring structural patterns, even in complex, articulated objects. We evaluate our model on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms existing unsupervised part discovery methods in both segmentation accuracy and interpretability. Furthermore, we show that the learned part representations are transferable to downstream tasks such as pose estimation and fine-grained recognition. Our results highlight the potential of unsupervised disentanglement as a powerful inductive bias for discovering meaningful object parts without any supervisory signals.
introduction: Understanding and representing objects in terms of their constituent parts is a fundamental problem in computer vision, with broad implications for recognition, manipulation, and reasoning. Traditional approaches often rely on supervised annotations, which are costly to obtain and may not generalize across domains. Recent advances in disentangled representation learning suggest that object factors such as shape, pose, and appearance can be separated without explicit supervision. However, most existing methods focus on global factors and do not explicitly address the discovery of semantically meaningful parts. In this work, we propose an unsupervised framework that leverages disentanglement to uncover object parts without any part-level labels. By encouraging independent variation across learned factors, our method isolates consistent spatial components corresponding to parts, enabling both interpretable analysis and downstream tasks. We evaluate our approach on diverse datasets, demonstrating that unsupervised part discovery emerges naturally from disentangled representations, offering a scalable path toward structured object understanding.
conclusion: In this work, we presented an unsupervised framework for discovering object parts through disentangled representation learning. By jointly learning to separate appearance and spatial factors without annotations, our approach enables the emergence of semantically meaningful parts across diverse object categories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the learned part representations are interpretable and transferable, supporting downstream tasks such as pose estimation and fine-grained recognition. Our results highlight the potential of unsupervised disentanglement for structured visual understanding, reducing reliance on costly supervision. Future work will explore scaling to more complex scenes and integrating temporal cues to further enhance part consistency and robustness.

title: Nonlinear Control of a DC MicroGrid for the Integration of Photovoltaic Panels
abstract: This paper presents a nonlinear control strategy for a DC microgrid integrating photovoltaic (PV) panels to ensure stable operation under varying irradiance and load conditions. The proposed approach employs a Lyapunov-based control design to regulate the DC bus voltage while coordinating power sharing among distributed generation units. The PV array is interfaced through a DC-DC converter with maximum power point tracking (MPPT) to optimize energy extraction. Nonlinear control laws are derived to handle system uncertainties and nonlinearities, enhancing robustness and dynamic performance. Simulation results demonstrate the ability of the controller to maintain voltage stability, achieve fast transient response, and improve power quality. The proposed method offers a practical solution for reliable PV integration in modern DC microgrids.
introduction:
The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources into modern power systems is transforming the architecture and operation of electrical networks. Among the various renewable technologies, photovoltaic (PV) energy has emerged as one of the most promising due to its scalability, declining cost, and environmental benefits. As PV generation becomes more widespread, the concept of direct current (DC) microgrids has gained significant attention. DC microgrids offer several advantages over their alternating current (AC) counterparts, particularly in applications where energy sources, storage systems, and loads inherently operate with DC voltages. These advantages include higher efficiency due to the elimination of multiple conversion stages, simpler control structures, and ease of integration with distributed energy resources (DERs) such as PV panels, batteries, and fuel cells.

However, the integration of PV systems into DC microgrids introduces several technical challenges. PV generation is inherently intermittent and nonlinear, as it is strongly influenced by environmental conditions such as solar irradiance and temperature. Furthermore, the power–voltage characteristics of PV modules require the implementation of maximum power point tracking (MPPT) algorithms to ensure optimal energy extraction. When interconnected within a DC microgrid, PV sources must also coordinate with other generation units, storage systems, and load demands to maintain power quality, voltage stability, and supply–demand balance. These requirements become more complex under varying operating conditions, load fluctuations, and potential faults.

Traditional linear control techniques, while effective for small-signal operation around a nominal operating point, often fail to provide adequate performance in the presence of the significant nonlinearities and uncertainties inherent in PV generation and power electronic converters. This limitation has motivated the exploration of nonlinear control strategies that can enhance system robustness, improve transient performance, and ensure stability over a wide range of operating conditions. Nonlinear control methods such as feedback linearization, sliding mode control, and adaptive control have been proposed to address these issues, allowing for more accurate tracking of reference signals and better disturbance rejection.

In the context of a DC microgrid with integrated PV panels, nonlinear control must address multiple objectives simultaneously: regulating the DC bus voltage, managing the power flow between sources and loads, and ensuring maximum power extraction from the PV arrays. These objectives are complicated by the presence of energy storage systems, which must be charged and discharged in a coordinated manner to smooth out the variability of renewable generation. Additionally, the coupling between the electrical and control subsystems, as mediated by power electronic interfaces such as DC–DC converters, adds further nonlinearities to the system dynamics.

Recent research has shown that model-based nonlinear control approaches can significantly improve the performance of DC microgrids with renewable integration. By explicitly accounting for the nonlinear dynamics of the converters and PV modules, these methods can provide more accurate control actions than conventional proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controllers. For example, sliding mode control offers robustness to parameter uncertainties and external disturbances, while backstepping control allows for a systematic design process that guarantees stability through Lyapunov-based analysis. Moreover, adaptive nonlinear control schemes can adjust their parameters in real time to compensate for unmodeled dynamics and time-varying conditions.

The deployment of nonlinear control strategies in DC microgrids also supports the broader objectives of smart grids, including enhanced resiliency, improved energy efficiency, and the facilitation of prosumer participation. By enabling stable and efficient operation under high renewable penetration, such control designs contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and supporting the global transition towards sustainable energy systems. Nonetheless, practical implementation requires careful consideration of computational complexity, measurement noise, switching constraints of power electronic devices, and the need for real-time operation.

This paper focuses on the development and analysis of a nonlinear control methodology for the integration of PV panels into a DC microgrid. The proposed approach aims to ensure stable DC bus voltage regulation, optimal PV power extraction, and coordinated operation with energy storage, under varying environmental and load conditions.
