The control design is validated through detailed simulation studies and experimental verification, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing system performance compared to conventional methods. The results contribute to the growing body of knowledge on advanced control strategies for renewable-based DC microgrids, offering a pathway for more reliable and efficient integration of solar energy into modern power systems.
conclusion: This work has presented a nonlinear control strategy for a DC microgrid integrating photovoltaic panels, aiming to ensure stable operation under varying irradiance and load conditions. By employing a Lyapunov-based design, the proposed controller guarantees voltage regulation and robust power sharing among distributed generation units. Simulation results have demonstrated improved dynamic response and resilience compared to conventional linear approaches. The method effectively accommodates nonlinearities inherent in PV generation and load variations, ensuring reliable energy management. Future research will focus on experimental validation and the extension of the control scheme to hybrid microgrids incorporating energy storage and additional renewable sources.

title: Beam-induced Back-streaming Electron Suppression Analysis for Accelerator Type Neutron Generators
abstract: Beam-induced back-streaming electron suppression is critical for maintaining operational stability and component longevity in accelerator-type neutron generators. In such systems, high-energy ion beams striking the target surface produce secondary electrons that can travel upstream, causing undesirable heating, electrical noise, and potential damage to accelerator components. This study presents a detailed analysis of suppression mechanisms, combining experimental measurements with particle-tracking simulations to evaluate the effectiveness of various electrode configurations and biasing schemes. The influence of beam energy, current density, and target geometry on electron trajectories was systematically investigated. Results demonstrate that optimized suppression electrode designs can significantly reduce back-streaming electron flux without adversely affecting neutron yield. The findings provide practical design guidelines for improved operational efficiency and reduced maintenance requirements in accelerator-based neutron sources, contributing to enhanced performance in applications such as materials characterization, medical isotope production, and security screening.
introduction:
Accelerator-type neutron generators (ATNGs) are widely employed in scientific research, industrial applications, and nuclear security due to their capability to produce neutrons with controllable energy spectra and intensities. These devices commonly utilize sealed-tube or open-structure designs in which accelerated deuterium or tritium ions impinge upon a target to induce fusion reactions such as D–T or D–D, generating neutrons. In typical configurations, the ion beam is accelerated through high-voltage potentials, and the target is housed in a high-vacuum environment to minimize beam scattering and maintain operational stability. While the primary design focus is on maximizing neutron yield and operational reliability, an important secondary phenomenon—beam-induced back-streaming electrons—can significantly impact performance, component longevity, and radiation safety.

Back-streaming electrons are generated when the incident ion beam interacts with the target surface, producing secondary electrons through processes such as kinetic emission, potential emission, and X-ray induced photoemission. These electrons can be accelerated upstream toward sensitive accelerator components by the same electric fields used to accelerate the ions. If not adequately suppressed, back-streaming electrons can cause undesirable effects including localized heating, surface erosion, vacuum degradation, high-voltage breakdown, and the generation of parasitic X-rays. In severe cases, they may limit the achievable beam current or pulse duration, thus constraining the neutron output and operational flexibility of the ATNG.

The mitigation of back-streaming electrons has been approached through a variety of suppression strategies, including the use of electrostatic suppressors, magnetic fields, biased electrodes, and geometric shielding of the target assembly. The choice and optimization of suppression techniques depend on multiple factors, such as beam energy, current density, target composition, and spatial constraints within the acceleration column. Despite the importance of this issue, comprehensive analyses tailored to the specific operating conditions of accelerator-type neutron generators remain limited, with much of the existing literature focused on general accelerator physics or other ion-beam systems.

This study presents a systematic analysis of beam-induced back-streaming electron suppression for accelerator-type neutron generators. The work integrates theoretical models, numerical simulations, and experimental validation to evaluate the efficiency of different suppression configurations under representative operating parameters. By quantifying the suppression effectiveness, examining the underlying physical mechanisms, and identifying design trade-offs, this investigation aims to provide practical guidelines for optimizing ATNG performance while reducing component degradation and operational hazards. The results are expected to contribute both to the fundamental understanding of electron back-streaming phenomena and to the applied engineering of more robust and efficient neutron generator systems.
conclusion:
The present study has examined the mechanisms and mitigation strategies for beam-induced back-streaming electron generation in accelerator-type neutron generators, with a focus on their impact on operational stability, component lifetime, and measurement accuracy. Through combined theoretical analysis and experimental validation, it was shown that back-streaming electrons originate primarily from secondary emission processes at the target surface under high-energy beam bombardment. These electrons, if unmitigated, can produce undesirable heating, induce noise in diagnostic systems, and degrade vacuum conditions.  

The evaluation of suppression techniques demonstrated that appropriately configured magnetic and electrostatic fields can significantly reduce electron flux toward upstream accelerator components. Magnetic deflection proved effective in altering electron trajectories away from sensitive regions, while optimized biasing potentials suppressed electron emission at the source. The results indicate that suppression efficiency is strongly dependent on field geometry, target bias voltage, and beam incidence parameters.  

Overall, the findings support the conclusion that integrated suppression designs, tailored to specific generator configurations, can substantially improve system reliability and performance. The interplay between suppression field strength and beam transport efficiency must be carefully balanced to avoid unintended beam perturbations. Future work will focus on refining suppression field models and incorporating real-time diagnostics for adaptive control, enabling next-generation neutron generators to operate at higher intensities with reduced electron-induced degradation.

title: Integrating Dictionary Feature into A Deep Learning Model for Disease Named Entity Recognition
abstract: This study presents a novel approach to disease named entity recognition (DNER) by integrating dictionary-based features into a deep learning framework. While recent neural models have achieved strong performance in biomedical text mining, they may struggle with rare or domain-specific terms. To address this, we incorporate curated disease lexicons as an auxiliary feature channel alongside contextual word embeddings in a bidirectional long short-term memory with conditional random fields (BiLSTM-CRF) architecture. The dictionary feature encodes binary matches and span-level cues, enhancing the model’s ability to detect low-frequency entities and reduce false negatives. Experiments on benchmark biomedical corpora demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model consistently outperforms baseline neural approaches, achieving notable gains in precision and recall. The results indicate that combining domain-specific lexical resources with deep contextual representations is an effective strategy for improving disease entity recognition, particularly in scenarios with limited annotated data.
introduction:
Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in biomedical natural language processing (BioNLP), aiming to automatically identify and classify entities such as diseases, genes, proteins, and chemicals from unstructured text. Accurate recognition of disease names is particularly critical, as it underpins downstream applications including clinical decision support, biomedical knowledge base construction, and literature curation. However, Disease Named Entity Recognition (DNER) remains challenging due to the complex morphology of disease terms, high variability in expression, use of synonyms and abbreviations, and the scarcity of annotated domain-specific corpora.

Traditional approaches to DNER have relied heavily on dictionary-based methods, which use curated lexicons to match terms in text. These methods offer high precision when comprehensive dictionaries are available, but they often lack the flexibility to capture unseen or contextually ambiguous disease mentions. Conversely, machine learning and, more recently, deep learning-based approaches, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and transformer-based architectures, have demonstrated strong capability in capturing contextual semantics and generalizing to previously unseen terms. Nevertheless, purely data-driven models can underperform when training data is limited, and may fail to leverage well-established biomedical knowledge embedded in expert-curated resources.

Integrating dictionary features into deep learning models presents a promising strategy to combine the strengths of both paradigms. Dictionaries, such as those derived from the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) or Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), contain standardized disease names and synonyms that encode domain expertise. When incorporated into neural architectures, these features can enhance entity boundary detection, disambiguation, and recognition of rare or long-tail terms. Several studies in related subdomains, such as chemical or gene NER, have demonstrated that hybrid models enriched with lexicon-derived signals often yield improvements in performance, particularly in recall, without significantly sacrificing precision.

In the context of disease entity recognition, the integration of dictionary features can be operationalized in multiple ways: as binary indicators of dictionary matches, as additional embedding channels, or as attention-guiding signals within transformer-based encoders. Such integration can mitigate the limitations of both dictionary-only and purely neural approaches by grounding statistical learning in curated biomedical knowledge. Furthermore, leveraging dictionary features can be particularly beneficial in cross-domain or low-resource scenarios, where model generalization is hindered by domain shift or insufficient annotated examples.

Despite these potential benefits, the systematic design, implementation, and evaluation of dictionary-augmented deep learning models for DNER remain underexplored. Key challenges include handling partial matches, managing overlapping entity spans, and preventing over-reliance on dictionary cues that may lead to false positives. This work aims to address these challenges by proposing and empirically evaluating a deep neural network architecture that seamlessly integrates dictionary-derived features into its representation learning process, thereby advancing the state of the art in disease named entity recognition.
conclusion: This work presented an approach to enhance disease named entity recognition by integrating a dictionary feature into a deep learning framework. Experimental results demonstrated that leveraging structured lexical knowledge improves both precision and recall, particularly for rare or ambiguous terms. The integration proved complementary to contextual embeddings, enabling more robust recognition across diverse biomedical texts. Future research will explore dynamic dictionary expansion and domain adaptation to further improve generalization and maintain performance in rapidly evolving biomedical literature.

title: Parton Energy Loss in the Extremely Prolate Quark-Gluon Plasma
abstract: We investigate the collisional energy loss of a high-energy parton traversing an extremely prolate quark–gluon plasma, characterized by strong momentum-space anisotropy. Using a hard-loop effective theory framework adapted to elongated momentum distributions, we analyze the impact of unstable chromomagnetic modes on the energy loss rate. Our results show that anisotropy significantly modifies both the magnitude and angular dependence of parton energy loss compared to isotropic media. In particular, plasma instabilities can lead to enhanced or suppressed energy dissipation depending on propagation direction, with potential implications for jet quenching phenomenology in early-stage quark–gluon plasma created in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.
introduction:
The study of parton energy loss in quark-gluon plasma (QGP) has become a central theme in exploring the properties of strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions. High-energy partons, produced in the early stages of relativistic heavy-ion collisions, traverse the deconfined medium and interact with its constituents, leading to the phenomenon of jet quenching. Measurements at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have provided compelling evidence for substantial partonic energy degradation, offering a sensitive probe of the QGP’s microscopic structure and transport properties. While much theoretical work has focused on equilibrated or nearly isotropic plasmas, the QGP generated in the earliest moments after a collision is expected to be highly anisotropic in momentum space due to rapid longitudinal expansion.

Anisotropies in the momentum distribution of plasma constituents can strongly influence the interaction dynamics between energetic partons and the medium. In particular, the extremely prolate configuration—characterized by a momentum distribution elongated along the beam (longitudinal) direction—represents a limiting case of momentum-space anisotropy that can arise immediately after the collision. Such a state may persist for a finite time before isotropization and thermalization occur. Understanding parton energy loss in this regime is crucial for establishing a coherent description of jet-medium interactions throughout the entire evolution of the QGP.

In anisotropic plasmas, the dispersion relations of collective excitations and the screening properties of chromodynamic fields differ substantially from those in isotropic systems. These modifications can alter both collisional and radiative energy loss mechanisms. In the extremely prolate limit, the gluon self-energy exhibits distinctive angular dependence, and unstable plasma modes—analogous to Weibel instabilities—can emerge and potentially enhance momentum broadening. A quantitative assessment of these effects requires theoretical frameworks capable of incorporating the full anisotropic structure of the medium.

This work investigates the collisional energy loss of a fast parton in an extremely prolate QGP, employing the hard-loop effective theory to describe the medium’s chromodynamic response. By focusing on this idealized but physically motivated limit, we aim to elucidate the qualitative and quantitative differences from isotropic energy loss scenarios and to provide insights relevant for modeling the early-time dynamics of heavy-ion collisions.
conclusion: In this study, we have analyzed the mechanisms of parton energy loss in an extremely prolate quark-gluon plasma, emphasizing the role of anisotropic momentum distributions. Our results indicate that the elongated momentum space geometry significantly modifies both collisional and radiative loss channels, enhancing direction-dependent effects. The energy loss exhibits pronounced angular dependence relative to the plasma’s symmetry axis, with potential implications for jet quenching observables in non-equilibrated stages of heavy-ion collisions. These findings highlight the necessity of incorporating extreme anisotropies into theoretical models for early-time quark-gluon plasma dynamics. Future work should extend this framework to evolving anisotropies and explore phenomenological consequences for experimental signatures.

title: Broader terms curriculum mapping: Using natural language processing and visual-supported communication to create representative program planning experiences
abstract: This study explores a novel approach to curriculum mapping by integrating natural language processing (NLP) with visual-supported communication to identify and connect broader curricular terms. By automating the extraction and clustering of related concepts from program documentation, the method enhances representativeness in program planning. Visual mapping tools are employed to facilitate shared understanding among stakeholders, promoting collaborative decision-making. Findings indicate that combining NLP-driven semantic analysis with interactive visualizations supports more coherent curriculum structures and fosters inclusive, transparent planning experiences across diverse educational contexts.
introduction:
Curriculum mapping has emerged as a critical process in higher education for ensuring coherence, transparency, and alignment between intended learning outcomes, instructional activities, and assessment strategies. By making explicit the relationships between courses, competencies, and program-level goals, curriculum maps help educators identify gaps, redundancies, and opportunities for pedagogical improvement. Traditional approaches to curriculum mapping, however, often rely on manual classification and interpretation of learning outcomes, which can be time-consuming, inconsistent, and susceptible to subjective bias. Furthermore, the increasing complexity of academic programs, coupled with diverse stakeholder perspectives, underscores the need for approaches that support both precision and inclusivity in mapping processes.

In recent years, natural language processing (NLP) has shown promise in educational contexts as a means of automating and enhancing the analysis of curricular data. By leveraging computational techniques to extract, categorize, and relate textual descriptions of learning outcomes, NLP offers opportunities to develop more representative and scalable curriculum maps. In particular, the use of broader terms—concepts that encapsulate multiple related competencies or topics—can help to bridge variations in terminology and disciplinary language. This approach can facilitate a more holistic view of program structure, enabling educators to identify thematic patterns that might be obscured by narrow or inconsistent phrasing.

In parallel, visual-supported communication has been recognized as a powerful tool for fostering shared understanding among faculty, administrators, and other stakeholders involved in curriculum design. Visual representations of curriculum data—such as network diagrams, heat maps, or hierarchical concept maps—can make complex relationships more accessible, support collaborative decision-making, and promote engagement in the planning process. When combined with NLP-driven identification of broader terms, visual tools can transform static curriculum maps into dynamic, interactive representations that better reflect the multifaceted nature of academic programs.

Despite these advancements, there remains limited research on integrating NLP techniques with visual-supported communication to create curriculum mapping experiences that are both analytically robust and inclusive of diverse perspectives. The potential to use broader terms as an intermediary layer in mapping—grouping related learning outcomes under shared conceptual categories—has been underexplored, especially in contexts where faculty with different disciplinary backgrounds must collaborate on program planning. Such integration could enhance the representativeness of curriculum maps, reduce cognitive load during analysis, and ultimately lead to more effective program-level decision-making.

This study addresses this gap by investigating the use of NLP for identifying broader terms in curriculum data and embedding these within visually mediated mapping environments. The goal is to create program planning experiences that are not only accurate and comprehensive but also accessible and meaningful to a wide range of educational stakeholders. Through this integrated approach, we aim to advance the field of curriculum mapping toward more inclusive, efficient, and strategically aligned practices.
conclusion:
The present study has explored the potential of integrating broader terms curriculum mapping with natural language processing (NLP) techniques and visual-supported communication to enhance the representativeness and inclusivity of program planning experiences. By situating curriculum mapping within a broader semantic framework, the approach enables a more holistic understanding of how learning outcomes, instructional activities, and assessment strategies are interconnected. This reconceptualization moves beyond rigid, prescriptive alignments toward a more dynamic, contextually responsive model that is capable of reflecting the complexity of contemporary educational programs.

The use of NLP has proven critical in operationalizing this vision. Automated analysis of curricular documents, program descriptions, and learning outcomes allows for the identification of thematic clusters, latent relationships, and broader conceptual categories that might otherwise be overlooked in manual mapping processes. Such computational methods not only improve efficiency but also reduce the risk of human bias in term selection and categorization, thereby supporting a more equitable representation of diverse disciplinary perspectives and pedagogical approaches. Furthermore, NLP’s capacity to process large-scale datasets affords curriculum planners a macro-level view of program coherence, gaps, and redundancies, which can inform both immediate adjustments and long-term strategic development.

Equally important is the integration of visual-supported communication in the curriculum mapping process. Translating complex, text-based analyses into intuitive visual formats fosters shared understanding among stakeholders with varying degrees of expertise in curriculum design. Interactive diagrams, semantic networks, and heat maps can make abstract relationships tangible, enabling faculty, administrators, and even students to engage meaningfully with the mapping outputs. Such visualizations act as boundary objects, facilitating dialogue across disciplinary and institutional boundaries, and supporting a participatory approach to program planning. When combined with NLP-driven insights, visual representations also enable iterative refinement, as stakeholders can quickly identify and address misalignments or emerging opportunities.

The findings from this investigation suggest that broader terms curriculum mapping, supported by NLP and visual communication tools, offers a more representative and adaptable model for educational program planning. This model is particularly responsive to the challenges of interdisciplinary curricula, where traditional, narrowly defined mapping approaches may fail to capture the depth and breadth of knowledge domains involved. By foregrounding connections across broader conceptual categories, the approach fosters curricular coherence without sacrificing flexibility, allowing programs to evolve in response to shifting societal needs, disciplinary advancements, and institutional priorities.

Nevertheless, the study also acknowledges certain limitations. The quality of NLP outputs remains dependent on the comprehensiveness and accuracy of source documents, as well as on the sophistication of the language models employed. Visualizations, while powerful, require careful design to avoid oversimplification or misinterpretation of complex data. Moreover, the successful implementation of such an approach presupposes a willingness among stakeholders to engage with computational methods and to adapt existing planning processes. Addressing these challenges will require capacity building, professional development, and ongoing evaluation of both technological tools and participatory practices.

Looking forward, future research should investigate the integration of broader terms curriculum mapping into institutional decision-making cycles, exploring its impact on program quality, student outcomes, and stakeholder engagement over time. Comparative studies across disciplines and educational contexts could further illuminate the adaptability and scalability of the approach. Additionally, advances in NLP—particularly in multilingual processing and context-aware semantic analysis—hold promise for extending the method to globalized curricula and diverse learner populations.

In sum, the convergence of broader terms curriculum mapping, NLP, and visual-supported communication represents a significant step toward more inclusive, transparent, and evidence-informed program planning. By harnessing computational analysis and accessible visualization, educational institutions can cultivate a richer understanding of their curricula, strengthen cross-disciplinary connections, and create planning experiences that more accurately reflect the complexity and diversity of contemporary higher education.

title: Controlling Photoluminescence Spectra of hBN Color Centers by Selective Phonon-Assisted Excitation: A Theoretical Proposal
abstract: We propose a theoretical framework for controlling the photoluminescence (PL) spectra of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) color centers through selective phonon-assisted excitation. By exploiting resonant coupling between defect electronic states and specific lattice vibrational modes, our approach enables targeted population of excited states that preferentially emit at desired wavelengths. Using a model incorporating electron–phonon interaction and phonon density of states, we predict that tuning the excitation energy to match sideband resonances can selectively enhance or suppress spectral features in the zero-phonon line and phonon sidebands. This method offers a pathway for engineered single-photon emission with tailored spectral profiles, relevant for quantum optics, nanoscale sensing, and photonic device integration based on solid-state defects in hBN.
introduction:
Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) has emerged as a promising two-dimensional (2D) wide-bandgap material for quantum photonics due to its ability to host stable, bright, room-temperature single-photon emitters (SPEs) embedded in its lattice. These emitters, often referred to as color centers, exhibit narrow zero-phonon lines (ZPLs) in the visible spectral range and possess photophysical properties that are robust against environmental perturbations, making them attractive for applications in quantum communication, sensing, and integrated photonic circuits. The layered nature of hBN allows for straightforward integration with other 2D materials and photonic platforms, while its large bandgap (~6 eV) ensures spectral isolation of defect-related optical transitions from the host material’s electronic states.

Despite substantial experimental progress in identifying and characterizing hBN color centers, a major challenge remains: the inhomogeneous distribution of emission wavelengths and line shapes across different emitters. This spectral variability arises from variations in local strain, dielectric environment, and defect configurations, which can hinder the scalability of quantum photonic devices relying on indistinguishable photons. Controlling the photoluminescence (PL) spectra in a deterministic and reversible manner is therefore a central goal for both fundamental studies and technological implementations.

One promising avenue for such control involves exploiting electron–phonon interactions. In hBN, lattice vibrations couple to defect electronic states, giving rise to phonon sidebands in the PL spectrum and influencing emission dynamics. This coupling is not merely a source of spectral broadening; it also offers a pathway for selective excitation schemes that can preferentially address specific optical transitions. Phonon-assisted excitation, in particular, has been demonstrated in other solid-state quantum emitters—such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond and semiconductor quantum dots—as an effective mechanism to tailor emission properties and enable spin–photon interfaces.

In the context of hBN color centers, phonon-assisted processes can be harnessed to achieve selective population of excited states associated with targeted ZPLs or to manipulate the spectral weight between the ZPL and phonon sidebands. By judiciously tuning the excitation wavelength to coincide with specific vibronic resonances, one can in principle enhance or suppress particular emission channels. This approach offers a degree of spectral control without the need for strong external fields or permanent material modification, thus preserving emitter stability.

Theoretical modeling of such selective phonon-assisted excitation in hBN defects requires a detailed understanding of the defect’s electronic structure, the symmetry and energy of relevant phonon modes, and the nature of electron–phonon coupling. The Huang–Rhys formalism provides a useful starting point for describing the phonon sideband structure, while more advanced ab initio calculations can yield quantitative predictions of coupling strengths and transition probabilities. Incorporating these elements into a coherent framework enables the exploration of excitation schemes that maximize emission into desired spectral windows.

In this work, we propose a theoretical strategy for controlling the PL spectra of hBN color centers by selective phonon-assisted excitation. We outline the underlying physical principles, describe a model for the electron–phonon interaction in representative defect systems, and predict how tailored excitation conditions can reshape the emission profile. Our proposal aims to bridge the gap between empirical observations of phonon sidebands in hBN and the practical implementation of spectral control protocols, thereby providing a route toward the deterministic engineering of quantum light sources in 2D materials.
conclusion:
In this work, we have proposed a theoretical framework for controlling the photoluminescence spectra of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) color centers through selective phonon-assisted excitation. By explicitly incorporating electron–phonon coupling into the excitation pathway, our model demonstrates that targeted stimulation of specific vibrational modes can preferentially populate distinct excited-state manifolds, thereby modifying the relative intensities and spectral positions of zero-phonon lines and phonon sidebands. This approach provides a route to spectral tailoring without the need for static structural modification or external cavity filtering, offering a dynamic and potentially reversible control mechanism.

The analysis indicates that the interplay between phonon mode symmetry, coupling strength, and excitation energy enables selective enhancement or suppression of emission channels. This selectivity arises from resonance conditions that match the excitation photon energy with vibrationally shifted electronic transitions, effectively steering the system’s relaxation dynamics. The proposed scheme could be implemented using narrowband, tunable light sources in conjunction with temperature or strain control to fine-tune phonon populations and coupling strengths.

Beyond its immediate implications for fundamental studies of defect–phonon interactions in van der Waals materials, this method suggests practical pathways for engineering emission properties in quantum photonic devices based on hBN. In particular, the ability to control linewidths, spectral purity, and emission wavelength on demand could benefit single-photon source optimization, multi-color quantum emitters, and integrated photonic circuitry.

While our proposal is grounded in theoretical modeling, it invites experimental verification using time-resolved and resonant photoluminescence spectroscopy. Future work should also explore the role of higher-order phonon processes and the influence of the dielectric environment. Overall, selective phonon-assisted excitation offers a promising and versatile tool for tailoring the optical response of hBN color centers, advancing both the understanding and application of solid-state quantum emitters.

title: Snitch: A tiny Pseudo Dual-Issue Processor for Area and Energy Efficient Execution of Floating-Point Intensive Workloads
abstract: This paper presents *Snitch*, a lightweight pseudo dual-issue RISC-V processor core optimized for area- and energy-efficient execution of floating-point (FP) intensive workloads. Snitch employs a minimalist microarchitectural approach that combines a simple in-order integer pipeline with a dedicated floating-point execution pipeline, enabling concurrent progress on integer and FP instructions without the complexity and overhead of a full dual-issue design. By decoupling integer and FP execution, the architecture sustains high utilization of the FP unit while maintaining a compact control structure, reducing both area and power consumption. The design leverages static scheduling and compiler-assisted instruction ordering to minimize structural hazards, allowing the hardware to remain simple while achieving high throughput for mixed integer/FP workloads. A small set of microarchitectural enhancements, including a lightweight instruction buffer and direct memory access support for FP operands, further improves performance for streaming and scientific kernels. Implemented in a 22 nm FD-SOI technology, Snitch achieves a core area of only 0.031 mm², delivering up to 4.8 GFLOPS/W on representative HPC and DSP workloads, significantly outperforming comparable single-issue embedded cores. The architecture is particularly well suited for integration into tightly coupled clusters, enabling scalable parallel systems for energy-constrained domains such as edge computing, sensor networks, and scientific accelerators. Experimental evaluation on a set of benchmarks, including dense linear algebra and stencil codes, demonstrates that Snitch attains between 85–95% of the throughput of more complex dual-issue cores while consuming less than half the area and energy. The results highlight the potential of pseudo dual-issue designs as an attractive middle ground between single-issue simplicity and superscalar performance for floating-point dominated applications.
introduction:
The demand for high-performance yet energy-efficient computing solutions continues to grow across a wide range of application domains, from scientific simulations to edge computing and embedded systems. In particular, workloads with a high proportion of floating-point operations present a significant challenge: they require substantial computational throughput, but are often constrained by stringent power and area budgets. While superscalar and out-of-order processors can deliver high performance through aggressive instruction-level parallelism (ILP) exploitation, their complexity and energy overhead make them ill-suited to cost-sensitive or resource-constrained environments. Conversely, simple in-order pipelines achieve excellent energy efficiency and small silicon footprints, but typically underutilize functional units when executing floating-point–intensive code, leading to poor performance.

Recent trends in processor design have sought to bridge this gap by introducing lightweight mechanisms to increase utilization without incurring the full cost of complex superscalar designs. One promising direction is pseudo dual-issue architectures, which allow limited concurrent execution of multiple instructions in a constrained and predictable manner. Such designs aim to deliver a subset of the performance benefits of dual-issue processors, while retaining the simplicity, low area, and energy efficiency of in-order pipelines. However, achieving these goals requires careful co-design of the microarchitecture, instruction scheduling, and memory system to balance throughput gains against hardware overheads.

In this work, we present **Snitch**, a tiny pseudo dual-issue processor optimized for floating-point–intensive workloads. Snitch employs a minimalist in-order core augmented with a tightly integrated floating-point unit (FPU) and an architecture that enables simultaneous execution of a scalar integer instruction and a floating-point instruction. This design choice leverages the natural decoupling between integer and floating-point execution paths, thereby increasing functional unit utilization without significantly enlarging the core’s critical path or control complexity. The processor is designed to be highly area- and energy-efficient, making it suitable for deployment in parallel many-core configurations, where aggregate performance and energy scalability are critical.

We evaluate Snitch across a range of floating-point–heavy benchmarks and compare it to both single-issue in-order processors and more complex dual-issue designs. Our results show that Snitch delivers substantial performance improvements over the baseline with minimal area and power overhead, achieving a favorable performance-per-watt profile. By demonstrating that pseudo dual-issue execution can be realized in an exceptionally compact and efficient form, this work contributes to the ongoing exploration of architectural techniques for bridging the performance–efficiency gap in modern processors, particularly in domains where floating-point throughput is a primary driver of application performance.
conclusion:
This work has presented Snitch, a lightweight pseudo dual-issue processor architecture designed to deliver high efficiency for floating-point intensive workloads while maintaining a minimal silicon footprint. By carefully balancing simplicity in control with targeted enhancements for parallelism, Snitch achieves execution characteristics that approach those of more complex superscalar designs, but at a fraction of the area and energy cost. The design philosophy emphasizes that many floating-point dominated applications do not require the full complexity of wide superscalar out-of-order architectures to achieve high throughput; instead, they benefit from a judicious combination of streamlined integer execution and dedicated floating-point capabilities.

Through detailed microarchitectural exploration and synthesis results, we have demonstrated that a pseudo dual-issue approach—allowing one floating-point and one integer instruction to be issued concurrently under specific conditions—can exploit the natural instruction-level parallelism present in scientific and signal processing kernels. The hardware overhead required to support this parallelism is minimal, preserving the compact nature of the core and enabling integration into resource-constrained systems such as embedded accelerators or manycore clusters.

Evaluation across a suite of representative benchmarks showed that Snitch attains substantial performance gains over strictly single-issue in-order cores, particularly in workloads with high floating-point density. At the same time, energy per operation is significantly reduced, owing both to the reduced execution time and the low static and dynamic power consumption of the lean design. These results underline the suitability of Snitch for deployment in domains where performance-per-watt is a critical metric, such as edge computing, autonomous systems, and high-performance embedded computing.

Moreover, the modularity of the architecture allows straightforward scaling and customization. The core can be paired with specialized functional units, tightly coupled scratchpad memories, or custom accelerators to further enhance domain-specific performance without incurring the costs of a general-purpose high-end core. This flexibility supports heterogeneous system-on-chip designs in which Snitch cores can serve as efficient compute tiles within a larger processing fabric.

In summary, Snitch represents a compelling alternative in the design space between minimalist single-issue microcontrollers and complex superscalar processors. By focusing on the specific needs of floating-point intensive workloads and embracing a pseudo dual-issue model, it delivers a favorable trade-off between performance, energy efficiency, and implementation cost. Future work will explore broader application domains, more aggressive clock gating strategies, and integration into multi-core and manycore systems, as well as potential ISA extensions to further increase floating-point throughput. The results presented here suggest that such targeted microarchitectural approaches can play a significant role in meeting the growing demand for efficient computation in both embedded and high-performance contexts.

title: Expansion Lensing (I) -- A new paradigm for cosmological luminosity-angular distances relation
abstract: We introduce *expansion lensing*, a novel conceptual framework that revisits the fundamental relation between luminosity distance and angular diameter distance in cosmology. In the standard formulation, these distances are linked by Etherington’s reciprocity theorem, assuming photon number conservation and a purely metric theory of gravity. However, recent high-precision observations suggest subtle deviations that cannot be fully reconciled with conventional explanations such as extinction, gravitational lensing, or cosmic opacity. We propose that the large-scale expansion of space itself can induce a systematic “lensing-like” effect, modifying the propagation of light independently of local curvature perturbations. By incorporating expansion-induced geodesic divergence into the photon trajectory analysis, we derive a generalized distance-duality relation that introduces a scale-dependent correction term. This formalism preserves compatibility with general relativity in the appropriate limit while offering a new interpretive tool for analyzing supernova, baryon acoustic oscillation, and strong-lensing time-delay data. We discuss the theoretical foundation of expansion lensing, outline its observational signatures, and present preliminary fits to current datasets. The results indicate that this paradigm may help resolve mild tensions in cosmological parameter estimates, opening a pathway toward a more nuanced understanding of photon propagation in an expanding universe.
introduction:
Over the past century, the measurement of cosmological distances has been central to our understanding of the structure, evolution, and ultimate fate of the Universe. Observational cosmology relies heavily on the relationship between luminosity distance, \(d_L\), and angular diameter distance, \(d_A\), as these quantities link intrinsic astrophysical properties to measurable fluxes and angular sizes. The conventional framework, grounded in the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric and the reciprocity relation established by Etherington (1933), asserts that \(d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A\) for any metric theory of gravity in which photons travel along null geodesics and their number is conserved. This distance duality relation underpins a vast range of cosmological measurements, from type Ia supernovae and baryon acoustic oscillations to the cosmic microwave background.

Despite its broad success, increasing observational precision has begun to reveal potential deviations from the standard distance duality relation. These discrepancies may stem from astrophysical effects such as intergalactic dust extinction, photon–axion conversion, or gravitational lensing, as well as from deeper departures from the assumptions of homogeneity, isotropy, or standard photon propagation. In particular, gravitational lensing by large-scale structure, usually treated as a perturbative effect in the standard model, can magnify or demagnify sources, altering the inferred distances in a redshift-dependent manner. While conventional analyses average over such effects, the cumulative impact of cosmic expansion itself on the propagation of light—beyond simple geometrical redshift—has not been fully explored in this context.

In this work, we propose *Expansion Lensing* as a new paradigm for understanding the luminosity–angular distance relation. The central idea is that the global expansion of space acts analogously to a lensing process, systematically modifying the observed flux and angular size of distant sources in a way that can be parameterised distinctly from standard gravitational lensing. This effect arises naturally when one considers the integrated influence of the evolving scale factor on the photon geodesics and their associated wavefronts, leading to corrections to the reciprocity relation that depend explicitly on the expansion history. Unlike conventional lensing, which is stochastic and tied to local inhomogeneities, expansion lensing is a deterministic, universal phenomenon that imprints a predictable signature on all light paths.

By formulating a covariant treatment of expansion lensing within the FLRW framework, we derive a generalised relation between \(d_L\) and \(d_A\) that reduces to Etherington’s expression in the appropriate limit but admits measurable deviations under realistic cosmological conditions. We explore the implications of this modified distance law for current and future surveys, and assess its potential to resolve existing tensions in cosmological parameter estimation. In doing so, we aim to open a new observational window on the interplay between cosmic expansion and light propagation, with the prospect of refining our grasp of cosmological geometry and dynamics.
conclusion: The analysis presented in this work introduces the concept of Expansion Lensing as a novel framework for relating cosmological luminosity and angular diameter distances. By accounting for the geometric and dynamical effects of cosmic expansion on the propagation of light, this approach offers an alternative interpretation of observational distance measures without invoking additional exotic physics. The formulation unifies these distance indicators through a modified reciprocity relation that naturally incorporates expansion-induced distortions, potentially resolving tensions observed in standard cosmological analyses. Our results suggest that certain discrepancies in supernova and baryon acoustic oscillation data may be addressed within this paradigm, offering new avenues for refining cosmological parameter estimates. While the present study establishes the theoretical foundation and basic phenomenology of Expansion Lensing, further work is needed to confront the model with a broader range of high-precision datasets and to explore its implications for the late-time acceleration problem. This framework thus opens a promising direction for re-examining fundamental cosmological relations.

title: Finite Size Effects in Highly Scaled Ruthenium Interconnects
abstract: We investigate finite size effects in highly scaled ruthenium (Ru) interconnects, focusing on their impact on electrical resistivity and performance at sub-20 nm dimensions. Experimental measurements and modeling reveal that grain boundary scattering and surface roughness significantly increase resistivity as linewidth decreases. Comparative analysis with copper interconnects highlights Ru’s reduced susceptibility to electromigration but greater sensitivity to boundary scattering. Our results indicate that optimizing microstructure and surface treatments can mitigate finite size penalties, enabling Ru to serve as a viable alternative for next-generation, high-density integrated circuit interconnects.
introduction:
As semiconductor technology nodes continue to scale beyond the limits of traditional copper interconnects, the impact of finite size effects on electrical performance has become increasingly significant. In highly scaled interconnects, where feature dimensions approach or fall below the electron mean free path, classical size-independent conduction models no longer provide accurate predictions. Instead, electron scattering at surfaces and grain boundaries, as described by models such as Fuchs–Sondheimer and Mayadas–Shatzkes, dominates resistivity behavior. These effects manifest as an increase in line resistance, which directly impacts signal delay, power dissipation, and overall chip performance.

Ruthenium (Ru) has emerged as a promising alternative to copper for next-generation interconnects due to its favorable size effect characteristics, relatively short bulk mean free path, and ability to maintain low resistivity at reduced dimensions. Unlike copper, Ru can be deposited without a thick diffusion barrier, allowing for a larger conductive cross-section at narrow pitches. Furthermore, its superior electromigration resistance offers enhanced reliability for advanced technology nodes. However, as line widths approach the deep nanoscale regime, finite size effects in Ru interconnects remain non-negligible and must be quantitatively understood to inform integration strategies.

Recent experimental and modeling studies have reported that Ru exhibits a weaker resistivity scaling penalty compared to copper, yet deviations from bulk behavior become substantial below ~20 nm linewidths. Factors such as surface roughness, interface chemistry with surrounding dielectrics, and grain structure critically influence electron scattering mechanisms. Accurate characterization of these effects is essential for predictive process design kits (PDKs) and for benchmarking Ru against other candidate metals such as cobalt or molybdenum.

This work investigates finite size effects in highly scaled Ru interconnects through a combination of experimental measurements and theoretical modeling. By elucidating the interplay between structural features and resistivity scaling, we aim to provide insight into the practical limits of Ru interconnect performance and guide material and process optimization for future technology nodes.
conclusion: This study has examined finite size effects in highly scaled ruthenium interconnects, elucidating their impact on electrical resistivity and performance at advanced technology nodes. The analysis shows that grain boundary scattering, surface roughness, and line edge disorder increasingly dominate as dimensions approach the electron mean free path, leading to deviations from bulk behavior. Ruthenium’s relatively short mean free path and favorable scattering characteristics mitigate some scaling-induced resistivity increases compared to copper, yet finite size effects remain non-negligible. These findings highlight the need for careful microstructural engineering and process optimization to fully exploit ruthenium’s potential. Future work should integrate experimental validation and modeling to guide interconnect design in sub-10 nm regimes.

title: Research Needs for Realization of Zero-Carbon Power Grids with Selected Case Studies
abstract: Achieving zero-carbon power grids is a critical objective for mitigating climate change and ensuring sustainable energy systems. This paper examines the technological, operational, and policy research needs required to realize such grids, with emphasis on integration of high shares of renewable energy, advanced storage solutions, and flexible demand-side management. Key challenges include ensuring grid stability under variable generation, developing cost-effective long-duration storage, enhancing forecasting accuracy, and upgrading transmission infrastructure. The study presents selected case studies from regions pursuing aggressive decarbonization targets, highlighting practical lessons, innovative approaches, and gaps in current strategies. Comparative analysis reveals that successful transitions depend on coordinated advancements in market design, digitalization, and sector coupling, alongside supportive regulatory frameworks. The findings underscore the necessity of interdisciplinary research integrating engineering, economics, and social sciences to address technical and societal barriers. This work provides a roadmap for targeted research priorities, aiming to accelerate the deployment of zero-carbon power systems globally.
introduction: Achieving zero-carbon power grids is a central objective in global efforts to mitigate climate change and ensure sustainable energy systems. Transitioning from fossil-fuel-based generation to renewable and low-carbon technologies requires overcoming significant technical, economic, and policy challenges. These include large-scale integration of variable renewable energy sources, advances in energy storage, grid flexibility, demand-side management, and robust regulatory frameworks. Furthermore, innovations in digitalization, smart grid technologies, and sector coupling are essential to ensure reliability and resilience. This paper examines critical research needs for realizing zero-carbon power grids, supported by selected case studies from different regions. By identifying key technological gaps and successful implementation strategies, the study aims to inform policymakers, researchers, and industry stakeholders in accelerating the decarbonization of electricity systems.
conclusion:
The transition toward zero-carbon power grids presents both formidable challenges and unprecedented opportunities for modern energy systems. This study has highlighted the technical, economic, and policy-oriented research priorities essential for achieving decarbonized electricity networks. Through the examination of selected case studies, it is evident that successful pathways rely on an integrated approach encompassing renewable generation expansion, advanced grid flexibility measures, energy storage deployment, and demand-side management. The experiences from diverse regions demonstrate that while technological maturity in wind, solar, and storage continues to advance, systemic transformation requires coordinated regulatory frameworks, innovative market designs, and robust investment strategies.  

Key research needs include improving forecasting and integration of variable renewable energy, enhancing transmission infrastructure, developing scalable storage solutions, and employing digitalization for real-time grid optimization. Equally critical are socio-economic studies that address equity, public acceptance, and workforce transitions in the context of deep decarbonization. The case studies underscore that no single blueprint exists; rather, context-specific solutions informed by local resources, policy environments, and stakeholder engagement are vital.  

Ultimately, realizing zero-carbon power grids demands sustained interdisciplinary research, cross-sector collaboration, and adaptive governance mechanisms. By addressing the identified gaps, future energy systems can achieve reliability, affordability, and sustainability, ensuring that the global pursuit of carbon neutrality is both technically feasible and socially equitable.

title: Survival Probability for Open Spherical Billiards
abstract: We investigate the survival probability of particles in open spherical billiards, where escape occurs through a finite aperture on the boundary. Using analytical approximations and numerical simulations, we examine the dependence of long-time decay rates on aperture size and initial conditions. Our results reveal distinct regimes characterized by algebraic and exponential decay, linked to underlying phase-space structures. The findings contribute to understanding escape dynamics in three-dimensional chaotic systems and have potential applications in optical and acoustic resonator design.
introduction:
The study of billiard systems has long occupied a central role in the investigation of deterministic dynamical systems, serving as paradigmatic models for exploring the interplay between geometry, chaos, and statistical behavior. In their simplest form, billiards consist of a point particle undergoing free motion within a bounded domain, reflecting elastically upon contact with the boundary. Despite their conceptual simplicity, billiards exhibit a rich variety of dynamical regimes, ranging from completely integrable to fully chaotic, depending on the shape of the confining region. This versatility has rendered billiard models indispensable in diverse areas of physics, from statistical mechanics and nonlinear dynamics to optical and quantum systems.

In recent years, increasing attention has been devoted to *open* billiard systems, in which a portion of the boundary is replaced by an aperture or “hole,” allowing the particle to escape. The resulting dynamics are transient in nature: trajectories persist in the system only for a finite time, and the statistical properties of escape become a central object of study. A fundamental quantity in this context is the *survival probability*, defined as the probability that a particle, initiated under a given distribution of initial conditions, remains within the billiard after a specified time. The survival probability encapsulates essential information about the transport and decay mechanisms in open systems and provides a direct link between the underlying dynamics and experimentally measurable escape rates in physical realizations.

While open billiard dynamics have been studied extensively in two-dimensional domains, comparatively less attention has been devoted to their three-dimensional counterparts. In particular, the case of *open spherical billiards*—systems in which a particle moves freely inside a sphere with a localized opening—offers a natural generalization of planar models but presents new challenges and opportunities. The spherical geometry preserves isotropy in the absence of openings, leading to integrable dynamics in the closed case. The introduction of an opening breaks this invariance, giving rise to a nontrivial interplay between geometry, initial condition distribution, and escape kinetics. Such models are not only of theoretical interest but are also relevant to practical contexts ranging from particle transport in porous media to photon leakage in optical microcavities.

Previous works on open billiards have revealed that the asymptotic decay of the survival probability often follows algebraic or exponential laws, depending on the degree of chaos, the nature of marginally stable orbits, and the size and position of the hole. In integrable systems such as the closed sphere, the decay is typically algebraic, governed by the phase-space structure and the measure of trajectories avoiding the hole for long times. Extending these results to the spherical case requires careful treatment of the angular momentum distribution, the geometry of the opening, and the projection of trajectories onto escape channels.

In this work, we analyze the survival probability in open spherical billiards with small apertures, focusing on the long-time asymptotic behavior and its dependence on the system’s geometric parameters. By combining analytical estimates with numerical simulations, we aim to provide a detailed characterization of escape statistics in this three-dimensional setting, thereby enriching the broader understanding of open dynamical systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the survival probability for open spherical billiards, focusing on the statistical properties of particle trajectories and the manner in which escape through an opening modifies the long-time dynamics. By combining analytical considerations with numerical simulations, we have characterized the interplay between geometry, initial conditions, and aperture size in determining the temporal decay of the survival probability. Our results provide a systematic framework for understanding escape processes in three-dimensional convex billiard systems, which have received comparatively less attention than their planar counterparts.

We have shown that, for small openings, the survival probability exhibits a clear separation of regimes. At short times, the decay is dominated by direct trajectories aimed toward the aperture, producing a rapid initial drop. This is followed by an intermediate regime in which the decay rate slows, reflecting the predominance of longer, more indirect trajectories that explore the spherical domain before escaping. Finally, at sufficiently long times, the survival probability approaches an asymptotic decay law that depends sensitively on the underlying phase-space structure. In particular, our analysis revealed the persistence of marginally trapped orbits arising from the perfect symmetry of the sphere, which yield deviations from a simple exponential decay and can be traced back to families of periodic and quasi-periodic trajectories that avoid the opening for extended durations.

By systematically varying the aperture size, we have quantified the relationship between geometric openness and escape rates. For very small apertures, the asymptotic decay rate scales proportionally to the aperture’s solid angle, consistent with a flux-based argument rooted in Liouville’s theorem. As the aperture enlarges, the decay becomes more strongly exponential, and correlations in the dynamics play a diminished role. Our numerical experiments confirm that the crossover between these regimes is smooth but depends on details of the initial condition ensemble, highlighting the importance of specifying both spatial and angular distributions when comparing theoretical predictions to simulations or experiments.

An important aspect of our work is the explicit comparison between the three-dimensional spherical billiard and analogous two-dimensional systems. While certain qualitative features, such as the existence of long-lived trajectories and non-exponential decay at small openings, carry over from the planar case, we have identified distinct quantitative differences in the scaling laws and correlation structures. These arise from the increased dimensionality of the phase space and the different topology of constant-energy surfaces, which allow for more intricate families of trajectories that can avoid the opening.

The implications of our findings extend beyond the idealized context of mathematical billiards. Open spherical geometries arise naturally in physical systems ranging from optical microcavities and acoustic resonators to models of planetary scattering and particle confinement in plasma devices. Understanding the survival probability in such settings provides insight into energy retention, signal decay, and transport properties, and can inform the design of devices to either minimize losses or, conversely, to facilitate efficient escape.

Future research could extend the present analysis by considering perturbations to the spherical geometry, such as slight deformations or refractive index variations, to explore the robustness of the observed decay laws. Similarly, incorporating weak external fields or stochastic perturbations would allow one to study the transition from deterministic to diffusive escape processes. Finally, experimental validation in controlled laboratory setups—such as optical or acoustic analogues—would provide a valuable test of the theoretical predictions and potentially reveal new dynamical phenomena not captured by the ideal model.

In summary, the present study establishes a detailed picture of escape dynamics in open spherical billiards, elucidating the dependence of survival probability on geometric and dynamical parameters. The combination of analytic scaling arguments, numerical verification, and comparative analysis with lower-dimensional systems advances our understanding of open Hamiltonian dynamics and sets the stage for further exploration of escape phenomena in higher-dimensional and more complex settings.

title: Polyphonic Piano Transcription Using Autoregressive Multi-State Note Model
abstract: We present a novel approach for automatic polyphonic piano transcription based on an autoregressive multi‑state note model that explicitly captures temporal dependencies and fine‑grained note evolution. Unlike conventional frame‑wise classification methods, our model represents each note as a sequence of discrete states corresponding to onset, sustain, and offset phases, enabling a more accurate reconstruction of note events in complex musical passages. The autoregressive framework conditions the prediction of each frame on previously estimated states, thereby modeling temporal context and reducing spurious activations. We employ a neural network architecture to parameterize state transition probabilities, trained end‑to‑end on aligned audio‑MIDI datasets. Evaluation on standard piano transcription benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed method achieves significant improvements in onset and offset detection accuracy compared to strong baselines, particularly in densely voiced segments. The multi‑state representation also facilitates expressive timing recovery and more natural transcription outputs. These results highlight the effectiveness of integrating structured note modeling with autoregressive temporal context for high‑fidelity polyphonic piano transcription.
introduction:
Automatic music transcription (AMT) is the task of converting an audio recording into a symbolic representation such as a musical score. For polyphonic instruments like the piano, this process involves detecting multiple simultaneously sounding notes, identifying their onsets and offsets, and capturing expressive nuances such as sustain pedal usage. Accurate polyphonic piano transcription has long been a challenging problem in music information retrieval, due to the complex acoustic interactions between notes, the wide dynamic range, and temporal variations in articulation. Overlapping harmonics, resonance, and non-linearities in the sound production mechanism make it difficult to isolate individual note events from a mixture, even for state-of-the-art computational models.

Recent advances in deep learning have substantially improved AMT performance. Convolutional and recurrent neural networks have been successfully applied to time–frequency representations of audio, enabling the modeling of both spectral patterns and temporal dependencies. More recently, sequence modeling architectures such as Transformers have further advanced the field by capturing long-range temporal relationships. However, many of these approaches treat note activation at each time frame as an independent classification problem, with limited explicit modeling of the temporal evolution of individual notes. This can lead to inconsistencies between predicted onsets, sustains, and offsets, and to errors in note duration estimation.

To address these limitations, note-level temporal modeling has emerged as a promising direction. Instead of predicting framewise activations independently, models can explicitly represent the progression of each note through a sequence of states, such as "off," "onset," "sustain," and "offset." This multi-state representation more closely mirrors the physical and perceptual processes underlying piano performance, where notes transition through distinct temporal phases. By constraining predictions to valid state sequences, such models can improve temporal coherence and reduce spurious activations.

Autoregressive sequence models are particularly well suited to this task, as they can condition each prediction on the sequence of past states, capturing dependencies both within and across notes. In the context of piano transcription, an autoregressive multi-state note model can generate note events in a temporally consistent manner, ensuring that onsets are followed by sustained activity and eventual offsets, while respecting the polyphonic structure of the music. This approach can also naturally incorporate prior musical knowledge, such as typical note durations, chordal structures, and rhythmic patterns.

In this work, we propose a novel framework for polyphonic piano transcription that integrates an autoregressive sequence model with a multi-state note representation. Our method operates directly on frame-level spectral features, predicting the state of each candidate note over time in an autoregressive fashion. By modeling the joint distribution over note states conditioned on past predictions, our system captures both the fine-grained temporal dynamics of individual notes and the higher-level musical context. We evaluate our approach on standard piano transcription benchmarks and demonstrate that it achieves improved onset, offset, and frame-level accuracy compared to strong baselines, particularly in challenging passages with dense polyphony and expressive timing. Furthermore, we analyze the contributions of the multi-state representation and the autoregressive decoding process, showing that both components are critical to the observed performance gains. Our results highlight the potential of structured, sequential note modeling for advancing the state of the art in automatic music transcription.
conclusion: This work presented an autoregressive multi-state note model for polyphonic piano transcription, integrating temporal dependencies and explicit note state transitions within a probabilistic framework. By modeling individual notes with multiple states and conditioning predictions on prior outputs, the approach effectively captured both onset-offset dynamics and inter-note correlations, leading to improved transcription accuracy over baseline framewise and non-autoregressive methods. Experiments on benchmark piano datasets demonstrated consistent gains in note-level precision and recall, particularly in complex passages with overlapping sustain and rapid articulation. The results highlight the benefits of combining autoregressive sequence modeling with structured state representations for music transcription tasks. While the current implementation focused on piano recordings with relatively clean acoustic conditions, future work may extend to more diverse instruments, incorporate richer timbral features, and explore integration with end-to-end neural front-ends. Overall, the proposed framework contributes a flexible and interpretable foundation for advancing polyphonic transcription, with potential applications in music information retrieval, education, and performance analysis.

title: Clustering Categorical Data: Soft Rounding k-modes
abstract: Clustering categorical data presents unique challenges due to the absence of inherent distance metrics and the prevalence of discrete attribute values. This paper introduces Soft Rounding k-modes, an extension of the traditional k-modes algorithm that incorporates probabilistic membership assignments and a soft rounding mechanism to improve cluster stability and interpretability. The proposed method refines mode updates by weighting attribute frequencies according to membership probabilities, reducing sensitivity to noise and initialization. Experimental evaluations on diverse categorical datasets demonstrate that Soft Rounding k-modes achieves higher clustering accuracy and lower variability compared to standard k-modes, offering a robust and flexible approach for categorical data analysis.
introduction: Clustering is a fundamental task in data analysis, aiming to uncover hidden structures by grouping similar objects together. While numerous clustering algorithms have been developed for numerical data, many real-world datasets are categorical in nature, such as demographic records, survey responses, and transaction logs. The k-means algorithm, widely used for numerical data, is unsuitable for categorical attributes due to its reliance on Euclidean distances and arithmetic means. The k-modes algorithm addresses this limitation by replacing means with modes and employing a simple matching dissimilarity measure, enabling efficient clustering of purely categorical data. However, the conventional k-modes approach assigns each object to exactly one cluster, which may be too restrictive when the underlying group memberships are uncertain or overlapping. In many applications, such as customer segmentation or document categorization, a soft assignment that reflects degrees of membership can provide richer insights and better downstream performance. In this work, we introduce the Soft Rounding k-modes algorithm, which extends traditional k-modes by incorporating a probabilistic, soft membership mechanism through a rounding strategy that balances interpretability with flexibility. This method preserves the efficiency of k-modes while capturing uncertainty in cluster assignments, offering a more nuanced representation of structure in categorical datasets.
conclusion: The proposed Soft Rounding k-modes algorithm extends traditional k-modes clustering by introducing a probabilistic membership update and a smooth mode estimation procedure, enabling more robust handling of categorical data with noise and ambiguity. Experimental results demonstrate improved clustering accuracy and stability compared to standard hard-assignment methods, particularly in datasets with overlapping category distributions. The soft rounding mechanism preserves interpretability while mitigating sensitivity to initialization. These findings suggest that incorporating soft assignments into k-modes offers a promising direction for categorical data analysis, with potential applications in domains where categorical attributes are prevalent and cluster boundaries are inherently uncertain.

title: Simplified dark matter models in the light of AMS-02 antiproton data
abstract: We investigate the implications of recent AMS-02 measurements of the cosmic-ray antiproton flux for simplified dark matter (DM) models. Employing a range of benchmark scenarios in which DM annihilates via s-channel mediators into Standard Model final states, we compute the resulting antiproton spectra using state-of-the-art cosmic-ray propagation models. Theoretical predictions are confronted with AMS-02 data, accounting for astrophysical background uncertainties and solar modulation effects. We explore both vector and scalar mediators, scanning over DM and mediator masses, as well as couplings to quarks and leptons. Our analysis identifies regions of parameter space where the predicted antiproton excess is compatible with observations, while remaining consistent with collider and direct detection bounds. We find that certain mediator masses in the few hundred GeV to multi-TeV range remain viable, with annihilation cross sections near the thermal relic benchmark. These results demonstrate the complementarity between cosmic-ray measurements and other probes, and highlight the potential of precision antiproton data to constrain or reveal new physics in the dark sector.
introduction:
The nature of dark matter (DM) remains one of the most compelling open questions in contemporary physics. A wide range of astrophysical and cosmological observations, from galactic rotation curves to the anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background, provide strong evidence for the existence of a non-luminous, non-baryonic component constituting about 27% of the total energy density of the Universe. Despite its gravitational imprint being well established, the particle properties of dark matter are still unknown. Among the various avenues to probe its nature, indirect detection seeks to observe the Standard Model particles produced by DM annihilation or decay in astrophysical environments. In this context, cosmic-ray antiprotons constitute a valuable probe, as they can be generated in hadronic final states and propagate relatively unaffected by energy losses over galactic scales.

Recent high-precision measurements from the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) aboard the International Space Station have significantly improved our knowledge of the cosmic-ray antiproton spectrum. The unprecedented precision and extended energy range of these data have opened new possibilities to search for subtle excesses above the astrophysical background that could hint at a DM contribution. However, interpreting the antiproton flux requires careful modelling of cosmic-ray production, propagation, and solar modulation, as well as a robust description of possible DM signals.

Simplified dark matter models provide a theoretically motivated yet flexible framework to explore DM phenomenology in light of current data. In these models, the complex structure of a full ultraviolet-complete theory is reduced to its essential degrees of freedom: the DM particle and a mediator connecting it to the Standard Model sector. By specifying the masses, spins, and couplings of these states, simplified models allow systematic studies of collider, direct, and indirect detection constraints, while remaining agnostic about the full high-energy theory. This approach has been widely adopted in the interpretation of LHC searches and is increasingly applied to indirect detection scenarios, enabling consistent comparisons between different experimental probes.

In this work, we investigate the implications of AMS-02 antiproton measurements for a representative set of simplified DM models. We consider both s-channel and t-channel mediators with various spin assignments, and explore a range of annihilation final states relevant for antiproton production. Our analysis incorporates state-of-the-art cosmic-ray propagation models and accounts for theoretical and experimental uncertainties. By confronting the predicted antiproton fluxes with AMS-02 data, we derive constraints on the parameter space of the models, and identify regions where a DM contribution could improve the fit to the observations. This study aims to bridge the gap between model-independent excess searches and more complete theoretical interpretations, shedding light on the role of current cosmic-ray data in the broader dark matter search program.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the implications of the latest AMS-02 antiproton flux measurements for a selection of simplified dark matter models. By focusing on representative scenarios with s-channel mediators coupling to quarks and/or gluons, we have explored the parameter space in which dark matter annihilation could account for a possible excess in the observed antiproton spectrum. Our analysis combined up-to-date cosmic-ray propagation models with a careful treatment of both experimental and theoretical uncertainties, allowing us to assess the robustness of the inferred constraints.
