Our contributions can be summarized as follows. First, we introduce a dual contrastive learning paradigm that decomposes the representation learning problem into two complementary contrastive tasks, each targeting a distinct dimension of spatio-temporal variation. Second, we design a set of spatio-temporal augmentations tailored to preserve semantic content while introducing controlled perturbations along spatial or temporal axes, enabling the model to learn invariances in a principled way. Third, we provide a unified architecture that accommodates both objectives efficiently, allowing for scalable training on large spatio-temporal datasets. Finally, through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets for action recognition, video retrieval, and motion prediction, we demonstrate that DCL outperforms strong baselines in both fully supervised and transfer learning settings, highlighting the versatility and effectiveness of our approach.

Beyond empirical performance, we also investigate the learned representations qualitatively and quantitatively, showing that DCL embeddings exhibit improved clustering of semantically related events, robustness to spatial occlusions and temporal jitter, and enhanced generalization to unseen tasks. These findings suggest that dual contrastive learning provides a principled and practical avenue for tackling the inherent complexities of spatio-temporal data.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in spatio-temporal representation learning, self-supervised methods, and contrastive learning paradigms. Section 3 details the proposed DCL framework, including architectural design, augmentation strategies, and optimization objectives. Section 4 describes the experimental setup, datasets, and evaluation metrics. Section 5 presents and discusses the results, and Section 6 concludes with a summary of contributions and potential directions for future research.
conclusion: In this work, we introduced a dual contrastive learning framework for spatio-temporal representation, leveraging complementary objectives to enhance both spatial and temporal feature discrimination. By jointly optimizing intra-modal and cross-modal contrastive losses, the proposed approach effectively captures fine-grained spatial structures while preserving temporal dynamics, leading to more robust and generalizable representations. Our experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrated consistent improvements over existing self-supervised and supervised baselines, confirming the effectiveness of the dual contrastive paradigm. Furthermore, ablation studies highlighted the critical role of balancing spatial and temporal contrastive components, as well as the benefits of the proposed sampling strategy in mitigating redundancy. The framework is flexible and can be readily integrated with diverse backbone architectures and extended to other spatio-temporal domains such as action recognition, trajectory prediction, and video retrieval. Future work will explore adaptive weighting mechanisms and incorporation of semantic priors to further enhance representation quality. Overall, this study underscores the potential of dual contrastive learning as a principled approach to spatio-temporal representation learning.

title: Compiling Finite Domain Constraints to SAT with BEE: the Director's Cut
abstract: We present an extended account of BEE, a compiler that translates finite domain constraint problems into Boolean satisfiability (SAT). BEE operates on a high-level declarative specification, applying a sequence of optimizations and encoding strategies to produce compact and efficient CNF formulas. Central to BEE’s approach is the use of order-encoding for integers, combined with equi-propagation and partial evaluation to simplify constraints prior to encoding. This “Director’s Cut” version expands upon earlier work by detailing the compilation pipeline, illustrating design choices, and reporting new empirical results. We discuss enhancements in constraint simplification, improved handling of symmetry, and refined encodings for global constraints. Experimental evaluation across a diverse benchmark suite demonstrates significant improvements in both CNF size and SAT solver runtimes. The results confirm that careful compilation from finite domain constraints to SAT, as implemented in BEE, can yield highly efficient encodings, advancing the practical applicability of SAT-based constraint solving.
introduction:
Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) over finite domains arise naturally in a wide range of combinatorial tasks, including scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Solving such problems efficiently is a central concern in Artificial Intelligence and Operations Research. One successful approach is to encode finite domain constraints into Boolean satisfiability (SAT), leveraging the remarkable progress in SAT solver performance over the past two decades. The quality of the encoding, in terms of size, structure, and propagation strength, plays a decisive role in the overall efficiency of the solution process.

BEE (Ben-Gurion University Equi-propagation Encoder) is a compiler that translates finite domain constraint models into SAT. It incorporates optimizations such as equi-propagation, partial evaluation, and symmetry breaking, producing compact and solver-friendly CNF formulas. Originally developed to facilitate experimental exploration of encodings and solver interactions, BEE has matured into a robust and versatile tool, used in both research and applied settings.

This paper presents an in-depth account of BEE’s architecture, encoding strategies, and optimization techniques—the “Director’s Cut” version, offering details that go beyond earlier descriptions. We discuss the principles behind its compilation pipeline, the trade-offs in representation choices, and the methods employed to preserve strong constraint propagation after translation. Special emphasis is placed on equi-propagation, a technique for simplifying constraints prior to SAT encoding by deducing and exploiting equalities between Boolean variables.

Furthermore, we evaluate BEE across diverse benchmarks, illustrating the impact of its optimizations on encoding size and solving time. Our results demonstrate that careful compilation from finite domain constraints to SAT can yield substantial performance gains, making SAT-based CSP solving a competitive alternative to dedicated constraint solvers. This work aims to provide both a comprehensive reference for researchers and practical guidance for practitioners seeking to harness SAT technology through effective compilation.
conclusion: We have presented an extended account of compiling finite domain constraints to SAT using BEE, highlighting both the underlying principles and novel optimizations. By refining constraint encodings, exploiting symmetry breaking, and applying equi-propagation, BEE achieves compact CNF representations that improve SAT solver performance. The “Director’s Cut” offers deeper insights into design choices and trade-offs, supported by experimental evidence across diverse benchmarks. Our findings demonstrate that careful compilation strategies can significantly enhance efficiency without sacrificing generality. Future work will explore broader classes of constraints, automated optimization selection, and tighter integration with modern SAT-based problem-solving frameworks.

title: Ground state of the one dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii equation with a Morse potential
abstract: We investigate the ground state of the one-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii equation in the presence of a Morse potential. Using a variational approach, we analyze the effect of varying interaction strength and potential parameters. Results reveal a transition from bound to unbound states, highlighting the interplay between nonlinearity and confinement in determining ground state properties.
introduction:
Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) has attracted considerable attention since its experimental realization in ultracold atomic gases, providing a macroscopic quantum system in which interactions and external potentials can be precisely controlled. The mean-field description of BECs at zero temperature is governed by the Gross–Pitaevskii equation (GPE), a nonlinear Schrödinger equation that incorporates both the kinetic energy of the condensate and the effects of inter-particle interactions via a cubic nonlinearity. Analytical and numerical studies of the GPE for various external potentials have revealed rich ground-state properties, nonlinear excitations, and dynamical behaviors. While the harmonic trap is the most common configuration in experiments, other trapping geometries are of both theoretical and practical interest, as they allow exploration of crossover regimes and the interplay between confinement and interactions.

The Morse potential, originally introduced in molecular physics to model the vibrational structure of diatomic molecules, offers a tunable form that interpolates between a harmonic-like well and an exponentially decaying potential. Its asymmetry and adjustable depth make it a useful model for studying systems where confinement can be gradually weakened, approaching free-particle behavior. In the context of the GPE, the Morse potential provides a tractable yet nontrivial setting for examining how the ground state evolves from a localized to a delocalized form as the potential parameters vary.

In this work, we investigate the ground-state properties of the one-dimensional GPE with a Morse potential using analytical variational methods. We analyze how the condensate’s spatial profile and energy depend on the interaction strength and potential parameters, revealing regimes of localization and delocalization, and discuss the implications for tunable trapping in ultracold gases.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the ground state properties of the one–dimensional Gross–Pitaevskii equation in the presence of a Morse potential by employing a variational approach. The Morse potential, with its tunable parameters, allowed us to interpolate smoothly between a tightly confining regime and a weakly bound or near–free particle regime. For the non–interacting case, the variational method reproduced the expected exact results, confirming the validity of our trial wave function. In the presence of repulsive interactions, we observed a qualitative change in behaviour: for small coupling strengths, localized bound states persist, whereas beyond a critical interaction strength the bound state ceases to exist, and the condensate becomes delocalized. This disappearance of the bound state with increasing nonlinearity reflects the competition between the trapping potential and the mean–field repulsion. Our analysis shows that the critical coupling is sensitive to the shape parameter of the Morse potential, providing a means to control localization–delocalization transitions. These results may have implications for manipulating Bose–Einstein condensates in tailored trapping potentials, and suggest that the Morse potential can serve as a useful model for exploring ground state properties across different confinement regimes.

title: Arrival statistics and exploration properties of mortal walkers
abstract: We investigate the statistical properties of arrival times and spatial exploration for mortal random walkers, i.e., stochastic walkers subject to a finite lifetime. By combining analytical methods with numerical simulations, we quantify how mortality modifies first-passage statistics, visitation patterns, and coverage of finite domains. We derive exact and asymptotic expressions for arrival probabilities and mean arrival times as functions of death rate, spatial dimension, and target geometry. Mortality introduces a competition between exploration and decay, leading to nontrivial scaling regimes absent in immortal walkers. In particular, we identify critical mortality thresholds beyond which long-range exploration is strongly suppressed, and arrival statistics become dominated by short trajectories. Our results establish a unified framework for understanding transport processes with finite lifetimes, with potential applications to chemical kinetics, biological search strategies, and transport in disordered or reactive media.
introduction:
Random walks and diffusion processes constitute a central paradigm in the description of transport phenomena across physics, chemistry, biology, and related disciplines. From the spread of molecules in a solvent to the migration of cells in tissues, and from the search strategies of foraging animals to the exploration of complex networks, stochastic motion models have provided deep insights into the interplay between dynamics and geometry. A key quantity of interest in these contexts is the arrival, or first-passage, statistics: the probability distribution of times at which a walker first reaches a target site or region. First-passage concepts are integral to understanding reaction kinetics, search efficiency, and survival probabilities, and have been studied extensively for a variety of geometries, boundary conditions, and types of random motion.

In the classical setting, walkers are assumed to be immortal: they persist indefinitely until they reach the target or explore the domain completely. However, in many realistic situations, the walk is terminated prematurely due to mortality, deactivation, or spontaneous disappearance. Mortality can arise from physical degradation (radioactive decay of diffusing nuclei), finite lifespan of reactive species (unstable molecules, excited states), biological death (microorganisms, cells), or imposed termination protocols (timeout in search algorithms). Introducing mortality fundamentally alters the statistics of arrival and exploration, as the walker may never reach the target. In such cases, the relevant observables shift from unconditional first-passage times to conditional statistics — given that arrival occurs — and to the probability of ever arriving at all.

The study of mortal walkers, also referred to as evanescent, decaying, or dying random walkers, has attracted increasing attention over the past decades. Early work examined the survival probability of particles subject to both diffusion and exponential decay, motivated by problems in chemical physics and radiative transfer. More recent research has extended these ideas to a broad range of mortality mechanisms, including deterministic finite lifetimes, stochastic resetting with absorption, and space- or time-dependent death rates. Mortality can regularize otherwise divergent mean first-passage times, influence the optimality of search strategies, and modify scaling relations that hold in the immortal case. The arrival statistics of mortal walkers thus encode a nontrivial interplay between motion, geometry, and the temporal window allowed for arrival.

Beyond arrival times, another important aspect of random motion is the exploration property — the extent to which a walker visits new sites or covers a domain over time. Measures such as the mean number of distinct sites visited, the coverage fraction, or the exploration rate quantify how effectively a walker probes its environment. For immortal walkers, exploration properties have been thoroughly characterised in various dimensions and for different motion models, revealing, for example, the recurrent nature of one- and two-dimensional random walks or the transient character in higher dimensions. Mortality, however, truncates the exploration process, leading to a finite and potentially small explored region. The statistical characterisation of exploration by mortal walkers remains less developed than for arrival statistics, despite its relevance in contexts where premature termination limits the information gathered or the resources discovered.

The coupling between arrival and exploration statistics becomes particularly significant when mortality is non-negligible. The probability of reaching a target depends not only on the dynamics of the walker but also on how the explored territory grows before termination. In sparse search problems, the likelihood of encountering the target is tied to the coverage achieved within the walker’s finite lifetime. Conversely, in dense or bounded domains, mortality may reduce the redundancy of visits and alter the spatial distribution of arrival events. Understanding this coupling is crucial for applications ranging from chemical reaction yields and ecological foraging success to the efficiency of search algorithms on networks.

In this work, we investigate the arrival statistics and exploration properties of mortal walkers in a unified framework. We consider random walkers subject to an exponential mortality process, whereby each walker has a constant rate of spontaneous death independent of its position or history. This simple yet widely applicable model permits analytical treatment while capturing the essential features of finite lifetime. We focus on two interrelated questions: (i) what is the distribution of arrival times, conditional and unconditional, in the presence of mortality, and how does mortality modify classic first-passage results? (ii) how does mortality affect the exploration of the domain, as quantified by the number of distinct sites visited and related measures?

By developing exact and asymptotic results for simple geometries, and complementing these with numerical simulations, we elucidate how mortality reshapes the statistical landscape of arrival and exploration. We show that even a small mortality rate can lead to significant changes in arrival probabilities and the scaling of exploration properties, and that these effects depend sensitively on the dimensionality and topology of the underlying space. Our analysis bridges the gap between the well-studied immortal case and the more realistic mortal scenario, providing insights relevant for diverse physical, biological, and computational systems. In doing so, we aim to contribute to a more complete statistical theory of random motion under finite lifetimes, with potential extensions to heterogeneous death rates, non-Markovian dynamics, and complex search environments.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the arrival statistics and exploration properties of mortal random walkers, focusing on the interplay between finite lifetime and stochastic motion in determining first-passage characteristics. By systematically comparing mortal and immortal walkers across a range of geometries and boundary conditions, we have shown that mortality introduces qualitative changes to both arrival-time distributions and spatial coverage. In particular, finite lifetimes truncate heavy-tailed first-passage distributions, leading to well-defined mean arrival times even in configurations where immortal walkers display diverging moments. This regularising effect is most pronounced in low-dimensional systems, where recurrence strongly influences the immortal case.

Our analysis of exploration properties reveals that mortality limits the extent of territory visited, producing a characteristic saturation in the number of distinct sites explored. The dependence of this saturation value on lifetime and diffusivity is captured by scaling forms that unify various regimes. These results highlight the subtle balance between stochastic search efficiency and survival probability, with direct implications for transport in reactive media, search processes in biological systems, and the modelling of diffusion-limited reactions where reactants may deactivate or decay.

The theoretical framework developed here can be extended to incorporate more complex dynamics, such as anisotropic motion, heterogeneous environments, or non-exponential lifetime distributions. Likewise, the methodology is broadly applicable to systems where termination events compete with exploration, including foraging models, epidemic spread with recovery or removal, and information propagation in finite-memory networks. The convergence of arrival statistics under mortality suggests new strategies for controlling search processes via lifetime tuning, potentially optimising performance in constrained or noisy environments.

Overall, our study deepens the understanding of how mortality reshapes the fundamental statistical properties of random walks, providing both conceptual insights and practical tools for analysing finite-lifetime stochastic transport.

title: Differentiable Multiple Shooting Layers
abstract: We introduce differentiable multiple shooting layers, a novel framework integrating multiple shooting methods into end-to-end trainable neural architectures. By discretizing dynamical systems into segments with learnable initial conditions, our approach enables stable gradient-based optimization while alleviating sensitivity to long-term dependencies. The proposed layers are compatible with automatic differentiation, allowing joint learning of system parameters and segment boundaries within deep learning pipelines. We present efficient implementations leveraging parallelized integration and constrained optimization to enforce continuity between segments. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dynamical systems demonstrate improved training stability, faster convergence, and enhanced predictive accuracy compared to single-shooting baselines. Our work bridges classical numerical methods and modern differentiable programming, enabling robust learning for complex time-dependent processes.
introduction:
The numerical solution of boundary value problems (BVPs) and optimal control problems (OCPs) is a cornerstone of scientific computing, with applications ranging from physics-based simulation to engineering design and data-driven modeling. Among the classical techniques for solving such problems, multiple shooting has emerged as a robust and efficient approach, particularly suitable for stiff or highly nonlinear dynamical systems. By decomposing the time domain into subintervals and solving initial value problems (IVPs) on each segment, multiple shooting mitigates the sensitivity to initial guesses and improves numerical stability compared to single shooting. The continuity constraints linking subintervals are then enforced through a nonlinear system of equations, whose solution yields the global trajectory.

In recent years, the growing integration of physical models into machine learning pipelines has created new opportunities and challenges at the intersection of numerical analysis and differentiable programming. In many applications, it is desirable to embed numerical solvers directly into computational graphs so that gradients can be propagated through them via automatic differentiation. This enables end-to-end training of hybrid models that combine data-driven components with physics-based priors, or that learn unknown parameters, controls, or system dynamics from observations. Such differentiable solvers have found applications in scientific machine learning, system identification, trajectory optimization, and control design.

Despite the well-established utility of multiple shooting in classical computational settings, its integration into differentiable programming frameworks has received comparatively little attention. Existing differentiable ODE solvers typically focus on single shooting or collocation-based methods, which may encounter numerical difficulties when applied to long time horizons, chaotic systems, or ill-conditioned problems. Extending multiple shooting to the differentiable setting is nontrivial, as it requires careful handling of both the forward simulation over subintervals and the coupled nonlinear constraints across shooting nodes, while maintaining computational efficiency and numerical stability in the computation of derivatives.

This work introduces differentiable multiple shooting layers—a novel formulation that embeds the multiple shooting method as a fully differentiable module within modern machine learning frameworks. Our approach preserves the algorithmic structure of classical multiple shooting, including the partitioned integration of subintervals and the enforcement of continuity constraints, while exposing all relevant components to automatic differentiation. We discuss strategies for implementing the layer efficiently, including the use of implicit differentiation for the nonlinear solve and adjoint-based sensitivity analysis for subinterval integrations. The resulting layers are compatible with gradient-based optimization routines and can be seamlessly integrated into end-to-end learning architectures.

By bridging the gap between robust numerical methods for dynamical systems and differentiable programming, differentiable multiple shooting layers enable a new class of hybrid algorithms that combine the stability and reliability of classical solvers with the flexibility and learning capacity of neural networks. We demonstrate their effectiveness on a range of challenging problems, showing improved convergence properties, better handling of long horizons, and enhanced robustness to poor initializations compared to differentiable single shooting approaches.
conclusion: We have presented differentiable multiple shooting layers as a flexible and efficient approach for embedding trajectory optimization and dynamic system constraints within end-to-end learning pipelines. By formulating the multiple shooting procedure as a differentiable module, our method enables gradient-based training while preserving the stability and convergence benefits of classical numerical techniques. Experimental results demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness over single shooting formulations, particularly in long-horizon and stiff-dynamics scenarios. Furthermore, the modular structure allows seamless integration with existing deep learning architectures, opening avenues for hybrid model-based and data-driven control. Future work will explore scaling to higher-dimensional systems, incorporating uncertainty quantification, and extending to implicit or adaptive integration schemes. Overall, differentiable multiple shooting layers provide a principled bridge between numerical optimal control and modern machine learning, enabling more reliable and interpretable solutions to complex dynamical problems.

title: On the road to percent accuracy: nonlinear reaction of the matter power spectrum to dark energy and modified gravity
abstract: We investigate the nonlinear response of the matter power spectrum to variations in dark energy and modified gravity models, with the aim of achieving percent-level accuracy across a broad range of cosmologies. Using a suite of high-resolution N-body simulations spanning dynamical dark energy equations of state and representative scalar–tensor gravity theories, we quantify deviations from the standard ΛCDM prediction in both amplitude and scale dependence. We extend the reaction framework, which models the nonlinear spectrum as a baseline ΛCDM prediction modified by a physically motivated response function, to incorporate time- and scale-dependent growth and screening effects. Calibration against simulations demonstrates that the extended formalism reproduces nonlinear power spectra to within 1–2% accuracy for wCDM and f(R) gravity models up to k ≈ 1 h Mpc⁻¹ at z ≤ 2. Our results enable precise and computationally efficient predictions for upcoming large-scale structure surveys, facilitating joint constraints on dark energy and gravity beyond general relativity, and providing a robust theoretical tool for testing the origin of cosmic acceleration.
introduction:
The accelerated expansion of the Universe, first revealed by observations of distant type Ia supernovae, remains one of the most profound puzzles in modern cosmology. Within the concordance ΛCDM framework, this phenomenon is attributed to a cosmological constant, yet its physical origin is poorly understood and its extreme fine-tuning poses deep theoretical challenges. Alternatives to a pure cosmological constant include dynamical dark energy models and theories of modified gravity, which alter the laws of gravitation on cosmological scales. Distinguishing between these possibilities requires precise predictions for large-scale structure observables across a wide range of scales.

The matter power spectrum, encoding the statistical distribution of density fluctuations, is a primary probe for constraining dark energy and testing gravity. While linear theory suffices on the largest scales, upcoming galaxy surveys such as Euclid, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will measure clustering deep into the nonlinear regime, where mode coupling and screening effects become important. Achieving percent-level accuracy in theoretical predictions in these regimes is essential to fully exploit the statistical power of forthcoming data.

In this work we investigate the nonlinear “reaction” of the matter power spectrum to deviations from ΛCDM caused by dark energy and modified gravity. The reaction formalism provides a flexible framework to map simulated or emulated ΛCDM results to alternative cosmologies, capturing their distinct growth histories and scale-dependent effects. By systematically assessing its accuracy against high-resolution N-body simulations, we aim to establish the viability of this approach for precision cosmology, thereby enabling robust constraints on the nature of cosmic acceleration.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the nonlinear response of the matter power spectrum to variations in dark energy and modified gravity models, with the aim of achieving percent-level accuracy in theoretical predictions for forthcoming large-scale structure surveys. By systematically comparing a diverse set of cosmological scenarios—including time-varying dark energy equations of state and representative classes of modified gravity theories—we have quantified how departures from the standard ΛCDM paradigm manifest across linear, quasi-linear, and fully nonlinear regimes. Our approach combined high-resolution N-body simulations with semi-analytical emulators, enabling us to disentangle the scale-dependent and redshift-dependent features induced by alternative gravitational dynamics.

A key result of our analysis is the identification of characteristic nonlinear signatures that persist even when models are tuned to match linear growth histories. This demonstrates that the nonlinear matter power spectrum contains distinctive information about the underlying theory of gravity and the properties of dark energy beyond what is accessible from linear observables alone. We have shown that neglecting such nonlinear imprints can lead to systematic biases in cosmological parameter inference, particularly for surveys targeting small-scale clustering with high precision.

We have also evaluated the performance of existing fitting functions and emulators, originally calibrated for ΛCDM cosmologies, when applied to non-standard models. While these tools retain reasonable accuracy in mildly nonlinear regimes, their performance degrades beyond \( k \gtrsim 0.5\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1} \) for certain classes of modified gravity, underscoring the need for extended calibration or new flexible frameworks. Our results indicate that percent-level accuracy is achievable if model-specific nonlinear effects are incorporated, either through targeted simulation campaigns or by augmenting existing emulators with physically motivated corrections.

Furthermore, we have assessed the interplay between baryonic feedback and gravitational modifications, finding that degeneracies can arise that complicate the interpretation of small-scale power. This highlights the importance of joint modeling efforts that consistently treat both astrophysical and gravitational sources of nonlinearity. We stress that future analyses should prioritise cross-validation between independent modeling approaches, as well as careful propagation of theoretical uncertainties into survey forecasts.

Looking ahead, the methodologies developed here can be extended to a broader range of theories and combined with higher-order statistics, such as the bispectrum, to further exploit the constraining power of nonlinear structure formation. As next-generation surveys, including Euclid, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, deliver unprecedented measurements of cosmic structure, the accurate modeling of the nonlinear matter power spectrum will be central to testing the physics of cosmic acceleration. Our findings provide both a cautionary note on the limitations of current tools and a roadmap for achieving the accuracy required to distinguish between dark energy and modified gravity scenarios in the coming decade.

title: A parameter study of the eclipsing CV in the Kepler field, KIS J192748.53+444724.5
abstract: We present a detailed parameter study of the eclipsing cataclysmic variable (CV) KIS J192748.53+444724.5, located in the *Kepler* field. Using high-cadence photometry from the *Kepler* spacecraft, supplemented by time-resolved ground-based spectroscopy, we model the system’s light curve to derive its fundamental parameters. The analysis incorporates a range of mass ratios, inclination angles, and accretion disc geometries to explore the parameter space consistent with the observed eclipse morphology. We find that the system exhibits deep, well-defined eclipses of both the white dwarf and the bright spot, enabling precise constraints on the binary configuration. Our best-fitting models suggest a mass ratio \(q = M_2/M_1\) of \(0.62 \pm 0.02\), an inclination of \(84.6^\circ \pm 0.3^\circ\), and a white dwarf mass of \(0.83 \pm 0.05\,M_\odot\). We also investigate the variability of the accretion disc radius across different orbital phases and brightness states, finding evidence for modest disc expansion during outburst episodes. These results place KIS J192748.53+444724.5 among the relatively few well-characterized eclipsing CVs in the *Kepler* field and provide a benchmark for testing models of accretion dynamics in compact binaries.
introduction:
Cataclysmic variables (CVs) are short-period interacting binary systems in which a white dwarf accretes material from a Roche-lobe–filling late-type companion star. The mass transfer typically proceeds via an accretion disc, unless strong magnetic fields disrupt its formation. These systems display a wide variety of photometric and spectroscopic variability, arising from orbital motion, accretion disc dynamics, and episodic outbursts. Among CVs, eclipsing systems are of particular importance because the geometry of the eclipse constrains the binary inclination, and high-time-resolution photometry can reveal the structure and evolution of the accretion flow. Detailed modelling of eclipse profiles allows precise determination of fundamental parameters such as component masses, radii, and the scale of the accretion disc.

The advent of high-precision, continuous photometry from the *Kepler* mission has opened new opportunities for studying CVs. Although *Kepler* was primarily designed for exoplanet detection, its long-term, uninterrupted light curves are ideally suited to the investigation of variability in compact binaries. Several CVs have been identified within the *Kepler* field of view, enabling unprecedented time-series data over months to years. This allows the detection of subtle periodicities, orbital modulations, and transient events that are often missed in ground-based observations due to diurnal gaps and weather interruptions.

KIS J192748.53+444724.5 (hereafter KIS J1927) is an eclipsing CV discovered in the course of the Kepler-INT Survey (KIS), which provided deep optical photometry of the *Kepler* field. Initial identification was based on its variability and blue colours, and subsequent time-resolved photometry confirmed the presence of deep eclipses, indicating a high-inclination configuration. The system’s orbital period of approximately 3.97 hours places it above the canonical 2–3 hour period gap for CVs, suggesting a relatively evolved donor star and a stable accretion disc.

Despite its favourable geometry and accessibility in the *Kepler* field, KIS J1927 has not yet been the subject of a comprehensive parameter study. Previous reports have focused on basic photometric characterisation, leaving the system’s physical parameters largely unconstrained. In this work, we combine *Kepler* long-cadence data with complementary ground-based observations to perform a detailed analysis of its eclipse morphology. By modelling the light curve with parameterised binary and disc models, we aim to derive robust estimates of the system’s key parameters, including inclination, mass ratio, and disc radius. Our study demonstrates the power of combining space-based photometry with targeted follow-up to characterise eclipsing CVs in unprecedented detail.
conclusion:
We have undertaken a detailed parameter study of the eclipsing cataclysmic variable KIS J192748.53+444724.5 using high-precision photometry from the *Kepler* mission, supplemented by ground-based follow-up. By modelling the eclipse profiles, we have constrained the system geometry, including the inclination, mass ratio, and component radii, and have examined their dependence on the adopted assumptions and modelling techniques. The results indicate a high inclination consistent with deep, well-defined eclipses, and a mass ratio placing the system among short-period CVs with a late-type donor. Our analysis shows that the white dwarf and accretion disc contributions to the optical light vary significantly between quiescent and outburst states, highlighting the importance of time-resolved, multi-epoch modelling to capture the range of system behaviour.

The parameter space exploration demonstrates that modest changes in limb-darkening coefficients, disc radial brightness profiles, and eclipse fitting methods can lead to measurable shifts in derived parameters, underscoring the need for consistent modelling frameworks when comparing different systems. The *Kepler* light curve’s continuous coverage allowed us to detect subtle features, such as ingress/egress asymmetries, that provide additional constraints on the disc structure.

This study adds to the small but growing sample of well-characterised eclipsing CVs in the *Kepler* field, offering a benchmark for testing accretion disc models and evolutionary tracks. Future work should combine high-speed spectroscopy with eclipse photometry to break remaining degeneracies in component masses and temperatures. The methodology developed here can be applied to other eclipsing CVs with high-quality light curves, enabling systematic comparisons and improved understanding of mass transfer and accretion dynamics in compact binaries.

title: Magnetic interactions in a proposed diluted magnetic semiconductor (Ba$_\text{1-x}$K$_\text{x}$)(Zn$_\text{1-y}$Mn$_\text{y}$)$_\text{2}$P$_\text{2}$
abstract: We investigate the electronic structure and magnetic interactions in the proposed diluted magnetic semiconductor (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)(Zn$_{1-y}$Mn$_y$)$_2$P$_2$ using density functional theory calculations. The host compound BaZn$_2$P$_2$ is a direct-gap semiconductor, and substitution of Mn for Zn introduces localized magnetic moments, while K substitution for Ba provides hole carriers. Our results reveal that in the absence of carrier doping, Mn–Mn coupling is dominated by short-range antiferromagnetic superexchange via P anions. Hole doping significantly modifies the magnetic interactions, promoting long-range ferromagnetic coupling mediated by the itinerant carriers, in line with the Zener p–d exchange mechanism. The competition between superexchange and carrier-mediated exchange leads to a tunable magnetic ground state dependent on doping concentrations and Mn–Mn separation. Electronic structure analysis shows strong hybridization between Mn 3d and P 3p states near the Fermi level, enhancing exchange pathways. These findings suggest that (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)(Zn$_{1-y}$Mn$_y$)$_2$P$_2$ is a promising platform for realizing high-temperature ferromagnetism in a bulk p-type semiconductor, and they provide microscopic insight into the interplay between carrier concentration and magnetic ordering in pnictide-based diluted magnetic semiconductors.
introduction:
Diluted magnetic semiconductors (DMSs) have attracted sustained interest over the past two decades due to their potential for integrating charge and spin degrees of freedom in a single material platform, thereby enabling spintronic devices that surpass the limitations of conventional electronics. In a DMS, a small fraction of the nonmagnetic cations in a semiconductor lattice is substituted by magnetic ions, typically transition metals with partially filled d shells, introducing local magnetic moments into an otherwise nonmagnetic host. The interplay between these localized spins and the itinerant carriers in the host lattice gives rise to novel magnetic phenomena, including carrier-mediated ferromagnetism, whose strength and character can be tuned through chemical substitution, carrier concentration, and external stimuli.

Early research on III–V-based DMSs such as (Ga,Mn)As demonstrated the feasibility of achieving ferromagnetic ordering with Curie temperatures up to ~200 K. However, the relatively low Curie temperatures and challenges in controlling both carrier and spin densities have motivated the search for alternative host lattices that can support robust magnetic interactions at or above room temperature. More recently, attention has turned to DMSs based on layered pnictide semiconductors, inspired in part by the structural and chemical flexibility of the ThCr$_2$Si$_2$-type framework, which has also been central to the development of iron-based superconductors. In these systems, the decoupling of charge and spin doping can be achieved by substituting alkali or alkaline-earth metals for carrier control, while independently introducing magnetic transition-metal ions into the Zn-based sublattice.

The compound (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)(Zn$_{1-y}$Mn$_y$)$_2$As$_2$ has emerged as a prototypical example of such a layered DMS. It crystallizes in the tetragonal ThCr$_2$Si$_2$-type structure, with Mn$^{2+}$ ions substituted on Zn sites providing localized $S = 5/2$ spins, and K$^+$ substitution for Ba$^{2+}$ introducing hole carriers into the Zn–As layers. This separation of spin and charge doping has been shown to facilitate higher solubility of magnetic ions and enhanced control over the exchange interactions, leading to Curie temperatures approaching 230 K in optimized compositions. Parallel investigations have considered replacing As with other group 15 elements to further tune the electronic structure and exchange pathways.

Phosphorus-based analogues offer a distinct platform for exploring magnetic interactions in DMSs. Compared to arsenides, phosphides generally exhibit wider band gaps, different covalency, and modified $p$–$d$ hybridization, all of which can influence the mediation of exchange interactions between localized spins. The substitution of P for As alters the lattice constants and bonding angles within the [Zn$_2$P$_2$] layers, potentially modifying both the superexchange pathways between nearest-neighbor Mn ions and the longer-range, carrier-mediated Ruderman–Kittel–Kasuya–Yosida (RKKY) interactions. These structural and electronic modifications may yield different magnetic ground states or enhance the stability of ferromagnetism.

In this context, the proposed material (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)(Zn$_{1-y}$Mn$_y$)$_2$P$_2$ presents an opportunity to investigate how replacing As with P in the ThCr$_2$Si$_2$-type DMS framework affects the balance between competing magnetic interactions. The layered structure provides spatial separation between the (Ba,K) layers, which act as a charge reservoir, and the (Zn,Mn)$_2$P$_2$ layers, which host the magnetic moments and itinerant carriers. By systematically varying the K and Mn concentrations, it is possible to probe the evolution of magnetic ordering from antiferromagnetic superexchange-dominated regimes at low carrier densities to ferromagnetic coupling mediated by itinerant holes at higher doping levels.

A detailed understanding of the magnetic interactions in (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)(Zn$_{1-y}$Mn$_y$)$_2$P$_2$ is essential for evaluating its potential as a functional DMS. This includes elucidating the role of lattice parameters, bond angles, and electronic structure in governing the strength and sign of exchange interactions, as well as determining the critical doping levels necessary for robust ferromagnetism. Moreover, comparison with the arsenide analogue can shed light on the influence of anion substitution on DMS behavior, offering guidelines for the rational design of new materials with tailored magnetic and electronic properties. In the present work, we combine experimental characterization and theoretical analysis to explore these aspects, aiming to clarify the mechanisms underlying magnetic ordering in this phosphorus-based DMS candidate.
conclusion:
In summary, we have carried out a comprehensive first-principles investigation of the magnetic interactions in the proposed diluted magnetic semiconductor (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)(Zn$_{1-y}$Mn$_y$)$_2$P$_2$, with the aim of elucidating the microscopic origin of its magnetic behavior and assessing its potential for spintronic applications. By systematically varying both the hole concentration, introduced via K substitution at the Ba site, and the magnetic impurity concentration, achieved through Mn substitution at the Zn site, we have identified clear trends in the magnetic coupling between Mn moments. Our results indicate that, in the absence of carrier doping, the Mn–Mn interaction is predominantly short-range and antiferromagnetic, consistent with superexchange mediated by the P anions. Upon hole doping, the magnetic coupling evolves toward long-range ferromagnetic alignment, a change we attribute to carrier-mediated exchange interactions of the Zener type.  

The calculated exchange parameters reveal that optimal ferromagnetic order emerges within a finite window of hole concentrations, beyond which competing interactions and magnetic frustration can reduce the net magnetization. Furthermore, the strength and sign of the coupling are sensitive to the Mn–Mn separation, with nearest-neighbor pairs tending toward antiferromagnetic alignment, while more distant pairs favor ferromagnetism under sufficient hole doping. This spatial dependence underscores the importance of controlling both the dopant distribution and the carrier density to achieve robust long-range magnetic order.

Our analysis also highlights the role of the host electronic structure in enabling carrier-mediated magnetism. The substitution of K shifts the Fermi level into the valence band, enhancing the overlap between Mn 3$d$ states and itinerant hole states derived from P 3$p$ orbitals. This hybridization facilitates effective spin polarization of the carriers and mediates ferromagnetic coupling over multiple coordination shells.

Taken together, these findings suggest that (Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$)(Zn$_{1-y}$Mn$_y$)$_2$P$_2$ shares key features with other 122-type diluted magnetic semiconductors, while offering tunability through independent control of charge and spin doping. The interplay between superexchange and carrier-mediated exchange provides a versatile route to engineering its magnetic ground state. This work establishes a theoretical foundation for targeted experimental synthesis and characterization, and points to the potential of this material system for integration into spin-based devices, provided that doping levels and dopant distributions are optimized to maximize ferromagnetic stability at technologically relevant temperatures.

title: Economic inequality and Islamic Charity: An exploratory agent-based modeling approach
abstract: This study explores the potential of Islamic charitable mechanisms, particularly zakat and sadaqah, in mitigating economic inequality through an agent-based modeling (ABM) approach. While economic inequality remains a persistent challenge in both developed and developing economies, Islamic economic thought offers a unique framework for redistribution grounded in moral and religious obligations. The paper develops an ABM to simulate interactions among heterogeneous agents differing in income, wealth, and compliance with Islamic charity principles. The model incorporates rules for earning, consumption, savings, and voluntary or obligatory charitable giving, allowing for dynamic feedback between economic behavior and wealth distribution. Various scenarios are tested, including differing rates of zakat compliance, varying levels of voluntary sadaqah, and alternative redistribution strategies for collected charity. Simulation results suggest that higher compliance with zakat obligations, coupled with targeted redistribution to the poorest agents, substantially reduces wealth inequality as measured by the Gini coefficient and other indicators. Voluntary sadaqah, while less predictable, contributes to additional reductions, particularly when directed toward agents with limited earning capacity. The findings highlight the importance of institutional mechanisms that ensure compliance and effective allocation of charitable funds. Moreover, the model illustrates that even modest increases in adherence to Islamic charitable principles can lead to measurable improvements in equity without significantly dampening aggregate economic activity. By integrating religiously motivated economic behavior into computational modeling, this study provides a novel methodological contribution to the literature on faith-based approaches to inequality reduction. The exploratory nature of the ABM underscores the need for further empirical calibration and validation, but the results point to the relevance of Islamic charitable instruments as viable components of broader economic policy aimed at fostering social justice and reducing disparities in wealth distribution.
introduction:
Economic inequality remains one of the most pressing socio-economic challenges of the twenty-first century, shaping patterns of poverty, social mobility, and political stability across both developed and developing nations. Despite sustained economic growth in many regions, disparities in wealth and income distribution persist, with significant consequences for social cohesion and well-being. In contemporary economic discourse, the persistence of inequality is often attributed to structural factors such as unequal access to education, labor market segmentation, and the concentration of capital. Yet, in many societies, particularly those with strong religious or cultural traditions, informal and religiously prescribed redistributive mechanisms play an important role in mitigating inequality. Among these, Islamic charity—primarily in the form of zakāt (obligatory almsgiving) and ṣadaqah (voluntary charity)—has long been regarded as a moral and institutional framework designed to promote economic justice and social solidarity.

Islamic charity represents a distinctive approach to redistribution, grounded in the ethical and theological principles of Islam. The Qurʾān and Hadith literature outline specific obligations for wealth-holders to transfer a portion of their assets to designated categories of recipients, including the poor, the indebted, and travelers in need. This form of redistribution is not merely an act of benevolence but a religious duty, embedded within the broader Islamic economic system, which emphasizes the circulation of wealth, prevention of hoarding, and reduction of socio-economic disparities. Historically, the institution of zakāt has functioned as both a spiritual practice and a socio-economic policy mechanism, contributing to the welfare of marginalized groups. However, the efficacy of Islamic charity in alleviating contemporary patterns of inequality remains a subject of debate, influenced by variations in institutional implementation, compliance, and socio-economic context.

While empirical studies have examined the scale, patterns, and socio-economic impacts of Islamic charitable practices, there remains a gap in understanding the dynamic processes through which such redistributive mechanisms influence broader economic systems over time. Traditional econometric approaches, while valuable, often rely on aggregate data and static models that may overlook the complex interactions between individual behavior, institutional settings, and macroeconomic outcomes. In this regard, computational approaches—particularly agent-based modeling (ABM)—offer a promising methodological avenue. ABM allows researchers to construct virtual societies composed of heterogeneous agents with distinct attributes, decision-making processes, and interaction rules. Such models can capture emergent phenomena, including the redistribution of wealth and the evolution of inequality, arising from the micro-level actions of individuals and institutions.

The application of ABM to the study of economic inequality has grown steadily in recent years, enabling the exploration of alternative policy interventions and behavioral assumptions. However, few studies have explicitly incorporated religiously motivated forms of redistribution into these models, despite their relevance in many parts of the world. Incorporating Islamic charity into an ABM framework allows for the simulation of how varying levels of compliance, different interpretations of eligibility, and alternative distribution strategies might influence inequality and poverty dynamics. Moreover, such an approach can illuminate the interaction between formal economic structures and faith-based practices, offering insights into how cultural and religious norms shape economic outcomes.

This paper explores the potential of Islamic charity as a mechanism for addressing economic inequality through an exploratory agent-based modeling approach. By operationalizing zakāt and voluntary charity within a simulated economy, the study examines how different parameters—such as the proportion of wealth subject to zakāt, the targeting efficiency of distribution, and the behavioral responses of both donors and recipients—affect the distribution of wealth over time. The objective is not to provide definitive empirical predictions, but rather to investigate plausible scenarios and identify patterns that may inform both policy and future research.

In doing so, this study contributes to three strands of literature: the economics of inequality, the role of religion in economic behavior, and the methodological development of computational social science. It highlights the importance of integrating culturally specific institutions into formal models of the economy and demonstrates the capacity of ABM to bridge micro-level motivations with macro-level outcomes. Ultimately, the findings aim to foster a deeper understanding of how Islamic charitable principles might operate within complex economic systems, and how such principles could complement broader strategies for reducing inequality in diverse socio-economic contexts.
conclusion:
This study set out to explore the potential of Islamic charitable mechanisms, particularly zakat and sadaqah, in mitigating economic inequality through an agent-based modeling (ABM) approach. By simulating heterogeneous agents with varying income levels, consumption patterns, and charitable behaviors within a simplified economic environment, we examined how the systematic redistribution of wealth in accordance with Islamic principles could influence income distribution dynamics over time. Our findings suggest that structured, obligatory charitable transfers such as zakat can substantially reduce income inequality, while voluntary contributions like sadaqah, though more variable in impact, can further enhance social welfare when embedded in a culture of altruism.

The ABM framework allowed us to capture emergent macro-level patterns arising from micro-level interactions, offering insights that would be challenging to obtain through purely analytical or aggregate models. In particular, the simulations demonstrated that when agents consistently fulfill their zakat obligations, wealth concentration diminishes and the lower-income segments experience measurable improvements in their economic standing. The inclusion of sadaqah introduced an additional layer of complexity, as its effects depended on individual preferences, social norms, and the perceived effectiveness of charitable giving. Nevertheless, in scenarios where voluntary giving was widespread, inequality measures such as the Gini coefficient showed further reductions beyond those achieved through zakat alone.

These results contribute to the growing body of literature that positions Islamic economic institutions not merely as religious or ethical imperatives, but as potentially effective policy instruments for addressing structural disparities. They also underscore the importance of compliance and enforcement mechanisms; the redistributive potential of zakat is only fully realized when participation is near-universal. Similarly, fostering a social environment that encourages voluntary giving can amplify the redistributive effects, particularly in contexts where state capacity to enforce obligatory contributions is limited.

The exploratory nature of our model necessarily entails several limitations. The economic environment we simulated was intentionally simplified, excluding factors such as production, investment, taxation beyond zakat, and broader macroeconomic shocks. Agent behaviors were parameterized in ways that may not capture the full diversity of motivations and constraints in real-world societies. Furthermore, our treatment of charitable distribution assumed efficient and need-based allocation, which in practice can be influenced by administrative inefficiencies, informational asymmetries, and socio-political biases. Future work could address these limitations by integrating more nuanced behavioral rules, incorporating network structures that shape giving and receiving patterns, and linking the ABM to empirical data from specific countries or communities.

Despite these constraints, the study offers valuable conceptual insights. It illustrates how ABM can serve as a flexible tool for testing the potential impacts of faith-based economic practices under diverse hypothetical scenarios. It also highlights the interplay between obligatory and voluntary forms of charity, suggesting that their combined application may yield more equitable and resilient economic systems. For policymakers and community leaders in Muslim-majority societies, the findings point to the potential benefits of reinforcing both institutional and cultural dimensions of charitable giving. More broadly, the research invites further interdisciplinary investigation into how religiously grounded economic norms can inform contemporary debates on inequality and redistribution, offering alternative frameworks that bridge ethical imperatives with practical policy design.

title: Influence of gravitational microlensing on broad absorption lines of QSOs: The case of the Fe K$\alpha$ line
abstract: We investigate the influence of gravitational microlensing on the broad absorption features of quasars (QSOs), with particular emphasis on the Fe K$\alpha$ emission line originating in the innermost regions of the accretion disk. Using a relativistic ray-tracing approach combined with microlensing magnification maps, we model spectral variations induced by lensing caustics crossing the disk. Our results show that microlensing can selectively amplify or suppress portions of the Fe K$\alpha$ profile, altering both line shape and equivalent width. These effects are most pronounced for compact X-ray emitting regions, offering a potential diagnostic for probing disk structure and testing strong gravity near supermassive black holes.
introduction:
Quasi-stellar objects (QSOs) are among the most luminous and distant sources in the Universe, powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) at the centres of active galactic nuclei (AGN). Their spectra often exhibit complex features, including broad emission and absorption lines that carry information about the physical conditions, kinematics, and geometry of the circumnuclear material. In particular, broad absorption lines (BALs) in the ultraviolet and X-ray regimes are widely interpreted as signatures of fast outflows originating from the inner regions of the accretion disk or from winds launched close to the SMBH. These outflows are believed to play a key role in AGN feedback processes, influencing both the evolution of the central engine and the host galaxy.

In the X-ray domain, the Fe K$\alpha$ emission line at $\sim$6.4 keV is one of the most prominent and diagnostically powerful spectral features in AGN. This line, produced by fluorescence following the irradiation of relatively cold material by hard X-rays, often displays broadened and skewed profiles in QSOs, indicative of relativistic effects in the strong gravitational field near the SMBH. The combination of BAL signatures with Fe K$\alpha$ line properties provides a unique window into the innermost regions of QSOs, potentially constraining the geometry, ionisation state, and velocity structure of the absorbing and emitting media.

Gravitational microlensing, the magnification of a background source by the gravitational field of a compact object in the foreground, offers a powerful probe of the unresolved structure of QSOs. When a QSO is gravitationally lensed by an intervening galaxy, individual stars or stellar remnants in the lensing galaxy can act as microlenses, producing wavelength- and time-dependent magnification patterns. Because microlensing preferentially amplifies emission from compact regions, it can differentially affect various spectral components depending on their size and location. This makes microlensing a valuable tool for studying both the continuum and line-emitting/absorbing regions at microarcsecond scales, beyond the reach of current direct imaging techniques.

Previous studies have demonstrated that microlensing can significantly modify the observed profiles of broad emission lines, including Fe K$\alpha$, and can reveal substructure in the accretion disk. However, the specific influence of microlensing on broad absorption lines, particularly in conjunction with the Fe K$\alpha$ feature, remains less well explored. Understanding these effects is crucial for interpreting spectra of lensed QSOs, where microlensing-induced distortions may mimic or obscure intrinsic variability, and for using microlensing as a diagnostic of BAL outflow geometry.

In this work, we investigate the effects of gravitational microlensing on the broad absorption line features of QSOs, focusing on the case of the Fe K$\alpha$ line. By modelling the combined emission and absorption processes in the vicinity of the SMBH and simulating microlensing magnification patterns, we aim to quantify how microlensing alters the line profile and absorption troughs, and to assess the implications for interpreting high-energy spectra of lensed BAL QSOs. This study contributes to disentangling intrinsic AGN physics from lensing-induced signatures, thereby refining our understanding of the small-scale structure and dynamics of quasar central regions.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the influence of gravitational microlensing on the broad absorption line (BAL) and emission features of quasars, with particular emphasis on the Fe K$\alpha$ line originating in the innermost regions of the accretion disk. By modeling the combined effects of the relativistic disk structure, the ionization state of the absorbing medium, and the magnification patterns produced by microlensing caustics, we have demonstrated that significant spectral distortions can arise when compact masses in a foreground lensing galaxy differentially amplify spatially distinct regions of the source.  

Our simulations show that microlensing can induce measurable changes in both the profile and equivalent width of the Fe K$\alpha$ line, as well as in the depth and shape of accompanying BAL features. The line profile modifications are sensitive to the relative orientation between the caustic structure and the velocity field of the disk, leading to asymmetric amplification of the red or blue wings. In particular, amplification of the innermost disk regions can enhance relativistic effects, producing transient shifts in the apparent centroid energy and altering the characteristic skewness of the line. These effects can mimic or obscure intrinsic variability, thereby complicating interpretations of reverberation mapping or disk tomography studies if microlensing is not accounted for.

We find that the magnitude of microlensing-induced variability in the Fe K$\alpha$ line is largest when the continuum and line-emitting regions have comparable projected sizes to the microlens Einstein radius. For realistic lens masses (0.1–1 M$_\odot$) and source redshifts typical of lensed QSOs, the X-ray emitting region is sufficiently compact for substantial amplification, while the BAL region, being more extended, experiences lower amplitude but still non-negligible differential magnification. This differential effect can lead to apparent changes in the BAL trough depth and velocity structure over timescales of months to years.

Our results underscore the importance of considering microlensing as a potential driver of short-term spectral variability in lensed quasars. In particular, high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy, combined with time-domain monitoring across multiple wavelengths, can disentangle microlensing signatures from intrinsic processes, offering unique constraints on the geometry and kinematics of both the inner accretion flow and the outflowing BAL wind. Future observational campaigns targeting strongly lensed QSOs with next-generation X-ray observatories will be crucial for exploiting microlensing as a natural probe of sub-parsec scale quasar structure.

title: Reconfigurable ASIC for a Low Level Trigger System in Cherenkov Telescope Cameras
abstract: We present the design and implementation of a reconfigurable application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) developed for low-level trigger systems in Cherenkov telescope cameras. The device integrates high-speed, low-noise analog signal processing with programmable logic resources to enable flexible trigger algorithms and adaptable coincidence patterns. Its reconfigurability allows optimization for varying observational conditions and camera configurations, reducing false triggers while maintaining high detection efficiency. The ASIC supports multi-channel inputs with precise timing alignment and low power consumption, making it suitable for large-scale telescope arrays. Laboratory and field tests demonstrate its robustness, scalability, and ability to enhance the performance of Cherenkov imaging systems in ground-based gamma-ray astronomy.
introduction:
Ground-based gamma-ray astronomy has undergone significant advances in recent decades, driven by the development of Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs) capable of detecting very-high-energy (VHE) photons through the faint Cherenkov light generated by extensive air showers in the atmosphere. The sensitivity, angular resolution, and energy threshold of these instruments depend critically on the performance of their cameras and, in particular, on the efficiency and reliability of their trigger systems. The trigger system must rapidly discriminate between genuine gamma-ray–induced events and the overwhelming background from cosmic rays and night-sky background (NSB) photons, while minimizing dead time and ensuring precise timing.

In current and next-generation IACT arrays, such as those envisioned for the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), the scale and complexity of the cameras pose new challenges for the design of the low-level (first-stage) trigger electronics. These systems must process signals from thousands of photodetector channels in parallel, delivering prompt and accurate trigger decisions under varying observational conditions. High channel counts demand compact, low-power, and cost-effective solutions, while the diversity of scientific goals requires flexibility in trigger algorithms and parameters. Conventional fixed-function trigger circuits, often implemented using discrete components or field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), offer certain advantages but can be limited by power consumption, physical footprint, and adaptability to evolving requirements.

Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) present a compelling alternative for implementing the low-level trigger stage. By integrating multiple processing channels and associated logic into a single chip, ASICs can achieve significant reductions in size, power usage, and interconnect complexity. Furthermore, modern ASIC design methodologies allow the incorporation of reconfigurable logic blocks, enabling the adjustment of trigger schemes, thresholds, and coincidence patterns in response to changes in observational strategy, background conditions, or hardware configuration. This reconfigurability bridges the gap between the efficiency of custom hardware and the versatility of programmable devices.

A reconfigurable ASIC-based trigger solution can also improve timing resolution and reduce latency due to the proximity of the trigger logic to the detector front-end. Precise timing is essential for stereoscopic reconstruction of air showers across multiple telescopes, as well as for rejecting short-duration background fluctuations. Moreover, the ability to tailor trigger algorithms to specific subarrays or observational campaigns can enhance sensitivity to transient or extended sources.

This work presents the design, implementation, and characterization of a reconfigurable ASIC developed for the low-level trigger system in Cherenkov telescope cameras. The device integrates multiple analog and digital processing stages, supports several trigger topologies, and allows dynamic parameter adjustments through a control interface. We describe the motivation and requirements for such a system, outline the architecture and key design choices, and report on laboratory and field tests demonstrating its performance under realistic conditions. The proposed ASIC addresses the stringent constraints of modern IACT facilities, offering a scalable and adaptable approach to first-stage triggering that can contribute to improved sensitivity and operational flexibility in VHE gamma-ray observations.
conclusion: The development and characterization of the reconfigurable ASIC for a low-level trigger system in Cherenkov telescope cameras have been presented. The device successfully integrates high-speed analog signal processing with flexible digital configuration, enabling its adaptation to different trigger schemes and operational conditions. Laboratory measurements and functional tests confirm that the ASIC meets the stringent requirements for timing precision, low noise, and low power consumption essential for large-area, multi-channel camera systems. The reconfigurable architecture allows for optimization of trigger thresholds, coincidence logic, and filtering parameters without hardware modifications, thereby extending the operational lifetime and scientific versatility of the instrument. Compared with conventional discrete-component solutions, the ASIC offers reduced size, power, and complexity, which are critical for large-scale telescope arrays. Its performance demonstrates suitability for next-generation Cherenkov telescopes, where scalability and maintainability are key factors. Future work will focus on extended field tests within prototype camera modules to assess robustness under real observational conditions and to refine firmware-based trigger algorithms. The presented results indicate that this ASIC constitutes a significant step toward more compact, efficient, and adaptive trigger systems, contributing to enhanced sensitivity and reliability in very-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy.

title: Low-Rank Modifications of Riccati Factorizations for Model Predictive Control
abstract: This paper investigates efficient techniques for updating Riccati factorizations in model predictive control (MPC) when problem data undergo low-rank modifications. Such updates arise frequently in real-time MPC, for example, due to changing constraints, horizon length adjustments, or warm-start strategies in embedded implementations. Standard approaches recompute the entire Riccati factorization at each iteration, incurring significant computational cost. We present a framework that exploits the structure of low-rank changes in the KKT system to perform targeted updates of the factorization, avoiding full recomputation. The method builds on backward and forward recursions of the Riccati algorithm, integrating low-rank matrix identities to adjust factor matrices efficiently. We analyse the computational complexity and demonstrate that the proposed scheme reduces the update cost to a fraction of the full factorization time, with negligible loss of numerical stability. Numerical experiments on linear MPC benchmarks illustrate substantial speed-ups for rank-one and small-rank modifications, enabling faster closed-loop performance and expanding the applicability of MPC to systems with stringent real-time requirements.
introduction:
Model Predictive Control (MPC) has emerged as a powerful and flexible methodology for controlling multivariable dynamical systems subject to operational constraints. By repeatedly solving a finite-horizon optimal control problem online, MPC can explicitly account for input and state constraints, incorporate predictions from process models, and handle multi-objective trade-offs in a systematic way. These features have led to its widespread adoption across diverse domains, including process control, robotics, automotive systems, and energy management. However, the main drawback of MPC is the substantial computational burden associated with solving a constrained optimization problem at every sampling instant, particularly when fast sampling rates, large horizons, or high-dimensional systems are involved.

For linear time-invariant systems with quadratic cost functions and linear constraints, the MPC optimization problem can be formulated as a quadratic program (QP). A widely used approach for solving such QPs is based on the *condensed* or *sparse* form of the problem. In the sparse formulation, efficient algorithms exploit the block-sparse structure arising from the system dynamics, frequently using interior-point or active-set methods. A key computational kernel in these methods is the repeated solution of linear systems derived from the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions. When exploiting the Riccati recursion, these systems can be factorized efficiently by leveraging the sequential structure of the prediction horizon, leading to a computational complexity that scales linearly with horizon length.

In many MPC applications, the problem data change only slightly from one sampling instant to the next. For example, changes in the active set of constraints between successive QP instances are often limited to a few constraints becoming active or inactive. Similarly, variations in the system model or cost function parameters may be small or localized. In such situations, it is advantageous to avoid recomputing the full Riccati factorization from scratch at each iteration. Instead, one can seek to update an existing factorization using low-rank modifications that reflect the changes in problem data. This approach has the potential to significantly reduce computational effort and enable MPC implementations for systems with stringent real-time requirements.

Low-rank modifications of matrix factorizations are a well-established tool in numerical linear algebra. For example, rank-one updates of Cholesky or QR factorizations have been extensively studied and applied in optimization algorithms, signal processing, and statistical estimation. In the context of MPC, low-rank updates can be used to adjust the KKT matrix factorization when the active set of constraints changes, without recomputing the entire factorization. However, the Riccati recursion used in sparse MPC algorithms involves a sequence of factorizations of reduced matrices that depend on each other through backward and forward passes. As a result, designing efficient and numerically stable low-rank update schemes for Riccati factorizations presents additional challenges compared to direct factorization updates.

Recent work has explored various strategies for exploiting problem structure and temporal coherence in MPC to achieve computational savings. Warm-starting primal-dual interior-point methods or active-set solvers with previous solution estimates, exploiting parametric QP structure, and implementing tailored Riccati recursions are examples of such strategies. Despite these advances, the systematic development of low-rank modification techniques specifically adapted to Riccati-based factorizations in sparse MPC has received comparatively less attention. In particular, there is a need for a clear characterization of the types of data changes that can be accommodated by low-rank updates, the associated computational complexity, and the implications for numerical stability.

This paper addresses these issues by developing a framework for low-rank modifications of Riccati factorizations in the context of linear MPC. We focus on situations where the active set changes by a small number of constraints between sampling instants, leading to local modifications of the KKT system. By interpreting these changes as low-rank perturbations of the matrices in the Riccati recursion, we derive efficient update and downdate formulas that preserve the block structure of the recursion and avoid redundant computations. The resulting algorithms can update the factorization in a fraction of the time required for a full recomputation, thereby enabling faster MPC iterations.

The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we present a detailed analysis of how changes in the active set translate into low-rank perturbations within the Riccati recursion framework. Second, we derive explicit update and downdate formulas for the relevant factorizations, together with complexity estimates. Third, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods through numerical experiments on representative MPC problems, showing substantial computational savings with minimal loss of numerical accuracy. We also discuss the trade-offs between update efficiency and stability, and outline guidelines for practical implementation.

By enhancing the efficiency of Riccati-based MPC solvers through low-rank modifications, this work aims to extend the applicability of MPC to faster systems, longer horizons, and more complex models. The proposed techniques are compatible with existing sparse QP solvers and can be integrated into real-time MPC frameworks with minimal modifications, offering a practical path toward improved performance in demanding control applications.
