In both cases, the dynamical disturbances can trigger non-equilibrium chemistry, enhancing the formation of cooling agents such as H₂ and, under certain conditions, HD. The latter, owing to its permanent dipole moment, can cool gas to temperatures approaching the cosmic microwave background (CMB) floor at the relevant redshifts. This raises the possibility that merging activity could, in some circumstances, promote the existence of extremely cold, dense primordial gas pockets, potentially altering the characteristic stellar mass spectrum.

The study of low-temperature primordial gas in merging halos is motivated by several key questions. First, under what conditions do mergers facilitate rather than hinder the cooling of baryons? Second, how do merger-driven shocks and turbulence compete with, or complement, molecular cooling processes? Third, what is the quantitative impact on the thermodynamic evolution, fragmentation scale, and star formation efficiency in the early Universe? Addressing these questions requires coupling cosmological structure formation models with detailed treatments of gas dynamics, non-equilibrium chemistry, and radiative processes.

Recent numerical simulations have begun to explore the complex interplay between mergers and primordial gas cooling, revealing a rich phenomenology that depends sensitively on merger mass ratios, relative velocities, and the ambient radiation field. Yet, a systematic characterization of the low-temperature phase in merging halos remains incomplete. In this work, we investigate the thermal and chemical evolution of primordial gas during halo mergers, focusing on the emergence and survival of cold gas components. By combining high-resolution cosmological simulations with a comprehensive microphysical network, we aim to quantify the prevalence and properties of such gas, and to assess its role in shaping the earliest stages of galaxy formation.
conclusion: Our investigation of low-temperature primordial gas in merging halos reveals that dynamical interactions in the early Universe can create conditions conducive to enhanced cooling below the canonical atomic hydrogen limit. By modeling the thermodynamic evolution of gas during halo mergers, we find that shock compression, combined with non-equilibrium chemistry, can promote the formation of molecular hydrogen and, in some cases, HD, enabling cooling to temperatures of a few tens of kelvin. Such low temperatures may significantly influence the initial mass function of the first stellar populations by reducing the Jeans mass and allowing for the formation of lower-mass stars than in isolated halos. The results suggest that mergers not only accelerate structure growth but also act as catalysts for chemical and thermal pathways otherwise inefficient in pristine environments. This interplay between gravitational dynamics and microphysical processes underscores the importance of considering environmental context when modeling Population III star formation. Future high-resolution simulations, incorporating radiative feedback and a broader range of merger parameters, will be crucial for quantifying the prevalence and impact of this mechanism. Observational constraints from forthcoming facilities may provide indirect signatures of such cold primordial gas in the high-redshift Universe.

title: Testing MOG, Non-Local Gravity and MOND with rotation curves of dwarf galaxies
abstract: We present a comparative analysis of Modified Gravity (MOG), Non-Local Gravity (NLG), and Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) using high-resolution rotation curves of a sample of nearby dwarf galaxies. Dwarf galaxies, being low-mass and dark-matter dominated in the standard cosmological framework, provide a sensitive testing ground for alternative theories of gravity. We employ a homogeneous set of photometric and kinematic data to derive mass models based on observed stellar and gas distributions, and fit the rotation curves within each theoretical framework without invoking cold dark matter halos. Parameter estimation is performed via χ² minimization, with systematic uncertainties assessed through Monte Carlo resampling. Our results show that all three models can reproduce the general shape of the rotation curves, though with differing parameter correlations and degrees of fine-tuning. MOG and MOND yield comparable fits for most galaxies, while NLG tends to underpredict velocities in the outer regions. We discuss the implications for the viability of these theories in explaining galactic dynamics without dark matter.
introduction:
The study of galactic rotation curves has long been a cornerstone in the investigation of the nature of gravity and the distribution of matter in the Universe. Observations beginning with the pioneering work of Rubin and collaborators revealed that the rotational velocities of spiral galaxies remain approximately constant well beyond the optical disk, in stark contrast with the predictions of Newtonian dynamics when applied to the luminous matter alone. This discrepancy has traditionally been attributed to the presence of a dominant, non-luminous dark matter component forming extended halos around galaxies. While the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm provides a successful large-scale structure formation framework, its direct detection remains elusive, and certain small-scale issues motivate the exploration of alternative theories of gravity.

Among the most discussed alternatives are Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND), Scalar-Tensor-Vector Gravity (STVG or MOG), and Non-Local Gravity (NLG). MOND, proposed by Milgrom, introduces a characteristic acceleration scale below which the effective gravitational attraction deviates from the Newtonian inverse-square law, thereby reproducing flat rotation curves without invoking dark matter. MOG, developed by Moffat and others, extends general relativity by incorporating scalar, tensor, and vector fields, leading to a modified gravitational potential that can enhance the effective gravitational coupling on galactic scales. Non-Local Gravity, motivated by attempts to address the cosmological constant problem and quantum gravity effects, modifies Einstein’s equations by introducing non-local terms, which can mimic dark matter effects in galaxy dynamics.

Dwarf galaxies are particularly valuable laboratories for testing such theories. Being low-mass systems with high mass-to-light ratios, their dynamics are often dominated by the discrepancy between visible matter and the observed gravitational effects. Moreover, dwarf galaxies are less affected by complexities such as prominent bulges or strong spiral arms, which can obscure dynamical interpretations in larger galaxies. Their relatively simple baryonic structure enables a cleaner comparison between theoretical predictions and observed rotation curves.

In recent years, high-resolution observations of dwarf galaxy kinematics, from surveys such as LITTLE THINGS, SPARC, and others, have provided precise rotation curves extending well into the low-acceleration regime where modified gravity effects should be most apparent. These datasets present an opportunity to rigorously test MOG, NLG, and MOND on the same footing, using consistent modeling of baryonic mass distributions and robust statistical methods to assess model performance.

The aim of this work is to compare the predictions of MOG, Non-Local Gravity, and MOND against the observed rotation curves of a representative sample of dwarf galaxies. We employ mass models derived from photometric and H I data to estimate the baryonic contribution to the gravitational potential, and then fit the rotation curves using each gravitational theory without invoking dark matter halos. For MOND, we adopt the standard interpolating functions and acceleration scale calibrated from previous studies. For MOG and NLG, we use parameter values constrained from earlier galactic and extragalactic analyses, assessing whether these can consistently reproduce the dwarf galaxy data.

By applying a uniform methodology across all three theories, we aim to quantify their relative successes and limitations, and to explore whether a single set of parameters within each framework can account for the diversity of dwarf galaxy rotation curves. Such a comparative analysis not only tests the viability of modified gravity theories in the low-mass regime, but also contributes to the broader effort to understand whether the missing mass problem signals the existence of dark matter particles or a need to revise our theory of gravity.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the capability of three alternative theories of gravity—Modified Gravity (MOG), Non-Local Gravity (NLG), and Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND)—to account for the observed rotation curves of a representative sample of dwarf galaxies without invoking non-baryonic dark matter. Using high-quality kinematic data, we performed systematic fits of each model to the rotation curves, exploring the parameter spaces allowed by theory and constrained by the data. Dwarf galaxies represent a stringent testing ground for modified gravity scenarios, given their low surface brightness, low mass-to-light ratios, and the fact that they are often dominated by dynamical effects attributed to dark matter in the standard ΛCDM framework.  

Our analysis shows that all three models can reproduce the general qualitative features of the rotation curves; however, notable differences emerge in their quantitative performance. MOND, with its single acceleration scale parameter, provides good fits for several galaxies in the sample, particularly those with well-constrained baryonic mass distributions. Nonetheless, its performance degrades for systems with irregular morphologies or those strongly affected by environmental perturbations, indicating a sensitivity to assumptions about the stellar and gas mass components. MOG, with its scale-dependent gravitational coupling, demonstrates flexibility in fitting the full radial extent of many rotation curves, though the required parameter values show some variance from galaxy to galaxy, suggesting a potential challenge to strict universality. NLG yields competitive fits, especially in the inner regions, but tends to over-predict velocities in the outer parts for some systems, pointing to possible refinements in its kernel form or application to low-mass systems.

A key finding is that no single model provides a universally superior fit across the entire sample. The residuals and reduced χ² values indicate that while modified gravity frameworks can, in principle, account for the observed dynamics without dark matter, the degree of fine-tuning or parameter adjustment required varies significantly. This raises important questions about the universality and predictive power of these theories, especially in light of the diversity of dwarf galaxy properties and the influence of environmental effects.

Future work should include expanding the sample size to incorporate galaxies with a wider range of baryonic masses, inclinations, and star formation histories, as well as employing more sophisticated modeling of gas dynamics and non-circular motions. Additional constraints from independent probes, such as stellar velocity dispersions and gravitational lensing, will be essential in assessing the viability of these alternative gravity models as comprehensive replacements for dark matter in explaining galactic dynamics.

title: 3D MHD simulations and synthetic radio emission from an oblique rotating magnetic massive star
abstract: We present three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of the circumstellar environment of an oblique, rotating, magnetic massive star, aimed at investigating the origin and variability of its non-thermal radio emission. The simulations employ a tilted dipolar magnetic field geometry relative to the stellar rotation axis, coupled with a line-driven stellar wind. This configuration produces a dynamic magnetosphere in which magnetically confined plasma is channeled toward the magnetic equator, forming complex, time-dependent density and velocity structures. Using the MHD outputs, we compute synthetic radio emission maps and light curves through radiative transfer calculations that include both thermal free–free and non-thermal gyrosynchrotron processes. The modeled radio flux exhibits rotational modulation arising from the changing orientation of magnetospheric structures relative to the observer. We explore the dependence of the synthetic light curves and spectra on magnetic obliquity, rotation rate, and viewing inclination, and compare them with observed variability patterns in known magnetic O- and B-type stars. Our results demonstrate that 3D MHD models with realistic obliquity reproduce key features of the observed radio behavior, highlighting the role of large-scale magnetic topology and rotational geometry in shaping the non-thermal emission from massive star magnetospheres.
introduction:
Massive stars with strong, organized magnetic fields constitute a distinct subclass of hot, luminous objects whose magnetospheres have a profound impact on their radiative and dynamical properties. In recent decades, high-resolution spectropolarimetric surveys have revealed that a small but significant fraction of O- and early B-type stars host large-scale, predominantly dipolar magnetic fields with strengths of the order of kilogauss. These fields channel the ionized stellar wind outflows, leading to the formation of structured, magnetically confined circumstellar environments. For oblique rotators—systems in which the magnetic axis is tilted with respect to the rotation axis—the interaction between rotation, wind driving, and magnetic confinement produces complex, time-dependent magnetospheric structures.  

Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) models have been instrumental in elucidating the global morphology of such magnetospheres, particularly in the context of the rigidly rotating magnetosphere (RRM) and dynamical magnetosphere (DM) frameworks. However, most previous studies have focused on axisymmetric or aligned configurations, whereas real systems often exhibit significant obliquity. Three-dimensional (3D) MHD simulations are therefore essential to capture the full spatial complexity of the plasma distribution, shock formation, and rotational modulation of observables in oblique magnetic massive stars.

Non-thermal radio emission provides a complementary diagnostic of magnetospheric physics. In these objects, the acceleration of electrons in current sheets or magnetically driven shocks can lead to gyrosynchrotron radiation detectable at centimeter wavelengths. The resulting light curves and spectra are sensitive to the geometry, density, and magnetic field topology of the emitting regions. Synthetic radio emission modeling, based on realistic 3D MHD simulations, enables direct comparison with observations, offering constraints on the physical processes governing particle acceleration and emission.

In this work, we present fully 3D MHD simulations of an oblique, rotating, magnetic massive star, coupled with radiative transfer calculations to predict synthetic radio emission. Our aim is to investigate the interplay between magnetic obliquity, rotation, and wind confinement in shaping the magnetosphere, and to assess how these factors influence the variability and morphology of the radio output. By comparing our synthetic diagnostics with observed radio light curves, we seek to advance the understanding of magnetospheric structure and emission processes in magnetic massive stars.
conclusion:
This work has presented three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of the circumstellar environment of an oblique, rotating, magnetic massive star, combined with detailed calculations of the corresponding synthetic radio emission. By employing a full 3D treatment of the magnetosphere, including the effects of stellar rotation and magnetic obliquity, we have been able to capture the complex interplay between the stellar wind, magnetic confinement, and rotational modulation of the circumstellar plasma. The results demonstrate that the oblique magnetic geometry produces a strongly asymmetric distribution of density and temperature, leading to significant rotational modulation in the predicted radio flux.

Our simulations reproduce key qualitative features observed in magnetic massive stars, including periodic variations in the radio light curve that arise from changes in the projected magnetospheric structure as the star rotates. The synthetic radio spectra reveal a dependence on both frequency and rotational phase, reflecting the variation in optical depth and emission measure along different lines of sight. In particular, the model naturally accounts for spectral flattening at higher frequencies and enhanced variability at lower frequencies, consistent with observational trends. These findings underscore the importance of considering full 3D structures, as axisymmetric models cannot capture the phase-dependent asymmetries that govern the radio emission.

An important outcome of this study is the identification of the role of magnetic obliquity in shaping the radio-emitting regions. Increased obliquity leads to more pronounced modulation amplitudes, as the densest magnetospheric sectors periodically move in and out of view. Furthermore, the simulations show that rotational effects, even at moderate velocities, can significantly distort the magnetosphere through centrifugal support and azimuthal flows, thereby influencing the spatial distribution of radio-emitting plasma. These results suggest that accurate interpretation of observed radio variability requires simultaneous constraints on both the magnetic geometry and the stellar rotation rate.

While our MHD models provide a physically consistent framework for predicting radio emission, several limitations remain. The treatment of non-thermal electron populations, which may contribute significantly to the observed emission at certain frequencies, has been simplified in the present work. Future studies should incorporate particle acceleration processes and non-thermal radiative transfer in order to achieve a more complete description. Additionally, exploring a wider parameter space in stellar mass-loss rates, magnetic field strengths, and inclination angles will help to assess the generality of the trends identified here.

In summary, this study highlights the diagnostic power of combining 3D MHD simulations with synthetic radio observations for probing the magnetospheres of massive stars. By linking the dynamical structure of the magnetised wind to observable signatures, we provide a pathway for interpreting current and forthcoming radio monitoring campaigns, and for constraining the fundamental physical parameters that govern the behaviour of magnetic massive stars.

title: Dear Sir or Madam, May I introduce the GYAFC Dataset: Corpus, Benchmarks and Metrics for Formality Style Transfer
abstract: We present the GYAFC dataset, a large-scale parallel corpus for formality style transfer, derived from informal and formal rewritings of user-generated content. Covering multiple domains, it enables systematic study of transforming text between informal and formal registers. We establish strong baselines using neural sequence-to-sequence models and evaluate them with automatic and human metrics. Our benchmarks highlight challenges in preserving meaning while adjusting style. The GYAFC dataset and evaluation framework aim to foster further research in controllable text generation and stylistic transformation.
introduction:
Formality style transfer is the task of automatically rewriting text to change its degree of formality while preserving its original meaning and fluency. This capability is relevant to many real‑world applications, including professional communication, customer service, educational tools, and the adaptation of user‑generated content for different audiences. For example, an informal sentence such as “Can you give me a hand with this?” might be transformed into the more formal “Could you assist me with this task?” without altering the underlying intent. Despite the growing interest in controllable text generation, research on formality style transfer has been hindered by the lack of large, high‑quality parallel corpora and standardized evaluation protocols. In the absence of such resources, models have often been trained on small, domain‑specific datasets or have relied on artificially constructed examples, leading to limited generalization and inconsistent comparisons across studies.

Prior work in style transfer has addressed various stylistic dimensions, including sentiment, politeness, and author imitation, often using monolingual parallel data or unsupervised approaches. However, formality stands out as a stylistic attribute that is both subjective and context‑dependent, requiring careful annotation and domain balance. The most commonly cited resources for this task have been limited in size, scope, or availability, thereby constraining progress toward robust, deployable systems. Furthermore, evaluation practices vary widely: some studies depend on automatic metrics such as BLEU or perplexity, which do not directly capture stylistic appropriateness, while others rely exclusively on small‑scale human judgments, which are costly and difficult to reproduce. This lack of standardized benchmarks and metrics has impeded meaningful comparison between competing approaches.

To address these gaps, we present the Grammarly’s Yahoo Answers Formality Corpus (GYAFC), a large‑scale, publicly available dataset specifically designed for training and evaluating formality style transfer systems. The dataset is constructed from the Yahoo Answers platform, which contains a wide variety of informal user‑generated text across numerous topics. We identify two distinct domains—Entertainment & Music and Family & Relationships—and for each, we collect parallel sentences where informal text has been rewritten into a formal variant by trained annotators. This results in over 100,000 sentence pairs, making GYAFC one of the largest resources of its kind. The corpus is split into training, development, and test sets, enabling reproducible experiments and fair comparisons.

Alongside the dataset, we establish benchmark results using several baseline and state‑of‑the‑art models, ranging from phrase‑based statistical machine translation to neural sequence‑to‑sequence architectures with attention. We also propose a set of evaluation metrics tailored to formality transfer, combining automatic measures of content preservation and fluency with human ratings of formality change. By releasing both the corpus and the accompanying benchmarks, we aim to provide the research community with a solid foundation for advancing the study of formality style transfer.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) the creation and public release of GYAFC, a large parallel corpus for formality transfer; (2) the establishment of standardized benchmarks across multiple models; and (3) the proposal of a comprehensive evaluation framework that integrates automatic and human assessments. We believe that these contributions will facilitate more rigorous, comparable, and impactful research in the field of stylistic text generation.
conclusion:
In this work, we introduced the GYAFC (Grammarly’s Yahoo Answers Formality Corpus) dataset, a large-scale resource designed to advance research in formality style transfer. By systematically collecting, cleaning, and annotating informal and formal sentence pairs from the Yahoo Answers platform, we created a corpus that addresses the scarcity of high-quality parallel data for this task. We further established rigorous training, validation, and test splits, and provided both automatic and human evaluation protocols to ensure consistent benchmarking.

We presented baseline results using neural sequence-to-sequence models, alongside traditional approaches, to illustrate the challenges inherent in capturing formality while preserving semantic content. Our experiments revealed that while current models can achieve reasonable improvements in formality, they often struggle to maintain meaning fidelity and fluency, particularly in cases involving idiomatic expressions, cultural references, or nuanced tone. These findings underscore the complexity of formality style transfer and the need for developing methods that go beyond surface-level lexical or syntactic changes.

In addition to releasing the dataset, we proposed a set of metrics tailored to this task, combining reference-based and reference-free measures to assess formality transformation, grammaticality, and semantic preservation. We demonstrated that relying solely on traditional text similarity metrics can be misleading, and that human evaluations remain indispensable for capturing subtleties of style.

By making the GYAFC dataset publicly available, along with standardized benchmarks and evaluation scripts, we aim to foster reproducibility and comparability across future studies. We believe that this resource will help unify the field, providing a shared foundation for developing and testing models that can perform style transfer in a controlled and interpretable manner.

Looking ahead, we envision several avenues for future work, including expanding the dataset to other stylistic dimensions, exploring multilingual formality transfer, and integrating contextual or pragmatic factors into model architectures. Ultimately, we hope that the GYAFC dataset will catalyze progress toward style transfer systems that are not only accurate and fluent, but also sensitive to the subtleties of linguistic register, making them more useful in real-world applications such as education, communication assistance, and content moderation.

title: Suppression of the Higgs Dimuon Decay
abstract: We investigate the suppression of the Higgs boson decay channel \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) within the framework of the Standard Model and selected extensions incorporating lepton-flavor-dependent couplings. The dimuon mode, though rare in the Standard Model with a branching ratio of approximately \(2.2 \times 10^{-4}\), provides a sensitive probe of the Higgs–muon Yukawa coupling and potential new physics effects. We analyze current LHC Run 2 measurements from ATLAS and CMS, which constrain deviations from the Standard Model prediction, and explore theoretical scenarios in which the dimuon decay width is significantly suppressed. Such suppression can arise from modified Yukawa structures, loop-induced cancellations, or mixing with additional scalar states. Using a combination of effective field theory techniques and explicit model realizations, we quantify the parameter space consistent with existing bounds from Higgs signal strengths in other channels and from electroweak precision observables. We find that sizeable reductions in the dimuon branching ratio can occur without conflicting with current experimental data, particularly in models with flavor-nonuniversal Higgs couplings. Our results highlight the importance of precision measurements of rare Higgs decays in testing the flavor structure of the Higgs sector, and they motivate targeted searches in forthcoming high-luminosity LHC datasets to further constrain or reveal such suppression mechanisms.
introduction:
The discovery of the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in 2012 marked a decisive milestone in particle physics, confirming the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking as formulated in the Standard Model (SM). Since then, a central focus of experimental and theoretical efforts has been the precise measurement of the Higgs boson’s properties, including its mass, spin-parity, and couplings to other particles. Such measurements serve not only as stringent tests of the SM but also as powerful probes of potential new physics beyond it. Among the various Higgs decay modes, those into fermion pairs offer direct access to its Yukawa couplings, which in the SM are predicted to scale with the fermion mass. While decays into heavy fermions such as bottom quarks and tau leptons have been observed and found broadly consistent with SM expectations, decays into lighter fermions remain more challenging to study and thus more susceptible to deviations induced by new dynamics.

The decay of the Higgs boson into a pair of muons, \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\), is particularly noteworthy in this regard. In the SM, the branching ratio for this process is predicted to be approximately \(2.18 \times 10^{-4}\), reflecting the small muon mass and, accordingly, its weak coupling to the Higgs field. Although rare, this channel is experimentally clean due to the distinct signature of muon pairs in the detector, offering a promising avenue for precision measurements at high luminosity. The ATLAS and CMS collaborations have recently reported evidence for this decay mode, with measured signal strengths consistent with SM expectations within current uncertainties. However, the precision of these measurements is still limited, leaving room for significant improvements in future LHC runs and at prospective future colliders.

Given its rarity and theoretical cleanliness, the \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) decay is highly sensitive to new physics effects that could suppress or enhance its rate. A suppression of the dimuon decay could arise from various scenarios, including modifications of the muon Yukawa coupling, mixing of the Higgs boson with additional scalar states, or the presence of higher-dimensional operators in the Higgs sector. Such effects could be generated in frameworks ranging from extended Higgs sectors and lepton-specific two-Higgs-doublet models to models with vector-like leptons or flavour-dependent couplings in the context of compositeness. Furthermore, loop-induced contributions from new particles could alter the effective coupling, leading to measurable deviations from the SM prediction.

The suppression of the Higgs dimuon decay is of particular theoretical interest because it would imply a violation of the simple mass proportionality of the Yukawa couplings, which is a cornerstone of the SM Higgs mechanism. This could point toward a more intricate origin of fermion masses, possibly linked to flavour symmetries, alignment mechanisms, or partial compositeness. In addition, precise measurements of the \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) branching ratio, when combined with those of other fermionic decay modes, could shed light on the universality of Yukawa couplings and reveal patterns indicative of specific classes of new physics models.

From the experimental side, probing a suppression of the Higgs dimuon decay requires not only large data samples but also careful control of backgrounds and systematic uncertainties. The dominant backgrounds arise from Drell–Yan production of muon pairs, diboson processes, and top-quark associated channels, all of which must be accurately modelled. Signal extraction typically relies on sophisticated multivariate analyses and precise muon momentum reconstruction. As the LHC transitions to the High-Luminosity phase (HL-LHC), the expected increase in dataset size by an order of magnitude will enable much more stringent tests, potentially reducing the uncertainty on the dimuon signal strength to the level where even modest suppressions relative to the SM can be detected.

In this work, we investigate the theoretical and phenomenological implications of a suppressed \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) decay rate. We examine the extent to which current measurements constrain such a suppression, explore representative new physics scenarios that can produce it, and assess the prospects for discovery or exclusion at future colliders. By confronting explicit models with existing and projected experimental sensitivities, we aim to clarify the role of the dimuon decay channel as a precision probe of Higgs sector dynamics and flavour structure. Our analysis underscores the importance of sustained efforts to measure this rare decay with ever-increasing precision, as it offers a unique window into possible departures from the Standard Model paradigm.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined in detail the theoretical and phenomenological implications of a suppressed branching ratio for the Higgs boson decay into a pair of muons, \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\), in light of current and projected collider sensitivities. The Standard Model (SM) predicts this channel to occur with a branching fraction of roughly \(2.2 \times 10^{-4}\), with the rate directly proportional to the muon Yukawa coupling. Consequently, any observed deviation from this prediction would constitute a clean and direct probe of the Higgs–lepton interaction sector. Our analysis has explored both model-independent parameterisations, through effective field theory (EFT) operators, and explicit new physics scenarios capable of producing such a suppression, while remaining consistent with other Higgs measurements and electroweak precision data.

We have argued that a significant suppression of the dimuon mode, in the absence of analogous effects in other fermionic decay channels, would require flavour-specific new physics. In the EFT framework, this can be realised through higher-dimensional operators that modify the muon Yukawa coupling without inducing large effects in the electron or tau sectors. We have quantified the degree to which current LHC data already constrain such operators, and shown that the present upper limits on \(\sigma \times \mathrm{BR}(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-)\) still allow for sizeable departures from the SM expectation. However, the projected sensitivities of the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) would be capable of probing suppressions of order 50% or more, thus providing a decisive test for many of the benchmark scenarios considered.

From the perspective of concrete models, we have discussed several mechanisms that can lead to reduced \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) rates. These include multi-Higgs doublet models with flavour-aligned Yukawa structures, radiative muon mass generation frameworks, and scenarios with partial compositeness in which the muon couples to the Higgs only via mixing with heavy fermions. In each case, we identified the parameter regions in which the dimuon suppression is pronounced, while other Higgs couplings remain SM-like. Such regions are often subject to complementary constraints from rare decays, lepton-flavour universality tests, and direct searches for new states. Our results highlight the importance of combining Higgs decay measurements with low-energy observables to disentangle the underlying dynamics.

We have also emphasised the role of correlations between \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) and other processes. In many new physics scenarios, modifications to the muon Yukawa coupling can be related to shifts in the muon anomalous magnetic moment, \(g-2\), or in rare meson decays involving muons. The possible connection to the longstanding \((g-2)_\mu\) anomaly provides an intriguing motivation for precision studies of Higgs decays to muons. Nonetheless, our analysis shows that achieving a large suppression in \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) while simultaneously explaining \((g-2)_\mu\) is challenging, often requiring fine-tuned parameter choices or additional new particles beyond the minimal setups.

Looking ahead, the measurement of the Higgs dimuon decay rate stands as a particularly clean window into the flavour structure of the Higgs sector. The modest SM branching ratio makes it experimentally challenging, but the same smallness also means that any statistically significant deviation will be difficult to attribute to systematic effects alone. The HL-LHC, and potentially future lepton colliders such as the FCC-ee or ILC, will push the precision on the muon Yukawa coupling to the few-percent level or better. Such accuracy would allow the discovery or exclusion of suppressions far smaller than those currently accessible, thereby providing a stringent test of both SM predictions and their possible extensions.

In conclusion, the suppression of the Higgs dimuon decay is a sensitive probe of lepton-specific new physics, with minimal contamination from hadronic uncertainties and clear theoretical interpretability. Our study underscores that a confirmed deviation from the SM rate in this channel would have profound implications for our understanding of fermion mass generation and the overall structure of the Higgs sector. The synergy between high-energy collider measurements, low-energy precision experiments, and global fits to Higgs couplings will be essential to fully exploit the discovery potential of this rare decay. Ultimately, the pursuit of precision in \(H \to \mu^+ \mu^-\) embodies the broader endeavour of particle physics: to use the rarest processes as guides toward the most fundamental laws of nature.

title: Thermodynamics of a dilute Bose gas: A path-integral Monte Carlo study
abstract: We present a comprehensive path-integral Monte Carlo investigation of the thermodynamic properties of a dilute, homogeneous Bose gas. Using high-precision simulations for systems with varying densities and temperatures, we extract the equation of state, superfluid fraction, and condensate fraction across the normal-to-superfluid transition. Finite-size scaling techniques are employed to accurately locate the critical temperature and to characterize universal behavior near the λ-transition. The results are compared with predictions from Bogoliubov theory and beyond-mean-field corrections, showing excellent agreement in the weakly interacting regime and quantifying deviations at higher densities. Our study highlights the role of quantum correlations in determining low-temperature thermodynamics and provides benchmark data for theoretical approaches. The methodology and results are directly relevant to ultracold atomic gas experiments and the exploration of quantum fluids in reduced dimensions.
introduction:
The study of dilute Bose gases has been a cornerstone in advancing our understanding of quantum many-body systems. Since the first experimental realizations of Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) in ultracold atomic vapors, there has been sustained theoretical and experimental interest in elucidating their thermodynamic properties across a range of interaction strengths and temperatures. The simplicity of the Bose gas model, combined with the richness of its quantum statistical behavior, makes it an ideal testbed for exploring fundamental aspects of quantum statistical mechanics, phase transitions, and collective excitations. In particular, dilute Bose gases provide a clean and highly controllable platform in which the interplay between quantum statistics and interparticle interactions can be studied with remarkable precision, both in laboratories and through advanced numerical simulations.

The thermodynamics of a dilute Bose gas is governed by a subtle balance between kinetic energy, which favors delocalization, and interaction energy, which can lead to significant correlations even in the low-density regime. At sufficiently low temperatures, Bose statistics lead to macroscopic occupation of the lowest-energy single-particle state, giving rise to Bose–Einstein condensation. While the ideal Bose gas already displays this remarkable phenomenon, interactions qualitatively modify the thermodynamic behavior, shifting the critical temperature, altering the condensate fraction, and influencing thermodynamic quantities such as the energy, pressure, and specific heat. A comprehensive and accurate description of these effects requires methods that can capture quantum fluctuations beyond mean-field theory, especially in regimes where perturbative approaches break down.

Analytical treatments of interacting Bose gases, such as Bogoliubov theory and its extensions, have been successful in describing the low-temperature limit and weakly interacting regime. However, these methods rely on expansions in the small parameter given by the gas parameter \( na^3 \), where \( n \) is the particle density and \( a \) is the \( s \)-wave scattering length, and they may lose accuracy near the critical region or at intermediate temperatures. More sophisticated field-theoretical approaches, including renormalization-group analyses and large-\( N \) expansions, have been developed to bridge these gaps, but they often require approximations whose validity can be difficult to assess quantitatively. In this context, unbiased numerical simulations play a crucial role in providing benchmark results that can both test and guide analytical theories.

The path-integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) method is particularly well-suited for studying the thermodynamic properties of bosonic systems at finite temperatures. By mapping the quantum many-body problem onto a classical system of polymers in imaginary time, PIMC enables exact sampling of the thermal density matrix, subject only to statistical and discretization errors that can be systematically controlled. For bosons, the method naturally incorporates exchange effects through the sampling of permutation cycles, allowing one to capture Bose–Einstein condensation and superfluidity on equal footing. In the dilute regime, PIMC can thus provide highly accurate predictions for observables such as the equation of state, condensate fraction, superfluid density, and correlation functions over a wide range of temperatures and interaction strengths.

Previous numerical studies using PIMC and related techniques have addressed various aspects of the dilute Bose gas, including critical behavior, finite-size scaling, and the role of interactions in modifying thermodynamic quantities. However, a systematic and high-precision investigation that spans from the noninteracting limit up to moderately strong interactions, while carefully resolving the temperature dependence across the BEC transition, remains of significant interest. Such a study not only refines our quantitative understanding of the dilute Bose gas but also provides essential input for interpreting ultracold atom experiments, where tunable interactions via Feshbach resonances and precise thermometry enable direct comparison with theoretical predictions.

In this work, we present a detailed path-integral Monte Carlo study of the thermodynamic properties of a homogeneous three-dimensional dilute Bose gas with short-range repulsive interactions. We focus on characterizing the temperature dependence of key observables across the normal and condensed phases, quantifying the effects of interactions on the critical temperature and other thermodynamic quantities. By performing simulations for various values of the gas parameter \( na^3 \), we map out the interaction-induced modifications in a controlled manner and compare our results with available analytical predictions and experimental data where applicable. Our approach emphasizes statistical accuracy and careful extrapolation to the continuum and thermodynamic limits, ensuring that the reported results can serve as reliable benchmarks for future theoretical developments.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section II we describe the model and outline the path-integral Monte Carlo methodology, including details of the interaction potential, discretization scheme, and finite-size analysis. Section III presents our results for the equation of state, condensate fraction, and superfluid density, along with a discussion of their dependence on temperature and interaction strength. In Section IV we compare our findings with analytical theories and previous numerical studies, highlighting agreements and discrepancies. Finally, Section V summarizes our conclusions and outlines potential directions for extending this work to more complex geometries and interaction models.
conclusion: We have investigated the thermodynamic properties of a dilute Bose gas using path-integral Monte Carlo simulations, obtaining accurate estimates of energy, pressure, and condensate fraction over a range of temperatures. The results demonstrate excellent agreement with known theoretical predictions in both the low-temperature condensed regime and the normal phase. Finite-size and statistical uncertainties were carefully analyzed, confirming the robustness of our approach. This study highlights the effectiveness of path-integral techniques for exploring quantum many-body systems with strong thermal and quantum fluctuations.

title: A sharp analysis on the asymptotic behavior of the Durbin-Watson statistic for the first-order autoregressive process
abstract: This paper presents a rigorous investigation into the asymptotic properties of the Durbin–Watson statistic in the context of a first-order autoregressive process. Focusing on both stationary and near-unit-root regimes, we derive precise limiting distributions under various assumptions on the error structure, including independence and weak dependence. The analysis employs advanced probabilistic tools to establish convergence rates and to characterize the influence of parameter estimation on the statistic’s behavior. Our results clarify subtle distinctions between the finite-sample and asymptotic frameworks, highlighting implications for statistical inference in autocorrelated environments. The findings provide sharper theoretical insight, improving the understanding of the Durbin–Watson test’s performance and guiding its application in econometric and time series modeling practice.
introduction:
The Durbin–Watson statistic is one of the most widely used tools for detecting the presence of serial correlation in the residuals of regression models, particularly in the context of time series data. Since its introduction by Durbin and Watson in the early 1950s, it has become a standard diagnostic in econometrics and applied statistics, owing to its simplicity and interpretability. A large body of literature has examined its distributional properties under various assumptions, as well as its performance in finite samples. However, the asymptotic behavior of the statistic, especially in the context of autoregressive processes, continues to attract theoretical interest.  

In this work, we focus on the first-order autoregressive process, AR(1), which serves as the canonical framework for modeling serial correlation. The AR(1) process is not only analytically tractable but also widely applicable in modeling economic, financial, and environmental time series. Understanding the asymptotic properties of the Durbin–Watson statistic in this setting is crucial for developing accurate inference procedures and for refining its use in large-sample contexts.  

Our analysis builds upon existing theoretical foundations, extending them to provide sharper characterizations of the limiting distribution and convergence rates. In particular, we examine how the statistic behaves under both stationary and near-unit-root regimes, highlighting differences that have important implications for hypothesis testing. This refined asymptotic perspective contributes to a deeper understanding of the Durbin–Watson test and its role in modern time series analysis.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined in detail the asymptotic behavior of the Durbin–Watson statistic in the context of a first-order autoregressive process. By establishing precise probabilistic limits and convergence rates, we provided a clearer understanding of how the statistic behaves under both the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation and alternative scenarios. Our analysis reveals that the limiting distribution depends critically on the magnitude of the autoregressive parameter, with distinct regimes emerging for stationary, unit root, and near-unit root cases. These results refine earlier asymptotic approximations and highlight conditions under which the Durbin–Watson statistic retains its diagnostic relevance or becomes unreliable. Furthermore, the theoretical findings suggest practical implications for inference, notably in finite samples where the asymptotic tendencies are only partially realized. This underscores the importance of complementing the Durbin–Watson statistic with alternative tests in near-nonstationary environments. Overall, our study contributes to the theoretical foundation for autocorrelation testing in time series analysis, offering both rigorous asymptotic characterizations and guidance for empirical application. Future research could extend these results to higher-order autoregressive structures and models with more complex error dynamics.

title: Statistical Analysis of High-Flow Traffic States
abstract: This study investigates the statistical properties of high-flow traffic states, defined as periods during which vehicular flow rates approach roadway capacity without immediate congestion onset. Using high-resolution traffic detector data from multiple highway segments, we apply time-series analysis and probabilistic modeling to characterize the frequency, duration, and stability of these states. The methodology integrates threshold-based state identification with distributional fitting to quantify the likelihood of transitions between high-flow and congested regimes. Results indicate that high-flow states exhibit distinct temporal clustering patterns, with durations following a heavy-tailed distribution, suggesting resilience against rapid breakdown under certain conditions. Furthermore, the probability of transition to congestion is shown to depend nonlinearly on both flow rate and occupancy, implying that deterministic thresholds may inadequately capture breakdown risk. Comparative analysis across sites demonstrates that roadway geometry and traffic composition significantly influence high-flow persistence. These findings contribute to the development of predictive traffic management strategies by improving the understanding of stability mechanisms in near-capacity operations, offering potential for refining congestion prevention measures and enhancing real-time traffic control systems.
introduction: The study of high-flow traffic states is essential for understanding the dynamics of modern transportation systems, particularly on highways and other high-capacity road networks. Such states are characterized by sustained vehicle flows approaching the theoretical maximum, where small perturbations can lead to significant changes in traffic stability and safety. Accurate statistical analysis of these conditions enables researchers and policymakers to anticipate congestion, optimize traffic control strategies, and improve infrastructure design. Previous research has examined high-flow states through deterministic models and simulation-based approaches; however, statistical methodologies provide complementary insights by capturing variability, uncertainty, and probabilistic patterns inherent in empirical traffic data. High-resolution traffic measurements, including vehicle counts, speeds, and headways, allow for the identification of statistical signatures that distinguish stable high-flow conditions from precursors to breakdown. By employing advanced statistical models, it becomes possible to quantify the likelihood of transitions between free flow, high-flow, and congested regimes, thereby enhancing predictive capabilities. This paper presents a comprehensive statistical investigation of high-flow traffic states, focusing on empirical data analysis, model development, and interpretation of findings within the broader context of traffic flow theory.
conclusion: The results of this study demonstrate that statistical analysis provides valuable insights into the dynamics of high-flow traffic states, enabling clearer identification of patterns and transitions within complex traffic systems. By applying rigorous quantitative methods, we revealed consistent relationships between flow intensity, variability, and the onset of congestion. These findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of traffic behavior under extreme demand conditions and offer a foundation for predictive modeling. The analytical framework presented here can support improved traffic management strategies, allowing for timely interventions to mitigate congestion. Future research should integrate additional real-time data sources and explore multi-scale modeling to further enhance prediction accuracy and operational efficiency in high-flow environments.

title: Recent, rapid advancement in visual question answering architecture: a review
abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) has emerged as a pivotal multimodal task, integrating computer vision and natural language processing to enable machines to answer questions about images. Recent years have witnessed rapid advancements in VQA architectures, driven by deep learning innovations, large-scale datasets, and transformer-based models. This review synthesizes recent progress, highlighting architectural trends, attention mechanisms, and multimodal fusion strategies that have significantly improved accuracy and reasoning capabilities. We examine benchmark performances, discuss limitations such as bias and interpretability, and outline emerging directions. The survey aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the evolving VQA landscape and its future research potential.
introduction: Visual Question Answering (VQA) has emerged as a prominent multidisciplinary research area at the intersection of computer vision, natural language processing, and machine learning. The task involves generating accurate answers to natural language questions about visual content, requiring systems to perform high-level reasoning over multimodal inputs. Since its formal introduction less than a decade ago, VQA has evolved rapidly, benefiting from advances in deep learning architectures, large-scale datasets, and computational resources. Early models often relied on separate pipelines for image and text processing, followed by simple fusion mechanisms. However, recent years have witnessed a surge in sophisticated architectures that employ attention mechanisms, multimodal transformers, and pretraining on vast image–text corpora, resulting in substantial performance improvements across benchmark datasets. These developments have been further accelerated by the integration of transfer learning from large vision-language models, enabling more robust generalization and reasoning capabilities. Despite impressive progress, challenges remain in areas such as commonsense reasoning, compositional generalization, and bias mitigation. This review aims to provide a comprehensive examination of the most recent and rapid advancements in VQA architectures, highlighting key innovations, trends, and open research directions. By synthesizing recent literature, we seek to offer insights into the evolving landscape of VQA and its potential for more sophisticated human–AI interaction.
conclusion: The rapid evolution of visual question answering (VQA) architectures in recent years reflects significant progress in bridging visual perception and natural language understanding. Advances in deep learning, particularly the integration of transformer-based models, cross-modal attention mechanisms, and large-scale pretraining on multimodal datasets, have led to substantial gains in accuracy, generalization, and robustness. These developments have been further supported by the availability of more diverse and challenging benchmarks, fostering innovation in model design and evaluation. Despite these achievements, several challenges remain. Current systems often struggle with complex reasoning, commonsense inference, and the handling of ambiguous or compositional queries. Moreover, issues related to bias, interpretability, and computational efficiency continue to limit the practical deployment of VQA models in real-world applications. Future research directions include the development of more explainable and resource-efficient architectures, integration of external knowledge sources, and improved mechanisms for reasoning over long context sequences. Additionally, advances in multimodal pretraining and self-supervised learning hold promise for further improving generalization across domains and tasks. Overall, the field is moving rapidly toward more sophisticated, context-aware, and trustworthy VQA systems, with the potential to play a central role in a wide range of interactive AI applications. Continued interdisciplinary efforts will be key to overcoming current limitations and unlocking the full potential of VQA technologies.

title: Condensation of actin filaments pushing against a barrier
abstract: We investigate the collective dynamics of actin filaments polymerizing against a rigid barrier, focusing on the phenomenon of filament tip condensation. Using a combination of stochastic simulations and analytical modeling, we explore how steric interactions and force generation lead to spatial clustering of filament tips near the barrier. Our results reveal a transition from a dispersed to a condensed state as the load force or filament density increases. In the condensed regime, a significant fraction of filaments share the leading edge, enhancing cooperative force production but reducing overall growth velocity. We quantify the dependence of condensation on filament number, polymerization rate, and barrier stiffness, and discuss implications for cellular processes such as lamellipodial protrusion. This work provides mechanistic insight into how actin networks regulate force output through self-organization at the nanoscale barrier interface.
introduction:
The dynamic remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton is a central driver of cell shape changes, motility, and force generation in a wide variety of biological contexts. Actin filaments, polymerizing from monomeric actin subunits, can exert pushing forces on intracellular structures or the plasma membrane, enabling processes such as lamellipodia extension, endocytosis, intracellular transport, and pathogen propulsion. When polymerizing against a physical barrier, actin filaments generate forces through the addition of new subunits at their barbed ends, which requires the thermal fluctuations of the barrier to create gaps large enough to accommodate monomer insertion. This so‑called Brownian ratchet mechanism has been extensively studied both theoretically and experimentally, providing a framework for understanding how actin polymerization can perform mechanical work.

In many physiological situations, actin filaments do not operate in isolation, but rather as part of dense, branched, or bundled arrays that interact with each other and with regulatory proteins. The spatial organization of filaments near a barrier can strongly influence the efficiency of force generation. One phenomenon of particular interest is the “condensation” of actin filaments against the barrier, whereby multiple filaments accumulate in close proximity to the load-bearing surface. Condensation can be driven by various factors, including geometric constraints, filament–filament interactions mediated by crosslinkers, or cooperative effects arising from load sharing. The resulting local increase in filament density can alter both the mechanical output and the kinetics of barrier advancement, potentially leading to regimes of collective force generation distinct from those of sparsely distributed filaments.

Previous theoretical treatments of polymerizing filament ensembles have highlighted the importance of load sharing in determining the force–velocity relationship of the system. In simple mean-field models, filaments in contact with the barrier share the load equally, leading to a smooth decrease in growth velocity as the opposing force increases. However, more detailed stochastic models suggest that filaments may distribute unevenly along the barrier, with some bearing a disproportionate share of the load while others remain behind and polymerize in relative freedom. This heterogeneity can give rise to intermittent dynamics and to fluctuations in the number of filaments in direct contact with the barrier. Under certain conditions, these fluctuations may be suppressed, and a large fraction of filaments may remain in close contact, forming a condensed layer. 

Experimentally, evidence for condensation has been observed in reconstituted actin networks growing against beads, vesicles, or synthetic membranes, where dense filament arrays form at the interface and collectively push the load. In living cells, high-resolution imaging has revealed regions of elevated filament density near the leading edge, consistent with the idea that condensation can occur in the lamellipodium or at endocytic sites. Nonetheless, a quantitative understanding of the mechanisms that lead to this phenomenon, and of its consequences for force generation, remains incomplete. The interplay between polymerization kinetics, filament elasticity, barrier fluctuations, and filament–filament interactions presents a complex problem that is not fully captured by existing models.

Addressing this gap requires combining theoretical analysis with simulations that can capture the stochastic nature of filament growth and the discrete nature of monomer addition. Such approaches can reveal how microscopic rules governing polymerization and load sharing translate into emergent collective behaviors such as condensation. In particular, it is important to delineate the conditions under which condensation occurs spontaneously, how it depends on parameters such as filament number, barrier stiffness, and monomer concentration, and what impact it has on the overall force–velocity characteristics of the system.

In this work, we investigate the condensation of actin filaments pushing against a barrier using a minimal stochastic model that incorporates the essential features of polymerization under load. We focus on the statistical distribution of filament–barrier distances, the dynamics of contact formation and loss, and the resulting collective force generation. By systematically varying key parameters, we identify regimes in which condensation is favored and analyze the mechanical and dynamical signatures of these regimes. Our results provide insight into the collective mechanics of actin filament ensembles and suggest testable predictions for in vitro and in vivo systems where actin-driven pushing plays a critical role.
conclusion:
In this study, we have investigated the physical and dynamical mechanisms underlying the condensation of actin filaments as they encounter and exert force upon a barrier. By combining theoretical modeling with quantitative analysis, we have shown that the interplay between filament growth, steric interactions, and load sharing leads to a highly non-uniform distribution of filament tips near the barrier. This “condensation” phenomenon—whereby filaments tend to accumulate at the barrier surface—emerges naturally from the stochastic dynamics of polymerization under load, and is robust across a range of parameter values relevant to cellular and in vitro systems.

Our analysis demonstrates that the condensation is not merely a trivial consequence of mechanical crowding, but is instead a collective effect arising from the balance between polymerization kinetics, thermal fluctuations, and force transmission through the filament network. When a subset of filaments makes contact with the barrier, they bear the mechanical load and slow their growth rate according to the force–velocity relationship of actin polymerization. This slowing increases the probability that trailing filaments will “catch up” to the barrier, thereby increasing the local filament density. Over time, this feedback loop reinforces the accumulation of filaments at the interface. The degree of condensation depends sensitively on both the stiffness of the barrier and the number of filaments in the bundle, with stiffer barriers and larger filament numbers promoting stronger accumulation.

We have further elucidated how condensation influences the force generation capabilities of the actin network. In regimes where condensation is significant, a larger fraction of filaments contribute directly to pushing the barrier, thereby increasing the effective load-bearing capacity. However, this comes at a cost: the high density of tips at the barrier may enhance lateral steric hindrance, potentially limiting the addition of new monomers and thereby reducing the overall polymerization rate per filament. This trade-off suggests that cells may regulate filament spacing and organization to optimize both the magnitude and efficiency of force production, depending on the mechanical task at hand.

Our findings also shed light on the transition between growth regimes dominated by a few leading filaments and those characterized by collective, synchronized advancement of many filaments. The condensation effect can be viewed as a precursor to such synchronization, as the narrowing of the tip distribution reduces the variability in individual filament lengths. In biological contexts, this could facilitate coordinated protrusion of lamellipodia or filopodia, where efficient load sharing and reduced length dispersion are advantageous for persistent movement against resistive environments.

Importantly, the theoretical framework developed here provides a basis for interpreting experimental observations of actin-driven motility. Electron microscopy and high-resolution fluorescence imaging have consistently reported dense zones of actin filaments adjacent to the leading edge in cells, as well as in reconstituted systems pushing against beads or membranes. Our results suggest that such structural features may not only be structural consequences of nucleation site proximity, but also dynamic outcomes of polymerization under load. The predicted dependence of condensation on barrier stiffness offers a potential avenue for experimental validation, for example by comparing filament distributions against deformable versus rigid obstacles.

Beyond the immediate scope of actin-based motility, the principles uncovered here may have broader relevance for other cytoskeletal systems where growing polymers interact with mechanical boundaries. Microtubule ensembles, bacterial actin homologs, or synthetic filamentous systems could all exhibit analogous condensation phenomena, with implications for intracellular transport, shape maintenance, and mechanosensing.

In conclusion, we have identified and characterized a robust condensation of actin filaments at barriers, arising from the coupled dynamics of polymerization and force generation. This effect enhances collective load sharing but introduces potential kinetic constraints, suggesting an inherent tension between maximizing force and maintaining high growth rates. By clarifying the mechanistic origins and consequences of filament condensation, this work provides a conceptual bridge between molecular-scale polymerization kinetics and mesoscopic force production in cytoskeletal networks. Future studies, combining precise experimental control of barrier properties with refined theoretical models incorporating filament flexibility, branching, and severing, will be essential to fully map the parameter space of this phenomenon and to understand its regulation in living cells.

title: End-to-end Music Remastering System Using Self-supervised and Adversarial Training
abstract: We present an end-to-end music remastering system that leverages self-supervised representation learning and adversarial training to enhance degraded audio recordings. The proposed framework operates directly on raw waveforms, jointly learning feature extraction and restoration without requiring paired high-quality references. A self-supervised pretraining stage captures rich musical structures by predicting masked audio segments, enabling the model to generalize across diverse genres and recording conditions. In the fine-tuning phase, a generative adversarial network refines spectral and temporal fidelity, with a discriminator trained to distinguish remastered outputs from professional-grade masters. This combination encourages perceptually convincing reconstructions while preserving artistic intent. Extensive experiments on a large collection of historical and contemporary tracks demonstrate significant improvements in objective metrics such as PESQ and STOI, as well as listener-rated quality. Our results suggest that integrating self-supervised pretraining with adversarial fine-tuning provides a powerful paradigm for automatic music remastering across heterogeneous and challenging audio sources.
introduction:
The process of music remastering aims to enhance the quality of existing audio recordings by improving clarity, balance, and overall listening experience, while preserving the artistic intent of the original work. Traditionally, remastering is performed manually by audio engineers, who apply a combination of equalization, dynamic range compression, stereo enhancement, and noise reduction techniques. While these manual approaches can produce high-quality results, they are inherently time-consuming, require domain expertise, and may be subject to subjective variation between practitioners.  

Recent advances in machine learning have opened new possibilities for automating complex audio processing tasks. In particular, deep learning models have demonstrated strong capabilities in speech enhancement, source separation, and music generation. However, automating end-to-end music remastering presents unique challenges due to the diversity of musical genres, recording conditions, and production styles. Moreover, the lack of large-scale paired datasets of low- and high-quality versions of the same track limits the applicability of conventional supervised learning approaches.  

Self-supervised learning offers a promising direction to address data scarcity by enabling models to learn robust audio representations from unlabeled music. Combined with adversarial training, which encourages outputs indistinguishable from professionally remastered audio, such methods can capture both low-level signal fidelity and high-level perceptual quality. An end-to-end system leveraging these techniques could learn to directly map degraded or unprocessed recordings to remastered outputs without the need for explicit intermediate processing steps.  

In this work, we propose a novel music remastering framework that integrates self-supervised representation learning with adversarial fine-tuning. Our approach aims to generalize across diverse musical content while preserving the nuances of the original performance. We evaluate the system on multiple objective and perceptual metrics, demonstrating its potential as a practical tool for automated, high-quality music restoration and enhancement.
conclusion: In this work, we presented an end-to-end music remastering system that integrates self-supervised feature learning with adversarial training to enhance audio quality. By leveraging self-supervision, the model learns robust, high-level representations from large unlabeled datasets, while adversarial objectives encourage perceptually convincing outputs. Experimental results demonstrated that our approach outperforms traditional signal processing and purely supervised baselines in both objective metrics and listener studies. Furthermore, the end-to-end design streamlines the remastering pipeline, reducing manual intervention and domain-specific tuning. These findings suggest that combining self-supervised and adversarial techniques offers a promising direction for high-fidelity audio restoration. Future work will explore broader musical genres, real-time processing capabilities, and integration with interactive production tools to further extend the system’s practical applicability.

title: Faster Parallel Multiterminal Cuts
abstract: We present new parallel algorithms for the multiterminal cut problem, achieving significant improvements in both work and depth compared to existing approaches. The multiterminal cut problem, a generalization of the classic s–t cut, has numerous applications in network design, VLSI layout, and computer vision. Our methods leverage recent advances in parallel graph processing, including efficient sparsification and flow-based decomposition techniques, to produce high-quality cuts with provable guarantees. We analyze the algorithms in the PRAM model, showing polylogarithmic depth and near-linear work for a fixed number of terminals. Experimental results on large-scale graphs demonstrate substantial speedups over sequential baselines, while maintaining comparable cut quality, thus enabling practical deployment of multiterminal cut computations in large parallel environments.
introduction:
The multiterminal cut problem is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem with numerous applications in network design, VLSI circuit layout, image segmentation, and data clustering. Given an undirected, edge-weighted graph and a set of designated terminal vertices, the goal is to remove a set of edges of minimum total weight so that each terminal is disconnected from all others. While the problem is NP-hard for three or more terminals, it has been extensively studied from the perspectives of exact algorithms, approximation schemes, and, increasingly, parallel computation.

As modern computing environments shift toward multi-core and many-core architectures, there is a growing demand for parallel algorithms that can handle large graph instances efficiently. Parallelization introduces new challenges: designing algorithms that minimize synchronization overhead, achieve good load balance across processing units, and maintain approximation quality or exactness guarantees. Existing parallel approaches to multiterminal cut often adapt sequential heuristics or approximation algorithms, but their scalability and performance vary significantly depending on graph structure and the number of terminals.

Recent advances in parallel graph algorithms—such as parallel minimum cut and maximum flow computations—suggest that substantial speedups are possible for multiterminal cut as well. However, directly extending these techniques is nontrivial because multiterminal cut requires simultaneously separating multiple terminals, and naive parallelization can lead to redundant work or degraded solution quality. This motivates the development of specialized parallel strategies that exploit both graph-theoretic properties and parallel hardware capabilities.

In this work, we present new parallel algorithms for the multiterminal cut problem that achieve faster running times while preserving solution quality. Our contributions include a refined decomposition strategy that reduces interdependence between subtasks, a parallel contraction framework that simplifies the graph without losing optimality, and an adaptive load-balancing scheme that ensures efficient utilization of processing resources. We evaluate our methods on a diverse set of benchmark graphs, demonstrating significant improvements in speed and scalability over existing approaches. The results indicate that carefully designed parallelism can make multiterminal cut computations feasible for large-scale instances, opening the door to broader applicability in real-time and data-intensive settings.
conclusion: In this work, we have presented new parallel algorithms for the multiterminal cut problem that achieve improved performance over existing approaches while preserving solution quality. By exploiting fine-grained parallelism and carefully balancing load across processing units, our methods substantially reduce execution time for large-scale instances. The algorithms integrate efficient graph partitioning strategies with parallel flow computations, yielding scalable performance on both shared-memory and distributed-memory architectures. Experimental results demonstrate speedups over state-of-the-art sequential and parallel baselines, particularly for graphs with millions of vertices and edges. Furthermore, our approach maintains competitive cut sizes, indicating that the acceleration does not compromise solution optimality. These results highlight the potential of combining algorithmic design with modern parallel computing techniques to address longstanding computational bottlenecks in combinatorial optimization. Future work will explore adaptive scheduling policies, heterogeneous architectures, and extensions to related cut and partitioning problems. We believe the principles outlined here can be generalized to other graph optimization tasks, enabling the efficient solution of increasingly large and complex instances and advancing the practical applicability of multiterminal cut algorithms in scientific, engineering, and data analysis domains.

title: On W-algebras and the symmetries of defects of 6d N=(2,0) theory
abstract: We investigate the emergence of W-algebras from codimension-two defects in the 6d \(\mathcal{N}=(2,0)\) theory. Using the correspondence with 4d class S theories, we analyze how defect data determine the associated chiral algebras and their symmetry structure. We propose a systematic characterization of the W-algebra generators and central charges, clarifying their relation to defect labels and uncovering new links between geometric engineering and quantum symmetries.
introduction: The study of codimension-two defects in the six-dimensional \( \mathcal{N}=(2,0) \) theory has revealed deep connections between higher-dimensional quantum field theories and two-dimensional conformal field theories. In particular, certain classes of defects preserve extended chiral algebras, often identified with \( W \)-algebras obtained via quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction. These structures encode nontrivial symmetry enhancements and provide a bridge to integrable systems and geometric representation theory. This work investigates the emergence of \( W \)-algebras from defect configurations, elucidating their role in organizing operator spectra and constraining correlation functions in the parent six-dimensional theory.
conclusion:
In this work we have explored the emergence and structure of \( W \)-algebras in the context of codimension-two defects in the six-dimensional \( \mathcal{N}=(2,0) \) theory, focusing on the interplay between defect data, symmetry algebras, and the geometric and algebraic structures that underpin them. By systematically examining the reductions of the parent theory along various directions and incorporating both the local and global properties of the defects, we have clarified how specific \( W \)-algebras arise as the natural symmetry algebras governing the protected operator subsectors associated to these defects.

Our analysis has shown that the correspondence between defect configurations and \( W \)-algebras is far from accidental: it follows from a chain of dualities and dimensional reductions that preserve a rich algebraic structure. In particular, the presence of codimension-two defects induces a nontrivial modification of the symmetry algebra of the parent theory, replacing the affine Kac–Moody symmetries that would appear in simpler setups with more intricate \( W \)-algebras obtained via quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction. This mechanism provides a unifying explanation for various observations scattered across the literature, from the appearance of Toda field theories in certain compactifications to the matching of conformal blocks with partition functions of supersymmetric gauge theories.
