An important aspect of our results is the elucidation of how the parameters of the defect — such as its type, embedding, and associated nilpotent orbit — dictate the precise form of the resulting \( W \)-algebra. The classification of these algebras can thus be traced back to the classification of defects themselves, offering a powerful dictionary between geometric data in six dimensions and algebraic data in two dimensions. This map not only deepens our understanding of the moduli of defects but also provides a concrete computational framework for extracting operator algebras in lower-dimensional effective theories.

We have also highlighted the role of protected correlation functions and their interpretation in terms of chiral algebras. The emergence of \( W \)-algebra symmetry in such correlators underscores the robust nature of these structures: they are insensitive to many of the deformations of the bulk theory, depending only on topological and holomorphic data. This robustness suggests that \( W \)-algebras associated with defects should be viewed as intrinsic invariants of the defect configuration, potentially serving as a key tool in the classification and study of defects in supersymmetric quantum field theories.

Our findings open several avenues for future work. One natural direction is to extend the analysis beyond the ADE classification of the \( \mathcal{N}=(2,0) \) theory, exploring whether analogous structures appear in less supersymmetric or non-simply-laced settings. Another is to investigate the implications for holography, where defects in the six-dimensional theory may have dual descriptions in terms of branes or geometries exhibiting \( W \)-symmetry. Furthermore, the connection to integrable systems, hinted at by the appearance of Toda theories, warrants a more detailed exploration, particularly in relation to quantization and the spectrum of protected operators.

In summary, the study of \( W \)-algebras in the presence of codimension-two defects in the \( \mathcal{N}=(2,0) \) theory provides a fertile intersection of geometry, representation theory, and quantum field theory. The correspondence we have developed not only unifies disparate observations but also equips us with new tools to probe the symmetries and dynamics of defects, broadening our understanding of the rich tapestry of structures arising from six-dimensional superconformal theories.

title: An Efficient Simulation of Quantum Secret Sharing
abstract: This paper presents an efficient simulation framework for quantum secret sharing (QSS) protocols, enabling the exploration of their performance and security in realistic conditions without requiring immediate access to quantum hardware. The proposed approach models qubit states, entanglement generation, and measurement processes while incorporating noise and decoherence effects. By optimizing state representation and computation, the simulator achieves significant reductions in runtime and memory usage compared to conventional methods. We validate the framework through simulations of well-known QSS schemes, demonstrating accurate reproduction of theoretical predictions and scalability to larger participant groups. The results provide insights into protocol robustness under various error models, guiding the design of more resilient quantum communication systems. This work offers a practical tool for researchers to investigate QSS implementations and to support the transition from theory to experimental realization.
introduction: Quantum secret sharing (QSS) enables secure distribution of confidential information among multiple parties using quantum resources. Efficient simulation of QSS is crucial for testing protocols before physical implementation. This work presents a novel simulation framework that reduces computational overhead while maintaining accuracy, facilitating practical evaluation of advanced quantum communication schemes.
conclusion: This work presented an efficient simulation framework for quantum secret sharing, enabling accurate modeling of quantum states and protocols with reduced computational overhead. The proposed approach enhances scalability while preserving fidelity, facilitating the study and optimization of multi-party quantum communication schemes. Future research may extend this framework to incorporate noise models and real-world constraints, bridging the gap between theoretical design and practical quantum network implementation.

title: Signal Processing on Graphs: Causal Modeling of Unstructured Data
abstract: The increasing prevalence of network-structured and irregularly sampled data in domains such as neuroscience, social networks, and sensor arrays has motivated the development of signal processing techniques on graphs. Traditional approaches often focus on spectral or spatial filtering, yet many real-world systems exhibit causal relationships that are not explicitly captured by these methods. This paper introduces a framework for causal modeling of unstructured data through graph signal processing (GSP), extending conventional time-series causality concepts to signals defined on arbitrary topologies. We formalize causal graph processes by integrating structural priors with probabilistic dependencies, enabling inference of both the underlying graph and directed causal interactions from observational data. The proposed methodology combines graph-based autoregressive models with sparsity-promoting regularization to ensure interpretability and robustness in high-dimensional settings. We evaluate our approach on synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating improved accuracy in recovering causal structure compared to baseline GSP and statistical methods. The results highlight the potential of causal GSP to advance understanding in applications where relational geometry and directional influence are intertwined, paving the way for more predictive and explainable analysis of complex networked systems.
introduction:
The proliferation of network-structured data across diverse scientific and engineering domains has motivated a growing interest in extending classical signal processing tools to irregular domains. Social networks, transportation systems, biological interaction networks, and sensor arrays are examples of systems in which the underlying support is naturally represented as a graph rather than a regular Euclidean grid. In such settings, the data of interest—often referred to as graph signals—are defined on the vertices of the graph, and their structure is dictated by the topology of the network. Traditional signal processing frameworks, which rely on notions of shift-invariance and regular sampling, are ill-suited to capture the irregular connectivity and heterogeneous relationships inherent in graph-structured data. This gap has spurred the emergence of signal processing on graphs (SPoG) as a principled methodology to generalize concepts such as filtering, spectral analysis, and sampling to unstructured domains.

While early work in SPoG has predominantly focused on descriptive and predictive tasks—such as denoising, interpolation, and classification—many real-world problems demand a deeper understanding of the generative mechanisms that govern the evolution of graph signals. In particular, causal modeling, which seeks to uncover directional, potentially asymmetric dependencies among variables, is of paramount importance in domains ranging from neuroscience and epidemiology to finance and climate science. Inferring causal structure from data enables not only improved prediction, but also intervention and control, as it reveals how changes in one part of the system propagate through the network.

Causal inference in the context of graph signals presents unique challenges. Unlike conventional multivariate time series, where the dependency structure is often assumed to be dense or structured according to temporal ordering, graph signals evolve over arbitrary topologies that may be unknown or partially observed. Moreover, dependencies can be both topological—arising from the graph edges—and functional—arising from latent processes that govern the signal dynamics. These complexities necessitate new models and analytical tools that integrate the representational power of SPoG with the inferential rigor of causal analysis.

Recent advances in graph signal models, including graph filters, graph autoregressive processes, and spectral-domain representations, provide a promising foundation for causal modeling on networks. By interpreting graph shifts and their polynomial expansions as localized linear operators, it becomes possible to encode directional dependencies and propagation delays across the graph. When combined with statistical frameworks for causal discovery—such as Granger causality, structural equation modeling, and constraint-based approaches—these models can be adapted to capture both the spatial and temporal aspects of causality in unstructured domains.

This work aims to bridge the gap between signal processing on graphs and causal inference by developing a unified framework for modeling, identifying, and interpreting causal relationships in graph-structured data. We explore how graph-based operators can be employed to represent causal interactions, how spectral and vertex-domain perspectives can be leveraged for efficient estimation, and how the resulting models can be validated against both synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets. By formalizing causal modeling in the SPoG context, we seek to enable more accurate, interpretable, and actionable insights into complex systems where structure and dynamics are intertwined, thereby extending the scope and impact of graph-based signal processing in scientific discovery and engineering applications.
conclusion: This work has explored the problem of causal modeling for unstructured data through the lens of signal processing on graphs. By leveraging the intrinsic topology encoded in graph structures, we have shown that it is possible to represent, analyze, and infer causal relationships in domains where the underlying system is irregular or non-Euclidean. The proposed framework integrates spectral and vertex-domain graph signal processing techniques with causal inference principles, enabling the identification of directional dependencies while accommodating complex connectivity patterns. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in revealing latent causal mechanisms and improving predictive performance. Beyond its immediate applications, the methodology provides a foundation for future research on dynamic and multiscale causal modeling in networked systems. As unstructured data continues to proliferate across scientific and engineering disciplines, the intersection of graph signal processing and causal analysis offers a promising direction for extracting interpretable, structure-aware insights from complex datasets.

title: Domain size and charge defects on the polarization switching of antiferroelectric domains
abstract: The influence of domain size and charge defects on polarization switching in antiferroelectric materials is investigated through combined experimental and phase-field simulation approaches. Results show that smaller domain sizes reduce the critical field required for switching, facilitating domain wall motion, whereas larger domains exhibit sluggish switching kinetics. Charged defects, introduced via controlled doping, are found to pin domain walls and locally alter the polarization pathway, leading to increased switching fields and hysteresis broadening. The interplay between domain size and defect concentration reveals a nontrivial dependence of switching dynamics on microstructural parameters. These findings provide insight into the nanoscale engineering of antiferroelectric materials for applications in energy storage, actuators, and electrocaloric devices, highlighting strategies to optimize their functional performance.
introduction:
Antiferroelectric (AFE) materials, characterized by an antiparallel alignment of neighboring dipoles in their ground state, have attracted significant attention due to their distinctive double hysteresis loops, high energy storage density, and field-induced phase transitions. Unlike ferroelectrics, where spontaneous polarization can be switched directly by an external electric field, AFEs undergo a field-driven transformation from the antipolar to a polar phase, enabling reversible control over their dielectric and electromechanical responses. This unique behavior has important implications for applications in energy storage capacitors, electrocaloric refrigeration, and high-strain actuators. Understanding the mechanisms that govern polarization switching in AFEs is thus a critical step toward optimizing their functional performance.

While much research has focused on the intrinsic crystallographic and thermodynamic aspects of the AFE–FE transition, recent studies have highlighted the crucial role of mesoscale features such as domain structure, domain wall mobility, and defect–dipole interactions. In particular, the size and arrangement of antiferroelectric domains can significantly influence the switching kinetics, coercive field, and stability of the induced ferroelectric phase. Smaller domains may facilitate rapid polarization changes due to shorter domain wall propagation distances, whereas larger domains can exhibit enhanced stability against back-switching. However, the quantitative relationship between domain size and polarization switching dynamics remains insufficiently understood, especially in the presence of real-material complexities.

Charge defects, including oxygen vacancies, cation non-stoichiometry, and impurity dopants, constitute another important factor affecting AFE switching. These defects can interact with domain walls, acting as pinning centers that impede wall motion, or in some cases, facilitate local nucleation of the polar phase. The defect–domain wall interaction strength depends not only on defect concentration and type but also on the spatial correlation between defects and the domain structure. Moreover, charge trapping at defects can locally modify the internal electric field, thereby altering the energy barrier for the antipolar-to-polar transformation. Despite their evident significance, the interplay between domain size and defect-mediated effects on the switching process has not been systematically addressed.

A comprehensive understanding of polarization switching in AFEs therefore requires an integrated view that accounts for both microstructural domain characteristics and defect chemistry. Recent advances in high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, piezoresponse force microscopy, and phase-field modeling now make it possible to examine these factors in combination, providing insights into the spatially resolved switching behavior. By correlating experimental observations with theoretical simulations, one can elucidate the mechanisms by which domain size and charge defects together regulate the kinetics, reversibility, and stability of polarization switching.

In this work, we investigate the coupled influence of domain size and charge defects on the polarization switching behavior of antiferroelectric domains. We aim to reveal how these two factors interact to determine the field thresholds, switching pathways, and fatigue resistance of AFE materials. Our findings contribute to a more complete framework for tailoring antiferroelectric properties through microstructural and defect engineering, thereby advancing the design of high-performance functional devices.
conclusion: In summary, this study has examined the influence of domain size and charge defects on the polarization switching behavior of antiferroelectric domains. Our results demonstrate that domain size plays a critical role in determining both the switching threshold and the stability of the antiferroelectric phase, with smaller domains exhibiting enhanced susceptibility to external fields. Charge defects, whether intrinsic or introduced during processing, were found to locally distort the electric field distribution, thereby facilitating or hindering domain wall motion depending on their configuration and density. The interplay between these two factors dictates the switching kinetics and can lead to pronounced asymmetries in the polarization–electric field response. These findings provide important insight into the microstructural and defect-mediated mechanisms governing antiferroelectric switching, offering potential strategies for optimizing material performance through controlled domain engineering and defect management. By tailoring domain architecture and minimizing detrimental defect states, it may be possible to achieve lower switching fields, improved endurance, and enhanced device efficiency in antiferroelectric-based applications such as energy storage capacitors and electrocaloric cooling systems.

title: A Corollary for Nonsmooth Systems
abstract: We present a corollary extending stability results to a class of nonsmooth dynamical systems. Using generalized Lyapunov methods, we establish sufficient conditions for asymptotic stability under discontinuous dynamics. The result unifies existing smooth and nonsmooth frameworks, offering broader applicability in control theory and engineering analysis.
introduction: Nonsmooth systems arise naturally in a wide range of applications, including mechanical systems with impacts, electrical circuits with switches, and control systems with saturation or hysteresis. The analysis of such systems presents unique challenges due to discontinuities and nondifferentiable dynamics, which render many classical smooth analysis tools inapplicable. Recent advances have extended stability, robustness, and performance results to nonsmooth settings, often by leveraging generalized derivatives or set-valued analysis. In this work, we present a corollary that refines existing theoretical frameworks, providing more accessible conditions for verifying critical properties of nonsmooth systems. This result not only simplifies analysis but also broadens applicability to practical engineering problems where nonsmooth behaviors are intrinsic.
conclusion: The corollary presented extends existing stability results to a broader class of nonsmooth systems, offering a unified framework for analysis. By accommodating discontinuities and non-differentiable dynamics, it enhances the applicability of Lyapunov-based methods. Theoretical developments were supported by illustrative examples, confirming practical relevance. These findings pave the way for future research on robust control and optimization in nonsmooth settings, potentially bridging gaps between theory and engineering applications.

title: The Potential of Spaced-based High-Energy Neutrino Measurements via the Airshower Cherenkov Signal
abstract: High-energy neutrinos offer a unique probe of the most energetic astrophysical processes and fundamental particle interactions at extreme energies. Detecting them from space enables vast target volumes and complements ground-based observatories. We investigate the feasibility of space-based measurements of high-energy neutrinos via detection of extensive air showers (EAS) induced by upward-going or horizontal secondary particles, observed through their Cherenkov emission in the atmosphere. Using simulated neutrino interaction geometries, atmospheric light transmission models, and realistic orbital parameters, we evaluate the expected photon yields, angular distributions, and background rejection capabilities for a satellite-borne optical system. Particular emphasis is placed on the discrimination of neutrino-induced upward-going showers from cosmic-ray-induced downward-going events, leveraging timing, directionality, and spectral signatures of the Cherenkov signal. Sensitivity estimates indicate that with a wide-field, high-speed photon detection system, event rates for ultra-high-energy neutrinos above ~10^17 eV could be competitive with current ground arrays, while achieving full-sky coverage over multi-year missions. We also discuss the implications for probing neutrino cross-sections at center-of-mass energies beyond terrestrial accelerators, and for identifying cosmic accelerators at redshifts inaccessible to gamma-ray observations. These results support the potential of orbital Cherenkov detection as a frontier technique in neutrino astronomy.
introduction:
High-energy neutrinos are unique astrophysical messengers, capable of traversing vast cosmic distances without significant deflection by magnetic fields or attenuation through interactions with matter and radiation. Their detection provides a direct probe of the most energetic and distant astrophysical phenomena, including active galactic nuclei, gamma-ray bursts, and potential sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. While ground-based observatories such as IceCube have made significant advances in the detection of TeV–PeV neutrinos, the limited instrumented volumes and duty cycles impose constraints on event statistics, particularly at energies above ~10 PeV. Extending sensitivity to the ultra-high-energy regime and increasing the effective target volume are critical for advancing neutrino astronomy.

Space-based detection concepts offer a promising pathway to address these limitations. By observing extensive air showers initiated by neutrino interactions in the Earth’s atmosphere or in dense media such as ice, space-based instruments can monitor vast surface areas and atmospheric volumes. Among the possible techniques, measurement of the Cherenkov emission from upward-going or Earth-skimming air showers has emerged as a compelling approach. Such signals, generated by secondary charged particles exceeding the local speed of light in air, produce fast, coherent optical flashes that can be detected from orbital or suborbital platforms. This method enables sensitivity to neutrinos of energies exceeding tens of PeV, expanding the observational window beyond the reach of current ground-based arrays.

Key advantages of a space-based Cherenkov detection system include the enormous instantaneous aperture achievable from orbit, the ability to monitor remote and otherwise inaccessible regions of the Earth, and the potential to operate continuously over extended observation periods. However, these benefits must be weighed against technical challenges, such as the attenuation of optical signals through the atmosphere, the need for precise background discrimination against cosmic-ray–induced showers, and the constraints imposed by satellite payload resources.

This work explores the potential of space-based high-energy neutrino measurements via the airshower Cherenkov signal, assessing the achievable sensitivity, event rates, and detection thresholds. We outline the physical principles underlying the method, describe feasible observational configurations, and evaluate the impact of instrumental and environmental factors on performance. By quantifying the scientific reach of such a system, we aim to inform the design and optimization of future orbital missions dedicated to high-energy neutrino astronomy.
conclusion:
The exploration of space-based detection of high-energy neutrinos through observation of the Cherenkov emission from extensive air showers offers a promising complement to current ground-based observatories. In this study, we have outlined the conceptual framework, detection geometry, and potential sensitivity of an orbital platform designed to register the optical signatures of upward-going showers initiated by neutrino interactions in the atmosphere or Earth’s crust. By capitalizing on the vast observational footprint afforded by satellite-based instruments, such an approach could substantially enlarge the effective target volume for neutrino interactions, particularly at energies beyond the reach of conventional detectors.

Our analysis indicates that the Cherenkov signal from these air showers, while subject to atmospheric attenuation and background contamination, remains within detectable limits for suitably optimized optical systems. Advances in low-noise, high-speed photon detectors, paired with wide-field optics and robust event reconstruction algorithms, would enable discrimination between neutrino-induced events and the more prevalent cosmic-ray background. The unique vantage point of space also mitigates some of the limitations imposed by ground-based operation, such as restricted horizon distance and weather-dependent duty cycles, thereby enhancing overall exposure.

Crucially, the feasibility of the proposed technique rests on accurate modeling of signal propagation, background light conditions, and the statistical characteristics of rare-event detection. Preliminary sensitivity estimates suggest that, with realistic instrument parameters, space-based Cherenkov observation could probe neutrino fluxes in the ultra-high-energy regime with competitive or superior reach compared to existing methods. Such measurements would not only provide valuable constraints on astrophysical source models but also open new windows for probing fundamental physics at extreme energies.

In summary, space-based high-energy neutrino measurements via the airshower Cherenkov signal represent a viable and potentially transformative avenue for neutrino astronomy. Continued development of this concept will require coordinated efforts in simulation, technology maturation, and mission design. Future work should focus on detailed trade studies of orbital configurations, detector architectures, and multi-messenger synergies, to fully realize the scientific return of such a mission. The integration of this technique into the broader neutrino detection landscape could significantly advance our understanding of the most energetic phenomena in the Universe and the role of neutrinos as cosmic messengers.

title: ANA at SemEval-2019 Task 3: Contextual Emotion detection in Conversations through hierarchical LSTMs and BERT
abstract: We present ANA’s system for SemEval-2019 Task 3: Contextual Emotion Detection in Conversations. Our approach combines hierarchical LSTMs to model conversational context with pretrained BERT embeddings for rich semantic representation. The hierarchical architecture captures utterance-level dependencies, while BERT encodes nuanced linguistic features. We fine-tune the model on task-specific data, leveraging both context and content to improve classification. Experimental results demonstrate that our system outperforms strong baselines, achieving competitive performance on the official leaderboard, highlighting the effectiveness of integrating contextual modeling with pretrained language representations.
introduction:
Detecting emotions in conversations is a crucial component in the development of intelligent dialogue systems, with applications ranging from empathetic virtual assistants to mental health support tools. Unlike sentiment analysis, which often focuses on the overall polarity of a text, emotion detection aims to capture nuanced affective states such as joy, sadness, anger, or surprise. The complexity of this task increases significantly when dealing with conversational data, where the meaning and emotional tone of an utterance often depend heavily on its preceding context. For instance, the same sentence may convey different emotions depending on the prior turns in the dialogue. This dependency on context poses unique challenges for computational models, necessitating methods that can effectively model inter-utterance relationships and contextual cues.

In recent years, advances in deep learning—particularly sequence models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their gated variants—have enabled significant progress in natural language understanding tasks. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, with their ability to capture long-range dependencies, have been widely adopted for sequential modelling in text. Hierarchical architectures, which process text at multiple levels (e.g., word-level and utterance-level), have shown particular promise for dialogue-related tasks, as they can explicitly model both the intra-utterance semantics and the inter-utterance context. At the same time, the emergence of large-scale pretrained language models such as BERT has transformed the landscape of natural language processing (NLP). By leveraging massive amounts of unlabeled data, these models learn rich contextual representations that can be fine-tuned for a variety of downstream tasks, including emotion classification.

The SemEval-2019 Task 3, “Contextual Emotion Detection in Text,” provides a benchmark for evaluating models that can detect emotions in conversational settings. The task involves classifying the emotion of the final utterance in a three-turn conversation, taking into account the preceding turns. The challenge lies in accurately modelling the conversational context to disambiguate emotions that may be subtle or implicit. For example, a short response such as “Fine.” could express resignation, sarcasm, or genuine contentment depending on the context provided by earlier turns.

In this work, we present ANA’s approach to SemEval-2019 Task 3, which combines the strengths of hierarchical LSTMs for structured context modelling with the powerful contextual embeddings provided by BERT. Our hierarchical framework first encodes each utterance through a word-level LSTM, then models the sequence of utterances using an utterance-level LSTM, thereby capturing both local semantic features and global conversational dynamics. To enhance the representational capacity of the model, we incorporate BERT embeddings as input features, allowing the system to benefit from deep contextual knowledge learned from large corpora. This combination aims to address two key challenges: (1) effectively representing the subtle emotional cues in individual utterances, and (2) integrating contextual information across multiple turns to ensure accurate emotion detection.

By integrating hierarchical LSTMs with BERT embeddings, our approach seeks to balance structured sequential modelling with rich pretrained representations. We evaluate our system on the official SemEval-2019 Task 3 dataset and demonstrate that this hybrid architecture achieves competitive performance, highlighting the importance of combining context-aware sequence models with state-of-the-art pretrained language models for conversational emotion detection.
conclusion: In this work, we presented ANA’s approach to SemEval-2019 Task 3 on Contextual Emotion Detection in Conversations, leveraging hierarchical LSTMs and BERT-based representations. Our method effectively captured contextual dependencies across conversational turns, enabling more accurate emotion classification. Experimental results demonstrated competitive performance, highlighting the complementary strengths of sequential modeling and pre-trained language representations. While our approach showed robustness, further improvements could be achieved by incorporating richer conversational features and external knowledge. Future work will explore multi-modal cues and advanced transformer architectures to enhance context understanding and generalization in emotion detection within complex, multi-turn dialogue scenarios.

title: Model of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction Part 2: Central role of the internal excitationgrowth rate
abstract: We investigate a refined mathematical model of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction, emphasizing the central role of the internal excitation–growth rate in generating and sustaining spatiotemporal patterns. Building on prior formulations, we extend the kinetic framework to incorporate nonlinear feedback between excitation dynamics and local reagent depletion. Numerical simulations reveal that variations in the excitation–growth parameter produce qualitative transitions between oscillatory, excitable, and damped regimes. Analytical stability analysis identifies thresholds that delimit self-organized wave propagation from pattern collapse. The results demonstrate that the internal excitation–growth rate acts as a primary control parameter governing the persistence, wavelength, and velocity of chemical waves. This work provides a deeper mechanistic understanding of the BZ reaction, with implications for reaction–diffusion systems across chemistry, biology, and materials science.
introduction: The Belousov–Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction is a prototypical example of non-equilibrium chemical oscillations, exhibiting striking spatiotemporal patterns such as target waves and spirals. Its study has provided fundamental insights into reaction–diffusion systems and the emergence of self-organization. Mathematical models, particularly the Oregonator, have captured many qualitative features, yet the quantitative determinants of pattern formation remain under investigation. Among these, the internal excitation growth rate plays a central role, governing both the onset and stability of oscillations. Understanding how this parameter influences wave dynamics is essential for linking microscopic reaction kinetics to macroscopic pattern behavior. In this work, we extend previous modeling efforts to examine systematically the effects of varying the internal excitation growth rate, providing new perspectives on the control and prediction of complex chemical wave phenomena.
conclusion:
In this study, we have extended the modeling of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction by focusing on the central role of the internal excitation–growth rate in shaping the system’s spatiotemporal dynamics. Building on the framework developed in Part 1, we demonstrated that the internal growth rate acts as a key control parameter governing both the amplitude and the persistence of oscillatory patterns. Numerical simulations and analytical considerations revealed that small variations in this rate can induce pronounced qualitative changes, including transitions between stationary wavefronts, rotating spirals, and fully developed turbulence. The sensitivity of the reaction–diffusion system to this parameter underscores its importance for understanding excitability thresholds and the onset of complex self-organization.

The analysis further showed that the growth rate influences not only the temporal frequency of oscillations but also the spatial coherence of emergent structures. This dual role highlights its function as a unifying factor linking microscopic reaction kinetics with macroscopic pattern formation. Moreover, our results suggest that experimentally accessible manipulations—such as adjusting reactant concentrations or temperature—can be interpreted as indirect means of tuning the internal excitation–growth rate, thereby providing a bridge between theoretical predictions and laboratory control strategies.

In conclusion, the internal excitation–growth rate emerges as a fundamental determinant of the BZ reaction’s dynamic regime. Recognizing and quantifying its influence offers a clearer path to predicting and controlling complex chemical wave phenomena, with potential implications for broader classes of excitable media in chemistry, biology, and materials science.

title: On the measurements regarding random observables
abstract: We investigate the statistical properties and measurement outcomes of random observables within finite- and infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. By employing probabilistic frameworks and spectral analysis, we characterize the distribution of eigenvalues and their influence on expectation values under repeated measurements. Our results reveal asymptotic behaviors linked to concentration phenomena and establish bounds on measurement uncertainties for ensembles of observables. Applications to quantum information theory and stochastic operator models are discussed, highlighting implications for both theoretical foundations and experimental implementations in systems dominated by inherent or engineered randomness.
introduction:
The study of measurements associated with random observables occupies a central position in both theoretical and applied branches of modern science. Random observables, broadly construed, are quantities whose values are governed by underlying probabilistic structures, and whose measurement outcomes exhibit inherent variability. They arise naturally in diverse contexts, ranging from quantum mechanical operators with stochastic parameters to classical random processes in signal analysis and statistical physics. Understanding the principles and limitations of measuring such observables is crucial not only for accurate characterization of physical systems, but also for the development of robust inference and prediction methods.

In many settings, the act of measurement itself interacts nontrivially with the randomness of the observable, introducing new layers of uncertainty and potential bias. This interplay complicates the interpretation of experimental data, especially when correlations exist between the measurement apparatus and the observable’s probabilistic nature. Furthermore, the finite resolution of measuring devices, environmental noise, and statistical sampling constraints all contribute to deviations between the measured values and the true statistical properties of the observable. Consequently, a rigorous framework for describing, quantifying, and mitigating these effects is of both fundamental and practical importance.

Recent developments in probability theory, statistical estimation, and operator analysis have provided new tools for addressing these challenges. These advances enable the formulation of precise conditions under which measurements of random observables can be considered reliable, as well as the derivation of bounds on the achievable accuracy. Moreover, the cross-fertilization between quantum measurement theory and classical stochastic analysis offers promising avenues for unifying disparate approaches. The present work aims to contribute to this growing body of knowledge by systematically analyzing measurement schemes for random observables, elucidating the relationships between measurement protocols, statistical properties, and operational constraints, and proposing methodologies for optimizing accuracy in the presence of intrinsic randomness.
conclusion:
In this work, we have examined the conceptual and operational aspects of measurements performed on random observables, with particular emphasis on the interplay between statistical uncertainty, measurement precision, and the underlying probabilistic structure of the observables themselves. Our analysis has been rooted in a framework that treats observables not as fixed, deterministic quantities, but as inherently stochastic entities whose properties are described by probability distributions rather than singular values. This perspective has allowed us to address both the theoretical underpinnings and the practical implications of working with random observables in a rigorous and systematic manner.

A central point emerging from our study is that the measurement of a random observable cannot be meaningfully discussed without a careful specification of its probability law, the space over which it is defined, and the statistical moments that are relevant to the physical or mathematical context. The standard notions of expectation value, variance, and higher-order cumulants acquire a dual role: they describe intrinsic features of the observable’s distribution, and they also dictate the achievable accuracy and reproducibility of measurement outcomes. In this sense, the act of measurement is inseparable from statistical estimation, and the performance of any measurement protocol is constrained by the same bounds—such as the Cramér–Rao inequality—that limit the estimation of parameters in classical and quantum statistics.

We have also clarified that, when observables are random, the notion of “measurement error” must be disentangled from the natural fluctuations of the quantity itself. In deterministic contexts, error is often conceptualised as an unwanted deviation from a fixed true value, attributable to imperfections in instruments or procedures. In contrast, for random observables, the dispersion of measurement results reflects both the variability intrinsic to the observable and the extrinsic inaccuracies of the measurement apparatus. Our treatment makes explicit how these contributions combine, and how their relative magnitudes can be assessed through repeated trials and appropriate statistical modelling.

Furthermore, our investigation has emphasised the nontrivial role of correlations—both temporal and cross-observable—in shaping measurement outcomes. When multiple random observables are measured jointly, or when a single observable is measured sequentially in time, correlation structures can either amplify or suppress the effective uncertainty, depending on their sign and magnitude. We have shown that neglecting such correlations can lead to systematic underestimation or overestimation of measurement variability, thereby distorting inferences drawn from the data. This is particularly significant in experimental regimes where environmental noise or intrinsic dynamical couplings impose long-range dependencies across observations.

From a methodological standpoint, we have discussed both model-based and nonparametric approaches to the analysis of measurement data for random observables. Model-based approaches, which assume a specified distributional form for the observable, permit the use of powerful parametric inference tools but are vulnerable to bias if the assumed model is incorrect. Nonparametric approaches, by contrast, make fewer assumptions but typically require larger datasets to achieve comparable precision. Our comparative discussion highlights that the optimal choice depends on the available prior knowledge, the cost of data acquisition, and the tolerance for model misspecification.

A notable implication of our findings is that the design of measurement protocols for random observables must be informed by an explicit trade-off between resolution and statistical stability. Increasing resolution—whether by refining instrument sensitivity or by narrowing sampling intervals—may reduce certain types of error but can also exacerbate the impact of intrinsic fluctuations, thereby increasing the total uncertainty. Similarly, averaging over larger ensembles can suppress random noise but may obscure fine-grained features of the observable’s distribution that are of scientific interest. Balancing these competing effects requires a clear articulation of the measurement’s objectives and the statistical characteristics most relevant to those objectives.

We have also touched upon the conceptual parallels between the measurement of classical random observables and the measurement of quantum observables described by mixed states. In both cases, the outcome statistics encode complete information about the system only in the limit of infinitely many trials, and in both cases, the uncertainty is an inextricable feature of the system’s description rather than merely an artefact of measurement imperfections. This analogy, while not exact, suggests that techniques developed in one domain—such as quantum tomography or Bayesian state reconstruction—may inspire novel strategies for measuring and interpreting random observables in other domains.

Looking forward, our analysis points to several promising directions for further research. One is the development of adaptive measurement schemes that dynamically adjust sampling parameters in response to real-time estimates of uncertainty, thereby optimising resource allocation. Another is the integration of robust statistical methods that remain effective under departures from idealised distributional assumptions, which is especially important in complex experimental settings where noise processes may be non-Gaussian or nonstationary. Finally, there is a need for deeper theoretical work to establish universal bounds on the precision of measurements for broad classes of random observables, extending existing results from estimation theory and information geometry.

In summary, the study of measurements regarding random observables requires a careful synthesis of statistical theory, measurement science, and domain-specific modelling. By explicitly recognising the stochastic nature of the quantities under investigation, we can better characterise the limits of measurement precision, design protocols that are fit for purpose, and interpret experimental data in a manner that respects both the intrinsic variability of the observable and the extrinsic imperfections of the measurement process. The framework and results presented here serve as a foundation for such endeavours, and it is our hope that they will inform both theoretical inquiry and practical experimentation across a range of disciplines where randomness is an essential feature of the observables of interest.

title: Solar wind collisional heating
abstract: The solar wind is a weakly collisional plasma whose thermodynamic evolution is governed by a complex interplay between adiabatic expansion, turbulent dissipation, and particle–particle collisions. While collisionless processes are widely recognized as the dominant heating mechanisms in the heliosphere, Coulomb collisions can still play a significant role in redistributing energy between particle species and regulating temperature anisotropies, particularly in the slow wind and near the Sun. In this study, we investigate the contribution of collisional heating to the large-scale energy budget of the solar wind using in situ measurements from multiple heliocentric distances combined with kinetic transport modeling. We quantify collisional energy exchange rates between protons and electrons, evaluate the dependence on heliocentric distance and solar wind speed, and assess the relative importance of collisions compared to turbulent dissipation. Our results indicate that collisional processes are non-negligible within ~0.3 AU, where they act to equilibrate temperatures and reduce heat fluxes, but become progressively less effective beyond 1 AU. We find that collisional heating can account for a measurable fraction of the observed proton and electron temperature profiles in the inner heliosphere, implying that accurate solar wind models must incorporate both collisional and collisionless heating to reproduce the observed thermodynamic evolution.
introduction: The solar wind is a continuous outflow of plasma from the Sun, composed primarily of protons, electrons, and alpha particles, propagating through interplanetary space. Its dynamics and thermodynamics are governed by a complex interplay of expansion, wave–particle interactions, turbulence, and collisional processes. While the solar wind is generally considered to be a weakly collisional medium, Coulomb collisions can still play a significant role in regulating particle distributions, facilitating energy exchange between species, and contributing to heating. Understanding the extent and mechanisms of collisional heating is essential for interpreting in situ spacecraft observations and for constraining models of solar wind acceleration and evolution. Previous studies have shown that the relative importance of collisional effects varies with heliocentric distance, solar wind speed, and plasma parameters such as density and temperature anisotropy. However, the quantitative contribution of collisions to the overall energy budget remains uncertain, particularly in the presence of competing kinetic and turbulent dissipation mechanisms. This work investigates the role of collisional heating in the solar wind by combining theoretical estimates with empirical constraints from spacecraft data, aiming to clarify its significance across different solar wind regimes and its implications for heliospheric plasma physics.
conclusion:
In this study, we have examined the role of collisional processes in the heating of the solar wind, with a particular emphasis on quantifying their contribution relative to collisionless mechanisms across different heliocentric distances. By combining theoretical considerations, observational constraints, and numerical modeling, we have provided a coherent framework for understanding how Coulomb collisions operate in a plasma that is often assumed to be nearly collisionless. Our analysis shows that while the mean free path of particles in the solar wind is generally large compared to characteristic system scales, collisional effects cannot be neglected entirely, especially in the near-Sun environment and in regions of enhanced density.

Our results indicate that collisional thermalization rates are strongly dependent on both local plasma parameters and the anisotropy of the particle velocity distributions. In particular, in the inner heliosphere, where densities are higher and temperatures lower, proton-proton and proton-electron collisions can contribute non-negligibly to the redistribution of energy among particle species. This collisional coupling tends to reduce temperature anisotropies and drive the system toward Maxwellian equilibrium, thereby modulating the efficiency of wave-particle interactions and turbulent dissipation processes. Farther from the Sun, the decreasing density and increasing temperature anisotropy lead to a rapid decline in collisional rates, rendering collisionless processes the dominant source of heating.

Our modeling also underscores the importance of considering the interplay between collisional and collisionless channels. The presence of collisions, even at low frequencies, can influence the cascade of turbulent energy by modifying the shape of particle distribution functions, which in turn affects the growth and damping rates of kinetic instabilities. This coupling suggests that heating in the solar wind cannot be fully understood by treating collisional and collisionless processes in isolation. Instead, a holistic description is required, in which the collisional relaxation of nonthermal features plays a complementary role to wave dissipation, stochastic heating, and reconnection-driven energization.

From an observational standpoint, our findings are consistent with in-situ measurements from missions such as Helios, Wind, and Parker Solar Probe, which reveal a gradual evolution of distribution functions and temperature ratios with radial distance. The agreement between modeled collisional relaxation rates and those inferred from data supports the view that collisional heating, while secondary in the outer heliosphere, has a measurable and sometimes significant impact closer to the Sun. This has implications for interpreting plasma diagnostics and for constraining the energy budget of the solar wind.

In summary, collisional heating in the solar wind is neither entirely negligible nor universally dominant; its significance varies with heliocentric distance, plasma conditions, and the relative strength of other dissipation mechanisms. Recognizing the nuanced role of Coulomb collisions offers a more complete picture of solar wind thermodynamics and provides essential context for upcoming high-resolution measurements. Future work should focus on integrating fully kinetic treatments of both collisional and collisionless processes into global solar wind models, enabling a more accurate prediction of plasma heating throughout the heliosphere.

title: A Decoupled Scheme to Solve the Mass and Momentum Conservation Equations of the Improved Darcy-Brinkman-Forchheimer Framework in Matrix Acidization
abstract: Matrix acidization is a key stimulation technique in petroleum engineering, where accurate modeling of fluid flow through porous media is essential for predicting treatment efficiency. In this work, we present a decoupled numerical scheme for solving the mass and momentum conservation equations within the improved Darcy–Brinkman–Forchheimer framework, which accounts for viscous, inertial, and permeability-dependent effects in acidizing processes. The proposed algorithm separates the pressure and velocity computations, enabling efficient and stable simulations over a wide range of flow regimes. By reformulating the coupled nonlinear system into sequential subproblems, the method reduces computational complexity while preserving second-order spatial accuracy. Numerical experiments demonstrate the scheme’s robustness in handling highly heterogeneous permeability fields and nonlinear drag terms induced by the Forchheimer correction. Comparisons with fully coupled solvers show that the decoupled approach achieves comparable accuracy with significantly reduced computational cost. This framework provides a reliable and efficient tool for simulating reactive flow in porous media, facilitating better design and optimization of matrix acidization treatments in complex reservoir conditions.
introduction:
Matrix acidization is a widely employed stimulation technique in petroleum engineering for enhancing the permeability of hydrocarbon-bearing formations. In carbonate and certain sandstone reservoirs, the injection of reactive acid solutions dissolves pore-blocking mineral constituents, creating or enlarging flow channels and thereby improving fluid transport. The design and optimization of such treatments require accurate mathematical models capable of representing the coupled processes of fluid flow, chemical reaction, and porous medium alteration. Among the various modeling approaches, continuum-scale flow models based on extensions of Darcy’s law are central to predicting the evolution of pressure, velocity, and porosity fields during acid injection.

The classical Darcy equation adequately describes creeping flows in porous media under low Reynolds number conditions, but it neglects important physical effects when inertial and viscous shear contributions become significant. The Darcy–Brinkman formulation extends the Darcy model by incorporating a viscous diffusion term, accounting for velocity gradients within the pore space. At higher injection rates, inertial effects further modify the flow resistance, necessitating the inclusion of a nonlinear Forchheimer term. The resulting Darcy–Brinkman–Forchheimer (DBF) framework provides a more comprehensive description of momentum transport in porous media, capturing a broader range of flow regimes relevant to acidization processes.

In the context of matrix acidization, additional complexities arise due to the evolving pore geometry as mineral dissolution progresses. Changes in porosity and permeability alter the coefficients in the governing equations, leading to strong coupling between the mass conservation equation and the nonlinear momentum equation. This coupling poses challenges for numerical simulation, as it can lead to stiff systems that are computationally demanding to solve, especially in three-dimensional domains or when fine spatial resolution is required to resolve wormholing patterns. Therefore, the development of efficient and stable numerical schemes that can handle the nonlinearities and couplings inherent in the improved DBF framework is an important research objective.

Traditional approaches to solving the coupled mass and momentum equations often employ fully implicit schemes that require the simultaneous solution of large, nonlinear algebraic systems. While robust, such methods can be computationally expensive and may face convergence difficulties when dealing with strong nonlinearities or large time steps. An alternative is to employ decoupling strategies, which separate the solution of the pressure (or mass conservation) equation from that of the velocity (momentum conservation) equation. By appropriately reformulating the governing equations, these methods can reduce computational cost and improve numerical stability, while retaining sufficient accuracy for engineering predictions.

The present work proposes and evaluates a decoupled numerical scheme tailored to the improved Darcy–Brinkman–Forchheimer model for matrix acidization. The scheme treats the mass and momentum conservation equations separately within each time step, allowing the efficient use of solvers optimized for each subproblem. Special attention is given to the treatment of the nonlinear Forchheimer term and to maintaining consistency between the decoupled fields. The proposed approach aims to provide a balance between computational efficiency and physical fidelity, making it suitable for large-scale simulations of acidization treatments where predictive capability and turnaround time are both critical.

In the following sections, the improved DBF framework is briefly reviewed, the decoupling strategy is described in detail, and the scheme’s performance is assessed through numerical experiments. The implications of the method for the design and optimization of acid stimulation treatments are also discussed.
conclusion:
In this work, a decoupled numerical scheme has been developed and assessed for solving the mass and momentum conservation equations arising from the improved Darcy–Brinkman–Forchheimer framework, with specific application to matrix acidization processes. By reformulating the coupled system into sequentially solvable subproblems, the proposed approach effectively isolates the pressure (mass conservation) and velocity (momentum conservation) computations, thereby reducing the complexity and computational cost typically associated with fully coupled solvers. The scheme accommodates the nonlinear Forchheimer term and the viscosity variations induced by acid–rock interactions, ensuring its applicability to realistic acidization scenarios.

Validation against benchmark solutions and available experimental trends demonstrated that the decoupled method maintains high accuracy in predicting pressure drops, velocity fields, and permeability evolution during acid injection. The algorithm exhibited robust convergence characteristics over a broad range of flow regimes, from Darcy-dominated to strongly inertial conditions, confirming its suitability for simulating the transitional behavior encountered in practice. Moreover, the flexibility of the formulation allows straightforward integration with reactive transport models, making it a promising tool for studying wormhole growth and optimizing acid placement.

The computational efficiency gained through decoupling was particularly evident in large-scale simulations, where reduced solution times were achieved without compromising numerical stability. This advantage is critical for iterative engineering workflows, such as sensitivity analysis and design optimization, where multiple realizations are required. Importantly, the method retains the physical completeness of the improved Darcy–Brinkman–Forchheimer framework, ensuring that both viscous and inertial effects, as well as microscale flow features, are adequately captured.

Overall, the proposed decoupled scheme constitutes a reliable and efficient alternative to monolithic solvers for the simulation of flow in porous media under acidizing conditions. Future work will focus on coupling the present approach with detailed geochemical reaction models and extending it to three-dimensional, heterogeneous formations to further enhance predictive capabilities for field-scale applications.

title: Synthesizing 3D Shapes from Silhouette Image Collections using Multi-projection Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: We present a novel framework for synthesizing high-quality 3D shapes from unstructured collections of silhouette images using a multi-projection generative adversarial network (MP-GAN). Unlike existing 3D reconstruction approaches that require dense multi-view correspondences or explicit 3D supervision, our method learns directly from independent silhouette images captured from diverse viewpoints. The core idea is to jointly model multiple orthogonal projections of a shape within a unified adversarial learning paradigm, enabling the network to capture consistent geometric structures across views while leveraging the simplicity of silhouette representations. The MP-GAN architecture incorporates a multi-branch generator that produces synchronized projections and a discriminator ensemble that enforces both intra-view fidelity and inter-view consistency. To recover full 3D geometry, we integrate the generated projections into a volumetric shape representation through a differentiable projection consistency module. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of shape plausibility, structural consistency, and generalization to unseen object categories. The proposed framework provides a scalable and annotation-efficient pathway for 3D shape synthesis from widely available silhouette image collections, opening new possibilities for applications in computer vision, graphics, and digital content creation.
introduction:
Recent advances in deep generative models have enabled significant progress in synthesizing realistic three-dimensional (3D) shapes from various forms of input data. Among these, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable capability in learning complex data distributions and producing high-fidelity samples in domains such as image synthesis, texture generation, and 3D shape modeling. However, synthesizing accurate and diverse 3D shapes remains challenging, particularly when only limited or partial observations are available. In many practical scenarios, obtaining dense 3D supervision requires expensive scanning equipment or labor-intensive manual modeling, making large-scale datasets of complete 3D geometry scarce. By contrast, silhouette images—binary masks capturing object outlines from different viewpoints—are often easier to acquire, for example from photographs, videos, or existing image collections. This motivates the exploration of silhouette-based 3D shape synthesis methods that can leverage such abundant yet weakly supervised data.

Silhouette images provide rich structural cues about object geometry, as the contours encode essential shape information across views. Nevertheless, inferring full 3D structure from silhouettes alone is inherently ill-posed: many distinct 3D shapes can produce identical 2D silhouettes under certain viewpoints. Overcoming this ambiguity requires models that can aggregate information from multiple silhouettes, reason about multi-view consistency, and learn powerful shape priors from data. Traditional multi-view reconstruction pipelines often rely on precise camera calibration and a dense set of viewpoints to resolve ambiguities, which may not be feasible in unstructured image collections. Recent neural approaches have attempted to relax these constraints by learning implicit shape representations from images, but many still depend on additional supervision such as depth maps, point clouds, or explicit 3D models.

In this work, we introduce a Multi-projection Generative Adversarial Network (MP-GAN) for synthesizing 3D shapes from unstructured collections of silhouette images. Our key insight is to integrate multi-view projection operations directly into the generative process, enabling the network to learn a 3D shape generator whose outputs are consistent with silhouettes from multiple viewpoints. The generator produces a volumetric or implicit shape representation, which is then projected into 2D silhouettes along several sampled camera poses. These projections are compared against real silhouette images by a discriminator that jointly considers both individual view realism and cross-view coherence. By training adversarially on diverse silhouette datasets without requiring explicit 3D ground truth, our approach learns to synthesize plausible and view-consistent 3D shapes that adhere to the structural constraints observed in the input image collection.

The proposed MP-GAN framework addresses several limitations of prior silhouette-based methods. First, by leveraging multiple projections during training, it enforces geometric consistency across viewpoints, reducing the likelihood of generating shapes that fit only a single view. Second, it naturally accommodates uncalibrated or sparsely sampled views, making it applicable to less controlled data sources. Finally, the adversarial objective encourages high-fidelity shape generation that captures fine-scale structural variations present in the training set. Experimental results on benchmark silhouette datasets demonstrate that MP-GAN produces more accurate and diverse 3D shapes than existing baselines, highlighting its potential for scalable 3D content creation from widely available 2D resources.
conclusion: In this work, we presented a novel framework for synthesizing 3D shapes from unstructured collections of silhouette images using a multi‑projection generative adversarial network. By leveraging multiple, complementary 2D projections during both training and inference, our method effectively learns a coherent implicit 3D representation without requiring explicit 3D supervision. The proposed architecture integrates a projection consistency module that enforces geometric plausibility across viewpoints, enabling the generation of shapes that preserve fine structural details while maintaining global shape fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing single‑view and multi‑view baselines in terms of visual realism, structural consistency, and shape diversity. Moreover, our framework exhibits strong generalization to novel categories and unseen viewpoints, highlighting its potential for scalable 3D content creation from readily available image data. While our current implementation focuses on binary silhouettes, future work could explore the integration of richer image cues such as shading, texture, and depth to further improve reconstruction accuracy. Additionally, extending the method to handle noisy or imperfect silhouettes would increase its applicability to real‑world scenarios. Overall, the proposed multi‑projection GAN framework provides an effective and flexible solution for bridging the gap between 2D image collections and high‑quality 3D shape synthesis.

title: A surviving disk from a galaxy collision at z=0.4
abstract: We report the discovery and analysis of a massive star-forming disk galaxy that has survived a recent major merger at redshift \( z = 0.4 \). Deep multi-band imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope, combined with integral-field spectroscopy from VLT/MUSE, reveals a prominent stellar disk embedded within an extended tidal envelope. Kinematic maps show ordered rotation with a maximum velocity of \( \sim 220 \) km s\(^{-1}\) and a low velocity dispersion, indicating that the disk has largely re-formed or survived despite the violent interaction. The surrounding low-surface-brightness features, including tidal tails and shells, suggest a mass ratio between 1:1 and 1:3, and dynamical modelling constrains the merger to have occurred within the past 1 Gyr. The galaxy exhibits ongoing star formation at a rate of \( \sim 15 \) M\(_\odot\) yr\(^{-1}\), concentrated along spiral arms, consistent with a replenished gas supply. This system provides direct evidence that massive stellar disks can persist or rapidly regenerate after major mergers at intermediate redshift, challenging models in which such events invariably destroy disk structures. Our findings have significant implications for the role of mergers in shaping the morphological evolution of galaxies over the past 4 Gyr.
introduction:
Galaxy interactions and mergers are fundamental drivers of galaxy evolution, capable of transforming morphology, redistributing angular momentum, and triggering enhanced star formation. In the hierarchical framework of structure formation, such events are expected to be common over cosmic time, with the frequency of major mergers peaking at intermediate redshifts (z ≈ 1–2) and declining toward the present epoch. While the most dramatic interactions can produce spheroidal remnants with little evidence of ordered rotation, observations and simulations increasingly suggest that disk components can sometimes survive, or be re-formed, following significant merger events. Identifying and characterizing such systems at different stages of their evolution provides important constraints on the timescales, physical conditions, and dynamical processes at play during and after galaxy collisions.

In the local Universe, post-merger galaxies exhibiting well-ordered disks are relatively rare, but carefully studied systems such as NGC 7252 demonstrate that large-scale, rotationally supported components can persist long after the initial coalescence. At higher redshifts, where the gas fractions of galaxies are typically larger, the dissipative nature of the interstellar medium may promote the survival or regrowth of disks following an encounter. Hydrodynamical simulations have shown that gas-rich major mergers can result in remnant galaxies with substantial disk components, particularly when orbital configurations and feedback processes are favorable. Nevertheless, the observational record of such systems at intermediate redshifts remains sparse, owing to the challenges of detecting both the kinematic signatures of ordered rotation and the morphological evidence of a recent collision.

At z ≈ 0.4, corresponding to a look-back time of roughly 4 Gyr, the Universe was transitioning from the more merger-rich environment of earlier epochs toward the relatively quiescent conditions we observe locally. This period offers a valuable window into the later stages of disk survival and reformation, where tidal features may still be visible and stellar populations retain a record of the interaction, yet the structural settling of the remnant may be well underway. Integral field spectroscopy and deep, high-resolution imaging are essential tools for probing such systems, enabling the simultaneous study of stellar and gas kinematics, star formation activity, and the distribution of tidal debris.

Previous surveys, including those conducted with the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based integral field units, have identified a small number of candidate post-merger disks at intermediate redshifts. These studies have begun to quantify the prevalence of disk survival, but questions remain regarding the detailed conditions that allow for the preservation of rotationally supported structures. The interplay between gas content, merger geometry, feedback efficiency, and the timescale for dynamical relaxation is complex, and direct observational constraints are critical for refining theoretical models.

In this work, we present the discovery and analysis of a galaxy at z = 0.4 that exhibits clear morphological evidence of a recent major merger, including extended tidal features, while simultaneously hosting a well-ordered, large-scale stellar and gaseous disk. Using a combination of deep optical imaging and spatially resolved spectroscopy, we investigate the structural, kinematic, and star-forming properties of this system. Our study provides new insight into the processes that enable disk survival in the aftermath of a galaxy collision, and contributes to a growing body of evidence that such outcomes may be more common than previously thought under certain physical conditions.
conclusion:
Our analysis of the system at \( z = 0.4 \) provides compelling evidence for the survival of a stellar disk following a significant galaxy–galaxy collision. High-resolution imaging and spectroscopic data reveal a coherent rotational component embedded within a disturbed stellar halo and tidal debris, indicating that the primary disk structure has persisted despite the disruptive encounter. The preservation of ordered kinematics, together with the asymmetric distribution of tidal features, supports a scenario in which the progenitor disk was only partially heated and thickened, rather than completely destroyed.  

These results challenge the traditional view that major mergers at intermediate redshift invariably lead to spheroidal remnants. Instead, they suggest that under certain orbital configurations, mass ratios, and gas fractions, disks can survive or be rapidly re-formed after the interaction. This has important implications for models of galaxy evolution, particularly in reproducing the observed fraction of disk galaxies at later epochs.  

The case studied here offers a valuable benchmark for testing hydrodynamical simulations of galaxy mergers, especially in constraining the physical conditions under which disk survival is possible. Future studies, combining deeper integral-field spectroscopy and higher-resolution imaging, will further elucidate the role of merger geometry and feedback in shaping the fate of galactic disks in the evolving universe. Our observations underscore the resilience of disk structures even in dynamically violent environments.

title: Effective Hamiltonians, prethermalization and slow energy absorption in periodically driven many-body systems
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of periodically driven interacting quantum many-body systems, focusing on the emergence of effective Hamiltonians, prethermalization, and slow energy absorption. Using high-frequency expansions and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that for sufficiently rapid driving, the system’s evolution is well captured by an effective static Hamiltonian over an extended intermediate time window. In this prethermal regime, local observables relax to quasi-stationary values distinct from infinite-temperature expectations, and heating to the featureless steady state is exponentially suppressed in the driving frequency. We analyze the breakdown of the prethermal plateau and quantify the heating rate, highlighting the role of resonances and many-body interactions. Our results provide a unified framework connecting Floquet theory, energy absorption bounds, and emergent conservation laws, offering guidance for experimental control of driven quantum matter in platforms ranging from cold atoms to solid-state systems.
introduction:
Periodically driven quantum many-body systems have emerged as a central theme in contemporary condensed matter physics, quantum optics, and cold atom research. By subjecting a system to a time-periodic modulation of its parameters, new dynamical regimes can be accessed that have no static analogues. This approach, often referred to within the Floquet framework, has enabled the engineering of artificial gauge fields, the realization of topological band structures, and the control of interaction strengths in ultracold atomic gases. The central theoretical construct underpinning much of this progress is the *effective Hamiltonian*, which governs the stroboscopic evolution of the system over one driving period. In the high-frequency limit, the effective Hamiltonian can be obtained via systematic expansions such as the Magnus or van Vleck expansions, and it often captures the essential physics over experimentally relevant timescales.

However, the utility of the effective Hamiltonian description in interacting systems is constrained by the fundamental fact that a generic periodically driven many-body system tends to absorb energy from the drive, ultimately heating up to a featureless infinite-temperature state. This energy absorption is an intrinsically non-equilibrium process, and it poses a challenge to the stabilization of non-trivial phases of matter under periodic driving. In the low-frequency regime, heating can be rapid, and the effective Hamiltonian picture breaks down quickly. In contrast, when the driving frequency is large compared to the characteristic local energy scales of the system, heating can be parametrically suppressed: the system exhibits a *prethermal regime* in which it evolves for a very long time under the governance of a quasi-conserved effective Hamiltonian before eventual thermalization sets in.

The phenomenon of prethermalization in Floquet systems has attracted significant attention in recent years. It connects to a broader set of ideas in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics concerning the emergence of long-lived quasi-stationary states in systems driven far from equilibrium. In the Floquet context, the prethermal regime offers a window in which novel steady states and phases can be stabilized and studied experimentally. Theoretically, this regime is characterized by an exponentially long heating time in the driving frequency, and the effective Hamiltonian can be constructed to high order in a controlled expansion. This leads to a remarkably accurate description of observables in the system up to the eventual heating time. Understanding the structure and limitations of such effective Hamiltonians, and quantifying the slow energy absorption that accompanies their breakdown, is thus a problem of both fundamental and practical importance.

A number of rigorous results have established bounds on the energy absorption rate in periodically driven many-body systems with local interactions. These works show that for sufficiently high driving frequencies, the heating rate is exponentially small in the ratio of the drive frequency to the local energy scale. The essential mechanism underlying this suppression is the locality of interactions, which constrains the many-body resonances responsible for energy absorption. In such settings, the effective Hamiltonian can be defined in a way that it is quasi-conserved over times that are exponentially long in the frequency. This provides a controlled setting in which to explore the interplay between coherent Hamiltonian dynamics and weak residual heating.

From a physical perspective, the prethermal regime can be viewed as an emergent equilibrium governed by the effective Hamiltonian, in which standard thermodynamic concepts apply, albeit with respect to quasi-conserved quantities. This picture has been corroborated by numerical simulations in spin systems, fermionic Hubbard models, and bosonic lattice models, as well as by experiments in ultracold atom setups. In these realizations, signatures of prethermalization include the persistence of order parameters, correlation functions, and topological invariants over long times, followed by a slow drift towards infinite temperature. The timescale of this drift is set by the exponentially small heating rate, which depends sensitively on the driving frequency and amplitude.

Despite these advances, several open questions remain. One central issue concerns the precise form and range of validity of the effective Hamiltonian beyond leading-order expansions, particularly in regimes where the drive frequency is not asymptotically large. Another challenge lies in understanding the crossover from the prethermal plateau to the eventual thermalized state, and in identifying universal features of this crossover. Moreover, in certain systems with additional conservation laws, disorder, or constraints, heating can be suppressed indefinitely, leading to genuinely non-thermal Floquet phases. Distinguishing such genuinely stable phases from long-lived prethermal ones is an important problem, both for theoretical classification and for experimental identification.
