In this work, we focus on the construction of effective Hamiltonians for periodically driven interacting systems in the high-frequency regime, and on the quantitative characterization of slow energy absorption. We aim to bridge rigorous bounds on heating with explicit calculations in concrete models, thereby elucidating the mechanisms controlling the onset and duration of the prethermal regime. Our approach combines analytical techniques for deriving effective Hamiltonians with numerical simulations to track the real-time evolution of observables and the growth of energy. By comparing the predictions of truncated effective Hamiltonians with exact dynamics, we assess the accuracy of the prethermal description and determine its breakdown time.

The results presented here contribute to a deeper understanding of how coherent many-body dynamics can persist in driven systems despite the generic tendency towards heating. They also inform the design of driving protocols that maximize the prethermal lifetime, which is of direct relevance to the realization of nontrivial Floquet phases in experiments. More broadly, our analysis sheds light on fundamental aspects of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, including the emergence of effective conservation laws and the mechanisms of their eventual violation. In doing so, we aim to provide a unified framework for thinking about effective Hamiltonians, prethermalization, and slow energy absorption in periodically driven many-body systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the emergence and applicability of effective Hamiltonians in the description of periodically driven many-body systems, with a particular focus on the regimes of prethermalization and slow energy absorption. By combining analytical insights with numerical evidence, we have elucidated how high-frequency driving can give rise to an extended temporal window in which the system’s dynamics are well captured by an effective static description, before eventual heating to an infinite-temperature state sets in. Our results underscore the central role of the drive frequency, interaction strength, and the structure of the underlying static Hamiltonian in determining the lifetime and properties of the prethermal regime.

We have shown that in the high-frequency limit, the Floquet-Magnus expansion offers a systematic route to constructing effective Hamiltonians that accurately reproduce the stroboscopic evolution over long timescales. Even when the expansion is truncated, the resulting effective model captures the essential features of local observables and correlation functions within a prethermal plateau. The breakdown of this description is governed by rare, higher-order processes that mediate energy absorption from the drive, and whose rates are exponentially suppressed in the ratio of the drive frequency to the characteristic local energy scales. This explains the observed separation of timescales between rapid relaxation to a quasi-steady state and the much slower heating towards infinite temperature.

Our analysis highlights that prethermalization in driven systems shares important similarities with its equilibrium counterpart in quenched dynamics, but is distinguished by the presence of a time-periodic Hamiltonian and the associated Floquet structure. In particular, the effective Hamiltonian is not simply a renormalized static Hamiltonian, but can contain qualitatively new terms reflecting the symmetry properties and micromotion induced by the drive. This opens up possibilities for engineering nontrivial phases of matter, including those without equilibrium analogues, within the prethermal window. The controlled suppression of heating is thus not only of fundamental interest for understanding nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, but also of practical relevance for quantum simulation and quantum control.

We have also discussed the dependence of the heating rate on system size and dimensionality, and the implications for both integrable and nonintegrable models. While integrable systems may exhibit additional constraints on heating due to conserved quantities, our results indicate that the qualitative picture of a long-lived prethermal regime at high frequencies remains robust in generic interacting systems, with the quantitative lifetime determined by the details of the microscopic processes that break integrability.

Looking forward, our findings suggest several promising directions. Extending the present framework to systems with disorder, long-range interactions, or coupling to external baths may reveal new mechanisms for stabilizing prethermal phases or modifying heating processes. Moreover, the interplay between topology, symmetry, and prethermalization in Floquet systems remains a fertile ground for exploration, with potential implications for realizing robust edge states or time-crystalline behavior over experimentally relevant timescales.

In summary, the concept of an effective Hamiltonian provides a powerful organizing principle for understanding the transient yet long-lived regimes of coherent dynamics in periodically driven many-body systems. The persistence of prethermalization and the exponential suppression of heating at high driving frequencies link microscopic dynamics to emergent nonequilibrium phenomena, offering both a deeper theoretical understanding and a toolbox for experimental control of complex quantum matter.

title: Simulations and interpretation of the 6-cm MERLIN images of the classical nova V723 Cas
abstract: We present simulations and an interpretation of the 6-cm MERLIN radio images of the classical nova V723 Cas, obtained over a four-year period following its 1995 outburst. The observations reveal evolving, partially resolved structures exhibiting changes in morphology, flux density, and angular size. To investigate the origin of these features, we employ three-dimensional hydrodynamical models of nova ejecta, incorporating both spherical and axisymmetric geometries, and generate synthetic radio images through radiative transfer calculations at the MERLIN observing wavelength and resolution. Comparison between model outputs and the observed data suggests that the radio emission is dominated by thermal bremsstrahlung from an expanding, clumpy shell with significant departures from spherical symmetry. The apparent asymmetries in the MERLIN maps can be reproduced by introducing modest bipolar elongations and density inhomogeneities into the ejecta. The simulated light curves and structural evolution are broadly consistent with observed trends, supporting a scenario in which the nova ejecta interact with pre-existing circumstellar material, enhancing anisotropy. Our results demonstrate the utility of combining high-resolution radio imaging with numerical modeling to probe the geometry, density distribution, and evolution of nova remnants.
introduction:
Classical novae are cataclysmic variable systems in which a white dwarf accretes material from a companion star, leading to a thermonuclear runaway on the surface of the white dwarf once sufficient hydrogen-rich material has accumulated. The resulting eruption ejects material into the surrounding space at velocities of several hundred to a few thousand kilometres per second, producing a rapidly evolving remnant whose emission can be studied across the electromagnetic spectrum. Radio observations provide a unique diagnostic of the ejecta, being sensitive to both the density distribution and ionisation state of the material, and are particularly valuable for constraining the geometry and physical parameters of the nova shell. 

V723 Cas, a slow nova discovered in August 1995, has been the subject of extensive multiwavelength monitoring due to its unusually prolonged optical light curve evolution and complex spectroscopic behaviour. Its relatively nearby distance and extended outburst timescale make it an excellent candidate for detailed imaging of the remnant structure. Observations at centimetre wavelengths can directly probe the thermal free–free emission from the ionised ejecta, allowing the morphology and expansion of the shell to be tracked over time. The Multi-Element Radio Linked Interferometer Network (MERLIN), with its high angular resolution at 6 cm, is particularly well suited to resolving structures on sub-arcsecond scales in such novae.

Previous studies of radio emission from classical novae have revealed a range of morphologies, including spherical shells, bipolar flows, and more complex asymmetric structures. Interpretation of these images, however, is not always straightforward due to projection effects, optical depth variations, and the limitations imposed by interferometric imaging. To disentangle these factors, numerical simulations of expanding ejecta with different geometries, density profiles, and inclination angles can be used to generate synthetic radio images for direct comparison with observations. By matching simulated morphologies to the data, it is possible to derive constraints on the intrinsic three-dimensional structure of the nova shell and on the physical processes shaping its evolution.

In this work, we present simulations and interpretations of the 6-cm MERLIN images of V723 Cas obtained during the years following its outburst. We describe the observational dataset, the modelling approach used to reproduce the observed structures, and the implications for the geometry and dynamics of the ejecta. Our aim is to assess the consistency of the radio morphology with simple geometric models and to explore the extent to which departures from spherical symmetry are required to explain the data.
conclusion:
The simulations and subsequent comparison with the 6-cm MERLIN observations of V723 Cas have provided valuable insight into the morphology and evolution of the nova remnant. By constructing model brightness distributions based on plausible geometries and physical parameters, and by subjecting these to the same sampling and imaging procedures as the actual MERLIN data, we have been able to disentangle genuine structural features from artefacts introduced by the interferometric response and sparse uv-coverage. The results demonstrate that even relatively simple axisymmetric shell models, when inclined appropriately to the line of sight, can reproduce several of the salient characteristics of the observed images, including the apparent clumpiness and asymmetry. At the same time, the simulations reveal that some of these apparent irregularities may arise from the incomplete Fourier sampling and deconvolution process, cautioning against overinterpretation of fine-scale structure in the maps.

The comparison between models and observations supports an interpretation in which the radio emission is dominated by a slowly expanding shell with modest equatorial enhancement, consistent with previous optical spectroscopy and imaging. The inferred expansion velocities and flux densities imply that the ejecta remain partially optically thick at 6 cm at the epochs observed, and the evolution of the brightness distribution can be understood in the context of free–free emission from a thermal plasma undergoing homologous expansion. The agreement between simulated and observed flux recovery also indicates that the MERLIN array, despite its limitations, is capable of capturing the bulk of the emission for sources of this angular scale.

These findings underline the importance of forward-modelling interferometric observations when interpreting complex, evolving astrophysical sources. For novae in particular, where rapid morphological changes occur on timescales of months to years, the combination of physically motivated models and realistic simulations of array performance provides a powerful tool for extracting reliable structural information. In the case of V723 Cas, the approach has allowed us to place constraints on the geometry and density distribution of the ejecta, assess the significance of apparent substructure, and better understand the imaging artefacts inherent in the data. Future high-sensitivity, higher-resolution observations with upgraded arrays, combined with multiwavelength monitoring, will further refine these models and help to build a comprehensive picture of the shaping processes in nova remnants.

title: On Representing Linear Programs by Graph Neural Networks
abstract: We investigate the representation of linear programs (LPs) within the framework of graph neural networks (GNNs). Linear programs, defined by linear objective functions and constraints, possess rich combinatorial and geometric structure that can be naturally encoded as bipartite graphs linking variables and constraints. We propose a methodology for mapping LP instances to graph-based representations that preserve problem-specific features such as sparsity patterns, constraint coefficients, and objective weights. Our approach enables GNNs to learn from both the topology and numerical attributes of LPs, supporting tasks such as solution prediction, feasibility classification, and warm-start generation for solvers. We analyze the expressive power of several GNN architectures in capturing LP structure, and evaluate performance on diverse benchmark datasets. Results indicate that graph-based models can effectively approximate LP solution properties, offering a promising direction for integrating machine learning with classical optimization techniques.
introduction:
Linear programming (LP) is a foundational tool in operations research, optimization, and decision-making, with applications ranging from supply chain management to machine learning. Classical algorithms such as the simplex method and interior-point methods offer exact solutions with well-understood theoretical guarantees. However, in large-scale and real-time scenarios, these methods may face computational limitations, motivating the exploration of alternative representations and solution strategies. Recent advances in machine learning, and in particular graph neural networks (GNNs), have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in learning from structured data. Since LP instances can be naturally expressed through the relationships between variables and constraints, graph-based representations offer a promising avenue for incorporating LP structure into neural models.

Graph neural networks have been successfully applied to combinatorial optimization problems, where they learn heuristics that generalize across problem instances. Extending these approaches to LPs raises key questions: how to encode continuous-valued coefficients and constraints into graph structures, how to preserve problem-specific symmetries, and how to ensure that learned models respect feasibility and optimality properties. In this work, we investigate principled methods for representing LPs as graphs suitable for GNN processing. We analyze different encoding schemes, study their expressive power, and evaluate their effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world LP benchmarks. Our goal is to bridge the gap between traditional LP solvers and modern graph-based learning frameworks, enabling new hybrid approaches to large-scale optimization.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated the representation of linear programs within the framework of graph neural networks, proposing a principled encoding that captures both structural and numerical properties of problem instances. Our approach enables learning-based models to exploit the inherent graph structure of linear programs, facilitating generalization across varied problem sizes and types. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed representation supports accurate prediction of solution properties and efficient approximation of optimization outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of graph-based learning for combinatorial optimization. Future research will explore scalability, integration with solver heuristics, and theoretical guarantees on representational fidelity.

title: Generalized Isotonic Regression
abstract: We present a unified framework for generalized isotonic regression that extends classical monotonic regression to a broad class of loss functions and constraints. Our formulation accommodates diverse error measures, including convex and certain non-convex losses, while preserving the monotonicity structure inherent in ordered data. We develop efficient optimization algorithms based on block coordinate descent and active set methods, ensuring scalability to large datasets. Theoretical analysis establishes existence, uniqueness, and convergence properties under mild conditions. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate superior predictive accuracy and robustness compared to standard isotonic regression, particularly in the presence of heteroscedastic noise and asymmetric error penalties. This work broadens the applicability of isotonic modeling in statistics, machine learning, and related fields requiring order-preserving prediction.
introduction: Generalized isotonic regression extends classical isotonic regression to accommodate complex constraints and loss functions, enabling broader applicability across diverse domains. By relaxing traditional assumptions, it addresses challenges in modeling monotonic relationships within high-dimensional or structured data, offering improved flexibility, interpretability, and predictive performance in statistical learning and applied data analysis.
conclusion: In this work, we have presented a generalized framework for isotonic regression that extends classical formulations to accommodate diverse loss functions, constraints, and data structures. By unifying existing approaches under a common theoretical perspective, our method enables flexible modeling while preserving the monotonicity property central to isotonic regression. Empirical evaluations demonstrate improved adaptability and robustness across varied application domains. The proposed framework also opens avenues for efficient algorithmic implementations and theoretical analysis of convergence properties. Future research may explore scalability to high-dimensional settings, integration with regularization techniques, and applications in emerging fields requiring structured monotonic relationships in predictive modeling.

title: Towards Automated Classification of Attackers' TTPs by combining NLP with ML Techniques
abstract: The increasing sophistication of cyber threats necessitates efficient methods for identifying and classifying attackers’ tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). This work proposes an automated framework that integrates natural language processing (NLP) with machine learning (ML) to extract and categorize TTPs from unstructured threat intelligence reports. Leveraging domain-specific embeddings and entity recognition, the system identifies key attack behaviors, which are then classified using supervised learning models trained on annotated cybersecurity corpora. Experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets demonstrates that combining contextual language representations with optimized classifiers significantly improves accuracy over baseline keyword-matching approaches. The proposed method enables rapid, scalable, and consistent TTP classification, supporting security analysts in threat hunting and incident response. Our results highlight the potential of NLP–ML synergy for advancing cyber threat intelligence automation and reducing the time-to-insight in operational cybersecurity environments.
introduction:
Cybersecurity has become an increasingly critical concern as the frequency, sophistication, and diversity of cyberattacks continue to escalate. Adversaries employ a broad spectrum of techniques, tactics, and procedures (TTPs) to compromise systems, exfiltrate data, and disrupt operations. Understanding and classifying these TTPs plays a central role in threat intelligence, enabling security analysts to anticipate attacker behavior, implement effective defenses, and accelerate incident response. However, the manual analysis of threat reports, incident logs, and other unstructured textual data is both time-consuming and prone to human bias, which limits scalability and timely decision-making in high-pressure security environments.

In practice, TTPs are often described in natural language within cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports, security blogs, and advisories. These descriptions vary widely in terminology, level of detail, and format, making automated extraction and classification a non-trivial task. While structured frameworks such as the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base provide standardized taxonomies for TTPs, mapping unstructured textual descriptions to these frameworks remains challenging. This difficulty arises from the inherent ambiguity of language, the use of domain-specific jargon, variations in attacker naming conventions, and the rapid evolution of threat techniques. Consequently, there is a growing need for methods that can bridge the gap between unstructured threat narratives and structured TTP classifications.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a promising avenue for addressing this challenge. By leveraging modern NLP techniques, textual descriptions of attacks can be automatically parsed, semantically analyzed, and transformed into representations suitable for downstream machine learning (ML) models. Recent advances in contextual embeddings, transformer architectures, and domain-adapted language models have shown significant potential in capturing nuanced meanings and relationships in technical cyber threat data. When combined with robust ML classification algorithms, these representations can enable automated, accurate, and scalable mapping of textual threat intelligence to standardized TTP categories.

Despite this promise, several research gaps remain. Prior work has often focused on either rule-based information extraction or traditional ML approaches with limited feature engineering, which may fail to generalize across heterogeneous threat reports. Moreover, many studies neglect the integration of domain-specific ontologies and structured knowledge bases, which could enhance classification accuracy and interpretability. The dynamic nature of cyber threats further compounds these challenges, as models must be adaptable to emerging TTPs and evolving linguistic patterns in attacker communications.

This study aims to address these gaps by proposing an approach that combines state-of-the-art NLP techniques with ML classification models to automate the categorization of attackers’ TTPs. Our method leverages pre-trained language models fine-tuned on cybersecurity corpora to generate contextual embeddings of threat descriptions, which are then processed by supervised classifiers trained to predict standardized TTP labels. By integrating domain knowledge from established frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK, the system is designed to improve both precision and recall in identifying relevant TTPs. We further explore techniques to handle class imbalance, deal with noisy or incomplete textual data, and adapt to novel attack techniques through incremental learning.

The contributions of this research are threefold. First, we present a comprehensive pipeline for processing unstructured threat intelligence using NLP and ML in an integrated fashion. Second, we empirically evaluate the performance of different NLP embeddings and classification algorithms on real-world cyber threat datasets. Third, we demonstrate how the incorporation of structured domain knowledge can enhance the robustness and interpretability of automated TTP classification. By advancing the automation of TTP classification, this work has the potential to support faster, more accurate threat analysis, ultimately strengthening the cyber defense posture of organizations.
conclusion: This work explored the potential of combining Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques to automate the classification of attackers’ Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs). By leveraging textual threat intelligence reports and structured frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK, the proposed approach demonstrated that NLP can effectively extract relevant semantic features, while ML models can classify TTPs with promising accuracy. The integration of these methods addresses the challenges posed by the unstructured nature of cyber threat data, enabling faster and more consistent analysis compared to manual processes. Experimental results indicate that the hybrid approach can reduce analyst workload, improve the timeliness of threat attribution, and enhance situational awareness in dynamic security environments. Furthermore, the methodology shows adaptability to evolving threat landscapes, provided that models are periodically retrained with up-to-date intelligence. While limitations remain, particularly in handling ambiguous or incomplete data, the results suggest a viable path towards scalable, automated TTP classification. Future work will focus on refining domain-specific language models, incorporating contextual threat indicators, and expanding evaluation across diverse intelligence sources to further strengthen the reliability and generalizability of the proposed framework.

title: OSIRIS-REx: Sample Return from Asteroid (101955) Bennu
abstract: The OSIRIS-REx (Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, and Security–Regolith Explorer) mission, launched by NASA in September 2016, was designed to rendezvous with, characterize, and return a sample from near-Earth asteroid (101955) Bennu. Bennu, a carbonaceous B-type asteroid, is of particular scientific interest due to its primitive composition, which may preserve materials from the early Solar System, including volatile- and organic-rich compounds. After arrival at Bennu in December 2018, OSIRIS-REx conducted detailed remote sensing and mapping, revealing a surface unexpectedly dominated by boulders and a highly porous regolith. High-resolution imaging, spectrometry, and laser altimetry informed the selection of the Nightingale sampling site, chosen for its fine-grained material and scientific potential. In October 2020, the Touch-and-Go Sample Acquisition Mechanism (TAGSAM) successfully collected an estimated 250 grams of regolith, exceeding mission requirements. The spacecraft departed Bennu in May 2021 and delivered the sample capsule to Earth in September 2023. Preliminary analyses indicate the presence of hydrated minerals, carbon-bearing compounds, and fine particulate matter consistent with minimal alteration since the Solar System’s formation. These findings have significant implications for understanding the distribution of volatiles and organics in the early protoplanetary disk, the processes governing asteroid surface evolution, and the potential delivery of prebiotic materials to early Earth. The OSIRIS-REx mission demonstrates the scientific value of sample return from primitive bodies and provides a foundation for comparative planetology, informing both planetary defense strategies and future exploration of asteroids as scientific and resource targets.
introduction: The Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, and Security–Regolith Explorer (OSIRIS-REx) mission, launched by NASA in September 2016, represents a landmark achievement in planetary science and asteroid research. Its primary objective was to rendezvous with the near-Earth asteroid (101955) Bennu, conduct detailed remote sensing and in situ measurements, and return a pristine sample to Earth for laboratory analysis. Bennu, a carbonaceous B-type asteroid, is considered a remnant from the early solar system, preserving materials that predate the formation of planets. Its composition offers critical insights into the distribution of organics, volatiles, and minerals that may have contributed to the emergence of life on Earth. Moreover, Bennu’s Earth-crossing orbit and potential impact hazard underscore the importance of characterizing its physical and dynamical properties. OSIRIS-REx successfully collected surface material using its Touch-And-Go Sample Acquisition Mechanism (TAGSAM) in October 2020, marking the first U.S. mission to return an asteroid sample. The returned material, delivered to Earth in September 2023, provides an unprecedented opportunity for high-precision laboratory studies under controlled conditions. Analyses of these samples will refine models of solar system evolution, advance our understanding of small-body processes, and support planetary defense strategies, thereby contributing substantially to planetary science and astrobiology.
conclusion: The OSIRIS-REx mission marks a significant milestone in planetary science and the exploration of near-Earth asteroids. By successfully collecting and returning samples from asteroid (101955) Bennu, the mission provides an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the composition, structure, and history of a primitive carbonaceous body. The returned material, preserved in pristine condition, offers insights into the early Solar System, the processes that governed planetary formation, and the potential delivery of prebiotic compounds to Earth. Moreover, the mission has advanced our understanding of asteroid dynamics, surface properties, and the influence of non-gravitational forces such as the Yarkovsky effect, contributing to improved models for impact risk assessment. Beyond its scientific achievements, OSIRIS-REx demonstrates the technical feasibility and value of complex sample-return missions, setting a precedent for future endeavors to other small bodies. The collaboration among international partners, along with the integration of ground- and space-based observations, underscores the importance of multi-faceted approaches in space exploration. As analyses of the Bennu samples proceed, the results will refine our knowledge of Solar System evolution and inform strategies for planetary defense. OSIRIS-REx thus stands as both a scientific triumph and a catalyst for future exploration, bridging curiosity-driven research with practical considerations for humanity’s long-term presence in space.

title: Recovering 0 Kelvin Effective Hamiltonian Parameters from High-Temperature Disordered Phases
abstract: Extracting effective Hamiltonian parameters that accurately describe the zero-temperature limit from measurements or simulations performed in high-temperature disordered phases presents a significant challenge, as thermal fluctuations obscure the underlying ground-state interactions. In this work, we develop and demonstrate a systematic framework for recovering 0 K effective Hamiltonian parameters from high-temperature data, without requiring direct access to ordered configurations. Our method leverages statistical mechanical relationships between correlation functions in the disordered regime and the microscopic interaction parameters of the Hamiltonian, employing inverse modeling and regularized fitting to mitigate the effects of noise and finite-size sampling. We validate the approach using both synthetic datasets generated from known model systems and first-principles simulations of representative materials. The recovered parameters are shown to reliably reproduce ground-state energies, ordering tendencies, and low-temperature phase behavior. This framework enables the extraction of accurate interaction models from experimentally accessible high-temperature phases, extending the applicability of effective Hamiltonian techniques to systems where ordered states are difficult to realize or observe directly.
introduction:
Understanding the fundamental interactions governing the behavior of condensed matter systems often relies on the construction of effective Hamiltonians that accurately describe the energetics of relevant degrees of freedom. At low temperatures, where thermal fluctuations are weak and long-range order may emerge, such Hamiltonians can be parametrized directly from experimental measurements or from first-principles calculations of ordered configurations. However, in many materials of current scientific and technological interest—such as high-entropy alloys, strongly correlated oxides, and frustrated magnets—the low-temperature ordered phase may be difficult to access experimentally or computationally. These systems may remain in a disordered phase down to relatively low temperatures, or exhibit sluggish kinetics that prevent equilibration into the ground state. As a result, extracting the effective Hamiltonian parameters corresponding to the idealized zero-Kelvin limit from data obtained in high-temperature disordered regimes presents a significant scientific challenge.

The ability to recover 0 K effective Hamiltonian parameters from high-temperature measurements or simulations has broad implications. For example, in alloys and solid solutions, knowledge of the interaction parameters at 0 K enables accurate predictions of phase stability, transition temperatures, and ordering tendencies. In correlated electron systems, it provides the foundation for constructing low-energy models such as Heisenberg, Hubbard, or t–J Hamiltonians, which in turn inform theoretical understanding of magnetism, superconductivity, and metal–insulator transitions. Similarly, in lattice-dynamical problems, force constants extracted at 0 K are crucial for predicting vibrational spectra, thermal transport, and structural phase transitions. In all these cases, the parameters of the effective Hamiltonian are defined in the absence of thermal excitations, yet experimental probes such as neutron or X-ray scattering, spectroscopies, and thermodynamic measurements often operate at finite, sometimes high, temperatures.

The primary difficulty in this inverse problem lies in the influence of thermal disorder on the observables from which Hamiltonian parameters are traditionally inferred. At elevated temperatures, occupation probabilities of different configurations are governed by the Boltzmann distribution, which integrates over a broad range of microstates. The resulting experimental signatures are therefore convolutions of the underlying zero-temperature energetics with thermal fluctuations. In addition, anharmonic effects, entropic contributions, and temperature-dependent renormalizations of the interactions can obscure the direct connection between measured quantities and the desired 0 K parameters. Standard fitting procedures that ignore these effects can yield temperature-dependent “effective” parameters, which may be unsuitable for describing ground-state behavior.

Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge. In the context of alloys, the cluster expansion formalism provides a systematic framework for representing the configurational energy as a sum over cluster interactions. Extensions of this method incorporate thermodynamic integration, inverse Monte Carlo, or regression techniques that account for finite-temperature sampling. In magnetic systems, inverse statistical-mechanical methods have been developed to extract exchange constants from spin correlation functions measured in the paramagnetic regime. Likewise, in lattice dynamics, temperature-dependent effective potential (TDEP) methods have been employed to fit force constants from molecular dynamics trajectories at elevated temperatures, with subsequent extrapolation toward 0 K. Despite these advances, accurately recovering the ground-state Hamiltonian from high-temperature data remains an open problem, especially when the thermal disorder is strong and the parameter space is high-dimensional.

A promising strategy is to exploit the statistical mechanics of the disordered phase more fully, using high-temperature correlation functions and fluctuation–dissipation relations to infer the zero-temperature interaction parameters. This requires careful modeling of the temperature dependence of the effective interactions, as well as robust statistical methods to disentangle genuine ground-state energetics from thermal renormalization effects. When successful, such approaches can enable high-fidelity reconstruction of the 0 K Hamiltonian without direct access to ordered configurations, thereby greatly expanding the range of systems amenable to quantitative modeling.

In this work, we address the problem of recovering zero-Kelvin effective Hamiltonian parameters from data obtained in high-temperature disordered phases. We focus on systems where the relevant degrees of freedom can be described by a discrete or continuous set of variables with short- or medium-range interactions, and where the disordered phase can be accessed experimentally or through atomistic simulations. By developing and applying a methodology that combines statistical-mechanical inversion with rigorous treatment of thermal effects, we aim to establish a general framework for extracting ground-state parameters from finite-temperature observations. This framework is validated against model systems with known Hamiltonians, and subsequently applied to realistic materials where direct low-temperature measurements are impractical. Through this approach, we demonstrate that accurate recovery of 0 K effective parameters is possible even in the presence of substantial thermal disorder, opening new avenues for the study and design of complex materials.
conclusion:
In this work, we have demonstrated a methodology for extracting effective Hamiltonian parameters representative of the 0 K limit from data obtained in high-temperature disordered phases. By systematically accounting for thermal fluctuations and configurational disorder, our approach bridges the gap between experimentally accessible regimes and the ground-state parameter space relevant for predictive modeling. The framework leverages statistical averaging and inverse modeling to disentangle temperature-induced renormalizations from the intrinsic interactions, enabling accurate recovery of low-temperature Hamiltonian coefficients without direct access to ordered-phase measurements.  

Our results indicate that even in the presence of substantial disorder, reliable parameter estimation is achievable, provided that sufficient configurational sampling and robust fitting strategies are employed. Comparisons with direct low-temperature calculations validate the approach, showing quantitative agreement across a range of systems and interaction types. This capability is particularly valuable for materials where low-temperature phases are experimentally inaccessible or metastable under ambient conditions.  

The presented methodology opens pathways for integrating high-throughput experimental or computational datasets from disordered phases into the construction of accurate, transferable effective models. Future work will extend these ideas to include quantum fluctuations and anharmonic effects, further enhancing the ability to connect finite-temperature observations with fundamental, ground-state descriptors of complex materials.

title: Learning Partially Known Stochastic Dynamics with Empirical PAC Bayes
abstract: We investigate the problem of learning stochastic dynamical systems when only partial knowledge of the underlying transition model is available. Building on the PAC Bayes framework, we propose an empirical methodology that integrates prior structural information with observed trajectories to obtain generalization guarantees for predictive models. Our approach accommodates model uncertainty, stochasticity, and limited data by deriving bounds that are both data-dependent and computationally tractable. We demonstrate how the resulting learning algorithm can adapt to unknown components of the dynamics while leveraging known structure for improved sample efficiency. Empirical studies on synthetic and real-world systems validate the theoretical results and highlight robustness to model misspecification.
introduction:
Many real-world systems evolve according to complex stochastic dynamics that are only partially known. Examples arise in fields as diverse as climate science, robotics, finance, and epidemiology, where the governing processes are affected by random perturbations, latent variables, and unobserved interactions. In such settings, complete mechanistic modeling is often infeasible due to missing knowledge or prohibitive data requirements. Instead, practitioners resort to learning from data while leveraging whatever partial knowledge is available—such as known physical laws, conservation constraints, or approximate parametric forms. This hybrid approach promises improved generalization and interpretability compared to purely data-driven methods, yet it also raises nontrivial statistical challenges.

A central difficulty lies in quantifying uncertainty and providing performance guarantees when both the model class and the data-generating process exhibit stochasticity. Classical statistical learning theory offers tools for bounding generalization error, but many of these results either assume independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data or require full specification of the model family. In contrast, partially known stochastic dynamics often generate dependent samples—due to temporal correlations—and the unknown components of the dynamics may not fit neatly into standard parametric frameworks. Moreover, the randomness in the system can be both intrinsic (process noise) and extrinsic (measurement noise), further complicating inference.

The Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) framework provides a formal basis for reasoning about learnability, offering high-probability guarantees on the deviation between empirical and true performance. PAC-Bayesian theory extends these ideas by incorporating prior knowledge in the form of distributions over hypotheses, leading to bounds that are often tighter and more flexible than classical uniform convergence results. In the PAC-Bayes setting, the learner chooses a posterior distribution over hypotheses after observing the data, and the generalization bound depends on both the empirical risk and the Kullback–Leibler divergence between posterior and prior. This framework is particularly attractive when partial knowledge of the dynamics can be encoded as a prior, enabling a principled trade-off between adherence to prior beliefs and adaptation to observed data.

Despite its promise, the application of PAC-Bayesian methods to learning partially known stochastic dynamics remains underexplored. Existing PAC-Bayes results typically focus on i.i.d. data or specific dependent processes with fully known structure, leaving a gap for the rich class of systems where only part of the transition law is known. Furthermore, most empirical PAC-Bayes approaches—where unknown quantities in the bound are estimated directly from finite data—have been developed for supervised learning tasks rather than stochastic dynamical systems.

In this work, we develop an empirical PAC-Bayesian framework tailored to learning in partially known stochastic dynamical systems. We consider settings where the known component of the dynamics can be explicitly modeled, while the unknown component is learned from data using flexible function approximators. We derive generalization bounds that account for temporal dependence and partial model knowledge, and we instantiate these bounds in algorithms that balance fidelity to prior structure with empirical performance. Through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, we demonstrate that our approach yields meaningful uncertainty quantification and improved predictive accuracy over purely data-driven baselines.
conclusion: We have introduced an empirical PAC-Bayes framework for learning partially known stochastic dynamics, leveraging prior structural knowledge while rigorously quantifying uncertainty from finite data. By combining model-based components with data-driven estimators, our approach provides generalization guarantees that hold with high probability, even when the underlying transition dynamics are only partially specified. The derived bounds adapt to both model uncertainty and stochastic variability, enabling principled selection among candidate models and guiding safe policy learning in sequential decision-making tasks. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that incorporating partial prior knowledge improves sample efficiency and predictive performance relative to purely model-free or fully model-based baselines. Furthermore, the PAC-Bayes formalism offers interpretable trade-offs between fit to observed data and adherence to prior structure. Future work will extend the framework to richer function classes, online adaptation, and interactive settings where the data collection policy co-evolves with the learned model. This work underscores the promise of PAC-Bayesian methods for robust learning in complex dynamical systems with incomplete prior knowledge.

title: A symplectic rearrangement of the four dimensional non-geometric scalar potential
abstract: We investigate a novel symplectic reformulation of the four-dimensional non-geometric scalar potential arising in type IIB superstring compactifications with generalized fluxes. Building on the framework of Double Field Theory and symplectic geometry, we reorganize the scalar potential into a manifestly symplectic invariant form, making explicit the role of electric–magnetic duality in the presence of non-geometric Q- and R-fluxes. Our construction employs a systematic decomposition of flux-induced terms in the effective \(\mathcal{N}=1\) supergravity, allowing the scalar potential to be expressed directly in terms of symplectic vectors and period matrices of the underlying Calabi–Yau threefold. This rearrangement not only streamlines the potential’s structure but also reveals hidden constraints and simplifications relevant for moduli stabilization. Furthermore, the symplectic formulation facilitates a more transparent comparison between geometric and non-geometric flux contributions. Potential implications for constructing consistent non-geometric vacua and for exploring duality covariant formulations of flux compactifications are discussed.
introduction:
The study of flux compactifications in string theory has revealed a rich landscape of effective four-dimensional theories, where a variety of geometric and non-geometric fluxes contribute to the scalar potential governing the low-energy dynamics. In particular, non-geometric fluxes, which arise naturally through successive T-duality transformations of geometric backgrounds, have attracted considerable attention due to their potential role in moduli stabilization, duality covariance, and the exploration of generalized notions of geometry. The resulting scalar potentials are often intricate, involving a large number of flux parameters and moduli fields, and their structure is constrained by the underlying symmetries of the theory, such as S- and T-duality.

A powerful framework for analyzing such potentials is provided by symplectic formulations of \(\mathcal{N}=2\) and \(\mathcal{N}=1\) supergravity theories, in which the scalar sector is encoded in terms of symplectic vectors of periods and their duals. This formalism makes duality properties manifest and often enables a more compact and transparent representation of the scalar potential. In the presence of generalized fluxes, however, the direct connection between the higher-dimensional origins of the potential and its symplectic structure is not always evident. This motivates the search for rearrangements of the scalar potential that manifest its symplectic covariance and clarify the role of different flux components.

In this work we focus on the four-dimensional scalar potential arising from type IIB flux compactifications on Calabi–Yau orientifolds with the full set of geometric and non-geometric fluxes, including \(H\)-flux, \(F\)-flux, and their T-duals \(Q\) and \(R\), as well as possible S-dual \(P\)-fluxes. Starting from the standard \(\mathcal{N}=1\) supergravity expression involving the Kähler potential and superpotential, we develop a systematic procedure to reorganize the potential into a manifestly symplectic form. This rearrangement is achieved by identifying appropriate symplectic vectors of generalized flux orbits, which combine the flux parameters in a manner consistent with duality transformations, and by expressing the potential in terms of symplectic inner products involving the period vector of the internal Calabi–Yau manifold.

The resulting formulation provides a compact and duality-covariant expression for the non-geometric scalar potential, in which the contributions of the different flux sectors are clearly separated. Such a symplectic rearrangement not only facilitates the analysis of moduli stabilization and vacuum structure, but also offers insight into the higher-dimensional origin of the effective theory and its embedding into generalized geometry and double field theory frameworks. Moreover, it may prove useful in extending the analysis to include non-perturbative effects or to explore more general non-geometric backgrounds beyond Calabi–Yau compactifications.
conclusion:
In this work we have undertaken a detailed reformulation of the four-dimensional non-geometric scalar potential arising in type II string compactifications, employing a symplectic framework that renders its structure more transparent and better suited for further analysis. Starting from the standard supergravity formulation, in which fluxes and moduli enter in a highly interwoven fashion, we have shown that the scalar potential can be rearranged into a manifestly symplectic invariant form. This reformulation exploits the underlying special Kähler geometry of the moduli space and the symplectic covariance of the flux-induced superpotential, allowing us to organise the various contributions—geometric, non-geometric, and their cross terms—into compact bilinear expressions.

A principal motivation for this rearrangement is to isolate and clarify the role of non-geometric fluxes, which in the traditional formulation appear entangled with geometric fluxes and moduli-dependent prefactors. By recasting the potential in terms of symplectic vectors of fluxes and period matrices, we have achieved a separation between the purely topological data of the compactification and the moduli-dependent couplings. The resulting expressions make explicit how the scalar potential depends on the symplectic pairing between flux quanta and moduli fields, and they reveal a high degree of structural similarity between the geometric and non-geometric sectors. This paves the way for a more unified treatment of moduli stabilisation, in which different classes of fluxes are handled on equal footing.

From a computational standpoint, the symplectic form of the potential offers a number of advantages. First, it significantly reduces the complexity of the expressions, replacing lengthy index contractions with compact vector–matrix–vector products. This not only aids in analytic manipulations, such as the derivation of extremum conditions, but also facilitates numerical studies, where the flux–moduli dependence can be implemented more efficiently. Second, the manifest symplectic covariance ensures that the potential transforms appropriately under electric–magnetic dualities of the underlying supergravity theory. This property is particularly relevant when exploring dual descriptions of non-geometric backgrounds, where such transformations can relate seemingly disparate flux configurations.

Our analysis confirms that the symplectic rearrangement preserves the full physical content of the original potential. All moduli couplings, including those induced by the non-trivial mixing between the complex structure and Kähler sectors in the presence of non-geometric fluxes, are faithfully retained. Moreover, the rearranged potential makes transparent certain symmetries and selection rules that are less evident in the conventional formulation. For example, the vanishing of specific flux combinations due to Bianchi identities or tadpole cancellation conditions is immediately reflected as orthogonality relations between symplectic vectors, allowing such constraints to be implemented at an early stage in model building.

Beyond its intrinsic formal appeal, the symplectic formulation has concrete implications for phenomenological applications. In flux compactifications aiming at realistic model building, one often seeks vacua with all moduli stabilised, controlled hierarchies, and possibly a small positive cosmological constant. The rearranged potential provides a cleaner starting point for scanning flux landscapes, as it disentangles the contributions from different flux sectors and organises them in a way that is directly amenable to optimisation algorithms. In particular, the bilinear structure suggests natural strategies for extremising the potential by varying fluxes and moduli in concert, guided by the geometry encoded in the period matrices.

Furthermore, our results are relevant for ongoing efforts to connect the low-energy effective description of non-geometric backgrounds with their higher-dimensional origins. The symplectic perspective aligns well with approaches based on generalised geometry and double field theory, in which fluxes are components of unified geometric objects transforming under duality groups. The compact form of the potential we have obtained may thus serve as a bridge between the four-dimensional supergravity description and the underlying ten-dimensional or doubled formulations, facilitating the matching of scalar potentials across frameworks.

In summary, we have provided a symplectic reorganisation of the four-dimensional non-geometric scalar potential that renders its structure more compact, transparent, and duality-covariant. This reformulation not only clarifies the interplay between geometric and non-geometric fluxes but also opens the way to more efficient analytic and numerical studies of moduli stabilisation. It harmonises with broader developments in the study of flux compactifications and non-geometric backgrounds, and offers a robust tool for probing the string theory landscape from a manifestly symplectic vantage point. Future work may extend this approach to include additional ingredients such as brane and orientifold contributions, quantum corrections, and more general duality groups, thereby further enhancing its applicability to realistic string phenomenology and the systematic exploration of non-geometric flux vacua.

title: NNLO Time-like Splitting Functions in QCD
abstract: We present the complete set of next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) time-like splitting functions governing the QCD evolution of fragmentation functions. Our results are obtained through analytic continuation from space-like processes, supplemented by independent cross-checks using physical evolution kernels. The NNLO corrections significantly improve perturbative precision, enabling more accurate predictions for hadron production in high-energy collisions and providing essential input for global analyses of fragmentation data.
introduction:
The precise understanding of parton fragmentation into hadrons is a cornerstone of perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and an essential ingredient in the theoretical description of high-energy processes. In this context, fragmentation functions (FFs) encode the nonperturbative dynamics of hadronization, while their scale evolution is governed by time-like splitting functions through the Dokshitzer–Gribov–Lipatov–Altarelli–Parisi (DGLAP) equations. Accurate determinations of these splitting functions are crucial for reliable predictions of observables in electron–positron annihilation, semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering, and hadron collider experiments.  

At leading and next-to-leading order (LO, NLO), the time-like splitting functions have been known for decades, enabling phenomenological analyses with controlled uncertainties. However, the increasing precision of experimental data, particularly from the LHC and future lepton colliders, demands theoretical predictions at next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO). On the space-like side, corresponding to parton distribution functions, the NNLO splitting functions have been computed and extensively applied. For the time-like case, progress has been more challenging due to the complexity of higher-order final-state corrections and analytic continuation from space-like kinematics.  

Recent advances in multi-loop techniques, Mellin-space methods, and analytic continuation have enabled the determination of the full set of NNLO time-like splitting functions. These results provide the last missing ingredient for fully consistent NNLO evolution of fragmentation functions. In this work, we present a comprehensive account of the NNLO time-like splitting functions in QCD, outlining their derivation, analytic structure, and phenomenological implications. Our results pave the way for improved precision in QCD analyses involving hadron production, thereby strengthening the bridge between theory and experiment in the study of strong interactions.
conclusion: In this work we have presented a detailed analysis of the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) time-like splitting functions in Quantum Chromodynamics, completing the perturbative description of parton fragmentation at this accuracy. By employing recent advances in analytic computation techniques, we have derived compact expressions for all relevant flavour-singlet and non-singlet components, ensuring consistency with known space-like results through analytic continuation and verifying the correctness via multiple independent checks. The improved precision of these splitting functions significantly reduces theoretical uncertainties in the evolution of fragmentation functions, with direct implications for high-energy collider phenomenology, particularly in processes dominated by hadronic final states. Our results provide essential input for global analyses aiming to extract fragmentation functions from experimental data, enabling a more accurate determination of parton-to-hadron transition dynamics. Furthermore, the availability of NNLO accuracy opens the door to systematically matching with resummed calculations in relevant kinematic regimes. Future work will explore numerical implementations and phenomenological applications, consolidating the role of NNLO time-like splitting functions as a cornerstone in precision QCD studies.

title: The Penrose Property with a Cosmological Constant
abstract: We investigate the formulation and implications of the Penrose property for asymptotically de Sitter and asymptotically anti–de Sitter spacetimes, incorporating the effects of a nonzero cosmological constant \(\Lambda\). The Penrose property, originally conceived in the context of asymptotically flat spacetimes, relates the causal structure at null infinity to global geometric constraints, with particular relevance to the validity of the Penrose inequality and cosmic censorship conjecture. Extending this framework to \(\Lambda \neq 0\) requires a careful re-examination of conformal compactification, the geometry of conformal boundaries, and the definition of energy-momentum in spacetimes with non-trivial asymptotics. We present a rigorous adaptation of the property, distinguishing between the \(\Lambda>0\) case, where future and past conformal infinities are spacelike, and the \(\Lambda<0\) case, where the boundary is timelike. In both regimes, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the Penrose property to hold, expressed in terms of curvature bounds and trapped surface formation. We further explore the interaction between the modified Penrose property and known mass inequalities, employing both analytical techniques and examples from exact solutions, including Schwarzschild–de Sitter and Kerr–anti–de Sitter metrics. Our results indicate that while the essence of the Penrose property survives the introduction of \(\Lambda\), its precise formulation and physical interpretation depend sensitively on the sign and magnitude of the cosmological constant. This work clarifies the role of \(\Lambda\) in global causal geometry and provides a foundation for testing the Penrose inequality in cosmological and anti-cosmological settings.
introduction: The Penrose property, originally formulated in the context of asymptotically flat spacetimes, provides a geometric criterion linking null geodesics and causal structure to the existence of trapped surfaces. Its relevance extends to cosmic censorship and singularity theorems, making it a foundational concept in mathematical relativity. Recent interest in cosmological models with a nonzero cosmological constant motivates examining how the Penrose property adapts in de Sitter or anti–de Sitter settings. The presence of a cosmological constant modifies asymptotic behavior and influences causal boundaries, requiring a careful reformulation. This work investigates these modifications, aiming to extend the Penrose property to such spacetimes.
conclusion:
In this work we have examined the Penrose property in the presence of a non-vanishing cosmological constant, extending previous analyses that have predominantly focused on the asymptotically flat case. By systematically incorporating the effects of a positive or negative cosmological constant into the geometric and causal structure of the spacetime, we have clarified the extent to which the original arguments supporting the Penrose inequality, and its related properties, can be adapted to de Sitter and anti–de Sitter asymptotics. Our approach has combined both analytic reasoning, grounded in the formalism of null hypersurfaces and trapped surface formation, and explicit model calculations that illuminate the role of the modified asymptotics in shaping global causal relations.

The principal outcome of our investigation is that the Penrose property, understood as a constraint linking the area of certain marginally trapped surfaces to a suitably defined mass functional, retains much of its conceptual force in the presence of a cosmological constant, but with important modifications. In particular, the value and sign of the cosmological constant enter not only through the asymptotic structure but also via the focusing properties of null congruences and the definition of total mass. For positive cosmological constant, the cosmological horizon imposes a natural cut-off that modifies the standard comparison between the area of the trapped surface and the ADM mass, necessitating a reformulation in terms of the mass contained within the cosmological domain of dependence. For negative cosmological constant, the conformal boundary at spatial infinity permits a more direct adaptation of the asymptotically flat formalism, but subtle boundary contributions and the choice of quasi-local mass definition become crucial.

We have shown that, in both regimes, a generalized Penrose-type inequality can be formulated, consistent with the known exact solutions such as Schwarzschild–de Sitter and Schwarzschild–anti–de Sitter spacetimes. The derivation relies on the interplay between the Raychaudhuri equation, the dominant energy condition, and the modified asymptotic geometry, and suggests that the physical intuition underlying the Penrose property—namely, that gravitational collapse cannot produce a black hole of area smaller than that corresponding to the total mass—remains valid beyond the asymptotically flat context. However, the precise numerical coefficients and the interpretation of the relevant mass parameter must be adapted to the cosmological setting.

Our results pave the way for several avenues of further research. A rigorous proof of the generalized inequality in full generality remains an open challenge, particularly in the de Sitter case, where the lack of a global timelike Killing field complicates the definition of mass. Numerical simulations of dynamical collapse in spacetimes with non-zero cosmological constant would provide valuable empirical support and could uncover regimes where the inequality approaches saturation. Moreover, the interplay between the Penrose property and holographic considerations in anti–de Sitter space suggests possible connections to gauge/gravity duality, offering a broader theoretical context. In sum, the inclusion of a cosmological constant enriches the mathematical structure of the Penrose property, preserves its core physical content, and underscores its universality as a guiding principle in gravitational theory.

title: Vicinity Effects of Field Free Point on the Relaxation Behavior of MNPs
abstract: The relaxation behavior of magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) in the vicinity of a field free point (FFP) is critical for optimizing magnetic particle imaging (MPI) performance. In this study, we investigate how spatially varying magnetic field gradients near the FFP influence Néel and Brownian relaxation mechanisms. Using a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental measurements, we quantify relaxation time variations as a function of distance from the FFP. Results reveal pronounced changes in relaxation dynamics within micrometer-scale proximity, offering insights for improving MPI spatial resolution and sensitivity through tailored magnetic field configurations.
introduction: Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) have attracted significant attention in recent years due to their promising applications in biomedical imaging, targeted drug delivery, and hyperthermia therapy. Their magnetic response is strongly dependent on both intrinsic properties, such as size, shape, and composition, and extrinsic factors, including the applied magnetic field configuration. Among various field geometries, the field free point (FFP) plays a central role in magnetic particle imaging (MPI), where spatial encoding is achieved by exploiting the nonlinear magnetization of MNPs in the presence of a strong magnetic field gradient. In the immediate vicinity of the FFP, the magnetic field approaches zero, and nanoparticles experience rapid changes in the local field strength as they move through this region. These variations can significantly influence the relaxation behavior of MNPs, including Néel and Brownian relaxation processes, which in turn affect the signal formation and spatial resolution in MPI. Understanding the vicinity effects of the FFP on relaxation dynamics is therefore crucial for optimizing particle design and imaging protocols. This work investigates how proximity to the FFP modifies the relaxation characteristics of MNPs, aiming to elucidate the interplay between local field gradients, particle properties, and thermal fluctuations that collectively govern their dynamic magnetic response.
conclusion: The investigation of the vicinity effects of the field-free point (FFP) on the relaxation behavior of magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) reveals that spatial variations in the local magnetic environment strongly influence their dynamic response. Experimental and theoretical analyses indicate that proximity to the FFP significantly modulates Néel and Brownian relaxation times, with measurable consequences for signal amplitude and phase in magnetic particle imaging applications. These findings underscore the importance of accurately modeling the field gradient distribution when interpreting relaxation-based measurements. Optimizing particle design and imaging protocols to account for these vicinity effects may enhance spatial resolution, sensitivity, and quantitative accuracy in future MNP-based diagnostic and therapeutic technologies.

title: Polarization in heavy ion collisions: a theoretical review
abstract: We review theoretical developments on polarization phenomena in relativistic heavy ion collisions, with emphasis on the spin polarization of hadrons emerging from the quark–gluon plasma. Recent measurements of global and local polarization, particularly of Λ hyperons, have revealed intriguing connections between spin degrees of freedom, vorticity, and the medium’s hydrodynamic evolution. We survey the main theoretical frameworks, including relativistic hydrodynamics with spin, statistical and kinetic approaches, and discuss their successes and limitations in describing experimental data. Special attention is given to the role of initial angular momentum, spin–orbit coupling, and possible magnetic field effects. Open questions and future directions toward a unified understanding of spin polarization in strongly interacting matter are outlined.
introduction:
The study of relativistic heavy ion collisions provides a unique opportunity to investigate strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions of temperature, density, and vorticity. Over the past decades, experiments at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have revealed a wealth of phenomena associated with the formation and evolution of the quark–gluon plasma (QGP). Among these, the observation of particle polarization, particularly the global polarization of hyperons, has opened a new window into the vortical structure and spin dynamics of the medium created in such collisions. Polarization measurements probe the interplay between the spin degrees of freedom of hadrons and the macroscopic properties of the fluid, offering insights into fundamental aspects of relativistic hydrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics (QCD).

The first experimental evidence of global Λ hyperon polarization in non-central heavy ion collisions indicated that the QGP can possess an exceptionally large vorticity, the largest ever observed in a fluid. This finding has stimulated intense theoretical activity aimed at understanding the mechanisms that transfer the initial orbital angular momentum of the colliding nuclei into the spin polarization of produced particles. Several frameworks have been developed, including relativistic hydrodynamic models with spin, kinetic theory approaches, and microscopic transport calculations, all of which seek to relate the measured polarization to the underlying local thermodynamic and dynamical properties of the system.

In addition to global polarization, more differential observables—such as spin alignment of vector mesons and local polarization patterns—have emerged as sensitive probes of the QGP’s space–time evolution, the role of magnetic fields, and possible manifestations of chiral and anomalous effects. This review summarizes the current theoretical understanding of polarization phenomena in heavy ion collisions, highlighting recent developments, open questions, and future directions in this rapidly evolving field.
conclusion: The study of polarization phenomena in heavy ion collisions offers valuable insights into the complex interplay between spin, vorticity, and the strongly interacting quark–gluon plasma. Theoretical developments have advanced our understanding of spin dynamics, revealing connections to local thermodynamic properties and the role of relativistic hydrodynamics with spin degrees of freedom. While significant progress has been made in interpreting experimental observations, open questions remain regarding the microscopic origins of global and local polarization patterns. Future work combining refined theoretical frameworks with high-precision measurements will be essential to fully uncover the mechanisms governing spin polarization in extreme nuclear matter conditions.

title: Research on the Design and Simulation of the CSRe Stochastic Cooling System
abstract: The stochastic cooling system of the Cooler Storage Ring experimental (CSRe) facility is designed to reduce beam emittance and momentum spread, thereby improving experimental precision in high-energy heavy-ion physics. This work presents the design principles, parameter optimization, and simulation studies of the CSRe stochastic cooling system. Key components, including pickups, kickers, and signal processing electronics, are modeled to evaluate system performance under various operational scenarios. Simulation results indicate that the proposed design achieves significant beam quality improvement within practical cooling times, meeting the requirements for rare isotope experiments. The influence of bandwidth, gain, and particle number on cooling efficiency is analyzed. These findings provide a theoretical and technical basis for the implementation of the stochastic cooling system at CSRe, supporting future high-precision experimental programs.
introduction:
Stochastic cooling is a powerful beam manipulation technique widely employed in storage rings to reduce the phase space volume of particle beams, thereby improving beam quality and extending experimental capabilities. Since its first successful implementation at CERN in the late 1970s, stochastic cooling has been developed into a mature technology with applications in high-energy physics, nuclear physics, and heavy-ion research. The Cooler Storage Ring experimental (CSRe) at the Institute of Modern Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, is dedicated to precision mass measurements and lifetime studies of exotic nuclei. For experiments involving short-lived, rare isotope beams, achieving high beam quality within limited storage times is crucial.  

The design of a stochastic cooling system for CSRe must address the specific requirements of its operational modes, beam parameters, and physical constraints. This includes optimizing the pickup and kicker structures, signal processing chain, and cooling bandwidth to achieve efficient cooling within the available lattice configuration. Simulation studies play an essential role in predicting system performance, guiding engineering design, and assessing feasibility before installation.  

This work presents the design considerations, simulation methodology, and expected performance of the CSRe stochastic cooling system. By integrating theoretical analysis with numerical modeling, the study aims to provide a reliable basis for system implementation and to enhance the experimental capabilities of CSRe in rare isotope research.
conclusion: The design and simulation of the CSRe stochastic cooling system have been carried out to meet the requirements of beam accumulation and quality improvement for experimental physics studies. Based on the lattice parameters of the CSRe, the system structure, pickup and kicker positions, and bandwidth configurations were optimized to achieve effective cooling performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed system can significantly reduce the momentum spread and transverse emittance of stored ions within reasonable cooling times, thereby enhancing luminosity and experimental precision. The influence of key parameters such as particle number, gain, and bandwidth on cooling efficiency was analyzed, providing guidance for practical implementation. The results confirm that the designed configuration meets the operational demands of the CSRe and offers a reliable basis for subsequent hardware construction and commissioning. Future work will focus on detailed engineering design, integration with existing accelerator systems, and experimental verification to validate the simulated performance under actual operating conditions.

title: Multiparty Session Types for Safe Runtime Adaptation in an Actor Language (Extended version)
abstract: We present an approach for ensuring safe runtime adaptation in actor-based systems by integrating multiparty session types (MPST) into the actor model. Modern distributed applications must adapt dynamically to changing requirements and environments, yet such adaptations risk violating communication safety and protocol compliance. Our work extends an actor language with MPST-based protocol specifications that govern inter-actor communication, enabling detection and prevention of protocol violations even during adaptation. We formalise an operational semantics that supports dynamic reconfiguration while preserving session fidelity, and introduce a type system that ensures actors adhere to their assigned roles across adaptations. The runtime monitors protocol conformance and coordinates adaptations through explicit reconfiguration primitives, ensuring that ongoing conversations are neither interrupted unsafely nor left in inconsistent states. We describe an implementation that integrates static type checking with lightweight runtime verification, balancing safety guarantees with flexibility. Through case studies, we demonstrate how the approach supports complex adaptation scenarios, such as dynamic role reassignment and protocol evolution, without compromising safety properties. This work advances the reliable engineering of adaptive distributed systems by combining the expressiveness of the actor model with the rigorous communication guarantees of multiparty session types.
introduction: The increasing complexity and dynamism of distributed systems demand programming abstractions that ensure correctness while supporting runtime adaptation. Actor-based languages offer a natural model for concurrency and distribution, encapsulating state and communicating via asynchronous message passing. However, ensuring that interacting actors adhere to intended communication protocols, particularly when the system evolves at runtime, remains challenging. Multiparty Session Types (MPST) provide a type-theoretic foundation for specifying and verifying structured communication among multiple participants, guaranteeing properties such as communication safety and deadlock freedom. While MPST have been successfully applied in static settings, their integration into adaptive actor systems raises new questions about type preservation and behavioural guarantees during reconfiguration. This work presents an extended framework that embeds MPST into an actor language, enabling safe runtime adaptation without compromising protocol conformance. We introduce language constructs and operational semantics that support reconfiguration, demonstrate how protocol safety is maintained, and evaluate the approach through examples and case studies, illustrating its expressiveness and practical applicability.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented an approach for ensuring safe runtime adaptation in an actor-based language by employing multiparty session types (MPST) as a formal foundation. By integrating MPST into the actor model, we enable the specification of global interaction protocols that can be projected into local types, ensuring that actors conform to prescribed communication patterns even as the system evolves dynamically. Our extended framework supports runtime adaptation by allowing protocol reconfiguration while preserving safety guarantees such as communication fidelity and progress.

We have shown how the combination of actor encapsulation, asynchronous message passing, and MPST verification can detect and prevent protocol violations both at design time and during execution. This capability is critical for long-lived, distributed applications that must adapt to environmental changes, failures, or evolving requirements without compromising correctness. The extended version of our work elaborates on the formal semantics, the adaptation mechanisms, and the verification process, providing rigorous proofs of safety properties and illustrating practical applicability through detailed examples.

Our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed approach can handle complex adaptation scenarios with minimal runtime overhead, enabling flexible yet dependable distributed systems.
