By avoiding ad-hoc adaptation strategies and grounding our solution in a well-understood type theory, we offer a path toward systematically engineering adaptive actor systems.

Future work will explore automated synthesis of adaptation strategies from protocol specifications, integration with fault-tolerant actor runtimes, and scaling to large multi-protocol systems. We believe that combining MPST with the actor paradigm offers a promising direction for building adaptive, robust, and maintainable distributed applications, bridging the gap between formal correctness and practical flexibility.

title: Agents that Listen: High-Throughput Reinforcement Learning with Multiple Sensory Systems
abstract: We present a high-throughput reinforcement learning framework that integrates multiple sensory modalities to enable agents to process and respond to complex, dynamic environments more effectively. Our approach, termed *Agents that Listen*, combines auditory, visual, and proprioceptive inputs within a unified policy architecture, leveraging parallelized simulation to accelerate training. By incorporating synchronized multimodal perception, the system improves situational awareness and decision-making under partial observability. We introduce a scalable training pipeline capable of processing millions of sensory-rich episodes per day, facilitated by optimized data streaming and batched environment interactions. Empirical evaluations on a suite of multimodal navigation and manipulation tasks demonstrate significant performance gains over unimodal baselines, particularly in environments where auditory cues provide critical, complementary information. The results indicate that listening—both literally, through audio sensing, and metaphorically, through richer environmental perception—is a key enabler for more adaptive, general-purpose agents. Our findings suggest that multimodal, high-throughput reinforcement learning can advance the robustness and versatility of embodied AI systems.
introduction:
The ability of artificial agents to operate effectively in complex, dynamic environments depends critically on their capacity to integrate and act upon information from multiple sensory modalities. In both natural and artificial systems, the fusion of complementary sensory inputs—such as vision, audition, and proprioception—enables more robust perception, richer situational awareness, and improved decision-making. While recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (RL) have yielded remarkable performance in domains ranging from game playing to robotic control, much of this progress has been achieved in settings where agents rely on a limited set of sensory channels, often dominated by visual data. This restriction can hinder performance in real-world scenarios, where information is inherently multimodal and temporal correlations across modalities play a critical role.

Incorporating multiple sensory systems into RL agents presents both opportunities and challenges. On one hand, modalities such as audio can provide complementary cues that are less susceptible to visual occlusion, lighting variation, or other perturbations. Auditory information, for example, can signal events outside the agent’s visual field, convey environmental dynamics, and facilitate spatial localization. On the other hand, the integration of multimodal data into high-throughput RL pipelines introduces additional complexity in data processing, synchronization, and representation learning. Furthermore, scaling such systems to train efficiently at the throughput levels demanded by contemporary RL research requires careful architectural and algorithmic design to avoid bottlenecks in computation and communication.

Prior work on multimodal reinforcement learning has demonstrated the potential benefits of combining sensory streams, yet these efforts often focus on proof-of-concept environments or small-scale training regimes. As a result, their applicability to large-scale settings remains underexplored. High-throughput RL frameworks, which leverage parallel simulation and distributed learning to accelerate policy optimization, have been predominantly developed with unimodal inputs in mind. Extending these frameworks to handle multiple sensory modalities—while preserving, or ideally improving, training efficiency—remains an open problem.

In this work, we investigate the integration of auditory perception into high-throughput RL agents, alongside existing visual and proprioceptive channels. We present a system architecture that enables scalable, synchronized processing of multi-sensory inputs without sacrificing training speed. Our approach leverages modality-specific encoders and a shared policy backbone, allowing the agent to learn unified representations while retaining the capacity to exploit modality-specific features. We evaluate our method across a suite of simulated tasks designed to test the complementary strengths of different sensory modalities, and we analyze the conditions under which additional sensory inputs yield measurable performance gains. By addressing the challenges of multimodal integration in a high-throughput RL context, we aim to advance the development of agents that can truly listen, see, and act in rich, dynamic environments.
conclusion:
In this work, we have presented a high-throughput reinforcement learning framework that integrates multiple sensory modalities into a unified agent architecture. By designing agents that can “listen” — in the sense of effectively attending to and integrating heterogeneous streams of perceptual information — we demonstrated that multi-sensory fusion can substantially improve both learning efficiency and task performance in complex environments. Our approach departs from conventional single-modality reinforcement learning by treating sensory channels not as isolated inputs but as interdependent sources of situational awareness, allowing the agent to dynamically adjust its policy in response to richer and more nuanced state representations.

The empirical results across diverse simulated and physical domains indicate that agents equipped with audio, visual, and proprioceptive sensing achieve higher sample efficiency and greater robustness to noise and perturbations than their single-sensory counterparts. Importantly, the high-throughput design of our training pipeline enabled parallelized experience collection and rapid policy updates, making it feasible to explore large state–action spaces without prohibitive computational cost. This combination of sensory integration and throughput optimization suggests a promising direction for scaling reinforcement learning to more realistic and demanding scenarios.

We also observed that multi-sensory agents exhibited emergent behaviors that were less brittle under partial sensory failure, suggesting that redundancy and cross-modal prediction are beneficial not only for performance but also for resilience. The framework’s flexibility allowed for varying the relative weighting of sensory channels, which in turn revealed interesting trade-offs between early convergence speed and long-term policy generalization. These findings underscore the importance of adaptive sensory attention mechanisms when designing agents for environments where the relevance and reliability of different modalities may shift over time.

While our results are encouraging, several limitations remain. The current implementation assumes synchronous sensory inputs with aligned temporal resolutions, which may not hold in many real-world settings. Moreover, the fusion strategies used here, though effective, are relatively simple compared to more sophisticated attention-based or graph-structured models that could capture complex inter-modal dependencies. Future work should investigate asynchronous and event-driven sensory processing, as well as hierarchical policies that can exploit modality-specific sub-policies within a unified control framework.

Beyond technical improvements, the broader implications of agents that can listen and perceive through multiple channels are significant. Such agents could be deployed in assistive robotics, autonomous vehicles, and interactive systems where understanding and responding to multi-sensory cues is essential. By demonstrating that high-throughput reinforcement learning can be effectively combined with multi-sensory integration, we provide a foundation for future research into agents that are not only faster learners but also more adaptable, robust, and capable of nuanced interaction with their environments. In doing so, we take a step toward bridging the gap between artificial and biological agents in their ability to learn from the rich tapestry of sensory information that defines the real world.

title: On the arcmin structure of the X-ray Universe
abstract: We present a systematic analysis of the arcminute-scale structure of the X-ray sky, combining archival data from *Chandra*, *XMM-Newton*, and *eROSITA*. By constructing mosaicked images over several deep and medium-deep extragalactic fields, we quantify the spatial clustering and surface brightness fluctuations of unresolved X-ray emission. Angular correlation functions and power spectra are derived in multiple energy bands, enabling separation of contributions from active galactic nuclei, galaxy clusters, and diffuse intergalactic gas. We find significant excess power on scales of 1–5 arcmin, consistent with the projected distribution of faint galaxy groups and the warm–hot intergalactic medium. Cross-correlation with optical and infrared catalogs strengthens this interpretation. Our results provide new constraints on the small-scale distribution of baryons and the link between X-ray background anisotropies and large-scale structure, demonstrating the potential of arcminute-resolution X-ray mapping for cosmological and astrophysical studies.
introduction: High-resolution X-ray observations have revealed the complex arcminute-scale structure of the Universe, offering crucial insight into the nature and distribution of cosmic sources. Such structures arise from a combination of diffuse emission, extended sources, and unresolved populations, each carrying signatures of astrophysical processes across diverse environments. Advances in instrumentation now allow systematic studies of these features, enabling constraints on source populations, clustering, and evolution. This work examines the arcminute-scale X-ray sky to probe the interplay between large-scale structure and high-energy phenomena.
conclusion:
Our investigation of the arcminute-scale structure of the X-ray sky reveals that significant spatial complexity persists at these intermediate angular resolutions, bridging the gap between the coarse all-sky surveys and the fine detail attainable with sub-arcsecond imaging. By combining archival datasets with targeted observations, we have demonstrated that both diffuse and compact components contribute measurably to the observed anisotropies. The statistical characterization of surface brightness fluctuations indicates that a substantial fraction of the arcminute-scale power arises from the clustering of unresolved extragalactic sources, primarily active galactic nuclei, with an additional contribution from diffuse Galactic emission and the outskirts of nearby galaxy clusters.  

The cross-correlation of X-ray intensity maps with multiwavelength tracers further supports a scenario in which the cosmic web’s hot baryons, residing in filamentary structures, play a non-negligible role at these scales. Our results also highlight the influence of energy band selection, with harder X-ray bands showing a stronger extragalactic signature, while softer bands are more affected by local and Galactic foregrounds.  

These findings underscore the importance of arcminute-resolution X-ray studies for constraining the distribution of matter and energy in the Universe. Such scales are particularly sensitive to the interplay between point-source populations and diffuse structures, offering a unique diagnostic of large-scale structure formation and feedback processes. The methodologies developed here provide a framework for disentangling the overlapping contributions to the X-ray background, and they will be directly applicable to forthcoming surveys from next-generation observatories.  

Future work will benefit from deeper exposures, wider fields, and improved spectral resolution, enabling a more precise separation of thermal and non-thermal components. Ultimately, mapping the X-ray Universe at arcminute scales will be essential for a comprehensive understanding of the high-energy cosmos, linking the fine detail of individual sources to the grand-scale architecture of the Universe.

title: Maxwell's fisheye lens as efficient power coupler between dissimilar photonic crystal waveguides
abstract: We propose and numerically investigate the use of a Maxwell’s fisheye (MFE) lens as an efficient power coupler between dissimilar photonic crystal waveguides. The MFE lens, known for its unique imaging properties, is employed to facilitate low-loss mode transformation between waveguides of differing lattice constants and guiding mechanisms. Full-wave simulations based on the finite-difference time-domain method demonstrate high transmission efficiency and minimal reflection over a broad wavelength range in the telecommunication band. The compact lens design ensures a small footprint while maintaining robust performance against structural imperfections. Our results indicate that the MFE lens offers a versatile and effective solution for photonic integration, enabling seamless interconnection between heterogeneous photonic crystal circuits.
introduction:
Efficient coupling of light between dissimilar photonic crystal waveguides (PCWs) is a critical challenge in the development of highly integrated photonic circuits. Photonic crystal technology offers unique advantages such as strong light confinement, engineered dispersion, and compact device footprints, which make it attractive for applications in optical communications, sensing, and on-chip signal processing. However, transitions between waveguides of different lattice constants, geometries, or modal properties often suffer from significant reflection and scattering losses due to impedance mismatch and mode-profile differences. Designing compact and broadband couplers that can bridge such dissimilar photonic structures remains an active area of research.

Conventional coupling schemes, including tapered waveguides, multimode interference devices, and transformation optics-based approaches, have demonstrated varying degrees of efficiency and footprint minimization. Nonetheless, each method faces trade-offs between fabrication complexity, operational bandwidth, and coupling performance. Transformation optics, in particular, offers a systematic way to control the trajectory of light, enabling low-loss, mode-matched transitions. Maxwell’s fisheye lens (MFL), a well-known gradient-index (GRIN) medium originally conceived for perfect imaging in geometrical optics, has recently attracted attention as a means of guiding light along curved paths or between mismatched modes without introducing abrupt discontinuities. Its refractive index profile, varying smoothly with position, can facilitate adiabatic mode conversion and minimize scattering losses.

The application of MFL concepts to photonic crystals is especially promising, as the GRIN profile can be implemented by locally varying the geometry or refractive index of the photonic crystal lattice. This approach allows the realisation of compact, planar couplers that are fully compatible with standard photonic crystal fabrication methods. Recent studies have demonstrated that GRIN-based devices can achieve high transmission efficiencies over relatively broad spectral ranges, even when coupling between waveguides with substantially different modal properties.

In this work, we propose and numerically investigate a Maxwell’s fisheye lens-based coupler for efficient power transfer between two dissimilar photonic crystal waveguides. By carefully tailoring the effective refractive index distribution through spatial variation of the photonic crystal parameters, we demonstrate that the MFL can serve as a compact, low-loss interface. The design achieves high transmission efficiency and low reflection, offering a practical solution for integrated photonic systems requiring interconnection between heterogeneous waveguide components.
conclusion: In summary, we have demonstrated that the Maxwell’s fisheye lens can serve as an efficient and compact power coupler between dissimilar photonic crystal waveguides. Numerical simulations confirm that its refractive index profile enables low-loss, broadband mode matching, overcoming limitations of conventional taper-based approaches. The design achieves high transmission efficiency while preserving structural compactness, making it attractive for densely integrated photonic circuits. Furthermore, the concept is adaptable to various lattice geometries and wavelength ranges, offering a versatile platform for heterogeneous photonic integration. Future work will explore experimental validation and optimization for fabrication tolerances to fully realize its potential in practical applications.

title: Scalar singlets at present and future colliders
abstract: We investigate the phenomenology of scalar singlets coupled to the Standard Model at present and future collider facilities. Focusing on both minimal extensions and scenarios with additional interactions, we analyze production mechanisms, decay channels, and signatures across a broad mass range. Current LHC constraints are compared with projected sensitivities from HL-LHC, FCC, and other proposed experiments. Our results highlight the discovery potential and parameter space coverage achievable, emphasizing complementarity between collider stages and search strategies.
introduction:
The addition of scalar singlets to the Standard Model (SM) constitutes one of the simplest and most widely studied extensions of the electroweak sector. Such states appear in a variety of theoretical frameworks, including models of electroweak baryogenesis, Higgs-portal dark matter, and solutions to the hierarchy problem. Being singlets under the SM gauge group, they can mix with the Higgs boson through renormalizable interactions, leading to modifications of Higgs couplings and opening new decay channels. This minimal extension can therefore be probed both through precision measurements of Higgs properties and via direct searches for additional scalar resonances.  

Current measurements from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) already place significant constraints on the scalar singlet parameter space, particularly for sizeable mixing angles and masses below the TeV scale. Nevertheless, substantial regions remain unexplored, especially in scenarios with suppressed couplings or unconventional decay modes. Upcoming data from the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and proposed future colliders—such as the FCC, ILC, or CLIC—promise significant advances in sensitivity. The interplay between precision Higgs physics and direct searches will be crucial in this endeavour. In this work, we review the current status of scalar singlet searches, discuss their phenomenology, and assess prospects at present and future collider facilities.
conclusion: In this work, we have examined the phenomenology of scalar singlets at current and proposed future collider facilities, assessing their discovery potential and constraints from existing data. Our analysis shows that present experiments already probe significant regions of parameter space, particularly through precision Higgs measurements and direct searches. Nonetheless, sizeable areas remain accessible only to next-generation colliders, where higher energies and luminosities will enable sensitivity to smaller mixing angles and heavier masses. Complementary channels, including exotic Higgs decays and vector boson fusion processes, will be essential to fully explore the singlet sector. These results underscore the importance of continued collider program development to elucidate possible scalar extensions of the Standard Model and their implications for fundamental physics.

title: Quantum mechanics? It's all fun and games until someone loses an $i$
abstract: Quantum mechanics, with its formalism grounded in complex-valued wavefunctions, rests critically on the mathematical constant \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) to encode phase relationships and superposition phenomena. This paper examines, through a combination of theoretical analysis and pedagogical reflection, the consequences—both humorous and profound—of “losing” the imaginary unit in quantum theory. We explore how the absence of \(i\) transforms the Schrödinger equation into a diffusion-like equation, erasing the oscillatory behavior essential for interference and coherence. By systematically replacing complex amplitudes with purely real quantities, we demonstrate the collapse of unitary time evolution and the emergence of irreversible dynamics. The thought experiment is framed as both a conceptual cautionary tale and a clarifying exercise for students and researchers seeking deeper intuition about the role of complex numbers in physical law. Alongside formal derivations, we discuss historical perspectives on the adoption of complex formalism and consider whether alternative mathematical structures could preserve quantum-like behavior without \(i\). The analysis underscores that while quantum mechanics may inspire playful metaphors, its mathematical architecture is delicately balanced; removing a single symbol can dismantle its foundational symmetries. Thus, “losing an \(i\)” serves as a vivid reminder of the intricate interplay between mathematical abstraction and physical reality.
introduction:
Quantum mechanics has long occupied a unique position in the landscape of modern physics, distinguished both by its unparalleled predictive power and the profound conceptual challenges it presents. Developed in the early twentieth century through the pioneering work of Planck, Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, and others, the theory has evolved into an indispensable framework for describing phenomena at the atomic and subatomic scales. Its formalism, built upon complex-valued wave functions, linear operators, and probabilistic interpretations, has demonstrated extraordinary empirical success, from explaining the stability of atoms to enabling technologies such as semiconductors, lasers, and quantum information processing. Yet, beneath this remarkable efficacy lies a set of mathematical and philosophical questions that continue to provoke debate. Among these is the role of the imaginary unit, \( i = \sqrt{-1} \), which permeates the theory’s structure and appears indispensable to its formulation.

The centrality of \(i\) in quantum mechanics is not merely a matter of mathematical convenience; it emerges naturally in the Schrödinger equation, in the unitary time evolution of states, and in the algebra of observables. The use of complex numbers allows for interference phenomena, a hallmark of quantum systems, and ensures the conservation of probability through the unitary nature of the evolution operator. In this sense, the presence of \(i\) is intimately linked to the dynamical and statistical consistency of the theory. Nevertheless, the reliance on complex quantities raises intriguing questions: Is the imaginary unit an essential ingredient of physical reality, or is it simply a calculational tool embedded in a formalism that could, in principle, be reformulated entirely in real terms? This question is not merely of abstract mathematical interest; it touches on the foundations of quantum theory, the nature of time, and the interpretation of the wave function.

The whimsical framing in the title—“It’s all fun and games until someone loses an \(i\)”—alludes to a serious inquiry: What happens to quantum mechanics when the imaginary unit is removed or altered in its role? A number of researchers have explored “real” formulations of quantum mechanics, in which the complex Hilbert space is replaced by a real Hilbert space or other algebraic structures. Such approaches often require compensating modifications, such as doubling the state space or introducing additional constraints, to recover the empirical predictions of the standard theory. Conversely, there are generalizations to quaternionic or other hypercomplex number systems, which extend the role of \(i\) rather than eliminate it. Each of these avenues sheds light on the interplay between mathematical representation and physical content, and on the extent to which our current formalism is uniquely determined by empirical adequacy.

The investigation of the necessity of \(i\) also intersects with broader foundational debates, including the measurement problem, the interpretation of the wave function, and the role of symmetry principles. In particular, time-reversal symmetry, CPT invariance, and the structure of quantum field theory all exhibit deep connections to the complex phase structure of quantum states. Removing or modifying \(i\) could have nontrivial consequences for these symmetries and for the correspondence between quantum and classical descriptions. Furthermore, in the context of quantum computing and quantum information theory, complex amplitudes are central to algorithms and protocols; understanding whether these amplitudes can be simulated or replaced in a real-number framework has practical as well as conceptual implications.

This paper aims to critically examine the role of the imaginary unit in quantum mechanics, with an emphasis on evaluating to what extent it is indispensable for the coherence, symmetry, and empirical adequacy of the theory. We will review the mathematical necessity of \(i\) in the standard formalism, survey alternative formulations, and assess their physical plausibility. By doing so, we hope to clarify whether the “loss” of an \(i\) in quantum mechanics is a mere change of mathematical language or a fundamental alteration of the theory’s structure. In pursuing this question, we seek not only to deepen our understanding of quantum theory’s mathematical underpinnings but also to probe the subtle boundary between mathematical representation and physical reality.
conclusion:
In bringing this discussion to a close, it is worth reflecting on the peculiar interplay between mathematical formalism and physical interpretation that has characterized the development of quantum mechanics. The tongue‑in‑cheek title of this work—suggesting that the “loss” of an imaginary unit \(i\) might have profound consequences—has served as a framing device for exploring the delicate role of complex numbers in the theory’s structure. We have shown that the ubiquitous presence of \(i\) in the Schrödinger equation is not merely a historical accident or a matter of mathematical convenience; rather, it encodes the deep connection between time evolution, unitarity, and the probabilistic interpretation of quantum states. When the \(i\) is altered, omitted, or replaced, the consequences propagate throughout the formalism, leading in many cases to violations of probability conservation or to dynamics incompatible with observed physical phenomena.

Our analysis has demonstrated that even seemingly minor modifications to the complex structure of quantum mechanics can have nontrivial ramifications for the symmetries and conservation laws upon which the theory depends. In particular, we have observed that removing the imaginary unit from the time‑evolution operator transforms the unitary flow on Hilbert space into a real exponential evolution, which generically leads to exponential growth or decay of norms. Such behavior is mathematically consistent in certain non‑Hermitian or open‑system frameworks, but it departs from the standard postulates that have been extensively confirmed in closed‑system experiments. This reinforces the idea that the complex phase, far from being a dispensable artifact, is integral to the coherent oscillatory behavior that underlies interference, superposition, and entanglement.

Beyond the technical consequences, the thought experiment of “losing an \(i\)” offers a pedagogical vantage point for appreciating the structural unity of quantum theory. By interrogating what breaks down when a single symbol is removed, we are compelled to revisit the web of interdependencies that tie together the mathematical language and the empirical content of the theory. This mode of inquiry reveals, perhaps more vividly than a conventional presentation, how quantum mechanics is less a patchwork of separate rules than a tightly interlocked system in which each postulate supports and constrains the others.

The metaphorical framing also invites reflection on the broader epistemological lesson: in theoretical physics, elegance and internal consistency are not merely aesthetic virtues, but indicators of deep compatibility between mathematics and nature. The imaginary unit’s role in quantum mechanics is emblematic of how abstract mathematical concepts can acquire physical necessity. That necessity is not imposed from outside the theory; it emerges organically from the requirement that predictions match experiments while respecting the symmetries we observe in the world.

In summary, the playful provocation of the title belies a serious conclusion: the “loss” of an \(i\) is not a benign modification, but a transformation that alters the very fabric of quantum theory. Preserving the imaginary unit is tantamount to preserving the core principles—unitarity, probability conservation, and coherent superposition—that give the theory its explanatory and predictive power. Any attempt to reformulate quantum mechanics without it must confront the formidable challenge of reconstructing these principles from alternative foundations. In this light, the imaginary unit stands not as an arbitrary symbol, but as a cornerstone of our most successful description of the microscopic world.

title: Reusing a Pretrained Language Model on Languages with Limited Corpora for Unsupervised NMT
abstract: We investigate the reuse of a pretrained language model to improve unsupervised neural machine translation (UNMT) for languages with limited monolingual resources. While UNMT relies heavily on large corpora for effective cross-lingual alignment, low-resource languages often suffer from poor initialization and inadequate shared representations. We propose leveraging a high-capacity pretrained model, originally trained on resource-rich languages, and adapting it through vocabulary augmentation and lightweight fine-tuning. Our method preserves general linguistic knowledge while incorporating language-specific features from scarce data. Experiments on several low-resource language pairs demonstrate substantial gains over standard UNMT baselines, with improvements in both BLEU and lexical diversity. These results indicate that reusing pretrained language models offers a practical and efficient pathway to enhance translation quality in low-data scenarios.
introduction:
Neural machine translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by the availability of large-scale parallel corpora and advances in deep learning architectures such as the Transformer. State-of-the-art NMT systems are capable of producing fluent and accurate translations for high-resource language pairs, where millions of aligned sentence pairs are available. However, for many of the world’s languages, parallel data is scarce or nonexistent, rendering supervised NMT approaches impractical. This poses a significant challenge for building translation systems that can serve speakers of low-resource languages, which constitute the vast majority of the world’s linguistic diversity.

Unsupervised NMT (UNMT) has emerged as a promising paradigm for overcoming the scarcity of parallel data. By relying on monolingual corpora in each language, UNMT systems learn to translate without direct supervision, typically through a combination of denoising autoencoding, back-translation, and shared latent representations. While UNMT has shown encouraging results for certain language pairs, its performance often lags behind supervised methods, especially when the available monolingual data is also limited in size or domain. This is a common situation for truly low-resource languages, where even monolingual corpora may be small, noisy, or domain-restricted, making it difficult to train robust models from scratch.

One promising direction for addressing this limitation is to reuse pretrained language models (PLMs) that have been trained on large-scale multilingual corpora. Multilingual PLMs such as mBERT, XLM-R, and mT5 capture rich syntactic and semantic knowledge across many languages, including some with relatively little data. Their contextualized representations can be adapted to downstream tasks with relatively small amounts of task-specific data. In the context of UNMT, a pretrained multilingual model can serve as a strong initialization, providing cross-lingual lexical and structural knowledge that reduces the burden on the training process. This approach can be particularly beneficial when one of the target languages has extremely limited resources.

However, directly applying a PLM to UNMT for low-resource languages presents several challenges. First, the PLM’s vocabulary and learned representations may not adequately cover the low-resource language, especially if it was underrepresented in pretraining. Second, the adaptation process must bridge discrepancies in domain, orthography, and morphology between the pretraining data and the target monolingual corpora. Third, ensuring that the model learns to align the two languages in a shared latent space without parallel supervision requires careful design of training objectives and initialization strategies.

In this work, we investigate methods for reusing a pretrained multilingual language model to improve UNMT for language pairs with limited monolingual corpora. We explore techniques for adapting the PLM to better represent low-resource languages, aligning cross-lingual embeddings, and fine-tuning for translation in an unsupervised setting. Our experiments focus on scenarios where both languages are low-resource or where one is low-resource and the other moderately resourced. The results demonstrate that strategic reuse and adaptation of PLMs can substantially improve translation quality over UNMT baselines trained from scratch, highlighting the potential of this approach for extending high-quality machine translation to the world’s underserved languages.
conclusion: In this work, we investigated the reuse of a pretrained language model for unsupervised neural machine translation in scenarios with limited monolingual data. By leveraging cross-lingual representations learned from high-resource languages, our approach effectively bridges the gap for low-resource language pairs without requiring parallel corpora. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline systems, highlighting the value of pretrained models as a foundation for adaptation. Furthermore, our findings suggest that careful fine-tuning and vocabulary alignment are critical to maximizing transfer performance. This study underscores the potential of pretrained language models to reduce the data barrier in low-resource translation and opens avenues for extending these methods to a wider range of typologically diverse languages and domains.

title: FILDNE: A Framework for Incremental Learning of Dynamic Networks Embeddings
abstract: Dynamic networks, such as evolving social or communication graphs, require representation learning methods that can adapt to structural changes over time without retraining from scratch. Existing dynamic network embedding approaches often struggle to balance efficiency, stability, and adaptability when new nodes, edges, or attributes emerge incrementally. We propose **FILDNE**, a novel framework for *Framework for Incremental Learning of Dynamic Networks Embeddings*, which updates node embeddings in an online manner while preserving previously learned structural patterns. FILDNE employs a hybrid update mechanism that leverages local neighborhood perturbations to efficiently adjust embeddings, combined with temporal regularization to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. The framework supports heterogeneous update scenarios, including node addition, edge modification, and weight adjustment, and operates with sub-linear complexity relative to network size. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world dynamic graph datasets demonstrate that FILDNE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in link prediction and node classification tasks, while achieving significant reductions in update time and memory consumption. Our results highlight FILDNE’s effectiveness in maintaining high-quality embeddings under continuous network evolution, making it suitable for large-scale, rapidly changing graph applications such as recommendation systems, fraud detection, and social network analysis.
introduction:
The rapid growth of networked data across diverse domains such as social media, citation networks, communication systems, and biological interactions has driven significant interest in developing methods for learning expressive representations of nodes, edges, and entire graphs. Network embedding techniques aim to map nodes in a graph to low-dimensional vector spaces while preserving the underlying structural and semantic properties. These learned embeddings have become a cornerstone for a wide range of downstream tasks, including node classification, link prediction, community detection, and anomaly detection. By enabling the transformation of complex, high-dimensional relational structures into more tractable continuous spaces, network embeddings facilitate the application of machine learning algorithms that operate effectively in vector spaces.

While the literature on network embedding has grown extensively, much of the early work has focused on static networks—networks whose topology does not change over time. In reality, however, many networks are inherently dynamic: new nodes and edges are continuously added, existing ones disappear, and the strength of relationships evolves. Social networks witness the formation and dissolution of friendships, citation networks expand as new papers are published, and communication networks fluctuate in response to human activity patterns. Such temporal evolution poses significant challenges for network embedding methods. Models trained on a static snapshot of the network quickly become outdated, losing their ability to accurately capture current structural features and relationships. This motivates the need for dynamic network embedding methods, which can adapt to topological changes and update node representations as the network evolves.

Dynamic network embedding methods can be broadly categorized into two approaches: retraining-based and incremental. Retraining-based methods periodically learn embeddings from scratch using the updated network structure. Although conceptually straightforward, these methods are computationally expensive and often infeasible for large-scale, rapidly evolving networks, as they require reprocessing the entire graph at each update step. Incremental methods, in contrast, update existing embeddings to reflect network changes without recomputing from scratch. Such methods promise substantial gains in efficiency and scalability, enabling near real-time adaptation to network dynamics. However, designing effective incremental learning strategies is challenging. The updated embeddings must remain consistent with previously learned representations while accurately reflecting new structural information. Additionally, they must balance computational efficiency with embedding quality, avoiding the accumulation of errors or drift over time.

Existing incremental dynamic network embedding approaches often face limitations in one or more dimensions. Some methods require extensive storage of past network states, which is impractical in memory-constrained environments. Others rely on restrictive assumptions about the nature of network evolution, such as the temporal smoothness of embeddings, which may not hold in domains with abrupt changes. Furthermore, many approaches lack a principled framework for integrating new information with prior knowledge, resulting in degraded performance in long-term deployments. There is thus a pressing need for a robust, generalizable, and efficient framework for incremental learning of dynamic network embeddings, capable of handling large-scale and rapidly evolving graphs without sacrificing representational quality.

In this work, we propose FILDNE, a *Framework for Incremental Learning of Dynamic Networks Embeddings*, which addresses these challenges by combining efficient update mechanisms with principled model adaptation. FILDNE is designed to incrementally adjust node embeddings as the network changes, leveraging both the local structural modifications and the global context of the network. By avoiding full retraining and instead focusing computation on affected regions of the graph, FILDNE achieves significant reductions in update time and resource consumption. At the same time, it employs a mechanism to preserve embedding stability, ensuring that representations remain comparable across time steps and suitable for longitudinal analysis.

The key contributions of this work are threefold. First, we introduce a general incremental learning framework that is compatible with a wide range of base embedding algorithms, enabling practitioners to extend existing methods to dynamic settings with minimal modification. Second, we develop an efficient update strategy that selectively processes changes in the graph, maintaining embedding quality while significantly reducing computational overhead. Third, we demonstrate through extensive experiments on multiple real-world dynamic networks that FILDNE outperforms baseline incremental and retraining-based methods in terms of both efficiency and predictive performance on downstream tasks.

By providing a scalable and adaptable approach to dynamic network embedding, FILDNE bridges the gap between static embedding methods and the demands of real-time, evolving network environments. Our framework offers a practical solution for applications where timely and accurate node representations are critical, including fraud detection in financial transaction networks, recommendation systems in social platforms, and monitoring of infrastructure or communication networks. In doing so, it contributes to the broader goal of enabling machine learning systems to operate effectively in settings characterized by continual change.
conclusion:
In this work, we introduced **FILDNE**, a novel framework for *incremental learning of dynamic network embeddings* that addresses the challenges posed by evolving graph structures in real-world applications. Unlike static embedding methods, which require complete retraining when network topology changes, FILDNE is designed to efficiently update node representations as new nodes, edges, and attributes arrive, while preserving previously learned structural and semantic information. This capability enables the framework to handle the temporal dimension of networks effectively, reducing computational costs and mitigating the risks of catastrophic forgetting.

FILDNE builds upon the principles of representation learning for graphs, but incorporates a carefully designed update mechanism that balances adaptation to new information with retention of historical patterns. By leveraging both local and global structural cues during updates, the framework maintains embedding stability over time while ensuring sensitivity to significant network changes. Our empirical evaluation across multiple real-world dynamic network datasets demonstrated that FILDNE achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines in tasks such as link prediction and node classification, while requiring significantly less retraining overhead. The results confirm that incremental learning strategies can substantially improve scalability and responsiveness in dynamic network analysis.

An important contribution of this study lies in the formulation of an embedding update strategy that integrates temporal smoothness regularization with selective neighborhood aggregation. This design allows the model to selectively adjust embeddings for affected regions of the graph without unnecessarily perturbing unaffected areas, thereby preserving the consistency of the learned representation space. Furthermore, the modular nature of FILDNE facilitates integration with a variety of base embedding models, making it adaptable to different domains and task requirements.

The experimental outcomes also highlight the importance of properly balancing historical context and new observations. We observed that excessive emphasis on either component can degrade performance: overly conservative updates may fail to capture emerging patterns, while overly aggressive updates risk discarding valuable historical structure. FILDNE’s parameterized update scheme offers a tunable solution to this trade-off, enabling practitioners to adapt the framework to the dynamics of their specific application domain.

While the proposed framework delivers notable improvements, several avenues remain for future research. One direction involves extending FILDNE to handle heterogeneous dynamic networks with multiple types of nodes and relations, which are common in knowledge graphs and multi-modal interaction networks. Another promising extension is the incorporation of attention mechanisms to automatically weight the relevance of historical versus recent information based on the evolving network context. Additionally, exploring distributed and streaming implementations would further enhance the scalability of the approach for massive, high-velocity networks.

In summary, FILDNE contributes a flexible, efficient, and effective solution for incremental embedding of dynamic networks, bridging the gap between the need for timely updates and the preservation of long-term structural knowledge. By enabling continuous learning from evolving data, it opens new opportunities for real-time analysis and decision-making in complex networked systems.

title: Hamilton's approach in cosmological inflation with an exponential potential and its observational constraints
abstract: We investigate cosmological inflation driven by a scalar field with an exponential potential within the Hamiltonian formalism, focusing on the advantages of this approach for both analytical treatment and comparison with observational data. By formulating the inflationary dynamics in terms of Hamilton’s equations, we obtain exact and approximate solutions for the scale factor and scalar field evolution, allowing a transparent characterization of the phase space structure. The exponential potential, motivated by high-energy theories and scaling solutions, yields a constant slow-roll parameter in the simplest case, but we extend the analysis to include deviations enabling a graceful exit from inflation. We compute inflationary observables, such as the scalar spectral index \(n_s\) and tensor-to-scalar ratio \(r\), directly from the Hamiltonian framework, and confront these predictions with the latest Planck and BICEP/Keck constraints. Our results show that pure exponential models are tightly constrained and often require modifications to remain viable, while generalized exponential forms can produce observationally consistent predictions. The Hamiltonian approach proves effective in unifying dynamical analysis and data confrontation, offering a robust tool for exploring inflationary scenarios and their theoretical underpinnings.
introduction: Cosmological inflation provides a compelling framework for addressing the horizon, flatness, and monopole problems of the standard Big Bang model, while offering a mechanism for the generation of primordial perturbations. Among the various inflationary models, those with exponential potentials have attracted sustained interest due to their analytical tractability and emergence in high-energy theories such as Kaluza–Klein and string-inspired scenarios. The Hamiltonian formulation offers an alternative approach to studying inflationary dynamics, enabling a clearer phase-space analysis and facilitating connections with canonical quantization. In this work, we apply Hamilton’s formalism to the case of a single scalar field with an exponential potential, deriving the corresponding dynamical equations and inflationary parameters. We then confront the model’s predictions with current observational constraints from cosmic microwave background measurements, examining its viability in light of recent Planck and related data.
conclusion: In this work, we have applied Hamilton’s formalism to study cosmological inflation driven by an exponential potential, deriving the dynamical equations and analyzing their implications for early-universe evolution. The Hamiltonian approach provides a transparent framework for identifying conserved quantities and exploring phase-space trajectories. Confronting the theoretical predictions with current observational constraints from CMB measurements, we find that viable parameter ranges remain, though tightly bounded. These results reinforce the consistency of exponential inflation within Hamilton’s framework and suggest directions for further refinement with future data.

title: Bi-convolution matrix factorization algorithm based on improved ConvMF
abstract: In recent years, matrix factorization methods have been widely applied in recommendation systems due to their effectiveness in capturing latent user–item interactions. Convolutional Matrix Factorization (ConvMF) integrates convolutional neural networks with probabilistic matrix factorization to exploit contextual information from item content. However, traditional ConvMF may suffer from limited feature extraction capability and insufficient modeling of complex correlations between users and items. To address these issues, this paper proposes a bi-convolution matrix factorization algorithm based on an improved ConvMF framework. The method employs dual convolutional modules to extract multi-scale semantic features from textual content, enhancing representation diversity. Furthermore, an adaptive weighting mechanism is introduced to balance user and item feature contributions, improving prediction accuracy. The proposed approach incorporates regularization strategies to mitigate overfitting and optimize convergence. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the bi-convolution model achieves superior performance compared to standard ConvMF and other baseline methods, particularly in scenarios with sparse rating data. The results verify the effectiveness of the improved architecture in leveraging rich content information for more accurate recommendations.
introduction:
In recent years, the rapid growth of digital information has led to an urgent need for efficient and accurate recommendation systems. These systems aim to predict user preferences by leveraging historical interaction data, thereby enabling personalized content delivery in domains such as e-commerce, online streaming, social media, and digital libraries. Among various approaches, collaborative filtering (CF) has been one of the most widely adopted techniques due to its effectiveness in uncovering latent patterns between users and items. Matrix factorization (MF) methods, in particular, have shown considerable success by decomposing the user–item interaction matrix into low-dimensional latent feature representations. Despite their popularity, traditional MF models often suffer from data sparsity and cold-start problems, which limit their predictive performance in real-world applications.

To address the limitations of standard MF, researchers have explored incorporating auxiliary information, such as item content and contextual features, into the recommendation process. Content-based extensions of MF, including convolutional matrix factorization (ConvMF), integrate textual or visual attributes of items into the latent feature learning process. ConvMF leverages convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract high-level semantic representations from item descriptions, which are then coupled with MF to improve recommendation accuracy, particularly under sparse interaction scenarios. By combining deep feature extraction with latent factor modeling, ConvMF has demonstrated improved performance compared to conventional MF and other hybrid approaches. However, existing ConvMF frameworks still face challenges in effectively capturing complex bidirectional relationships between users and items, as well as in fully utilizing the deep semantic information derived from content features.

A primary limitation of traditional ConvMF lies in its one-sided convolutional feature extraction, where convolutional operations are typically applied only to item content and not to user-related attributes. This asymmetry can result in suboptimal latent representations, as the model fails to exploit potential structural patterns on the user side. Furthermore, the integration between CNN-extracted features and matrix factorization is often linear and shallow, which may restrict the model’s ability to capture higher-order interactions. In many recommendation contexts, user preferences are shaped not only by item content but also by complex co-occurrence patterns and contextual signals that require more sophisticated modeling techniques.

To better address these issues, bi-convolution matrix factorization offers a promising direction. The core idea is to perform convolutional feature extraction on both user and item domains, thereby achieving a more balanced and comprehensive representation learning framework. By applying convolutional operations to user-related data—such as demographic attributes, historical interaction sequences, or social network information—alongside item content, it becomes possible to model richer interactions in the latent space. This dual feature extraction strategy can capture bidirectional semantic structures and improve the alignment between user and item latent factors.

Building upon this motivation, this work proposes a bi-convolution matrix factorization algorithm based on an improved ConvMF architecture. The proposed method enhances the original ConvMF in several key aspects. Firstly, it incorporates convolutional neural networks on both the user and item sides, enabling simultaneous extraction of high-level user and item features before latent factor integration. Secondly, it introduces an improved fusion mechanism that combines deep semantic features with MF in a nonlinear manner, allowing for the capture of more complex user–item interaction patterns. Thirdly, the model integrates a refined regularization strategy to prevent overfitting and to ensure robustness in sparse data environments.

The contributions of this work are threefold. (1) We extend the conventional ConvMF framework to a bi-convolutional structure, achieving symmetric and richer representation learning for both users and items. (2) We design an improved feature fusion approach that leverages nonlinear transformations to more effectively integrate deep convolutional features with latent factor models. (3) We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, comparing it with state-of-the-art MF-based and deep learning-based recommendation methods.

By bridging the gap between deep semantic feature extraction and collaborative latent factor modeling in a bidirectional manner, the proposed bi-convolution matrix factorization algorithm aims to enhance recommendation accuracy, particularly in scenarios with sparse data and heterogeneous auxiliary information. The improved ConvMF architecture not only strengthens the expressiveness of latent representations but also provides a flexible framework for integrating diverse types of user and item side information. This research contributes to the ongoing development of hybrid recommendation models that combine the strengths of collaborative filtering and deep learning, offering new insights into the design of more effective and generalizable recommendation systems.
conclusion: In this paper, we proposed a bi-convolution matrix factorization algorithm based on an improved ConvMF framework to enhance recommendation accuracy and robustness. By introducing dual convolution operations, the method effectively captures both local and global contextual features in user–item interaction data. The improved architecture incorporates optimized feature extraction and adaptive weight learning, enabling better integration of side information and alleviating sparsity issues. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms traditional matrix factorization and standard ConvMF approaches in terms of prediction accuracy and generalization. The findings confirm the effectiveness of combining bi-convolution structures with enhanced feature modeling for recommendation tasks. Future work will explore scalability to larger datasets, integration with heterogeneous information networks, and application to dynamic recommendation scenarios.

title: Frequency Dependent Specific Heat from Thermal Effusion in Spherical Geometry
abstract: We present a theoretical and experimental investigation of frequency-dependent specific heat measurements using thermal effusion in spherical geometry. The method exploits periodic heating of a spherical surface embedded in a surrounding medium, with the resulting temperature response analyzed in the frequency domain. By solving the heat diffusion equation for spherical symmetry, we derive expressions linking the complex thermal impedance to the dynamic specific heat of the material. The spherical geometry minimizes boundary effects and enables probing of bulk-like response over a wide frequency range. Experiments were performed on viscous liquids near the glass transition, where the specific heat exhibits pronounced dispersion. The measured thermal effusivity agrees with model predictions, and the extracted frequency-dependent specific heat matches independent calorimetric data. Our results demonstrate that spherical thermal effusion provides an accurate and versatile tool for characterizing thermally activated relaxation processes in complex materials.
introduction:
The measurement of specific heat is a cornerstone in the characterization of thermal properties of materials. In its most familiar form, specific heat is treated as a static quantity, reflecting the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass by one degree under equilibrium conditions. However, in systems where thermal energy exchange involves internal degrees of freedom with finite relaxation times—such as molecular reorientations, conformational changes, or structural relaxations—the specific heat becomes frequency dependent. This so-called “dynamic” or “complex” specific heat contains information not only about the total heat capacity but also about the kinetics of underlying energy exchange processes. Over the past decades, frequency-dependent calorimetry has therefore emerged as a powerful tool for probing relaxation phenomena in liquids, polymers, glasses, and other complex materials.

One experimental approach to frequency-dependent calorimetry is thermal effusion, in which a small temperature oscillation is imposed on a heater in contact with the sample, and the resulting heat flux is measured. The ratio of temperature oscillation to heat flux, as a function of frequency, yields information about the thermal impedance of the system. Through appropriate modeling, this impedance can be related to the complex specific heat. Thermal effusion has been implemented in various geometries, most notably planar, cylindrical, and spherical. Each geometry imposes a characteristic spatial profile on the oscillating temperature field, leading to different sensitivities to the thermal parameters of interest. Planar geometries have been widely studied and are well-suited for probing bulk materials with relatively simple boundary conditions. Cylindrical and spherical geometries, on the other hand, arise naturally in situations involving wires, fibers, beads, or particles, and their inherently nonuniform temperature fields can offer distinct advantages for certain measurement contexts.

Spherical geometry is particularly relevant in experiments where the heat source is a small particle embedded in the sample or where the sensing element itself is spherical, such as in the transient hot bead method. In such cases, the radial symmetry simplifies the mathematical description of heat diffusion while simultaneously allowing the sample to be probed in all directions from the source. Thermal effusion in spherical geometry differs fundamentally from the planar case in that the thermal wave amplitude decays not only because of intrinsic thermal diffusion but also due to geometric spreading. This leads to a modified relationship between thermal impedance and the material’s thermal properties. For frequency-dependent specific heat measurements, it is therefore essential to account for the combined effects of geometry, thermal conductivity, and the relaxation dynamics of internal degrees of freedom.

In the frequency domain, heat diffusion in a medium with complex specific heat is described by a diffusion equation in which the thermal diffusivity becomes complex-valued. The penetration depth of the oscillating thermal wave is then frequency dependent, shrinking as the frequency increases. When the thermal penetration depth is comparable to or smaller than the characteristic size of the system, finite-size effects and boundary conditions must be carefully considered. In spherical geometry, the interplay between penetration depth and radius of the source or sensor defines the operational frequency window over which reliable extraction of the complex specific heat is possible. Moreover, the interpretation of experimental data requires an explicit inversion from the measured thermal impedance to the underlying frequency-dependent specific heat, which can be nontrivial when geometry and material dispersion are coupled.

Previous studies have developed theoretical frameworks for thermal effusion in planar and cylindrical geometries, often under simplifying assumptions such as purely real specific heat or negligible thermal contact resistance. Extensions to spherical geometry have also been reported, but in many cases the treatment of frequency-dependent specific heat has been limited or approximate. A systematic derivation of the relationship between the measurable thermal impedance in spherical effusion and the complex specific heat, valid across a broad frequency range, has been lacking. Such a derivation is not only of theoretical interest but also of practical importance for the design and interpretation of experiments involving microspheres, nanoparticles, or bead-based sensors, especially in soft matter and complex fluids where relaxation phenomena are prominent.

In this work we present a detailed analysis of frequency-dependent specific heat determination from thermal effusion in spherical geometry. Starting from the heat diffusion equation with a complex heat capacity, we derive the exact expression for the thermal impedance of a sphere in contact with a surrounding medium. We examine the asymptotic limits of low and high frequency, elucidating the roles of thermal conductivity, particle radius, and penetration depth. We also discuss the inversion procedure for extracting the complex specific heat from experimental impedance data, highlighting potential sources of error and strategies for their mitigation. The theoretical results are illustrated with model calculations and compared, where possible, with existing experimental data. By providing a rigorous and comprehensive treatment, we aim to establish spherical thermal effusion as a robust method for probing dynamic calorimetric properties, thereby extending the toolbox available for the study of relaxation phenomena in condensed matter systems.
conclusion:
In this work, we have investigated the determination of frequency-dependent specific heat by means of thermal effusion in a spherical geometry. Building upon the theoretical framework of heat transport in materials exhibiting thermal relaxation phenomena, we have derived and analyzed the relationships between the measurable effusivity in oscillatory heating experiments and the underlying complex, frequency-dependent specific heat. The spherical geometry, in contrast to the planar case more commonly treated in the literature, offers distinct advantages for certain experimental configurations, particularly in cases where the heater or sensor naturally assumes a compact, isotropic form such as a bead, droplet, or encapsulated thermistor. Moreover, the geometry mitigates some of the edge effects or lateral losses that can complicate planar measurements, while introducing its own characteristic radial heat flow profile.

Our analysis has shown that, under the constraints of linear response theory and assuming homogeneous, isotropic material properties in the region of interest, the governing heat diffusion equation in spherical coordinates admits analytic solutions in the frequency domain that explicitly connect the thermal admittance to the complex specific heat. In the low-frequency limit, the measured effusivity approaches the value determined by the equilibrium, static specific heat and thermal conductivity, recovering the well-known steady-state behavior. In the high-frequency limit, the penetration depth of the thermal wave becomes small compared to the sphere radius, and the response reflects primarily the high-frequency limiting value of the specific heat, which may differ significantly from the static value in materials with slow internal degrees of freedom.

An important outcome of the present study is the clarification of how the finite size of the spherical effusing body influences the interpretation of the measured data. Unlike in planar effusion, where the thermal wave penetrates semi-infinitely into the material, in a finite sphere the interplay between penetration depth and sphere radius produces a crossover in the frequency dependence of the thermal response. This crossover contains valuable information about both the thermal diffusivity and the dispersion of specific heat, but also requires careful modeling to avoid systematic errors in parameter extraction. The derived expressions and asymptotic limits provide a practical basis for such modeling, and can be adapted to experimental data analysis across a range of frequencies.

We have further discussed the implications of the frequency-dependent specific heat for characterizing complex fluids, polymers, and other materials in which structural relaxation or other slow processes contribute significantly to the thermal response. By resolving the specific heat into its real and imaginary components as a function of frequency, one gains direct insight into the timescales and magnitudes of these processes. The spherical thermal effusion method, as formulated here, thus offers a complementary approach to more established calorimetric techniques, with the potential to probe frequency ranges that are difficult to access otherwise.

From an experimental standpoint, the spherical configuration lends itself well to setups where the heating element is embedded within or in intimate contact with the material under study. The symmetry simplifies the boundary conditions and can reduce the influence of thermal contact resistances, provided that the interface is well-controlled. Nevertheless, practical measurements must account for additional factors such as radiation losses at elevated temperatures, deviations from perfect sphericity, and possible anisotropy in the sample. Our theoretical treatment provides a framework for estimating and correcting for such effects when they are small; in cases where they are not negligible, numerical simulation may be required to complement the analytic results.

In summary, the present work extends the theory of thermal effusion to spherical geometry with explicit inclusion of frequency-dependent specific heat, yielding analytic expressions that connect measurable quantities to the underlying thermophysical properties. The results underscore the sensitivity of the method to both the equilibrium and dynamic aspects of specific heat, and point to the importance of considering finite-size effects in the interpretation of data. The approach is applicable to a broad variety of materials, particularly those with pronounced thermal relaxation phenomena, and offers a pathway to richer characterization than is possible with frequency-independent models. Future work could focus on experimental validation of the theory across different materials systems, exploration of non-linear effects at higher excitation amplitudes, and extension to non-homogeneous or multi-phase materials where the spherical thermal effusion method may reveal additional complexities. By combining careful experimental design with the theoretical insights presented here, spherical thermal effusion promises to be a powerful tool in the study of frequency-dependent thermal properties.

title: Distinguishing among dark matter annihilation channels with neutrino telescopes
abstract: We investigate the potential of neutrino telescopes to discriminate among dark matter annihilation channels by analyzing the resulting neutrino energy spectra. Using simulated signals from benchmark dark matter masses and annihilation modes, including leptonic, hadronic, and gauge boson final states, we model neutrino propagation through the Sun and Earth, incorporating oscillations, absorption, and regeneration effects. We evaluate the sensitivity of current and next-generation detectors to spectral features that distinguish channels, focusing on energy resolution, background rejection, and statistical inference. Our results indicate that, for dark matter masses above several hundred GeV, characteristic spectral shapes enable channel identification at high significance, particularly for hard versus soft spectra. These findings highlight the role of neutrino telescopes as complementary probes of dark matter particle properties beyond detection of total flux alone.
introduction:
The existence of dark matter is supported by a wide range of astrophysical and cosmological observations, from galactic rotation curves and gravitational lensing to the anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background. Despite its inferred abundance—constituting roughly 27% of the total energy density of the Universe—the nature of dark matter remains one of the most pressing open questions in modern physics. A broad class of candidates, including weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), axions, and sterile neutrinos, has been proposed to explain its properties. Among these, WIMPs are particularly well-motivated, as they naturally arise in several extensions of the Standard Model and can achieve the correct relic abundance through thermal freeze-out in the early Universe.

If dark matter is composed of WIMPs or other particles capable of self-annihilation, their mutual annihilation in regions of high density could produce Standard Model particles, including high-energy neutrinos. Neutrino telescopes, such as IceCube at the South Pole, ANTARES in the Mediterranean Sea, and the upcoming KM3NeT, are designed to detect these neutrino signals. Unlike charged cosmic rays and photons, neutrinos propagate in straight trajectories largely unaffected by intervening matter and radiation fields, allowing them to carry direct information from dense astrophysical environments such as the Galactic Center, the Sun, and dwarf spheroidal galaxies. In particular, the Sun is an especially promising target: dark matter particles gravitationally captured in its core can accumulate over time, leading to an equilibrium between capture and annihilation. The resulting neutrino flux would be a unique indirect signature of dark matter.

A key challenge in interpreting any potential neutrino signal is distinguishing among the possible annihilation channels of dark matter. Depending on the underlying particle physics model, dark matter may annihilate into a variety of Standard Model final states, such as \(b\bar{b}\), \(W^+W^-\), \(\tau^+\tau^-\), or directly into neutrino–antineutrino pairs. Each channel produces a characteristic neutrino energy spectrum, shaped by the decay chains and interactions of the primary annihilation products. For example, annihilation into heavy quarks yields a softer neutrino spectrum due to hadronization and subsequent meson decays, while annihilation into leptonic channels can produce harder spectra with higher-energy neutrinos. Direct annihilation into neutrinos would generate a monochromatic line at an energy close to the dark matter particle mass. Identifying the dominant annihilation channel is crucial for constraining the properties of the dark matter particle, such as its mass, couplings, and possible mediators.

Neutrino telescopes measure the energy and arrival direction of neutrinos primarily through the Cherenkov light emitted by charged leptons produced in neutrino–nucleon interactions. The energy resolution, angular resolution, and background rejection capabilities of these detectors play a central role in the ability to discriminate between different annihilation channels. Atmospheric neutrinos constitute the dominant background, with additional contributions from cosmic-ray–induced muons. Statistical techniques are therefore required to extract a potential dark matter signal from the background and to assess the likelihood that a given spectral and angular distribution corresponds to a specific annihilation channel. 

Recent analyses have demonstrated that with sufficient statistics, differences in the spectral shape of neutrinos from various channels can indeed be resolved. For example, simulations indicate that IceCube is sensitive to the spectral hardening characteristic of leptonic channels compared to hadronic ones, particularly for dark matter masses above a few hundred GeV. Furthermore, combining data from multiple neutrino observatories with complementary sky coverage and detector characteristics can enhance the ability to distinguish between channels, especially when combined with multi-messenger observations in gamma rays or charged cosmic rays.

Theoretical models predict correlations between the branching ratios of different annihilation channels and other observables, such as the spin-dependent or spin-independent scattering cross section with nucleons. Consequently, the ability to identify the dominant annihilation channel not only informs the particle physics nature of dark matter but also constrains the viable parameter space of candidate models. In scenarios where multiple channels contribute significantly, a spectral decomposition of the neutrino flux may reveal the relative weights of each channel, offering further clues about the underlying interactions.

In this work, we investigate the prospects for distinguishing among dark matter annihilation channels using current and next-generation neutrino telescopes. We focus on the neutrino spectra expected from a set of representative channels and assess the statistical significance with which they can be discriminated under realistic detector conditions. By quantifying the impact of energy resolution, exposure time, and background modeling, we aim to provide a framework for interpreting possible future neutrino signals in terms of the underlying dark matter physics. This approach has the potential to bridge the gap between indirect detection experiments and theoretical models, offering a pathway toward identifying the fundamental nature of dark matter.
conclusion:
In this work we have investigated the potential of neutrino telescopes to distinguish among different dark matter annihilation channels by exploiting the spectral and angular features of the resulting neutrino flux. Using a range of representative annihilation final states, including both leptonic and hadronic channels, we have modelled the expected neutrino energy spectra for dark matter masses spanning the sub-TeV to multi-TeV regime. By propagating these spectra through realistic detector response models, we have assessed the degree to which neutrino observatories such as IceCube and KM3NeT can discriminate between channels under plausible astrophysical and experimental conditions.  

Our results demonstrate that the shape of the neutrino energy spectrum, particularly the presence or absence of sharp cutoffs and hard components, carries substantial discriminatory power. Leptonic channels, such as \(\chi\chi \rightarrow \nu\bar{\nu}\) or \(\chi\chi \rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-\), tend to produce harder spectra with more pronounced high-energy features, whereas hadronic channels, such as \(\chi\chi \rightarrow b\bar{b}\) or \(\chi\chi \rightarrow W^+W^-\), yield softer, broader distributions due to hadronization and subsequent decay chains. These differences persist even after accounting for neutrino oscillations en route to the detector.  

We have further shown that the inclusion of angular information, particularly for annihilation in the Galactic Center or in nearby dwarf spheroidal galaxies, can enhance channel separation. The combination of spectral and directional likelihood analyses increases the statistical significance with which one can reject incorrect channel hypotheses, especially when the signal-to-background ratio is modest. While atmospheric neutrinos remain the dominant background, their smoother energy dependence and isotropic distribution make them less likely to mimic the distinctive features of certain dark matter–induced spectra.  

Our study also highlights the importance of detector energy resolution and flavor identification capability. Improved resolution not only sharpens spectral features, aiding in channel discrimination, but also reduces degeneracy between different dark matter masses and annihilation channels. Although current large-volume Cherenkov detectors have limited flavor sensitivity, even partial separation of muon tracks from cascade events can provide valuable additional constraints.  

We emphasize that our conclusions are based on idealized signal injections and do not account for all possible systematic uncertainties, such as those arising from the dark matter density profile, neutrino–nucleon cross-section modeling, or detector calibration. Nonetheless, the qualitative trends we identify are robust: more precise energy measurements, larger effective volumes, and the combination of spectral and angular analyses will significantly improve the ability of neutrino telescopes to probe the particle physics nature of dark matter.
