Incorporating microscopic defect models and interface state distributions into such simulations can further improve their predictive power.

In this work, we present a comparative study of photoconversion in HIT solar cells from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We employ state‑of‑the‑art modeling tools to simulate the optical and electrical behavior of representative device structures, using input parameters derived from independent measurements wherever possible. We then fabricate and characterize HIT devices under conditions matched to the simulations, allowing for a direct comparison between predicted and observed performance metrics. By systematically varying key structural parameters such as intrinsic layer thickness, doped layer properties, and TCO characteristics, we investigate the origins of discrepancies between theory and experiment and assess the validity of common modeling assumptions.

Our aim is to provide an integrated picture of how photoconversion in HIT solar cells is influenced by the interplay of optical and electrical factors, and to identify the dominant loss mechanisms that limit real‑world device performance relative to theoretical limits. The insights gained from this study are expected to inform both the refinement of physical models and the development of improved fabrication strategies, thereby contributing to the continued advancement of high‑efficiency silicon heterojunction photovoltaics.
conclusion:
The comparative analysis of theoretical predictions and experimental results for photoconversion in HIT solar cells demonstrates a generally good agreement in the trends of efficiency, open-circuit voltage, and fill factor, particularly under standard test conditions. The theoretical model, incorporating carrier transport across the heterointerface, recombination processes, and optical absorption in both crystalline and amorphous layers, successfully captures the essential mechanisms governing device performance. Discrepancies between calculated and measured values are attributed primarily to variations in interface quality, localized defect states, and non-uniformities in the thin amorphous layers, which are challenging to parameterize precisely.  

Experimental data confirm the high potential of HIT structures to maintain high efficiency at elevated temperatures, consistent with model expectations derived from the reduced temperature coefficient of the open-circuit voltage. However, deviations under low-light conditions suggest that additional loss channels, not fully accounted for in the model, may play a significant role.  

Overall, the study reinforces the validity of the theoretical framework while highlighting the importance of accurate material and interface characterization for predictive modeling. Further refinement of the model to incorporate spatial inhomogeneities, advanced recombination kinetics, and realistic surface passivation parameters will enhance its predictive power. Such improvements will be essential for guiding the optimization of HIT solar cells toward their theoretical performance limits.

title: A Universal Part-of-Speech Tagset
abstract: We present a universal part-of-speech (POS) tagset designed to facilitate cross-linguistic natural language processing and corpus annotation. Existing tagsets vary widely across languages, hindering multilingual applications and comparative linguistic studies. Our proposed tagset defines a small, consistent inventory of POS categories that balances linguistic adequacy with practical applicability. We describe the mapping of diverse language-specific tags to this universal set and evaluate its coverage on multiple annotated corpora. Results demonstrate improved interoperability, enabling more effective transfer learning, multilingual parsing, and cross-lingual evaluation, while maintaining sufficient granularity for diverse linguistic and computational tasks.
introduction:
Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), providing crucial syntactic information that supports a wide range of downstream applications, including parsing, machine translation, information extraction, and sentiment analysis. POS tags indicate the grammatical category of each word in a text—such as noun, verb, adjective, or adverb—thereby enabling computational systems to capture structural relationships and to generalize across linguistic contexts. Over the past decades, numerous tagsets have been developed for specific languages and corpora, each tailored to the linguistic characteristics, orthographic conventions, and annotation goals of a given community. While this diversity has facilitated detailed and language-specific analysis, it has also led to fragmentation: tagsets vary widely in size, granularity, and theoretical underpinnings, making it difficult to compare results across languages, reuse annotated resources, or train multilingual models effectively.

The increasing availability of multilingual corpora and the growing emphasis on cross-linguistic research have amplified the need for a standardized POS tagset that can be applied consistently to many languages. Such a universal tagset would enable direct comparison of linguistic phenomena across typologically diverse languages, facilitate transfer learning between resource-rich and resource-poor languages, and support the development of interoperable NLP tools. Furthermore, it would simplify the integration of heterogeneous datasets into unified multilingual models, thereby advancing research in areas such as cross-lingual parsing and machine translation. However, designing a universal tagset poses significant challenges. Languages differ not only in their inventories of lexical categories but also in their morphological and syntactic systems. Some languages mark grammatical categories such as case, gender, and number morphologically, while others rely heavily on word order or auxiliary words. This diversity complicates the creation of a single tagset that is both sufficiently general to apply across languages and sufficiently expressive to capture meaningful distinctions.

Previous efforts toward universal POS tagging have made important strides. Initiatives such as the Universal Dependencies (UD) project have proposed standardized tagsets and annotation guidelines to promote cross-linguistic consistency. Nonetheless, existing universal tagsets often must strike a delicate balance between theoretical rigor and practical applicability. On one hand, overly coarse tagsets risk losing linguistically significant distinctions, potentially limiting their utility for certain applications. On the other hand, overly fine-grained tagsets may introduce categories that are not applicable to all languages, thereby undermining the goal of universality. Moreover, mapping from language-specific tagsets to a universal scheme is not always straightforward; it requires careful consideration of linguistic theory, annotation practices, and the intended use cases.

In this context, the present work introduces a universal part-of-speech tagset designed to provide a common framework for POS annotation across a wide range of languages, while remaining compatible with existing resources. The proposed tagset focuses on a core set of categories that are both cross-linguistically attested and computationally useful. By abstracting away from language-specific morphological details, it aims to facilitate interoperability and comparability without sacrificing essential grammatical information. To support adoption, we outline systematic mapping procedures from common language-specific tagsets to the universal scheme, and we provide examples from multiple languages representing different typological profiles.

The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we define a concise and interpretable inventory of POS categories grounded in cross-linguistic research and computational needs. Second, we demonstrate how existing annotated corpora in various languages can be mapped to this scheme with minimal loss of information. Third, we evaluate the utility of the universal tagset in multilingual and cross-lingual NLP tasks, highlighting its potential to improve performance and resource sharing. By establishing a shared POS annotation standard, we aim to advance the development of truly multilingual language technologies and to foster deeper comparative linguistic analysis.
conclusion: This work has presented a universal part-of-speech tagset designed to facilitate cross-linguistic consistency and interoperability among natural language processing tools. By mapping diverse language-specific tags to a shared inventory, the proposed framework enables more effective multilingual evaluation, transfer learning, and comparative linguistic analysis. The tagset balances granularity with broad applicability, supporting both fine-grained annotation and cross-language generalization. While challenges remain in handling language-specific phenomena, our approach provides a principled foundation for harmonizing POS annotation. Future work will focus on refining mappings, extending coverage to under-resourced languages, and exploring integration with other universal linguistic representation frameworks.

title: Complexes of Discrete Distributional Differential Forms and their Homology Theory
abstract: We develop a comprehensive framework for complexes of discrete distributional differential forms, unifying concepts from finite element differential forms and distribution theory. By extending discrete exterior calculus to distributional settings, we construct chain complexes that accommodate irregular data and discontinuities across simplicial decompositions. We establish fundamental properties, including well-defined coboundary operators and exactness criteria, and formulate a corresponding homology theory. This approach enables robust analysis of generalized differential form fields in numerical contexts, providing a foundation for stable discretisations of partial differential equations on manifolds with singularities or non-smooth structures, and clarifying connections to classical de Rham cohomology.
introduction:
The theory of differential forms plays a central role in modern geometry, topology, and the analysis of partial differential equations. In recent decades, the discretization of differential forms has emerged as a powerful framework for numerical methods that preserve key geometric and topological structures, notably within finite element exterior calculus and discrete exterior calculus. These approaches replace smooth manifolds and smooth forms by combinatorial analogues, often defined on simplicial or cubical complexes, while retaining algebraic structures such as the exterior derivative, wedge product, and Hodge star in an appropriate discrete sense. The resulting methods have found applications in computational electromagnetics, fluid dynamics, elasticity, and other areas where the preservation of conservation laws and invariants is crucial.

A natural extension of this framework arises when one considers discrete distributional differential forms. These are discrete analogues of distributional (or generalized) differential forms, which allow for singularities and discontinuities in the underlying data. Such objects appear, for example, when modeling sources concentrated on lower-dimensional substructures, in the treatment of interface problems, or in the formulation of weak solutions to PDEs. In the discrete setting, distributional forms can be represented by cochains of mixed dimensionality, possibly supported on the skeleton of the underlying mesh, and their calculus requires a careful adaptation of the exterior derivative and other operators.

The aim of this work is to develop a systematic homology theory for complexes of discrete distributional differential forms. We construct chain complexes that generalize the standard discrete de Rham complex to incorporate distributional degrees of freedom, and we investigate their algebraic and topological properties. In particular, we establish conditions under which the homology of such complexes coincides with classical topological invariants of the underlying space, and we analyze the impact of distributional components on these invariants. This provides a unifying perspective linking smooth, discrete, and distributional theories within a single homological framework.

Our approach draws on tools from algebraic topology, functional analysis, and numerical analysis, combining combinatorial constructions with concepts from the theory of currents and generalized functions. The resulting theory not only clarifies the structure of discrete distributional forms but also opens the way to novel discretization strategies for problems with singularities, complex boundary conditions, or heterogeneous media. By situating distributional phenomena within a precise homological setting, we aim to enrich both the theoretical foundations and the computational methodologies of discrete differential geometry.
conclusion:
In this work we have developed a systematic framework for complexes of discrete distributional differential forms and established their associated homology theory. Building on the interplay between combinatorial topology, functional analysis, and finite element exterior calculus, we have shown how discrete distributional forms, defined over simplicial complexes, can be organized into chain complexes that faithfully reflect the geometric and topological structure of the underlying domain. By extending the notion of differential operators to distributional settings, we have been able to incorporate singularities and irregular data while retaining a coherent algebraic structure.

Our analysis demonstrates that these complexes admit well-defined homology groups, which are naturally isomorphic to the simplicial homology of the mesh. This provides a rigorous justification for viewing discrete distributional forms as a unifying language bridging classical smooth differential forms and combinatorial representations. Furthermore, the homological framework allows for a transparent characterization of kernels, ranges, and cohomology classes within discrete distributional settings, offering new tools for the study of numerical methods for partial differential equations.

An important consequence of our results is the compatibility of the discrete distributional complex with standard finite element subcomplexes, ensuring that approximation spaces retain the desired topological properties. This compatibility opens the possibility of designing numerical schemes capable of handling domains with nontrivial topology and data with singular support, without sacrificing stability or convergence.

Looking forward, the abstract theory developed here invites several directions of further research. One avenue is the extension to non-simplicial meshes and higher-order distributional forms, potentially relevant for polyhedral discretizations. Another is the investigation of discrete Hodge theory in the distributional setting, aiming to connect our homological results with discrete harmonic analysis. Finally, applications to computational electromagnetism, elasticity, and flow problems in complex geometries may benefit from the robustness and flexibility of the proposed framework. We hope that the concepts introduced here will serve as a foundation for further exploration of discrete distributional methods in both theoretical and applied contexts.

title: Euler/X: A Toolkit for Logic-based Taxonomy Integration
abstract: Euler/X is a toolkit for logic-based taxonomy integration, enabling the reconciliation and alignment of multiple, potentially conflicting biological classifications. It employs formal reasoning techniques to detect inconsistencies, infer implied relationships, and generate consistent merged taxonomies. The system supports interactive exploration of alternative alignments, provenance tracking, and visualization of results. Euler/X integrates multiple reasoning approaches, offering scalability and flexibility for diverse datasets. By combining automated reasoning with user guidance, it facilitates accurate, transparent, and reproducible taxonomy integration for biodiversity and related research domains.
introduction:
The integration of biological taxonomies is a critical challenge in biodiversity informatics, systematics, and related domains. Taxonomies—structured representations of biological classification—are often developed independently by different research communities, institutions, or projects, and consequently exhibit differences in scope, granularity, nomenclature, and classification criteria. Merging such heterogeneous taxonomies is essential for synthesizing knowledge, enabling data interoperability, and supporting large-scale biodiversity analyses. However, integration is non-trivial: taxonomic concepts may overlap only partially, differ in circumscription, or be related in ways that are not captured by simple name matching. Furthermore, historical changes in classification, synonymy, and divergent expert opinions complicate the task. Robust solutions require methods that can explicitly represent and reason over complex relationships among taxonomic entities.

Logic-based approaches offer a principled framework for addressing these challenges. By representing taxonomic concepts and their relationships in formal logical languages, it becomes possible to express nuanced articulations—such as congruence, proper inclusion, overlap, or disjointness—and to use automated reasoning to detect inconsistencies, infer additional relationships, and generate merged taxonomies that are both logically consistent and maximally informative. Previous work has demonstrated the feasibility of applying formal logic, particularly variants of first-order logic and description logic, to taxonomy alignment, yet practical adoption has been hindered by the lack of accessible, scalable, and versatile toolkits that bridge the gap between theoretical methods and the needs of taxonomic practitioners.

Euler/X is a new toolkit designed to address this gap by providing an integrated environment for logic-based taxonomy integration. Building on the principles of formal articulation and reasoning, Euler/X supports the specification of alignments between taxonomies using expressive relationship vocabularies, and applies multiple reasoning engines to analyze, diagnose, and reconcile differences. The toolkit accommodates alternative reasoning backends—including first-order logic provers and Answer Set Programming solvers—allowing users to balance expressivity, performance, and scalability according to their needs. Euler/X further integrates facilities for inconsistency explanation and repair, enabling users to identify conflicting articulations and explore minimal changes that restore consistency. This emphasis on transparency and diagnostic feedback is critical for fostering trust and facilitating collaboration among taxonomic experts.

A distinguishing feature of Euler/X is its capacity to generate multiple consistent “possible worlds” when alignments are underspecified or ambiguous, reflecting alternative interpretations of the relationships between taxonomic concepts. This capability acknowledges the reality of uncertainty in taxonomy and provides a structured way to explore and communicate it. In addition, Euler/X offers visualization tools that help users navigate complex merged taxonomies and understand the logical inferences underlying the integration.

By combining expressive logical formalisms, a choice of reasoning paradigms, and user-oriented diagnostic and visualization capabilities, Euler/X advances the state of the art in taxonomy integration. It is designed to serve both as a research platform for experimenting with new reasoning strategies and as a practical toolkit for biodiversity informatics projects requiring robust, transparent, and reproducible taxonomy alignment. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of Euler/X, illustrate its functionality through case studies, and evaluate its performance and utility in real-world integration scenarios.
conclusion: Euler/X provides a robust, logic-based framework for integrating diverse taxonomies, enabling consistent reasoning and conflict resolution. Its modular design and automated inference capabilities support scalable, transparent taxonomy management. Future developments will enhance usability, broaden data compatibility, and strengthen its role in biodiversity informatics and other knowledge integration domains.

title: Double Parton Distributions of the Pion
abstract: We investigate the double parton distributions (dPDFs) of the pion within a light-front constituent quark model framework, providing insight into the spatial and momentum correlations between partons in a mesonic bound state. The formalism incorporates relativistic effects and ensures proper support properties of the distributions. We analyze the dependence of dPDFs on longitudinal momentum fractions and transverse separation, highlighting deviations from simple factorized approximations. The results are evolved perturbatively to higher scales using leading-order QCD evolution, facilitating comparison with phenomenological expectations and lattice QCD calculations. Our study offers a quantitative description of two-parton correlations in the pion and contributes to the theoretical foundation for interpreting double parton scattering processes involving mesonic targets.
introduction: The study of double parton distributions (dPDFs) has gained increasing attention as a means to probe the three-dimensional structure of hadrons and to understand multi-parton correlations beyond the single parton picture. While much of the existing work focuses on the proton, the pion, as the lightest QCD bound state and a key mediator of the strong force, offers a unique testing ground for nonperturbative dynamics. dPDFs encode the joint probability of finding two partons with specified longitudinal momentum fractions and transverse separation inside the hadron, thus providing insight into spatial and momentum correlations. For the pion, these distributions are relevant both for interpreting double parton scattering in high-energy collisions and for constraining models of its internal structure. Recent advances in lattice QCD, phenomenological modeling, and perturbative evolution make it timely to investigate pion dPDFs systematically. This work aims to explore their properties, theoretical constraints, and potential phenomenological implications within a consistent QCD framework.
conclusion: In this work, we have investigated the double parton distributions (DPDs) of the pion within a specified theoretical framework, emphasizing their role in describing multiparton correlations in hadronic structure. Our analysis demonstrates how the spatial and momentum correlations between partons in the pion emerge from its nonperturbative dynamics, and how model predictions compare with existing constraints from QCD symmetries and lattice results. We have highlighted the sensitivity of DPDs to both longitudinal momentum fractions and transverse separation, providing insights relevant for phenomenological applications in double parton scattering processes. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the pion’s internal structure and offer a basis for future studies, including higher-order corrections and potential experimental extractions in forthcoming high-energy facilities.
